Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkā

Commentary on the Abhidhānappadīpikā

Ganthārambha

Beginning of the Work

Yassa [M 0.0001] ñāṇaṃ sadā ñāṇaṃ, nāññeyyā ñāṇakaṃ vinā;

Nissesaguṇayuttassa, tassa natvā mahesino.

To Him whose knowledge is ever knowledge, without whose knowledge there is nothing to be known; endowed with all virtues, to that Great Sage I pay homage.

Satthantarā samādāya, sāraṃ sabbadharā tathā;

Kariyyate’bhidhānappa-dīpakassatthavaṇṇanā.

Taking the essence from various treatises, and bearing all doctrines, thus an explanation of the meaning of the Abhidhānappadīpikā is made.

Paṇāmādivaṇṇanā

Explanation of the Preliminary Homage

[Ka] idhāyaṃ ganthakāro paṭhamamattano paresampi sammā hitatthanipphādanatthaṃ puññasampada’mācinoti “tathāgato”ccādinā. Tattha karuṇākaro mahākaruṇāya uppattiṭṭhānabhūto yo tathāgato bhagavā karopayātaṃ attano hatthagataṃ sukhappadaṃ sukhassa patiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ sukhakāraṇaṃ vā sukhadāyakaṃ vā padaṃ nibbānaṃ osajja cajitvā kalisambhave dukkhakāraṇabhūte [M 0.0002] bhave saṃsāre kevaladukkaraṃ sukarenāsammissaṃ accantadukkaraṃ pañcavidhapariccāgādikaṃ karaṃ karonto paratthaṃ paresamatthaṃyeva akā katavā, tamedisaṃ tathāgataṃ ahaṃ namāmi.

[Ka] Here, this author first accumulates a wealth of merit for the purpose of accomplishing the true welfare of himself and others, with the words 'Tathāgata,' etc. Therein, the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, the compassionate one, who is the origin of great compassion, performed a deed for the welfare of others, for their benefit alone. He did so having abandoned and relinquished the state of Nibbāna, which was within his grasp and was a giver of happiness, the basis of happiness, the cause of happiness, or the bestower of happiness. This deed, undertaken in existence, in saṃsāra, which is the cause of suffering arising from defilements, was utterly difficult, unmixed with ease, and extremely difficult, involving such things as the fivefold renunciation and so forth. To such a Tathāgata I pay homage.

[Kha] yañca dhammaṃ jarārujādimuttā jarārogādīhi vimuttā munikuñjarā muniseṭṭhā bhagavanto apūjayuṃ pūjitavanto, tathā uttare uttame sattānaṃ vā saṃsāramahoghapakkhandānaṃ tato uttaraṇasamatthe yahiṃ tare yasmiṃ dhammaplave ṭhitā sammāpaṭipajjanavasena ārūḷhā narānarā manussā ca devā ca tivaṭṭambunidhiṃ kilesakammavipākavaṭṭasaṅkhātehi tīhi vaṭṭehi ākulitaṃ saṃsāramahamburāsiṃ tariṃsu tiṇṇā, aghappahaṃ kilesappahānakaraṃ, saṃsāradukkhappahānakaraṃ vā taṃ dhammamapi ahaṃ namāmi.

[Kha] And that Dhamma, which the elephant-like sages, the foremost of sages, the Blessed Ones—who are free from aging and sickness, liberated from the afflictions of aging and disease—revered and honored. It is also the supreme means for beings who have fallen into the great flood of saṃsāra to cross over from it. Standing on that raft of Dhamma and having ascended by way of proper practice, humans and non-humans, humans and devas, have crossed the great ocean of saṃsāra, which is a sea of three rounds, agitated by the three rounds of defilements, kamma, and results. To that Dhamma, which is the abandoner of afflictions, the cause of abandoning defilements, or the remover of the suffering of saṃsāra, I also pay homage.

[Ga] munindorasasūnutaṃ bhagavato ure sambhavadhammadesanāya ariyabhāvappattatāya munindassa orasaputtabhāvaṃ gataṃ pattaṃ nutaṃ kilesakhepanakaṃ supuññakhettaṃ puññatthikānaṃ puññabījaviruhanaṭṭhānaṃ sukhettabhūtaṃ bhuvane loke sutaṃ vissutaṃ[M 0.0003], sutadharaṃ vā kilesasavanābhāvena assutaṃ apāṇopi pāṇo karīyitthāti pāṇīkato, pātimokkhasaṃvaro, sova saṃvaro etassatthīti pāṇīkatasaṃvaro, taṃ pāṇīkatasaṃvaraṃ, varaṃ sīlādiguṇehi sadevakehi lokehi patthanīyaṃ. “Devāpi tassa pihayanti tādino”ti udā. 27 hi vuttaṃ. Sadā sabbasmiṃ kāle guṇoghena sīlādiguṇasamūhena nirantarantaraṃ avicchinnamānasaṃ, paripuṇṇacittaṃ vā gaṇampi aṭṭhannaṃ ariyapuggalānaṃ samūhaṃ api ahaṃ namāmīti evamettha tiṇṇampi saṅkhepato atthayojanā daṭṭhabbā.

[Ga] To the Sangha, praised as the true sons of the Muninda, having attained the status of the Muninda’s own son by attaining the noble state through the teaching of the Dhamma born from the breast of the Blessed One—the dispeller of defilements, a supreme field of merit for those seeking merit, a place where the seeds of merit sprout, a good field in the world, heard of and renowned. Or, one who upholds the teachings, who is 'unheard of' due to the absence of the flowing of defilements. He is called 'Pāṇīkata' because, though without breath, he was made into a living being. The Pātimokkha restraint is his restraint; because he possesses this restraint, he is called 'Pāṇīkatasaṃvara.' To that one of Pātimokkha restraint, who is supreme, to be aspired to by the world with its devas on account of virtues like morality. For it is said, 'Even the devas envy such a one.' To the assembly also, the community of the eight noble individuals, whose minds are always, at all times, uninterrupted and continuous, or fulfilled, by a flood of virtues, a collection of virtues like morality—I pay homage. Thus, here, the connection of the meaning of the three should be seen in brief.

[Gha-ṅa] evaṃ puññasampadamācinitvā kimabhimataṃ sādhanīyamiccāha “pakāsissamabhidhānappadīpika”nti. Buddhādīnamabhidhānānaṃ sarūpavasena, liṅgavasena ca paridīpanato pakāsanato “abhidhānappadīpika”nti laddhanāmaṃ satthaṃ pakāsissaṃ antobhāvena nipphannaṃ bahibhāvena pakāsissaṃ. Antobhāvassa hi bahibhāvamapekkhitvā bhāvitamupapannaṃ. Nanu santeva pubbācariyānaṃ nāmaliṅgappakāsanānyamarakosatikaṇḍoppalinyādyabhidhānasatthāni, pāṇini byāḍivararucicandagomi ruddavāmanādivihitāni ca liṅgasatthāni, tato kimidamuccate iccāha “nāmaliṅgāni buddhabhāsitassārahāni dassayanto”ti. Etena santesvapi pubbācariyānaṃ satthesu yasmā na tesu nāmaliṅgāni buddhavacanānurūpāni honti[M 0.0004], tasmā tadanurūpāni nāmaliṅgāni dassayanto abhidhānasatthaṃ pakāsissāmīti etamatthaṃ dīpeti. Namyate abhidhīyate attho anenāti nāmaṃ, saddasatthe namudhātuvasena. Liṅgayate “itthiyamato āpaccayo”tyādinā vibhajjateti, itthādayo vānena liṅgīyante byañjīyanteti liṅgaṃ, itthipumanapuṃsakaṃ. Kimetassa abhidhānasatthassa karaṇe payojananti pucchāyaṃ yasmiṃ sati taṃ sotāro sotumussahanti, taṃ dassetumāha “nāmaliṅgesvi”ccādi. Yato buddhavacane paṭuno bhāvo pāṭavaṃ, tadeva attho payojanaṃ, taṃ icchantīti pāṭavatthino, tesaṃ pāṭavatthīnaṃ sotūnaṃ nāmaliṅgesu kosallaṃ kusalatā chekabhāvo buddhavacane mahabbalaṃ atthassa nicchayakāraṇaṃ hoti, ato tasmā kāraṇā buddhabhāsitassārahāni nāmaliṅgāni dassayanto abhidhānappadīpikaṃ satthaṃ pakāsissanti sambandho.

[Gha-ṅa] Having thus accumulated a wealth of merit, he declares what he intends to accomplish, saying, "I will illuminate the Abhidhānappadīpikā." Because it illuminates and explains the names (abhidhāna) of the Buddha and others by way of their forms and genders, the text has obtained the name "Abhidhānappadīpikā." I will illuminate the text that is complete internally and make manifest externally. For the internal essence, being cultivated, becomes manifest in dependence on the external manifestation. But surely, there already exist explanations of names and genders by previous teachers—such as the Amarakośa, Tikaṇḍa, Uppalinī, and other abhidhāna texts—as well as gender treatises composed by Pāṇini, Vyāḍi, Vararuci, Candragomin, Ruddha, Vāmana, and others. So why is this being said? He explains: "Showing the names and genders that are appropriate to the Buddha's words." By this, he indicates that even though the works of previous teachers exist, the names and genders in them are not in accordance with the Buddha's words. Therefore, showing names and genders that are in accordance with them, he will illuminate the abhidhāna text. That by which a meaning is signified is a "name" (nāma), according to the verbal root nam in the science of sounds. "Gender" (liṅga) is that which is distinguished by markers such as "from this, in the feminine, the affix āp," etc.; or, feminine and other genders are indicated and made clear by this, hence "gender" refers to feminine, masculine, and neuter. What is the purpose of composing this abhidhāna text? In response to this question, in order to show that which makes listeners eager to listen, he says: "In names and genders..." Since the state of being skilled in the Buddha's words, namely proficiency, is itself the aim and purpose, those who desire it are seekers of proficiency. For such listeners, skill in names and genders—expertise and mastery—in the Buddha's words becomes a powerful cause for determining the meaning. Therefore, for this reason, revealing names and genders that are appropriate to the Buddha's speech, he will illuminate the Abhidhānappadīpikā—this is the connection.

[Ca] idāni satthalahubhāvatthamāha “bhiyyo”ccādi. Bhiyyo bāhullena rūpantarā rūpabhedena itthipaccayapumbhāvādikāriyakatena thīpunnapuṃsakaṃ ñeyyaṃ, so ca nāmānaṃ nāmavisesanassa, nāmaparāmasisabbanāmasaddassa ca ñeyyo pakārantarābhāvā. Tatra nāmānaṃ rūpabhedo yathā – churikā satya’siputti abhidhāna 392 gāthā. Asi khaggo ca sāyako abhidhāna 391 gāthā. Pānīyaṃ salilaṃ dakanti abhidhāna 661 gāthā. Nāmavisesanassa yathā – nisītho majjhimā rattīti abhidhāna 70 gāthā. Nāmaparāmasisabbanāmasaddassa yathā – [M 0.0005] ākaṅkhā ruci vuttā sā, tvadhikā lālasā dvisūti abhidhāna 163 gāthā. Sāhacariyena niyataliṅgenāvippayogato thīpunnapuṃsakaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Katthacīti yatra rūpabhedo natthi, taṃ yathā – marīci migataṇhikā abhidhāna 65 gāthā. Raṃsimā bhākaro bhānu abhidhāna 63 gāthā. Āpo payo jalaṃ vāri abhidhāna 661 gāthā. Marījhādayo hyabhinnarūpattā liṅgantarepi sambhāviyantehi niyataliṅgehi migataṇhikābhākarajalādisaddehi sāhacariyena taṃliṅge nicchīyante. Āhaccavidhānena itthipumanapuṃsakānaṃ visesetvā kathanena thīpunnapuṃsakaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Kvacīti yatra na rūpabhedo liṅganiṇṇayassa nimittaṃ, na ca sāhacariyaṃ liṅgabhedobhimato, nekameva vā liṅgamicchate, taṃ yathā – vallarī mañjarī nārī abhidhāna 550 gāthā. Viṭapo viṭabhītthiyaṃ abhidhāna 547 gāthā. Bhītitthī bhayamuttāso abhidhāna 166 gāthā. Vajiraṃ punnapuṃsakeccādi abhidhāna 24 gāthā.

[Ca] Now, for the sake of the treatise's brevity, he says 'bhiyyo,' etc. Mostly, the feminine, masculine, and neuter genders are to be known by the difference of form, that is, by the application of feminine affixes, masculine state, and so forth. And that gender is to be known for nouns, adjectives, and pronouns that refer to nouns, as there is no other way. Among these, the differentiation of forms in nouns is as follows: - "Churikā" (knife), "satya" (truth), "asiputti" (small sword). - "Asi" (sword), "khaggo" (sword), "sāyako" (arrow). - "Pānīyaṃ" (drink), "salilaṃ" (water), "dakaṃ" (water). The differentiation in adjectives is as follows: - "Nisītho" (midnight), "majjhimā rattī" (middle of the night). The differentiation in pronouns referring to nouns is as follows: - "Ākaṅkhā" (desire) and "ruci" (liking) are said to be feminine; "adhikā" (excessive) and "lālasā" (longing) are in two genders. Through association, from non-separation with a fixed gender, the feminine, masculine, and neuter are to be known. Where? In cases where there is no difference of form, such as: - "Marīci" (mirage), "migataṇhikā" (deer’s thirst). - "Raṃsimā" (radiant), "bhākaro" (sun), "bhānu" (sun). - "Āpo" (water), "payo" (water), "jalaṃ" (water), "vāri" (water). For 'marīci,' etc., having indistinct forms, though possible in other genders, are determined in a specific gender by association with words of fixed gender like 'migataṇhikā,' 'bhākara,' 'jala,' etc. By explicit statement, by stating the feminine, masculine, and neuter specifically, they are to be known. Where? In cases where difference of form is not the cause for determining gender, nor is association, and a difference of gender is intended, or not just one gender is desired, such as: - "Vallarī" (creeper), "mañjarī" (cluster), "nārī" (woman). - "Viṭapo" (tree), "viṭabhī" (branch) in the feminine. - "Bhīti" (fear) is feminine, "bhayaṃ" (fear), "uttāso" (terror). - "Vajiraṃ" (diamond) is in masculine and neuter, etc.

[Cha] idāni rūpabhedoti liṅganiṇṇayassa paṭipattihetuko yo bhinnaliṅgānaṃ dvando, takkaraṇapaṭisedhena abhinnaliṅgānameva dvando katoti paribhāsitumupakkamate “abhinnaliṅgina”miccādi. Abhinnaliṅgīnaṃyeva nāmānaṃ dvando kato, na bhinnaliṅgīnaṃ, yathā – vimutyasaṅkhatadhātu, suddhinibbutiyo siyunti abhidhāna 9 gāthā. Na kevalaṃ dvandoyeva, atha kho ekasesopyabhinnaliṅgānaṃyeva kato, yathā – naggo digambarāvatthā. abhidhāna 734 gāthā Sabbadharakate pana “jīmūtā meghapabbatā” iccudāhaṭaṃ. Nanu ca bhinnaliṅgānampi ekaseso kato, yathā [M 0.0006] – mātā pitā tu pitaro, puttā tu puttadhītaro abhidhāna 249 gāthā. Sasurā sassu sasurā, bhātubhagini bhātaroti abhidhāna 250 gāthā. Ettha hi mātā ca pitā ca pitaro, putto ca dhītā ca puttā, sassu ca sasuro ca sasurā, bhātā ca bhaginī ca bhātaroti bhinnaliṅgānampi ekaseso dassitoti. Ṭhānantare tesaṃ bhinnaliṅgatāya dassitattā na doso. Tāto tu janako pitā abhidhāna 243 gāthā. Ammā’mbā jananī mātā abhidhāna 244 gāthā. Apaccaṃ puttotrajo suto abhidhāna 240 gāthā. Nāriyaṃ duhitā dhītā abhidhāna 241 gāthā. Jāyāpatīnaṃ jananī, sassu vuttātha tappitā. Sasuroti iccādikañhi tesaṃ abhidhāna 246 gāthā ṭhānantaranti. Tathā ettha kamaṃ vinā bhinnaliṅgānaṃ gaṇanapāṭho viya saṅkaropi na kato. Tatra hi saggadisādayo atthā yathākkamaṃ taṃsambandhā ca sakkavidisādayo atthā sakasakasambandhasahitā yathābhidhānaṃ sarūpapaṭipatyamatthabhidheyyā, tathā tappariyāyasambandhāni ca yāni nāmāni, tāni sabbāni tadabhidhānāvasare abhidheyyānīti sukhenekatreva sakalanāmapaṭipatti sarūpapaṭipatti ca yathā siyāticcetadatthaṃ kamo abhyupagamyate, tathā ca satyāvassaṃ saggādipariyāye divasaddādayo, harādyavasare kumārādayo abhidheyyā iti kamānurodhena liṅgasaṅkaro pariharitumasakkuṇeyyo, yathāvuttantu kamaṃ vinā neha saṅkaro kato, iti pariyāyena itthippakaraṇādikkamena yathāsambhavamabhidhānato, taṃ yathā – īti tvitthī ajaññañca, upasaggo upaddavoti abhidhāna 401 gāthā. Atra hi ye tiliṅgā, te tiliṅgāvasare eva nibaddhā, na gaṇanapāṭhā viya uccāraṇavasena, evaṃ sabbatra yathāsambhavaṃ nīyate. Vuttañca –

[Cha] Now, in the section on the distinction of forms, regarding the determination of gender, it begins to define the reason for the practice of forming a dvanda compound of words with different genders. By prohibiting the formation of such, it states that a dvanda compound is made only of words with the same gender, beginning with 'of the same gender,' etc. A dvanda compound is made only of nouns of the same gender, not of different genders, as for example: 'vimutyasaṅkhatadhātu' and 'suddhinibbutiyo.' Not only a dvanda compound, but also an ekasesa is made only from words of the same gender, as for example: 'naggo digambarāvatthā.' In the Sabbadharakata, however, 'jīmūtā meghapabbatā' is cited as an example. But is it not so that an ekasesa is also made from words of different genders? For example: 'mātā pitā' (mother and father) become 'pitaro' (parents); 'putto dhītā' (son and daughter) become 'puttā' (children); 'sassu sasuro' (mother-in-law and father-in-law) become 'sasurā' (parents-in-law); and 'bhātā bhaginī' (brother and sister) become 'bhātaro' (siblings). Here, indeed, an ekasesa of words of different genders is shown. There is no fault, as their differing genders are shown in other contexts. For example: 'tāto tu janako pitā' (father, begetter, is father); 'ammā ambā jananī mātā' (mother, the bearer, is mother); 'apaccaṃ putto atrajo suto' (offspring, son, born of him, is son); 'nāriyaṃ duhitā dhītā' (in a woman, daughter is daughter); 'jāyāpatīnaṃ jananī, sassu vuttātha tappitā. Sasuroti' (the mother of the husband and wife is called mother-in-law, and the father thereof, father-in-law), and so forth are their other contexts. Similarly, here, without a fixed order, no mixture is made, unlike in an enumeration. For there, the meanings of 'heaven, directions, etc.' and their related meanings 'Sakka, intermediate directions, etc.,' together with their respective connections, are to be expressed according to their designation, in conformity with their form and meaning. Likewise, all nouns related as synonyms are to be expressed at the time of their designation, so that the complete understanding of the nouns and the understanding of their forms may easily occur in one place. For this purpose, a specific order is adopted. And so, in the section on synonyms for heaven, etc., words like 'diva,' etc., and in the section on Hara, etc., words like 'kumāra,' etc., must be expressed. Thus, by following the order, the mixture of genders cannot be avoided. However, as has been said, without such an order, no mixture is made here. Thus, by means of a sequence, such as the order of the section on the feminine gender, the designation is made as is possible. For example: 'īti tvitthī ajaññañca, upasaggo upaddavoti.' Here, those words that are of three genders are included only in the section on the three genders, not by way of utterance as in an enumeration. Thus, everywhere, this is to be applied as is possible. And it has been said—

“Bhedākhyānāya [M 0.0007] na dvando, nekaseso na saṅkaro;

Katotra bhinnaliṅgāna-mavuttānaṃ kamaṃ vinā”ti amara 1.4.

A dvanda compound is not for stating difference, nor is an ekasesa for creating a mixture. Here, for words of different genders and for those unstated, this is done without a fixed order.

Idāni liṅgavācakānaṃ ṭhānavasenatthesu gamanaṃ dassetumāha “liṅgavācake”ccādi. Gāthāpādantamajjhaṭṭhā gāthānaṃ pādānañca antamajjhaṭṭhā liṅgavācakā anekatthaliṅgavācakāni ñāṇadassanādīni liṅgāni pubbamatthaṃ vācakavasena yanti gacchanti. Apare gāthāpādānamādiṭṭhā liṅgavācakā paramatthaṃ yanti gacchanti. Taṃ yathā –

Now, to show how meanings are conveyed by gender-indicating words according to their position, it is stated: 'gender-indicating words,' etc. Gender-indicating words situated at the end and in the middle of the lines of a verse convey the prior meaning by way of their designation. Other gender-indicating words situated at the beginning of the lines of a verse convey the subsequent meaning. For example—

Phale vipassanādibba-cakkhusabbaññutāsu ca;

Paccavekkhaṇañāṇamhi, magge ca ñāṇadassanaṃ abhidhāna 794 gāthā.

The term 'ñāṇadassana' applies to the fruit, to insight, the divine eye, and omniscience; and to the knowledge of reviewing, and to the path.

Ṇādo saddhācīvarādi-hetvādhāresu paccayo;

Kīḷādibbavihārādo, vihāro sugatālaye abhidhāna 857 gāthā.

The term 'paccayo' is used for the supporting causes such as faith, robes, and so forth. The term 'vihāro' is used for play, divine abiding, and so forth, and for the abode of the Sugata.

Khagge kurūre nettiṃso, parasmiñcātra tīsvamu abhidhāna 1089 gāthā;

Kusale sukataṃ suṭṭhu-kate ca sukato tisu abhidhāna 938 gāthā.

The word 'nettiṃso' is used in the sense of a sword and what is cruel; and here, in another sense, this word is in three genders. The word 'sukato' is used in the sense of what is skillful, well-done, and well-made, and it is in three genders.

Samayo samavāye ca, samūhe kāraṇe khaṇe;

Paṭivedhe siyā kāle, pahāne lābhadiṭṭhisu abhidhāna 778 gāthā.

The term 'samayo' is used for an assembly, a gathering, a cause, and a moment; it may also be used for penetration, time, abandonment, gain, and views.

Kantāro vanaduggesu abhidhāna 1107 gāthā.

'Kantāro' is used for a wilderness or a difficult path through a forest.

Ettha ca –

And here—

Yebhuyyatābyāmissesu, visaṃyoge ca kevalaṃ;

Daḷhatthenatireke cā-navasesamhi taṃ tisu abhidhāna 786 gāthā.

The word 'kevalaṃ' is used in the sense of majority, in what is unmixed, and in disjunction; in the sense of firmness, in excess, and in remainderlessness—that word is in three genders.

Samādhismiṃ pumekaggo-nākule vāccaliṅgiko abhidhāna 1035 gāthā.

In the sense of concentration, 'ekaggo' is masculine; in the sense of 'unconfused,' it is adjectival in gender.

Jaḷe thūlo mahatyapi abhidhāna 1066 gāthā ccādīsu

The word 'thūlo' is used in the sense of 'dull' and also 'great,' and so forth.

Gāthāmajjhaṭṭhānaṃ[M 0.0008], pādantamajjhaṭṭhānañca liṅgavācakānaṃ pubbaparatthesvapi gamanabhāvato “pubbaṃ yantī”ti idaṃ yebhuyyavasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā gāthānaṃ majjhantaṭṭhā pubbaṃ yanti, gāthāmajjhaṭṭhā, pādantamajjhaṭṭhā ca pubbāparañca yantīti yathālābhayojanā daṭṭhabbā.

Because gender-indicating words situated in the middle of verses, and at the end and in the middle of lines, also convey both prior and subsequent meanings, the statement 'they convey the prior meaning' should be understood as having been stated as a general rule. Alternatively, it should be understood that those situated in the middle and at the end of verses convey the prior meaning, while those situated in the middle of verses, and at the end and in the middle of lines, convey both prior and subsequent meanings; this application should be understood as is appropriate.

[Ja] idāni visesavidhimhi satthalahubhāvatthaṃ paribhāsate “pumitthiya”miccādi. Pumitthiyaṃ “dvīsū”ti padaṃ ñeyyaṃ, yathā – asani dvīsu abhidhāna 24 gāthā. Sabbaliṅge liṅgattaye “tīsū”ti padaṃ ñeyyaṃ, yathā – sattannaṃ pūraṇe seṭṭhe’tisante sattamo tisu abhidhāna 942 gāthā. Ettha ca nisiddhaliṅganāmaṃ pārisesato “sesaliṅga”nti ñeyyaṃ nisiddhaliṅga sesatthaṃ (amara 1.5.), yathā – vassa saṃvaccharā nitthīti abhidhāna 81 gāthā. Atra cekaliṅganisedhabyākhyānena liṅgadvayavidhānanti ekaliṅganisedhabyājena liṅgadvayābhidhānamiti (amarakosacintāmaṇiṭīkā).

[Ja] Now, in the section on special rules, for the sake of the treatise's brevity, it is defined with 'masculine, feminine,' etc. The word 'dvīsu' (in two) should be understood in the context of 'masculine and feminine,' as in: 'asani dvīsu' (lightning in two). In the context of all genders, that is, in the three genders, the word 'tīsū' (in three) should be understood, as in: 'sattannaṃ pūraṇe seṭṭhe’tisante sattamo tisu' (the seventh, best among seven, is in three). And here, a noun of a prohibited gender should be understood by the principle of remainder as being of the 'remaining gender,' as in: 'vassa saṃvaccharā nitthī' (vassa and saṃvaccharā are not feminine). Here, by the explanation of the prohibition of one gender, the establishment of two genders is to be understood.

Ganthalāhavaṃ vidhāyedāni paṭipattilāhavatthamāha “abhidhānantarārambhe”iccādi. Abhidhānantarassa aññassa abhidhānassa ārambhe sati, tu anto yassa abhidhānassa, atha ādi yassa abhidhānassāti idaṃ abhidhānadvayañca ñeyyaṃ. Tvantamathādikaṃ nāmādipadaṃ pubbena na sambajjhateti bhāvo. Tatra nāmapadaṃ yathā – jino sakko tu siddhattho abhidhāna 4 gāthā. Kesavo cakkapāṇyatha abhidhāna 16 gāthā. Mahissaro sivo sūlī abhidhāna 16 gāthā. Liṅgapadaṃ yathā – pume tu paṇhi pāsaṇi abhidhāna 277 gāthā. Pume tūtu rajo pupphaṃ abhidhāna 238 gāthā. Sā tirokaraṇīpyatha [M 0.0009] abhidhāna 298 gāthā. Punnapuṃsakamullocaṃ abhidhāna 299 gāthā. Atthapadaṃ yathā – udare tu tathā pācā’nalasmiṃ gahaṇītthiyaṃ abhidhāna 973 gāthā. Paṇīto tīsu madhure, uttame vihitepyatha. Añjase visikhāyañca, pantiyaṃ vīthi nāriyaṃ abhidhāna 940 gāthā. Athasaddena catra anantariyatthena sakapariyāyopalakkhaṇato atho saddādīsu ca na pubbena sambajjhate. Pāṇako cāpyatho uccāliṅgo lomasapāṇakoti abhidhāna 623 gāthā.

Having established the brevity of the text, it now speaks for the sake of ease of practice, saying: 'At the beginning of another designation,' etc. When there is the beginning of another designation, these two designations should be understood: the one ending with 'tu' and the one beginning with 'atha'. The meaning is that a word such as a name, etc., which ends in 'tu' or begins with 'atha', is not connected with what precedes. There, as an example of a noun: 'jino sakko tu siddhattho' (the Victor, Sakka, but Siddhattha); 'kesavo cakkapāṇyatha' (and Kesava, Cakkapāṇi); 'mahissaro sivo sūlī' (the Great Lord, Siva, Sūlin). As an example of a gender word: 'pume tu paṇhi pāsaṇi' (but in the masculine, 'paṇhi' and 'pāsaṇi'); 'pume tūtu rajo pupphaṃ' (but in the masculine, 'utu', 'rajo', 'pupphaṃ'); 'sā tirokaraṇīpyatha' (and that 'tirokaraṇī' is also feminine); 'punnapuṃsakamullocaṃ' ('ulloca' is masculine and neuter). As an example of a meaning word: 'udare tu tathā pācā’nalasmiṃ gahaṇītthiyaṃ' (but in the sense of belly, and likewise digestive fire, 'gahaṇī' is feminine); 'paṇīto tīsu madhure, uttame vihitepyatha' (and 'paṇīta' is in three genders for sweet, supreme, and prepared); 'vīthi nāriyaṃ añjase visikhāyañca pantiyaṃ' (the word 'vīthi' is feminine in the sense of a straight path, a street, and a row). And here, by the word 'atha', due to its meaning of immediate sequence, and by indicating its own synonyms, words like 'atho' also do not connect with what precedes. For example: 'Pāṇako cāpyatho uccāliṅgo lomasapāṇakoti' (A living being, and also a kind of worm and a hairy creature).

[Jha] idāni buddhavacanānamanurūpānampi pacurappayogānameva kesañci gahaṇaṃ attano satthantarāpasayhatāvasena ahaṃkārapubbikābhāvañca dassetumāha “bhiyyo payoga”miccādi. Sogate sugatassa vacanabhūte āgame piṭakattaye, tañhi āgacchanti tividhasampattiyo etenāti āgamoti vuccati. Tasmiṃ bhiyyo payogaṃ bāhullena payujjateti payogo, taṃ āgamma gahetvā kvaci araññavaggādīsu nighaṇṭuyuttiñca nighaṇṭunāmake satthe āgataṃ buddhavacanānurūpaṃ yuttiñca ānīya ānetvā nāmaliṅgaṃ kathīyati antobhāvena nipphannaṃ bahibhāvena pakāsīyate. Āvibhāvattameva hi jaññattaṃ santakāriyakārino. Āsīsāyaṃ vā avassambhāvinopi vacanassa vattamānatthavatticchāya vattamānattaṃ, tathā hi loke avassambhāvino siddhimabhisandhāya bhāvinamappattaṃ vattamānattena vā atītattena vā vattumicchati, taṃ yathā – “idaṃ mamamapāpaye”ti koci kenacābhihito santo avassaṃ taṃ bhavissatīti maññamāno pāpiyamānaṃ pattaṃ vā vattumicchati[M 0.0010], tatoyeva “āsīsāyaṃ bhūtamiva ce”ti pāṇini 3.3.132 tadatidesavacanaṃ paccākhyāyate.

[Jha] Now, to show that some accept only frequently used words, even those in conformity with the Buddha's word, due to their inability to bear other treatises and the absence of a preceding egoism, it is said: 'bhiyyo payoga' (more frequent usage), and so on. In the dispensation of the Sugata, in the scriptures of the three baskets—for the threefold attainments come from this, hence they are called 'āgama.' In that, 'bhiyyo payoga' means it is used abundantly. Based on that, having taken it, sometimes in the Araññavagga and so on, having brought the reasoning found in the lexicon named 'Nighaṇṭu' and the reasoning that is in conformity with the Buddha’s words, the name and gender are spoken of, produced internally and manifested externally. For manifestation itself is the state of being known for one who acts rightly. Or, in the optative, even an inevitable statement has the sense of the present due to the desire to speak of the present meaning. For in the world, one who desires inevitable success wishes to speak of the future, which has not yet arrived, as if it were present or past. For example, when someone is told by another, 'May this not reach me,' thinking, 'Surely this will happen,' he wishes to speak of it as being reached or attained. Therefore, the statement of extended application, 'and in the optative, it is like the past,' is rejected.

Paṇāmādivaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of salutation, etc., is concluded.

1. Saggakaṇḍavaṇṇanā

1. The Exposition of the Heaven Chapter.

1. Idāni yasmā abhidheyyattho nāma paññattiparamatthatthavasena duvidho, tesu yebhuyyena paññattatthato paramatthatthova seṭṭho, tesupi odhiso kilesānaṃ samucchedapaṭippassaddhikarattā yathākkamaṃ aṭṭha dhammā seṭṭhā, tatopi nibbānameva seṭṭhaṃ, tesaṃ sabbesampi dhammānaṃ sammāsambuddhova seṭṭho. Vuttañhi bhagavatā “virāgo seṭṭho dhammānaṃ, dvipadānañca cakkhumā”ti dha. pa. 273; netti. 125. Ettha hi “yāvatā, bhikkhave, dhammā saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā, virāgo tesaṃ dhammānaṃ aggamakkhāyatī”ti a. ni. 4.34; 5.32; itivu. 90 vacanato sabbesampi saṅkhatāsaṅkhatadhammānaṃ virāgasaṅkhāto nibbānameva seṭṭho, cakkhumā pana sammāsambuddho tesaṃ sabbesampi dhammānaṃ, devamanussādibhedānaṃ dvipadānañca paññattatthānaṃ seṭṭhoti ayamattho vutto bhagavatā, tasmā sabbatthaseṭṭhatthābhidhāyakābhidhānabhūtaṃ buddhātidhānameva paṭhamaṃ saggakaṇḍassa ādimhi patthiyavasena satthiyavasena (ka.) dassetumāha “buddho”ccādi. Tattha jinasaddantaṃ sabbabuddhassa nāmaṃ. Sabbaṃ buddhavāti buddho, sakammakā kattari tapaccayo. Visiṭṭhā buddhi assatthīti buddho, pasaṃsāyaṃ yadādinā ṇapaccayo. Dānasīlakkhandhādayo ṭhānāṭṭhānañāṇādayo vā dasa [M 0.0011] balāni yasseti dasabalo. Sāsati vinayati satteti satthā. Sabbadhammajānanasīlatāya sabbaññū. Dvipadānaṃ, dvipadesu vā uttamo dvipaduttamo, buddhavaṃsavaṇṇanāyaṃ bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 37 nidānakathā niddhāraṇalakkhaṇāya chaṭṭhiyā samāsassa paṭisiddhattā nedisī niddhāraṇalakkhaṇā chaṭṭhī gamyate. Kasmā pana so tattha paṭisiddhoti? Samāse yebhuyyena niddhāraṇalakkhaṇattayassa vikalābhāvato. Kiñcāpi hi tattha chaṭṭhiyāyeva paṭisiddho, sattamiyā pana niddhāraṇalakkhaṇāya vijjamānattā tassāpi so paṭisedhanīyoyeva. Munīnaṃ indo rājā munindo. Puññañāṇabhāgyādayo bhagaṃ nāma, taṃyogā bhagavā. Nāthati sattānaṃ hitaṃ yācati, kilese vā upatāpeti, sattesu vā issariyaṃ karoti, tesaṃ vā hitaṃ āsīsatīti nātho. Buddhadhammasamantañāṇadibbacakkhusaṅkhātehi pañcahi cakkhūhi samannāgatattā cakkhumā. Sabbadā byāmappabhāya kāyato niccharaṇavasena aṅgīraso. Sabbākārena sabbadhammānaṃ munanato muni, dhammavādesu vā monakaraṇato muni.

1. Now, since the meaning to be expressed is twofold—as conventional meaning and ultimate meaning—among these, the ultimate meaning is generally superior to the conventional meaning. Even among these, specifically, eight phenomena are supreme in order due to their role in cutting off and pacifying defilements, and among them, Nibbāna is the supreme. Of all these phenomena, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is the supreme. For it was said by the Blessed One: "Dispassion is the best of phenomena, and among two-footed beings, the One with Vision." Here, the statement "Monks, among all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the highest" means that among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, Nibbāna, called dispassion, is indeed the supreme. But the One with Vision, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, is supreme among all these phenomena, and among two-footed beings, such as gods and humans, who are conventional designations. This is the meaning conveyed by the Blessed One. Therefore, to first indicate the meaning of the supreme in all respects, the very designation 'Buddha' is mentioned at the beginning of the Heaven Chapter, with the words 'Buddho' and so on, by way of introduction. Here, the term 'Jina' (Conqueror) is a name for all Buddhas. 'Buddha' means 'one who has awakened to everything', formed by the suffix 'ta' in the agentive sense, indicating action. 'Buddha' means 'one who possesses distinguished wisdom', formed by the suffix 'ṇa' in the sense of praise, beginning with 'ya'. Dasabala (the Ten-Powered One) is one who possesses the ten powers, such as the aggregates of generosity and virtue, or the knowledge of what is possible and impossible. Satthā (the Teacher) is one who instructs and disciplines beings. Sabbaññū (the Omniscient One) is one who knows all phenomena by virtue of his nature. Dvipaduttama (the Supreme Among Bipeds) is the best among two-footed beings or the supreme among bipeds. In the commentary on the Buddhavaṃsa, due to the prohibition of the sixth case having a determining sense in the compound, that specifying sixth case is not used here. Why is it prohibited here? Because in compounds, the triple characteristic of determination is mostly absent. Even though the sixth case is prohibited here, since the specifying characteristic of the seventh case exists, it too must be prohibited. Muninda (the Sage-King) is the lord of sages, the king. Bhagavā (the Blessed One) is one endowed with 'bhaga', which refers to merit, knowledge, good fortune, and other excellent qualities. Nātha (the Protector) is one who seeks the welfare of beings, or torments defilements, or exercises lordship over beings, or wishes for their welfare. Cakkhumā (the One with Vision) is one endowed with five eyes, namely, the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the wisdom-eye, the divine eye, and the eye of universal knowledge. Aṅgīrasa (the Radiant One) is one from whose body a fathom-wide aura constantly emanates. Muni (the Sage) is one who knows all phenomena in every way, or one who causes silence in Dhamma discussions.

2. Lokānaṃ, lokesu vā nātho lokanātho. Attano adhikassa kassacipi uttamapuggalassa abhāvato anadhivaro, sabbapariyantagatattabhāvattā vā natthi etassa ito añño adhiko patthetabbo attabhāvoti anadhivaro. Mahantānaṃ sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ esanato gavesanato mahesi, mahanto vā īso vibhūti etassāti mahesi. Hitaṃ vinayati anusāsatīti vināyako, visiṭṭhaṃ vā nibbānaṃ satte netīti vināyako. Sabbadhammadassanasīlatāya [M 0.0012] “samantacakkhū’ti laddhanāmena sabbaññutaññāṇena samannāgatattā samantacakkhu. Sobhanaṃ gataṃ ñāṇamassa, saṃsārā vā suṭṭhu apunarāvattiyā gatavāti sugato, saparasukhasiddhatthaṃ vā sammā gatavāti sugato. Bhūri bahukā paññā yassa, anantattā vā bhūrisamā paññā etassāti bhūripañño, anantāya mahāpathaviyā sadisapaññotyattho. Kilesādipañcavidhaṃ māraṃ jitavāti māraji.

2. Lokanātha (the Lord of the Worlds) is the lord of the worlds, or the lord in the worlds. Anadhivara (the Unsurpassed) is one for whom there is no superior individual, or because he has reached the ultimate boundary of existence, or because there is no other state beyond this that he should seek. Mahesi (the Great Sage) is one who seeks and explores great aggregates of virtue and so on, or one who possesses great power and majesty. Vināyaka (the Guide) is one who disciplines and instructs for welfare, or one who leads beings to the distinguished state of Nibbāna. Samantacakkhu (the All-Seeing One) is one endowed with the knowledge of omniscience, known as 'the All-Seeing Eye,' by virtue of his nature of seeing all phenomena. Sugata (the Well-Gone One) is one whose knowledge has gone well, or one who has gone well from saṃsāra, never to return, or one who has rightly gone for the accomplishment of his own and others' happiness. Bhūripañña (the One of Vast Wisdom) is one whose wisdom is abundant and vast, or one whose wisdom is immeasurable, like the great earth; this means his wisdom is like the immeasurable great earth. Māraji (the Conqueror of Māra) is one who has conquered the fivefold Māra, consisting of defilements and so on.

3. Narānaṃ sīho seṭṭho, parappavādamaddanasahanato vā naro ca so sīho cāti narasīho, sahatīti sīho, niruttinayena pubbavaṇṇākārassīkāro, sīhasadisattā vā naro ca so sīho cāti narasīho. Yathā hi sīho migarājā catūhi dāṭhāhi sabbasatte hiṃsati abhibhavati, tathā bhagavāpi sīlapaññāpuññiddhisaṅkhātehi catūhi dhammehi sabbaṃ lokaṃ hiṃsati abhibhavatīti opammasaṃsandanaṃ. Sabbapurisānaṃ seṭṭhattā naravaro, narānaṃ vā devamanussānaṃ seṭṭhattā naravaro, “sīle patiṭṭhāya naro sapañño”ti saṃ. ni. 1.23 ettha viya narasaddena sabbe devamanussā saṅgahitā. Dhammassa rājapavattakattā dhammarājā, dhammato vā sadevakassa lokassa rājā jāto, nādhammatoti dhammarājā, dhammena rājatīti vā dhammarājā, dhammapālako vā rājā dhammarājā. Munīnaṃ seṭṭhattā mahāmuni. Devānaṃ atidevoti devadevo, devānaṃ adhiko vā devo devadevo. Lokānaṃ garu ācariyo lokagaru, lokānaṃ garubhājanattā vā lokagaru. Dhammassa sāmi yathāvuttanayena dhammassāmī. Yathā purimakā sammāsambuddhā [M 0.0013] sabbaññubhāvaṃ gatā, tathā ayampi gatoti tathāgato, tathā vā sammā gataṃ ñāṇamassāti tathāgatotyādinā tathāgatasaddassa atthapapañco tattha tattha dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.12; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.78; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.70; udā. aṭṭha. 18; itivu. aṭṭha. 38; theragā. aṭṭha. 1.3; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 2 nidāna kathā; mahāni. aṭṭha. 14; paṭi. sa. aṭṭha. 1.1.37; dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7; dī. ni. abhi. ṭī. 1.7; ma. ni. ṭī. 1.12; a. ni. ṭī. 1.1.170 vuttanayena veditabbo.

3. Narasīha (the Lion among Men) is the best among men, or because he is a man capable of crushing the doctrines of others, hence he is the Lion among Men. He conquers, thus he is a lion; by the method of etymology, the initial vowel is changed to 'ī' (sīho), or because he is like a lion, hence he is the Lion among Men. Just as the lion, the king of beasts, subdues and overcomes all beings with his four fangs, so too the Blessed One subdues and overcomes the entire world with the four qualities known as virtue, wisdom, merit, and power—this is the connection by analogy. Naravara (the Best of Men) is the foremost of all men, or because he is the best among gods and humans. Here, as in the phrase "a wise man established in virtue," the term "man" includes all gods and humans. Dhammarājā (the King of Dhamma) is one who initiates the reign of the Dhamma, or one who is born as the king of the world with its gods through Dhamma, not through unrighteousness, or one who reigns by Dhamma, or a king who protects the Dhamma. Mahāmuni (the Great Sage) is the foremost among sages. Devadeva (the God of Gods) is a god beyond the gods, or a god superior to the gods. Lokagaru (the World-Teacher) is the teacher revered by the worlds, or one who is worthy of reverence from the worlds. Dhammassāmī (the Master of the Dhamma) is the master of the Dhamma in the manner previously described. Tathāgata (the Thus-Gone One) is one who has attained the state of omniscience just as the former Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones attained it, or one whose knowledge has rightly gone. The detailed explanation of the meaning of the term 'Tathāgata' should be understood in each instance according to the method explained in the respective contexts.

4. Sayameva sammāsambuddho bhavati, anaññabodhitoti sayambhū. Sammā aviparītena sa’mattanāyeva sabbadhamme bujjhati abujjhi bujjhissatīti sammāsambuddho. Seṭṭhapaññāya samannāgatattā varapañño. Satte saṃsāraṇṇavato nibbānapāraṃ netīti nāyako. Jitapañcamārattā jino. Ettha ca samantabhadra, lokaji, chaḷabhiñña, advayavādī, sirīghana, akaniṭṭhaga akaniṭṭhaka (ka.), dhammacakka, rāgāsani rāgāri (ka.), tisaraṇa, khasama khaṇasama (ka.) khena ākāsena samā tulyā guṇā yassa so (tikaṇḍasesaṭīkā 1.1.8), guṇākara, mahāsukha, vajira, mettābala, asama, jitāri, mahābodhi, dhammadhātu, setaketu, khaji, timutti khajiravimutti (ka.) khena ākāsajjhānena – suññabhāvanāyāti bhāvo – jayati saṃsārabhāvaṃ yo, ji+ kvipa suññavādīnaṃ boddhānaṃ “suññaṃ sabbameva” ityākārabhāvanāya saṃsārabhāvajayanato tathābhāvo (saddakappadduma), dasabhūmissara, pañcañāṇa, bahukkhama, sambuddha, sabbadassī, mahābala, sabbabodha [M 0.0014] sambodhadhamma (ka.), dhammakāya, saṃgutta, araha, dvādasakkha, vītarāgādīnipi anekāni buddhassa nāmāni imāni pariyāyavacanāni pāyaso amarakosato, tikaṇḍasesābhidhānato ca gahitāni. Samantato puññasambhārato ca ñāṇasambhārato ca bhadro seṭṭhoti samantabhadrotyādīni ca nibbacanāni veditabbāni. Vuttañca –

4. Sayambhū (the Self-Existent) is one who himself becomes the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, not enlightened by another. Sammāsambuddha (the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One) is one who rightly comprehends all phenomena without error, by his own accord, having awakened, awakening, and who will awaken. Varapañña (the One of Excellent Wisdom) is one endowed with supreme wisdom. Nāyaka (the Leader) is one who leads beings across the ocean of saṃsāra to the further shore of Nibbāna. Jina (the Conqueror) is one who has conquered the five Māras. Here, names of the Buddha also include Samantabhadra, Lokaji, Chaḷabhiñña (Possessor of the Six Super-Knowledges), Advayavādī (the Non-Dualist), Sirīghana, Akaniṭṭhaga, Dhammacakka (the Wheel of Dhamma), Rāgāsani (the Thunderbolt against Passion), Tisaraṇa (the Triple Refuge), Khasama (the Forbearing One), Guṇākara (the Abode of Virtues), Mahāsukha (the Great Bliss), Vajira, Mettābala (the Power of Loving-Kindness), Asama (the Unequalled), Jitāri (the Conqueror of Foes), Mahābodhi (the Great Enlightenment), Dhammadhātu (the Dhamma-Element), Setaketu (the White Banner), Khaji, Timutti (the Triple Deliverance), Dasabhūmissara (the Lord of the Ten Grounds), Pañcañāṇa (the Possessor of Five Knowledges), Bahukkhama (the Very Forbearing), Sambuddha (the Fully Awakened), Sabbadassī (the All-Seeing), Mahābala (the Great Power), Sabbabodha (the All-Knowing), Dhammakāya (the Dhamma-Body), Saṃgutta (the Well-Guarded), Araha (the Worthy One), Dvādasakkha (the Twelve-Eyed), Vītarāga (the Free from Passion), and many others. And derivations such as Samantabhadra, meaning 'from all sides, he is auspicious and excellent due to the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wisdom,' should be understood. And it is said—

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāmasahassato”ti dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1313; udā. aṭṭha. 53; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.76; netti. aṭṭha. 38.

"Innumerable are the names of the great sage endowed with virtues; one should discern a name by its virtue, even from a thousand names."

Tattha uddheyyanti uddharitabbaṃ. Api nāmasahassatoti anekehi nāmasahassehītyattho. Sabbabuddhanāmakathā.

There, 'uddheyyaṃ' means 'should be discerned.' 'Api nāmasahassato' means 'from many thousands of names.' This is the discourse on the names of all Buddhas.

Sakkādisattakaṃ amhākaṃ buddhassa nāmaṃ. Pañcamāre jetuṃ sakkotīti sakko, bhaginīhi saddhiṃ saṃvāsakaraṇato vā lokamariyādaṃ chindituṃ sakkuṇantīti sakkā, sākiyarājūnaṃ pubbarājāno, tesaṃ vaṃsabhūtattā bhagavā “sakko”ti vuccati. Assa ca jātisamanantaraṃ nidhayo ratanāni ca uppannānīti siddhatthoti nāmaṃ kataṃ, sabbesaṃ vā lokānaṃ siddhā atthā etena hetubhūtenāti siddhattho. Suddhaṃ odanaṃ assāti suddhodano, tassa apaccaṃ suddhodani. Gotamavaṃsassa kapilassa munino sissatāya sakyā gotamā, bhagavā pana gotamavaṃse uppannattā gotamassa munino apaccaṃ gotamo.

The set of seven names beginning with Sakka belongs to our Buddha. Sakka (the Able One) is one who is able to conquer the five Māras; or because the Sakyas, the former kings of the Sakyan lineage, were able to break worldly conventions by living with their sisters, they are called 'Sakkā,' and since the Blessed One was born in their lineage, he is called 'Sakka.' Siddhattha (He Whose Aim is Accomplished) is the name given to him because immediately after his birth, treasures and jewels arose; or because the aims of all beings were accomplished through him as the cause. Suddhodana (He of Pure Rice) is one who has pure rice; his descendant is called Suddhodani. Gotama (of the Gotama Clan) is the name given to the Sakyas because they were disciples of the sage Kapila of the Gotama lineage; but the Blessed One is Gotama because he was born in the Gotama lineage and is a descendant of the sage Gotama.

5. Sakyavaṃsāvatiṇṇo sakyavaṃsā pitthiṇṇo (ka.) sakyamuni yo buddho so sakyasīho, sakyānaṃ vā seṭṭhattā sakyasīho. Sakyakulato [M 0.0015] jāto muni sakyamuni. Sūriyadevaputtassa sotāpannattā bhagavā ādiccabandhūti vuccati, ādiccassa bandhu ñātīti nibbacanaṃ katvā. Etthapi māyādevīsuta, mahāsamaṇa, kalisāsanādīni kulisāsanādīni (ka.) kalimhi yuge sāsanaṃ anusāsanaṃ yassa so, athavā kalimhi pāpe vivāde vā sāsanaṃ hitasādhanaṃ yassa so (tikaṇḍasesaṭīkā 1.1.11) gotamapariyāyāni veditabbāni.

5. Sakyasīha (the Lion of the Sakyas) is the Buddha, the Sakya sage who descended from the Sakya lineage; or he is so called because he is the chief among the Sakyas. Sakyamuni (the Sage of the Sakyas) is the sage born from the Sakya clan. The Blessed One is called Ādiccabandhu (Kinsman of the Sun) because the son of the Sun deity became a stream-enterer, the name being derived from 'a kinsman and relative of the sun.' Here too, the designations Māyādevīsuta (Son of Māyādevī), Mahāsamaṇa (Great Ascetic), Kalisāsana (Dispeller of Evil), and others, should be understood as epithets of Gotama.

6. Mokkhādīni nibbutipariyantāni chacattālīsa nāmāni nibbānassa nāmāni. Muccanti ettha, etena vā rāgādīhīti mokkho. Nirujjhanti ettha rāgādayoti nirodho, rundhati vā nibbānanti rodho, kileso, so ettha natthīti nirodho. Vānasaṅkhātāya taṇhāya nikkhantattā, nibbāti vā etena rāgaggiādikoti nibbānaṃ. Yathā pakatidīpo nadīsotena vuyhamānānaṃ patiṭṭhā hoti, evamidampi nibbānaṃ saṃsāramahoghena vuyhamānānaṃ patiṭṭhāti dīpo viyāti dīpo, nikkilesānaṃ vā padīpasadisabhāvakaraṇato dīpo viyāti dīpo, “nibbanti dhīrā yathayaṃ padīpo”ti hi vuttaṃ, dippati vā ariyānaṃ ñāṇacakkhusseva pakāsatīti dīpo. Taṇhānaṃ khayahetuttā taṇhakkhayo. Rāgādīnaṃ paṭipakkhattā, uttamaṭṭhena vā paraṃ. Tāyati rakkhati apāyāditoti tāṇaṃ. Nilīyanti ettha saṃsārabhayabhīrukāti leṇaṃ. Natthi dīgharassādikaṃ rūpaṃ saṇṭhānametassāti arūpaṃ, appaccayattā vā arūpaṃ. Rāgādīnaṃ santakaraṇattā santaṃ. Rāgakkhayahetubhāvena aviparītattā, catusaccapariyāpannattā [M 0.0016] vā saccaṃ. Natthi ālayo taṇhā etthāti anālayaṃ.

6. The forty-six names for Nibbāna, beginning with Mokkha and ending with Nibbūti, are names of Nibbāna. It is called Mokkha (Liberation) because beings are freed here, or by this, from lust and so forth. It is called Nirodha (Cessation) because lust and other defilements cease here; or, 'rodha' is defilement, which obstructs, and since that is not present here, it is 'nirodha'. It is called Nibbāna because one has gone forth from craving, which is called 'vāna', or because by it the fires of lust and so forth are extinguished. Just as a natural island is a support for those swept away by a river’s current, so too does Nibbāna serve as a support for those swept away by the great flood of saṃsāra—thus it is called Dīpa (Island). Or because it makes those without defilements like a lamp, it is called Dīpa (Lamp)—for it is said, 'The wise are extinguished like this lamp.' Or because it shines, illuminating the wisdom-eye of the noble ones, it is called Dīpa (Light). It is called Taṇhakkhaya (Destruction of Craving) because it is the cause for the destruction of craving. It is called Paraṃ (The Beyond) because it is the opposite of lust and so forth, or because of its supreme meaning. It is called Tāṇa (Refuge) because it protects from dangers such as the lower realms. It is called Leṇa (Shelter) because those fearful of the dangers of saṃsāra take shelter here. It is called Arūpa (Formless) because it has no form or shape, such as long or short; or it is called Arūpa because it is unconditioned. It is called Santaṃ (Peace) because it pacifies lust and so forth. It is called Saccaṃ (Truth) because, as the cause for the destruction of lust, it is unperverted, or because it is encompassed by the Four Noble Truths. It is called Anālayaṃ (Non-clinging) because there is no clinging, that is, craving, here.

7. Paccayehi na saṅkarīyateti asaṅkhataṃ. Sivaṃ khemabhāvaṃ karotīti sivaṃ, saṃsārabhīrukehi sevitabbattā vā sivaṃ, yadādinā vapaccayo. Natthi ettha mataṃ maraṇaṃ, etasmiṃ vā adhigate puggalassa matanti amataṃ. Passituṃ sudukkaratāya sududdasaṃ. Parehi uttamehi ariyapuggalehi ayitabbaṃ gantabbanti parāyaṇaṃ, parato vā ayitabbaṃ gantabbanti parāyaṇaṃ, saṃsārasabhāvato aññasabhāvavasena bujjhitabbantyattho, paresaṃ vā ariyapuggalānaṃ patiṭṭhānattā parāyaṇaṃ. Yena cattāro maggā odhiso kilese saranti hiṃsanti taṃ dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ, ariyānaṃ vasitagehattā vā saraṇaṃ. Īti upaddavo pavāso ca te yattha na santi, taṃ anītikaṃ, satte saṃsāraṃ netīti “nītī”ti laddhanāmāya taṇhāya abhāvato vā anītikaṃ. Āsavānaṃ anārammaṇatāya anāsavaṃ. Niccaṭṭhena dhuvaṃ, dhavati vā maggānamārammaṇabhāvaṃ gacchatīti dhuvaṃ, “dhu gatitheriyesū”ti hi kātantadhātu. Daṭṭhabbasabhāvassa natthitāya anidassanaṃ. Paccayehi akatattā akataṃ. Sadā vijjamānattā apalujjanasabhāvaṃ gacchati, tena vā viññāyatīti apalokitaṃ. “Itaṃ gate ca viññāte”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe vuttaṃ. Lokasabhāvena vā viññāyatīti lokitaṃ, tabbhāvāpagamanato apalokitaṃ. Saṇhaṭṭhena nipuṇaṃ, yena vā cattāro maggā odhiso kilese nissesato punanti sodhenti, taṃ nipuṇaṃ. Na kadācipi yassa anto vināso atthi, taṃ anantaṃ. Kharanti [M 0.0017] vinassantīti kharā, saṅkhatā, te yattha na santi, taṃ akkharaṃ, kharasaṅkhātānaṃ vā saṅkhatānaṃ paṭipakkhattā akkharaṃ. Ettha ca asaṅkhatantyādikā gāthā rucirā nāma.

7. It is called Asaṅkhata (Unconditioned) because it is not compounded by conditions. It is called Siva (Auspicious/Safe) because it brings about a state of safety, or because it should be resorted to by those who fear saṃsāra. There is no death or dying here, or when this is attained, there is no death for the person—thus it is Amata (Deathless). It is Sududdasa (Very Hard to See) because it is extremely difficult to perceive. It is called Parāyaṇa (Ultimate Goal/Refuge) because it is to be approached and gone to by the supreme noble persons; or it is to be approached and gone to from beyond, meaning it is to be understood as a nature different from the nature of saṃsāra; or it is the foundation for the supreme noble persons. That Dhamma by which the four paths, cutting them off, injure and destroy defilements is called Saraṇa (Refuge), or it is Saraṇa because it is the dwelling place of the noble ones. Where calamity, affliction, and exile do not exist, that is Anītika (Free from Calamity). Or it is Anītika because of the absence of craving, which has gained the name 'nīti' (leading) because it leads beings through saṃsāra. It is Anāsava (Taintless) because it is not an object for the taints. It is Dhuva (Stable) because of its constant nature, or because it moves towards becoming the object of the paths—for the root 'dhu' in the Kātantra grammar means 'to go' or 'to be firm.' It is Anidassana (Invisible) because the nature of what can be seen does not exist there. It is Akata (Uncreated) because it is not made by conditions. It is Apalokita (Unseen/Unperishing) because it always exists and undergoes no destruction, or because it is known by that. Indeed, in the Nānārthasaṅgaha, it is stated: 'Itaṃ means gone to and known.' Or it is called Lokita (Seen) because it is known by the nature of the world; because it departs from that nature, it is Apalokita. It is Nipuṇa (Subtle) because of its refined nature, or because it is that by which the four paths, having cut them off, completely cleanse and purify the defilements. It is Ananta (Endless) because there is never any end or destruction of it. The conditioned are called 'kharā' (perishable) because they perish; where these do not exist, that is Akkhara (Imperishable), or it is Akkhara because it is the opposite of the perishable, called the conditioned. And here, the verse beginning 'the unconditioned' is indeed called Rucirā (Delightful).

8. Sabbadukkhānaṃ khayakāraṇattā dukkhakkhayo. Byābādhatīti byābādho, so eva byābādo, dukkhasaccaṃ, tassa bhāvo byābajjaṃ, dukkhassa pīḷanādyattho, taṃ yattha natthi, taṃ abyābajjaṃ, abyāpajjhantipi pāṭho, tattha byāpajjanti vinassantīti byāpādā, saṅkhatā, tesaṃ bhāvo byāpajjhaṃ, saṅkhatānaṃ vinassanabhāvo, taṃ yattha natthi, taṃ abyāpajjhanti evamattho veditabbo, niruttinayena ca dyassa jjhakāro. Kilesakammavipākavaṭṭānamabhāvato vivaṭṭaṃ. Nibbhayaṭṭhena khemaṃ, khayanti vā etena rāgaggiādayoti khemaṃ. Saṅkhārehi asammissatāya, visaṃyogatāya ca kevalaṃ. Apavajjanti saṅkhārā etasmāti apavaggo. Yasmā rāgo vigato, so virāgo. Padhānabhāvaṃ nītaṃ paṇītaṃ. Natthi etasmiṃ adhigate ariyānaṃ cutaṃ cavananti accutaṃ. Ariyehi pajjitabbattā gantabbattā padaṃ.

8. It is the Destruction of Suffering (dukkhakkhaya) because it is the cause for the destruction of all suffering. That which afflicts is an affliction (byābādha); that very thing is an affliction (byābāda), the truth of suffering. Its state is affliction (byābajja), meaning the oppression of suffering and so forth. Where that is absent, it is Non-affliction (abyābajja). There is also the reading 'abyāpajjhaṃ.' Therein, 'byāpādā' means 'they perish,' referring to conditioned things. Their state is 'byāpajjhaṃ,' the state of perishing of conditioned things. Where that is absent, it is 'abyāpajjhaṃ'—this is the meaning to be understood. And according to the etymological method, 'dya' becomes 'jjha.' It is the Unrolling (vivaṭṭa) due to the absence of the cycle of defilements, kamma, and results. It is Safety (khema) in the sense of being without fear, or because the fires of lust and so forth are extinguished by it, it is Safety. It is Solitary (kevala) because of its being unmixed with and disconnected from formations. It is Release (apavagga) because formations fall away from it. Because lust is gone from it, it is Dispassion (virāga). Brought to a state of pre-eminence, it is Excellent (paṇīta). When this is attained, there is no falling or passing away for the noble ones; thus, it is the Unfailing (accuta). It is the State (pada) because it is to be reached and gone to by the noble ones.

9. Cattāro yogā khayanti etenāti yogakkhemo. Pāreti sakkoti saṃsāradukkhasantāpaṃ sametunti pāraṃ, “saṃsāradukkhasantāpatattassā’laṃ sametave”ti hi vuttaṃ. Pagatā saṃsāracakkassa arā etasmāti vā pāraṃ. Kilesehi muccanato mutti, nikāyantariyā pana “sarīrendriyehi attano muttattā muttī”ti vadanti. Kilesasamanato santi. Visujjhanti sattā etāya rāgādimalehīti visuddhi[M 0.0018]. Sabbasaṅkhārā vimuccanato vimutti. Asaṅkhatameva nissattanijjīvaṭṭhena, santilakkhaṇadhāraṇato vā dhātūti asaṅkhatadhātu. Sujjhanti sattā etāya rāgādimalehīti suddhi. Āvuṇoti saṃsārato nikkhantumappadānavasenāti vuti, taṇhā, tato nikkhantattā nibbuti.

9. It is Security from Yokes (yogakkhema) because the four yokes are destroyed by this. It is the Further Shore (pāra) because it is able to quell the burning of suffering in saṃsāra; for it has been said, 'It is sufficient to quell the burning of one afflicted by the suffering of saṃsāra.' Or, it is the Further Shore (pāra) because the spokes (arā) of the wheel of saṃsāra are gone from it. It is Liberation (mutti) because of being freed from defilements; other schools, however, say, 'Liberation is being free from one’s own body and faculties.' It is Peace (santi) because of the pacification of defilements. It is Purity (visuddhi) because beings are purified from the stains of lust and so forth by this. It is Deliverance (vimutti) because of being completely released from all formations. The Unconditioned Element (asaṅkhatadhātu) is so called in the sense of being without a being and without a soul, or because it bears the characteristic of peace. It is Purity (suddhi) because beings are cleansed from the stains of lust and so forth by this. Craving is an Obstruction (vuti) because it obstructs by not affording an opportunity to exit from saṃsāra; because one has gone forth from that, it is Extinction (nibbuti).

10. Khīṇāsavādicatukkaṃ arahante. Khīṇā āsavā yassa so khīṇāsavo. Tato uttari karaṇīyābhāvato natthi sikkhā etassāti asekkho. Vigato rāgo yasmāti vītarāgo. Saṃsāracakkassa are hatavāti arahā, “araha”ntipi pāṭho.

10. The quartet of terms beginning with 'khīṇāsava' refers to the Arahant. One whose taints are destroyed is a Khīṇāsava. Because there is nothing further to be done, there is no training for him; thus, he is an Asekkha (One with No More Training). One from whom lust has departed is a Vītarāga. One who has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra is an Arahā; 'arahaṃ' is also a reading.

Devalokādipañcakaṃ saggassa nāmaṃ. Devānaṃ loko bhavanaṃ devaloko. Dibbantyatra divo. Aja gatiyaṃ, anekatthattā ṭhitiyaṃ, ciraṃ ṭhiyate asminti aggo, ṭhānaṃ, sobhano aggo saggo, puññena vā suṭṭhu ajīyateti saggo. Tayo devā dibbantyatreti tidivo. Padhānato hi tīhi hariharabrahmehi byapadeso. Tidasānaṃ devānaṃ ālayo ṭhānanti tidasālayo. Keci pana “devalokādittayaṃ saggasāmaññassa nāmaṃ, tidivādidvayaṃ tāvatiṃsassā”ti vadanti, taṃ amarakosādīsu sāmaññasmiṃyeva dvinnampi gahaṇato na sārato paccetabbaṃ. Etthāpi nāka, suraloka, tipiṭṭhapa visanti sukatino asmiṃ iti piṭṭhapaṃ pisodarādi tidasānaṃ piṭṭhapadhiti dasasaddalopo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), avaroha, phalodaya [M 0.0019] phalassa kammaphalassa udayo diṭṭhiyogyaṭṭhānaṃ (tikaṇḍaṭīkā), mandara, serika, sakkabhavana, khaṃ, nabhādīni devalokasāmaññāni idhānāgatānipi gahetabbāni.

The pentad of terms beginning with 'devaloka' are names for heaven. Devaloka is the world of the gods, their abode. They shine here; thus, it is Divo. The root 'aj' means 'to go'; due to its many meanings, it also means 'to stay.' That in which one stays for a long time is 'agga,' a place. A beautiful place (sobhano aggo) is Sagga. Or, because it is well attained (suṭṭhu ajīyate) through merit, it is Sagga. Three gods shine here; thus, it is Tidivo. Indeed, the designation is primarily by the three: Hari, Hara, and Brahma. Tidasālaya is the abode, the dwelling place, of the Tidasā gods. Some, however, say, 'The three terms beginning with devaloka are general names for heaven, while the two beginning with tidiva are for the Tāvatiṃsa realm.' This should not be accepted as authoritative, since in the Amarakośa and other lexicons, both are taken in a general sense. Here, too, names such as nāka, suraloka, tipiṭṭhapa, avaroha, phalodaya, mandara, serika, Sakka’s abode, khaṃ, nabha, and others—even those not mentioned here—should be taken as general names for the heavenly world.

11-12. Tidasādicatuddasakaṃ devatāsāmaññassa nāmaṃ. Jātīsu jātijātīsu (ka.) vuttāsu byattipi vuccatīti byattīnaṃ bahuttā bahuvacananiddeso. Jātisattāvināsasaṅkhātā tisso dasā parimāṇā etesanti tidasā. Ete hi manussādayo viya buddhivipariṇāmakhayehi na yujjanti, pañcavīsativassuddesiyā eva uppajjanti santi vinassanti ca. Maraṇaṃ maro, so yesaṃ natthi, te amarā. Dibbanti pañcakāmaguṇādīhi kīḷantīti devā. Vibujjhanti na supantīti vibudhā, atītānāgatajātiṃ vibujjhantīti vā vibudhā. Sudhābhojanabhuñjanasīlatāya sudhāsino. Samudduṭṭhā amatamathanoṭṭhā (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) surā atthi yesaṃ, te surā, suranti vā kīḷantīti surā, sukhena ramantīti vā surā. Dīghāyukāpi samānā yathāparicchedaṃ sampattakāle maranti sīlenāti marū. Divo devaloko oko āsayo yesaṃ te divokā. Sudhāhārassa pātabbassapi sambhavato amataṃ pivantīti amatapā, amatosadhaṃ vā pivantīti amatapā. Sagge vasanasīlattā saggavāsino. Sadā pañcavīsativassuddesiyattā nirākatā jarā etesanti nijjarā. Na nimisantīti animisā, bhamukā niccalaṃ karontītyattho. Dive vasantīti dibbā. Devā eva devatā, sakatthe devasaddato tāpaccayo, devatā eva devatāni, sakatthe nipaccayo. “Apume”ti ettha paṭhamasakatthikavasena itthiliṅgattaṃ, dutiyasakatthikavasena [M 0.0020] napuṃsakaliṅgattaṃ veditabbaṃ, dutiyasakatthikavaseneva vā dviliṅgattaṃ, tattha itthiliṅgapakkhe yadādinā nikārādeso. Amarakose pana “devatāni pume vā”ti amara 1.9 vuttaṃ. Tassattho – devatānisaddo vikappena pulliṅge, niccaṃ napuṃsaketi. Ṭīkāyañca “sakatthikā pakatito liṅgavacanāni ativattantīti punnapuṃsakatta”nti devo eva devatā, sakatthe tā, sakatthikā api paccayā pakatito liṅgavacanādyativattante, apīti itthittaṃ devatā eva devataṃ paññādittā aṇa (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) vuttaṃ. Tattha sakatthikāti dutiyasakatthikaṃ vuttaṃ, pakatitoti paṭhamasakatthikaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ “punnapuṃsakatta”nti, itarathā tāpaccayantassa niccaṃ itthiliṅgatāya itthiliṅgattameva vadeyya. Supabbā, sumanā, tidivesā, āditeyyā, divisadā, lekhā, aditinandanā, ādiccā, ribhavo vibhavā (ka.), rikāro devamātā siyā iti tikaṇḍe, tato bhavantīti (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) asoppā, amaccā maraṇaṃ mati iti ti, matiyaṃ bhavā maccā… na maccā amaccā (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), amatāsanā, aggimukhā, havibhojanā, girabbāṇā, dānavārayo, bindārakā, pūjiyā, cirāyukā, saggino, nabhosadāiccādīnipi devatānaṃ sāmaññanāmāneva.

11-12. The set of fourteen terms beginning with Tidasā are general names for deities. Since among the classes (jāti) mentioned, individuals (byatti) are also spoken of, the plural is used because of the multitude of individuals. Those for whom the three stages known as birth, existence, and destruction are the measure are the Tidasā. For these, unlike humans and others, are not subject to changes and decay of intellect; they arise, exist, and pass away always appearing as twenty-five years old. Death is 'mara'; those who are without it are the Amarā (Immortals). They play (dibbanti) with the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth; thus, they are Devā. They are awake (vibujjhanti) and do not sleep; thus, they are Vibudhā. Or, they awaken to past and future lives; thus, they are Vibudhā. Because of their nature of partaking of nectar-food, they are Sudhāsino. Those who possess the liquor (surā) that arose from the ocean are the Surā; or, they play (suranti); thus, they are Surā; or, they delight (ramanti) in happiness; thus, they are Surā. Though long-lived, they die by nature at the appointed time according to their limit; thus, they are Marū. Those for whom heaven (divo), the devaloka, is their home (oko) and abode (āsayo) are the Divokā. Because it is possible for them to drink the deathless nectar, they are Amatapā (Nectar-Drinkers); or, they drink the medicine of deathlessness; thus, they are Amatapā. Because of their nature of dwelling in heaven, they are Saggavāsino. Because they always appear as twenty-five years old, old age is rejected for them; thus, they are Nijjarā (Ageless). They do not blink (na nimisanti); thus, they are Animisā, meaning they keep their eyebrows motionless. They dwell in heaven (dive); thus, they are Dibbā. Devatā is simply Deva; the suffix -tā is added to the word 'deva' in the reflexive sense. Devatāni is simply Devatā; the suffix -ni is added in the reflexive sense. Regarding the word 'apume,' it should be understood that based on the first reflexive suffix [-tā], the gender is feminine, while based on the second reflexive suffix [-ni], it is neuter; or, based on the second reflexive suffix, it can have two genders. In that case, for the feminine gender, there is a substitution involving the letter 'n' according to the rule beginning 'yadādinā.' In the Amarakośa, however, it is said, 'devatāni is also masculine.' The meaning is that the word 'devatāni' is optionally masculine and always neuter. And in the subcommentary it is said: 'Reflexive suffixes transcend the gender and number of the base form, hence it is masculine-neuter.' There, 'reflexive suffix' refers to the second one [-ni], and 'base form' refers to the first one [-tā]. Therefore, 'masculine-neuter' is stated; otherwise, since a word ending in the suffix -tā is always feminine, only 'feminine' would have been stated. Supabbā, Sumanā, Tidivesā, Āditeyyā, Divisadā, Lekhā, Aditinandanā, Ādiccā, Ribhavo, Asoppā, Amaccā, Amatāsanā, Aggimukhā, Havibhojanā, Girabbāṇā, Dānavārayo, Bindārakā, Pūjiyā, Cirāyukā, Saggino, Nabhosadā, and others are also general names for deities.

13. Siddhādayo ime devayoniyo devappabhavā devavaṃsā etesamuppattiyaṃ devānameva ādikāraṇattā. Aṇimādiguṇopetattā sijjhanti etassa yathicchitā atthāti siddho. Yassa bhāsāya brūhati kathā, so bhūto[M 0.0021], pisācappabhedo adhomukhādi. Vacanattho pana bhavanti brūhanti kathā etasmāti bhūtoti. Gandhaṃ abbati paribhuñjatīti gandhabbo, devagāyanā “hāhā hūhū” pabhutayo amara 1.55. Nidhayo guyhatīti guyhako, saññāyaṃ ko, maṇibhadrādiko kuverānucaro. Yakkha pūjāyaṃ, yakkhīyate pūjīyateti yakkho, kuverādiko. Rakkhanti attānaṃ etasmāti rakkhaso, vibhīsaṇādi. Kumbhappamāṇaṇḍatāya kumbhaṇḍo. Pisitaṃ maṃsaṃ asati bhakkhatīti pisāco, sakuni sakuntiādiko kuverānucaro, yadādinā pisitassa pibhāvo, asassa ca sācādesabhāvo pāṇini 6.3.109; moggallānapañcikā 1.47. Ādisaddena vijjādhara, apasara, kinnare ca saṅgaṇhāti. Vijjaṃ guḷikāñjanamantādikaṃ dharatīti vijjādharo. Apasārayanti khalayantīti apasarā, ubbasyādikā suravesiyo amara 1.55, apasarasaddassa jātiyaṃ sayaṃ bahuttaṃ, byattiyantu tadavayavaṃ vā sayaṃ, tathā ca bahuttaṃva. Vanādisaddo kadāci jātiyaṃ payujjate, kadāci byattiyaṃ. Tatra yadā jātiyaṃ, tadā byattigataṃ saṅkhyamādāya pavattati. Yadā byattiyaṃ payujjate, tadā taṃbyattāvayavānaṃ pāṇipādādīnaṃ bahuttasaṅkhyamādāya pavattati. Vanasaddo tu jātigatekasaṅkhyāvisiṭṭhadabbābhidhānato dhavādibyattigatajātyābhidhānato vā ekavacananti apasarasaddo vāmanādimatena itthiyaṃ bahuvacane ca, tadaññesaṃ pana matena pumitthiyaṃ vacanadvaye ca daṭṭhabbo. Assamukhanarasarīrattā kucchito naro, kiñci vā naro, narasadisattā vā kinnaro. Etā devayoniyo. Gaṇadevatā pana –

13. These divine beings, such as the Siddhas, are of divine birth, of divine origin, and of divine lineage, because the gods are the primary cause of their arising. Because they possess qualities such as the power of becoming minute (aṇimā), they succeed in achieving whatever they desire; hence they are called Siddhas. One by whose speech words flourish is called a Bhūta, a type of Pisāca, characterized by being downward-faced, etc. The meaning of the word, however, is that speech flourishes from them; hence they are called Bhūtas. One who enjoys fragrance is called a Gandhabba, such as the divine singers Hāhā and Hūhū. One who conceals treasures is called a Guhyaka; 'ko' is a suffix in this term, such as Maṇibhadra, a follower of Kuvera. 'Yakkha' is in the sense of worship; because one is worshipped, he is called a Yakkha, such as Kuvera. A Rakkhasa is so called because one protects oneself from him, such as Vibhīṣaṇa. A Kumbhaṇḍa is so called for having testicles the size of pots. A Pisāca is one who eats raw flesh; by a grammatical rule, 'pisita' becomes 'pi' and 'asa' becomes 'sāca', such as Sakunī and Sakunti, followers of Kuvera. The term 'ādi' (etc.) also includes Vidyādharas, Apsarās, and Kinnaras. A Vidyādhara is one who holds knowledge, such as pills, collyrium, spells, etc. Apsarās are celestial nymphs who distract and agitate, such as Urvaśī. The word 'apasarā' is inherently plural when referring to the class, but when referring to an individual, it can be singular or plural based on its parts. Similarly, words like 'vana' (forest) can refer to a class or an individual. When referring to a class, the number is determined by the individual instances. When referring to an individual, the number is determined by its constituent parts, such as hands and feet. The word 'vana' itself, however, is singular when denoting a substance characterized by a single class-nature, or denoting the class-nature inherent in individuals like the Dhava tree. Thus, the word 'apasarā' is feminine and plural according to Vāmana's view, but according to the view of others, it is to be understood as being in both masculine and feminine genders and in both numbers. A Kinnara is so called for having a horse's face and a human body, or for being a 'deformed human,' or 'somewhat human,' or for resembling a human. These are the divine beings. As for the Gaṇadevatās—

“Ādiccā visu vasavo, tusitā’bhassarā’nilā;

Mahārājikā sādhyā ca, ruddā ca gaṇadevatā”ti amara 1.10.

"The Ādiccas, the Visus, the Vasus, the Tusitas, the Ābhassaras, the Anilas, the Mahārājikas, the Sādhyas, and the Ruddas; these are the host of deities."

Amarakose [M 0.0022] kathitā.

These are mentioned in the Amarakośa.

Tatrādiccā dvādasakā, visudevā dasa ṭhitā;

Vasavo aṭṭhasaṅkhyātā, chattiṃsa tusitā matā.

Therein, the Ādiccas are twelve, the Visudevas stand at ten; the Vasus are reckoned as eight, and the Tusitas are held to be thirty-six.

Ābhassarā catusaṭṭhi, vātā paṇṇāsekūnakā;

Mahārājikanāmāyo, dvisataṃ vīsatādhikā.

The Ābhassaras are sixty-four, the Vātas are forty-nine; those named Mahārājika are two hundred and twenty.

Sādhyā dvādasa vikhyātā, ruddā cekādasa ṭhitā;

Samayantarato etā, viññeyyā gaṇadevatā.

Twelve are known as the Sādhyas, and eleven stand as the Ruddas; these hosts of deities are to be understood according to different traditions.

14. Pubbadevādicatukkaṃ asure. Pubbaṃ devā pubbadevā, dutiyāsamāso, pubbe vā devā pubbadevā, pubbe hyete devapure ṭhitā, anantaraṃ sakkādīhi tato cālitā. Surānaṃ ripū sattavo suraripū. Surānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato asurā, devā viya na suranti na kīḷantīti vā asurā, samudduṭṭhā vā surā devehi abhyupagatā, nāsurehīti natthi surā etesanti asurāti nikāyantariyā. Danunāmāya mātuyā apaccaṃ dānavā. Danu nāma terasasu rakkhasaduhitīsu ekissā duhitu nāmaṃ. Ete pubbadevādayo sadā pume pulliṅge vattanti. Deccā, deteyyā, danujā, indārī, suradisā, sukkasissā, ditisutā, pubbajāiccādīnipi asurassa sāmaññanāmāni.

14. The group of four beginning with the Former Devas refers to the Asuras. "Pubbadevā" means "former devas," which is a second-case compound. Or, they are called Former Devas because they formerly dwelt in the city of the devas, but were later displaced from there by Sakka and others. The enemies of the Suras are the Suraripus. Because they are the opposition of the Suras, they are Asuras; or, unlike the devas they do not rejoice or play, hence they are Asuras; or, according to another school, the liquor surā arose from the ocean and was accepted by the devas, but not by the Asuras, hence, "there is no surā for them," thus they are Asuras. The offspring of the mother named Danu are the Dānavas. Danu is the name of one of the thirteen daughters of a Rakkhasa. These Former Devas and others are always used in the masculine gender. Deccā, Deteyyā, Danujā, Indārī, Suradisā, Sukkasissā, Ditisutā, Pubbajā, and others are also common names for Asuras.

Tabbisesā asurappabhedā. Surehi saddhiṃ saṅgāmatthaṃ attano balakāyānaṃ pahāraṃ āyudhaṃ dadātīti pahārado, so eva pahārādo. Saṃ pasattho varo jāmātā yassa [M 0.0023] so sambaro, tassa hi sakko jāmātā saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.256, puññāharīsu vā indriyāni saṃvuṇotīti sambaro. Balametassatthīti balī, atisayabalakāyattā vā balī, so eva bali, “baliādayo”ti iminā samāsepi sandhi natthīti dīpeti. Ādinā macchasakuṇādikepi kuñcādikepi asurabhede saṅgaṇhāti.

Their particulars are the varieties of Asuras. Pahārada is one who gives blows and weapons to his own army for battle with the Suras; he is also Pahārāda. Sambara is one whose son-in-law is excellent and well-praised, for Sakka is his son-in-law; or because he restrains the senses in meritorious deeds, he is Sambara. Balī is one who has strength, or because he possesses an exceedingly powerful body, he is Balī; he is also Bali. The grammatical rule "baliādayo" indicates that there is no sandhi here even in a compound. By "ādi" he includes other varieties of Asuras like Macchasakuṇa and Kuñca.

15. Pitāmahādyaṭṭhakaṃ brahmani. Pitūnaṃ pajāpatīnaṃ lokapitūnampi pitā pitāmaho, āmahapaccayo moggallāna 4.38. Sabbalokānaṃ pituṭṭhāniyattā pitā, sabbalokaṃ vā pāti rakkhatīti pitā, ritupaccayo. Mahantasarīratāya brahmā, braha vuḍḍhiyaṃ mapaccayo. Lokānaṃ īso indo lokeso. Kamalasambhavattā kamalaṃ, padmaṃ. Taṃ āsanamuppattiṭṭhānamassa kamalāsano. Hiraññaṃ suvaṇṇamayaṃ aṇḍaṃ hiraññaṃ, tassa gabbho bhūṇo guṇo (ka.) hiraññagabbho. Jhānādiguṇehi surānaṃ jeṭṭhattā surajeṭṭho. Pajānaṃ sattānaṃ pati sāmibhūto pajāpati, pajaṃ pāletīti vā pajāpati. Attabhū, parameṭṭhi, sayambhū, caturānano, dhātā, kamalayoni, duhiṇo, viriñci, sajitā, vedhā, vidhātā, vidhi, haṃsaratho, viriñco, papitāmaho iccādayopi brahmanāmāni.

15. The group of eight beginning with Pitāmaha are names for Brahmā. Pitāmaha is the father of fathers, of the lords of creatures, and even of the world-fathers; the suffix 'āmaha' is used. He is called Pitā (Father) because he is in the position of a father to all worlds, or because he protects (pāti) the entire world; the suffix 'ritu' is used. Brahmā is so called because of his immense body, from the root 'brah' meaning 'to grow,' with the suffix 'ma'. Lokesa is the lord, the chief, of the worlds. Kamalāsana is so called because he arose from a lotus (kamala, also known as padma), which is his seat and place of origin. Hiraññagabbha is so called because he is the embryo (gabbho, bhūṇo) of the golden egg (hiraññaṃ, suvaṇṇamayaṃ aṇḍaṃ). Surajeṭṭho is the eldest of the Suras due to his qualities like jhāna. Pajāpati is the lord, the master of beings, or because he protects (pāleti) beings. Other names for Brahmā include Attabhū, Parameṭṭhi, Sayambhū, Caturānano, Dhātā, Kamalayoni, Duhiṇo, Viriñci, Sajitā, Vedhā, Vidhātā, Vidhi, Haṃsaratho, Viriñco, Papitāmaho, and others.

16-17. Vāsudevādipañcakaṃ [M 0.0024] kaṇhe. Vasudevassa apaccaṃ vāsudevo. Maccānaṃ jīvitaṃ harati sīlenāti hari. Kaṇhaguṇayogato kaṇho. Kesiṃ nāma asuraṃ hatavāti kesavo, īkārassa akāro, hanassa ca vo. Vuttañca –

16-17. The group of five beginning with Vāsudeva are names for Kaṇha. Vāsudeva means the descendant of Vasudeva. Hari means he who takes away the life of mortals by his nature. Kaṇha is so called because of his dark qualities. Kesava means he who slew the Asura named Kesi; the 'ī' becomes 'a,' and 'han' becomes 'va.' And it was said—

“Yasmā tayā hato kesī,

Tasmā me sāsanaṃ suṇa;

Kesavo nāma nāmena,

Seyyo loke bhavissasī”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkāyampi.

"Since you have slain Kesī,

Therefore, listen to my command;

By the name of Kesava,

You shall be the best in the world."

Cakkaṃ pāṇimhi assa cakkapāṇi. Visaṇu piṇhu (ka.), nārāyano, vekuṇṭho, dāmodaro, mādhavo, sambhū, deccāri, puṇḍarīkakkho, govindo, garuḷaddhajo, pītambaro, accuto, maṅgalo, siṅgī, janāddano, upendo, indāvarajo, catubhujo, padmanābho, madhuripu, tivikkamo, devakīnandano, sorī, sirīpati, purisottamo, vanamālī, balidhaṃsī, kaṃsārāti, adhokkhajo, sabbambharo, keṭabhaji keṭabhaṃ jitavā (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), vidhu, sasabindu, sirīkaro, sirīvarāho, ajito, parapuriso, sirīgabbho, chabindu, ananto, narakaji, kesaro, jātikīlo, narasīho, purāṇapuriso, nalinesayo, vāsu, narāyano, punabbasu, sabbarūpo, dharaṇīdharo, vāmano, ekasiṅgo, somagabbho, ādidevo, ādivarāho, suvaṇṇabindu, sadāyogī, sanātano, rāhumuddhabhido[M 0.0025], kāḷanemi, paṇḍavo, vaḍḍhamāno, satānando, pajānātho, suyāmunoiccādīni visaṇunāmāni. Assa pana pitu nāmāni vasudevo, ānakadundubhi amara 1.23 iccādīni. Rathavāho panassa dāruko nāma tikaṇḍasesa 1.1.34. Mantī pana pavanabyādhi nāma mantī pavanabyāmi uddhavo (titaṇḍasesa 1.1.35) pavanabyādhi… uddhavo iti dve piṇhussa mantino (kaṭṭīkā).

He who has a wheel in his hand is Cakkapāṇi. Visaṇu, Nārāyano, Vekuṇṭho, Dāmodaro, Mādhava, Sambhū, Deccāri, Puṇḍarīkakkho, Govindo, Garuḷaddhajo, Pītambaro, Accuto, Maṅgalo, Siṅgī, Janāddano, Upendo, Indāvarajo, Catubhujo, Padmanābho, Madhuripu, Tivikkamo, Devakīnandano, Sorī, Sirīpati, Purisottamo, Vanamālī, Balidhaṃsī, Kaṃsārāti, Adhokkhajo, Sabbambharo, Keṭabhaji, Vidhu, Sasabindu, Sirīkaro, Sirīvarāho, Ajito, Parapuriso, Sirīgabbho, Chabindu, Ananto, Narakaji, Kesaro, Jātikīlo, Narasīho, Purāṇapuriso, Nalinesayo, Vāsu, Narāyano, Punabbasu, Sabbarūpo, Dharaṇīdharo, Vāmano, Ekasiṅgo, Somagabbho, Ādidevo, Ādivarāho, Suvaṇṇabindu, Sadāyogī, Sanātano, Rāhumuddhabhido, Kāḷanemi, Paṇḍavo, Vaḍḍhamāno, Satānando, Pajānātho, Suyāmuno—these and other names belong to Visaṇu. Moreover, his father’s names are Vasudeva, Ānakadundubhi, and so forth. His charioteer is named Dāruka. His minister is named Pavanabyādhi.

Mahissarādichakkaṃ hare. Mahanto issaro vibhūti etassāti mahissaro. Guṇāvatthārahito sampati paramānandarūpattā nibbikāro samati bhavatīti sivo, niruttinayena akārassa ittaṃ, massa vo ca. Evaṃ sabbattha yadādinā vā niruttinayena vā saddasiddhi veditabbāti. Sūlapāṇittā sūlī. Iṭṭhe pabhavatīti issaro, issati abhibhavatīti vā issaro. Pasūnaṃ pamathānaṃ pati pasupati. “Pasu migādo chagale, pamathepi pasu pume”ti ruddo rabhaso (ka.). ( ) (guṇe) (ka.) Visiṭṭhatamoguṇattā sabbaṃ haratīti haro. Vuttoti kriyāpadaṃ. Sambhu, īso, sabbo, īsāno, saṅkaro, candasekharo, bhūteso, khaṇḍaparasu, girīso, maccuñjayo, pinākī, pamathādhipo, uggo, kapaddi, sirīkaṇṭho, kāḷakaṇṭho, kapālabharo, vāmadevo, mahādevo, virūpakkho, tilocano, sabbaññū, nīlalohito, māraharo, bhaggo, tyambako, tipurantako, gaṅgādharo, andhakaripu, byomakeso, bhavo, bhīmo, ruddo, umāpati, bhagālī, kapisañjano, hīro, pañcānano, khakuntalo, gopālako, piṅgakkho vibhaṅgo (ka.), kūṭakaro, candāpīḷo, mahānaṭo, samīro, ho, nandivaḍḍhano, guḷākeso migūho (ka.), mihirāṇo, meghavāhano, suppatāpo suppasādo (ka.), u, thāṇu upāṇḍo (ka.), sipiviṭṭho, kīlo, dhammavāhanoiccādīnipi haranāmāni.

The group of six, beginning with Mahissara, belong to Hara. He is Mahissara because great lordship and power belong to him. He is Siva because, being free from states of qualities and attachments, he is blissful and undisturbed, being of the nature of supreme bliss. By the rule of etymology, 'a' becomes 'i' and 'ma' becomes 'va'. Thus, in all cases, whether by derivation or by the rule of etymology, the word formation should be understood. He is Sūlī because he has a trident in his hand. He is Issara because he arises in what is desired, or because he overpowers. He is Pasupati, the lord of beings and goblins. For it is said, 'Pasu means deer, goats, and also the hosts of goblins; pasu, masculine gender,' in the Rudda. He is Hara because he removes all things due to his supreme and excellent qualities. 'Vutto' is a verb. The following are names of Hara: Sambhu, Īsa, Sabba, Īsāna, Saṅkara, Candasekhara, Bhūtesa, Khaṇḍaparasu, Girīsa, Maccuñjaya, Pinākī, Pamathādhipa, Ugga, Kapaddī, Sirīkaṇṭha, Kāḷakaṇṭha, Kapālabhara, Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, Virūpakkha, Tilocana, Sabbaññū, Nīlalohita, Mārahara, Bhagga, Tyambaka, Tipurantaka, Gaṅgādhara, the enemy of Andhaka, Byomakesa, Bhava, Bhīma, Rudda, Umāpati, Bhagālī, Kapisañjana, Hīra, Pañcānana, Khakuntala, Gopālaka, Piṅgakkha, Kūṭakara, Candāpīḷa, Mahānaṭa, Samīra, Ho, Nandivaḍḍhana, Guḷākesa, Mihirāṇa, Meghavāhana, Suppatāpa, U, Thāṇu, Sipiviṭṭha, Kīla, Dhammavāhana, and so forth are also names of Hara.

Kumārādittayaṃ [M 0.0026] harassa putte. Kumāra kīḷāyaṃ, kumāreti kīḷatīti kumāro, soḷasavassiko, ayañca soḷasavassiko. “Bālo ca soḷasa bhave”ti hi vuttaṃ. Khaṇḍati dānavabalanti khando, ṇḍassa ndo. Sattiṃpaharaṇavisesaṃ dharatīti sattidharo, pabhāvussāhamantasaṅkhātaṃ vā sattittayaṃ dharatīti sattidharo. Amarakose pana –

The group of three, beginning with Kumāra, are Hara's sons. He is Kumāra because he plays (kīḷati) in play (kīḷāyaṃ); he is sixteen years old, and this one is also sixteen years old. For it is said, 'A boy is even sixteen.' He is Khaṇḍa because he breaks the strength of the Dānavas; 'ṇḍa' becomes 'nda'. He is Sattidhara because he bears a special weapon called Satti, or because he bears the threefold power known as influence, effort, and counsel. But in the Amarakośa—

“Kattikeyyo mahāseno,

Sarajāto chaḷānano;

Pabbatīnandano khando,

Senānī aggibhū guho.

"Kattikeyya, Mahāsena, Sarajāta, Chaḷānana; Pabbatīnandana, Khaṇḍa, Senānī, Aggibhū, Guha.

Bāhuleyyo tārakaji,

Visākho sikhivāhano;

Chamāturo sattidharo,

Kumāro koñcadāraṇo”ti amara 1.41-2 vuttaṃ.

Bāhuleyya, Tārakaji, Visākha, Sikhivāhana; Chamātura, Sattidhara, Kumāra, Koñcadāraṇa—thus it is said.

18-21. Sakkādīni vīsati sakkassa nāmāni. Asure jetuṃ sakkuṇātīti sakko. Pure, puraṃ vā dadātīti purindado[M 0.0027]. Devānaṃ rājā devarājā. Vajiraṃ pāṇimhi assa vajirapāṇi. Sujāya asurakaññāya pati sujampati. Bahūnaṃ devamanussānaṃ cintitatthassa dassanasamatthatāya sahassakkho. Mahataṃ devānaṃ indo rājā mahindo, devehi mahitabbo vā indo rājā mahindo, mahanto ca so indo cāti vā mahindo. Vajiraṃ āvudhaṃ yassa vajirāvudho, “vajirāyudho”tipi pāṭho. Vasūni ratanāni santyasseti vāsavo. Dasasatāni nayanāni yassa so dasasatanayano. Dvinnaṃ devalokānaṃ adhipatibhūtattā tidivādhibhū. Surānaṃ nātho suranātho. Vajiraṃ hatthe yassa so vajirahattho. Bhūtānaṃ sattānaṃ pati bhūtapati. Mahitabbattā maghavā. Maha pūjāyaṃ, hassa ghavo. Kosasaṅkhātāni dhanāni santi yassa, so kosiyo, “kosiyagottatāya kosiyo”ti ca vadanti. Indati paramissariyena yujjateti indo. Vatraṃ nāma asuraṃ abhibhavatīti vatrabhū. Pāko nāmavatrāsurassa bhātā, tassa sāsanato niggahato pākasāsano. Viḍaṃ byāpakaṃ ojo etassa viḍojo. Sunāsīro, purandaro, lekhāsabho lekhanaṃ devānaṃ usato uttamo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), divapati, surapati, balārāti, sacīpati, jambhabhedī, harihayo, namucisūdano, saṃkandano, meghavāhano, ākhaṇḍalo ākhaṇḍayati parabalaṃ usādittā kalaca (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), kosiko, suragāmaṇī, nākanātho, harī iccādīnipi sakkassa nāmāni.
