18-21. These are the twenty names of Sakka, beginning with Sakka. He is Sakka because he is able to conquer the Asuras. He is Purindada because he gives in the city or gives a city. He is Devarāja, the king of the devas. He is Vajirapāṇi because he has a thunderbolt in his hand. He is Sujampati, the husband of Sujā, the Asura maiden. He is Sahassakkha because he is capable of seeing the desired aims of many devas and humans. He is Mahinda, the great king of the devas, or the king who should be honored by the devas, or because he is both great and a lord. He is Vajirāvudha because his weapon is the thunderbolt; 'Vajirāyudha' is also a reading. He is Vāsava because he possesses treasures. He is Dasasatanayana because he has ten hundred eyes. He is Tidivādhibhū because he is the overlord of the two devalokas. He is Suranātha, the lord of the Suras. He is Vajirahattha because he has a thunderbolt in his hand. He is Bhūtapati, the lord of beings. He is Maghavā because he is worthy of honor (from the root mah, 'to worship', with 'ha' becoming 'ghava'). He is Kosiya because he possesses wealth called 'kosa,' or they say he is Kosiya because he is of the Kosiya clan. He is Inda because he is endowed with supreme sovereignty. He is Vatrabhū because he overcomes the Asura named Vatra. He is Pākasāsana because he subdues Pāka, the brother of the Asura Vatra, by his command. He is Viḍoja because his power is extensive. Sunāsīra, Purandara, Lekhāsabha, Divapati, Surapati, Balārāti, Sacīpati, Jambhabhedī, Harihaya, Namucisūdana, Saṃkandana, Meghavāhana, Ākhaṇḍala, Kosika, Suragāmaṇī, Nākanātha, Harī, and so forth are also names of Sakka.

Assa sakkassa bhariyā sujātā nāma. Sukhena jātā, sundarā vā jāti yassā sā sujātā. Pulomajā, sacī, indānī iccādīnipi sakkabhariyāya nāmāni.

Sakka’s wife is named Sujātā. She is Sujātā because she was born happily, or because her birth is beautiful. Pulomajā, Sacī, Indānī, and so forth are also names of Sakka’s wife.

Assa sakkassa puraṃ masakkasārādayo tayo bhave. Mo ca sakko ca masakkā, te saranti gacchanti ettha kīḷāvasenāti masakkasārā, mahissarādīnaṃ parisānaṃ, sakkassa ca kīḷānubhavanaṭṭhānantyatthoti [M 0.0028] cintāmaṇithutiṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Saṅgahaṭīkāyaṃ pana “masakkanti vā vasokanti vā asurapurassa nāmaṃ, idaṃ pana tesaṃ uttamattā masakkasāro, vasokasāroti ca vutta”nti vuttaṃ. Amarā etissaṃ santi amaravatī, sā eva amarāvatī, rassassa dīghatā pāṇinī 6.3.119.

Sakka’s city has three names, beginning with Masakkasārā. It is called Masakkasārā because Mo and Sakka are Masakkas, and they frequent this place for play; or it is the place where the assemblies of great lords and Sakka’s pastimes occur, as stated in the Cintāmaṇithutiṭīkā. However, in the Saṅgahaṭīkā, it is stated that 'Masakka' or 'Vasoka' is the name of an Asura city, but this city is called Masakkasāra or Vasokasāra because it is superior among them. It is Amaravatī because the deathless ones (amarā) exist in it; this becomes Amarāvatī by the lengthening of the short vowel.

Assa sakkassa pāsādo vejayanto nāma. Vejayantī paṭākā pasatthā, bhūtā vā assa atthīti vejayanto.

Sakka’s palace is named Vejayanta. It is Vejayanta because it possesses the Vejayantī banner, which is praised or which exists.

Assa sakkassa sabhā sudhammā matā. Sobhano dhammo assāti sudhammā, devamaṇḍapo.

Sakka’s assembly hall is known as Sudhammā. It is Sudhammā because it has excellent Dhamma; it is the pavilion of the devas.

22. Tassa sakkassa ratho vejayanto nāma. Vejayantīnāmāya paṭākāya yogato vejayanto. Tassa sakkassa sārathi sūto mātalināma. Matalassa mātalāya (ka.) apaccaṃ mātali, tassa sakkassa gajo erāvaṇo nāma, irāvaṇo samuddo, tatrajāto erāvaṇo irāvati samudde jāto (erāvato), sese aṇa… pisodarādittā ṇatte erāvaṇo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā). Tassa sakkassa silāsanaṃ paṇḍukambalo nāma. Paṇḍuvaṇṇakambalasadisattā paṇḍukambalo. Silā pāsāṇo eva āsanaṃ silāsanaṃ.

22. That Sakka’s chariot is named Vejayanta. It is Vejayanta due to its connection with the banner named Vejayantī. That Sakka’s charioteer is named Mātali. Mātali is the descendant of Matala. That Sakka’s elephant is named Erāvaṇa. Irāvaṇa is the ocean, and Erāvaṇa is born there. That Sakka’s stone seat is named Paṇḍukambala. It is Paṇḍukambala because it resembles a pale-colored blanket. Silā means stone and āsana means seat; thus, it is Silāsana.

23. Tassa sakkassa puttā suvīra, jayantaiccādayo. Atisayena sūrattā suvīro. Asure jayatīti jayanto. Tassa sakkassa pokkharaṇī nandā nāma bhave. Nandīyatīti nandā. Pokkharaṃ vuccati padumaṃ, salilañca, tehi sattānaṃ [M 0.0029] manaṃ attānaṃ nayatīti pokkharaṇī, pokkharena vā sundarena aṇṇena jalena sahitattā pokkharaṇṇī, sā eva pokkharaṇī. Tassa sakkassa vanāni uyyānāni nandanādīni cattāri. Nandayatīti nandanaṃ. Nānādibbarukkhehi missakattā missakaṃ. Nānālatāhi vallīhi cittattā cittalatā, nānāvirāgavaṇṇavicittāya vā latāya samannāgatattā cittalatā, devatānaṃ vā cittāsā ettha atthīti cittā, āsāvatī nāma latā, sā yassa atthi, taṃ cittalatā. Devatānaṃ vā cittaṃ lanti gaṇhantīti cittalā, dibbarukkhā, tesaṃ samūho cittalatā, itthiliṅgena tassa vanassa nāmaṃ, yathā “khuddasikkhā”ti. Phārusakāni yattha santi, taṃ phārusakaṃ.

23. That Sakka’s sons are Suvīra, Jayanta, and so forth. He is Suvīra because he is exceedingly brave. He is Jayanta because he conquers the Asuras. That Sakka’s pond is named Nandā. It is Nandā because it delights. Pokkhara means lotus and also water; thus, it is Pokkharaṇī because it draws the minds or selves of beings by means of these, or because it is endowed with beautiful water by means of lotuses; that very Pokkharaṇṇī is Pokkharaṇī. That Sakka’s forests and parks are four, beginning with Nandana. It is Nandana because it delights. It is Missaka because it is mixed with various divine trees. It is Cittalatā because it is variegated with various creepers and vines, or because it is endowed with a creeper of various beautiful colors, or because the deities have their diverse hopes (citta-āsā) here; or it is Cittalatā because it has a creeper named Āsāvatī. Or, it is a collection of divine trees (cittalā) that take or grasp the minds of the deities, and their collection is Cittalatā. The name of that forest is in the feminine gender, like 'Khuddasikkhā'. Where Phārusaka trees exist, that is Phārusaka.

24. Asanyādittayaṃ tassa sakkassa āyudhaṃ. Assate bhujjate lokadhātukamanenāyudhenāti asani, ayaṃ asanisaddo dvīsu pumitthiliṅgesu vattati. Kulimhi sakkassa hatthe seti tiṭṭhatīti kulisaṃ, kuli hattho bhujādaloti hi tikaṇḍaseso tikaṇḍasesa 2.6.26. Kuyaṃ vā pathaviyaṃ lisati tanu bhavatīti kulisaṃ. Vaja gatiyaṃ, vajateva na paṭihaññate yassa gamanaṃ kenacīti vajiraṃ, irapaccayo. Vajirasahacaraṇato kulisasaddopi punnapuṃsake. Bhiduraṃ, pavi, satakoṭi, suru, sambo, dambholiiccādīnipi vajirassa nāmāni. Tatra bhiduraṃ punnapuṃsake, paviādayo pume.

24. Asani, Kulisa, and Vajira are the three names for Sakka's weapon. Asani is so called because it strikes and consumes world-spheres. The word 'asani' is used in both the masculine and feminine genders. Kulisa is so named because it rests in Sakka's hand; 'kuli' means hand or arm, according to the Tikaṇḍasesa. Alternatively, 'kulisa' means it becomes thin when it touches the earth. Vajira is so named because its motion is unimpeded by anything; the suffix 'ira' is added. Because of its association with 'vajira,' the word 'kulisa' is also used in the neuter gender. Other names for the thunderbolt include Bhidura, Pavi, Satakoṭi, Suru, Sambo, and Dambholi. Of these, Bhidura is neuter, while Pavi and the others are masculine.

Rambhā [M 0.0030] ca alambusā ca iccādikā devitthiyo accharāyo nāmāti vuttā. Accharāvisesā hi etā. Accho nimmalavaṇṇo etāsamatthīti accharāyo. “Apasarā”tipi etāsameva sāmaññasaññā. Devaputtānaṃ ratiṃ bhāventi vaḍḍhentīti rambhā, raṃ kāmaggiṃ bhanti dīpayanti jālentīti vā rambhā, niggahītāgamo. Kāmarativasena devaputte attani vasāpetuṃ alaṃ samatthāti alambusā, assukāro. Devānaṃ devaputtānaṃ, devībhūtā vā itthiyo devitthiyo.

Rambhā, Alambusā, and other such divine women are called Apsarās. These are indeed special kinds of Apsarās. They are called Apsarās because they possess a pure, stainless complexion. 'Apasarā' is also a general designation for them. Rambhā is so called because she cultivates and increases the delight of the sons of the gods, or because she illuminates, kindles, and ignites 'raṃ,' the fire of passion; this is due to the insertion of a nasal sound. Alambusā is so called because she is able and capable of bringing the sons of the gods under her control through sensual pleasure; this is due to the insertion of 'a'. Divine women are the women of the gods and the sons of the gods, or women who have become goddesses.

“Pañcasikho, hāhā, hūhū”iccādayo gandhabbā nāma. Pañca sikhā cūḷā yassa so pañcasikho. “Hā”ti ananditaṃ dhaniṃ nindibhaddhaniṃ (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) jahatīti hāhā. “Hū”ti gītavisesasaddaṃ hūyateti hūhū. Gandhaṃ abbanti bhuñjantīti gandhabbā, gāyanaṃ vā dhammo etesaṃ gandhabbā, mmassa bbo.

'Pañcasikha, Hāhā, Hūhū,' and so forth, are called Gandharvas. Pañcasikha is he who has five crests or topknots. Hāhā is so called because he abandons a joyless sound. Hūhū is so called because he utters a special musical sound, 'hū.' Gandharvas are those who consume fragrances, or singing is their nature; 'mm' becomes 'bb'.

25. Vimānādidvayaṃ vimāne. Devānamākāse gamanaṃ yena taṃ vimānaṃ, vigataṃ vinā (ka.) mānaṃ upamānamassa vimānaṃ. Vihe ākāse gacchatīti byamhaṃ, hakārato pubbe amapaccayo. Ettha ca vimānabyamhasaddā dvepi anitthiyaṃ punnapuṃsake vattanti.

25. The two terms, beginning with vimāna, refer to a celestial mansion. Vimāna is that by which the gods travel in the sky; or, it is that for which measure or comparison is gone. Byamha is so called because it moves through the sky; the suffix 'ama' comes before the letter 'ha'. Here, both the words 'vimāna' and 'byamha' are used in the masculine and neuter genders.

Pīyusādittayaṃ amate. Pīyateti pīyusaṃ, “amatapā”ti hi vuttaṃ, usapaccayo uṇādi 4.76 ṇvādi 215 suttesu pana “pīyūsa”miti dissati. “Peyuso”tipi nāmamassa. Na mataṃ maraṇamanena amataṃ. Sukhena dhayanti pivanti taṃ iti sudhā. Ettha ca amatasaddo yaññasesapīyusasalilaghatādīsu napuṃsake[M 0.0031], dhanvantaridevādīsu pulliṅge, gaḷojhābhayāmalakyādīsu itthiliṅgeti tīsu vattati amataṃ yaññasese ca, pīyūse salile ghate ayācite ca mokkhe ca, nā dhanvantaridevasu amatā māgadhīpathyā guḷucyāmalakīsu ca (medinīkosa 16 77-8), taṃsahacaraṇato pīyusasaddopi tīsu liṅgesu. Sudhāsaddo pana amatanuhīlepādīsupi niccamitthiliṅgova sudhā lepo’mataṃ nuhī (amara 23.101).

The three terms beginning with pīyusa signify amata, the nectar of immortality. Pīyusa is so called because it is drunk, for it is said to be 'the drink of immortality'; the suffix is '-usa.' 'Peyusa' is also a name for it. Amata is so called because by it there is no death. Sudhā is so called because it is drunk with ease and pleasure. Here, the word 'amata' is used in the neuter gender for sacrificial remnants, nectar, water, ghee, and the like; in the masculine gender for gods like Dhanvantari and others; and in the feminine gender for Galojhā, Abhayā, Āmalakī, and the like, thus appearing in all three genders. Due to its association, the word 'pīyusa' also appears in all three genders. The word 'sudhā,' however, is always in the feminine gender, even when referring to nectar, the snuhī plant, plaster, and so forth.

Sineruādipañcakaṃ pabbatarāje. Sinā soceyye, sināti soceti deveti sineru, erupaccayo. Mī hiṃsāyaṃ, mināti hiṃsati sabbe pabbate attano uccataraṭṭhenāti meru, rupaccayo. Tidivānaṃ dvinnaṃ devalokānaṃ ādhāro patiṭṭhāti tidivādhāro. Deve nayatīti neru. Sumerūti upasaggena nāmaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Hemaddi, ratanasānu, surālayādīnipi pabbatarājassa nāmāni.

The five terms, Sineru, Meru, Tidivādhāra, Neru, and Sumeru, refer to the king of mountains. Sineru is from the root 'sinā' in the sense of purifying; it purifies the gods, thus it is 'sineru'; the suffix is '-eru'. Meru is from the root 'mī' in the sense of harming; it harms or surpasses all other mountains by its greater height, thus it is 'meru'; the suffix is '-ru'. Tidivādhāra is so called because it is the support and foundation of the two divine worlds. Neru is so called because it leads the gods. Sumeru is the name augmented with the prefix 'su-'. Hemaddi, Ratanasānu, Surālaya, and others are also names for the king of mountains.

26. Yugandharādīni sinerussa parivārabhūtānaṃ sattannaṃ paribhaṇḍapabbatānaṃ nāmāni. Candasūriyasaṅkhātaṃ yugaṃ dhāreti tadubbedhamaggacārittāti yugandharo. Īsaṃ mahissaraṃ dhāreti tassa nivāsaṭṭhānattāti īsadharo. Karavīrā assamārakā bahavo ettha santīti karavīro, ke vā mayūrā ravanti etthāti karavīro, “karavīko”tipi pāṭho, idhāpi pacchimoyevattho, karavīkasakuṇā vā bahavo ettha santīti karavīko. Sudassanā osadhivisesā bahukā ettha santīti sudassano, sukhena passitabbattā vā sudassano[M 0.0032], sundaraṃ vā dassanaṃ etthāti sudassano. Pañcannaṃ pabbatacakkānaṃ nemisadisaṃ katvā attānaṃ dhāretīti nemindharo, nemibhāvena vā dhāretabbo upalakkhetabboti nemindharo, nemiṃvā rathaddumaṃ dhāreti yebhuyyenāti nemindharo. Vinatā nāma supaṇṇamātā, tassā nivāsaṭṭhānattā vinatakoti cintāmaṇiṭīkā. Vitthiṇṇā vā natā nadiyo etthāti vinatako. Assakaṇṇā sajjadumā bahavo ettha santīti assakaṇṇo, assakaṇṇasadisakūṭattā vā assakaṇṇo. Kulācalāti ete sineruādayo aṭṭha pabbatā acalasaṅkhātānaṃ pabbatānaṃ kulāni yoniyo pabhavā, ete ca sineruādayo anupubbasamuggatā, sabbabāhiro cettha assakaṇṇo. Nimijātake pana –

26. The names of the seven surrounding mountains of Sineru, known as the Paribhaṇḍa mountains, are Yugandhara and the others. Yugandhara is so called because it bears the yoke known as the sun and moon, its path having that height. Isadhara is so called because it bears Īsa, the great lord, as it is his dwelling place. Karavīra is so called because many Karavīra or Assamāraka trees grow there, or because peacocks cry there. There is also a variant reading 'Karavīka,' in which case the latter meaning still applies, or it is so called because many Karavīka birds dwell there. Sudassana is so called because many excellent medicinal plants grow there, or because it is easily seen, or because it has a beautiful appearance. Nemindhara is so called because it holds itself like the rim of the five mountain ranges, or because it should be regarded as a rim, or because it mostly bears a rim or chariot-wood. Vinataka, according to the Cintāmaṇi commentary, is the dwelling place of Vinatā, the mother of the Supaṇṇas. Alternatively, it is so called because the rivers there are wide and winding. Assakaṇṇa is so called because many horse-ear (assakaṇṇa) or Sajja trees grow there, or because its peaks resemble a horse's ears. These eight mountains, beginning with Sineru, are called Kulācalas, as they are the families, origins, or sources of the immovable mountains. These, beginning with Sineru, arise in succession, with Assakaṇṇa being the outermost. However, in the Nimi Jātaka—

“Sudassano karavīko, īsadharo yugandharo;

Nemindharo vinatako, assakaṇṇo giri brahā”ti jā. 2.22.568.

'Sudassana, Karavīka, Īsadhara, Yugandhara; Nemindhara, Vinataka, Assakaṇṇa, the great mountain.'

Vatvā sineruṃ parikkhipitvā assakaṇṇo nāma pabbato patiṭṭhito, taṃ parikkhipitvā vinatako nāma pabbatoti evamaññoyevānukkamo kathito. Kiñcāpi kathito, nāmabhedamattakatoyeva panettha bhedo, nātthabhedakatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

It is said that the mountain named Assakaṇṇa is established, encircling Mount Sineru. Encircling that, the mountain named Vinataka is established. Thus, a different sequence has been recounted. Although it has been recounted, it should be understood that the difference here is merely one of names, not a difference in substance.

27. Ākāsavāhīgaṅgāyaṃ merusiṅgobbhavāyaṃ mandākinyādināmattayaṃ. Mandaṃ akituṃ sīlamassāti mandākinī. Ākāse sandamānā gaṅgā ākāsagaṅgā. Surānaṃ devānaṃ nadī suranadī. Suradīghikātipi etissā nāmaṃ.

27. The sky-flowing Ganges, which originates from the peak of Mount Meru, has three names, beginning with Mandākinī. Mandākinī is so called because its nature is to flow slowly. The Ganges flowing in the sky is the Ākāsagaṅgā. The river of the gods is the Suranadī. Suradīghikā is also a name for it.

28. Koviḷārādittayaṃ [M 0.0033] “phalaharo”tikhyāte pāricchattake. Kuṃ pathaviṃ vidārayati mūlenāti koviḷāro, dassa ḷo. Pari samantato chattaṃ viya tiṭṭhatīti pāricchattako. Pārino samuddassa jāto apaccaṃ pārijātako, sakatthe ko. Pāribhaddo, nimbataru, mandāroiccādīnipi pāricchattakassa nāmāni.

28. The three terms beginning with Koviḷāra are names for the Pāricchattaka tree, which is known as 'Phalahara'. Koviḷāra is so called because it splits the earth with its roots; 'd' becomes 'ḷ'. Pāricchattaka is so called because it stands all around like an umbrella. Pārijātaka is so called because it is born as an offspring on the far shore of the ocean; the suffix 'ka' is used in its own sense. Pāribhadda, Nimbataru, Mandāra, and others are also names for the Pāricchattaka.

Kapparukkho ca santāno ca ādinā mandāro pārijātako ca haricandanañca ete pañca devaddumā amara 1.53 devataravo devabhūmīsveva sambhavato. Kappo saṅkappito attho, tassa rukkho jaññajanakabhāvena sambandho, kappaṃ vā ṭhito rukkho kapparukkho. Tananaṃ tāno, bhāve ṇo. Gandhassa sammā tāno asseti santāno, sirīsarukkho. Mandante modante devā anenāti mandāro, ārapaccayo. Harimindaṃ cadayati sukhayatīti haricandanaṃ. Ete pañca devataravo amarakosanayena vuttā, sogatanayena pana satta devataravo. Vuttañca –

The Kapparukkha, the Santāna, and also the Mandāra, Pārijātaka, and Haricandana—these five are divine trees because they arise only in the celestial realms. 'Kappo' signifies a conceived purpose, and its tree is related as a generator of what is wished for; or, a tree that stands for an aeon is a Kapparukkha. 'Tananaṃ' means expansion ('tāno'); the suffix 'ṇa' is used in the sense of state. The Santāna tree is so called because it has a proper spreading of fragrance; it is the Sirīsa tree. The Mandāra is so called because the gods delight and rejoice by means of it; the suffix is 'āra'. Haricandana is that which pleases and delights Hariminda. These five divine trees are described according to the Amarakośa, but according to the way of the Sugata, there are seven divine trees. And it is said—

“Pāṭalī simbalī jambū, devānaṃ pārichattako;

Kadambo kapparukkho ca, sirīsena bhavati sattama”nti dha. sa. aṭṭha. 584; sārattha. ṭī. 1.1verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā.

'The Pāṭalī, the Simbalī, the Jambū, the Devas' Pārichattaka; The Kadamba and the Kappa-tree, and with the Sirīsa it is the seventh.'

Tattha pāṭalīti citrapāṭalī, sā asuraloke tiṭṭhati. Tathā simbalī garuḷesu, jambū jambudīpe, pāricchattako tāvatiṃse, kadambo aparagoyāne. Kapparukkho uttarakurūsu[M 0.0034], sirīso pubbavideheti. Ete satta devānameva patiṭṭhānabhūmīsu sambhavato devataravotveva vuccanti.

Therein, the pāṭalī refers to the variegated pāṭalī, which stands in the realm of the asuras. Similarly, the simbalī tree is among the garuḷas, the jambū tree in Jambudīpa, the pāricchattaka tree in Tāvatiṃsa, and the kadamba tree in Aparagoyāna. The kappa tree is in Uttarakuru, and the sirīsa tree is in Pubbavideha. These seven are called divine trees because they arise in the very places that are the abodes of the devas.

Saggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The description of the heavens is complete.

29. Pubbapacchimauttarā disā yathākkamaṃ pācī patīcī udīcī nāma bhavanti. Paṭhamaṃ pāto ancati ravi yassaṃ sā pācī, nakāralopo. Pacchā divāvasāne ancati ravi yassaṃ sā patīcī. Uddhaṃ ancati ravi yassaṃ sā udīcī, yassaṃ vā sītaviyogaṃ datvā ancati sā udīcī, viyogatthavācako hettha ukāro, dasaddo dānattho. Atha vā pancati pubbabhāvamāpajjateti pācī. Patincati pacchābhāvamāpajjateti patīcī. Udañcati sītaviyogadānattamāpajjateti udīcī. Ettha ca udīcīsahacaraṇato patīcī itthiyaṃ, patīcīsahacaraṇato pācī itthiyaṃ vattatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ taṃtaṃsahacaraṇabhāvena tassa tassa taṃtaṃliṅgattamupaneyyuṃ. Pubbapacchimauttarāti sabbanāmassa vuttamatte pumbhāvo.

29. The eastern, western, and northern directions are named pācī, patīcī, and udīcī respectively. First, that in which the sun moves in the morning is pācī (eastern), with the elision of the letter 'na'. Later, that in which the sun moves at the end of the day is patīcī (western). That in which the sun moves upwards is udīcī (northern), or it is called udīcī because it gives separation from the cold—here, the letter 'u' conveys the meaning of separation, and the syllable 'da' conveys the meaning of giving. Alternatively, pācī is so called because it approaches a prior state. Patīcī is so called because it approaches a later state. Udīcī is so called because it attains the state of giving separation from the cold. And here, it should be noted that due to association with udīcī, patīcī is feminine, and due to association with patīcī, pācī is feminine. Thus, through association with each, the respective genders should be understood. When the pronoun 'pubbapacchimauttarā' is merely stated, it is in the masculine gender.

Dakkhiṇādidvayaṃ dakkhiṇadisāyaṃ. Majjhe apāyaṃ añcati yassaṃ ravi, sā apācī. Majjhatthoyaṃ apasaddo, yathā “apadisa”nti, “avācī”tipi pāṭho, avapubbo añca adhomukhībhāve. Avañcati adhomukhī bhavati yassaṃ ravi, sā avācī. Uṇhādike vā tabbiyoge karonto yassaṃ ravi añcati, sā avācī. Vidisādidvayaṃ disāmajjhe. Disāhi viniggatā vidisā. Disānamanurūpā, anuvattakā vā disā anudisā. Apadisantipi vidisāya nāmaṃ napuṃsakābyayaṃ tva’padisaṃ (amara 3.6).

The two terms beginning with 'dakkhiṇā' refer to the southern direction. That direction in which the sun moves towards its decline in the middle is called Apācī (South). Here, the word 'apa' has the meaning of 'middle', as in 'apadisa.' There is also the reading 'avācī'; the prefix 'ava' with the root 'añc' is in the sense of facing downwards. That direction in which the sun moves or faces downwards is Avācī (South). Or, that direction in which the sun moves, causing separation from heat and so forth, is Avācī. The two terms beginning with 'vidisā' refer to the intermediate directions. Those that have come forth from the cardinal directions are called Vidisā (Intermediate Directions). The directions that are similar to or follow the cardinal directions are called Anudisā (Sub-directions). Apadisa is also a name for an intermediate direction.

30. Erāvatādayo [M 0.0035] aṭṭha gajā pubbādīnaṃ disānaṃ rakkhaṇato disāgajā nāma, puṇḍarīkaṃ nāma sitambojaṃ, taṃsadisavaṇṇatāya puṇḍarīko. Rassasarīratāya vāmano. Kuyaṃ pathaviyaṃ modate kumudo. Añjanavaṇṇatāya añjano. Pupphā pakāsamānā dantā assa pupphadanto. Sabbabhūmiyaṃ caratīti sabbabhummo, sabbabhummo vā cakkavattī tassānurūpattā sabbabhummo. Sobhanadantāvayavattā suppatīko sobhanā patīkā avayavā’ssa suppatīko (ka.). “Suppatīko sobhanaṅge, bhave īsānadisāgaje”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe vuttaṃ. Erāvatādīnaṃ disānaṃ sambandhakathanaṃ pācīvāraṇādināmasūcanatthaṃ, esaṃ kareṇuyo pana –

30. The eight elephants beginning with Erāvata are called directional elephants because they protect the eastern and other directions. Puṇḍarīka is the name of a white lotus; because its color resembles that, it is called Puṇḍarīka. Because of its short body, it is called Vāmana. It delights in the earth, hence Kumuda. Because of its añjana (collyrium) color, it is called Añjana. Its teeth shine like flowers, so it is named Pupphadanta. It roams over all the earth, thus Sabbabhumma; or, because it is analogous to a universal monarch, who is also called Sabbabhumma, it is named Sabbabhumma. Because of its beautiful teeth and limbs, it is called Suppatīka. As stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: 'Suppatīka, with beautiful limbs, is the directional elephant in the northeast.' The mention of Erāvata and others and their connection to the directions is for the purpose of suggesting names like Pācīvāraṇa (Eastern Elephant), etc. Their female elephants, however, are as follows:

Abbhamu kapilā ceva, piṅgalā nupamā matā;

Tambakaṇṇī subhadantī, aṅganā añjanāvatī amara 3.5.

Abbhamu, Kapilā, Piṅgalā, and Anupamā are known; Tambakaṇṇī, Subhadantī, Aṅganā, and Añjanāvatī.

31. Dhataraṭṭhādidvayaṃ pubbadisādhipatideve. Dhāritaṃ raṭṭhamanenāti dhataraṭṭho, rassa to. Pañcasikhādīnaṃ gandhabbānaṃ adhipo nāyako gandhabbādhipo. Kumbhaṇḍasāmyādidvayaṃ dakkhiṇadisādhipatideve. Kumbhaṇḍānaṃ sāmi nāyako kumbhaṇḍasāmi. Viruhanti vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhimāpajjanti etasmiṃ kumbhaṇḍāti virūḷhako. Virūḷhaṃ vuḍḍhippattaṃ vā kaṃ sukhametassāti virūḷhako. Virūpakkhādidvayaṃ pacchimadisādhipatideve. Virūpāni akkhīni yassa virūpakkho, vividhasaṇṭhānāni akkhīni yassa vā virūpakkho. Nāgānaṃ adhipati nāgādhipati.

31. The two terms, Dhataraṭṭha and so forth, refer to the deity ruling the eastern direction. He is called Dhataraṭṭha because the kingdom is upheld by him; the 'a' is short. The chief and leader of the Gandhabhas, such as Pañcasikha, is called Gandhabādhipa. The two terms, Kumbhaṇḍasāmi and so forth, refer to the deity ruling the southern direction. The lord and leader of the Kumbhaṇḍas is called Kumbhaṇḍasāmi. He is Virūḷhaka because the Kumbhaṇḍas grow and attain growth in him. Or he is Virūḷhaka because he has attained growth and has happiness therein. The two terms, Virūpakkha and so forth, refer to the deity ruling the western direction. He whose eyes are deformed is called Virūpakkha, or he whose eyes are of various shapes. The lord of the Nāgas is called Nāgādhipati.

32. Yakkhādhipādicatukkaṃ [M 0.0036] kuvere. Āḷavakādiyakkhānaṃ adhipo yakkhādhipo. Vissavaṇassa apaccaṃ vessavaṇo. Ticaraṇāṭṭhadāṭhābhayānakamatthitāya kucchitaṃ vero sarīramassa kuvero. Khuddenāssa narayuttā sivikāratheti naro vāhanamassa naravāhano. Tyambakasakho, yakkharājo, guyhakesaro, manussadhammā, dhanado, rājarājo, dhanādhipo, kinnareso, yakkho, ekapiṅgalo, sirido, puññajanessaroiccādīnipi kuverassa nāmāni.

32. The four names beginning with Yakkhādhipa refer to Kuvera. The lord of Yakkhas such as Āḷavaka is called Yakkhādhipa. The offspring of Vissavaṇa is called Vessavaṇa. He is called Kuvera because his body is disgusting, having three feet, eight tusks, and a terrifying appearance. Because men are yoked to his small palanquin, he has men as his vehicle, hence Naravāhana. Other names of Kuvera include Tyambakasakha, Yakkharāja, Guyhakesara, Manussadhamma, Dhanada, Rājarāja, Dhanādhipa, Kinnaresa, Yakkha, Ekapiṅgala, Sirida, and Puññajanessara.

Assa kuverassa purī “aḷakā, aḷakamandā”ti ca vuccati. Alaṃ vibhūsane, alaṃ vibhūsanaṃ karotīti alakā, sā eva aḷakā. Aḷakā eva modakaraṇato aḷakamandā, ukārassa akāro, nāgamo ca. Kelāsotipi tassa nāmaṃ, keli payojanaṃ assa kelo, āsate asminti āso, kelo ca so āso ceti kelāso, kaṇhasappādi viya niccaṃ kammadhārayo. Assa kuverassa paharaṇaṃ āyudhaṃ gadā, gaṃ vuccati vajiraṃ, taṃ viya dukkhaṃ dadātīti gadā. Ime cattāro yathāvuttā dhataraṭṭhādayo devā kamato pubbādīnaṃ catuddisānaṃ adhipā adhipatayo nāma. Amarakose pana –

The city of this Kuvera is also called 'Aḷakā' and 'Aḷakamandā'. It is called Aḷakā because it is sufficient for adornment, or because it causes adornment. Aḷakamandā is so called because Aḷakā itself causes delight; the 'u' becomes 'a', and there is an insertion of 'n'. Kelāsa is also its name. That which has play (keli) as its purpose is 'kelo'; that in which one dwells (āsate) is 'āso'. 'Kelo' and that 'āso' together form 'Kelāso', which is always a karmadhāraya compound, like 'kaṇhasappa' (black serpent). The weapon of this Kuvera is the mace (gadā). 'Gaṃ' is said to be a thunderbolt (vajira), and since it gives pain like that, it is called 'gadā'. These four deities, Dhataraṭṭha and so forth, as mentioned, are in order the lords and rulers of the four directions, beginning with the eastern. However, in the Amarakosa, it is said:

“Indo aggi pitupati, nerito varuṇo’nilo;

Kuvero īso patayo, pubbādīnaṃ ime kamā.

"Indra, Agni, Pitupati, Nerita, Varuṇa, Anila, Kuvera, and Īsa are the lords, these in order, of the eastern and other directions."

Ravi [M 0.0037] sukko mahīsūnu, tamo ca bhānujo vidhu;

Budho suraguru ceti, disādhipā tathā gahā”ti amara 3.3-4.

"The Sun, Venus, the son of the earth (Mars), Tamas (Rāhu), the son of the sun (Saturn), the Moon, Mercury, and the teacher of the gods (Jupiter); these are the lords of the directions and also the planets."

Aññeyeva disādhipatayo kathitā, indaravimādīnañca disādhipaccakathanaṃ pājhādīnaṃ indadisāravidisādināmasūcanaphalaṃ.

Other lords of the directions have indeed been mentioned, and the explanation of the lordship of the directions by Indra, Ravi, and others has the result of indicating names such as Pājhā, Indra's direction, Ravi's direction, and so forth.

33-34. Jātavedādyaṭṭhārasakaṃ aggimhi. Jāte uppanne vindati ghātayatīti jātavedo. Andhakāre jātaṃ vijjamānaṃ vindati labhati, vidati jānāti etenāti vā jātavedo, jananaṃ jātaṃ vedo pākaṭo yassa vā so jātavedo. Sikhā vuccati jālā, tāya yogato sikhī. Jotati dippatīti joti. Punātīti pāvako, ṇvu. Dahatīti dahano. Ananti pālentyaneneti analo, alapaccayo. Vede hutaṃ vahati pāpayati, sayaṃ vā labhateti hutāvaho. Acci vuccati jālā, tāya yogato accimā. Dhūmo ketu dhajo yassāti dhūmaketu. Ajati jalamāno kuṭilaṃ gacchatīti aggi, i. Go raṃsi etassatthīti gini, assatthyatthe ini, agginītipi pāṭho, so aggisadiso. Bhānu pabhā yassatthi, so bhānumā. Tejeti sesabhūtopādārūpānīti tejo. Dhūmo sikhā cūḷā yassa dhūmasikho. Vāyu sakhā assa vāyusakho. Dahitvā dahato (ka.) gacchato kaṇhā vattanī maggo yassa kaṇhavattanī. Vissānarassa isino apaccaṃ vessānaro. Hutaṃ [M 0.0038] haviṃ asati bhuñjatīti hutāso. Dhanañjayo, jalano, āsayāso, rohitasso, sattācci, sukko, citrabhānu, vibhāvasu, suciiccādīnipi aggissa nāmāni.

33-34. The eighteen names beginning with Jātaveda refer to fire. Jātaveda: because it finds and destroys what is born or arisen. Or, it finds or obtains what is born and existing in darkness, or one knows by means of this—thus, Jātaveda. Or, it is called Jātaveda because its birth is manifest. Sikhī: because it is connected with the flame (sikhā), which is called jālā. Joti: because it shines and blazes. Pāvako: because it purifies (punāti), with the suffix ṇvu. Dahano: because it burns (dahati). Analo: because beings live (ananti) or are sustained (pālenti) by it, with the suffix 'ala'. Hutāvaho: because it carries (vahati) or conveys (pāpayati) the oblation (hutaṃ) in the Veda, or because it obtains it for itself. Accimā: because it is connected with the flame (acci), which is called jālā. Dhūmaketu: because it has smoke (dhūma) as its banner or flag (ketu dhajo). Aggi: because it moves (gacchati) crookedly (kuṭilaṃ) while blazing (ajati), with the suffix 'i'. Gini: because it has rays (go raṃsi), with the suffix 'ini' in the sense of 'possessing'; 'agginī' is also a reading, meaning 'similar to fire'. Bhānumā: because it has radiance (bhānu pabhā). Tejo: because it sharpens (tejeti) the remaining primary elements and derived matter. Dhūmasikho: because it has smoke (dhūma) and a flame or crest (sikhā cūḷā). Vāyusakho: because wind (vāyu) is its companion (sakhā). Kaṇhavattanī: because it has a dark (kaṇha) path (vattanī maggo) as it burns and moves. Vessānaro: a descendant (apaccaṃ) of the sage Vissānara. Hutāso: because it consumes (asati bhuñjati) the oblation (hutaṃ). Other names of fire include Dhanañjayo, Jalano, Āsayāso, Rohitasso, Sattācci, Sukko, Citrabhānu, Vibhāvasu, and Suci.

Sikhādittayaṃ aggijālāyaṃ. Sinoti nisānī bhavatīti sikhā, “si nisāne”ti kātanta dhātu, khapaccayo. Jalatīti jālā. Accate pujjate aneneti acci. Sikhā jālā bhiyyo rūpantarā itthiyaṃ, acci pana apume.

The three terms, beginning with sikhā, refer to the flame of fire. It is called 'sikhā' because it marks (sinoti) or is a sign (nisānī bhavati); the root 'si' is in the sense of 'marking', according to the Kātanta grammar, with the suffix 'kha'. It is called 'jālā' because it burns (jalati). It is called 'acci' because it is honored or worshipped (accate pujjate) by this. 'Sikhā' and 'jālā' are feminine, being further forms, while 'acci' is neuter.

35. Dvayaṃ aggikaṇe tīsu phuliṅgo’ggikaṇo (amara 1.60) phuliṅgānīti aggikaṇāni (ma. ni. ṭī. 3.65). Vividhāsu disāsu phullaṃ gacchatīti vipphuliṅgaṃ. Tathā phuliṅgaṃ. Sabbadharakate pana “phuliṃ gacchatīti phuliṅgo”ti vuttaṃ. Tikaṃ chārikāyaṃ. Malīnakaṃsavatthādīnaṃ taṃ dittiṃ seti pavattetīti bhasmaṃ, mapaccayo, bhasati vā adho patati vatthādīnaṃ malametenāti bhasmaṃ. Kaṃsādīnaṃ sukkabhāvatthaṃ icchitabbattā iṭṭhi abhilāso sobhanaṃ etassā atthīti seṭṭhi, “sapakkhako salomako”tyādīsu viya sasaddassa vijjamānatthattā. Malassa saraṇaṃ karotīti sārikā, sā eva chārikā, yathā “saḷāyatana”ntyādīsu.

35. These two refer to a spark of fire. It is called 'vipphuliṅga' because it goes forth blooming in various directions. Similarly, 'phuliṅga'. However, in the Sabbadharakata, it is said: 'It is called 'phuliṅgo' because it goes forth as a spark.' These three refer to ash. It is called 'bhasma' because it deposits or establishes luster on tarnished metal vessels and so forth, with the suffix 'ma'; or, it is called 'bhasma' because it shines, or because the dirt of cloth and so forth falls down by it. Because a white state for metal vessels and so forth is to be wished for, it is 'iṭṭhi' (desire); it is 'seṭṭhi' because it possesses beauty, the prefix 'sa' having the sense of 'possessing', as in such examples as 'with wings, with hair'. It is called 'sārikā' because it makes a resort for the stain; that is the same as 'chārikā', just as in the case of 'saḷāyatana' and so forth.

36. Dvayaṃ uṇhachārikāyaṃ. Uṇhattā kukkuṃ kucchitaṃ lātīti kukkulo, “kukku vidatthiyaṃ hatthe, pakoṭṭhe kucchitepi ce”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe vuttaṃ. Kukkuṃ vā hatthaṃ lunāti chindati dahatīti kukkulo, so eva kukkuḷo[M 0.0039]. Uṇhameva bhasmaṃ uṇhabhasmaṃ, tasmiṃ. Tikaṃ dittakaṭṭhādindhane. Aṅgati hāniṃ gacchatīti aṅgāro, ārapaccayo, punnapuṃsakoyaṃ. “Alāte’nitthi kuje’ṅgāro”ti hi tikaṇḍasese tikaṇḍasesa 3.329 vuttaṃ. Hānimeva lāti, na ṭhitiṃ visesañcāti alātaṃ. Uddhaṃ dhūmaṃ muñcatīti ummutaṃ, tadeva ummukaṃ. Pañcakaṃ kaṭṭhādindhane. Santamaggiṃ edhayati vaḍḍhayatīti samidhā. Edhayatīti idhumaṃ, umo. Edhayatīti idho. Upādiyate aggineti upādānaṃ. Edhayatīti indhanaṃ.

36. These two refer to hot ash. It is called 'kukkulo' because, being hot, it takes (lāti) the 'kukku' (a span or a despised thing). Indeed, in the collection of diverse meanings, it is said that 'kukku' means a span, hand, wrist, or despised. Or, it is called 'kukkulo' because it cuts off, severs, or burns the hand; that is the same as 'kukkuḷo'. Hot ash is 'uṇhabhasma'. These three refer to burning wood and fuel. It is called 'aṅgāra' because it goes to destruction (aṅgati hāniṃ gacchati), with the suffix 'āra'; this is masculine or neuter. Indeed, in the Tikaṇḍaśesa, it is said: 'Alāta is not feminine; kuja and aṅgāra are masculine.' It is called 'alāta' because it takes only destruction, not stability or distinction. It is called 'ummuta' because it releases smoke upwards; that is the same as 'ummuka'. These five refer to wood and fuel. It is called 'samidhā' because it kindles and increases the existing fire. It is called 'idhuma' because it kindles, with the suffix 'umo'. It is called 'idho' because it kindles. It is called 'upādāna' because it is taken up by the fire. It is called 'indhana' because it kindles.

37. Pañcakaṃ āloke. Obhāsati dippatīti obhāso. Pakāsati dippatīti pakāso. Ālocayati passati etenāti āloko, āloketi vā etenāti āloko, “loka, loca dassane”ti dhātudvayapāṭhato. Ujjotatīti ujjoto, andhakāraṃ viddhaṃsento jotatīti vā ujjoto. Ā samantato tapati dippatīti ātapo. Samāti ete pañca tulyatthāti bhāvo.

37. These five refer to light. It is called 'obhāso' because it shines and gleams. It is called 'pakāso' because it illuminates and gleams. It is called 'āloko' because one considers or sees by it, or because it illuminates by it, derived from the two roots 'loka' and 'loca' in the sense of 'to see'. It is called 'ujjoto' because it shines brightly, or because it destroys darkness and shines. It is called 'ātapo' because it heats and gleams all around. The meaning is that these five are similar in meaning.

Dasakaṃ vāte. Āhāro viya pāṇabhūtopi kadāci satte māretīti māruto, sova māluto. Punāti saṅkārādikanti pavano. Vāyati gacchatīti vāyu, vāyati vā pupphādīnaṃ gandho yena so vāyu. Tathā vāto. Ananti pāṇantyaneneti anilo, ilo. Santaṃ niccalaṃ [M 0.0040] īrayati kampetīti samīraṇo, samīrituṃ kampituṃ sīlamassāti vā samīraṇo. Gandhaṃ vahatīti gandhavāho, ṇo. Vāyo vāyusadiso, ubhayatrāpi yāgamo. Samantato īrati khipati rukkhādayoti samīro. Sadā sabbadā gati yassa sadāgati. Sasano, gandhavaho, āsugo, maruto, jagatipāṇo, pavamāno, pabhañjano iccādīnipi vātanāmāni.

These ten refer to wind. It is called 'māruta' because, although it is the very breath of life like food, it sometimes kills living beings; that is the same as 'māluta'. It is called 'pavana' because it purifies impurities and so forth. It is called 'vāyu' because it moves (vāyati gacchati), or because the fragrance of flowers and so forth moves by it. Similarly, 'vāta'. It is called 'anila' because beings breathe (ananti pāṇanti) by it, with the suffix 'ila'. It is called 'samīraṇa' because it stirs or shakes what is still and motionless; or because its nature is to stir or shake. It is called 'gandhavāha' because it carries fragrance, with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Vāyo' is similar to 'vāyu', with the insertion of 'y' in both cases. It is called 'samīra' because it stirs or scatters trees and so forth in all directions. It is called 'sadāgati' because it always moves (sadā sabbadā gati yassa). Other names for wind include Sasana, Gandhavaha, Āsuga, Maruta, Jagatipāṇa, Pavamāna, Pabhañjana, and so forth.

38. Ime cha vakkhamānā vāyubhedā vāyuvisesā, uddhaṃ gacchatīti uddhaṅgamo, uccārapassāvādīnaṃ nīharaṇavasena adhobhāgaṃ gacchatīti adhogamo. Kucchimhi udare tiṭṭhatīti kucchiṭṭho. Koṭṭhe ante seti tiṭṭhatīti koṭṭhāsayo. Punappunaṃ sasanti yena assāso, bahinikkhantavāto. Passāsoti antopavisanakavātopi “assāso”ti etena saṅgayhate sahacāritattā. Sabbaṅgesu anusarati sīlena sedalohitādisampādanatoti aṅgānusārī. Amarakose panāyaṃ vāto ṭhānabyāpārabhedena pañcadhā kathito pāṇo’pāno samānocodānabyānā ca vāyavo sarīraṭṭhā ime (amara 1.67), ṭīkāyañcassa –

38. These six kinds of wind, which will be explained, are specific types of wind: 'uddhaṅgama' (rising upward), 'adhogama' (descending downward, expelling excrement, urine, etc.), 'kucchiṭṭha' (dwelling in the belly), 'koṭṭhāsaya' (resting in the intestines). That by which they breathe repeatedly is 'assāsa', the outward-moving wind. And 'passāsa' (the inward-moving wind) is also encompassed by the term 'assāsa' due to their co-occurrence. It is called 'aṅgānusārī' because it circulates through all limbs by its nature, producing sweat, blood, etc. However, in the Amarakosa, this wind is said to be of five kinds, distinguished by location and function, and in its commentary it is said:

“Hadaye pāṇo gude’pāno, samāno nābhimajjhaṭṭho;

Udāno kaṇṭhadese tu, byāno sabbaṅgasandhisu hadaye pāṇo gude’pāno, samāno nābhisaṇṭhito; udāno kaṇṭhadesaṭṭho, byāno sabbasarīrago iti ṭhānaniṇṇayo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā).

"In the heart, it is the prāṇa; in the rectum, the apāna; samāna in the middle of the navel; udāna, in the throat region; and vyāna in all the joints."

Tatrapāṇoannappavesādikaro[M 0.0041]. Apāno muttakarīsasukkavisaṭṭhikaro. Samāno majjhe annapacanādikaro. Udāno bhāsitagītādikaro. Byāno sedarattasavanummesanimesagatyādikaro khedaceṭṭhāummesanimmesagatyādikaro (ka.). Pakaṭṭhena anantyanena bhattādippavesanatoti pāṇo. Muttādikaṃ apanetvā anantyanenāti apāno. Sammā ananti anena bhuttaparipācanatoti samāno. Uddhamanantyanena bhāsitādo sāmatthiyajananatoti udāno. Visesena anantyanena sedarattasemhādi khedaceṭṭhādi (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) sampādanatoti byāno”ti taṃbyāpārā ca yathā – annappavesanaṃ muttā-dyussaggo’nnavipācanaṃ bhāsaṇādi nimesādi, taṃbyāpārā kamā ime (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) vuttaṃ.

Here, 'pāṇa' facilitates the intake of food, etc. 'Apāna' eliminates urine, feces, and semen. 'Samāna' aids in digesting food in the middle. 'Udāna' enables speech and singing, etc. 'Vyāna' produces sweat, blood flow, opening and closing of the eyes, movement, etc. 'Pāṇa' is so called because it brings in food, etc., by means of breathing. 'Apāna' because it removes urine, etc., by means of breathing. 'Samāna' because it digests consumed food evenly by means of breathing. 'Udāna' because it generates the ability for speech, etc., by means of breathing upward. 'Vyāna' because it specifically produces sweat, blood, phlegm, etc., by means of breathing.

39. Dvayaṃ antopavisanakavāte. Ānaṃ vuccati bahinikkhamanavāto, tato apagataṃ apānaṃ. Assāsato apagato passāso. Dvayaṃ bahinikkhamanavāte. Ādimhi pavatto sāso assāso. Ananti pāṇantyaneneti ānaṃ, ādimhi pavattaṃ ānaṃ ānaṃ, ekassākārassa lopo.

39. Two types are for the inward-moving wind. 'Āna' is called the outward-moving wind, and 'apāna' is that which has departed from it. 'Passāsa' is that which has departed from 'assāsa'. Two types are for the outward-moving wind. The breath (sāsa) that occurs at the beginning is 'assāsa'. 'Āna' is so called because living beings breathe by it; the initial 'āna' is 'āna', with the elision of one 'a' sound.

40. Vegakhippādayo vātadhammattena niccappavattikā iti tappakkame tappakkamena takkamena (ka.) uccante. Tatra rayantaṃ vege. Sabbatra karaṇasādhanaṃ. Icchitaṭṭhānaṃ vajanti pāpuṇanti etenāti vego.

40. Vega, khippa, etc., are constantly active due to the nature of wind; thus they are mentioned in that sequence. There, 'rayantaṃ' (moving swiftly) is in the sense of speed (vega). Everywhere the derivation is in the instrumental sense. It is called 'vega' because they go to, or reach, desired places by it.

“Kriyāvācittamākhyātuṃ[M 0.0042], ekekattho nidassito;

Payogatonugantabbā, anekatthā hi dhātavo”ti candradhātupāṭhe.

"To explain what expresses action, each single meaning is shown; for verbal roots have many meanings and should be understood according to usage."

Vuttattā vajadhātu pāpuṇanepi pavattati, evaṃ sabbatra, akārassa e. Javanti etenāti javo, rayanti gacchanti etenāti rayo.

Because it is stated, the root 'vaj' also occurs in the sense of reaching. Thus everywhere, 'a' becomes 'e'. It is called 'java' because they go swiftly by it; it is called 'raya' because they go by it.

Khippādinavakaṃ sīghe. Atha javasīghānaṃ ko bhedo? Savegagativacanā javādayo, sīghādayo tu dhammavacanā, tathā ca “sīghaṃ pacati passati (ka.), sīghaṃ gacchatī”ti payogo, na tu “javaṃ pacati, javaṃgacchatī”ti pana payogo. “Vegena gacchati, javena gacchatī”tyādīsu kathaṃ? Tatra bhedassa vattumicchitattā na doso. Khippati peratīti khippaṃ, khipa peraṇe. Sayatīti sīghaṃ, sī saye, ghapaccayo. Byuppatti hi yathā kathañcipi bhavati, saññā tu lokatovāvagantabbā, sabbatrevaṃ. Taratīti turitaṃ. Laṅghatīti lahu, laṅgha gatisosanesu, ghassa ho, niggahītalopo, upaccayo ca, lahupariyāyo laghusaddopyatthi. Asati khepatīti āsu, u. Taratīti tuṇṇaṃ, rassa ṇo. Arati gacchatīti araṃ. Na vilambīyati na ohīyatīti avilambitaṃ, labi avasaṃsane. Tuvaṭṭati sayatīti tuvaṭṭaṃ, turitabhāvena vattatīti vā tuvaṭṭaṃ, ritalopo.

The group of nine beginning with 'khippa' are in the sense of 'sīgha' (quick). Then what is the difference between 'java' and 'sīgha'? 'Java' and similar terms denote speed of movement, while 'sīgha' and similar terms denote a quality. Thus, the usage is 'sīghaṃ pacati' (cooks quickly) or 'sīghaṃ gacchati' (goes quickly), but not 'javaṃ pacati' or 'javaṃ gacchati'. But how is it in cases like 'vegena gacchati' (goes swiftly) or 'javena gacchati' (goes speedily)? There, because the distinction is intended to be expressed, there is no fault. 'Khippa' is so called because it sends forth (khipati), from the root 'khip' in the sense of sending forth. 'Sīgha' is so called because it lies down (sayati), from the root 'sī' in the sense of lying, with the suffix 'gha'. Indeed, etymology can occur in any way, but the conventional meaning must be understood from worldly usage—this applies everywhere. 'Turita' is so called because it crosses (tarati). 'Lahu' is so called because it leaps (laṅghati), from the root 'laṅgha' in the sense of movement and drying, with 'gha' becoming 'ha', elision of the nasal, and the suffix 'u'. There is also the word 'laghu', synonymous with 'lahu'. 'Āsu' is so called because it throws (asati, khepati), with suffix 'u'. 'Tuṇṇaṃ' is so called because it crosses (tarati), with 'ra' becoming 'ṇa'. 'Araṃ' is so called because it goes (arati). 'Avilambita' is so called because it is not delayed, not left behind, from the root 'labi' in the sense of hanging back. 'Tuvaṭṭaṃ' is so called because it quickly lies down (tuvaṭṭati sayati), or it is 'tuvaṭṭaṃ' because it behaves with speed, with the elision of 'rita'.

41. Ariyāsāmaññassa pubbaḍḍhaṃ santate. Ettha ca aṭṭhasu gaṇesu chaṭṭho sabbalahuko, tatopare chaggaṇā sa[M 0.0043], bha, sa, bha, bha, bhā, aṭṭhamo go. Samantato tanotīti satataṃ. Nāsabhāvena na iccaṃ na gantabbaṃ niccaṃ, nāsaṃ vā na gacchatīti niccaṃ. “Nāgo”tyādīsu viyāti etthāpi na doso, tassa co. Na viramatīti avirataṃ. Na āramatīti anārataṃ. Samantato, punappunaṃ vā tanotīti santataṃ. Na avaramatīti anavarataṃ. Sadā dhavati gacchatīti dhuvaṃ. “Dhu gatitheriyesū”ti kātantadhātu.

41. The first half of the Ariyā-sāmañña meter is an example for the meaning 'continuous'. Here, among the eight feet, the sixth is all-light; after that, the six feet are sa, bha, sa, bha, bha, bhā, and the eighth is a long syllable. 'Satataṃ' is so called because it stretches continuously on all sides. 'Niccaṃ' is so called because it is not to be desired or gone to by way of destruction, or it does not go to destruction. As in 'nāgo' and similar words, there is no fault here either, with its 'ca' (particle). 'Avirataṃ' is so called because it does not cease. 'Anārataṃ' is so called because it does not desist. 'Santataṃ' is so called because it stretches continuously, or repeatedly. 'Anavarataṃ' is so called because it does not stop. 'Dhuvaṃ' is so called because it always runs, always moves. The root 'dhu' is in the sense of 'going' and 'stability' in the Kātantra grammar.

Vipulāḍḍhaṃ atisaye. Ettha hi ayugapāde dvādasamattā, yuge aṭṭhārasamattā, sabbāsu ariyāsu paṭhame pāde dvādasamattā, dutiye aṭṭhārasa, tatiye dvādasa, catutthe pañcadasa. Yadā pana paṭhamatatiyesu parihāyanti, tadā yuge adhikā honti, idaṃ vipulālakkhaṇaṃ. Atha satatātisayānaṃ ko bhedo? Satataṃ santati avicchedokriyantarehi abyavadhānaṃ, atisayo tu ponopuññaṃ, pakaṭṭho ca. Tesu ponopuññaṃ kriyābyāvutti, pakaṭṭho tu kriyāvayavānaṃ ukkaṃsatā. Bhāsati sabbesanti bhusaṃ, āssa u. Bhassati adho patatīti vā bhusaṃ. Bhasa adhopatane, assa u. Atisayanaṃ atisayo, atikkamitvā vāsayanaṃ pavattanaṃ atisayo. Dahati sabbanti daḷhaṃ, hato pubbe ḷo, dalati vidārayatīti vā daḷhaṃ, hapaccayo, dahanto lātīti vā daḷhaṃ, vaṇṇavipariyayo, abhisayo ca daḷhañca atisayadaḷhā. Tarati atikkamatīti tibbaṃ, rassa vo, assa i. Eti gacchatīti eko, so eva ekantaṃ, ekaṃ tarati atikkamatīti vā ekantaṃ. Mattato atikkantaṃ atimattaṃ. Bahuṃ lātīti bāḷhaṃ, ulopo, vaṇṇavipariyayo ca hasaddo. Ativelaṃ, accatthaṃ, nibbharaṃ, nitantaṃ, gāḷhaṃiccādīnipi atisaye.

The 'vipulā' half-verse is in the sense of excess. Here indeed, in the odd pādas, there are twelve mātrās; in the even, eighteen mātrās. In all Āryā meters, in the first pāda, there are twelve mātrās; in the second, eighteen; in the third, twelve; in the fourth, fifteen. But when they are deficient in the first and third, then they are greater in the even pādas—this is the characteristic of the vipulā. Now, what is the distinction between 'satata' (continuous) and 'atisaya' (excess)? 'Satata' is continuity, uninterrupted, without intervention by other actions; 'atisaya', however, is frequency and excellence. Among these, frequency is the repetition of an action, while excellence is the superiority of the components of the action. 'Bhusaṃ' is so called because it shines for all (bhāsati), with 'ā' becoming 'u'. Or 'bhusaṃ' is so called because it falls downwards (bhassati), from the root 'bhas' in the sense of falling downwards, with 'a' becoming 'u'. 'Atisayo' is the act of surpassing, or 'atisayo' is the proceeding or dwelling after having surpassed. 'Daḷhaṃ' is so called because it burns all (dahati), with 'ha' previously becoming 'ḷa'. Or 'daḷhaṃ' is so called because it splits (dalati) or tears apart, with the suffix 'ha'. Or 'daḷhaṃ' is so called because it takes while burning (dahanto lāti), with transposition of letters. 'Abhisayo' and 'daḷhaṃ' are used in the sense of 'atisayadaḷhā' (excessively firm). 'Tibbaṃ' is so called because it crosses or surpasses (tarati), with 'ra' becoming 'va', and 'a' becoming 'i'. 'Eko' is so called because it goes (eti). That very 'eko' is 'ekantaṃ'. Or 'ekantaṃ' is so called because it surpasses one (ekaṃ tarati). That which has surpassed the measure is 'atimattaṃ'. 'Bāḷhaṃ' is so called because it takes much (bahuṃ lāti), with elision of 'u', and transposition of letters and the sound 'ha'. 'Ativelaṃ', 'accatthaṃ', 'nibbharaṃ', 'nitantaṃ', 'gāḷhaṃ', and so on, are also in the sense of excess.

Dabbaṃ satvaṃ, taṃviparīte dhammamatte vattamānā bāḷhapariyantā khippādayo atisayaṃ vinā paṇḍake napuṃsake vattanti[M 0.0044]. Khippaṃ bhavati “khippa bhavabhī”ti padadvayaṃ adhikaṃ viya dissati, atisayo pulliṅgo, assa guṇassātisayo, assa dabbassātisayo iti. “Khippaṃ bhuñjati, satataṃ juhoti, satataṃ ramaṇīyo”iccatra tu kriyāvisesanattāyeva paṇḍakattaṃ. Tesu khippādīsu ye dabbagā dabbābhidhāyino, te tīsu liṅgesu. “Dabbadhammo liṅga”nti dassanantaraṃ. Yathā khippā jarā, khippo maccu, khippaṃ gamanaṃ. Santatā taṇhā, santataṃ dukkhaṃ, santato ākāso. Atimattā kriyā, atimatto naro, atimattaṃ padaṃ iccādi.

A substance is a being. In the opposite case, when referring to a mere phenomenon, 'khippa' and similar terms up to 'bāḷha' occur in the neuter gender, without being the word 'atisaya' itself. For example, 'khippaṃ bhavati' (it happens quickly). 'Atisayo' is masculine, as in 'assa guṇassātisayo' (the excess of this quality), 'assa dabbassātisayo' (the excess of this substance). However, in 'khippaṃ bhuñjati' (he eats quickly), 'satataṃ juhoti' (he constantly sacrifices), 'satataṃ ramaṇīyo' (he is constantly delightful), the neuter gender occurs precisely because they are adverbs of action. Among these 'khippa' and similar terms, those that refer to a substance or denote a substance exist in all three genders, following the view that 'gender is a property of a substance'. For example: 'khippā jarā' (quick decay), 'khippo maccu' (quick death), 'khippaṃ gamanaṃ' (quick going). 'Santatā taṇhā' (continuous craving), 'santataṃ dukkhaṃ' (continuous suffering), 'santato ākāso' (continuous space). 'Atimattā kriyā' (excessive action), 'atimatto naro' (excessive man), 'atimattaṃ padaṃ' (excessive word), and so on.

42-43. Dvādasakaṃ māre. Haranayanaggidaḍḍhattā tinayanaggidaḍḍhattā (ka.) natthi viggaho sarīrametassa aviggaho. Kāmayati raticchaṃ uppādayatīti kāmo, kāritantā apaccayo. Siṅgārarūpena pāṇīnaṃ manasi bhavatīti manobhū. Pañcakāmaguṇesu madayatīti madano. Lokānaṃ antaṃ vināsaṃ karotīti antako. Vase vatteti sīlenāti vasavattī. Pāpaṃ icchati karoti, tena yuttoti vā pāpimā. Parato jāyatīti pajā, acchandikā, tāsaṃ pati pajāpati. Ye kusaladhammesu pamattā, tesameva bandhu pamattabandhu. Kaṇhadhammayuttatāya kaṇho. Kusaladhamme māretīti māro. Akusaladhamme na muñcatīti namuci. Mīnaketano, kandappo, dappako, anaṅgo, pañcasaro, sambarāri, manasijo, kusumesu[M 0.0045], anaññajo, pupphadhanvā, ratipati, makaraddhajoiccādīnipi viṇhusutassa kāmassa nāmāni.

42-43. Twelve names for Māra: Because he was burned by the fire of Hara's eye, he has no body (viggaha); he is bodiless (aviggaho). 'Kāma' is so called because he desires (kāmayati) and produces the desire for pleasure; the suffix 'a' is from the causative root. 'Manobhū' is so called because he arises (bhavatīti) in the minds (manasi) of beings through alluring forms. 'Madano' is so called because he intoxicates (madayati) with the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Antako' is so called because he brings an end (antaṃ), destruction, to beings. 'Vasavattī' is so called because by his nature (sīlena) he wields power (vatteti) over others (vase). 'Pāpimā' is so called because he desires and does evil (pāpaṃ), or is associated with it. 'Pajā' (progeny) are so called because they are born from others, they are without free will; their lord is 'Pajāpati'. 'Pamattabandhu' is so called because he is a friend (bandhu) only to those who are heedless (pamattā) in wholesome qualities. 'Kaṇho' is so called because he is associated with dark (kaṇha) qualities. 'Māro' is so called because he kills (māreti) wholesome qualities. 'Namuci' is so called because he does not release (na muñcati) from unwholesome qualities. Mīnaketana, Kandappa, Dappaka, Anaṅga, Pañcasara, Sambarāri, Manasija, Kusumesu, Anaññaja, Pupphadhanvā, Ratipati, Makaraddhaja, and so on, are also names of Kāma, the son of Viṣṇu.

Taṇhā aratī ragā ceti etā tisso tassa mārassa dhītaro. Yo taṃ passati, taṃ tasitaṃ karotīti taṇhā, salopo, ṇhā ca. Paresaṃ kusaladhammesu aratiṃ karotīti aratī. Rajjanti etthāti ragā. Tassa mārassa hatthī girimekhalo nāma. Sarīramahantabhāvena girisadisattā giri viyāti giri. Mārena mamāyanavasena “ayaṃ me hatthī mekhalo nāma hotū”ti katanāmattā mekhalā viyāti mekhaloti samuditanāmadvayena ekameva hatthiṃ vadati, yathā “vajirāsani, sītuṇha”nti.

Craving (Taṇhā), Discontent (Aratī), and Lust (Ragā)—these are the three daughters of that Māra. 'Taṇhā' is so called because for one who sees her, she makes them thirsty (tasitaṃ karoti); with elision of 'sa' and the suffix 'ṇhā'. 'Aratī' is so called because it causes discontent (aratiṃ) in others regarding wholesome qualities. 'Ragā' is so called because beings are impassioned (rajjanti) by it. That Māra's elephant is named Girimekhala. Because of its massive body, it is like a mountain (giri viya), hence 'Giri'. Because Māra, out of possessiveness, named it, saying, 'Let this be my elephant named Mekhala'—it is like a girdle (mekhalā viya), hence 'Mekhala'. Thus, by the two names combined, it refers to a single elephant, just as in 'vajirāsani' (thunderbolt-weapon) and 'sītuṇha' (cold-and-hot).

44. Tikaṃ yame. Pajāsaṃyamanato yamā, maccuppabhutayo assa kiṅkārā, tesu rājateti yamarājā. Tedhātukesupi āṇāpavattakattā mahanto visayo etassa visayī, ṇī, so eva vesāyī. Yattha lakkhaṇena na sijjhati, tattha sabbatra “yadādinā vā niruttinayena vā saddasiddhi veditabbā”ti hi pubbe vuttaṃ, dukkhajanakattā vā visadisaṭṭhānaṃ gacchantīti vesā, nerayikā, tesaṃ adhipatibhāvena ayati pavattatīti vesāyī, ī. Yamānaṃ rājā yamo. Dhammarājo, katanto, samavattī, kālo, daṇḍadharo, antakoiccādīnipi yamassa nāmāni. Assa yamassa āvudhaṃ nayanameva. Tena kira kodhacittena olokitamattena sattānaṃ sarīrāni ātape khittaghatapiṇḍāni viya vilīyantīti.

44. A triad concerning Yama. From restraining (saṃyamana) beings, he is Yama. Death and others are his servants (kiṅkārā); because he is king (rājā) among them, he is Yama-rāja. Because he exercises authority over the three realms, his domain (visayo) is vast; he is one with a domain (visayī), hence he is Vesāyī. Where a derivation is not successful by the given characteristic, it has been previously stated that 'the formation of a word should be understood by means of 'yad' and so on, or by etymological method.' Alternatively, because they go to a disparate place that generates suffering, they are 'vesā', the hell-beings; because he proceeds as their lord (adhipati), he is Vesāyī. The king of those who restrain (yamānaṃ) is Yama. Dhammarāja, Katanta, Samavattī, Kāla, Daṇḍadhara, and Antaka are also names of Yama. This Yama's weapon is his gaze alone. It is said that merely by his looking at beings with an angry mind, their bodies dissolve like lumps of ghee thrown into the heat of the sun.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0046] asurabhede. Etesañhi satipi devabhāve heṭṭhā nivāsitabhāvasāmaññato ettha vacanaṃ, mārassa pana sattānamanatthakārakatāsāmaññena yamena saddhiṃ vacanaṃ takkarattā. Yuddhādīsu vepitaṃ kampitaṃ cittametassa vepacitti saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.256. Puṇṇaṃ lomaṃ yassa so pulomo, pulāmahatī umā kitti, kanti vā yassāti pulomo. “Umātasīhemavati-haliddākittikantisū”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ pana sakkassa bhariyāya sujātāya pitā. Dvayaṃ kinnare. Assamukhanarasarīratāya kucchito puriso, kiñci vā puriso, purisasadisoti vā kimpuriso. Evaṃ kinnaro. Turaṅgavadana, assamukhādīnipi kinnarassa nāmāni.

A pair concerning a type of asura. Although these beings possess a divine state, they are mentioned here due to the commonality of their dwelling in a lower abode. Māra, however, is mentioned with Yama because of the commonality of causing harm to beings and because of his evil nature. One whose mind (citta) is agitated (vepitaṃ) and shaken in battles and the like—he is Vepacitti. He whose hair (loma) is full (puṇṇa) is Puloma; or he who has great (pulā) splendor (umā), fame (kitti), or radiance (kanti) is Puloma. For in the Nānatthasaṅgaha it is said: 'Umā, atasī, hemavatī, haliddā, kitti, and kanti.' This Puloma was the father of Sujātā, the wife of Sakka. A pair concerning the kinnaras. A despised man (kucchito puriso); or, somewhat a man (kiñci puriso); or one similar to a man (purisasadiso)—thus, he is called a kimpurisa. Similarly, a kinnara. Turaṅgavadana (horse-faced), Assamukha (horse-faced) and others are also names of the kinnara.

45-46. Addhapajjena ākāsassa nāmāni. Tesaṃ tesaṃ vatthūnaṃ antaraṃ nānattaṃ ikkhate loko ettha, anenāti vā antalikkhaṃ, rassa lo. Ikkhanaṃ vā dassanaṃ ikkhā, tassa antaraṃ kāraṇaṃ antalikkhaṃ. Khanati byavadhānanti khaṃ, kvi. Sabbagahagāmaṇino ādiccassa patho maggo ādiccapatho. Na bhavatīti abbhaṃ. Gacchantyanena devāti gaganaṃ, yu, massa go. Ambate saddāyate atrāti ambaraṃ, ro. Haya gatimhi, visesena hayati gacchati sabbatrāti vehāso, yassa so, vigato vā hāso cittassa etthārammaṇālābhatoti vehāso. Anilassa vātassa patho anilapatho. Bhusaṃ kāsante dippante padatthā etenāti ākāso, na kassati na vilekhīyatīti vā ākāso. Na bhavati [M 0.0047] ettha kiñcipi vatthūti nabhaṃ, natthi bhūmi etthāti vā nabhaṃ, na bhāyanti pakkhino anena, etthāti vā nabhaṃ. Vino pakkhino hayanti gacchanti etthāti vehāyasaṃ, aso. Tārā vuccanti nakkhattādayo, tesaṃ patho tārāpatho. Surānaṃ devānaṃ patho surapatho. Na haññateti aghaṃ, hanassa gho. Anantaṃ, visaṇupadaṃiccādīnipi ākāsassa nāmāni.

45-46. The names of the sky in a half-verse. The world sees (ikkhate) the diversity in the interval (antaraṃ) between various objects here, or by means of this, hence it is called 'antalikkhaṃ', with 'ra' becoming 'la'. Or, 'ikkhā' is seeing (dassanaṃ), and the intermediate cause of that is 'antalikkhaṃ'. It digs out (khanati) a separation, hence 'khaṃ'. The path (patho) of the sun (ādicca), the leader of all celestial bodies, is 'ādiccapatho'. It does not exist (na bhavati), hence 'abbhaṃ' (cloud). The gods go (gacchanti) by means of it, hence 'gaganaṃ'. Sound is made (ambate saddāyate) herein, hence 'ambaraṃ'. It moves (hayati) or goes everywhere with distinction, hence 'vehāso'; or, joy (hāso) of the mind is gone (vigato) here due to the lack of an object, hence 'vehāso'. The path of the wind (anila) is 'anilapatho'. Objects shine (kāsante) brightly herein, hence 'ākāso'; or, it is not ploughed (na kassati) or scratched, hence 'ākāso'. Nothing whatsoever exists (na bhavati) here, hence 'nabhaṃ'; or, there is no earth (bhūmi) here, hence 'nabhaṃ'; or, birds (pakkhino) do not fear (na bhāyanti) by means of it or in it, hence 'nabhaṃ'. Birds (vino) move (hayanti) or go herein, hence 'vehāyasaṃ'. The stars (tārā), that is, the constellations and so on, their path is 'tārāpatho'. The path of the gods (surā) is 'surapatho'. It is not harmed (na haññati), hence 'aghaṃ'. Anantaṃ (endless), visaṇupadaṃ (Vishnu's place), and so on, are also names for the sky.

47-48. Meghādyekādasakaṃ meghe. Mehati gharati secatīti megho. Vāriṃ vahatīti valāhako, vārisaddassa vo, vassa lo pāṇini 6.3.109; moggallānapañcikā 1.47; nīti-sutta 1340, 1343. Dibbanti vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ gacchanti lokā anenāti devo. Pajānaṃ lokānaṃ annaṃ bhojanaṃ bhavati etenāti pajjunno, akārassukāro. Ambuṃ udakaṃ dhāretīti ambudharo. Lokānaṃ santāpaṃ hantīti ghano, hassa gho. Jaladhāraṃ dhāretīti dhārādharo. Jīvanaṃ jalaṃ mūtaṃ bandhamaneneti jīmūto, vanasaddalopo, lokānaṃ vā jīvitaṃ munāti bandhatīti jīmūto, vitalopo, jīvitassa jī ādeso vā pāṇini 6.3.109; moggallānapañcikā 1.47; nīti-sutta 1340, 1343. Evaṃ aññatra. Vāriṃ vahatīti vārivāho. Ambuṃ dadātīti ambudo. Āpaṃ bharatīti abbhaṃ, kvi, passa bo.

47-48. The group of eleven, beginning with megha, concerning clouds. Mehati, it sprinkles; gharati, it thunders; secati, it pours; thus it is called megho. It carries water (vāriṃ vahati), hence valāhako; from the word vāri comes vo, from vassa comes lo. Because beings attain growth and increase through it, it is called devo. It becomes the food and sustenance of beings, hence pajjunno, with the vowel 'a' becoming 'u'. It holds water (ambuṃ dhāreti), hence ambudharo. It destroys the world's affliction, hence ghano, with 'h' becoming 'gh'. It holds streams of water (jaladhāraṃ dhāreti), hence dhārādharo. By this, life-giving water is bound, hence jīmūto, with the elision of the word 'vana'; or, it binds the life of beings, hence jīmūto, with the elision of 'vita', or with 'jī' as a substitute for 'jīvita'. Thus elsewhere. It carries water (vāriṃ vahati), hence vārivāho. It gives water (ambuṃ dadāti), hence ambudo. It bears water (āpaṃ bharati), hence abbhaṃ, with the kvi suffix, and 'p' becoming 'b'.

Tikaṃ vuṭṭhiyaṃ. Vassati siñcatīti vassaṃ, vassa secane. Evaṃ vassanavuṭṭhiyo.

The triad concerning rain. It rains (vassati), it sprinkles (siñcati), hence vassaṃ; from the root vass, in the sense of sprinkling. Likewise are vassana and vuṭṭhi.

Pañcakaṃ [M 0.0048] vijjuyaṃ. Satataṃ īrati kampatīti satero, talopo, so eva sateritā. Khaṇamattampi na tiṭṭhatīti akkhaṇā. Kuṭilaṃ aciraṭṭhāyitattā virūpaṃ hutvā javatīti vijju. Vijjotatīti vijjutā. Aciraṃ pabhā yassa acirappabhā.

The pentad concerning lightning. It constantly moves and trembles (satataṃ īrati kampati), hence satero, with the elision of 'ta'; this itself is sateritā. It does not last even for a moment, hence akkhaṇā. It moves swiftly (javati), being crooked (kuṭilaṃ) and misshapen (virūpaṃ) on account of its brief duration, hence vijju. It flashes, hence vijjutā. That which has a brief radiance is acirappabhā.

49. Catukkaṃ meghanāde. Meghānaṃ nādo meghanādo. Dhanīyate dhanitaṃthanitaṃ (sī.), dhana sadde. Gajjanaṃ gajjitaṃ, gajja sadde. Rasīyate rasitaṃ. Ādinā harādādi sabbatra napuṃsakebhāve to, ādinā svanitadhanitādayo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), ādinā dhanitaharādarāsādayo (byākhyāsudhāṭīkā). Dvayaṃ sakkadhanumhi. Indassa āvudhaṃ dhanu ca indāvudhaṃ, indadhanu ca. Vātena khittamambu vātakkhittambu, bindu. Sītaṃ karotīti sīkaro, siñcatīti vā sīkaro, cassa ko, aro ca, vātavasena vā tato tato saratīti sīkaro, assa ī, majjhe kāgamo ca.

49. The tetrad concerning thunder. The sound of clouds is meghanādo. It is sounded, hence dhanitaṃ, from the root dhan, in the sense of sound. A roaring is gajjanaṃ or gajjitaṃ, from the root gajja, in the sense of sound. It is resounded, hence rasitaṃ. By `ādi` (etc.), `harā` and so on are included. The pair concerning Sakka's bow. The weapon and bow of Inda is indāvudhaṃ, and also indadhanu. Water thrown by the wind is vātakkhittambu; a drop (bindu). It makes cold (sītaṃ karoti), hence sīkaro; or it sprinkles (siñcati), hence sīkaro, where 'c' becomes 'k' and 'aro' is added; or by the force of the wind it moves (sarati) here and there, hence sīkaro, where 'a' becomes 'ī' and there is the augment 'k' in the middle.

50. Tikaṃ jaladhārāyaṃ. Vegato jaladhārānaṃ saṃ bhusaṃ patanaṃ āsāro, punappunaṃ saratīti āsāro. Vegaṃ dhāretīti dhārā. Adho patatīti sampāto, saṃsaddo adhobhāge vegato jaladhārānaṃ sambhūya patanaṃ dhārāsampāto, sara gatiyaṃ ghau iti āsāro (cintāmaṇiṭīkā). Dvayaṃ vassopale. Karena hatthena gayhupagattā karakā, jalaṃ piṇḍaṃ karotīti vā karakā, “vassopale [M 0.0049] tu karakā, karakopi ca dissate”ti ruddo, karasaddotra. “Karo vassopale pāṇi-soṇḍāpaccāyaraṃsisū”ti nānatthasaṅgahe vuttaṃ. Ghanato, ghanakāle vā sañjātaṃ upalaṃ silā ghanopalaṃ. Duṭṭhu dinaṃ duddinaṃ, ayaṃ duddinasaddo meghacchannāhe vattati, asobhanatthopyatthi duddinasaddo, aguṇavacanatāyaṃ vāccaliṅgo.

50. The triad concerning streams of water. The forceful falling down of streams of water is āsāro; or because it flows repeatedly (punappunaṃ sarati), it is āsāro. It holds the force (vegaṃ dhāreti), hence dhārā. It falls downwards (adho patati), hence sampāto; the word saṃ is in the sense of 'downwards'. The pair concerning hailstones. Because it is taken up and held by the hand (karena hatthena), it is karakā; or because it makes water into a lump (jalaṃ piṇḍaṃ karoti), it is karakā. According to Rudra: 'Regarding a hailstone, karakā, and also karako is seen'; here the word is kara. In the Nānatthasaṅgaha it is said: 'Kara is used for a hailstone, a hand, an elephant's trunk, a tax, and a ray of light.' A stone (upalaṃ) born from a cloud (ghanato), or at the time of a cloud (ghanakāle), is ghanopalaṃ. A bad day is duddinaṃ; this word duddina is used for a day covered by clouds. The word duddina also has an inauspicious meaning; and because it is a word expressing a bad quality, it is an adjective (of indeterminate gender).

51-52. Chakkaṃ tirodhāne. Dhara āvaraṇe, apādipubbo. Apidharati āvuṇotīti pidhānaṃ, alopo. Apadharatīti apadhāraṇaṃ. Tiro dharati pidahatīti tirodhānaṃ. Antaraṃ dharatīti antaradhānaṃ, niggahītalopo. Apidharatīti apidhānaṃ. Ettha ca apādiupasaggā dhātuno āvaraṇatthajotakā. Chādayatīti chādanaṃ. Byavadhā, antaradhiiccādayopi tirodhāne.

51-52. The hexad concerning concealment. The root dhar is in the sense of covering, preceded by prefixes such as api. Apidharati means it covers, hence pidhānaṃ, with the elision of 'a'. From apadharati comes apadhāraṇaṃ. Tiro dharati means it covers, hence tirodhānaṃ. Antaraṃ dharati, it holds within, hence antaradhānaṃ, with the elision of the niggahīta. From apidharati comes apidhānaṃ. And here, the prefixes such as api indicate the meaning of 'covering' for the root. Chādayati, it covers, hence chādanaṃ. Byavadhā, antaradhi, and so on, are also in the sense of concealment.

Sāddhapajjena candassa nāmāni. Indati nakkhattānaṃ paramissariyaṃ karotīti indu. Candati hilādayati sukhayati pajanti cando. Nakkhattānaṃ rājā nakkhattarājā. Umā kanti, tāya saha vijjatīti somo, sukhaṃ abhissavatīti vā somo, mapaccayo. Nisaṃ rattiṃ karoti, tattha vā karo raṃsi etassa nisākaro. Andhakāraṃ usenti dahanti vināsentīti osā, raṃsayo, te ettha dhiyanti patiṭṭhahantīti osadhi, tārāviseso, tassa īso pati osadhīso. Himo sītalo raṃsi yassa himaraṃsi. Saso aṅko lakkhaṇaṃ yassa sasaṅko. Candaṃ kappūraṃ māti sadisaṃ nayatīti candimā. Ikārādeso. Sasalakkhaṇamettha atthi sasī[M 0.0050]. Sasati vā hiṃsati uṇhaguṇanti sasī, īpaccayo tadupalakkhite tadupacāraṃ. Sītā raṃsayo yassatthīti sītaraṃsi. Nisāya rattiyā nātho tadālaṅkārabhāvatoti nisānātho. Uḷūnaṃ tārānaṃ rājā uḷurājā. Māti attānaṃ kappūrena sadisaṃ karotīti mā, māsaddoyaṃ pume, taṃsahacaraṇato uḷurājādayopi. Himaṃsu, kumudabandhu, vidhu, sudhaṃsu, subbhaṃsu, nisāpati, migaṅko, kalānidhi, dvijarājo, sasadharo, nakkhattesoiccādīnipi candassa nāmāni.

The names of the moon, in a verse and a half. It exercises supreme lordship over the stars, hence indu. It shines, gladdens, and makes beings happy, hence cando. King of the stars is nakkhattarājā. Umā means beauty; it exists together with that, hence somo; or, it pours forth happiness, hence somo, with the suffix ma. It makes the night (nisaṃ karoti), or its rays (karo) are therein, hence nisākaro. They burn and destroy the darkness, hence osā, meaning rays; these are placed and established therein, hence osadhi, a particular star; its lord and master is osadhīso. He whose rays (raṃsi) are cool (himo) is himaraṃsi. He whose mark (aṅko) is a hare (saso) is sasaṅko. It is like camphor, hence candamā, with the substitution of the vowel 'i' making it candimā. The hare-mark is present in it, hence sasī. Or, it harms the quality of heat, hence sasī, with the suffix ī; this is a metaphorical usage for that which is characterized by it. He who has cool rays is sītaraṃsi. He is the lord of the night (nisāya nātho) because he is its adornment, hence nisānātho. King of the stars (uḷūnaṃ rājā) is uḷurājā. It makes itself like camphor, hence mā; this word mā is masculine, and due to association with it, uḷurājā and so on are also masculine. Himaṃsu, kumudabandhu, vidhu, sudhaṃsu, subbhaṃsu, nisāpati, migaṅko, kalānidhi, dvijarājo, sasadharo, nakkhatteso—these and others are also names of the moon.

53-54. Soḷasannaṃ bhāgānaṃ pūraṇo soḷasamo bhāgo candassa kalā, kala saṅkhyāne, kalīyate ekādinā saṅkhyāyateti kalā. Dvayaṃ candassa sarīre. Maññate ñāyate aneneti bimbaṃ. Manato vapaccayo, nipātanā massa bo, assi, nassa mo, vassa bo, bimbasaddo anitthiyaṃ. Maṇḍayateti maṇḍalaṃ, alo, itthiyaṃ maṇḍalī, ayaṃ tīsvapi bimbo anitthī, maṇḍalaṃ tīsu (amara 3.15).

53-54. The sixteenth part, which is the completion of the sixteen parts of the moon, is a kalā. The root kal is in the sense of counting; because it is counted by one and so on, it is called kalā. The pair concerning the moon's body. That by which it is perceived or known is bimbaṃ. From the root man, the suffix va is added; by irregular formation, 'm' becomes 'b', 'a' becomes 'i', 'n' becomes 'm', and 'v' becomes 'b'; the word bimba is not feminine. It adorns, hence maṇḍalaṃ, with the suffix ala; in the feminine, it is maṇḍalī. This word exists in all three genders.

Pādahīnapajjena addhabhāgo. Asati khepeti samudāyanti aḍḍho, to. Tathā addho. Upaḍḍhoti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ, ete tayo pume. Khaṇḍayati samudāyanti khaṇḍaṃ. Sakyate [M 0.0051] ubbāhanādīsu thokattāti sakalaṃ, alo, khaṇḍasakalā vā pume, satthe rūpabhedato napuṃsake. Ete ca aḍḍhādayo tayo asame bhāge pume, same tu napuṃsaketi rūpabhedenāha “addhaṃ vuttaṃ same bhāge”ti. Khaṇḍādidvayaṃ pana asamepi vattamānaṃ punnapuṃsake vattati, tasmā “addhaṃ vuttaṃ same bhāge”ti ettha “aḍḍhaṃ, upaḍḍha”nti idaṃ dvayampi saṅgahitaṃ asamabhāge pumāni, same aṃse napuṃsakattaṃ rūpabhedato, upacārato tabbhāgavati vāccaliṅgo – addhā sāṭī, addhaṃ vatthaṃ addho kambalo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā).

A half-portion, by a verse lacking a quarter. When it is not present, it diminishes the whole, hence aḍḍho, with the suffix to. Likewise, addho. Upaḍḍho is a word augmented by the prefix upa. These three are masculine. It breaks the whole, hence khaṇḍaṃ. Because it is able, on account of its smallness, to be lifted and so on, it is sakalaṃ, with the suffix ala. Khaṇḍa and sakala are masculine, or in treatises, due to difference in form, they are neuter. And these three, aḍḍha and so on, are masculine when referring to unequal parts, but neuter for equal parts; thus, due to this difference in form, it is said: 'addhaṃ is stated for an equal part.' The pair khaṇḍa and so on, however, even when referring to unequal parts, is used in the masculine and neuter. Therefore, in the statement 'addhaṃ is stated for an equal part,' both aḍḍhaṃ and upaḍḍhaṃ are included.

Pasādādayo cande avassambhāvino, aññatra tu pāsaṅgikā iti candapakkame uccante. Visesena sādayati pasādayatīti pasādo. Evaṃ pasanno, so eva pasannatā.

Clarity, serenity, and so forth are necessarily present in the moon, but elsewhere are incidental; thus they are mentioned in the section on the moon. It especially pleases and clarifies, hence pasādo. Likewise, pasanno, and that very state is pasannatā.

Tikaṃ candappabhāyaṃ. Kumudassāyaṃ vikāso vikāro (ka.) komudī. Candaṃ ācikkhati paṭipādayatīti candikā. Juti assātthīti juṇhā. Tassa ṇo, hapaccayo ca, candassa vā jutiṃ sobhaṃ nayhati bandhatīti juṇhā.

The triad concerning the moon's radiance. This blossoming of the water lily is komudī. It indicates or makes known the moon, hence candikā. It has brightness, hence juṇhā. From that, there is the suffix ṇa and the suffix ha; or, it binds the brightness and beauty of the moon, hence juṇhā.

Catukkaṃ sobhanamatte. Kanati dippatīti kanti, kana dittiyaṃ, kāmīyatīti vā kanti. Sundaraṃ bhāti dippatīti sobhā. Jotayatīti juti. Chādayatīti chavi. Chada saṃvaraṇe, vipaccayo, dalopo.

The tetrad concerning mere beauty. It shines, it gleams, hence kanti; from the root kan, in the sense of shining; or, it is desired, hence kanti. It shines beautifully, it gleams, hence sobhā. It illuminates, hence juti. It covers, hence chavi; from the root chad, in the sense of covering, with the suffix vi and the elision of 'd'.

55. Sattakaṃ lakkhaṇe. Kaṃ attānaṃ laṅkayati hīnaṃ karotīti kalaṅko. Lañchate lakkhate aneneti lañchanaṃ[M 0.0052]. Lakkhyate aneneti lakkhaṃ. Tathā lakkhaṇaṃ. Aṅkīyate lakkhyate aneneti aṅko. Abhi visesaṃ jānāti etenāti abhiññāṇaṃ. Cihīyati lakkhīyati aneneti cihanaṃ. Ciha lakkhaṇe.

55. The heptad concerning a mark. It marks oneself (kaṃ attānaṃ), making one inferior, hence kalaṅko. By this it is marked or characterized, hence lañchanaṃ. By this it is indicated, hence lakkhaṃ. Likewise, lakkhaṇaṃ. By this it is branded or marked, hence aṅko. Through this one knows distinctly, hence abhiññāṇaṃ. By this it is marked or characterized, hence cihanaṃ; from the root cih, in the sense of marking.

Sabbāsaṃ sobhānaṃ majjhe paramā sobhā susamā nāma, sobhanaṃ samaṃ sabbaṃ assaṃ susamā, seṭṭhā sobhā.

Among all beauties, the supreme beauty is named Susamā. In her, everything beautiful is harmonious and even, hence Susamā; the most excellent beauty.

56. Guṇe phoṭṭhabbavisese sītanti napuṃsakaṃ bhavati. Devadattassa sītaṃ vattati. Sītādayo tayo guṇīliṅgā guṇino liṅgaṃ gaṇhanti, taṃ yathā – sītalā bhūmi, sītalaṃ jalaṃ, sītalo vāto. Uṇhābhitattehi sevīyatīti sītaṃ, tena yutto sīto. Sasa gatiyaṃ, iro, ittañca, sītatthikena sarīyatīti vā sisiraṃ. Sītaṃ guṇaṃ lātīti sītalo.

56. In the sense of a specific tangible quality, 'sīta' is neuter. Devadatta experiences cold. The three, 'sīta' and so forth, being adjectives of quality, take the gender of the qualified noun, for example: 'sītalā bhūmi' (cold earth), 'sītalaṃ jalaṃ' (cold water), 'sītalo vāto' (cold wind). It is resorted to by those afflicted by heat, hence 'sītaṃ'; one endowed with that is 'sīto'. The root 'sasa' is in the sense of movement, with the suffixes 'ira' and 'itta'; or, it is resorted to by one desiring cold, hence 'sisiraṃ'. It takes the quality of cold, hence 'sītalo'.

Mahikāntaṃ hime. Hiṃsatīti himaṃ, sassa mo,niggahītalopo ca. Tuha adane, tohati hiṃsatīti tuhinaṃ, ino. Uparito savatīti ussāvo. Nīharanti nissasantyaneneti nīhāro, natthi īhā vā etasmā hetubhūtāti nīhāro, āro. Mahīyate rāgīhīti vācābhi (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) mahikā, ṇvu.

The terms ending with 'mahikā' are for frost. It harms, hence 'himaṃ'; with 'sa' becoming 'ma' and the elision of the niggahīta. The root 'tuha' is in the sense of devouring; it devours, that is, it harms, hence 'tuhinaṃ'; with the suffix 'ina'. It flows from above, hence 'ussāvo'. They bring forth or breathe out through this, hence 'nīhāro'; or, there is no effort ('īhā') because of it, hence 'nīhāro'; with the suffix 'āra'. It is honored by the passionate, hence 'mahikā'; with the suffix 'ṇvu'.

57. Chakkaṃ nakkhatte. Punappunaṃ udayattā na khīyate nakkhattaṃ, attano gamanaṭṭhānaṃ na kharati na vināsetīti vā nakkhattaṃ, atha [M 0.0053] vā nakkha gatiyaṃ, nakkhatīti nakkhattaṃ. Jotati subhāsubhanimittaṃ pakāsetīti joti, nakkhatta bhaṃsaddehi sahacaraṇato napuṃsake. Yathāvuttaṃ nimittaṃ bhāti pakāsetīti bhaṃ. Kattabbaṃ taranti lokā etāyāti tārā, attano vīthiṃ tāyati arati gacchatīti vā tārā, tāreti vā loke ahitatoti tārā, ayañca tārakā, uḷu ca ete tayo apume. Tarā eva ṇvu, tārakā tārā eva tārakā ṇvu (ka.). Uccaṃ lavati ulayati (ka.) gacchatīti ulu. So eva uḷu. Na kevalaṃ tārakā eva apume, atha kho uḷu cāti casaddattho. Uḷusahacariyato pakkhe napuṃsake ca.

57. Six terms for a constellation. It is called 'nakkhattaṃ' because it does not wane from rising again and again; or it does not wear away or destroy its own path; or, from the root 'nakkha' in the sense of movement, it moves. It shines, revealing auspicious and inauspicious signs, hence 'joti'; it is neuter due to its association with the words 'nakkhatta' and 'bhaṃ'. It shines, revealing the aforementioned signs, hence 'bhaṃ'. People cross over what is to be done by means of it, hence 'tārā'; or it protects its own path and moves without fatigue; or it helps the world cross over from harm. And this is 'tārakā', and 'uḷu'; these three are not masculine. From 'tarā' with the suffix 'ṇvu' comes 'tārakā'. It moves high above, hence 'uḷu'. That very one is 'uḷu'. Not only 'tārakā' is non-masculine, but also 'uḷu'—this is the meaning of the word 'ca'. Due to association with 'uḷu', it is alternatively also neuter.

58-60. Assayujādayo revatyantā sattādhikavīsatārakā nakkhattā nāma honti. Tāni ca nakkhattāni ākāse yathāṭhitāni kamatoyeva ettha kathitāni, na uppaṭipāṭiyā. Vakkhati ca “kamato sattādhikavīsati nakkhattā”ti. Assarūpayogato assayujo. Yamasadisattāsabbatra bharatīti bharaṇī. Yu, ī. Aggisadisattā kantati chindatīti kattikā, karoti tasmā vā katthikā, kattikāya sahitā sakattikā. Bharaṇī, rohiṇī vā. Kamalasambhavattā kamale ruhati vaḍḍhatīti rohiṇī. Migasīsaṇṭhānattā [M 0.0054] tārāpuñjo migasiraṃ, chaṭṭhīsamāso uttarappadhānattā napuṃsakattaṃ. Ruddarasāvaṭṭhitakodharuddasadisattā kadāci adati ghasatīti addā. Punappunaṃ sattesu hitaṃ vassatīti punabbasu, vassa secane. Poseti kriyāni, posentyasminti vā pusso. Bhujagasadisattā na silisyate nāliṅgyateti asileso.

58-60. The twenty-seven star constellations, beginning with Assayuja and ending with Revatī, are known as the lunar mansions. These constellations are described here in the order they are situated in the sky, not in reverse order. And it will be said: 'the twenty-seven constellations in order.' Due to its connection with the form of a horse, it is 'Assayujo'. Because it bears everywhere, being similar to Yama, it is 'Bharaṇī'; with suffixes 'yu' and 'ī'. Because it cuts or divides, being similar to fire, it is 'Kattikā'; or because it acts, it is 'Katthikā'; that which is with Kattikā is 'Sakattikā'. Or it is Bharaṇī or Rohiṇī. Because it grows or increases in a lotus, being born from a lotus, it is 'Rohiṇī'. Because the star cluster has the shape of a deer's head, it is 'Migasiraṃ'; this is a genitive compound, and it is neuter due to the prominence of the final member. Because it sometimes eats or consumes, being similar to a wrathful Rudra whose anger is aroused and established in fury, it is 'Addā'. Because it repeatedly rains benefit upon beings, it is 'Punabbasu'; the root 'vassa' is in the sense of pouring. It nourishes actions, or actions are nourished in it, hence 'Pusso'. Because it is not clung to or embraced, being similar to a serpent, it is 'Asileso'.

Mahīyate kāriyatthikehīti maghā māghā (ka.), hassa gho. Phalaṃ gaṇhāpetīti phaggunī, yu, ī. Dveti pubbaphaggunī, uttaraphaggunī ceti dve. Hatthasaṇṭhānatāya hattho. Tacchakasadisattā vicittaṃ phalaṃ dadātīti cittā. Sobhanā āti, sāti vā tanuṃ karoti subhāsubhanti sāti svāti (ka.), subhāsubhaphaladānato vā sāti, “sāti dānāvasānesū”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe vuttaṃ, ayaṃ dvīsu. Visadisaṃ phalaṃ khaṇatīti visākhā, vividhā vā sakhā mittā yassā sā visākhā. Anurādhayati saṃsijjhati subhāsubhaphalametāyāti anurādhā. Guṇehi sabbāsaṃ vuḍḍhattā jeṭṭhā. Mūlati patiṭṭhāti subhāsubhaphalametthāti mūlaṃ. Āsāḷho nāma bhatīnaṃ daṇḍo, taṃsaṇṭhānattā āsāḷhā nāma dve nakkhattā pubbāsāḷhauttarāsāḷhavasena.
