It is honored by those who have a purpose to accomplish, hence 'Maghā'; with 'ha' becoming 'gha'. It causes fruit to be obtained, hence 'Phaggunī'; with suffixes 'yu' and 'ī'. There are two: 'Pubbaphaggunī' and 'Uttaraphaggunī'. Due to its shape like a hand, it is 'Hattho'. Because it gives varied fruit, being similar to a carpenter, it is 'Cittā'. It is beautiful; or 'sāti' makes the body good and bad; or from giving good and bad fruit, it is 'Sāti'; for in the Nānārthasaṅgaha it is said, 'sāti is in the sense of giving and ending'; this one is in two genders. It digs up dissimilar fruit, hence 'Visākhā'; or she who has diverse friends is 'Visākhā'. Good and bad fruit is accomplished or succeeds through it, hence 'Anurādhā'. Because it is the eldest of all in virtues, it is 'Jeṭṭhā'. Good and bad fruit is rooted or established in it, hence 'Mūlaṃ'. 'Āsāḷho' is the name of a wanderer's staff; due to its shape, there are two constellations named 'Āsāḷhā', by way of 'Pubbāsāḷhā' and 'Uttarāsāḷhā'.

Savati subhāsubhaphalametenāti savaṇo, savaṇaṃ vā. Dhanamesanti etthāti dhaniṭṭhā, dhanati vā vibhūti nidhānaṃ dhaniṭṭhā. Sataṃ bhisajā ettha, satabhisajānaṃ vā adhipati satabhisajo. Bhaddo go, tasseva padāni pādā assaṃ bhaddapadā, pubbabhaddapadā dve, uttarabhaddapadā dve, samūho cesaṃ catusaṅkhyāti bahuvacanaṃ. Rā vuccati dhanaṃ, tabbantatāya revatī, ākārasse, revato vā isibhedo, tassa apaccaṃ revatī.

Good and bad fruit flows by means of it, hence 'Savaṇo', or 'Savaṇaṃ'. Wealth is sought here, hence 'Dhaniṭṭhā'; or it holds prosperity and treasure, hence 'Dhaniṭṭhā'. A hundred physicians are here, or it is the lord of a hundred physicians, hence 'Satabhisajo'. 'Bhaddo' is an ox; its feet are 'pādā', hence 'Bhaddapadā'; there are two 'Pubbabhaddapadā' and two 'Uttarabhaddapadā', and since their group is four in number, the plural is used. 'Rā' is called wealth; from possessing that, it is 'Revatī'; with the form of 'ā'; or 'Revato' is a particular sage, and his descendant is 'Revatī'.

61. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0055] rāhuggahe. So vuccati saggo, tattha bhātīti sobbhānu. Rahati candādīnaṃ sobhaṃ jahāpetīti rāhu. Tamo, vidhuntudo, candādo, sehikeyotipi rāhussa nāmāni.

61. Two terms for Rāhu's seizing. Heaven is called 'so'; it shines there, hence 'Sobhānu'. It abandons, that is, it causes the radiance of the moon and others to be abandoned, hence 'Rāhu'. 'Tamo', 'Vidhuntudo', 'Candādo', and 'Sehikeyo' are also names of Rāhu.

Sūra, canda, aṅgāraka, budha, jīva, sukka, asita, rāhu, ketūti ete sūrādayo navaggahā nāma.

The sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—these, beginning with the sun, are called the nine planets.

Mesādiko dvādasakoṭṭhāso rāsi nāma. Ādinā usabha, methuna, kakkaṭa, sīha, kaññā, tulā, vicchika, dhanu, makara, kumbha, mīne saṅgaṇhāti.

The twelve-part division beginning with Aries is called a zodiacal sign. By 'beginning with', it includes Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.

Dvayaṃ bhaddapadanakkhattānaṃ nāmaṃ. Poṭṭho go pāṭho bhaddo go (ka.), tasseva padāni pādā assaṃ poṭṭhapadā.

Two names for the Bhaddapada constellations. 'Poṭṭho' is an ox; its feet are 'pādā', hence 'Poṭṭhapadā'.

62-63. Pajjadvayena sūriyassa nāmāni. Ā bhuso dippatīti ādicco, ppassa cco. Lokānaṃ sūrabhāvaṃ janetīti sūriyo. Tathā sūro. Sataṃ bahavo raṃsayo yassa sataraṃsi. Divā divasaṃ karotīti divākaro, divase vā karo [M 0.0056] ābhā yassa divākaro, divāsaddoyaṃ sabbakārakavacano, na tu ādhāravacano eva. Visesena rocate dippateti verocano. Dinaṃ karoti, kumudānaṃ vā dinaṃ mākulyaṃ karotīti dinakaro, uṇho raṃsi yassa uṇharaṃsi. Pabhaṃ karotīti pabhaṅkaro.

62-63. The names of the sun in two verses. It shines intensely, hence 'Ādicco'; with 'ppa' becoming 'cca'. It generates brilliance for the worlds, hence 'Sūriyo'. Likewise, 'Sūro'. He whose rays are many hundreds is 'Sataraṃsi'. It makes the day, hence 'Divākaro'; or he whose radiance makes the day is 'Divākaro'; this word 'divā' is expressive of all grammatical cases, not only the locative. It shines or gleams especially, hence 'Verocano'. It makes the day, or it causes the water lilies to close, hence 'Dinakaro'. He whose rays are hot is 'Uṇharaṃsi'. It makes light, hence 'Pabhaṅkaro'.

Aṃsuno mālā, sā yattha atthi aṃsumālī. Dinānaṃ pati dinapati. Tapatīti tapano. Ravanti etena sattā pabhāvittāti ravi. Bhānu yassa atthīti bhānumā. Raṃsi yassa atthīti raṃsimā. Bhaṃ ābhaṃ karoti, tāsaṃ vā ākaro uppattiṭṭhānaṃ bhākaro. Bhāti dippatīti bhānu. Devehipi accate pūjīyateti akko. Sahassaṃ bahavo raṃsayo yassa sahassaraṃsi. Dvādasattā, pabhākaro, vibhākaro, vikattano vissakammunā vikattito, kammani yu (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), mattaṇḍo, divamaṇi, taraṇi, mitto, citrabhānu, vibhāvasu, gahappati, haṃso, savitāiccādīnipi sūriyassa nāmāni.

A garland of rays; he who has this is 'Aṃsumālī'. The lord of days is 'Dinapati'. It heats, hence 'Tapano'. Beings are made to resound or are illuminated by it, hence 'Ravi'. He who has light is 'Bhānumā'. He who has rays is 'Raṃsimā'. It makes radiance, or it is the mine or place of origin for them, hence 'Bhākaro'. It shines or gleams, hence 'Bhānu'. It is honored and worshipped even by the gods, hence 'Akko'. He whose rays are many thousands is 'Sahassaraṃsi'. Being the twelve Ādityas, 'Pabhākaro', 'Vibhākaro', 'Vikattano', 'Mattaṇḍo', 'Divamaṇi', 'Taraṇi', 'Mitto', 'Citrabhānu', 'Vibhāvasu', 'Gahappati', 'Haṃso', 'Savitā'—these and others are also names of the sun.

64. Pajjena sūriyādīnaṃ raṃsippabhānaṃ nāmāni. Rasanti taṃ sattāti raṃsi. Ā bhuso bhātīti ābhā. Pakārena bhātīti pabhā. Dippatīti ditti. Rocate dippateti ruci. Dīdhyati dippatīti dīdhiti. Dippatīti vā dīdhiti, passa dho, ikārāgamo. Miyyante khuddajantavo aneneti marīci, īci. Asati gacchati disantanti aṃsu, ussāgamo. Marīcisahacaraṇato dīdhityādayo khalitapāṭho (?), savarasāmī tu aṅguli kākalisāri sarāri tumbiari susi dīmityattayo thīpumesu iccāha (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) bhānu aṃsu ca dvīsu. Maya gamanattho [M 0.0057] daṇḍako dhātu daṇḍakappakaraṇe āgatadhātūti attho, niruttisāramañjusāṭīkāyaṃ 253.413 piṭṭhesu passitabbaṃ, khapaccayo ūkārāgamo, atha vā mā māne, ukha gatyattho daṇḍako dhātu daṇḍakappakaraṇe āgatadhātūti attho, niruttisāramañjusāṭīkāyaṃ 253.413 piṭṭhesu passitabbaṃ, māya mānāya ukhatīti mayūkho māpasaṃ gaganaṃ pamāṇayaṃ ukhati gacchatīti pisodarādi (cintāmaṇiṭīkā). Kirati timiraṃ kiraṇo. Kirati timiraṃ karo.

64. In a verse, the names of the rays and radiances of the sun and others. Beings delight in it, hence 'raṃsi'. It shines intensely, hence 'ābhā'. It shines in a special way, hence 'pabhā'. It gleams, hence 'ditti'. It pleases and gleams, hence 'ruci'. It shines brightly, hence 'dīdhiti'. Or, it gleams, hence 'dīdhiti'; with 'p' becoming 'dh' and the addition of 'i'. Small creatures die by this, hence 'marīci'; with the suffix 'īci'. It exists and goes in all directions, hence 'aṃsu'; with the addition of 'u'. Due to association with 'marīci', 'dīdhiti', and others, 'bhānu' and 'aṃsu' are in two genders. The Daṇḍaka root 'maya' is in the sense of going, with the suffix 'kha' and the addition of 'ū'; or alternatively, from 'mā' in the sense of measuring, and the Daṇḍaka root 'ukha' in the sense of going; it goes while measuring, hence 'mayūkho'. It scatters darkness, hence 'kiraṇo'. It scatters darkness, hence 'karo'.

65. Dvayaṃ ādiccamaṇḍalotikhyāte uppātādijāte raṃsimaṇḍale. Sūriyassa pari samantato dhīyate paridhī, pari samantato visatīti pariveso, sūriyaṃ vā pariveṭhayatīti pariveso. Ṭhassa so. Upasūriyakaṃ, maṇḍalanti dvepi paridhino nāmāni.

65. Two [terms] for the circle of rays, known as the solar orb, which arises from atmospheric phenomena and so forth. Around the sun, a boundary is discerned; that is paridhi. Spreading all around, it is parivesa. Or, that which surrounds the sun is parivesa. The letter ṭh [changes to] s. Upasūriyaka and maṇḍala are both names for the halo.

Dvayaṃ marīcikāyaṃ. Marīcisadisatāya marīci. Migānaṃ taṇhā pipāsā yassaṃ jalābhāsattā sā migataṇhikā.

Two [terms] for a mirage. Because of its likeness to a ray of light, it is called marīci. That in which there is the appearance of water, causing the thirst and craving of deer—that is migataṇhikā.

Sūriyassa udayato pubbe uṭṭhitaraṃsi uggataraṃsi aruṇo nāma siyā. Aruṇavaṇṇatāya arati gacchatīti aruṇo. Sūrasūto, anūru, kassapeyyo, kassapi, garuḍāggajotipi aruṇassa nāmānīti. Ākāsavaṇṇanā.

Before the rising of the sun, the rays that have risen, the foremost rays, are called Aruṇa. Because of its reddish hue, it goes toward, or dispels, dislike (arati)—thus Aruṇa. Sūrasūta, Anūru, Kassapeyya, Kassapi, and Garuḍāggaja are also names of Aruṇa. This is the description of the sky.

66-67. Catukkaṃ [M 0.0058] kāle. Kalyante saṅkhyāyante āyuppamāṇādayo anenāti kālo, karaṇaṃ vā kāro, bhāve ṇo, so eva kālo, na hi kriyāvinimutto kālo nāma koci atthi, mahākālassa pana sassatabhāvato atītādivohāro natthevāti avayavakālānaṃ samūhabhāvato sopi “kālo”ti vutto. Sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ asati khepetīti addhā, tassa dho, ākārantoyaṃ addhāsaddo pume. Punappunaṃ etīti samayo. Vināsaṃ lātīti velā, vaṇṇalopo. Diṭṭho, anehotipi kālassevanāmāni.

66-67. Four [terms] for time. It is called 'kāla' because things like lifespan and so forth are reckoned or enumerated by it; or, it is an action (karaṇa) or 'kāra,' with the suffix 'ṇo' in the sense of 'bhāva' (state of being); that itself is kāla, for there is no time apart from action. However, since Great Time (mahākāla) is eternal, designations such as past, etc., do not exist for it; but because it is spoken of as the aggregate of divisions of time, it also is called 'kāla.' 'Addhā' is that which wastes away the life of beings by consuming it; 'dho' is its suffix, and this word 'addhā' is masculine in gender. 'Samaya' is that which comes again and again. 'Velā' is that which obtains destruction, with the elision of a letter. 'Diṭṭha' and 'aneha' are also names for time.

Khaṇādayo pana tabbisesā tassa kālassa visesā bhedā. Ke te, kittakappamāṇā cetyāha “khaṇo”iccādi. Dasahi accharāhi aṅguliphoṭanehi lakkhito kālo khaṇo nāma, khaṇu hiṃsāyaṃ, khaṇotīti khaṇo, a. Dasa khaṇā layo nāma bhave bhavanti, etena vā vacanena vikabhisaṅkhyāpekkhinopi vācakā santīti gamyate. Layati gacchati, sattānaṃ jīvitaṃ lunanto vā ayati gacchatīti layo. Dasa layā khaṇalayo nāma, khaṇalayānaṃ samūhabhāvato. Te dasa khaṇalayā muhutto nāma siyā siyuṃ vā, ayamanitthī. Huccha koṭilye[M 0.0059], kuṭilayati rattidivase subhāsubhadassanatoti muhutto, to, dhātuyādimhi mukārāgamo, cchalopo ca. Te dasa muhuttā khaṇamuhutto nāma.

Moments and so forth, however, are its particulars, the specific divisions of that time. What are they, and what are their measures? It is said: 'A moment (khaṇa)' and so on. A moment (khaṇa) is the time marked by ten finger-snaps. The root 'khaṇ' is in the sense of harming; it harms, therefore it is a moment (khaṇa). Ten moments become a laya. Or, by this statement, it is understood that there are also terms that depend on conventional counting. A laya is so called because it passes (layati), or because it cuts off (lunanto) the life of beings as it goes (ayati). Ten layas constitute a khaṇalaya, because it is a collection of khaṇalayas. Those ten khaṇalayas are a muhutta. This word is not feminine. The root 'hucch' is in the sense of crookedness; it makes the day and night crooked by showing the auspicious and inauspicious, therefore it is a muhutta. The initial 'mu' is an augment to the root, and the 'ccha' is elided. Ten muhuttas make up a khaṇamuhutta.

Tikaṃ dine. Dibbanti kīḷantyasmiṃ divaso, so. Na jahāti paccāgamanaṃ ahaṃ. Ādadāti nibyāpāranti dinaṃ, ino, ālopo ca, dibbati vā etthāti dinaṃ, vassa no. Ghasaro ghasati andhakāraṃ ro (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), vāsarotipi dinassa nāmāni.

Three [terms] for day. They shine and play in this, therefore it is 'divasa.' It does not abandon returning—thus 'ahaṃ.' It takes away inactivity—thus 'dinaṃ,' with the suffix 'ina' and elision of 'ā'; or, one shines in this, therefore 'dinaṃ,' with the 'v' becoming 'n'.

68. Kallantaṃ paccūse. Pabhātyasmiṃ lokoti pabhātaṃ. Tathā vibhātaṃ. Usa rujāyaṃ, paccūsati vināseti timiranti paccūso. Kalyante saṅkhyāyante anena saṅkhyādayoti kallaṃ. Ahomukhaṃ, ūsotipi paccūsassa nāmāni.

68. Kalla and so forth are [terms] for dawn. The world shines forth in this, so it is 'pabhāta.' Similarly, 'vibhāta.' The root 'us' is in the sense of 'ruj' (to destroy); it destroys darkness, therefore 'paccūsa.' That by which numbers and so forth are reckoned or counted is 'kalla.' 'Ahomukha' and 'ūso' are also names for 'paccūsa' (dawn).

Dvayaṃ padose. Dosāya rattiyā ārambho abhidoso. Dosāya rattiyā pārambho padoso. Abhidhānato pāsaddassa pubbanipāto, appadhānarasso ca, atha vā abhidussanti padussanti ca yattha sabbakammāni abhidoso padoso ca.

Two [terms] for evening. The beginning of the night is abhidosa. The beginning of the night is padosa. In terms of expression, the prefix 'pa' is placed first, and the short vowel is not prominent; or alternatively, it is where all actions are corrupted, hence abhidosa and padosa.

Tikaṃ sāyanhe. Sāyati dinaṃ avasāyatīti sāyo, sāyanto vā dinantaṃ karonto ayatīti sāyo, punnapuṃsake. Sammājhāyanti taṃ sañjhā, (“brahmuno tanu pitā lokassa janettī”ti hi āgamo nikāyantarikānaṃ.) [M 0.0060] ( ) etthantare pāṭho adhiko viya dissati Dinānaṃ accayo atikkamo, avasānaṃ vā dinaccayo. Dinantotipi tasseva nāmaṃ.

Three [terms] for evening. The day ends, it comes to a close, thus it is 'sāya'; or, coming, it brings the day to an end, thus 'sāya.' It is in the masculine and neuter genders. That which is properly meditated upon is 'sañjhā.' (For, among other schools, there is the scripture: "Brahmā's son is the father, the world's progenitor.") The passing of the day, that is, its lapse or end, is 'dinaccayo.' 'Dinanta' is also a name for that.

Pubbaṇhāparaṇhamajjhanhavasena tividhā sañjhā amara 4.3. Pubbañca taṃ ahañcāti pubbaṇhaṃ. Aparañca taṃ majjhañca taṃ ahañceti aparaṇhaṃ majjhanhaṃ. Sabbatrāvayave samudāyopacārato ahassekadese ahasaddoti kammadhārayo, tāsaṃ tissannaṃ sañjhānaṃ samāhāroti sañjhamityuccate. Samāharaṇaṃ samāhāro, ekībhāvo, so ca bhinnakālānaṃ na bhavatīti buddhiyā samakālaggahaṇato ekakālattā tasmiṃ abhidheyye digusamāso, tathā hi samāhāro samūho taṃsambandhe chaṭṭhiyāyeva bhavitabbanti cintento ācariyo na aññapadatthasamāso ayanti ākārassāppadhāne rassattanti sañjhaṃ. Samāhāro bhāvo tassekattā ekavacanaṃ, kammavacane tu samāhāre tisso sañjhā samāhaṭāti paṭhamantānaṃ samāse sapadatthapādhānyā bahuvacanaṃ, rassābhāvo ca.

Twilight is threefold: morning, afternoon, and midday. 'That which is the first part of the day' is 'pubbaṇha.' 'That which is the latter part of the day' and 'that which is the middle part of the day' are 'aparaṇha' and 'majjhanha.' In all cases, by metaphorical application of the whole to a part, the word 'aha' (day) is used for a single part of the day; thus, these are kammadhāraya compounds. The aggregation of these three twilights is called 'sañjhaṃ.' Aggregation is 'samāhāra,' a state of unity; and since that does not occur for different times, due to the conceptual apprehension of them as simultaneous, it is a digu compound referring to a single time. Thus, indeed, the teacher, thinking that 'samāhāra' is a group and should be in the genitive case in relation to it, says this is not a compound with another meaning, and because of the shortening of the 'ā' vowel in a non-primary position, it is 'sañjhaṃ.' Since 'samāhāra' denotes a state, which is single, it is in the singular. However, in the passive voice, when the three twilights are aggregated, the plural form is used ('tisso sañjhā samāhaṭā'), with the first term in the nominative case, because in the compound, the meaning of each component remains prominent, hence the plural and the absence of shortening.

69. Pañcakaṃ rattiyaṃ. Nisati tanuṃ karoti sabbabyāpāraṃ nisā. Rajjanti rāgino atra rajanī, yu, ī. Rāti gaṇhāti abyāpāranti ratti,ti, rajjanti vā ettha ratti. Paṭhamamajjhimapacchimayāmavasena tayo yāmā pahārā yassā tiyāmā. Saṃvuṇoti dinaṃ saṃvarī. Nisīthinī, khaṇadā, khapā, vibhāvarī, tamassinī, yāminī, tamīiccādīnipi rattiyā nāmāni.

69. Five [terms] for night. It settles down, it makes all activity slight—thus 'nisā.' The passionate delight in it—thus 'rajanī,' with suffixes 'yu' and 'ī.' It takes away activity—thus 'ratti,' with suffix 'ti'; or, they delight in it—thus 'ratti.' That which has three watches (yāma) or beats (pahāra), by way of the first, middle, and last watches, is 'tiyāmā.' It covers the day—thus 'saṃvarī.' Nisīthinī, khaṇadā, khapā, vibhāvarī, tamassinī, yāminī, and tamī are also names for night.

Candikāyuttā [M 0.0061] candappabhāya yuttā ratti juṇhā nāma, juṇhāyogato juṇhā. Tamo ussanno yassaṃ sā tamussannā ratti timisikā nāma, timisaṃ ussannaṃ etthāti timisikā, upadhāya ittañca.

A night endowed with moonlight, endowed with the moon's radiance, is called 'juṇhā'; because of its connection with moonlight, it is 'juṇhā.' That night in which darkness is abundant is 'tamussannā'; it is called 'timisikā' because darkness is abundant in it, with 'i' for the penultimate vowel.

70. Tikaṃ aḍḍharattiyaṃ. Majjhimāratti kammabhūtā “nisītho, aḍḍharatto, mahānisā”ti ca vuccati. Nissate sayate asmiṃ nisītho. Aḍḍhañca taṃ ratti cāti aḍḍharatto, rattekadese rattisaddo, rattiyā aḍḍhanti vā aḍḍharatto. Mahatī ca sā nisā cāti mahānisā.

70. Three [terms] for midnight. The middle of the night is referred to as 'nisītha,' 'aḍḍharatta,' and 'mahānisā.' One sits down, one lies down at this time—thus 'nisītha.' It is half the night—thus 'aḍḍharatta'; the word 'ratti' is used for a part of the night, or it is half of the night—thus 'aḍḍharatta.' It is a great night—thus 'mahānisā.'

Catukkaṃ andhakāre. Andhaṃ hataṃ diṭṭhasattikaṃ lokaṃ karotīti andhakāro. Tamatīti tamo, atha vā tamanti ākaṅkhanti ratiṃ lokā ettha tamo, tamu ākaṅkhāyaṃ, tamasaddo anitthī, taṃsahacaraṇato andhakāropi. Timisaṃ iso, atha vā timu temane, timanti ettha rāgenāti timisaṃ. Timiraṃ, pubbeva irapaccayo.

Four [terms] for darkness. It makes the world blind, whose power of sight is destroyed—thus 'andhakāra.' It darkens—thus 'tamo'; or alternatively, beings desire delight in it—thus 'tamo,' from the root 'tamu' in the sense of 'desire.' The word 'tamas' is not feminine, and by association with it, neither is 'andhakāra.' 'Timisa' is 'isa' (lord); or alternatively, it is from 'timu' meaning 'to be wet,' as 'they are wetted here by passion'—thus, 'timisa.' For 'timira,' the suffix 'ira' is as before.

71. Catuddasannaṃ rattīnaṃ pūraṇī catuddasīsaṅkhāto kāḷapakkho ca ekagghano vanasaṇḍo ca meghapaṭalañca aḍḍharatti ca etehi catūhi samannāgato tamo caturaṅgatamaṃ nāma.

71. The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, a dense forest grove, a thick covering of clouds, and midnight—the darkness endowed with these four is called 'caturaṅgatama.'

72. Andhañca taṃ tamañcāti andhatamaṃ, yaṃ lokaṃ andhakāraṃ karoti. Ayaṃ andhatamasaddo ghanatame bāḷhatame vattati.

72. 'That which is blind darkness' is 'andhatamaṃ,' which makes the world dark. This term 'andhatama' is used for the densest, the most intense darkness.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0062] pahāre. Paharīyate bheriyādi atrāti pahāro, pume saññāyaṃ apaccayo. Yā pāpuṇe mo, upayameti vā aho ratti cānena yāmo, yamito ṇo. Pahāro eva yāmo iti saññito yāmasaññito.

Two [terms] for a watch. A drum and so forth is struck at this time—thus 'pahāro'; it is a masculine noun with the suffix 'a.' That which reaches, with the suffix 'mo' from the root 'yā' in the sense of 'pāpuṇe'; or, day and night are controlled by it—thus 'yāmo,' from the root 'yam' with the suffix 'ṇo.' A 'pahāra' is a 'yāma'; thus it is designated 'yāmasaññita.'

Dutiyā tithi pāṭipado nāma. Paṭipajjate cando khayaṃ, udayaṃ vā yassaṃ pāṭipado. Tatiyādī tithiyeva, na pāṭipado. Tanotīti tithi, atha vā tā pālane ithi. Tithisaddo dvīsu.

The first lunar day is called pāṭipada. The moon enters into its waning or waxing phase on that day, which is why it is called pāṭipada. The third and subsequent lunar days are simply tithi, not pāṭipada. It extends—thus 'tithi'; or from the root 'tā' in the sense of protection, with the suffix 'ithi.' The word tithi is [used] in two genders.

73. Dvayaṃ pannarasiyaṃ, pannarasannaṃ tithīnaṃ pūraṇī pannarasī, paṇṇarasītipi pāṭho atthi. Dvayaṃ puṇṇamāyaṃ tithiyaṃ. Miyyate tithīnaṃ khayo vuḍḍhi cānena māso, cando, puṇṇo ca so māso cāti puṇṇamāso, tassāyaṃ tithi, puṇṇamāso yassamatthīti vā puṇṇamāsī. Puṇṇo mā cando yattha, puṇṇamassāyaṃ vā tithi puṇṇamā, “puṇṇimā”ti pāṭhe pana sati candassa puṇṇabhāvo puṇṇo, tena nibbattā bhāvapaccayantā tena nibbatte imo dissati, lokāsayattā liṅgassa itthiliṅgattaṃ, sā puṇṇamā ekakalāhīne cande sati anumati nāma, anumaññante anugacchante devatāpitūhi saha yassaṃ sā anumati. Puṇṇe pana cande sā puṇṇamā rākā nāma, rāti dassanāvakāsaṃ rākā, ko kalāhīne sā’numati puṇṇe rākā nisākare (amara 4.8).

73. These two refer to the fifteenth day. 'Pannarasī' is the completion of the fifteen lunar days; there is also the reading 'paṇṇarasī'. These two refer to the full moon day. The month and the moon are measured by the decrease and increase of the lunar days. It is a full month, hence 'puṇṇamāso'. The lunar day belonging to that is 'puṇṇamāsī', or it is 'puṇṇamāsī' because it possesses the full moon. Where the moon (mā, cando) is full, that lunar day is 'puṇṇamā'. However, if there is the reading 'puṇṇimā', the state of fullness of the moon is 'puṇṇa'; produced from that, ending in a 'bhāva' suffix, 'ima' is seen. Due to worldly convention, the gender is feminine. That full moon is called 'Anumati' when the moon is deficient by one digit; Anumati is so called because on that day, one is approved of and followed by the deities and ancestors. But when the moon is full, that full moon is called 'Rākā'. Rākā is so called because it gives (rāti) an opportunity for seeing; the suffix is 'ka'.

Aparā kāḷapakkhasambhūtāpannarasī pana amāvasī, amāvāsītipi uccate. Amā saha vasanti ravicandā yassaṃ amāvasī, amāvāsī ca dīghaṃ katvā, amāsaddo sahattho abyayaṃ. Dasso dassalā (ka.), dissante ravicandā atra, “gaṇakehī”ti gha (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), sūriyindusaṅgamoti tassāyeva nāmāni.

However, the other fifteenth day, born from the dark fortnight, is called 'Amāvasī', or 'Amāvāsī'. It is called 'Amāvasī' because the sun and moon dwell together (amā saha vasanti) on this day; 'Amāvāsī' is formed by lengthening the 'ā'. The word 'amā' is an indeclinable meaning 'together'. 'Dasso' and 'Sūriyindusaṅgamo' (the meeting of the sun and moon) are other names for it.

74. Saṭṭhighaṭikāhi [M 0.0063] lakkhito kālo ahoratto nāma. Ghaṭenti ahorattiyoti ghaṭikā. Aho ca ratti ca ahoratto, pume. Adiguttepi ahorattanti napuṃsakepi. Te pañcadasa ahorattā pakkho nāma. Pacanti pariṇamanti bhūtānyaneneti pakkho. Pubbāparabhūtā te ca pakkhā yathākkamaṃ sukkakāḷā sukkapakkhakāḷapakkhā nāma. Jotisatthakkamena sukkapakkho pubbasaññito, kaṇhapakkho aparasaññito. Tato eva māsavisese loke sakaparapakkhoti lokepyaparapakkhoti (ka.) rūḷhī. Suca soke, sukko, socanti ettha andhakārābhilāsinoti katvā, sūceti pakāsetīti vā sukko. Kirati sukkanti kāro, ṇo, sova kāḷo, kena vā jotinā arati ettha kāro, sova kāḷo. Te duve sukkakāḷapakkhā samuditā māso nāma. Masi parimāṇe, kammaniṇo.

74. A period of time marked by sixty ghaṭikās is called a day and night (ahoratta). They are called ghaṭikās because they measure (ghaṭenti) a day and night. 'Aho' (day) and 'ratti' (night) together make 'ahoratta,' in the masculine gender. It is also 'ahoratta' in the neuter gender, according to Adigutta. Fifteen such days and nights make a fortnight (pakkha). It is called pakkha because beings (bhūtāni) ripen (pacanti) and transform (pariṇamanti) by it. These fortnights, being earlier and later, are respectively called the bright and dark fortnights (sukkakāḷā), or the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight (sukkapakkhakāḷapakkhā). According to the science of astronomy, the bright fortnight (sukkapakkha) is known as the earlier, and the dark fortnight (kaṇhapakkha) as the later. Thus, in the world, in specific months, it is conventionally known as 'one's own fortnight' (sakapakkha) and 'another's fortnight' (parapakkha). Sukka (bright) is from the root 'suc' (to grieve), because those who desire darkness grieve in it; alternatively, sukka is so called because it illuminates (sūceti, pakāseti). Kāḷo (dark) is from 'kāra', derived from 'kirati' (to scatter) brightness, with the suffix 'ṇa'; thus it is kāḷo. Or, it is kāḷo because light (jotinā) is absent (arati) from it, hence 'kāra'. These two fortnights, the bright and the dark, together make a month (māsa). Māsa is derived from 'masi' (to measure), with the passive suffix 'ṇa'.

75-76. Sāddhapajjena dvādasamāsānaṃ nāmāni. Cittāya paripuṇṇenduyuttāya yutto, upalakkhito vā māso citto[M 0.0064], saṃyogantattā na vuddhi, evaṃ sabbatra. Paripuṇṇenduyuttataṃtaṃnakkhattanāmavasena dvādasannaṃ māsānaṃ nāmāni veditabbāni. Cittamāsādayo phaggunamāsapariyantā dvādasa koṭṭhāsā kamena māsāti ñeyyā. Pasatthatamattā jeṭṭhā, taṃyogā jeṭṭho. Asayho ravi atreti āsāḷho. Yassa ḷo, savantyasmiṃ sāvaṇo, yu. Phalantyatra phagguno, yu, lassa go, assa u. Kattikamāso pacchimakattiko nāma. Assayujamāso pubbakattiko nāma.

75-76. The names of the twelve months are given by a half-verse. The month associated with the Citta constellation, conjoined with or marked by the full moon, is Citta. Due to the ending in a conjunct consonant, there is no vowel lengthening; this applies everywhere. The names of the twelve months should be understood according to the names of the respective constellations conjoined with the full moon. The twelve divisions, beginning with the month of Citta and ending with the month of Phagguna, should be known as months in order. Jeṭṭhā means most excellent; from its connection with that, the month is Jeṭṭho. Āsāḷho is so called because the unbearable (asayho) sun is here (atra). Sāvaṇo is so called because waters flow (savanti) in it, with the suffix 'yu'. Phagguno is so called because fruits ripen (phalanti) there, with the suffix 'yu', 'l' becoming 'g', and 'a' becoming 'u'. The month of Kattika is called Pacchimakattika. The month of Assayuja is called Pubbakattika.

77. Dvayaṃ sāvaṇamāse. Antovīthito bahi nikkhamati sūriyo ettha, adhikaraṇe anīyo. Dvayaṃ cittamāse. Nānāpupphaphalavicittatāya lokānaṃ rammaṃ karoti, ramanti vā etthāti rammako.

77. There are two terms for the month of Sāvaṇa. In this month, the sun moves out from its inner orbit; the suffix 'anīya' is used in the locative sense. There are two terms for the month of Citta. Due to the diversity of flowers and fruits, it makes the world delightful, or people rejoice here, therefore it is called Rammaka.

78. Kattikakāḷapakkhato pacchimakattikato paṭṭhāya caturo caturo māsā kamā kamato hemantagimhānavassānasaññitā utuyo nāma honti. Himāni ettha santi hemo, so eva hemanto, “suttanto vananto”ti yathā, hinoti vā hāniṃ gacchati sabbametthāti hemanto, antapaccayo, māgamo ca. Girati pīḷayatīti gimhāno, māno, rassa ho, vaṇṇavipariyayo ca. Vassati ettha vassānoyu. Utuyo dvīsūti paccāsatyā utusaddo eva dvīsu, na hemantādayo, amarakose pana utusaddo pume vutto amara 4.20.

78. Starting from the dark fortnight of Kattika, that is, from Pacchimakattika, four months each, in order, are the seasons named Hemanta (winter), Gimhāna (summer), and Vassāna (rainy season). Hema is so called because cold (himāni) exists here; that itself is Hemanta, just as in 'suttanto' and 'vananto'. Or, it is Hemanta because everything here declines (hinoti vā hāniṃ gacchati), with the suffix 'anta' and the augment 'ma'. Gimhāna is so called because it oppresses (girati, pīḷayati), with the suffix 'māna', 'r' becoming 'h', and a transposition of letters. Vassāna is so called because it rains (vassati) here, with the suffix 'yu'. Regarding 'Utuyo dvīsu' (seasons in two genders), by proximity, the word 'utu' itself is in two genders, not Hemanta and the others. However, in the Amarakośa, the word 'utu' is stated to be in the masculine gender.

79. Aññathāpi [M 0.0065] utubhedaṃ dassetuṃ ariyasāmaññamāha “hemanto”iccādi. Vā atha vā vuttānusārena ututtayapabhede vuttavacanassānusārena. Idaṃ pana “kattikakāḷapakkhato”ti vacanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, tasmā kattikakāḷapakkhato pabhuti dve dve māsā kamā kamato hemanto, sisiro, vasanto, gimho, vassāno, sarado utūti cha utū bhavanti, punappunaṃ etīti katvā, tu, issa u. Sisiraṃ sītalaṃ, taṃyogā sisiraṃ, vāvidhānato na vuddhi, makāro padasandhikaro. Vasa kantiyaṃ. Vasīyateti vasanto. Pupphadhanuttā pupphavantattā (ka.) vā vasati kāmo ettha vasanto. Sarati pīḷayati asminti sarado, tassa do. Sā sunakhā ramanti etthāti vā sarado, massa do.

79. Alternatively, to show another division of seasons, it states the noble convention, 'Hemanta,' etc. Or else, it is according to the statement made regarding the division into three seasons. This, however, is said with reference to the phrase 'from the dark fortnight of Kattika.' Therefore, starting from the dark fortnight of Kattika, two months each, in order, are Hemanta, Sisira, Vasanta, Gimha, Vassāna, and Sarada—thus there are six seasons. Utu is so called because it comes again and again (punappunaṃ eti), with the suffix 'tu', and 'i' becoming 'u'. Sisira means cold; from its connection with that, it is Sisira. Due to the optional rule, there is no vowel lengthening; the 'm' is for euphonic conjunction. The root 'vasa' is in the sense of 'to shine'. It is 'Vasanta' because it is dwelt in (vasīyati). Or, it is 'Vasanta' because Kāma, he who has a bow of flowers, dwells (vasati) here. Sarada is so called because it oppresses (sarati, pīḷayati) in this season, with 't' becoming 'd'. Or, it is Sarada because dogs (sā, sunakhā) rejoice (ramanti) here, with 'm' becoming 'd'.

80-81. Tikaṃ gimhe. Usati dahatīti uṇho, ṇho, salopo ca. Nidahante yasminti nidāgho, hassa gho. Girati [M 0.0066] pīḷayatīti gimho, mo, rassa ho, vaṇṇavipariyayo ca. Tikaṃ vassānotumhi. Vassati pavassati etthāti vasso, vassāno, pāvuso ca. Assa u, saṃyogalopo ca.

80-81. There are three terms for summer. Uṇho (hot) is so called because it burns (usati, dahati), with the suffix 'ṇha', and elision of 's'. Nidāgho (scorching heat) is so called because it burns down (nidahante) in this season, with 'h' becoming 'gh'. Gimho (summer) is so called because it oppresses (girati, pīḷayati), with the suffix 'ma', 'r' becoming 'h', and a transposition of letters. There are three terms for the rainy season. Vasso, Vassāno, and Pāvuso are so called because it rains (vassati, pavassati) here. For Pāvuso, 'a' becomes 'u', and there is elision of the conjunct consonant.

Vassānādikehi tīhi utūhi dakkhiṇāyanaṃ sūriyassa dakkhiṇadisāgamanaṃ bhavati, aññehi tīhi sisiravasantagimhehi uttarāyanaṃ uttaradisāgamanaṃ bhavati. I gatiyaṃ, bhāve yu, ayanaṃ. Pussasaṅkantimārabbha āsāḷhaṃ yāva ādiccassa uttarā gati uttarāyanaṃ. Āsāḷhasaṅkantimārabbha pussaṃ yāva dakkhiṇā gati dakkhiṇāyanaṃ. Vassoyanadvayanti idaṃ ayanadvayaṃ sampiṇḍitaṃ vasso nāma. Vassanti etthāti vasso, vassakālena vā upalakkhito vasso, “citto, cakkhudasaka”nti yathā.

During the three seasons beginning with the rainy season, the southern course of the sun (dakkhiṇāyana), its movement towards the southern direction, occurs. During the other three seasons—Sisira, Vasanta, and Gimha—the northern course (uttarāyana), its movement towards the northern direction, occurs. The root 'i' means 'to go'; with the suffix 'yu' in the sense of state, it becomes 'ayana'. From the sun's transition into the constellation of Pussa until Āsāḷha, the sun’s northern course is uttarāyana. From the sun's transition into Āsāḷha until Pussa, the southern course is dakkhiṇāyana. This pair of courses (ayanadvaya), when combined, is called 'vassa' (year). Vassa (year) is so called because beings dwell (vassanti) in it, or it is characterized by the rainy season (vassakālena), just as in 'Citto' and 'Cakkhudasaka'.

Pajjaddhaṃ vasse. Saṃvasati ettha saṃvaccharo, charo, sassa co, “vaccharo”tipi tasseva nāmaṃ. Natthi itthiliṅgattametesu anitthī. Paccāsatyā saradopi taṃpaccāsatyā hāyanopi. Saradakālena lakkhito sarado, yathā “sotadasakaṃ, vesākho”ti. Jahāti bhāveti hāyano, padatthe vā jahanto ayatīti hāyano. Samayati vikalayati bhāveti samā, sama vekalye. “Samā vasse thīliṅgo tu, samaṃ sabbasamānesū”ti ruddo.

A half-verse on the year. Saṃvaccharo (year) is so called because beings dwell (saṃvasati) here, with the suffix 'chara', and 's' becoming 'c'; 'Vaccharo' is also a name for the same. Among these terms, there is no feminine gender; they are non-feminine. By association, 'sarado' (autumn) also refers to the year, and by further association, 'hāyano' also. Sarado, as a year, is characterized by the autumn season, just as in 'sotadasakaṃ' and 'vesākho'. Hāyano is so called because it abandons (jahāti) or produces (bhāveti); or, in terms of its components, it is Hāyano because abandoning (jahanto), it goes (ayati). Samā is so called because it disjoins (samayati, vikalayati) or produces (bhāveti); the root 'sama' is in the sense of 'disjunction'. Rudda says: "'Samā' is feminine for 'year', but 'samaṃ' is for all things equal."

Sabbasattānaṃ sabbapārisadattā sabbapaṭipadattā (ka.) sabbavohārakusalatthaṃ kālādhikārattā parasamaye kathitaṃ devānaṃ vassappamāṇampi idhāharitvā dīpetabbaṃ. Tathā hi manussānaṃ māsena pitūnaṃ ahoratto, evaṃ manussānaṃ vassena devānaṃ ahoratto, tatrottarāyanaṃ devānaṃ dinaṃ, ratti pana dakkhiṇāyanaṃ, devatānaṃ saṭṭhyādhikāhorattisatattayena vassena dvādasavassasahassāni devānaṃ yugaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ –

For the benefit of all beings, for the sake of skill in all communication in all assemblies, and because time is the main subject, even the measure of the gods' year, spoken of in other traditions, should be brought here and explained. For indeed, a month of humans is a day and night for the ancestors. Likewise, a year of humans is a day and night for the gods. Therein, the northern course of the sun is the day for the gods, and the southern course is their night. By a year of the deities, consisting of three hundred and sixty days and nights, twelve thousand such years make a yuga of the gods. Therefore, it is said:

“Esā [M 0.0067] dvādasasahassī, yugākhyā parikittitā;

Etaṃ sahassaguṇitaṃ, aho brahmamudāhaṭa”nti “vedadīpakaganthe”ti nissaye.

"This twelve-thousandfold period is proclaimed as a yuga; this, multiplied by a thousand, is said to be a day of Brahma."

Tañca narānaṃ catuyugaṃ dibbasahassadvayena brahmuno dve diveti. Kata, tetā, dvāpara, kalivasena catuyugaṃ. Tatra katayugassa manussasaṅkhyāya pamāṇaṃ aṭṭhavīsatisahassādhikāni sattarasavassalakkhāni, tetāya channavutisahassādhikāni dvādasavassalakkhāni, dvāparassa catusaṭṭhisahassādhikāni aṭṭhavassalakkhāni, kalissa bāttiṃsasahassādhikāni cattāri vassalakkhāni. Vuttañca –

And that four-yuga period of humans is two thousand divine years, which is two days for Brahmā. The four yugas are Krita, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali. Therein, the measure of the Krita Yuga in human years is 1,728,000 years. For Tretā, it is 1,296,000 years. For Dvāpara, it is 864,000 years. For Kali, it is 432,000 years. And it is said:

“Suññaṃ suññaṃ khaṃ nāgā, karamunisasino;

Māna’mādo yugassa, tetāya khaṃkhaṃsuññaṃ.

"(The years for Krita Yuga are encoded as) Empty (0), empty (0), void (0), Nāgas (8), hands (2), sages (7), moon (1) [i.e., 1,728,000]. Pride and intoxication of the age. For Tretā, void (0), void (0), empty (0)."

Rasanavasūriyā, vassasaṅkhyā pasiddhā;

Suññaṃ suññaṃ khaṃ vedā, rasabhujagamiti.

"Flavors (6), nine (9), suns (12)—(thus 1,296,000) is the well-known number of years (for Tretā). Empty (0), empty (0), void (0), Vedas (4), flavors (6), serpents (8)—(thus 864,000 for Dvāpara)."

Dvāpare vassasaṅkhyā, suññākāsaṃkhaṃnetta-;

Guṇajalanidhayo, vassasaṅkhyā kalisse”ti.

"After the number of years in Dvāpara, (the number for Kali is encoded as) empty (0), sky (0), void (0), eyes (2); qualities (3), oceans (4)—(thus 432,000) is the number of years for Kali."

Piṇḍo cesa vīsativassasahassādhikāni tecattālīsavassalakkhāni. Vuttañca “khākāsasuññambaradantasāgarā catuyugānaṃ parimāṇasaṅgaho”ti. Brahmuno ahorattena narānaṃ dve kappā.

The total is 4,320,000 years. And it is said: "Void (0), sky (0), empty (0), atmosphere (0), teeth (32), oceans (4)—(thus 4,320,000) is the collection of the measures of the four yugas." A day and night of Brahmā is two aeons for humans.

Tatra aṭṭha nāgā, dve karā, satta munayo, eko sasī, cha rasā, dvādasa sūriyā, cattāro vedā jalanidhayo ca. Dve nettāni, tayo guṇā, bāttiṃsa dantā, saṅkhyāya pasiddhehetehi saṅkhyā gahetabbā. Khākāsambarasaddā suññapariyāyā. Suññañca gaṇite bindunā saṅgahitaṃ. Sabbañcetaṃ paṭiyugaṃ paṭilomena patthāraye. Tatra katayugassa patthāro yathā – 1728000. Tetāya yathā – 1296000[M 0.0068]. Dvāparassa yathā – 864000. Kalissa yathā – 432000. Catuyugapiṇḍassa ca yathā – 4320000. Yugānaṃ paṭipatthārañca piṇḍassa ca yathākkamaṃ antimaṃ bindumādāya paṭilomena gaṇaye. Taṃ yathā –

Therein are eight nāgas, two hands, seven sages, one moon, six tastes, twelve suns, four Vedas, and oceans. Two eyes, three qualities, thirty-two teeth—from these well-known numbers, the calculation is to be taken. The terms 'kha,' 'ākāsa,' and 'ambara' are synonyms for emptiness. And emptiness in calculation is represented by a dot. All this should be expanded in reverse for each age. Therein, the expansion of the Krita age is as follows: 1,728,000. For the Tretā age it is: 1,296,000. For the Dvāpara age it is: 864,000. For the Kali age it is: 432,000. And the total of the four ages is: 4,320,000. The reverse expansion of the ages and their total should be calculated sequentially, taking the last zero and proceeding in reverse. That is as follows—

“Ekaṃ dasa satañceva, sahassa’mayutaṃ tathā;

Lakkhañca niyutañceva, kamā dasaguṇottara”nti.

"One, ten, a hundred, and a thousand, and also ten thousand; a hundred thousand and a million, in sequence, each ten times the previous."

Tatra dasasahassāni ayutaṃ. Dasalakkhāni niyutaṃ. Tañca kalidvāparesu natthīti lakkhapariyantameva tatra gaṇaye, tadevaṃ yugānaṃ, taṃpiṇḍassa ca aṅkato pubbavuttā vassasaṅkhyā saññātā bhavatīti.

Therein, ten thousand is an ayuta. Ten hundred thousands are a niyuta. And since this does not exist in the Kali and Dvāpara ages, one should count only up to a hundred thousand there. Thus, the previously stated number of years for the ages and their total becomes known numerically.

Tatra brahmuno dinaṃ narānaṃ udayakappo, ratti pana khayakappo. Ekasmiñca brahmadine manusaññitā catuddasa brahmasutā bhavanti. Tatrekassa manvantarassa ekasattatidibbayugāni pamāṇaṃ, tañca mānusaṃ catuddasabhi uttaraṃ caturāsītiuttaraṃ (?) yugasatadvayaṃ. Tadevaṃ catuddasabhi manvantarehi catunavutyuttarāni navadibbayugasatāni bhavanti. Mānusaṃ tu catuvīsatiyugasahassacatukkaṃ. Esañca chasattatyādhikanavatiṃsayugasataṃ (?) manvantarānaṃ aṭṭhavīsasahassādhikasattarasamānusavassalakkhasaṅkhyā vā katayugappamāṇakā pañca sandhayo bhavanti. Tena vuttaṃ sūriyasiddhante 1.18-19 –

Therein, a day of Brahmā is an aeon of arising for humans, and the night is an aeon of dissolution. In one day of Brahmā, fourteen sons of Brahmā known as Manus arise. Therein, one Manvantara is the measure of seventy-one divine ages, and in human terms, it is two hundred and fourteen ages. Thus, with fourteen Manvantaras, there are nine hundred and ninety-four divine ages. In human terms, it is ninety-six thousand ages. And for these Manvantaras, there are five junctures, which are of the measure of a Krita age, or of the number of one million seven hundred and twenty-eight thousand human years. Thus, it is said in the Sūryasiddhānta—

“Yugānaṃ sattati sekā, manvantara’miho’ccate;

Katassa saṅkhyā tassante, sandhi vutto jalaplavo.

"Seventy-one ages are said to be one Manvantara here; at its end, a juncture, called a flood, is stated, having the duration of a Krita yuga."

Sasandhayo te manavo, kappe ñeyyā catuddasa;

Katappamāṇā kappādo, sandhī pañcadasaṭṭhitā”ti.

Those Manus, together with their junctures, are to be known as fourteen in an aeon; at the beginning of the aeon, fifteen junctures, of the measure of a Krita age, are established."

Katayugassa ca pādena kalino pamāṇaṃ, pādadvayena dvāparassa, pādattayena tetāya. Catuyugañcetaṃ cakkamiva bhamatīti pañcadasahi sandhīhi narānaṃ yugāni catuvīsati bhavanti. Devānaṃ [M 0.0069] tu yugacakkaṃ. Etāni ca sasandhicatuddasamanvantarānyekatopi piṇḍitāni devānaṃ yugasahassaṃ bhavati, narānaṃ catuyugasahassaṃ, tañca brahmuno dinamekaṃ. Añño manu asmiṃ manvantaraṃ, brahmasutā eva manavo.

The measure of the Kali Yuga is by one quarter of the Krita Yuga, by two quarters for the Dvāpara Yuga, and by three quarters for the Tretā Yuga. And this cycle of four ages revolves like a wheel. Thus, with fifteen junctures, the ages of humans become twenty-four. For the gods, it is a cycle of ages. And these fourteen Manvantaras together with their junctures, when combined, become a thousand ages of the gods, or four thousand ages of men; and that is one day of Brahmā. In this Manvantara there is another Manu; the Manus are indeed the sons of Brahmā.

82. Pañcakaṃ khayakappe. Kappate jagatī vinassateti kappo. Khayanti ettha khayo. Kappo ca khayo cāti kappakkhayā. Saṃvattate uparamate, vinassate vā jagatī asminti saṃvaṭṭo. Catuyugānamante jāto yuganto. Palīyate khīyate yattha lokoti palayo, pume, saññāyaṃ ṇo. Keci panettha “kappakkhayo tū”ti pāṭhaṃ vatvā dvinnamekābhidhānattaṃ kappenti, taṃ amarakosena ca taṭṭīkāya ca na sameti. Vuttañhi tattha “saṃvaṭṭo, palayo, kappo, khayo, kappantamiccapī”ti amara 4.22 ca “pañcakaṃ khayakappe”ti ca.

82. The five terms for the aeon of destruction. The world is destroyed, thus it is 'kappa'. Herein, things are destroyed, thus 'khaya'. And 'kappa' and 'khaya' together are 'kappakkhaya'. The world evolves, ceases, or is destroyed in this, thus 'saṃvaṭṭa'. That which arises at the end of the four ages is 'yuganta'. Where the world decays and wastes away, thus 'palayo'; it is masculine, with 'ṇo' as a designation. Some, however, saying the reading here is 'kappakkhayo tu', make the two terms synonymous, but this does not agree with the Amarakośa or its commentary. For it is stated there: 'saṃvaṭṭa, palaya, kappa, khaya, kappanta'—these too, and 'the group of five in the aeon of destruction'.

Dvayaṃ kāḷakaṇṇiyaṃ. Ninditabbattā na lakkhīyateti alakkhī. Attano nissayaṃ kāḷavaṇṇasadisaṃ karoti appakāsakattāti kāḷakaṇṇī, karato ṇo, rassa ṇo, ī ca. Dvayaṃ siriyaṃ. Pasaṃsitabbattā lakkhīyateti lakkhī. Katapuññehi sevīyate, te vā sevatīti sirī, ro, ī ca.

The two terms for inauspiciousness. Because it is blameworthy, it is not marked (by good fortune), thus 'alakkhī'. Because it makes its basis similar to a dark color, being unilluminating, it is called 'kāḷakaṇṇī'; from the root 'kar' with the agent suffix 'ṇa', and the feminine suffix 'ī'. The two terms for prosperity. Because it is praiseworthy, it is marked (by good fortune), thus 'lakkhī'. It is served by those who have done meritorious deeds, or it serves them—hence 'sirī', from the root 'si' with the suffix 'ri', and 'ī'.

83. Dvayaṃ dānavānaṃ mātari. Dā avakhaṇḍane, dāyatīti danu. Dvayaṃ devānaṃ mātari. Ditīti asurānameva vemātikā mātā, tassā paṭipakkhabhāvena aditi.

83. The two terms for the mother of the Dānavas. 'Dā' is in the sense of cutting; she cuts, thus 'Danu'. The two terms for the mother of the Devas. 'Diti' is indeed the stepmother of the Asuras; 'Aditi' is so called by virtue of being her opposite.

84. Āguntaṃ [M 0.0070] pāpe. Pānti rakkhanti attānamasmāti pāpaṃ, pakāravaṇṇāgamo, duggatiṃ pāpanato vā pāpaṃ. Kilyate sithilī kariyyate yeneti kibbisaṃ, lassa vo, iso ca, karoti aniṭṭhaphalanti vā kibbisaṃ, ibbiso. Virūpena gacchatīti veraṃ. Na hanti dhaññanti aghaṃ, hanassa gho, sādhūhi agantabbattā vā aghaṃ, hana gatiyaṃ. Kucchitaṃ caritaṃ duccaritaṃ. Du ninditaṃ karaṇamassa dukkaṭaṃ. Na punātīti apuññaṃ. Kusalānaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ akusalaṃ. Kaṃ sukhaṃ hanatīti kaṇhaṃ, vaṇṇavipariyayo. Kalyate anena kalusaṃ, uso, kaṃ vā sukhaṃ lunanto setīti kalusaṃ. Du ninditaṃ itaṃ gamanamassa duritaṃ. Agantabbaṃ gacchati etenāti āgu, ā pīḷayaṃ gacchatīti vā āgu, “ā tu kodhamudāṭṭīsū”ti hi ekakkharakose vuttaṃ.

84. The term 'āgu' is for evil. From this, they protect themselves, thus 'pāpa', with an augmentation of the syllable 'pa'. Or, it leads to a bad destination, thus 'pāpa'. That by which one is wearied and made slack, thus 'kibbisa', with 'la' becoming 'va', and the suffix 'isa'. Or, it produces undesirable results, thus 'kibbisa', or 'ibbisa'. It proceeds in an ugly manner, thus 'vera'. It does not strike grain, thus 'agha', with 'han' becoming 'gha'. Or, it is not to be gone to by the good, thus 'agha', from 'han' meaning 'to go'. Bad conduct is 'duccarita'. Its doing is blameworthy, thus 'dukkaṭa'. It does not purify, thus 'apuñña'. The opposite of the wholesome is 'akusala'. It destroys happiness, thus 'kaṇha', with a reversal of letters. One is stained by this, thus 'kalusa', with the suffix 'usa'. Or, cutting off happiness, it settles, thus 'kalusa'. Its movement is blameworthy, thus 'durita'. By this, one goes where one should not go, thus 'āgu'. Or, it goes oppressing, thus 'āgu'; for in the single-letter lexicon, it is said: 'ā' is for anger, joy, and pride.

85-86. Chakkaṃ dhamme. Kucchitenākārena santāne sentīti kusā, rāgādayo, te lunāti chindatīti kusalaṃ. Sukhaṃ karoti, sobhanaṃ vā karaṇamassa sukataṃ. Sukhaṃ karotīti sukkaṃ. Punātīti puññaṃ. Dharati sabbanti dhammaṃ. Apare panidaṃ “puññadhamma”mityekapadaṃ vadanti, taṃ amarakosena amara 4.24 virujjhanato na gahetabbaṃ. Sundaraṃ caraṇamassa sucaritaṃ.

85-86. The group of six terms for the wholesome. Because they lie in the continuum in a reprehensible manner, they are called 'kusā'—that is, the passions, etc. That which cuts off or severs them is 'kusalaṃ' (skillful). It makes happiness, or its making is beautiful, thus 'sukataṃ' (well-done). It makes happiness, thus 'sukkaṃ' (bright). It purifies, thus 'puññaṃ' (merit). It bears or supports all, thus 'dhammaṃ' (the Dhamma). But others say that 'puññadhamma' is one word; however, that should not be taken, since it is contrary to the Amarakośa. Its conduct is beautiful, thus 'sucaritaṃ' (good conduct).

Tikaṃ [M 0.0071] diṭṭhadhammike. Diṭṭhadhammo nāma paccakkho attabhāvo, tattha nibbattaṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ. Ihaloke jātaṃ ihalokikaṃ. Sandiṭṭhe paccakkhe attabhāve jātaṃ sandiṭṭhikaṃ. Dvayaṃ samparāyike. Taṃ vacanatthato suviññeyyaṃ.

The three terms for 'in this very life'. The 'diṭṭhadhamma' is the directly visible individual existence; what arises there is 'diṭṭhadhammikaṃ' (relating to this very life). What is born in this world is 'ihalokikaṃ' (relating to this world). What arises in the directly visible individual existence is 'sandiṭṭhikaṃ' (directly visible). The two terms for 'in the future life'. That is easily understood from the meaning of the words.

Dvayaṃ takkāle. Tasmiṃyeva kāle jātaṃ, nāsannakālādīsūti takkālaṃ. Tadā tasmiṃyeva kāle jātaṃ tadātvaṃ, tvaṃ, tadāttantipi pāṭho. Dvayaṃ āyatikāle. Uttarakālo pacchimo kālo. Āgamissatīti āyati, āpubbo i gatimhi. Ettha ca yaṃ imasmiṃ attabhāve dūramāsannaṃ vā, taṃ diṭṭhadhammikaṃ. Yaṃ pana imasmiṃ attabhāve vā samparāye vā dūrataraṃ, taṃ āyati.

Two terms for 'at that time'. That which arises at that very time, not in a near time and so forth, is 'takkālaṃ'. That which arises at that very time is 'tadātvaṃ'; 'tvaṃ' and 'tadāttanti' are also readings. Two terms for 'in the future'. The subsequent time, the later time. It will come, thus 'āyati', from the root 'i' meaning 'to go', with the prefix 'ā'. And here, whatever is distant or near in this present existence is 'diṭṭhadhammikaṃ'. But whatever is much further, either in this present existence or in a future existence, is 'āyati'.

87-88. Pamodantaṃ pāmojje. Hasati yenāti hāso. Attā mano yassa attamano. Duṭṭhassa hi mano attā nāma na hoti, tassa bhāvo attamanatā, pāmojjaṃ. Pīṇeti tappetīti pīti. Vindati sukhaṃ etāyāti vitti. Tussanti etāyāti tuṭṭhi, taṃsahacaraṇato vitti, taṃsahacaraṇato pīti ca nāriyaṃ, attamanatā pana niddesato rūpabhedo. Ā bhuso nandayatīti ānando. Muda hāse, pamudo, āmodopi. Santussanaṃ santoso[M 0.0072]. Nandanaṃ nandi. Sammado sammadāpi sammudo, sammadopi (?), ukārassa a. Pamoditassa puggalassa, cittassa vā bhāvo pāmojjaṃ.

87-88. The term 'pamodantaṃ' is used in the sense of 'pāmojja'. That by which one laughs is 'hāso'. One whose mind is pleased is 'attamano'. Indeed, for a corrupt person, the mind is not pleased; the state of that is 'attamanatā', which is 'pāmojjaṃ'. It satisfies and pleases, thus 'pīti'. One finds happiness by this, thus 'vitti'. They are content by this, thus 'tuṭṭhi'. Due to association with it, 'vitti' and 'pīti' are in the feminine gender, but 'attamanatā' is a difference of form according to the exposition. It greatly delights, thus 'ānando'. The root 'mud' is in the sense of joy; 'pamudo' and 'āmodo' also. Being content is 'santoso'. Delighting is 'nandi'. 'Sammado' and also 'sammadā', with the 'u' becoming 'a'. The state of a delighted person or mind is 'pāmojjaṃ'.

Tikaṃ sukhe. Suṭṭhu khaṇatīti sukhaṃ, kvi. Sādīyati assādīyatīti sātaṃ. Phassati sinehatīti phāsu, phusati vā bādhati dukkhanti phāsu. Sattakaṃ kalyāṇe. Bhadi kalyāṇe, bhaddatīti bhaddaṃ. Pasatthatarattā seyyo. Sobhatīti sobhaṃ. Khī khaye, khepeti asukhaṃ khemaṃ, mo. Kalyaṃ nirogaṃ aṇati gacchati, kalyaṃ vā hitaṃ aṇayati pāpayatīti kalyāṇaṃ, kammani ṇo kammani upapade ṇapaccayoti adhippāyo. Maṅga gatyattho, maṅgati dhaññaṃ maṅgalaṃ, alo. Sameti dukkhanti sivaṃ, vo.

A triad of terms for happiness. It digs well, thus 'sukhaṃ', with the 'kvi' suffix. It is tasted and enjoyed, thus 'sātaṃ'. It touches and endears, thus 'phāsu'; or, that which touches, that is, afflicts suffering, is 'phāsu'. A septad of terms for the auspicious. The root 'bhad' is in the sense of 'auspicious'; it prospers, thus 'bhaddaṃ'. Because it is more praised, it is 'seyyo'. It shines, thus 'sobhaṃ'. The root 'khī' is in the sense of 'destruction'; it destroys unhappiness, thus 'khemaṃ', with the 'mo' suffix. One goes in health, free from disease; or, it brings what is auspicious or beneficial, thus 'kalyāṇaṃ', with 'ṇo' in the sense of the object. The root 'maṅg' is in the sense of 'going'; it goes to fortune, thus 'maṅgalaṃ', with the 'alo' suffix. It appeases suffering, thus 'sivaṃ', with the 'vo' suffix.

89. Chakkaṃ dukkhe. Dukkaraṃ khamanamettha dukkhaṃ. Kasa gamane, kasati apuññanti kasiraṃ, iro, kucchitenākārena setīti vā kasiraṃ. Kira vikkhipane, kirati sukhanti kicchaṃ, katā vā puññakaraṇicchā yenāti kicchaṃ, “dukkhūpanisā saddhā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Natthi adhigamanatthaṃ īhā etthāti nīgho, hassa gho, atha vā nihantyapuññaṃ hiṃsati gacchatīti vā nīgho, puññaṃ vā na hanti na gacchatīti nīgho. Virūpamasati yenāti byasanaṃ, visiṭṭhaṃ vā asati khepetīti byasanaṃ. Na hanti dhaññanti aghaṃ. Ete pāpādayo guṇe yathāvuttaliṅgā. Pāpapuññāni sukhādi ca ākicchaṃ kicchantaṃ guṇayogato dabbe visesye vattamānāni tīsu. Yathā –

89. A hexad of terms for suffering. Difficult to endure, thus 'dukkhaṃ'. The root 'kas' is in the sense of 'going'; it plows, i.e., produces, demerit, thus 'kasiraṃ', with the 'iro' suffix. Or, one lies in a contemptible manner, thus 'kasiraṃ'. The root 'kir' is in the sense of 'scattering'; it scatters happiness, thus 'kicchaṃ'. Or, that by which the desire to perform merit is made is 'kicchaṃ', for it is said: "Faith has suffering as its prerequisite." There is no striving for attainment herein, thus 'nīgho', with 'h' becoming 'gh'. Or, it destroys demerit, harms, and goes, thus 'nīgho'. Or, it does not strike, does not go to, merit, thus 'nīgho'. That by which one is deformed is 'byasanaṃ'. Or, it throws away or destroys what is excellent, thus 'byasanaṃ'. It strikes the fortunate, thus 'aghaṃ'. These, beginning with 'pāpa', are qualities with genders as stated. Evil and merit, and happiness and so forth up to difficulty, when they exist as adjectives qualifying a substance by connection with a quality, are in the three genders. For example:

Pāpā utumatī kaññā, pāpo rājāpyarakkhako;

Pāpaṃ byādhakulaṃ hiṃsaṃ, pāpo vippo ca sevako;

Puññaṃ titthamidaṃ puññā, nadī puñño’ya’massamo.

An evil one is a maiden in her season; an evil one is a king who does not protect; an evil thing is a hunter's family given to violence; and an evil one is a brahmin who is a servant. Meritorious is this ford, meritorious is this river, meritorious is this hermitage.

Sukhaṃ [M 0.0073] kāmikulaṃ dabbaṃ sabbaṃ (?), sukho vāso sahā’mbayā sahānvayo (ka.);

Sukhā yuvati’ricchantī, sukhā ve maghavaggahā sukhā yuvatikā gahā (ka.).

Happy is a family with desires and wealth; happy is dwelling with one's mother; happy is a young woman who is desiring; happy indeed is the capture of Maghavan.

Yadā tu sakatthappadhānaṃ sukhādikameva visesyattena vattumicchate, na tu dabbaṃ (pubbamiva visesanaṃ,) ( ) cintāmaṇiṭīkāyaṃ na dissati tadā rūpabhedottameva liṅgaṃ. Yathā –

But when one wishes to speak of happiness and so forth itself as the principal thing, as a noun, and not as qualifying a substance (as before, as an adjective), then the gender is only that stated by the difference in form. For example:

“Dāliddepi valittepi (ka.) dhanittepi, vaso parijano sukhaṃ;

Sukhaṃ sajjanavāso ca, sukhaṃ santi anuttarā”ti.

"Whether in poverty or in wealth, dwelling with one's retinue is happiness; and dwelling with good people is happiness; unsurpassed peace is happiness."

Nanu “dukkaṭoyaṃ byāpāro, sukataṃ kammaṃ, kalusoyaṃ me byāpāro”ti aññesampi tīsu vutti attheveti kiṃ pāpapuññānameva gahaṇaṃ bhavatīti? Vuccate – “duṭṭhu kato dukkaṭo, suṭṭhu kataṃ sukata”miccevaṃ kriyānibandhanāpi tīsu vutti sambhavati, nāvassaṃ guṇanibandhanā eva. Kalusassapi yadā siṭṭhapayogesu visesyavutti tiliṅgatā upalabbhate, tadā pāpaggahaṇa’matthappadhānaṃ byākhyātabbaṃ.

Is it not the case that for other terms also, such as 'this action is ill-done (dukkaṭa),' 'the deed is well-done (sukata),' 'this action of mine is defiled (kalusa),' there is usage in the three genders? Why then is only 'evil' and 'merit' taken as examples? It is said: 'Badly done is ill-done (dukkaṭo), well done is well-done (sukataṃ)'—thus, a usage in the three genders based on action is also possible, not necessarily one based on quality alone. In the case of 'kalusa' too, when its adjectival usage in three genders is found in the applications of the learned, then the taking of 'pāpa' should be explained as being primary in meaning.

90. Pañcakaṃ subhāsubhakammamatte. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhavipākabhāgo yattha atthīti bhāgyaṃ. Subhāsubhaphalaṃ netīti niyati,ti. Subhāsubhaphalaṃ bhājetīti bhāgo. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhavibhāgabhāgodhīyati etthāti bhāgadheyyaṃ. Subhāsubhaphalaṃ vidadhātīti vidhi. Ayo, subhāvaho, devaṃ, diṭṭhaṃiccādīnipi subhāsubhakammamattassa nāmāni. Pañcakaṃ jātiyaṃ. Uppajjanaṃ uppatti, nippajjanaṃ nibbatti, pada gatiyaṃ, nipubbo,ti, passa bo. Jananaṃ jāti. Janīyate jananaṃ. Uddhaṃ bhavanaṃ ubbhavo.

90. A pentad of terms for wholesome and unwholesome kamma itself. Where there is a share of agreeable and disagreeable results, that is 'bhāgyaṃ'. That which leads to wholesome and unwholesome results is 'niyati'. That which distributes wholesome and unwholesome results is 'bhāgo'. Because the share of the division of agreeable and disagreeable is placed herein, that is 'bhāgadheyyaṃ'. That which arranges wholesome and unwholesome results is 'vidhi'. 'Ayo', 'subhāvaho', 'devaṃ', 'diṭṭhaṃ', and so forth are also names for wholesome and unwholesome kamma itself. A pentad of terms for birth. Arising is 'uppatti'. Coming into being is 'nibbatti', from the root 'pad' meaning 'to go', with the prefix 'ni' and the suffix 'ti', where 'p' becomes 'b'. Generating is 'jāti'. Being generated is 'jananaṃ'. Arising upwards is 'ubbhavo'.

91. Pajjaṃ [M 0.0074] hetumhi. Attano phalaṃ niminātīti nimittaṃ, mā parimāṇe, nipubbo. Karoti phalanti kāraṇaṃ. Tiṭṭhati phalametthāti ṭhānaṃ. Pajjati nipajjati phalametenāti padaṃ, visesena jāyateti bījaṃ, rassassa dīghatā. Nissesena attano phalaṃ bandhati pavattetīti nibandhanaṃ. Nidīyate nicchīyate aneneti nidānaṃ, yu, nidadāti phalanti vā nidānaṃ. Pabhavati phalametasmāti pabhavo, hinoti gacchati pariṇamati kāriyarūpatanti hetu, tu, hinoti vā patiṭṭhāti phalametthāti hetu, hi patiṭṭhāyaṃ. Sambhavati yena phalanti sambhavo. Sinoti phalaṃ bandhatīti setu. Paṭicca phalametasmā etīti paccayo.

91. A collection of terms for cause. It measures out its own fruit, thus 'nimittaṃ', from the root 'mā' meaning 'to measure', with the prefix 'ni'. It produces fruit, thus 'kāraṇaṃ'. The fruit stands herein, thus 'ṭhānaṃ'. The fruit proceeds or comes forth by this, thus 'padaṃ'. It is born in a special way, thus 'bījaṃ', with the short vowel being lengthened. It binds and brings forth its own fruit without remainder, thus 'nibandhanaṃ'. By this it is laid down and determined, thus 'nidānaṃ', with the 'yu' suffix; or, it lays down the fruit, thus 'nidānaṃ'. The fruit originates from this, thus 'pabhavo'. It impels, goes, or transforms into the state of an effect, thus 'hetu', with the 'tu' suffix; or, the fruit is impelled or established herein, thus 'hetu', from the root 'hi' meaning 'to be established'. That by which the fruit comes into being is 'sambhavo'. It binds the fruit, thus 'setu'. Depending on this, the fruit comes, thus 'paccayo'.

92. Yaṃ kāraṇaṃ samāsannaṃ āsannataraṃ phalena, taṃ padaṭṭhānanti mataṃ. Padānaṃ hetūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, yathā “rājarājā”ti. Tividhaṃ kāraṇaṃ upādānakāraṇaṃ sahakārīkāraṇaṃ kāraṇakāraṇanti. Yathā bījaṃ aṅkurassa upādānakāraṇasaṅkhātaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, bhūmijalādi sahakārīkāraṇaṃ, “kammassa kampassa (?) kāraṇaṃ jaro, tassa kāraṇaṃ kapho”ti kapho kāraṇakāraṇaṃ kammassa kampassa (?).

92. That cause which is proximate, very near to the result, is considered the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). 'Padaṭṭhāna' means the basis of causes, like 'rājarājā' means 'king of kings'. The cause is threefold: the material cause (upādānakāraṇa), the auxiliary cause (sahakārīkāraṇa), and the cause of the cause (kāraṇakāraṇa). For example, the seed is the proximate cause, known as the material cause of the sprout; earth, water, and so forth are auxiliary causes. In the phrase, "The cause of the affliction is fever, and its cause is phlegm," phlegm is the cause of the cause of the affliction.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0075] sarīrādhipatideve. Jīvanti sattā yenāti jīvo. Pūreti nissayassābhilāsanti puriso, iso. Atanti satataṃ gacchanti sattā yenāti attā. Dvayaṃ sattarajotamosāmyāvatthāyaṃ. Padhīyante palīyante atra guṇā sattarajotamo rūpāti padhānaṃ, yu. Pakaroti purisopabhogatthaṃ saddādikāriyanti pakati,ti. Moharāgadosānaṃ yathāsaṅkhyaṃ sattarajotamānīti saññā. Sato bhāvo sattaṃ, ṭhitiparatā. Rajjantyatrāti rajo, saṭṭhiparatā. Tamantyatrāti tamo, palayaparatā.

A triad of terms for the body, the lord, and a god. That by which beings live is 'jīvo'. It fulfills the desire of its support, thus 'puriso', and 'iso'. That by which beings constantly go is 'attā'. A pair of terms for the state of equilibrium of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Herein the qualities in the form of sattva, rajas, and tamas are put forth and dissolved, thus 'padhānaṃ', with the 'yu' suffix. It produces effects such as sound for the enjoyment of the person, thus 'pakati', with the 'ti' suffix. The designations for delusion, lust, and hatred are respectively sattva, rajas, and tamas. The state of being is 'sattaṃ', being intent on stability. They are impassioned herein, thus 'rajo', being intent on attachment. They are suffocated herein, thus 'tamo', being intent on dissolution.

93. Pajjena pāṇino nāmāni. Paṇanti jīvanti sattā yenāti pāṇo, so yassatthi, so pāṇo. Sarīrasaṅkhāto kāyo yassatthi, so sarīrī. Kammena bhavatīti bhūtaṃ, napuṃsake, pumevāti vāsaddattho. Rūpādīsu sañjatīti satto, nicchandarāgāpi rūḷhiyā sattāti vuccanti. Deho kāyo yassatthīti dehī. Pūretīti pūti, pūtisaṅkhātaṃ āhāraṃ gilati adatīti puggalo, tissa lopo, sattānaṃ āyuṃ pūrento gacchatīti puggo, taṃ lāti bhakkhatīti puggalo. Jīvanti yenāti jīvaṃ, tamassatthīti jīvo. Yathāvuttattho pāṇo yassatthīti pāṇī. Pakārena jātattā pajā. Jāyatīti jantu, tu. Kusalākusalaṃ janetīti jano. Lujjatīti loko, luja vināse, jassa ko. Yathā purimakā sattā jātijarāmaraṇaṃ gacchanti, tathā ayampi gacchatīti tathāgato.

93. By this verse, the names of living beings. That by which beings breathe and live is 'pāṇa'; he who possesses that is a 'pāṇo'. He who has a body, designated as 'sarīra', is a 'sarīrī'. 'Bhūtaṃ' is that which comes to be through kamma; it is in the neuter, or in the masculine, where 'vā' has the sense of 'eva' (indeed). 'Satto' is one who clings to forms and so forth; even those without desire and passion are, by convention, called 'sattā'. 'Dehī' is one who has a body. 'Pūti' is that which fills; 'puggalo' is one who swallows or eats food designated as 'pūti', with the elision of 'ti'. Or, 'puggo' is one who goes on filling the lifespan of beings, and 'puggalo' is one who takes or devours that. 'Jīvaṃ' is that by which one lives; he who possesses that is a 'jīvo'. He who possesses 'pāṇa' in the sense previously stated is a 'pāṇī'. 'Pajā' are those born in a particular manner. 'Jantu' is one who is born, with the suffix 'tu'. 'Jano' is one who generates the skillful and unskillful. 'Loko' is that which is destroyed, from the root 'luja' in the sense of destruction, with 'j' becoming 'k'. Just as former beings go to birth, aging, and death, so too does this one go; thus, 'tathāgato'.

94. Rūpādayo [M 0.0076] cha cakkhādigayhā dhammā “gocarā”ti “ālambā”ti “visayā”ti “ārammaṇānī”ti “ālambaṇānī”ti ca vuccante. Rūpayati pakāseti attano sabhāvanti rūpaṃ. Sappati uccārīyatīti saddo, sappa gatiyaṃ vā, sappate ñāyate yeneti saddo. Gandha addane, addanaṃ hiṃsanaṃ, yācanañca, hiṃsate abhilasīyate vā gandho, gandheti vā attano vatthuṃ sūceti pakāseti “idamettha atthī”ti pesuññaṃ karonto viya hotīti gandho. Rasanti taṃ sattā assādentīti raso. Phusīyatīti phasso. Gāvo indriyāni carantyetesu gocarā. Cittacetasikehi ālambīyanteti ālambā. Si bandhane vipubbo, visinonti vibandhanti indriyānīti visayā. Āgantvā cittacetasikā ramanti etthāti ārammaṇāni, yu. Ete indriyatthātipyuccante, indriyehi atthyante abhilasīyanteti katvā.

94. The six objects—forms and so on—grasped by the eye and other faculties are called 'gocarā,' 'ālambā,' 'visayā,' 'ārammaṇāni,' and 'ālambaṇāni.' 'Rūpa' is that which manifests its own nature. 'Saddo' is that which is sounded or uttered; or from the root 'sappa' in the sense of 'going', it is that by which one approaches and knows. 'Gandha' is from 'addana', meaning 'harming' or 'requesting'; 'gandha' is that which is harmed or desired; or it is that which indicates and reveals its own substance, like one engaging in slander, intimating, 'This is here.' 'Raso' is that which beings taste and savor. 'Phasso' is that which is touched. 'Gocarā' are the fields where the faculties roam. 'Ālambā' are those things which are grasped by the mind and mental factors. 'Visayā' are so called because they bind or fetter the faculties, from the root 'si' (to bind) with the prefix 'vi'. 'Ārammaṇāni' are those things wherein the mind and mental factors delight upon arriving, with the suffix 'yu'. These are also called 'indriyatthā', because they are sought after and desired by the faculties.

95. Pajjaddhaṃ sukke. Suca soke, socanti etena tadatthikāti sukko, a. Gu sadde, guyate kittīyateti goro, ro. Si sevāyaṃ, sevīyateti sito, sinoti vā bandhati cittanti sito. Avadāyati sabbavaṇṇeti odāto. Dā avakhaṇḍane avapubbo. Dhāvati sujjhatyaneneti dhavalo, alo. Sita vaṇṇe, ṇo, seto[M 0.0077]. Paḍi gatiyaṃ, paṇḍati pakāsetīti paṇḍaro, aro. Suci, visado, ajjunotipi sukkanāmāni.

95. Half a verse on white. 'Sukka' is from the root 'suca' in the sense of 'sorrow', meaning 'those who desire it sorrow by this', with the suffix 'a'. 'Goro' is that which is praised, from the root 'gu' in the sense of 'sound', with the suffix 'ro'. 'Sito' is that which is resorted to, from the root 'si' in the sense of 'service'; or it is that which binds the mind. 'Odāto' is that which purifies all colors, from the root 'dā' in the sense of 'cleansing', with the prefix 'ava'. 'Dhavalo' is that by which one is cleansed or purified, with the suffix 'alo'. 'Seto' is from 'sita' in the sense of 'color', with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Paṇḍaro' is that which shines forth, from 'paḍi' in the sense of 'going', with the suffix 'aro'. 'Suci', 'visado', and 'ajjuno' are also names for white.

Chakkaṃ ratte. Soṇa vaṇṇe, ṇo, rattuppalavaṇṇo, ruha janane, ito, latte lohito. Rañjantyaneneti ratto, ranja raṅge. Tambo udumbarasaṅkhāto lohaviseso, tabbaṇṇatāya tambo. Mañjeṭṭhā nāma rattavalli, yāya hatthidantādivikatiyo rattā bhavanti, tabbaṇṇatāya mañjeṭṭho. Rohito lohitasamo, alattameva viseso.

A set of six on red. 'Soṇo' is from 'soṇa' in the sense of 'color', with the suffix 'ṇo'; it is the color of a red lotus. 'Lohito' is from the root 'ruha' in the sense of 'generating', with the suffix 'ito', and with 'la' for 'ra'. 'Ratto' is that by which one is dyed, from the root 'ranja' in the sense of 'dyeing'. 'Tambo' is a particular metal, copper, which is the color of the udumbara fruit; it is called 'tambo' due to that color. 'Mañjeṭṭhā' is the name of a red creeper by which things made of ivory and so forth are dyed red; it is called 'mañjeṭṭho' due to that color. 'Rohito' is the same as 'lohito'; the specific instance is the color of lac.

96. Sāmalantaṃ kaṇhe. Nīla vaṇṇe, a. Kassateti kaṇho, kasa vilekhane, ṇho. Na sito asito. Vaṇṇesu ekakoṭṭhāsabhāvena kalyateti kālo, so eva kāḷo. Maca, maci kakkane, kakkanaṃ pisanaṃ, setādikaṃ macatīti mecako, ṇvu, assettaṃ. Sā tanukaraṇe, sāyati tanukarīyati paṭipakkhavaṇṇehīti sāmo. Sāmalo sāmasadiso, malapaccayova viseso.

96. Terms for black, ending with 'sāmala'. 'Nīla' is from the root 'nīla' in the sense of 'color', with the suffix 'a'. 'Kaṇho' is that which scratches, from the root 'kasa' in the sense of 'scratching', with the suffix 'ṇho'. 'Asito' is 'not white'. 'Kālo' is that which is counted among colors as having a single portion; this is also 'kāḷo'. 'Mecako' is from the roots 'maca' and 'maci' in the sense of 'rubbing' ('kakkanaṃ'), which means 'crushing'; it is that which crushes white and so forth, with the suffix 'ṇvu'; it is unmixed. 'Sāmo' is from the root 'sā' in the sense of 'thinning'; it is that which is thinned by opposing colors. 'Sāmalo' is similar to 'sāma'; the suffix 'mala' is the only difference.

Paṇḍusaddo sitapīte utto, sitapītasammissitavaṇṇe paṇḍusaddo vuttotyattho. Vuttañca “sitapītasamāyutto, paṇḍuvaṇṇo pakittito”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 5.13. Paṇḍati ekagaṇanaṃ gacchatīti paṇḍu, paḍi gatiyaṃ, u. Hariṇo, paṇḍurotipi paṇḍuvaṇṇanāmāni. Īsaṃpaṇḍu abyattapaṇḍuvaṇṇo dhūsaro nāma, yathā dhūlivaṇṇo. Dhūsa kantikaraṇe, curādi, aro.

The term 'paṇḍu' is used for white-and-yellow, meaning it is used for a color mixed of white and yellow. And it is said: 'Associated with white and yellow, the paṇḍu color is proclaimed.' 'Paṇḍu' is that which goes to a single count, from the root 'paḍi' in the sense of 'going', with the suffix 'u'. 'Hariṇa' and 'paṇḍura' are also names for the paṇḍu color. A slightly paṇḍu, an indistinct paṇḍu color, is called 'dhūsara', like the color of dust. It is from the root 'dhūsa' in the sense of 'making bright', of the curādi class, with the suffix 'aro'.

97. Kiñciratto [M 0.0078] abyattarattavaṇṇo aruṇo nāma, yathā macchassa cakkhu yathā madamattassa cakkhurāgo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 5.15), sūriyādo taruṇo vutto.

97. A somewhat red, indistinctly red color is called 'aruṇa', like the eye of a fish; it is said to be the young dawn, the beginning of the sun.

Setalohito setarattamisso vaṇṇo pāṭalo nāma, yathā pāṭalakusumaṃ. Pāṭayateti pāṭalo, alo, paṭa vibhājane.

White-red, a mixed color of white and red, is called 'pāṭala', like the pāṭala flower. 'Pāṭalo' is so called because it divides, from the root 'paṭa' in the sense of 'dividing', with the suffix 'alo'.

Dvikaṃ pīte. Pā pāne, kammani to, īttañca. Haliddiyā iva ābhā yassa halidyābho.

A pair of terms for yellow. 'Pīta' is from the root 'pā' in the sense of 'drinking', with the suffix 'ta' in the passive sense, and with lengthening of the vowel. 'Halidyābho' is that which has a radiance like turmeric.

Tikaṃ tiṇapattādigate vaṇṇe. Lasa kantiyaṃ, atisayena lasyateti palāso. “Pālāso”ti pāṭhe tu rassassa dīghatā. Hara haraṇe, manaṃ haratīti harito, ito. I, hari.

A set of three for the color found in grass, leaves, and so on. 'Palāsa' is from the root 'lasa' in the sense of 'shining', meaning 'that which shines exceedingly'. In the reading 'pālāso', the short vowel is lengthened. 'Harita' is from the root 'hara' in the sense of 'taking away'; it is that which takes away the mind, with the suffix 'ito'. Also, 'hari'.

98. Nīlapītasammissavaṇṇe kaḷāro, kapilo ca vattanti. Kala saṅkhyāne. Aro, lassa ḷo, kaḷāro. Kaba vaṇṇe, ilo, bassa po, kapilo.

98. For the mixed color of blue and yellow, 'kaḷāro' and 'kapilo' are used. 'Kaḷāro' is from the root 'kala' in the sense of 'counting', with the suffix 'aro', and 'l' becoming 'ḷ'. 'Kapilo' is from the root 'kaba' in the sense of 'color', with the suffix 'ilo', and 'b' becoming 'p'.

Rocanappabhe gorocanasadisappabhāyaṃ piṅgo, pisaṅgo ca vattanti. Pabhāsaddassa dviliṅgattameva. Piji bhāsattho, piṅgo. Paratra sakāravaṇṇāgamo, pisaṅgo.

For a radiance like that of gorocana, the terms 'piṅga' and 'pisaṅga' are used. The word 'pabhā' has two genders. 'Piṅga' is from the root 'piji' in the sense of 'to shine'. For the other term, 'pisaṅga', there is the addition of the letter 's'.

Kaḷārādīnaṃ [M 0.0079] catunnaṃ piṅgalavisesatthavācakataṃ dassetvā piṅgalasāmaññatthavācakattampi dassetumāha “kaḷārādi”ccādi. Tassāyamattho – na kevalaṃ kaḷārādayo piṅgalavisesattheyeva pavattanti, atha kho piṅgalasāmaññatthepi vattantīti. Vuttañhi amarakose “kaḷāro kapilo piṅgo, pisaṅgo kaddu piṅgalo”ti amara 5.16. Keci pana kaḷārādayo pisaṅgapariyantā cattāro saddā piṅgalaguṇe vattamānā pume vattanti, guṇini pana vāccaliṅgāti evaṃ pacchimena sambandhaṃ katvā vadanti, taṃ amarakosena virujjhanato idha ca “sukkādayo”ti sabbesaṃyeva gahaṇato na gahetabbaṃ.

Having shown that the four terms beginning with 'kaḷāra' denote specific meanings of 'tawny,' the text now states 'kaḷārādi,' etc., to show that they also denote the general meaning of 'tawny.' The meaning here is this: not only do the terms starting with 'kaḷāra' apply to specific nuances of tawny, but they also apply to the general sense of tawny. For it is stated in the Amarakośa: 'Kaḷāro kapilo piṅgo, pisaṅgo kaddu piṅgalo.' However, some say that the four words from 'kaḷāra' up to 'pisaṅga,' when referring to the quality of tawny, are used in the masculine gender, but when referring to the possessor of that quality, they take the gender of the word they describe, thus making a connection with the latter rule. This should not be accepted because it contradicts the Amarakośa, and because here the phrase 'sukkādayo' includes all of them.

99. Tikaṃ sabale kokilakaṇṭhasadise. Kalyateti kalo, masi parimāṇe, kammani ṇo, kalo eva māso kammāso, lassa mo, kalanaṃ vā kalo, taṃ masatīti kammāso, yathā “kumbhakāro”ti. Saba gatiyaṃ, sabatīti sabalo, alo. Ciyyateti citto, ta. Traṇapaccaye citro. Kammīro, kabburotipi sabalassa nāmāni.

99. A set of three for 'variegated', like the throat of a cuckoo. 'Kammāso': 'Kalo' (a spot) is so called because it is counted. From the root 'masi' in the sense of 'to measure', with the suffix 'ṇa' in the passive, 'kalo' itself is 'māso', becoming 'kammāso', with 'l' becoming 'm'. Or, 'kalo' is a spot, and 'kammāso' is that which measures it, like 'kumbhakāro' (pot-maker). 'Sabalo' is from the root 'saba' in the sense of 'going'; it is that which goes, with the suffix 'alo'. 'Citto' is that which is arranged, with the suffix 'ta'. With the suffix 'traṇa', it is 'citro'. 'Kammīro' and 'kabburo' are also names for 'sabala'.

Kaṇhapītamisse sāvo vutto. Se gatimhi, sayatīti sāvo, avo. Kapisotipi sāvassa nāmaṃ. Kaṇhalohitamisse dhūmābhe pana dhūma, dhūmalā vattanti. Dhūmo viyāti dhūmo. Dhūmaṃ lātīti dhūmalo. Ete sukkādayo sāvantā yadā abhedopacārā guṇini guṇimhi vattanti, tadā vāccaliṅgā, yathā sukko haṃso, sukkā haṃsī[M 0.0080], sukkaṃ haṃsakulaṃiccādi yojjaṃ. Yadā guṇe guṇamatte vattanti, tadā pume, yathā haṃsassa sukko, mayūrassa citto iccādi yojjaṃ.

For a mixture of black and yellow, the term 'sāvo' is used. It is from the root 'se' in the sense of 'going'; 'sāvo' is that which goes, with the suffix 'avo'. 'Kapiso' is also a name for 'sāvo'. However, for a mixture of black and red, which has the appearance of smoke, 'dhūma' and 'dhūmalo' are used. 'Dhūmo' is so called because it is like smoke. 'Dhūmalo' is that which takes on smoke. When these terms from 'sukka' to 'sāva', by means of non-differentiated application, refer to a qualified object, they take the gender of that object; for example, one should apply this as: 'sukko haṃso' (a white swan), 'sukkā haṃsī' (a white female swan), 'sukkaṃ haṃsakulaṃ' (a white flock of swans). When they refer to the quality alone, they are in the masculine; for example, one should apply this as: 'haṃsassa sukko' (the white of the swan), 'mayūrassa citto' (the variegation of the peacock).

100. Lāsanantaṃ nacce. Nata gattavināme, pabbajjādittā naccādeso. Natanaṃ naccaṃ, naṭanaṃ vā naccaṃ, sabbatra bhāvasādhanaṃ. Natīyate nattanaṃ. Lasyate lāsanaṃ, lasa kantiyaṃ, lasitabbanti vā lāsanaṃ.

100. Terms for dancing, ending with 'lāsana'. From the root 'nata' in the sense of 'bending the limbs'. Due to its inclusion in the 'pabbajjādi' group of words, there is the substitution 'nacca'. 'Naccaṃ' is 'natanaṃ' or 'naṭanaṃ'; in all cases, it is formed in the abstract sense of the action. 'Nattanaṃ' is 'that which is danced'. 'Lāsanaṃ' is derived from 'lasyate' (it is danced gracefully). It is from the root 'lasa' in the sense of 'shining'; or 'lāsanaṃ' is 'shining'.

Naccaṃ, vāditaṃ, gītaṃ iti idaṃ bhoriyattikaṃ nāṭyaṃ nāmetyuccate amara 7.10. Tura turaṇahiṃsāsu. Turīyanteneneti tūriyaṃ, murajādi. Tabbhavo saddo toriyo, ṇo. Tena lakkhitaṃ tikaṃ toriyattikaṃ. Naṭassedaṃ nāṭyaṃ. Tatiyassa toriyasāmaññassa tu pāsaṅgā nāṭakā.

Dancing, instrumental music, and singing—this triad of performance is called `nāṭya`. The root `tura` is used in the sense of swiftness and violence. That by which one is made swift is `tūriya`, such as drums and so on. A sound arising from that is `toriya`, with the suffix `ṇa`. The triad characterized by that is the `toriyattika`. This `nāṭya` belongs to the actor (`naṭa`). As for the third, the general category of instrumental music (`toriya`), the `nāṭaka` (dramas) are incidental.

101. Naccaṭṭhānaṃ rājaṅgaṇādi raṅgo nāma siyā “ramantā gacchanti ettha, rajjanti etthā”ti vā katvā. Sūjhasūcanaṃ hatthādīhi sūcitabbassa pakāsetabbassa satthappahārādino sūcanaṃ pakāsanaṃ abhinayo nāma “nayanaṃ nayo, passantānaṃ abhimukhaṃ nayo”ti katvā. Byañjakotipi tasseva nāmaṃ.

101. A place for dancing, such as a royal courtyard, may be called `raṅga` (stage), because ‘they go there rejoicing’ or ‘they are delighted there’. The indication or revelation of what is to be indicated or revealed by means of hands and so on, such as striking with a weapon, is called `abhinaya`, because it is a ‘leading’ (`nayana`) or ‘method’ (`naya`), a ‘leading towards those who are watching’. `Byañjaka` is also a name for the same.

Bharatasatthavuttaaṭṭhuttarasatakaraṇanipphannathirahatthapariyatthakādināmako dvattiṃ sappakāro vitthāro bharatamunikate nāṭyasatthe catuttha ajjhāye passitabbo naccaviseso aṅgavikkhepo, aṅgahāro nāma “aṅgassa hāro, vikkhepo”ti katvā[M 0.0081]. Tikaṃ naṭe. Sabbatra kattusādhanaṃ, “naccatīti naṭṭako”tyādinā.

A special kind of dance, consisting of thirty-two types of limb movements (`aṅgavikkhepo`), called `aṅgahāra`, which is produced from the one hundred and eight `karaṇas` mentioned in the treatise of Bharata, and which includes `thirahatthapariyatthaka` and so on, is so called because it is ‘the carrying’ (`hāro`) or ‘the movement’ (`vikkhepo`) of the limbs (`aṅga`). The triad refers to the actor. In all cases, the derivation is in the agent sense, as in ‘one who dances is a dancer (`naṭṭako`)’ and so on.

102. Siṅgārādayo nava rasā nāṭyarasā assādanīyattā. Yathā hi nānābyañjanasaṅkhatamannaṃ bhuñjantā rase assādayanti sumanā purisā hāsaṃva adhigacchanti, tathā nānābhinayabyañjite aṅgasattopete ṭhāyībhāve assādayanti sumanāti subodhālaṅkārassa mahāsāmiṭīkāya 352 gāthāvaṇṇanāyampi.

102. The nine `rasas`, beginning with the erotic sentiment (`siṅgāra`), are the dramatic sentiments because they are to be savored. Just as cheerful people, while eating food prepared with various seasonings, savor the flavors and attain happiness, so too, cheerful people savor the abiding emotion (`ṭhāyībhāva`), which is manifested through various expressions and endowed with physical and mental states.

103. Tesu siṅgārasseva sarūpaṃ, pabhedañca dassetumāha “posasse”ccādi. Nāriyaṃ saṅgamaṃ paṭicca kāraṇaṃ katvā posassa purisassa yā pihā icchā manovikāraviseso pose ca purise saṅgamaṃ paṭicca kāraṇaṃ katvā itthiyā yā pihā icchā manovikāraviseso, eso ratikīḷādīnaṃ kāraṇabhūto, ratikīḷādikāraṇasahito vā raso siṅgāro nāma. Ettha ca itthipurisānaṃ dassanasavanaphusanavasena vā vippayogavasena vā yā pihā sañjātā, so raso nāma. Yaṃ pana taṃ kāraṇaṃ katvā pavattaṃ gītaṃ, tameva lokānaṃ assādajanakattā raso nāma. Phalūpacāravasena pana pihā rasoti vuttā, sabbatrevaṃ.

103. Among these, to show the nature and distinctions of the erotic sentiment (`siṅgāra`), it is said: ‘of a man’ and so on. The desire (`pihā`), wish (`icchā`), or particular mental modification (`manovikāraviseso`) that arises in a man (`posassa purisassa`) on account of union with a woman, and the desire, wish, or particular mental modification that arises in a woman (`itthiyā`) on account of union with a man—this, being the cause of amorous play and the like, or accompanied by the cause of amorous play and similar activities, is what is called the erotic sentiment (`siṅgāra`). Here, the desire that arises in men and women through seeing, hearing, touching, or through separation is what is called sentiment (`rasa`). Moreover, the song that is performed having that as its cause is called sentiment (`rasa`), because it generates delight in people. However, desire (`pihā`) is called sentiment (`rasa`) by way of a figurative usage based on the effect. This applies in all cases.

104. Uttamānaṃ [M 0.0082] itthipurisānaṃ pakati saṃyogaviyogasabhāvo sā ettha siṅgāre pāyo bahulanti uttamapakatippāyo, yebhuyyena uttamānaṃ saṃyogaviyogappavattaṃ gītameva siṅgāro nāmātyattho. Itthipurisānaṃ pihā hetu etassāti itthipurisahetuko. So siṅgāro sambhogo, viyogoti iminā pabhedena duvidho mato. Tatra ca –

104. The natural state of excellent men and women is characterized by union and separation; since this is predominant in the erotic sentiment (`siṅgāra`), it is called ‘predominantly of excellent nature’ (`uttamapakatippāyo`). The meaning is that, generally, songs arising from the union and separation of excellent beings are indeed called the erotic sentiment (`siṅgāra`). The desire (`pihā`) of men and women is the cause of this, hence it is called ‘having men and women as its cause’ (`itthipurisahetuko`). That erotic sentiment (`siṅgāra`) is considered twofold by this distinction: union (`sambhoga`) and separation (`viyoga`). And in that regard:

Vāpivanagehuyyāna-mālācandanādayo;

Sambhogassa vibhāvā te, ye caññe lalitaṅkarā.
