Ponds, forests, houses, gardens, garlands, sandalwood, and so on; these are the stimuli (`vibhāva`) for union (`sambhoga`), and whatever else is conducive to pleasure.

Viyogassa tu piyādassanaṃ vibhāvo, rasajanako ca vibhāvo. Vuttañca –

For separation, however, the non-seeing of the beloved is the stimulus (`vibhāva`), and a stimulus is that which generates sentiment (`rasa`). And it is said:

“Jayante ca rasā yena,

Sa vibhāvo pakittito;

Tesamevā’nubhāvo’yaṃ,

Khyāto kavīhi byañjako”ti.

“That by which sentiments (`rasā`) are produced is declared to be the stimulus (`vibhāva`); this effect (`anubhāva`) of theirs, which is expressive (`byañjaka`), is proclaimed by the poets.”

Saha bhuñjanamanubhavanaṃ sambhogo. Viyujjanaṃ nānābhavanaṃ viyogo. Siṅgaṃ nāmadhātu, vijjhanaṭṭhena siṅgaṃ, nāgarikabhāvasaṅkhātassa kilesasiṅgassetaṃ nāmaṃ, taṃ karoti, siṅgaṃ vā pabhuttaṃ, taṃ karoti rāgīsūti siṅgāro, āro, kilesasiṅgakaraṇaṃ vilāsoti vuttaṃ. Suci, ujjalotipi siṅgārassa nāmāni.

Enjoying or experiencing together is union (`sambhoga`). Being separated, being apart, is separation (`viyoga`). `Siṅga` is a nominal root. In the sense of piercing, it is `siṅga`. It is a name for the ‘horn of defilements’ (`kilesasiṅga`), which is known as ‘urbanity’ (`nāgarikabhāva`); it produces that. Or `siṅga` means ‘eminence’; it produces that in those who are lustful, hence `siṅgāra`, with the suffix `āro`. The act of producing the horn of defilements is called `vilāsa` (playful grace). `Suci` (pure) and `ujjala` (bright) are also names for `siṅgāra`.

Sokopacayasabhāvo [M 0.0083] karuṇo.

The compassionate sentiment (`karuṇa`) has the nature of an accumulation of sorrow.

Iṭṭhanāsaṅganāsāya iṭṭhanāsadhanāpāya (cintāmaṇiṭīkā),

Vadhabandhanatāḷanā;

Sāpaklesopatāpehi,

Jāyate karuṇo raso.

From the loss of a loved one and the loss of a limb, from killing, imprisonment, and beating; from curses, defilements, and torments, the compassionate sentiment (`karuṇo raso`) arises.

Ussāhavaddhano vīro. Vibhāvā tassa vinayupatāpabalavikkamā. Sa cāyaṃ dānavīro dhammavīro yuddhavīroti tividho.

The heroic sentiment (`vīra`) is that which increases effort. Its stimuli (`vibhāva`) are discipline, affliction, strength, and prowess. And it is threefold: a hero in giving, a hero in Dhamma, and a hero in battle.

Vimhayopacayasabhāvo abbhuto.

The wondrous sentiment (`abbhuta`) has the nature of an accumulation of amazement.

Pāsāduyyānaselādi-gamanā dibbadassanā;

Sabhāvimānamāyenda-jālasippādidassanā jālavijjādidassanā (ka.);

Hadayecchitalābhehi, vibhāvehissa sambhavo.

From going to palaces, gardens, mountains, and so on; from witnessing divine sights; from seeing assembly halls, celestial chariots, magic, illusion, craftsmanship, and so on; from the attainment of the heart's desired gains—its arising is due to these stimuli (`vibhāva`).

Hāsopacayasabhāvo hāso.

The comical sentiment (`hāsa`) has the nature of an accumulation of mirth.

Sābahitthā savikatā, nepathyā byaṅgadassanā;

Asambandhakathālāpā, hāso so kuhakādibhi.

From jests and strange behavior, from seeing odd costumes and deformities, from incoherent talk and chatter, that comical sentiment (`hāsa`) arises from deceivers and the like.

Bhayopacayasabhāvo bhayānako.

The fearful sentiment (`bhayānaka`) has the nature of an accumulation of fear.

Uccabheravasaṃrāva-yakkhapetādidassanā;

Suññāgāramahārañña-vadhabandhanadassanā.

From high places and terrifying sounds, from seeing spirits, ghosts, and the like; from seeing empty houses, great forests, killing, and imprisonment:

Tāsāyāsaṅkatobbego, sivolūkaruṇādibhi;

Vibhāvehi ca itthīnaṃ, nīcānañca bhayānako.

From trembling, distress, anxiety, and agitation; from the cries of jackals, owls, and the like; and from such stimuli, for women and the base, the fearful sentiment (`bhayānaka`) arises.

Samaṇopacayasabhāvo santo.

The peaceful sentiment (`santa`) has the nature of an accumulation of serenity.

Dassanā santavesānaṃ, santacittāna tādinaṃ;

Santakāraṇadhammānaṃ, santo nāma raso bhave.

From seeing those of peaceful demeanor, those with peaceful minds, the stable ones, and things that are causes of peace, the sentiment called peace (`santa`) arises.

Jigucchopacayasabhāvo [M 0.0084] bībhaccho.

The disgusting sentiment (`bībhaccha`) has the nature of an accumulation of revulsion.

Pūtimaṃsādikānaṃ tu, dassanasutikittanā;

Vigatehi vibhāvehi, bībhacco jāyate raso.

From seeing, hearing, or speaking of rotten flesh and the like, through particular stimuli (`vibhāva`), the sentiment of disgust (`bībhaccha`) arises.

Kodhopacayasabhāvo ruddaṃ.

The furious sentiment (`rudda`) has the nature of an accumulation of anger.

Tañca saṅgāmahetukaṃ, uggakammaupaghāta-;

Musāvādādipharusā, vacanādīhi bhavati.

And it arises from causes connected with battle, from violent acts and injury, and from harsh speech such as falsehood and so on.

Etesu ca bībhaccharuddāni napuṃsake, aññe tu pume rūpabhedā. Ete ca nava nāṭyarasā ratanakosanayena vuttā. Vuttañhi tattha –

Among these, `bībhaccha` and `rudda` are neuter, while the others are masculine in form. These nine dramatic sentiments (`nāṭyarasā`) are stated according to the Ratanakośa. For it is said there:

“Siṅgāravīra bībhaccha-rudda hāsa bhayānakā;

Karuṇā’bbhuta santāca, nava nāṭyarasā ime”ti.

“The erotic (`siṅgāra`), heroic (`vīra`), disgusting (`bībhaccha`), furious (`rudda`), comical (`hāsa`), fearful (`bhayānaka`), compassionate (`karuṇā`), wondrous (`abbhuta`), and peaceful (`santa`)—these are the nine dramatic sentiments.”

Amarakose pana –

In the Amarakośa, however:

“Siṅgāravīra karuṇā-bbhuta hāsa bhayānakā;

Bībhaccha ruddāti rasā”ti amara 7.17.

“The erotic (`siṅgāra`), heroic (`vīra`), compassionate (`karuṇā`), wondrous (`abbhuta`), comical (`hāsa`), fearful (`bhayānaka`), disgusting (`bībhaccha`), and furious (`rudda`)—these are the sentiments (`rasā`).”

Aṭṭheva rasā vuttā. Atheha navamo santo raso kasmā na vuttoti? Vuccate –

Only eight sentiments (rasa) are mentioned. Why is the ninth, the sentiment of peace (santa rasa), not mentioned here? It is explained:

Hāso rati ca kāruññaṃ,

Kodhussāhabhayaṃ tathā;

Jigucchā vimhayo ceti,

Ṭhāyībhāvā pakittitā.

Laughter (hāsa), delight (rati), compassion (kāruñña), anger (kodha), energy (ussāha), fear (bhaya), disgust (jigucchā), and astonishment (vimhaya)—these are declared as abiding emotions (ṭhāyībhāva).

Ṭhāyī eva tu rasībhavatipyāgamo, tasmā pakatiyā aṭṭhasaṅkhyattā aṭṭheva tu te vuttāti na vutto. Santaraso cāyaṃ dhammasiṅgārattā siṅgārarase evānupaviṭṭho. Dhammayuddhakāmattena tividho hi siṅgāro. Keci pana piyasamāgamādivibhāvajaparamaṃ vassalyākhyaṃ rasamāhu.

Indeed, the abiding emotion (ṭhāyī) transforms into a sentiment (rasa), thus is the tradition; therefore, by nature, being eight in number, only eight are mentioned, and the ninth is not. And this sentiment of peace (santarasa) is included within the erotic sentiment (siṅgārarasa) because it has the charm of the Dhamma. For the erotic sentiment (siṅgāra) is threefold, by way of the desire for Dhamma-combat. However, some speak of a supreme sentiment called vassalya (affection), which arises from stimuli such as reunion with the beloved and so on.

Rabhasopyāha [M 0.0085] –

Rabhasa also says:

“Siṅgāra vīra bībhaccha-rudda hāsa bhayānakā;

Karuṇā’bbhutasantā ca, vassalyañca rasā dase”ti.

“The erotic (siṅgāra), heroic (vīra), disgusting (bībhaccha), furious (rudda), comic (hāsa), fearful (bhayānaka), compassionate (karuṇā), wondrous (abbhuta), peaceful (santa), and also affectionate (vassalya)—these are the ten sentiments (rasa).”

Aññe tu –

Others, however, say:

“Siṅgārānugato hāso,

Karuṇo ruddakammajo;

Vīrato abbhuto jāto,

Bībhacchā ca bhayānako”ti –

“Laughter follows the erotic sentiment; compassion is born of cruel action; wonder is born of the heroic; and the fearful is born from the disgusting.”

Cattāro rasā iccāhu.

Thus, they say there are four sentiments (rasa).

Bībhacchanti vadha bandhane, cho, abbhāsikārassa dīgho. Vassa bho, dhassa co bībhaccho. Ruddo devatā asseti ruddaṃ. Vuttañca –

Killing and imprisonment are considered disgusting. [The text continues with an obscure grammatical analysis.] The deity Rudra is its presiding deity, hence it is called 'rudraṃ'. And it is said:

“Siṅgāro haridevohi, hāso pamathadevato;

Karuṇo yamadevo tu, ruddo ruddādhidevato”ti saddakappaddume rodrapadepi.

“The erotic sentiment has Hari as its deity, laughter has the Pramathas as its deities; compassion has Yama as its deity, and the furious sentiment has Rudra as its chief deity.”

Ettha ca kāmakodhahāsādikato cittavikāro bhāvo “bhāvayati pakāsayati kavino adhippāya”nti katvā. So ca ṭhāyī byabhicārī sāttiko ceti tividho. Tatra –

Here, the mental modification arising from lust, anger, laughter, and so on, is called a 'bhāva' (state), because it 'develops and manifests the poet's intention'. And that bhāva is threefold: stable, transient, and affective. Among these:

Hāso rati ca kāruññaṃ,

Kodhu’ssāha bhayaṃ tathā;

Jigucchā vimhayo ceti,

Ṭhāyībhāvā pakittitā.

Laughter, delight, and compassion, anger, energy, and fear as well, disgust and wonder—these are declared to be the stable states.

Byabhicārī tu tettiṃsappabhedā. Yathā –

The transient states, however, are of thirty-three kinds, as follows:

Saṅkā gilāni nibbedo,

Tathā issā mado samo;

Ālasyaṃ dīnatā cintā,

Moho sati matī dhiti.

Doubt, sickness, and weariness, likewise envy, pride, and exhaustion; sloth, dejection, anxious thought, delusion, mindfulness, wisdom, and resolve.

Cāpalyaṃ [M 0.0086] hariso pīḷā,

Āvego jaḷatu’ggatā;

Suttaṃ vitakko tāso ca,

Gabbhu’ssukko visādatā.

Restlessness, gaiety, oppression, excitement, stupor, harshness; sleep, thought, and terror, conceit, eagerness, and despondency.

Niddā’bahitthā’marisā,

Maraṇaṃ byādhireva ca;

Apamāro ca ummādo,

Vibodho tiṃsa tuttarā.

Drowsiness, concealment, and impatience, death and disease as well; epilepsy and madness, and awakening—thirty-three in total.

Sāttiko aṭṭhavidho. Yathā –

The affective states are of eight kinds, as follows:

Thambho sedo ca romañco,

Sarabhedo tu vepathu;

Vevaṇṇa’massupalayā,

Iccete aṭṭha sāttikāti.

Stiffness, sweat, and hairs standing on end, breaking of voice, and trembling; change of color, tears, and fainting—thus, these are the eight affective states.

Thirattā ekantikattā ṭhāyī. Byabhicārī anekantikattā. Yathā nāṭikāya siṅgāro ṭhāyī, tadupakārā hāsādayo byabhicārino, moharāgadosā eva saṅkhyabhāsāya sattarajotamānītyuccante. Tatra sattena āsayena nibbatto sāttiko. Bhāvassa bodhako abhinayo anubhāvo “anu pacchā bhāvayati pakāsayatī”ti katvā.

A stable state is so called because of its permanence and singularity. A transient state is so called because of its non-singularity. Just as in a drama, the erotic sentiment is stable, while laughter and other emotions that support it are transient. Delusion, lust, and hatred are called sattva, rajas, and tamas in the language of Sāṅkhya. Among them, that which arises from the disposition (āsaya) characterized by sattva is called sāttika. The expression (abhinaya) that reveals a bhāva is an anubhāva, because it 'causes the bhāva to arise and manifest afterwards'.

Tatra sambhogasabhāvo yo ratyākhyo bhāvo, tassa locanacāturiyabhamukkhepamihitavibbhamacittaṅgahārivākyādi anubhāvo. Vuttañca –

Therein, for the state called 'rati' (delight), which is of the nature of enjoyment, its anubhāva (expression) consists of skillful eye movements, raising of eyebrows, smiles, affected gestures, heart-stealing words, and so on. And it is said:

“Tassa locanacātura-bhamukkhepasitavibbhamo;

Cittaṅgahārivākyādi, anubhāvo pakittito”ti.

“Skillful eye movements, raising of eyebrows, smiles, and affected gestures, heart-stealing words, and so on—these are proclaimed as its anubhāva.”

Viyogassa [M 0.0087] tu anubhāvo –

The anubhāva (expression) of separation, however, is:

Abhilāpo tathā cintā,

Tassa saraṇakittanā;

Ubbego ca vilāpo ca,

Ummādo byādhireva ca;

Jaḷatā maraṇañceva,

Dasevettha pakittitā.

Longing and also anxiety, recollection and praise of that person; agitation and lamentation, madness and disease as well; stupor and death—these ten are proclaimed here.

Hāsassa tu vikārakālādi anubhāvo, yo tu karuṇo.

The anubhāva (expression) of laughter, however, is distortion, untimely actions, and so on, while that of compassion is:

Assusāsehi vevaṇṇa-

Thambhagattasatikkhayā;

Paridevitasokehi,

Abhinayo sasūribhi.

With tears and sighs, discoloration, stiffness of body, and loss of memory; with lamentation and sorrow, the performance is by the wise.

Karacaraṇavadanavepathugattathambhahadayakampanasukkhoṭṭhatālukaṇṭhehi bhayānako niccamabhinayo.

The fearful sentiment is always expressed through trembling of hands, feet, and face, stiffness of body, pounding of the heart, and dryness of the lips, palate, and throat.

Ruddassa tu bhūkuṭyādi anubhāvo.

The anubhāva (expression) of the furious sentiment, however, is frowning and so on.

Vīro’bhinīyate cāga-

Vesārajjādito tathā;

Akkhepasūcatādīhi,

Therasorādito bhave.

The heroic sentiment is expressed through generosity, confidence, and so on; and also through hints, indications, and the like, as befits elders and the brave.

Bībhacchassa tu –

For the disgusting sentiment, however:

Ayaṃ pacchādanā byatta-

Pādabāhacchikūlanā;

Ubbejanādīhi mato,

Tajjehi’bhinayo sadā.

This performance is understood to consist of covering oneself, drawing back the feet and arms, frightening actions, and so on; the performance is always with actions born thereof.

Abbhutaṃ [M 0.0088] pana –

The wondrous sentiment, however, is:

Dantalocanavitthārā,

Pasādopasamādihi;

Romañcasedatāsassu,

Sādhuvādehi dassaye.

With wide eyes and baring of teeth, with joy, tranquility, and so on, with goosebumps, sweat, and tears, it should be shown with words of approval.

Sāttikānaṃ tvaṭṭhannaṃ thambhasedaromañcasarabhedavepathuvevaṇṇamassupalayānaṃ yathākkamaṃ nikriyatā, vāta, ccāsīta, dobhaggaḷā’pāṅgapūraṇa, mukhacchāyāvipallāsa, locanamajjana, mahipātādayo abhinayā.

For the eight affective states—stiffness, sweat, goosebumps, breaking of voice, trembling, discoloration, tears, and fainting—their respective performances (abhinayā) are, in order: inactivity, wind, extreme cold, crookedness, filling of the eye's corners, change of facial complexion, eye-rolling, falling to the ground, and so on.

Evaṃ byabhicārīnampi nibbeda, gilāni, saṅki’ssā, mada, samā’lasyādīnaṃ yathākkamaṃ sāsa, santāpa, disāvalokana, guṇamacchera, bhīta, ṅgamaddana, samādayo abhinayāti.

Thus, for the transient states as well, such as weariness, sickness, doubt, envy, pride, fatigue, sloth, and so on, their respective performances (abhinayā) are, in order: sighing, torment, looking in all directions, begrudging of virtues, fear, massaging the limbs, fatigue, and so on.

Byabhicārīsu saṅkā nāma āsaṅkacittatā. Gilāni gelaññatā. Nibbedo attāvamānanaṃ. Mado pamādukkaṃso. Samo khedo. Dīnatā cetaso dukkhatā. Dhiti santoso. Hariso cetopasādo. Pīḷā ruddācārādīhi mukhavikāro. Āvego sambhamo. Jaḷatā appaṭipatti, uggatā dāruṇattaṃ. Suttaṃ supanaṃ. Tāso cittakkhobho. Ussāho ussukkaṃ. Visādo khedo. Abahitthā ākāraguttatā. Amariso akkhamatā. Vibodho viniddatā. Sesā papañcabhayā na vitthāritāti. Rasavaṇṇanā.

Among the transient states, doubt (saṅkā) is a suspicious mind. Sickness (gilāni) is illness. Weariness (nibbeda) is self-contempt. Pride (mada) is excessive negligence. Fatigue (samo) is weariness. Dejection (dīnatā) is mental unhappiness. Resolve (dhiti) is contentment. Joy (hariso) is mental serenity. Oppression (pīḷā) is facial distortion due to harsh behavior and so on. Excitement (āvego) is flurry. Stupor (jaḷatā) is non-comprehension; harshness (uggatā) is severity. Sleep (suttaṃ) is slumber. Terror (tāso) is mental agitation. Eagerness (ussāho) is zeal. Despondency (visādo) is weariness. Concealment (abahitthā) is guarding one's demeanor. Impatience (amariso) is intolerance. Awakening (vibodho) is wakefulness. The rest are not elaborated for fear of prolixity. This is the description of sentiments.

105. Silokena vacaso nāmāni. Bhāsitabbanti bhāsitaṃ. Lapa vacane, lapitaṃ. Bhāsīyateti bhāsā. Voharīyateti [M 0.0089] vohāro, hara haraṇe vipubbo, “vohāra vacane”ti vā dhātu. Vuccateti vacanaṃ. Vacopi, manogaṇoyaṃ. Uccateti utti,ti. Vuccateti vācā, a. Giṇanti saddāyanti tanti girā, ge sadde, iro, gāyitabbāti vā girā. Vāyate saddāyateti vāṇī, yu, ī ca, paresaṃ mammavijjhanaṭṭhena vāṇo viyāti vā vāṇī, ī. Bharato nāma satthakāro isi, tassesā bhāratī. Kathīyateti kathitā. Vuccateti vacī, ī. Brahmī, sarovatītipi vacaso nāmāni.

105. The names of speech, by verse. That which is spoken is 'bhāsita'. From 'lapa' (to speak), 'lapita'. That which is uttered is 'bhāsā'. That which is expressed is 'vohāra', from 'hara' (to carry) with the prefix 'vi', or from the root 'vohāra' meaning 'to speak'. That which is said is 'vacana'. Also 'vaco'; this belongs to the manas-group. That which is uttered is 'utti'. That which is said is 'vācā', with suffix 'a'. Because they sing or make a sound, it is 'girā'; from 'ge' (to sound), with suffix 'iro', or 'that which is to be sung' is 'girā'. Because it sounds or makes a sound, it is 'vāṇī', with suffixes 'yu' and 'ī'; or like an arrow ('vāṇa') in piercing the vital points of others, it is 'vāṇī', with 'ī'. Bharata is the name of a sage, a composer of treatises; his speech is 'bhāratī'. That which is told is 'kathitā'. That which is said is 'vacī', with 'ī'. Brahmī and Sarasvatī are also names of speech.

106. Ekamevākhyātapadaṃ yattha ekākhyāto savisesanena kārakapadena sahitattā sakārako padacayo sambandhattho padasamudāyo vākyaṃ nāma siyā, yathā – vessantaro rājā sukhavipākaṃ kammaṃ karoti, puriso gacchati. Ākhyātaggahaṇañcettha kriyāsaddopalakkhaṇaṃ, tena devadatto kaṭaṃ katavā iccādīnipi vākyaṃ nāma siyā. Amarakose pana – “tisyādyantacayo vākyaṃ, kriyā vā kārakānvitā”ti amara 6.2 dvīhi lakkhaṇehi vākyamāha. Tassattho – tisyādyantacayo tyādisyādyantapadānaṃ cayo samūho sambandhattho vākyaṃ, taṃ yathā – uccaṃ paṭhati, odanaṃ pacati. Tathā ca bhāvākhyaṃ ākhyātaṃ sābyayakārakavisesanaṃ vākyaṃ, ākhyātaṃ tyādyantaṃ sābyayaṃ vā sakārakaṃ vā savisesanaṃ vā vākyamuccate. Tyādiggahaṇaṃ kriyāsaddopalakkhaṇaṃ, tena devadatto [M 0.0090] kaṭaṃ katavā iccādīnipi vākyaṃ. Upalakkhaṇanirapekkhaṃ aparaṃ vākyalakkhaṇamāha “kriyā vā kārakānvitā”ti. Kriyāpadaṃ vā kārakasambandhaṃ vākyaṃ, yathā – rājā gacchati, rājā gato. Imasmiṃ pakkhe sābyayassapi anabyayassapi sabbassa kriyākārakapadasamūhassa vākyattamāha.

106. A collection of words having a single finite verb, accompanied by words indicating syntactic roles with their modifiers, and possessing a connected meaning, may be called a sentence (vākya). For example: 'King Vessantara performs a deed with a happy result,' or 'A man goes.' Here, the term 'finite verb' is indicative of any action-word; therefore, 'Devadatta made a mat' and so on may also be called a sentence. In the Amarakośa, however, a sentence is described by two characteristics: 'a collection of words ending in ti, sya, etc.' or 'an action connected with syntactic roles.' Its meaning is: a collection of words ending in ti, sya, etc., with a connected meaning, is a sentence, for example: 'He recites aloud,' 'He cooks rice.' Similarly, a finite verb ending in ti, etc., whether with an indeclinable, a syntactic role, or a modifier, is called a sentence. The mention of ti, etc., is indicative of any action-word, so 'Devadatta made a mat' is also a sentence. Another definition, independent of indicative markers, is 'an action connected with syntactic roles.' A verb-word connected with syntactic roles is a sentence, for example: 'The king goes,' 'The king has gone.' In this view, any collection of words indicating actions and syntactic roles, with or without indeclinables, is considered a sentence.

Bhayādīhi yaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vā tikkhattuṃ vā udīraṇaṃ kathanaṃ “sappo sappo, vijjha vijjhā”tyādikaṃ, taṃ āmeḍitaṃ ñeyyaṃ. Meḍi ummādane, āpubbo dvattikkhattumuccāraṇe vattati. Yathā “etadeva yadā vākyaṃ, āmeḍayati vāsavo” “harivaṃse”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ. “Devadattenāmeḍo kato” iccatrāpyayamevattho, sokādinā hi “bhātā bhātā”ityuccārīyate, bhāve kammani ca to. Kammañca padaṃ vākyamhā.

That which is uttered or spoken twice or thrice out of fear and so on, such as 'A snake! A snake!' or 'Pierce! Pierce!', should be known as āmeḍita (repetition). The root 'meḍi' is in the sense of agitation; with the prefix 'ā', it is used in the sense of uttering two or three times. As in: 'When Vāsava repeats this very speech.' In 'A repetition was made by Devadatta,' here too the meaning is the same. For due to sorrow and so on, one cries out, 'Brother! Brother!' The suffix 'ta' is used in the sense of state (bhāva) and action (kammani). And the action (kamma) is a word from the sentence.

107. Āmeḍitassa visayaṃ dassetumāha “bhaye”ccādi. “Sappo sappo, coro coro”tyādīsu bhaye. “Vijjha vijjha, pahara paharā”tyādīsu kodhe. “Sādhu sādhū”tyādīsu pasaṃsāyaṃ. “Gaccha gaccha, lunāhi lunāhī”tyādīsu turite. “Āgaccha āgacchā”tyādīsu kotūhale. “Buddho buddhoti cintayanto”tyādīsu acchare. “Abhikkamathāyasmanto abhikkamathāyasmanto”tyādīsu hāse. “Kahaṃ ekaputtaka, kahaṃ ekaputtakā”tyādīsu soke. “Aho sukhaṃ aho sukha”ntyādīsu pasāde. Casaddo avuttasamuccayattho, tena garahā’sammānādīnaṃ saṅgaho [M 0.0091] daṭṭhabbo. Tattha “pāpo pāpo”tyādīsu garahāyaṃ. “Abhirūpaka, abhirūpakā”tyādīsu asammāne. Evametesu navasu, aññesu ca āmeḍitavacanaṃ budho paṇḍito kare kareyya yojeyya āmeḍanaṃ punappunuccāraṇaṃ āmeḍiyati vā punappunuccārīyatīti āmeḍitanti katvā.

107. To show the scope of repetition, it is said: 'in fear,' and so on. In cases like 'A snake! A snake!' or 'A thief! A thief!', it is for fear. In 'Pierce! Pierce!' or 'Strike! Strike!', it is for anger. In 'Good! Good!', it is for praise. In 'Go! Go!' or 'Cut! Cut!', it is for urgency. In 'Come! Come!', it is for curiosity. In 'Thinking, "The Buddha! The Buddha!"', it is for wonder. In 'Come forth, Venerables! Come forth, Venerables!', it is for laughter. In 'Where is my only child? Where is my only child?', it is for sorrow. In 'Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness!', it is for joy. The particle 'ca' (and) serves to include what is unstated, and thus it should be understood as encompassing blame, disrespect, and so on. Here, in cases like 'Wicked! Wicked!', it is for blame. In 'Handsome one! Handsome one!', it is for disrespect. Thus, in these nine and other instances, a wise and learned person should employ the repeated utterance, considering that repetition is repeated utterance, or that which is repeatedly uttered is called āmeḍita.

108. Iru, yaju, sāmanti tayo vedā siyuṃ, tatra irusaddo nārī itthiliṅgo. Ica thutiyaṃ, iccante devā etāyāti iru, u, cassa ro. Yajante aneneti yaju, u. So antakammani, karaṇe mo, soyanti pāpamaneneti sāmaṃ, ossā, “sā tanukaraṇāvasānesū”ti vā dhātvattho. Vidanti dhammametehīti vedā.

108. The three Vedas are 'Iru', 'Yaju', and 'Sāma'. Among these, the word 'Iru' is feminine in gender. From 'ic' in the sense of praise; 'the gods praise by this', hence 'Iru', with the suffix 'u' and 'c' changing to 'r'. They sacrifice by this, hence 'yaju', with the suffix 'u'. From the root 'so' in the sense of ending, with 'mo' as the instrumental suffix, 'sāmaṃ' means 'they destroy evil by this'; or alternatively, the root meaning is from 'sā' meaning 'to make subtle or to conclude'. They know the Dhamma through these, hence 'vedā'.

Ete eva tayo vedā tayī nāma, tayo avayavā assāti tayī. Ayaṃ tayīsaddo nārī itthiliṅgo. Tikaṃ vede. Munāti jānāti dhammaṃ anenāti manto, to, ussa a. Suyyate dhammaṃ etāyāti suti. Itthiyaṃ sutisaddo.

These same three Vedas are called 'Tayī', meaning 'having three parts'. This word 'Tayī' is feminine in gender. The three Vedas are a 'Tika' (triad). One knows the Dhamma through this, hence 'manto' (from the root man, 'to know'); the suffix is 'ta', and 'u' becomes 'a'. The Dhamma is heard through this, hence 'suti'. The word 'suti' is feminine.

109. Vedasatthakārake dasa isayodassetumāha “aṭṭhako”ccādi. Atthaṃ hitaṃ, atthe vā satthe karotīti aṭṭhako. Vāmaṃ kalyāṇavacanaṃ karotīti vāmako, rassasarīrattā [M 0.0092] vā vāmano, so eva vāmako, nassa kakārattaṃ katvā. Vāmo nāma haro, so devo assa vāmadevo.

109. To point out the ten sages who composed the Vedic texts, it is said: 'Aṭṭhaka' and so on. 'Aṭṭhaka' means 'one who makes what is beneficial,' or 'one who makes meaning in the teaching.' 'Vāmaka' means 'one who makes auspicious speech,' or because of his short body, he is called 'Vāmana,' and that is the same as 'Vāmaka' by changing 'na' to 'ka'. 'Vāma' is a name of Hara; that god is his, hence Vāmadeva.

“Vāmaṃ sabye patīpe patīpeti paṭikūle ca, daviṇe daviṇeti dhane cātisundare;

Payodhare hare kāme, jaññā vāma’mapitthiya”nti.

Know 'vāma' in the sense of left and opposite, in wealth and extreme beauty, in breasts, in Hara, in desire, and also as unfavorable.

Hi nānatthasaṅgahe.

This is from the Nānatthasaṅgaha (Collection of Various Meanings).

Aṅgirasassa isino apaccaṃ aṅgiraso, citrasikhaṇḍino apaccaṃ putto. Atha vā aṅgimhi kāye raso siddhippatto pārado yassāti aṅgiraso. Teneva tassa puttaṃ surācariyaṃ “jīvo”ti vadati. Jīvayati raṇe asuranihate deveti jīvo amara 3.24 cintāmaṇiṭīkā oloketabbā. Bharatīti bhagu, bhaṃ vānakkhattaṃ gacchati jānātīti bhagu, u. Yamaṃ saṃyamaṃ dadāti paresanti yamado ca so dakkhiṇeyyaggittā aggi ceti yamadaggi, rāmassa pitā parasurāmassa pitā (saddakappaddume). Vasiṭṭhassa apaccaṃ vāsiṭṭho. Bhāradvājassa apaccaṃ bhāradvājo. Kassapassa apaccaṃ kassapo. Vessāmittassa apaccaṃ vessāmitto. Iti ime dasa isayo mantānaṃ vedānaṃ kattāro kārakā.

The descendant of the sage Aṅgirasa is Aṅgirasa, the son and descendant of Citrasikhaṇḍin. Or, he for whom mercury, the essence, attained perfection in his fiery body is Aṅgirasa. For that reason, his son, the teacher of the gods, is called 'Jīva.' He brings the gods to life when the asuras are slain in battle—thus, Jīva. As for Bhagu: he who goes to or knows the constellation Bha is Bhagu. As for Yamadaggi: he who gives restraint to others is Yamada, and because he is a fire worthy of offerings, he is also Agni; hence Yamadaggi, the father of Rāma. The descendant of Vasiṭṭha is Vāsiṭṭha. The descendant of Bhāradvāja is Bhāradvāja. The descendant of Kassapa is Kassapa. The descendant of Vessāmitta is Vessāmitto. Thus, these ten sages are the authors and makers of the mantras and the Vedas.

110. Vede dassetvā tassa chaḷaṅgāni dassetumāha “kappo”ccādi. Yaññakammānamupadesako kappo “kappate pabhavatī”ti katvā. Sādhusaddānamanvākhyāyakaṃ byākaraṇaṃ visesena ākarīyante pakaticcādinā ābyāpādyante anena [M 0.0093] saddāti, yu. Jotisatthaṃ gaṇanasatthaṃ subhāsubhakammaphalajotanakaṃ. Sikkhyante abbhasyante ajjhayante (ka.) etāyāti sikkhā, akārādivaṇṇānaṃ ṭhānakaraṇapayatanānaṃ paṭipādikā. Nicchayena, nissesato vā utti nirutti, vaṇṇāgamo vaṇṇavipariyayoccādikā. Chandasi anuṭṭhubhādivuttānaṃ paṭipādikā chandoviciti, etāni cha vedānaṃ aṅgānīti vadanti.

110. Having shown the Vedas, to show its six limbs, he says, 'Kappo,' etc. Kalpa is the instructor of sacrificial acts, because it is established and originates. Grammar is the explainer of correct words, because by this, words are specifically formed and derived by means of the base, etc. Astrology is the science of calculation, which illuminates the results of auspicious and inauspicious actions. That by which one learns and practices is called Śikṣā; it explains the place of articulation, the articulator, and the effort for letters such as 'a.' Nirutti is a certain or complete utterance, including letter augmentation, letter inversion, and so on. Chandoviciti explains meters such as Anuṣṭubh in prosody. These, they say, are the six limbs of the Vedas.

111. Purāvuttanibandhanapāyattā purāvuttaṃ, tassa pabandho vitthāro, santāno vā bhāratādiko bhāratayuddhakathādiko byāsādipakato gantho itihāso nāma, itihasaddo pārampariyopadese nipāto, itihā’tthi asminti itihāso.

111. Itihāsa is the name for a text of ancient accounts, so called because it depends on compositions of what was said in the past. It is a composition, elaboration, or lineage, such as the Bhārata and others—a text composed by Vyāsa and others concerning the story of the Bhārata war and so on. The word 'itiha' is an indeclinable particle in the sense of traditional instruction; because 'iti ha āsa' ('thus indeed it was') is in it, it is Itihāsa.

Rukkhādīnaṃ nāmapariyāyehi nāmappakāsakaṃ ratanamālādikaṃ satthaṃ nighaṇṭu nāma, sotiminā nighaṇṭusaddassa pulliṅgattaṃ dīpeti, sabbatrevaṃ. Tattha tatthāgatāni nāmāni nissesato ghaṭenti rāsīkaronti etthāti nighaṇṭu, bindāgamo, vacanīyavācakabhāvena atthaṃ saddañca nikhaṇḍati bhindati vibhajja dassetīti vā nikhaṇṭu, so eva khassa ghakāraṃ katvā nighaṇṭūti vutto. Rukkhādīnaṃ nāmappakāsakantiminā ekekassa atthassa anekapariyāyanāmappakāsakattaṃ vuttaṃ, nidassanamattañcetaṃ, anekesaṃ atthānaṃ ekasaddavacanīyatāpakāsakavasenapi [M 0.0094] tassa ganthassa pavattattā dī. ni. ṭī. 1.256; ma. ni. ṭī. 1.22; a. ni. ṭī. 2.3.59; sārattha. ṭī. 1.tatiyasaṅgītikathāvaṇṇanā.

A treatise such as the Ratnamālā, which makes known the names of trees and other things by way of synonyms, is called a Nighaṇṭu (lexicon). By the word 'so' [in the verse], he indicates the masculine gender of the word 'nighaṇṭu'; this is so everywhere. Because names that occur in various places are completely collected and amassed herein, it is a Nighaṇṭu; there is a nasal insertion. Or, because it analyzes, breaks down, and shows by dividing the meaning and the word through the relationship of the signified and the signifier, it is a Nikhaṇṭu. That very word, with 'kh' changed to 'gh', is called Nighaṇṭu. By this phrase, 'which makes known the names of trees and other things,' it is said that it makes known the many synonymous names for each single meaning. And this is merely an indication, for that text also proceeds by way of showing that many meanings can be expressed by a single word.

112. Loke yaṃ vitaṇḍavādīnaṃ satthaṃ, taṃ lokāyatanti viññeyyaṃ. Tanu vitthāre, aññamaññaviruddhaṃ, saggamokkhaviruddhaṃ vā tanonti etthāti vitaṇḍo, ḍo, ṇattaṃ, viruddhena vā vādadaṇḍena tāḷenti ettha vādinoti vitaṇḍo, taḍi tāḷane, adesampi hi yaṃ nissāya vādīnaṃ vādo pavatto, taṃ tesaṃ desatopi upacāravasena vuccati, yathā “cakkhuṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, etthesā taṇhā pahīyamānā pahīyati, ettha nirujjhamānā nirujjhatī”ti dī. ni. 2.401; ma. ni. 1.134; vibha. 204. Lokāti bālalokā, te ettha āyatanti ussahanti vāyamanti vādassādenāti lokāyataṃ, āyatiṃ hitaṃ tena loko na yatati na īhatīti vā lokāyataṃ, tañhi ganthaṃ nissāya sattā puññakriyāya cittampi na uppādenti.

112. Whatever is the treatise of the sophists in the world, that should be known as Lokāyata. The root 'tanu' is in the sense of 'to spread.' Because they spread herein what is mutually contradictory, or what is opposed to heaven and liberation, it is Vitaṇḍa. Or, because they strike the debaters herein with the rod of contradictory argument, it is Vitaṇḍa; the root 'taḍi' is in the sense of 'to strike.' Indeed, even a non-place which debaters rely on for their debate to proceed is metaphorically called their place, just as it is said: 'The eye in the world is a dear and delightful form; herein this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; herein, when ceasing, it ceases.' 'Loka' means the world of foolish people. Because they strive, exert themselves, and make an effort herein for the pleasure of debate, it is Lokāyata. Or, because by means of it the world does not strive or endeavor for future welfare, it is Lokāyata. For, relying on that text, beings do not even give rise to the thought of meritorious action.

Yo kavīnaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ hito kavittabhogasampattādipayojanakaro kriyākappavikappo kavīnaṃ kriyāsaṅkhātakappabandhanavidhividhāyako subodhālaṅkārādiko gantho, so keṭubhaṃ nāma, kiṭanti gacchanti kosallaṃ kavayo bandhanesu etenāti keṭubhaṃ, kiṭa gatiyaṃ, abho, assukāro, atha vā kiṭati gameti kriyādivibhāgaṃ, taṃ vā anavasesena pariyādānato gamento pūretīti keṭubhaṃ, ubha, umbha pūraṇe.

That text which is beneficial to poets and scholars, which serves the purpose of attaining poetic wealth and other benefits, which is the arrangement and diversification of poetic works, which prescribes the method for the composition of poetic works for poets, such as the Subodhālaṅkāra and others, is named Keṭubha. Because poets go to skill in compositions by means of this, it is Keṭubha; the root 'kiṭa' is in the sense of 'to go.' Alternatively, it causes the division of poetic works and so on to be understood; or, causing it to be completely comprehended, it fills, hence Keṭubha; the roots 'ubha' and 'umbha' are in the sense of 'to fill'.

Vacībhedādilakkhaṇā [M 0.0095] kriyā kappīyati vikappīyati etenāti kriyākappo. So pana vaṇṇapadasambandhapadatthādivibhāgato atibahu vikappoti āha “kriyākappavikappo”ti, idañca mūlakriyākappaganthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. So hi mahāvisayo satasahassaparimāṇo nayacaritādipakaraṇaṃ nalacaritādipakaraṇaṃ (?).

A poetic work, characterized by divisions of speech and so on, is arranged and diversified by this, hence it is called 'Kriyākappo.' However, because it is greatly diversified due to divisions of letters, words, connections, word-meanings, and so on, he said 'Kriyākappavikappo.' This is said with reference to the root text, the Kriyākappagantha. Indeed, it has a vast scope, a measure of a hundred thousand, and is a treatise on method, conduct, and so on.

113. Upaladdho kenapyattho yassaṃ sā upaladdhatthā, iti ākhyāyikātyuccate ākhyāyate nāyakānusāsakacaritamassanti, saññāyaṃ ṇvu.

113. That in which a subject matter has been obtained by someone is 'upaladdhatthā.' Thus it is called an Ākhyāyikā (narrative), because the conduct of the hero-instructor is related in it. In the sense of a name, the suffix is 'ṇvu'.

Pabandheneva ca savitthārena kappanaṃ yassaṃ sā pabandhakappanā, kādambarīpabhuti. Kathīyatīti kathā.

And that which is a detailed compositional arrangement is a 'pabandhakappanā,' such as the Kādambarī and so on. That which is narrated is a Kathā.

Atthā bhūmihiraññādayo, tatra padhānaṃ bhūmi itaresaṃ tappabhavattā, tesaṃ ajjane pālane ca upāyabhūtaṃ satthaṃ atthasatthaṃ, payānakyādipaṇītaṃ bahasvaticābbīkyādipraṇītaṃ (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 6.5), tasmiṃ daṇḍanītisaddo pavatto. Sāmādīnaṃ catutthopāyo vadhabandhanādilakkhaṇo daṇḍo, tassa nīti paṇayanaṃ daṇḍanīti, pāyena nītissa daṇḍena byappadeso, vadhadosabāhulyena pāyaso daṇḍassa paṇayanato, daṇḍanītyatthattā satthañca daṇḍanīti.

The objects of wealth are land, gold, and so on; among them, land is primary because the others originate from it. The treatise that is a means for acquiring and protecting them is the Arthasāstra, expounded by Cāṇakya and others. In that context, the term 'Daṇḍanīti' is current. The fourth means among conciliation and others is 'Daṇḍa' (punishment), characterized by execution, imprisonment, etc. The application of that policy is 'Daṇḍanīti.' Generally, the policy is designated by punishment because punishment is generally applied due to the abundance of faults deserving of execution. And because the treatise has the meaning of 'Daṇḍanīti,' the treatise is also 'Daṇḍanīti'.

Dvayaṃ kathāyaṃ. Vutto anuvattanīyo anto parisamatti yassa attano kāriyabhāgassa pāpanatoti vuttanto. Pavattante kāriyā yassaṃ pavatti,ti. Cakārena vuttaudantādayo gahitā. Kāriyassa vutti atratthīti assatthyatthe [M 0.0096] ṇo. Uggato anto parisamatti yassa udanto.

A dyad for 'story.' Vuttanta is that of which the end or conclusion is spoken and to be followed, because it leads to the attainment of one's own share of action. Pavatti is that in which actions proceed. By the word 'ca,' 'vutta,' 'udanta,' and so on are included. Because the occurrence of an action is herein, the suffix 'ṇo' is in the sense of 'possessing that.' Udanta is that of which the end or conclusion has arisen.

114. Adhivacanantaṃ nāme. Sañjānanti etāyāti saññā, a. Ākhyāyate etāyāti ākhyā. Ahvayate etāyāti avhā, hu sadde, vhe avhāneti vā dhātu, a. Sammā ājānāti, samaṃ vā jānāti etāyāti samaññā. Abhidhīyate yena, yu. Namyate abbhassate asminti nāmaṃ, namati nāmayatīti vā nāmaṃ. Ahvāyateti avhayo, kamme yo. Nāmameva nāmadheyyaṃ. Nāmarūpehi nāmasaddehi (ka.) bhāgarūpanāmehi dheyyo (pāṇini 5.4.36 vā) sakatthe dheyyo yadādinā, tiṭṭhati vā ettha atthoti dheyyaṃ, dharīyate uccāriyateti vā dheyyaṃ, nāmameva dheyyaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ. Adhīnaṃ vacanaṃ adhivacanaṃ, kena adhīnaṃ? Atthena. Puṭṭhassa paṭivacanaṃ paṭivākyaṃ. Paṭigataṃ pacchāgataṃ vākyaṃ paṭivākyaṃ. Uttarīyate atikkamyate yenāti uttaraṃ.

114. The list ending with 'adhivacana' are synonyms for 'name.' One perceives by this, hence Saññā. It is declared by this, hence Ākhyā. It is called by this, hence Avhā; from the root 'hu' in the sense of 'sound,' or the root 'vhe' in the sense of 'to call.' One knows rightly or knows equally by this, hence Samaññā. That by which it is expressed is Abhidhāna. Meaning inclines towards or resorts to this, hence Nāma; or it inclines or causes to incline, hence Nāma. It is called, hence Avhayo; with the suffix 'yo' in the passive sense. Name itself is Nāmadheyya. Meaning is placed (dheyya) herein, or it is held and uttered, hence Dheyya; name itself is Dheyya, hence Nāmadheyya. Speech that is governed by meaning is Adhivacana. The reply to what is asked is Paṭivākya. Speech that comes after is Paṭivākya. That by which one gets beyond is Uttara.

115. Tikaṃ pucchāyaṃ. Pucchitabboti pañho, ñātumicchito hi attho pañho nāma. Puccha pucchane, cassa ño, chassa ho, ussa a, pañha pucchanetipi dhātu. Yuja yoge, anuyuñjitabbo [M 0.0097] pucchitabboti anuyogo. Pucchanaṃ, pucchitabbāti vā pucchā. Eteneva nayena dvīsupi bhāvasādhanampi kattabbameva.

115. A triad for 'question.' What should be asked is a Pañha; for a matter that one wishes to know is called a question. The root 'puccha' is in the sense of 'to ask'; its 'c' becomes 'ñ,' 'ch' becomes 'h,' and 'u' becomes 'a'; there is also a root 'pañha' in the sense of 'to ask.' The root 'yuj' is in the sense of 'to join'; what should be inquired into or asked is an Anuyoga. The act of asking, or what should be asked, is Pucchā. In this same way, for both of these, the derivation in the abstract sense should also be made.

Catukkaṃ nidassane. Pakatena sadisaṃ nidasseti etenāti nidassanaṃ, pakatassopapādanaṃ vākyaṃ. Upogghaññate upohaññate (?) paṭipādīyate anenāti upogghāto. Upa upubbo hanadhātu paṭipādanattho. Dassīyate anenāti diṭṭhanto, anto, diṭṭho vā pakatassa anto parisamatti yenāti diṭṭhanto. Sabbatrāpi vā kammasādhanampi kattabbaṃ. Udāharīyati pakatassopapādanāyāti udāharaṇaṃ.

A tetrad for 'illustration.' By this one points out what is similar to the subject at hand, hence Nidassana (illustration); a statement that supports the subject at hand. By this one is led to the topic, hence Upogghāta (introduction). The root 'han' with the prefix 'upa' is in the sense of 'to lead to.' It is shown by this, hence Diṭṭhanta (example); or, that by which the end or conclusion of the subject at hand is seen, hence Diṭṭhanta. Or in all cases, the derivation in the passive sense should also be made. It is brought forth for the support of the subject at hand, hence Udāharaṇa (citation).

116. Catukkaṃ saṅkhepe. Samāti tulyatthā. Saṅkhipīyate ekadesato kathīyatīti saṅkhepo, khipa peraṇe. Saṃharīyate saṅkhepena paccākhyāyate etenāti saṃhāro. Samasyate saṅkhipīyateti samāso, asu khepane. Saṅkhepena gayhate anenāti saṅgaho.

116. A tetrad for 'abridgement.' It is abridged, spoken of in part, hence Saṅkhepa (summary); from 'khipa' in the sense of 'to throw.' By this it is collected or concisely explained, hence Saṃhāro (compendium). It is compounded or abridged, hence Samāso (combination); from 'asu' in the sense of 'to throw.' By this it is grasped concisely, hence Saṅgaho (collection).

“Tvaṃ sataṃ suvaṇṇaṃ dhārayasi”ityādikaṃ tucchabhāsanaṃ abhūtabhāsanaṃ abbhakkhānaṃ nāma. Asaccena akkhānaṃ bhāsanaṃ abbhakkhānaṃ.

'You possess a hundred gold coins,' and so forth, such empty speech, such false speech, is called 'unfounded accusation.' Speech that is an accusation based on untruth is an 'unfounded accusation.'

117. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0098] vivādāya vibhāgavisaye iṇavādādivisaye (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 6.9). Viruddhaṃ katvā avaharati vadati yanti vohāro. Viruddhaṃ katvā vadati yanti vivādo. Sabbatra bhāvasādhanaṃ vā yujjati. “Musāvādaṃ vadanto ghorāni tvaṃ narakāni yassasī”tyādisarūpaṃ sapanaṃ. Sapa akkose, tho, sapatho.

117. Two terms for dispute in the matter of division. When one acts or speaks contrarily, that is 'vohāro' (conduct). When one speaks contrarily, that is 'vivādo' (dispute). Everywhere, the abstract noun form is also applicable. An oath is of such a nature as, 'Speaking falsehood, you will go to terrible hells.' 'Sapatho' (oath) is from the root 'sapa' in the sense of 'to curse,' with the suffix 'tho'.

Tikaṃ khyāte. Yajati etenāthi yaso, jassa so, sabbattha yātīti vā yaso, so, yasati payasatīti vā yaso. Silokati pattharatīti siloko, siloka saṅghāte. Kitta saddane, kittīyate kathīyateti kitti, i. Samaññā ca khyāte, saṃ āpubbo jānāti khyāte. Tathā hi “ñāto, abhiññāto, saṅkhyāto, vissuto, samaññāto”ti ratanakose vuttaṃ. Uccadhaninā saddanaṃ ghosanā nāma, ghusa sadde, ghusanaṃ saddanaṃ ghosanā.

Three terms for 'renowned.' One sacrifices through this, hence 'yaso' (fame); or, it goes everywhere, hence 'yaso'; or, one strives or prospers, hence 'yaso.' It spreads, hence 'siloko' (renown); the root 'siloka' is in the sense of 'to compose.' The root 'kitta' is in the sense of 'to praise'; it is praised, it is spoken of, hence 'kitti' (reputation), with the suffix 'i.' And 'samaññā' (designation) is also for 'renowned'; the root 'jānāti' (to know) with the prefixes 'saṃ' and 'ā' means 'renowned.' Thus it is said in the Ratanakosa: 'known, well-known, reckoned, celebrated, designated.' A loud sound is called 'ghosanā' (proclamation); the root 'ghusa' is in the sense of 'to sound'; 'ghusanaṃ' (sounding) is 'ghosanā.'

118-119. Dvayaṃ paṭisadde. Ghusanaṃ ghoso, taṃ paṭigato, dutiyāsamāso. Evaṃ ravaṃ paṭigato paṭiravo. Atha [M 0.0099] vā ghosassa patirūpo paṭighoso. Ravassa patirūpo paṭiravo. Paṭisuti, paṭiddhanītipi paṭisaddassa nāmāni, vacīmukhaṃ vacanopakkamo upaññāso nāma, upanipubbo āsa upavesane, upa paṭhamaṃ purimavacanassa samīpaṃ vā nyāso ṭhapanaṃ upaññāso, nyassa ño.

118-119. Two terms for 'echo.' A sounding is 'ghoso'; that which has returned to it is 'paṭighoso,' a compound of the second case. Similarly, that which has returned to a noise is 'paṭiravo.' Alternatively, that which is similar to a sound is 'paṭighoso.' That which is similar to a noise is 'paṭiravo.' 'Paṭisuti' and 'paṭiddhanī' are also names for 'paṭisadda' (echo). The beginning of speech, the commencement of speaking, is called 'upaññāso.' The root 'āsa' with the prefixes 'upa' and 'ni' is in the sense of 'placing.' Or, 'upaññāso' is the placing or setting down of the first utterance near the prior speech; the 'ny' of 'nyāso' becomes 'ñ'.

Sattakaṃ thutiyaṃ. Kattha silāghāyaṃ, yu, kathanaṃ vāasarūpadvibhāvavasena katthanā. Silāgha katthane, silāghā. Sīlassa vā sabhāgaguṇassa āhananaṃ sīlāghā, sā eva rassaṃ katvā silāghā. Vaṇṇa pasaṃsāyaṃ, vaṇṇīyateti vaṇṇanā. Nu thutiyaṃ,ti, nuti. Thu abhitthave,ti, thuti. Thoma silāghāyaṃ, thomanaṃ. Papubbo saṃsa pasaṃsane, a.

Seven terms for 'praise.' The root 'kattha' is in the sense of 'to boast'; with the suffix 'yu,' it becomes 'katthanā,' a form of speaking. The root 'silāgha' is in the sense of 'to praise,' hence 'silāghā.' Or, the extolling of virtue or a similar quality is 'sīlāghā'; that same word, when shortened, becomes 'silāghā.' The root 'vaṇṇa' is in the sense of 'to praise'; it is praised, hence 'vaṇṇanā.' The root 'nu' is in the sense of 'to praise'; with the suffix 'ti,' it becomes 'nuti.' The root 'thu' is in the sense of 'to extol'; with the suffix 'ti,' it becomes 'thuti.' The root 'thoma' is in the sense of 'to praise,' hence 'thomanaṃ.' The root 'saṃsa' with the prefix 'pa' is in the sense of 'to praise,' with the suffix 'a.'

Sikhaṇḍīnaṃ mayūrānaṃ nādo nadaravo kekā nāma, kā sadde, keiti kāyatīti kekā, kammani a, atha vā kāyati, kāyanaṃ vā kā, ke mayūre pavattā kā kekā, aluttasamāso. Gajānaṃ nādo koñcanādo nāma, koñcasakuṇanādasadiso nādo koñcanādo. Hayānaṃ assānaṃ dhani saddo hesā nāma, hesa abrattasadde, hesanaṃ hesā, he iti pavattatīti vā hesā.

The sound or cry of crested peacocks is called 'kekā.' The root 'kā' is in the sense of 'to sound'; it sounds 'ke,' hence 'kekā,' with the suffix 'a' in the sense of the object. Alternatively, it sounds; the act of sounding is 'kā'; the sound 'kā' that occurs in peacocks is 'kekā,' a non-elided compound. The sound of elephants is called 'koñcanādo'; a sound similar to the cry of the koñca bird is 'koñcanādo.' The sound or cry of horses, of steeds, is called 'hesā'; the root 'hesa' is in the sense of 'to make an unarticulated sound'; 'hesanaṃ' (neighing) is 'hesā,' or it is called 'hesā' because the sound 'he' occurs.

120-121. Dvayaṃ pariyāye. Paribyattamatthaṃ ayanti gacchanti bujjhanti etenāti pariyāyo. Eko attho punappunaṃ vuccati [M 0.0100] yenāti vevacanaṃ. Dvayaṃ sākacchāyaṃ. Saha, sammā vā avirodhena kathā sākacchā, saṃkathā ca. To, thassa co, tassa cho.

120-121. Two terms for 'synonym' or 'mode.' They go to or understand a well-explained meaning by this, hence 'pariyāyo.' That by which one meaning is repeatedly said is 'vevacanaṃ.' Two terms for 'conversation.' Talk together, or rightly, or without opposition, is 'sākacchā,' and also 'saṃkathā'.

Sāddhapajjena garahassa nāmāni. Dosakkhānena vadanaṃ upavādo. Kusa avhāne bhedane ca, kvaci “apakkoso”ti pāṭho, ṇo. Vaṇṇo thuti, tassa avadanaṃ avaṇṇavādo. Hīḷanena vadanaṃ anuvādo. Janānaṃ vādo garahaṇaṃ janavādo. Garahaṇena vādo apavādo. Parivadanaṃ parivādo, rassassa dīghatā. Ete upavādādayo tulyatthā samānatthā. Visamavuttappabhedesu vattamidaṃ. Khipa peraṇe, khipanaṃ bahikaraṇaṃ khepo. Nidi kucchāyaṃ, a, nindā. Yathā upavādādayo garahatthā, kucchādayopi tathāti tathāttho. Kuccha avakkhepane, curādi, kusa akkosetimassa vā pabbajjādittā “kucchā”ti rūpaṃ nipphajjati. Gupa, gopa kucchanesu, “tijagupakitamānehi khachasā vā”ti cho. Garaha kucchane. Tattha keci “upavādādayo abbhakkhānatthā, khepādayo nindatthā”ti vadanti, taṃ amarakosena virujjhanato abbhakkhānatthassa ca vuttattā na gahetabbaṃ. Ete upavādādayo satta abbhakkhānepi vattanti.

The names for 'censure' are given with their derivations. Speaking with a declaration of faults is 'upavādo.' The root 'kusa' is in the sense of 'to scold' and 'to divide'; sometimes the reading is 'apakkoso,' with the suffix 'ṇa.' 'Vaṇṇo' is praise; speaking ill of that is 'avaṇṇavādo.' Speaking with contempt is 'anuvādo.' The talk of people, which is censure, is 'janavādo.' Speaking with censure is 'apavādo.' Reproaching is 'parivādo,' with the lengthening of the short vowel. These terms, 'upavādo' and the rest, are synonymous, having the same meaning. This applies in cases of irregular usage. The root 'khipa' is in the sense of 'to throw'; 'khipanaṃ' (throwing) or 'bahikaraṇaṃ' (expulsion) is 'khepo.' The root 'nidi' is in the sense of 'to despise'; with the suffix 'a,' it becomes 'nindā.' Just as 'upavādo' and the like have the meaning of censure, so too do 'kucchā' and the like; such is their meaning. The root 'kuccha' of the curādi class is in the sense of 'to disparage'; or, from the root 'kusa' meaning 'to scold,' the form 'kucchā' is produced due to rules concerning 'pabbajjā' and so forth. The roots 'gupa' and 'gopa' are in the sense of 'to despise'; the suffix 'cha' is applied according to the rule 'tijagupakitamānehi khachasā vā.' The root 'garaha' is in the sense of 'to censure.' Here, some say that 'upavādo' and the like mean 'accusation,' while 'khepo' and the like mean 'blame'; but this should not be accepted, as it contradicts the Amarakośa and because the meaning of 'accusation' has already been stated. These seven terms, 'upavādo' and the rest, are also used to mean 'accusation.'

Vivādakāmassa dubbādo upārambho, so ca īdise sabbalokacūḷāmaṇibhūte sakyakule sambhūtassa bhagavato kimidaṃ kammamucitanti guṇāvikaraṇapubbakopyatthi, bandhakīsutassa tavedamucitamevāti nindāpubbakopi upārambho. Tatra yo nindāpubbo sanindo upārambho, so paribhāsanamuccate. Upagantvā paresaṃ cittassa ārambhanaṃ vikopanaṃ upārambho. Dosakkhānena bhāsanaṃ paribhāsanaṃ.

For one who desires disputes, harsh speech is 'upārambho' (reproach). This can be preceded by a finding of fault with virtues, as in: 'What deed is fitting for the Blessed One, born in such a Sakyan clan, who is the crest-jewel of the entire world?' It can also be preceded by blame, as in: 'This is indeed fitting for you, the son of a bondwoman!' Among these, the reproach that is preceded by blame and includes blame is called 'paribhāsanaṃ' (reviling). Approaching others and agitating their minds is 'upārambho.' Speaking with a declaration of faults is 'paribhāsanaṃ.'

122. Anariyānaṃ [M 0.0101] lāmakānaṃ vohārato, ariyānaṃ uttamajanānaṃ vā avohārato anariyavohāroti saṅkhātānaṃ adiṭṭhe diṭṭhavādādīnaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ vohārānaṃ vasena yā vācā lāmakajanehi pavattitā vuttā, vītikkamadīpanī ajjhācāravītikkamasādhanī sā vācā ariyajanehi vattabbamariyādātikkamattā abhivākyaṃ nāma siyā.

122. Speech uttered by base people—which is reckoned as 'ignoble speech' because it is the conduct of ignoble, inferior people, or the non-conduct of noble, superior people, and which consists of the eight types of conduct such as claiming to have seen what one has not seen—that speech, which indicates transgression and establishes misconduct, would be called 'abhivākyaṃ' by noble people, because it exceeds the bounds of what should be spoken.

123. Muhuṃbhāsā bahuso abhidhānaṃ anulāpo nāma, anu punappunaṃ lāpo anulāpo. Anatthikā girā nippayojanaṃ ummattādivacanaṃ palāpo, payojanarahito lāpo palāpo, pasaddo viyogatthajotako.

123. Frequent speaking, speaking much, is called 'anulāpo' (repetitious talk); 'anu' means 'again and again,' and 'lāpo' is talk, hence 'anulāpo.' Useless speech, the purposeless talk of madmen and the like, is 'palāpo' (babble); talk devoid of purpose is 'palāpo'; the prefix 'pa' indicates separation.

Gamanāgamanādisamaye ādimhi bhāsanaṃ piyavacanaṃ ālāpo, ādimhi lāpo ālāpo, āpucchāsaddopyatra. Dosena patiṭṭhito pariddavo paridevanaṃ anusocanaṃ atikkamalāpo vilāpo nāma, vividhena, vividhaṃ vā lāpo vilāpo. Paridevanaṃ paridevo, so eva pariddavo, deva paridevane.

Pleasant speech or conversation at the beginning, at the time of coming and going and so forth, is 'ālāpo'; talk at the beginning is 'ālāpo'; the word for asking leave is also included here. Lamentation established in fault, wailing, sorrowing, or talk that transgresses is called 'vilāpo' (lament); talk of various kinds, or in various ways, is 'vilāpo.' Lamentation is 'paridevo'; that itself is 'pariddavo'; the root 'deva' is in the sense of 'to lament.'

124. Viruddhaṃ [M 0.0102] vacanaṃ virodhotti. Viruddhaṃ palāpo vippalāpo. Sandissateti sandeso, sandissamāno attho, tassotti. Yāya sandiṭṭho attho abhidhīyate, sā sandesotti vācikamuccate. Vaca sandese, sakatthe ṇiko, sandiṭṭhatthā vācā eva vācikamiccattho.

124. Contradictory speech is 'virodho.' Contradictory babble is 'vippalāpo.' That which is communicated is 'sandeso' (message); it has the meaning of 'that which is communicated.' That speech by which a communicated meaning is expressed is called 'vācikaṃ' (verbal message), which is a synonym for 'sandeso.' The root 'vaca' is in the sense of 'to communicate'; with the suffix 'ṇika' in its own sense, the meaning is that speech with a communicated meaning is 'vācikaṃ.'

Mithu aññamaññaṃ virodharahitaṃ vacanaṃ “sambhāsanaṃ, sallāpo”ti ca vuccati. Yathā eko brūte “ajja sobhanaṃ nakkhatta”nti, itaropyāha “tathevā”ti.

Mutual speech, free from contradiction, is called 'sambhāsanaṃ' (conversation) and 'sallāpo' (discussion). For example, one says, 'Today the constellation is auspicious,' and the other replies, 'So it is.'

125. Niṭṭhuraṃ vākyaṃ kakkasavacanaṃ pharusaṃ nāma, pare jane ussāpeti dāhetīti parusaṃ, tadeva passa phakāraṃ katvā pharusaṃ. Asavanīyattā na icchitabbanti niṭṭhuraṃ, uro, yathā “nāgo”ti. Dvayaṃ kaṇṇasukhavacane. Manaṃ ā bhusaṃ ñāpeti tosetīti manuññaṃ, ñā parimāṇatosananisānesu, assukāro. Hadayaṃ manaṃ gacchati pavisatīti hadayaṅgamaṃ.

125. Harsh speech, rough language, is called 'pharusaṃ.' It provokes and burns other people, hence 'parusaṃ'; that same word, by changing 'pa' to 'pha,' becomes 'pharusaṃ.' Because it is unpleasant to hear and undesired, it is called 'niṭṭhuraṃ' (harsh), with the suffix 'ura,' as in 'nāgo.' Two terms for 'ear-pleasing speech.' That which greatly pleases and satisfies the mind is 'manuññaṃ'; the root 'ñā' is in the sense of 'to measure,' 'to satisfy,' and 'to sharpen,' with the suffix 'uṇṇa.' That which goes to and enters the heart or mind is 'hadayaṅgamaṃ' (heart-pleasing).

Saṃkulādidvayaṃ pubbāparavirodhini pubbāparaviruddhe vākye, yathā –

The two terms beginning with 'saṃkula' refer to a statement where the former and latter parts are contradictory, such as:

Yāvajīvamahaṃ monī, brahmacārī ca me pitā;

Mātā ca mama vañjhāsi, aputto ca pitāmaho.

For all my life I am a silent sage, and my father is a celibate; my mother was barren, and my grandfather is without a son.

Saṃkulanti jaḷībhavantyanenāti saṃkulaṃ. Kilissante etthāti kiliṭṭhaṃ.

That by which things become confused is 'saṃkulaṃ.' That in which one is afflicted is 'kiliṭṭhaṃ.'

126. Samudāyattharahitaṃ [M 0.0103] dasadāḷimādivākyaṃ dasa dāṭhimāni ṭhaḷapūpā kuṇḍa’ majājinaṃ palālapiṇḍā (nyāyabhāssa 5.2.10 moggallānapañcikāṭīkā 1.1) asambaddhattā abaddhamiti kittitaṃ kathitaṃ, na bajjhate hadayamatrāti abaddhaṃ, to.

126. A statement devoid of coherent meaning, such as 'ten pomegranates' and so forth, is called 'abaddhaṃ' (unconnected) because it is incoherent. It does not bind the heart, hence 'abaddhaṃ'.

Natthi tathaṃ saccamatrāti vitathaṃ. Pharusādayo vitathasaddaṃ yāva tiliṅgikā.

That in which there is no truth or reality is 'vitathaṃ' (false). The words from 'pharusa' up to 'vitatha' are used in all three genders.

127. Pajjaddhaṃ saccavacane. Sammāsaddoyaṃ abyayaṃ, sabbaliṅgavibhattivacanesu ca samāno. Na vitathaṃ avitathaṃ. Santesu sādhūsu bhavaṃ saccaṃ. Sata sātacche vā, vajādinā yo, saccaṃ. Tathasaddo bhūtapariyāyo, “tathena maggena yathātthabhājinā”ti tathāgatā jināti (ka.) payogo. Tathe sādhu tacchaṃ, sādhvatthe yo. Yathātathasaddāpi ca saccatthā aliṅgā. Tabbantā saccavacanavantavācakā sammā saccaṃ yathātathaṃsaddavajjitā sesā avitathādayo tīsu liṅgesu vattanti. Saccaṃsaddo tu aliṅgo. Amarakose pana sammā saccasaddānampi tabbati tiliṅgattaṃ vuttaṃ, yathā – saccaṃ tacchaṃ ritaṃ sammā, amūni tīsu tabbati amara 6.22. Yathā – sacco brāhmaṇo, saccā nārī, saccaṃ vippakulaṃ. Idha pana sabbaliṅgavacanavibhattīsu rūpabhedābhāvā sammāsaddassa abyayattaṃ, tiliṅgesvapi rūpabhedābhāvā saccaṃsaddassa aliṅgattañca vuttaṃ. Yathā – sammā vācā, sammā vohāro, sammā vacanaṃ. Saccaṃ brāhmaṇo, saccaṃ nārī, saccaṃ vippakulaṃ. Micchāmusāsaddā pana sabbatrāpi abyayameva bhavanti. Yathā [M 0.0104] – micchā vācā, micchā vohāro, micchā vacanaṃ. Musā vācā, musā vohāro, musā vacanaṃ.

127. A half-verse on truthful speech. The word 'sammā' is an indeclinable, being the same in all genders, cases, and numbers. That which is not false is 'avitathaṃ'. That which is among the good and virtuous is 'saccaṃ'. Or, from 'sata' in the sense of continuity, with the suffix 'yo' from the 'vajādi' group, it becomes 'saccaṃ'. The word 'tatha' is a synonym for 'bhūta' (reality), as in the usage, 'by that true path, which partakes of the real meaning'. That which is good in the sense of 'tatha' is 'tacchaṃ', with the suffix 'yo' in the sense of 'good'. The words 'yathātatha' also have the meaning of 'sacca' (truth) and are genderless. The remaining words, such as 'avitatha', which denote one who possesses truthful speech—excluding the words 'sammā', 'saccaṃ', and 'yathātathaṃ'—occur in the three genders. The word 'saccaṃ', however, is genderless. In the Amarakośa, on the other hand, it is said that the words 'sammā' and 'sacca' are used in the three genders, for example: 'sacco brāhmaṇo' (a truthful brahmin), 'saccā nārī' (a truthful woman), 'saccaṃ vippakulaṃ' (a truthful family of priests). Here, however, the word 'sammā' is stated to be indeclinable because it has no variation in form in any gender, number, or case, and the word 'saccaṃ' is stated to be genderless because it has no variation in form even in the three genders. For example: 'sammā vācā' (right speech), 'sammā vohāro' (right conduct), 'sammā vacanaṃ' (right utterance); 'saccaṃ brāhmaṇo' (a truthful brahmin), 'saccaṃ nārī' (a truthful woman), 'saccaṃ vippakulaṃ' (a truthful family of priests). The words 'micchā' and 'musā', however, are always indeclinable in all instances. For example: 'micchā vācā' (false speech), 'micchā vohāro' (false conduct), 'micchā vacanaṃ' (false utterance); 'musā vācā' (false speech), 'musā vohāro' (false conduct), 'musā vacanaṃ' (false utterance).

128. Soḷasa saddamattapariyāye dassetuṃ upajātiṃ “ravo”iccādimāha. Ruyate saddāyateti ravo, ru sadde. Nadanaṃ nādo, nirattho nādo ninādo, nada abyattasadde. Evaṃ ninado, rassattameva viseso. Sappati uccārīyatīti saddo. Ghusa sadde, pātubhāvo ghoso nigghoso. Nadanaṃ nādo. Dhana sadde, dhanīyatīti dhani. Nigghoso ca nādo ca dhani ca nigghosanādadhanayo. Ravo eva rāvo. Ārāvoti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Tathā saṃrāvavirāvaāravā. Ghusanaṃ ghoso. Ārāvo ca saṃrāvo ca virāvo ca ghoso ca āravo cāti dvando. Su savane, suyyateti suti. Sarati suyyamānataṃ gacchatīti saro. Nissanati etenāti nissano, sana sambhattiyaṃ nipubbo. Saro ca nissano cāti dvando.

128. To show the sixteen terms for sound, he states the Upajāti verse beginning with 'ravo'. 'Ruyate saddāyateti ravo' (it is sounded, it makes a sound, therefore it is 'ravo'), from the root 'ru' (to sound). 'Nadanaṃ nādo' (sounding is 'nāda'); 'nirattho nādo ninādo' (a meaningless sound is 'nināda'), from 'nada' (to sound indistinctly). Thus 'ninado'; the only difference is the shortness of the vowel. 'Sappati uccārīyatīti saddo' (that which is uttered is 'saddo'). From 'ghusa' (to sound), its manifestation is 'ghoso' or 'nigghoso'. 'Nadanaṃ nādo' (sounding is 'nāda'). From 'dhana' (to sound), 'dhanīyatīti dhani' (that which is sounded is 'dhani'). 'Nigghoso ca nādo ca dhani ca' forms the compound 'nigghosanādadhanayo'. 'Ravo' is also 'rāvo'. 'Ārāvo': the word is extended with a prefix. Similarly, 'saṃrāva', 'virāva', and 'āravā'. 'Ghusanaṃ ghoso' (sounding is 'ghosa'). 'Ārāvo ca saṃrāvo ca virāvo ca ghoso ca āravo cāti dvando' (a dvandva compound of ārāva, saṃrāva, virāva, ghosa, and ārāva). From 'su' (to hear), 'suyyateti suti' (that which is heard is 'suti'). 'Sarati suyyamānataṃ gacchatīti saro' (it proceeds to a state of being heard, therefore it is 'saro'). 'Nissanati etenāti nissano' (that by which it issues forth is 'nissano'), from the root 'sana' in the sense of 'sambhatti', with the prefix 'ni'. 'Saro ca nissano cāti dvando' (a dvandva compound of saro and nissano).

129. Visajjīyate na laggīyate semhādīhīti visaṭṭho. Manitabbanti mañju, ju, mana ñāṇe, suṇantānaṃ vā manaṃ rañjetīti mañju, u, na ralopo. Sukheneva vijānitabbattā viññeyyo. Hitasukhanipphādanato sotabboti savanīyo. Bahiddhāparisā aṅgulimattampi na visarati na gacchatīti avisārī[M 0.0105], tassīlatthe ṇī, vividhena vā na saratīti avisārī, chinnassarānaṃ viya dvedhā na hotītyattho. Vindyate labbhateti bindu, vassa bo, niggahītāgamo, u ca, vaṭṭattā vā bindu, imasmiṃ pakkhe pabbajjādinā rūpasiddhi. Pañcannaṃ ṭhānagatīnaṃ dūraṭṭhānato jātattā gambhīro. Punappunaṃ nādo ninnādo, kriyābhikkhaññattā dvittaṃ, assa i, niggahītāgamo, so ettha atthīti ninnādī. Iccevaṃ bhagavato aṭṭhaṅgiko saro hoti.

129. It is emitted, not clinging like phlegm and so forth, hence 'visaṭṭha' (clear). That which is to be esteemed is 'mañju'; from the root 'ju', or from the root 'mana' in the sense of 'knowledge'; or because it delights the minds of listeners, it is 'mañju'; formed with the suffix 'u', and there is no elision of 'r'. Because it is easily understood, it is 'viññeyya' (comprehensible). Because it produces welfare and happiness, it is to be heard, hence 'savanīya' (pleasant to hear). Not even a finger's breadth of it strays outside the assembly, hence 'avisārī' (non-diffuse); the suffix 'ṇī' is in the sense of 'having the nature of', or it does not scatter in various ways—thus 'avisārī'; the meaning is that it does not become twofold like a broken sound. It is obtained, thus 'bindu' (from the root 'vid'); 'v' becomes 'b', a niggahīta is inserted, and the suffix is 'u'; or, due to its roundness, it is 'bindu'; in this view, the word is formed according to the 'pabbajjādi' group. Because it arises from a deep source within the five places of articulation, it is 'gambhīra' (profound). A repeated sound is 'ninnāda'; due to the repetition of the action, there is doubling, 'a' becomes 'i', and a niggahīta is inserted; because that is present in the voice, it is 'ninnādī' (resonant). Thus, the voice of the Blessed One has eight qualities.

130. Khaggādīnaṃ tiracchānagatānaṃ rutaṃ vassitantyuccate. Ru sadde, rutaṃ. Vassa sadde, vassanaṃ ravanaṃ vassitaṃ.

130. The cry of animals such as rhinoceroses is called 'rutaṃ' and 'vassitaṃ'. From 'ru' (to sound), 'rutaṃ'. From 'vassa' (to sound), 'vassanaṃ', 'ravanaṃ', and 'vassitaṃ'.

Kolāhalādidvayaṃ bahūhi sambhūya kate abyattasadde. Kula saṅghāte saṅkhyāne (ka.), kolanaṃ kolo, ekībhāvo, taṃ āhalati vindatīti kolāhalo. Karoti hiṃsati madhuranti kalo, taṃ halatīti kalahalo. Hala vilekhane.

The two terms 'kolāhala' and 'kalahala' refer to indistinct sounds produced by many together. From 'kula' (assembly); 'kolanaṃ' is 'kolo'—unity, and that which brings it about is 'kolāhala'. 'Kala' means to make, to injure, or to be sweet; that which carries it away is 'kalahala'. From 'hala' (to scratch or plow).

Tikaṃ gāyane. Ge sadde, getabbaṃ gītaṃ gānaṃ gītikā ca. Sabbatra bhāvasādhanaṃ.

The triad concerns singing. From 'ge' (to sing), 'getabbaṃ' (to be sung), 'gītaṃ' (song), 'gānaṃ' (singing), and 'gītikā' (a little song) are derived. In every case, the formation is in the sense of the action.

131. Tantikaṇṭhoṭṭhitā amara 7.1 usabhādayo satta sarā. Chajjādayo tayo gāmā samūhātyattho. Vuttañca “gāmo nāma sarasamūhassa sandhāna”nti. Manussalokavādanavidhinā ekekassa [M 0.0106] sarassa vasena tayo tayo mucchanā katvā ekavīsati mucchanā, devalokavādanavidhinā pana samapaññāsa mucchanā vadanti. Tattha hi ekekassa sarassa vasena satta satta mucchanā, antasarassa ca ekāti samapaññāsa mucchanā āgatā, teneva sakkapañhasuttasaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ “samapaññāsa mucchanā mucchitvā”ti dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.345 pañcasikhassa vīṇāvādanaṃ dassentena vuttaṃ. Muccha mohasamussayesu, yu, mucchanā. Yathā kamena vīṇā vādituṃ sakkā, evaṃ sajjanāhi mucchanaṭṭhānāni ekūnapaññāsātyattho. Ekekassa sarassa satta satta ṭhānāni. Yato sarassa mandatāravavatthānaṃ hoti, tena ekūnapaññāsa ṭhānāni. Iccetaṃ saramaṇḍalaṃ sarasamūho.

131. The seven notes, beginning with Usabha, are produced from stringed instruments and the throat. The three gāmas, beginning with Chajja, have the meaning of 'collection'. And it is said, 'A gāma is the connection of a collection of notes'. According to the method of playing in the human world, by making three modulations for each note, there are twenty-one modulations; but according to the method of playing in the world of the devas, they speak of fifty modulations. For there, for each note, there are seven modulations, and one for the final note—thus fifty modulations are arrived at. Therefore, in the commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta, when describing Pañcasikha's lute-playing, it is said, 'having modulated fifty modulations'. From the root 'muccha' (in the sense of delusion and accumulation), with the suffix 'yu', comes 'mucchanā'. Just as one can play the lute in sequence, so the meaning is that there are forty-nine places of modulation for the virtuous. Each note has seven positions. Since there is the establishment of the softness and loudness of a note, there are forty-nine positions. Thus, this is the circle of notes, the collection of notes.

132. Sarādīnaṃ nāmasarūpappabhedaṃ dassetumāha “usabho”ccādi. Isa gatiyaṃ. Isati cittaṃ pavisatīti usabho, abho, issu ca. “Usa dāhe”ti vā dhātvattho. Yasmā pana so saro usabho viya nadati, tasmā usabhoti vuccati. Dhīmantehi gīyateti dhevato, vaṇṇavikāro, vattaṃ.

132. To show the distinctions of name and form among the notes, he says 'usabho' and so on. From the root 'isa' in the sense of motion. Because it enters the mind, it is 'usabho'; formed with the suffix 'abho', and 'issu'. Or alternatively, the meaning of the root is 'usa' (to burn). And because that note sounds like a bull (usabha), therefore it is called 'usabho'.

Nāsaṃ kaṇṭhamuro tāluṃ,

Jivhaṃ dante ca nissito;

Chadhā sañjāyate yasmā,

Tasmā chajjo sa uccate cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.1.

Dependent on the nose, throat, chest, palate,

Tongue, and teeth;

Because it arises in six ways,

Therefore it is called 'Chajja'.

Gandhaṃ [M 0.0107] lesaṃ aratīti gandharo, rassassa dīghatte gandhāro cetyaññe aññesamapīti (pāṇini 3.137) dīgho (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.1), gandhārā nāma janapadā, tehyayaṃ gīyateti gandhāro, ṇo. Majjhe layavisese bhavo majjhimo. Pañcannampi dhevatādīnaṃ pūraṇo pañcamo, (pañcannaṃ vā mahābhūtānaṃ pūraṇo pañcamo.) ( ) etthantare pāṭho adhiko viya dissati Nissesato sīdanti sarā yasminti yasmāti (ka.) – sadato adhikaraṇe ghau (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.1), ṇo. “Nisīdanti sarā yasmiṃ, nisādo tena hetunā”ti hi vuttaṃ. Ete satta sarāti gaditā kathitā.

It goes against even a trace of smell, hence 'Gandharo'; or, according to others, 'Gandhāro' due to the lengthening of the short vowel; or because it is sung by the people of the country named Gandhārā, hence 'Gandhāro', with the suffix 'ṇo'. That which exists in a specific tempo in the middle is 'Majjhimo'. The completion of the five notes beginning with Dhevata is 'Pañcamo' (the fifth), (or it is the completion of the five great elements). That in which the notes completely subside is 'Nisādo', with the suffix 'ṇo'. For it is said: 'Sounds settle in him, hence for that reason he is called Nisādo'. These seven notes have been spoken of and declared.

133-135. Usabhādayo ye nadanti, te dassetumāha “nadanti”ccādi. Usabhaṃ nāma saraṃ gāvo nadanti. Tathā dhevataṃ turaṅgā assā, chajjaṃ mayūrā sikhaṇḍino, gandhāraṃ ajā, majjhimaṃ koñcā sakuṇavisesā, pañcamaṃ parapuṭṭhādī kokilādayo, nisādaṃ vāraṇā hatthino nadanti. Vuttañca nāradamuninā –

To show which creatures sound the notes Usabha and so forth, he says 'nadanti' etc. Cows sound the note called 'usabha'. Similarly, horses sound 'dhevata'; peacocks, the crested ones, 'chajja'; goats, 'gandhāra'; certain birds, like herons, 'majjhima'; cuckoos and others, 'pañcama'; and elephants, 'nisāda'. And it was said by the sage Nārada –

“Chajjaṃ [M 0.0108] nadati mayūro, gāvo nadanti usabhaṃ;

Ajo roti ca ajāvikā tu (ka.) gandhāraṃ, koñcā nadanti majjhimaṃ.

"The peacock sounds the Chajja, the cows sound the Usabha;

The goat cries the Gandhāra, the herons sound the Majjhima."

Pupphasādhārane kāle, kokilo roti pañcamaṃ;

Asso tu dhevataṃ roti, nisādaṃ roti kuñjaro”ti.

"In the season of flowers, the cuckoo cries the Pañcama;

The horse cries the Dhevata, the elephant cries the Nisāda."

Mayūrādayopi sabbe ime sattā samadā santo (ka.) ete ca samadā pañcamaṃ gāyanti (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.1) pañcamaṃ nadanti.

All these beings, peacocks and others, when impassioned, also sound the fifth note.

Chajjo gāmo, majjhimo gāmo, sādhāraṇo gāmoti tayo gāmā. Tatra vīṇādaṇḍaṃ vibhāgaṃ katvā adhobhāgassa “chajjagāmo”ti saññā, majjhabhāgassa “majjhimagāmo”ti, uparibhāgassa “sādhāraṇagāmo”ti saññā. Kiṃ pana gāmabhede kāraṇaṃ? Yasmā ekasseva sarassa gāmantare bhedo, taṃbhede gāmānampibhedo. Māghaṭīkāyaṃ pana sādhāraṇagāmaṭṭhāne gandhāragāmo kathito, ekekasmiñca gāme satta satta mucchanā. Idha pana usabhādīsu sattasu saresu paccekaṃ tisso tisso mucchanā kathitā. Kiṃkāraṇā? Idha manussalokavādanavidhinā, tattha ca devalokavādanavidhinā kathitattā tatheva ṭhānāni satta satteva labbhareti. Yathā usabhādīsu tesu yathāvuttesu saresu paccekaṃ ekekasmiṃ sare tisso tisso mucchanā siyuṃ, tatheva ṭhānānipi satta satteva labbharetyattho.

The Chajja gāma, the Majjhima gāma, and the Sādhāraṇa gāma—these are the three gāmas. There, having divided the neck of the lute, the lower part is designated 'Chajjagāma', the middle part 'Majjhimagāma', and the upper part 'Sādhāraṇagāma'. But what is the reason for the distinction of gāmas? Because there is a distinction of a single note within another gāma, due to that distinction, there is also a distinction of gāmas. In the Māghaṭīkā, however, Gandhāragāma is mentioned in place of Sādhāraṇagāma, and in each gāma, there are seven modulations each. Here, however, in the seven notes beginning with Usabha, three modulations each are mentioned for each note. What is the reason? Because here it is explained according to the method of playing in the human world, and there according to the method of playing in the divine world, the positions are thus obtained as only seven each. Just as in those notes beginning with Usabha, in those notes as described, there would be three modulations each in every single note, so too the positions are obtained as only seven each—that is the meaning.

136. Sarānaṃ gāmesu bhinnasutittaṃ dassetumāha “tisso”iccādi. Usabhassa sarassa tārakalamandavasena tisso sutiyo. Dhevatassa sarassa tāra mandavasena [M 0.0109] duve. Chajjassa tārakala manda kākalīvasena catasso. Gandhārassa ca tathā. Majjhimassa tārakala kākalīvasena tisso. Pañcamassa kala kākalīvasena duve. Nisādassa tārādivasena catasso sutiyo. Iccevaṃ sattasu saresu kamato sampiṇḍitā dvāvīsati sutiyo siyuṃ. Māghaṭīkāyaṃ pana aññathā sutibhedo vutto. Vuttañhi tattha –

136. To show the distinct subtle tones of the notes in the gāmas, he says 'three' and so on. For the note Usabha, there are three subtle tones, corresponding to the high, medium, and low registers. For the note Dhevata, there are two, corresponding to the high and low registers. For the note Chajja, there are four, corresponding to the high, medium, low, and kākalī registers. The same applies to the note Gandhāra. For the note Majjhima, there are three, corresponding to the high, medium, and kākalī registers. For the note Pañcama, there are two, corresponding to the medium and kākalī registers. For the note Nisāda, there are four subtle tones, corresponding to the high and other registers. Thus, in the seven notes, when combined in order, there would be twenty-two subtle tones. In the Māghaṭīkā, however, a different classification of subtle tones is mentioned. For it is stated there:

“Catussuti suviññeyyo, majjhimo majjimaṭṭhito;

Dvissuti cāpi gandhāro, tissuti usabho tathā.

“The Majjhima, standing in the middle, is to be known as having four śrutis; the Gandhāra also has two śrutis, and likewise the Usabha has three śrutis.”

Chajjo catussuti ñeyyo, nisādo dvissutī tathā;

Catussuti dhevato tu, pañcamo tissutī mato”ti.

“The Chajja is to be known as having four śrutis, the Nisāda likewise as having two śrutis. The Dhevata, however, has four śrutis, and the Pañcama is considered to have three śrutis.”

Sabbametaṃ nāṭakasatthato gahetabbaṃ.

All this should be taken from the science of dramaturgy.

137. “Uccatare”tyādinā sutibhede sarūpato dasseti. Uccatare rave atyuccadhanimhi tāro, tārayati bodhayatīti tāro. Abyatte abyattakkhare madhure sutisukhe kalo, kala made. Gambhīre dhanimhi mando. Madi thutimodamadamohasupanagatīsu. Mandayate bujjhatenenāti mando.

137. By ‘higher’ and so on, he shows the distinction in subtle tones according to their intrinsic nature. In a higher sound, a very high tone, it is ‘tāra’; it is ‘tāra’ because it causes one to cross over and awaken. In an indistinct, unarticulated, sweet, and ear-pleasing sound, it is ‘kala’; from the root ‘kal’ in the sense of delight. In a deep tone, it is ‘manda’; from the root ‘mad’ in the senses of praise, joy, intoxication, delusion, sleep, and movement. It is called ‘manda’ because one understands by it slowly.

Tārādayo tayo vāccaliṅgattā tīsu. Tāro dhani, tārā vāṇī, tāraṃ rutaṃ iccādi. Abyattamadhurasaddo kalo. Tatra kale sukhume kākalīsaddo, īpaccayanto, īsaṃ [M 0.0110] kalā vāṇī kākalī nāma, kāsaddoyamīsattho. Kriyādisamatāti gītavāditapādanyāsādikriyānaṃ, kālassa ca samattaṃ layo nāma, laya sāmyagatīsu, ādhāre apaccayo, sabbābhinayānampi sāmyaṃ layoti keci.

The words beginning with ‘tāra’ are three because they are adjectives of three genders. ‘Tāro’ (masc.) is a tone, ‘tārā’ (fem.) is speech, ‘tāraṃ’ (neut.) is a cry, and so on. An indistinct, sweet sound is ‘kala’. Therein, a subtle ‘kala’ sound is ‘kākalī’, a word ending with the suffix ‘ī’. Or, ‘kākalī’ is a voice that is slightly ‘kala’; the word ‘kā’ here has the meaning of ‘slightly’. The equilibrium of actions and so on, that is, the evenness of actions such as singing, instrumental music, and footwork, and also of time, is called ‘laya’. From the root ‘laya’ in the senses of equilibrium and movement; the suffix ‘a’ is used in the sense of a locus. Some say that ‘laya’ is the equilibrium of all expressions.

138. Dvayaṃ vīṇāyaṃ. Vi janane, to, īṇattaṃ, vīṇa veṭhaneti vā dhātu, ā, vīṇā. Valla saṃvaraṇe, vallate dhanivisesaṃ, ṇvu, vallakī, nadādi. Vipañcītipi vīṇāya nāmaṃ. Vipañcayatīti vipañcī vipañcayati vitthārayatisaddaṃ (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.3), nadādi.

138. There are two terms for the lute. From the root ‘vi’ in the sense of generating, with the suffix ‘to’, and the state of being ‘īṇa’; or from the root ‘vīṇa’ in the sense of enveloping, with the suffix ‘ā’, comes ‘vīṇā’. From the root ‘valla’ in the sense of covering; it covers a special sound, with the suffix ‘ṇvu’, making ‘vallakī’, a word of the nadādi group. ‘Vipañcī’ is also a name for the lute. It is ‘vipañcī’ because it elaborates, a word of the nadādi group.

Sā vīṇā sattatantī sattahi tantīhi visiṭṭhā parivādinī nāma, parito vadatīti parivādinī, inī. Vīṇādayo cattāropi vīṇāsāmaññavācakā icceke, tesaṃ mate sāsaddassa catunnampi itthiliṅgatthadīpakatā viññeyyā, tathāpi amarakosena amara 7.3 virujjhanato tesaṃ mataṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

That lute, distinguished by seven strings, is called ‘parivādinī’; it is ‘parivādinī’ because it sounds all around, with the suffix ‘inī’. Some say that the four terms beginning with ‘vīṇā’ are general designations for a lute. In their opinion, it should be understood that the word ‘sā’ indicates the feminine gender for all four terms. However, since this contradicts the Amarakośa, their view should not be accepted.

Kaṭṭhādīhi doṇisaṇṭhānena kataṃ vajjabhaṇḍaṃ vīṇāya pokkharo nāma, poseti vaḍḍheti saddeti pokkharo, kharo, vuddhi, vaṇṇavikāro ca. Du gamane, ṇi, doṇi. Kakubho, pasevakotipi pokkharassa nāmāni. Kaṃ vātaṃ kubhati bandhatīti kakubho. Pasibbanti tamiti pasevako.

The musical instrument made of wood and so on, in the shape of a trough, is called the ‘pokkhara’ of the lute. It is ‘pokkhara’ because it nourishes (poseti) and increases (vaḍḍheti) the sound; it is formed with the suffix ‘kharo’, involving vowel gradation and letter change. From the root ‘du’ in the sense of going, with the suffix ‘ṇi’, comes ‘doṇi’ (trough). ‘Kakubho’ and ‘pasevako’ are also names for ‘pokkhara’. It is ‘kakubho’ because it restrains the wind (‘kaṃ vātaṃ kubhati bandhati’). It is ‘pasevako’ because they sew it (‘pasibbanti tamiti’).

Dvayaṃ pokkharaveṭhake cammani. Vīṇābhāvaṃ upagacchati yenāti upavīṇo. Veṭhati pokkharanti veṭhako, ṇvu.

There are two terms for the hide covering the resonator. It is ‘upavīṇo’ because by it one approaches the state of a lute. It is ‘veṭhako’ because it covers the resonator, with the suffix ‘ṇvu’.

139. Ātatādipañcakaṃ [M 0.0111] pañcaṅgikatūriyassa nāmāni.

139. The group of five terms beginning with ‘ātata’ are names for the five-limbed musical instrument.

140. Cammāvanaddhesu cammena bandhanīyesu bheriyādīsu majjhe talekekayutaṃ ekekena talena yuttaṃ kumbhathuṇadaddarikādikaṃ tūriyaṃ ātataṃ nāma, ātanotīti ātataṃ, tanu vitthāre. Mahatīādivīṇāvisesopi “mahatī”ti nāradassa vīṇā (saddakappaddume) ātatamevāti “cammāvanaddhesū”ti visesanaṃ kataṃ. Kumbhasaṇṭhānattā kumbho ca taṃ thunanagarasambhūtattā thunañceti kumbhathunaṃ. Tadeva kumbhathuṇaṃ, atha vā thu abhitthave, kammani ṇo. Kumbho ca so thuṇo ceti kumbhathuṇo, thuṇa pūraṇeti vā dhātvattho. Dara vidāraṇadāhesu, dvebhāvo, kāpubbassikāro ca, daddarasaddaṃ karotīti vā daddarikā.

140. Among the hide-covered instruments, those which are to be bound with hide, such as drums and so on, a musical instrument like the kumbhathuṇa and daddarikā, which is endowed with a single face, is called ‘ātata’. It is ‘ātata’ because it stretches, from the root ‘tanu’ in the sense of stretching. Even a special kind of lute like the Mahatī and so on is also ‘ātata’; hence the specification ‘among the hide-covered instruments’ is made. Due to its pot-like shape, it is ‘kumbha’, and because it originates from the city of Thuṇa, it is ‘thuṇa’; thus it is ‘kumbhathuṇa’. That itself is ‘kumbhathuṇa’. Alternatively, from the root ‘thu’ in the sense of praising, with the suffix ‘ṇo’ in the objective sense. Or, it is ‘kumbhathuṇa’ because it is a pot and it is ‘thuṇa’; or the meaning of the root ‘thuṇa’ is to fill. From the root ‘dara’ in the senses of splitting and burning; there is doubling, and the change of the preceding vowel to ‘i’; or it is ‘daddarikā’ because it produces the sound ‘daddara’.

141. Ubhayatalaṃ murajādikaṃ tūriyaṃ vitataṃ nāma, visesena saddaṃ tanotīti vitataṃ, sabbavinaddhaṃ sabbapassesu, pubbapacchābhāgesu ca pariyonaddhaṃ paṇavādikaṃ, ādinā caturassaālambaragomukhīādayo ātatavitataṃ nāma, “cammapariyonaddhaṃ hutvā tantibaddhaṃ ātatavitata”nti hi vuttaṃ. Paṇa byavahārathutīsu, paṇīyatīti paṇavo, avo.

141. A musical instrument with two faces, like the muraja and so on, is called ‘vitata’; it is ‘vitata’ because it stretches sound extensively. An instrument like the paṇava and so on, which is covered all over, on all sides, and on the front and back portions—and by ‘and so on’ are included instruments like the caturassa, ālambara, and gomukhī—is called ‘ātatavitata’; for it is said: “That which is covered with hide and bound with strings is ‘ātatavitata’.” From the root ‘paṇa’ in the senses of usage and praise; it is ‘paṇavo’ because it is praised, with the suffix ‘avo’.

142. Vaṃsasaṅkhādikaṃ [M 0.0112] susiraṃ nāma, randhaṃ susiraṃ, taṃyogā susiraṃ. Vana, sana sambhattiyaṃ, so, vaṃso. Sama upasamakhedesu, kho, saṅkho. Sammatāḷādikaṃ accantaṃ pīḷanato, analasaṃyogato vā dravībhūtaṃ puna ghanāyateti ghanākhyaṃ. Hana hiṃsāyaṃ, kammani ṇo, hassa gho. Ghanabhāvena samaṃ bhavatīti sammaṃ, daṇḍādīhi tāḷitabbato tāḷaṃ, taḷa tāḷane, sammañca taṃ tāḷañceti sammatāḷaṃ. Ādinā kaṃsatāḷasilātāḷādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tattha sammatāḷaṃ nāma kaṭṭhamayatāḷaṃ. Kaṃsatāḷaṃ nāma lohamayaṃ. Silāya ca ayopaṭṭena ca vādanatāḷaṃ silātāḷaṃ.

142. A bamboo flute, conch, and so on, are called ‘susira’; a hole is ‘susira’, and due to connection with that, it is ‘susira’. From the roots ‘vana’ and ‘sana’ in the sense of service, with the suffix ‘so’, comes ‘vaṃso’ (bamboo). From the root ‘sama’ in the senses of calming and weariness, with the suffix ‘kho’, comes ‘saṅkho’ (conch). An instrument like the sammatāḷa and so on is called ‘ghana’ because from being thoroughly pressed, or because having become liquid from contact with fire it solidifies again.
