From the root ‘han’ in the sense of harming, with the suffix ‘ṇo’ in the objective sense, and ‘h’ becomes ‘gh’. It is ‘samma’ because it is equal in solidity. It is ‘tāḷa’ because it is to be struck with sticks and so on; from the root ‘taḷa’ in the sense of striking. Thus, ‘sammatāḷa’ is ‘samma’ and ‘tāḷa’. By ‘and so on’ the kaṃsatāḷa, silātāḷa, and so on are included. Among these, ‘sammatāḷa’ refers to a wooden cymbal. ‘Kaṃsatāḷa’ refers to a metal one. ‘Silātāḷa’ is a cymbal played with a stone or an iron plate.

Catukkaṃ ātatādīnaṃ nāmaṃ. Ā samantato tujjate tāḷīyateti ātojjaṃ. Vaṃsādikepi mukhavāyunā ātojjanamattheva. Vādayanti dhanayanti tanti vādittaṃ vāditañca, itto, to ca. Vādayanti tanti vajjaṃ, yo.

The group of four are names for ‘ātata’ and so on. It is ‘ātojja’ because it is struck all around and beaten. Even in the case of bamboo instruments and so on, it is simply a matter of being struck by the wind from the mouth. They play and they sound, thus it is ‘vāditta’ and ‘vādita’, with the suffixes ‘itto’ and ‘to’ respectively. They play, thus it is ‘vajja’, with the suffix ‘yo’.

143. Dvayaṃ bheriyaṃ. Bhāyanti sattujanā etenāti bheri, ri. Ubha pūraṇe, ubhanaṃ ubhi. “Dunda”iti saddena ubhi yatra sa dundubhi. Pumitthiyamete dve serī thī, dundubhi pumā (amara 7.6). Dvayaṃ mudiṅge. Mudaṃ modaṃ iṅgati gacchati yenāti mudiṅgo. Murā asurā jāto murajo.

143. There are two terms for the drum. It is ‘bheri’ because beings fear by it, with the suffix ‘ri’. From the root ‘ubha’ in the sense of filling; ‘ubhanaṃ’ means both. That is ‘dundubhi’ where both are sounded with the sound ‘dunda’. These two are masculine and feminine. There are two terms for the mudiṅga. It is ‘mudiṅga’ because joy and delight move and go by it. It is ‘muraja’ because it is born from the asura Mura.

Assa [M 0.0113] murajassa bhedā visesā āliṅgaṅkyoddhakā bhavanti. Vuttañca –

The distinctions and varieties of this muraja are the āliṅgya, aṅkya, and ūrdhvaka. And it is said:

“Haritakyākati tvaṅkyo,

Yavamajjho tatho’ddhako;

Āliṅgyo ceva gopuccho,

Ākatyā sampakittito”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkāyampi.

“The aṅkya has the shape of a harītakī fruit, and the ūrdhvaka is like a barley grain in the middle. The āliṅgya and the gopuccha are proclaimed by their shape.”

Āliṅgyateti āliṅgo, ṇo. Ucchaṅke bhavo akyo. Uddhaṃ katvā ekena mukhena vādanato uddho santo kāyati saddāyatīti uddhako, uddhasaddoyaṃ tiliṅgiko. Uggacchatīti uddho, to, gamissa do, nerutto. Yo tu uparipariyāyo uddhaṃsaddo, so abyayameva.

It is ‘āliṅga’ because it is embraced (āliṅgyate), with the suffix ‘ṇo’. It is ‘aṅkya’ because it is in the lap (ucchaṅke bhavo). It is ‘uddhaka’ because, being held upwards and played with one mouth, it sounds while being upright; this word ‘uddha’ is of three genders. It is ‘uddha’ because it goes upwards (uggacchati), with the suffix ‘to’, and ‘ga’ becomes ‘da’, according to etymology. But the word ‘uddhaṃ’, which is a synonym for ‘above’, is indeed an indeclinable.

Tiṇavādīni cattāri paṇavassa nāmāni. Tanu vitthāre, avo, assa ittaṃ, ṇattañca, tiṇavo. Mā māne sadde ca, “ḍiṇḍi”iti māyate saddāyateti ḍiṇḍimo, ṇo.

The four, tiṇava and so on, are names for the paṇava. From the root ‘tanu’ in the sense of extension, with the suffix ‘avo’, with ‘a’ becoming ‘i’, and with the retroflexion of ‘n’, it is ‘tiṇavo’. From the root ‘mā’ in the senses of measurement and sound; it is ‘ḍiṇḍima’ because it sounds as ‘ḍiṇḍi’ (māyate saddāyati), with the suffix ‘ṇo’.

144. “Ālamba”iti saddāyateti ālambaro. “Ālambaro tūriyarave, gajendānañca gajjite”ti amara 23.167 hi amarakosa nānatthasaṅgahesu.

144. It is ‘ālambara’ because it sounds as ‘ālamba’. For it is said in the Amarakosa and other collections of various meanings: “Ālambara is used for the sound of musical instruments and the roar of elephants.”

Vīṇādīnaṃ vādanakaṭṭhakuṭilādikaṃ koṇo, kuṇyate saddāyatenenāti koṇo, ṇo. “Dadda”iti saddaṃ karotīti daddari, daddati vā saddavisesena pariṇamatīti daddari, ri. “Paṭa”iti saddaṃ jahātīti paṭaho, paṭaṃ hantīti vā paṭaho. Hana hiṃsāgatīsu, kvi. Apare maddalādayo bherippabhedā[M 0.0114]. “Madda”iti saddaṃ lātīti maddalā, lā ādāne, a. “Mandalā”tipi pāṭho, mandaṃ saddaṃ lātīti mandalā. Ādinā ḍamaruādayopi bherippabhedā viññeyyā.

The curved wooden stick and so on for playing lutes and other instruments is called a ‘koṇa’; it is ‘koṇa’ because a sound is made with it (kuṇyate anena), with the suffix ‘ṇo’. It is ‘daddarī’ because it makes the sound ‘dadda’, or it is ‘daddarī’ because it transforms with a distinct sound, with the suffix ‘ri’. It is ‘paṭaha’ because it emits the sound ‘paṭa’, or it is ‘paṭaha’ because it strikes a surface. The root ‘han’ is in the senses of harming and going, with the suffix ‘kvi’. Other varieties of drums are the maddalā and so on. It is ‘maddalā’ because it takes the sound ‘madda’; the root ‘lā’ is in the sense of taking, with the suffix ‘a’. There is also a reading ‘mandalā’; it is ‘mandalā’ because it takes a slow sound (‘manda’). By ‘and so on’ are also to be understood other varieties of drums like the ḍamaru and so on.

145. Janappiye janehi piyāyitabbe vimaddoṭṭhe vilepanakuṅkumādīnaṃ, nānāgandhadabbānañca vimaddanobbhūte parimalo bhave, parimajjati pavattayatyāsayanti, a, nerutto, mala, malla dhāraṇe vā. Parimalyate dhārīyateti, ṇo. Vimaddaggahaṇena vāpikūpādino vimaddagandhādino (ka.) nirāso, janaggahaṇena makkhikādino. So parimalo gandho dūragāmī atinihārī atidūrapātī āmodo vuccate, āmodante anena, ṇo. Ito paraṃ iṭṭhagandhādayo vissasaddapariyantā tīsu liṅgesu vattante.

145. A perfume, dear to people and to be cherished by them, may arise from the crushing of unguents like saffron and various fragrant substances. It is ‘parimala’ because it pervades (parimajjati) or spreads (pavattayati); this is an etymological derivation. Alternatively, it is from the roots ‘mala’ or ‘malla’ in the sense of holding. Or, it is ‘parimala’ because it is worn or carried (parimalyate dhārīyate), with the suffix ‘ṇo’. By the mention of ‘crushing’ (vimadda) are excluded scents from ponds, wells, and so on; by the mention of ‘people’ (jana) are excluded those from flies and so on. That perfume, a scent which is far-reaching, extremely diffusive, and travels a great distance, is called ‘āmoda’; it is ‘āmoda’ because one delights in it (āmodante anena), with the suffix ‘ṇo’. From this point onward, the words for pleasant scents and so on, up to the word ‘vissa’, occur in all three genders.

146. Catukkaṃ iṭṭhagandhe. Iṭṭho gandho iṭṭhagandho, atha vā iṭṭho gandho assa iṭṭhagandho. Suṭṭhu rabhanti tussantyanenāti surabhi, i. Sundaro gandho assa sugandho, sugandhi ca, antassikārādeso.

146. There are four terms for an agreeable scent. ‘Iṭṭhagandha’ means an agreeable scent, or alternatively, it is ‘iṭṭhagandha’ because it has an agreeable scent. It is ‘surabhi’ because one is greatly delighted and satisfied by it (suṭṭhu rabhanti tussanti anena), with the suffix ‘i’. It is ‘sugandha’ because it has a beautiful scent, and also ‘sugandhi’, with the substitution of ‘i’ for the final vowel.

Dvayaṃ duggandhe. Pūti gandho assa, pubbe viya ikārādeso, kammadhārayasamāsaṃ assatthyatthepi kattumicchanti, pakriyālāghavatthaṃ bahubbīhiyeva nyāyoti. Duṭṭhu gandho assāti [M 0.0115] duggandho, tena vuttaṃ kaccāyanena – “kammadhārayamantatthiyehi bahubbīhi laghutaro”ti. Aññe tu lāghava’manādaramānā icchanteva mantatthiyaṃ. Duvidho vā vāccadhammo lahu garu ca, tatra bahubbīhinā lahu, kammadhārayamantatthiyenagaru. Kiñca bahubbīhinā atisāyanādyattho na gamyateti avassaṃ tappaṭipādanāya kammadhārayapubbako mantatthiyeva daṭṭhabbo.

There are two terms for a bad smell. It has a putrid smell; as before, there is the substitution of ‘i’. Some wish to form a karmadhāraya compound even in the sense of possession, but for the sake of brevity in derivation, the bahubbīhi is indeed more logical. It is ‘duggandha’ because it has a bad smell. Therefore, it was said by Kaccāyana: “The bahubbīhi is briefer than the karmadhāraya with a possessive suffix.” Others, however, disregarding brevity, still prefer the form with a possessive suffix. Or, the expressed meaning is twofold: light and heavy. In that case, the bahubbīhi is light, while the karmadhāraya with a possessive suffix is heavy. Moreover, with the bahubbīhi, the sense of excessiveness and so on is not conveyed, so for the sake of expressing that, the form with a possessive suffix, preceded by a karmadhāraya, should indeed be used.

Dvayaṃ citādhūmādigandhe. Visa vippayoge, so. Āmassa vasādivatthuno gandho taṃyogā, i, yaṃsaddo tassa napuṃsakattadīpako.

There are two terms for the smell of things like smoke from a pyre. From the root ‘visa’ in the sense of separation, with the suffix ‘so’, comes ‘vissa’. The smell of a raw substance, such as fat, is so called from its connection with that raw thing, with the suffix ‘i’; the word ‘yaṃ’ indicates its neuter gender.

147. Kuṅkumādayo cattāro catujjātigandho nāma. Kuka, vaka ādāne, umo, niggahītāgamo ca, kuṅkumaṃ, lohitacandanaṃ, yaṃ “kasmīraja”nti vuccati, kamissa vā kuṅkādeso, kuṅkumaṃ. Yu missane, yu, yavanaṃ, tassa pupphaṃ yavanapupphaṃ, devakusumaṃ, yavanadese jātaṃ pupphanti vā yavanapupphaṃ. Yaṃ “lavaṅga”ntipi vuccati, yaṃ pupphaṃ nuhīpupphasamānaṃ. Tagi gatyattho daṇḍako dhātu, aro, tagaraṃ, kuṭilaṃ. Taruto jāto turukkho, kho, uttañca, sallakīdavo hi “turukkho”ti vutto.

147. Saffron and the like are the four called the fourfold scents. From the root ‘kuka’ or ‘vaka’ in the sense of ‘taking’, with the suffix ‘uma’ and the augment of niggahīta, comes ‘kuṅkumaṃ’ (saffron), which is red sandalwood, also called ‘Kashmiri-born’. Or, from the root ‘kam’, with the substitution ‘kuṅka’, comes ‘kuṅkumaṃ’. From the root ‘yu’ in the sense of ‘mixing’, with the suffix ‘yu’, comes ‘yavanaṃ’ (foreign); its flower is ‘yavanapupphaṃ’ (foreign flower), a divine flower, or it is ‘yavanapupphaṃ’ because it is a flower born in a foreign land. This is also called ‘lavaṅga’ (clove), a flower resembling the ‘nuhī’ flower. From ‘tagi’, a ‘daṇḍaka’ root meaning ‘to go’, with the suffix ‘aro’, comes ‘tagaraṃ’ (a fragrant plant), which is crooked. Born from ‘taru’ (tree) is ‘turukkho’, with the suffix ‘kho’ and the substitution of ‘u’ for ‘a’; for the resin of the Sallakī tree is called ‘turukkho’.

148. Pajjena charasānaṃ nāmāni. Kaṃ pānīyaṃ sevateti kasāvo, avo, atha vā kaṃ savāpetīti kasāvo su [M 0.0116] savane. Tuvaropi kasāyopi kasāvapariyāyo. Tija nisāne, to, titto, kaṭu. Madhu mādhuriyaṃ, taṃyogā madhuro. Lunāti jaḷattanti lavaṇo, yu. Ambasadde, aro, ittaṃ, lattañca. Kaṭa gatiyaṃ, ṇvu, uttaṃ. Ime cha rasā nāma vuccanti. Tabbati dabbe kasāvādisaddā tīsu liṅgesu vattanti.

148. The names of the six tastes are given in this section. It is ‘kasāva’ (astringent) because it serves water (kaṃ sevati), with the suffix ‘avo’; or, because it causes water to flow (kaṃ savāpeti), from the root ‘su’ in the sense of flowing. ‘Tuvara’ and ‘kasāya’ are also synonyms for ‘kasāva’. From the root ‘tija’ in the sense of sharpening, with the suffix ‘to’, comes ‘titto’ (bitter). ‘Kaṭu’ (pungent) is also a taste. ‘Madhu’ is sweetness; from its association, comes ‘madhuro’ (sweet). It is ‘lavaṇo’ (salty) because it cuts (lunāti) dullness, with the suffix ‘yu’. From the word ‘amba’, with the suffix ‘aro’, the substitution of ‘i’, and the substitution of ‘l’, comes ‘ambila’ (sour). From the root ‘kaṭa’ in the sense of movement, with the suffix ‘ṇvu’ and the substitution of ‘u’, comes ‘kaṭuka’ (pungent). These six are called tastes. These words, such as ‘kasāva’, when referring to substances, occur in all three genders.

149. Dvayaṃ phoṭṭhabbe. Phusitabbo phasso, phoṭṭhabbo ca, tabbo, sassa ṭo, tassa ṭho. Tikaṃ visayimhi. Visayo assa gayhaṭṭhenātthīti visayi. Ukhati gacchati visayeti akkhaṃ, ussattaṃ dvittañca, natthi khaṃ vedanā etthāti vā akkhaṃ, na hi sukhavedanādayo sampayogavasena pañcasu indriyesu uppajjanti, javanādīsu eva pana uppajjantīti tathā vuttaṃ, manindriye tūpacārā manindriyesupacārā (ka.) akkhaṃ. Indo attā, tassa liṅgaṃ indriyaṃ, iyo. Nā’nantarena payojakaṃ cakkhādayo byāpārayante, tasmā atthi attā cakkhādīnaṃ payojakoti cakkhādikaṃ liṅgamattano bhavatīti nikāyantarikā. Sayaṃ tikkhamandādibhāve cakkhuviññāṇādīnaṃ tikkhamandādibhāvasambhavato tesu indati paramissariyaṃ karotīti vā indriyaṃ.

149. There are two terms for the tangible. That which is to be touched (phusitabbo) is ‘phassa’ and ‘phoṭṭhabba’. The derivation of ‘phoṭṭhabba’ is from ‘phusitabba’, where ‘s’ becomes ‘ṭ’ and ‘t’ becomes ‘ṭh’. There are three terms for the sense faculty. It is ‘visayī’ because it has an object (visayo assa atthi) in the sense of being grasped. It is ‘akkhaṃ’ because it goes (ukhati) to the object; this involves phonetic changes. Or, it is ‘akkhaṃ’ because there is no opening (khaṃ) for feeling (vedanā) in it; for pleasant feelings and the like do not arise in connection with the five senses, but only during the impulsion phase—thus it is said. In the case of the mind faculty, ‘akkhaṃ’ is used figuratively. It is ‘indriyaṃ’ because it is a mark (liṅgaṃ) of the lord (indo), that is, the self (attā), with the suffix ‘iyo’. For the sectarians say: “Because the eye and the like do not function without a director, there is a self that directs the eye and the like; thus, the eye and the like are a mark of the self.” Or, it is ‘indriyaṃ’ because it exercises supreme lordship (indati paramissariyaṃ karoti) over consciousness, since the sharpness or dullness of eye-consciousness and the like arises from the sharpness or dullness of the faculties themselves.

Chakkaṃ nayane. Neti attano nissitaṃ puggalanti nayanaṃ, yu. Asu byāpane, asati visayesu byāpī viya bhavatīti akkhi, sassa ko, atha vā akkha byāpanadassanesu, akkhati visayesu byāpībhavati, akkhati vā passati etenāti [M 0.0117] akkhi. Netīti nettaṃ. Locati passati etenāti locanaṃ. Accha dassanabyāpanesu, i, acchi. Cakkhati assādeti rūpanti cakkhu, u, cakkhati passatīti vā cakkhu.

There are six terms for the eye. It is ‘nayanaṃ’ because it leads (neti) the person dependent on it, with the suffix ‘yu’. From the root ‘asu’ in the sense of ‘pervading’: it is ‘akkhi’ because it becomes as if pervading objects when they are present, with ‘s’ becoming ‘k’. Or, from the root ‘akkha’ in the senses of ‘pervading’ and ‘seeing’: it is ‘akkhi’ because it pervades objects, or because one sees with it. It is ‘nettaṃ’ because it leads (neti). It is ‘locanaṃ’ because one sees (locati) with it. From the root ‘accha’ in the senses of ‘seeing’ and ‘pervading’, with the suffix ‘i’, comes ‘acchi’. It is ‘cakkhu’ because it experiences (cakkhati) forms, with the suffix ‘u’; or, it is ‘cakkhu’ because it sees (cakkhati).

150. Pañcakaṃ sote. Suṇāti etenāti sotaṃ. Saddo gayhate anenāti saddaggaho. Kara karaṇe, ṇo, kaṇṇo, kaṇṇati suṇāti etenāti vā kaṇṇo, kaṇṇa savane. Suṇāti yenāti savanaṃ, suti ca, yu,ti ca.

150. There are five terms for the ear. It is ‘sotaṃ’ because one hears (suṇāti) with it. It is ‘saddaggaho’ because sound is grasped (gayhate) by it. From the root ‘kara’ in the sense of ‘doing’, with the suffix ‘ṇo’, comes ‘kaṇṇo’. Or, it is ‘kaṇṇo’ because one hears (kaṇṇati) with it, from the root ‘kaṇṇa’ in the sense of ‘hearing’. It is ‘savanaṃ’ and ‘suti’ because one hears (suṇāti) with it, with the suffixes ‘yu’ and ‘ti’ respectively.

Catukkaṃ ghāne. Nasanti etāyāti natthu, thu, ā, nāsā. Ṇvu, aka ca ikāro ca nāsikā. Ghā gandhopādāne, ghāyati gandhopādānaṃ karotīti ghānaṃ, yu, ghāyantyanenāti vā ghānaṃ.

There are four terms for the nose. It is ‘natthu’ because one smells (nasanti) with it, with the suffix ‘thu’; with the suffix ‘ā’, it is ‘nāsā’. From ‘nāsa’, with the suffix ‘ṇvu’ (which becomes ‘aka’) and the feminine suffix ‘ikā’, comes ‘nāsikā’. From the root ‘ghā’ in the sense of ‘taking scent’: it is ‘ghānaṃ’ because it takes scent, with the suffix ‘yu’; or, it is ‘ghānaṃ’ because one smells with it.

Dvayaṃ jivhāyaṃ. Jīvati etāyāti jivhā, ho, jīva pāṇadhāraṇe. Jīvitanimittaṃ raso jīvitaṃ nāma, taṃ avhāyatīti vā jivhā, vaṇṇalopo. Rasanti etāyāti rasanā, rasa assādane, rasaṃ jānātīti vā rasanā, ñāssa nā, nī naye vā, a.

There are two terms for the tongue. It is ‘jivhā’ because one lives (jīvati) by it, with the suffix ‘ho’, from the root ‘jīva’ in the sense of ‘sustaining life’. Or, taste, being the cause of life, is called ‘jīvita’; it is ‘jivhā’ because it calls for (avhāyati) that, with the elision of a letter. It is ‘rasanā’ because one savours (rasanti) with it, from the root ‘rasa’ in the sense of ‘savouring’. Or, it is ‘rasanā’ because it knows (jānāti) flavour, with ‘ñā’ becoming ‘nā’; or from the root ‘nī’ in the sense of ‘leading’, with the suffix ‘a’.

151. Pajjaṃ sarīre. Sarati gacchati, saranti vā taṃ hiṃsantīti sarīraṃ, īro. Vapa bījasantāne. Vapati kusalākusalabījametthāti vapu, u. Gacchati, gaṇhāti vā kusalākusalametenāti [M 0.0118] gattaṃ, gamu gatiyaṃ, gaha upādāne vā. “Attā”ti abhidhānaṃ, buddhi ca bhavanti etasmāti attabhāvo. Vuṇoti saṃvarati etthāti bondi, vu saṃvaraṇe, di, niggahītāgamo. Vividhaṃ gaṇhāti etthāti viggaho. Diha upacaye, dihati vaḍḍhati ettha kusalākusalanti dehaṃ. Ayaṃ dehasaddo purise pulliṅgevattati. Kucchitānaṃ āyo uppattiṭṭhānanti kāyo. Tanu vitthāre, u, tanu, tanusaddoyaṃ itthiyaṃ. Etthāpi vāsaddo sambandhitabbo. “Aṅgenāṅgaṃ tanu ca tanunā gāḷhatattena tatta”nti uttaramegha 42 hi meghadūte vuttaṃ. Kaḷe retasi varaṃ kaḷevaraṃ, aluttasamāsoyaṃ.

151. A verse on the body. From 'sarati' (it moves, it goes), or because they harm it ('saranti taṃ hiṃsanti'), it is 'sarīraṃ', with the suffix 'īra'. From 'vapa' in the sense of 'sowing seed': because it sows the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome states herein, it is 'vapu', with the suffix 'u'. Because one goes ('gacchati') or grasps ('gaṇhāti') wholesome and unwholesome states by this, it is 'gattaṃ', from 'gamu' in the sense of 'going', or 'gaha' in the sense of 'grasping'. Because the designation 'attā' (self) and intelligence arise from this, it is 'attabhāvo' (existence). Because one covers ('vuṇoti') or restrains ('saṃvarati') herein, it is 'bondi', from 'vu' in the sense of 'covering', with the suffix 'di' and the augment 'niggahīta'. Because it takes various things herein, it is 'viggaho'. From 'diha' in the sense of 'accumulation': because wholesome and unwholesome states accumulate and grow herein, it is 'dehaṃ'. This word 'deha' is used in the masculine gender when referring to a man. Because it is the origin ('āyo') or place of arising for vile things, it is 'kāyo'. From 'tanu' in the sense of 'spreading', with the suffix 'u', comes 'tanu'; this word 'tanu' is feminine. Here too, the word 'vā' (or) should be connected. For it is said in the Meghadūta: 'Limb with limb, and the slender with the slender, heated by intense firmness'. The best ('varaṃ') in filth ('kaḷe') or semen ('retasi') is 'kaḷevaraṃ'; this is an 'aluttasamāsa', a compound where the case ending is not elided.

152-154. Chakkaṃ citte. Cintetīti cittaṃ. Ceto ca, nalopo. Manati jānātīti mano. Vijānātīti viññāṇaṃ, yu. Harati attano ādhāranti hadayaṃ, yo, rassa do ca. Mano eva mānasaṃ, sakatthe saṇa.

Six terms for the mind. Because it thinks ('cinteti'), it is 'cittaṃ'. And 'ceto', with the elision of 'na'. Because it thinks ('manati') or knows ('jānāti'), it is 'mano'. Because it discerns ('vijānāti'), it is 'viññāṇaṃ', with the suffix 'yu'. Because it carries ('harati') its own support, it is 'hadayaṃ', with the suffix 'yo', and the change of 'ra' to 'da'. 'Mānasaṃ' is simply 'mano', with the suffix 'aṇa' used in the reflexive sense.

Cuddasa buddhākhyassa guṇassa nāmāni. Jhāyatīti dhī, jhe cintāyaṃ, jhassa dho, nadādi, dhī, dhāretīti vā dhī, kvi, nadādi, dhī[M 0.0119], saṅkhāresu dhīkāro jāyati etāyāti vā dhī, nadādi. Paññāyate etāyāti paññā, a. Bujjhate tāyāti buddhi,ti. Medha hiṃ sāsaṅgamesu, karaṇe a, mi hiṃsāyaṃ vā, dho, medhā. Manati jānātīti mati, muti ca, uttaṃ, munātīti vā muti, muna ñāṇe,ti, muti. Bhū sattāyaṃ, ri, nadādi, bhūrī, bhūsaṅkhāte atthe ramatīti vā bhūrī, kvi, nadādi. Manati jānātīti mantā, anta, ā. Vidati jānātīti vijjā, pabbajjādinā siddhaṃ. Yu missane. Yamati missībhavati ñeyyesūti yoni. Paṭimukhaṃ bhanti upaṭṭhahanti ñeyyā etenāti paṭibhānaṃ, yu. Na muyhati etenāti amoho. Vīmaṃsā vicayo samupekkhā upaladdhi paṭipatti utticetanādīnipi buddhināmāni.

Fourteen names for the quality called 'buddhi' (wisdom). Because one contemplates ('jhāyati'), it is 'dhī'; from the root 'jhe' in the sense of 'contemplation', 'jha' becomes 'dho'; it is in the 'nadī' class. Or, because one upholds ('dhāreti'), it is 'dhī', with the 'kvi' suffix, in the 'nadī' class. Or, because by this the sound 'dhī' is born in formations, it is 'dhī', in the 'nadī' class. Because it is known ('paññāyate') by this, it is 'paññā', with the suffix 'a'. Because one awakens ('bujjhate') by this, it is 'buddhi', with the suffix 'ti'. From the root 'medha' in the sense of 'harming' and 'conflict', with the suffix 'a' in the instrumental sense; or from 'mi' in the sense of 'harming', with the suffix 'dha', comes 'medhā'. Because one thinks ('manati') or knows ('jānāti'), it is 'mati'; and 'muti', with the vowel 'u'. Or, because one knows ('munāti'), it is 'muti', from 'muna' in the sense of 'knowledge', with the suffix 'ti'. From 'bhū' in the sense of 'existence', with the suffix 'ri', in the 'nadī' class, comes 'bhūrī'. Or, because it delights in the thing called 'bhū' (existence), it is 'bhūrī', with the 'kvi' suffix, in the 'nadī' class. Because one thinks ('manati') or knows ('jānāti'), it is 'mantā', with the suffix 'tṛ' and feminine 'ā'. Because one knows ('vidati' or 'jānāti'), it is 'vijjā', a term established through renunciation and so on. From 'yu' in the sense of 'mixing'. Because it restrains ('yamati') or becomes mixed ('missībhavati') with knowables, it is 'yoni'. Because knowables shine forth ('bhanti') or present themselves ('upaṭṭhahanti') before one ('paṭimukhaṃ') by this, it is 'paṭibhānaṃ', with the suffix 'yu'. Because one is not deluded ('na muyhati') by this, it is 'amoho'. Investigation ('vīmaṃsā'), analysis ('vicayo'), equanimity ('samupekkhā'), attainment ('upaladdhi'), practice ('paṭipatti'), higher volition ('utticetanā'), and so on, are also names for wisdom ('buddhi').

Vipassanādayo nepakkantā pariyāyā paññābhedā paññāvisesā. Tattha vividhaṃ aniccādikaṃ saṅkhāresu passatīti vipassanā, yu. Sammādassanalakkhaṇā sammādiṭṭhi, sā duvidhā lokiyalokuttaravasena. Tattha purimā chabbisuddhippavattikāle, itarā ñāṇadassanavisuddhikāle labbhati. Ādipariyāyena pabhutinā anaññātaññassāmītindriyādayo gahitā. Tattha tattha kāriyesu vicāraṇā. Māna vīmaṃsāyaṃ, so, cittābhogādi. Vicārayate etāyāti vicāraṇā, cara sañcaye, curādigaṇo, yu. Sampajānātīti sampajāno, puggalo, dhammasamūho vā, ñāssa jā, tassa bhāvo sampajaññaṃ, nyassa ño, dvittaṃ, taṃ sātthakasampajaññādivasena catubbidhaṃ. Nissesato pāceti kusaladhammeti nipako, ñāṇī puggalo, tassa bhāvo nepakkaṃ. Dvayaṃ vedanāyaṃ. Vedayatīti vedayitaṃ, vida anubhavane, curādittā ṇayo, to, ikārāgamo ca. Vedayatīti vedanā, yu.

Insight and so on, ending with proficiency, are synonyms, divisions of wisdom, and specific kinds of wisdom. Therein, because one sees in various ways the impermanent and other characteristics in formations, it is 'vipassanā', with the suffix 'yu'. 'Sammādiṭṭhi' (right view) is characterized by correct seeing; it is twofold, mundane and supramundane. The former is obtained during the period of the six purifications, the latter during the purification of knowledge and vision. By the term 'ādi' (and so on), in its various applications, the faculty of 'I will know the unknown' and others are included. Investigation in various tasks. From 'māna' in the sense of 'vīmaṃsā' (investigation), with the suffix 'sa'; e.g., 'cittābhoga' (mental application) and so on. Because one investigates by this, it is 'vicāraṇā', from the root 'cara' in the sense of 'to accumulate' (of the 'curādi' group), with the suffix 'yu'. One who knows clearly ('sampajānāti') is 'sampajāno', a person or a collection of states; 'ñā' becomes 'jā'; the state of that is 'sampajaññaṃ', where 'nya' becomes 'ñña' with doubling. This is fourfold, by way of purposeful awareness and so on. Because one brings wholesome states to maturity without remainder, one is 'nipako' (proficient), a wise person; the state of that is 'nepakkaṃ' (proficiency). Two terms for feeling: 'vedayitaṃ' (that which is felt), from 'vida' in the sense of 'experiencing' (of the 'curādi' group), with the causative suffix 'ṇaya', the suffix 'ta', and the augment 'i'. And 'vedanā' (feeling), from 'vedayati' (it feels), with the suffix 'yu'.

155. Pañcakaṃ [M 0.0120] vitakke. Takka vitakke. Takketi sampayuttadhamme ārammaṇaṃ abhiniropetīti takko. Vitakkoti upasaggamattameva viseso. Saṅkappanti pabhavantyanenāti saṅkappo, ṇo, kappa vitakke, kappa sāmatthiye vā, bhūvādi, saṅkappayanti pabhavantyanenāti vā saṅkappo, kappa vitakke, curādi. Apa pāpuṇane, appeti sampayuttadhamme pāpeti ārammaṇanti appanā, yu, ā. Ūha vitakke. Ūhantyanenāti ūho. Takkaūhasaddā cettha ajjhāhāravācakāpi bhavanti, ajjhāhāraṃ nāma ūnapūraṇatthamadhikappabhedāharaṇaṃ madhikopādānaṃ (cintāmaṇiṭīkā). “Ajjhāhāro takka ūhā”ti amara 5.3 hi amarakose vuttaṃ. Dvayaṃ jīvitindriye. Ayaiti gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu. Ayati addhānaṃ gacchati yenāti āyu, ṇu, eti etenāti vā āyu, i gatimhi, ṇu, isse, e aya. Jīvanti anenāti jīvitaṃ, jīva pāṇadhāraṇe.

155. A set of five on initial application ('vitakka'). The root 'takka' is in the sense of 'initial application'. Because it directs ('abhiniropeti') associated states towards an object, it is 'takko' (reasoning). In 'vitakka', the difference is merely the prefix. Because they intend ('saṅkappanti') or arise ('pabhavanti') by this, it is 'saṅkappo' (intention), with the suffix 'ṇa', from 'kappa' in the sense of 'initial application' or 'capability' (of the 'bhūvādi' group). Or, because they intend ('saṅkappayanti') or arise ('pabhavanti') by this, it is 'saṅkappo', from 'kappa' in the sense of 'initial application' (of the 'curādi' group). From 'apa' in the sense of 'attaining': because it makes associated states attain the object, it is 'appanā' (absorption), with the suffix 'yu' and feminine 'ā'. The root 'ūha' is in the sense of 'initial application'. Because one reflects ('ūhanti') by this, it is 'ūho' (reflection). Here, the words 'takka' and 'ūha' can also denote supplementation ('ajjhāhāra'); supplementation is the supplying of an additional distinction to fill a deficiency. For it is said in the Amarakośa: 'Supplementation is reasoning and reflection'. Two terms for the life faculty. From 'aya', a 'daṇḍaka' root meaning 'to go': because one goes ('ayati') through time ('addhānaṃ') by this, it is 'āyu' (life-span), with the suffix 'ṇu'. Or, because one goes ('eti') by this, it is 'āyu', from 'i' in the sense of 'motion', with the suffix 'ṇu'; 'i' becomes 'e', then 'aya'. Because they live ('jīvanti') by this, it is 'jīvitaṃ' (life), from 'jīva' in the sense of 'sustaining life'.

Catukkaṃ samādhimhi. Nānālambaṇavisāraṇābhāvato ekaṃ aggaṃ ārammaṇametassāti ekaggaṃ, cittaṃ, “aggasaddo cettha ālambaṇavācako”ti hi saddhammaṭīkāyaṃ vuttaṃ, tassa bhāvo ekaggatā, ekaṃ vā ārammaṇaṃ ajati gacchatīti ekaggaṃ, tassa bhāvo ekaggatā. Kāmacchandaṃ sametīti samatho, tho, samu upasame, “samādhi kāmacchandassa paṭipakkho”ti pārā. aṭṭha. 1.11; dha. sa. aṭṭha. 160 hi vuttaṃ. Vikkhipanaṃ nānārammaṇaperaṇaṃ vikkhepo, so natthi etthāti avikkhepo. Ekārammaṇe suṭṭhu ādhānaṃ [M 0.0121] samādhi, saññāyami, nānālambaṇavikkhepavasappavattaṃ adhisaṅkhātaṃ cittabyadhaṃ sametīti vā samādhi, nerutto.

A set of four on concentration. Because there is no scattering to various objects, it has one supreme object—thus, it is 'ekaggaṃ' (one-pointed), that is, the mind. For it is said in a Saddhammaṭīkā: 'Here, the word agga refers to the object.' The state of this is 'ekaggatā' (one-pointedness). Or, because it goes ('ajati') to one object, it is 'ekaggaṃ'; the state of this is 'ekaggatā'. Because it appeases ('sameti') sensual desire, it is 'samatho' (tranquility), with the suffix 'tha', from the root 'samu' in the sense of 'to appease'. For it is said: 'Concentration is the opponent of sensual desire.' Scattering, the impelling towards various objects, is 'vikkhepo' (distraction). That is not present herein, thus 'avikkhepo' (non-distraction). The firm placing ('suṭṭhu ādhānaṃ') on a single object is 'samādhi' (concentration), in the conventional sense. Or, because it appeases ('sameti') the mental affliction known as proceeding under the influence of distraction towards various objects, it is 'samādhi', according to the etymologists.

156. Pajjena vīriyassa nāmāni. U dukkhalābhaṃ, uddhaṃ vā sahati khamatīti ussāho, ṇo. Ā bhuso kāyaṃ, cittañca tāpetīti ātappo ātāpo (?) abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkā 1135 gāthāyaṃ passitabbaṃ, tapa santāpe. Līnaṃ cittaṃ paggaṇhāti ukkhipatīti paggaho. Attano nissayaṃ paramatthaṃ gaṇhāpetīti vā paggaho. “Pasaddo paramatthepī”ti hi ekakkharakose vuttaṃ. Vāyamanti yenāti vāyāmo, vāyama ussāhane, atha vā vaya gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu, vayati sabbakālanti vāyāmo, amo, vāyo viya sadā amati gacchatīti vā vāyāmo. Paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamatīti parakkamo, paraṃ paccanīkabhūtaṃ kosajjaṃ akkamatīti vā parakkamo. Padahati yenāti padhānaṃ, yu. Dahassa dho, daha bhasmīkaraṇe papubbadhādhātunā sādhetabbaṃ maññe. Vīre sādhu, vīrānaṃ vā kammaṃ, vidhinā vā īrayitabbaṃ pavattetabbanti vīriyaṃ, īra gatiyaṃ, īhati eti vā yāya subhāsubhaphalanti īhā, īha ceṭṭhāyaṃ, i vā gatimhi, pacchime hapaccayo, uddhaṃ yanti yenāti uyyāmo, amo. Tiṭṭhati ettha subhāsubhaphalanti dhiti,ti, ṭhā gatinivattiyaṃ.

156. The names of energy ('vīriya'), in verse. Because it endures ('sahati') or bears ('khamati') hardship ('u' for 'dukkhalābhaṃ') or upward movement ('uddhaṃ'), it is 'ussāho' (effort), with the suffix 'ṇa'. Because it greatly ('ā' for 'bhuso') heats ('tāpeti') the body and mind, it is 'ātappo' (ardor), from the root 'tapa' in the sense of 'to heat'. Because it lifts up ('paggṇhāti' or 'ukkhipati') the sluggish mind, it is 'paggaho' (exertion). Or, because it causes one to grasp ('gaṇhāpeti') the ultimate goal ('paramatthaṃ'), which is its support, it is 'paggaho'. For it is said in the Ekakkharakosa: 'The prefix pa is also used in the ultimate sense.' Because one strives ('vāyamanti') by it, it is 'vāyāmo' (endeavor), from the root 'vāyama' in the sense of 'to exert'. Or, 'vaya' is a 'daṇḍaka' root meaning 'to go'; because it always goes ('vayati'), it is 'vāyāma', with the suffix 'ama'. Or, because it always goes ('amati') like the wind ('vāyo'), it is 'vāyāma'. Because it overcomes ('akkamati') one state after another, it is 'parakkamo' (exertion). Or, because it overcomes laziness ('kosajjaṃ'), which is its opposite, it is 'parakkamo'. Because one strives ('padahati') by it, it is 'padhānaṃ' (striving), with the suffix 'yu'; the 'dha' comes from 'daha', from the root 'daha' in the sense of 'to reduce to ashes'. It is good for heroes ('vīre sādhu'), or it is the action of heroes ('vīrānaṃ kammaṃ'), or it should be set in motion ('īrayitabbaṃ') according to rule ('vidhinā'), thus 'vīriyaṃ' (energy), from the root 'īra' in the sense of 'to move'. Because one strives ('īhati') or goes ('eti') by it towards good and bad results, it is 'īhā' (exertion), from the root 'īha' in the sense of 'to strive', or from 'i' in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix 'ha' at the end. Because one goes upward ('uddhaṃ yanti') by it, it is 'uyyāmo' (exertion), with the suffix 'ama'. Because good and bad results stand firm ('tiṭṭhati') herein, it is 'dhiti' (steadfastness), with the suffix 'ti', from the root 'ṭhā' in the sense of 'cessation of movement'.

157. Pajjena vuttapariyāyassa vīriyassa cattāri aṅgāni dasseti. Tacādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ avasissanaṃ avasesatā maṃsalohitehi avadhibhūtehi, maṃsalohitānaṃ pana sussanaṃ sukkhatā[M 0.0122]. Etāni cattāri adhiṭṭhānavasappavattāni vīriyassa aṅgāni kāraṇāni honti. Aṅga gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu. Aṅgati siddhiṃ gacchati vīriyaphalametehīti aṅgāni. Taca pālane, ṇo, taco. Naha bandhane āru. Nhārūtipi pāṭho. Tattha nantassa lopo. Sisa asabbappayoge, yu, dvittaṃ. Asati khepeti addhānanti aṭṭhi,ti, napuṃsake, nerutto, ā bhuso tiṭṭhati etenāti vā aṭṭhi, i. Mana ñāṇe, so, nassa niggahītaṃ, maṃsaṃ. Ruha janane, ito, lattaṃ, lohitaṃ.

157. By this verse, he shows the four limbs of energy, which were described previously. The remaining of the three, beginning with skin, has flesh and blood as its limit; for flesh and blood, however, the drying up is dryness. These four, proceeding by way of resolve, are the limbs and causes of energy. The root aṅga is in the sense of ‘to go’; it is a daṇḍaka root. Because the fruit of energy is achieved (aṅgati siddhiṃ gacchati) by these, they are called aṅgāni (limbs). Taco (skin) is from the root taca in the sense of ‘to protect’, with the suffix ṇo. Nahāru (sinew) is from the root naha in the sense of ‘to bind’, with the suffix āru. Nhāru is also a reading; there, the n is elided. Aṭṭhi (bone) is from the root sisa in the sense of ‘improper usage’, with the suffix yu and doubling. Because it wastes away (khepeti) over time (addhānaṃ), it is aṭṭhi; it is neuter, with the suffix ti, according to the etymologists. Or, because one stands firm (tiṭṭhati) greatly (bhuso) by this, it is aṭṭhi, with the suffix i. Maṃsaṃ (flesh) is from the root mana in the sense of ‘to know’, with the suffix so, and the n becomes a niggahīta. Lohitaṃ (blood) is from the root ruha in the sense of ‘to generate’, with the suffix ita, and the r becomes l.

158. Asājhasādhanepi yassā vasena uyyāmo, sā adhimattehā adhikasattiyuttā īhā ussoḷhī nāma, u pabalaṃ dukkarakammaṃ sahati yāyāti ussoḷī, sahassa soḷho, nadādi, ussāhānaṃ ūhāti vā ussoḷī, yathā “padaṭṭhāna”nti, ākārasso, hassa ḷo, ūlopo, nadādi, vāyāmamattepi. Dvayaṃ satiyaṃ. Sarati, saranti vā tāya, saraṇamattameva vā esāti sati,ti, pamādaṃ vā sarati hiṃsatīti sati. Anu punappunaṃ sati anussati, upasaggamattameva vā viseso, dvepi itthiyaṃ.

158. Even in accomplishing what is not easy, that exertion (uyyāmo) by means of which there is an intense striving (adhimattehā īhā) endowed with superior strength (adhikasattiyuttā), is called ussoḷhī. Because one endures (sahati) difficult tasks (dukkarakammaṃ) with great strength (pabalaṃ) by it, it is ussoḷī. (Soḷho is from sah, like in the nadādi group). Or, because it gathers (ūhāti) efforts (ussāhānaṃ), it is ussoḷī, like padaṭṭhāna. (Here, ā becomes o, h becomes ḷ, and ū is elided, like in the nadādi group). This applies even to mere exertion. There are two terms for mindfulness (sati). Because one remembers (sarati), or because beings remember by it, or because it is merely remembering, it is sati (with the suffix ti). Or, because it destroys (sarati), that is, harms (hiṃsati), negligence (pamādaṃ), it is sati. Repeated mindfulness (punappunaṃ sati) is anussati (recollection). Or, the difference is merely the prefix (anu). Both are feminine.

Dvayaṃ lajjāyaṃ. Laji pīḷe, kātantadhātu. Lajja lajjane, moggallānadhātu, lajjati pāpāti lajjā, a. Hirī lajjiyaṃ, i. Hiriyati pāpāti hirī. Samānā tulyatthā dve. Dvayaṃ ottappe. Ottappati bhāyati pāpatoti ottappaṃ, tapa bhaye avapubbo. Pāpato bhāyati sīlenāti pāpabhīru, puggalo, cittaṃ vā, tassa bhāvo tathā.

There are two terms for shame (lajjā). Lajjā is from the root laji in the sense of ‘to torment’, a Kātantadhātu root; or, from the root lajja in the sense of ‘to be ashamed’, a Moggallānadhātu root. Because one is ashamed of evil (pāpaṃ lajjati), it is lajjā, with the suffix a. Hirī is from the root hirī in the sense of ‘to be ashamed’, with the suffix i. Because one is ashamed of evil (pāpaṃ hiriyati), it is hirī. The two are similar in meaning. There are two terms for fear of wrongdoing (ottappa). Because one fears (bhāyati) wrongdoing (pāpato), it is ottappa (fear of wrongdoing), from the root tapa in the sense of ‘to fear’, preceded by ava. One who fears evil (pāpato bhāyati) through virtue (sīlena) is called pāpabhīru (one who fears evil), referring to a person or the mind. The state of such a one is likewise.

159. Pajjaddhena [M 0.0123] upekkhāya vedanāya nāmāni. Majjhatte majjhattasabhāve pavattā majjhattikā. Dvinnaṃ vedanānaṃ samīpe pavattā ikkhā anubhavananti upekkhā, ikkha dassane. Adukkhā ca sā asukhā ceti adukkhamasukhā, makāro padasandhikaro.

159. In this half-stanza, the names for the feeling of equanimity (upekkhā vedanā) are given. Occurring in a neutral state, with a neutral nature, it is majjhattikā (neutral). Because it is an observation (ikkhā) occurring near (samīpe) the two feelings, it is upekkhā (equanimity), from the root ikkha in the sense of ‘to see’. And because it is neither painful nor pleasant, it is adukkhamasukhā (neither-painful-nor-pleasant). The letter m is inserted for euphonic connection.

Dvayaṃ manasikāre. Bhavaṅgavasena pavattassa cittassa ābhujanato āvaṭṭāpanato cittābhogo. Pālanajjhohārattho cettha bhujadhātu āvaṭṭanattho āpubbattā, idaṃ pana vīthijavanapaṭipādake sandhāya vuttaṃ, cittassārammaṇe ābhujanaṃ pavattanaṃ vā cittābhogo, idaṃ pana ārammaṇapaṭipādakavasena vuttaṃ. Bhavaṅgamanato visadisaṃ manaṃ karotīti manakkāro, karaṇaṃ vā kāro, manasmiṃ kāro manakkāro. Ettha ca paṭhamavikappena dve paṭipādakā vuttā, pacchimena tu itaro.

There are two terms for attention (manasikāra). The turning (ābhujanato) and directing (āvaṭṭāpanato) of the mind that proceeds by way of the life-continuum is cittābhoga (engagement of mind). Here, the root bhuj has the meaning of ‘to protect’ or ‘to consume’, but when preceded by ā, it means ‘to turn towards’. This, however, is said with reference to the establishing of the cognitive process and impulsion. Or, the bending (ābhujanaṃ) or directing (pavattanaṃ) of the mind towards an object is cittābhoga. This, however, is said by way of establishing the object. Because it makes the mind distinct from the flow of the life-continuum, it is manakkāra (attention). Or, the act of making is kāra; the making in the mind is manakkāra. And here, by the first alternative, two establishers are stated, while by the latter, the other.

Dvayaṃ adhimokkhe. Muca mocane, adhimuccanaṃ “idamevā”ti sanniṭṭhānakaraṇaṃ adhimokkho. Nicchayanaṃ niṇṇayanaṃ nicchayo, caya gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu, cassa dvittaṃ, chattaṃ, ni bhusaṃ chedanaṃ vā nicchayo, chidi dvidhākaraṇe, issattaṃ, dassa yo, asarūpadvittaṃ.

There are two terms for resolve (adhimokkha). Adhimokkha is from the root muca in the sense of ‘to release’. Adhimuccana, the act of making a firm decision, ‘This indeed is it,’ is adhimokkha. Discrimination (nicchayanaṃ) and determination (niṇṇayanaṃ) is nicchaya. The root caya is in the sense of ‘to go’; it is a daṇḍaka root. The doubling of ca produces ccha. Or, nicchaya is from ni (meaning ‘intensely’) and chedana (‘cutting’), from the root chidi in the sense of ‘to split’. Here, the i becomes a, the d becomes y, and there is dissimilar doubling.

160. Pajjaddhaṃ dayāyaṃ. Daya dānagatihiṃsārakkhaṇesu. Dayati paradukkhaṃ, attasukhañca hiṃsatīti dayā, a. Kapi [M 0.0124] calane, anu punappunaṃ kampeti attādhārassa cittanti anukampā. Kaṃ sukhaṃ rundhatīti karuṇā, rudhi āvaraṇe, dhassa ṇo, atha vā karonti attānamadhīnametāyāti karuṇā, yu, ā, karuṇā, sā eva kāruññaṃ. Anuddayāti upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ.

160. This half-stanza concerns compassion (dayā). The root daya is used in the senses of ‘giving’, ‘going’, ‘harming’, and ‘protecting’. Because it feels (dayati) the suffering of others and harms (hiṃsati) one’s own happiness, it is dayā (compassion), with the suffix a. Anukampā is from the root kapi in the sense of ‘to tremble’. Because it repeatedly makes the mind of oneself tremble, it is anukampā (sympathy). Because it obstructs (rundhati) happiness (kaṃ sukhaṃ), it is karuṇā (pity), from the root rudhi in the sense of ‘to obstruct’, with dha becoming ṇa. Or, because they make themselves dependent on it, it is karuṇā, with the suffixes yu and ā. Karuṇā is indeed kāruñña (compassion). The word anuddayā is augmented by the prefix anu.

Pajjaddhaṃ viratiyaṃ. Ramu uparame vipubbo, viramaṇaṃ veramaṇī, yu, nadādi, veraṃ maṇati vināsetīti vā veramaṇī. Viramaṇaṃ virati,ti. Dūrato viramaṇaṃ ārati.

This half-stanza concerns abstinence (virati). Veramaṇī is from the root ramu in the sense of ‘to cease’, preceded by vi. The act of ceasing (viramaṇaṃ) is veramaṇī, with the suffix yu, like in the nadādi group. Or, because it destroys (vināseti) enmity (veraṃ), it is veramaṇī. The act of ceasing (viramaṇaṃ) is virati (abstinence), with the suffix ti. Ceasing from afar is ārati (aversion).

161. Catukkaṃ khantiyaṃ. Titikkhanaṃ khamanaṃ titikkhā, tija khantiyaṃ, kho, dvittaṃ, kattādi, ā. Khamanaṃ sahanaṃ khanti,ti. Khamate khamanaṃ, khamā ca, khamu sahane. Dvayaṃ mettiyaṃ. Mida snehe, mijjati sinehatīti mettā, ta, ā. Metti,ti. Atha vā mitte bhavā mettā, metti ca.

161. There are four terms for patience (khanti). Endurance (titikkhanaṃ) and forbearance (khamanaṃ) are called titikkhā. Titikkhā is from the root tija in the sense of ‘to be patient’, with the suffix kho, doubling of the consonant, and like kattādi, with the suffix ā. Forbearance (khamanaṃ) and endurance (sahanaṃ) are called khanti (patience), with the suffix ti. It endures (khamate), it is endurance (khamanaṃ), and it is khamā (patience), from the root khamu in the sense of ‘to endure’. There are two terms for loving-kindness (mettā). Mettā is from the root mida in the sense of ‘to be affectionate’. Because one is affectionate (mijjati sinehati), it is mettā, with the suffixes ta and ā. Metti is with the suffix ti. Or, because it exists in a friend (mitte bhavā), it is mettā and metti.

Pajjaddhaṃ diṭṭhiyaṃ. Dassīyate dassanaṃ, disa pekkhane, yu. Dassanaṃ diṭṭhi. Labha lābhe,ti, laddhi, micchādiṭṭhiyameva. Sesā tu ubhayatra. Ṭhitapakkho siddhanto ṭhito pakkho siddhanto, pubbapakkhaṃ nirasya siddhapakkhaṭṭhāpane iti bhāvo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā), siddho anto anenāti viggaho. Samantato ayanaṃ gati samayo.

This half-stanza concerns view (diṭṭhi). It is seen, it is seeing (dassanaṃ), from the root disa in the sense of ‘to see’, with the suffix yu. Seeing is diṭṭhi (view). Laddhi is from the root labha in the sense of ‘to gain’, with the suffix ti. Laddhi (attainment) refers specifically to wrong view. The rest, however, apply in both cases, i.e., to right and wrong view. An established position is siddhanta (doctrine). The analysis is: ‘The end (anto) is accomplished (siddho) by this (anena).’ Movement (ayanaṃ) or going (gati) all around (samantato) is samaya (convention).

162. Dohaḷantaṃ taṇhāyaṃ. Tasa pipāsāyaṃ, yāya tasanti, sā taṇhā, ṇho. Iṇamhi tasiṇā. Eja kampane, ejā[M 0.0125]. Saṃsārato nissaritumappadānavasena jālasadisattā jālinī, upamāne inī. Visa pavesane, sabbatra visatā patthatāti visattikā, sakatthe ṇiko. Chanda icchāyaṃ, chandanaṃ chando, kattukamyatāpi. Tesu tesvārammaṇesu ākulībhūtattā jaṭā viyāti jaṭā. Kamu icchāyaṃ,ti, nikanti. Isu icchāyaṃ, a, issa ā, āsā. Sivu tantasantāne, bhavādīhi bhavādayo sibbatīti sibbinī, a, inī. Satte bhavaṃ netīti bhavanetti,ti.

162. The section ending with dohaḷa concerns craving (taṇhā). From the root tasa in the sense of ‘to thirst’: because beings thirst (tasanti) on account of it, it is taṇhā (craving), with the suffix ṇho. Tasiṇā is craving in the sense of a debt. From the root eja in the sense of ‘to tremble’, comes ejā. Because it is like a net (jālasadisattā) in that it does not allow (appadānavasena) one to escape from saṃsāra, it is jālinī (net-like), with the suffix inī in the sense of comparison. From the root visa in the sense of ‘to enter’: because it spreads (patthatāti) everywhere like poison (visatā), it is visattikā (attachment), with the suffix ṇiko in its own sense. From the root chanda in the sense of ‘to desire’: the act of desiring is chando (desire); it is also the desire to act (kattukamyatā). Because it is entangled in those various objects like matted hair (jaṭā viya), it is jaṭā (tangle). From the root kamu in the sense of ‘to desire’, with the suffix ti, comes nikanti. From the root isu in the sense of ‘to desire’, with the suffix a, and the i becoming ā, comes āsā (hope). From the root sivu in the sense of ‘to sew a continuous thread’: because it sews existences to other existences, it is sibbinī (the sewer), with the suffixes a and inī. Because it leads beings to existence, it is bhavanetti (leader to existence), with the suffix ti.

163. Jhecintāyaṃ, ārammaṇābhimukhaṃ jhāyatīti abhijjhā, ā. Vana sambhattiyaṃ, vanati yena so vanatho, tho. Vā gatiyaṃ, vāti ārammaṇanti vānaṃ, yu. Lubha icchāyaṃ, lubbhanaṃ lobho, ṇo. Ranja rāge, rajjanaṃ, rajjanti vā yena so rāgo, ṇo. Laya gatiyaṃ, ā punappunaṃ layatyārammaṇesūti ālayo, punappunaṃ layati saṃsilesati yenāti vā ālayo. “Layo vināse saṃsilese, sāmye toriyattikassa ce”ti nānatthasaṅgahe. Piha icchāyaṃ, curādi, a, pihayati yāyāti pihā. Cittassa nānārammaṇesu vibbhamakaraṇato manaso ratho iva manoratho, mano eva ratho viyāti vā manoratho. Isu icchāyaṃ, a, sassa cchādeso. Lasa kantiyaṃ, abhimukhaṃ katvā lasati yenāti abhilāso, ṇo. Kamu icchāyaṃ, ṇo, kāmo[M 0.0126]. Duha papūraṇe, duhanaṃ doho, taṃ lātīti dohaḷo, duṭṭhaṃ hadayametenāti vā dohaḷo, hadayassa haḷo, hala kampane dvisaddūpapado, dvīhi halati kampatīti vā dohaḷo, a, dvissa do, lassa ḷo. Dve hadayā assa paramatthassāti vā dohaḷo. A, dvissa do, hadayassa haḷo, dassa ḷo vā, yalopo, icchāvisesattepi dohaḷassa sāmaññavatticchāya niddeso.

163. From the root jhe in the sense of ‘to long for’: because it longs for an object, it is abhijjhā, with the suffix ā. From the root vana in the sense of ‘to be devoted to’: that by which one is devoted is vanatho, with the suffix tho. From the root vā in the sense of ‘to go’: because it goes towards an object, it is vānaṃ, with the suffix yu. From the root lubha in the sense of ‘to desire’: the act of desiring is lobho, with the suffix ṇo. From the root rañja in the sense of ‘passion’: the act of being impassioned, or that by which beings are impassioned, is rāgo, with the suffix ṇo. From the root laya in the sense of ‘to go’: because it repeatedly clings to objects, it is ālayo; or, that by which one repeatedly clings and adheres is ālayo. In the Nānātthasaṅgaha it is said: ‘Laya means destruction, adhesion, sameness, and also the three kinds of musical instruments.’ From the root piha of the curādi group, in the sense of ‘to desire’: that by which one longs is pihā, with the suffix a. Because it causes the mind to wander among various objects, it is like a chariot of the mind, thus manoratho; or, the mind itself is like a chariot, thus manoratho. From the root isu in the sense of ‘to desire’, with the suffix a, and the substitution of ccha for sa. From the root lasa in the sense of ‘to desire’: that by which one desires, having turned towards, is abhilāso, with the suffix ṇo. From the root kamu in the sense of ‘to desire’, with the suffix ṇo, comes kāmo. From the root duha in the sense of ‘to fill’: the act of filling is doho; because it takes that, it is dohaḷo. Or, because the heart is corrupted by it, it is dohaḷo. Or, haḷa from hadaya, from the root hala ‘to shake’, with the word dvi as a prefix; because it shakes in two ways, it is dohaḷo, with the suffix a, where dvi becomes do and l becomes ḷ. Or, because it has two hearts in the ultimate sense, it is dohaḷo, with the suffix a, where dvi becomes do, hadaya becomes haḷa, or da becomes ḷ with the elision of ya. Although dohaḷa is a specific kind of desire, it is mentioned here as a general desire.

Ataṇhāsabhāvampi ruciṃ ālambaṇicchāsabhāvasāmaññena idheva vattumāha “ākaṅkhātu”iccādi. Kaṅkha icchāyaṃ, a. Ruca rocane, rocanaṃ kattukāmatā, i, ruca dittiyaṃ vā, ruci. Kattukāmateva. Sā ruci adhikā lālasā nāma, lasa kantiyaṃ, punappunaṃ, atisayaṃ vā lasatīti lālasā, dvittaṃ, assā. “Yācanāyaṃ mahicchāyaṃ taṇhātireke yācanāyaṃ (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.28), ussukke lālasā dvisū”ti ruddo.

Even a liking (ruci) that is not of the nature of craving is mentioned here in the general sense of the nature of desire for an object, as in 'ākaṅkhātu' (let him wish), etc. The root is kaṅkh in the sense of 'to desire', with suffix a. The root is ruc in the sense of 'to shine' or 'to please'; rocana is the desire to do, with suffix i. Or the root is ruc in the sense of 'to shine', thus ruci. It is indeed the desire to do. That ruci, when excessive, is called lālasā. The root is las in the sense of 'to shine' or 'to be beautiful'. It shines repeatedly or excessively, thus lālasā, with reduplication and lengthening of the vowel. Rudda states: 'Lālasā is used in two senses: in begging, in great desire, and in eagerness.'

164. Tikaṃ virodhe. Pāyena vīresu bhavaṃ veraṃ, paṭighapāpesupi. Rudha paṭighāte, virujjhanaṃ virodho. Disa appītiyaṃ, viddesanaṃ viddeso.

164. Three terms in the sense of opposition. Vera (enmity) generally arises among the brave, and also in connection with aversion and evil deeds. The root is rudh in the sense of 'to obstruct'; virujjhanaṃ is virodho (opposition). The root is dis in the sense of 'to be displeased'; viddesanaṃ is viddeso (hatred).

Rosantaṃ kodhe. Dusa appītiyaṃ, dussanaṃ doso. Ārammaṇe paṭihaññatīti paṭighaṃ, hana hiṃsāyaṃ, paṭighasaddoyaṃ pulliṅge vā bhavati. Kudha kope, kujjhanaṃ kodho. Āgantvā haññatīti āghāto. Kupa kope, kuppatīti kopo, kopayati vā cittanti kopo. Rusa rosane, rusanaṃ dussanaṃ roso.

The set ending with rosa is used in the sense of anger. The root is dus in the sense of 'displeasure'; dussanaṃ is doso (anger/fault). That which strikes against an object is paṭigha; the root is han in the sense of 'to injure'. This word paṭigha can also be masculine. The root is kudh in the sense of 'anger'; kujjhanaṃ is kodho (anger). That which strikes upon approach is āghāto. The root is kup in the sense of 'anger'; that which is agitated is kopo, or that which agitates the mind is kopo. The root is rus in the sense of 'irritation'; rusanaṃ or dussanaṃ is roso (anger/irritation).

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0127] parānatthacintane. Byāpajjati vinassati cittametenāti byāpādo, paṭighepi. Pada gatimhi. Parasampattīsu nābhiramatīti anabhirati, ramu ramaṇe,ti.

Two terms in the sense of thinking of harm to others. That by which the mind is afflicted and ruined is byāpāda, which is also used in the sense of aversion; the root is pad in the sense of 'movement'. Not delighting in the success of others is anabhirati; the root is ram in the sense of 'to delight', with suffix ti.

165. Dvayaṃ upanāhe. Naha bandhane, punappunaṃ, upagantvā vā nayhati cittanti upanāho. Bajjhati veramanenāti baddhaveraṃ. Dvayaṃ soke. Suca soke, ṇo, sucanaṃ soko. Sucate socanaṃ.

165. Two terms in the sense of resentment. The root is nah in the sense of 'to bind'; that which binds the mind repeatedly or upon approach is upanāho. That which is bound by enmity is baddhaveraṃ (bound enmity). Two terms in the sense of sorrow. The root is suc in the sense of 'to sorrow'; with suffix ṇo, sucanaṃ is soko (sorrow). Sucate means 'one sorrows'; socanaṃ is 'sorrowing'.

Tikaṃ rudite. Rudi assuvimocane, sabbatra bhāve to. Kadi avhāne, rodane ca, tapaccayassa aṇṇādese ruṇṇaṃ. Dvayaṃ paridevane. Devanaṃ sokena vilāpo, punappunaṃ, samantato vā devo paridevo, pariddavo ca.

Three terms in the sense of crying. The root is rud in the sense of 'shedding tears'; in all cases, the suffix is ta in the sense of 'state'. The root is kad in the sense of 'calling out' and 'weeping'; with the substitution of aṇṇa for the suffix ta, it becomes ruṇṇaṃ. Two terms in the sense of lamentation. Devanaṃ is wailing with sorrow. Or, wailing repeatedly or completely is paridevo (lamentation), and also pariddavo.

166. Tikaṃ bhaye cittutrāsasaṅkhāte. Sabbatra bhāvasādhanaṃ. Bhī bhaye, bhāyanaṃ bhīti,ti. Bhayaṃ, ṇo. Tasa ubbeje, uttasate uttāso, ṇo. Dvayaṃ mahati bhaye. Bhīruno idaṃ bheravaṃ, ṇo. Mahantañca taṃ bhayajanakattā bhayañcāti mahabbhayaṃ. Mahābhayantipi pāṭho.

166. Three terms in the sense of fear, designated as mental terror. In all cases, they are formed in the sense of 'state'. The root is bhī in the sense of 'to fear'; bhāyanaṃ is bhīti (fear), with suffix ti. Bhayaṃ (fear), with suffix ṇo. The root is tas in the sense of 'to be agitated'; uttasate means 'one is terrified', and uttāso (terror) is formed with suffix ṇo. Two terms in the sense of great fear. That which belongs to the fearful is bheravaṃ (terrifying), with suffix ṇo. And because it is great and generates fear, it is mahabbhayaṃ (great fear). The reading mahābhayaṃ is also found.

167. Pajjaṃ bhāyitabbasāmaññe. Bheravasaddoyaṃ sāmaññavācakopi atthīti idha niddeso. Bhāyati yasmāti bhiṃsanaṃ, so, yu, bindāgamo. Bhāyati yasmāti bhīmaṃ, mo. Dara vidāraṇe, darīyatīti dāruṇaṃ, uṇo. Bhāyati yasmāti [M 0.0128] bhayānakaṃ, ṇvu, anakādeso. Ghura bhīme, ghurati bhiṃsatīti ghoraṃ, ṇo. Paṭivattati bhayaṃ cittutrāso yasmāti paṭibhayaṃ. Bhāyati yasmāti bhesmaṃ, smapaccayo. Bhayaṃ karotīti bhayaṅkaraṃ, aluttasamāsoyaṃ. Ime nava bheravādayo bhayabheravādihetumhi dabbe visesanabhāvena vattante, tadā tīsu liṅgesu, sāmaññena tu napuṃsake.

167. This verse is in the general sense of what is to be feared. This word bherava also has a general meaning, hence its explanation here. That from which one fears is bhiṃsanaṃ (frightening), with suffixes so and yu, and a nasal augment. That from which one fears is bhīmaṃ (dreadful), with suffix mo. The root is dar in the sense of 'to split'; that which is split is dāruṇaṃ (cruel/harsh), with suffix uṇo. That from which one fears is bhayānakaṃ (fearful), with suffix ṇvu and the substitution anaka. The root is ghur in the sense of 'to be terrifying'; it terrifies, thus ghoraṃ (horrible), with suffix ṇo. That from which fear and mental terror turn back is paṭibhayaṃ (dreadful). That from which one fears is bhesmaṃ (terrible), with suffix sma. That which causes fear is bhayaṅkaraṃ (fear-inducing); this is an unelided compound. These nine terms, beginning with bherava, function as qualifiers for a thing that is the cause of fear, terror, and so on. In that case, they are in all three genders, but in a general sense, they are neuter.

168. Dvayaṃ parābhyudayāsahane. Issa issatthe, issa issāyanti vā dhātvattho, issati santesupi guṇesu vacasā, manasā vā dosāropanaṃ karotīti issā, a. Ussuya usūya (?) dosāvikaraṇe. Tikaṃ macchere. Masu āmasane, ccheraccharapaccayā, maccharameva macchariyaṃ, sakatthe iyo, atha vā masuiccetassa pāṭipadikassa sussa ṇamhi ccheraccharā, masu maccheretipi dhātu.

168. Two terms in the sense of intolerance of others' success. The root is iss in the sense of 'envy', or the root meaning is 'to be envious'; that by which one imputes faults by speech or mind, even when virtues are present, is issā (envy), with suffix a. The root is ussuy in the sense of 'manifesting faults'. Three terms in the sense of stinginess. The root is mas in the sense of 'to touch'; with suffixes cchera and cchara. Macchara itself becomes macchariyaṃ, with the suffix iya in its own meaning. Alternatively, for the nominal stem masu, when su becomes ṇa, the suffixes are cchera and cchara. The root mas also means 'to be stingy'.

Tikaṃ aññāṇe. Mūha vecitte, muyhanti tena sampayuttadhammā, sayaṃ vā muyhati, muyhanamattameva vā tanti moho. Vida ñāṇe, na vidatīti avijjā. Na vijānātīti aññāṇaṃ. Tikaṃ māne. Bhūtenābhūtena vā parato ukkaṃsakappanena cetaso unnati māno, yathā “sūro atthavāha’masmi sīlavā buddhisampanno”ti avehi bhalavā asmi, sīlavā buddhisaṃyuto (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.22). Māna pūjāyaṃ, curādi, a. Dhāraṇattho dhādhātu, karotyatthe vipubbo, seyyādibhāve attānaṃ vidadhāti yāya sā vidhā, tīsu. Uddhaṃ namati yāya sā unnati, itthiyanti.

Three terms in the sense of ignorance. The root is muh in the sense of 'to be bewildered'; the associated states are bewildered by it, or one is bewildered oneself, or it is merely bewilderment—thus moho (delusion). The root is vid in the sense of 'to know'; not knowing is avijjā (ignorance). Not understanding is aññāṇaṃ (unknowing). Three terms in the sense of conceit. The elevation of mind by imagining oneself superior to others, whether truly or falsely, is māno (conceit), as in: 'I am heroic, wealthy, virtuous, and intelligent.' The root is mān in the sense of 'to honor', from the curādi class, with suffix a. The root dhā has the meaning of 'upholding'; with the prefix vi in the sense of 'doing', that by which one places oneself in a state of superiority, etc., is vidhā (disposition), in three genders. That by which one is uplifted is unnati (elevation), in the feminine.

169. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0129] uddhacce. Hana gatiyaṃ, uddhaṃ uddhaṃ hanati gacchatīti uddhato, to, hanassa dho, asarūpadvittaṃ, cittaṃ, uddhatassa bhāvo uddhaccaṃ. Dhāva gatiyaṃ, uddhaṃ dhāvati cittametenāti uddhavaṃ, a, rasso.

169. Two terms in the sense of restlessness. The root is han in the sense of 'to move'; one who moves or goes upward and upward is uddhato (agitated), with suffix ta. The ta of hata becomes dha, with doubling of the dissimilar consonant. The state of being agitated is uddhaccaṃ (restlessness). The root is dhāv in the sense of 'to run'; that by which the mind runs upward is uddhavaṃ (agitation), with suffix a and shortening of the vowel.

Tāpādipañcakaṃ kukkucce. Tapa, dhupa santāpe, tapati cittametenāti tāpo, ṇo. Kucchitaṃ karotīti kukkutaṃ, cittaṃ, taṃsamaṅgī vā, tassa bhāvo kukkuccaṃ. Pacchā tapati etenāti pacchātāpo. Anu pacchā tapati yena so anutāpo. Sara gatiyaṃ, virūpena pati punappunaṃ sarati cittametenāti vippaṭisāro, tassa ṭo.

The pentad beginning with tāpa is used in the sense of remorse. The roots are tap and dhup in the sense of 'to burn' or 'to torment'; that by which the mind is tormented is tāpo (torment), with suffix ṇo. A blameworthy deed is kukataṃ; the state of having done such is kukkuccaṃ (remorse). That by which one is tormented afterwards is pacchātāpo (remorse). That by which one is subsequently tormented is anutāpo (remorse). The root is sar in the sense of 'to move'; that by which the mind repeatedly moves improperly towards an object is vippaṭisāro (regret), with suffix a.

170. Pajjaṃ vicikicchāyaṃ. Likha lekhane, manaṃ vilekhati dvidhākaraṇavasenāti manovilekho. Diha upacaye. Idha pana saṃpubbattā saṃsaye, karaṇe ṇo. Sī saye, idha saṃpubbattā kaṅkhāyaṃ, sabbatrevaṃ. “Kathamida”miti kathayati yāya sā kathaṃkathā. Kita rogāpanayane, chapaccayo, dvittādi, vigatā cikicchā ñāṇappaṭikāro etāyāti vicikicchā. Ila gatikampanesu, dvidhā ilati cittametenāti dveḷhakaṃ, hapaccayo, sakatthe ko ca. Kaṅkha vicikicchāyaṃ, a, itthiyaṃ. Saṅka saṅkāyaṃ. Vividhenākārena maññati yasmā, sā vimati. Mana ñāṇe, itthiyanti.

170. This verse is in the sense of doubt. The root is likh in the sense of 'to scratch'; that which scratches the mind, by way of making it twofold, is manovilekho (mental vacillation). The root is dih in the sense of 'to accumulate'; here, however, with the prefix saṃ, it is in the sense of doubt (sandeha), with suffix ṇo in the instrumental sense. The root is sī in the sense of 'to lie'; here, with the prefix saṃ, it is in the sense of hesitation (saṃsaya), and so on everywhere. That by which one asks, 'How is this?' is kathaṃkathā (questioning). The root is kit in the sense of 'removing disease'; with suffix cha, reduplication, etc. That by which the remedy (cikicchā), the counteraction of knowledge, is gone is vicikicchā (doubt). The root is il in the sense of 'moving and shaking'; that by which the mind wavers in two ways is dveḷhakaṃ (vacillation), with suffix ha, and also ka in its own meaning. The root is kaṅkh in the sense of 'doubt', with suffix a, feminine. The root is saṅk in the sense of 'doubt'. Because one thinks in various ways, it is vimati (wrong view/doubt); from the root man in the sense of 'to know', feminine.

171. Tikaṃ [M 0.0130] nīcapakatidosasambhūtarūpissariyādinimittike made, yasmiṃ sati uttaradānasādarolokanādivimukho puriso jāyate. Madopyatra “katthūrīgabbaretesu, madohassebhadānesū”ti kattari gabbharetesu, mado purisamānesūti (nissaya) rabhaso. Gabba māne, curādi, a, atha vā gara secane, bo. Māna pūjāyaṃ, visesato mānetīti abhimāno. Ahaṃkāre ahaṃsaddo nipāto, amhasaddopyatra, “aha”miti attānaṃ karoti yenāti ahaṃkāro. Dvayaṃ cintāyaṃ. Cinta cintāyaṃ, a. Jhe cintāyaṃ, jhāyate jhānaṃ, dvīsupi bhāvasādhanaṃ, a. Vitakkacintānaṃ ko bhedo? Vitakko tāva vācāya pubbabhāgappavatto, “pubbeva kho, gahapati, vitakketvā vicāretvā pacchā vācaṃ bhindatī”ti saṃ. ni. 4.348 hi vuttaṃ. Itarā pana tassā apubbabhāgappavattāpīti ayametāsaṃ viseso. Atha vā vitakko pakiṇṇakapariyāpanno eko cetasikadhammo, itarā pana sabbasādhāraṇapariyāpanno manasikāranāmako eko cetasikadhammoti ayametāsaṃ viseso.

171. Three terms in the sense of intoxication (mada), which is caused by things such as low birth, faults, beauty, wealth, etc., and in the presence of which a person becomes averse to giving gifts, showing respect, and so on. Here mada is also defined by Rabhasa as: 'Intoxication is found in musk, in the womb, in joy, and in the rut of an elephant.' The root is gabb in the sense of 'pride', from the curādi class, with suffix a; or the root is gar in the sense of 'to secrete', with suffix ba. The root is mān in the sense of 'to honor'; that by which one honors oneself specifically is abhimāno (pride). In ahaṃkāra, the word ahaṃ is a particle; the word amha is also used here. That by which one makes the self into an 'I' is ahaṃkāro (egoism). Two terms in the sense of thought. The root is cint in the sense of 'to think', with suffix a. The root is jhe in the sense of 'to think'; that which is thought upon is jhānaṃ (meditation); in both cases, they are formed in the sense of 'state', with suffix a. What is the difference between vitakka and cintā? Vitakka, for one, is the preliminary stage of speech, for it is said: 'First, householder, having applied thought and sustained thought, one then breaks forth into speech.' The other (cintā), however, can also arise without being a preliminary stage of speech; this is their distinction. Alternatively, vitakka is a particular mental factor, while the other, named manasikāra, is a universal mental factor; this is their distinction.

Dvayaṃ nicchaye. Naya gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu, ārammaṇaṃ nicchinanto nayatīti niṇṇayo, nassa ṇattaṃ. Atha adhimokkhaniṇṇayānaṃ ko bhedo? Adhimokkho ārammaṇaṃ ajjhogāhetvā tiṭṭhati, niṇṇayo vinicchayamattamevāti ayametesaṃ viseso. Atha vā adhimokkho pasādepi sambhavati, itaro pana na tathāti ayaṃpyetesaṃ bhedo[M 0.0131]. Tatra nicchayasaddo idhāpi pavattatīti dvīsupi vutto.

Two [terms] for certainty (nicchaya). The root 'naya' (√nī) has the meaning of 'going'; 'niṇṇaya' is that which leads (nayati) by determining an object, with 'na' becoming 'ṇa'. Now, what is the difference between adhimokkha and niṇṇaya? Adhimokkha, having thoroughly penetrated the object, remains [fixed]; niṇṇaya is merely a decision—this is their distinction. Alternatively, adhimokkha can also occur with confidence (pasāda), but the other does not—this is also their difference. Here, the word 'certainty' (nicchaya) also applies, thus it is stated for both.

Pādena abhyupagamassa nāmāni. Patipubbo jānāti abhyupagame, itthiyaṃ a, paṭiññā. Tathā suṇoti ca, a, paṭissavo, dvīsupi bhāvasādhanaṃ. Saṃvidā’gū, paṭiññānaṃ, niyamo, assavo, saṃsavo, aṅgīkāro, abhyupagamo, samādhiiccādīnipi abhyupagamassa nāmāni amara 5.5.

Names for agreement (abhyupagama) by way of etymology. The root jānāti (to know), prefixed with paṭi, in the sense of agreement, with the feminine suffix 'a', forms paṭiññā (acknowledgment). Similarly, suṇoti (to hear), with 'a', forms paṭissava (assent); in both cases, they are derived in the sense of a state (bhāvasādhana). Also, saṃvidā, āgū, paṭiññāna, niyama, assava, saṃsava, aṅgīkāra, abhyupagama, samādhi, etc., are names for agreement.

172. Chahi padehi anādarassa nāmāni. Māna pūjāyaṃ, curādi, mana ñāṇe vā, heṭṭhā katvā jānanaṃ avamānaṃ, bhāve yu. Yo yenānādarito, sa tato avassameva kāyavacīmanānaṃ aññatarenāvadhīyateti anādarepi byavadhānābhicārato tirasaddo antaradhāne vattamāno sambajjhateti tirodhānakaraṇaṃ tirakkāro. Pari parāpubbo bhūdhātu avaññāṇe, avapubbo jānāti ca, sabbatra bhāve ṇo, a ca. Dara ādare, ādaro sakkāro, tabbiparīto anādaro. Parābhavanaṃ parābhavo. Avajānanaṃ avaññā.

172. Names for disregard (anādara) by way of six terms. The root māna (to honor), from the curādi class, or mana (to know); knowing by putting down is avamāna (contempt), with the suffix yu in the sense of a state. One who is disregarded by another is inevitably harmed by one of body, speech, or mind—thus, in the sense of disregard, the word tira, signifying disappearance, which is present in obstruction and sorcery, becomes connected [to this meaning], hence tirakkāra (rejection), meaning causing disappearance. The root bhū, prefixed with pari or parā, means disrespect (avaññāṇa); and jānāti, prefixed with ava, also [means disrespect]. In all cases, the suffixes ṇo and a are used in the sense of a state. The root dara means regard; ādara is respect, and its opposite is anādara (disregard). Parābhavana is causing downfall; parābhava is downfall. Avajānana is contempt (avaññā).

Dvayaṃ ummāde. Cittassa vibbhamo bhanti ummādo. Mada ummāde, uggatehi, ummaggasaṇṭhitehi vā dosehi madanaṃ ummādo.

Two [terms] for madness (ummāda). The aberration of the mind, a delusion, is ummāda. The root mada means madness; ummāda is the state of being mad (madanaṃ) due to defilements (dosehi) that have arisen (uggatehi) or are established on the wrong path (ummaggasaṇṭhitehi).

173. Snehantaṃ [M 0.0132] snehe. Piyassa bhāvo pemaṃ, imo, piyassa pattaṃ, pīnayatīti vāpī, pino bhāvo pemaṃ, imo. Siniha, sniha pītiyaṃ, bhāve ṇo. Dvayaṃ mucchāyaṃ. Pīḷa vibādhāyaṃ, cittassa pīḷā cittapīḷā, vigatā nīlādisañjānanalakkhaṇā saññā etasmāti visaññī, tassa bhāvo visaññitā.

173. For affection (sneha), [the terms are as follows], ending with sneha. The state of being dear is pema (love), with the suffix 'imo'; or, it is the attainment of what is dear; or, because it satisfies (pīnayati), it is pī, and the state of being satisfied is pema, with the suffix 'imo'. The roots siniha and sniha mean joy; with the suffix ṇo in the sense of a state. Two [terms] for fainting (mucchā). The root pīḷa means oppression; oppression of the mind is cittapīḷā. One from whom perception, characterized by the recognition of blue, etc., has departed, is visaññī (unconscious); its state is visaññitā (unconsciousness).

Dvayaṃ pamāde. Yena sakko samāno sayaṃ kattabbaṃ na karoti, so pamādo, mada pamāde papubbo, pamajjanaṃ pamādo, ṇo. Saja visajjanāliṅgananimmānesu. Satiyā visajjanaṃ sativosaggo, issa o. Apubbavatthuparikkhātisaye kotūhalādidvayaṃ. Tuja hiṃsāyaṃ, kuṃ pāpaṃ tojatīti kotūhalaṃ, alo, vaṇṇavikāro ca. Tula nikkase, kuṃ pāpaṃ tulayatīti kutūhalaṃ, a, hakāravaṇṇāgamo. Kotukaṃ, kutukañca etesaṃ pariyāyāni.

Two [terms] for heedlessness (pamāda). That by which one, though capable, does not do what should be done, is pamāda. The root mada means heedlessness; prefixed with pa, pamajjana becomes pamāda, with the suffix ṇo. The root saja means releasing, embracing, or creating. The release of mindfulness is sativosagga; 'i' becomes 'o'. The pair kotūhala and the like [refer to] excessive examination of an unprecedented object. The root tuja means harming; kotūhala is that which harms evil (kuṃ pāpaṃ tojati), with the suffix ala, and a change of vowel. The root tula means assaying; kutūhala is that which weighs evil (kuṃ pāpaṃ tulayati), with the suffix a, and the addition of the letter ha. Kotuka and kutuka are synonyms of these.

174. Vilāsādayo kriyā ceṭṭhā, kiṃvisiṭṭhā? Sā kriyā nārisiṅgārabhāvajā itthīnaṃ ratibhāvajā, yā hāvasaddenoccante. Huyante rāgino atrāti hāvo, hu havane, ṇo. Ādinā vicchittipabhutīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ, tathā hi vuttaṃ nāṭakaratanakose –

174. Actions such as vilāsa and so forth are gestures; what are their distinguishing characteristics? That action arises from the amorous state of women, born from the nature of passion, which is expressed by the term hāva. The passionate are called to this, hence hāva; the root hu means to call, with the suffix ṇo. By 'and so forth' (ādinā), vicchitti and others are included. Thus it is stated in the Nāṭakaratnakośa:

“Līlā [M 0.0133] vilāso vicchitti, vibbhamo kilakiñcitaṃ;

Moṭṭāyitaṃ kuṭṭamitaṃ, vibboko lalitaṃ tathā.

"Playfulness (līlā), dalliance (vilāsa), coquetry (vicchitti), amorous confusion (vibbhamo), feigned agitation (kilakiñcita); involuntary affection (moṭṭāyita), feigned refusal (kuṭṭamita), proud indifference (vibboko), and grace (lalita) as well.

Vikatañceti viññeyyā, dasa thīnaṃ thīnaṃ ceṭṭhā (ka.) sabhāvajā;

Hāvo ca helā vikkhepa-sammūḷhamadakapaṇya”nti.

And `vikata` should be understood, completing the ten states natural to women; also hāva, helā, vikkhepa, sammūḷha, mada, and kapaṇya.'"

Tatra piyasamīpagamane yo ṭhānāsanagamanavilokitesu vikāro, akasmā ca kodhamihitacamakkāramukhavikūṇanaṃ, so vilāso, vipubbā lasadhātumhā ṇo. Sukumāravidhānena bhamukanettādikriyāsacivakaracaraṇaṅgavinyāso lalitaṃ, lala vilāse, to. Aladdhapiyasamāgamena kucittavinodanatthaṃ piyassa yā vesagatidiṭṭhihasitabhaṇitehānukati karīyate, sā līlā, lala vilāse, lala upasevāyanti vā dhātvattho, a. Surate pavaḍḍhecchā heḷā, helā vā, hila hāvakaraṇe, a. Madarāgahassajanito vipariyāso vibbhamo. Ābharaṇavilepanādīnaṃ kutoci piyāparādhato issāyānādarena cattānaṃ sakhīnaṃ payatanena vāraṇaṃ vicchitti, chidi dvedhākaraṇe,ti. Piyena dattaṃ pītinibandhanaṃ svappamapi bhūsanaṃ vicchittītyaññe. Kilakiñcitādayo nāṭakasatthānusārato byākhyāsudhāṭīkāṭīppaṇe ñeyyā.

Among these, vilāsa is a change in posture, sitting, movement, or gaze when approaching the beloved, and also a sudden anger, feigned smile, sidelong glance, or frowning of the face; it is derived from the root las prefixed with vi, with the suffix ṇo. Lalita is the delicate arrangement of brows, eyes, and other actions, accompanied by movements of hands, feet, and limbs; the root lala means to flirt, with the suffix to. Līlā is the imitation of the beloved's dress, gait, gaze, smile, or speech, done to dispel mental distress when unable to meet the beloved; the root lala means to flirt, or the meaning of the root lala is to serve, with the suffix a. Heḷā (or helā) is increased desire in sexual intercourse; the root hila means to make an amorous gesture, with the suffix a. Vibbhamo is a reversal caused by intoxication, passion, or laughter. Vicchitti is the casting aside of ornaments, perfumes, etc., out of jealousy or disregard due to some offense by the beloved, or the prevention of this by friends; the root chidi means to split in two, with the suffix ti. Others say vicchitti is even a small ornament given by the beloved as a token of affection. Kilakiñcita and others should be understood according to the treatises on dramatic art.

175. Tikaṃ hasite. Hasa hasane, sabbatra bhāvasādhanaṃ. So hāso mando samāno mihitaṃ, sitañcuccate. Miha īsaṃhasane. Mandassitaṃ mhitantipi pāṭho, mhi [M 0.0134] īsaṃhasanetipi dhātu, mhissa, mihissa vā syādeso, sitaṃ. Sabbatra bhāve to.

175. Three [terms] for laughter. The root hasa means to laugh; in all cases, it is derived in the sense of a state. That laughter, when gentle, is called mihita or sita. The root miha means to laugh faintly. The reading 'mandassitaṃ mhitaṃ' is also found; the root mhi also means to laugh faintly; mhissa or mihissa is a substitute for sita. In all cases, the suffix to is used in the sense of a state.

Īsaṃphullitadantehi, kaṭākkhehi soṭṭhavehi ca;

Alakkhitadvijadvāraṃ, sitamicchanti sūrayo cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.34.

With teeth slightly blossoming, with sidelong glances and grace, the wise desire a smile wherein the opening of the teeth is unperceived.

Dvayaṃ mahāhasite. Aṭa gatiyaṃ, dūragāmihāso aṭahāso, atikkanto vā hāso aṭahāso, tassa ṭo, ikārassattañca. Sitātihasitānaṃ antarāḷikaṃ vihasitaṃ.

Two [terms] for loud laughter. The root aṭa means going; aṭṭahāsa is laughter that goes far, or laughter that is excessive; the suffix ṭo is added to it, and 'i' becomes 'a'. Vihasita is the intermediate [laughter] between a smile (sita) and loud laughter (atihasita).

Ākuñcitakapola’kkhaṃ, sassanaṃ nissanaṃ tathā;

Patthāvotthaṃ sānurāgaṃ, āhu vihasitaṃ budhā cintāmaṇiṭīkā 7.35.

The wise say vihasita is when the cheeks and eyes are slightly drawn in, with a soft sound and also a hissing sound, with lips slightly parted, accompanied by affection.

Dvayaṃ lomuggame. Romānaṃ añcanaṃ romañco, añca gamane, ṇo. Lomānaṃ haṃsanaṃ uddhaggabhāvo lomahaṃsano.

Two [terms] for horripilation (lomuggama). Romañca is the bristling of the hairs; the root añca means to go, with the suffix ṇo. Lomahaṃsana is the bristling of the hairs, the state of being erect.

176. Parihāsādichakkaṃ vallabhādīnaṃ parihāse. Parihasantyatrāti parihāso, ṇo, paribhavitukāmena hāsoti vā parihāso. Du parihāse, du anādareti vā dhātu, a, dava dāheti vā dhātu. Khiḍa kīḷāyaṃ, khiḍḍā, khiddātipi pāṭho, atha vā khaṃ tucchaṃ iḍḍā vācā, sā etthāti khiḍḍā. Kīḷa pītiyakīḷanesu, kīḷa vihāreti vā, kīḷanaṃ keḷi kīḷā ca kīḷitañca. Parihāsādichakkesupi adhikaraṇasādhanampi ācariyā vadanti.

176. The group of six terms beginning with parihāsa [refer to] mockery of intimates and others. Parihāsa is that wherein one mocks, with the suffix ṇo; or, parihāsa is laughter intended to deride. The root du means to mock, or du means to disrespect, with the suffix a; or the root dava means to burn. The root khiḍa means to play; khiḍḍā (or khiddā is also a reading); alternatively, khiḍḍā is that where empty speech (khaṃ tucchaṃ iḍḍā vācā) is present. The root kīḷa means joyful play; or kīḷa means to dwell; kīḷana, keḷi, kīḷā, and kīḷita are [forms of] play. The teachers also say that in the group of six terms beginning with parihāsa, the locative derivation is also applicable.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0135] niddāyaṃ. Nipubbo dā supane, a. Supa saye, ino, supinaṃ. A, soppaṃ. Accantaparissamādikāraṇā sabbaṅganimīlanaṃ middhaṃ. Mucchāpāyaṃ middhaṃ. Mida kāriyakkhamane, to. Medhayati vā middhaṃ, akammaññabhāvena vihiṃ satītyattho, kampanattho caladhātu mucchāpāye papubbo. Akkhidalānaṃ pacalabhāvena ayati pavattatīti pacalāyikā, ṇvu, assittaṃ.

Three [terms] for sleep. The root dā, prefixed with ni, in the sense of sleeping, with the suffix a [forms niddā]. The root supa means to sleep; with ino, it forms supina (dream); with a, it forms soppa (sleep). Middha is the complete closing of all limbs due to extreme exhaustion and other causes. Middha is in the category of fainting. The root mida means to be incapable of action, with the suffix to. Or, middha stupefies, meaning it harms by causing unfitness for work. The root cala (to shake), prefixed with pa, has the meaning of shaking in the context of fainting. Pacalāyikā is that which occurs due to the shaking of the eyelids, formed with the suffix ṇvu in the feminine.

177-178. Ketavantaṃ kūṭe. Karaṇaṃ kati, ninditā kati nikati. Aṭa gamane, kucchitenākārena aṭatīti kūṭaṃ. Kuṭa chedaneti vā dhātu saddanītidhātumālāyaṃ pana “kūṭa appasāde”ti dhātunā sādhitaṃ. Rabhi byāje, byājo nāma ketavaṃ. Saṭha ketave, saṭhaṃ, saṭhayati na sammā bhāsati yenāti vā saṭhaṃ. Kitavassa dhammo ketavaṃ, kitavo nāma jūtakāro, coro vā, kita nivāse, avo. Kapaṭo, byājo, upadhi, kusati iccādīnipi ketavassa nāmāni.

177-178. Terms for deceit (kūṭa), ending with ketava. Doing is kati; despised kati is nikati. The root aṭa means going; kūṭa is that which goes in a crooked manner. Or, the root kuṭa means cutting. The root rabhi means pretense; byājo is indeed ketava. The root saṭha means deceit; saṭhaṃ is deceit, or that by which one does not speak rightly. The characteristic of a cheat (kitava) is ketava. A kitava is a gambler or a thief; the root kita means to dwell, with the suffix avo. Kapaṭo, byājo, upadhi, kusati, etc., are also names for deceit.

Sattakaṃ sabhāve. Bhavanaṃ bhāvo, sassa attano, santo vā saṃvijjamāno bhāvo sabhāvo. Saja visajjanāliṅgananimmānesu, natthi visajjanametassāti nissaggo. Rūpa pakāsane, saṃvijjamānaṃ rūpaṃ sarūpaṃ. Karaṇaṃ bhavanaṃ kati, paṭhamaṃ kati pakati. Yathā paṭhamakāle sambhūtā, tatheva sabbadāpītyattho. Sīla samādhimhi, samādhi niyamo. Lakkha dassanaṅkesu, tatheva lakkhitabbanti lakkhaṇaṃ, yu. Tatheva bhavatīti bhāvo.

The group of seven terms for nature. Bhavana is bhāva; sabhāva is one's own nature, or existing nature. The root saja means releasing, embracing, or creating; nissagga is that of which there is no abandonment. The root rūpa means to manifest; sarūpa is existing form. Karaṇa is bhavana, kati; pakati is the first kati. The meaning is that as it arose in the first instance, so it remains always. The root sīla means concentration; samādhi is a rule. The root lakkha means to see or mark; lakkhaṇa is that which is marked thus, with the suffix yu. Thus it exists, hence bhāva.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0136] ussave. Usa dāhe. Kaṃ usavanti uggirayantyatrāti ussavo, nānāsamiddhīhi savanti etthāti vā ussavo. Chi chedane, chindati sokametthāti chaṇo. Yu. Issa lopo. Sokaṃ, pāpañca chindantā aṇanti saddāyanti etthāti vā chaṇo. Chi chedane. Aṇa saddattho daṇḍako dhātu.

Two terms for festivity. The root usa means to burn. Ussava is that where they kindle or emit joy; or, ussava is that where they flow with various successes. The root chi means to cut; chaṇa is that which cuts sorrow here, with the suffix yu, and the elision of i. Or, chaṇa is that where, cutting sorrow and evil, they make a sound. The root chi means to cut. The root aṇa has the meaning of sound; it is a primary root.

179. Yathā sasnehaṃ pakatitilatelādisnehasahitaṃ dīpakaṃ pajjotaṃ dhārento jantu naro atyandhakāragabbhādīsvapi ṭhitāni khuddakānyatthajātāni atisukhumānipi nānādabbasamūhāni sukhaṃva sampassati, tathā sasnehaṃ buddhapariyāyādianekapariyāyasnehasahitaṃ imaṃ abhidhānappadīpikaṃ ganthaṃ uggahaṇadhāraṇādinā dhārento jantu sotujano khuddakāni atthajātāni nānāsatthesu āgatāni atigambhīrāni atthajātāni sukhaṃ sampassatīti yojanā.

179. Just as a person, holding a lamp or light that is provided with oil, such as sesame oil, easily perceives even the smallest objects, extremely subtle things, and various collections of substances, even those located in extremely dark chambers and so forth; so too, a person, that is, a listener, holding this Abhidhānappadīpikā text, which is provided with the oil of the Buddha's teachings and many other explanations, by way of learning and memorizing it, easily perceives the subtle meanings and extremely profound meanings that have come down in various scriptures—this is the connection.

Iti sakalabyākaraṇamahāvanāsaṅgañāṇacārinā kavikuñjarakesarinā sirimahācaturaṅgabalena mahāmaccena viracitāyaṃ abhidhānappadīpikāvaṇṇanāyaṃ saggakaṇḍavaṇṇanā samattā.

Thus concludes the commentary on the Saggakaṇḍa, within this commentary on the Abhidhānappadīpikā, composed by the great minister Sirimahācaturaṅgabala, who wandered with unimpeded knowledge through the great forest of all grammar, a lion to the elephant-like poets.

Saggakaṇḍavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Saggakaṇḍa is finished.

2. Bhūkaṇḍa

2. The Earth Section

1. Bhūmivaggavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Earth Chapter

180. Idha [M 0.0137] bhūkaṇḍe sāṅgopāṅgehi bhūmyādīhi dasahi, pātālena cāti ekādasahi koṭṭhāsehi kamato vaggā bhūmivaggādināmakā vaggā vuccante. Sappadhānopakārakāni aṅgāni khārādīni, aṅgānaṃ upakārakāni ca upaṅgāni addhādīni.

180. Here, in the Earth Section, the chapters, named the Earth Chapter and so on, are sequentially explained with their main and subsidiary constituents in eleven divisions: the ten beginning with the earth, and also the nether region.
