The main constituents (aṅga) are those like alkali, which are primarily supportive; and the subsidiary constituents (upaṅga), which are supportive of the main constituents, are those like paths.

181. Sāddhapajjena bhūmiyā nāmāni. Vasūni ratanāni dhārayatīti vasundharā. Khamu sahane, khassa cho, chamā, atha vā chi chedane, sattānamadhopatanaṃ chindatīti chamā, mo, itthiyamā ca. Bhavantyassaṃ bhūtānīti bhūmi. Bhū sattāyaṃ, mi. Puthaiti pāṭipadike ṭhite nadādi, ī, puthassa puthuādese, vuddhimhi ca kate puthavī. Ussuvādese puthuvī. Pathādese tu pathavī, imasmiṃ pakkhe avāgamo, atha vā thava gatiyaṃ, pathavati etthāti pathavī, nadādi, sabbattha pattharatīti vā pathavī, thara santharaṇe papubbo, rassa vo, nadādi, puthavī, assu.

181. The names of the earth with their etymologies. Vasundharā is so called because it bears treasures (vasu) and jewels (ratana). Chamā is from the root khamu, to endure, with kha becoming cha; or from the root chi, to cut, because it cuts off beings from falling downward, with the suffix ma and the feminine ending ā. Bhūmi is so called because beings (bhūta) exist (bhavanti) upon it; from the root bhū, to be, with the suffix mi. From the stem putha, with the suffix ī according to the nadādi rules, the substitution of puthu for putha, and vowel gradation (vuddhi), puthavī is formed. With the substitution of u, it becomes puthuvī. With the substitution of patha, it becomes pathavī, in which case there is the augment ava. Or, from the root thava, to go, it is pathavī because one goes (pathavati) upon it, with the nadādi rules; or it is pathavī because it spreads (pattharati) everywhere, from the root thara, to spread, with the prefix pa, ra becoming va, and the nadādi rules; hence also puthavī, with the suffix u.

“Madhuno keṭabhassāpi, medamaṃsapariplutā;

Tenāyaṃ medinī devī, vuccate brahmavādibhī”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 11.3. –

“Because she was inundated with the fat and flesh of Madhu and Keṭabha, therefore this goddess is called Medinī by the proclaimers of Brahman.”

Vacanato medayogā medinī, ī, inī ca. Mida snehane vā, yu, nadādi, issettañca. Maha pūjāyaṃ, nadādi. Vitthiṇṇattā [M 0.0138] ubbī, nadādi, avati bhūtānīti vā ubbī, assu. Vasūni santyassaṃ vasumatī. Gacchanti yassaṃ lokā, sā go, pumitthiyaṃ. Kā sadde, kāyati ettha, kāyati māravijayakāleti vā ku, u. Vasūni dhārayatīti vasudhā. Sabbaṃ lokaṃ dharayatīti dharaṇī, yu, nadādi. Dharatīti dharā, itthiyaṃ ā. Gamu gamane, gacchantyassaṃ jagatī, antapaccayo, gassa dvittaṃ, jattañca, nalopo, nadādi. Bhū sattāyaṃ, ri, nadādi, kvimhi bhū. Bhūte satte dharatīti bhūtaro. Ava rakkhaṇe, yu, nadādi, avanī.

From the preceding verse, by connection with meda (fat), medinī is derived, with the suffixes ī and inī. Or it is from the root mida, to be unctuous, with the yu suffix, nadādi rules, and the change of i to e. From maha, to worship, with nadādi rules. Due to its expansiveness, it is ubbī, with nadādi rules; or because it protects (avati) beings, it is ubbī, with the suffix u. Because treasures (vasu) are in it, it is vasumatī. Because the worlds (lokā) go (gacchanti) upon it, it is go, in both masculine and feminine genders. From the root kā, to sound, because it sounds (kāyati) here, or because it sounds at the time of Māra's defeat, it is ku, with the suffix u. Because it bears treasures (vasu), it is vasudhā. Because it upholds (dharayati) the whole world, it is dharaṇī, with the yu suffix and nadādi rules. Because it sustains (dharati), it is dharā, with the feminine suffix ā. From the root gamu, to go, because they go upon it, it is jagatī, with the anta suffix, the doubling of ga, the substitution of ja, the elision of na, and nadādi rules. From the root bhū, to exist, with the ri suffix and nadādi rules, or bhū with the kvi suffix. Because it upholds existing beings (bhūte satte), it is bhūtaro. From the root ava, to protect, with the yu suffix and nadādi rules, it is avanī.

182. Khārā lavaṇarasā mattikā ūsotyuccate. Khādatīti khārā, dassa ro. Padesakattā mattena pamāṇena yuttā mattikā. Ūsa rujāyaṃ, ūso. Ūsayogā ūsavā, vantu. Rapaccaye ūsaro. Dvepi tīsu vattante.

182. Alkaline earth, having a salty taste, is called ūsa. Because it is eaten (khādati), it is called khārā, with da becoming ra. Because it constitutes a place, mattikā is that which is endowed with a measure (matta) or quantity (pamāṇa). The root ūsa is in the sense of disease; hence, ūso. By connection with ūsa, it is ūsavā, with the vantu suffix. With the ra suffix, it is ūsaro. Both of these apply in the three genders.

Thala ṭhāne, adhikaraṇe a. Kittimaṃ thalaṃ, akittimā thalī, nadādi. Thaddhalūkhamhi bhūbhāge bhūmippadese jaṅgalasaddo vattati. Tattha nijjalattā kakkhaḷattā thaddho. Tikkhasakkharādividāragavādikhuragaṇḍuppādavaccādisahitattā lūkho veditabbo. Gala cavanādhopatanādanesu. Jalaṃ galati ettha, jalena vā galanti etthāti jaṅgalo, nijjalo deso, “jaṅgalo nijjale dese, tiliṅgo pisite thiya”nti tikaṇḍasesa 3.3.393 hi tikaṇḍaseso, lassa lopo, niggahītāgamo ca.

The root thala is in the sense of ṭhāna (place), with the suffix a in the sense of location. Artificial ground is thalaṃ; natural ground is thalī, with nadādi rules. The term jaṅgala is used for a hard and rough region of land. There, it is hard (thaddha) due to being waterless and firm. It should be understood as rough (lūkha) because it contains sharp pebbles, fissures, the hooves of cattle, anthills, thorny plants, and so forth. The root gala is in the sense of falling, descending, and so on. Water drips away from here, or beings are separated from water here, hence jaṅgalo, a waterless region. As the Tikaṇḍaśeṣa states: “Jaṅgalo is used for a waterless region; it is three-gendered, but in the sense of flesh, it is feminine.” This involves the elision of la and the augment of the niggahīta.

183. Vedena [M 0.0139] paññāya īhanti etthāti vedeho. So eva videho, imaṃ dīpamupādāya sineruno pubbadisābhāgattā pubbo ca so videho ceti pubbavideho. Evamaparuttaresu. Gavena yantyetthāti goyāno. Aparo ca so goyāno ceti aparagoyāno. Jambuyā lakkhito, kappaṭṭhāyitādippabhāvena vā tappadhānodīpoti jambudīpo. Dhammatāsiddhassa pañcasīlassa ānubhāvena kaṃ sukhaṃ uru mahantametthāti kuru, kuṃ pāpaṃ rundhanti etthāti vā kuru, kvi. Dīpa dittippakāsanesu, jalamajjhe dippantīti dīpā, dippanti ettha saddhammāti vā dīpā, pamāṇato mahantā dīpā mahādīpā.

183. They strive here with knowledge (veda) and wisdom (paññā), hence Vedeho. That same is Videho. Relative to this island, due to being in the eastern direction of Sineru, it is Pubbavideho (Eastern Videho). Similarly for the western and northern regions. They go here by means of cattle (gava), hence Goyāno. The other one is Aparagoyāno (Western Goyāno). Jambudīpo is so called because it is marked by the Jambu tree, or because it is the principal island due to the power of its lasting for an aeon and so forth. Because of the power of the five precepts, which are established by nature, happiness (kaṃ sukhaṃ) is great (uru mahantaṃ) here, hence Kuru. Or, evil (kuṃ pāpaṃ) is obstructed (rundhanti) here, hence Kuru, with the kvi suffix. The root dīpa is in the sense of shining and illumination. They shine (dippanti) in the midst of the water, hence they are islands (dīpā); or the true Dhamma shines here, hence they are islands. Because they are great in extent, they are great islands (mahādīpā).

184. Kuruādayo ekavīsati janapadantarā janapadavisesā, ādinā suramahapaccuggatā talakuṭā asmākādayo ca pumbahutte pulliṅge bahutte ca siyuṃ. Kuru nāma jānapadino rājakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso ekopi janapado rūḷhīsaddena “kurū”ti bahuvacanena vuccati, evaṃ sabbatra. Kuṃ pāpaṃ rundhatīti kuru, khattiyakumārā, tesaṃ nivāso kurū, paccayalopato na vuddhi, sabbatrevaṃ pāṇini 1.2.52 4.2.81 suttesu passitabbaṃ. Arivijayalokamariyādātikkamādīsu sakkontīti sakkā. Kosaṃ lanti gaṇhanti, kusalaṃ pucchantīti vā kosalā. Magena saddhiṃ dhāvantīti magadhā, kvi, maṃsesu gijjhantīti vā magadhā. Gidha abhikaṅkhāyaṃ. Sevanti yenāti sivi, si sevāyaṃ, vi. Sivaṃ karontīti vā sivī, aññatthe i. Kala sadde, iṅgapaccayo, kaliṅgā[M 0.0140], tesaṃ nivāso kaliṅgā, uttarāpatho “jagannāthā pubbabhāge kaṇhātīrantaraṃ sive kaliṅgadeso saṃvutto” ityuttadese (thomanidhi), kaliṃ gaṇhantīti vā kaliṅgā, kvi, kalaṃ madhurasaddaṃ gāyantītivā kaliṅgā, assittaṃ, kena sukhena liṅgantīti vā kaliṅgā, liṅga gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu. Attanā khāditaṃ lañjaṃ parājitehi yācitepi puna na vamantīti avantī. Pañcālassa puttā pañcālā. Vajjetabbāti vajjī, “vajjetabbā ime”tyādinā pavattavacanamupādāya vajjīti laddhanāmā rājāno. Vajjīraṭṭhassa vā rājāno vajjī. Raṭṭhassa vā pana taṃsamaññā taṃnivāsirājakumāravasena veditabbā. Gaṃ pathaviṃ dhārentīti gandhārā, kittigandhena arantīti vā gandhārā. Cita ussāhane, cetanti ussahanti yuddhakammādīsūti cetayo.

184. The twenty-one different regions, including Kuru and others, are specific countries. By 'and others' are meant Surasena, Mahāpaccuggata, Talakuṭa, Asmāka, and so on. These are masculine and plural. The Kuru are princely people of the country; their dwelling, though a single country, is called “Kurū” in the plural by common usage, and so everywhere. They restrain evil (kuṃ pāpaṃ), hence Kuru, the Khattiya princes; their dwelling is Kurū. Due to the elision of the suffix, there is no vowel gradation; this applies everywhere. They are capable (sakkā) in conquering enemies, transgressing worldly conventions, and so on. They grasp wealth (kosaṃ lanti gaṇhanti), or they ask about what is skillful (kusalaṃ pucchanti), hence Kosalā. They run along with the path (magena saddhiṃ dhāvanti), hence Magadhā, with the kvi suffix; or they are greedy for meat (maṃsesu gijjhanti), hence Magadhā. The root Gidha is in the sense of abhikaṅkhā (longing). They resort to that (sevanti yena), hence Sivi; the root si is in the sense of sevā (service), with the vi suffix. Or, they bring about welfare (sivaṃ karonti), hence Sivī; here, i is the suffix in another sense. From the root kala (to sound), with the iṅga suffix, hence Kaliṅgā. Their dwelling is Kaliṅgā, the northern region. Or, they seize strife (kaliṃ gaṇhanti), hence Kaliṅgā, with the kvi suffix. Or, they sing a sweet sound (kalaṃ madhurasaddaṃ gāyanti), hence Kaliṅgā, without the s-augment. Or, with what pleasure do they go (kena sukhena liṅganti), hence Kaliṅgā. Liṅga is a daṇḍaka root meaning 'to go'. Even when asked by the defeated, they do not vomit up the bribe they themselves have taken (attanā khāditaṃ lañjaṃ parājitehi yācitepi puna na vamanti), hence Avantī. The sons of Pañcāla are the Pañcālā. They are to be avoided (vajjetabbā), hence Vajjī. By adopting the statement “these are to be avoided” (vajjetabbā ime), etc., the kings acquired the name Vajjī. Or, the kings of the Vajji country are the Vajjī. Alternatively, the name of the country is to be understood in terms of the princes dwelling there. They uphold the earth (gaṃ pathaviṃ dhārenti), hence Gandhārā; or they go about with the fragrance of fame (kittigandhena aranti), hence Gandhārā. From the root cita (to exert), they exert themselves (cetanti ussahanti) in acts of war, etc., hence Cetayo.

185. Vaṅga gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu. Visiṭṭhāni dehāni yesaṃ videhā, pubbavidehadīpato āgatattā vā videhā. Oja dittiyaṃ, kambunā sambukena ojanti tassaṃ vohārakaraṇatoti kambojā, kambukajo ojo balametesanti vā kambojā. Mada maddane, maddantīti vā maddā, maṃ sivaṃ dadantīti vā maddā, pañcakāmaguṇādīhi modantīti vā maddā, mada hāse. Bhañja avamaddane, bhaggā. Aṅga gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu. Sīhaṃ lantīti sīhaḷā. Kāsa dittiyaṃ, sampattiyā kāsantīti kasmīrā, mīro. Kāsa dittiyaṃ, i, kāsī. Paḍi gatiyaṃ, paṇḍu, u. Atha vā kuṃ pāpaṃ rundhati etthāti kuru, iti ekopi janapado nissitānaṃ bahuttā bahuvacanena vuccati. Evaṃ sabbattha.

185. Vaṅga is a daṇḍaka root meaning 'to go'. Those whose bodies are distinguished are Videhā; or they are called Videhā because they came from the island of Pubbavideha. The root Oja is in the sense of ditti (shining). They are called Kambojā because they shine in that land through trade with conch shells and oysters, or because the strength born of conch shells belongs to them. The root Mada is in the sense of maddana (crushing); or they crush, hence Maddā; or they give welfare, hence Maddā; or they delight in the five strands of sensual pleasure, hence Maddā. The root Mada is also in the sense of hāsa (joy). The root Bhañja is in the sense of avamaddana (crushing), hence Bhaggā. Aṅga is a daṇḍaka root meaning 'to go'. They take lions (sīhaṃ lanti), hence Sīhaḷā. The root Kāsa is in the sense of ditti (shining). They shine with prosperity (sampattiyā kāsanti), hence Kasmīrā, with the mīra suffix. The root Kāsa is in the sense of ditti (shining), with the i suffix, hence Kāsī. The root Paḍi is in the sense of gati (going), hence Paṇḍu, with the u suffix. Alternatively, evil (kuṃ pāpaṃ) is restrained here, hence Kuru; thus even a single region is referred to in the plural due to the multitude of those who depend on it. So it is everywhere.

186. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0141] bhuvane. Luja adassane, lujjatīti loko, gassa ko, jassa vo. Bhavanti etthāti bhuvanaṃ, yu. Jagati, viṭṭhapādīnipi bhuvanapariyāyāni. Dvayaṃ desasāmaññe. Disa atisajjane, atisajjanaṃ pabodhanaṃ, “ayaṃ itthannāmo”ti disati apadisatīti deso. Si sevāyaṃ, saññāyaṃ a, visayo.

186. Two words for 'world'. The root Luja is in the sense of adassana (disappearing). It crumbles, hence loko, with ga becoming ka, and ja becoming va. Beings exist here, hence bhuvanaṃ, with the yu suffix. Jagati and terms like viṭṭhapa are synonyms for bhuvana. Two words in the general sense of 'region'. The root Disa is in the sense of atisajjana (pointing out). Atisajjana means 'making known'. It points out, 'This is so-and-so,' hence deso. The root Si is in the sense of sevā (service), with a in the sense of 'designation', hence visayo (sphere).

Siṭṭhācārarahito milakkhadeso kāmarūpādi paccanto nāma. Milakkha abyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, milakkhanti abyattavācaṃ bhāsantīti milakkhā. Siṭṭhācāramaggadassanatthāya paññācakkhuno abhāvā rāgādimalaṃ akkhimhi yesanti vā milakkhā, assittaṃ, tesaṃ nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ milakkhadeso. Paccante majjhimadesassa bahiddhābhāge jāto paccanto.

A place devoid of the conduct of the civilized, such as Kāmarūpa and other borderlands, is called a milakkhadesa. The root Milakkha is in the sense of abyatti (unintelligibility) in speech. Those who speak unintelligible speech are called milakkhā. Or, because they lack the eye of wisdom to see the path of proper conduct, their eyes are stained with lust and other defilements, hence milakkhā, without the s-augment. Their dwelling place is milakkhadesa. Paccanta refers to a borderland that has arisen in the outer part of the Middle Country.

Byavatthā catuvaṇṇānaṃ, yasmiṃ dese na vijjate;

Milakkhadeso so vutto, majjhabhūmi tato paraṃ cintāmaṇiṭīkā 11.7.

A country where the system of the four castes is not found is called a milakkhadesa (a barbarian land); beyond that is the Middle Land.

Ariyācārabhūmittā majjho ca so deso ceti majjhadeso, navayojanasataparikkhepo majjhimadeso.

Because it is the ground of noble conduct and is a central region, it is called majjhadesa (Middle Country). The Middle Country has a circumference of nine hundred yojanas.

187. Salilappāyo bahūdako deso anūpo nāma, anugatā āpā atrāti anūpo, āpassa ādino [M 0.0142] uttaṃ, paralopo vā. Kaca bandhane, cho, kacchaṃ. Anūpadeso ca. Abhinavoggamanena tiṇena lakkhite harite dese saddalo, dala dittiyaṃ, bhāve a. Vijjati dalo yattha saddalo.

187. A place abundant with water, a watery region, is called anūpa. Water has gone into it (anugatā āpā), hence anūpo; or the initial ā of āpa becomes u, or there is elision of the latter part. The root Kaca is in the sense of bandhana (binding), with the cha suffix, hence kacchaṃ. It is also an anūpadesa (a watery region). A green place marked by freshly grown grass is saddalo. The root Dala is in the sense of ditti (shining), with a in the sense of 'state of being'. Where shining exists, that is saddalo.

188. Nadiyā ābhatena ambunā udakena jīvanti etthāti nadyambujīvano deso nadī mātā assāti nadīmātikoti vuccati, bahubbīhimhi ko. Vuṭṭhiyā vassena nipphajjati sassametthāti vuṭṭhinipphajjasassako deso devo mātā assāti devamātikoti vuccati, bahubbīhimhiyeva ko, devasaddo cettha vuṭṭhimāha.

188. A place where life is sustained by water brought by the river is a nadyambujīvano deso. A place where the river is its mother is called nadīmātika, a bahubbīhi compound with the suffix ka. A place where crops are produced by rainfall is a vuṭṭhinipphajjasassako deso. A place where the deva (god of rain) is its mother is called devamātika, also a bahubbīhi compound with the suffix ka; here the word deva means rain.

189. Anūpādayo devamātikāntā tīsu liṅgesu. Candasūrādo candasūriyasinerupabbatādimhi sassatisaddo īrito kathito. Sabbadā saranti gacchantīti sassatiyo, sara gatiyaṃ, sarasaddassa so,ti.

189. The words from anūpa up to devamātika can be in all three genders. The word sassati is stated in reference to the moon, sun, Mount Sineru, and so on. Because they always move or go (saranti), they are called sassatiyo. This is from the root sara (to go); so is substituted for sara, with the ti suffix.

Raṭha gatiyaṃ, raṭhanti ettha nagarādayoti raṭṭhaṃ, to. Nāgarehi vijinitabbanti vijitaṃ. Āḷiyaṃ pavattamāno yo setu, so purise pulliṅge vattati. Si bandhane, tu. Ala bhūsane, i, āḷi, tassaṃ āḷiyaṃ.

The root Raṭha is in the sense of gati (going). Raṭṭhaṃ (a kingdom) is so called because cities and the like are established therein, with the suffix to. Vijitaṃ (conquered territory) means that which is conquered by the citizens. A setu (bridge) that exists on an āḷi (causeway) is in the masculine gender. The root Si is in the sense of bandhana (to bind), with the suffix tu. The root Ala is in the sense of bhūsana (to adorn), with the suffix i, forming āḷi; on that āḷi is āḷiyaṃ.

Nagarapabbatādino [M 0.0143] upāntabhū samīpabhūmi parisaro parito sarantyatrāti, ṇo.

The land near cities, mountains, and so forth, the adjacent land, is called parisaro (surrounding area), because one goes around it (parito sarati), with the suffix ṇo.

Tikaṃ vaje. Gāvo tiṭṭhantyatrāti goṭṭhaṃ. Kula saṅkhyāne, gāvo kulantyetthāti gokulaṃ, gunnaṃ kulaṃ gharanti vā gokulaṃ. Vaja gatiyaṃ, vajanti yaṃ gāvo nivāsanatthāyāti vajo. Goṭṭhānakaṃ, goṭṭhānantipi vajassa nāmāni.

There are three terms for vaja (cowpen). Goṭṭhaṃ (cowpen) is where cows stand. The root Kula is in the sense of saṅkhyāna (gathering). Gokulaṃ (herd of cattle) is where cows gather, or it is the family of cows, or their dwelling. The root Vaja is in the sense of gati (going). Vajo (cowpen) is where cows go for shelter. Goṭṭhānakaṃ and goṭṭhānaṃ are also names for a vaja.

190. Silokena maggassa nāmāni. Pathikehi majjate nittiṇaṃ karīyateti maggo, majja suddhiyaṃ, ṇo, jassa gattaṃ, pathikehi maggīyateti vā maggo, magga anvesane, maṃ sivaṃ gacchati ettha, etenāti vā maggo, “mo sive parisāyañce”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe, sivaṃ gamanaṃ karotītyattho, kriyāvisesanametaṃ. Pathi gatiyaṃ, curādi, nāgamo. Panthayanti yantyanenāti pantho, a, kāritalopo. Pathati yātyanenāti patho. Ada gamane, adati yattha sā addhā, dho, addhā maggo, addhāsaddoyaṃ kālepi, samabhāgatthavacane tu addhaṃ, tasmā addhasaddo pumanapuṃsakavasena dviliṅgo, rājāditte addhā, arājāditte addhaṃ. Añja gatiyaṃ, aso. Vaja gatiyaṃ, umo, jassa ṭo. Pada gatiyaṃ, a, dassa jo, dvittaṃ, pajjo. Aya gatiyaṃ, yu, pada gatiyaṃ, avo, nadādi. Vatta vattane, vattanaṃ gamanādi, ani, nadādi, vattanī. Kantanadaṇḍe punnapuṃsakaṃ. Pathikehi pādehi haññateti paddhati. Pādasaddasamānatthena padasaddena niyatappayogato vuttinā siddho, padasaddūpapado hanadhātu,ti, hanassa dho, alopo. Paddhatisahacaraṇato vattanī, taṃsahacaraṇato padavī ca itthiyaṃ.

190. The names of a path are given by these synonyms. Maggo (path) is so called because it is cleansed and cleared of grass by travelers; from the root majja (to cleanse), with the suffix ṇo, and j becoming g. Or, maggo is so called because it is sought by travelers; from the root magga (to seek). Or, maggo is so called because one goes to welfare (maṃ sivaṃ) by it; as stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha, 'ma is for welfare and for an assembly', meaning it causes the going to welfare. This is an adverbial usage. The root Pathi is in the sense of gati (going), from the curādi group, without augment. Pantho (path) is that by which one goes, from panthayati, with the suffix a and elision of the causative marker. Patho is that by which one goes, from pathati. The root Ada is in the sense of gamana (going). Addhā (road) is where one goes, with the suffix dho. Addhā is a road. This word addhā is also used for 'time'. But in the sense of a half, addhaṃ is used. Therefore, the word addha is of two genders, masculine and neuter: addhā when referring to a king's road, addhaṃ otherwise. The root Añja is in the sense of gati (going), with the suffix aso. The root Vaja is in the sense of gati (going), with the suffix umo, and j becomes ṭ. The root Pada is in the sense of gati (going), with the suffix a, d becomes j, and the consonant is doubled, forming pajjo. The root Aya is in the sense of gati (going), with the suffix yu. The root Pada is in the sense of gati (going), with the suffix avo, from the nadādi group. The root Vatta is in the sense of vattana (turning); vattanaṃ denotes movement, etc., with the suffix ani, from the nadādi group, forming vattanī. In Kantanadaṇḍa, it is masculine and neuter. Paddhati (path) is where it is trodden by the feet of travelers. It is established by usage with the word pada having the same meaning as pāda (foot), from the root han (to strike) preceded by pada, with the ti suffix, the h of han becoming dh, and elision of the root's vowel. Due to its association with paddhati, vattanī is feminine; and due to its association with vattanī, padavī is also feminine.

191-192. Tabbhedā [M 0.0144] tassa maggassa visesā jaṅghamaggādayo apathantā. Jaṅghāhi gato maggo jaṅghamaggo. Sakaṭehi gato maggo sakaṭamaggo. Te jaṅghamaggasakaṭamaggā mahāmagge vattanti.

191-192. The distinctions of that path are footpaths and so forth, which are secondary paths. A footpath ('jaṅghamaggo') is a path traversed by feet; a cart-track ('sakaṭamaggo') is a path used by carts. These footpaths and cart-tracks are found on the main road.

Ettha ca “tethā”ti athasaddo na vattabbo, “te cā”ti pana vattabbo. “Matāddhanī”ti pāṭhe pana sati “tethā”ti vattabboyeva, tadā ekapadike addhani magge ekapadī matāti yojanā kātabbā. Gacchataṃ eko asahāyo pādo yassaṃ, na nisinnasseva yamakoti ekapadī, samāsante niccamīpaccayo, kapaccaye ekapadiko, īssa rassattaṃ.

Here, the word 'tethā' should not be spoken; rather, 'te cā' should be spoken. However, if the reading is 'matāddhanī', then 'tethā' is indeed to be spoken. In that case, the interpretation should be that on a single-track road ('ekapadike addhani'), one track ('ekapadī') is dead ('matā'). 'Ekapadī' means that on which one foot of a walking person goes alone, not like the pair of feet of one who is sitting. At the end of a compound, the suffix 'ī' is always used; with the suffix 'ka', it becomes 'ekapadiko', and the 'ī' is shortened.

Corakaṇṭakādidose duggame pathe kantāro, punnapuṃsake, kena pānīyena taranti atikkamanti yanti kantāro, tara taraṇe, corakantārādīsu panāyaṃ rūḷhivasena vutto, atha vā kati chedane, sappaṭibhayattā kantati niccagamanāgamanametthāti kantāro, āro, nāgamo ca. Dukkhena gacchantyetthāti duggamo.

A 'kantāra' (wilderness) is a difficult path with dangers such as thieves and thorns; it is masculine and neuter. It is called 'kantāra' because by what water ('kena pānīyena') do they cross ('taranti'), pass over, and go through it? The root 'tara' is in the sense of 'to cross'. However, in the context of a wilderness of thieves and so forth, this term is used by convention. Alternatively, the root 'kati' is in the sense of 'to cut'. Because it is full of danger, it is called 'kantāra' as it cuts off constant coming and going there, with the suffix 'āro' and no augment. 'Duggama' (difficult to access) is so called because one goes there with difficulty.

193. Dvayaṃ paṭimagge. Paṭi abhimukhena gantabbo maggo, patho ca paṭimaggo, paṭipatho ca. Dīghamañjasaṃ atidūro maggo [M 0.0145] addhānanti vuccate. Addhānaṃ ayanaṃ addhānaṃ, accāyato maggo, yathā “padaṭṭhāna”nti, yalopo.

193. There are two terms for 'paṭimagga'. A 'paṭimagga' or 'paṭipatha' is a path to be traveled towards or head-on. A long, straight, and very distant path is called 'addhāna'. 'Addhāna' is from 'addhā' and 'ayana' (a long going); it is an exceedingly long path, just as in 'padaṭṭhāna', there is an elision of 'ya'.

Dvayaṃ pasattheddhani. Sobhano patho, pantho cāti viggaho. Gantabbapathabhāvato apetaṃ uppathaṃ, apathañca, abyayībhāvasamāso, asaddo atra nipāto.

There are two terms for an excellent path. The analysis is 'a good path' ('sobhano patho') and 'a path' ('pantho'). That which is devoid of the quality of a path to be traveled is 'uppatha' (a wrong path) and 'apatha' (a non-path); this is an 'avyayībhāva' compound, and the word 'a' here is an indeclinable particle.

194-196. Paramāṇūnaṃ chattiṃsa eko aṇu nāma, aṇutopi aṇutarattā paramo aṇu, aṇuto vā paramoti paramāṇu, aṇa saddattho daṇḍako dhātu, u. Te aṇavo chattiṃsa tajjārī nāma, taṃ taṃ attano nissayaṃ malīnakaraṇavasena jarāpetīti tajjārī, jara jīraṇe, jara vayohānimhi vā, a, nadādi. Tāpi tajjāriyo chattiṃsa rathareṇu nāma, rathānaṃ sañcaraṇavasena pavatto reṇu rathareṇu. Te rathareṇavo chattiṃsa likkhā nāma. Lakkha dassane, pakaticakkhunāpi lakkhyateti likkhā, assittaṃ.

194-196. Thirty-six 'paramāṇus' make one 'aṇu'. A 'paramāṇu' is 'paramo aṇu' (supreme particle) because it is even subtler than an 'aṇu', or it is supreme over the 'aṇu'. The root 'aṇa' has the meaning of 'sound'; it is a 'daṇḍaka' root, with the suffix 'u'. Thirty-six of these 'aṇus' are called 'tajjārī'. A 'tajjārī' is so called because it causes its respective support to decay by making it impure; from the root 'jara' in the sense of 'to decay', or 'jīraṇa' in the sense of 'to waste away', or 'jara' in the sense of 'decline of age', with the suffix 'a' from the 'nadādi' group. Thirty-six of these 'tajjārīs' are called 'rathareṇu' (chariot-dust particle). 'Rathareṇu' is dust ('reṇu') that arises from the movement of chariots. Thirty-six of these 'rathareṇus' are called 'likkhā' (a nit). The root 'lakkha' is in the sense of 'to see'. A 'likkhā' is so called because it can be seen even by the ordinary eye; it is related to 'assittaṃ' (adhering).

Tā [M 0.0146] likkhā satta ūkā nāma, ūkāti vuccati sirovattakimi, tappamāṇattā ūkā. Tā satta ūkā dhaññamāso nāma, dhañño vīhiyeva parimāṇitabbattā māso cāti dhaññamāso, masi parimāṇe. Te satta dhaññamāsā aṅgulaṃ nāma, aṅga gamanattho, ulo, aṅgulaṃ, pamāṇaṃ, ulipaccaye aṅguli, karasākhā. Amudviccheti aduṃ dvādasaṅgulaṃ vidatthi nāma, kaṇiṭṭhasahitenaṅguṭṭhena vitthārīyate, vidhīyateti vā vidatthi, vipubbo tanu vitthāre. Dhā dhāraṇe, ubhayatrāpiti, pubbapakkhe tassa tho, nassa to, tassa do. Pacchime dhassa do, tassa tho, asarūpadvibhāvo ca. Tā duve vidatthī ratanaṃ siyuṃ, ramu kīḷāyaṃ, tano, malopo. Tāni satteva ratanāni yaṭṭhi nāma, yata payatane,ti, tassa ṭho, tassa ṭo. Tā vīsati yaṭṭhiyo usabhaṃ nāma, usa dāhe, abho. Ettha pana usabhanadantaraṃ usabhaṃ. Usabhānaṃ asītippamāṇaṃ gāvutaṃ nāma, gavaṃ, gavehi vā yutaṃ gāvutaṃ. Yuja samādhimhi, gonadantarehi gahitappamāṇasamādhānantyattho, taṃ catugāvutaṃ yojanaṃ nāma, yuja samādhimhi, yu, “ettakaṃ yojanaṃ nāma hotū”ti catugāvutehi samādhānantyattho.

Seven of these 'likkhā' are called 'ūkā' (lice). An 'ūkā' is said to be a head-louse; it is called 'ūkā' because of its size. Seven of these 'ūkā' are called a 'dhaññamāsa' (grain-measure). It is called 'dhaññamāsa' because 'dhañña' (grain), specifically rice, is to be measured, and it is a 'māsa' (measure); from the root 'masi' in the sense of 'to measure'. Seven of these 'dhaññamāsas' are called an 'aṅgula' (finger-breadth). The root 'aṅga' is in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix 'ula'. 'Aṅgula' is a measure. With the suffix 'uli', it becomes 'aṅguli' (finger), a branch of the hand. The phrase 'amudviccheti aduṃ' refers to a 'vidatthi' (span), which is twelve 'aṅgulas'. It is called 'vidatthi' because it is spread out ('vitthārīyate') with the thumb and little finger, or it is arranged ('vidhīyate'); from the root 'tanu' (to extend) preceded by 'vi', or from the root 'dhā' (to hold). The commentary then explains the complex phonetic changes. Two of these 'vidatthīs' make a 'ratana' (cubit); from the root 'ramu' (to play), with the suffix 'tana', and elision of 'ma'. Seven of these 'ratanas' are called a 'yaṭṭhi' (rod); from the root 'yata' (to strive), with the suffix 'ti', and subsequent phonetic changes. Twenty of these 'yaṭṭhis' are called an 'usabha'; from the root 'usa' (to burn), with the suffix 'abha'. Here, however, an 'usabha' is the distance between two bulls. A measure of eighty 'usabhas' is called a 'gāvuta'. It is called 'gāvuta' because it is yoked ('yutaṃ') with or by cows ('gava'); from the root 'yuja' (to concentrate). The meaning is the establishment of a measure taken by the intervals between oxen. Four 'gāvutas' are called a 'yojana'; from the root 'yuja' (to concentrate), with the suffix 'yu'. The meaning is that it is established by four 'gāvutas' as 'let this much be a yojana'.

197. Āropitānaṃ ācariyadhanūnaṃ pañcasataṃ koso nāma, anāropitānantyapare. Kusa avhāne, ṇo, kusanaṃ avhānaṃ koso, idha pana kosappamāṇattā koso, dvisahassakarappamāṇo. Aññattha pana –

197. Five hundred strung master-bows are called a 'kosa'; others say it refers to unstrung ones. The root 'kusa' is in the sense of 'to call', with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Kusana' or 'avhāna' is 'kosa' (calling). But here, it is called 'kosa' because it is a measure, being a measure of two thousand 'karas'. Elsewhere, however—

“Catukkādhivīsatiyā[M 0.0147], aṅgulehi karo bhave;

Khyātamaṭṭhasahassehi, kosamānaṃ vibhāvinā”tyuttaṃ.

“A 'kara' (hand) should be of twenty-four 'aṅgulas'; the 'kosa' measure is known by the wise as eight thousand,” thus it is stated.

Caturambaṇanti caturambaṇavīhibījajātaropanayogyo bhūmippadeso karīsaṃ nāma, karonti ettha kasanaropanādikanti karīsaṃ, īso. Caturambaṇabījajātāni ropentyetthāti caturambaṇaṃ, ambaṇaṃ ekādasadoṇamattaṃ, aññe pana “caturambaṇaṃ catuyaṭṭhikaṃ ṭhānaṃ karīsaṃ nāmā”ti vadanti, taṃ karīsabbhantarānaṃ pariyāyabhāvappasaṅgā na gahetabbaṃ.

A land area suitable for planting what is grown from four 'ambaṇas' of rice seed is called a 'karīsa'. It is called 'karīsa' because plowing, planting, and so forth are done ('karonti') there, with the suffix 'īsa'. It is called 'caturambaṇa' because what is grown from four 'ambaṇas' of seed is planted there. An 'ambaṇa' is a measure of eleven 'doṇas'. Others, however, say that a 'caturambaṇa' is a space of four 'yaṭṭhis' called a 'karīsa'. That, however, should not be accepted because it would lead to the consequence of it being a synonym for the internal parts of a 'karīsa'.

Pamāṇato hatthānamaṭṭhavīsappamāṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ abbhantaraṃ nāma, abbhantare antokoṭṭhāse jātaṃ, na bahikoṭṭhāseti abbhantaraṃ. Yattha yattha hi yo yo ṭhito, nisinno vā, tattha tattha samantā aṭṭhavīsatihatthappamāṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ tassa tassa abbhantaraṃ ṭhānaṃ nāma. Bhūmyādittā bhūmivaggo, atha vā aṅgāpekkhāya bhūmiyeva padhānaṃ, padhānena ca byappadeso bhavatīti bhūmivaggabyappadeso.

By measure, a space measuring twenty-eight 'hatthas' (cubits) is called 'abbhantara' (inner space). It is called 'abbhantara' because it arises within the inner part ('abbhantare'), not the outer part. Indeed, wherever anyone stands or sits, the space all around them measuring twenty-eight 'hatthas' is called their 'abbhantara' space. Because it begins with 'bhūmi' (earth), it is the 'Earth Section'. Or alternatively, with reference to the parts, earth itself is primary, and the designation is made according to what is primary; thus, it is designated the 'Earth Section'.

Bhūmivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Earth Section is finished.

2. Puravaggavaṇṇanā

2. Explanation of the City Section

198. Chakkaṃ nagare.

198. A hexad for a city.

“Paṭṭanañca adhiṭṭhānaṃ, nagaraṃ puṭabhedanaṃ;

Thiyo pū nagarī pūriyo, ṭhānīyaṃ kabbaṭaṃ puṭa”nti.

“'Paṭṭana' (port), 'adhiṭṭhāna' (capital), 'nagara' (city), 'puṭabhedana' (market town); 'thī', 'pū', 'nagarī', 'pūrī', 'ṭhānīya' (capital), 'kabbaṭa' (town), 'puṭa'.”

Hi silokapariyāyesu vopālito.

Indeed, Vopālita was skilled in the ways of verses.

“Vicittadevāyatanaṃ[M 0.0148], pāsādāpaṇamandiraṃ;

Nagaraṃ dassaye vidvā, rājamaggopasobhita”nti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 1.2.1. –

“A wise one should point out a city with its various temples, palaces, shops, and mansions, graced by the royal road.”

Nagaralakkhaṇaṃ. Pu pālane, pura pālaneti ca, punāti pureti ca rakkhati paracakkā duggatāyāti puraṃ, ro, a ca, pura aggagamanetipi dhātvattho. Nagā pāsādādayo assa santi nagaraṃ, ro. Vākārena nagarasaddassa pulliṅgattaṃ samuccinoti nagariyo vā pattanaṃ (amara 1.2.1) pakkhe pattanasāhacariyā napuṃsakattaṃ. (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 1.2.1), purasaddassāpītyācariyā. Akutobhayattā ṭhānāya hitaṃ ṭhānīyaṃ, īyo. Paṇikānaṃ puṭā bhijjante atrāti puṭabhedanaṃ.

The characteristic of a city. The root ‘pu’ is in the sense of protecting, and ‘pura’ is also in the sense of protecting. It purifies ('punāti'), fills ('pureti'), and protects ('rakkhati') from hostile armies and misfortune, therefore it is called ‘puraṃ’, with the suffixes 'ra' and 'a'. The root meaning of 'pura' also implies 'going foremost'. It has 'nagā' (mountains), that is, palaces and other buildings, hence it is called ‘nagaraṃ’, with the suffix 'ra'. By means of the letter 'va', it indicates the masculine gender of the word ‘nagara’; teachers say this is also so for the word ‘pura’. Being without fear from any quarter, it is beneficial for staying, thus it is called ‘ṭhānīyaṃ’, with the suffix 'īya'. Here, the bundles ('puṭa') of merchants are broken open, thus it is called ‘puṭabhedanaṃ’.

Niccanivāsanaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā itaraṃ dassetumāha “thiya”miccādi. Rājā tiṭṭhati etthāti rājaṭhānī, yu, nadādi, niccanivāsanaṭṭhānepi “caturāsītinagarasahassāni kusavatīrājaṭhānīpamukhānī”tyādīsu dī. ni. 2.263. Dārukkhandhādīhi ā samantato varanti parikkhipīyanti etthāti khandhāvāro, patthanattho varadhātu āpubbattā parikkhipanattho hoti. Pañcakaṃ nagare, “khandhāvāro”ti pana ekameva aciranivāsanaṭṭhānassa nāmaṃ.

Having shown the permanent dwelling place, to show the other, it says “thiya” and so on. The king stands ('tiṭṭhati') here ('ettha'), hence ‘rājaṭhānī’ (royal capital), with the suffix 'yu' of the 'nadādi' group. It also refers to a permanent dwelling place, as in the example: ‘Eighty-four thousand cities, with the royal capital Kusavatī as the foremost’. They enclose or surround it here on all sides with logs of wood and the like, hence ‘khandhāvāra’ (camp, stockade). The root ‘vara’, which means ‘to desire’, takes the meaning of ‘to enclose’ when preceded by the prefix ‘ā’. The pentad of terms applies to a city, but ‘khandhāvāra’ is solely the name for a temporary dwelling place.

199. Mūlapurā aññatra mūlapuraṃ vajjetvā yaṃ puramatthi yojanavitthiṇṇapākārādiparikkhittaṃ, taṃ mūlapurassa taruṭṭhāniyassa sākhāsadisattā sākhānagaraṃ nāma.

199. Apart from the root city—that is, excluding the root city—whatever city there is that is surrounded by walls and other defenses a yojana in breadth, that is called a branch city ('sākhānagara') because of its similarity to a branch of the root city, which is like a tree.

200-201. Sāddhapajjadvayena [M 0.0149] mūlapurassa nāmāni. Vānarasīsaṃ, taṃsaṇṭhāno vā pāsāṇo ettha atthīti “vānarasīsa”nti vattabbe vassa battaṃ, vaṇṇavipariyayaṃ, dīghaṃ, ṇattaṃ, sassa lopañca katvā “bārāṇasī”ti vuttaṃ. Savatthassa isino nivāsanaṭṭhānattā sāvatthi, sabbaṃ dhanamettha atthīti vā sāvatthi ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.14, sabbassa sāvo, dhanavācako atthasaddo, i. Tikkhattuṃ visālībhūtattā vesālī, assatthutthe ī. Mathi hiṃsāyaṃ, ilo, assittaṃ, mithilā. Alaṃ bhūsanametthāti āḷavī, vī, ḷattañca. Kusa avhāne, “khādatha pivathā”tyādīhi dasahi saddehi kosanti etthāti kosambī, bo, nadādi, kusambarukkhavantatāya vā kosambī, kusambassa isino assamato avidūre māpitattāti eke udā. aṭṭha. 35; ma. ni. ṭī. 1.14; 2.284. Uggaṃ ripuṃ jayati yattha, sā ujjenī, yu, nadādi. Takka ūhe, ūho ūnapūraṇaṃ, takkanaṃ takko, so sīlaṃ sabhāvo yattha sā takkasīlā, yo hi purisakārena ūno, so tattha gantvā tamūnaṃ pūretīti. Cama adane, po, campā. Sānaṃ dhanānaṃ ākaraṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ sākaro, so eva sāgalaṃ. Saṃsumārasaṇṭhāno giri etthāti saṃsumāragiraṃ, saṃsumāro gāyati etassa māpitakāleti vā saṃsumāragiraṃ, ge sadde, iro. Rājūnameva ādhipaccavasena pariggahitabbattā rājagahaṃ. Ādikāle kapilanāmassa isino nivāsanaṭṭhānattā kapilavatthu, pumanapuṃsake.

200-201. The names of the principal cities are given in two and a half verses. Vānarasīsaṃ: It should be called ‘Vānarasīsa’ because a stone shaped like a monkey’s head exists here, but by the change of ‘v’ to ‘b’, metathesis, lengthening, the retroflexion of ‘n’, and the elision of ‘s’, it is called ‘Bārāṇasī’. Sāvatthī: It is so named because it was the dwelling place of the sage Savattha, or because all wealth exists there; ‘sāva’ is from ‘sabba’ (all), and ‘attha’ is the word denoting wealth. Vesālī: It is so called because it became vast threefold. Mithilā: From the root ‘mathi’ (to harm), with the suffix ‘ila’; it is feminine. Āḷavī: From ‘alaṃ bhūsanam ettha’ (sufficient adornment is here), with the suffix ‘vī’ and the change to retroflex ‘ḷ’. Kosambī: From the root ‘kusa’ (to call), because they call out here with the ten sounds such as ‘eat, drink’, or because it has many kusamba trees. Some say it was built not far from the hermitage of the sage Kusamba. Ujjenī: It is where one conquers a formidable enemy. Takkasīlā: ‘Takka’ is in the sense of reasoning; reasoning is the filling of a deficiency. The act of reasoning is ‘takka’; that which has this as its nature is Takkasīlā. For, whoever is deficient through personal effort goes there to complete that deficiency. Campā: From the root ‘cama’ (to eat), with the suffix ‘pa’. Sāgala: The source, the place of origin, of wealth is ‘sākaro’; that itself is Sāgalaṃ. Saṃsumāragira: A mountain shaped like a crocodile exists here, or a crocodile sang at the time of its construction; from the root ‘ge’ (to sound), with the suffix ‘ira’. Rājagaha: It is so named because it is to be held by kings by right of their sovereignty. Kapilavatthu: It was the dwelling place of the sage Kapila in ancient times; the word is masculine and neuter.

Sāko rājūnaṃ yuddhādīsu satti sañjātā etthāti sāketaṃ, “sāko sattimhi bhūpāle, dumadīpantaresu ce”ti nānatthasaṅgahe. Sañjātatthe ito, sāko nāma rājā, dumo vā ettha ādikāle sañjātoti vā sāketaṃ. Indaṃ paramissariyabhāvaṃ pāpuṇanti etthāti indapattaṃ, indo vā [M 0.0150] sakko devarājā, so patto etthāti indapattaṃ. Ukkaṃ dhārayati etassa māpitakāleti ukkaṭṭhā, vaṇṇavikāro. Yassa māpitaṭṭhāne pāṭalīnāmako eko taruṇarukkho atthīti taṃ pāṭaliputtakaṃ, atha vā paṭali nāma eko gāmaṇī, tassa putto ettha vasatiādikāleti pāṭaliputtakaṃ. Cetiyaraṭṭhe uttamattā cetuttaraṃ, “jetuttara”nti pāṭhe pana vaṇṇavikāro, verijayaṭṭhānattā jetañca taṃ uttamattā uttarañceti vā jetuttaraṃ. Yassa māpitakāle dīpo dippati, taṃ saṅkassaṃ, kāsa dittiyaṃ, dvittaṃ, sammā kasanti etthāti vā saṅkassaṃ, kasa vilekhane, yassa māpitakāle nimittamolokentā brāhmaṇā kusahatthaṃ naraṃ passitvā māpenti, taṃ kusināraṃ. Ādinā mathura madhura, mādhura (ka.) pāsāṇapurasoṇikādayopyanekapuravisesā saṅgahitā.

Sāketa: It is so called because the power of kings, known as ‘sāka’, arose there in battles and other such events; as it is said in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: “‘Sāka’ is used for power, a king, a tree, and an island.” Or, it is called Sāketa because a king named Sāka, or a sāka tree, first arose there. Indapatta: It is so called because one attains ‘inda’, that is, supreme sovereignty, there; or, because Inda, that is, Sakka, king of the gods, arrived there. Ukkaṭṭhā: It is so called because a torch was held at the time of its founding; there is a phonetic change. Pāṭaliputta: It is so called because at the place of its founding there was a young pāṭali tree; or, because the son of a village headman named Paṭali lived there in ancient times. Cetuttara: It is so called because of its excellence in the Cetiya country. In the reading ‘Jetuttara’, there is a phonetic change; or, it is Jetuttara because it is a place of victory over enemies and it is excellent, thus supreme. Saṅkassa: It is so called because a lamp shone at the time of its founding, from the root ‘kāsa’ (to shine), with reduplication; or, because they plow well there, from the root ‘kasa’ (to plow). Kusināra: It is so called because at the time of its founding, brahmins observing omens saw a man with kusa grass in his hand and had it built. By ‘etcetera’, many other specific cities such as Mathurā, Pāsāṇapura, Soṇikā, and others are included.

202. Catukkaṃ abbhantaragāmamagge. Rathassa hitā racchā, pabbajjādi. Visayante pakāsayante vikkayena dabbāni yassaṃ, sā visikhā, vipubbo si sevāyaṃ, kho, visanti etthāti vā visikhā, visa pavesane, kho. Rathassa hitā rathikā, iko. Vī gamane, thi, vīthi.

202. The fourfold group of terms for inner village paths. Racchā: That which is suitable for chariots. Visikhā: The street where they spread out and display goods for sale; this is from the root `si` (to resort to) with the prefix `vi` and the suffix `kha`. Alternatively, it is where they enter, from the root `visa` (to enter), with the suffix `kha`. Rathikā: That which is suitable for chariots, with the suffix `ika`. Vīthi: From the root `vī` (to go), with the suffix `thi`.

Anibbiddhā racchantarena majjhe anibbiddhā racchā byūho nāma. Byūheti sampiṇḍeti jane aññatra gantumappadānavasenāti byūho, ūha sampiṇḍane vipubbattā. Na nibbijjhate racchantarenāti anibbiddho, vidha sampahāre, a. Nibbiddhā racchantarena racchā patho, addhīti ca vuccati. Patha gamane, patho. Ada gamane,ti, addhi.

A street unpierced in the middle by another street is called a ‘byūha’. It is called ‘byūha’ because it gathers people together by not affording them a way to go elsewhere; this is from the root ‘ūha’ (to gather) with the prefix ‘vi’. It is called ‘anibbiddha’ (unpierced) because it is not pierced by another street; this is from the root ‘vidha’ (to strike), with the negative prefix ‘a’. A street pierced by another street is called ‘patho’ and also ‘addhi’. Patho: From the root ‘patha’ (to go). Addhi: From the root ‘ada’ (to go), with the suffix ‘ti’.

203. Catukkaṃ [M 0.0151] caccare. Catunnaṃ pathānaṃ samāhāro catukkaṃ, cara gatibhakkhanesu, caro, rassa co, caccaraṃ, aṅgaṇavācako cāyaṃ. Dvinnaṃ, catunnaṃ vā maggānaṃ sandhi maggasandhi. Siṅgha ghāyane, āṭako.

203. The fourfold group of terms for a public square. Catukkaṃ: A combination of four paths. Caccaraṃ: From the root ‘cara’ (to move, to eat), comes ‘cara’; the ‘r’ becomes ‘c’, hence ‘caccaraṃ’. This is also a word for a courtyard. Maggasandhi: The junction of two or four roads. Āṭako: From the root ‘siṅgha’ (to smell), with the suffix ‘āṭaka’.

Dvayaṃ vappassopari iṭṭhakādiracite veṭhane. Vappaṃ nāma dugganagare parikhāmattikaṃ kūṭaṃ kuṭiṃ (ka.) katvā gohi, hatthīhi ca vimaddāpetvā tiṃsahatthappamāṇaṃ pākārassa heṭṭhimatalaṃ, tathā hatthasataṃ tato uddharitvā paṃsunā vappaṃ kāraye, tassopari pākāranti, pakubbanti tanti pākāro, samantato karīyateti vā pākāro, akattari ca kārake saññāyaṃ ṇo, rassassa dīghatā. Vu saṃvaraṇe, vuṇotīti varaṇo, yu, rāgamo ca. “Sālo”tipi pākārassa nāmaṃ.

Two terms for the enclosure made of bricks and the like above the rampart. Vappa: In a fortified city, this is the lower level of the wall, thirty cubits in measure, made by forming a heap of clay from the moat and having it trampled by cows and elephants. Likewise, one should have the rampart made with earth, raising it a hundred cubits from there, and above that is the wall. Pākāro (wall): It is so called because they construct it, or because it is made all around; the suffix ‘ṇa’ is used for a noun in a non-agentive sense, and the short vowel is lengthened. Varaṇo (wall): From the root ‘vu’ (to enclose), because it encloses; the suffix is ‘yu’, with the augment ‘r’. ‘Sālo’ is also a name for a wall.

Dvayaṃ rājabhavanasāmaññe. Sabbagehānaṃ visesena pakāsanato uddāpo, dīpa pakāsane, īssākāro. Saṅgamma karonti tanti upakārikā, ṇvu. Ke paccaye thīkatākārapare pubbo akāro dīghaṃ kātanta 2.2.65, akādesopi hi “ko”ti vuccati, yathā devadatto “datto”ti. Kapaccayo vā.

Two terms for royal buildings in general. Uddāpo: From its special manifestation among all houses; from the root `dīpa` (to shine), with the change of `ī` to `ā`. Upakārikā: It is made by assembling; the suffix is `ṇvu`. When the suffix `ka` follows, which has been made feminine with `ā`, the preceding `a` is lengthened. The substitution `aka` is also called `ka`, just as Devadatta is called Datta. Or the suffix is `ka`.

204. Dvayaṃ gehādino mattikeṭṭhakādimayabhittiyaṃ. Kuṭa chedane, kuṭati chindati magganti kuṭṭaṃ. Bhidi dvidhākaraṇe,ti, [M 0.0152] bhitti. Gunnaṃ vācānaṃ puraṃ gopuraṃ. Dvārasamīpe kato koṭṭhako dvārakoṭṭhako, kusa akkose, ṭhako, koṭṭhakoti gehaviseso.

204. Two terms for a wall made of clay, bricks, and the like in a house or other structure. Kuṭṭa: From the root ‘kuṭa’ (to cut), because it cuts off the path. Bhitti: From the root ‘bhidi’ (to divide in two), with the suffix ‘ti’. Gopura: The foremost of words for ‘go’. Dvārakoṭṭhako: A chamber made near a door. Koṭṭhako is a particular kind of house, derived from the root `kusa` (to revile) with the suffix `ṭhaka`.

Dvayaṃ indakhīle. Isa icchāyaṃ, esa gavesane vā, iko. Indassa sakkassa khīlo kaṇṭako indakhīlo. Dvayaṃ dvārapassopasālāyaṃ’hamyādipiṭṭhe ca vātakuṭikāyaṃ. Aḍḍa atikkamahiṃsāsu, a. Ālakapaccaye aṭṭālako.

Two terms for the city pillar. It is derived from the root ‘isa’ (to desire) or ‘esa’ (to seek), with the suffix ‘ika’. Indakhīla: The stake or thorn of Indra, that is, Sakka. Two terms for the side-hall beside the door, and for the wind-chamber on the back of a mansion or other such building. Aṭṭālako: From the root ‘aḍḍa’ (to transgress, to harm), with the suffix ‘a’; with the suffix ‘ālaka’, it becomes ‘aṭṭālako’.

205. Upari mālādiyuttaṃ sobhanathambhadvayamubhayato nikhanitvā yaṃ bahidvāraṃ kappīyate, taṃ toraṇaṃ. Tura vāraṇe, yu, thavantā vā raṇantyatrāti toraṇaṃ, tu abhitthave. Raṇa saddattho, vaṇṇavikāro. Dvārassa bahi bahidvāraṃ. Pari samantato khaññateti parikhā. Dīghabhāvena yuttā dīghikā.

205. Toraṇa (gateway): That which is constructed as an outer gate by planting two beautiful pillars on both sides, adorned above with garlands and the like. It is derived from the root `tura` (to ward off), with the suffix `yu`. Or, it is called ‘toraṇa’ because they praise and make sound here; `tu` is in the sense of praising, and `raṇa` has the meaning of sound, with a phonetic change. Bahidvāra (outer door): That which is outside the door. Parikhā (moat): It is so called because it is dug all around. Dīghikā (long pond): It is so called because it is endowed with length.

206-207. Sadumantaṃ gehe. Manda modanathutijaḷattesu, mandante yatthāti mandiraṃ, iro. Sīdanti tatthāti sadanaṃ, yu. Sada [M 0.0153] visaraṇagatyāvasānesu. Na gacchantīti agā, thambhādayo, te rāti gaṇhātīti agāraṃ. Rassassa dīghatte āgāraṃ. Ci caye, nicīyate chādīyateti nikāyo, yamhi cissa kādeso nipātanā. Lī silesane, ṇo, nilayo, ālayo ca. Vasa nivāse, āvasantyatrāti āvāso, ṇo. Bhū sattāyaṃ, bhavantyatrāti bhavanaṃ. Visanti tanti vesmaṃ, mo. Kita nivāse, adhikaraṇe yu, niketanaṃ. Nivisanti, nivasanti vā yatra, taṃ nivesanaṃ. Ghara secane, gharati kilesametthāti gharaṃ, gayhatīti vā gharaṃ, ṇo. Gahassa gharādeso. Gaṇhāti purisena ānītaṃ dhananti gahaṃ. Adhikaraṇe tho, āvasatho. Sara gaticintāhiṃsāsu, saranti cintenti ettha subhāsubhakammāni, sarati vā sūriyasantāpādikanti saraṇaṃ. Si sevāyaṃ, ṇo, patissayo. Uca samavāye, okaṃ. Sala gamane, “itthiyamatiyavo vā”ti a, sālā, saradhātumhi sati lattameva viseso. Ci caye, kammani ṇo, cayo. Kuṭa chedane, i. Vasa nivāse,ti. Upadhassa ette gehaṃ. Sadadhātumhā umo, sadumaṃ.

206-207. [The word] `Sadumantaṃ` [is a synonym] for `gehe` (a house). The root `mand` is used in the senses of delighting, praising, and being dull; because one delights (`mandante`) therein, it is `mandiraṃ`, with the suffix `ira`. Because one settles (`sīdanti`) therein, it is `sadanaṃ`, with the suffix `yu`. The root `sada` is used in the senses of spreading, moving, and coming to rest. That which does not move (`na gacchanti`), such as pillars, is `agā`; it takes (`rāti`) them (`te`), hence `agāraṃ`. When the short vowel is lengthened, it becomes `āgāraṃ`. From the root `ci`, in the sense of accumulating, because things are accumulated (`nicīyate`) or covered (`chādīyate`) therein, it is `nikāyo`, wherein `kā` is substituted for `ci` by special rule. From the root `lī`, in the sense of adhering, with the suffix `ṇo`, come `nilayo` and `ālayo`. From `vasa`, in the sense of dwelling, because one dwells (`āvasanti`) therein, it is `āvāso`, with the suffix `ṇo`. From `bhū`, in the sense of being, because beings exist (`bhavanti`) therein, it is `bhavanaṃ`. Because one enters (`visanti`) it, it is `vesmaṃ`, with the suffix `ma`. From `kita`, in the sense of dwelling, in the locative sense with the suffix `yu`, is `niketanaṃ`. Where one settles (`nivisanti`) or dwells (`nivasanti`), that is `nivesanaṃ`. The root `ghara` is in the sense of sprinkling; because it sprinkles away (`gharati`) defilements therein, or because it is taken (`gayhatīti`), it is `gharaṃ`, with the suffix `ṇo`. `Ghara` is a substitute for `gaha`. Because it takes (`gaṇhāti`) the wealth brought by a man, it is `gahaṃ`. In the locative sense with the suffix `tha`, is `āvasatho`. The root `sara` is in the senses of moving, thinking, and harming; because one thinks (`saranti cintenti`) about good and bad deeds therein, or because it protects from (`sarati`) the sun's heat and so forth, it is `saraṇaṃ`. From `si`, in the sense of serving, with the suffix `ṇo`, is `patissayo`. From `uca`, in the sense of assembling, is `okaṃ`. From `sala`, in the sense of going, with the suffix `a` according to the rule `itthiyamatiyavo vā`, is `sālā`; when the root is `sara`, the change to `la` is a special case. From `ci`, in the sense of accumulating, in the objective sense with the suffix `ṇo`, is `cayo`. From `kuṭa`, in the sense of cutting, with the suffix `i`, [is `kuṭi`]. From `vasa`, in the sense of dwelling, with the suffix `ti`, [is `vasati`]. With `e` replacing the penultimate vowel, `gehaṃ` [is formed]. From the root `sada`, with the suffix `uma`, is `sadumaṃ`.

Dvayaṃ mukharahitadevakulasadise yaññāyatane. Cita pūjāyaṃ, kammani iyo. Yata yatane, āyatanti vāyamanti ettha phalakāmāti āyatanaṃ, atha vā āyantīti āyāni, tāni tanotīti āyatanaṃ, phalakārakantyattho. Ettha tusaddo samāgatānaṃ dvinnaṃ pubbāparagamanattho. “Cetiyāyatanāni cā”tipi pāṭho.

A pair of terms for a sacrificial site resembling a shrine without an entrance. [The word `cetiya` is derived from] the root `cit`, in the sense of worship, with the suffix `iya` in the objective sense. [The word `āyatana` is derived from] the root `yat`, in the sense of striving; because those desiring a result strive (`āyatanti vāyamanti`) here, it is called `āyatanaṃ`. Alternatively, things that come (`āyanti`) are offerings (`āyāni`); it extends (`tanoti`) them, hence `āyatanaṃ`, meaning that which produces a result. Here, the word `tu` indicates the sequence of the two terms that have been presented. There is also the reading, `Cetiyāyatanāni ca`.

208. Dvayaṃ devānaṃ, narapatīnañca iṭṭhakādimaye bhavane. Aññassāpi sādisyā. Pasīdanti nayanamanānyatrāti pāsādo. Yu [M 0.0154] missane, po, dīgho ca, dīghavidhānasāmatthiyā ottābhāvo.

208. A pair of terms for a dwelling of gods and kings made of bricks and the like. By similarity, it may also apply to others. `Pāsādo` is so called because the eyes and mind are pleased (`pasīdanti`) therein. [Alternatively, from the root] `yu`, in the sense of mixing, with the prefix `pa`, and with lengthening; due to the force of the rule prescribing lengthening, the change to `o` does not occur.

Dvayaṃ rājato aññesaṃ dhanīnaṃ byavahārakādīnaṃ bhavane. Muṇḍo chadanametassa, na pāsādassa viyāti muṇḍacchado, dvittaṃ. Hara haraṇe, yo, yamhi miāgamo ca.

A pair of terms for the dwelling of wealthy people other than kings, such as merchants and so forth. Its roof is bare (`muṇḍo`), not like that of a palace, hence it is called `muṇḍacchado`. This is a pair. [The second term, `hammiya`, is derived from] the root `har`, in the sense of taking, with the suffix `ya`, and with the augment `mi`.

Duggapuradvāre vā, yattha katthaci vā mattikādimaye gajakumbhamhi yo yūpo pāsādo patiṭṭhito, so hatthinakho nāma, hatthisseva nakho yassāti hatthinakho, nakhasaddena vā nakhasahito pāsādo gayhate.

A pillar or turret established on a model of an elephant's frontal globe made of clay or other materials, at the gate of a fortified city or elsewhere, is called `hatthinakho`. It is `hatthinakho` because it has what is like an elephant's nail. Alternatively, by the word `nakha` (nail), a turret associated with a nail is understood.

209. Supaṇṇassa garuḷassa vaṅkena pakkhena sadisachadanaṃ gehaṃ suvaṇṇavaṅkacchadanaṃ. Vaṅka gamane. Ekapasseyeva chadanato aḍḍhayogo.

209. A house with a roof resembling the curved wing of Supaṇṇa, the Garuḷa, is called a `suvaṇṇavaṅkacchadanaṃ` (golden-curved roof). The root `vaṅk` is in the sense of going. Because the roofing is on one side only, it is an `aḍḍhayogo` (half-structure).

Ekeneva kūṭena yutto anekakoṇo patissayaviseso māḷo nāma, vaṭṭākārena katasenāsananti keci. Mā māne, ḷo, māḷo.

A particular type of lodging, having many corners and joined with a single peak, is called a `māḷo`. Some say it is a seating place made in a circular shape. `Māḷo` is derived from the root `mā`, in the sense of measuring, with the suffix `ḷo`.

Caturasso patissayaviseso pāsādo nāma, āyatacaturassapāsādoti keci.

A particular type of four-cornered lodging is called a `pāsādo`. Some say it is an oblong, four-cornered `pāsādo`.

210. Santehi bhāti dibbatīti sabhāyaṃ, sabhā ca, purime yapaccayo, santassa sādeso tūbhayatra. Maṇḍā raviraṃsayo, te pivati nāsayatīti maṇḍapo, vāsaddena maṇḍapapadassa [M 0.0155] pulliṅgattaṃ samuccinoti, janānaṃ ālayo sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ janālayo. Āsanatthāya katā sālā āsanasālā. Paṭikkamanti etthāti paṭikkamanaṃ, kamu padavikkhepe, adhikaraṇe yu.

210. Because it shines (`bhāti`) with the virtuous (`santehi`), it is called `sabhā`. In the former derivation, the suffix is `ya`; the substitution of `sā` for `santa` occurs in both. `Maṇḍā` are the rays of the sun; because it drinks (`pivati`) or dispels (`nāsayatī`) them, it is `maṇḍapo`. By the word `vā`, it also indicates the masculine gender of the word `maṇḍapa`. An abode for people, a place of assembly, is `janālayo`. A hall made for seating is `āsanasālā`. Because one walks back and forth (`paṭikkamanti`) therein, it is `paṭikkamanaṃ`; the root `kam` is in the sense of stepping, and the suffix `yu` is in the locative sense.

211. Jinassa vāsabhūtaṃ bhavanaṃ gandhakuṭi nāma, dibbagandhehi paribhāvitā kuṭi gandhakuṭi.

211. The dwelling that is the abode of the Conqueror is called the `gandhakuṭi` (Perfumed Chamber). A chamber imbued with divine fragrances is a `gandhakuṭi`.

Tikaṃ pākaṭṭhāne. Rasāni santyassaṃ rasavatī, pacanaṃ pāko, tassa ṭhānaṃ pākaṭṭhānaṃ. Mahantāni bahūni asitabbāni santettha mahānasaṃ, asa bhakkhane, yu, vaṇṇavipariyayo.

A triad of terms for a cooking place. Because it has flavors, it is called `rasavatī`. `Pāka` is cooking, and its place is the `pākaṭṭhānaṃ`. Because many great things to be eaten are here, it is called `mahānasaṃ`; this is from the root `as`, in the sense of eating, with the suffix `yu` and a metathesis of letters.

212. Suvaṇṇakārādisippīnaṃ kammasālā āvesanaṃ. Āvisantyasmiṃ āvesanaṃ, yu. Pānamandiraṃ surāpānatthaṃ katamandiraṃ soṇḍā nāma, kattabbākattabbaṃ vicāretvā attanā icchitavatthukāraṇā sabbaṃ deyyadhammaṃ sanontīti soṇḍā, sana dāne, tanādi. Ḍo, assottaṃ, vaṇṇavikāro ca, tesaṃ esā vasati soṇḍā. Pānasaddasannidhānā surāsoṇḍāyevidha gahitā. Vaccassa gūthassa visajjanaṭṭhānaṃ vaccaṭṭhānaṃ. Vaccassa visajjanaṭṭhānā kuṭi vaccakuṭi. Munīnaṃ isīnaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ assamo nāma, ā kodhaṃ samenti etthāti assamo, ā bhuso samenti ettha rāgādayoti vā assamo.

212. The workshop of craftsmen such as goldsmiths is an `āvesanaṃ`. Because they enter (`āvisanti`) it, it is `āvesanaṃ`, with the suffix `yu`. A drinking hall, a hall made for drinking liquor, is called a `soṇḍā`. Because, having considered what should and should not be done, they give (`sanonti`) away all their wealth for the sake of desired things, they are called `soṇḍā`; from the root `san`, in the sense of giving, of the `tanādi` class, with the suffix `ḍa`, a change of the vowel to `o`, and a modification of a letter. This dwelling of theirs is a `soṇḍā`. Due to the proximity of the word 'drinking', it is understood here as a liquor tavern. The place for voiding excrement is `vaccaṭṭhānaṃ`. A hut that is a place for voiding excrement is `vaccakuṭi`. The dwelling place of sages and seers is called an `assamo`. Because anger is allayed (`ā-samenti`) here, it is `assamo`; or, because passions and so forth are thoroughly allayed here, it is `assamo`.

213. Tikaṃ [M 0.0156] paṇyavikkayasālāyaṃ. Paṇa byavahāre, paṇitabbāti paṇyā, vatthādayo, te ettha vikkiṇantīti paṇyavikkayo, kī dabbavinimaye, so eva sālā gehanti paṇyavikkayasālā. Āpaṇayante byavaharante asminti āpaṇo, ṇo. Paṇyānaṃ vikkayāya nīyamānānaṃ vīthi pantho paṇyavīthikā. Vasa acchādane, to, udakaṃ vasitaṃ acchādanaṃ katamanenāti udosito, vassottaṃ, bhaṇḍaṭṭhapanassa sālā bhaṇḍasālā. Kamu padavikkhepe, caṅkamatyatrāti caṅkamanaṃ, caṅkamo ca, dvittādi.

213. A triad of terms for a hall for selling merchandise. The root `paṇ` is in the sense of trade. Things to be traded (`paṇitabbā`) are goods (`paṇyā`), such as cloth. Because they are sold here, it is a `paṇyavikkayo` (sale of goods); the root `kī` is in the sense of exchanging goods. That very hall or house is a `paṇyavikkayasālā`. Because they trade (`āpaṇayante`) in it, it is an `āpaṇo`, with the suffix `ṇo`. A street or path for goods being taken for sale is a `paṇyavīthikā`. From the root `vas`, in the sense of covering, with the suffix `ta`; because water is covered by it, it is `udosito`; the `a` of `vas` is changed to `o`. A hall for storing goods is a `bhaṇḍasālā`. The root `kam` is in the sense of stepping; because one walks (`caṅkamati`) there, it is `caṅkamanaṃ` and `caṅkamo`, formed with reduplication and so forth.

214. Jalanti etthāti jantā, jala dittiyaṃ, anto, “itthiyamatiyavo vā”ti a, ā, lalopo, janetyatra agginti vā jantā, jana janane, anto, sā eva gharaṃ jantāgharaṃ. Aggino sālā aggisālā. Pā pivane, papivantyassanti papā, a. Pānīyaṭṭhā sālā pānīyasālā, sā eva pānīyasālikā.

214. Because it burns (`jalanti`) here, it is `jantā`; from the root `jal`, in the sense of shining, with the suffix `anta`, and according to the rule `itthiyamatiyavo vā`, the suffix is `a` or `ā`, and the `l` is elided. Alternatively, because one generates fire here, it is `jantā`; from the root `jan`, in the sense of generating, with the suffix `anta`. That very house is a `jantāgharaṃ`. A hall for fire is an `aggisālā`. The root `pā` is in the sense of drinking; because they drink from it, it is `papā`, with the suffix `a`. A hall for drinking water is a `pānīyasālā`; that same hall is also a `pānīyasālikā`.

Gasa gamane, bho, sassa bo. Avati rakkhatīti ovarako, aro, sakatthe ko, assottañca. Vasanaṃ vāso, tadatthaṃ agāraṃ vāsāgāraṃ. Sayati etthāti sayanī, yu, nadādi, sā eva gahaṃ sayaniggahaṃ.

From the root `gas`, in the sense of going, with the suffix `bha`; the `s` is changed to `b` [forming `gabbho`]. Because it protects (`avati rakkhati`), it is `ovarako`; the suffix is `ara`, `ka` is pleonastic, and the `a` is changed to `o`. `Vāso` is a dwelling; a house for that purpose is a `vāsāgāraṃ`. Because one lies down (`sayati`) here, it is `sayanī`, with the suffix `yu`, belonging to the `nadādi` group; that very house is a `sayaniggahaṃ`.

215. Catukkaṃ [M 0.0157] rājitthāgāre, tadatthiyato tadaṭṭhiyato (ka.) upacārena rājitthīsupi. Rājitthīnamagāraṃ itthāgāraṃ. Avarundhīyante rājitthiyo anenāti orodho, rudha āvaraṇe. Suddhā kāmāpagamattā parisuddhā rakkhakā ante samīpe yassāti suddhanto. Ante abbhantare puraṃ gehaṃ antepuraṃ, purassa anteti vā antepuraṃ. “Antopura”ntipi pāṭho.

215. A quartet of terms for the royal women's quarters; and by metaphorical extension, for the royal women themselves. The house of the royal women is `itthāgāraṃ`. Because the royal women are confined (`avarundhīyante`) by it, it is `orodho`, from the root `rudh` in the sense of obstructing. That which has pure, completely pure guards within or near it, due to the absence of sensual desire, is `suddhanto`. A city or house that is inside is `antepuraṃ`; or, it is the interior of the city. There is also the reading `Antopura`.

Raññaṃ rājūnaṃ asabbavisayaṭṭhānaṃ sabbehyasādhāraṇaṭṭhānaṃ “kacchantara”nti mataṃ kathitaṃ, yaṃ “pamadavana”nti vuccati, pamadavanaṃ nāma upakārikāsannihitaṃ vā purasannihitaṃ vā antepurocitaṃ, yatra antepurasahito eva rājā viharati, nāññajanappaveso amara 14.3. Pamadānaṃ vanaṃ pamadavanaṃ. Nipātanā yākārānaṃ īkāra ākārānanti attho itthigatānaṃ rasso kvacītirasso. Kacchassa pakoṭṭhassa antaraṃ abbhantaraṃ kacchantaraṃ. Pakoṭṭhaṃ nāma abbhantaradvāraṃ.

A place for kings that is not the domain of everyone, a place not common to all, is known as `kacchantaraṃ`. This is also called `pamadavanaṃ`. A `pamadavanaṃ` is situated near a royal outbuilding, or near the city, or is suitable for the inner quarters; it is where the king dwells only with the residents of the inner quarters, and no other person may enter. A grove for the delightful women is `pamadavanaṃ`. By special rule, the final `ā` of feminine words is sometimes short, sometimes long. The interior of an enclosure (`kaccha` or `pakoṭṭha`) is `kacchantaraṃ`. A `pakoṭṭha` is an inner door.

216. Dvayaṃ iṭṭhakādiracite ārohane. Upānena saha vattateti sopāno, sopānaṃ vā napuṃsakepi. Ārūyhate yena taṃ ārohanaṃ, yu, ruha janane.

216. A pair of terms for an ascent made of bricks and so forth. `Sopāno` is that which exists together with steps; or `sopānaṃ` also in the neuter. `Ārohanaṃ` is that by which one ascends; from the root `ruha`, to grow, with the suffix `yu`.

Dvayaṃ kaṭṭhādiracitāyaṃ. Nicchayena sayanti pākārādikametāyāti nisseṇī, si sevāyaṃ, ṇī, nadādi. Uddhamārohate etāyāti adhirohiṇī, sāsaddo dvinnampi itthiliṅgattaṃ joteti.

A pair of terms for that which is made of wood and so forth. `Nisseṇī` is that by which one certainly goes upon walls and so forth; from the root `si`, to serve, with the suffix `ṇī`, of the `nadādi` class. `Adhirohiṇī` is that by which one ascends upward; the word `sā` indicates that both are of the feminine gender.

217. Pañcakaṃ [M 0.0158] jālake. Vātaṃ pivatīti vātapānaṃ. Gavaṃ akkhi gavakkho, samāsantattā a, saññāsaddato pulliṅgattaṃ, akkhi sadde vā, gavaṃ akkhi gavakkhīti viggaho. Jala dittiyaṃ, jālaṃ. Sīharūpayuttaṃ pañjaraṃ sīhapañjaraṃ. Ālokānaṃ ātapānaṃ pavisanaṭṭhānaṃ sandhi chiddanti ālokasandhi, ālokīyanti etenāti āloko, so eva sandhīti vā ālokasandhi.

217. A group of five terms for a lattice. `Vātapānaṃ` is that which drinks the wind. `Gavakkho` is from `gavaṃ akkhi`, a cow's eye; the final `a` is due to the compound; its masculine gender is from being a conventional term, or from the word `akkhi`; the analysis is `gavaṃ akkhi gavakkhīti`. From the root `jala`, to shine, comes `jālaṃ`. `Sīhapañjaraṃ` is a cage endowed with a lion figure. `Ālokasandhi` is an opening, a fissure, a place for light and heat to enter; or, `āloko` is that by which one is illuminated, and that very opening is `ālokasandhi`.

Dvayaṃ laṅgiyaṃ. Lagi gatyattho, a, nadādi. Pari punappunaṃ gamanāgamanavasena hantīti paligho, ṇo. Kapirūpamatthakattā kapisīso. Aggaḷaṃ nāma kavāṭako kavāṭaphalavidhāraṇo (ka.), tassa thambho aggaḷatthambho, “aggaḷaṃ tīsu kallole, daṇḍe cāntakavāṭesū”ti rabhaso, itthiyamato āpaccayo, aggaḷā. Nissesato abbati vassodakamanenāti nibbaṃ, abba gatihiṃsāsu. Chaddassa chadanassa koṭi heṭṭhimāvasānaṃ chaddakoṭi, tassaṃ.

A pair of terms for a bolt. From the root `lagi`, to go, with the suffix `a`, of the `nadādi` class. `Paligho` is that which repeatedly strikes against coming and going; with the suffix `ṇo`. `Kapisīso` is so called because its head has the form of a monkey. `Aggaḷaṃ` is a door-panel; its post is `aggaḷatthambho`. According to Rabhasa: '`aggaḷaṃ` is used for three things: a wave, a staff, and an inner door-leaf'; from this, in the feminine, the suffix `ā` is applied, making `aggaḷā`. `Nibbaṃ` is that by which rainwater goes without remainder; from the root `abba` in the senses of going and harming. `Chaddakoṭi` is the edge of the roof, the lower end of the covering; `tassaṃ` refers to that.

218. Tikaṃ gehacchadane. Chādeti etenāti chadanaṃ, chada saṃvaraṇe, curādi. Paṭagamane, “paṭyādīhyala”nti alo. Chādeti etenāti chaddaṃ, dvittādi.

218. A group of three terms for a house covering. `Chadanaṃ` is that by which one covers; from the root `chada`, to cover, of the `curādi` class. From `paṭa`, to go, the suffix `alo` is added according to the rule `paṭyādīhyala`. `Chaddaṃ` is that by which one covers; formed by reduplication and so forth.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0159] gehaṅgaṇe. Aja gatimhi, iro, ajiraṃ. Cara gatibhakkhanesu, caro. Aṅga gamane, karaṇādhikaraṇesu yu, vaṇṇavikāro, ṇattaṃ.

A group of three terms for a house courtyard. From the root `aja`, to go, with the suffix `iro`, comes `ajiraṃ`. From the root `cara`, in the senses of going and eating, comes `caro`. From the root `aṅga`, to go, with the suffix `yu` in the sense of instrument or location, with phonetic change and nasalization, comes `aṅgaṇaṃ`.

Pañcakaṃ gehadvārato bahipakoṭṭhake, vīthiyaṃ dvārapiṇḍake ca. Alindo tvaññapiṇḍakepicchate. Paṭhamaṃ hananti gacchanti etthāti paghāṇo, paghaṇo ca, hanassa ghaṇādeso. Ali sakhā indo etthāti alindo, “gehekadese alindo, paghāṇo paghaṇobhave”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 12.12 amaramālāyaṃ. Ālindo, dīghādi. Padhānaṃ mukhaṃ pamukhaṃ, gehassa hi catūsu mukhesu tadeva padhānaṃ, yattha sādhujanāpi āgantukāpi nisīdanti. Dvāraṃ bandhati pidahati etthāti dvārabandhanaṃ.

A group of five terms for the outer enclosure from the house door, for the street, and for the door-terrace. `Alindo` is also desired for another terrace. `Paghāṇo` is where one first strikes or goes; also `paghaṇo`, with `ghaṇa` as a substitute for `han`. `Alindo` is where friends (`ali`) and lords (`indo`) are; as stated in the Amarāmālā: 'In a part of the house, there may be an `alindo`, `paghāṇo`, or `paghaṇo`'. `Ālindo` has a long initial vowel. `Pamukhaṃ` is the principal face; for of a house's four faces, that is the principal one, where good people and guests sit. `Dvārabandhanaṃ` is where one binds or shuts the door.

219. Dvayaṃ dvārabāhāyaṃ. Pīṭhāni lohavikatiādīhi saṅghaṭīyanti etthāti pīṭhasaṅghāṭakaṃ, pīṭhehi saṅghaṭīyatīti vā pīṭhasaṅghāṭakaṃ, ghaṭa ghaṭane. Dvibhāgena bāhāsadisattā bāhā, dvārassa bāhā dvārabāhā. “Kapāṭaṃ, kavāṭa”ntipi dvārabāhāya nāmāni, kaṃ vātaṃ pāṭayati, vāṭayati ceti kammani ṇo, itthiyaṃ kapāṭī.

219. A pair of terms for a door-post. `Pīṭhasaṅghāṭakaṃ` is where panels are joined by means of ironwork and so forth; or that which is joined with panels; from the root `ghaṭa`, to join. `Bāhā` is so called because of its resemblance to an arm in having two parts; the arm of the door is `dvārabāhā`. `Kapāṭaṃ` and `kavāṭaṃ` are also names for a door-post; because it splits or encloses the air (`kaṃ vātaṃ`); with the suffix `ṇo` in the objective sense; in the feminine, it is `kapāṭī`.

Dvayaṃ gehādīnaṃ kūṭe. Kuṭa chedane, kammani ṇo. Naya gamanattho, ke sīse nayatīti kaṇṇīkā, ṇvu, ittaṃ, ṇattañca.

A pair of terms for the peak of houses and so forth. From the root `kuṭa`, to cut, with the suffix `ṇo` in the objective sense, comes `kūṭa`. The root `naya` is in the sense of going. `Kaṇṇīkā` is that which leads at the head (`ke sīse`); with the suffix `ṇvu`, the feminine ending `ikā`, and nasalization.

220. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0160] dvāre. Dve arantyatrāti dvāraṃ, dujjane vārayantyasmā rakkhakāti vā dvāraṃ, ulopo. Paṭiharanti apanenti etasmā rakkhakā aññātanti paṭiharo, paṭipakkhe harati etasmāti vā paṭiharo, rassassa dīghatte paṭihāro.

220. A pair of terms for a door. `Dvāraṃ` is where two go; or, where guards keep out wicked people; with elision. `Paṭiharo` is that from which guards ward off or remove strangers; or, that from which one removes the opposition; `paṭihāro` is with the lengthening of the short vowel.

Catukkaṃ ummāre, yaṃ “dvārapiṇḍikā”ti vuccati. Ura gatimhi, māro karaṇe. Dehaṃ neti pavesenāti dehanī, “dehalī”tipi pāṭho, dehaṃ lāti pavesenāti dehalī. Ila gatimhi, ṇvu. Indo eva pādaṃ khipati etthāti indakhīlo, khipa peraṇe. Passa lopo, atha vā iṃ gamanaṃ dadātīti indo, dvāraṃ, tattha ṭhapito khīlo kaṇṭakoti indakhīlo, vegagabhighātanato hi so khīlo viya hoti.

A group of four terms for the threshold, which is called `dvārapiṇḍikā`. From the root `ura`, to go, with the suffix `māra` in the instrumental sense, comes `ummāra`. `Dehanī` is that which leads the body in; the reading `dehalī` is also found, meaning that which takes the body in. From the root `ila`, to go, with the suffix `ṇvu`. `Indakhīlo` is where Indra himself places his foot; from the root `khipa`, to cast, with elision of `pa`. Or else, `indo` is that which gives passage, i.e., the door; `indakhīlo` is a post, a stake, placed there, for it is like a post because it obstructs a sudden rush.

Thambha paṭibandhane, thambho, dhāretīti vā thambho, dhara dharaṇe, rambhapaccayo, vaṇṇavikāro ca. Thu abhitthave, uṇo, yu vā, dhāretīti vā thūṇo, yu, ralopo, assū.

From the root `thambha`, to obstruct, comes `thambho`; or, `thambho` is that which supports, from the root `dhara`, to hold, with the suffix `rambha` and phonetic change. From the root `thu`, to praise, with the suffix `uṇo` or `yu`, comes `thūṇo`; or, `thūṇo` is that which supports, from the root `dhara` with the suffix `yu`, elision of `ra`, and `ū` for `a`.

Aḍḍhendupāsāṇe addhacandākāre pāsāṇe paṭikāsaddo vattati. Paṭa gatiyaṃ, ṇvu. Itthikatākārapare ke assittaṃ. Gaji sadde, ṇvu, assittaṃ, bindāgamo ca. Isa icchāyaṃ, ṭhako.

For the half-moon stone, a stone in the shape of a half-moon, the word `paṭikā` is used. From the root `paṭa`, to go, with the suffix `ṇvu`. [The following grammatical note is obscure.] From the root `gaji`, to sound, with the suffix `ṇvu`, `assittaṃ`, and the insertion of a nasal. From the root `isa`, to desire, with the suffix `ṭhako`.

221. Valabhīti [M 0.0161] cūḷā, “sikhāyaṃ valabhī cūḷe”ti ruddo rassantā ca, sikhāyaṃ vaḷabhiyaṃ cūḷeti ruddo (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 12.15). Tacchādane dārumhi kaṭṭhe gopānasī matā. Vaṅketi dāruvisesanaṃ. Gaṃ vassodakaṃ, sūriyādikiraṇañca pivanti vināsayanti abbhantaramappavesanavasenāti gopānā, iṭṭhakādayo, tāni sinonti bandhanti etthāti gopānasī.

221. `Valabhī` is a pinnacle; according to Rudra: '`valabhī` is a crest on a pinnacle'. `Gopānasī` is considered to be a curved piece of wood in a roof. `Vaṅka` (curved) is an adjective for the wood. `Gopānā` are those (bricks, etc.) which 'drink' (i.e., protect from) water—rainwater—and the rays of the sun, etc., by not letting them inside; `gopānasī` is that which binds them.

Sodhādigehesu chekapakkhāvāsatthaṃ yo bahi kariya kaṭṭhekadeso ṭhapīyate, so viṭaṅko. Kapote pālayatīti kapotapālikā, kammani ṇvu. Ṭaki nivāsagatīsu. Vino pakkhino ṭaṅkanti etthāti viṭaṅko. Ṇo.

In plastered houses and so forth, that part of a wooden structure which is made externally and placed for the dwelling of domestic birds is a `viṭaṅko`. `Kapotapālikā` is that which protects pigeons; with the suffix `ṇvu` in the objective sense. The root `ṭaki` is in the senses of dwelling and going. `Viṭaṅko` is where birds perch; with the suffix `ṇo`.

222. Dvayaṃ kuñcikāchidde. Kuñcikāya vivaraṃ chiddaṃ kuñcikāvivaraṃ. Tāḷassa pavesanaṭṭhānabhūto chiggaḷo chiddaṃ tāḷacchiggaḷo.

222. A pair of terms for a keyhole. `Kuñcikāvivaraṃ` is the opening, the hole, for the key. `Tāḷacchiggaḷo` is the hole which is the place of entry for the lock.

Tikaṃ kuñcikāyaṃ. Kuñca koṭilye, ṇvu. Tāyati rakkhatīti tālo. Alo, talati tiṭṭhati etenāti vā tālo, tala patiṭṭhāyaṃ. Avāpurati vivarati yenāti avāpuraṇaṃ, vara saṃvaraṇe, yu, vassa po, uttaṃ, upasaggassa dīghatā ca, “apārutā tesaṃ amatassa [M 0.0162] dvārā”ti dī. ni. 2.71; ma. ni. 1.283 vacanato pura, pāra saṃvaraṇetipi dhātvatthaṃ paṭhanti. Avapubbo vu saṃvaraṇetipi dhātvatthe pana sati vassa rattaṃ, upasaggassa dīghatā ca, “apārutā, saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā”tyādīsu pana pakāravaṇṇāgamena siddho. Vida lābhe, imhi vedikā, sakatthe ko. Itarattha iyeva.

A group of three terms for a key. From the root `kuñca`, to be crooked, with the suffix `ṇvu`, comes `kuñcikā`. `Tālo` is that which protects; with the suffix `alo`. Or, `tālo` is that by which one is established; from the root `tala`, to be established. `Avāpuraṇaṃ` is that by which one opens; from the root `vara`, to cover, with the suffix `yu`, `v` becoming `p`, `a` becoming `u`, and lengthening of the prefix, as in the quote: 'Opened are the doors of the Deathless for them'. They also read the root meaning as `pura` or `pāra`, to cover. Alternatively, from the root `vu`, to cover, preceded by `ava`, `v` becomes `r` and the prefix is lengthened; but in examples like `apārutā` and `saṅghāṭiṃ pārupitvā`, the form is achieved by the insertion of the letter `p`. From the root `vida`, to find, with the suffix `i`, comes `vedi`; with the suffix `ka` in its own sense, it becomes `vedikā`. The rest is as before.

223. Saṅghāṭādayo mandiraṅgā gehaṅgavisesā. Sammā ghaṭenti ettha gopānasyādayoti saṅghāṭo, pubbapacchimadakkhiṇuttarāyāmavasena thambhānamupari ṭhito kaṭṭhaviseso, te pana pubbapacchimayāmā tayo kaṭṭhā, dakkhiṇuttarayāmā pana heṭṭhimaparicchedato tayo kaṭṭhā, ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena pana pañcasattanavādayopi. Dvinnaṃ pakkhānaṃ apatanatthaṃ bandhanato pāso viyāti pakkhapāso. Tulati saṅghāṭesu patiṭṭhatīti tulā, tala patiṭṭhāyaṃ, assuttaṃ, pakkhānaṃ vā samavāhitabhāvakaraṇato tulayati mināti etāyāti tulā, tula ummāne.

223. `Saṅghāṭa` and so forth are parts of a building, special components of a house. `Saṅghāṭo` is where rafters and the like are properly fitted together; it is a particular piece of wood placed atop the pillars, according to the east-west and north-south dimensions. For the east-west dimension, there are three pieces of wood; for the north-south dimension, from the lower section, there are three pieces of wood, but in the upper section, there may be five, seven, nine, or more. `Pakkhapāso` is so called because it is like a bond, for binding the two sides to prevent them from falling. `Tulā` is that which is established on the `saṅghāṭa`; from the root `tala`, to be established, with `u` for `a`. Or, `tulā` is that by which one weighs or measures, because it makes the sides evenly balanced; from the root `tula`, to weigh.

Tikaṃ sammajjaniyaṃ. Muji sodhane, yu. Majja saṃsuddhiyaṃ, yu. Sudha suddhiyaṃ, sabbatra karaṇe yu.

A group of three terms for a broom. From the root `muji`, to clean, with the suffix `yu`. From the root `majja`, to be pure, with the suffix `yu`. From the root `sudha`, to be pure, with the suffix `yu`. In all cases, the suffix `yu` is in the instrumental sense.

224. Tikaṃ saṅkārachaḍḍanappadese. Kaṭa chaḍḍanamaddanesu, saṅkaṭanti etthāti saṅkaṭīraṃ, īro, “saṅkaṭo”ti vā saṅkāro vuccati, taṃ īrayanti khipanti etthāti saṅkaṭīraṃ, īra khepe. Saṅkārassa ṭhānaṃ saṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ. Saṅkāraṃ kaṭati [M 0.0163] chaḍḍeti etthāti saṅkārakūṭaṃ, assū, sakatthe ko.

224. A triad of terms for a place where refuse is discarded. The root `kaṭa` is in the sense of discarding and throwing away. Because they discard here, it is `saṅkaṭīraṃ`; the suffix is `īro`. Or, `saṅkaṭo` is also called `saṅkāro`. Because they throw or discard it here, it is `saṅkaṭīraṃ`; the root `īra` is in the sense of throwing. The place for refuse is `saṅkāraṭṭhānaṃ`. Because one discards refuse here, it is `saṅkārakūṭaṃ`; [the term] `assū` [is noted]; the suffix `ko` is in its own sense.

Catukkaṃ sammajjaniyā nirākate nirassate (ka.) thusādimhi. Nānāvidhe saṅkāre rāsīkaraṇavasena kacati bandhati etenāti kaco, so ettha icchitabboti kacavaro, vara icchāyaṃ. Ucchiṭṭho kalāpo samūho uklāpo, kassākāralopo. Nānāvidhehi tiṇādīhi saṅkarīyate missīkarīyateti saṅkāro, ṇo. Avakarotipyatra. Avakarīyate nirassateti, a. “Sammajjo majjanī ceva, saṅkāro’vakaro mato”ti halāyudho. Kasa vilekhane, ambu.

A tetrad of terms for husks and the like swept away by a broom. Because it binds or gathers various kinds of refuse into a pile, it is `kaco`. That which is to be desired here is `kacavaro`; the root `vara` is in the sense of desiring. `Uklāpo` means leftover scraps, a bundle, or a heap; it is formed by the elision of the letter `ka` and the vowel `ā`. Because it is mixed with various things such as grass, it is `saṅkāro`; the suffix is `ṇo`. `Avakaro` is also used here. Because it is discarded or cast away, it is `avakaro`; the suffix is `a`. Halāyudha states: '`Sammajjo` and `majjanī` are for sweeping, and `saṅkāro` and `avakaro` are considered rubbish.' The root `kasa` is in the sense of scratching; `ambu`.

225. Gharādibhūmi gharakhettavihārādīnaṃ yo bhūmippadeso vatthu nāma, taṃ napuṃsake, vasanti etthāti vatthu, ratthu. Gasa madane, gasanti etthāti gāmo, mo. Saṃvasantyatrāti saṃvasatho, atho.

225. The ground of a house, etc. That region of ground of a house, field, monastery, and so on, is named `vatthu`; it is in the neuter gender. Because they dwell here, it is `vatthu`; the suffix is `ratthu`. The root `gasa` is in the sense of eating. Because they eat here, it is `gāmo`; the suffix is `mo`. Because they live together here, it is `saṃvasatho`; the suffix is `atho`.

Pākaṭo khyāto gāmo, so nigamo nāma, atireko gāmo nigamo, bhusattho ni, saññāsaddattā rasso.

A manifest, famous village is named a `nigamo`. A `nigamo` is an excellent village; the prefix `ni` is in the sense of abundance. The vowel is short because it is a designation.

Upabhuñjitabbabhogamanussādīhi ( ) (ibhyo) (?) vaḍḍhito adhiko gāmo nigamatopi adhikatarattā “adhibhū”ti īrito kathito, adhiko bhavatīti adhibhū.

A village that is grown and superior with consumable wealth, people, and so on, is called `adhibhū` because it is more superior even than a market town; `adhibhū` means it becomes superior.

226. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0164] gāmādipariyantabhāge. Si bandhane, mo. Paricchinditvā ādīyateti mariyādā, passa mo.

226. A dyad of terms for the boundary of a village, etc. The root `si` is in the sense of binding; the suffix is `mo`. Because it is established after having been demarcated, it is `mariyādā`; the `p` becomes `m`.

Dvayaṃ ābhīrakuṭiyaṃ ghoso ābhīrapallī siyā (amara 12.20). Ghu sadde, ghosantyatrāti ghoso. Gopālānaṃ gāmo gopālagāmako, sakatthe ko.

A dyad of terms for a cowherd's hut. The root `ghu` is in the sense of sound; because they make sounds here, it is called `ghoso`. The village of cowherds is `gopālagāmako`; the suffix `ko` is used in its own sense.

Puravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the chapter on towns is completed.

3. Naravaggavaṇṇanā

3. The Explanation of the Chapter on Men
