227-228. Porisantāni manussajātiyā nāmāni. Mano ussannamassāti manusso, satisūrabhāvabrahmacariyayogyatādiguṇavasena upacitamānasā ukkaṭṭhaguṇacittā, ke pana te? Jambudīpavāsino sattavisesā. Tenāha bhagavā – [M 0.0165] “tīhi, bhikkhave, ṭhānehi jambudīpakā manussā uttarakuruke manusse adhiggaṇhanti deve ca tāvatiṃse. Katamehi tīhi, sūrā satimanto idha brahmacariyavāso”ti a. ni. 9.21. Tathā hi buddhā bhagavanto paccekabuddhā aggasāvakamahāsāvakacakkavattino ca aññe ca mahānubhāvā sattā tattheva uppajjanti. Samānarūpāditāya pana saddhiṃ parittadīpavāsīhi itaramahādīpavāsinopi manussātveva paññāyiṃsūti eke, apare pana bhaṇanti “lobhādīhi, alobhādīhi ca sahitassa manassa ussadatāya manussā, ye hi sattā manussajātikā, tesu visesato lobhādayo, alobhādayo ca ussadā, te lobhādīhi ussadatāya apāyamaggaṃ, alobhādīhi ussadatāya sugatimaggaṃ, nibbānagāmimaggañca pūrenti, tasmā lobhādīhi, alobhādīhi ca sahitassa manassa ussadatāya parittadīpavāsīhi saddhiṃ catumahādīpavāsino sattavisesā manussāti vuccantī”ti. Lokiyā pana manuno apaccabhāvena manussāti vadanti, manu nāma paṭhamakappiko lokamariyādāya ādibhūto hitāhitavidhāyako sattānaṃ pituṭṭhāniyo, yo sāsane “mahāsammato”ti vuccati, paccakkhato, paramparatāya ca tassa ovādānusāsaniyaṃ ṭhitā tassa puttasadisatāya manussāti vuccanti, tato eva hi te “mānavā, manujā”ti ca voharīyanti, ussapaccayo. Manuno apaccaṃ mānuso, uso. Mara pāṇacāge, co, macco, pabbajjādinā vā tyapaccayo, dhātvantassa lopo ca. Tato “yavata”miccādinā co, dvittaṃ. Manuno apaccaṃ mānavo. Māṇavopyatra, ṇavo. Manumhā jāto manujo. Nī naye, netīti naro, aro. Pusa posane, ṇo, puretīti vā poso. Pura pūraṇe, so, ussottaṃ, ralopo. Punātīti pumā, pu [M 0.0166] pavane, mo, sissā. Puretīti puriso, poriso ca, iso, rassassa dīghatāya pūriso ca. Ettha ca manussādipañcakaṃ itthiyampi vattate, narādayo tu pumeyeva visiṭṭhaliṅgattā. Tatra manussa mānusa manuja māṇavehi nadādittā īpaccayo, ekasakāralopo, manusī, mānusī, manujī, māṇavī. Maccā, itthiyamato āpaccayo.

227-228. The names for the human race, ending with `porisa`. “Manussa” (human being) is so called because the mind (mano) is prominent (ussanna) in them—those with a developed mind, that is, a distinguished mind due to qualities such as mindfulness, courage, and suitability for the holy life. But who are they? The distinguished beings dwelling in Jambudīpa. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “Monks, in three respects, the people of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the gods of Tāvatiṃsa. What three? They are courageous, they are mindful, and the holy life is lived here.” Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, great disciples, wheel-turning monarchs, and other beings of great power arise only there. Some say that due to similarity in form and other attributes, the inhabitants of the minor continents along with the inhabitants of the other major continents are also known as humans. Others, however, state: “Humans are so called because of the prominence of a mind associated with greed and non-greed, etc. For in those beings who are of human birth, greed and so on, and non-greed and so on, are especially prominent. Through the prominence of greed and so on, they fulfill the path to a woeful state; through the prominence of non-greed and so on, they fulfill the path to a happy state and the path leading to Nibbāna. Therefore, the distinguished beings of the four great continents, along with the inhabitants of the minor continents, are called `manussā` because of the prominence of a mind associated with greed and so on, and non-greed and so on.” Worldly people, however, say they are `manussā` because they are the descendants of Manu. Manu was the first of the cosmic age, the originator of worldly conventions, the prescriber of what is beneficial and harmful, a father-figure to beings, who in the Dispensation is called 'Mahāsammata'. Because they abide by his advice and instruction, either directly or through tradition, they are called `manussā` due to their resemblance to his sons. For this very reason they are also called `mānavā` and `manujā`; the suffix is `ussa`. The descendant of Manu is `mānuso`; the suffix is `uso`. From the root `mara`, in the sense of abandoning life, with the suffix `co`, comes `macco`; or from `pabbajjā`, etc., the suffix is `tya`, with elision of the end of the root. Then, by the rule beginning 'yavata', the suffix is `co`, with doubling. The descendant of Manu is `mānavo`. `Māṇavo` is also used here; the suffix is `ṇavo`. Born from Manu is `manujo`. From the root `nī`, in the sense of leading; because he leads, he is `naro`; the suffix is `aro`. From the root `pusa`, in the sense of nourishing, with the suffix `ṇo`, comes `poso`; or, because he fills, he is `poso`. From the root `pura`, in the sense of filling, with the suffix `so`, the vowel `u` becomes `o`, and there is elision of `r`. Because he purifies, he is `pumā`, from the root `pu` in the sense of purifying, with the suffix `mo`, and elision of `s`. Because he fills, he is `puriso`, and also `poriso`; the suffix is `iso`. And by the lengthening of the short vowel, also `pūriso`. Herein, the five terms beginning with `manussa` also apply to the feminine. But `nara` and the others are only masculine because they have a specific gender. In that case, for `manussa`, `mānusa`, `manuja`, and `māṇava`, the suffix `ī` is used because they belong to the `nadādi` group, with the elision of one `s`, resulting in `manusī`, `mānusī`, `manujī`, and `māṇavī`. For `macco`, the feminine is `maccā`; the suffix `ā` is used after a stem ending in `a`.

Viddasupariyantaṃ paṇḍite. Paṇḍā buddhi sañjātā assāti paṇḍito, taratyādi. Paḍi gatiyaṃ vā, to. Bujjhatīti budho. Vidati jānātīti vidvā, vida ñāṇe, vo, sissā. Bhū sattāyaṃ, atthe vibhāveti pakāseti sīlenāti vibhāvī, ṇī. Rāgādayo sametīti santo, to, sundaro anto avasānametassāti vā santo. Sundarā paññā yassa sappañño. Kinnāma na vindatīti kovido, nerutto, kuṃ pāpaṃ vindatīti vā kovido. Dhī paññā yassatthīti so dhīmā, sobhanaṃ jhāyatīti sudhī, jhe cintāyaṃ. Jhassa dho, ī, sundarā dhī yassāti vā sudhī. Kavi vaṇṇe, i, itthiyaṃ kavī ca, ku sadde vā, i, kavi. Byañjayatīti byatto, añja gatiyaṃ, to. Bhujādīnamanto no dvi ca. Visiṭṭho attā yassāti vā byatto. Cakkha dassane, yu, vicakkhaṇo, vicāretīti vā vicakkhaṇo, nerutto. Vigato sārado etasmāti visārado.

The terms ending with `viddasu` are for a wise person. “Paṇḍita” is so called because wisdom (paṇḍā) is born (sañjātā) in him; or because he crosses over (tarati), etc. Or, “paṇḍita” comes from “paḍi” in the sense of “going,” with the suffix “to.” One who understands is called “budho.” “Vidvā” means one who knows (vidati, jānāti), from the root “vida” meaning knowledge, with the suffix “vo,” and elision of “s.” “Vibhāvī” is one who clarifies or reveals meaning by his nature, from the root “bhū” meaning existence, with the suffix “ṇī.” “Santo” is one who has calmed passions, etc., with the suffix “to,” or because their end (anta) is beautiful (sundara). “Sappañño” is one whose wisdom (paññā) is beautiful (sundarā). “Kovido” (expert) is so called because 'what indeed does he not find?'; this is an irregular formation. Or because he finds evil (kuṃ pāpaṃ), he is `kovido`. “Dhīmā” is one who possesses wisdom (dhī). “Sudhī” is one who thinks beautifully (sobhanaṃ jhāyati), from “jhe” (to think), with “dho” for “jha” and “ī,” or because their wisdom (dhī) is beautiful (sundarā). “Kavi” is from the root `kavi` in the sense of describing, with the suffix “i”; in the feminine form it is `kavī`. Or from the root `ku` in the sense of sound, with the suffix “i.” “Byatto” is one who makes manifest (byañjayati), from “añja” (to go), with the suffix “to.” For roots of the `bhujādi` group, the final is `no` and it is doubled. Or, “byatto” is one whose self (attā) is distinguished (visiṭṭho). “Vicakkhaṇo” is from the root “cakkha” (to see), with the suffix “yu,” or one who investigates (vicāreti); this is an irregular formation. “Visārado” is one from whom timidity (sārada) has departed (vigato).

229. Medhā dhāraṇā mati paññā yassāti medhāvī, vī. Atisayamatiyuttatāya matimā. Paññāya yogato pañño. Visesaṃ jānāti sīlenāti viññū, rū. Vida ñāṇe, uro, viduro vidūro (ka.). Rūpaccaye vidū. Dhīyogā dhīro, ro. Visiṭṭhadassanasīlatāya [M 0.0167] vipassī, ṇī. Dosaṃ jānātīti dosaññū, rū. Bujjhatīti buddho, to. Du gatiyaṃ, a, ussāvo du gatiyaṃ abbo (sūci), dabbo. Vida ñāṇe, dasu.

229. One who possesses `medhā` (retention), `mati` (intelligence), and `paññā` (wisdom) is called “medhāvī”; the suffix is “vī.” One having exceeding intelligence is called “matimā.” One who is connected with wisdom is called “pañño.” One who knows distinctions by nature is called “viññū”; the suffix is “rū.” “Viduro” is from the root “vida” in the sense of knowledge, with the suffix “uro.” “Vidū” is from `rūpaccaye`. One devoted to wisdom is called “dhīro”; the suffix is “ro.” One distinguished by the nature of seeing is called “vipassī”; the suffix is “ṇī.” One who knows faults is called “dosaññū”; the suffix is “rū.” One who awakens is called “buddho”; the suffix is “to.” “Dabbo” (capable) is from the root “du” in the sense of going, with the suffix “a,” and the sound change `ussāvo`. From the root “vida” in the sense of knowledge, with the suffix “dasu.”

230-231. Mahilāntaṃ itthisāmaññe. Isu icchāyaṃ, to, nadādi. Sīmassa anto sīmanto, kesaveso, taṃyogā sīmantinī, inī. Narassāyaṃ nārī, idamatthe ṇo. Tiṭṭhati gabbho yassaṃ, sā thī. Dhā dhāraṇe vā, vaṇṇavikāro, ī. Bandha bandhane, ū, bandhassa vadhādeso ca ṇvādi 3, vadhūsaddo suṇisābhariyānampi vācako. Vana sambhattiyaṃ, to, ikārāgamo ca. Aṅga gamanattho, yu, aṅganā, visiṭṭhanāriyampi aṅganā, tadā kalyāṇaṅganārīlakkhaṇopetaṃ pasatthaṃ hatthapādādikamaṅgamassatthīti assatthyatthe aṅgā kalyāṇe napaccayo moggallāna 4.92. Virūpesupi mado rāgamado yassā sā pamadā, visiṭṭhanāriyaṃpyatra pamadā, tadā pakaṭṭho mado rūpasobhaggajanito cetovikāro yassā sā pamadā. Rūpalāvaṇyasampannatāya sundarī, visiṭṭhāyampi. Kamanīyavuttitāya kantā, kamu kantiyaṃ, to. Kantiyogā vā kantā, visiṭṭhāyampi. Ramayati vinodayati nāyakaṃ, sā ramaṇī, nandādīhi yu, nadādi, visiṭṭhāyampi. Daya rakkhaṇe, kammani to. Appaṃ balaṃ yassā sā abalā, appatthoyaṃ akāro. Mātuyā gāmo viya gāmo yassā [M 0.0168] sā mātugāmo, mātā viya gacchatīti vā mātugāmo, gamu gamane, ṇo, mātā viya gasatīti vā mātugāmo, gasa adane, mo, mātā viya gāyatīti vā mātugāmo, gā sadde, mo. Mahī viya suciṃ asucimpi lātīti mahilā, mahantesu bahūsupi rattacittesu ilati gacchatīti vā mahilā, ila gamane, maha pūjāyaṃ vā, iro, lattaṃ, ā, mahilā. Mahelāpyatra.

230-231. The terms up to `mahilā` are for women in general. `Isu` is in the sense of desire (`icchāyaṃ`), with the suffix `ta`; it belongs to the `nadī` group. The inner limit of a boundary (`sīmassa anto`) is `sīmanto`, the parting of the hair (`kesaveso`); from connection with this, she is `sīmantinī`, with the suffix `inī`. `Nārī` means 'of a man' (`narassa ayaṃ`); `ṇa` is in the sense of 'this'. She in whom an embryo stands (`tiṭṭhati gabbho yassaṃ`) is `thī`. Or, it is from `dhā` (to hold, `dhāraṇe`), with a vowel change (`vaṇṇavikāro`) and the suffix `ī`. From `bandha` (to bind, `bandhane`), with `ū`, and the substitution of `vadha` for `bandha`; the word `vadhū` also denotes a daughter-in-law (`suṇisā`) and a wife (`bhariyā`). From `vana` (to serve, `sambhattiyaṃ`), with `ta`, and the insertion of `i` (`ikārāgamo`). `Aṅganā` is from `aṅga` in the sense of going (`gamanattho`), with the suffix `yu`. `Aṅganā` is also a distinguished woman; in that case, it means she who possesses excellent, praiseworthy limbs such as hands and feet, endowed with the marks of a beautiful woman; it is from `aṅga` in the sense of 'beautiful' with the suffix `na` in the sense of 'possessing'. She in whom there is the intoxication of passion (`rāgamado`), even if she is unattractive (`virūpesu`), is `pamadā`. `Pamadā` is also a distinguished woman; in that case, it means she in whom there is an excellent intoxication (`pakaṭṭho mado`), a mental alteration produced by beauty and good fortune (`rūpasobhaggajanito cetovikāro`). Because she is endowed with beauty and charm (`rūpalāvaṇyasampannatāya`), she is `sundarī`; this also applies to a distinguished woman. Because of her desirable conduct (`kamanīyavuttitāya`), she is `kantā`, from `kamu` (to desire, `kantiyaṃ`), with the suffix `ta`. Or, from her connection with desirability (`kantiyogā`), she is `kantā`; this also applies to a distinguished woman. She who delights and entertains her lord (`ramayati vinodayati nāyakaṃ`) is `ramaṇī`; it is from the `nandādi` group with the suffix `yu`, and belongs to the `nadī` group; this also applies to a distinguished woman. From `daya` (to protect, `rakkhaṇe`), with `ta` in the passive sense (`kammani`). She whose strength is small (`appaṃ balaṃ yassā`) is `abalā`; the `a` here is in the sense of 'small' (`appattho ayaṃ akāro`). She whose community is like her mother's (`mātuyā gāmo viya gāmo yassā sā`) is `mātugāmo`; or, she who goes like a mother (`mātā viya gacchati`), from `gamu` (to go), with `ṇa`; or, she who eats like a mother (`mātā viya gasati`), from `gasa` (to eat), with `ma`; or, she who sounds like a mother (`mātā viya gāyati`), from `gā` (to make a sound), with `ma`. She who, like the earth (`mahī`), receives (`lāti`) both the pure and impure (`suciṃ asucim pi`) is `mahilā`; or, she who goes (`ilati`) among many great (`mahantesu`) men with impassioned minds (`rattacittesu`) is `mahilā`, from `ila` (to go); or from `maha` (to honor, `pūjāyaṃ`), with the suffix `ira`, which becomes `ila`, and the feminine suffix `ā`. `Mahelā` is also used here.

Tikaṃ visiṭṭhanāriyameva. Lala vilāse, nandādīhi yu. Lala icchāyanti curādigaṇato vā yu. Bhayapakati bhīru, bhī bhaye, ru, “bhīru atte jane’tthiya”nti rabhaso. Atisayitakāmā kāminī, kāmo siṅgārarūpo mado yassātthīti inī, sabbatrevaṃ. Vāmalocanā, bhāvinī, nitambinī, rāmāiccādīnipi visiṭṭhanārīnāmāni.

This triad of terms is for a distinguished woman. `Lalanā` is from `lala` (to sport, `vilāse`), with the suffix `yu` from the `nandādi` group. Or, it is from `lala` (to desire, `icchāyam`), from the `curādi` group, with the suffix `yu`. One whose nature is fear (`bhayapakati`) is `bhīru`, from `bhī` (to fear, `bhaye`), with the suffix `ru`. Rabhasa says: '`Bhīru` is used for oneself, for people, and for women.' One with excessive desire (`atisayitakāmā`) is `kāminī`; or, she who has passion (`kāma`), which is the intoxication in the form of erotic love (`siṅgārarūpo mado`), with the suffix `inī`; this is so in all cases. `Vāmalocanā`, `bhāvinī`, `nitambinī`, `rāmā`, and so on, are also names for distinguished women.

Dvayaṃ paṭhamavayasi vattamānāyaṃ.

This pair of terms is for one who is in the first stage of life.

Aṭṭhavassā bhave gorī, dasavassā tu kaññakā;

Sampatte dvādase vasse, kumārītya’bhidhīyate cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.8.

At eight years of age, she is a `gorī`; at ten years, a `kaññakā`; upon reaching the twelfth year, she is called a `kumārī`.

Iha tvabhedopacārenekattaṃ. Aññe panāhu “kaññāsaddoyaṃ pumunābhisambandhapubbake sampayoge nivattetī”ti. Kumāra kīḷāyaṃ, curādi, kumārayatīti kumārī, a, nadādi, sakatthe ko, ṇvunā vā siddho. Kamanīyateti kaññā, kana dittikantigatīsu, yo, nyassa ñattaṃ, a, ā.

Here, however, through the figurative application of non-distinction, they are treated as one. But others say: 'The word `kaññā` denotes one who has not previously had sexual union with a man.' `Kumārī` is from `kumāra` (to play, `kīḷāyaṃ`), of the `curādi` group; she is `kumārī` because she plays (`kumārayati`), with the suffix `a`, belonging to the `nadī` group; or it is formed with `ka` in its own sense, or with `ṇvu`. `Kaññā` is so called because she is desirable (`kamanīyatā`); it is from `kana` (in the senses of shining, desiring, or going), with the suffix `ya`, where `ny` becomes `ññ`, and the final vowel is `a` or `ā`.

Yuvasaddato [M 0.0169] pāṭipadikatoti, yuvati. Varitthipariyāyasāmaññepi yuvatisaddo pakatyantaramatthīti. Tara taraṇe, yu, uttaṃ, ī ca.

`Yuvati` (a young woman) is from the nominal stem `yuvan`. Even among the general synonyms for a noble woman, the word `yuvati` has another derivation. [The word `taruṇī` is derived] from `tara` (to cross, `taraṇe`), with the suffix `u`, vowel strengthening (`uttaṃ`), and `ī`.

232. Sābhisekā laddhābhisekā rājitthī mahesī nāma, maha pūjāyaṃ, kammani iso, isse, tato ī, mahatiyo rājitthiyo īsati abhibhavatīti vā mahesī, īsa issariye, ī. Mahesito aññā rājanāriyo bhoginiyo bhogayogā, ī, inī ca. Yānārī purisassa saṅketaṃ yāti, sā “dhavatthinī, abhisārikā”ti coccate. Dhavaṃ patiṃ atthayati icchatīti dhavatthinī, attha yācanicchāsu, inī, asatīviseso. Sara gatiyaṃ, abhisarati saṅketanti, ṇvu.

232. A royal woman who is consecrated, who has received the consecration, is called `mahesī`. It is derived from `maha` (to honor, `pūjāyaṃ`), with the suffix `isa` in the passive sense, which becomes `īsa`, and then `ī`. Or, she who rules over or surpasses (`īsati abhibhavati`) great royal ladies is `mahesī`, from `īsa` (to rule, `issariye`), with the suffix `ī`. Royal women other than the `mahesī` are `bhoginiyo`, from their connection with enjoyment (`bhogayogā`), with the suffixes `ī` and `inī`. The woman who goes to a man's rendezvous (`saṅketaṃ`) is called `dhavatthinī` or `abhisārikā`. She who desires or seeks (`atthayati icchati`) her husband (`dhavaṃ patiṃ`) is `dhavatthinī`, from `attha` (to ask or desire, `yācanicchāsu`), with the suffix `inī`; this is a type of unchaste woman (`asatīviseso`). From `sara` (to go, `gatiyaṃ`), she goes towards (`abhisarati`) a rendezvous (`saṅketaṃ`), hence `abhisārikā`, with the suffix `ṇvu`.

233. Chakkaṃ vesiyaṃ. Catusaṭṭhikalākusalatāya, sīlarūpādimattāya ca gaṇyate ādīyate gaṇikā, gaṇa saṅkhyāne, ṇvu. Veso ākappo, tenātisobhate, kammavesehi vā icchīyateti. Atisobhane, icchatthe vā yapaccayo. Vaṇṇasampannā dāsī vaṇṇadāsī, dāsimpi hi vaṇṇasampannaṃ keci sāmikā dhanalobhena gaṇikaṃ karonti. Nagaraṃ sobhetīti nagarasobhinī. Rūpena upajīvatīti rūpūpajīvinī. Atisayavesayuttatāya vesī.

233. This set of six terms is for a courtesan. She is called `gaṇikā` because she is counted (`gaṇyate`) or regarded (`ādīyate`) for her skill in the sixty-four arts and for the measure of her virtue, beauty, and so on; it is from `gaṇa` (to count, `saṅkhyāne`), with the suffix `ṇvu`. `Vesa` means adornment (`ākappo`); she shines exceedingly with it (`tena atisobhate`), or she is desired (`icchīyati`) for her professional attire (`kammavesehi`), hence `vesiyā`. Or, the suffix `ya` is used in the sense of 'shining exceedingly' (`atisobhane`) or 'desire' (`icchatthe`). A slave woman endowed with beauty is a `vaṇṇadāsī`, for some masters, out of greed for wealth, make even a beautiful slave woman into a courtesan. She who makes the city beautiful (`nagaraṃ sobheti`) is a `nagarasobhinī`. She who makes a living by her beauty (`rūpena upajīvati`) is a `rūpūpajīvinī`. Because she is endowed with excessive adornment (`atisayavesayuttatāya`), she is a `vesī`.

Dvayaṃ asatīsāmaññe. Kulāni aṭati nāsayatīti kulaṭā. Bandhamanubandhaṃ kāyatīti bandhakī, nadādi.

This pair of terms is for an unchaste woman in general. She who wanders among and destroys families (`kulāni aṭati nāsayatīti`) is a `kulaṭā`. She who proclaims bondage and attachment (`bandham anubandhaṃ kāyati`) is a `bandhakī`; it belongs to the `nadī` group.

234. Catukkaṃ uttamanāriyaṃ. Varo āroho soṇi yassā sā varārohā. Uttamaguṇayogā uttamā. Soṇigāravena [M 0.0170] mattagajo viya bandhanagāminī mattakāsinī, kasa gatiyaṃ. Varavaṇṇayogā varavaṇṇinī, inī.

234. This set of four terms is for a supreme woman. She whose hips (`soṇi`) are of excellent proportion (`varo āroho`) is a `varārohā`. Because of her connection with the highest qualities (`uttamaguṇayogā`), she is `uttamā`. Like an intoxicated elephant proceeding to its binding post due to the heaviness of its hindquarters (`soṇigāravena`), she is a `mattakāsinī`; from `kasa` (to go, `gatiyaṃ`). Because of her connection with an excellent complexion (`varavaṇṇayogā`), she is a `varavaṇṇinī`, with the suffix `inī`.

“Sīte sukhoṇhasabbaṅgī, gimhe yā sukhasītalā;

Bhattu bhattā ca yā nārī, sā bhave varavaṇṇinī”ti. ruddo;

Rudra says: 'She whose whole body is pleasantly warm in the cold, and who is pleasantly cool in the heat; the woman who is devoted to her husband, she is a `varavaṇṇinī`.'

Dvayaṃ akhaṇḍitacaritrāyaṃ. Pati sāmikova kamanīyo yassā patibbatā, patimhi vatamassāti vā patibbatā. Asa bhuvi, anto, ī, ādilopo. Sametīti vā satī, samu upasame, anto, ī.

This pair of terms is for a woman of unbroken conduct. She for whom her husband alone is desirable (`pati sāmiko eva kamanīyo`) is a `patibbatā`; or, she whose vow is directed towards her husband (`patimhi vatam assā`) is a `patibbatā`. [The word `satī` is derived] from `asa` (to be, `bhuvi`), with the suffix `ant`, the feminine suffix `ī`, and elision of the initial vowel (`ādilopo`). Or, she who is composed (`sameti`) is `satī`, from `samu` (to be calm, `upasame`), with the suffix `ant` and `ī`.

Dvayaṃ kāmarattarājaputtādino kulassa niyatapatiyaṃ. Kulānurūpā itthī kulitthī, kulaṃ pāleti rakkhatīti kulapālikā, ṇvu.

This pair of terms is for the designated wife of a family, such as that of a prince impassioned with desire. A woman suitable for the family (`kulānurūpā`) is a `kulitthī`. She who protects or guards (`pāleti rakkhati`) the family (`kulaṃ`) is a `kulapālikā`, with the suffix `ṇvu`.

235. Dvayaṃ matabhattikāyaṃ. Vigato dhavo bhattā yassā vidhavā. Pati suñño naṭṭho yassāti patisuññā.

235. This pair of terms is for a woman whose husband is dead. She whose husband (`dhavo bhattā`) has departed (`vigato`) is a `vidhavā`. She whose husband is absent (`suñño`) or lost (`naṭṭho`) is a `patisuññā`.

Dvayaṃ atticchāya patyanvesiniyaṃ kaññāyaṃ. Patiṃ varati gavesatīti patimbarā, dutiyāyālopo. Sayameva patiṃ varatīti sayambarā, paṭhamāyālopo, vara patthanāyaṃ.

This pair of terms is for a maiden who, with excessive desire, seeks a husband. She who chooses (`varati`) or seeks (`gavesati`) a husband (`patiṃ`) is a `patimbarā`, with the elision of the accusative case ending. She who chooses a husband herself (`sayameva`) is a `sayambarā`, with the elision of the nominative case ending; from `vara` (to wish for, `patthanāyaṃ`).

Catukkaṃ vijātāyaṃ. Vijanī gabbhavimokkhane, to, vijāyitthāti vijātā. Sū abhisave, to. Jātaṃ apaccaṃ putto etissāti jātāpaccā. Pasūtāva pasūtikā, kapaccayo, ittañca.

This set of four terms is for a woman who has given birth. `Vijananaṃ` is the release from the womb (`gabbhavimokkhanaṃ`); she who has given birth (`vijāyitthā`) is `vijātā`, from `vi-jan` with the suffix `ta`. [The word `pasūtā` is] from `sū` (to bring forth, `abhisave`), with the suffix `ta`. She whose offspring (`apaccaṃ`), a son (`putto`), is born (`jātaṃ`) is `jātāpaccā`. `Pasūtikā` is the same as `pasūtā`, with the suffix `ka` and the insertion of `i`.

236. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0171] dūtiyaṃ. Yā pesīyate, sā dūtī, du gamane,ti, īmhi dūtī. Sañcārayati yathābhimatanti, ṇvu.

236. This pair of terms is for a female messenger. She who is sent (`pesīyate`) is a `dūtī`. It is from `du` (to go, `gamane`), with the suffix `ti`, and the feminine `ī`. She who causes to proceed according to what is desired (`sañcārayati yathābhimataṃ`) is a `sañcārikā`, with the suffix `ṇvu`.

Tikaṃ dāsiyaṃ. Du kucchitaṃ asati bhakkhatīti dāsī, ī, dīyante tāyāti vā dāsī, dā dāne, so, ī ca. Ciṭa pesane, kammani ṇo, ī. Kuṭaṃ udakakumbhaṃ dhāretīti kuṭadhārikā, ṇvu.

This triad of terms is for a female slave. She who eats (`bhakkhati`) what is contemptible (`du kucchitaṃ`) unjustly (`asati`) is a `dāsī`, with the suffix `ī`. Or, because things are given by her (`dīyante tāyā`), she is a `dāsī`, from `dā` (to give, `dāne`), with the suffix `sa` and `ī`. [The word `ceṭī` is] from `ciṭa` (to send, `pesane`), with `ṇa` in the passive sense (`kammani`), and `ī`. She who carries a water pot (`kuṭaṃ udakakumbhaṃ`) is a `kuṭadhārikā`, with the suffix `ṇvu`.

Dvayaṃ subhāsubhanirūpiniyaṃ saṃvarikādimhi. Vara gatiyaṃ, kattari inī. Subhāsubhassa ikkhaṇaṃ nirūpanaṃ yassātthīti, i, sakatthe ko. Ime dve saddā tulyatthā.

This pair of terms is for one who discerns good and bad, such as a `saṃvarikā`. [The word `vārinī` is] from `vara` (to go, `gatiyaṃ`), with the suffix `inī` in the agent sense (`kattari`). She who possesses the seeing (`ikkhaṇaṃ`) or discernment (`nirūpanaṃ`) of good and bad (`subhāsubhassa`) is an `ikkhinikā`, with the suffix `in`, and `ka` in its own sense (`sakatthe`). These two words have the same meaning.

Yā sayaṃ khattiyajāti yassa kassaci bhariyā, sā khattiyānī, khattiyā ca. Khattiyassāpaccaṃ khattiyānī, āno, ī. Ṇamhi khattiyā.

She who is herself of the khattiya birth and is the wife of anyone whatsoever is called a `khattiyānī` and also a `khattiyā`. The female offspring of a khattiya is a `khattiyānī`, from the suffix `āna` with `ī`. With the suffix `ṇa`, it is `khattiyā`.

237. Pajjaṃ aggisakkhipubbakatapāṇigahitāyaṃ bhariyāyaṃ, aññatra tūpacārā. Dārayante yenāti dāro, dara vidāraṇe, akattari ca kārake saññāyaṃ ṇo. Jāyati putto yāyāti jāyā, jana janane, yo, janissa jā ca, ā, jayatīti vā jāyā, ji jaye, yo, jissa jā, ā, jāyā. Kala saṅkhyāne, atto. Gharaṃ netīti gharaṇī, ṇattaṃ. Bharitabbato bhariyā, bhara bharaṇe, yo. Piyāyitabbato piyā,pī tappanakantīsu, yo. Pajaṃ puttaṃ pāletīti pajāpati, pā pālane,ti, āttaṃ, rassattañca[M 0.0172]. Dvinnaṃ pūraṇī dutiyā. Paṭhamo bhattā, bhariyā dutiyā. Sāmikassa pāde paricaratīti pādaparicārikā, ṇvu. Patinī, pāṇigahitā, sahadhamminītipi tassāyeva nāmāni.

237. A verse on a wife taken by the hand with fire as a prior witness, other than a concubine. She by whom one is torn is 'dāro', from the root 'dara' (to split), with the suffix 'ṇo' in a non-agentive case, as a noun. She from whom a son is born is 'jāyā', from the root 'jana' (to be born), with the suffix 'yo', where 'jan' becomes 'jā', and with 'ā'. Or, she who conquers is 'jāyā', from the root 'ji' (to conquer), with the suffix 'yo', where 'ji' becomes 'jā', and with 'ā'. From 'kala' (to count), with the suffix 'atta' [forms 'kalatta']. She who leads the household is 'gharaṇī', with the nasalization to 'ṇ'. She who is to be supported is 'bhariyā', from the root 'bhara' (to support), with the suffix 'yo'. She who is to be cherished is 'piyā', from the root 'pī' (to please, to cherish), with the suffix 'yo'. She who protects progeny, a son, is 'pajāpati', from the root 'pā' (to protect), with the suffix 'ti', with lengthening and shortening. She who is the completion of two is 'dutiyā' (the second). The first is the husband, the wife is the second. She who serves at her master's feet is 'pādaparicārikā', with the suffix 'ṇvu'. 'Patinī', 'pāṇigahitā', and 'sahadhamminī' are also her names.

238. Tikaṃ sakhiyaṃ. Tesu tesu kiccesu saha khāyati pakāsatīti sakhī, sahapubbo khā pakāsanakathanesu, ī. Ala bhūsane āpubbo, i. Vayasā tulyā vayasā, tulye saññāyaṃ so pāṇini 4.4.91 sutte yapaccayo dissati.

238. A triad of terms for a female friend. She who is known or shines forth together in various duties is 'sakhī', from the root 'khā' (to be known, to speak) with the prefix 'saha', and the suffix 'ī'. From the root 'ala' (to adorn) with the prefix 'ā' and the suffix 'i' is formed 'ālī'. She who is equal in age is 'vayassā'; from 'tulya' (equal) as a noun with the suffix 'sa'.

Jarovuccati corassāmiko, tassāyaṃ jārī, ṇo, ī. Sāmikaṃ atikkamma aññatra caratīti, inī.

'Jāro' is said to be a clandestine lover; from this, 'jārī' (a female clandestine lover) is formed, with the suffix 'ṇo' and 'ī'. She who, transgressing against her husband, consorts with another, is 'jārinī', with the suffix 'inī'.

239. Pume tūti liṅganto tusaddo na pubbaṃ bhajate. Ara gamane, tu, arassuttaṃ. Ratiyā jāyatīti rajo, tilopo. Puppha vikasane, pupphaṃ.

239. In the masculine, the word 'tu' ending a gendered term does not take precedence. From the root 'ara' (to go), with the suffix 'tu', and 'ara' becoming 'u', is formed 'utu'. That which is born of passion is 'rajo', with the elision of 'ti'. From the root 'puppha' (to blossom), is formed 'pupphaṃ'.

Tikaṃ rajassalāyaṃ. Utuyogāutunī, inī. Rajayogā rajassalā, salo. Pupphavantatāya pupphavatī. Thīdhamminī, avī, atteyī, malinī, utumatī, udakīiccādīnipi tassā nāmāni.

A triad of terms for a menstruating woman. Due to her connection with her season, she is 'utunī', with the suffix 'inī'. Due to her connection with menses, she is 'rajassalā', with the suffix 'sala'. Due to possessing the 'flower', she is 'pupphavatī'. 'Thīdhamminī', 'avī', 'atteyī', 'malinī', 'utumatī', and 'udakī' are also names for her.

Tikaṃ gabbhiniyaṃ. Garu alahuko gabbho kucchi etissāti garugabbhā. Āpanno patto gabbhaṭṭho satto etāyāti āpannasattā. Gabbhayogā gabbhinī.

A triad of terms for a pregnant woman. She who has a heavy, not light, fetus in her womb is 'garugabbhā'. She who has a being that has entered, arrived, and is established in the womb is 'āpannasattā'. Due to her connection with a fetus, she is 'gabbhinī'.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0173] yena veṭhito gabbho kucchiyaṃ tiṭṭhati, tatrāsayeti khyāte. Gabbho āsayate tiṭṭhatyatrāti, ṇo. Jaraṃ etīti jalābu. U, rassa lo, yassa bo, jarāpubbo i gatiyaṃ. Kalaṃ jarataṃ lātīti kalalo, kala saṅkhyāne vā, alo.

A triad of terms for that in which the fetus is enveloped and remains in the womb, known as the receptacle. That wherein the fetus lies and abides is 'gabbhāsayo', with the suffix 'ṇo'. That which goes to decay is 'jalābu'; from the root 'i' (to go) with the prefix 'jarā', with 'u', 'r' becoming 'l', and 'y' becoming 'b'. That which receives a particle of what is decaying is 'kalalo'; or from 'kala' (to count), with the suffix 'ala'.

240-241. Sattakaṃ bhattari. Dhū kampane, santāsaṃ dhunotīti dhavo, a. Saṃ etassatthīti sāmiko, āmipaccayo, sakatthe ko, ipaccayo vā, niggahītassa mo, assa ca dīgho, sāmiko. Bhara bharaṇe, bharatīti bhattā, ritu. Kamu icchāyaṃ, to, “pakkamādīhi nto cā”ti ntattaṃ. Pā rakkhaṇe, ati, pati. Vara icchāyaṃ, a, varo. Pī tappanakantīsu, yo.

A heptad of terms for a husband. He who shakes off terror is 'dhavo', from the root 'dhū' (to shake), with the suffix 'a'. He who possesses wealth is 'sāmiko'; from 'saṃ' with the suffix 'āmi', and 'ka' in its own sense; or with the suffix 'i', the niggahīta becoming 'ma', and the preceding 'a' being lengthened. He who supports is 'bhattā', from the root 'bhara' (to support), with the suffix 'ritu'. He who desires is 'kantu', from the root 'kamu' (to desire), with the suffix 'to', which becomes 'nta' according to the rule 'pakkamādīhi nto cā'. He who protects is 'pati', from the root 'pā' (to protect), with the suffix 'ati'. He who chooses is 'varo', from the root 'vara' (to choose), with the suffix 'a'. He who is cherished is 'piyo', from the root 'pī' (to please, to cherish), with the suffix 'yo'.

Ratikāraṇattā patino upa upapati, samāse kate abhidhānato pubbanipāto, appadhānabhūto vā pati upapati. Jara vayohānimhi, jīyante anenāti jāro, dāro ca.

Because he is a cause of pleasure, a secondary husband is an 'upapati'. When a compound is formed, the prior member is determined by the lexicon; or, a husband who is secondary is an 'upapati'. From the root 'jara' (to waste away with age), he by whom one is made to waste away is a 'jāro', and also 'dāro'.

Sattakaṃ putte. Narake na patantyanena jātenāti apaccaṃ, pata gatiyaṃ, yo, tyassa co, na patati na vicchindati vaṃso [M 0.0174] etenāti vā apaccaṃ, putte, dhītari ca niccanapuṃsakoyaṃ. Pū pavane. Punāti pitaro tenāti putto. “Chadādīhi tatraṇa”ti to. Pūretīti vā putto. Attato jāto atrajo, “attajo”tipi pāṭho. Suyateti suto. Su abhisave, suṇātīti vā suto, to, su savane. Tanumhā jāto tanujo, tanayo ca, yo, tanoti mudanti vā tanayo, ayo. Sūyateti sūnu, kammani nu, sū pasave.

A heptad of terms for a son. Because they do not fall into hell on account of one who is born, he is 'apaccaṃ' (offspring); from the root 'pata' (to fall), with the suffix 'yo', and 'tya' becoming 'ca'. Or, because the family line does not fall or is not cut off by him, he is 'apaccaṃ'. This term is always neuter, for a son and a daughter. He who purifies the ancestors is 'putto', from the root 'pū' (to purify), with the suffix 'to' according to the rule 'chadādīhi tatraṇa'. Or, he who fulfills is 'putto'. Born from oneself is 'atrajo'; 'attajo' is also a reading. He who is brought forth is 'suto', from the root 'su' (to bring forth); or he who hears is 'suto', from the root 'su' (to hear), with the suffix 'to'. Born from the body is 'tanujo', and also 'tanayo', with the suffix 'yo'; or he who extends or gladdens is 'tanayo', with the suffix 'ayo'. He who is brought forth is 'sūnu', from the root 'sū' (to give birth), with the suffix 'nu' in the passive sense.

Puttādayo sūnupariyantā dhītari vattamānā itthiyaṃ vattanti. Duhitā, dhītā ca sadā nāriyameva. Duha papūraṇe, rātu, ottābhāvo, ikārāgamo ca. Dhā dhāraṇe, rātu, āssī. Puttādayo ca te sāmaññeneva kuṇḍagolakādīnaṃ vācakā. Savaṇṇāyaṃ tu ūḍhāyaṃ sajāto sayaṃ janito suto oraso nāma. Sajātasaddena kuṇḍakagolakakhattādibyavacchedo. Jīvati bhattari jārajo suto kuṇḍākhyo. Mate bhattari jārajo golakākhyo. Ariyāsuddajo suto khattā nāma khattā ariyāsuddānaṃ (amara 20.3). Ādinā māgadhādīnaṃ gahaṇaṃ. Vuttañhi –

The terms from 'putta' to 'sūnu', when referring to a daughter, are used in the feminine. 'Duhitā' and 'dhītā', however, always refer to a female. 'Duhitā' is from the root 'duha' (to fill), with the suffix 'rātu', the absence of 'o', and the insertion of 'i'. 'Dhītā' is from the root 'dhā' (to hold), with the suffix 'rātu', and 'ā' becoming 'ī'. And those terms beginning with 'putta' are also general designators for sons such as 'kuṇḍa', 'golaka', and so on. However, a son born to a married wife of the same caste is called 'sajāta', 'sayaṃjanita', 'suto', or 'oraso'. By the word 'sajāta', a distinction is made from 'kuṇḍaka', 'golaka', 'khatta', and others. A son born of a paramour while the husband is alive is named 'kuṇḍa'. A son born of a paramour when the husband is dead is named 'golaka'. A son born of an Aryan and a śūdra is named 'khattā'. By 'and others', 'māgadha' and so on are included. For it is said:

“Amate jārajo kuṇḍo,

Mate bhattari golako”ti amara 16.36.

“When the husband is not dead, the son of a paramour is a 'kuṇḍa'; when the husband is dead, he is a 'golaka'.”

“Māgadho suddakhattājo”ti abhidhānu 503 gāthā ca.

And: “A 'māgadha' is one born of a śūdra and a kṣatriya.”

Urasā manasā nimmito, urasaddā tatiyantā nimmitatthe ṇo, niviṭṭhattā tena nimmitoti vuccati. Urasi bhavoti vā oraso.

He who is created from the chest and by the mind. From the word 'ura', in the third (instrumental) case, with the suffix 'ṇo' in the sense of 'created'. Because he is established therein, he is said to be 'created by that'. Or, he who comes to be in the chest is 'oraso'.

242. Catukkaṃpatipatinīnaṃ [M 0.0175] yuge, “dārā pume bahutte ca, daṃ kalatre napuṃsake”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.38 amaramālā, jaṃsaddo tvabyayo dāravacano. Tasmā “jampati, dampatī”tipi bhavitabbaṃ, idha pana kaccāyanamatenodāhaṭā. Jāyā ca pati ca jāyāpati. Itarītarayogadvando. Jāyā ca pati ca jānipati, tathā jāyampatiādayo, jāyāsaddassa patimhi pare jāni, tudañca, jāyañca yadādinā.

242. A tetrad of terms for a couple of husband and wife. In the Amaramālā: 'dārā' is masculine and plural, and 'daṃ' is neuter for 'kalatra' (wife). The word 'jaṃ', however, is an indeclinable meaning 'dāra'. Therefore, 'jampati' and 'dampatī' should also be formed, but here the examples are cited according to the view of Kaccāyana. 'Jāyā ca pati ca' is 'jāyāpati'; it is a mutual copulative compound. 'Jāyā ca pati ca' is 'jānipati', and likewise 'jāyampati' and so on; the word 'jāyā', when followed by 'pati', becomes 'jāni', 'tudaṃ', and 'jāyaṃ' according to the rule beginning 'yadā'.

Tikaṃ napuṃsake. Vigato rāgassavo yasmā vassavaro. Su savane, aro. Paṇa byavahāre, ḍo, paḍi liṅgavekalye vā, bhūvādi. Na itthī na pumā napuṃsakaṃ, niruttinayena itthipumānaṃ puṃsakabhāvo, nassa ca pakati. Tatiyāpakati, saṇḍo, kalībantipi tassa nāmāni. Tatiyā pakati tatiyappakāro, samajātike itthipurise apekkhitvā tatiyattaṃ pakārassa. Paṭhamā hi pakati itthī, dutiyā pakati puriso, itarapakati tatiyā pakati.

A triad of terms for a person of neuter gender. One from whom the outflow of passion has departed is a 'vassavaro'. From the root 'paṇa' (to transact), with the suffix 'ḍo'; or from 'paḍi' (gender deficiency), of the 'bhū' class, is formed 'paṇḍaka'. Not a woman, not a man, is 'napuṃsakaṃ'; by etymological analysis, it is the state of being neither woman nor man, with 'na' as the base. 'Tatiyāpakati', 'saṇḍo', and 'kalība' are also its names. 'Tatiyā pakati' means the third kind; with respect to females and males of the same species, the kind is the third. For the first nature is female, the second nature is male; the other nature is the third nature.

243. Chakkaṃ ñātimatte, bandhuyeva bandhavo, a, ussāvo. Bandhatīti bandhu, u. Sassa attano jano sajano. Samānaṃ gottaṃ kulaṃ assāti sagotto, samānassa sabhāvo. Ñā avabodhane, kammeti, ñātiyeva ñātako, attaṃ, sakatthe ko ca. Susaddopyatra sva (amara 16.36).

243. A hexad of terms for a kinsman. 'Bandhu' itself is 'bandhavo', with the suffix 'a' by general rule. He who binds is 'bandhu', with the suffix 'u'. One's own people are 'sajano'. He who has the same clan is 'sagotto'; 'sa' is used for 'samāna'. From the root 'ñā' (to know), with the suffix 'ti' in the objective sense, is 'ñāti'; 'ñāti' itself is 'ñātako', with 'ka' in its own sense. The word 'su' is also used here.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0176] sattapurisāvadhikesu nikaṭañātīsu. Lohitena sambandho sālohito, sambandhassa sādeso, pubbanipāto ca, samānaṃ piṇḍadānaṃ yassa sapiṇḍo, sanābhayopyatra nābhi sattapurisāvadhikakule (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.33). Tikaṃ pitari. Tā pālane, to kattari. Janayatīti janako, ṇvu. Pā rakkhaṇe, ritu, assittaṃ.

A dyad of terms for close kinsmen within seven generations. One connected by blood is 'sālohito'; 'sa' is a substitute for 'samāna', and it is a prefix. One who shares the same rice-ball offering is 'sapiṇḍo'; 'sanābhayo' is also used here. A triad of terms for the father. From the root 'tā' (to protect), with the agentive suffix 'to', is formed 'tāto'. He who generates is 'janako', with the suffix 'ṇvu'. From the root 'pā' (to protect), with the suffix 'ritu', and the 'a' becoming 'i', is formed 'pitā'.

244. Chakkaṃ mātari. Ama pūjāyaṃ, kammani mo, bo ca, ammā, ambā. Janayatīti jananī, yu, nadādi. Māna pūjāyaṃ, puttaṃ mānetīti mātā, rātu, pātīti vā mātā, pātissa mo. Janetīti janetti,ti. Janetīti janikā, ṇvu, ittaṃ.

244. A hexad of terms for the mother. From the root 'ama' (to honor), in the passive sense with the suffixes 'ma' and 'ba', are formed 'ammā' and 'ambā'. She who gives birth is 'jananī', with the suffix 'yu', of the 'nadādi' group. From the root 'māna' (to honor), she who honors her son is 'mātā', with the suffix 'rātu'; or, she who protects is 'mātā', with 'pā' becoming 'mā'. She who gives birth is 'janetti', with the suffix 'ti'. She who gives birth is 'janikā', with the suffix 'ṇvu' and the feminine form 'ikā'.

Appadhānabhūtā mātā upamātā, kumāre dhāretīti dhāti. Dhā dhāraṇe,ti. Jāyāya bhariyāya bhātiko kaniṭṭho ca jeṭṭho ca sālo nāma, sassa attano esā sā, bhariyā, tassā bhātā sālo, jāyāya bhātari alo. Sara gaticintāhiṃsāsu vā, ṇo, lattaṃ, sāla vitakke vā, curādi.

A secondary mother is an 'upamātā'. She who nurtures a child is a 'dhāti' (wet-nurse), from the root 'dhā' (to hold), with the suffix 'ti'. The younger and elder brother of one's wife is named 'sālo'. 'Sa' means 'his own', 'sā' is she, the wife; her brother is 'sālo'. In the sense of 'wife's brother', the suffix is 'alo'. Or, from the root 'sara' (to move, think, or harm), with the suffix 'ṇo', and 'r' becoming 'l'. Or, from the root 'sāla' (to consider), of the 'curādi' class.

245. Sāmino bhattu bhaginī nanandā nāma, na nandatīti nanandā, attābhāvo nassa vibhāsādhikārā. Nanda samiddhiyaṃ, bhūvādi.

245. The sister of one's master, the husband, is named 'nanandā'. 'Na nandati' means 'she does not rejoice', hence 'nanandā'. The absence of the 'na' is due to the governing rule of option. The root 'nanda' means 'to prosper', and is of the 'bhū' class.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0177] ayyikāyaṃ. Mātuyā mātā mātāmahī. Pitūnaṃ pitari ca mātari ca āmahaṃ yadādinā, nadādi. Araha pūjāyaṃ, ṇvu, rahassa yo, aya gatimhi vā, ṇvu, ayyikā.

The twofold pertains to the grandmother. The mother's mother is mātāmahī. For the father's father and mother, the suffix is āmaha, by rules such as yadādi and from the nadādi group. Ayyikā is derived from the root arah, in the sense of honoring, with the suffix ṇvu, and yo for raha; or from the root aya, in the sense of going, with the suffix ṇvu.

Mātuyā bhātā mātulo nāma, mātuyā bhātā mātulo, mātu bhātari ulapaccayo. Assa mātulassa pajāpati jāyā mātulānī nāma, mātulassa bhariyā mātulānī, mātulabhariyāyaṃ āno, nadādi, atha vā mātulassa esā mātulānī, ī, assa āno.

The mother's brother is called mātulo; for the mother's brother, the suffix ula is applied. The wife of that maternal uncle is called mātulānī; for the maternal uncle's wife, the suffix āna from the nadādi group is applied. Or, she is the mātulānī of the mātula, with the suffix ī from that āna.

246. Jāyāpatīnaṃ dvinnaṃ jananī mātā sassu vuttā, sasa gatihiṃsāpānesu. Tappitā tesaṃ jāyāpatīnaṃ pitā pana sasuro nāma, sasadhātumhā uro. Bhaginiyā putto pana bhāgineyyo nāma, bhaginiyā apaccaṃ bhāgineyyo, ṇeyyo.

246. For both husband and wife, the mother is called sassu, from the root sasa in the sense of going, harming, or breathing. The father of those husband and wife is called sasuro, from the root sasa and the suffix uro. The sister's son is called bhāgineyyo; the offspring of the sister is bhāgineyyo, with the suffix ṇeyya.

247. Dvayaṃ sutassa, sutāya ca puttesu. Naha bandhane, ritu, nī naye vā. Puttassa putto paputto, ttalopo, ussattañca. Sāmibhātā devaro nāma, atha vā sāmibhātā kaniṭṭho sāmino bhātā devaro nāma. Jeṭṭho tu sasuro evoccate. Divu kīḷāyaṃ, aro.

247. The twofold pertains to the sons of a son and of a daughter. The root nah is in the sense of binding, with the suffix ritu; or the root nī is in the sense of leading. The son of a son is paputto, with the elision of tta and the addition of ussa. The husband's brother is called devaro; or the husband's younger brother, the master's brother, is called devaro. The elder, however, is called sasuro. The root divu is in the sense of playing, with the suffix aro.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0178] dhītupatimhi. Jana janane, ritu, assāttaṃ, nassa mādeso ca. Dvayaṃ pitupitari. Pituno pitā pitāmaho.

The twofold pertains to the son-in-law. The root jan is in the sense of generating, with the suffix ritu, assāttaṃ, and the substitution of m for n. The twofold pertains to the father's father. The father's father is pitāmaho.

248. Husāntāni padena padena nāmāni. Mātuyā bhaginī mātucchā, ccho. Pituno bhaginī pitucchā, pitubhaginī pitucchā bhavetyattho.

248. The names ending in husā are explained word by word. The mother's sister is mātucchā, with the suffix ccha. The father's sister is pitucchā; the meaning is 'the father's sister is pitucchā'.

Pitāmahasaddo na kevalaṃ janakapitarameva vadati, atha kho janakapitupitādayopīti etthāpi “papitāmaho” iccudāhaṭo. Pituno ayyako payyako, tulopo. Su savane, ṇhā. Ṇisamhi suṇisā. Samhi husā, hattaṃ. Sabbatra “itthiyamato āpaccayo”ti ā.

The term pitāmaha does not only refer to the father's father, but also to the father's father's father and so on; hence, here too, papitāmaho is cited as an example. The father's grandfather is payyako, with the elision of tu. The root su is in the sense of hearing, with the suffix ṇhā. With the suffix ṇisa, it forms suṇisā. With the suffix sa, it forms husā, with the change to ha. Everywhere, the suffix ā is applied according to the rule 'itthiyamato āpaccayo'.

249. Catukkaṃ ekodare bhātari. Samānodare ṭhito sodariyo, samānassa so. Samāno gabbho sagabbho, tatra bhavo sagabbho, ṇo. Samānodare jāto sodaro. Samānodare jāto sahajo. Sahasaddo tulyavacano.

249. The fourfold pertains to a brother born of one womb. One who stands in the same womb is sodariyo, where so is a substitute for samāna. The same womb is sagabbho; one existing there is sagabbho, with the suffix ṇa. Born of the same womb is sodaro. Born of the same womb is sahajo. The word saha expresses equality.

Mātāpitū te dve janā pitaro vuccante. Ubhinnampi janakabyappadesaniyatattā abhedavacanicchāyaṃ pituttamattheva. Nanvabhedā jāti, tassā cobhayatra sattādekattaṃ, na ca jātiyā [M 0.0179] liṅgasaṅkhyā bhavanti, adabbattā bahuvacanaṃ na siyāti? Nesa doso, na hi jātipadatthikassa na dabbaṃ, dabbapadatthikassa vā na jātīti. Kintubhayesaṃpyubhayapadattho ihātthaviseso. Jātipadatthikassa jāti padhānabhūtā dabbaṃ guṇabhūtaṃ, dabbapadatthikassa tu vipariyayo, tatra jātivacanicchāyaṃ dabbe viya liṅgasaṅkhyā vattabbā, tassa ca bahuttā bahuvacanaṃ. Pubbe viyābhedavacanicchāyaṃ putto ca dhītā ca puttā vuccante, jaññattañhi puttabyapadesaniyataṃ dhītaripyatthi, vipariyaye tu na bhavatyanabhidhānato. Bhedavacanicchāyaṃ puttadhītaroti bhavati.

Mother and father, these two people, are called pitaro. Since both are invariably designated as progenitors, with the intention of non-distinction, the term pitaro itself is used. But is not genus (jāti) undifferentiated? And since its existence is the same in both cases, and genus has no gender or number, should not the plural be inapplicable, since it is not a substance? This is no fault, for it is not that for one whose meaning is based on genus there is no substance, or for one whose meaning is based on substance there is no genus. But here, for both, the meaning of both words is a particular meaning. For one whose meaning is based on genus, genus is primary and substance is secondary; for one whose meaning is based on substance, the reverse is true. There, when intending to express genus, gender and number should be stated as with the substance, and its plurality justifies the plural. Just as before, when intending non-distinction, both son and daughter are called puttā, for the state of being offspring, which is invariably designated by putta, also exists in a daughter. But in the reverse case, it does not apply due to non-expression. When intending distinction, puttadhītaro occurs.

250. Sassu ca sasuro ca sasurāti vuccante. Tadapaccohanasambandhinibandhanā hi byappadeso sassuyampi ṭhito. Bhedavacanicchāyaṃ tu pubbe viya paccatthaṃ saddaniveso. Bhātā ca bhaginī ca bhātaro vuccante. Ekagabbhositattaṃ bhātubyappadesaniyataṃ bhaginiyaṃpyatthi. Tato ekagabbhositattassābhedavacanicchāyaṃ ubho bhātaro vuccante. Ettha ca sabbatrāpi virūpekaseso daṭṭhabbo. Duvidho hi ekaseso sarūpāsarūpavasena. Tatra sarūpekasese bahuvacanameva, itaratra pana dvivacanaṃ, yathā puriso ca puriso ca purisā, nāmañca rūpañca nāmarūpañca nāmarūpaṃ, mātā ca pitā ca pitaroti.

250. Mother-in-law and father-in-law are called sasurā. Indeed, the designation, which is based on the connection to their offspring, also applies to the mother-in-law. But with the intention of expressing distinction, the words are placed separately, as before. Brother and sister are called bhātaro. The state of being from the same womb, which is invariably designated by bhātu, is also present in the sister. Therefore, with the intention of non-distinction regarding the state of being from the same womb, both are called bhātaro. And here, in all cases, dissimilar ellipsis (virūpekaseso) should be understood. Indeed, ellipsis is of two kinds, according to similarity and dissimilarity. There, in similar ellipsis, only the plural is used; but in the other, the dual is used, as for example: puriso ca puriso ca becomes purisā; nāmañca rūpañca becomes nāmarūpañca or nāmarūpaṃ; mātā ca pitā ca becomes pitaro.

Bālyayobbanavuḍḍhattāni tīṇi vayāni. Tatra tikaṃ bālye. Dvayaṃ yobbane. Bālassa bhāvo bālattaṃ, ttaṃ. Tāpaccaye bālatā. Ṇyamhi bālyaṃ, atha vā bala pāṇane, balanti assasitapassasitamattena [M 0.0180] paṇantīti bālā, balyante saṃvarīyanteti vā bālā, bala saṃvaraṇe. Tesaṃ bhāvo bālattādi. Yuvassa bhāvo yobbaññaṃ, yobbanañca, bhāve ṇyo, ṇo ca, atha vā yu missane, yu, ussa uvādeso, vuddhi. Tesaṃ bhāvo yobbaññādi.

Childhood, youth, and old age are the three ages. Of these, there is a threefold set of terms for childhood, and a twofold for youth. The state of a child is bālattaṃ, with the suffix ttaṃ. With the suffix tā, it becomes bālatā. With the suffix ṇya, it becomes bālyaṃ. Or alternatively, from the root bal in the sense of breathing: they are bālā because they live (balanti) merely by inhaling and exhaling; or they are bālā because they are restrained (balyante), from the root bal in the sense of restraint. Their state is bālattādi. The state of a youth is yobbaññaṃ and yobbanaṃ, with the suffixes ṇya and ṇa respectively, in the sense of 'state'. Or alternatively, from the root yu in the sense of mixing: from yu, there is substitution of uva for u, and vowel gradation (vuddhi). Their state is yobbaññādi.

251. Ye jarākatā sukkā kesādayo, te palitaṃ nāma siyuṃ, tesaṃ vā yaṃ sukkattaṃ, taṃ palitaṃ nāma. Paca pāke, ito, cassa lattañca.

251. Those hairs and so on that are aged and white may be called palitaṃ; or their whiteness is called palitaṃ. It is derived from the root pac in the sense of ripening, with the suffix ita, and the change of c to l.

Dvayaṃ valipalitādimati kāyaparipāke. Jīyanti vuḍḍhā bhavanti assaṃ jarā, jara vayohānimhi, jarā eva jaratā, sakatthe tāpaccayo. Vissasātipi jarāya nāmaṃ. Visesena saṃsate adho pātayatīti vissasā. Saṃsati’rayaṃ pamādattho, avasaṃsanattho ca, iha avasaṃsanattho, niggahītalopo, dvittañca.

The twofold pertains to the body's decay, characterized by wrinkles, gray hair, and so on. That in which beings decay and become old is jarā, from the root jar in the sense of the decline of life. Jarā itself is jaratā, with the suffix tā used in its own sense. Vissasā is also a name for old age. It is vissasā because it especially causes one to sink (saṃsate) or fall downwards. This verb saṃsati can mean heedlessness or decline; here it means decline. The derivation involves the elision of the nasal consonant and reduplication.

Bālyayobbanavuḍḍhattāni pubbe vuttāni. Idāni tabbatināmānyāha. Tatra addhaṃ chāpasāmaññe. Putha, patha vitthāre, uko, puthuko, pala gamane, ṇvu, assittaṃ, dvittañca, pillako. Chupa samphasse, ussāttaṃ, chāpo. Kumāra kīḷāyaṃ, kumāro. Bala pāṇane, ṇo, bālo, pū pavane, to, sakatthe ko, potako, itthiyaṃ potakī. Poto, sāvo, sāvako, abbhako, ḍimbho, susuko, susuiccādīnipi chāpasāmaññatthāni.

Childhood, youth, and old age have been previously mentioned. Now, the names of those possessing these states are stated. Among them, half are in the general sense of a young animal or child. From the root puth or path in the sense of expansion, with the suffix uka, comes puthuko. From the root pal in the sense of going, with the suffix ṇvu, assittaṃ, and reduplication, comes pillako. From the root chup in the sense of touching, with ussāttaṃ, comes chāpo. From the root kumār in the sense of playing, comes kumāro. From the root bal in the sense of breathing, with the suffix ṇa, comes bālo. From the root pū in the sense of purifying, with the suffix ta, and ka in its own sense, comes potako; in the feminine, potakī. Poto, sāvo, sāvako, abbhako, ḍimbho, susuko, susu, and so on, also have the general meaning of a young animal or child.

252. Bālasāmaññavācakāni [M 0.0181] dassetvā visesabālanāmāni dassetumāha “athu”ccādi. Uttāno, uttānaṃ vā sayatīti uttānasayo. Kapaccaye uttānaseyyako. Thanaṃ pivatīti thanapo, ḍimbhasaddopyatra.

252. Having shown the general terms for a child, the text proceeds to show specific names for children, beginning with 'now' (athu), and so on. One who lies supine, or lies on his back, is uttānasayo. With the suffix ka, this becomes uttānaseyyako. One who drinks from the breast is thanapo. The word ḍimbha is also applicable here.

253. Sattakaṃ taruṇe.

253. The sevenfold pertains to a youth.

Āsoḷasā bhave bālo,

Taruṇo tu tato bhave;

Vuddho tu sattatyāyumhā,

Tīṇi vayāni lakkhaye.

Up to sixteen years, one is a child; then one becomes a youth; but one is old from the age of seventy. One should thus discern the three ages.

Tara taraṇe, uṇo. Vayasi yobbane tiṭṭhatīti vayaṭṭho, to, “vayo bālyādi pakkhī ca, yobbanañca vayo kvacī”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.42 ruddo, daha bhasmīkaraṇe, aro, yu missane, a, uvādeso, sissākāro. Sasa plutagatimhi, u, assuttaṃ, susu, taruṇassa vā pāṭipadikassa susvādeso. Manuno apaccaṃ mānavo, vaṇṇavikāro, nassa ṇattaṃ, māṇavo. Kucchāyaṃ kapaccayo, māṇavakoti siddhaṃ. Vuttañca –

From the root tar in the sense of crossing, with the suffix uṇa, comes taruṇa. One who stands (ṭṭha) in the age (vaya) of youth is vayaṭṭho, with the suffix ta. Rudda says: 'Vayo means childhood and so on, and also a bird; and sometimes vayo means youth.' From the root dah in the sense of burning, with the suffix ara, comes dahara. From the root yu in the sense of mixing, with the suffix a, substitution of uv, and sissākāro, comes yuva. From the root sas in the sense of leaping, with the suffix u and assuttaṃ, comes susu; or there is the substitution of susu for the base form of taruṇa. The offspring of Manu is mānavo, with vowel modification and the change of n to ṇ, becoming māṇavo. With the suffix ka in the sense of contempt, māṇavako is established. And it is said:

“Apacce kucchite mūḷhe, manutossaggiko mato”ti mahābhāssa 4.1.161 dara vidāraṇe, ṇvu.

'The generic suffix from Manu is held to apply in the sense of offspring, contempt, or foolishness.' From the root dar in the sense of tearing, with the suffix ṇvu, comes dāraka.

Dvayaṃ sukhavaḍḍhite kumāre, sukho kumāro sukumāro, khalopo, sukhena edhati vaddhatīti sukhedhito. “Sukhocito”tipi [M 0.0182] pāṭho, sukhaṃ ucitaṃ sampiṇḍitaṃ etthāti sukhocito, uca samavāye.

The twofold pertains to a child raised in comfort. A happy child is sukumāro, with the elision of kha. One who thrives and grows with ease (sukhena) is sukhedhito. Sukhocito is also a reading; it means one in whom happiness (sukhaṃ) is gathered (ucitaṃ) and accumulated, from the root uc in the sense of accumulation.

254-255. Dvipādena vuḍḍhassa nāmāni. Āyumahattaṃ lātīti mahallako, ṇvu, dvittaṃ. Vaḍḍha vaḍḍhane, kattari to, tassa ḍho, ḍḍhassa ḍo, assuttaṃ, dhā gatinivattiyaṃ, iro, dhassa thattaṃ, issa ettaṃ. Jara vayohānimhi, kattari to, tassa innādeso, dhātvantalopo, ṇattañca, jiṇṇo, sakatthe kamhi jiṇṇako. Pakataṃ vayo yobbanamassāti pavayotipi vuḍḍhassa nāmaṃ.

254-255. Names for an elder among bipeds. One who receives greatness of age is mahallako; the suffix is ṇvu, with doubling of the consonant. From the root vaḍḍh, 'to grow', with the agent suffix ta; for this ta, there is ḍha; for ḍḍh, there is ḍa; and the vowel a becomes u. From the root dhā, 'to go or to stop', with the suffix ira; for dh, there is th; for i, there is e. From the root jar, 'in the sense of the decay of age', with the agent suffix ta; for this ta, there is the substitution inna, elision of the final vowel of the root, and cerebralization of n; thus, jiṇṇo. In its own sense, with the suffix ka, it becomes jiṇṇako. One whose age, that is, youth, has passed is pavayo; this is also a name for an elder.

Valinantāni pādena nāmāni. Tatra tikaṃ jeṭṭhabhātari. Agge pure kāle, pubbe ca kāle jāyatīti aggajo, pubbajo ca. Ayañca vuḍḍho ayañca vuḍḍho, ayamimesaṃ visesena vuḍḍhoti jeṭṭho, vuḍḍhasaddā iṭṭhapaccayo, “vuḍḍhassa jo iyiṭṭhesū”ti vuḍḍhassa jo. Alope parassāsavaṇṇattaṃ.

Therein, a triad for an elder brother. One who is born at the beginning, at a former time, or at an earlier time is aggajo and pubbajo. 'This one is old, and this one is old; this one among them is especially old,' thus jeṭṭho. From the word vuḍḍha with the suffix iṭṭha; according to the rule "vuḍḍhassa jo iyiṭṭhesū," ja is substituted for vuḍḍha. Upon elision of the preceding vowel, the following vowel is not heard.

Tikaṃ pacchājāte bhātari. Ayañca yuvā ayañca yuvā, ayamimesaṃ visesena yuvāti kaniṭṭho, kaniyo kaṇiṭṭho kaṇiyo (ka.) ca. Iyiṭṭhesu yuvasaddassa kanādeso kaṇādeso (ka.). Anu pacchākāle jāto anujo. Jaghaññe pacchākāle jāto jaghaññajo. Aparasmiṃ pacchākāle jāto aparajoti dvepyatra.

A triad for a brother born later. 'This one is young, and this one is young; this one among them is especially young,' thus kaniṭṭho and kaniyo. When the suffixes iy or iṭṭha follow, the substitute kana replaces the word yuva. Born later in time (anu) is anujo. Born at the last time is jaghaññajo. Born at a later time is aparajo; these two are also included here.

Vali [M 0.0183] sithilaṃ taco cammaṃ yassa valittaco, dvittaṃ. Vali cammametassatthīti valino, ino. Uttānasayādayo valinantā vāccaliṅgattā tīsu liṅgesu vattanti, yathā – uttānasayo bālo, uttānasayā kumārī, uttānasayaṃ napuṃsakaṃ.

Vali means a wrinkle; one whose skin (taco, cammaṃ) is loose (sithilaṃ) is valittaco; with doubling of the consonant. One who has wrinkled skin (vali cammaṃ) is valino; the suffix is in. Words such as uttānasayo and those ending in valin function in all three genders because they take the gender of the noun they qualify, for example: uttānasayo bālo (a boy lying on his back), uttānasayā kumārī (a girl lying on her back), uttānasayaṃ napuṃsakaṃ (a neuter being lying on its back).

256. Pañcakaṃ matthake. Si saye, so, dīgho ca, aṅgesu uttamaṅgattā uttamaṅgaṃ, uttamo ca taṃ aṅgañcātipi uttamaṅgaṃ. Sīsañca uttamaṅgañca sīsottamaṅgāni. Si sevāyaṃ, ro, sevanti etenāti siro. Muda tose, dho. Sissākāro. Masa āmasane, ttho, sakatthe ko ca, masi parimāṇe vā.

256. A pentad for the head. From the root si, 'to lie', with the suffix sa, and lengthening of the vowel. Because it is the highest limb among the limbs, it is uttamaṅgaṃ; or, it is the highest (uttamo) and it is a limb (aṅgaṃ), thus also uttamaṅgaṃ. Sīsaṃ and uttamaṅgaṃ are sīsottamaṅgāni. From the root si, 'in the sense of service', with the suffix ra; 'they serve with it', thus siro. From the root mud, 'to rejoice', with the suffix dha. The shape of an ear of corn. From the root mas, 'to touch', with the suffix tha, and ka in its own sense; or from the root mas, 'to measure'.

Pajjaddhaṃ kese. Ke matthake seti tiṭṭhatīti keso. Sattamiyālopo, kati chedane, alo, assuttaṃ. Vala saṃvaraṇe, kammani ṇapaccayo, vālo. Uttamaṅge sīse ruhatīti uttamaṅgaruho. Muddhani jāyatīti muddhajo. Vālo ca uttamaṅgaruho ca muddhajo ceti itarītarayogadvando. Cikuro, kacotipyatra. Ci cayane, kura sadde, anekatthattā chedane. Vaḍḍhamāno cikarīyateti cikuro, kaca bandhane, a.

Half a verse on hair. 'It lies (seti) or stands (tiṭṭhati) on the head (ke, matthake)', thus keso. Elision of the locative. From the root kat, 'to cut', with the suffix ala, and the vowel a becomes u. From the root val, 'to cover', with the suffix ṇa in the passive sense, thus vālo. 'It grows (ruhati) on the highest limb, the head', thus uttamaṅgaruho. 'It is born (jāyati) on the crown of the head', thus muddhajo. Vālo, uttamaṅgaruho, and muddhajo form an itarītarayoga dvanda compound. Cikuro and kaco are also here. From the root ci, 'to pile up'; from the root kur, 'to sound', or, due to having many meanings, 'to cut'. 'Growing, it is cut (cikarīyate)', thus cikuro. From the root kac, 'to bind', with the suffix a.

257. Kusumagabbhā kesā kesacūḷā muttikādinā bahi saṃyatā santhatā dhammilo nāma. Ekato katvā dharīyati [M 0.0184] bandhīyatīti dhammilo, kammani ilo. Dhammena nānādesiyamanussānaṃ samācārena ilatīti vā dhammilo, ila gamane.

257. Hair containing flowers, a topknot of hair, bound and arranged on the outside with pearls and so on, is called a dhammilo. 'It is held and bound, having been gathered together,' thus dhammilo; with the suffix ila in the passive sense. Or, 'it goes (ilati) according to custom (dhammena), that is, the practice of people from various regions,' thus dhammilo; from the root il, 'to go'.

Dvayaṃ kumārānaṃ sikhāpañcake, cūḷattayeti keci. Kākānaṃ pakkhasaṇṭhānattā kākapakkho. Sikhā eva sikhaṇḍako, sakatthe ko. Sikhāsikhaṇḍasaddānamabhedattāyeva hi “sikhaṇḍī, sikhī cā”ti moro vutto.

A dyad for the five-fold topknot of boys; some say for the three-fold topknot. Because it has the shape of a crow's wings, it is kākapakkho. A crest (sikhā) itself is sikhaṇḍako; the suffix ka is in its own sense. Indeed, it is because of the non-difference between the words sikhā and sikhaṇḍa that the peacock is called sikhaṇḍī and sikhī.

Pāso, hattho ca ime dve kesacaye kesapariyāyato pare hutvā kesānaṃ kalāpe vattanti, na kevalā, yathā – kesapāso kesahattho iccādi. Pā rakkhaṇe, pāti rakkhati avayaveti pāso, so, pasa bandhaneti keci, ṇo. Hana gatiyaṃ, avayavā nihananti etthāti hattho, tho, pakkhopyatra.

Pāso and hattho, these two, when following a synonym for hair, refer to a bundle of hair, not by themselves; for example, kesapāso, kesahattho, etc. From the root pā, 'to protect'; 'it protects the parts', thus pāso; the suffix is sa. Some say it is from the root pas, 'to bind', with the suffix ṇa. From the root han, 'to go'; 'the parts are bound together in it', thus hattho; the suffix is tha. Pakkho is also here.

Tāpasānaṃ vatīnaṃ tahiṃ kesacaye jaṭāsaddo vuccati, jaṭa jaṭane, jaṭa saṅghāte vā, “itthiyamatiyavo vā”ti a.

For ascetics and those who have vows, the word jaṭā is used for that mass of hair. It is from the root jaṭ, 'to entwine', or from the root jaṭ, 'to heap together'; the suffix is a, according to the rule "itthiyamatiyavo vā".

258. Positabhattādīhi yā banjhate, tatra veṇī, paveṇī ca. Vī pajane, pajanaṃ gabbhavimokkho, vī tantasantāne vā, ṇī. Pakkhe paveṇī.

258. That which is bound by well-fed persons and so on is called veṇī and paveṇī. From the root vī, 'to produce'—producing means release from the womb—or from the root vī, 'to weave'; the suffix is ṇī. Alternatively, with the prefix pa, it is paveṇī.

Dvayaṃ sīsamajjhaṭṭhacūḷāyaṃ. Cūḷa sañcodane, cūḷa hāvakaraṇe vā, a. Sikhā vuttā. Kesapāsīpyatra, nadādi.

A dyad for the topknot situated in the middle of the head. From the root cūḷ, 'to incite', or from the root cūḷ, 'to act coquettishly'; the suffix is a. Sikhā has been mentioned. Kesapāsī is also here, belonging to the nadādi group.

Nārīnaṃ [M 0.0185] kesamajjhamhi paddhati ujugatamaggo sīmantoti mato kathito. Sīmassa anto sīmanto, sī saye vā, anto, majjhe makāravaṇṇāgamo.

The path, the straight-gone way, in the middle of women's hair is considered and called sīmanto. It means the end (anto) of the boundary (sīmā). Or, it is from the root sī, 'to lie', with the suffix anta, and the insertion of the letter ma in the middle.

259. Tikaṃ lome. Lū chedane, vaḍḍhamānaṃ lūyateti lomaṃ, mo. Tanumhi ruhatīti tanuruhaṃ, a. Ruha janane, rūha pātubhāve vā, mo, halopo, ottañca, lū chedane vā, mo, lassa rattaṃ, romaṃ. Akkhimhi jātaṃ lomaṃ pamhaṃ, pakhumañcoccate. Paminoti tenāti pamhaṃ, papubbo mā parimāṇe, hapaccayo. Akkhino pakkhadvaye jātaṃ pakhumaṃ, umo, kalopo ca.

259. A triad for body-hair. From the root lū, 'to cut'; 'what grows is cut', thus lomaṃ; the suffix is ma. 'It grows on the body', thus tanuruhaṃ; the suffix is a. From the root ruh, 'to be born', or rūh, 'to appear', with the suffix ma, elision of h, and the vowel u becomes o; or, from the root lū, 'to cut', with the suffix ma, and l becomes r; thus romaṃ. The hair born on the eye is called pamhaṃ and pakhumaṃ. 'One measures with it', thus pamhaṃ; from the root mā, 'to measure', with the prefix pa, and the suffix ha. 'It is born on the two sides of the eye', thus pakhumaṃ; the suffix is uma, with elision of ka.

Pumamukhe purisānaṃ mukhe vuttaṃ pavuṭṭhaṃ (ka.) lomaṃ massu nāma, masa āmasane, su, massu.

The hair on the face of a male, that is, on the face of men, is called massu. It is from the root mas, 'to touch', with the suffix su; thus massu.

Tikaṃ bhamumhi. Bhama anavaṭṭhāne, ū, malopo, bhū. Umhi bhamu, kapaccaye bhamuko. Bhamukasahacaraṇato bhamu pulliṅgo.

A triad for the eyebrow. From the root bham, 'to be unsteady', with the suffix ū and elision of m, thus bhū. With the suffix u, it is bhamu. With the suffix ka, it is bhamuko. Due to its association with bhamuka, bhamu is masculine.

260. Tikaṃ nettodake. Khipa peraṇe, po, issattaṃ. Nette jātaṃ jalaṃ nettajalaṃ. Asa adhopatane, su, assu. Nettajalañca assu cāti dvando. Assu napuṃsake.

260. A triad for tears. From the root khip, 'to throw', with the suffix pa, and the vowel i becomes a. 'Water born in the eye' is nettajalaṃ. From the root as, 'to fall down', with the suffix su, thus assu. Nettajalaṃ and assu form a dvanda compound. Assu is neuter.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0186] akkhiputtalikāyaṃ. Nette dissamānā tārā nettatārā. Kaññāsaddato taddhito apaccayo, kaññāsaddassa kanīnādeso, itthikatākārapare ke pubbo akāro ikāramāpajjate kātanta 2.2.65, kanīnikā. Tārakāpyatra.

A dyad for the pupil of the eye. 'The star seen in the eye' is nettatārā. From the word kaññā, with a taddhita suffix in the sense of 'descendant'; for the word kaññā there is the substitution kanīna; when the feminine suffix ikā follows, the preceding vowel a becomes i; thus kanīnikā. Tārakā is also here.

Chakkaṃ mukhavivare, kavayo pana tadupalakkhitepi samudāye yujjante. Vada viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, karaṇe yu. Mu bandhane, kho, ottābhāvo nipātanā, mukhaṃ. Sabbadharakate pana khaññateti dhātunā mukhanti nipātitaṃ, khanu avadāraṇe. Tuḍi toḍane, a. Tanu vitthāre vā, ḍo, assuttaṃ. Vadati tenāti vattaṃ, to, vuccate anenāti vā vattaṃ. Vada viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, to. Lapa vacane, karaṇe yu. Ānanti asanti anenāti ānanaṃ, ana pāṇane, yu. Assaṃpyatra. Asa bhakkhane. Karaṇe so.

A hexad for the mouth-opening; poets, however, use them also for the whole face which is characterized by it. From the root vad, 'in distinct speech', with the instrumental suffix yu. From the root mu, 'to bind', with the suffix kha; mukhaṃ is an irregular formation due to the absence of the vowel o. However, mukhaṃ is irregularly formed from the root khan, 'to dig', because 'it digs all that is brought to it'. From the root tuḍ, 'to strike', with the suffix a. Or from the root tan, 'to spread', with the suffix ḍa, and the vowel a becomes u. 'One speaks with it', thus vattaṃ; the suffix is ta. Or, 'it is spoken with', thus vattaṃ. From the root vad, 'in distinct speech', with the suffix ta. From the root lap, 'to speak', with the instrumental suffix yu. 'They breathe with it', thus ānanaṃ; from the root an, 'to breathe', with the suffix yu. Āsaṃ is also here; from the root as, 'to eat', with the instrumental suffix sa.

261. Aḍḍhaṃ dante. Dvīsu ṭhānesu dvikkhattuṃ vā jāyateti dvijo. Lapane mukhe jāyatīti lapanajo. Dā avakhaṇḍane, dāyati bhakkhamanenāti danto, anto, dasa adane vā, dasanti bhojjamanenāti danto, anto, dhātvantalopo. Damu damane vā, to. Daṃsa daṃsane, daṃsate vilikhyate bhakkhamanenāti daṃsano, yu. Rada vilekhane, yu, radano. Amhi rado.

261. A half-verse on the tooth. 'It is born in two places or twice', thus dvijo. 'It is born in the mouth (lapane)', thus lapanajo. From the root dā, 'to cut'; 'it cuts what is eaten', thus danto; the suffix is anta. Or from the root das, 'to eat'; 'they eat what is to be eaten with it', thus danto; the suffix is anta, with elision of the final vowel of the root. Or from the root dam, 'to tame', with the suffix ta. From the root daṃs, 'to bite'; 'it bites or scratches what is eaten', thus daṃsano; the suffix is yu. From the root rad, 'to scratch', with the suffix yu; thus radano. In me, rado.

Dantabhedasmiṃ dantavisese dāṭhāsaddo. Itthiliṅgoyaṃ. Daṃsadhātuto ṭho, daṃsissa ca dā, dāṭhā, muddhajadutiyoyaṃ. Akkhikoṭīsu [M 0.0187] vāmadakkhiṇanettānaṃ antesu apāṅgo vattati, sarīraṅgasaṅkhātassa kaṇṇassa apa samīpaṃ apāṅgo.

The word dāṭhā refers to a type of tooth, a specific kind of tooth. This is feminine in gender. From the root daṃs, with the suffix ṭha, and for daṃs there is the substitute dā; thus dāṭhā. This is the second cerebral. At the corners of the eyes, at the ends of the left and right eyes, the term apāṅgo is used. Apāṅgo also means near (apa samīpaṃ) the ear, which is counted as a part of the body.

262. Catukkaṃ oṭṭhe. Dante āvarati chādayatīti dantāvaraṇaṃ. Usa dāhe, to, “sādisantapucchabhanjahaṃsādīhi ṭṭho”ti sahādibyañjanena ṭṭho, ottadvittāni, oṭṭho. Gadrabhepyayaṃ. Atha vā usa dāhe, ṭṭho, ottadvittādi, ubhayatrāpi muddhajadutiyo, īsaṃ kiñci kālaṃ dhāreti bhakkhametthāti adharo, īsattho hyatra akāro.

262. Four terms for the lip. It is dantāvaraṇaṃ because it covers or conceals the teeth. From the root us, 'to burn', with the suffix to; according to the rule 'sādisantapucchabhanjahaṃsādīhi ṭṭho', the suffix is ṭṭha with an initial consonant like sa, etc.; with the vowel becoming o and the consonant doubled, it becomes oṭṭha. This word also applies to a donkey. Alternatively, from the root us, 'to burn', with the suffix ṭṭha, with the vowel becoming o and the consonant doubled, etc. In both cases, the second consonant is a cerebral. It is adharo because food is held here for a little while, for here the letter 'a' has the meaning of 'a little'.

“A pume mādhave ñeyyo,

Paṭisedhe tadabyayaṃ;

Īsatthe ca viruddhatthe,

Sadisatthe payogato”ti. –

The letter 'a' in the masculine should be known as Mādhava; as an indeclinable, it is used for negation; and it is employed in the sense of 'a little', 'opposite', and 'similar'.

Hi ekakkharakose vuttaṃ. Dasane dante chādayatīti dasanacchado. Ettha keci adharasaddena heṭṭhimoṭṭhamevāhu, tesaṃ vacanaṃ “nettantādharapāṇipādayugalehi”ccādīhi mahākavipayogehi asaṃsandanato na gahetabbaṃ.

Indeed, it is said in the Ekakkharakosa. It covers the teeth; hence, it is called dasanacchado. Here, some say that the word adhara refers only to the lower lip, but their statement should not be accepted because it does not accord with the usage of great poets, as in such phrases as 'nettantādharapāṇipādayugalehi' (with the corners of the eyes, lips, hands, and pairs of feet).

Tikaṃ kapole. Gaḍi vadanekadese, a, dhātuppakriyatthañhi dhātupāṭhavacanaṃ, sabbatrāpyevaṃ. Kena jalena pūriyateti kapolo, alo, kapa acchādane vā, olo, kapolo, nadādi. Gaṇḍī. Adharā adhobhāgo cubukaṃ nāma, cibukaṃpyatra. Cibu olambake, ṇvu, assuttaṃ.

Three terms for the cheek. From the root gaḍi, 'in a part of the face', with the suffix a; indeed, the statement in the Dhātupāṭha is for the purpose of root derivation, and this is so everywhere. Because it is filled with water (kena), it is kapolo, with the suffix alo; or from the root kapa, 'to cover', with the suffix olo, it becomes kapolo, belonging to the nadādi group. Gaṇḍī. The lower part below is called cubukaṃ; cibukaṃ is also found here. From the root cibu, 'to hang down', with the suffix ṇvu; it is an underived word.

263. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0188] gīvāya purobhāge. Gala adane, karaṇe a, gila gilane vā, gilati anenāti galo, issattaṃ. Kaṇa saddattho daṇḍako dhātu, ṭho, kaṇṭho, muddhajadutiyoyaṃ.

263. Two terms for the front part of the neck. From the root gal, 'to eat', with the suffix a in the sense of instrument; or from the root gil, 'to swallow'—that by which one swallows is galo, with a vowel change. The root kaṇ, meaning 'sound', is a daṇḍaka root; with the suffix ṭho, it becomes kaṇṭho; this has the second cerebral consonant.

Tikaṃ ekatthaṃ. Gā sadde, īvo. Kaṃ sīsaṃ dharatīti kandharā. Siraṃ dharatīti sirodharā, siro dhiyyate assanti vā sirodharā, dhā gatinivattiyaṃ, aro.

Three terms with one meaning. From the root gā, 'to sound', with the suffix īvo. Because it bears the head (kaṃ), it is called kandharā. Because it bears the head (siraṃ), it is sirodharā; or sirodharā because the head is placed upon it. From the root dhā, 'to go or to stop', with the suffix aro.

Suvaṇṇamayo āliṅgo murajabhedo, tena sannibhā sadisā yā gīvā, sā kambugīvā matā, mahāpurisalakkhaṇametaṃ. Atha vā yā gīvā tīhi lekhāhi aṅkitā lakkhitā, sā kambugīvā matā, mahāpurisalakkhaṇametañca. Kambu vuccati suvaṇṇaṃ, kambumayena āliṅgena sannibhā gīvā kambugīvā, kamba saṃvaraṇe, u, kambu.

A golden āliṅga is a type of drum; a neck that resembles it is considered a kambugīvā. This is a mark of a Great Man. Alternatively, a neck marked with three lines is considered a kambugīvā, and this too is a mark of a Great Man. Kambu is said to mean gold; a neck resembling a golden āliṅga is a kambugīvā. From the root kamb, 'to cover', with the suffix u, it becomes kambu.

264. Tikaṃ khandhe. Ana gatiyaṃ, so. Bhujānaṃ siro matthakaṃ bhujasiro. Kaṃ matthakaṃ dadhātīti kandho, so eva khandho kakārassa khakārakaraṇavasena, khamati bhāranti vā khandho, khamu sahane, to, tassa dho, massa no, niggahītaṃ vā[M 0.0189]. Tassandhi tassa khandhassa majjhaṃ jattu nāma, yaṃ khandhānaṃ majjhe tiṭṭhati. Jana janane, jara vayohānimhi vā, tu, jattu, taṃ napuṃsakaṃ.

264. Three terms for the shoulder. From the root an, 'to go', with the suffix so, forming aṃso. The head or top of the arms is bhujasiro. Because it bears the head (kaṃ), it is kandho; this same word becomes khandho by changing the letter 'k' to 'kh'. Alternatively, because it endures a burden, it is khandho; from the root kham, 'to endure', with the suffix to, its t becomes dh, and its m becomes n, or a nasal. The joint in the middle of that shoulder is called jattu, which stands between the shoulders. From the root jan, 'to generate', or from jar, 'to decay', with the suffix tu, it becomes jattu; it is neuter.

Dvayaṃ bāhumūle. Bāhūnaṃ bhujānaṃ mūlaṃ bāhumūlaṃ. Kaca bandhane, cho. Assa kacchassa adhobhāgaṭṭhānaṃ passaṃ vuccati, disa pekkhane, apaccayo, disassa passādeso.

Two terms for the armpit. The root of the arms or limbs is bāhumūlaṃ. From the root kac, 'to bind', with the suffix cho, forming kaccho. The place that is the lower part of the armpit is called passaṃ; it is derived from the root dis, 'to see', with the suffix a, and the substitution of passa for disa.

265. Tikaṃ bāhumhi. Vahati anenāti vāhu, vāhu eva bāhu, ku ṇvādi 6. Bhuñjate anenāti bhujo. Bhuja pālanajjhohāresu. Bāhu ca bhujo ceti dvando, ete dve dvīsu, itthiyaṃ bhujā. Vahati yāyāti bāhā. Aparosaddopyatra a pārosaddopyatra (ka.), a paveṭṭhasaddopyatra (?).

265. Three terms for the arm. That by which one carries is vāhu; vāhu itself becomes bāhu, with the suffix ku. That by which one enjoys is bhujo. The root bhuj means 'to protect' or 'to consume'. Bāhu and bhujo form a dvanda compound; these two are in the dual, while bhujā is feminine. That by which one carries is bāhā. The word apara is also used here.

Tikaṃ hatthe. Hasa hasane, tho. Hara haraṇe vā. Nakkhattepyayaṃ. Kara karaṇe, a. Paṇa byavahārathutīsu, i. Pā rakkhane vā, ṇi. Karo ca pāṇi ca karapāṇayo. Pañcasākho, sayopyatra.

Three terms for the hand. From the root has, 'to laugh', with the suffix tho, forming hattho. Or from har, 'to take'. This word also applies to a constellation. From the root kar, 'to do', with the suffix a, forming karo. From the root paṇ, 'to transact' or 'to praise', with the suffix i, forming pāṇi. Or from pā, 'to protect', with the suffix ṇi. Karo and pāṇi form karapāṇayo. Pañcasākho is also a word used here.

Pakoṭṭhanto hatthagaṇṭhi maṇibandho nāma. Pakoṭṭho nāma āmaṇibandhaṃ kapparassa adhobhāgo. Maṇivikatiṃ bandhati etthāti maṇibandho. Kusa akkose, ṭho, pakoṭṭho.

The end of the forearm, the joint of the hand, is called maṇibandho. Pakoṭṭho is the name for the lower part of the arm from the elbow down to the wrist. Because a jeweled ornament is bound here, it is maṇibandho. From the root kus, 'to revile', with the suffix ṭho, it becomes pakoṭṭho.

Dvayaṃ bhujamajjhagaṇṭhimhi. Kapu hiṃsāyaṃ, aro. Kupparotipi pāṭho, tadā assuttaṃ. Kapu hiṃsāyaṃ, oṇi, kapoṇi, itthiyaṃ. Kaphoṇīpyatra, tattha passa phattaṃ.

Two terms for the middle joint of the arm, the elbow. From the root kapu, 'to harm', with the suffix aro, forming kapparo. Kupparo is also a reading; in that case, it is an underived word. From the root kapu, 'to harm', with the suffix oṇi, it becomes kapoṇi; it is feminine. Kaphoṇī is also found here; in that case, note the change of p to ph.

266. Pāṇissa [M 0.0190] pāṇitalassa sambandhīnaṃ maṇibandhakaniṭṭhānaṃ dvinnaṃ antaraṃ bahiṭṭhānaṃ karabho vuccati, yena kumārakā satthaṃ katvā aññamaññaṃ paharanti, kara hiṃsāyaṃ, abho, kara karaṇe vā.

266. The outer part of the hand, between the wrist and the little finger, is called karabho; with this, boys make a weapon and strike one another. It is from the root kar, 'to harm', with the suffix abho; or from kar, 'to do'.

Dvayaṃ aṅgulimatte. Karassa pāṇissa sākhā karasākhā. Agi gatyattho, aṅga gamanattho vā, uli. Itthiliṅgoyaṃ (nadādi) (ka.), aṅguli.

Two terms for the finger. The branches of the hand or palm are karasākhā. From the root agi, meaning 'to go', or from aṅg, meaning 'to go', with the suffix uli, forming aṅguli. This word, aṅguli, is feminine.

Tā aṅguliyo pañcappabhedā, yathā – aṅguṭṭho tajjanī majjhimā anāmikā kaniṭṭhā ceti kamā siyuṃ. Aṅga gamanattho, assuttaṃ, agge pure tiṭṭhatīti vā aṅguṭṭho, niggahītāgamo, assuttañca. Tajja hiṃsāyaṃ, tajjeti yāya, sā tajjanī, yu, nadādi. Majjhe tiṭṭhatīti majjhimā. Natthi nāmamassāti anāmikā, sakatthe ko. Atisayena khuddakāti kaniṭṭhā. Yuvappānaṃ kana, kaṇa vā iyiṭṭhesu.

Those fingers are of five kinds, which are, in order: the thumb (aṅguṭṭho), the index finger (tajjanī), the middle finger (majjhimā), the ring finger (anāmikā), and the little finger (kaniṭṭhā). Aṅguṭṭho is from the root aṅg, 'to go'; it is an underived word. Or because it stands at the front, it is aṅguṭṭho, with the insertion of a nasal and also being an underived word. Tajjanī is from the root tajj, 'to harm'; that by which one threatens is tajjanī, with the suffix yu, belonging to the nadādi group. Because it stands in the middle, it is majjhimā. Because it has no name, it is anāmikā, with the suffix ka in its own sense. Because it is exceedingly small, it is kaniṭṭhā. For young things, kana or kaṇa is used with the comparative and superlative suffixes.

267. Tajjanyādīhi yute aṅguṭṭhe tate pasārite sati padesādikā catasso saññā kamato siyuṃ, yathā – tajjanīyute [M 0.0191] aṅguṭṭhe tate padeso. Disa pekkhane. Majjhimayute aṅguṭṭhe tate tālo, tala patiṭṭhāyaṃ. Anāmikāsahite aṅguṭṭhe tate gokaṇṇo, gokaṇṇasadisattā, tappamāṇattā vā gokaṇṇo, atha vā gokaṇṇo nāma eko migaviseso, takkaṇṇasadisappamāṇattā gokaṇṇo, tālo ca gokaṇṇo ca tālagokaṇṇā. Liṅgabhedā “tālagokaṇṇavidatthī”ti na vuttaṃ, kaniṭṭhāyute aṅguṭṭhe tate vidatthi, vitanotīti vitatthi, vitatthi eva vidatthi, tanu vitthāre,ti, tassa tho. Vidatthi. “Kamā tato”tipi pāṭho.

267. When the thumb is extended and spread out along with the index finger and others, four designations, beginning with padeso, occur in order. For example, when the thumb is extended along with the index finger, it is a padeso. This is from the root dis, 'to see'. When the thumb is extended along with the middle finger, it is a tālo; from the root tal, 'to be established'. When the thumb is extended along with the ring finger, it is a gokaṇṇo, because of its resemblance to a cow's ear or because its measure is that of a cow's ear. Alternatively, gokaṇṇo is the name of a particular kind of deer, and it is so called because its measure resembles that deer's ear. Tālo and gokaṇṇo together are tālagokaṇṇā. Due to the difference in gender, tālagokaṇṇavidatthī is not stated. When the thumb is extended along with the little finger, it is a vidatthi. Because it stretches out, it is vitatthi, and vitatthi itself becomes vidatthi. It is from the root tan, 'to spread', with the suffix ti, which becomes thi. Kamā tato is also a reading.
