Kuñcito saṅkocito pāṇi pasatākhyo, papubbo sara gatiyaṃ, to. Pamāṇappakaraṇato vitatañjaliyevāyaṃ kavīhi icchito. Sampuṭañjali panāyaṃ, pasāritasahitā pasāritasahitattā (ka.) yassa aṅguliyo bhavantīti.

A cupped or hollowed hand is called pasata. It is from the root sar, 'to go', with the prefix pa and the suffix to. In the context of measurement, this is what is intended by poets as vitatañjali. A sampuṭañjali, however, is that in which the fingers are extended and joined.

Kuñcito ca tataṅguṭṭho, sapatākoti sammato;

Patākehi tu hatthehi, sampuṭañjali icchito.

A hand with bent fingers and an extended thumb is considered sapatāka. But a sampuṭañjali is desired with patāka (flag-like) hands.

Devatānaṃ garūnañca, pitūnañce’cchito pure;

Atthappakaraṇādīhi, bhedo ñeyyo tahiṃ tahiṃ.

For deities, teachers, and ancestors, this was desired of old. The distinction should be known in each case according to the meaning, context, and other factors.

Yathā jalañjaliṃ dadāti, añjalinā pivati, devoyaṃ katañjaliriti. Puṭañjalissa vā vakkhamānattā idha vitatañjaliyeva.

For example: 'one gives a water-offering (jalañjali)', 'one drinks with cupped hands (añjalinā)', 'this deity has his hands joined in reverence (katañjali)'. Or, because puṭañjali will be spoken of, here only vitatañjali is meant.

268. Tikaṃ sappakoṭṭhe vitatakare. Ramu kīḷāyaṃ, tano, malopo, ratanaṃ, maṇibuddhādīsu ca. Kuka ādāne, u[M 0.0192], dvittaṃ. Hasa dhātumhā tho, to vā, hattho, hatthasahitattā vā pakoṭṭho hattho.

268. Three terms for the outstretched hand including the forearm. From the root ram, 'to play', with the suffix tana and the elision of m, it becomes ratanaṃ; it is also used for 'jewel', 'Buddha', etc. From the root kuk, 'to take', with the suffix u and doubling, it becomes kukku. From the root has, with the suffix tho or to, it becomes hattho; or the forearm (pakoṭṭho) is called hattho because it is together with the hand.

Dvayaṃ sampuṭañjalimhi. Karamayo puṭo karapuṭo, añja byattigatikantīsu, ali, añjali. Karapuṭo ca añjali ceti karapuṭañjalī.

Two terms for cupped hands in reverence. A hollow (puṭo) made of the hands (karamayo) is karapuṭo. From the root añj, 'to make clear', 'to go', or 'to adorn', with the suffix ali, it becomes añjali. Karapuṭo and añjali together form karapuṭañjalī.

Dvayaṃ nakhe. Kare jāyati ruhatīti karajo. Natthi khaṃ indriyaṃ etthāti nakho, saññāsaddattā na attaṃ, avisayattā vā. Punabbhavo, kararuho, nakharotipi nakhassa nāmāni.

Two terms for the nail. Because it is born or grows on the hand, it is called karajo. Because there is no sense faculty (khaṃ indriyaṃ) here, it is nakho. Because it is a conventional term, it is not the self, or because it is not an object of the senses. Punabbhavo, kararuho, and nakharo are also names for the nail.

Dvayaṃ puṭaṅgulikaretikhyāte muṭṭhimhi. Khaṭa icchāyaṃ, ṇvu, khada hiṃsāyaṃ vā, dassa ṭo. Mu bandhane,ti, tassa ṭho, dvittaṃ.

Two terms for the fist, which is known as puṭaṅgulikara (a hand with enclosed fingers). From the root khaṭ, 'to desire', with the suffix ṇvu; or from khad, 'to harm', with its d becoming ṭ. From the root mu, 'to bind', with the suffix ti, its t becoming ṭh, with doubling, it becomes muṭṭhi.

269. Passadvayavitthatā passadvayepi vitatā pasāritā sahakarā sapāṇayo dve bāhū byāmo nāma, byāmīyate anenāti byāmo, vipubbo yāma añche. Uddhaṃ upari tatā vitatā bhujā ca poso ca tesaṃ samuditānaṃ pamāṇasadisaṃ pamāṇaṃ yassa tasmiṃ uddhantatabhujaposappamāṇe porisasaddo vattati. Bhujasaddena sahakarā bhujā gayhate, ekassa pamāṇasaddassa lopo, purisassa pamāṇaṃ porisaṃ. Purisasaddo cettha sakarabhujapurisaṃ vadati, tīsu, yathā – porisaṃ jalaṃ, poriso hatthī, porisī yaṭṭhi.

269. The two arms, extended and spread out on both sides, together with the hands, are called a 'byāma'. It is called 'byāma' because one measures with it; it is from the root 'yāma' with the prefix 'vi', in the sense of stretching. The word 'porisa' is used for that which has a measure equal to the combined measure of the arms stretched and extended upwards and the man himself. By the word 'bhuja', the arms together with the hands are taken; there is an elision of one word for 'measure'; thus, 'purisassa pamāṇaṃ' (a man's measure) becomes 'porisaṃ'. Here, the word 'purisa' refers to a man with his arms and hands, in three genders, for example: 'porisaṃ jalaṃ' (water a man's depth), 'poriso hatthī' (an elephant a man's height), 'porisī yaṭṭhi' (a staff a man's length).

270. Dvayaṃ urasi. Usa dāhe, ro, salopo, ara gatimhi vā, assukāro. Hara haraṇe, yo, rassa do. Koḷaṃ koṭṭha (ka.)[M 0.0193], bhujantaraṃ, vakkhotipi uronāmāni. Tikaṃ uroje. Tanu vitthāre, tanoti icchanti thano, tassa tho, thana devasadde, thana coriye vā. Kuca saṅkocane, kuco. Payo khīraṃ dhāretīti payodharo. Kuco ca payodharo cāti dvando.

270. Two terms for the chest. [The word 'ura'] is from the root 'usa' in the sense of 'burning,' with the suffix 'ro,' and elision of 'sa'; or from 'ara' in the sense of 'going,' with 'a' becoming 'u'. [The word 'hadaya' is from the root] 'hara' in the sense of 'carrying away,' with the suffix 'yo,' and 'ra' becoming 'da'. 'Koḷa,' 'bhujantara' (space between the arms), and 'vakkha' are also names for the chest. Three terms for the breast. [The word] 'thana' is from the root 'tanu' in the sense of 'spreading'; 'it spreads' or 'they desire it', hence 'thana', with its 'ta' becoming 'tha'; or from the root 'thana' in the sense of 'divine sound' or 'theft'. [The word] 'kuco' is from the root 'kuca' in the sense of 'contracting'. That which holds milk ('payo') is 'payodharo'. 'Kuco' and 'payodharo' form a dvanda compound.

Thanaggasmiṃ thanassa agge cūcukaṃ, napuṃsake. “Cūcuko so kucānana”nti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.77 tu ratanakoso, cu cavane, uko, dvittaṃ, dīgho ca, cūcukaṃ, cancu gatiyaṃ vā, uko, nalopo, assūkāro, cūcukaṃ.

For the tip of the breast, the summit of the breast, 'cūcukaṃ' is used; it is neuter. However, the Ratanakosa has: 'cūcuko so kucānanaṃ' (that nipple is the face of the breast). [The word] 'cūcukaṃ' is from the root 'cu' in the sense of 'moving,' with the suffix 'uko,' with doubling and lengthening; or from 'cancu' in the sense of 'going,' with the suffix 'uko,' with elision of 'n,' and 'a' becoming 'ū'.

Dvayaṃ piṭṭhe kāyassa pacchābhāge. Piṭa saddasaṅghātesu, to. Itaratra ti, pisu secane vā.

Two terms for the back, the rear part of the body. [The word 'piṭṭha'] is from the root 'piṭa' in the senses of 'sound' and 'collection,' with the suffix 'to'. For the other word ['piṭṭhi'], the suffix is 'ti'; or it is from the root 'pisu' in the sense of 'sprinkling'.

271. Tikaṃ tanumajjhe. Majjhe bhavo majjho. Laga saṅge, a. Majjhe bhavaṃ majjhimaṃ. Catukkaṃ udare. Kusa akkose, chi, sassa co. Gaha upādāne, ani, īmhi gahaṇī, gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti dhāretīti vā gahaṇī, gabbhāsayasaññito mātukucchippadeso, tejodhātumhi pana yathābhuttāhārassa vipācanavasena gaṇhanato achaḍḍanato gahaṇī. Upubbo dara gamane. Udarati uddhaṃ gacchati vāyu yatrāti udaraṃ. Gu sadde, abho, dvittādi, gabbho. Picaṇḍa jaṭhara tundāpyatra.

271. Three terms for the middle of the body. 'Majjho' is that which is in the middle. [The word 'lagga'] is from the root 'laga' in the sense of 'attachment,' with the suffix 'a'. 'Majjhimaṃ' is that which is in the middle. Four terms for the abdomen. [The word 'kucchi'] is from the root 'kusa' in the sense of 'reproaching,' with the suffix 'chi,' with 'sa' becoming 'ca'. [The word] 'gahaṇī' is from the root 'gaha' in the sense of 'taking,' with the suffix 'ani,' becoming 'ī' in the feminine; or 'gahaṇī' is so called because it takes and holds the embryo, being the region of the mother's belly known as the womb. However, in the context of the fire element, 'gahaṇī' is so called because it takes and does not discard the eaten food, by way of digestion. [The word] 'udara' is from the root 'dara' in the sense of 'going,' with the prefix 'u'; 'udara' is where the wind goes upwards. [The word] 'gabbho' is from the root 'gu' in the sense of 'sounding,' with the suffix 'abho,' with doubling, etc. 'Picaṇḍa,' 'jaṭhara,' and 'tunda' are also found here.

Kucchisambhave kucchiṭṭhe koṭṭho, anto cāti ime dve vattanti, kusa akkose, to, ṭho vā. Ama gamanattho, to.

For that which arises in the belly or is situated in the belly, these two terms, 'koṭṭho' and 'anto' (interior), are used. [The word 'koṭṭho'] is from the root 'kusa' in the sense of 'reproaching,' with the suffix 'to' or 'ṭho'. [The word 'anto'] is from the root 'ama' in the sense of 'going,' with the suffix 'to'.

272. Catukkaṃ [M 0.0194] kaṭiyaṃ. Hanadhātumhā yu, hassa dvittaṃ, hassa jo, hanassa gho ca, jaghanaṃ. Nicchayena tamatīti nitambo, tamudhātumhā bo. Sū pasave, ṇi. Kaṭa vassāvaraṇesu, kaṭyate āvarīyate vatthādīhi kaṭi, i, ete dve nāriyaṃ. Ettha ca jaghanasaddena itthikaṭiyā aggabhāgo, nitambasaddena itthikaṭiyā pacchābhāgo, sesadvayena kaṭisāmaññaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, vuttañca “pacchā nitambo thīkaṭyā, jaghanaṃ tu puro bhave”ti amara 16.74.

272. Four terms for the hip. [The word] 'jaghanaṃ' is from the root 'han,' with the suffix 'yu,' with doubling of 'ha,' 'ha' becoming 'ja,' and 'han' becoming 'gha'. [The word] 'nitambo' is so called because 'it is certainly dark'; it is from the root 'tamu' with the suffix 'bo'. [The word 'soṇi'] is from the root 'sū' in the sense of 'giving birth,' with the suffix 'ṇi'. [The word] 'kaṭi' is from the root 'kaṭa' in the senses of 'rain' and 'covering'; 'kaṭi' is that which is covered by garments and so on, with the suffix 'i'. These two terms, 'jaghana' and 'nitamba', are used for a woman. Here, it should be understood that by the word 'jaghana,' the front part of a woman's hip is meant; by the word 'nitambo,' the rear part of a woman's hip; and by the remaining two, the hip in general is stated. And it is said: 'The nitamba is the rear of a woman's hip, while the jaghana is in the front.'

273. Liṅgantaṃ liṅgasāmaññe. Aṅge sarīre jāyatīti aṅgajātaṃ, aṅgasaddo sarīravācako, aṅgametassatthīti katvā. Rahasi ṭhāne jātaṃ aṅgaṃ rahassaṅgaṃ, sattamiyālopo, issattaṃ, sassa dvittañca. Vatthena guyhitabbanti vatthaguyhaṃ. Miha secane, karaṇe yu, mihati retomuttāni yenāti mehanaṃ. Nipubbo miha secane, to, nimittaṃ. Uttamaṅgattā varaṅgaṃ. Vaja gatiyaṃ, assīkāro, paccayehi vinā jāyatīti vā bījaṃ, virahattajotako hyettha vikāro. Phala nipphattiyaṃ, phalati etena puttanti phalaṃ. Liṅgati “itthī, puriso”ti vibhāgaṃ gacchati yenāti liṅgaṃ. Liṅga [M 0.0195] gamane, līnaṃ apākaṭaṃ aṅganti vā liṅgaṃ. Etesu bījaphalasaddā aṇḍepi vattanti.

273. The section on the genital organ in general. 'Aṅgajāta' is that which is born on a limb ('aṅga'), that is, the body; the word 'aṅga' denotes the body, based on the derivation 'it has a part'. 'Rahassaṅga' is the organ born in a secret place, with elision of the locative, 'a' becoming 'i', and doubling of 's'. 'Vatthaguyha' is that which should be concealed by a cloth. From the root 'miha' in the sense of 'sprinkling', with the instrumental suffix 'yu'; 'mehana' is that by which one sprinkles semen and urine. From the root 'miha' in the sense of 'sprinkling', with the prefix 'ni' and the suffix 'to', comes 'nimitta'. 'Varaṅga' because it is the best organ. 'Bīja' is from the root 'vaja' in the sense of 'going', with 'a' becoming 'ī'; or 'bīja' is that which is born without causes, for here the phonetic modification indicates separation. From the root 'phala' in the sense of 'production'; 'phala' is that by which one produces offspring. 'Liṅga' is that by which one arrives at the distinction 'woman' or 'man'; from the root 'liṅga' in the sense of 'going'. Or 'liṅga' is a hidden, unmanifest organ. Among these terms, the words 'bīja' and 'phala' are also used for the testicles.

Dvayaṃ purisaliṅgapasibbake. Ama gamane, ḍo, aṇasaddattho vā, ḍo, aḍi aṇḍatthe vā, to. Kusa akkose, ṇo. Aṇḍasaddo cettha bījepi, aṇḍakosoti samuditampi kosassa nāmaṃ, “kukkuṭacchāpakasseva aṇḍakosamhā”ti pārā. 13, 14 hi vuttaṃ, amarakosepi amarakose 16.76 aṇḍakosoti samuditeneva nāmaṃ vuttaṃ. Ettha ca aṇḍassa bījassa koso aṇḍakosoti viggaho kātabbo.

Two terms for the scrotum of the male organ. [The word 'aṇḍa' is derived] from the root 'ama' in the sense of 'going,' with the suffix 'ḍo'; or from the root 'aṇa' in the sense of 'sound,' with 'ḍo'; or from 'aḍi' in the sense of 'aṇḍa,' with 'to'. [The word 'kosa' is derived] from the root 'kusa' in the sense of 'reproaching,' with the suffix 'ṇo'. Here, the word 'aṇḍa' is also used for seed. 'Aṇḍakosa', even as a compound, is a name for 'kosa', for it is said, 'as from the egg-sac of a young chicken'. In the Amarakosa too, 'aṇḍakosa' is stated as a compound name. And here the analysis should be made: 'aṇḍakosa' is the sheath ('kosa') of the seed ('aṇḍa').

Dvayaṃ itthiyā aṅgajāte. Yu missane, adhikaraṇeni, yoni, itthiyaṃ pume cāyaṃ, itthī ca pumā ca itthipumaṃ, tasmiṃ. Bhajanti asminti bhagaṃ. Māramandira mārakūpā cātra.

Two terms for the female genital organ. 'Yoni' is from the root 'yu' in the sense of 'mixing', with the locative suffix 'ni'; this word is used for both female and male, that is, in the sense of 'itthipumaṃ' (female-and-male). 'Bhaga' is that in which they enjoy. 'Māramandira' (Māra's mansion) and 'mārakūpa' (Māra's pit) are also used here.

274-275. Tikaṃ itthipurisānaṃ sambhave. Sucissa paṭipakkho asuci, ikāranto, dvīsu, sambhavaliṅgo vā. Saṃpubbā bhūdhātumhā a. Saka sāmatthiyaṃ, to, tassa ko, assuttaṃ, suca soke vā, ko.

274-275. Three terms for the generative fluid of women and men. 'Asuci' is the opposite of 'suci'; it ends in 'i'; it is used in two genders, or it has the gender of its origin. 'Sambhava' is from the root 'bhū' with the prefix 'saṃ', with the suffix 'a'. 'Sukka' is from the root 'saka' in the sense of 'ability', with the suffix 'to', which becomes 'ko'; it means 'not flowed' ('asuttaṃ'); or it is from the root 'suca' in the sense of 'grieving', with the suffix 'ko'.

Dvayaṃ vaccamagge. Punanti anenāti pāyu. Pū pavane, u, ūssāyo, paya gamanattho vā, payati vaccamanenāti pāyu, [M 0.0196] karaṇe u, ayaṃ purise pulliṅge vattati. Guda kīḷāyaṃ, a. Apānaṃpyatra.

Two terms for the excretory passage. 'Pāyu' is that by which one is purified. It is from the root 'pū' in the sense of 'purifying', with the suffix 'u', and the vowel is modified to 'āyu'; or from 'paya' in the sense of 'going', 'pāyu' is that by which one goes for excrement, with the instrumental suffix 'u'. This word is used in the masculine gender for a man. 'Guda' is from the root 'guda' in the sense of 'playing', with the suffix 'a'. 'Apāna' is also used here.

Aṭṭhakaṃ vacce. Gūtha karīsossagge, gupa gopane vā, tho. Kira vikiraṇe, īso, karīsaṃ. Vara varaṇasambhattīsu, co, gūthañca karīsañca vaccañceti dvando, tāni vikappena pume vattanti, niccaṃ napuṃsake, pulliṅgattaṃ tesaṃ katthaciyeva, sabbatra napuṃsakattameva bahulantyattho. Mala calane, a, mala dhāraṇe vā. Saka sattiyaṃ, sassa cho. Uccārīyate jahyateti uccāro, upubbo caradhātu cajane, ukkhipane ca vattati. Miha secane, lo, vaṇṇavipariyayo, ḷattañca. Avakarīyateti ukkāro, avassuttaṃ, kira vikkhipane. Samalaṃpyatra. Samu upasame, alo.

Eight terms for excrement. 'Gūtha' is from the root 'gūtha' in the sense of 'excreting dung', or from 'gupa' in the sense of 'concealing', with the suffix 'tho'. 'Karīsaṃ' is from the root 'kira' in the sense of 'scattering', with the suffix 'īso'. 'Vacca' is from the root 'vara' in the senses of 'choosing' and 'serving', with the suffix 'co'. 'Gūtha', 'karīsa', and 'vacca' form a dvanda compound; they are optionally used in the masculine gender, but always in the neuter. Their use in the masculine is only in some places; the meaning is that the neuter gender is predominant everywhere. 'Mala' is from the root 'mala' in the sense of 'moving', with the suffix 'a', or from 'mala' in the sense of 'holding'. 'Chakaṇa' is from the root 'saka' in the sense of 'ability', with 's' becoming 'ch'. 'Uccāro' is that which is expelled or abandoned; it is from the root 'car' with the prefix 'u', used in the senses of 'abandoning' and 'expelling'. 'Mīḷha' is from the root 'miha' in the sense of 'sprinkling', with the suffix 'lo', with metathesis and the change to 'ḷ'. 'Ukkāro' is that which is thrown down, from the root 'kira' in the sense of 'scattering' with the prefix 'ava'. 'Avassuttaṃ' is also a term here. 'Samalaṃ' is also here, from the root 'samu' in the sense of 'appeasing', with the suffix 'alo'.

Dvayaṃ mutte. Su savane, savanaṃ sandanaṃ, curādi, ṇo. Muca mocane, to, mutta passāve vā. Uccate kathīyate. Gomutte gavaṃ sambandhini mutte pūtimuttasaddo vattati. Ajja pavattampi hi taṃ duggandhabhāvena pūtimuttantveva vuccati, yathā “pūtikāyo”ti. Assādīnaṃ male chakaṇasaddo, saka sattiyaṃ, yu, sassa cho.

Two terms for urine. 'Passāva' is from the root 'su' in the sense of 'flowing'; 'savana' (flowing) means 'sandana' (trickling); it is from the curādi group, with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Mutta' is from the root 'muca' in the sense of 'releasing', with the suffix 'to'; or 'mutta' is used in the sense of 'passāva' (urination). It is said, it is spoken. For cow urine, that is, urine related to cows, the word 'pūtimutta' is used. For even today it is called 'pūtimutta' because of its foul smell, just as one says 'pūtikāya' (foul body). For the excrement of horses and so on, the word 'chakaṇa' is used; it is from the root 'saka' in the sense of 'ability', with the suffix 'yu', and 's' becoming 'ch'.

276. Nābhiyā adhobhāgo vatthi nāma, so dvīsu. Vatthi muttapuṭaṃ. “Muttāsayapuṭo vatthi”riti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.73 ratanamālā. Vasati muttametthāti vatthi, vasa nivāse,ti, tassa tho, tthipaccayena vā siddhaṃ. Ucchaṅgaṃ aṅkañca ime dve ubho saddā [M 0.0197] pume vattanti. Ussajjati etthāti ucchaṅgaṃ, saja saṅge, sassa cho, dvittaṃ. Aṅka gamanattho, a, aṅko, atha vā aṅka lakkhaṇe, a, aṅko, “ucchaṅgacihanesva’ṅko”ti amarakose amara kose 23.4.

276. The part below the navel is called 'vatthi'; it is used in two genders. 'Vatthi' is the urine-pouch. The Ratanamālā states: 'Vatthi is the receptacle for the reservoir of urine'. 'Vatthi' is so called because urine dwells there; it is from the root 'vasa' in the sense of 'dwelling', with the suffix 'ti', its 't' becoming 'th'; or it is formed with the suffix 'tthi'. These two words, 'ucchaṅga' and 'aṅka', are both used in the masculine gender. 'Ucchaṅga' is where one places something; it is from the root 'saja' in the sense of 'attachment', with 's' becoming 'ch', and doubling. 'Aṅka' is from the root 'aṅka' in the sense of 'going', with the suffix 'a', hence 'aṅko'; or from 'aṅka' in the sense of 'marking', with the suffix 'a', hence 'aṅko'. In the Amarakosa it is stated: 'aṅka is used for lap and sign'.

Dvayaṃ jāṇūparibhāge. Ara gamane, u, assūkāro. Sanja saṅge, āsajjati vatthamatrāti satthi, thi. Ūru ca satthi ceti dvando, napuṃsakepi.

Two terms for the part above the knee. 'Ūru' is from the root 'ara' in the sense of 'going', with the suffix 'u', and 'a' becoming 'ū'. 'Satthi' is from the root 'sanja' in the sense of 'clinging'; 'satthi' is that to which a cloth clings, with the suffix 'thi'. 'Ūru' and 'satthi' form a dvanda compound; they are also used in the neuter gender.

Tikaṃ jāṇumhi, ūruno pabbaṃ gaṇṭhi ūrupabbaṃ. Jana janane, ṇu. Dvitte jaṇṇu.

Three terms for the knee. 'Ūrupabbaṃ' is the joint or knot of the thigh. 'Jāṇu' is from the root 'jana' in the sense of 'producing', with the suffix 'ṇu'. With doubling, it is 'jaṇṇu'.

277. Dvayaṃ pādagaṇṭhimhi. Gupa rakkhaṇe pho, sakatthe ko. Pādassa gaṇṭhi pādagaṇṭhi. Ghuṭikāpyatra. Ghuṭa parivattane, ghuṭyate aneneti ghuṭikā, ṇvu.

277. Two terms for the ankle joint. ('Gopphaka' is derived from) the root 'Gup' (to protect), with the suffix 'pha', and 'ka' in its own sense. The joint of the foot is 'pādagaṇṭhi' (foot-joint). 'Ghuṭikā' is also found here. ('Ghuṭikā' is derived from) the root 'Ghuṭa' (to turn or revolve); 'ghuṭikā' is that by which one turns, with the suffix 'ṇvu'.

Dvayaṃ pādassa pacchābhāge gopphakassādho bhāge. Pume tūti tvantaṃ liṅgapadaṃ. Pasa bādhanaphusanesu,ti, tassa ṇo, sassa ho, vaṇṇavipariyayo, ṇipaccayena vā siddhaṃ. Sakāravaṇṇāgame vuddhiyañca pāsaṇhi. Elipyatra, ila gatiyaṃ,ti, talopo.

Two terms for the back part of the foot, below the ankle. The word ending in 'tu' is masculine. ('Pāsaṇhi' is derived from) the root 'Pasa' (in the sense of binding or touching), with the suffix 'ti', its 't' becoming 'ṇ', 's' becoming 'h', and with metathesis; or it is formed by the suffix 'ṇi'. With the addition of the letter 'sa' and vowel lengthening, it becomes 'pāsaṇhi'. 'Eḷi' is also found here, (derived from) the root 'Ila' (to go), with the suffix 'ti', and the elision of 't'.

Dvayaṃ pādagge. Pādassa aggaṃ pādaggaṃ. Pakaṭṭhaṃ padaṃ papadanti kammadhārayo. “Papado”tipi pāṭho. Tikaṃ pāde. Pada gatimhi, ṇo, pajjateti pādo. Pajjate gacchatīti, a. Caramhā karaṇe yu, caraṇaṃ, idaṃ pume vikappena, niccaṃ napuṃsake. Aṅghipyatra, ahi gatiyaṃ. I, hassa gho.

Two terms for the front of the foot. The front of the foot is 'pādaggaṃ'. 'Pakaṭṭhaṃ padaṃ' (prominent foot) is 'papada', a karmadhāraya compound. The reading 'papado' is also found. Three terms for the foot. ('Pāda' is derived from) the root 'Pada' (in motion), with the suffix 'ṇa'; 'pādo' is that which goes. It goes, it moves, with the suffix 'a'. ('Caraṇaṃ' is derived from) the root 'Car' (to move), with the instrumental suffix 'yu'; this is optionally masculine and also neuter. 'Aṅghi' is also found here, (derived from) the root 'Ahi' (to go), with the suffix 'i', and 'h' becoming 'gh'.

278. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0198] hatthādyavayave. Aṅgi gatyattho, a. Avapubbo yu missane, a. Patīko, apaghanopyatra. Patipubbā imhā ko. Apapubbā hanimhā a, ghanādeso ca.

278. Two terms for a limb, such as the hand. ('Aṅga' is derived from) the root 'Aṅgi' (to go), with the suffix 'a'. ('Avayava' is derived from) the root 'Yu' (to mix), prefixed by 'ava', with the suffix 'a'. 'Patīka' and 'apaghana' are also found here. ('Patīka' is derived from) the root 'I' prefixed by 'pati', with the suffix 'ka'. ('Apaghana' is derived from) the root 'Han' prefixed by 'apa', with the suffix 'a', and the substitution of 'ghana'.

Dvayaṃ passaṭṭhimhi. Pā rakkhaṇe, su, ḷikāravaṇṇāgamo, sakatthe ko, passa pho. Aḷāgame phāsukā. “Pāsuḷikā, pāsukā”tipi pāṭho. Phusa samphassetipi dhātu, tadā upaccayādi.

Two terms for the rib bone. ('Pāsuḷikā' is derived from) the root 'Pā' (to protect), with the suffix 'su', the addition of the letters 'ḷikā', and 'ka' in its own sense. ('Phāsukā' is derived from the same root), with 'p' becoming 'ph'. The readings 'pāsuḷikā' and 'pāsukā' are also found. The root 'Phusa' also means 'to touch'; in that case, it is formed by 'upaccaya' and so forth.

Dvayaṃ aṭṭhimatte. Asu khepane, i, sassa ṭṭho, aṭṭhi, idaṃ paṇḍake napuṃsake vattati. Dhā dhāraṇe, tu, itthī. Kīkasaṃ, kullaṃpyatra. Galassa kaṇṭhassa heṭṭhimante jātamaṭṭhi galantaṭṭhi. Aka gamane, kho, sakatthe ko.

Two terms for bone. ('Aṭṭhi' is derived from) the root 'Asu' (to throw or cast), with the suffix 'i', and 's' becoming 'ṭṭh'. This word 'aṭṭhi' is used in the neuter gender. ('Dhātu' is derived from) the root 'Dhā' (to hold), with the suffix 'tu', and is feminine. 'Kīkasaṃ' and 'kullaṃ' are also found here. The bone born at the lower end of the throat is 'galantaṭṭhi' (collarbone). ('Akkha' is derived from) the root 'Aka' (to go), with the suffix 'kha', and 'ka' in its own sense.

279-280. Dvayaṃ sirasoṭṭhikhaṇḍe. Samudite tu karoṭi, itthī amara 16.69. Kapu sāmatthiye, aro, kaṃ sīsaṃ pāletīti vā kapparo, rasso, lassa rattañca. Kaṃ pālayatīti[M 0.0199], kammādimhi ṇo. “Siroṭṭhimhi kapālo’thī, ghaṭādisakalepice”ti ruddo cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.68. Kapālo athīti anitthīti attho chedo. Kapālasaddo vikappena pulliṅgo. Kaḍi chede, aro. Mahatī sirā mahāsirā, sirāti ca. Si bandhane, ro.

279-280. Two terms for a piece of the skull bone. When combined, it is 'karoṭi', which is feminine. ('Kappara' is derived from) the root 'Kapu' (in capability), with the suffix 'ara'; or 'kappara' is that which protects the head, with shortening of the vowel and 'l' becoming 'r'. ('Kapāla' is derived from) 'Kaṃ' (head) and the root 'pāl' (to protect), with the suffix 'ṇa' in the sense of agent. Rudra says, "'Kapāla' refers to the skull bone, and also to fragments of pots and so forth." The analysis is 'kapālo athi' (kapāla is bone). The word 'kapāla' is optionally masculine. ('Kaḍara' is derived from) the root 'Kaḍi' (to cut), with the suffix 'ara'. A large vein is 'mahāsirā', and also 'sirā'. ('Sirā' is derived from) the root 'Si' (to bind), with the suffix 'ra'.

Tikaṃ susiravatyaṃ vāyuvahantasirāyaṃ. Tividhā hi kāyasirā ekā vāyuvahā, aparā suttamivāṭṭhibandhinī, aññā āhāravāhinī antakhyā. Tatra tatiyena paṭhamā, paṭhamadutiyehi dutiyā ca dīpitā, tatiyā pana parato vakkhati. Naha bandhane, aru. Si bandhane, ro. Dhama sadde, yu. Nadādi, ani vā, dhamanī.

Three terms for a hollow or wind-carrying channel. Indeed, there are three kinds of channels in the body: one carries wind, another binds the bones like a thread, and another, called 'antakhyā' (internal), carries nutrients. Among these, the first type of channel is indicated by the third term, and the second type by the first and second terms; the third type, however, will be explained later. ('Nahāru' is derived from) the root 'Naha' (to bind), with the suffix 'aru'. ('Sirā' is derived from) the root 'Si' (to bind), with the suffix 'ra'. ('Dhamanī' is derived from) the root 'Dhama' (to sound or blow), with the suffix 'yu'; or from the 'nadādi' group of words, or with the suffix 'ani', it forms 'dhamanī'.

Tatiyaṃ dassetumāha “rasaggasā”tyādi. Rasaṃ gasatīti rasaggasā, gasa adane. Rasaṃ harati netīti rasaharaṇī, yu, nadādi.

To show the third type of channel, he says 'rasaggasā' and so forth. 'Rasaggasā' is that which consumes essence; from the root 'gasa' (to eat). 'Rasaharaṇī' is that which carries and conveys essence; it is derived with the suffix 'yu', from the 'nadādi' group of words.

Tikaṃ maṃse. Mana ñāṇe, so. Misa sadde, āpubbo āmasane vā. Pisa avayave, to. Palalaṃ, kabbaṃpyatra.

Three terms for flesh. ('Maṃsa' is derived from) the root 'Mana' (to know), with the suffix 'sa'. ('Āmisa' is derived from) the root 'Misa' (to sound), or prefixed by 'ā' in the sense of 'āmasana' (touching). ('Pesi' is derived from) the root 'Pisa' (in limbs or parts), with the suffix 'ta'. 'Palalaṃ' and 'kabbaṃ' are also found here.

Dvayaṃ ātapādinā sukkhamaṃse. Tiliṅgakantūti tvantaṃ liṅgapadaṃ. Vala, valla saṃvaraṇe, ūro, itthiyaṃ “itthiyamato āpaccayo”ti ā, vallūrā. Uddhaṃ tattaṃ uttattaṃ. Tapa santāpe, to.

Two terms for meat dried by the sun and so forth. The word ending in 'tu' is of three genders. ('Vallūra' is derived from) the root 'Vala' or 'valla' (to cover), with the suffix 'ūra'; in the feminine, the suffix 'ā' is added, thus 'vallūrā'. 'Uttattaṃ' means heated up. ('Uttatta' is derived from) the root 'Tapa' (to heat), with the suffix 'ta'.

281. Catukkaṃ lohite. Ruha janane, to, ito vā. Runjhate cammenāti rudhiraṃ, iro. Soṇa vaṇṇe, to. Rañja rāge, to. Asaṃ, khatajaṃpyatra khatā jāyate (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.64).

281. Four terms for blood. ('Lohita' is derived from) the root 'Ruha' (to produce), with the suffix 'ta' or 'ita'. 'Rudhiraṃ' is that which stains the skin, from the root 'rudh' (to obstruct), with the suffix 'ira'. ('Soṇita' is derived from) 'Soṇa' (in color), with the suffix 'ta'. ('Ratta' is derived from) the root 'Rañja' (to color or dye), with the suffix 'ta'. 'Asaṃ' and 'khatajaṃ' are also found here.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0200] kheḷe. Lā ādāne, alo, itthiyamā, lala icchāyaṃ vā, itthiyamā. Khela gatiyaṃ, a. Khala calane, sañcaye vā, ṇo, ḷattaṃ, khaṃ vā ākāsaṃ ilatīti kheḷo. Ila gatiyaṃ, kammani ṇo, ila gatimhi vā, a, isse.

Three terms for saliva. ('Lālā' is derived from) the root 'Lā' (to take), with the suffix 'ala', and in the feminine, 'ā'; or from the root 'lala' (in desire), and in the feminine, 'ā'. ('Kheḷa' is derived from) the root 'Khela' (to move), with the suffix 'a'. ('Kheḷa' is also derived from) the root 'Khala' (to move) or (to gather), with the suffix 'ṇa', and the change of 'l' to 'ḷ'; or 'kheḷo' is that which moves in space ('khaṃ') or the sky ('ākāsaṃ'). ('Kheḷa' is also derived from) the root 'Ila' (to move), with the suffix 'ṇa' in the passive sense; or from the root 'ila' (in motion), with the suffix 'a', and 'i' becoming 'e'.

Dvayaṃ pitte. Mā parimāṇe, dhu. Mada ummāde vā, ṇu, dassa dho. Māyūti pāṭhe maya gatiyaṃ, ṇu. Mādhumāyusaddā dve purise pulliṅge. Apidadhātīti pittaṃ. Apipubbo dhā pidhāne, to, alopo, bhujādi, pittaṃ, napuṃsake.

Two terms for bile. ('Madhu' is derived from) the root 'Mā' (to measure), with the suffix 'dhu'; or from the root 'Mada' (in intoxication), with the suffix 'ṇu', and 'd' becoming 'dh'. If the reading is 'māyu', it is derived from the root 'maya' (to go), with the suffix 'ṇu'. The words 'madhu' and 'māyu' are masculine. 'Pittaṃ' is that which covers. ('Pittaṃ' is derived from) the root 'Dhā' (to cover), prefixed by 'api', with the suffix 'ta', elision of 'a', from the 'bhujādi' group; 'pittaṃ' is neuter.

Dvayaṃ semhe. Silisa silesane, curādi, silisyate atreti semho, mana, lisassa ho, vaṇṇavipariyayo. Itaratra umo, silesumo. Kaphopyatra, kena toyena phāti vuddhi yassa kapho, nerutto.

Two terms for phlegm. ('Semha' is derived from) the root 'Silisa' (to adhere), from the 'curādi' group; 'semha' is that which adheres here, with the suffix 'man', 'lis' becoming 'h', and metathesis. Elsewhere, with the suffix 'uma', it forms 'silesuma'. 'Kapha' is also found here. 'Kapha' is that whose growth swells by water, according to a Nirukta etymology.

282-283. Vilīno vibhūto sneho vasātyuccate, vasa nivāse, ā. Dvayaṃ avilīnasnehe. Mida snehane, ṇo. Vapa bījasantāne, a, vapā. “Vapā vivaramedesū”ti nānatthasaṅgahe, amarakose pana medādīnamekatthatā dīpitā, vuttañhi tattha “medo tu vapā vasā”ti amara 16.64.

282-283. Melted or liquid fat is called 'vasā'; it is derived from the root 'vasa' (to dwell), with the suffix 'ā'. Two terms for unmelted fat. ('Meda' is derived from) the root 'Mida' (to be unctuous), with the suffix 'ṇa'. ('Vapā' is derived from) the root 'Vapa' (to sow seed), with the suffix 'a'. The word 'vapā' is found in the Nānatthasaṅgaha in the sense of 'cavity' and 'fat', but in the Amarakośa, 'meda' and so forth are shown to have a single meaning, for it is said there: 'medo tu vapā vasā' (fat, indeed, is vapā and vasā).

Tikaṃ candanasuvaṇṇādyalaṅkārakatasarīrasobhāyaṃ. Kapu sāmatthiye, ākappanaṃ ākappo, ṇo. “Nepacche gehamatte [M 0.0201] ca, veso vesyāgahepi vessagahepi (ka.) ce”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.99 rabhaso. Vasa kantiyaṃ, visi byāpane vā, ṇo. Nissesato pathanaṃ pakhyānaṃ nepacchaṃ, patha pakhyāne ghyaṇa. Paṭikammaṃ, pasādhanaṃpyatra.

Three terms for the bodily beauty created by adornments such as sandalwood and gold. ('Ākappa' is derived from) the root 'Kapu' (in capability); 'ākappanaṃ' (arranging) becomes 'ākappo' (adornment), with the suffix 'ṇa'. The Rabhasa dictionary states: "'Nepaccha' is used in the sense of adornment and a house, and 'vesa' also in the sense of a prostitute's house." ('Vesa' is derived from) the root 'Vasa' (in brightness), or 'visi' (to pervade), with the suffix 'ṇa'. That which is a complete spreading out is 'nepacchaṃ'; it is derived from the root 'patha' (to proclaim or spread), with the suffix 'ghyaṇa'. 'Paṭikammaṃ' and 'pasādhanaṃ' are also found here.

Chakkaṃ hārādyābharaṇe. Maḍi bhūsāyaṃ, karaṇe yu. Sādha saṃsiddhiyaṃ, yu, sāṭha saṅkhāragatīsu vā, pasāṭhanaṃ, muddhajadutiyotra. Bhūsa alaṅkāre, karaṇeyeva yu. Ābhariyyate tanti ābharaṇaṃ, bhara bharaṇe, kammani yu. Alaṃ vibhūsanaṃ kariyyateneneti alaṅkāro, ṇo. Piḷandha bhūsane, karaṇe yu. Parikkhāropyatra parikaropyatra (ka.).

Six terms for ornaments such as necklaces. ('Maṇḍana' is derived from) the root 'Maḍi' (to adorn), with the suffix 'yu' in the instrumental sense. ('Pasādhana' is derived from) the root 'Sādha' (to accomplish), with the suffix 'yu'; or from the root 'sāṭha' (in arrangement or movement), it becomes 'pasāṭhanaṃ'; here the second consonant is a cerebral. ('Bhūsana' is derived from) the root 'Bhūsa' (to adorn), with the suffix 'yu' in the instrumental sense. That which is worn is 'ābharaṇaṃ' (ornament), from the root 'bhara' (to bear), with the suffix 'yu' in the passive sense. That by which adornment is done is 'alaṅkāro' (ornament), with the suffix 'ṇa'. ('Piḷandhana' is derived from) the root 'Piḷandha' (to adorn), with the suffix 'yu' in the instrumental sense. 'Parikkhāro' is also found here.

Dvayaṃ makuṭe. Kira vikiraṇe, īṭo. Maki maṇḍane, uṭo. Mukuṭotipi pāṭho, ete dve anitthī.

Two terms for a crown. ('Kirīṭa' is derived from) the root 'Kira' (to scatter), with the suffix 'īṭa'. ('Makuṭa' is derived from) the root 'Maki' (to decorate), with the suffix 'uṭa'. 'Mukuṭo' is also a reading. These two words are not feminine.

Dvayaṃ makuṭaggaṭṭhe nāyakamaṇimhi. Makuṭacūḷāyaṃ cumbitā maṇi cūḷāmaṇi. Makuṭasirasi cumbitā maṇi siromaṇi.

Two terms for the chief jewel placed on the crest of a crown. The jewel that touches the crest of the crown is 'cūḷāmaṇi'. The jewel that touches the head of the crown is 'siromaṇi'.

284. Dvayaṃ uṇhīsapaṭṭe. Siraso veṭhanaṃ siroveṭhanaṃ. Upubbo naha bandhane, īso, vaṇṇavikāro. Yaṃ bahukālaṃ debyāmanussesvapi bhavati, tatra kaṇṇābharaṇe kuṇḍalādidvayaṃ. Kuḍi dāhe, alo. Veṭha veṭhane, kaṇṇassa veṭhanaṃ kaṇṇaveṭhanaṃ, muddhajadutiyoyaṃ.

284. Two terms for a turban-band. A wrapping for the head is 'siroveṭhanaṃ'. ('Uṇhīsa' is derived from) the root 'naha' (to bind) with the prefix 'u', and the suffix 'īsa', with a change of vowel. Regarding that which is worn for a long time by both deities and humans, there are two terms for ear ornaments, 'kuṇḍala' and so on. ('Kuṇḍala' is derived from) the root 'Kuḍi' (to burn), with the suffix 'ala'. ('Kaṇṇaveṭhana' is derived from) the root 'Veṭha' (to wrap); a wrapping for the ear is 'kaṇṇaveṭhanaṃ'; this is the second word with a cerebral consonant.

Tikaṃ tāḷakākhye kaṇṇābharaṇe. Kaṇṇānaṃ bhūsanaṃ kaṇṇikā, kaṇṇā bhūsane bahulalakkhaṇe ṇiko. Kaṇṇacchadanaṃ [M 0.0202] pūrati yena so kaṇṇapūro. Kaṇṇassa vibhūsanaṃ kaṇṇavibhūsanaṃ, karaṇe yu. Tālapattaṃpyatra.

Three terms for the ear ornament called 'tāḷaka'. An ornament for the ears is 'kaṇṇikā'; the suffix 'ṇika' is applied to 'kaṇṇa' in the sense of 'ornament' due to the principle of multiple applications. That by which the ear is filled is 'kaṇṇapūro'. An adornment for the ear is 'kaṇṇavibhūsanaṃ', with the suffix 'yu' in the instrumental sense. 'Tālapattaṃ' is also found here.

285. Dvayaṃ gīvābharaṇe. Kaṇṭhassa bhūsā kaṇṭhabhūsā, thī. Gīvāyaṃ bhavaṃ gīveyyaṃ, bhavatthe eyyo, gīvāya ābharaṇaṃ vā gīveyyaṃ, gīvato ābharaṇe eyyo.

285. Two terms for neck ornaments. An adornment for the throat is 'kaṇṭhabhūsā'; it is feminine. That which is on the neck is 'gīveyyaṃ', with the suffix 'eyya' in the sense of 'being there'. Or 'gīveyyaṃ' is an ornament of the neck, with the suffix 'eyya' added to 'gīvā' in the sense of 'ornament'.

Dvayaṃ muttāvaliyaṃ. Harīyate mano yena hāro. Muttānaṃ āvali panti muttāvali. Hārāsaddopyatra.

Two terms for a string of pearls. That by which the mind is captivated is 'hāro' (a necklace). A string or row of pearls is 'muttāvali' (a pearl necklace). The word 'hārā' is also found here.

Catukkaṃ pakoṭṭhābharaṇe. Pakoṭṭho nāma kapparassādhobhāgo. Nī naye, uro, iyādeso. Vala saṃvaraṇe, ayo, anitthī, niyuropi. Kaṭa vasāvaraṇagatīsu, ṇvu. Pari samantato harati cittaṃ yanti parihārakaṃ, ṇvu. Avāpakopyatra.

Four terms for forearm ornaments. 'Pakoṭṭho' means the lower part of the elbow. ('Keyūra' is derived from) the root 'nī' (to lead), with the suffix 'ura', and the substitution 'īya'. ('Valaya' is derived from) the root 'Vala' (to cover), with the suffix 'aya'; it is not feminine. 'Niyuro' is also a form. ('Kaṭaka' is derived from) the root 'Kaṭa' (in dwelling, covering, or moving), with the suffix 'ṇvu'. That which captivates the mind all around is 'parihārakaṃ', with the suffix 'ṇvu'. 'Avāpako' is also found here.

286-287. Dvayaṃ muttādighaṭitavalayavikatyābharaṇe. Kā sadde, kaṇapaccayo, kaṇa sadde vā, dvittaṃ, kaṅkaṇaṃ, kaki gatyatthe [M 0.0203] vā, yu, kaki lolye vā, kaṅkati yenāti kaṅkaṇaṃ, karaṇe yu. Karassa bhūsā karabhūsā, thī.

286-287. Two terms for an ornament that is a type of bracelet fashioned from pearls and the like. From the root `kā` meaning 'sound', with the suffix `kaṇa`; or from the root `kaṇa` meaning 'sound', with reduplication, it becomes `kaṅkaṇaṃ`. Or from the root `kaki` meaning 'motion', with the suffix `yu`; or from the root `kaki` meaning 'unsteadiness', that by which it makes a 'kaṅka' sound is `kaṅkaṇaṃ`, with the suffix `yu` in the instrumental sense. An adornment for the hand is `karabhūsā`; it is feminine.

Dvayaṃ khuddaghaṇṭikāyaṃ. Kiṃ kucchitaṃ kaṇatīti kiṅkaṇī, nadādi. Kiṅkiṇītipi pāṭhantaraṃ, tadā yadādi. Khuddā eva ghaṇṭā khuddaghaṇṭikā, sakatthe ko, ghaṭa calane.

Two terms for a small bell. That which makes a slight, tinkling sound is `kiṅkaṇī`; it is formed according to the `nadādi` group. `Kiṅkiṇī` is also an alternative reading; in that case, it is formed according to the `yadādi` group. A small bell itself is `khuddaghaṇṭikā`, with the suffix `ko` in its own sense; the root `ghaṭa` means 'to move'.

Dvayaṃ aṅgulyābharaṇe. Aṅguliyaṃ bhavaṃ aṅgulīyakaṃ, īyo, sakatthe ko, aṅgulīnamābharaṇaṃ aṅgulyābharaṇaṃ. Ummikāpyatra. Tamevāṅgulīyakaṃ sākkharamakkharavantaṃ “muddikā, aṅgulimuddā”ti coccate. Muda tose, ṇvu, ā, muddikā, phalavisesepyayaṃ. Aṅguliyaṃ bhavā muddā aṅgulimuddā.

Two terms for a finger ornament. That which is on the finger is `aṅgulīyakaṃ`, with the suffix `īya`, and the suffix `ko` in its own sense. An ornament for the fingers is `aṅgulyābharaṇaṃ`. `Ummikā` is also used here. That same finger-ring, when engraved with letters, is called `muddikā` or `aṅgulimuddā`. From the root `muda` meaning 'joy', with the suffix `ṇvu` and `ā`, it becomes `muddikā`; this term also refers to a specific fruit. A seal that is on the finger is `aṅgulimuddā`.

Dvayaṃ itthikaṭyābharaṇe. Rasa sadde, kattari yu, ā, rasanā. Sāyeva inīmhi rasanī. “Sāre dhanimhi rasanaṃ, jivhāyaṃ rasanā na so”ti ruddo. Mehanassa khassa mālā mekhalāti nirutti, mehanindriyassa mālātyattho. Kāñcī sattakī, sārasanaṃpyatra.

Two terms for a woman's hip ornament. From the root `rasa` meaning 'sound', with the suffix `yu` in the agentive sense and `ā`, it becomes `rasanā`. That same word with the suffix `inī` becomes `rasanī`. Rudda says: '`rasanaṃ` is used for essence or wealth; `rasanā` is used for the tongue, not for that ornament.' The etymology of `mekhalā` is `mehanassa khassa mālā` (a garland for the region of the penis), meaning a garland for the generative organ. `Kāñcī` is a seven-stringed ornament; `sārasanaṃ` is also used here.

Ekayaṭṭhi bhave kāñcī, mekhalā tva’ṭṭhayaṭṭhikā;

Rasanā soḷasā ñeyyā, kalāpā pañcavīsati kalāpo pañcavīsako (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.108).

A `kāñcī` should be of one string, while a `mekhalā` is of eight strings. A `rasanā` should be known as having sixteen strings, and a `kalāpā` as having twenty-five.

Tikaṃ sovaṇṇe pagaṇḍabhūsane. Pagaṇḍo nāma kapparassoparibhāgo. Ke sadde, uro, yāgamo. Aṅga gamane. Do. Bāhumūlassa, bāhumūle vā bhavaṃ vibhūsanaṃ bāhumūlavibhūsanaṃ.

Three terms for a golden upper-arm ornament. `Pagaṇḍa` is the name for the part of the arm above the elbow. From the root `ke` meaning 'sound', with the suffix `uro` and the augment `yā`, comes `keyūra`. From the root `aṅga` meaning 'going', with the suffix `do`, comes `aṅgada`. An adornment of the shoulder, or an adornment that is on the shoulder, is `bāhumūlavibhūsanaṃ`.

288. Catukkaṃ itthicaraṇavibhūsane. Aṅgadākāraṃ pādabhūsanaṃ pādaṅgadaṃ. Maji saddattho, īro, pāde kaṭakaṃ pādakaṭakaṃ. Ūnaṃ pādaṃ pūretīti nūpuro, vaṇṇavipariyayo. Pādakaṭako ca nūpuro ceti kaṭakasaddassa pulliṅgepi pavattanato [M 0.0204] dvandasamāso. Tulākoṭi, haṃsakopyatra. Tula gatikoṭilye. Kuṭilakoṭittā tulākoṭi, pume. Haṃsagatittā haṃsako.

288. Four terms for a woman's foot ornament. A foot ornament shaped like an armlet is `pādaṅgadaṃ`. From the root `maji` meaning 'sound', with the suffix `īro`, comes `mañjīra`. A bracelet for the foot is `pādakaṭakaṃ`. That which completes a deficient foot is `nūpuro`, formed by a transposition of letters. The dvandva compound `pādakaṭako ca nūpuro ca` is formed because the word `kaṭaka` also occurs in the masculine gender. `Tulākoṭi` and `haṃsako` are also used here. The root `tula` means 'crooked movement'. Because of its crooked tip, it is `tulākoṭi`; it is masculine. Because it produces a swan-like gait, it is `haṃsako`.

289. Mukhaphullādayo alaṅkārappabhedā siyuṃ. Mukhaphullaṃ nāma suvaṇṇamayo mukhālaṅkāro, mukhe phullatīti mukhaphullaṃ, phulla vikasane, dantādīsu suvaṇṇamayālaṅkāropi mukhaphullameva. Uṇṇataṃ suvaṇṇādiracitaṃ nalāṭābharaṇaṃ, upubbo namu namane. Ettha ca mukhaphulluṇṇatānaṃ visesaṃ vipariyayenāpīti vadanti. Gāvīnaṃ thanākārattā gatthanaṃ, ossattaṃ, tameva uttamattā uggatthanaṃ, catuyaṭṭhiko hārabhedo. Gamu gamane, ṇvu, dvittaṃ, assittañca, giṅgamakaṃ, bāttiṃsayaṭṭhiko hārabhedova. Ādinā addhahāro, māṇavako, ekāvalī, nakkhattamālādayo hārabhedā ca saṅgayhanti amara 16.106.

289. There may be various types of ornaments such as `mukhaphulla`. `Mukhaphullaṃ` is a golden facial ornament; that which blossoms on the face is `mukhaphullaṃ`, from the root `phulla` meaning 'to blossom'. A golden ornament on the teeth and so on is also `mukhaphullaṃ`. `Uṇṇataṃ` is a forehead ornament made of gold and the like, from the root `namu` meaning 'to bend' with the prefix `u-`. And here, some say that the distinction between `mukhaphulla` and `uṇṇata` can also be reversed. Because it is in the shape of cows' udders, it is called `gatthanaṃ`; it is an `ossattaṃ`. That same ornament, due to its superiority, is called `uggatthanaṃ`; it is a type of necklace with four strands. From the root `gamu` meaning 'to go', with the suffix `ṇvu` and reduplication, comes `giṅgamakaṃ`; it is also an `assittaṃ`, a type of necklace with thirty-two strands. By 'and so on', types of necklaces such as `addhahāra` (half-necklace), `māṇavaka` (youth's necklace), `ekāvalī` (single-string necklace), `nakkhattamālā` (star-necklace), and others are also included.

290. Pajjaṃ vatthamatte. Cila vassane, cilyate acchādīyateti, ṇo, thiyaṃ celī. Chada saṃvaraṇe, āpubbo karaṇe, yu. Vasa acchādane, vasyate acchādīyateti vatthaṃ, tho. Ṇamhi vāso. Yumhi vasanaṃ. Ama gamane, karaṇe yu, aṃsukaṃ, raṃsipariyāyopyayaṃ. Amba sadde, kattari aro. Paṭa gamane, karaṇe a, sobhanacelepyayaṃ. Du gamane, karaṇe so, dvittaṃ, durūpaṃ asati khepatīti vā dussaṃ, durūpaṃ asati dīpetīti vā dussaṃ, dupubbo asa dittiyaṃ[M 0.0205]. Cala vasane, assottaṃ, ḷattañca. Saṭa rujāvisaraṇagatyāvasānesu, ṇvu.

290. A verse on cloth in general. From the root `cila` meaning 'to dress'; that which is covered or clothed is `celī`, with the suffix `ṇo`; it is feminine. From the root `chada` meaning 'to cover', with the prefix `ā-` and the suffix `yu` in the instrumental sense, comes `acchādana`. From the root `vasa` meaning 'to cover'; that which is covered or clothed is `vatthaṃ`, with the suffix `tho`. With the suffix `ṇa`, it becomes `vāso`. With the suffix `yu`, it becomes `vasanaṃ`. From the root `ama` meaning 'to go', with the suffix `yu` in the instrumental sense, comes `aṃsukaṃ`; this is also a synonym for 'ray'. From the root `amba` meaning 'sound', with the suffix `aro` in the agentive sense, comes `ambara`. From the root `paṭa` meaning 'to go', with the suffix `a` in the instrumental sense, comes `paṭa`; this also means a beautiful cloth. From the root `du` meaning 'to go', with the suffix `so` and reduplication, comes `dussaṃ`; or `dussaṃ` because it removes a bad appearance; or `dussaṃ` because it makes a bad appearance shine, from the root `asa` meaning 'to shine' with the prefix `du-`. From the root `cala` meaning 'to dress', with the vowel `a` changing to `o` and `l` changing to `ḷ`, comes `coḷa`. From the root `saṭa` meaning 'to break', 'to spread', 'to move', or 'to end', with the suffix `ṇvu`, comes `sāṭaka`.

291. Pajjaṃ vatthabhede. Tatrādidvayaṃ dukūlakhye vatthe. Khu sadde, mo, khumasaddā vikāre ṇo, khumāya vikāro khomaṃ, khumā nāma atasī, tabbakkalasambhavaṃ vatthaṃ, vāccaliṅgoyaṃ. Kūla āvaraṇe, dukkhena kulyateti dukūlaṃ, dumehi jātaṃ kūlanti vā dukūlaṃ. Keci pana “dukūlampi ekaṃ vatthantaraṃ, na khomanāma”nti vadanti. Taṃ “khoma’maṭṭe dukūle ca, atasīvasanepi ca”, “khoma’maṭṭe dukūlecā”ti nānatthasaṅgahatikaṇḍasesesu nānatthasaṅgaha 3.3.295 vuttattā na gahetabbaṃ. Koso nāma kimigabbho, tato jātattā koseyyaṃ, eyyo, “koseyyaṃ kimikosottha”nti amara 16.111 hi vuttaṃ. Koseyyameva dhotaṃ paṭṭuṇṇaṃ nāma, vuttañca “paṭṭuṇṇaṃ dhotakoseyya”nti amara 16.113. Pattuṇṇantipi pāṭhantaraṃ. Paṭṭuṇṇaraṭṭhe jātattā paṭṭuṇṇantipi vadanti. Kamu kantiyaṃ, kamanīyattā kambalo, raṅkunāmakassa hariṇavisesassa lomenasañjātavatthaṃ rāṅkavaṃ vigaromajaṃ (amara 16.111), alo, vāgamo ca majjhe. Vāsaddo kambalasaddassa napuṃsakattaṃ samuccinoti. Rallakopi amara 16.116 kambalapariyāyo. Saṇa sadde, kattari a, saṇo nāma thirattaco eko rukkhayoni, yassa tacena kevaṭṭādayo jālādīni karonti, saṇassa vikāro sāṇaṃ, vatthaṃ. Migalomāni koṭṭetvā sukhumāni katvā katamambaraṃ koṭumbaraṃ, kuṭa chedane, usso, assu, koṭumbaraṭṭhejātattā vā koṭumbaraṃ. Bhaṅgaṃ nāma khomādīni sabbāni [M 0.0206] ekajjhāni vomissetvā katavatthaṃ, bhanja avamaddane, atha vā bhaṅgaṃ nāma sāṇaphalaṃ, tabbikārattā vatthaṃ bhaṅgaṃ, vuttañca nānatthasaṅgahe “bhaṅgā sāṇākhyasassepī”ti. Sassasaddena cettha phalaṃ vuttaṃ, “rukkhādīnaṃ phalaṃ sassa”nti amara 14.15 vacanato. Bhaṅgampi vākamayamevāti keci. Vatthantaraṃ vatthaviseso. Ādinā kappāsādayopi gahitā.

291. A verse on types of cloth. Among these, the first two terms are for the cloth known as `dukūla`. From the root `khu` meaning 'sound', with the suffix `mo`, comes `khuma`; from the word `khuma`, with the suffix `ṇo` in the sense of 'product', the product of `khumā` is `khomaṃ`. `Khumā` is the name for flax (`atasī`); it is a cloth produced from its bark. This word is of variable gender. From the root `kūla` meaning 'to cover'; `dukūlaṃ` is so called because it is covered with difficulty, or because it is a covering produced from trees. However, some say, '`dukūla` is another type of cloth, not what is called `khoma`.' This view should not be accepted, because it is stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha and the Tikaṇḍasesa that '`khoma` means flax, and also `dukūla` and linen cloth,' and '`khoma` means flax and also `dukūla`.' `Kosa` is the name for a silkworm's cocoon; because it is produced from that, it is `koseyyaṃ` (silk), with the suffix `eyya`. Indeed, it is said: '`koseyyaṃ` is produced from the silkworm's `kosa`.' Washed `koseyyaṃ` itself is called `paṭṭuṇṇaṃ`, and it is said: '`paṭṭuṇṇaṃ` is washed silk.' `Pattuṇṇaṃ` is also an alternative reading. Some also say it is called `paṭṭuṇṇaṃ` because it is produced in the Paṭṭuṇṇa country. From the root `kamu` meaning 'to desire'; because it is desirable, it is `kambalo`. It is a cloth produced from the hair of a special deer called `raṅku`, with the suffix `alo` and the augment `vā` in the middle. The particle `vā` also indicates that the word `kambala` can be neuter. `Rallako` is also a synonym for `kambala`. From the root `saṇa` meaning 'sound', with the suffix `a` in the agentive sense; `saṇo` is a type of tree with tough bark, from which fishermen and others make nets and so on. The product of `saṇa` is `sāṇaṃ`, a cloth. A cloth made by pounding and softening animal hairs is `koṭumbaraṃ`, from the root `kuṭa` meaning 'to cut', with the suffix `usso` or `assu`; or it is `koṭumbaraṃ` because it is produced in the Koṭumbara country. `Bhaṅgaṃ` is a cloth made by mixing all types of flax and so on together, from the root `bhanja` meaning 'to crush'. Alternatively, `bhaṅgaṃ` is the name for the fruit of the `sāṇa` plant, and because it is a product of that, the cloth is `bhaṅgaṃ`. It is also stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: '`bhaṅgā` refers to the `sāṇa` plant and also to grain.' Here, by the word `sassa` (grain), 'fruit' is meant, according to the saying: 'The fruit of trees and so on is called `sassa`.' Some say `bhaṅgaṃ` is made only of bark. `Vatthantaraṃ` means a specific type of cloth. By 'and so on', cotton and other types are also included.

292-293. Catukkaṃ paridhānabhūte adhovatthe. Adhobhāge vasīyateti nivāsanaṃ, nisaddo adhobhāgassa jotako. Vasa acchādane, kammani yu. Bāhulyena antare majjhe bhavaṃ antarīyaṃ, īyo. Samānaliṅgattā dvando. Antare bhavaṃ antaraṃ, ṇo. Antare majjhe bhavo vāso antaravāsako, sakatthe ko. Upasaṃbyānaṃpyatra amara 16.117.

292-293. Four terms for the lower garment, which is worn. That which is worn on the lower part is `nivāsanaṃ`; the prefix `ni-` indicates the lower part. It is from the root `vasa`, 'to cover', with the suffix `yu` in the passive sense. That which is mostly on the inside or in the middle is `antarīyaṃ`, with the suffix `īyo`. Because of having the same gender, a dvandva compound is formed. That which is on the inside is `antaraṃ`, with the suffix `ṇo`. A garment that is on the inside or in the middle is `antaravāsako`, with the suffix `ko` in its own sense. `Upasaṃbyānaṃ` is also used here.

Pañcakaṃ uparidhāne. Vara acchādane, papubbo, kammani ṇo, ubhayatrāpi vuddhi, pāvāro. Uttarasmiṃ dehabhāge āsajjateti uttarāsaṅgo, ā pubbo sañja saṅge. Upari saṃvīyate pidhīyate bāhulyenāti, yu. Upasaṃpubbo vī tantasantāne. Uttarasmiṃ dehabhāge bhavaṃ vijjamānaṃ uttaraṃ, uttarīyañca, ṇo, īyo ca. Saṃbyānaṃpyatra.

Five terms for the upper garment. From the root `vara`, 'to cover', with the prefix `pa-` and the suffix `ṇo` in the passive sense, with vowel strengthening in both places, it becomes `pāvāro`. That which is attached to the upper part of the body is `uttarāsaṅgo`, from the root `sañja`, 'to attach', with the prefix `ā-`. That by which one is mostly wrapped or covered above is `upasaṃvyāna`, from the root `vī`, 'to weave', with the prefix `upasaṃ-` and the suffix `yu`. That which is or exists on the upper part of the body is `uttaraṃ` and `uttarīyaṃ`, with the suffixes `ṇo` and `īyo` respectively. `Saṃbyānaṃ` is also used here.

Navaṃ vatthaṃ ahatanti mataṃ kathitaṃ, na haññati yaṃ pāsāṇādīhīti ahataṃ. Tantato aciramāharitaṃ vatthaṃ. Anāhataṃ, nippavāṇi, tantakaṃpyatra. Vuttañca “anāhataṃ nippavāṇi, tantakañca navambare”ti amara 16.112.

New cloth is considered and said to be `ahataṃ`, meaning that which is not beaten by stones and the like. It is cloth recently brought from the loom. `Anāhataṃ`, `nippavāṇi`, and `tantakaṃ` are also used here. And it is said: '`Anāhataṃ`, `nippavāṇi`, and `tantakaṃ` are terms for a new garment.'

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0207] cirakālattā niddase jiṇṇavatthe. Natthi anto dasā yassa nantakaṃ, sakatthe ko. Kucchito paṭo kappaṭo, kappa vitakke vā, aṭo. Dvayaṃ athiravatthe, jiṇṇavasanaṃ athiraṃ vatthaṃ. “Paṭa”iti carati phoṭatīti paṭaccaraṃ, paṭaccarameva paḷaccaraṃ, ḷattaṃ.

The two terms refer to worn-out cloth due to long use. That which has no end or edge is nantaka, with the suffix -ka in its own sense. A wretched cloth is kappaṭo, or from kappa 'to think,' with the suffix -aṭo. The two terms refer to unstable cloth, meaning worn-out cloth is unstable cloth. That which moves and rustles is paṭaccara; paḷaccara is the same as paṭaccara, due to the change to ḷ.

294. Dvayaṃ koṭikādisannāhe, coḷe ca. Kaca bandhane, uko, niggahītāgamo ca. Vāṇaṃ saraṃ vārayatīti vāravāṇo, kammani ṇo, abhidhānato vārassa pubbanipāto, anitthiyamete. Vatthassa avayave dasāsaddo itthī. “Dasā vatyamavatthāyaṃ, vatthaṃse bahumhi dvisū”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.114 rabhaso. Dā chedane, kammani so, rasso.

294. The two terms refer to armor-like coverings and cloaks. From the root kaca 'to bind,' with the suffix -uko, and the insertion of niggahīta. That which wards off arrows is vāravāṇo, with the suffix -ṇa in the object sense; by convention, vāra comes first; these terms are not feminine. In a part of a cloth, the word dasā is feminine. And Rabhasa says: 'Dasā is used for a tattered cloth, for a piece of cloth, and in the plural for two pieces.' From the root dā 'to cut,' with the suffix -so in the object sense, and shortening.

Uttamaṅgamhi sīse yo kañcuko suvaṇṇādimayo, so “nāḷipatto”ti kathito. Nāḷipatto taṃsaṇṭhāno suvaṇṇādipaṭo nāḷipatto. Sīsakaṃ, siriyaṃ, sirohantipi tassa nāmāni.

The golden or similar covering on the head, the uppermost part, is called nāḷipatta. A nāḷipatta is a golden plate or similar object of that shape. Sīsaka, siriya, and sirohanti are also its names.

295. Tikaṃ dīghatte. Āpubbo yamu uparame, ṇo. Ā bhuso yāti gacchatīti vā āyāmo, yā gatipāpuṇesu, mo. Dīghassa bhāvo dīghatā. Ruha janane, ṇo.

295. The three terms refer to length. From the root yamu 'to cease' with the prefix ā-, and the suffix -ṇa. Or āyāma is that which goes far, from the root yā 'to go or reach,' with the suffix -mo. The state of being long is dīghatā. From the root ruha 'to be produced,' with the suffix -ṇa.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0208] vitthāre. Vatthavisaye “osāro”ti rūḷhe. Samantato nayhatīti pariṇāho, naha bandhane, ṇo. Vitthārena saraṇaṃ visāro, so eva visālatā.

The two terms refer to breadth. In the context of cloth, osāro is a conventional term. That which is bound all around is pariṇāho, from the root naha 'to bind,' with the suffix -ṇa. An expanse in breadth is visāro; that itself is visālatā.

296. Catukkaṃ cīvare. Arahataṃ dhajo arahaddhajo, rūḷhiyā tadaññacīvaresu. Kasāyena, kasāvena ca rattaṃ kāsāyaṃ, kāsāvañca, samānaliṅgattā dvando. Ci caye, īvaro. Vatthakhandhehi cīyateti cīvaraṃ.

296. The four terms refer to the robe. The banner of the arahants is arahaddhajo, by convention also used for other robes. That which is dyed with kasāya or kasāva is kāsāya and kāsāva; they form a dvanda compound due to having the same gender. From the root ci 'to accumulate,' with the suffix -īvara. That which is accumulated from pieces of cloth is cīvara.

Maṇḍalādayo tadaṅgāni samūhabhūtassa cīvarassa avayavāni. Maḍi bhūsāyaṃ, alo, maṇḍalaṃ. Cīvarapariyantoyaṃ mahāpathaviyā cakkavāḷapabbato viya cīvarassa samantato tiṭṭhati. Vivaṭṭo nāma cīvaramajjhagatamaggo, so hi visuṃ visuṃ vaṭṭatīti vivaṭṭoti vuccati, vaṭṭa āvaṭṭane. Kusi nāma maggānaṃ majjhagatavatthakhaṇḍaṃ, kusa chedane, kammani i, kusi, pumitthiyaṃ.

The maṇḍala and others are component parts of the robe, which exists as a composite whole. From the root maḍi 'to adorn,' with the suffix -ala, forming maṇḍala. This border of the robe stands all around the robe, like the Cakkavāḷa mountains around the great earth. Vivaṭṭa is the path running through the middle of the robe; it is called vivaṭṭa because it turns separately, from the root vaṭṭa 'to turn' or 'to revolve'. Kusi is the piece of cloth in the middle of the paths; from the root kusa 'to cut,' with the suffix -i in the object sense, forming kusi, which is both masculine and feminine.

297. Phalādīnaṃ yāni cattāri santi, etā vatthassa yoniyo kāraṇāni tato taduppattito. Kappāsikaṃ vatthaṃ phālaṃ nāma phalavikārattā, vikāre ṇo, tīsu. Yathā – phālo paṭo, phālā celī, phālaṃ vatthaṃ. Khomādayo pana paṭā tacabbhavā tacato sañjātā.

297. There are four sources for fabrics; these are the origins and causes of cloth, from which they arise. Cotton cloth is called phāla because it is a modification of fruit (phala), with the suffix -ṇa indicating modification, in the three genders. For example: phālo paṭo (masculine), phālā celī (feminine), phālaṃ vatthaṃ (neuter). Fabrics like khomā, however, are cloths born from bark, originating from bark.

298. Koseyyaṃ [M 0.0209] vatthaṃ kimijaṃ nāma. Migalomamayantu kambalaṃ. Dvayaṃ byavadhāyakapaṭe, kaṇḍapaṭepīti keci. Samānatthā ete dve tulyatthātyattho. Ju gatiyaṃ, bhūvādi, ju bandhane vā, yu, anakādeso, sā itthī. Tiro karīyati pidhīyati yāya, sā tirokaraṇī, yu. Patisīrāpyatra. Patipubbo si bandhane, ro.

298. Silk cloth is called kimija. A woolen blanket is made from animal hair. The two terms refer to a screen-cloth; some say kaṇḍapaṭa also. These two terms are synonymous, meaning they have the same meaning. From the root ju 'to move' (bhūvādi class), or ju 'to bind,' with the suffix -yu and the substitution of -anaka, forming a feminine word. That by which something is hidden or concealed is tirokaraṇī, with the suffix -yu. Here also is patisīrā. From the root si 'to bind' with the prefix pati-, and the suffix -ro.

299. Dvayaṃ uparibandhapaṭe, athasaddotra liṅgādijotako. Uddhaṃ locate bandhīyateti ullocaṃ, luca dassane. Candātape vitanyateti vitānaṃ, tanu vitthāre, ṇo, curādi. Dvayampi punnapuṃsakanti īritaṃ kathitaṃ.

299. The two terms refer to an upper binding cloth; the word atha here indicates the gender and so forth. That which is seen or bound above is ullocaṃ, from the root luca 'to see'. That which is spread out in moonlight or sunlight is vitānaṃ, from the root tanu 'to extend,' with the suffix -ṇa, from the curādi class. Both are said to be in the masculine and neuter genders.

Dvayaṃ sināne. Naha soce, karaṇe yu, sinā soce, karaṇe yu, “sināne”ti sattamyantaṃ padaṃ. Dvayaṃ kulyādinā kuṭyādinā (ka.), kujjanādinā (nissaya), kuṅkumahaliddādinā (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.121) aṅganimmalīkaraṇe. Ubbattīyate visārīyate malamaneneti ubbattanaṃ, vatu vattane, bhūvādi. Majja suddhiyaṃ, yu. Samanti dvayamidaṃ samānatthaṃ.

The two terms refer to bathing. From the root naha 'to purify,' with the suffix -yu in the instrumental sense; from sinā 'to purify,' with the suffix -yu in the instrumental sense; sināne is a word in the locative case. The two terms refer to cleansing the body with water from a canal, etc. That by which dirt is rubbed off or spread out is ubbattanaṃ, from the root vatu 'to exist,' from the bhūvādi class. From the root majja 'to purify,' with the suffix -yu. These two terms are synonymous.

300. Tikaṃ nalāṭakate cittake. Tilakākati tilako. Cittakākati cittakaṃ. Cakārena tamālapattākati tamālapattaṃ[M 0.0210]. Sāmaññena visesakaṃ, ubho visesakatilakā anitthī, sesadvayaṃ napuṃsakaṃ amara 16.123.

300. The three terms refer to a mark made upon the forehead. That which has the form of a sesame seed is tilako. That which has a variegated form is cittakaṃ. By the particle 'ca', that which has the form of a tamāla leaf is tamālapattaṃ. Visesaka is the general term; both visesaka and tilaka are not feminine, while the remaining two are neuter.

Tikaṃ candane, cadi hilādane, hilādanaṃ sukhāpanaṃ, yu. Gandhānaṃ sāro uttamo gandhasāro, gandhayutto sāro thiraṃso vā gandhasāro. Malayadīpagirimhi jāyatīti malayajo. Bhaddasirīpyatra.

The three terms refer to sandalwood. From the root cadi 'to delight,' meaning 'to give pleasure,' with the suffix -yu. The best essence of fragrances is gandhasāro, or gandhasāro is a fragrant, firm essence. That which is born on the Malaya island-mountain is malayajo. Here also is bhaddasirī.

301. Tikaṃ pītacandane. “Gosīsa”iti pabbate malaye dese jātaṃ gosīsaṃ, go viya jalaṃ viya sītanti vā gosītaṃ, tadeva tassa sakāraṃ katvā gosīsaṃ. Tilapaṇṇappamāṇapaṇṇayuttatāya telapaṇṇikaṃ. Manaṃ haratīti hari, tameva candananti haricandanaṃ. Pītasāru, susītaṃpyatra. Gosīsādayo tayo pume, napuṃsake ca vattanti.

301. The three terms refer to yellow sandalwood. Gosīsa is that which is born in the region of the Malaya mountain; or, it is gosīta (cool like a cow or like water), which becomes gosīsa by changing its 'ta' to 'sa'. Due to having leaves the size of sesame leaves, it is called telapaṇṇika. That which captivates the mind is hari; that same sandalwood is haricandana. Here also are pītasāru and susītaṃ. The three terms, gosīsa and the others, are used in the masculine and neuter genders.

Catukkaṃ rattacandane. Tilapaṇṇappamāṇapaṇṇayuttatāya tilapaṇṇī. Purimena bhedakaraṇatthaṃ na vuddhi. Pattamaṅgamasseti pattaṅgaṃ, khuddapaṇṇatāya appadhānapattamiccattho. “Aṅgaṃ gattanti kopāya-patīkesvappadhānake”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe. Rañja rāge, hetukattari yu. Rattavaṇṇatāya rattañca taṃ candanañceti rattacandanaṃ, amarakose pana “gosīsādīni rattacandanantāni visese vattantī”ti amara 16.131 vuttāni. Tatra gosīsassa yathāvuttoyevattho. Dhavalaṃ, susītalaṃ, candanaṃ, telapaṇṇikaṃ malayapabbatadesajameva. Hari maṇḍūko, tadākāre pabbate jātaṃ candanaṃ haricandanaṃ. Pakkambaphalagandhi pītavaṇṇaṃ. Tilapaṇṇīpattaṅgāni rattacandanasadisassa rattasārassa ekassa candanassa nāmāni.

The four terms refer to red sandalwood. Due to having leaves the size of sesame leaves, it is called tilapaṇṇī. There is no vṛddhi here to distinguish it from the previous term. That which has leaves as its secondary part is pattaṅga, meaning it has small leaves, hence leaves of minor importance. Indeed, in the Nānatthasaṅgaha, it is said: 'Aṅga means body, and also, in the sense of a secondary part, anger or retaliation.' From the root rañja 'to color,' with the suffix -yu. Due to its red color, it is rattaṃ and it is candanaṃ, hence rattacandanaṃ. In the Amarakośa, however, it is stated: 'Gosīsa and others ending in rattacandana are used in specific contexts.' There, the meaning of gosīsa is as previously explained. Dhavala (white), susītala (very cool), candana (sandalwood), and telapaṇṇika are all born in the Malaya mountain region. Hari means frog; haricandana is sandalwood born on a mountain resembling its shape. It has the fragrance of ripe mango fruit and is yellow in color. Tilapaṇṇī and pattaṅga are names for one type of sandalwood, rattasāra, which resembles red sandalwood.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0211] rattacandane. Atha vā tilapaṇyādīni cattāri lohitacandanasadisassa rattasārassa ekassa candanavisesassa nāmāni. Kucandanaṃpyatra. “Pattaṅgaṃ rañjanaṃ rattaṃ, patraṅgañca kucandana”nti ratanamālāyaṃ.

The two terms refer to red sandalwood. Alternatively, the four terms beginning with tilapaṇṇī are names for a specific type of sandalwood, rattasāra, which is similar to lohitacandana (red sandalwood). Here also is kucandana. In the Ratnamālā, it is said: 'Pattaṅga, rañjana, ratta, and patraṅga are also kucandana.'

302. Dvayaṃ vaṇijādīnaṃ “kāḷeyā”iti rūḷhepītakaṭṭhe. Kāḷavaṇṇaṃ anusarati sīlenāti kāḷānusārī, kāḷavaṇṇajanakotyattho. Kāḷaṃ janetīti kāḷiyaṃ, “kāḷīyakantu kāḷeyaṃ, vaṇṇadaṃ kantijāsaka”nti jāsakaṃ kantidāyakaṃ (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.126) byāḍi.

302. The two terms refer to yellow wood, conventionally called kāḷeyā by merchants and others. That which habitually follows the black color is kāḷānusārī, meaning it produces black color. That which generates black is kāḷiyaṃ. Byāḍi says: 'Kāḷīyaka is kāḷeya, a color-giver, a luster-producer.'

Tikaṃ agarusāmaññe. Lū chedane, ho. Lahunāmattā agaru. Rassa latte agalu, dvayaṃ pume. Vaṃsikaṃ, rājārahaṃ, kimijaṃ, joṅgakaṃpyatra.

The three terms refer to agaru in general. From the root lū 'to cut,' with the suffix -ho. It is agaru (not heavy) on account of its lightness. Agalu is formed by the change of 'ra' to 'la'; these two are masculine. Here also are vaṃsika, rājāraha, kimija, and joṅgaka.

Asmiṃ agarumhi kāḷe sati “kāḷāgarū”tyuccate. Mallikāpupphagandhi agaru pana maṅgalyoccate.

When this agaru is black, it is called kāḷāgaru. But agaru with the fragrance of jasmine flowers is called maṅgalya.

Dvayaṃ sallakīdave. Turukkho vutto. Piḍi saṅghāte, ṇvu. Sihalo, yāvaṇopyatra.

The two terms refer to the resin of the sallakī tree. Turukkho is mentioned. From the root piḍi 'to collect,' with the suffix -ṇvu. Here also are sihalo and yāvaṇo.

303. Dvayaṃ miganābhiyaṃ. Kattha silāghāyaṃ, ūro, nadādi, sakatthe ko. Migassa mado migamado, migo marati yenāti vā migamaro, so eva migamado.

303. The two terms refer to musk. From the root kattha 'to praise,' with the suffix -ūro; from the nadādi group of roots, with the suffix -ka in its own sense. The musk of a deer is migamado, or migamaro is that by which a deer dies; that itself is migamado.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0212] kuṭṭhe. Kuṭa chedane, ṭho, to vā, “kuṭādīhi ṭho”ti ṭho, kuṭṭhaṃ, rogabhedepi. Attano chāyūpagate aje pāletīti ajapālakaṃ, ṇvu. Pāribhābyaṃ, pākalaṃ phālakī (ka.), uppalaṃ, vāppaṃpyatra.

The two terms refer to kuṭṭha (costus). From the root kuṭa 'to cut,' with the suffix -ṭha or -ta; or, by the rule 'kuṭādīhi ṭho', the suffix is -ṭha, forming kuṭṭhaṃ, which also refers to a type of disease. That which protects goats that have come into its shade is ajapālakaṃ, with the suffix -ṇvu. Here also are pāribhābyaṃ, pākalaṃ, uppalaṃ, and vāppaṃ.

Dvayaṃ piḍaṅge. Rogaṃ lunanto aṅgati gacchatīti lavaṅgo. Devānaṃ kusumaṃ pupphaṃ devakusumaṃ. Sirisaññaṃpyatra.

Two [terms] for piḍaṅga. That which goes, cutting disease, is lavaṅga. The flower of the gods is devakusuma. Here also is sirisañña.

Dvayaṃ kuṅkume. Kasmīraraṭṭhe jātaṃ kasmīrajaṃ. Aggisikhaṃ, varaṃ, vallīkaṃ, pītanaṃ, rattasaṅkocaṃ, pisunaṃ, dhīraṃ lohitacandanaṃpyatra.

Two [terms] for saffron. That which is born in the land of Kashmir is kasmīrajaṃ. Here also are aggisikhaṃ, varaṃ, vallīkaṃ, pītanaṃ, rattasaṅkocaṃ, pisunaṃ, dhīraṃ, and lohitacandanaṃ.

304. Dvayaṃ dhunake. Yakkhehi kato dhūpo yakkhadhūpo, yakkho devo. Sajjarukkhassa sileso sajjulaso. Assu, silopo, essattañca, sajjassa raso davo sajjulaso, assu, lattañca. Sajjarasotipi pāṭho. Rālo, sabbaraso, bahurūpopyatra.

304. Two [terms] for dhunaka. Incense made by yakkhas is yakkhadhūpa; a yakkha is a deity. The resin of the sajja tree is sajjulaso. [The derivation involves] assu, elision, and essatta; and the liquid sap of the sajja tree is sajjulaso, [involving] assu and latta. Sajjaraso is also a reading. Here also are rāla, sabbarasa, and bahurūpa.

Tikaṃ takkole. Takka vitakke, olo. Kula saṅkhyāne, ṇvu. Kosayuttaṃ phalametassāti kosaphalaṃ. Dvayaṃ jātiphale. Kosasahitaṃ jātiphalametassāti jātikosaṃ. Jātiphalametassa, na kittimanti jātiphalaṃ.

Three [terms] for takkola. [The root] takka [is in the sense of] reasoning, [with suffix] olo. [The root] kula [is in the sense of] counting, [with suffix] ṇvu. That which has a fruit joined with a sheath is kosaphala. Two [terms] for jātiphala. That which has a jāti fruit together with a sheath is jātikosa. Its fruit is by birth, not artificial, thus it is jātiphala.

305. Pajjaddhaṃ kappūre, ghano hutvā saratīti ghanasāro. Abbhamiva sitaṃ sitabbho, abhidhānato pubbanipāto, kappa [M 0.0213] sāmatthiye, ūro. Candasañño, himavāluko, himāvhayopyatra.

305. A half-verse for camphor. Becoming dense, it flows, thus it is ghanasāra. White like a cloud, it is sitabbha; the pre-posing [of sita] is due to lexical authority. [The root] kappa [is in the sense of] capability, [with suffix] ūro. Here also are candasañña, himavāluka, and himāvhaya.

Pajjaddhaṃ lākhāyaṃ, ā bhuso rattaṃ karotīti alattako, lattaṃ, kvi. Yu missane, ṇvu. Lākha sosane, a, lā ādāne vā, kho. Jana janane, tu, nalopo. Dumāmayopyatra.

A half-verse for lac. That which makes things very red is alattaka, from latta, with suffix kvi. [The root] yu [is in the sense of] mixing, [with suffix] ṇvu. [The root] lākha [is in the sense of] drying, [with suffix] a; or [the root] lā [is in the sense of] taking, [with suffix] kho. [The root] jana [is in the sense of] producing, [with suffix] tu, with elision of 'na'. Here also is dumāmaya.

306. Dvayaṃ saraladdave. Siriyā lakkhiyā āvāso sirivāso. Saralanāmakassa rukkhassa davo raso saraladdavo. Pāyaso, vakadhūpo, siriveṭṭhopyatra. “Sirivāse paramanne ca, pāyaso sammato pume”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 16.129 ruddo. Dvayaṃ añjane. Añju byattimakkhanagatikantīsu, yu. Kajja byasane. Kajjati roganti kajjalaṃ, alo.

306. Two [terms] for saraladdava. The abode of glory and fortune is sirivāsa. The liquid sap of the tree named sarala is saraladdava. Here also are pāyasa, vakadhūpa, and siriveṭṭha. Rudda says: 'The word pāyasa is considered masculine when it means sirivāsa and excellent food.' Two [terms] for añjana. [The root] añju [is in the senses of] manifestation, smearing, movement, or beauty, [with suffix] yu. [The root] kajja [is in the sense of] affliction. That which afflicts disease is kajjala, [with suffix] alo.

Dvayaṃ gandhagāhāpanacuṇṇe, vasa hiṃsattho, vasati duggandhanti vāso, ṇo, vāsa upasevāyaṃ vā, vasa nivāse vā. So eva cuṇṇaṃ. Yuja yoge, kammani ṇo, vāso eva yogo vāsayogo. Dvayaṃ vilepanamatte. Vaṇṇa vaṇṇakriyāvitthāraguṇavacanesu, curādi. Vaṇṇayatīti vaṇṇakaṃ. Ṇvu. Lipa upadehe. Vilepīyateti vilepanaṃ, kammani yu.

Two [terms] for fragrance-imparting powder. [The root] vasa [is in the sense of] harming; or, it harms a bad smell, thus vāso, [with suffix] ṇo; or [the root] vāsa [is in the sense of] perfuming; or vasa [in the sense of] dwelling. That itself is the powder. [The root] yuja [is in the sense of] joining, [with suffix] ṇo in the passive sense; or vāso itself is the mixture, thus vāsayogo. Two [terms] for a mere smearing substance. [The root] vaṇṇa [is in the senses of] coloring, the act of coloring, explaining, qualities, or speech, of the curādi group. That which colors is vaṇṇaka, [with suffix] ṇvu. [The root] lipa [is in the sense of] smearing. That which is smeared is vilepana, [with suffix] yu in the passive sense.

307. Yo gandhamālyadhūpādīhi vatthatambulādīnaṃ saṅkhāro, taṃ “vāsana”mityuccate, vāsa upasevāyaṃ, vāsīyate saṅkharīyateti vāsanaṃ, yu.

307. The preparation of garments, betel, and so forth, with perfumes, garlands, incense, and the like, is called vāsana. [It is derived from the root] vāsa [in the sense of] perfuming; that which is perfumed or prepared is vāsana, [with suffix] yu.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0214] pupphadāme. Mā māne, lo, mala dhāraṇe vā, a. Mālova mālyaṃ. Dama gatiyaṃ, pupphāni damantyatreti pupphadāmaṃ, pupphānaṃ rāsikaraṇaṭṭhānamiccattho. Dā lavane vā, mo. Amarakose pana “mālāmālyāni muddhani pavattāya mālāya nāmānī”ti amara 16.135 vadati. Mālamālyasaddā pupphepi, “mālā mālyaṃ pasune”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe. Dvayaṃ gandhaggāhite vatthādo. Bhū sattāyaṃ, kammani to, vuddhādi. Vāsāpeti gandhaṃ gāhāpeti yanti vāsitaṃ, vasa nivāse, kamme to, tīsu, yathā – bhāvito paṭo, bhāvitā celī, bhāvitaṃ vatthaṃ. Vāsito, vāsitā, vāsitaṃ vatthaṃ.

Three [terms] for a flower garland. [The root] mā [is in the sense of] measuring, [with suffix] lo; or mala [in the sense of] wearing, [with suffix] a. Mālova is mālya. [The root] dama [is in the sense of] subduing; flowers are strung here, hence pupphadāma, meaning the place where flowers are piled up. Or [the root] dā [is in the sense of] cutting, [with suffix] mo. However, in the Amarakosa, it is said: 'Mālā and mālya are names for a garland worn on the head.' The words mālā and mālya also apply to flowers, as indeed it is stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: 'Mālā and mālya [are used] for a flower.' Two [terms] for cloth, etc., that has absorbed fragrance. [The root] bhū [is in the sense of] being, [with suffix] to in the passive, with vṛddhi, etc. That which is caused to be perfumed, caused to absorb fragrance, is vāsita; [from the root] vasa [in the sense of] dwelling, [with suffix] to in the passive, in three genders, for example: bhāvito paṭo, bhāvitā celī, bhāvitaṃ vatthaṃ. Thus: vāsito, vāsitā, vāsitaṃ.

308. Pañcakaṃ muddhamālāyaṃ. Tasi alaṅkāre, bhūvādi. Uddhaṃ tasīyateti uttaṃso. Sikhāyaṃ jāto sekharo, ro. Muddhaṃ avati rakkhatīti aveḷā, ava rakkhaṇe, elo, ḷattaṃ. “Āveḷā”tipi pāṭho, dīghattaṃ. Sekharo ca āveḷā cāti dvando. Muddhani alaṅkataṃ mālyaṃ muddhamālyaṃ, tasmiṃ. Avapubbo tasi alaṅkāre, uddhaṃ tasīyateti avataṃso, so eva vaṭaṃsako, sakatthe ko, tassa ṭo, anekatthattā upasagganipātānaṃ uddhaṃbhāvajotako cettha avasaddoti tathottaṃ.

308. Five [terms] for a head garland. [The root] tasi [is in the sense of] adorning, of the bhūvādi group. It is adorned above, hence uttaṃsa. Born on the crest, it is sekharo, [with suffix] ro. It protects the head, hence aveḷā; [from the root] ava [in the sense of] protecting, [with suffix] elo, and the state of being ḷ. Āveḷā is also a reading, with lengthening. A garland adorned on the head is muddhamālya; in that [sense]. With ava prefixed to [the root] tasi [in the sense of] adorning, it is adorned above, hence avataṃso. That itself is vaṭaṃsako, with ko in its own sense, and ṭa for ta. Due to the multiple meanings of prefixes and particles, the word ava here indicates upwardness, and thus it is so stated.

Tikaṃ seyyāyaṃ. Sayantyassaṃ seyyā, yo. Sayantyatreti sayanaṃ, senañca. Ubhayatrapi adhikaraṇe yu, isse, e aya, itaratra ettaṃ, “vā paro asarūpā”ti alopo ca, sayanīpyatra.

Three [terms] for a bed. One lies in it, hence seyyā, [with suffix] yo. One lies here, hence sayana, and sena. In both cases, [the suffix] yu [is used] in the locative sense; [from the root sī,] i becomes e, e becomes aya; elsewhere, e remains e; and there is elision of a according to the rule 'vā paro asarūpā'. Here also is sayanī.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0215] mañce. Paripubbo aki lakkhaṇe, ṇo, ilopo, rassa lattaṃ. Maci dhāraṇocchāyapūjanesu, bhūvādi a, sakatthe ko. Khaṭāpyatra, khaṭyate ākaṅkhate sayanatthikehīti khaṭā, khaṭa ākaṅkhāyaṃ.

Two [terms] for a couch. [The root] aki [is in the sense of] marking, with pari prefixed, [suffix] ṇo, elision of i, and la for ra. [The root] maci [is in the senses of] bearing, elevating, and honoring, of the bhūvādi group, [with suffix] a, and ko in its own sense. Here also is khaṭā; it is desired by those who wish to lie down, hence khaṭā, [from the root] khaṭa [in the sense of] desiring.

309. Dvayaṃ mañcādhāre. Mañcassa ādhāro mañcādhāro. Paṭipajjati pavattati seyyā yena, so paṭipādo. Mañcaṅge mañcāvayave aṭanisaddo itthiyaṃ, aṭa gamanattho, ani, yu vā, nadādi, rasso.

309. Two [terms] for a couch support. The support of the couch is mañcādhāra. That by which the bed proceeds or functions is paṭipāda. Regarding a couch-part or component, the word aṭani is feminine; [the root] aṭa [is in the sense of] going, [with suffix] ani, or yu; of the nadādi group, with a short vowel.

310. Kuḷīrapādādayo ime cattāro mañcantarā mañcabhedā siyuṃ. Tattha kuḷīro kakkaṭako tassa saṇṭhānapādattā kuḷīrapādo. Aṭaniyaṃ āhacco, āhacca vā pādo tiṭṭhati yassāti āhaccapādo, pubbapakkhe “riccā”ti yogavibhāgena riccapaccayanto āhaccasaddo, parapakkhe tu tvāpaccayanto, yassa aṭanichidde pādo pavisitvā tiṭṭhati, so āhaccapādo. Masa āmasane, āro, sakatthe ko. Yassa pādacchidde aṭani pavisitvā tiṭṭhati, so masārako. Bundena pādena saha ekābaddhā aṭani yassa so bundikābaddho, ekārassittaṃ. Ettha ca majjhe dvinnaṃ mañcānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vipariyayenāpi vadanti.

310. These four, beginning with kuḷīrapāda, are types or varieties of couches. Among them, a kuḷīra is a crab; it is a kuḷīrapāda because its legs have that shape. That whose leg stands having struck an aṭani, or having struck, is an āhaccapāda; in the first case, the word āhacca ends in the suffix ricca by yogavibhāga, but in the second case, it ends in the suffix tvā. That whose leg stands having entered a hole in the aṭani is an āhaccapāda. [The root] masa [is in the sense of] touching, [with suffix] āra, and ko in its own sense. That in whose leg-hole an aṭani enters and stands, is a masāraka. That whose aṭani is bound as one with its base-leg is a bundikābaddha; the 'i' is short. And here, the characteristics of the two middle couches are also described in reverse.

311. Dvayaṃ sīsādhāre. Visesena sīsaṃ vahatīti bibbohanaṃ, yu, battaṃ, assottañca. Upadhīyate sīsāsanaṃ karīyateti upadhānaṃ, yu, dhā dhāraṇe.

311. Two [terms] for a head support. It bears the head in a special way, thus bibbohana, [with suffix] yu, and with the change of 'v' to 'b' and 'a' to 'o'. That which is placed under, on which the head is made to rest, is upadhāna, [with suffix] yu; [from the root] dhā [in the sense of] holding.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0216] sāmaññapīṭhe. Pīṭha hiṃsāsaṃkilesesu, bhūvādi, ṇvu, ā. Yadādinā ke paccaye itthikatākāre pare pubbo akāro ikāramāpajjate, “ke”ti kiṃ? Cetanā. “Paccaye”ti kiṃ? Bakā. “Itthī”ti kiṃ? Pācakā. “Kata”iti kiṃ? Vuttakammā, kammapaccayoyaṃ, tapaccaye pīṭhaṃ moggallāna 4.142 suttampi passitabbaṃ. Āsate asminti āsanaṃ.

Three [terms] for a common seat. [The root] pīṭha [is in the senses of] harming or defiling, of the bhūvādi group, [with suffixes] ṇvu or ā. By the yadādi rule, when the suffix ka and the feminine ā follow, the preceding a becomes i. Why specify 'ka'? For example, cetanā. Why 'suffix'? For example, bakā. Why 'feminine'? For example, pācakā. Why 'made'? For example, vuttakammā. This is a passive suffix; with the ta suffix, it becomes pīṭhaṃ. One sits in it, hence āsana.

Dvayaṃ uttamārahapīṭhe. Kuca saṃpaccanakoṭilyapatithambhavilekhanesu, cho. Bhaddaṃ kalyāṇaṃ pīṭhaṃ bhaddapīṭhaṃ. Gajadantādimayakesamajjaniyampi dvayamidamāhu. Tadā pasādhanī, kaṅkatikāpyatra. Pīṭhantare dīghapīṭhe āsandī matā. Sada visaraṇagatyāvasānesu, nadādi, bindāgamo ca.

Two [terms] for a supreme, worthy seat. [The root] kuca [is in the senses of] contracting, crookedness, supporting, or engraving, [with suffix] cho. A good, beautiful seat is bhaddapīṭha. This pair of terms is also said to refer to a hair-comb made of ivory and so forth. In that case, here also are pasādhanī and kaṅkatikā. Among other seats, a long seat is considered an āsandī. [The root] sada [is in the senses of] perishing, movement, or ending, of the nadādi group, and with the insertion of a nasal.

312. Āyāmavitthāravasena mahanto āsanappabhedo “kojavo”ti mato, kuju theyyakaraṇe, ṇo, kuyaṃ pathaviyaṃ javatīti vā kojavo, ju gatiyaṃ. Dīghena lomena yutto āsanappabhedo “gonako”ti mato, gu sadde, yu, sakatthe ko, ussottaṃ.

312. A large type of seat, in terms of length and breadth, is known as a kojavo. [It is derived from the root] kuju [in the sense of] acting crookedly, [with suffix] ṇo; or, it goes on the bad earth, thus kojavo, [from the root] ju [in the sense of] going. A type of seat endowed with long fleece is known as a gonako; [it is from the root] gu [in the sense of] sounding, [with suffix] yu, and ko in its own sense, and the vowel 'u' becomes 'o'.

Dvayaṃ attharaṇe. Migalomapuṇṇatāya jātaṃ uṇṇāmayaṃ. Thara santharaṇe, pādipubbova, na kadācipi pādirahito, ā bhuso tharīyateti attharaṇaṃ, yu.

Two [terms] for a spread. One is woollen, being filled with the hair of deer. The root thara is in the sense of spreading; it is always preceded by a prefix like pā, never without one. It is spread out abundantly, hence attharaṇa, [with suffix] yu.

Dvayaṃ saṃsibbanacittake. Cittarūpamassatthīti cittakaṃ. Bāhulyena na ikārāgamo. Vānena saṃsibbanena sañjātaṃ cittarūpamassāti vānacittakaṃ, sakatthe ko.

Two terms for a stitched and decorated cover. It has decorated patterns, hence 'cittaka'. Generally, the 'i' vowel is not added. It has decorated patterns arising from stitching, hence 'vānacittaka', with the suffix 'ko' in its own sense.

313. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0217] nirantarapupphapaṭe. Ghanaṃ sandhibhūtaṃ puppharūpametthāti ghanapupphaṃ. Paṭalametissātthīti paṭalikā, iko. Dvayaṃ bahumudulome setavatthe. Si sevāyaṃ, sivatthikehi sevīyateti seto, to. Paṭa gamane, ṇvu, paṭikā, addhendupāsāṇepi.

313. Two terms for a continuous flower cloth. It has dense, joined flower patterns, hence 'ghanapuppha'. It possesses layers, hence 'paṭalikā', with the suffix 'ika'. Two terms for a white cloth with abundant soft hair. The root 'si' is in the sense of service; it is served by those who desire service, hence 'seto', with the suffix 'to'. The root 'paṭa' is in the sense of going; with the suffix 'ṇvu', it forms 'paṭikā'; it is also used for a half-moon-shaped stone.

Dvīsupi pariyantesu yassā dasā santi, sā uddalomī, uditaṃ dvīsu lomaṃ dasā yassā sā uddalomī, issattaṃ, dvittañca. Ekasmiṃ pariyanteyeva dasā yassā ekantalomī, ekasmiṃ ante pariyante lomaṃ dasā yassātthīti ekantalomī, uddalomī ca ekantalomī ceti uddalomiekantalomino, “padānaṃ sandhi vatticchāto, na samāsantaragesū”ti vuttepi gāthābhāvato chandohānibhayā visandhi.
