Yattha pana gāthāyampi agāthāyampi (?) visandhi “dhammasaṃvaṇṇanāya’ntiādimāhā”tyādīsu, tattha kathanti? “Na samāsantaraṅgesū”ti imassāniccattā tatthāpi na doso, “nena niddiṭṭhamanicca”nti hi paribhāsitaṃ naghaṭitaṃ aniccaṃ (paribhāsendusekhara 97).

That which has fringes (dasā) at both ends is 'uddalomī'; that which has risen hair (loma) or fringes at both ends is 'uddalomī', with the feminine suffix 'ī' and doubling of the consonant. That which has fringes at only one end is 'ekantalomī'; that which has hair or fringes at one end is 'ekantalomī'. 'Uddalomī' and 'ekantalomī' together form 'uddalomiekantalomino'; although it is stated, 'Sandhi of words is optional, but not within compounds', here the sandhi is broken because it is a verse and for fear of disrupting the meter. But where sandhi is broken even in a verse, as in 'dhammasaṃvaṇṇanāya'ntiādimāhā' and so forth, what is said there? There is no fault even there, because the rule 'not within compounds' is not absolute, for it is indeed stated as a maxim: 'What is indicated by this is not absolute'.

314. Tadeva yathāvuttadvayameva soḷasannaṃ itthīnaṃ naccayoggaṃ naccassa yogyaṭṭhānabhūtaṃ “kuttaka”mityuccate. Hi padapūraṇe. “Naccayogyamhī”tipi pāṭho, tadā bhāvasattamī. Karonti [M 0.0218] ettha naccanti kuttakaṃ, kara karaṇe, to, assu, bhujādi, sakatthe ko.

314. That very pair, as described, which is suitable for the dancing of sixteen women, being the appropriate place for dance, is called 'kuttaka'. 'Hi' is a particle for filling out the line. 'Naccayogyamhī' is also a reading, in which case it is a locative absolute. Here they perform and dance, hence 'kuttaka'; it is from the root 'kara' in the sense of doing, with the suffix 'to', with substitution of 'u' for 'a', like in the bhujādi class, and with the suffix 'ko' in its own sense.

Sīhādirūpehi vicittarūpaṃ vatthaṃ, āsanaṃ vā vikatikā nāma bhave, ekasseva hi kattuno pakativikatisaṅkhātāvatthāvasena dvittaṃ, vatticchāvasena liṅgasaṅkhyāvibhattibhedañca hoti, yathā – manussā yakkhabhattaṃ ahesuṃ, sattappakaraṇāni abhidhammo nāma bhavanti, devadatto rajjaṃ pāpuṇātīti. Yatra hi pakatiyā vā vikatiyā vāti dvinnampi vuttatā siyā, tatra vācako pakatiyāyeva saṅkhyaṃ gaṇhāti, netarassa tannissitabhāvenāppadhānato kaccāyanasāre 6-7 gāthāsu passitabbaṃ. Yadā pana pakatiyā sambandhādibhāvaṃ vattumicchati, tadā attanā vattabbassa aññatthassābhāvā vikatipyuccate vācakena, yathā – devadattassa rajjaṃ pāpuṇāti, idha pana liṅgabhedeneva vuttaṃ “cittaṃ vikatikā bhave”ti. Vikarīyateti vikati.

A garment or seat with variegated forms such as lions is called 'vikatikā'. For a single agent, there is a duality of state, designated as original and altered; and depending on the intention of speaking, there is a difference in gender, number, and case, as in: 'Men became food for yakkhas,' 'The seven treatises are called Abhidhamma,' 'Devadatta attains kingship.' Where both the original and altered states could be mentioned, the predicate takes the number of the original state, not of the other, as it is dependent and thus subordinate. But when one wishes to express a relation with the original state, and there is no other meaning to be expressed by itself, the altered state is also expressed by the predicate, as in: 'Kingship comes to Devadatta.' Here, however, it is expressed merely by a difference of gender: 'A variegated pattern becomes an adornment (vikatikā).' That which is altered is 'vikati'.

315. Kaṭṭissakoseyyasaṅkhātānaṃ dvinnamattharaṇānaṃ karaṇappakāraṃ dassetuṃ ariyāsāmaññamāha “kaṭṭissa”miccādi. Kosiyakaṭṭissamayaṃ kosiyasuttakaṭṭissavākehi pakatamattharaṇaṃ kaṭṭissaṃ nāma, virūpekasesavasena kosiyañca kaṭṭissañca kaṭṭissāni, tehi pakataṃ attharaṇaṃ kaṭṭissaṃ. Kosiyasuttena pakatantu attharaṇaṃ koseyyaṃ nāma. Ratanapatisibbitanti idaṃ dvinnampi visesanaṃ, attharaṇañca iti kamā kamato “bhave”ti ajjhāharitabbaṃ. Attharaṇasaddassānuṇṇāmayesvapi pavattanato etthāpi “attharaṇa”nti [M 0.0219] vuttaṃ, yathā – suttaṃ kammanti. Ettha ca cakāro pādantattā garūsu gaṇhitabbo, teneva hi sattapaññāsamattā paripuṇṇā honti, ariyāya hi paṭhamapāde dvādasamattā, tathā tatiye, dutiye aṭṭhārasa, catutthe pannarasamattāti sampiṇḍitā sattapaññāsamattā honti.

315. To explain the method of making the two kinds of coverings known as 'kaṭṭissa' and 'koseyya', he states in general in the Āriyā meter: 'kaṭṭissa,' etc. A covering made from silk threads and wood-bark is called 'kaṭṭissa'. By the principle of 'virūpekasesa' (retention of one of dissimilar members), 'kosiya' (silken) and 'kaṭṭissa' (of wood-bark) become 'kaṭṭissāni'; a covering made from these is 'kaṭṭissa'. But a covering made from silk thread is called 'koseyya'. The phrase 'ratanapatisibbitaṃ' (interwoven with jewels) is an adjective for both. The words 'attharaṇaṃ' (covering) and 'bhave' (it would be) should be supplied in due order. The word 'attharaṇa' is used here because it also applies to non-woolen items. Here, the syllable 'ca', being at the end of a line, is to be counted as long; only then are the fifty-seven mātrās complete. For in the Āriyā meter, the first line has twelve mātrās, as does the third; the second has eighteen, and the fourth fifteen, totaling fifty-seven mātrās when combined.

316. Tikaṃ dīpe. Dīpa dittiyaṃ, divādi. Dippatīti dīpo, ṇo. “Padīpo”ti aññapadanivattanatthaṃ upasaggena padaṃ vaḍḍhitaṃ. Juti dittiyaṃ, bhūvādi, ṇo.

316. Three terms for a lamp. 'Dīpa' is derived from the root 'dip' in the sense of shining, belonging to the divādi class. That which shines is 'dīpo', with the suffix 'ṇa'. The word 'padīpo' is augmented with a prefix to exclude other meanings. 'Juti' is from the root 'jut' in the sense of shining, belonging to the bhūvādi class, with the suffix 'ṇa'.

Dvayaṃ ādāse. “Pume tū”ti tvantaṃ liṅgapadaṃ. Ādissate asminti ādāso, ṇo, āpubbo disa pekkhane, issā. Dippati etthāti dappaṇo, yu, issattaṃ. Makuropyatra.

Two terms for a mirror. The word is masculine. That in which one is seen is 'ādāso', with the suffix 'ṇa', from the root 'dis' with the prefix 'ā' in the sense of seeing. That in which one shines is 'dappaṇo', with the suffix 'yu'. 'Makura' is also used here.

Dvayaṃ cammamayakīḷāguḷake. Vāsabhavanehi yuvatīhi saha kīḷāsambhavā ñeyyā, tappakkamenassābhidhānaṃ. Guḍi vedhane, ṇuko, usse, gudda kīḷāyameva vā, tadā dassa ṇḍo. Kadi avhāne rodane ca, ṇuko, kudda kīḷāyameva vā, ussattaṃ, pubbadassa no.

Two terms for a leather play-ball. They are known to arise from the play of young women in the dwellings of Vāsava; hence their designation by this method. 'Guṇḍaka' is from the root 'guḍ' in the sense of piercing, with the suffix 'ṇuka'; or from the root 'gudda' in the sense of play itself, in which case 'da' becomes 'ṇḍa'. 'Kanduka' is from the root 'kad' in the sense of calling and crying, with the suffix 'ṇuka'; or from the root 'kudda' in the sense of play itself, with a sound change, and the preceding 'da' is elided.

Dvayaṃ bījanīmatte. Vaṭi vibhājane, tālavaṇṭehi katattā tālavaṇṭaṃ. Vaṇṭaṃ nāma bījanādikaraṇatthaṃ visuṃ bhājito tālapattāvayavo, tālavaṇṭasaddassa yathāvuttavacanatthayogepi sati saññāsaddattā bījanīsāmaññe pavatti veditabbā. Yadā pana tālavaṇṭehi katabījanimeva vattumicchati, tadā ekena tālasaddena visesetvā “tālatālavaṇṭa”nti vattabbaṃ. Yathā – tilassa telaṃ, sugatassa sugatacīvaranti. Bijanti vāyunā yojayanti yāya[M 0.0220], sā bījanī, yu, nadādi, yuja yoge, yassa vo, ussī, vaja gatiyaṃ vā assī. Byajanaṃpyatra.

Two terms for a fan. 'Vaṇṭa' is from the root 'vaṭ' in the sense of dividing. 'Tālavaṇṭa' is so called because it is made from palm-leaf segments. A 'vaṇṭa' is a part of a palm leaf separated for the purpose of making fans and so forth. Even though the word 'tālavaṇṭa' has the meaning stated, it should be understood to function as a general term for 'bījanī' (fan) due to its being a conventional term. But when one wishes to specifically state a fan made of palm-leaf segments, then one should say 'tālatālavaṇṭa', qualifying it with the word 'tāla', as in 'oil of sesame' (tilassa telaṃ), or 'the Sugata's robe' (sugatassa sugatacīvaraṃ). That by which they cause wind or join with wind is 'bījanī', with the suffix 'yu', belonging to the nadādi class; or from 'yuj' in the sense of joining, where 'ya' becomes 'va'; or from 'vaj' in the sense of going. 'Byajana' is also used here.

317. Dvayaṃ caṅkoṭake. Kuṭa chedane, sakatthe ko. Karaḍi bhājanatthe, ko. Dvayaṃ kappūrādisampuṭe sarūpakādisampuṭe (ka.). Samuggacchatīti samuggo, kvi. Puṭa saṃsilesane, bhūvādi, a.

317. Two terms for a casket. 'Koṭaka' is from the root 'kuṭ' in the sense of cutting, with the suffix 'ka' in its own sense. 'Karaṇḍaka' is from the root 'karaḍ' in the sense of a vessel, with the suffix 'ka'. Two terms for a container for camphor and so forth. That which goes up together is 'samuggo', with the suffix 'kvi'. 'Puṭa' is from the root 'puṭ' in the sense of joining together, belonging to the bhūvādi class, with the suffix 'a'.

Pajjaddhaṃ methune. Gāmavāsīnaṃ dhammo ācāro gāmadhammo, gāmasaddena cettha gāmavāsino vuttā, yathā “gāmo āgato”ti. Asataṃ asappurisānaṃ dhammo, saddhammapaṭipakkhattā vā asaddhammo. Byaya khaye, byayati balametenāti byavāyo, majjhe vāgamo, atha vā vigato ayo vuḍḍhi tasmāti avāyo, atisayo avāyo byavāyo. Mithunānaṃ itthipurisānaṃ samānacchandānaṃ ācāro methunaṃ, tadaññesu upacāro, ramu ramane, bhāve, karaṇe vāti.

Half a verse on sexual intercourse. The custom or practice of villagers is 'gāmadhammo'; here, by the word 'gāma' (village) are meant villagers, as in 'the village has come'. The practice of the bad and unprincipled is 'asaddhammo', or so called because it is opposed to the true Dhamma. 'Byavāyo' is from the root 'byay' in the sense of decay. That by which strength decays is 'byavāyo', with the insertion of 'v' in the middle. Or, that from which increase (ayo) has gone is 'avāyo'; excessive 'avāyo' is 'byavāyo'. The practice of couples—men and women who share the same desire—is 'methuna'; in other contexts, this is a metaphorical usage. 'Rati' is from the root 'ram' in the sense of delighting, forming a noun of state (bhāva) or instrument (karaṇa).

318. Catukkaṃ vivāhe. Vaha pāpuṇe, ṇo. Upapubbo yamu uparame, a. Aññamaññassa pāṇino gahaṇaṃ pāṇiggaho. Nī naye, a. Ubbāho, pāṇipīḷanaṃpyatra.

318. Four terms for marriage. 'Vivāha' is from the root 'vah' in the sense of obtaining, with the suffix 'ṇa'. 'Upayama' is from the root 'yam' with the prefix 'upa' in the sense of restraint, with the suffix 'a'. The mutual taking of hands is 'pāṇiggaho'. 'Pariṇaya' is from the root 'nī' in the sense of leading, with the suffix 'a'. 'Ubbāho' and 'pāṇipīḷanaṃ' are also used here.

Dhammakāmatthā tayo vaggā vuccante. Āgamaniddiṭṭho samācāro dhammo. Visayavisayisannipātajaṃ sukhaṃ kāmo. Sabbopakaraṇaṃ [M 0.0221] attho. Samokkhakā mokkhasahitā dhammakāmatthā catubbaggo vuccante. Tivaggena visaṃyutto mokkho nibbānaṃ. Tulyabalehi pana dhammādīhi catūhi padhānehi catubhadra amara 17.57 muccate.

The three groups, namely Dhamma, Kāma, and Attha, are spoken of. Right conduct indicated by tradition is Dhamma. Pleasure born from the conjunction of object and sense-faculty is Kāma. All that is of use is Attha. Dhamma, Kāma, and Attha, together with liberation (mokkha), are called the fourfold group. Liberation, disconnected from this threefold group, is Nibbāna. But when the four principal factors beginning with Dhamma are of equal strength, this is called the 'fourfold good' (catubhadra).

319-320. Dvayaṃ khujje. Kucchitaṃ vajjatīti khujjo, kassa kho, valopo, ṇo. Gaḍi nindāyaṃ, ulo.

Two terms for a hunchback. One who avoids what is blameworthy (kucchitaṃ) is 'khujjo'; 'ka' becomes 'kha', 'va' is elided, and the suffix is 'ṇa'. 'Gullako' is from the root 'gaḍ' in the sense of blaming, with the suffix 'ula'.

Tikaṃ rassasarīre puggale. Rasa sadde, so. Byāmappamāṇaṃ na lātīti vāmano, nerutto. Rasso ca vāmano ceti dvando. Lakuḍi vāmanatthe, a, sakatthe ko, laku viya ghaṭikā viya ḍeti pavattetīti vā lakuṇḍako.

Three terms for a short-bodied person. 'Rasso' is from the root 'ras' in the sense of sounding, with the suffix 'sa'. One who does not attain the measure of a fathom is 'vāmano' (dwarf); this is an etymological explanation. 'Rasso' (short) and 'vāmano' (dwarf) form a compound. 'Lakuṇḍako' is from the root 'lakuḍ' in the sense of dwarf, with the suffix 'a', and 'ka' in its own sense. Or, 'lakuṇḍako' is so called because it moves or turns like a stick (laku) or like a pot (ghaṭikā).

Pañcakaṃ paṅguḷajane. Parena aṅgatīti paṅguḷo, ulo. Pīṭhena sappati sīlenāti pīṭhasappī, sappa gamane, upaccaye paṅgu, dvīsu. Chinno gamanādiiriyāpatho yassāti so chinniriyāpatho. Vigatā akkhasadisā jaṅghā yassāti pakkho, yathā hi rathassa akkhe bhinne gamanaṃ na sijjhati, tatheva tassāpi akkhajaṅghāya bhinnāyāti opammasaṃsandanaṃ.

Five terms for a lame person. One who goes by means of another's limb is 'paṅguḷo', with the suffix 'ulo'. One who creeps with the buttocks or by habit is 'pīṭhasappī'; 'sappati' is from the root 'sapp' in the sense of going; 'paṅgu' is derived in two ways by accumulation. One whose gait and other postures are cut off is 'chinniriyāpatho'. One whose leg, like an axle, is gone is 'pakkho'; just as a chariot cannot move when its axle is broken, so too for him whose axle-like leg is broken—thus the comparison of the simile.

Dvayaṃ khañje. Khaji gativekalye, bhūvādi, khañjatīti, a. Khoḍi gatipaṭighāte, ko.

Two terms for 'lame' or 'limping'. The root 'khaj' is in the sense of defective movement, of the bhūvādi class; from this comes 'khañjati' (he limps), with the suffix 'a'. The root 'khoḍ' is in the sense of obstruction of movement, with the suffix 'ko'.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0222] avākye. Vattumasakkuṇeyyattā migasadisoti mūgo, issū. Suññaṃ vaco yassāti so suññavaco.

Two terms for 'mute' or 'speechless'. Because he is unable to speak, he is like a deer, hence 'mūgo' (mute), with the suffix 'issū'. One whose speech is empty is 'suññavaco'.

Hatthādivaṅko puriso “kuṇī”tyuccate. Kuṇanaṃ kuṇo hatthādivekalyaṃ, tametassatthīti kuṇī, atha vā kuṇa saṅkocane, ī, kucchitaṃ nayatīti vā kuṇī, ṇattaṃ, “hatthena kuṇī, pādena kuṇī”iccādipayogā. Dvayaṃ apāṅgadassane jane. Vala saṃvaraṇe, iro. Kucchitaṃ karotīti kekaro, usse.

A man with a crooked hand, etc., is called 'kuṇī'. The bending is 'kuṇa', a disability of the hand, etc.; one who has this is 'kuṇī'. Alternatively, the root 'kuṇ' is in the sense of contracting, with the suffix 'ī'. Or, one who leads defectively is 'kuṇī', with 'ṇattaṃ' (a grammatical change), as in usages like 'kuṇī by hand', 'kuṇī by foot'. Two terms for a person with a squinting eye. The root 'val' is in the sense of covering or restraining, with the suffix 'iro'. One who acts defectively is 'kekaro', with the suffix 'usse'.

321. Dvayaṃ nikkesasīse. Nikkesaṃ sīsametassa, khala khalane, sañcaye ca, āṭo, nikkesattā khaṃ tucchaṃ sīsaṃ lātīti khallāṭo, ṭo.

321. Two terms for a bald head. One whose head is without hair is 'nikkesa'. The root 'khal' is in the sense of shaking or stumbling, and accumulating, with the suffix 'āṭo'. Alternatively, 'khallāṭo' is so called because, due to being hairless, it takes on an empty head, with the suffix 'ṭo'.

Tikaṃ khuramuṇḍasīse. Muṇḍa khaṇḍane, bhūvādi, a. Bhaṇḍa paribhāsane, u, sakatthe ko, muṇḍako, muṇḍikopyatra.

Three terms for a shaven head. The root 'muṇḍ' is in the sense of cutting, of the bhūvādi class, with the suffix 'a'. The root 'bhaṇḍ' is in the sense of speaking or reviling, with the suffix 'u', and 'ko' in its own sense, hence 'muṇḍako'. 'Muṇḍiko' is also applicable here.

Akkhīnaṃ majjhe ekenākkhinā suñño kāṇo nāma, kaṇa saddagatinimīlanesu, ṇo, kaṇati nimīlatīti kāṇo, taṃ panassa nimīlanaṃ ekenevakkhinā. Aṭṭhakathādīsu pana “kāṇoti ekacchikāṇo, ubhayacchikāṇo vā”ti saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.132 vuttaṃ. Dvayena akkhidvayena suñño andho nāma, andha dassanūpasaṃhāre, a.

One who is deficient in one eye is called 'kāṇa'. The root 'kaṇ' is in the sense of sounding, going, or closing, with the suffix 'ṇo'. One who closes an eye is 'kāṇa', and that closing of his is with one eye. However, in commentaries, etc., it is said: 'kāṇa' means one-eyed or blind in both eyes. One who is deficient in both eyes is called 'andha', from the root 'andh' in the sense of loss of sight, with the suffix 'a'.

322. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0223] naṭṭhasotappasāde. Bandha bandhane, iro. Nalopo. Suti kaṇṇo hīno vikalo yassāti sutihīno. Eḷopyatra.

322. Two terms for one with impaired hearing. From the root 'bandh' in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'iro' and elision of 'na', comes 'badhira'. One whose ear (suti/kaṇṇa) is deficient or impaired is 'sutihīno'. 'Eḷa' is also applicable here.

Tikaṃ gilānasāmaññe. Gila hāsakkhaye, yu, byādhirogosañjāto yassa byādhito. Ata sātaccagamane, adhikaraṇe, kattari vā uro, āturo, dīghādi. Āmayāvī, vikato, apaṭu, abbhamito, abbhāntopyatra.

Three terms for general sickness. From the root 'gil' in the sense of wasting away, with the suffix 'yu', comes 'gilāna'. One in whom disease and sickness have arisen is 'byādhito'. From the root 'at' in the sense of continuous going, with the suffix 'uro' in the locative or agent case, comes 'āturo', with lengthening, etc. 'Āmayāvī', 'vikato', 'apaṭu', 'abbhamito', and 'abbhānto' are also applicable here.

Ummādo vātādipakopo rogaviseso, tabbati ummatto, mada ummāde, uggatehi vātādidosehi madayatīti ummādo, ṇo. Khujjādayo ummattantā vāccaliṅge yuttatāya vāccaliṅgikā, yathā – khujjo puriso, khujjā itthī, khujjaṃ napuṃsakaṃ. Ummatto puriso, ummattā itthī, ummattaṃ napuṃsakaṃ.

'Ummāda' is a specific disease, a derangement caused by the disturbance of wind, etc. One afflicted by it is 'ummatta'. The root 'mad' is in the sense of madness; 'ummāda' is so called because it maddens due to aggravated humours such as wind, etc., with the suffix 'ṇo'. The words from 'khujja' to 'ummatta' take the gender of the noun they qualify; for example: 'khujjo puriso' (a hunchbacked man), 'khujjā itthī' (a hunchbacked woman), 'khujjaṃ napuṃsakaṃ' (a hunchbacked neuter thing); 'ummatto puriso' (a mad man), 'ummattā itthī' (a mad woman), 'ummattaṃ napuṃsakaṃ' (a mad neuter thing).

323. Navakaṃ rogamatte. Taki kicchajīvane, bhūvādi, ā bhuso taṅkatīti ātaṅko, a. Ama roge, yo, maya gatimhi vā, atha vā ama roge, curādi, āmayati rujjatīti āmayo, a, kāritalopābhāvo. Vidha vijjhane, vijjhatīti byādhi, i, akāravaṇṇāgamo, bādha vibādhāyaṃ vā, tadā yāgamo, vividhā vā ādhayo manopīḷā yasmiṃsa [M 0.0224] byādhi, “pume ādhi mānasī byathā”ti amara 8.28 hi amarakose vuttaṃ. Rogegado, kuverāyudhe gadā, gado bhātharikaṇhassa, “āmaye cāyudhe gadā”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe. Ruja roge, kattari ṇo, rujā itthī. Gilānassa bhāvo gelaññaṃ. Kala gatisaṅkhyānesu, na kalati yena taṃ akalaṃ, tameva akallaṃ, lo. Bādha vibādhāyaṃ, bhūvādi, a. Upatāpopyatra.

323. Nine terms regarding disease. The root 'tak' is in the sense of difficult living, of the bhūvādi class; 'ātaṅka' (affliction) is so called because it greatly afflicts (ā taṅkati), with the suffix 'a'. 'Āmaya' (disease) is from the root 'am' (to be sick), with the suffix 'yo'; or from 'may' (to go); or again from 'am' (to be sick), of the curādi class, meaning it causes pain (āmayati), with the suffix 'a', and without the elision of the causative sign. 'Byādhi' (sickness) is from 'vidh' (to pierce), meaning it pierces (vijjhati), with the suffix 'i' and the addition of the vowel 'a'; or from 'bādh' (to obstruct), in which case there is the addition of 'yā'. Or 'byādhi' is that in which there are various mental afflictions (ādhi), as it is said in the Amarakośa: “In the masculine, 'ādhi' means mental pain.” 'Roga' and 'gada' (disease). 'Gadā' also refers to Kubera's weapon, and 'Gada' is the brother of Kaṇha, as it is said in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: “'Gadā' means disease and weapon.” 'Rujā' (pain) is from 'ruj' (to be sick), with the suffix 'ṇo' in the agentive sense; 'rujā' is feminine. 'Gelañña' is the state of being sick. 'Akalla' (unfit) is from 'kal' (to move, to count), meaning that by which one does not move; from 'akalaṃ' it becomes 'akallaṃ', with the suffix 'la'. 'Ābādha' (affliction) is from 'bādh' (to obstruct), of the bhūvādi class, with the suffix 'a'. 'Upatāpa' (affliction) is also included here.

Dvayaṃ khayaroge, rasādisattadhātuyo sosayatīti soso, susa sosane, divādi, ṇo. Khi khaye, khayatīti, a. Yakkhā, rājayakkhāpyatra. Yakkha pūjāyaṃ, curādi.

Two terms for wasting disease. 'Sosa' (consumption) is so called because it dries up the seven bodily elements beginning with 'rasa'; from the root 'sus' (to dry), of the divādi class, with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Khaya' (wasting) is from the root 'khi' (to waste), meaning it wastes away, with the suffix 'a'. 'Yakkha' and 'rājayakkha' are also included here. The root 'yakkha' is in the sense of worship, of the curādi class.

324. Dvayaṃ nāsaroge. Apihitā nāsā anenāti pīnāso, pīnasopi. Upasaggato nāsāya bahubbīhimhi nasādesaṃ kubbanti pāṇini 5.4.119, apissākāralopo vaṇṇanāso, rassassa dīghatā. “Soso yakkhā rājayakkhā, patīssāyo tu pīnaso, āpīnaso patissāyo”ti rabhaso. Patissayopyatra. Vejjaganthe imesaṃ pīnasapatissāyānaṃ bhedo abhihito –

324. Two terms for nasal disease. 'Pīnāsa' (nasal catarrh) is so called because the nose is obstructed by it (apihitā nāsā anena); 'pīnasa' is also used. Due to a prefix, in a bahubbīhi compound, 'nāsā' is replaced by 'nasa'; there is also elision of a vowel, loss of a letter, and lengthening of the short vowel. Rabhasa says: “Sosa, yakkha, rājayakkha; patissāya, however, is pīnasa; āpīnasa is patissāya.” 'Patissayo' is also included here. In medical texts, the distinction between 'pīnāsa' and 'patissāya' is explained as follows:

Ānahyate yassa visussate ca,

Kilidyate dhūpati ceva nāsā;

Na ñāyate gandharase ca jantu,

Duṭṭhaṃ vijaññā tamapīnasenāti.

“Whose nose is obstructed and dries up, whose nose becomes wet and emits vapor, and a person cannot perceive scents or tastes—one should know that person to be afflicted with apīnasa.”

Ānaddhā [M 0.0225] pihitā nāsā,

Tanusāvappasekinī;

Galatāloṭṭhasoso ca,

Nittodo saṅkhakadvaye;

Bhave saro paghāto ca,

Patissāyoti lakkhitoti.

“Nose obstructed and blocked, with thin and sparse discharge; and dryness of the throat, palate, and lips; constant pain in both temples; and there is loss of voice—these are known as the signs of patissāya.”

Iha tvabhedenottaṃ. Patipubbo sidhātu rujatyattho. Nāsikāya jāto rogo nāsikārogo.

Here, however, it is stated without distinction. The root 'si' preceded by 'pati' has the meaning of ‘to be sick’. A disease arising in the nose is 'nāsikārogo'.

Ghāne pavatto assavo siṅghānikā nāma, siṅgha āghāne, bhūvādi, siṅghatīti siṅghānaṃ, yu, tattha jātā siṅghānikā. Ā punappunaṃ savati sandatīti assavo, sū abhisave. Dvayaṃ vaṇamatte. Ara gamane, u, aru, napuṃsakeyeva. Vaṇa gattavicuṇṇane, curādi, a, vaṇo, anitthī. Dvayaṃ phoṭe. Phuṭa saṃsilesane, bhūvādi, phoṭo, ṇo. Pīḷa vibādhāyaṃ, curādi, ṇvu, “itthiyamato āpaccayo”ti ā, pīḷako, pīḷakā, pīḷakaṃ, tīsvapi, tathā phoṭo.

A discharge occurring in the nose is called 'siṅghānikā'. From the root 'siṅgh' (to sniff), of the bhūvādi class; 'siṅghānaṃ' is so called because it is sniffed (siṅghati), with the suffix 'yu'; 'siṅghānikā' is that which arises there. 'Assavo' (discharge) is so called because it flows and streams repeatedly (ā punappunaṃ savati sandati), from the root 'sū' (to flow). Two terms for a wound. 'Aru' (wound) is from the root 'ar' (to go), with the suffix 'u'; it is only neuter. 'Vaṇa' (wound) is from the root 'vaṇ' (to tear the body), of the curādi class, with the suffix 'a'; 'vaṇo' is not feminine. Two terms for a blister. 'Phoṭo' (blister) is from the root 'phuṭ' (to adhere), of the bhūvādi class, with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Pīḷaka' (pustule) is from the root 'pīḷ' (to afflict), of the curādi class, with the suffix 'ṇvu'; by the rule “in the feminine, the suffix 'ā' follows a stem ending in 'a',” the feminine form is 'pīḷakā'. The word can be in all three genders, and likewise 'phoṭo'.

325. Dvayaṃ pakkavaṇādīsu sañjātaduggandhavisese. Pubba pūraṇe, bhūvādi, a. Pūya visaraṇe, duggandhe ca, bhūvādi.

325. Two terms for the particular foul-smelling substance that arises in festering sores, etc. 'Pubba' (pus) is from the root 'pubb' (to fill), of the bhūvādi class, with the suffix 'a'. 'Pūya' (pus) is from the root 'pūy' (to spread, and to be foul-smelling), of the bhūvādi class.

Dvayaṃ lohitanissaraṇaroge. Rattassa lohitassa saṇṭhānamatikkamitvā saraṇaṃ gamanaṃ rattātisāro. Pakkhandati nissaratīti pakkhandikā. Kamu padavikkhepe. “Itthiyamatiyavo vā”titi. “Pakkamādīhinto ce”ti ettha cakārena tissanti, dhātvantalopo ca, sakatthe ko. Dvitte. Yadādinā parakakārassa kho, pakkhandikā.

Two terms for diseases involving bloody discharge. 'Rattātisāro' (bloody dysentery) is the flowing of red blood, going beyond its normal state. 'Pakkhandikā' (dysentery) is so called because it discharges (pakkhandati) and flows out (nissarati). The root 'kamu' is in the sense of striding. By the rule “Itthiyamatiyavo vā”. Here, by the 'ca' in “Pakkamādīhinto ce,” 'tissa' is understood, and there is elision of the root-ending, and the suffix 'ko' in its own sense. In reduplication, by the rule beginning “yadādinā,” the following 'ka' becomes 'kha'; hence 'pakkhandikā'.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0226] apamāre. Saraṇaṃ sāro, apagato sāro yena apamāro, sassa mo. Itaratra makārāgamo. Dvayaṃ pādabhede. Pādassa phoṭo bhedanaṃ daraṇaṃ pādaphoṭo, phuṭa bhede. Virūpo pādo etāya hetubhūtāyāti vipādikā. Samāsante ko, pubbākārassittaṃ, vidārīyamānattā vipajjamāno pādo assanti vā vipādikā.

Two terms for epilepsy. 'Saraṇaṃ' means 'sāro' (essence); 'apamāro' (epilepsy) is so called because its essence is gone (apagato sāro yena), with 'sa' becoming 'ma'. Elsewhere, there is the addition of the letter 'ma'. Two terms for foot ailments. 'Pādaphoṭo' (cracked foot) is the breaking, splitting, or tearing of the foot, from the root 'phuṭ' (to break). 'Vipādikā' (fissured foot) is so called because the foot becomes deformed due to it. At the end of a compound, the suffix 'ko' is used, and the preceding 'ā' becomes 'i'. Alternatively, 'vipādikā' is so called because one's foot is being torn and ruined.

326. Dvayaṃ vuḍḍhippattaṇḍakosaroge. Vuḍḍhippatto rogo vuḍḍhirogo. Vātapūritaṃ aṇḍaṃ koso vātaṇḍaṃ. Dvayaṃ thūlapādaroge. Ghanābhāvato sithilaṃ padaṃ sīpadaṃ, vaṇṇanāso, dīghādi. Bhāro pādo yassa, tassa bhāvo bhārapādatā.

326. Two terms for diseases involving swelling and scrotal enlargement. 'Vuḍḍhirogo' (swelling disease) is a disease that has attained swelling. 'Vātaṇḍaṃ' (wind-scrotum) is a scrotum inflated by wind. Two terms for elephantiasis. 'Sīpadaṃ' (elephantiasis) is a foot that is loose due to lack of density, with loss of a letter, and lengthening, etc. 'Bhārapādatā' (heaviness of foot) is the state of one whose foot is heavy.

Pañcakaṃ kaṇḍuyaṃ. Kaṇḍa bhedane, u, dīghe kaṇḍū, vadhūsaddova. Timhi kaṇḍūti, assū, curādittā yamhi kaṇḍūyā, yalopābhāvo. Khajja theyyakaraṇabyathanesu, bhūvādi, u. Yumhi kaṇḍūvanaṃ, assū. Uvādeso, dīgho ca.

Five terms for itching. 'Kaṇḍū' (itching) is from the root 'kaṇḍ' (to break), with the suffix 'u', and the vowel is lengthened, like the word 'vadhū'. With the suffix 'ti', it becomes 'kaṇḍūti'; with the suffix 'assū'. From the curādi class comes 'kaṇḍūyā' (itching), where there is no elision of 'ya'. 'Khajja' (itching) is from the root 'khajj' (to chew, to steal, to cause pain), of the bhūvādi class, with the suffix 'u'. With the suffix 'yu', it becomes 'kaṇḍūvanaṃ' (itching); with the suffix 'assū'. There is the substitution of 'va' for 'u', and lengthening.

327. Tikaṃ kacchuyaṃ. Yā “khasurogo”ti vuccati. Pātyattānanti pāmaṃ, mana, pāmāpyatthi, pulliṅgo, rājādi, visesena tacchati kāsanti vitacchikā, taccha tanukaraṇe, ṇvu[M 0.0227], “vivacchikā” viccaccikā (amara 16.53) tipi pāṭho. Vaccha paribhāsanatajjanesu, bhūvādi. Kaca bandhane, u, cassa chattaṃ, dvittādi. Tilakāḷakantaṃ dvayaṃ dvayaṃ samatthaṃ. Tatra dvayaṃ sothe. Su gativuḍḍhīsu, bhūvādi, tho. Thupaccaye sayathu, ussattaṃ, yāgamo ca. Sophopyatra. Sokaṃ phāyati bahulaṃ karotīti sopho, phāya vuḍḍhiyaṃ, phāyassa pho, nerutto.

327. Three terms for scabies, which is also called 'khasuroga'. 'Pāmaṃ' (scabies) is so called because it causes one to fall (pātyattānaṃ); it is also 'pāmā', masculine, of the rājādi group. 'Vitacchikā' (scabies) is so called because it especially scratches (visesena tacchati kāsanti); from the root 'taccha' (to thin), with the suffix ṇvu; there is also the reading 'vivacchikā'. The root 'vaccha' is in the sense of reproaching and threatening, of the bhūvādi class. 'Kacchu' is from the root 'kaca' (to bind), with the suffix u; 'ca' becomes 'cha', with reduplication, etc. The two terms, 'tilaka' and 'kāḷaka', are each competent. Therein, two terms for swelling. 'Sotha' (swelling) is from the root 'su' (to move, to grow), of the bhūvādi class, with the suffix 'tho'. With the suffix 'thu', 'sayathu' (swelling) is formed; there is the raising of the vowel to 'u' and the insertion of 'y'. 'Sopho' is also included here. 'Sopho' (swelling) is so called because it greatly increases sorrow (sokaṃ phāyati); from the root 'phāya' (to grow), 'phāya' becomes 'pho', an etymological formation.

Dvayaṃ arisaroge. Amaṅgalatāya du ninditaṃ nāmamassa dunnāmaṃ, sakatthe, kucchāyaṃ vā ko, dīghakosikāyaṃ dunnāmā, itthī. Ari viya sasati hiṃ satīti arisaṃ, sasa hiṃsāyaṃ, kvi, ara gamane vā, iso. Dvayaṃ vamanaroge. Chadda vamane, curādi, ṇvu. Vamu uggiraṇe, thu. Vamidhupyatra. Chaddikā, vami itthiyaṃ, vamathu pume.

Two terms for hemorrhoids. 'Dunnāmaṃ' (hemorrhoids) is so called because its name is censured due to its inauspiciousness; this is in its own sense, or with the suffix 'ko' in the sense of 'bad'. 'Dunnāmā', feminine, is found in the Dīghakosikā. 'Arisaṃ' (hemorrhoids) is so called because it harms like an enemy (ari viya sasati hiṃsati); from the root 'sasa' (to harm), with the suffix kvi; or from the root 'ara' (to go), with the suffix 'isa'. Two terms for the disease of vomiting. 'Chaddana' is from the root 'chadda' (to vomit), of the curādi class, with the suffix ṇvu. 'Vamathu' is from the root 'vamu' (to eject), with the suffix 'thu'. 'Vamathu' is also included here. 'Chaddikā' and 'vami' are feminine; 'vamathu' is masculine.

328-329. Dvayaṃ paritāpe. Du paritāpe, tanādi, thu. Paritapanaṃ santāpanaṃ paritāpo. Dvayaṃ tilakāḷake. Tilasaṇṭhānaṃ viya jāyatīti tilako. Tilaṃ viya kāḷo hutvā jāyatīti tilakāḷako.

328-329. Two terms for distress. The root 'du' is in the sense of distress, of the tanādi class, with the suffix 'thu'. 'Paritāpo' (distress) is heating and burning. Two terms for moles or dark spots. 'Tilako' (mole) is so called because it arises with the appearance of a sesame seed. 'Tilakāḷako' (dark mole) is so called because it arises, being black like a sesame seed.

Mahāvireko “visūcikā”tyuccate. Nissesato sucati gacchatīti sūcikā. Suci, suca gatiyaṃ, bhūvādi. Suca soceyye [M 0.0228] vā, nissesato socetīti visūcikā, visesena sūci viya vijjhatīti vā visūcikā. Bahumosaraṇattā mahanto vireko mahāvireko, rica viyojanasampucchanesu, ṇo.

Severe purging (mahāvireko) is called 'visūcikā'. 'Sūcikā' is so called because it passes away or goes completely (nissesato sucati gacchati). This is from the root 'suci' or 'suca' (to go), of the bhūvādi class. Or, from the root 'suca' (to purify), 'visūcikā' is so called because it completely purifies (nissesato soceti); or 'visūcikā' is so called because it pierces intensely, like a needle (visesena sūci viya vijjhati). 'Mahāvireko' is a great purging due to profuse discharge (bahumosaraṇattā); it is from the root 'rica' (to separate, to mix), with the suffix 'ṇo'.

Bhagandalādayo satta āmayantarā rogabhedā bhavanti. Tatra gudasamīpajo vaṇaviseso bhagandalā, itthī. Bhagaṃ yoni, taṃ dārayatīti rūḷhīto apaccayanto nipātito. Dara vidāraṇe, bhūvādi, latte bhagandalā. Bhagandaropyatra. Meho muttameho, so ca bahumuttatāya madhumeho, rattameho, sukkamehotyanekavidho. Miha secane, bhūvādi, mihati muttanti meho, ṇo. Jara roge. Bhūvādi, jaratīti, a. Jaro pasiddho. Kāsa saddakucchāyaṃ, dittiyañca, bhūvādi, kāsatīti kāso, ṇo, kucchitaṃ asatīti vā kāso, kuāpubbo. Sasa pāṇane, sasanaṃ sāso, bhusaṃ sasanametassatthīti vā sāso, kuṭa chedane, ṭho, kuṭṭhaṃ. Sāmaññena tacovikāre. Sukke tu sittaṃ. Sūla rujāyaṃ, bhūvādi, sūlaṃ. Viddadhi, asmarī, muttakicchādayopyanekā rogabhedā.

Fistula and others are seven further types of disease. Among them, 'bhagandalā' (fistula) is a particular kind of sore arising near the anus; it is feminine. 'Bhaga' means vulva; the word is derived by convention (rūḷhīto) as an irregular formation without a suffix (apaccayanto nipātito) from the notion that it tears it (taṃ dārayati). From the root 'dara' (to tear), of the bhūvādi class, 'bhagandalā' is formed with the addition of 'la'. 'Bhagandara' is also included here. 'Meho' (urinary disease) is 'muttameho', and due to excessive urination, it is of many kinds, such as 'madhumeho' (diabetes mellitus), 'rattameho' (hematuria), and 'sukkameho' (spermatorrhea). The root 'miha' is in the sense of wetting, of the bhūvādi class; 'meho' is so called because one urinates (mihati muttanti), with the suffix 'ṇo'. The root 'jara' is in the sense of disease. Of the bhūvādi class, from 'jarati' (it decays/makes ill), with the suffix 'a', comes 'jaro'. 'Jaro' (fever) is well-known. The root 'kāsa' is in the sense of making a sound, being bad, and also shining, of the bhūvādi class; 'kāso' (cough) is so called because one coughs (kāsatīti), with the suffix 'ṇo'. Or 'kāso' is so called because it badly consumes (kucchitaṃ asati), with 'ku' as a prefix. The root 'sasa' is in the sense of breathing; 'sasanaṃ' is breathing. Or 'sāso' (asthma) is so called because one has much breathing (bhusaṃ sasanam etassa atthi). 'Kuṭṭhaṃ' (leprosy) is from the root 'kuṭa' (to cut), with the suffix 'ṭho'. Generally, it refers to skin disorders. In the case of white leprosy, it is 'sittaṃ'. 'Sūlaṃ' (colic) is from the root 'sūla' (to cause pain), of the bhūvādi class. Abscess (viddadhi), calculus (asmarī), dysuria (muttakicchā), and many other types of diseases are also included.

Pajjaddhaṃ vejje. Āyubbedasaṅkhātaṃ vijjaṃ jānātīti vejjo, “ṇa rāgā tassedamaññatthesu cā”ti ṇo, vida ñāṇe vā, vindatīti vejjo, ṇyo, dyassa jo. Bhisajjati cikicchatīti bhisakko, a, jassa ko. Rogaṃ harati sīlenāti rogahārī, ṇī. Harasaddoyaṃ kevalopi ānayanāpanayanesu vattati “manoharo, dukkhaharo”iccādīsu, idha apanayane. Kita rogāpanayane, bhūvādi. Tikicchatīti tikicchako, chapaccayo, ṇvu, dvittādi. Agadakaropyatra, agadaṃ arogaṃ pāṇīnaṃ karotīti agadakaro, kammādimhi ṇo.

Half a verse on the physician. 'Vejjo' (physician) is so called because he knows the science (vijjaṃ) called Ayurveda. Or, from the root 'vida' (to know), 'vejjo' is so called because he finds (vindati), with the suffix 'ṇya', where 'dy' becomes 'j'. 'Bhisakko' (physician) is so called because he heals or treats (bhisajjati cikicchati), with the suffix 'a', where 'j' becomes 'k'. 'Rogahārī' (remover of disease) is so called because it is his nature to remove disease (rogaṃ harati sīlena), with the suffix 'ṇī'. This word 'hara' (remover), even by itself, is used in the senses of bringing and taking away, as in 'manoharo' (charming) and 'dukkhaharo' (remover of suffering); here, it is in the sense of taking away. The root 'kita' is in the sense of removing disease, of the bhūvādi class. 'Tikicchako' (healer) is so called because he treats (tikicchati), formed with the desiderative suffix 'cha', the agent suffix 'ṇvu', reduplication, etc. 'Agadakaro' is also included here; 'agadakaro' is so called because he makes beings free from disease (agadaṃ arogaṃ pāṇīnaṃ karoti), with the suffix 'ṇo' in the sense of agent, etc.

330. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0229] sallanīharaṇe vejje. Kāye paviṭṭhasarādisallassa nīharaṇo vejjo sallavejjo. Yathāvuttaṃ sallaṃ nīharaṇavasena kantati chindatīti sallakatto, kati chedane, to. Dvayaṃ paṭikāre. Tikicchanaṃ tikicchā, bhāve a. Patipubbo karoti tikicchāyaṃ, karato ririyā.

330. Two terms for a physician who removes foreign objects. 'Sallavejjo' (surgeon) is a physician who removes foreign objects, such as arrows, that have entered the body. 'Sallakatto' (surgeon) is so called because he cuts (kantati) or severs (chindati) the aforementioned foreign object in order to remove it; from the root 'kati' (to cut), with the suffix 'to'. Two terms for remedy or treatment. 'Tikicchā' (treatment) is the act of treating, with the suffix 'a' in the abstract sense. The root 'kar' preceded by 'paṭi' is used in the sense of treatment.

Catukkaṃ osadhe. Bhisajānamidaṃ bhesajjaṃ, ṇya. Na vijjate gado yasminti agado. Bhisajānamidaṃ bhesajaṃ, ṇo. Usa dāhe. Rogamosāpetīti osadhaṃ, dho, atha vā osadhī nāma asaṃyogadabbaṃ, tehi saṃyojitaṃ osadhaṃ. Jāyupyatra. Ji jaye, ṇu.

Four terms for medicine. 'Bhesajjaṃ' (medicine) is that which belongs to physicians, with the suffix 'ṇya'. 'Agado' (medicine) is so called because by means of it, there is no disease. 'Bhesajaṃ' (medicine) is that which belongs to physicians, with the suffix 'ṇo'. The root 'usa' is in the sense of burning. 'Osadhaṃ' (medicine) is so called because it burns away disease (rogam osāpeti), with the suffix 'dha'. Alternatively, 'osadhī' is an uncompounded substance, whereas 'osadhaṃ' is that which is compounded from them. 'Jāyu' is also included here. It is from the root 'ji' (to conquer), with the suffix 'ṇu'.

331. Tikaṃ ārogye. Anatthakārakattā kucchitākārena sarīre sentīti kusā, rogā, te lunāti chindatīti kusalaṃ. Āmayassābhāvo anāmayaṃ, abyayībhāvo. Arogassa bhāvo ārogyaṃ. Kusalānāmayārogyanti samāhāradvando. Dvayaṃ anāmayajane. Kala gatisaṅkhyānesu. Kalati yathāsukhaṃ sabbiriyāpathesūti kallo, lo. “Kālaṃ khamatīti kalyaṃ, arogatā, tassaṃ niyutto kalyo”ti aṅguttaranikāyaṭīkāyaṃ. Natthi āmayo yasmiṃ nirāmayo. Vuttopyatra. Vutti jīvitavutti pasatthā assatthīti vutto. Rogato niggatajane pana ullāgho, lāgha sāmatthiye, usaddoyaṃ rogavimutyattho. Narādittā, narappadhānattā ca naravaggo.

331. A triad of terms for health. Diseases (rogā) are called 'kusā' because they cause harm and lie in the body in a despicable manner. That which cuts or severs them is 'kusalaṃ' (health). The absence of illness is 'anāmayaṃ'; it is an indeclinable compound. The state of being without disease is 'ārogyaṃ'. 'Kusalānāmayārogyāni' is a collective compound. Two terms for a person free from illness. The root 'kala' is in the sense of movement and calculation. One who moves comfortably in all postures is 'kallo', with the suffix 'lo'. As stated in the Aṅguttaranikāya commentary: 'That which is fit for the time is 'kalyaṃ', meaning health; one endowed with that is 'kalyo'.' One in whom there is no illness is 'nirāmayo'. 'Vutto' is also a term here. 'Vutti' is livelihood; one who has a praised livelihood is 'vutto'. For a person who has recovered from disease, the term is 'ullāgho'; from the root 'lāgha' (to be able), with the prefix 'u' signifying freedom from disease. Because it begins with 'nara' and because humans are its main subject, this is the Naravagga (Chapter on Humans).

Naravaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The exposition of the Naravagga is concluded.

4. Catubbaṇṇavaggavaṇṇanā

4. Exposition of the Catubbaṇṇavagga.

332. Santatipariyantaṃ vaṃse. Kula santānabandhūsu, bhūvādi, ṇo, kulaṃ, vana sambhattiyaṃ, so. Saṃtanu vitthāre, ṇo. Abhimukhaṃ janetīti abhijano, ṇo. Go vuccati abhidhānaṃ, buddhi ca, te tāyatīti gottaṃ. Gotrampi. Gavaṃ saddaṃ tāyatīti vā gottaṃ, tā pālane. Anupubbo i gatiyaṃ, karaṇe a. Tanotismāti, santati, nalopo, itthiyaṃ.

332. The terms up to 'santati' are synonyms for lineage. The root 'kula' is in the sense of lineage and relatives, of the bhūvādi class; with the suffix 'ṇa', it becomes 'kulaṃ'. From the root 'vana' (to serve), in the sense of sharing, with the suffix 'sa', comes 'vaṃsa'. From the root 'tanu' with the prefix 'saṃ', in the sense of spreading, with the suffix 'ṇa', comes 'santāna'. 'Abhijano' (noble birth) is so called because one is born into a high station, with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Go' means name and also intellect; 'gottaṃ' (clan) is so called because it protects them. 'Gotraṃ' is also a valid form. Or, 'gottaṃ' is so called because it protects the name of the progenitor; from the root 'tā' (to protect). From the root 'i' (to go) with the prefix 'anu', in the sense of succession, with the suffix 'a', comes 'anvayo'. Because it extends, it is 'santati'; the 'na' is elided, and it is feminine.

Santati pantivitthāra-gottesu kavibhī matā;

Paramparā bhave cāpi, puttakaññāsu santati.

'Santati' is understood by poets to mean a line, expansion, and lineage; also succession, worldly existence, and offspring, both sons and daughters.

Khattiyādayo khattiyabrāhmaṇavessasuddā cattāro vaṇṇā kulāni bhavanti, ete hi aññamaññamasaṅkarato vaṇṇetabbato ṭhapetabbato vaṇṇāti vuccante. Vaṇṇa ṭhapane.

The khattiyas and others—khattiyas, brāhmaṇas, vessas, and suddas—are the four castes or families. They are called 'vaṇṇā' because they are to be described or established as unmixed with one another. The root 'vaṇṇa' is in the sense of establishing.

333-334. Chakkaṃ [M 0.0231] kulīne. Kulassāpaccaṃ kulino, ino apacce. Sobhano jano sajjano. Saparatthaṃ sādhetīti sādhu, sādha saṃsiddhimhi, u. Sabhāyaṃ sādhu sabhyo. Sādhvatthe yo. Aya gatiyaṃ. Ayitabbo upagantabboti ayyo, kammani yo. Mahākulassāpaccaṃ mahākulo, ṇo.

333-334. A set of six terms for one of high birth. 'Kulino' is an offspring of a family, with the suffix 'ina' in the sense of 'offspring'. A good person is a 'sajjano'. One who accomplishes their own and others' welfare is a 'sādhu'; from the root 'sādha' (to accomplish), with the suffix 'u'. One who is good in an assembly is a 'sabhyo', with the suffix 'yo' in the sense of 'good'. The root 'aya' is in the sense of movement. One who is to be approached or resorted to is an 'ayyo', with the suffix 'yo' in the passive sense. An offspring of a great family is a 'mahākulo', with the suffix 'ṇa'.

Bhūbhujantaṃ rājasāmaññe. Atitejavantatāya visesena rājate dibbateti rājā, rāja dittiyaṃ. Bhuyā bhūmiyā pati bhūpati, bhuṃ pāletīti vā bhūpati, pā rakkhaṇe,ti, rasso. Pathaviyā issaro patthivo, ṇo, dvittaṃ, ittañca. Jagatiṃ bhūmiṃ pāletīti jagatipālo, kammani ṇo. Disānaṃ pati disampati, disā, disaṭṭhe vā pāletīti disampati, rassattaṃ, niggahītāgamo ca. Bhuṃ bhūmiṃ bhuñjatīti bhūbhujo, bhuja pālanajjhoharaṇesu, idha pālane, rudhādi. Mahikhitopyatra. Khi nivāsagatīsu, mahiṃ akhi gatavā mahīkhito.

The terms up to 'bhūbhuja' are general terms for a king. Because of his great majesty, he shines and is resplendent with distinction, hence 'rājā' (king); from the root 'rāja' (to shine). 'Bhūpati' is the lord of the earth, or one who protects the earth; from the root 'pā' (to protect), with the suffix 'ti' and shortening of the vowel. The ruler of the earth is 'patthivo', with the suffix 'ṇa', doubling of the consonant, and the change of 'a' to 'i'. One who protects the world or the earth is 'jagatipālo', with the suffix 'ṇo' in the agent sense. The lord of the directions is 'disampati'; or one who protects the directions, with shortening of the vowel and the insertion of a nasal. One who protects or enjoys the earth is 'bhūbhujo'; from the root 'bhuja' (to protect or enjoy), here in the sense of protection, of the rudhādi class. 'Mahīkhito' is also a term here. The root 'khi' is in the sense of dwelling or movement; 'mahīkhito' means one who possesses the earth.

335. Pajjaddhaṃ muddhābhisitte jātikhattiye, “rājajacce ca khattiye”ti vacanato. Rañño khattiyassāpaccaṃ rājañño, ñño [M 0.0232] apacce. “Khattiyo tu virā khattaṃ, rājaññadvijaliṅgano”ti rabhasa, ratanakosesu pariyāyā. Khattassāpaccaṃ khattiyo, apacce iyapaccayo dissate, khettānaṃ adhipatibhūtattā vā khattiyotiādikappikarājā vuccati, tappabhavattā pana muddhābhisittesvapi taṃsamaññā, essattaṃ. Khattassāpaccaṃ khattaṃ, ṇo. Rajjāropanasamaye dakkhiṇāvaṭṭasaṅkhodakena gaṅgānītena muddhani khattiyakaññādīhi abhisittattā muddhābhisitto, paṭhamakhattiyo. Tappabhavatāya pana anabhisittā ca muddhābhisittākhyā, yathā – brahmabāhujassa vaṃse jātassāpi brahmabāhujo. Brahmabāhuto jātattā bāhujoti hi nikāyantarikānaṃ laddhi. Yasmiṃ pana rājini asesā sāmantā paṇamanti, so adhissarākhyo amara 18.2. Saṃ satto laggo anto yassā sā samantā, savisayānantarā bhūmi, samantāya ime sāmantā, anantararājāno.

335. A half-verse on the consecrated khattiya of noble birth, according to the phrase, "of royal birth and a khattiya." The offspring of a khattiya king is a rājañño; the suffix 'ñño' is in the sense of offspring. The phrases, "The khattiya is indeed a heroic protector, the royal noble marked as a twice-born," are synonyms in the Rabhasa and Ratanakosa. The offspring of a khatta is a khattiyo; the suffix 'iya' is seen in the sense of offspring. Or, because he is the lord of the fields, the primordial king is called a khattiyo. Due to that origin, however, this designation also applies to the consecrated ones; it is their essence. The offspring of a khatta is khattaṃ, with the suffix 'ṇo'. At the time of enthronement, because of being anointed on the head with water from a right-spiraling conch brought from the Gaṅgā by khattiya maidens and others, the first khattiya is a muddhābhisitto. Due to that origin, however, even the unconsecrated are named muddhābhisitta, just as one born in the lineage of Brahmabāhuja is also called Brahmabāhuja. Indeed, the doctrine of other schools is that one is a bāhuja because of being born from the arm of Brahmā. Moreover, the king to whom all neighboring rulers bow down is called an adhissara. That which has its interior connected and attached is samantā, the land immediately surrounding one's own domain. Those of the surrounding land are sāmantā, the adjacent kings.

Dvayaṃ cakkavattini. Sabbabhūmiyā issaro sabbabhummo, ṇyo. Puññopanītena cakkaratanena vattate asādhudamanikādirājavattaṃ anutiṭṭhatīti cakkavattī, ṇī, cakkaratanaṃ vatteti ākāse attano purato gamayatīti vā cakkavattī, puññacakkaṃ, catucakkaṃ vā sattesu vatteti, te vā asmiṃ vattetīti cakkavattī, cakkaratanuppādanatthaṃ dvādasavassacaritaṃ dasarājadhammaṃ vattametassatthīti vā cakkavattī. Tattha antojanasmiṃ balakāye dhammikārakkhāvaraṇaguttiyā saṃvidhānaṃ, khattiyesu, anuyuttesu, brāhmaṇagahapatikesu, negamajānapadesu, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu, migapakkhīsu, adhammakārapaṭikkhepo, adhanānaṃ dhanuppādanaṃ, samaṇabrāhmaṇe upasaṅkamitvā pañhapucchananti idaṃ dasavidhaṃ cakkavattivattaṃ, idameva ca gahapatike, pakkhijāte ca visuṃ katvā gahaṇavasena dvādasavidhampi dīpesu. Catūsvapi dīpesu āṇādhammacakkāni sattesu [M 0.0233] pavattetīti vā cakkavattī. Añño asabbabhummo anavakāso sāmanto bhūpo maṇḍalissaro nāma. Sayamāṇāpavattiṭṭhānavasena paricchinnasseva maṇḍalassa issaro, na sabbamaṇḍalassāti maṇḍalissarotipi. Ettha ca “sabbabhummo, cakkavattī”ti dvīhi nāmehi catudīpissaro rājā dīpito, idhānāgatepi saṅgahetvā kathitena adhissarapadena ekadīpissaro rājā, maṇḍalissarapadena padesissaro rājā dīpito. Atha vā maṇḍalissarapadena ekadīpissaro rājā, sesehi rājarājaññādīhi bāhujapariyantehi padesissaro dīpito.

Two terms for a wheel-turning monarch. The lord of all the earth is a sabbabhummo, with the suffix 'ṇyo'. He is called a cakkavattī because he rules by means of the wheel-treasure produced by his merit, and he observes the royal duties such as the subduing of the unrighteous; or because he causes the wheel-treasure to turn, making it go before him in the sky; or because he sets in motion the wheel of merit or the four wheels among beings, or they revolve for him; or because he possesses the twelve-year conduct and the ten royal virtues for the sake of producing the wheel-treasure. Herein, the tenfold duty of a wheel-turning monarch is: providing righteous protection, ward, and guard for his own people and his army; for khattiyas, attendants, brahmins and householders, town and country folk, ascetics and brahmins, and beasts and birds; the prevention of unrighteous action; providing wealth for the destitute; and approaching ascetics and brahmins to ask questions. This very duty, by taking householders and the class of birds separately, is also explained as twelvefold in the continents. Or, he is a cakkavattī because he sets in motion the wheels of command and Dhamma among beings in the four continents. Another, who is not a universal sovereign, a subordinate king, is a regional lord named maṇḍalissara. He is the lord of only a limited domain where his own command prevails, not of the entire domain, hence he is also called a maṇḍalissara. Herein, by the two names sabbabhummo and cakkavattī, the king who is lord of the four continents is indicated. By the term adhissara, stated by way of inclusion of what is not mentioned here, the king who is lord of a single continent is indicated. By the term maṇḍalissara, a regional ruler is indicated. Alternatively, by the term maṇḍalissara, the king who is lord of a single continent is indicated, and by the remaining terms from rāja and rājañña up to bāhuja, a regional ruler is indicated.

336. Dvayaṃ rājabhede. Sukhumatāya līnā apākaṭā chaviyo yesaṃ te licchavino. Licchavī ca vajjī cāti dvando. Dvayaṃ sammāsambuddhakule rājini. Purimatarasambhūte sakyakule sañjātattā sakyo, ṇo. Sakkopi. Sakye bhavo sākiyo, iyo, yalopo, dīgho ca.

336. Two terms in the classification of kings. Those whose skins are delicate, smooth, and not coarse are the Licchavino. Licchavī and Vajjī—this is a dvanda compound. Two terms for the king in the clan of the Perfectly Enlightened One. Because he was born in the Sakyan clan, which arose earlier, he is Sakyo, with the suffix 'ṇo'. Also Sakko. One who is of the Sakyans is Sākiyo, with the suffix 'iyo', the elision of 'ya', and lengthening.

Pañcakaṃ buddhaputtassāyasmato rāhulassa mātari. Bhadda kalyāṇe, sokhye ca. Kulācārarūpādivasena kalyāṇattā bhaddā. Kaccassāpaccaṃ kaccānā, apaccasaddoyaṃ niccaṃ napuṃsake putte, puttiyañca bhavatīti. “Rāhu viya candaṃ mama nikkhamanaṃ lātukāmo cāyaṃ me puttoti rāhuloti nāmena bhavitabba”nti manasi katvā “rāhu jāto, bandhanaṃ jāta”nti pitarā vutto sikkhākāmo āyasmā rāhuloyevettha rāhulo, tassa mātā rāhulamātā, bimbaṃ vuccati sarīraṃ, atisayavaṇṇasarīrayuttatāya bimbā, vamidhātumhā vā [M 0.0234] bo, vassa battaṃ. Yaso vuccati parivāro, kitti ca, te dhāretīti yasodharā, manādittā asso.

A pentad of terms for the mother of the Venerable Rāhula, the Buddha's son. Bhaddā is in the sense of kalyāṇa (auspicious) and sokhya (happiness). Because of her excellence in terms of family conduct, appearance, and so forth, she is Bhaddā. The offspring of Kacca is Kaccānā; this word for offspring is always neuter, and it occurs for a son and for a daughter. Having thought, "This son of mine desires to seize my going forth like Rāhu seizing the moon, therefore he should be named Rāhula," his father said, "A Rāhu is born, a fetter is born." The Venerable Rāhula, desirous of the training, is here called Rāhula. His mother is Rāhulamātā. Bimba means body; because she possessed a body of excellent complexion, she is Bimbā. Or, from the root 'vam', the suffix is 'ba', and 'va' becomes 'ba'. Yasa means retinue and also fame; because she bears them, she is Yasodharā. She has a pleasing splendor.

337-339. Yesaṃ khattiyānaṃ dhanaṃ sataṃ hoti, kīdisaṃ taṃ dhanaṃ? Nidhānagaṃ pathavādīsu nidhānavasena gataṃ pavattaṃ, tesaṃ dhanānaṃ sataṃ kahāpaṇānaṃ, kittakappamāṇānaṃ? Koṭīnaṃ sataṃ. Kena paricchedena? Heṭṭhimantena heṭṭhimakoṭṭhāsena, heṭṭhimaparicchedena vā koṭīnaṃ sataṃ hoti. Divasavaḷañjo divase divase vaḷañjitabbo pana kahāpaṇo vīsatambaṇamattaṃ hoti, te khattiyā “khattiyamahāsālā”tyuccante. Mahanto dhanasāro yesante mahāsālā, lattaṃ, ambaṇamatra ekādasadoṇamattaṃ.

337-339. For those khattiyas whose wealth is a hundred koṭis: what kind of wealth is that? Treasure gone to a treasury, that is, existing as treasure in the earth and so on. A hundred of their wealth in kahāpaṇas. Of what amount? A hundred koṭis. By what measure? By the lowest limit, by the lowest portion, or by the lowest measure, it is a hundred koṭis. However, the daily expenditure, the kahāpaṇa to be spent day by day, is the equivalent of twenty ambaṇas. Those khattiyas are called khattiyamahāsālas. Those who have great essential wealth are mahāsālas; the 'ra' becomes 'la'. Here, an ambaṇa is the measure of eleven doṇas.

Yesaṃ dvijānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ nidhānagāni nidhānavasena pavattāni asītikoṭidhanāni honti, divasavaḷañjo pana kahāpaṇo dasambaṇamattaṃ hoti, te dvijā “dvijamahāsālā”tyuccante.

For those twice-born, that is, brahmins, whose wealth, gone to a treasury and existing as treasure, amounts to eighty koṭis, and whose daily expenditure in kahāpaṇas is the equivalent of ten ambaṇas, those twice-born are called dvijamahāsālas.

Nidhānage, vaḷañje ca dhane tadupaḍḍhe tesaṃ dvijamahāsālānaṃ dhanassa upaḍḍhabhāge sati gahapatimahāsālā nāma siyuṃ, ubhayatrāpi heṭṭhimanteneva dhanaparicchedo.

When the wealth in the treasury and for expenditure is half, that is, a half-portion of the wealth of those dvijamahāsālas, they are called gahapatimahāsālas. In both cases, the measure of wealth is by the lowest limit.

340. Yo [M 0.0235] na hīno, na cukkaṭṭho, majjhimādhikārabyavaṭṭhito rājaputtasenāpatimahākaṇittharādi, so mahāmatto. Mahatī mattā paricchedo yassa mahāmatto, rūpabhedena paṭṭhānaṃ klīvaṃ.

340. He who is not inferior, not of low status, but is established in middle authority, such as a prince, a general, or a chief accountant, is a mahāmatta. A mahāmatta is one whose measure or limit is great. Due to a difference in form, the word paṭṭhānaṃ is neuter.

“Pakatiyaṃ mahāmatte, paññāyaṃ paramattani;

Napuṃsakaṃ padhānaṃ taṃ, ekatte tu’ttame sadā”ti.

"Regarding the great minister by nature, and the supreme meaning by wisdom; that principal term is neuter, but in the singular it is always supreme."

Rabhaso ca. “Mahāmatto, paṭṭhāno cā”ti tu puṃsakaṇḍe vopālito. Pakaṭṭhe tiṭṭhatīti paṭṭhānaṃ, yu abhidhānappadīpikā ṭīkā 983, 1123 gāthāsupi passitabbaṃ.

And Rabhasa. However, in Vopālita's masculine section, it is given as "mahāmatto and paṭṭhāno". Because it stands out prominently, it is paṭṭhānaṃ, with the suffix 'yu'.

Pañcakaṃ mantinimhi. Matippadhāno sacivo sahāyo. Itikattabbatāvadhāraṇaṃ manto, taṃyogā mantinī. Assatthyatthe inī, atha vā mantena nayatīti mantinī, atha vā mantayogā manti, netīti nī, manti ca nī cāti mantinī. “Matisacivamantinī”tipi pāṭho, tadā dvinnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vā dvando. Raññā saha jīvatīti sajīvo. Sacate samaveto bhavatīti sacivo. Saca samavāye, vo, ikārāgamo ca. Sabbakiccesu raññā mantena amā saha bhavatīti amacco, amāsaddoyaṃ nipāto sahatthe ccapaccayo. Sajīvamatte cāmaccasaddo vattati. Dvayaṃ senāpatimhi. Senaṃ nayatīti senānī. Camūnaṃ senānaṃ pati camūpati.

A pentad of terms for a minister. A companion, a friend, whose main quality is intelligence. Counsel (manta) is the determination of what is to be done; one connected with it is a mantinī. The suffix 'inī' is in the sense of 'possessing it'. Alternatively, one who leads by counsel is a mantinī. Or again, one connected with counsel is a manti, and one who leads is a nī; thus manti and nī make mantinī. There is also the reading 'matisacivamantinī'; in that case, it is a dvanda compound of two or three terms. One who lives with the king is a sajīvo. One who associates, is united, is a sacivo; from the root 'saca' (to associate), with the suffix 'vo' and the augment 'i'. In all affairs, one who is with (saha) the king through counsel, together (amā), is an amacco; this word 'amā' is an indeclinable in the sense of 'together', with the suffix 'cca'. The word amacco also applies to a mere companion. A dyad of terms for a general. One who leads the army is a senānī. The lord of the troops, that is, armies, is a camūpati.

341. Nyāsādīnaṃ [M 0.0236] iṇādānadāyavibhāgādīnaṃ vivādānaṃ vohārānaṃ upadaṭṭhari upadassite akkhadasso, akkhe vohāre passatīti akkhadasso, ṇo, dhammādhikaraṇiyo. Pucchāvivāko, pañhavivākopyatra.

341. Regarding the observer, the one who examines disputes and legal cases concerning deposits, the taking on of debt, the division of inheritance, and so on, he is an akkhadasso. He who sees into legal cases is an akkhadasso, with the suffix 'ṇo'; a judicial officer. Pucchāvivāko and pañhavivāko are also included here.

Pajjaḍḍhaṃ paṭihāre. Dvāre niyutto dovāriko, ṇiko, okārāgamo. Paṭiharati viññāyati tenāti paṭihāro, ṇo. Dvāre tiṭṭhatīti dvāraṭṭho, sakatthe ko. Dvārapālako. Dvāraṭṭhito, dassakopyatra.

The first half of the verse is about a doorkeeper. One appointed at the door is a 'dovārika', [formed with the] 'ṇika' [suffix], with the augment 'o'. He guards, he is known by that—thus he is a 'paṭihāra', [formed with the] 'ṇa' [suffix]. One who stands at the door is a 'dvāraṭṭha', [with the] 'ka' [suffix] in its own sense. 'Dvārapālaka', 'dvāraṭṭhita', and 'dassaka' are also here.

342. Rājūnaṃ aṅgarakkhagaṇo anīkaṭṭhoti mato. “Rakkhivaggo tu yo raññaṃ, so’nīkaṭṭho’bhidhīyate”ti amaramālāyañca, anīkena samūhena tiṭṭhatīti anīkaṭṭho, ṇo.

342. The troop of kings' bodyguards is considered 'anīkaṭṭha'. And in the Amarāmālā it is said: "That guard division of the king is called 'anīkaṭṭha'." One who stands with an army or troop is an 'anīkaṭṭha', [formed with the] 'ṇa' [suffix].

Dvayaṃ mahallake. Kañcukaṃ coḷaṃ, taṃyogā kañcukī. Sokaṃ vindatīti sovidallo. Vida lobhe, lo, kalopo. Thāpati, sovidopyatra. Dvayaṃ sevake. Pabhuno pacchā jīvatīti anujīvī, ṇī. Seva sevane, bhū, ṇvu. Atthīpyatra. Attha yācanāyaṃ. Atthanamattho, āsīso, taṃyogā atthī.

Two terms for a chamberlain. A 'kañcuka' is a tunic; from connection with that, [one is called] 'kañcukī'. One who gets sorrow is a 'sovidalla'. [From the root] 'vid' in the sense of 'to get', [with the suffix] 'la', and elision of 'ka'. 'Thāpati' and 'sovido' are also here. Two terms for a servant. One who lives in dependence on a master is an 'anujīvī', [formed with the] 'ṇī' [suffix]. [From the root] 'sev' in the sense of 'to serve', of the 'bhū' class, [with the] 'ṇvu' [suffix]. 'Atthī' is also here. [The root] 'atth' is in the sense of 'requesting'. 'Atthana' is a request, a blessing; from connection with that, [one is called] 'atthī'.

343. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0237] adhikamatte. Gāmesu adhikattā adhikā ikkhā anubhavanametassa ajjhakkho, issattaṃ. Adhikaṃ karotīti adhikato. Idaṃ dvayaṃ thāyukagopānaṃ dvinnampi nāmaṃ. Tatra ekagāme adhikato thāyuko, bahūsu gāmesvadhikato gopo. Vuttañcāmarakose “thāyukodhikato gāme, gopo gāmesu bhūrisū”ti. amara 18.7 Ruddenāpi vuttaṃ “gāmesvadhikate gopo, goṭṭhajjhakkhepi vallabho”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.7.

343. Two terms in the sense of 'superior'. Because of superiority in villages, this one's observation and experience is superior, [hence he is] an 'ajjhakkha' (overseer), [which implies] lordship. One who acts as a superior is an 'adhikato'. These two are names for both the 'thāyuka' and the 'gopa'. Among them, one in charge of one village is a 'thāyuka', and one in charge of many villages is a 'gopa'. And it is said in the Amarakosha: 'A 'thāyuka' is one in charge of a village, a 'gopa' in many villages.' By Rudra it is also said: 'A 'gopa' is one in charge of villages, and a 'vallabha' is an overseer of cow-pens'.

Dvayaṃ suvaṇṇarajatajjhakkhānaṃ dvinnampi nāmaṃ. Hiraññaṃ vuccati akatasuvaṇṇādi, tatra niyutto heraññiko. Kana dittigatikantīsu, nipubbo, kho, nikkho, suvaṇṇādivikāro, tatra niyogo nikkhiko. Visesato pana suvaṇṇajjhakkhe bhoriko. Bhūrisaddo suvaṇṇe, taṃyogā bhoriko. Rūpyājjhakkhenikkhiko, tasmā’ya’mubhayatrāpi heraññikoti sāmaññasmiṃyeva. Vuttañca –

Two names for both the overseers of gold and silver. 'Hirañña' is said to be unwrought gold, etc.; one appointed over that is a 'heraññika'. [From the root] 'kan' in the senses of 'luster, movement, and beauty', with the prefix 'ni', [and the suffix] 'kha', [it becomes] 'nikkha', a product of gold, etc.; one appointed over that is a 'nikkhika'. Specifically, however, the overseer of gold is a 'bhorika'. The word 'bhūri' is in the sense of gold; from connection with that, [one is called] 'bhorika'. The overseer of silver is a 'nikkhika'; therefore, 'heraññika' is indeed a general term for both. And it is said—

“Bhoriko kanakājjhakkho,

Rūpyā’jjhakkho tu nikkhiko”ti amara 18.7.

"A 'bhorika' is the gold superintendent, while a 'nikkhika' is the silver superintendent."

Sassa attano vijigīsabhūtassa desānantaro samantato maṇḍalībhūto rājā satturuccate ekatthābhinivesitattā. Tato paraṃ vijigīsabhūmyekantariko mitto ekatthakārittanopakārattā. Arivijigīsamittānaṃ pana maṇḍalānaṃ bahibhūto dūramaṇḍalaṭṭho vijigīsabhūmiyā accantabyavahito balādhikopi yo nāpakarotyupakāroti vā, sa udāsīno dūramaṇḍalattenopakārattā. Dūramaṇḍale [M 0.0238] āsatīti udāsīno, upubbo āsa upasevane, yu, assi, dāgamo ca. Sattumabhiyuñjamānassa vijigīsassa sattuhitāya yo paṇhiṃ gaṇhati piṭṭhito vattati, so paṇhiggāho. “Paṇhi pacchā padaṃ vijigīsassā”ti ratanakose. “Paṇhipāde byūhapiṭṭhe”ti tikaṇḍasesa 3.3.134 tikaṇḍaseso. “Paṇhi pacchimabhāge ca, pādamūlomadiṭṭhisu. Senāpiṭṭhe kumbhiyañce”ti tu nānatthasaṅgahe.

The king whose territory is immediately adjacent to one's own, who is a would-be conqueror, and who forms a circle all around, is called an enemy because he is intent on the same object. Beyond that, the one whose territory is separated by one from the land of the would-be conqueror is a friend, because he acts for the same purpose and renders assistance. But one who is outside the circles of the enemy, the conqueror, and the friend, standing in a distant territory, very far removed from the land of the would-be conqueror, who, even if more powerful, neither harms nor helps, is called neutral because of his position in a distant territory and his non-assistance. One who resides in a distant territory is 'udāsīna'; [from the root] 'ās' in the sense of 'to attend' with the prefix 'u', [the suffix] 'yu', [which becomes] 'asi', and the augment 'dā'. When a conqueror is attacking an enemy, one who seizes the rear or operates from behind for the enemy's benefit is called a 'pāṇhiggāha'. 'Paṇhi' (the rear) is the hindmost foot of the conqueror, states the Ratanakośa. 'Paṇhi' and 'pāda' (foot) [mean] the back of the battle array, says the Tikaṇḍaśeṣa. 'Paṇhi' [means] in the back part, and at the base of the foot and in unseen places; [also] the back of the army and the flank, according to the Nānātthasaṅgraha.

344-345. Diṭṭhantaṃ ripumhi. Mittapaṭipakkhattā amitto, rapatyavaṇṇaṃ rajateti ripu, u, ittaṃ, rapa, lapa, japa, jappa vacane vā. Veraṃ virodho yassatthīti verī, ī, dukkhahetuttā sapatti iva sapatto, ivatthe akārapaccayo. Ara gamane,ti, bhūvādittā āgamo. Sada sādane, tu, bhūvādi, sattu, yavādicuṇṇepi. Ara gamane, veramaratīti ari, rassanto i. Sapattādīnaṃ catunnaṃ dvando, “byañjano ca visaṃyogo”ti sutte caggahaṇena ekatakārassa lopo ca. Patiyamatthanaṃ paccattho, taṃyogā paccatthiko, patiyaṃ viparītagamanaṃ. Pantha gatiyaṃ, curādi. Paripantho parissavaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃyogā paripanthī. Paṭiviruddho pakkho sahāyo paṭipakkho, tathā vipakkho. Na hito ahito. Hiṃsāyaṃ ramatīti paratīti (?) paro, kvi. Paṭipakkhabhāvena amati gacchatīti paccāmitto, ama gamane, to, dvittaṃ. Natthi etasmā īti upaddavoti anīto[M 0.0239], mitto, tappaṭipakkho paccanīto, so eva paccanīko, tassa ko, yathā niyako. Virodhossatthīti virodhī, ī. Disa, dusa appītiyaṃ, divādi. Vidussanasīlatāya viddesī, dvittaṃ, issettaṃ. Dussatīti diso, a. Tapaccaye diṭṭho, dhātvantena saha ṭṭhādeso. Dvesaṇo, duhadayo, dassu, sāttavo, abhighātīpyatra.

344-345. An example concerning the enemy. Because of being opposed to a friend, [he is] an 'amitta' (non-friend). One who speaks ill or sullies is a 'ripu', [with the suffix] 'u', and the insertion of 'i'; or from the roots 'rap', 'lap', 'jap', 'japp' in the sense of 'speaking'. One who has enmity or opposition is a 'verī', [formed with the] 'ī' [suffix]. Because of being a cause of suffering, he is like a rival (sapatti), hence 'sapatta'; the 'a' suffix is in the sense of 'like'. [From the root] 'ar' in the sense of 'to go', [with the suffix] 'ti', and the augment 'ā' because it belongs to the 'bhūvādi' class. [From the root] 'sad' in the sense of 'to crush', [with the suffix] 'tu', of the 'bhūvādi' class, [it becomes] 'sattu', also [meaning] powder of barley, etc. [From the root] 'ar' in the sense of 'to go', one who goes to enmity is an 'ari', ending in a short 'i'. A dvanda compound of the four, 'sapatta' etc.; and by the 'ca' in the rule 'byañjano ca visaṃyogo', there is elision of one 'ta'. Opposition is 'paccattha'; one connected with that is 'paccatthika'; 'patiyaṃ' means going against. [From the root] 'panth' in the sense of 'to go', of the 'curādi' class. An obstacle or place of danger is a 'paripantha'; one connected with that is a 'paripanthī'. An opposing faction or companion is a 'paṭipakkha', likewise a 'vipakkha'. One who is not beneficial is an 'ahita'. One who delights in harming is a 'para', [formed with the] 'kvi' [suffix]. One who goes as an opposing party is a 'paccāmitta', [from the root] 'am' in the sense of 'to go', [with the suffix] 'ta', with doubling [of 'm']. There is no calamity from this one, hence 'anīti', a friend; its opposite is 'paccanīti', which is also 'paccanīka', [with the suffix] 'ka', like 'niyaka'. One who has opposition is a 'virodhī', [formed with the] 'ī' [suffix]. [From the roots] 'dis', 'dus' in the sense of 'dislike', of the 'divādi' class. Because of a nature of hating, [he is] a 'viddesī', with doubling [of 'd'], and the vowel 'i'. One who hates is a 'diso', [formed with the] 'a' [suffix]. With the 'ta' suffix, it becomes 'diṭṭha', with 'ṭṭha' replacing the end of the root. 'Dvesaṇa', 'duhadaya', 'dassu', 'sāttava', and 'abhighātī' are also here.

Dvayaṃ anukūlane. Anurodhanaṃ anurodho, ṇo. Rudha āvaraṇe. Anurūpaṃ pavattanaṃ anuvattanaṃ, vatu vattane, bhū, yu.

Two terms in the sense of 'compliance'. Complying is 'anurodha', [formed with the] 'ṇa' [suffix]. [From the root] 'rudh' in the sense of 'to obstruct'. Acting conformably is 'anuvattana', [from the root] 'vat' in the sense of 'to act', of the 'bhū' class, [with the] 'yu' [suffix].

346. Pañcakaṃ mittasāmaññe. Mida snehe, bhūvādi, to, vayasā tulyo vayaso, mūlavayosaddehi saññāyaṃ sapaccayo yapaccayo (?) pāṇini 4.4.91 suttaṃ passitabbaṃ, sabbakāriyesu saha vayatīti vā vayaso, vaya gamane, sahassa so vaṇṇavipariyayo. Saha ayati kiccesūti sahāyo, aya gamane, sahassa sābhāvo, yathā sahadhammiko. Saha vā hāni, ayo vā vuḍḍhi yassa sahāyo, tipadabahubbīhi, yathā parakkamādhigatasampadā. Atha vā hāni ca āyo ca hāyā, nilopo, te yassa atthi, so sahāyo, “sapakkhako, salomako”tyādīsu viya sasaddassa vijjamānatthattā. Sundaraṃ hadayametassāti suhadayo, alopo, dyassa jo, sova suhajjo. Saha parisahane. Parisahanaṃ adussanaṃ, kho, halopo, sakhā, rājādi, samāno khyāto patīto vā sakhā, yalopo, samānassa [M 0.0240] ca sabhāvo. Siniddho, sniddho, savayopyatra. Sakhyasattapadinā pana mettiyaṃ vattanti. Sakhimhi bhavaṃ sakhyaṃ. Sattahi padehi avagamyateti sattapadinaṃ sattapadīna (amara 18.12), ino.

346. Five terms in the general sense of 'friend'. [From the root] 'mid' in the sense of 'to be affectionate', of the 'bhūvādi' class, [with the] 'ta' [suffix]. One equal in age is a 'vayasa'; the 'sa' suffix is used with the root 'vaya' and the word 'sadda' in the sense of 'designation'. Or, one who goes together in all actions is a 'vayasa', [from the root] 'vaya' in the sense of 'to go'; for 'saha', there is 'so' by metathesis. One who goes together in affairs is a 'sahāya', [from the root] 'ay' in the sense of 'to go'; 'saha' becomes 'sā', as in 'sahadhammika'. Or, one for whom there is loss and gain together is a 'sahāya'; [this is] a three-term bahubbīhi compound, like 'parakkamādhigatasampadā'. Or, loss (hāni) and gain (āyo) are 'hāyā', with elision of 'ni'; one who has these is a 'sahāya', just as in 'sapakkhako', 'salomako', etc., where the word 'sa' has the meaning of 'existing'. One whose heart is good is a 'suhadaya', with elision of 'a', and 'dy' becoming 'jo'; this itself is 'suhajja'. [From the root] 'sah' in the sense of 'to endure'. Enduring is not being vexed; [with the suffix] 'kha', elision of 'ha', [it becomes] 'sakhā', of the 'rājādi' [class]. Or, one who is equal, famous, or trusted is a 'sakhā', with elision of 'ya', and 'samāna' becomes 'sa'. 'Siniddha', 'sniddha', and 'savaya' are also here. But 'sakhya' and 'sattapadina' are used in the sense of 'friendship'. That which pertains to a friend is 'sakhya'. That which is understood by seven steps is 'sattapadina', [formed with the] 'ina' [suffix].

Dvayaṃ abhejjamitte. Sabbakālaṃ bhajatīti sambhatto, bhaja sevāyaṃ, bhūvādi. Daḷho thiro mitto daḷhamitto. Dvayaṃ diṭṭhamattamitte. Kiñci kālaṃ passitabboti sandiṭṭho. Saṃsaddoyamappattho. Disa pekkhane, dassanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, taṃ mattā pamāṇametassa diṭṭhamattako, sakatthe ko.

Two terms for an inseparable friend. One who always attends upon is a 'sambhatta', [from the root] 'bhaj' in the sense of 'to serve', of the 'bhūvādi' class. A firm, steadfast friend is a 'daḷhamitta'. Two terms for a mere acquaintance. One who is seen for some time is a 'sandiṭṭha'. The word 'saṃ' here has the sense of 'a little'. [From the root] 'dis' in the sense of 'to see'; seeing is 'dassana', seen is 'diṭṭha'; one whose measure is merely that (being seen) is a 'diṭṭhamattaka', [with the] 'ka' [suffix] in its own sense.

347. Dvayaṃ carapurise tāpasādirūpena caramatte. Carati jānāti paracakkanti caro, a, cāropi, ṇo. Guḷhapuriso guttapuriso. Yathārahavaṇṇo, paṇidhi, appasapo, phassopyatra. Tatrādidvayaṃ vāṇijakasibalaliṅgabhikkhukaccāyanādilesena thāyinicare. Itare idhāgatasadisatthe. Vaṇṇo pakāro, yathārahavaṇṇo yathārahappakāro. Yena paracakkaṃ sakkā ñātuṃ tappakāravā iccattho. Paṇidhiyyate ñeyyamasmiṃ paṇidhi, i. Apakaṭṭhaṃ sappati caratīti apasappo, a. Phusa bādhanaphusanesu, a, phasso.

347. Two terms for a spy, in the sense of one merely wandering in the guise of an ascetic, etc. One who wanders and knows the enemy's circle is a 'cara', [formed with the] 'a' [suffix]; also 'cāra', [with the] 'ṇa' [suffix]. A secret person, a guarded person. 'Yathārahavaṇṇa', 'paṇidhi', 'apasappa', and 'phassa' are also here. Among these, the first two refer to a resident spy in the guise of a merchant, hunter, monk, teacher, etc. The others are in the sense of a non-resident spy. 'Vaṇṇa' means type; 'yathārahavaṇṇa' means of a suitable type. The meaning is: possessing that type by which the enemy's circle can be known. That which is to be known is placed in this, hence 'paṇidhi', [formed with the] 'i' [suffix]. One who moves or wanders secretly is an 'apasappa', [formed with the] 'a' [suffix]. [From the root] 'phus' in the sense of 'harming' or 'touching', [with the] 'a' [suffix, it becomes] 'phassa'.

Tikaṃ pathike. Pathe gacchatīti pathāvī, vī, dīgho. Iko, pathiko. Addhani magge gacchati sīlenāti addhagū. Addhagopyatra.

Three terms for a traveler. One who goes on the path is a 'pathāvī', [formed with the] 'vī' [suffix], with lengthening. [With the suffix] 'ika', [it becomes] 'pathika'. One who habitually goes on the road is an 'addhagū'. 'Addhagu' is also here.

Dvayaṃ dūte. Du paritāpe, to. Sandesaṃ vācikaṃ haratyaneneti haratīti (?).

Two terms for a messenger. From the root du in the sense of torment, with the suffix to. By this one, a verbal message is carried.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0241] jotisike. Gaṇayatīti gaṇako, ṇvu. Muhuttaṃ kālavisesaṃ jānātīti muhuttiko, vāggahaṇena na vuddhi. Saṃvaccharo, jotisiko, devaññū, mohutto, ñāṇiko, kātantikopyatra. Katanto devamattaṃ, taṃ jānātīti kātantiko.

Two terms for an astrologer. He counts, thus he is a gaṇaka, with the suffix ṇvu. He knows a muhutta, a specific time, thus he is a muhuttika; due to the inclusion of vā in the grammatical rule, there is no vowel strengthening. Saṃvacchara, jotisika, devaññū, mohutta, ñāṇika, and also kātantika are used here. Katanta is the divine measure; one who knows that is a kātantika.

348. Dvayaṃ lekhake. Likha lekhane, bhū, ṇvu. Lipena masyopadesena bhavatīti lipi, i, vaṇṇasaṇṭhāno, taṃ karotīti lipikāro. Akkharacaṇo, akkharacuñcupyatra. Cana dāne, bhū. Cañcu gatiyaṃ.

348. Two terms for a scribe. From the root likha in the sense of writing, of the bhū class, with the suffix ṇvu. That which comes into being by smearing, by the application of ink, is lipi, with the suffix i; it is the form of letters. One who makes that is a lipikāra. Akkharacaṇa and akkharacuñcu are also used here. The root cana is in the sense of giving, of the bhū class. The root cañcu is in the sense of movement.

Melānandā masimaṇi, melandhu vaṇṇakūpikā;

Masijalantu melā ca, pattañjanaṃ masi dvisu.

Melānandā is an ink-stone; melandhu is an ink-pot. Masijala and melā are ink. Pattañjana is collyrium. Masi is used in two senses.

Lekhanī vaṇṇatūlī ca, vaṇṇakakkharatūlikā;

Vaṇṇadūto sotthimukho, lekho vācikahārako.

Lekhanī, vaṇṇatūlī, and vaṇṇakakkharatūlikā are terms for a pen or brush. Vaṇṇadūta and sotthimukha are terms for a messenger. Lekha is a letter; vācikahāraka is a bearer of a verbal message.

Kācanakitaliko ca, kācanaṃ tannibandhanaṃ;

Lekhyaṭṭhānaṃ ganthakuṭi, muddā paccayakārinī tikaṇḍasesa 2.8.27, 28, 29.

A kācanakitalika is a golden casket, and kācana is its binding. Lekhyaṭṭhāna and ganthakuṭi are a place for writing. A muddā is a seal, which produces conviction.

Dvayaṃ vaṇṇe. Vaṇṇīyati pakāsīyati attho yena, so vaṇṇo, vaṇṇa pakāsane. Na kharati na khīyatīti akkharo, khara vināse, khi khaye vā, tadā aro. Likhanaṃ, lipi, likhi ime vaṇṇasaṇṭhāne vattanti. Lipilikhiyo itthiyaṃ.

Two terms for a letter. That by which a meaning is described or illuminated is a vaṇṇa, from the root vaṇṇa in the sense of making clear. That which does not perish or decay is an akkhara, from the root khara in the sense of destruction, or khi in the sense of decay, with the suffix ara. Likhana, lipi, and likhi are used in the sense of the form of a letter. Lipi and likhi are feminine.

Bhedādayo ime caturo upāyā sattuvijayakāraṇāni. Sattuvijayamupagacchanti etehīti upāyā. Parasmā visilesanaṃ bhedo.

These four means, beginning with division (bheda), are the causes for conquering an enemy. One approaches the conquest of an enemy by these, hence they are called means (upāya). Division (bheda) is separation from another.

Sneharāgāpanayanaṃ[M 0.0242], saṃhāsoppādanaṃ tathā;

Santajjanañca bhedoyaṃ, viññūhi tividho mato kāmandakīyanītisāra 17.8.

The removal of affection and passion, the generation of ridicule, and also intimidation—this division (bheda) is considered threefold by the wise.

Tatrāyaṃ tavānuggatena pavuddho pāsādataravo viya attānañcocchindissatīti saṅkāyaṃ janitāyaṃ snehabhattiñcāpanayati. Abhibhavanañcopādayati paddhañcopādayati (ka.). Aññassa ca pariyapaccāmittānuggahaṇassa maraṇamevanto bhavissatītyevaṃpakāramabhibhayanaṃ santajjanaṃ.

Therein, when the doubt is generated that, 'This one, having grown strong through your support, will destroy you yourself like a palace tree,' this removes affection and devotion and produces subjugation. And intimidation (santajjana) is a kind of threatening of this sort: 'For another who supports a hostile relative, death alone will be the end.'

Vadhotthaggahaṇañceva, parikleso tatheva ca;

Iti daṇḍavidhaññūhi, daṇḍopi tividho mato kāmandakīyanītisāra 17.9.

Killing, the taking up of a weapon, and likewise torment; thus, by those who know the methods of punishment, punishment (daṇḍa) is also considered threefold.

Parikleso bandhanatāḷanādi.

Torment (pariklesa) is binding, beating, and so forth.

Aññamaññopakārānaṃ, dassanaṃ guṇakittanaṃ;

Sambandhassa samakkhānaṃ, āyatiṃ sampakāsanaṃ.

Showing mutual benefits, praising qualities, declaring a relationship, and illuminating the future.

Vācā pesalayā sādhu, tavāhamiti cappaṇaṃ;

Iti sāmavidhaññūhi, sāmaṃ pañcavidhaṃ mataṃ kāmandakīyanītisāra 17.4-5.

Offering oneself with gentle speech, saying, 'I am yours'; thus, by those who know the methods of conciliation, conciliation (sāma) is considered fivefold.

“Asmiṃ evaṃ kate idaṃ amhākaṃ bhavissatī”ti āsādassanaṃ āyatisampakāsanaṃ. Appaṇamityaṅgassa dānaṃ.

Illuminating the future (āyatisampakāsana) is the showing of a prospect by saying, 'When this is done thus, this will be ours.' Appaṇa is the giving of oneself.

Dānañca pañcadhā sārassāsārassa ca dabbassa gahitassa samappaṇaṃ, tathāgahitassānumodanaṃ, tathā apubbadānaṃ, tathā “amussa dabbaṃ gaṇhāhi, tatheva bhavissatī”ti parasesu sayaṃ gāhappavattanaṃ, tathā iṇappamocanañceti. Yathāha –

And giving (dāna) is fivefold: the bestowal of received goods, both essential and non-essential; likewise, rejoicing in what has been received; likewise, an unprecedented gift; likewise, personally instigating others to take by saying, 'Take the goods for so-and-so; it will be just so for you'; and likewise, release from debt. As it is said:

“Yo sampattadhanossaggo, uttamamajjhimādhamo;

Patidānaṃ tathā tassa, gahitassānumodanaṃ.

The relinquishing of acquired wealth—superior, middling, or inferior; likewise, giving in return for that, and rejoicing in what has been received.

Dabbadāna’mapubbañca[M 0.0243], sayaṃ gāhappavattanaṃ;

Deyyassa paṭimokkho ca, dānaṃ pañcavidhaṃ mata”nti kāmandakīyanītisāra 17.6-7.

Unprecedented giving of goods, personally initiating the taking, and the release of what is to be given—giving is considered fivefold.

Ete cattāro upāyā māyādīsvevantogadhā, tathā hi māyopekkhā ca daṇḍantogadhā. Indajālañca bhede antogadhaṃ. Keci panāhu

These four means are included in deceit (māyā) and so forth; for indeed, deceit and indifference (upekkhā) are included in punishment (daṇḍa), and illusion (indajāla) is included in division (bheda). But some say:

“Sāmaṃ dānañca bhedo ca, daṇḍo ceti catukkakaṃ;

Māyopekkhindajālañca, sattopāyā pakittitā”ti kāmandakīyanītisāra 17.3.

Conciliation, giving, division, and punishment—this is a set of four; and with deceit, indifference, and illusion, seven means are proclaimed.

349. Nāmamattena vuttānaṃ bhedādīnamidāni pariyāyānyāha. Tatra dvayaṃ bhede. Japa mānase ca japo cintanavācāsu (dhātvatthasaṅgaha, 135 gāthā), bhū, ṇo. Bhidi dvidhākaraṇe, ṇo.

349. Now he states the synonyms for division (bheda) and so forth, which were mentioned only by name. Therein, there are two terms for division. From the root jap in the sense of mental action, of the bhū class, with the suffix ṇo. From the root bhid in the sense of making twofold, with the suffix ṇo.

Tikaṃ daṇḍe. Daṇḍa nipātane, curādi. Saho vuccati balaṃ, tabbhavaṃ sāhasaṃ. Damanaṃ damo, dīghapaṭisedho.

Three terms for punishment (daṇḍa). From the root daṇḍ in the sense of striking down, of the curādi class. Strength is called saha; that which is derived from it is sāhasa. Taming (damana) is dama; the lengthening of the vowel is prohibited.

350. Sāmaṃ suddavagge, dānañca brāhmaṇavagge kathessati. Sāmyādayo sattarevācariyamate. Paramparopakārittā rajjassaṅgāni. Pakaṭṭhamupakubbanti rajjanti pakatiyoti coccante. Vuttañca kāmandakīye –

350. He will speak of conciliation (sāma) in the Suddhavagga, and of giving (dāna) in the Brāhmaṇavagga. The seven constituents, beginning with the sovereign (sāmī), are indeed according to the teacher's view. They are the limbs of the kingdom due to their successive mutual helpfulness. And they are called the natural constituents (pakati) because they greatly assist and rule. And it is said in the Kāmandakīya:

“Sāmya’maccañca raṭṭhañca, duggaṃ koso balaṃ sakhā;

Paramparopakārīdaṃ, sattaṅgaṃ rajjamuccate kāmandakīyanītisāra 4.1.

The sovereign, minister, kingdom, fortress, treasury, army, and friend; this, being successively mutually helpful, is called the seven-limbed kingdom.

Amaccaraṭṭhaduggāni[M 0.0244], koso daṇḍo ca pañcamo;
