Etā pakatiyo vuttā, vijigīsassa rājino.

Minister, kingdom, fortress, treasury, and the army as the fifth; these are said to be the natural constituents (pakati) for a king who seeks victory.

Etā pañca tathā mittaṃ, sattamo pathavīpati;

Sattappakatikaṃ rajjaṃ, iccāha sūrapūjito”ti.

These five, and likewise a friend, with the lord of the earth as the seventh; a kingdom has seven constituents—thus spoke the one honored by heroes.

Tatra poraseṇīnaṃ padhānabhāvepi sati raṭṭhaggahaṇena, balaggahaṇena vā gahaṇasiddhanti neha visuṃ gahaṇaṃ kataṃ, amarakose pana dvīhi gahaṇe siddhepi padhānattākhyāpanatthaṃ visuṃ gahitā. Vuttañhi tatra –

Therein, although citizens (pora) and guilds (seṇī) are primary, their inclusion is accomplished by the inclusion of the kingdom or the army; therefore, they are not mentioned separately here. In the Amarakośa, however, although their inclusion is accomplished by these two, they are mentioned separately to declare their primacy. For it is said there:

“Sāmya’macco sakhā koso, rajjaduggabalāni ca;

Rajjaṅgāni pakatayo, porānaṃ seṇiyopi ce”ti amara 18.17.

The sovereign, minister, friend, treasury, and the kingdom, fortress, and army; these are the limbs of the kingdom, the natural constituents, and also the citizens (pora) and the guilds (seṇī).

Esañca sāmyamaccaraṭṭhaduggakosabalasakhīnaṃ pubbatarassa garuttaṃ viññeyyaṃ, iha tu nāmaliṅgānusāsane abhidhānasatthe anupayogato yathākkamaṃ garuttaṃ na vattumicchatīti byatikkamenopaññāso kato.

And among these—the sovereign, minister, kingdom, fortress, treasury, army, and friend—the greater importance of each preceding one should be understood. But here, in this treatise on lexicography, a teaching on names and genders, because it is not applicable, the author does not wish to state their importance in sequential order; therefore, the enumeration has been made out of that order.

Suvaṇṇādimayabhaṇḍāgāraṃ koso, pabbatodakarukkhādīhi duggamaṃ puraṃ duggaṃ, vijitaṃ janapadavatī bhūmi, balaṃ cakkaṃ, tañca molabhataseṇisahāyāmittāṭavikabhedena chabbidhaṃ. Tatra kamāgataṃ molaṃ, vetanasambandhaṃ bhataṃ, poraṃ balaṃ seṇī, sahāyabhūtaṃ sahāyo, amittabhūtaṃ amittaṃ, aṭavikaṃ aṭavisahāyo mittaṃ. Tadapi sahajjaṃ, pākataṃ, kittimañceti tividhaṃ. “Liṅge sabhāve pakati, porāmaccādiyonisu. Tiliṅgaṃ guṇasāmyepī”ti byākhyāsudhā 1.4.29 ruddo.

A treasury (kosa) is a storehouse for goods made of gold and so forth. A fortress (dugga) is a city difficult to access because of mountains, water, trees, and so forth. A conquered territory (vijita) is a land possessing inhabitants. An army (bala) is a wheel. And it is sixfold, distinguished as hereditary troops (mola), hired soldiers (bhata), guild troops (seṇī), allied troops (sahāya), enemy troops (amitta), and forest tribes (aṭavika). Therein, mola are those who have come in succession; bhata are those connected by wages; seṇī is the citizen army; sahāya are those who have become allies; amitta are those who have become enemies; aṭavika are forest tribes. A friend (mitta) is also threefold: inborn (sahajja), natural (pākata), and artificial (kittima). Rudda says: 'Pakati means gender, inherent nature, and the origins of citizens, ministers, and so forth. It is also of three genders in the equilibrium of the primary qualities (guṇa).'

351. Pabhāvādīnaṃ [M 0.0245] vasā sattiyo nāma tisso bhavanti. Saka sattiyaṃ,ti. Tatra yaṃ sandhādīnaṃ, bhedādīnañca yāthāvato avaṭṭhāpanaṃ, taṃ ñāṇabalaṃ mantasatti, sakasampattuppattiyaṃ kosadaṇḍā pabhūsatti, tesaṃyeva pabhuttasampādane sāmatthiyato. Vuttañca “kosadaṇḍabalaṃ pabhūsatti”riti cintāmaṇiṭīkāyampi. Balavatī ussāhaceṭṭhā ussāhasatti. Vuttañca “vikkamabalamussāhasatti”riti byākhyāsudhā 2.8.19 cintāmaṇiṭīkāyampi.

351. By virtue of power and so forth, there are three kinds of powers. Concerning 'one's own power': among these, the accurate establishment of alliances, divisions, and so forth, is the strength of wisdom, the power of counsel. The treasury and army, in the production of one's own prosperity, are the power of dominion, due to their capacity to achieve mastery. And it is said: 'The power of treasury and army is the power of dominion.' Vigorous effort is the power of exertion. And it is said: 'The strength of valor is the power of exertion.'

Pabhāvādīnaṃ sakāraṇaṃ sarūpaṃ dassetumāha “pabhāvo”ccādi. Damanaṃ daṇḍo, tadatthiyā balampi daṇḍo. Tato jātaṃ yaṃ tejo, taṃ pabhāvo. Tato jāto yo tejo, so “pabhāvo”tipi pulliṅgena yojanīyaṃ. Pabhavanti tejassino aneneti pabhāvo, ṇo. Pakaṭṭho vā bhāvo pabhāvo. Koso dhanaṃ, tato jāto yo tejo, so pabhāvo nāma. Tathā kosajo tejo dhanena sattūnamupakaraṇaṃ. Patapanti tejassino bhavantyaneneti patāpo, ṇo.

To show the cause and nature of 'pabhāva' and so forth, he says 'pabhāvo' and so on. 'Discipline' is 'punishment'; the force for that purpose is also 'punishment'. The energy that arises from that is 'pabhāva'. The energy that is born from that, that too should be construed as 'pabhāva' in the masculine gender. It is 'pabhāva' because the powerful arise through it, with the suffix ṇo. Or, the pre-eminent state is 'pabhāva'. 'Treasury' is wealth; the energy born from it is called 'pabhāva'. Similarly, the energy born from the treasury is an instrument against enemies by means of wealth. It is 'patāpa' because the powerful shine and exist through it, with the suffix ṇo.

352. Dvayaṃ mante. Mantā vuccati paññā, sā etasmiṃ vijjati tāya nipphādetabbattāti manto, atha vā manta guttabhāsane, bhāve ṇo. Itaratra bhāve yu.

352. Two terms for 'manta'. Wisdom is called 'mantā'; it is 'manto' because it exists in this matter and by it the matter is to be accomplished. Alternatively, the root 'manta' is in the sense of 'guarded speech', with the suffix ṇo in the sense of 'state'. Elsewhere, the suffix yu is in the sense of 'state'.

So [M 0.0246] manto dvigocaro dvinnaṃ janānaṃ visayabhūto catukkaṇṇo nāma. Cattāro kaṇṇā ettha catukkaṇṇo. So manto tigocaro tiṇṇaṃ janānaṃ visayabhūto chakkaṇṇo nāma. Manto nāma catukkaṇṇo vā chakkaṇṇo vā kattabbo, na tato paranti dvinnamevettha gahaṇaṃ. Amarakose pana chakkaṇṇopi paṭikkhitto. Vuttañhi tattha “achakkaṇṇo, yo tatiyādyagocaro”ti amara 18.22.

That counsel which has two spheres, being the domain of two people, is called 'catukkaṇṇa' (four-eared). 'Catukkaṇṇa' means 'four ears are here'. That counsel which has three spheres, being the domain of three people, is called 'chakkaṇṇa' (six-eared). Counsel should be made either 'catukkaṇṇa' or 'chakkaṇṇa', not more than that; thus only these two are taken here. However, in the Amarakośa, even 'chakkaṇṇa' is rejected. For it is said there: 'Not six-eared, which is beyond the domain of a third party and so forth.'

Sabbapārisadattā sabbapāṭhipadattā (ka.) byākaraṇassa sotūnaṃ samayantaresvapi paṭubhāvajananatthaṃ idhānāgatāpi chagguṇādayo ānetvā kathetabbā. Vuttañhi –

Since the explanation is for the entire assembly, in order to generate quick understanding for the listeners even at other times, the six qualities and so forth, even if not mentioned here, should be brought up and explained. For it is said:

“Sabbapārisadaṃ sabbapāṭipadaṃ (ka.) hidaṃ, sabbasattha’mato mataṃ;

Nissīyate kvaci kiñci, sabbesa’matra vādina”nti.

Indeed, this is for the entire assembly, held as the view of all teachers; something is relied upon in a certain place, and here all are proponents.

Yathā chagguṇā sandhi viggahayānāsanadvedhāsayā amara 18.18-9. Tatra sandhi upahāralakkhaṇo tividho kosadaṇḍabhūmippadānahetuko. Apahāralakkhaṇo viggaho, sopi tividho pakāsayuddhaṃ kūṭayuddhaṃ tuṇhiyuddhanti.

For example, the six qualities are: alliance, conflict, marching, halting, duplicity, and seeking shelter. Among these, alliance is characterized by gifts, and is threefold, caused by the giving of treasury, army, or land. Conflict is characterized by hostility; it too is threefold: open warfare, treacherous warfare, and silent warfare.

Parabyasanatāsapattidesakālātyudayāvāpayānamattena sāddhe parasmiṃ katācarassa guṇānurattapakatissa vijigīsassa yātrā yānaṃ kāmandakīyanītisāre 11 sagge passitabbaṃ, tañca viggayhayānaṃ sandhāyayānaṃ sambhūyayānaṃ pasaṅgayānaṃ upekkhiyayānamiti pañcavidhaṃ. Patiggāhīnaṃ niggayha, sandhāya, upekkhiya vā yaṃ yānaṃ, taṃ viggayhayānādi. Yadā na sakkoti, tadā sāmantehi sahekībhūya yānaṃ sambhūyayānaṃ. Aññatra gantabbe aññasmiṃ pasaṅgato gamanaṃ pasaṅgayānaṃ.

When an enemy can be overcome by means of their misfortune, fear, gain, place, time, excessive prosperity, or decline, the march of a would-be conqueror—who has acted accordingly and whose nature is devoted to virtue—is 'marching'. It is fivefold: marching after declaring war, marching after making an alliance, marching in combination, marching by chance, and marching with indifference. The march undertaken after either subduing, allying with, or being indifferent towards one's rear-guard is 'marching after declaring war', and so on. When one is unable to proceed alone, marching in unity with neighboring rulers is 'marching in combination'. When one must go elsewhere, going to another place by chance is 'marching by chance'.

“Na maṃ paro hantuṃ samattho, nāhampi para”miti kālādike parikkhitvā vijigīsassa duggādīni vaḍḍhayato ṭhiti āsanaṃ, tadapi viggayhāsanasandhāyāsanādibhedena pañcavidhaṃ. Balīnaṃ [M 0.0247] sattūnaṃ majjhe kākakkhivā’lakkhitasso’bhayatra vacanenattano samappaṇaṃ dvedhaṃ. Aññatarena vā balavatarena sandhi, aññatarena abalena viggaho dvedhaṃ. Sattuno vā pakatīhi sandhāya yo tena viggaho, sattuneva vā yo sandhiviggahasamudāyahetuko sattunova vā sandhiviggahasamudāyahetuno (byākhyāsudhā 1.8.18) duggāsayassa byāpāro, sopi dvedhaṃ. Parasantānamapyobhayavedanānaṃ ubhayato vutti dvedhamuccate.

'Another is not able to destroy me, nor am I able to destroy another'—having examined time and other factors, the staying of a would-be conqueror who is strengthening strongholds and so on is 'halting'. That too is fivefold, with divisions such as halting after declaring war, halting after making an alliance, and so on. In the midst of powerful enemies, the commitment of oneself through speech in both directions by one who is observant in both directions like a crow's eye is 'duplicity'. Or, an alliance with a stronger party and conflict with a weaker one is 'duplicity'. Or, the conflict with an enemy that arises from an alliance with his ministers, or the activity of one relying on a stronghold which is caused by the combination of alliance and conflict with the enemy himself, that too is 'duplicity'. Furthermore, even concerning the continuums of others, the functioning in both ways of both feelings is called 'duplicity'.

“Ucchijjamāno ripunā nirupāya patikriyo. Sattihīno samāsiyate”ti byākhyāsudhā 1.8.18 hīnenāññassa balavatarassa dhammavijayino samāsayanaṃ balavatā arinā ucchijjamānassa hīnasattino yaṃ balavadhammavijayisamāsayanaṃ (byākhyāsudhā 1.8.18), tasseva vā balino sattuno kosādippadānena āsayanaṃ āsayo vuccate. Ete chagguṇā.

'Being destroyed by an enemy, without means of counteraction, devoid of power, one seeks shelter.' Thus, the seeking of shelter by a weaker person from another who is stronger and a righteous conqueror, or seeking shelter from that very powerful enemy by giving one's treasury and so on, is called 'shelter'. These are the six qualities.

Yasmiñca guṇe ṭhito vijigīso sakkotyattano aṭṭhavaggiyakammāni pavattayituṃ, parassa cetānyupahantuṃ, guṇamādhiṭṭheyya, sā vuḍḍhi.

And in whatever quality a would-be conqueror, while standing, is able to carry on his own eightfold group of actions and to obstruct those same actions of another, he should establish that quality; that is growth.

Kasi vaṇijjaṃ patho duggaṃ, setu kuñjarabandhanaṃ;

Khanyākaradhanādānaṃ, suññānañca nivesanaṃ kāmandakīyanītisāra 5.78.

Agriculture, trade, paths, strongholds, bridges, the capturing of elephants; the acquisition of wealth from mines and other sources, and the settlement of uninhabited lands.

Ityeso aṭṭhavaggo.

This is the eightfold group.

Yasmiṃ vā guṇe ṭhito sakammānaṃ vuḍḍhi, khayaṃ vā nābhipassati, taṃ ṭhānaṃ, yasmiṃ vā guṇe ṭhito sakammānamupaghātaṃ passati, tasmiṃ na tiṭṭheyya, so khayo, ayaṃ nītivedīnaṃ tivaggo amara 18.19. Itaresaṃ dhammatthakāmā tivaggo.

Or in whatever quality one stands, if one does not perceive growth or decline in one's own actions, that is 'stationariness'. Or in whatever quality one stands, if one perceives harm to one's own actions, one should not remain in it—that is decline. This is the threefold group for those skilled in policy. For others, the threefold group is Dhamma, wealth, and desire.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0248] guyhe. Rahasi bhavaṃ rahassaṃ, so, rahe vā bhavaṃ rahassaṃ. Guha saṃvaraṇe, kammani yo. Idaṃ dvayaṃ tīsu. Rahasso manto, rahassā vācā, rahassaṃ mantanaṃ.

Two terms for 'secret'. 'That which is in secret' is 'rahassaṃ'; or 'that which is in a secluded place' is 'rahassaṃ'. The root 'guha' is in the sense of 'concealing'; the suffix 'yo' is in the sense of 'action'. This pair of terms is used in three genders: a secret counsel, secret speech, a secret deliberation.

353. Pañcakaṃ vijane. Viji puthabhāve, bhū, to ca. Vici vivecane, puthubhāve ca vā. “Vivittaṃ tīsu vijane, asaṃpakkapavittesū”ti ruddo. Vigato jano asmāti vijano. Chādetīti channo. Chada saṃvaraṇe. Vittamarahatīti raho, raha cāge, ramante asminti vā raho, vaṇṇavikāro. “Raho nidhuvane cāpi, raho guyhe napuṃsaka”nti byākhyāsudhā 2.8.22 rabhaso. Dutiyo rahosaddo abyayaṃ. Nissalākā, upāsupyatra. Nissalākā thī, upāsu abyayaṃ.

353. A pentad for 'in solitude'. The root 'viji' is in the sense of 'separation'; and 'bhū' (being), and 'to' (suffix). Or the root 'vici' is in the sense of 'discernment' and 'separation'. Rudda says: 'Vivittaṃ' is in three genders for 'vijane', and for 'unmixed' and 'pure'. Because people are gone from it, it is 'vijano'. Because it covers, it is 'channo'. The root 'chada' is in the sense of 'concealment'. Because it deserves to be deserted, it is 'raho'; or the root 'raha' is in the sense of 'abandonment'; or because people delight in it, it is 'raho', with a modification of a letter. Rabhasa says: 'Raho' is also in the sense of 'coitus', and 'raho' is 'secret' in the neuter. The second word 'raho' is an indeclinable. 'Nissalākā' and 'upāsu' are also here. 'Nissalākā' is feminine; 'upāsu' is an indeclinable.

Dvayaṃ vissāse. Sasa pālane, ṇo. Sambha vissāse. “Vissambho kelikalahe, vissāse’paṇayepi ce”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkāyampi ruddo.

Two terms for 'trust'. The root 'sasa' is in the sense of 'protecting', with the suffix 'ṇo'. The root 'sambha' is in the sense of 'trust'. Rudda says: 'Vissambho' is used in the sense of 'playful quarrel', 'trust', and also 'affection'.

Dvayaṃ nyāye. Yuja samādhimhi, samādhi abhyupagamo, to. Upagantabbattā upāyikaṃ. Upāyā sakatthe iko, opāyikaṃ, opayikampi pāṇini 5.4.34 (gaṇa), labbhaṃ, bhajamānaṃ, abhinītaṃ, nyāyaṃ, ñāyaṃpyatra.

Two terms for 'method'. The root 'yuja' is in the sense of 'concentration'; 'samādhi' is 'agreement'; with the suffix 'to'. Because it is to be approached, it is 'upāyikaṃ'. From 'upāya', with the suffix 'ika' in its own sense, comes 'opāyikaṃ', and also 'opayikaṃ'. Also here are: 'labbhaṃ', 'bhajamānaṃ', 'abhinītaṃ', 'nyāyaṃ', and 'ñāyaṃ'.

354. Silokaṃ ovāde. Avapubbo vada viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, bhāve ṇo. Sāsa anusiṭṭhimhi,ti, āssi, anusiṭṭhi[M 0.0249]. Anusāsate anusāsanaṃ. Pumavajje itthiyaṃ, napuṃsake ca. Ettha ca ekassevatthassa bhinnaliṅgehi tīhi nāmehi kathanaṃ na kevalaṃ vāccaliṅgoyeva saddo, atha kho vācakaliṅgopyatthīti dīpanatthaṃ.

354. 'Siloka' is in the sense of 'instruction'. The root 'vada', preceded by 'ava', is in the sense of 'clear speech', with the suffix 'ṇo' in the sense of 'state'. The root 'sāsa' is in the sense of 'instruction'; forms are 'ti', 'āssi', 'anusiṭṭhi'. 'He instructs' (anusāsate), 'instruction' (anusāsanaṃ). In feminine and neuter, excluding masculine. And here, the stating of a single meaning by three names with different genders is for the purpose of showing that a word is not only gendered according to the thing signified, but also has its own grammatical gender.

Dvayaṃ āṇāyaṃ. Āṇa pesane, bhāve a, āṇā, itthī. Avavādo, niddeso, siṭṭhipyatra. Dvayaṃ bandhane. Dā dāne, bhāve yu, dā avakhaṇḍane vā, viyogadānato uddānaṃ.

Two terms for 'command'. The root 'āṇa' is in the sense of 'sending'; with the suffix 'a' in the sense of 'state'; 'āṇā' is feminine. 'Avavādo', 'niddeso', and 'siṭṭhi' are also here. Two terms for 'binding'. The root 'dā' is in the sense of 'giving', with the suffix 'yu' in the sense of 'state'; or 'dā' is in the sense of 'cutting off'; 'uddānaṃ' comes from 'giving separation'.

355-356. Dvayaṃ aparādhe. Apagacchantyanenāti āgu, ṇu, palopo, rassassa dīghatā, napuṃsake āgu. Apagato rādho yena aparādho, rādha saṃsiddhimhi. Dvayaṃ rājagayhe. Kira vikiraṇe, kattari a, attaṃ. Bala pāṇane, i. Karasāhacariyato bali pulliṅge. Bhāgadheyyopyatra. Bhāgāsakatthe dheyyo pāṇini 5.4.36 (vā.), bhāgattena tiṭṭhatīti vā bhāgadheyyo, iyo.

355-356. Two terms for 'offence'. 'Because one goes away by it', it is 'āgu'; with the suffix 'ṇu', elision, and lengthening of the short vowel; 'āgu' is neuter. 'Because accomplishment is gone from it', it is 'aparādho'; the root 'rādha' is in the sense of 'accomplishment'. Two terms for 'royal share'. The root 'kira' is in the sense of 'scattering'; with the suffix 'a' in the sense of 'agent', forming 'kara'. The root 'bala' is in the sense of 'living'; with the suffix 'i'. Because of its association with 'kara', 'bali' is masculine. 'Bhāgadheyyo' is also here. 'Dheyya' is in the sense of 'one's own portion'; or 'because it stands as a portion', it is 'bhāgadheyyo', with the suffix 'iyo'.

Dvayaṃ tuṭṭhidāye. Manorathapuṇṇattā pattabbo bhāgo puṇṇapatto. Tussanaṃ tuṭṭho, sossatthīti tuṭṭhī, tena dātabbo dāyo tuṭṭhidāyo, ākārantānamāyo.

Two terms for 'gift of satisfaction'. Because it is a share to be obtained due to the fulfillment of a wish, it is 'puṇṇapatto'. 'Tuṭṭho' means satisfied; 'tussanaṃ' is satisfaction. 'Tuṭṭhī' is that which brings satisfaction; hence, the gift to be given by it is 'tuṭṭhidāyo'. For nouns ending in 'ā', 'āyo' is a suffix.

Chakkaṃ [M 0.0250] pābhate. Tathā hi –

Six terms for 'gift' or 'present'. For thus it is said:

“Hemaṃ sīhāsanaṃ vesaṃ, vuttaṃ bhaddāsanaṃ tathā;

Upāyana’mupaggayhaṃ, pābhatañco’padā thiya”nti.

"Gold, a lion-throne, attire, and likewise the said auspicious seat; 'upāyana', 'upaggayha', 'pābhata', and 'upadā' in the feminine."

Silokāddhaṃ nāma amaramālā.

This half-verse is from the work named Amaramālā.

Upagantvādātabbāti upadā, a, itthī, taṃ tamatthaṃ patthentehi ābharīyate ānīyateti pābhataṃ, patthanatthajotakoyaṃ pasaddo. Upeyyateti upāyanaṃ, ito yu, upagacchati yenāti vā upāyanaṃ. Kuca saṅkocane, ṇo, vigato koco yena ukkoco. Paṇṇena satthapaṇṇena saddhiṃ ākarīyate ānīyateti paṇṇākāro, aññatra upacārā. Pahiṇantyaneneti paheṇakaṃ, hi gatiyaṃ, yu, sakatthe ko. Padesanaṃ, upaggayhaṃ, upahāropyatra.

Because it is to be approached and taken, it is 'upadā'; the suffix is 'a'; it is feminine. Because it is brought and carried by those who desire a particular purpose, it is 'pābhataṃ'; this prefix 'pa' indicates the meaning of desire. Because it is approached, it is 'upāyanaṃ'; from the root 'i' with the suffix 'yu'; or, 'upāyanaṃ' is that by which one approaches. The root 'kuca' is in the sense of 'shrinking'; with the suffix 'ṇo'; that from which shrinking has departed is 'ukkoco'. Because it is brought together with a leaf or a written message, it is 'paṇṇākāro'; elsewhere it is used metaphorically. Because one sends by means of it, it is 'paheṇakaṃ'; from the root 'hi' in the sense of 'going', with the suffix 'yu'; the suffix 'ko' is pleonastic. 'Padesanaṃ', 'upaggayhaṃ', and 'upahāro' are also included here.

Gumbādideyyo gumbaghaṭādiko gumbaghaṭādito (?) deyyosuṅkaṃ, anitthī, gumbo nāma jalathalamaggādīsu laddhabbabhāgo, tathā ghaṭṭopi, samānatthā hete. Ādinā pābhatampi saṅgaṇhāti. Suṅka gamane, suṅkati yena, taṃ suṅkaṃ. Gamu gamane, bo, assu, gumbo. Dvayaṃ gāmajanapadādito laddhabbabhāge. Aya gamane, ṇo, āyo. Apaccaye ayo. Dhanānaṃ sampattakāle āgamo dhanāgamo.

For 'taxable due', there are 'gumba', 'ghaṭa', and so on; it is not feminine. 'Gumbo' is a share obtainable from water, land, roads, and so on; likewise 'ghaṭṭo'; for these have the same meaning. By 'and so on', 'pābhata' is also included. The root 'suṅka' is in the sense of 'going'; that by which one goes is 'suṅkaṃ'. The root 'gamu' is in the sense of 'going'; with the suffix 'bo', and 'a' becoming 'u', it forms 'gumbo'. Two terms for 'a share obtainable from villages, districts, and so on'. The root 'aya' is in the sense of 'going'; with the suffix 'ṇo', it becomes 'āyo'. Without a suffix, it is 'ayo'. The arrival of wealth at a time of prosperity is 'dhanāgamo'.

357. Dvayaṃ chattasāmaññe. Ātapato sūriyālokato tāyatīti ātapattaṃ, to. Chādayatīti chattaṃ, chada [M 0.0251] apavāraṇe, to, traṇapaccaye chatraṃ, hemaṃ suvaṇṇakhacitaṃ raññaṃ rājūnaṃ āsanaṃ sīhāsanākhyaṃ. Sīhākatippadhānattā sīhākatippadhānaṃ āsananti viggaho.

357. Two terms for 'umbrella' in general. Because it protects from heat and sunlight, it is 'ātapattaṃ'; with the suffix 'ta'. Because it covers, it is 'chattaṃ'; from the root 'chada' in the sense of 'covering', with the suffix 'ta'; with the suffix 'traṇa', it forms 'chatraṃ'. A golden seat, inlaid with gold, for kings is called 'sīhāsana'. Because its lion-shape is prominent, the analysis is 'sīhākatippadhānaṃ āsanaṃ' (a seat with a prominent lion-shape).

Dvayaṃ cāmare. Vālena katā bījanī vālabījanī. Camaro migo tassedaṃ cāmarī. “Cāmarā cāmaraṃ romaṃ, gucchakañcāvacūlaka”nti tikaṇḍasesa 2.8.406 tikaṇḍaseso. Pakiṇṇakaṃpyatra. Pakarīyate vikkhipate pakiṇṇakaṃ, sakatthe ko.

Two terms for 'chowrie'. A fan made of hair is 'vālabījanī'. The 'camara' is a type of deer; this item belonging to it is 'cāmarī'. The Tikaṇḍasesa states: "'Cāmarā', 'cāmaraṃ', 'romaṃ', 'gucchakaṃ', and 'avacūlakaṃ'." 'Pakiṇṇakaṃ' is also included here. That which is scattered or dispersed is 'pakiṇṇakaṃ'; the suffix 'ko' is pleonastic.

358. Khaggādayo ime pañca rājūnaṃ kakudhabhaṇḍāni bhavanti. Kuka ādāne, dho, vaṇṇavipariyayo. Rañño gamanakāle sadā ādātabbato kakudhāni ca tāni rājadhanattā bhaṇḍāni ceti kakudhabhaṇḍāni.

358. These five—sword, parasol, crown, sandals, and fan—are the royal insignia of kings. From the root 'kuka' in the sense of 'taking', with the suffix 'dha' and a transposition of letters. Because they must always be taken when the king travels, they are 'kakudhāni'; and because they are goods that are the king's property, they are 'kakudhabhaṇḍāni'.

359. Dvayaṃ puṇṇaghaṭe. Jalapuṇṇattā bhaddo kalyāṇo kumbho bhaddakumbho. Dvayaṃ hemabhājane. Bhara bharaṇe, bharaṇaṃ dhāraṇaṃ posanañca, dhāraṇatthassa bharatissa bhiṅgādeso, bharati dadhāti udakanti bhiṅgāro, āro. Karako, kuṇḍikāpyatra.

359. Two terms for 'full pot'. Because it is filled with water, an auspicious and good pot is a 'bhaddakumbho'. Two terms for 'golden vessel'. The root 'bhara' is in the sense of 'bearing'; 'bearing' means holding and nourishing. For 'bharati' in the sense of 'holding', 'bhiṅga' is the substitute. Because it holds water, it is 'bhiṅgāro'; the suffix is 'āro'. 'Karako' and 'kuṇḍikā' are also included here.

Hatthī [M 0.0252] ca asso ca ratho ca patti ca, tesaṃ samūho hatthissarathapatti caturaṅginī senātyuccate, senaṅgattā samāhāradvandoyaṃ. Cattāri aṅgāni yassaṃ saṃvijjanti, sā caturaṅginī, ī, inī.

The elephant, the horse, the chariot, and the foot soldier—their collection is called the four-limbed army. Because it is a component of the army, this is a collective compound. That in which four components are present is 'caturaṅginī'; with the suffixes 'ī' or 'inī'.

360. Dantyantaṃ hatthini. Kuñjo hanu, danto ca, taṃyogā kuñjaro, atisaye ro, kuṃ pathaviṃ jarāpetīti vā kuñjaro, aluttasamāso, kuñje vā girikūṭe ramati, koñcanādaṃ nadanto vā carati, kuṃ vā pathaviṃ tadāghātena jarayatīti kuñjaro. Vārayati parabalaṃ vāraṇo, nandādīhi yu. Hatthayogā hatthī. Mataṅgassa isino apaccaṃ mātaṅgo, mahantaṃ aṅgaṃ sarīrametassāti vā mātaṅgo, ha nalopo, assākāro ca. Dve radā dantā yassa dvirado, “rada vilekhane dante”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe. Gaja sadde, gajatīti, a. Nago pabbato, so viya dissatīti nāgo, ṇo. Karena, mukhena cāti dvīhi pivatīti dvipo. I gamane, bho. Dantayogā dantī. Saṭṭhihāyano, dantāvalo, anekapo, mataṅgajo, karī, thambheramo, padmī, mahāmigo, pīlu, sindhuro, dīghamāruto, rājīvo, jalakakkho, nilluro, karaṭī, varaṅgo, suppakaṇṇo iccādīnipi hatthino nāmāni. Saṭṭhivassikattā, jātiyā saṭṭhivassakāle thāmena hāyanato vā saṭṭhihāyano.

360. The following terms, up to 'dantī', are for the elephant. 'Kuñja' means jaw, and 'danta' means tusk; from their connection, it is 'kuñjaro'; the 'ra' is for emphasis. Or, because it makes the earth old, it is 'kuñjaro', an irregular compound. Or, because it delights on mountain peaks. Or, because it moves while making a trumpeting sound. Or, because it wears out the earth with its impact, it is 'kuñjaro'. Because it wards off the enemy's force, it is 'vāraṇo'; from the nandādi group with the suffix 'yu'. From its trunk, it is 'hatthī'. The offspring of the sage Mataṅga is 'mātaṅgo'; or, because it has a large body, it is 'mātaṅgo', with elision of 'ha' and lengthening of 'a'. That which has two tusks is 'dvirado'; for in the Nānatthasaṅgaha it is said: 'rada for carving and for tusk'. The root 'gaja' is in the sense of 'to sound'; because it makes a sound, it is 'gaja', with the suffix 'a'. 'Nāga' means mountain; because it looks like one, it is 'nāgo', with the suffix 'ṇa'. Because it drinks with two—that is, with its trunk and mouth—it is 'dvipo'. The root 'i' is in the sense of 'going'; with the suffix 'bha', it forms 'ibha'. From its tusks, it is 'dantī'. Other names for the elephant are also: Saṭṭhihāyano, Dantāvalo, Anekapo, Mataṅgajo, Karī, Thambheramo, Padmī, Mahāmigo, Pīlu, Sindhuro, Dīghamāruto, Rājīvo, Jalakakkho, Nilluro, Karaṭī, Varaṅgo, and Suppakaṇṇo. Because it is sixty years old, or because its strength declines at the age of sixty, it is 'saṭṭhihāyano'.

Vanakarīnaṃ yo yūthajeṭṭho, so sayūthānaṃ jeṭṭhattā yūthajeṭṭho. Sayūthe pāti rakkhatīti yūthapoti coccate.

Among forest elephants, the one who is the leader of a herd is 'yūthajeṭṭho' because he is the foremost of his herd. He is also called 'yūthapo' because he protects his herd.

361. Kāḷāvakādīni [M 0.0253] etāni hatthirājānaṃ kulāni. Kalambate saddāyateti kāḷāvako, ṇvu, malopo. Gaṅgāyaṃ jāto gaṅgeyyo, ṭhānavasena sā saññā. Paṇḍaravaṇṇatāya paṇḍaro. Vaṇṇavasena tambavaṇṇatāya tambo. Piṅgalavaṇṇatāya piṅgalo. Gandhayuttatāya gandho. Maṅga gamanattho, sobhanagamanayuttatāya maṅgalo, atisāyane, pasaṃsāyaṃ vā lo. Hemavaṇṇatāya hemo. Uposathakule jātattā uposatho, upagantvā arayo usatīti vā uposatho, tho, usa dāhe, upapubbo vasa nivāse vā, vasso, uposatho, tithīviseso ca. Chabbaṇṇadantatāya chaddanto. Etesañca kāḷāvako dasannaṃ purisānaṃ balaṃ dhāreti, gaṅgeyyo dasannaṃ kāḷāvakānaṃ, evaṃ yāvachaddantā netabbo, sammāsambuddho pana dasannaṃ chaddantānaṃ balaṃ dhāreti, teneva bhagavā kāḷāvakahatthigaṇanāya koṭisahassabalaṃ dhāreti, purisagaṇanāya dasannaṃ purisakoṭisahassānaṃ balaṃ.

361. These, beginning with Kāḷāvaka, are the clans of the elephant kings. 'Kāḷāvaka' is so called because it makes a sound. 'Gaṅgeyya' is born in the Ganges; that name is based on its place. 'Paṇḍara' is so named because of its white color. 'Tamba' is so named because of its copper color. 'Piṅgala' is so named because of its tawny color. 'Gandha' is so named because it is fragrant. 'Maṅgala' is so named for having an auspicious gait, or because it is exceedingly auspicious or praiseworthy. 'Hema' is so named because of its golden color. 'Uposatha' is so named because it was born in the Uposatha clan, or because it approaches and burns its enemies; it is also a specific lunar day. 'Chaddanta' is so named for having six-colored tusks. Among these, a Kāḷāvaka possesses the strength of ten men; a Gaṅgeyya, the strength of ten Kāḷāvakas, and so this should be understood up to the Chaddanta. The Perfectly Enlightened One, however, possesses the strength of ten Chaddantas. Therefore, the Blessed One, by the measure of Kāḷāvaka elephants, possesses the strength of a thousand crores, and by the measure of men, the strength of ten thousand crores of men.

362. Pādo karipote. Pañcavassāni yāva kalabho, kala saṅkhyāne, abho, kalabho, ḷatte kaḷabho, mātāpitūhi [M 0.0254] bharitabbattā bhiṅko, bharatissa bhiṅko. Karisāvakopyatra. Pādo mattamātaṅge. Dānaṃ pabhinno yassa pabhinno. Majjatīti matto, mada ummāde. Gaje jāyatīti gajjo, ṇyo, mado. So sañjāto yassa gajjito.

362. A section on the elephant calf. Up to five years of age, it is a 'kalabho' or 'kaḷabho'. Because it is to be nourished by its parents, it is 'bhiṅko'. 'Karisāvako' is also included here. A section on the rutting elephant. One from whom rut-fluid has burst forth is 'pabhinno'. Because it is intoxicated, it is 'matto'; from the root 'mada' in the sense of 'intoxication'. That which is born in an elephant is 'gajjo', meaning rut-fluid. One in whom that has arisen is 'gajjito'.

Dvayaṃ hatthisamūhe. Hatthīnaṃ samūho hatthighaṭā. Gajānaṃ samūho gajatā, gāmajanabandhusahāyādīhi tā. Pādo hatthiniyaṃ. Hatthayogā hatthinī, ī, inī. Kaṇa sadde, iru, sakatthe ko. Kareṇukātipi, tadā karayogā kareṇukā, iṇu. Kariṇī, dhenukā, vasā, kareṇupyatra.

Two terms for 'a group of elephants'. A group of elephants is 'hatthighaṭā'. A herd of elephants is 'gajatā'; the suffix 'tā' is from the group beginning with 'gāma'. A section on the female elephant. From 'hatthī', the feminine is 'hatthinī', with the suffixes 'ī' or 'inī'. Also 'kareṇukā'; from the root 'kaṇa' in the sense of 'to sound', with the suffix 'iru' and a pleonastic 'ka'. Alternatively, from its trunk, it is 'kareṇukā', with the suffix 'iṇu'. 'Kariṇī', 'dhenukā', 'vasā', and 'kareṇu' are also included here.

363. Hatthisiropiṇḍā hatthino sirasi dve piṇḍā kumbhākhyā. Ke sirasi bhavatīti kumbho, assu, niggahītāgamo ca. Dvinnaṃ pana kumbhānaṃ majjhimaṃ vidu nāma amara 18.37. Aṅkusasaṅghātaṃ vindatyasminti vidu, pume, u. Dvayaṃ kaṇṇamūle. Cūḷa nimajjane, ṇvu, cūḷikā, cuda sañcodane vā, codenti ettha aṅkusādīhi adantanti cūḷikā, dassa ḷo, ṇvu.

363. The lumps on an elephant's head: on an elephant's head are two lumps called 'kumbhā'. Because it is on the head, it is 'kumbho'. The space between the two 'kumbhas' is named 'vidu'. Because the strike of the goad is found there, it is 'vidu'; it is masculine. Two terms for 'the base of the ear'. From the root 'cūḷa' in the sense of 'sinking', it is 'cūḷikā'. Or, from the root 'cuda' in the sense of 'urging', because they urge the untamed elephant there with goads and so on, it is 'cūḷikā'.

Āsate asminti āsanaṃ, khandhadeso. Khandho eva deso khandhadeso, tasmiṃ. Dvayaṃ pucchamūle. Pucchassa mūlaṃ heṭṭhimabhāgo.

That on which one sits is 'āsanaṃ', the shoulder region. The shoulder itself is the region, 'khandhadeso'. Two terms for 'the base of the tail'. The base of the tail is its lower part.

364. Tikaṃ gajabandhanathambhe. Ālantyasmiṃ, anena vā bandhanti ālānaṃ, yu. Āpubbo bandhanattho lādhātu. Āhananti [M 0.0255] bandhantyasmiṃ, anena vā āḷhako, hanadhātu, nassa ḷo, vaṇṇavipariyayo ca, ṇvu. Thambha paṭibandhane. Bandhopyatra.

364. Three terms for an elephant's binding post. That in which they bind, or by which they bind, is 'ālāna', from the root 'lā' with the prefix 'ā' in the sense of binding. That in which they fasten, or by which they fasten, is 'āḷhaka', from the root 'han', where 'n' becomes 'ḷ' and there is a metathesis of letters. 'Thambha' is in the sense of obstructing. 'Bandha' is also used here.

Tikaṃ saṅkhale. Anitthī tūti tvantaṃ liṅgapadaṃ. Gala secane. Nigaḷati bandhati yenāti nigaḷo, a, kattusādhanaṃ vā. Adi bandhane, andatīti anduko. Ṇvu, assu. Bhusaṃ khalatyanena saṅkhalaṃ, kaṭi vatthabandhanepi, “thīkaṭīvatthabandhepi, nigaḷe saṅkhalaṃ tisū”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.41 rabhaso. Saṅkhalikāpyatra.

Three terms for a fetter. The phrase 'but not feminine' is a term indicating gender. From the root 'gala' (to drip), that by which one binds is 'nigaḷa'. From 'adi' (to bind), that which binds is 'anduka'. That by which one is strongly bound is 'saṅkhalaṃ'; it is also used for a waist-garment. As Rabhasa states: 'For a woman's waist-garment and for a fetter, 'saṅkhalaṃ' is used in the three genders.' 'Saṅkhalikā' is also used here.

Dvayaṃ gajagaṇḍe. Gaṇḍa vadanekadese, adhātūnampi dhātūsu pāṭho, dhātu hi kriyattho. Gaṇḍo kapolasāmaññepi. Kaṭa vassāvaraṇesu, a. Dvayaṃ karimadajale. Dīyateti dānaṃ. Mada ummāde, karaṇe a.

Two terms for an elephant's cheek. 'Gaṇḍa' is for a part of the face; even non-roots are read among the roots, for a root indeed has the meaning of action. 'Gaṇḍa' is also generally for the cheek. 'Kaṭa' is from the root 'kaṭ' in the sense of raining and covering. Two terms for an elephant's rut-fluid. That which is exuded is 'dāna'. From the root 'mad' (to be intoxicated), in the instrumental sense, comes 'mada'.

365. Dvayaṃ hatthikare. Soṇa vaṇṇagatīsu, ḍo, soḍa gabbe vā, niggahītāgamo, ṇo ca. Dvīsu dvepi.

365. Two terms for an elephant's trunk. From the root 'soṇa' in the sense of color or movement, comes 'soṇḍa'; or from 'soḍa' in the sense of pride, with a nasal augment and the letter 'ṇ'. Both terms are used in two genders.

Dvayaṃ soṇḍagge. Karassa soṇḍassa aggaṃ. Pusa posane. Kharo, sassa ko, ussottaṃ, pusa vuḍḍhimhi vā, bhū, pusa snehasecanapūraṇesu vā, kiyādi, pusa dhāraṇe vā, curādi.

Two terms for the tip of the trunk. The tip of the 'kara' or 'soṇḍa' (trunk). From the root 'pus' (to nourish) comes 'pokkhara'; 's' becomes 'k', and 'u' becomes 'o'. Or it is from 'pus' in the sense of growth; or from 'pus' in the sense of anointing, sprinkling, or filling; or from 'pus' in the sense of holding.

Hatthissa kāyamajjhamhi bandhanarajju kacchā nāma. Kaca bandhane, cho. Dūsā, varatrāpyatra. Kutho nāma hatthipiṭṭhattharitacitrakambalaṃ, so ādi yesante kuthādayo. Kuthādayo eva kappano nāma bhavanti. Kappa sāmatthiye, sajjanāyañca[M 0.0256], karaṇe yu. Kappanāpi. Kaca sajjanāyaṃ, tho, kutho, tīsu. “Napuṃsakamattharaṇaṃ, thī paveṇī kuthaṃ tisū”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.42 hi vopālito. Paveṇī, attharaṇaṃ, vaṇṇo, paritthomoti ete kuthapariyāyā.

The binding rope around the middle of the elephant's body is named 'kacchā'. It is from the root 'kac' (to bind). 'Dūsā' and 'varatrā' are also used here. 'Kutha' is the name for the decorated blanket spread on the elephant's back; 'kutha' and so forth are 'kuthādayo'. These 'kuthādayo' are also named 'kappana'. From the root 'kapp' (to be able, and to adorn), in the instrumental sense, comes 'kappana'. Also 'kappanā'. From the root 'kac' (to adorn) comes 'kutha', which is in three genders. For Vopālita states: ''Attharaṇa' is neuter, 'paveṇī' is feminine, and 'kutha' is in three genders.' 'Paveṇī', 'attharaṇa', 'vaṇṇa', and 'paritthoma'—these are synonyms for 'kutha'.

366. Dvayaṃ rājārahe hatthini. Rājānamupagantvā vahitumarahatīti opavayho, arahatthe ṇyo. Rājānaṃ vahituṃ arahatīti rājavayho, ṇyo. Dvayaṃ kappitahatthini. Sajjā sajjanā sañjātā yasmiṃ sajjito. Kappā kappanā sañjātā yasmiṃ kappito. Etasmāyeva pāṭhā sajjakappā sajjanākappanānaṃ pariyāyāti ñeyyā.

366. Two terms for an elephant worthy of a king. Because it is fit to carry the king, having approached him, it is 'opavayha'. Because it is fit to carry the king, it is 'rājavayha'. Two terms for a caparisoned elephant. He in whom preparation ('sajjanā') has arisen is 'sajjita'. He in whom caparisoning ('kappanā') has arisen is 'kappita'. From this very text, it should be known that 'sajja' and 'kappa' are synonyms for 'sajjanā' and 'kappanā'.

Hatthino pāde vijjhanakaṇṭako “tomaro”tyuccate. Tujjateneneti tomaro, tuda byathane, aro, dassa mo, ottaṃ. Veṇukaṃpyatra kotraṃ veṇukamālānaṃ (amara 18.41), kvaci veḷukantipi pāṭho.

The piercing spike for an elephant's foot is called a 'tomara'. Because one pierces with it, it is 'tomara', from the root 'tud' (to vex), where 'd' becomes 'm' and the vowel becomes 'o'. 'Veṇuka' is also used here; in some places, the reading is 'veḷuka'.

367. Hatthino kaṇṇamūlamhi vijjhanakaṇṭako “tutta”mityuccate. Tujjateneneti tuttaṃ, to. Hatthino matthakamhi vijjhanakaṇṭako “aṅkuso”tyuccate. Aṅkate aneneti aṅkuso, aṅka lakkhaṇe, so, assu.

367. The piercing spike at the root of the elephant's ear is called 'tutta'. It is called 'tutta' because one pierces with it. The piercing spike on the top of the elephant's head is called 'aṅkusa'. It is called 'aṅkusa' because one marks with it, from the root 'aṅk' (to mark).

Pajjaddhaṃ [M 0.0257] hatthārohe. Maḍi bhūsāyaṃ, hatthiṃ maṇḍayati rakkhatīti hatthimaṇḍo, sova hatthimeṇḍo, mi hiṃsāyaṃ vā, ḍo, niggahītāgamo. Hatthiṃ pāti rakkhatīti hatthipo, kammani ṇo. Hatthiṃ gopayati rakkhatīti hatthigopako. Gupa rakkhaṇe, sakatthe ko. Ādhoraṇo, nisādinopyatra.

A half-verse on the elephant rider. From the root 'maḍi' (to adorn), one who adorns and protects the elephant is 'hatthimaṇḍa'; this same is 'hatthimeṇḍa', or it is from the root 'mi' (to harm). One who protects the elephant is 'hatthipa'. One who guards the elephant is 'hatthigopaka', from the root 'gup' (to protect). 'Ādhoraṇa' and 'nisādin' are also used here.

368. Mātaṅgahayādīnaṃ gamanādikriyāsikkhāpako ācariyo “gāmaṇīyo”tyuccate. Gamanaṃ gāmo, bhāve ṇo. Hatthādīnaṃ gamanakriyā gāmo, taṃ neti sikkhāpetīti gāmaṇīyo, aññakriyāsikkhāpanetūpacārā, gāmaṃ vā hatthādisamūhaṃ netīti gāmaṇīyo, gamanaṃ vā sikkhāpetīti gāmaṇīyo, sabbatra nassa ṇattaṃ.

368. The teacher who instructs in movement and other actions for elephants, horses, and the like is called 'gāmaṇīya'. 'Gamana' (movement) becomes 'gāma'. The action of movement for elephants and others is 'gāma', and one who leads or teaches that is 'gāmaṇīya'; this is used metaphorically for teaching other actions. Alternatively, 'gāmaṇīya' is one who leads a 'gāma' (group) of elephants and the like, or one who teaches movement. In all cases, 'n' becomes 'ṇ'.

Pādadvayaṃ asse. Haya gatiyaṃ, a. Turaṃ sīghaṃ gacchatīti turaṅgo, kvi, bindālopo, lope sati turago. Vāha payatane, a. Asa bhakkhane, a. Sindhūnamadūrabhavo janapadopi sindhavo, tatra bhavo sindhavo, saṃyogantattā na vuddhi. Ghoṭako, pīti, turaṅgamo, vājī, gandhabbo, sattiriccādīnipi asse. Ghuṭa parivattane, ṇvu. Pā pāne,ti. “Pāne thī pīti asse so”ti ruddo. Vājayogā vājī, ī. “Esañca pubbaṃ pakkho āsi, sa tu devetyatyatthitena sālībhūtamuninā sakkaṃ payojetvā vajirachedito”ti nikāyantariyā. Sapa samavāye,ti, satti, sāmatthiyepi.

Two quarter-verses on the horse. 'Haya' is from the root 'hay' (to go). One that goes quickly is 'turaṅga'; with elision of the nasal, it is 'turaga'. 'Vāha' is from the root 'vah' (to strive). 'Asa' is from the root 'as' (to eat). One born in the country of Sindhu is 'sindhava'. 'Ghoṭaka', 'pīti', 'turaṅgama', 'vājī', 'gandhabba', 'satti', and so on are also for a horse. 'Ghoṭaka' is from the root 'ghuṭ' (to turn). 'Pīti' is from the root 'pā' (to drink). As Rudra states: ''Pīti' is feminine for drinking, but masculine for a horse.' From its connection with speed ('vāja'), it is 'vājī'. Followers of another school say: 'And this one previously had wings, but they were cut off by the thunderbolt, after Sakka was employed by the sage Sālībhūta at the excessive request of the gods.' 'Satti' is from the root 'sap' (to be connected); also in the sense of capability.

369. Tassa [M 0.0258] assassa bhedo viseso assataro, assaṃ taratīti assataro, tara atikkamane, tarapaccayenāpi siddhaṃ. Padhānassabhūmibhavo sujātiko avikārī kulīnako asso ājānīyo nāma, ā bhuso kāraṇākāraṇaṃ jānātīti ājānīyo, anīyo, ṇyapaccayena vā siddhaṃ, tadā “kiyādito nā”ti nāgamo, īkārāgamo ca cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.44 gāthāyampi passitabbaṃ. Kule sambhūto kulīnako, īno, sakatthe ko. Saṅgāme garusatthappahārena nihato santo piyo sāmikaṃ na jahati sukhaṃ vahanasīlo yo asso, so vinītasaddenoccate. Visesena dammataṃ neti yanti vinīto.

369. A particular type of that horse is the 'assatara' (mule); it surpasses a horse, thus 'assatara', from the root 'tara' (to surpass). A horse born in a land of excellent horses, well-bred, faultless, and of noble family, is named 'ājānīya'. Because it thoroughly knows cause and non-cause, it is 'ājānīya'; or it is formed with the suffix 'ṇya', in which case there is no 'nā' augment and there is an 'ī' augment. Born in a noble family is 'kulīnaka'. That horse which, though struck by a heavy weapon in battle, does not abandon its beloved master and is disposed to carrying comfortably, is called by the word 'vinīta'. It is 'vinīta' because it is led to a special state of tameness.

Dvayaṃ assapote. Kasa gamane, oro, assi, kiñci saratīti vā kisoro, bindulopo, asso ca, hayo eva bālattā hayapotako, appatthe ko.

Two terms for a colt. From the root 'kas' (to go) comes 'kisora'; or, because it remembers something, it is 'kisora'. A horse, due to its youth, is a 'hayapotaka'; the suffix 'ka' is in the sense of diminution.

370. Dvayaṃ athāmasse. Ghuṭa parivattane, ṇvu, ghoṭako, assasāmaññepyayaṃ, kharaṃ gacchatīti khaluṅgo, so eva khaḷuṅko, gakārassa kakāraṃ katvā, rassa lo, ḷattamuttañca, khaḷukotipi. Javena sabbesamadhiko asso javano, yu.

370. Two terms for an inferior horse. From the root 'ghuṭ' (to turn) comes 'ghoṭaka'; this is also a general term for a horse. One that goes harshly is 'khaluṅga'; this same is 'khaḷuṅka', by changing 'ga' to 'ka' and 'ra' to 'la'; also 'khaḷuko'. A horse superior to all in speed is 'javana'.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0259] kavītikhyāte mukhabandhane. Mukhamātiṭṭhatīti mukhāṭhānaṃ. Khe mukhavivare līno khalīno. “Kavikā tu khalīnoti khalīne thī (?), kaviyaṃ kathanaṃtyapī”ti rabhaso. Kavi, kavikāpyatra. Ku sadde. I, ī ca, sakatthe ko. Vāsaddena napuṃsakattaṃ samuccinoti. Vuttañca amarakose “kavikā tu khalīno’nitthī”ti amara 18.49.

Two terms for a bridle-bit, known as 'kavīti'. That which stays on the mouth is 'mukhāṭhāna'. That which is attached in the mouth-opening is 'khalīna'. Rabhasa says: ''Kavikā' is 'khalīna', and 'kaviyaṃ' is also a term.' 'Kavi' and 'kavikā' are also used here. From the root 'ku' (to sound). By the word 'vā' (or), the neuter gender is included. And it is said in the Amarakośa: ''Kavikā' is 'khalīna', not feminine.'

Assābhitāḷinī vettavikatādi kasā nāma. Kasa gamane, a, karaṇasādhanaṃ.

That which strikes a horse, made of cane and so forth, is named 'kasā'. It is from the root 'kas' (to go), formed in the instrumental sense.

371. Assassa nāsāgatarajjumhi kusā, kusa silesane. Dvayaṃ assāyaṃ. Vala saṃvaraṇe, vo, ḷattaṃ, ā, vaḷavā. Asatīti assā, “itthiyamatiyavo vā”ti a, ā ca, assā. Vāmīpyatra. Dvayaṃ khure. Khura chedane. Saṃ sukhaṃ pharatyanena saphaṃ, nerutto. “Saphaṃ klīve khuro pumā”ti amara 18.49 amarakoso.

371. The rope going through a horse's nose is 'kusā', from the root 'kus' (to join). Two terms for a mare. From the root 'vala' (to cover), comes 'vaḷavā'. She who eats is 'assā'. 'Vāmī' is also used here. Two terms for a hoof. 'Khura' is from the root 'khur' (to cut). That by which one moves with ease is 'saphaṃ'; this is an etymological explanation. The Amarakośa states: ''Saphaṃ' is neuter, 'khuro' is masculine.'

Dvayaṃ pucchamatte. Puccha pamāde. Na gacchatīti naṅguṭṭho, aṅga gamane, ṭho, assu, dvepi anitthiyaṃ. Lūmaṃpyatra. Dvayaṃ kesavati naṅguṭṭhamatte, na tu hatthino eva. Vālasamūhayogā vālahattho, yathā kesahattho caye, tathātrāpi. Vālo dhiyyate asminti vāladhi, i.

Two terms for a tail. 'Puccha' is from the root 'pucch' (to be heedless). 'Naṅguṭṭha' is that which does not go, from the root 'aṅg' (to go); both terms are not feminine. 'Lūma' is also used here. Two terms for a hairy tail, not only an elephant's. From its connection with a collection of hair, it is 'vālahattha', just as 'kesahattha' means a mass of hair. That in which hair is placed is 'vāladhi'.

Etthānāgatāpi assassa dhārākhyā dhāvākhyā (ka.) pañca gatiyo kathetabbā. Yathā –

Here, the five gaits of a horse, known as 'dhārā', though not included in the verse, should also be described. As follows:

Akkanditaṃ [M 0.0260] dhoritakaṃ, recitaṃ vaggitaṃ plutaṃ;

Gatiyome pañca dhārā dhāvā (ka.), assānaṃ viññunā matā amara 18.48-9.

Akkandita, dhoritaka, recita, vaggita, and pluta; these five gaits are the 'dhārā' of horses, as known by the wise.

Tattha vitthambhā samāvagati akkanditaṃ, kandi gatisosanesu, to. Tato adhikā caturāgati dhoritakaṃ, dhora gaticāturiye, to, sakatthe ko. Maṇḍalikāyānena gamanaṃ recitaṃ, rica viyojanasambajjhanesu, sambajjhanaṃ missanaṃ. Vegena parikkhitto paricaraṇaṃ vaggitaṃ, vagga gamanattho. Turaṃ samena gamanaṃ plutaṃ, plu gatiyaṃ. Ta’dutta’massasatthe “samo’dhiko layo vegī, turitasso bhave kamā”ti.

There, 'akkandita' is a gait of equal pace with a firm stance; from 'kandi' (to move and dry up), with the suffix 'ta'. Then, 'dhoritaka' is a fourfold gait that is more than that; from 'dhora' (clever movement), with the suffix 'ta', and 'ka' in its own sense. 'Recita' is going in circles; from 'ric' (to separate and join), where 'sambajjhana' is mixing. 'Vaggita' is moving swiftly in circles; from 'vagga' in the sense of going. 'Pluta' is going quickly and evenly; from 'plu' (to go). It is said in the treatise on horses: "Let the horse be in stages: even, excessive, slow, swift, hurried."

372. Dvayaṃ yuddhatthe cakkayuttayāne. Sanda gamane, sandate gamyateneneti sandano, yu. Ramateneneti ratho, tho, malopo. Sataṅgopyatra. Satamaṅgānyassa.

372. These two are for a wheeled vehicle used in battle. From 'sand' (to go), 'sandano' means that by which one goes; with the suffix 'yu'. 'Ratho' means that by which one delights; with the suffix 'tha', and elision of 'ma'. 'Sataṅga' is also here. It has a hundred parts.

Yaṃ na raṇāya yuddhatthaṃ cakkayuttaṃ yānaṃ, api tu kīḷābhamanādyatthaṃ, so pussaratho. Vuttañca amarakose “ayaṃ pussaratho cakka-yānaṃ na samarāya ya”nti amara 18.51. Pusa pāsane, so, pusanāmakena phalavisesena yutto ratho pussaratho, pussanakkhattena kato, sajjito vā rathoti pussaratho.

That wheeled vehicle which is not for strife or battle, but for the sake of play and amusement, is a 'pussaratho'. And it is said in the Amarakośa: "This 'pussaratho' is a wheeled vehicle not for battle." From 'pus' (to adorn), with the suffix 'sa'. A chariot connected with a particular fruit called 'pusa' is a 'pussaratho', or a chariot made or equipped under the constellation Pushya is a 'pussaratho'.

Byagghassa cammāvuto parikkhitto ratho veyyaggho nāma, byagghassa vikāro cammaṃ veyyagghaṃ, ṇo, tena parivuto ratho veyyaggho, ṇo, ubhayatrāpi vuḍḍhāgamo. “Paccattaṃ paccatthaṃ (ka.) ayanti [M 0.0261] gacchantīti paccayā”ti vacanatthato paccattameva paccatthameva (?) paccayā bhavanti, yathā kāritantasmāpi payojakavasena anekakāritapaccayā. Dīpino cammāvuto ratho dīpo nāma, dīpino vikāro cammaṃ dīpaṃ, ṇo, tena parivuto ratho dīpo, ṇo.

The chariot covered and surrounded by a tiger's skin is called a 'veyyaggha'; the product of a tiger, its skin, is 'veyyaggha', formed with the suffix 'ṇa'; the chariot surrounded by that is 'veyyaggha', formed with the suffix 'ṇa'; in both cases, there is the vṛddhi augment. According to the meaning of the statement, 'Because they go towards the individual (paccattaṃ ayanti), they are called suffixes (paccayā),' suffixes are indeed individual, just as from a causative form, many causative suffixes arise through the agency of the instigator. The chariot covered with a leopard's skin is called a 'dīpa'; the product of a leopard, its skin, is 'dīpa', formed with the suffix 'ṇa'; the chariot surrounded by that is 'dīpa', formed with the suffix 'ṇa'.

373. Dvayaṃ purisayuttayāne. Si sevāyaṃ. Sukhatthikehi sevīyateti sivikā, ṇvu, vāgamo, ittaṃ, kitapaccayā hi yebhuyyena kammādīsupi vattanti, kiccapaccayā ca kattaripi, yathā “vinayo, nissayo, tapanīyā dhammā”tyādīsu, mahāpadesena vā kitakiccapaccayānaṃ kattukammādīsvapi pavatti veditabbā, sivaṃ karotīti vā sivikā, iko. Yāpyehi adhamehi yāyate niyyateti yāpyayānaṃ. “Yāpya pānīyake nindye”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe.

373. These two are for a vehicle drawn by men. From 'si' (to serve). The 'sivikā' is that which is served by those seeking comfort; with the suffix 'ṇvu', the augment 'va', and the feminine ending 'itta'. Indeed, 'kita' suffixes generally apply to the object of an action, etc., and 'kicca' suffixes to the agent, as in 'vinayo', 'nissayo', 'tapanīyā dhammā', etc. Or, by the great rule, the application of 'kita' and 'kicca' suffixes to agent, object, etc., should be understood. Or, 'sivikā' means 'that which does good' (sivaṃ karoti), with the suffix 'ika'. 'Yāpyayāna' is that which is drawn or conveyed by inferior or lowly beings. Indeed, in the Nānatthasaṅgaha, it is said: "'Yāpya' is for water and for what is blameworthy."

Dvayaṃ sakaṭe. Anitthī tūti tvantaṃ liṅgapadaṃ. Saka sattiyaṃ, aṭo. Ana pāṇane, karaṇasādhanaṃ, natthi nāsā yassāti vā anaṃ, sālopo, rasso ca. Klīve’naṃ, sakaṭo, nitthītyamarakoso amara 18.52.

These two are for a cart. The term 'anitthī' indicates the gender is not feminine. From 'sak' (in power), with the suffix 'aṭa'. From 'an' (to breathe), it is formed as an instrument; or 'anaṃ' means 'that which has no nose' (natthi nāsā yassa), with elision of 'sa' and shortening. 'Anaṃ' is neuter; 'sakaṭo' is not feminine, according to the Amarakośa.

Dvayaṃ cakke. Karoti gamanamaneneti cakkaṃ, dvittaṃ, cakkādi. Rathassa aṅgaṃ rathaṅgaṃ. Tassa cakkassa anto avasānaṃ nemi, sā nāriyaṃ itthiyaṃ. Nayati cakkaṃ nemi. Yā bhūmiṃ phusati, nī naye, mi, īpaccaye nemī ca. Padhipyatra.

These two are for the wheel. 'Cakkaṃ' is that by which movement is made; with doubling of the consonant, and so forth. A part of a chariot is 'rathaṅga'. The rim of that wheel is the 'nemi'; it is feminine. The 'nemi' guides the wheel, that which touches the ground; from 'nī' (to lead), with the suffix 'mi', and with the 'ī' suffix, also 'nemī'. 'Padhi' is also here.

374. Tammajjhe [M 0.0262] tassa rathassa, cakkassa vā majjhe cakkākāro piṇḍikā, yassaṃ sabbāni kaṭṭhāni āsajjante. Piṇḍikāsāhacariyā nābhi itthī, īpaccaye nābhī ca. Sabbāni kaṭṭhāni piṇḍetīti piṇḍikā, piṇḍa saṅghāte, a, sakatthe ko. Piṇḍīpi, nābhi viyāti nābhi.

374. In the middle of that chariot, or in the middle of the wheel, there is the hub, a round mass, where all the spokes are attached. Associated with 'piṇḍikā' is 'nābhi', which is feminine, and with the 'ī' suffix, also 'nābhī'. 'Piṇḍikā' means that which gathers all the spokes into a mass; from 'piṇḍ' (to gather), with the suffix 'a', and 'ka' in its own sense. 'Piṇḍī' is also here; 'nābhi' is like the navel, hence 'nābhi'.

Rathassa yugakaṭṭhaṃ yatra āsajjate, sa yugandharo. Kuṃ pathaviṃ vuṇoti acchādayatīti kubbaro, vu saṃvaraṇe, ro, ussattaṃ. Yugaṃ dhāretīti yugandharo, saññāyaṃ a, abhidhānā rasso.

That part of the chariot where the yoke-wood is attached is the 'yugandharo'. 'Kubbaro' is so called because it covers the earth (kuṃ vuṇoti); from 'vu' (to cover), with the suffix 'ra', and raising of the vowel. 'Yugandharo' is that which bears the yoke (yugaṃ dhāreti); with the suffix 'a' as it is a name, and the preceding vowel is shortened by rule.

Akkho sakaṭaṃ, tadavayavo vā, tathā cāhājayācariyo –

'Akkho' means a cart, or its part; and so says the teacher Ajaya –

“Akkho vibhīṭake nimbe, sakaṭe ca byavahāre;

Rathassāvayave kasse, pāsakepya’kkha’mindriye”ti.

The word 'akkha' means 'vibhīṭaka' (Beleric myrobalan), 'nimba' (neem tree), a cart, in trade; a part of a chariot, in agriculture, in dice, and a sense faculty.

Tassaggagate kīle āṇī, itthī. Aṇipi, “sīmāssikkhaggakīlesu, aṇī āṇī ime dvisū”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.56 hi ruddo dvidhā paṭhati. “Aṇī āṇī ca akkhaggakīle sīmāssisu matā”ti ca nānatthasaṅgahopi. Assi koṇo. Aṇa sadde, ṇi. Pubbapakkhe na vuḍḍhi, ana pāṇane vā, ṇattaṃ. Kaṇḍakādisatthehi parirakkhaṇatthaṃ kato rathāvaraṇo varutho, yo “rathaguttī”ti khyāto. Vara varaṇe, varaṇametthāvaraṇaṃ, yathā rathaṃ thiratthaṃ taṭṭhañca gopatīti rathagutti, itthī, “gutti kārāgāre vuttā, bhūgate rakkhaṇe yame”ti nānatthasaṅgahe.

The peg at its tip is 'āṇī', which is feminine. Also 'aṇī'. Indeed, Rudda reads these two, 'aṇī' and 'āṇī', in two ways: "in boundary pegs, corner pegs, and axle-tip pegs." And the Nānatthasaṅgaha also states: "'Aṇī' and 'āṇī' are understood as the peg at the axle-tip, and in boundaries and corners." 'Assi' is a corner. From 'aṇ' (to sound), with the suffix 'ṇi'. In the former case, there is no vṛddhi; or from 'an' (to breathe), with 'ṇattaṃ'. The chariot's covering, made for protection against thorns and other weapons, is called 'varutha', which is known as 'rathagutti'. From 'var' (to cover), here 'varaṇa' is the covering; 'rathagutti' is so called because it guards the chariot for firmness and stability; it is feminine. In the Nānatthasaṅgaha, 'gutti' is mentioned in the sense of a prison, and in the sense of protection, restraint, and Yama.

375. Rathādīnaṃ [M 0.0263] purobhāgasaṅkhāte mukhe dhuro. Dhara dhāraṇe, assu, yānamukhaṃpyatra. Akkhopakkharādayo rathassa aṅgā nāma. Aka gamane, kho, akkho, dvinnaṃ rathacakkānaṃ antaragato kaṭṭhaviseso. Upari karīyateti upakkharo, akkhassopari kaṭṭhaviseso. Amarakose pana upakkharasaddassa sabbarathāvayavavācakattaṃ vuttaṃ “rathaṅgantu upakkharo”ti amara 18.55. “Apakkharo”tipi pāṭho.

375. The pole ('dhura') is in the front part of chariots and other vehicles, designated as the mouth. From 'dhar' (to bear), with the suffix 'assu'; 'yānamukha' (front of the vehicle) is also here. The axle, 'upakkhara', etc., are called parts of the chariot. From 'ak' (to go), with the suffix 'kha', 'akkho' is a specific wooden piece placed between the two wheels of the chariot. 'Upakkharo' means that which is made above, a specific wooden piece above the axle. However, in the Amarakośa, the term 'upakkharo' is said to denote all parts of the chariot: "'Rathaṅga' is 'upakkharo'." There is also the reading 'apakkharo'.

Sabbasmiṃ hatthādike vāhane yānādittayaṃ, sabbatra karaṇasādhanaṃ. Yojanīyaṃ yujjatenenāti yoggaṃ, ṇyo. Pattaṃ dhoraṇañcātra. Pata gatiyaṃ. Dhora gaticāturiye, etthāpi karaṇasādhanaṃ.

For all conveyances, such as elephants, etc., the three terms beginning with 'yāna' apply, and in every case it is formed as an instrument. 'Yoggaṃ' means that which is to be yoked, or that by which one yokes; with the suffix 'ṇya'. 'Pattaṃ' and 'dhoraṇaṃ' are also here. From 'pat' (to go). From 'dhor' (clever movement); here too, it is formed as an instrument.

376. Catukkaṃ sārathimhi. Rathena carati sīlenāti rathacārī. Savati perayatīti sūto, sū peraṇe, to. Aja gamane. Pājetīti pājitā, ritu, dīghādi. Sara gatiyaṃ, thi, rathena saha gacchatīti vā sārathi, iṇa, aññatropacārā. Niyantā, yantā, khattā, sabyaṭṭho, dakkhiṇattho, rathakuṭumbīpyatra.

376. Four terms are for the charioteer. 'Rathacārī' means one who moves by chariot by habit. 'Sūto' means one who drives or conveys; from 'sū' (to convey), with the suffix 'ta'. From 'aj' (to go). 'Pājitā' means one who drives; from 'pājeti', with the suffix 'ritu', lengthening, etc. 'Sārathi' comes from 'sar' (to go), with the suffix 'thi'; or one who goes with the chariot, from 'i' (to go) with the suffix 'ṇa', by metaphorical usage elsewhere. 'Niyantā', 'yantā', 'khattā', 'sabyaṭṭho', 'dakkhiṇattho', and 'rathakuṭumbī' are also here.

“Niyantā pājitā yantā, sūto khattā ca sārathi;

Sabyaṭṭho dakkhiṇattho ca, saññā rathakuṭumbino”ti amara 18.56-60. –

It is said: "'Niyantā', 'pājitā', 'yantā', 'sūto', 'khattā', and 'sārathi'; 'sabyaṭṭho' and 'dakkhiṇattho'—these are designations of the charioteer."

Vuttaṃ[M 0.0264]. Atthato sārathino rathakuṭumbī ca nāmaṃ. Rathanāyake tu “rathāroho ca rathiko rathī”ti pacchā vakkhati. Khudi saṃpesane, tu, dassa to, ussattañca, khattā.

It is said. In meaning, 'rathakuṭumbī' is a name for a charioteer. But regarding the chariot-warrior, he will explain later with the terms 'rathāroho,' 'rathiko,' and 'rathī.' The root 'khud' is in the sense of impelling; from this is formed 'khattā', with the suffix 'tu', the change of 'da' to 'ta', and the raising of the vowel.

Tikaṃ rathe pājitatarā aññe yodhā, atra ye “rathanāyakā”tipyuccante. Rathamārohatīti rathiko, rathī ca. Rathena yujjatīti vā rathiko, rathī ca. Rathino, sandanārohopyatra. Dvayaṃ yodhe. Yudha sampahāre, ṇo. Bhaṭati yujjatīti bhaṭo, a. Kvaci yoddhopi.

Three terms are for warriors in a chariot other than the driver, who are also called 'rathanāyakā' here. 'Rathiko' and 'rathī' are so called because they mount a chariot. Alternatively, 'rathiko' and 'rathī' are so called because they are engaged with a chariot. 'Rathino' and 'sandanāroho' are also here. Two terms are for warriors. From 'yudh' (to fight), in the sense of conflict, with the suffix 'ṇa'. 'Bhaṭo' is so called because he fights or is engaged; with the suffix 'a'. Sometimes 'yoddho' also occurs.

377-379. Catukkaṃ padātike. Padehi atati ajatīti padāti, ata sātaccagamane, i. Pada gamane. Padatīti patti, i, dvittaṃ. Padena adatīti vā patti, alopo, dassa to, ime dve, vakkhamānā dve ca pume. Padehi gacchatīti padago, padiko. Pādātiko, padājayopyatra pādehi ajati ī, rasso ca padājiṃ (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.66).

377-379. Four terms are for foot soldiers. 'Padāti' is so called because he goes or moves with his feet; from 'at' (in the sense of continuous going), with the suffix 'i'. From 'pad' (in the sense of going). 'Patti' is so called because he goes; with the suffix 'i' and doubling of the consonant. Alternatively, 'patti' is so called because he takes with his feet, with elision of 'a' and the change of 'da' to 'ta'. These two, and the two to be mentioned, are masculine. 'Padago' and 'padiko' are so called because they go with their feet. 'Pādātiko' and 'padājayo' are also here.

Chakkaṃ [M 0.0265] kavace. Naha bandhane, karaṇe ṇo. Kaṅka gatyattho, aṭo. Varīyate tanti vammaṃ, vara varaṇe, vara icchāyaṃ vā, mo, rassa mo. Kaca bandhane, a, vakāravaṇṇāgamo. Uro chādayantyanenāti uracchado. Vāsaddo dvinnaṃ punnapuṃsakattaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Jala dittiyaṃ, ṇvu. Tanuttaṃ, daṃsanaṃ, jagaropyatra. “Jagaro kaṅkaṭo yogo, sannāho ca uracchado”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.64 byākhyāsudhā 2.8.64 vopālito.

Six terms are for armor. 'Naha' is in the sense of binding; the suffix 'ṇo' is used in the sense of instrument. 'Kaṅka' has the meaning of movement; the suffix is 'aṭa'. 'Vamma' is so called because it is chosen; 'vara' is in the sense of choosing, or 'vara' in the sense of desiring, with the suffix 'ma', and 'ma' for 'ra'. 'Kaca' is in the sense of binding; the suffix is 'a', with the addition of the letter 'va'. 'Uracchado' is so called because the chest is covered by it. The word 'vā' combines the two, masculine and neuter genders. 'Jala' is in the sense of shining; the suffix is 'ṇvu'. 'Tanuttaṃ', 'daṃsanaṃ', and 'jagaro' are also here. As Vopālita said: 'Jagaro, kaṅkaṭo, yogo, sannāho, and uracchado'.

Tikaṃ katasannāhe. Cammena sammā naddhavāti sannaddho, dho. Sajju gatiyaṃ, a. Vammena naddhavā vammiko. Daṃsito, uracchadiko, byūḷhakaṅkaṭo, jagarikopyatra.

Three terms are for one who is clad in armor. 'Sannaddho' is so called because he is properly bound with leather; the suffix is 'ta'. 'Sajju' is in the sense of movement; the suffix is 'a'. 'Vammiko' is so called because he is bound with mail. 'Daṃsito' (armored), 'uracchadiko' (one wearing a breastplate), 'byūḷhakaṅkaṭo' (one with a broad cuirass), and 'jagariko' (a watchman) are also here.

Dvayaṃ paridahite vatthādo. Āpatipubbo mucadhātu paridahane, ubhayattha to, bhūjādi. Pakkhe “susapacasakato kkhakkā ce”ti sutte cakārena tapaccayassa kko, dhātvantalopo ca. Pinaddho, apinaddhopyatra. Pubbapakkhe apissākāralopo.

Two terms are for one clothed in garments and so forth. The root 'muc', preceded by 'ā' and 'paṭi', is in the sense of wearing; in both cases the suffix is 'ta', as with 'bhū' and others. Alternatively, in the rule 'susapacasakato kkhakkā ce', by 'ca', the suffix 'ta' becomes 'kka', and the final letter of the root is elided. 'Pinaddho' (girded) and 'apinaddho' (girded) are also here. In the former case, the 'a' of 'api' is elided.

Catukkaṃ abhicārapadātimhi. Pure caraṇasīlo, sattamiyā alopo ubhayatrāpi. Pubbe ṇī. Parapakkhe a, pubbaṃ, pubbe vā gacchatīti pubbaṅgamo, dutiyāyālopo. Purogo, aggesaro, paṭṭho, aggatosaro, purassaro, purogamopyatra.

Four terms are for a vanguard foot soldier. One whose habit is to go before; the elision of the seventh case ending occurs in both instances. Previously, the suffix is 'ṇī'. In the other alternative, the suffix is 'a'; 'pubbaṅgamo' is so called because one goes before ('pubbaṃ' or 'pubbe'), with the elision of the second case ending. 'Purogo' (leader), 'aggesaro' (foremost), 'paṭṭho' (chief), 'aggatosaro' (preeminent), 'purassaro' (vanguard), and 'purogamo' (forerunner) are also here.

Dvayaṃ asīghagāmini. Mandaṃ gacchati sīlenāti mandagāmī, ṇī. Mantha viloḷane, anekatthattā saṃkilese ca. Saṃkilissateti mantharo, aro.

Two terms are for one who goes slowly. 'Mandagāmī' is so called because he goes slowly by nature; the suffix is 'ṇī'. The root 'mantha' is in the sense of churning, and due to having many meanings, also in the sense of defilement. 'Mantharo' is so called because one becomes defiled; the suffix is 'ara'.

Tikaṃ vegini. Turameti gacchatīti turito, i gatiyaṃ, to. Turassi, pajavī, javopyatra. Dvayaṃ jetuyoggatāmatte. Ji jaye, tabbo, jetabbaṃ, ṇyapaccaye jeyyaṃ.

Three terms are for one who is swift. 'Turito' is so called because he goes quickly; the root 'i' is in the sense of going, with the suffix 'ta'. 'Turassi' (swift), 'pajavī' (fleet), and 'javo' (speedy) are also here. Two terms are for mere conquerability. The root 'ji' is in the sense of conquering; with the suffix 'tabba' it becomes 'jetabbaṃ' (that which is to be conquered); with the suffix 'ṇya' it becomes 'jeyyaṃ' (that which should be conquered).

380. Tikaṃ [M 0.0266] sūre. Sura vīra vikkanteti curādidhātu. Surayati, vīrayatīti sūro, vīro ca, a, dīghādi, kanta chedane. Vikkanto. Dvayaṃ sahāyamatte. Saha eti gacchatīti sahāyo, sabbatra kattari ca a. Anusaddo pacchāttho. Samāti ete dve tulyatthā. Anuplapo, abhisaropi. Sannaddhappabhutī sannaddhasaddādayo anucarantā tīsu.

380. Three terms are for a brave one. The roots 'sura', 'vīra', and 'vikkanta' are from the 'curādi' group. 'Sūro' and 'vīro' are so called because one acts boldly or heroically; the suffix is 'a', with lengthening and so on. 'Kanta' is in the sense of cutting. 'Vikkanto'. Two terms are for a mere companion. 'Sahāyo' is so called because one goes together with another; the suffix 'a' is used in all agent nouns. The word 'anu' has the meaning of 'following'. These two, 'sama' and 'iti', have similar meanings. 'Anuplapo' and 'abhisaro' are also here. The words beginning with 'sannaddha', being adjectives, are used in the three genders.

Pātheyyaṃ nāma rājādīnaṃ yātrāsveva bahulaṃ pavattatīti idha taṃ vuttaṃ, pathe hitaṃ pātheyyaṃ, eyyo. Samba maṇḍale, alo, sameti addhānaparissamametenāti vā sambalaṃ, alo, bāgamo ca.

'Pātheyya' is mentioned here because it commonly occurs for kings and others on journeys; 'pātheyyaṃ' is so called because it is beneficial on the path ('pathe'), with the suffix 'eyya'. The root 'samba' is in the sense of a collection; the suffix is 'ala'. Or 'sambalaṃ' is so called because it alleviates ('sameti') the fatigue of the journey; the suffix is 'ala', and there is an augment 'ba'.

381. Catukkaṃ senāyaṃ. Vāhayogā vāhinī. Dhajayogā dhajinī. Si bandhane, no, senā. Camu adane, ū. Camati bhīrunti camū. Putanā, anīkinī, varūthinīpyatra. Ettha ca putanā anīkinī vāhinī camū senābhedepi. “Putanā’nīkinī camū, senā senāntarepi ce”ti ruddo, “senāpabhede senāyaṃ, savantyamapi vāhinī”ti rabhaso ca. Cakkāditikaṃ sāmaññena senāyaṃ, senaṅge ca. Cāṇakye tu senāvisese anīko vutto “tīṇi tikānyanīka”nti.

381. Four terms are for an army. 'Vāhinī' is so called because it is connected with vehicles ('vāha'). 'Dhajinī' is so called because it is connected with banners ('dhaja'). The root 'si' is in the sense of binding; with the suffix 'no', it becomes 'senā'. The root 'camu' is in the sense of eating; the suffix is 'ū'. 'Camū' is so called because it devours the timid ('bhīru'). 'Putanā', 'anīkinī', and 'varūthinī' are also here. And here, 'putanā', 'anīkinī', 'vāhinī', and 'camū' are also used for divisions of an army. As Rudda said: 'Putanā, anīkinī, camū, and senā are also used for divisions of an army'; and Rabhasa said: ''Vāhinī' is used for divisions of an army, and also for a river.' The triad beginning with 'cakka' refers generally to an army and its components. But in Cāṇakya, 'anīka' is mentioned as a specific type of army: 'Three groups of three constitute an anīka'.

Asseva [M 0.0267] kāmandakīye vivaraṇaṃ, yathā –

Of this, the explanation is given in the Kāmandakīya, as follows:

“Assassa pattiyodhā ye, bhaveyyuṃ purisā tayo;

Iti kappā tu pañcassā, vidheyyā kuñjarassa tu;

Pādaṅgo pājitāvanto, purisā dasa pañca ca;

Vidhānamiti nāgassa, catukkaṃ sandanassa ca;

Anīkamiti viññeyya-miti kappā nava dvipā”ti.

'For a horse, there should be three foot soldiers; thus five such units should be assigned to an elephant; fifteen men are to be arranged as foot soldiers; such is the arrangement for an elephant, and four for a chariot; an 'anīka' should be known as nine units of men.'

Karīyate viggaho yeneti cakkaṃ. Bala saṃvaraṇe, a. Aṇa sadde, iko. Vākāro napuṃsakattaṃ samuccinoti.

'Cakkaṃ' is that by which strife ('viggaho') is made ('karīyate'). The root 'bala' is in the sense of restraining; the suffix is 'a'. The root 'aṇa' is in the sense of sound; the suffix is 'ika'. The word 'vā' combines the neuter gender.

Caturaṅgabalāya susannaddhāya senāya yuddhatthaṃ desavidese vinyāso vibhajitvā nyasanaṃ ṭhapanaṃ byūho kathyate. Vibhajitvā ūhanaṃ ṭhapanaṃ byūho. Tabbhedā daṇḍabhogamaṇḍalāsaṃhatā cattāro pakatibyūhā. Tatra anīkānaṃ tiriyato vutti daṇḍo. Samatthānamanīkānamanvāvutti aññoññato vutti bhogo. Maṇḍalaracanāya sarantānamanīkānaṃ sabbato vutti sappasarīramiva maṇḍalo. Ṭhitānamitaretarāsaṃ hatānaṃ visiliṭṭhatarānaṃ anīkānaṃ puthuvutti asaṃhato. Taduttaṃ kāmandakena –

The deployment ('vinyāso') of a well-equipped fourfold army for battle in various regions, which is a dividing, arranging, and positioning, is called a formation ('byūho'). Dividing, arranging, and positioning is a formation. Its types are four basic formations: the staff ('daṇḍa'), the coil ('bhoga'), the circle ('maṇḍala'), and the scattered ('asaṃhata'). Among these, the linear disposition of troops is the staff. The successive disposition of capable troops, one after another, is the coil. The disposition of troops on all sides, moving in a circular formation like a serpent's body, is the circle. The separate disposition of troops standing uncombined and rather loosely connected is the scattered. As stated by Kāmandaka:

“Tiriyato vutti daṇḍākhyā, bhogonvāvuttireva ca;

Maṇḍalo sabbatovutti, puthuvutti asaṃhato”ti.

'The linear disposition is called 'daṇḍa', and 'bhoga' is the successive disposition; 'maṇḍala' is the all-around disposition, 'asaṃhata' is the separate disposition.'

Byūhasamaveto eva byūhassekadeso pacchābhāgo byūhapaṇhi, byūhassa pacchā, byūhantarameva vā. Yatra ṭhito rājā sasenaṃ paṭiggaṇhati, taṃ senāya pacchā dhanusatadvayantarena ṭhitaparisasahitaṃ anīkaṃ “paṭiggaho”tyuccate.

The 'byūhapaṇhi' is the rear part of the formation, which is itself part of the formation, or the rear of the formation, or even the interior of the formation. That unit where the king stands with his army to provide support, which is located at a distance of two hundred bow-lengths behind the army, along with his retinue, is called 'paṭiggaho' (reserve).

382-383. Eko [M 0.0268] hatthī dvādasapurisasahito “eko hatthī”tyuccate, etena lakkhaṇena adhamantato heṭṭhimaparicchedena tayo hatthino hatthānīkaṃ nāma, tathā eko turaṅgo tipurisasahito, eko ca ratho catupurisasahito eko hayo, eko rathoti etena lakkhaṇena adhamantato tayo hayā ca tayo rathā ca hayānīkaṃ, rathānīkaṃ nāma, tenāha “tayo tayo gajādayo”ti. Sasatthā khaggādisatthahatthā catujjanā cattāro purisā pattānīkaṃ nāma vuttā. Heṭṭhimantatoyevetthāpi paricchedo. Amarakose tvaññathā kathitā –

A single elephant accompanied by twelve men is called 'one elephant'. By this characteristic, with the lowest limit as the minimum measure, three elephants constitute an elephant unit ('hatthānīkaṃ'). Similarly, a single horse accompanied by three men, and a single chariot accompanied by four men—one horse and one chariot—by this characteristic, from the lowest limit, three horses and three chariots constitute a horse unit ('hayānīkaṃ') and a chariot unit ('rathānīkaṃ'). Hence it is said, 'three each of elephants and so forth'. Four men, armed, with swords and other weapons in hand, are called a foot-soldier unit ('pattānīkaṃ'). Here too, the lowest limit is the measure. In the Amarakośa, however, it is explained differently:

“Ekakebharathā tyassā, patti pañcapadātikā;

Patyaṅgehi tiguṇehi, kamā saññā yathottaraṃ.

'One elephant, one chariot, three horses, and five foot soldiers make a 'patti'; with the components of a 'patti' multiplied by three, the designations of larger units follow in successive order.'

Senāmukhaṃ gumbagaṇā, vāhinī putanā camū;

Anīkinī ca tāsantu, dasa akkhobhinī mata”nti amara 18.80-1.

'Senāmukha', 'gumba', 'gaṇa', 'vāhinī', 'putanā', 'camū', and 'anīkinī'; and ten of those 'anīkinīs' are considered an 'akkhobhinī'.

Tassattho – tīhi assehi gajenekena rathena ca padātībhi ca pañcahi patti nāma senantaraṃ. Patyaṅgehi sabbehi gajādīhi [M 0.0269] yathāpubbaṃ guṇehi yathottaraṃ kamena senāmukhādikā saññā bhavati. Yathottaranti vacanena yathāpubbamityatthamāha, tenedaṃ vuttaṃ “bhavati tayo pattino senāmukhaṃ. Tīhi senāmukhehi gumbo. Gumbattayena gaṇo. Gaṇattayaṃ vāhinī. Vāhinittayaṃ putanā. Putanattayaṃ camū. Camuttayaṃ anīkinī. Tāsaṃ anīkinīnaṃ dasa akkhobhinī”ti.

The meaning of that is: a division of an army called a 'patti' consists of three horses, one elephant, one chariot, and five foot soldiers. With all the components of a 'patti', such as elephants and so on, multiplied as before, the designations such as 'senāmukha' arise in successive order. By the word 'successively' he stated the meaning 'as before'; thus it is said: 'Three 'pattis' form a 'senāmukha'. Three 'senāmukhas' form a 'gumba'. Three 'gumbas' form a 'gaṇa'. Three 'gaṇas' form a 'vāhinī'. Three 'vāhinīs' form a 'putanā'. Three 'putanās' form a 'camū'. Three 'camūs' form an 'anīkinī'. Ten of these 'anīkinīs' make an 'akkhobhinī'.

Tatra rathānaṃ saṅkhyā sattatisahitehi aṭṭhasatehādhikānyekavīsatisahassāni, evameva gajānampi saṅkhyā, tathā ca –

Therein, the number of chariots is twenty-one thousand, eight hundred and seventy. Likewise, the number of elephants is the same, and so:

Pañcasaṭṭhisahassāni, chasatāni daseva tu;

Saṅkhyā tā turaṅgānañhi, vinā rathe turaṅgame.

Sixty-five thousand, six hundred and ten was indeed the count of horses, excluding chariot horses.

Narānaṃ satasahassaṃ, sahassāni naveva ca;

Satāni tīṇi ca’ññāni, paññāsañca padātayoti byākhyāsudhā 2.8.80.

The number of men is one hundred and nine thousand, three hundred and fifty foot soldiers.

384. Heṭṭhimaparicchedena senaṃ dassetvā ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena dassetumāha “saṭṭhi…pe… yanti”ccādi. Yantiyā yānaṃ kubbantiyā senāya kattubhūtāya dhūlīkatesu santesu. Kesu? Saṭṭhivaṃsakalāpesu. Kittakappamāṇesu? Paccekaṃ saṭṭhidaṇḍavantesu, esā akkhobhinī nāma senā ukkaṭṭhaparicchedena. Kenaci khobhetumasakkuṇeyyatāya akkhobhinī, yu, nadādi. Khubha calane.

384. Having shown the army by the lower measure, in order to show it by the higher measure, he says: 'sixty... etc.... they go.' When dust has been raised by the army, which is the agent, as it makes its movement. Among what? Among sixty clumps of bamboo. Of what measure? Each having sixty staffs. This army, named 'akkhobhinī,' is by the higher measure. Because it cannot be shaken by anyone, it is 'akkhobhinī'; formed with the suffix 'yu,' like 'nadī,' etc. The root 'khubh' is in the sense of 'to tremble'.

385. Catukkaṃ [M 0.0270] sampattiyaṃ. Dhanukkaṃso sampatti. Pada gamane, bhāveti. Yupakkhe “itthiyamatiyavo vā”ti a. Lakkha dassanaṅkesu, ī, lakkhī, sirī ca pubbe devatāvasena vuttā, idha dhanukkaṃsavasena.

385. Four terms are for prosperity. Excellence in archery is prosperity. The root 'pad' is in the sense of 'to go'; it is in the causative sense. In the case of the suffix 'yu,' 'a' is used, as in the rule 'itthiyamatiyavo vā.' The root 'lakkh' is in the sense of 'to see' and 'to mark'; with the suffix 'ī,' it becomes 'lakkhī.' Both 'sirī' and 'lakkhī' were previously mentioned in the sense of deities, but here in the sense of excellence in archery.

Dvayaṃ sampattiviparītāyaṃ. Virūpaṃ pajjatīti vipatti, padimhā kattariti. Virūpaṃ pajjanaṃ vā vipatti, bhāveti. Āpadāsahacaraṇato vipatti thiyaṃ.

Two terms are for the opposite of prosperity. 'Vipatti' is so called because 'it falls into a bad state' (virūpaṃ pajjati); it is formed from the root 'pad' with the suffix 'ti' in the agent sense. Alternatively, 'vipatti' means 'a falling into a bad state' (virūpaṃ pajjanaṃ); it is in the sense of the action. 'Vipatti' is feminine because it is associated with calamities.

Catukkaṃ satthamatte. Ādāya yujjhante yanti āvudhaṃ, yassa vo. Āyudhaṃ vā. Hara haraṇe. Harati jīvitanti heti,ti, asse, ralopo, hanativasena vā siddhaṃ. Sasa hiṃsāyaṃ, tho. Atthaṃpyatra. Asu khepane.

Four terms are for a weapon in general. 'Āvudhaṃ' or 'āyudhaṃ' is so called because they go (yanti) to fight (yujjhante) taking it (ādāya). The root 'har' is in the sense of 'to carry away.' 'Heti' is so called because 'it carries away life' (harati jīvitaṃ); it is formed with the suffix 'ti,' the change of 'a' to 'e,' and the elision of 'ra'; or it is derived from 'hanati' (to strike). The root 'sas' is in the sense of 'to harm,' with the suffix 'tha.' The word 'attha' is also used here. The root 'as' is in the sense of 'to throw'.

386-387. Saṅkhepenāyudhaṃ dassetumāha. Muttāmuttañca amuttañca pāṇito muttañca yantamuttañceti sakalaṃ taṃ āyudhaṃ catubbidhaṃ bahūnampi tabbhedānativattanato.

386-387. To explain weapons briefly, it is stated: All those weapons are fourfold—those that are both thrown and not thrown (muttāmutta), those that are not thrown (amutta), those thrown by hand (pāṇito mutta), and those thrown by machine (yantamutta)—since even many other distinctions do not go beyond these.

Catunnaṃ sarūpamāha “muttāmuttañcā”di. Yaṭṭhi nāma satthaviseso, na kattaradaṇḍo.

The nature of the four types is stated, beginning with 'muttāmuttañca.' 'Yaṭṭhi' is a specific kind of weapon, not a driver's goad.

“Yaṭṭhi hāralatāsattha-bhedesu dhanudaṇḍake”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe.

For it is said in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: 'Yaṭṭhi is used in the senses of a pearl necklace, types of weapons, a bow, and a staff.'

Tadādi [M 0.0271] āyudhaṃ muttañca taṃ amuttañceti muttāmuttaṃ, kammadhārayo, yathā katākataṃ. Churikā asiputti, tadādikaṃ amuttaṃ. Yanta saṅkocane, yantaṃ, dhanvādi.

A weapon such as a staff, which is both thrown and not thrown, is called 'muttāmuttaṃ'; it is a kammadhāraya compound, like 'katākataṃ' (done and not done). A dagger (churikā), a small sword (asiputti), and the like are not thrown (amutta). The root 'yant' is in the sense of 'to restrain,' hence 'yantaṃ' (a machine), such as a bow and so forth.

388-389. Pañcakaṃ dhanumhi. Usuṃ asati khipatīti, kammani ṇo, ussi. Dhana dhaññe, u, hana hiṃsāyaṃ vā, u, hassa dho, dhanu. “Dhanu vaṃsavisuddhopi, nigguṇo kiṃ karissatī”ti hitopadesa kathāmukha 23 pume payogo. “Sarā vāpo dhanu itthī, tuṇatā tiṇatāpice”ti tikaṇḍasesa 2.8.51 tikaṇḍaseso. Kiṃ nāmena daṇḍayatīti kodaṇḍaṃ, daṇḍa nipātane, kiṃ nāmena damyatīti vā kodaṇḍaṃ, damudhātumhā ḍo, kiṃ nāmena dunotīti vā kodaṇḍaṃ, du paritāpe, ḍo nipātito, kuṭilattā vā kucchito daṇḍo yassatthīti kodaṇḍaṃ. Capa santāpe, a, capo, vaṃsabhedo, tabbikāro cāpo, ṇo. Saramasati khipatīti sarāsanaṃ. Kammukampi. Kammāya pabhavatīti kammukaṃ.

388-389. Five terms are for the bow. 'Ussi' is so called because it throws (asati, i.e., khipati) an arrow (usuṃ); it is formed with the suffix 'ṇa' in the sense of object. 'Dhanu' is from the root 'dhan' (to produce grain) with the suffix 'u'; or from 'han' (to harm) with 'u,' where 'h' becomes 'dh.' Its usage in the masculine gender is shown: 'Even a bow of pure bamboo, if unstrung, what can it do?' The Tikaṇḍasesa states: 'Sarā, vāpo, and dhanu are feminine, as are tuṇatā and tiṇatā.' 'Kodaṇḍaṃ' is so called because 'it punishes with what?' (kiṃ daṇḍayati), from the root 'daṇḍ' (to strike down); or 'it is tamed with what?' (kiṃ damyati), from the root 'dam' with the suffix 'ḍo'; or 'it torments with what?' (kiṃ dunoti), from 'du' (to torment), with 'ḍo' irregularly inserted; or it is that which has a contemptible (kucchito) staff (daṇḍo) because of its crookedness. 'Capo' is from the root 'cap' (to torment) with the suffix 'a'; it is a type of bamboo, and its product is 'cāpo,' formed with 'ṇa.' 'Sarāsanaṃ' is so called because it throws (asati) arrows (sara). 'Kammukaṃ' is also a term; it is so called because it is suitable for work (kammāya pabhavati).

Tikaṃ guṇe. Gacchati saro yenāti guṇo, massa ṇo, assu, gu sadde vā, gavati etenāti guṇo, yu, ṇattaṃ. Jara vayohānimhi, a, jiyādeso. Pakkhe ikāralopo, jayā. “Jiyā cāthā”tipi pāṭho, tadā dvayaṃ [M 0.0272] guṇe. Mubbī, siñjinīpyatra. Mubbavikāro mubbī. Siñja abyattasadde, inī.

Three terms are for the bowstring. 'Guṇa' is so called because the arrow goes (gacchati saro) along it (yena); it is formed from the root 'gam' with the suffix 'u,' where 'm' becomes 'ṇ'; or from the root 'gu' (to sound), because one makes a sound (gavati) with it (etena), with the suffix 'yu' and the change to 'ṇ.' 'Jiyā' is from the root 'jar' (to grow old), with the suffix 'a' and the substitution of 'jiyā.' Alternatively, with the elision of 'i,' it becomes 'jayā.' There is also the reading 'jiyā cāthā,' in which case there are two terms for bowstring. 'Mubbī' and 'siñjinī' are also used here. 'Mubbī' is a product of the 'mubba' plant. 'Siñjinī' is from the root 'siñj' (to make an indistinct sound), with the suffix 'inī'.

Tipādo kaṇḍe. Sara hiṃsāyaṃ. Sarantyanenāti, pume, saññāyaṃ ṇo. Pattaṃ vājo, taṃyogā pattī, ī. Sā tanukaraṇāvasānesu, divādi, ṇvu, yassālopo. Vaṇyate saddāyateneneti vāṇo, ṇo, vaṇa sadde. Kaṇyateneneti kaṇḍaṃ, kaṇa sadde, ḍo, kaṇḍa bhede vā. Isa gamane, u, issu, usa dāhe vā. Khura chedane, apo, atha vā khe arati gacchatīti khuro, assu, taṃ pātīti khurappo. Tija nisāne, yu. Asa khipane, kamme yu. Visikho, ajimhago, khago, āsugo, kalambo, maggaṇo, ropopyatra. Visanto khaṇatīti visikho. Kala made, ambo. Magga anvesane, yu. Rupa vimohane, divādi, a, ropo. “Thūlakheḍo vipāṭo ca, citrapuṅkho saropi ce”ti tikaṇḍasesa 2.8.52 tikaṇḍasese.

Three verses are on the arrow. The root 'sar' is in the sense of 'to harm.' 'Sara' is so called because one moves (sarati) with it (anena); it is masculine, a noun formed with the suffix 'ṇa.' 'Pattaṃ' means a feather or wing (vājo); from its connection with this, an arrow is called 'pattī,' with the suffix 'ī.' 'Sāyaka' is from the root 'sā' (to thin, to finish), of the Divādi class, with the suffix 'ṇvu' and elision of 'ya.' 'Vāṇo' is so called because a sound is made (vaṇyate saddāyate) by it (anena); it is from the root 'vaṇ' (to sound) with the suffix 'ṇa.' 'Kaṇḍaṃ' is so called because a sound is made (kaṇyate) by it (anena), from the root 'kaṇ' (to sound) with the suffix 'ḍa'; or from 'kaṇḍ' (to break). 'Issu' is from the root 'is' (to go) with 'u'; or from 'us' (to burn).
