'Khurappo' is from the root 'khur' (to cut) with the suffix 'appa'; or, 'khuro' is that which goes (arati) in the sky (khe), formed with 'a,' and 'khurappo' is that which protects it. 'Tejana' is from the root 'tij' (to sharpen) with 'yu.' 'Asana' is from the root 'as' (to throw), with 'yu' in the sense of object. 'Visikho,' 'ajimhago,' 'khago,' 'āsugo,' 'kalambo,' 'maggaṇo,' and 'ropo' are also used here. 'Visikho' is so called because, having entered (visanto), it cuts (khaṇati). 'Kalambo' is from the root 'kal' (to be intoxicated) with the suffix 'amba.' 'Maggaṇo' is from the root 'magg' (to seek) with 'yu.' 'Ropo' is from the root 'rup' (to confuse), of the Divādi class, with 'a.' In the Tikaṇḍasesa it is said: 'Thūlakheḍo, vipāṭo, citrapuṅkho, and also sara.'

Pañcakaṃ kalāpe. Tūṇa pūraṇe, curādi, nadādi. “Tūṇo nisaṅgo tūṇiro, upāsaṅgo ca vāṇadhi”riti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 18.88 amaramālāyaṃ puṃsakaṇḍe. “Tūṇā”tipi itthiliṅgappakaraṇe vutto, idha pana “tuṇī, tūṇo”ti dvīsu, sarasamūhānaṃ ṭhānattā kalāpo. Irapaccaye tūṇiro. Vāṇā sarā dhiyantetreti vāṇadhi. “Tūṇo pasaṅga tūṇira-nisaṅgā vāṇadhi dvisū”tyamarasīhe.

Five terms are for the quiver. The root 'tūṇ' is in the sense of 'to fill,' of the Curādi or Nadādi class. As stated in the masculine section of the Amaramālā: 'Tūṇa, nisaṅga, tūṇira, upāsaṅga, and vāṇadhi are terms for a quiver.' 'Tūṇā' is also mentioned in the section on feminine gender; however, here 'tuṇī' and 'tūṇo' are in both genders. 'Kalāpo' is so called because it is the place for a collection of arrows. With the suffix 'ira,' it becomes 'tūṇiro.' 'Vāṇadhi' is that in which arrows (vāṇā) are held (dhīyante). According to Amarasīha: 'Tūṇa, pasaṅga, tūṇira, nisaṅga, and vāṇadhi are used in two genders.'

390. Dvayaṃ vāje, yaṃ “kaṇḍapatta”mityuccate. Pata gamane, karaṇe kho, tassa ko, pakkhena katattā vā pakkho[M 0.0273]. Vajatyanenāti vājo, ṇo. Visamapivitthāti visappīto saro diddho nāma. Disa appītiyaṃ, to. Littopyatra.

390. Two terms are for the feather (vāja), which is called 'kaṇḍapatta' (arrow-feather). 'Pakkha' is from the root 'pat' (to go), with the suffix 'kha' in the instrumental sense, which becomes 'ka'; or it is 'pakkha' because it is made from a wing (pakkha). 'Vājo' is so called because one goes (vajati) by means of it (anena), with the suffix 'ṇa.' An arrow that is smeared with poison is called 'visappīto' or 'diddho.' 'Diddho' is from the root 'dih' (to smear), with the suffix 'ta.' 'Litta' (smeared) is also used here.

Tikaṃ vijjhitabbe. Vijjhanatthaṃ lakkhyateti lakkhaṃ. Vijjhitabbanti vejjhaṃ, ṇyo, jhassa jjho, isse. Saro vayati gacchati yasmiṃ sarabyaṃ, vassākāralopo. Niccaṃ sarānamabhyāsanaṃ vasīkaraṇaṃ sarābhyāso. “Byādhepyupāsanāyañca, vāṇābhyāsepyupāsana”nti ruddo. Lakkhamupagantvā asanaṃ khipanaṃ upāsanaṃ.

Three terms are for that which is to be pierced. 'Lakkhaṃ' (target) is that which is aimed at (lakkhiyati) for the purpose of piercing. 'Vejjhaṃ' is that which is to be pierced (vijjhitabbaṃ), formed with the suffix 'ṇya,' where 'jh' becomes 'jjh,' and 'i' becomes 'e.' 'Sarabyaṃ' is that toward which an arrow (saro) goes (vayati, i.e., gacchati), with the elision of the letter 'va.' Constant practice with arrows, which leads to mastery (vasīkaraṇaṃ), is 'sarābhyāsa.' Rudda states: ''Upāsana' is used in the sense of hunting and the practice of archery.' 'Upāsana' is approaching the target and shooting.

391. Pañcakaṃ khagge. Maṇḍalaṃ aggaṃ yassa. Niggato tiṃsato’ṅgulito nettiṃso. Asa khepane, asate khippateti asi, i. Khagga khaṇḍabhede. Sāyako sarepi. Candahāso, riṭṭhi, kakkhalako, karavālopyatra. Tassa khaggassa pidhāne kosi, itthī. Kusa silesane, i, kosi, rassanto. Khaggachurikādīnaṃ muṭṭhiyaṃ tharusaddo. Thara satthagatiyaṃ, u.

391. Five terms are for the sword. 'Maṇḍalāgga' is that which has a circular (maṇḍala) tip (agga). 'Nettiṃso' is that which extends beyond (niggato) thirty (tiṃsato) finger-breadths. 'Asi' is from the root 'as' (to throw), because it is thrown (asati, i.e., khippati), with the suffix 'i.' The root 'khagg' is in the sense of 'to break into pieces.' 'Sāyaka' is also a term for an arrow. 'Candahāsa,' 'riṭṭhi,' 'kakkhalaka,' and 'karavāla' are also used here. The scabbard (pidhāna) of that sword is 'kosi,' which is feminine. 'Kosi' is from the root 'kus' (to embrace) with 'i'; it ends in a short vowel. The word for the hilt (muṭṭhi) of swords, daggers, and so forth is 'tharu.' 'Tharu' is from the root 'thar' (to move in a heap) with 'u'.

392. Tikaṃ khaggādīnaṃ satthānaṃ vāraṇaphalake. Kheṭa bhakkhane, ṇvu. Phala visāraṇe, ṇvu. Phalatīti phalakaṃ, anitthī. Cara gatibhakkhanesu, mo, camu adane vā, a. Phalampi.

392. Three terms are for the shield (vāraṇaphalaka) that wards off swords and other weapons. 'Kheṭaka' is from the root 'kheṭ' (to eat) with the suffix 'ṇvu.' 'Phalaka' is from the root 'phal' (to spread out) with 'ṇvu.' 'Phalakaṃ' is so called because it spreads out (phalati); it is not feminine. 'Camma' is from the root 'car' (to move, to eat) with the suffix 'ma'; or from 'cam' (to eat) with 'a.' 'Phala' is also used.

Vaṇṭānihārassākhaggākati [M 0.0274] hatthakuṇḍādi illī, ilīpi, ila gatiyaṃ, nadādi. Karaṃ pālayatīti karapālikā, ṇvu.

'Illī,' and also 'ilī,' is a term for a hand-guard and the like, such as a handle-guard, having the shape of a sword, or a hand-ring; it is from the root 'il' (to go), of the Nadādi class. 'Karapālikā' is so called because it protects (pālayati) the hand (karaṃ); it is formed with the suffix 'ṇvu'.

Dvayaṃ asiputtiyaṃ. Chura chedane, ṇvu. Sasu hiṃsāyaṃ,ti, nadādi. Asino puttī, asidhenukāpi.

Two terms are for the dagger (asiputti). 'Churikā' is from the root 'chur' (to cut) with the suffix 'ṇvu.' 'Satti' is from the root 'sas' (to harm) with 'ti,' of the Nadādi class. 'Asiputti' means the 'daughter of a sword' (asino puttī); 'asidhenukā' is also used.

Dvayaṃ vaḍḍhakīnaṃ muggarehi samānākārāyudhabhede. Laga saṅge, alo, assu, ḷattañca. Muraṃ giratīti muggaro, rassa go, gira niggiraṇe, muccatīti vā muggaro, aro. Dughaṇo, ghanopi.

Two terms are for a type of weapon similar in shape to a carpenter's mallet. 'Laguḷa' is from the root 'lag' (to attach) with the suffixes 'ula' and 'a,' and the change of 'g' to 'ḷ.' 'Muggara' is so called because it envelops and swallows (muraṃ girati), with 'g' replacing 'r,' from the root 'gir' (to swallow); or it is so called because it is released (muccati), with the suffix 'ara.' 'Dughaṇa' and 'ghana' are also used.

393. Dvayaṃ salle. Sala āsugatiyaṃ, a, sara hiṃsāyaṃ vā, lo, rassa lo. Saṅka saṅkāyaṃ, u. Sūlampi. Sūla rujāyaṃ.

393. Two terms are for the dart or stake. 'Salla' is from the root 'sal' (to move swiftly) with the suffix 'a'; or from 'sar' (to harm) with 'la,' where 'r' becomes 'l.' 'Saṅku' is from the root 'saṅk' (to doubt) with 'u.' 'Sūla' is also used. The root 'sūl' is in the sense of 'to cause pain'.

Dvayaṃ vāsiyaṃ. Vasa chedanasnehāvahāraṇesu, ṇī. Taccha tanukaraṇe, yu, nadādi.

Two terms are for the adze. 'Vāsi' is from the root 'vas' (to cut, to extract oil, to remove) with the suffix 'ṇī.' 'Tacchanī' is from the root 'tacch' (to pare, to thin) with 'yu,' of the Nadādi class.

Dvayaṃ pharasumhi. Chedakattā kucchitā dhārā yassāti kudhārī. Kudhāropi. Paraṃ sasati hiṃsatīti pharasu. U, passa pho, salopo ca. Parasupi, so parasusaddo napuṃsako. Parasudhopyatra.

Two terms are for the axe. 'Kudhārī' is so called because it has a contemptible edge (kucchitā dhārā) due to its cutting nature. 'Kudhāro' is also used. 'Pharasu' is so called because it harms (sasati, i.e., hiṃsati) another (paraṃ); it is formed with the suffix 'u,' the change of 'p' to 'ph,' and the elision of 's.' 'Parasu' is also used; the word 'parasu' is neuter. 'Parasudha' is also used here.

Dvayaṃ pāsāṇavidāraṇe. Ṭaṅka bandhane. Dara vidāraṇe. Pāsāṇaṃ dārayatīti pāsāṇadāraṇo, yu. Pāsāṇadārakopi.

Two terms for a stone-splitting instrument. The root `ṭaṅka` is in the sense of fastening. The root `dara` is in the sense of splitting. `Pāsāṇadāraṇo` is 'that which splits stone' (pāsāṇaṃ dārayati), formed with the suffix 'yu'. `Pāsāṇadāraka` is also a term.

394. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0275] hatthappamāṇe kaṇaye kaṇḍe (cintāmaṇiṭīkā). Cakkapūraṇādivāyuvasena khippate. Kaṇa sadde, ayo. Bhindanasīlatāya bhindī, vāti gacchati tenāti vālo, alo, bhindī ca so vālo cāti bhindivālo, ḷatte bhindivāḷo, rasso.

394. Two terms for a hand-sized `kaṇaya`. It is thrown by the force of wind from a blowpipe or similar device. The root `kaṇa` is in the sense of sounding, with the suffix `ayo`. `Bhindī` is so called because of its nature of breaking. `Vālo` is 'that by which it goes' (vāti gacchati tena), with the suffix `alo`. `Bhindivālo` is a compound of `bhindī` and `vālo`; with the change to `ḷ`, it becomes `bhindivāḷo`, with a short vowel.

Cakkādayo satthabhedā. Tatra cakkākāro āyudhaviseso cakkaṃ. Kanta chedane, assu, kunto dīghadaṇḍo. Gadā, satti ca pasiddhā.

`Cakka` and so forth are types of weapons. Among them, `cakkaṃ` is a particular weapon in the shape of a wheel. `Kunto`, a long staff, is from the root `kant` in the sense of cutting, with the suffix `assu`. `Gadā` (mace) and `satti` (spear) are well-known.

Tikaṃ koṇabhāge. Kuṇa saddopakaraṇesu, kuṇa saṅkocane vā, ṇo. Si sevāyaṃ, a, rasso, asso. Kuṭa koṭille, iṇa.

Three terms for a corner. `Koṇa` is from the root `kuṇa` in the sense of 'sounding' or 'being an instrument', or from `kuṇa` in the sense of 'contracting', with the suffix `ṇo`. `Asso` is from the root `si` in the sense of serving, with the suffix `a`, and the vowel is shortened. `Koṭi` is from the root `kuṭa` in the sense of being crooked, with the suffix `iṇa`.

395. Dvipādaṃ vijigīsassa yātrāyaṃ, sabbatra bhāvasādhanaṃ. Yā pāpuṇe, nikkhamitvā yāyate niyyānaṃ, yu. “Chadādīhi tatraṇa”ti traṇa. Yātrā, ā. Nadādino ākatigaṇattā īpaccayābhāvo. Ṭhā gatinivattiyaṃ, papubbo yāne, yu, patiṭṭhīyate paṭṭhānaṃ, purecārimhi paṭṭho.

395. Two terms for the journey of one who desires victory; in all cases, they are abstract nouns of action. `Niyyānaṃ` is 'one goes forth' (nikkhamitvā yāyate), from the root `yā` in the sense of reaching, with the suffix `yu`. `Yātrā` is from the root `yā` with the suffix `tra` and the feminine ending `ā`. Because it belongs to the `nadādi` class, which is an open class, the suffix `ī` is not applied. `Paṭṭhānaṃ` means 'one sets forth' (patiṭṭhīyate), from the root `ṭhā` in the sense of ceasing motion, with the prefix `pa` used here in the sense of going, with the suffix `yu`. `Paṭṭho` means a forerunner.

Pañcakaṃ dhūlīmatte. Tathā ca “paṃsu khodo mato reṇu, cuṇṇo dhūli’tthiyaṃ bhave”tyamaramālā. Cuṇṇa pisane, cuṇṇa sañcuṇṇane vā. Paṃsa nāsane, u. Ranja rāge, rajo, manogaṇopi napuṃsake, taṃsahacaraṇato paṃsupi. “Klivaṃ’parādhe reṇumhī”ti [M 0.0276] rabhaso. Atha vā cuṇṇarajosahacaraṇato paṃsu napuṃsake. Dhū vidhunane, dhū kampane vā, li, nadādi. Ri gatiyaṃ, ṇu, isse.

Five terms for dust. As stated in the Amaramālā: '`Paṃsu`, `khodo`, `mato`, `reṇu`, and `cuṇṇo` are terms for dust; `dhūli` is feminine.' `Cuṇṇa` is from the root `cuṇṇ` in the sense of grinding or pulverizing. `Paṃsu` is from the root `paṃs` in the sense of destroying, with the suffix `u`. `Rajo` is from the root `rañj` in the sense of coloring; it belongs to the `manogaṇa` group and is neuter, and due to its association, `paṃsu` is also neuter. According to Rabhasa: 'The neuter gender is used for a fault and for `reṇu`.' Alternatively, `paṃsu` is neuter due to its association with `cuṇṇa` and `rajo`. `Dhūli` is from the root `dhū` in the sense of shaking or trembling, with the suffix `li`, and belongs to the `nadādi` class. `Reṇu` is from the root `ri` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ṇu`, and the vowel of the root is changed.

396. Vaṃsakkamavedīvaṃsathutiṃ yo kubbati, so māgadho. Tasmiṃ madhuko vutto. So ca khattiyāvessasambhavo bhavati, vaṃsamaggaṃ thavatīti māgadho, thassa dho. Maggaṃ dhavatīti madhuko, ṇvu, ggalopo.

396. One who, knowing the succession of the lineage, offers praise of the lineage is a `māgadha`. In that sense, `madhuka` is also used. He is born from a Khattiya father and a Vessa mother. `Māgadha` is so called because 'he praises the path of the lineage' (vaṃsamaggaṃ thavati), with `th` changing to `dh`. `Madhuka` is so called because 'he runs along the path' (maggaṃ dhavati), with the suffix `ṇvu` and the elision of `gga`.

Vīriyādithutiṃ sīlena yo paṭhati, so vandī, tassīlādīsu ṇī.

One who recites praises of heroism and so forth as a profession is a `vandī`; the suffix `ṇī` is used in the sense of 'one whose habit it is', and so forth.

Yo nisāvasānaṃ vibhāvento bodhayati, so vetāḷiko, vibhāvento tāḷasaddena bodhayatīti vetāḷiko, ṇiko.

One who awakens people by announcing the end of the night is a `vetāḷika`. He is so called because 'he awakens by announcing with the sound of music' (vibhāvento tāḷasaddena bodhayati), with the suffix `ṇika`.

Cakkena caranto bahūhi pīḷetvā yo paṭhati, so cakkiko, ubhayatra caratyatthe iko. Ghaṇṭa bhāsattho, curādi.

One who wanders with a wheel, oppressing many, and recites is a `cakkika`. The suffix `ika` has the sense of 'one who goes about'. The root `ghaṇṭ` is in the sense of speaking, belonging to the `curādi` class.

397. Pañcakaṃ dhaje. Kita nivāse, rogāpanayane ca, u, kitati apaneti etenāti ketu. Dhaja gamane, a. Uppatatīti paṭākā, āko, paṭa gatiyaṃ vā, paṭākā. Kena vātena dalīyate vidārīyateti kadalī, nadādi, chinnabhinnattā [M 0.0277] kucchitaṃ dalaṃ pattametissātthīti vā kadalī, paṭākā sahacaraṇato itthiyaṃ. Kadalī mocepi. Yumhi ketanaṃ. Ettha ca dhajasahacaraṇato ketu punnapuṃsake. “Paṭākā vejayantī ca, ketanaṃ dhaja’manitthī”tya amara 18.99 marakose.

397. Five terms for a banner. `Ketu` is from the root `kit` in the sense of 'dwelling' or 'removing disease', with the suffix `u`; it is so called because 'one removes disease with it' (kitati apaneti etena). `Dhaja` is from the root `dhaj` in the sense of going, with the suffix `a`. `Paṭākā` is so called because 'it flies up' (uppatati), with the suffix `āka`; or it is from the root `paṭa` in the sense of going. `Kadalī` is so called because 'it is split or torn by the wind' (kena vātena dalīyate vidārīyate), and it belongs to the `nadādi` class; or it is so called because 'it has a contemptible leaf that is cut and broken'; it is feminine due to its association with `paṭākā`. `Kadalī` also means a banana tree. `Ketanaṃ` is formed with the suffix `yu`. Here, due to its association with `dhaja`, `ketu` is masculine or neuter. In the Amarakośa it is said: '`Paṭākā`, `vejayantī`, `ketanaṃ`, and `dhaja` are not feminine.'

Aññamaññasseti ekamapekkhitvā aparassāparaṃ apekkhitvā aññassa. Yo ahaṃkāro abhimāno, so “ahaṃ aha”miti karotīti ahamahamikā bhave. “Ahaṃ aggo bhavāmi, ahaṃ aggo bhavāmī”ti aññamaññamatikkamma yodhānaṃ samagge dhāvanaṃ, tatra tu ahaṃpubbikā. Ahaṃsaddo vibhattipatirūpako nipāto, sakatthe kapaccaye kate vicchāyaṃ gamyamānattā dvittābhāvo.

The term `aññamaññassa` means: with respect to one, then with respect to another, and that other with respect to the first. `Ahamahamikā` is the egoism and conceit that makes one act thinking, 'It is I! It is I!'. `Ahaṃpubbikā` is when warriors, seeking to surpass one another, charge all together thinking, 'I will be first! I will be first!'. The word `ahaṃ` is an indeclinable that has the form of an inflected word; when the suffix `ka` is added in its own sense, there is no reduplication because a sense of rivalry is understood.

398. Catukkaṃ bale. Bala pāṇane, karaṇe a. Dhā gatinivattiyaṃ, karaṇe mo, dhassa tho. Sahatenenāti sahaṃ, sahopi. Saka sattiyaṃ,ti. Draviṇaṃ, taro, parakkamo, pāṇopi.

398. Four terms for strength. `Bala` is from the root `bal` in the sense of living, with the suffix `a` in the instrumental sense. `Thāma` is from the root `dhā` in the sense of ceasing motion, with the suffix `mo` in the instrumental sense, and `dh` becomes `th`. `Sahaṃ` is so called because 'one endures with it' (sahate anena); also `saho`. `Satti` is from the root `sak` in the sense of being able, with the suffix `ti`. `Draviṇa`, `taro`, `parakkamo`, and `pāṇa` are also terms for strength.

Atisūratā vikkamo nāma.

Great bravery is called `vikkama`.

Jaye jite sati, kāraṇabhūte vā kataṃ pānaṃ jayapānaṃ. Amarakose pana “vīrapānaṃ tu yaṃ pānaṃ, jāte bhāvini vā raṇe”ti amara 18.103 vuttaṃ. Tassattho – bhavissatiraṇe jīvitasaṃsayā saṃhāsuppādanatthaṃ, devatāyācanapubbakaṃ sajātiyehi saha sambhūya yodhānaṃ yaṃ pānaṃ jāte ca raṇe vijayassa sandassanatthaṃ, taṃ vīrapānamuccate.

`Jayapāna` is a drink taken when victory has been won, or when there is a cause for it. In the Amarakośa, however, it is stated: 'The hero's drink is that which is drunk when a battle has occurred or is imminent.' The meaning of this is: that which is called the 'hero's drink' is the drink that warriors, having first invoked the deities, gather and consume together with their kinsmen to generate courage when a future battle involves danger to life; and also the drink taken when a battle has occurred to demonstrate victory.

399-400. Sāḍḍhapajjaṃ [M 0.0278] yuddhe. Saṅgāma yuddhe, curādi, a. Hara haraṇe, pasayhakaraṇe ca. Ara gamane, a. Samaraṃ. Raṇa sadde, dvepyanitthiyaṃ. Aja gamane, ṇi, āji, rassanto. Āhuyyante asmiṃyodhā, hu sadde, a. Yudha sampahāre, to. Ādāya yujjhantetra āyodhanaṃ, yu. Yuja yoge, saṃyugaṃ, saṃyuttampi. Bhaṇḍa paribhāsane, yu. Viggayhanti yujjhantyasmiṃ viggaho. Kalahantyasmiṃ kalaho. Medha medhāhiṃsāsaṅgamesu, ṇvu. Jaññaṃ, pavidāraṇaṃ, akkandanaṃ, saṅkhyaṃ, samīkaṃ, samparāyakaṃ, anīkaṃ, abhisampāto, kalisaṃ, phoṭo, atyāmaddoiccādayopi yuddhe. Keci pana “bhaṇḍanādipañcakaṃ kalahe, na yuddhe”ti vadanti, taṃ “bhaṇḍanaṃ kavace yuddhe, khalikārepi vattate”ti nānatthasaṅgahe vuttattā na gahetabbaṃ.

One and a half verses on battle. `Saṅgāma` is from the root `saṅgāma` of the `curādi` class, in the sense of battle, with the suffix `a`. `Samaraṃ` is from the root `har` in the sense of taking or overpowering, and from the root `ar` in the sense of going, with the suffix `a`. `Raṇa` is from the root `raṇ` in the sense of sounding; both `samaraṃ` and `raṇa` are not feminine. `Āji` is from the root `aj` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ṇi`, and the final vowel is short. `Āhava` is from the root `hu` in the sense of calling, with the suffix `a`, because 'warriors are called together in it'. `Yuddha` is from the root `yudh` in the sense of conflict, with the suffix `ta`. `Āyodhanaṃ` is so called because 'they fight there, having taken up arms', with the suffix `yu`. `Saṃyugaṃ` and `saṃyuttaṃ` are from the root `yuj` in the sense of joining. `Bhaṇḍanaṃ` is from the root `bhaṇḍ` in the sense of reproaching, with the suffix `yu`. `Viggaho` is so called because 'they fight by grappling with one another'. `Kalaho` is so called because 'they quarrel in it'. `Medhaga` is from the root `medh` in the senses of killing or conflict, with the suffix `ṇvu`. `Jaññaṃ`, `pavidāraṇaṃ`, `akkandanaṃ`, `saṅkhyaṃ`, `samīkaṃ`, `samparāyakaṃ`, `anīkaṃ`, `abhisampāto`, `kalisaṃ`, `phoṭo`, and `atyāmaddo` are also terms for battle. Some say that the five terms beginning with `bhaṇḍana` refer to a quarrel, not a battle, but this should not be accepted, because it is stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha that '`bhaṇḍana` is used for armor, battle, and also dispute'.

Dvayaṃ mucchāyaṃ. Muccha mohasamussayesu. Muha vecitte. Tikaṃ balakkāre. Pasahanaṃ pasayho, saha sattiyaṃ, ṇyo. Balino, balena vā karaṇaṃ balakkāro. Haṭha balakkāre, ṇo. Pasaṅgopi.

Two terms for fainting. The root `mucch` is in the senses of delusion and fainting. The root `muh` is in the sense of bewilderment. Three terms for violence. `Pasayho` means overpowering; it is from the root `sah` in the sense of being able, with the suffix `ṇya`. `Balakkāro` is an act done by the strong or by force. `Haṭho` is from the root `haṭh` in the sense of violence, with the suffix `ṇa`. `Pasaṅga` is also a term.

401. Subhāsubhānaṃ phalānaṃ sūcikā pakāsakā yā bhūtassa vatthuno vikati aññathā uppatti, sā uppāto. Subhāsubhaphalaṃ [M 0.0279] pakāsento patati gacchatīti uppāto. Uppādopi. Tasaddo’yaṃ pubbapadassa, aparapadassa vā liṅgamādatte. “Avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo, viggaho ca taṃ vākyañceti viggahavākya”ntyādīsu, idha pana pubbapadassa liṅgamādatte. Uppātassa tatra yuddhapakkamenābhidhānaṃ.

401. An `uppāta` (portent) is an alteration or unusual occurrence in a physical object which indicates and reveals good or bad results. It is so called because 'it arises while revealing a good or bad result'. `Uppāda` is also a term. The pronoun `ta` may take the gender of either the preceding or the following word in a compound, for example, in `avijjāpaccayo` (from `avijjā ca so paccayo`) and `viggahavākyaṃ` (from `viggaho ca taṃ vākyaṃ`). Here, however, it takes the gender of the preceding word. The mention of `uppāta` here is in the context of the section on war.

Catukkaṃ uppātassa pariyāye. I gamane,ti, dīghādi. Sabbakālaṃ na jāyatīti ajaññaṃ, ṇyo, phalaṃ na janetīti vā ajaññaṃ, tañhi dhūmo viya aggissa kammaphalassa pakāsanamattameva karoti, na taṃ janetīti ajaññaṃ nāma. Upagantvā sajjati pakāsetīti upasaggo, ṇo. Upagantvā dunotīti upaddavo, du paritāpe, a. Ettha ca ītyādayo janakepi vattanti, yathā jarādīnamupaddavā.

Four synonyms for `uppāta`. `Īti` is from the root `i` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ti`, and the initial vowel is lengthened. `Ajaññaṃ` is so called because 'it is not born at all times', with the suffix `ṇya`; or because 'it does not generate a result', for it only reveals the result of kamma, just as smoke reveals fire, but does not generate it. `Upasaggo` is so called because 'it approaches and attaches itself' or 'reveals', with the suffix `ṇa`. `Upaddavo` is so called because 'it approaches and torments', from the root `du` in the sense of tormenting, with the suffix `a`. Here, `īti` and other such terms also refer to the cause, as in 'the afflictions of old age, etc.'.

402. Mallayuddhamhi bāhuyuddhamhi nibbuddhaṃ. Adhobhāgaṃ bandhanaṃ vā katvā yujjhantyatra nibbuddhaṃ, yassa bo, aññamaññassa vedhaṃ nibbedhentyatreti vā nibbuddhaṃ. Vedha vedhane, to, essu, aññatropacārā. Dvayaṃ jayakriyāyaṃ. Ji jaye, “bhāve cā”ti ṇo. Raṇe yuddhe yo bhaṅgo, so parājayo. Parāpubbo ji yuddhabhaṅge. Dvayaṃ palāyanamatte, na tu saṅgāmatoyeva palāyane. Parivajjetvā ayanaṃ gamanaṃ palāyanaṃ. Apavajjetvā gamanaṃ apakkamo. Padāvo, dāvo, sandāvo, viddavo, davo, apayānaṃpyatra.

402. `Nibbuddhaṃ` refers to wrestling or hand-to-hand combat. It is so called because 'they fight there having bound the lower part', with `b` replacing `y` in `yuddha`; or because 'they pierce each other's vital points there'. The word `vedha` is from the root `vidh` in the sense of piercing, with the suffix `ta`; this is a metaphorical usage. Two terms for the act of victory. `Jayo` is from the root `ji` in the sense of conquering, with the suffix `ṇa` in the abstract sense. `Parājayo` is the rout in battle; the root `ji` with the prefix `parā` is in the sense of a rout in battle. Two terms for mere flight, not necessarily flight from battle. `Palāyanaṃ` is 'going away while avoiding'. `Apakkamo` is 'going away while leaving behind'. `Padāvo`, `dāvo`, `sandāvo`, `viddavo`, `davo`, and `apayānaṃ` are also terms here.

403. Pajjaṃ [M 0.0280] māraṇe. Mara pāṇacāge, sabbattha bhāvasādhanaṃ. Mārīyate māraṇaṃ, yu. Hana hiṃsāyaṃ, ṇamhi “hanassa ghāto”ti ghātādeso. Nasa adassane. Sūda dhāraṇe. Hiṃsa hiṃsāyaṃ. Sara hiṃsāyaṃ, itthiyamāpaccayo, hiṃsā. Ṇamhi hanassa vadhādeso. Sasa hiṃsāyaṃ. Yumhi hanassa ghāto, ghātanaṃ, nibbarahanaṃ, nikāraṇaṃ, pavāsanaṃ, saññāpanaṃ, pamathanaṃ, kathanaṃ, ujjāsanaṃ, ārambho, piñjopyatra. Varaha bādhānyaparibhāsanahiṃsādānesu. Kara hiṃsāyaṃ. Vasa nivāse, papubbo hiṃsattho. Ñā māraṇatosananisāmanesu, pāgamo, saññāpanaṃ. Matha viloḷane. Katha hiṃsattho. Jasu hiṃsāyaṃ, jasi tāḷane vā, curādi. Āpubbo rabhi māraṇe. Piñja hiṃsābaladānaniketanesu. Ete yathākkamamidhānāgatānaṃ dhātavo.

403. A verse on killing. The root 'mar' is in the sense of abandoning life; everywhere it is formed to denote the action. Māraṇaṃ (killing) is so called because one is killed (mārīyate); the suffix is 'yu'. The root 'han' is in the sense of harming; when the suffix 'ṇa' is used, 'ghāta' is the substitute for 'han', as in the rule 'hanassa ghāto'. The root 'nas' is in the sense of disappearance. The root 'sūd' is in the sense of holding. The root 'hiṃs' is in the sense of harming. The root 'sar' is in the sense of harming; in the feminine, with the suffix 'ā', it becomes hiṃsā. When the suffix 'ṇa' is used, 'vadha' is the substitute for 'han'. The root 'sas' is in the sense of harming. When the suffix 'yu' is used, 'ghāta' is the substitute for 'han', forming ghātanaṃ; also nibbarahanaṃ, nikāraṇaṃ, pavāsanaṃ, saññāpanaṃ, pamathanaṃ, kathanaṃ, ujjāsanaṃ, ārambho, and piñja are here. The root 'varah' is in the senses of affliction, censure, harming, and giving. The root 'kar' is in the sense of harming. The root 'vas' is in the sense of dwelling; preceded by 'pa', it has the meaning of harming. The root 'ñā' is in the senses of killing, pleasing, and observing; with the augment 'pa', it forms saññāpanaṃ. The root 'math' is in the sense of churning. The root 'kath' has the meaning of harming. The root 'jasu' is in the sense of harming, or 'jasi' in the sense of beating, of the curādi class. The root 'rabh' preceded by 'ā' is in the sense of killing. The root 'piñj' is in the senses of harming, strength, giving, and dwellings. These are the roots, in their respective order, for the words that have appeared here.

404. Pajjaṃ maraṇe. Kālo atītādi, tassa kiriyā, “kālo ghasati bhūtānī”ti jā. 1.2.190 hi vuttaṃ. Maratito cu, maccu, vajādinā vā tyu. Tato maccusadiso dvīsu. Atikkamitvā ayanaṃ accayo. Dhana dhaññe. Kālassa kiriyattā [M 0.0281] kālo, attabhāvassa antaṃ karotīti vā kālo, ṇo. Amati gacchatīti anto. Cu cavane.

404. A verse on death. Time is the past, and so forth; it is its action, for it is said: 'Time devours beings.' From 'marati' with the suffix 'cu' comes maccu; or from the root 'vaj' and others with the suffix 'tyu'. Therefore, 'maccusadiso' (like death) is in two genders. Accayo (passing away) is a going (ayanaṃ) beyond (atikkamitvā). The root 'dhan' is in the sense of grain. Kāla (time) is so called because it is the action of time, or because it makes an end (antaṃ karoti) to individual existence; the suffix is 'ṇo'. Anto (end) is so called because one goes (amati = gacchati) towards it. The root 'cu' is in the sense of falling away.

405. Tikaṃ mate. Paraṃ lokaṃ eti gacchatīti peto, pareto ca, to, pubbe ralopo. Maratīti mato. Parāsu, pattapañcattopyatra. Dvayaṃ matadahanakaṭṭharāsimhi, yā “phullī”ti vuccati. Cīyate yatthāti citako, cito ca, to. Pubbatra sakatthe ko. Citā, cityā, citipyatra.

405. A triad on the dead. Peto (departed) is so called because one goes (eti = gacchati) to the other world (paraṃ lokaṃ); also pareto, with the suffix 'to', and in the former, there is elision of 'ra'. Mato (dead) is so called because one dies (marati). Parāsu and pattapañcatta are also here. A pair on the pile of wood for burning the dead, which is called 'phullī'. Citako (funeral pyre) is so called because things are piled up (cīyate) there; also cito, with the suffix 'to'. In the former case, the suffix 'ka' is in its own sense. Citā, cityā, and citi are also here.

Dvayaṃ susāne, āgantvā dahanti atra āḷahanaṃ. Daha bhasmīkaraṇe, yu, dassa ḷo. Āḷāhanampi. Chavassa sayanaṭṭhānaṃ susānaṃ, chavassa su, sayanassa ca sāno, atha vā senti atrāti sānaṃ, yu, chavassa sānaṃ susānaṃ. Chavassa su. Pituvanampi. Dvayaṃ matasarīre, kuṇapa pūtigandhatthe. Kucchitaṃ netīti vā kuṇapo, apo, ṇattaṃ. Chava gatiyaṃ, a.

A pair on the cemetery. Āḷahanaṃ (cremation ground) is so called because they come and burn here. The root 'dah' is in the sense of reducing to ashes; the suffix is 'yu', and 'ḷa' is the substitute for 'da'. Also āḷāhana. Susānaṃ (cemetery) is the resting place (sayanaṭṭhānaṃ) of a corpse (chavassa), from 'su' of 'chavassa' and 'sāna' of 'sayanassa'; or alternatively, sānaṃ is so called because they lie (senti) here, with the suffix 'yu', thus 'sāna' of a corpse (chavassa) is susānaṃ. From 'su' of 'chavassa'. Also pituvanam. A pair on the dead body. Kuṇapa is in the sense of a foul smell. Or, kuṇapo is so called because it leads to (neti) what is vile (kucchitaṃ); the suffix is 'apa', with the insertion of 'ṇ'. The root 'chav' is in the sense of movement; the suffix is 'a'.

406. Asīsakattā sirosuñño naccanādikriyāsahitattā sahakriyo deho kāyo kabandho “yuddhe yodhesu sūresu sahassaṃ katta (khaṇḍa) muddhasu tadāvesā kabandho tu eko’muddhā kriyāndhito”ti kabandhalakkhaṇaṃ, yuddhe sahassapūraṇo kabandho. “Naccatī”ti vuttattā naccanādikriyārahite tūpacāro. Avijjamānena kena sirasā andho kabandho, vakāramajjho. Avijjamānassāpi hi kāraṇabhāvo [M 0.0282] loke diṭṭho, yathā vassena kato subhikkho, dubbhikkho ca, yathā loke, tathā sāsanepi, yathā anantarapaccayādīni.

406. A kabandha is a body (deho, kāyo) that, being headless (asīsakattā), is void of a head (sirosuñño), and being associated with actions like dancing (naccanādikriyāsahitattā), is with action (sahakriyo); in battle, a kabandha is one who completes a thousand. Because it is said 'it dances', its application to that which is devoid of actions like dancing is metaphorical (upacāro). A kabandha is blind (andho) due to a non-existent (avijjamānena) head (sirasā), which is 'ka' (kena); with 'va' in the middle. Indeed, the causality of something non-existent is seen in the world, just as abundance and famine are caused by rain; as in the world, so too in the Dispensation, as with the immediate condition and so forth.

Āmakehi kucchitehi apūtigatamatasarīrehi sampuṇṇe āmake susānasmiṃ sivathikā vuttā, atthappadhānaniddesena cettha saddo niddiṭṭho, yathā “sato sampajāno”ti puggalappadhānaniddesena dhammoti. Chavā dhiyyantetra sivathikā, ṇvu, chassa so, thattaṃ, ittañca. Chavathikāpi.

A sivathikā (charnel ground) is said to be a 'raw' cemetery (āmake susānasmiṃ) filled with raw (āmakehi), vile (kucchitehi), unputrefied (apūtigata) dead bodies (matasarīrehi); and here the word is indicated with the meaning as primary (atthappadhānaniddesena), just as in 'mindful and clearly comprehending' (sato sampajāno), the dhamma is indicated with the person as primary (puggalappadhānaniddesena). Sivathikā is so called because corpses (chavā) are placed (dhiyyante) here; the suffix is 'ṇvu', 'sa' is the substitute for 'cha', and there is the insertion of 'tha' and 'i'. Also chavathikā.

407. Dvayaṃ ākaḍḍhitamanussagavādo. Muñcanasaññāya vandatīti vandī. Vanda abhivādanathutīsu, ī, rassopi, vandi. Sattūnaṃ karena hatthena maritabbattā karamaro. Paggaho, upaggahopi. Dvayaṃ jīvite, ana pāṇane, pāṇanti anenāti pāṇo, ṇo. Bhavati yenāti asu. Asa bhuvi, u, āsupi, asu khubhane vā.

407. A pair on one who drags away humans, cattle, and so on. Vandī (captive) is so called because one praises (vandati) with the perception of being released (muñcanasaññāya). The root 'vand' is in the senses of paying homage and praising; the suffix is 'ī', or also the short 'i', forming vandi. Karamaro is so called because enemies are to be killed (maritabbattā) by hand (karena = hatthena). Also paggaho and upaggaho. A pair on life. The root 'an' is in the sense of breathing; pāṇo (breath) is so called because one breathes (pāṇanti) with it; the suffix is 'ṇo'. Asu (life-breath) is so called because one exists (bhavati) by it. The root 'as' is in the sense of being, with the suffix 'u'; also āsu; or the root 'asu' is in the sense of throwing.

Bandhanāgāraṃ bandhanagehaṃ kārā nāma. Karonti hiṃsanti atra kārā, a. Kara hiṃsāyaṃ. Bandhanālayopi. Kara hiṃsāyaṃ, yata niyyātane. Kāraṇā, yatanā ca. Tibbavedanāpyatra.

A house of bondage (bandhanāgāraṃ, bandhanagehaṃ) is named kārā (prison). Kārā is so called because they inflict harm (karonti = hiṃsanti) here; the suffix is 'a'. The root 'kar' is in the sense of harming. Also bandhanālaya. The root 'kar' is in the sense of harming; the root 'yat' is in the sense of restraining. And from these come kāraṇā and yatanā (torment). Intense suffering is also a meaning here.

Khattiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Khattiya section is finished.

408. Dvipādaṃ [M 0.0283] brāhmaṇe, brahmuno bandhu, brahmā bandhu yassa vā brahmabandhu. Kulācārabrāhmaṇabhāvavasena dvikkhattuṃ jātattā dvijo, ekaje tūpacārā. Vapismā po, assi. Brahmuno apaccaṃ brahmā, brāhmaṇo ca, nāgamo, ṇattaṃ, dīghādi. Sutāyutakathanatthaṃ “bhobho”ti vacanaṃ vadati sīlena, ṇī.

408. A couplet on the brahmin. A kinsman of Brahmā, or one whose kinsman is Brahmā, is a brahmabandhu. Because of being born twice by way of family, conduct, and brahminhood, one is a dvija (twice-born); but for an ekaja (once-born), this is a metaphorical usage. From 'vapu', the suffixes 'po' and 'assi'. A descendant of Brahmā is a brahmā, and also a brāhmaṇa, with the augment 'na', the suffix 'ṇa', vowel lengthening, and so on. One who by nature speaks the address 'bhobho' for the purpose of speaking in a manner connected with learning is a bhovādī; the suffix is 'ṇī'.

Dvayaṃ chandojjhetari. Brahmasuttaṃ adhīte sottiyo, “nena niddiṭṭhamanicca”nti kātanta 1.2.18 naghaṭitaṃ aniccaṃ (paribhāsendusekhara 97) vuttattā vuddhi, yadādinā vā chandasaddassa sottiyādeso pāṇini 5.2.84. Chandaṃ adhīte chandaso, so pulliṅgo.

A pair on one who studies the Vedas. One who studies the sacred texts (brahmasuttaṃ) is a sottiyo; there is vuddhi (vowel gradation) due to the rule 'nena niddiṭṭhamanicca', or alternatively, by the rule beginning with 'yad', 'sottiya' is the substitute for the word 'chandas'. One who studies the Vedas (chandaṃ) is a chandaso; it is masculine.

Dvayaṃ sisse. Sotuṃ icchantīti sissā, su savane, so, ussi. Ācariyassa ante samīpe vasanasīlo, saññāsaddattā sattamiyā alopo.

A pair on the disciple. Sissā (disciples) are so called because they wish to hear (sotuṃ icchanti); from the root 'su' (to hear), with the suffixes 'sa' and 'ussa'. An antevāsī is one who is accustomed to dwelling near (ante = samīpe) the teacher; because it is a conventional term, there is non-elision (alopo) of the seventh case ending.

409. Brahmacārīādayo ete caturo janā assamā nāma bhavanti, assamasaddoyaṃ punnapuṃsake. Tatra muñjamekhalādiyutto vedajjhāyako brahmacariyāyaṃ ṭhito brahmacārī. Vedajjhayanaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caratīti, ṇī. Dhammatthakāmesu ṭhito pañcamahāyaññakārī gahaṭṭho, gahā dārā [M 0.0284] tatra tiṭṭhantīti gahaṭṭho. Gahaṭṭho paro tatiyassapi vānapattho. Vanapatthe vanekadese, dūravane vā bhavo vānapattho, assa bhūmiseyyājaṭājinadhāraṇavanavāsonyahārabhojitādi dhammo. Vānapatthassameva tatiyamāyuso bhāgaṃ khepayitvā gahitakāsāvadaṇḍo bhikkho sabbabhūtesu samo jhānāyatanavaro bhikkhu. Samu tapasi, khede ca, āsammanti atrāti, akattari kārake saññāyaṃ ṇo. “Assamo brahmacariyādi- catukkepi maṭhepi ce”ti nānatthasaṅgahe.

409. These four persons, beginning with the student of the holy life (brahmacārī), are called assama (stages of life); and this word assama is in the masculine and neuter genders. Among them, one who wears the muñja grass girdle and so on, who recites the Vedas, and is established in the holy life, is a brahmacārī. One who practices the holy life (brahmacariyaṃ), which is the study of the Vedas; the suffix is 'ṇī'. A householder (gahaṭṭho) is one who performs the five great sacrifices, established in righteousness, wealth, and sensual pleasures; gahaṭṭho is so called because wives (gahā = dārā) dwell (tiṭṭhanti) there. After the householder is the forest-dweller (vānapattho), the third stage. Vānapattho is one who is in a part of the forest (vanapatthe = vanekadese) or in a remote forest; his practice consists of sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair and animal skins, dwelling in the forest, eating gleaned food, and so on. Having spent the third portion of life as a forest-dweller, one who has taken up the ochre robe and staff, is equal towards all beings, and is supreme in jhāna and its base, is a bhikkhu (mendicant). The root 'sam' is in the sense of austerity and exertion. Assama is so called because they exert themselves (āsammanti) here; the suffix is 'ṇa' for a name in a case other than the agent. As stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: 'Assama is used for the four stages beginning with the holy life, and also for a hermitage'.

410. Sīlādayo tayo sikkhādhamme saha ekato carantā mithu aññamaññaṃ sabrahmacārino nāma, brahmacārīhi saha carantīti sabrahmacārino. “Mithū”ti iminā sabrahmacārīsaddassa tagguṇasaṃviññāṇattaṃ dīpitaṃ, tena brahmacārīnampi sabrahmacārittamupapannaṃ.

410. Those who practice the three training principles beginning with virtue together, as one, and mutually with one another, are called sabrahmacārino (fellows in the holy life); they are sabrahmacārino because they fare together with practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārīhi). By this word 'mithu' (mutually), it is shown that the word sabrahmacārī implies the possession of the same qualities; thereby, the state of being a sabrahmacārī is also established for brahmacārins themselves.

Dvayaṃ upasampadādāyake. Manasā upecca sissānaṃ vajjāvajjaṃ jhāyatīti upajjhāyo, upajjhā ca. Jhe cintāyaṃ, ṇo, pubbatra e aya, pakkhe rājādipakkhepena upajjhā, parasamaye pana vedādipāṭhayitā “upajjhāyo, upajjhā”ti coccate, upecca adhīyate asmāti katvā.

A pair on the giver of higher ordination. An upajjhāyo, and also an upajjhā, is so called because, having mentally approached, one reflects upon the faults and faultlessness of disciples. The root 'jhe' is in the sense of thinking; the suffix is 'ṇa'; in the former, 'e' becomes 'aya'. Alternatively, by inclusion in the 'rājādi' group, the form is upajjhā. However, in other traditions, one who recites the Vedas and so on is called 'upajjhāyo' or 'upajjhā', because one learns from him, having approached him.

Dvayaṃ nissayadāyake. Sissānaṃ hitaṃ ācaratīti ācariyo, ṇyo. Nissayaṃ dadātīti, kammādimhi ṇvu.

A pair on the giver of dependence. An ācariyo is so called because one practices what is for the welfare of disciples; the suffix is 'ṇya'. A nissayadāyako is one who gives dependence; the suffix 'ṇvu' is used in the sense of agent and so on.

411. Sāsane [M 0.0285] ācariyaṃ dassetvā parasamayepi dassetumāha “upanīye”ccādi. Atha vā yo dvijo brāhmaṇo yaṃkiñci brāhmaṇaṃ upanīya attano santikaṃ ānetvā kappādichaḷaṅgikattā sāṅgaṃ saguyhattā rahassañca vedaṃ kammabhūtaṃ pubbaṃ paṭhamameva kenaci asikkhāpiteyeva ajjhāpaye sikkhāpeyya, so brāhmaṇesu “ācariyo”ti vuccati, ādito cāreti sikkhāpetīti ācariyoti katvā, ṇyo. Yathāvuttā aññe upajjhāyā.

411. Having shown the teacher in the Dispensation, in order to show the teacher in other traditions as well, he says 'upanīya', and so on. Or, whichever twice-born brahmin, having led near any brahmin, bringing him into his presence, should teach or instruct him in the Veda—which is complete with its limbs (sāṅgaṃ) as it has the six limbs beginning with Kalpa, and is secret (rahassaṃ) as it contains esoteric teachings, and which is his duty—for the very first time, it not having been taught by anyone else, he is called an 'ācariya' among brahmins. This is because from the beginning (ādito) he makes him practice (cāreti) and instructs (sikkhāpeti); the suffix is 'ṇya'. Other preceptors (upajjhāyā) are as previously described.

412. Pajjaddhaṃ upadesaparamparāyaṃ. Pare ca pare ca paramparā, pubbācariyā. Tato ābhataṃ pārampariyaṃ. Itihasaddo nipātasamudāyo. “Itiha pubbācariyehi vuttamida”nti kathetabbaṃ vacanaṃ etihyaṃ, ṇyo. Ṇamhi etihaṃ. Ācariyaṃ upagantvā dissati uccārīyatīti upadeso, disī uccāraṇe, ṇo.

412. A half-verse on the succession of teaching. Others and others in succession form a tradition; these are the former teachers. That which is handed down from them is traditional lore. The word 'itiha' is a collection of particles. The statement to be said, 'Thus, indeed, this was said by the former teachers,' is 'etihyaṃ,' with the suffix 'ṇya.' With the suffix 'ṇa,' it is 'etihaṃ.' Having approached a teacher, it is pointed out or uttered, thus it is 'upadeso,' from the root 'dis' in the sense of 'to utter,' with the suffix 'ṇa.'

Tikaṃ yaññe. Yaja devapūjāsaṅgahakaraṇadānadhammesu, yajanaṃ yāgo, ṇo. Saggatthikehi karīyateti katu, tu. Jassa ññatte yañño. Yāgatthaṃ mantādinā parikkhatā parisaṅkhatā bhū bhūmi vedi nāma, īpaccaye vedī ca. Vindati assaṃ lābhasakkāranti vedi, vida lābhe, iṇa.

A triad of terms for sacrifice. The root 'yaj' is used in the senses of honoring deities, beneficence, giving, and righteous acts; 'yajanaṃ' and 'yāgo' are derived from it, with the suffix 'ṇa.' Because it is performed by those desiring heaven, it is 'katu,' with the suffix 'tu.' From the root 'yaj,' with the transformation of 'j' to 'ññ,' it is 'yañño.' The ground ('bhū,' 'bhūmi') prepared or consecrated with mantras and so on for the sake of sacrifice is called 'vedi'; with the suffix 'ī,' it is also 'vedī.' One obtains gain and honor on it, hence 'vedi,' from the root 'vid' in the sense of 'to obtain,' with the suffix 'i.'

413. Assamedhādayo [M 0.0286] pañca “mahāyāgā”tyuccante. Porāṇakarājakāle kira sassamedhaṃ purisamedhaṃ sammāpāsaṃ vācāpeyyanti cattāri saṅgahavatthūni ahesuṃ, yehi rājāno lokaṃ saṅgaṇhiṃsu, tattha nipphannasassato dasamabhāgaggahaṇaṃ sassamedhaṃ nāma, sassasampādane medhāvitā sassamedhaṃ nāmātyattho. Mahāyodhānaṃ chamāsikabhattavetanānuppadānaṃ purisamedhaṃ nāma, purisassa saṅgaṇhane medhāvitā purisamedhaṃ nāmātyattho. Daliddamanussānaṃ hatthato lekhaṃ gahetvā tīṇi vassāni vinā vaḍḍhiyā sahassadvisahassamattadhanānuppadānaṃ sammāpāsaṃ nāma. Tañhi sammā manusse pāseti hadaye bandhitā viya ṭhapeti, tasmā “sammāpāsa”nti vuccati. “Tāta mātulā”tyādinā pana saṇhavācāya bhaṇanaṃ vācāpeyyaṃ nāma, peyye vajjapiyavacanatātyattho. Evaṃ catūhi vatthūhi saṅgahitaṃ raṭṭhaṃ iddhañceva hoti phītañca pahūtannapānaṃ khemaṃ nirabbudaṃ. Manussā mudā pamodamānā ure putte naccentā apārutagharadvārā viharanti, idaṃ gharadvāresu aggaḷānaṃ abhāvato niraggaḷanti vuccati, ayaṃ porāṇikapaveṇī, aparabhāge pana okkākarājakāle brāhmaṇā imāni cattāri saṅgahavatthūni, imañca raṭṭhasampattiṃ parivattentā uddhaṃ mūlaṃ katvā “assamedha”ntiādike pañca yaññe nāma akaṃsu, vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā brāhmaṇadhammikasutte –

413. The five sacrifices beginning with the horse sacrifice are called 'great sacrifices.' Indeed, in the time of ancient kings, there were four means of beneficence—the sassamedha, purisamedha, sammāpāsa, and vācāpeyya—by which kings sustained the world. Therein, the taking of a tenth portion from the produced harvest was called sassamedha; the meaning is that wisdom in ensuring the abundance of crops is sassamedha. The provision of six-monthly food and wages to great warriors was called purisamedha; the meaning is that wisdom in gathering people is purisamedha. Taking a written pledge from poor people and providing wealth of one or two thousand without interest for three years was called sammāpāsa. For it properly ensnares people, holding them in the heart as if tied; therefore it is called sammāpāsa. Speaking gentle words such as 'dear father, dear uncle' and so on, was called vācāpeyya; the meaning is the uttering of pleasing and affectionate speech. Thus, a kingdom sustained by these four means became prosperous and flourishing, with plentiful food and drink, secure, and free from calamity. People lived joyfully, making their children dance on their laps, with the doors of their houses open—this is called 'without bolts' (niraggaḷa) due to the absence of bolts on doors. This was the ancient custom. Later, however, in the time of King Okkāka, the brahmins, subverting these four means of beneficence and this prosperity of the kingdom, turning them upside down, instituted five so-called sacrifices beginning with the horse sacrifice. This was stated by the Blessed One in the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta:

“Tesaṃ āsi vipallāso, disvāna aṇunā aṇuṃ;

Te tattha mante ganthetvā, okkākaṃ tadupāgamu”nti su. ni. 301, 304.

"There arose in them a perversion of mind, seeing things change little by little; having composed mantras, they then approached King Okkāka."

Idāni [M 0.0287] tehi parivattetvā ṭhapitamatthaṃ dassento “assamedho”ccādimāha. Tattha assaṃ ettha medhanti vadhantīti assamedho. Purisaṃ ettha medhanti vadhantīti purisamedho. Sammā yugacchidde pakkhipitabbadaṇḍakaṃ pāsenti khipenti ettha sammāpāso. Mantapadābhisaṅkhatānaṃ sappimadhūnaṃ “vāja”nti samaññā, tamettha pivayantīti vājapeyyo. Sabbassa attano sāpateyyassa anigūhitvā niravasesato dinnattā natthi ettha aggaḷāti niraggaḷo, ayaṃ pāḷiyā āgatakkamato atthavaṇṇanā, idhāgatakkamena pana assamedhapurisamedhaniraggaḷasammāpāsavājapeyyānaṃ atthavaṇṇanā likhitabbā.

Now, showing the meaning established by their subversion, he speaks of 'horse sacrifice' and so on. Therein, 'assamedha' is where they sacrifice (medhanti) or kill (vadhanti) a horse. 'Purisamedha' is where they sacrifice or kill a person. 'Sammāpāsa' is where they cast (pāsenti) or throw (khipenti) the pin that is to be placed correctly in the yoke-hole. 'Vāja' is a designation for clarified butter and honey consecrated with mantras; 'vājapeyya' is where they cause that to be drunk. 'Niraggaḷa' means 'without a bolt,' because one gives all of one’s possessions entirely without concealment, so there is no bolt (aggaḷa) there. This is the explanation of the meaning according to the order found in the Pāli canon. Here, however, the explanations of the meanings of assamedha, purisamedha, niraggaḷa, sammāpāsa, and vājapeyya should be written according to the order in which they appear here.

414. Tikaṃ yājake. Yajanasīlo idi, yassi, jassa do. Yajatīti ijo, a. Atha vā itthiyā utumhi jāte jāyatīti itthītujo. “Nārītvijo”tipi pāṭho. “Utujo yājako tathā”tipi pāṭho, sundaro. Parasamayaṃ amanasi katvā pana ācariyena itidvijasaddo iditvijasaddo ca samānatthāti maññamānena “idi tvijo”ti vuttaṃ siyā, ṇvumhi yājako amara 17.17 gāthā passitabbā.

414. A triad of terms for the sacrificer. One whose nature is to sacrifice is 'yajanasīlo'; also 'idi,' 'yassi,' 'jassa do.' One who sacrifices is 'ijo,' with the suffix 'a.' Alternatively, one who is born when a woman's season arises is 'itthītujo.' There is also the reading 'nārītvijo.' There is also the reading 'utujo yājako tathā' (a seasonal sacrificer, likewise), which is excellent. However, disregarding other traditions, the teacher, thinking that the words 'itidvija' and 'iditvija' have the same meaning, might have said 'idi tvijo.' With the suffix 'ṇvu,' it is 'yājako.'

Dvayaṃ yāgasabhāyaṃ, aññasabhāyañcārambhake. Sabhāyaṃ sādhu sabhyo, yo. Samājaṃ janasaṅghātaṃ samāvasanti āgantvā ekadesī bhavantīti samājā, tehi samaṃ ekībhavatīti [M 0.0288] sāmājiko, ṇiko. Sabhāsado, sabhātāropyatra.

A pair of terms for a member of a sacrificial assembly and of another assembly. One who is fit for the assembly ('sabhā') is 'sabhyo,' with the suffix 'ya.' A gathering of people is a 'samāja'; they come together, arriving and becoming one group. One who joins in with them is a 'sāmājiko,' with the suffix 'ṇika.' 'Sabhāsado' and 'sabhātāro' are also used here.

Pañcakaṃ sabhāsāmaññe. Pari samantato sentyassaṃ parisā, si sevāyaṃ. Saha bhāsantyassaṃ sabhā, halopo, sabbhi bhātīti vā sabhā. Samajjanti saṃgacchanti milantyassaṃ samajjā, aja gamane. Samayanti milantyassaṃ samiti, i gatimhi, itthiyanti. Milanamekībhāvo. Samantato sīdantyasmiṃ saṃsado, itthinapuṃsakesu. Goṭṭhī, aṭṭhānīpyatra. Gāvovācā tiṭṭhanti bhavantyassaṃ goṭṭhī. Āgantvā tiṭṭhantyassaṃ aṭṭhānī, yu, nadādi, rassādi.

Five terms for assemblies in general. That in which they sit around is a 'parisā,' from 'pari' (around) and the root 'si' in the sense of 'to attend.' That in which they speak together ('saha bhāsanti') is a 'sabhā,' with elision of the 'ha'; or, it is a 'sabhā' because it shines ('bhāti') with the virtuous ('sabbhi'). That in which they assemble ('samajjanti'), come together ('saṅgacchanti'), and meet ('milanti') is a 'samajjā,' from the root 'aj' in the sense of 'to go.' That in which they come together ('samayanti') and meet ('milanti') is a 'samiti,' from the root 'i' in the sense of 'to go'; it is feminine. Meeting is unification. That in which they sit around is a 'saṃsado,' used in the feminine and neuter genders. 'Goṭṭhī' and 'aṭṭhānī' are also used here. That in which speech ('gāvo,' i.e., 'vācā') stands or occurs is a 'goṭṭhī.' That in which they arrive and stand is an 'aṭṭhānī,' with the suffix 'yu,' and following the rules of 'nadādi' and 'rassādi.'

415-416. Bhikkhuādikā imā catasso parisā nāma. Bhikkhanasīlatādīhi bhikkhu. “Uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā”ti jā. 1.7.59 hi vuttaṃ. Bhikkha yācane, rū. Yomhi bhikkhū. Inīpaccaye bhikkhunī, yossa lopo. Ratanattayamupagantvā āsayantīti upāsakā, ṇvu, āsa upavesane. Itte upāsikāyo. Ettha ca pabbajjāsāmaññato, liṅgasāmaññato ca sāmaṇerā bhikkhūsu, sāmaṇeriyādayo, ca bhikkhunīsu saṅgahitā, tato, avasesā pana sabbepi devamanussādayo itthipurisavasena dve koṭṭhāse katvā liṅgasabhāgavasena dvīsu saṅgahitā, brahmāno pana liṅgābhāvepi purisasaṇṭhānattā purisesu saṅgahitā, tathā paṇḍakāpi, ubhatobyañjanesu pana [M 0.0289] purisaubhatobyañjanaṃ purisesu, itthiubhatobyañjanaṃ itthīsu saṅgahitanti veditabbaṃ.

415-416. These four, beginning with the monks, are called the assemblies. A 'bhikkhu' is so called from his disposition to beg, etc. For it is said: “The noble ones stand with a purpose; this is the asking of the noble ones.” The word is from the root 'bhikkh' in the sense of 'to beg,' with the suffix 'u.' When the nominative singular ending 'o' is applied, it becomes 'bhikkhu.' With the suffix 'inī,' it is 'bhikkhunī,' with the elision of the 'o.' 'Upāsakas' are those who, having approached the Triple Gem, attend upon it, from the root 'ās' in the sense of 'to sit near,' with the suffix 'ṇvu.' In the feminine, they are 'upāsikāyo.' Here, on account of the commonality of their going forth and their gender, male novices are included among the monks, and female novices and others among the nuns. Then, all remaining beings, such as gods and humans, are made into two categories according to male and female and are included in these two on the basis of their shared gender. Brahmās, however, despite their lack of gender, are included among males due to their masculine form; likewise for eunuchs. But among hermaphrodites, a male hermaphrodite is included among males, and a female hermaphrodite among females; this should be understood.

Evaṃ catūhi koṭṭhāsehi parisaṃ dassetvā aṭṭhahipi dassetumāha “athave”ccādi. Tassattho – parisā nāma aṭṭha siyuṃ, kesaṃ vasenā’ṭṭha siyuṃ? Tāvatiṃsānaṃ dvijānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ khattānaṃ khattiyānaṃ mārassa gahapatissa samaṇānaṃ cātumahārājikānaṃ brahmūnañca vasenāti imā cā’ṭṭhaparisā pākaṭavasena, seṭṭhavasena ca vuttāti na ettha pubbe viya sabbā saṅgahitā, tāvatiṃsādikā hi pākaṭavasena vuttā, samaṇā pana pākaṭavasena, seṭṭhavasena ca vuttā.

Having thus shown the assembly in four categories, to show it in eight, he says 'or' and so on. Its meaning is: there may be eight assemblies. On what basis might there be eight? On the basis of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, the twice-born brahmins, the khattiya warriors, Māra, householders, ascetics, the Four Great Kings, and the Brahmās. These eight assemblies are spoken of in terms of being well-known and in terms of being superior. Thus, not all are included here as before. The Tāvatiṃsa and others are mentioned in terms of being well-known, whereas the ascetics are mentioned in terms of being both well-known and superior.

417. Gāyatti nāma yassa catūsu pādesu paṭipādaṃ chaḷakkharāni santi, sā pamukhamādi yassa utthādīnaṃ pāyenānupayogattā gāyattipamukhaṃ chandaṃ nāma. Gāyateti gāyatti, ge sadde, tti, e aya. Vajjaṃ chādayatīti chandaṃ, chada saṃvaraṇe, vuttañhi pajjaviveke buddhaguttena bhikkhunā –

417. The meter called Gāyattī is that which has six syllables in each of its four lines. It is the chief and first of the meters, because meters such as Uṭṭhā are generally not in use; hence the meters are named 'those with Gāyattī as chief.' It is called 'gāyattī' because one sings with it ('gāyati'), from the root 'ge' in the sense of 'to sound,' with the suffix 'tti' and the substitution of 'aya' for 'e.' It is called 'chanda' because it covers faults ('vajjaṃ chādayati'), from the root 'chad' in the sense of 'to cover.' For it was stated in the Pajjaviveka by the monk Buddhagutta:

“Uttha’maccutthakaṃ majjhaṃ, patiṭṭhā suppatiṭṭhakā;

Pāyo payogabāhyatthā, abhabbattā ca neritā”ti.

“Uṭṭhā, Accuṭṭhakā, Majjhā, Patiṭṭhā, and Suppatiṭṭhakā are generally not mentioned because they are outside the scope of usage and are unsuitable.”

Yaṃ pana catuvīsakkharavantaṃ, vedānaṃ ādibhūtañca gāyatti viya chandānaṃ nāpi catuppadaṃ, atha kho tipadameva siyā, sā sāvitti nāma, sāvittisaddo gāyattipariyāyopyatthi, “sāvitti chandaso mukhaṃ” ma. ni. 2.400; su. ni. 573, “gāyatti tu ca sāvittī”ti ca vuttattā. Idha pana bhedena vuttaṃ, yathā “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammaṃ [M 0.0290] saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti. Savitussa isino ayaṃ vācā sāvitti, iṇa.

That which consists of twenty-four syllables, is the origin of the Vedas, and like the Gāyattī among meters, is not four-footed but rather three-footed—that is called Sāvittī. The word ‘Sāvittī’ also exists as a synonym for ‘Gāyattī’, as it is stated: “Sāvittī is the face of meters,” and “Gāyattī is indeed Sāvittī.” Here, however, it is stated distinctly, just as in, “I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.” This saying of the seer Savitu is Sāvittī, from the suffix ‘iṇa’.

418. Habyaṃ devatātthamannaṃ, tassa pāke tadādhāre thālyādimhi caru, tattha ṭhitattā upacārena habyampi caru, caratismā u, caru pume. “Habyapāke caru pumā”ti amara 17.22 hyamarakose. Homadabbiyaṃ homakammani habyannādīnamuddharaṇatthaṃ katāyaṃ kaṭacchuyaṃ sujā, itthī, habyannādīnaṃ sukhaggahaṇatthaṃ jāyatīti sujā.

418. Habya is food intended for deities. Caru is the pot or other such vessel, its container during cooking. By extension, the offering itself is also called caru because it is situated therein. Caru is derived from the root ‘car’ with the suffix ‘u’, and is masculine. For it is stated in the Amarakośa: “Caru is masculine in the context of cooking the offering.” Sujā is the sacrificial ladle, the spoon made for lifting offerings such as cooked rice in the sacrificial rite; it is feminine. It is called sujā because it is produced (jāyati) for the easy grasping of offerings such as cooked rice.

Dvayaṃ khīranne, devannattā paramaṃ annaṃ. Pātabbassa, asitabbassa cāti dvinnampi bhāvānaṃ sambhavato pāyāso, ākārantānamāyo. Pāyasopyatra. Dvayaṃ devanne. Hu dāne, ṇyo. Imhi havi, napuṃsake.

There are two terms for milk-rice; as it is food for devas, it is the supreme food. Pāyāsa is so called from the occurrence of both states, that of being drinkable and that of being eatable; the suffix ‘āya’ is for roots ending in ‘ā’. Pāyāsa is also a term here. There are two terms for divine food. From the root ‘hu’ in the sense of giving, with the suffix ‘ṇya’, comes havi, which is neuter.

419. Thūṇāyaṃ yaññathambhe yūpo. Beluvo vā khādiro vā. Ālambapasubandhaneyaṭṭhi, samattayaññe vā yaṃ yaṭṭhimāropayati, sa yūpo yūpa… yaññīyapasubandhanakaṭṭhabhede… yāgasamatticihnatthe thambhe ca (vācappati), yu missane, po, dīghādi. Thu abhitthave, ṇo, dīghādi. Yaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ kaṭṭhantarenā’gginipphādanatthaṃ ghaṃsate, tasmiṃ nimmanthyadārumhi araṇī, ara gamane, aṇi, īmhi araṇī.

419. Yūpa is a term for a sacrificial post or pillar. It may be of beluva wood or khādira wood. It is the post for tying the animal to be sacrificed, or the post that is erected in a completed sacrifice; that is the yūpa. It is derived from the root ‘yu’ in the sense of mixing, with the suffix ‘po’, and lengthening of the vowel, etc. Thūṇā is derived from the root ‘thu’ in the sense of extolling, with the suffix ‘ṇo’, and lengthening of the vowel, etc. The piece of wood that is rubbed against another piece of wood for the purpose of producing fire, that kindling-wood, is called araṇī. It is derived from the root ‘ara’ in the sense of going, with the suffix ‘aṇi’, and with the feminine suffix ‘ī’ it becomes araṇī.

Gāhapaccādayo [M 0.0291] tayo aggayo. Gahapatinā saṃyutto gāhapacco, aggi, ṇyo. Taṃyoniyaṃrevāhavanīyo hutabbaggiāhavanamarahatīti āhavanīyo. Dakkhiṇaggi pana taṃyoni aññayonipi. Dakkhiṇaṃ deyyadhammaṃ agganti vissajjantyasminti dakkhiṇaggi, agga dāne, dānaṃ aggīyati dīyatyasminti dānaggaṃ, “parivesanaṭṭhāna”nti a. ni. ṭī. 3.9.20 hi aṅguttaranikāyaṭīkā. Ettha ca gāhapaccaggādīnaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vippaṭipajjantānaṃ vināsahetubhāvato aggitādaṭṭhabbā. Sattakanipātaaṅguttaranikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana –

There are three fires, beginning with the Gāhapaccaggi. The Gāhapaccaggi is connected with the householder. The Āhavanīyaggi has that as its source and is so called because it is worthy of oblations and offerings. The Dakkhiṇaggi, however, has that as its source and also another source. The Dakkhiṇaggi is so called because one distributes gifts (deyyadhamma) as foremost (agga) in it. The root ‘agg’ is in the sense of giving; a gift is given in it, hence it is the foremost place for gifts (dānaggaṃ), for it is stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya subcommentary: “the place of distribution.” Here, the nature of fire should be understood as being the cause of destruction for those who act contrary to the three fires, beginning with the Gāhapaccaggi. Moreover, in the commentary on the Sattaka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, it is said:—

Āhunaṃ vuccati sakkāro, āhunaṃ arahantīti āhuneyyā, mātāpitaro, mātāpitaro hi puttānaṃ bahūpakāratāya āhunaṃ arahanti, tesu vippaṭipajjamānā puttā nirayādīsu pavattanti, tasmā kiñcāpi mātāpitaro nānudahanti, anudahamānassa pana paccayo hotīti anudahanaṭṭheneva “āhuneyyaggī”ti vuccati. Yo mātugāmassa sayanavatthālaṅkārādianuppadānena bahūpakāro, taṃ aticaranto mātugāmo nirayādīsu nibbattati, tasmā sopi purimanayeneva anudahanaṭṭhena “gahapataggī”ti vutto. “Dakkhiṇeyyaggī”ti ettha pana “dakkhiṇā”ti cattāro paccayā, bhikkhusaṅgho dakkhiṇeyyo, so gihīnaṃ tīsu saraṇesu, pañcasu sīlesu, dasasu sīlesu, mātāpitupaṭṭhāne, dhammikasamaṇabrāhmaṇūpaṭṭhāneti evamādīsu kalyāṇadhammesu niyojanena bahūpakāro, tasmiṃ micchāpaṭipanno gihī bhikkhusaṅghaṃ akkositvā nirayādīsu nibbattati, tasmā sopi purimanayeneva anudahanaṭṭhena

Āhuna is said to be honor. Āhuneyyā are those worthy of honor, namely, mother and father. For parents are worthy of honor because of their great service to their children. Children who act wrongly towards them proceed to hell and other such states. Therefore, although parents do not burn, they are a cause for burning; thus, in the sense of burning, they are called the ‘āhuneyyaggi’. A man who is of great service to a woman by providing her with a bed, clothing, ornaments, and so on—if that woman transgresses against him, she is reborn in hell and other such states. Therefore, he too, in the same way as before, is called the ‘gahapataggi’ in the sense of burning. Regarding the ‘dakkhiṇeyyaggi’, here ‘dakkhiṇā’ refers to the four requisites, and the community of bhikkhus is worthy of offerings. It is of great service to householders by engaging them in wholesome states such as the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten precepts, attendance on parents, and attendance on righteous ascetics and brahmins. A householder who acts wrongly towards the community, having reviled the community of bhikkhus, is reborn in hell and other such states. Therefore, it too, in the same way as before, in the sense of burning,

“Dakkhiṇeyyaggī”ti [M 0.0292] vutto. Kaṭṭhato nibbatto pākatikova aggi kaṭṭhaggi nāmāti a. ni. aṭṭha. 3.7.46 vutto.

is called the ‘dakkhiṇeyyaggi’. Fire produced from wood, which is just ordinary fire, is called the ‘kaṭṭhaggi’.

420. Siloko dāne. Hā cāge, ṇo, dvittacattagattāni, caja hānimhi vā. Saja visagge, visaggo dānaṃ, upubbo saja visajje, ṇo, pubbe vāgamo, vosaggo. Disa atisajjane, atisajjanaṃ dānaṃ, pabodhanañca, iha dānaṃ padesanaṃ. Saṇa dāne, yu. Tara plavanataraṇesu, maccherasotātikkamanamettha taraṇaṃ. Hā cāge, curādi, to, yālopo, bhūvādimhi pana “ākārantānamāyo”ti āyo, vihāyitaṃ. Vajja vajjane, sabbatra bhāvasādhanaṃ. Upasaggavisesenete dānatthābhidhāyino. Phassanaṃ, patipādanaṃpyatra.

420. A verse on giving. From the root ‘hā’ in the sense of abandoning (cāga), with the suffix ‘ṇo’... Or from the root ‘caj’ in the sense of loss (hāni). From the root ‘saj’ in the sense of releasing (visagga); visagga means giving. From the root ‘saj’ with the prefix ‘vi’, in the sense of releasing, with the suffix ‘ṇo’, and with ‘ava’ as a prefix, comes vosagga. From the root ‘dis’ in the sense of bestowing (atisajjana); atisajjana means giving and also awakening; here giving is pointing out (padesanaṃ). From the root ‘saṇ’ in the sense of giving, with the suffix ‘yu’. From the root ‘tar’ in the sense of floating and crossing; here, crossing means overcoming the stream of stinginess. From the root ‘hā’ in the sense of abandoning, of the curādi class, with the suffix ‘ta’, and elision of ‘yā’; but in the bhūvādi class, with the suffix ‘āya’ according to the rule ‘ākārantānamāyo’, it becomes vihāyitaṃ. From the root ‘vad’ in the sense of speaking (vajjana). In all cases, the derivation is as an abstract noun. These words, with various prefixes, denote the meaning of giving. Phassana and paṭipādana are also included here.

421. Seṭṭhadhanassa, puttānaṃ, dārānaṃ, rajjassa, aṅgānañca vasena pañcamahāpariccāgo vutto. Tatra seṭṭhadhanaṃ setahatthādiratanaṃ. Puttā orasā, atha vā puttadhītaro. Dāro patibbatā piyabhariyā. Rajjaṃ pakatirajjaṃ, taduṭṭhito vā āyo. Aṅgaṃ cakkhādi. Mahantehi uttamapuriseheva kato, mahantānaṃ vā pariccāgo mahāpariccāgo, mahatthaṃ vā buddhabhāvatthaṃ kato pariccāgo mahāpariccāgo, kāpurisehi dukkarattā mahanto vā seṭṭho pariccāgo mahāpariccāgo.

421. The five great relinquishments are stated in terms of supreme wealth, sons, wives, kingdom, and limbs. Therein, supreme wealth refers to precious things such as a white elephant. Sons are one’s own natural offspring, or sons and daughters. A wife is a devoted, beloved spouse. A kingdom is the natural kingdom, or the revenue derived from it. A limb is the eye, and so on. It is called a great relinquishment because it is performed by great and excellent persons, or it is a relinquishment of great things, or it is a relinquishment performed for the great purpose of attaining Buddhahood, or it is a great or supreme relinquishment because it is difficult for ignoble persons to perform.

422. Dānapāramīādikānaṃ [M 0.0293] tissannaṃ pāramīnaṃ vasena asādhāraṇadānavatthuṃ dassetvā sādhāraṇadānavatthuṃ dassetumāha “annaṃ pāna”miccādi. Tatra annaṃ pānavajjitaṃ yaṃ kiñci khādanīyādikaṃ. Pānaṃ pātabbaṃ udakādi. Yānaṃ hatthyādi antamaso upāhanaṃ upādāya gamanasādhanaṃ. Mālā mālyaṃ, pupphañca. Vilepanaṃ chavirāgakaraṇaṃ, vibhūto sugandho vā. Gandho tadaññagandho. Seyyā mañcādi, seyyāggahaṇena cettha āsanampi gahitaṃ. Padīpeyyaṃ padīpassa hitaṃ yaṃ kiñci telādi, ime dasa dānavatthū nāma siyuṃ. Dīyante yāyāti dānaṃ. Tassa vatthu kāraṇaṃ, taduppattiyā uppajjanatoti dānavatthu, dātabbaṃ vā dānaṃ, annādi, tadeva vatthu. Etāni pana dasa dānavatthūni suttantanayena kathitāni. Vinayābhidhammanayavasenāpi pana kathetabbāni, rūpādichaḷārammaṇadānavasena hi abhidhamme cha dānavatthūni āgatāni, vinaye cīvarapiṇḍapātabhesajjasenāsanavasena cattāri āgatāni. Tatthevamācariyā vadanti “suttantanayadānato vinayadānameva mahapphalaṃ, kasmā? Annādidānamattavaseneva yassa kassaci dussīlādikassa dātabbanti anujānitvā piṇḍapātādikappiyavohāravasena sīlavantādikasseva ca dātabbanti anuññātattā. Sāmaññadānato hi visesadānameva mahapphalaṃ, tatopi abhidhammanayadānameva mahapphalaṃ, kasmā? Rūpādīsu paramatthavaseneva abhinivisitvā dānavasena tatopi atisayadānattā”ti. Mayaṃ pana suttantanayadānaṃ vā hotu vinayābhidhammanayadānaṃ vā, yaṃ khettāditividhasampadāyuttaṃ, tameva mahapphalaṃ karotīti vadāma.

422. Having shown the uncommon objects of giving in terms of the three perfections beginning with the perfection of giving, to show the common objects of giving he says, “food, drink,” and so on. Therein, food is any kind of edible item, excluding drink. Drink is that which is drinkable, such as water. A vehicle is a means of conveyance, from an elephant down to a sandal. A garland is a floral wreath, and also flowers. An unguent is that which makes the skin radiant, or a pleasant fragrance. Perfume is any other kind of scent. A bed includes couches and the like; by the inclusion of ‘bed’, a seat is also included. A lamp-offering is anything useful for a lamp, such as oil. These are said to be the ten objects of giving. Dāna is that by which things are given. Its object (vatthu) is the cause, that from which it arises; thus it is a dānavatthu (an object of giving). Or, dāna is that which is to be given, such as food, and that itself is the object. These ten objects of giving are spoken of according to the Suttanta method. They should, however, also be spoken of according to the methods of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma. For in the Abhidhamma, six objects of giving are mentioned, in terms of giving the six sense-objects such as form. In the Vinaya, four are mentioned, in terms of robes, almsfood, medicine, and lodging. Regarding this, the teachers say: “Giving according to the Vinaya method is of greater fruit than giving according to the Suttanta method. Why? Because while it is permitted to give food and so on to anyone at all, such as an immoral person, it is permitted to give almsfood and so on only to a virtuous person, in accordance with the proper designation. For a specific gift is of greater fruit than a general gift. And giving according to the Abhidhamma method is of even greater fruit than that. Why? Because it is giving with conviction based on the ultimate realities of form and so on, and is thus a superior gift.” We, however, say that whether it is giving according to the Suttanta, Vinaya, or Abhidhamma method, only that which is endowed with the threefold excellence of the field and so on brings great fruit.

423. Tadahe [M 0.0294] matadivase matatthaṃ yaṃ piṇḍapātajalāñjalyādidānaṃ, etaṃ dānaṃ dehā uddhe bhavaṃ uddhadehikaṃ nāma. Pitaraṃ uddissa jalāñjalisuvaṇṇādidānaṃ nivāpo, vapa bījasantāne, ṇo. Kālapattādiniyamena rājamattaṇḍavisottarādisatthato vihitaṃ, taṃva tameva pitudānaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇabhojanādi saddhaṃ nāma, saddhā assa dānassatthīti, ṇo. Satthatoti hetumhi avadhyatthavatticchāya pañcamī.

423. On the very day of death, the offering of almsfood, water libations, and so forth, made for the deceased—this gift, being for one who has gone beyond the body, is called 'uddhadehika'. The offering of water libations, gold, and so forth, dedicated to the ancestors is called 'nivāpa'; from the root 'vapa' in the sense of 'to scatter seeds', with the suffix 'ṇo'. That same ancestral offering, such as the feeding of ascetics and brahmins, prescribed by rules of time, circumstance, and so forth, from texts like the Rājamattaṇḍa and Visottara, is called 'saddha', because faith is present for this gift, with the suffix 'ṇo'. The word `satthato` is in the fifth case (ablative) in the sense of a reason, with the desire for the meaning of 'not to be killed'.

424. Catukkaṃ gehāgate. Ata sātaccagamane, ithi, atithi, “atithi dvīsū”ti tikaṇḍasese tikaṇḍasesa 2.7.9. Itthiyaṃ atithī ca. Āgacchatīti āgantu, tu. Āhunaṃ vuccati gehāgatānaṃ dātabbabhattādi, taṃ paṭiggaṇhituṃ arahatīti pāhuno. Visa pavesane, āvesanaṃ āveso, tamarahatīti āvesiko. Atyāgatopyatra. Gantumicchatīti gamiko, iko. Dvayaṃ pūjitapupphadabbakkhatādimhi. Aggha pūjāyaṃ, a. Ṇyamhi agghiyaṃ, agghayampi. Agghato vā tadatthiye iyo.

424. A set of four for one who has come to the house. From the root 'ata' in the sense of 'constant coming', with the suffix 'ithi', is formed 'atithi'. In the Tikaṇḍasesa it is said, 'atithi is in two genders'. And in the feminine, 'atithī'. One who comes is 'āgantu', from the suffix 'tu'. 'Āhunaṃ' is said of food and so forth to be given to those who have come to the house; one who is worthy to receive it is 'pāhuno'. From the root 'visa' in the sense of 'entering', 'āvesanaṃ' is 'āveso'; one who is worthy of it is 'āvesiko'. 'Atyāgato' is also included here. One who wishes to go is 'gamiko', from the suffix 'iko'. A pair for honored flowers, substances, uncooked rice, and so forth. From the root 'aggha' in the sense of 'to honor', with the suffix 'a'. With the suffix 'ṇya', 'agghiyaṃ', and also 'agghayaṃ'. Or from 'agghato' (from value), in the sense of 'for that purpose', with the suffix 'iyo'.

425. Pādatthe pādaddhe (ka.) udakādimhi pajjaṃ. Padassa hitaṃ pajjaṃ. Āgantvādayo pajjapariyantā satta saddā tīsu liṅgesu.

425. Water and so forth for the feet is 'pajja'. What is beneficial for the feet is 'pajja'. The seven words beginning with 'āgantu' and ending with 'pajja' are in the three genders.

Chakkaṃ [M 0.0295] pūjāyaṃ. Ci caye,ti. Acca pūjāyaṃ, yu. Pūja pūjāyaṃ, itthiyamati a. Hara haraṇe, upapubbo hara pūjāyaṃ, ṇo, upahāro, pume. Bala pāṇanapūjāsaṃvaraṇesu, i, bali dvīsu. Māna pūjāyaṃ, yu. Namassāpyatra, namassa pūjāyaṃ, itthiyaṃ a.

A set of six for worship. From the root 'ci' in the sense of 'to accumulate', with the suffix 'ti'. From the root 'acca' in the sense of 'to worship', with the suffix 'yu'. From the root 'pūja' in the sense of 'to worship', in the feminine, with the suffix 'a'. From the root 'hara' in the sense of 'to carry'; the root 'hara' preceded by 'upa' is in the sense of 'to worship', with the suffix 'ṇo', forming 'upahāro', in the masculine. From the root 'bala' in the senses of 'breathing, worship, and restraint', with the suffix 'i', forming 'bali' in two genders. From the root 'māna' in the sense of 'to worship', with the suffix 'yu'. 'Namassā' is also included here; from the root 'namassa' in the sense of 'to worship', in the feminine, with the suffix 'a'.

426. Catukkaṃ vandanāyaṃ. Namassa vandane, pubbeva, namu namane vā, ssapaccayo. Namo karaṇaṃ namakkāro, ṇo. Namoto chaṭṭhīlopo, “lopañca tatrākāro”ti okāralope akārāgamo, atha vā namanaṃ namo, tassa karaṇaṃ namakkāro, rahosaddo viya hi namosaddotra dvidhā vattati. Eko akāranto saliṅgo, eko aliṅgo okārantoti. Vanda abhivādanathutīsu, yu, vandanā, nalope, dīghe ca abhivādanaṃ.

426. A set of four for veneration. From the root 'namassa' in the sense of 'to venerate', as stated before; or from 'namu' in the sense of 'to bow', with the 'ssa' suffix. The doing of 'namo' is 'namakkāro', with the suffix 'ṇo'. From 'namo', the sixth case ending is elided; when the 'o' is elided, the letter 'a' is inserted. Alternatively, 'namanaṃ' (bowing) is 'namo'; the doing of that is 'namakkāro'. Indeed, like the word 'raho', the word 'namo' here functions in two ways: one form ends in 'a' and has gender, the other is genderless and ends in 'o'. From the root 'vanda' in the senses of 'salutation' and 'praise', with the suffix 'yu', 'vandanā' is formed; with the elision of 'n' and lengthening, 'abhivādanaṃ' is also formed.

Tikaṃ patthanāmatte. Attha yācanāyaṃ, yu, patthanā. Atthanāpi. Ṭhā gatinivattimhi. Panidvayapubbo patthanāyaṃ, yu, ṇattaṃ, dhattaṃ. Imhi paṇidhi. Ayaṃ purise pulliṅge. Yācanāpyatra.

A set of three for mere aspiration. From the root 'attha' in the sense of 'to request', with the suffix 'yu', is formed 'patthanā'. Also 'atthanā'. From the root 'ṭhā' in the sense of 'cessation of motion', when preceded by the double prefix 'pa-ni', in the sense of 'aspiration', with the suffix 'yu', the 'n' becomes 'ṇ' and the 'dh' becomes 'dh'. From this root is also formed 'paṇidhi'. This word is in the masculine gender when referring to a man. 'Yācanā' is also included here.

427. Sakkārapubbaṅgamaṃ katvā garuādīnaṃ ārādhanīyānaṃ kvaci atthe niyojanaṃ patthanāviseso ajjhesanā, isa gavesane, isa gatihiṃsāvadānesuvā, yu, ajjhesanā, yathā “desetu bhagavā dhammaṃ, desetu sugato dhamma”nti mahāva. 8.

427. Having made respect foremost, the appointment of those worthy of veneration, such as teachers, to some task is a special kind of aspiration called 'ajjhesanā'. From the root 'isa' in the sense of 'to seek', or from 'isa' in the senses of 'going, harming, and giving', with the suffix 'yu', is formed 'ajjhesanā', as in: 'May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma, may the Sugata teach the Dhamma'.

428. Catukkaṃ [M 0.0296] anussaraṇe. Esa gavesane, yāgame pariyesanā. Timhi pariyeṭṭhi. Gavesa maggane.

428. A set of four for investigation. From the root 'esa' in the sense of 'to seek', with the augment 'yā', is formed 'pariyesanā'. With the suffix 'ti', is formed 'pariyeṭṭhi'. From the root 'gavesa' in the sense of 'to search for'.

Tikaṃ ārādhanīyassa cittānukūle. Āsa upavesane, yu, upāsanaṃ. Su savane. Sotumicchā sussūsā, “bhujaghasaharasupādīhi tumicchatthesū”ti sapaccayo, dvittādi, sussūsā, sā itthī. Caratito bhāve ṇyo, pāricariyā.

A set of three for what is agreeable to the mind of one worthy of veneration. From the root 'āsa' in the sense of 'to sit near', with the suffix 'yu', is formed 'upāsanaṃ'. From the root 'su' in the sense of 'to hear'. The desire to hear is 'sussūsā'; according to the rule 'from roots like bhuj, ghas, har, su, and so forth, in the sense of desiring to...', the 'sa' suffix is used; with doubling and so forth, 'sussūsā' is formed; it is feminine. From 'carati', in the sense of 'state', with the suffix 'ṇya', is formed 'pāricariyā'.

429. Tikaṃ tuṇhībhāve. Munino kammaṃ monaṃ, ṇo. Tuha adane, ṇhapaccayo, halopo ca, tuṇho monametassatthīti tuṇhī, tassa bhāvo tuṇhībhāvo, atuṇhassa vā tuṇhībhavanaṃ tuṇhībhāvo, atha vā tohatīti tuṇhī, tuha adane, adanaṃ hiṃsā, ṇīpaccayo, vaṇṇavipariyayo, tuṇhino bhāvo tuṇhībhāvo.

429. A set of three for the state of silence. The deed of a sage is 'monaṃ', with the suffix 'ṇo'. From the root 'tuha' in the sense of 'to consume', with the suffix 'ṇha' and elision of 'h', is formed 'tuṇho'; one for whom this silence exists is 'tuṇhī'; the state of that is 'tuṇhībhāvo'. Or, the becoming silent of one who is not silent is 'tuṇhībhāvo'. Alternatively, 'that which strikes' is 'tuṇhī'; from the root 'tuha' in the sense of 'to consume', where 'consuming' is 'harming'; with the suffix 'ṇī' and metathesis of letters. The state of a silent one is 'tuṇhībhāvo'.

Pañcakaṃ anukkame. Patirūpena patanaṃ paṭipāṭi, pata gamane, ubhayatrāpi tassa ṭo, i. Sā itthī. Anurūpo kamo, kamo eva vā anukkamo. Pari anatikkamena ayanaṃ pavattanaṃ pariyāyo. Pubbassānurūpā anupubbī, nadādi. Ayaṃ apume. Anupubbampi. Kamu icchākantīsu, ṇo.

A set of five for sequence. Proceeding in a suitable manner is 'paṭipāṭi'; from the root 'pata' in the sense of 'to go', in both cases the suffix is 'ṭo' or 'i'. It is feminine. A suitable order is 'kamo', or 'kamo' itself is 'anukkamo'. Going on or proceeding without transgression is 'pariyāyo'. That which is in conformity with what precedes is 'anupubbī'; it belongs to the `nadādi` group of nouns. This word is not masculine. Also 'anupubbaṃ'. From the root 'kamu' in the senses of 'desire' and 'beauty', with the suffix 'ṇo'.

430. Tikaṃ sīle. Tapa santāpe. Kilese tāpetīti tapo, a. Yamu uparame, uparamo viramaṇaṃ, bhāve ṇo[M 0.0297]. Si bandhane, sinoti cittametenāti sīlaṃ, lo, sīla samādhāne vā, samādhānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvo. Sīla samādhimhi vā, samādhiratra kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhyupagamo, aññatra sīle tupacārā, atha vā attānaṃ, parañca nirayādīsu tāpetīti tapo. Kusaladhammato saṃyamanaṃ viramaṇaṃ saṃyamo, samādhānañcātrākusaladhammavasenevāti ayaṃ aññatra sīle nibbacanaṃ.

430. A set of three for virtue. From the root 'tapa' in the sense of 'to burn'. Because it burns the defilements, it is 'tapo', with the suffix 'a'. From the root 'yamu' in the sense of 'to restrain'; restraint is abstaining; with the suffix 'ṇo' in the sense of 'state'. From the root 'si' in the sense of 'to bind'; because the mind is bound by this, it is 'sīlaṃ', with the suffix 'lo'. Or from 'sīla' in the sense of 'composing'; composing is the state of being established in wholesome qualities. Or from 'sīla' in the sense of 'concentration'; concentration here is the undertaking of wholesome qualities; in other contexts, 'sīla' is used figuratively. Alternatively, because it burns oneself and others in hell and so forth, it is 'tapo'. Restraint or abstaining from unwholesome qualities is 'saṃyamo'; and composing here is precisely through the power of unwholesome qualities—this is the derivation in contexts other than virtue.

Satthavihito niyamo vataṃ. “Mantanāyaṃ paṭiññāyaṃ, niyamo nicchaye vate”ti rabhaso. Tañca vataṃ upavāsādilakkhaṇaṃ puññamuccate. “Sīlaṃ cārittaṃ vārittamupavāsādipuññaka”ntyamaramālā. Ādinā akkhāralavaṇāsanādi akhādanābhojanādi (ka.). Ettha ca tapādayo mukhyavasena kusalasīle vattanti, rūḷhīvasena akusalasīlepi. Niyamādayo mukhyavasena akusalasīle vattanti, rūḷhīvasena kusalasīleti ayaṃ sīlabbatānaṃ viseso. Yamu uparame. Vatu vattane, vattanañcātra caraṇaṃ, samādhānaṃ vā. Vā pulliṅgepi.

A rule prescribed by scripture is 'vataṃ'. Rabhasa says: 'Niyama is used in the sense of incantation, promise, decision, and vow.' And that vow, characterized by fasting and so forth, is called merit. The Amaramālā says: 'Sīla is conduct, avoidance, and the merit of fasting, etc.' By 'and so forth' is meant abstaining from pungent and salty food, etc. Here, 'tapo' and the like apply primarily to wholesome virtue, and conventionally to unwholesome virtue as well. 'Niyama' and the like apply primarily to unwholesome virtue, and conventionally to wholesome virtue—this is the distinction between precepts (`sīla`) and vows (`vata`). From 'yamu' in the sense of 'to restrain'. From 'vatu' in the sense of 'to be'; 'being' here is conduct or composure. The word `vata` is also in the masculine gender.

Dvayaṃ mariyādātikkame. Kamu padavikkhepe, virūpo atikka mo vītikkamo. Mariyādātikkamo ācāro ajjhācāro. Kāyavivekādayo tayo ettha viveko. Vica vivecane, puthabhāve ca, bhāve ṇo, dvittādi. Puthu visuṃbhūto gaṇādīhi attā sarīraṃ mano sabhāvo ca etesanti puthugattā, tesaṃ bhāvo puthugattatā puthagattatā (ka.) kāyavivekādayo, majjhe gāgamo. “Evaṃsarūpoyaṃ puriso, evaṃsarūpā vā amhepi nesaṃ pakati”riti pakatipurisānaṃ vibhāgena ñāṇaviveko. Attā buddhi, so puthubhāvena yassa, tabbhāvo puthugattatātyaññe. Aññato vilakkhaṇassa bhāvo puthugattatātyaññe.

A pair of terms for transgression of limits. From the root 'kamu' in the sense of 'stepping'; an improper transgression is 'vītikkamo'. A transgression of the limits of conduct is 'ajjhācāro'. Here, 'viveko' refers to the three kinds: bodily seclusion and so forth. From the root 'vica' in the sense of 'to discern' and 'to be separate'; with the suffix 'ṇo' in the sense of 'state', with doubling and so forth. Those for whom the self, body, mind, and nature are separate and distinct from groups and so forth are 'puthugattā'; their state is 'puthugattatā', which refers to bodily seclusion and so forth, with the insertion of 'gā' in the middle. 'This person is of such a nature', or 'we too are of their nature'—discerning the nature of ordinary people by way of distinction is 'ñāṇaviveko' (discernment of knowledge). Others say: 'attā' is intellect; the state of one for whom that is separate is 'puthugattatā'. Still others say: the state of being distinct from another is 'puthugattatā'.

431. Khuddānukhuddakaṃ [M 0.0298] cūḷavattaṃ, mahāvattañca, vattapaṭipatti vā “ābhisamācārika”mityuccate, abhisamācāre uttamasamācāre bhavaṃ ābhisamācārikanti katvā, tadaññaṃ khuddānukhuddakato aññaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlādikaṃ sīlaṃ brahmacariyassāriyamaggassa ādimhi tadatthāya caritabbattā ādibrahmacariyamityuccate.
