431. The minor and lesser rules, the minor observances, and the major observances, or the practice of the observances, are called 'ābhisamācārika'. This is because 'ābhisamācārika' is that which pertains to 'abhisamācāra', which is supreme conduct. Virtue other than this, that is, different from the minor and lesser rules, such as the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint and so forth, is called 'ādibrahmacariya' (the beginning of the holy life), because it is to be practiced for the sake of the Noble Path at the beginning of the holy life.

432. Pāpehi akusaladhammehi upāvatto upāvuto (ka.) anāvuto vigato sabbannapānabhogādīhi vivajjitova hutvā guṇehi sīlādīhi saddhiṃ yo vāso vasanaṃ thambhanamatthi, so “upavāso”ti vijānitabbo. Vasu thambhe, divādi, upavasanaṃ upavāso, ṇo, vigato, upeto ca vāsoti vā upavāso.

432. That which is a dwelling, living, or abiding—being turned away from, uncovered by, and departed from evil, unwholesome states; having abstained from all food, drink, enjoyments, and so forth; and being together with qualities such as virtue—should be known as 'upavāso'. From the root 'vasu' in the sense of 'to abide firmly', of the `divādi` class. 'Upavasanaṃ' becomes 'upavāso', with the suffix 'ṇo'. Alternatively, 'upavāso' is a dwelling (`vāso`) that is departed from (`vigato`) evil and endowed with (`upeto`) virtue.

433. Pajjaddhaṃ bhikkhumhi. Tapo kammamassatthīti tapassī, tapādito sī, dvittaṃ. Bhayadassanasīlo bhikkhu, rū, rasso. Sametīti samaṇo, yu. Pabbajā sañjātā yassāti pabbajito, sañjātatthe ito, seṭṭhattaṃ vajatīti vā [M 0.0299] pabbajito, vaja gamane, to. Tapokammaṃ dhanaṃ yassāti tapodhano.

433. The term pajjaddha is used for a monk. He is called tapassī because austerity (tapa) is his practice (kamma); it is derived from tapa with the suffix sī and doubling of the consonant. A monk is one whose nature is to see fear (bhayadassanasīlo); it is derived from rū with shortening of the vowel. He is called samaṇa because he is tranquil (sameti); it is derived with the suffix yu. He is called pabbajita because ‘going forth’ (pabbajā) has arisen for him; it is derived with ito in the sense of ‘arisen’. Or he is pabbajita because he goes to the highest state (seṭṭhattaṃ vajatīti); it is derived from vaja (to go) with the suffix to. He is called tapodhana because ascetic practice (tapokamma) is his wealth (dhana).

Dvayaṃ monabbate. Vācato yamatīti vācaṃyamo, niggahītāgamo, rasso ca. Monamassatthīti muni, rasso, ossu. Dvayaṃ ābhusopavāsanabrahmacariyādiyutte. Tapoyogā tāpaso, saṇa. Isa gavesane, i, isi, isa gatiyaṃ vā, ñāṇassa, saṃsārassa vā pāraṃ gamanato isi, i. Pārikaṅkhīpyatra, pāramassatthīti pārī, brahmañāṇaṃ, taṃ kaṅkhatīti pārikaṅkhī.

Two terms are for one who has taken a vow (monabbate). He is called vācaṃyamo because he restrains his speech (vācato yamatīti); it involves the insertion of a niggahīta and shortening of the vowel. He is called muni because he possesses silence (mona); it involves shortening of the vowel, and the o becomes u. Two terms are used for one endowed with ascetic practices, fasting, the holy life, and so on. From the practice of austerity (tapoyoga), one is called tāpasa, with the suffix saṇa. The root isa is in the sense of ‘seeking’; with the suffix i, it forms isi. Or the root isa is in the sense of ‘going’; because of going to the other shore of knowledge or of saṃsāra, one is called isi, with the suffix i. Here also, pārikaṅkhī is used. He is called pārī because he possesses the far shore (pāra), which is the knowledge of Brahma; and he who longs for that is called pārikaṅkhī.

434. Dvayaṃ jitindriyagaṇe. Yesaṃ saṃyatā indriyānaṃ gaṇā, te yatino, vasino ca nāma. Yataṃ indriyasaṃyamo niccametesamatthīti yatino, ī. Yatayopi, yata payatane, i. Vasa pāguṇye, vaso yesamatthīti vasino, ī.

434. There are two terms for the group of those who have conquered their senses. Those whose groups of senses are restrained are called yatino (ascetics) and vasino (masters). They are called yatino because they constantly possess restraint (yataṃ), that is, restraint of the senses (indriyasaṃyamo); the suffix ī is added. Also, yatayo (ascetics) is from the root yata in the sense of ‘exertion,’ with the suffix i. They are called vasino because they possess mastery (vasa), from the root vasa in the sense of ‘skill’ (pāguṇye); the suffix ī is added.

Tikaṃ dhammasenāpatimhi. Sārī nāma brāhmaṇī, tassā putto sāriputto. Tussantyasmiṃ atthasiddhitoti tisso, so, tussi ca. Pūjito tisso upatisso, atha vā “tisso”ti vā “phusso”ti vā “upatisso”ti vā daharakāle mātāpitūhi yadicchāya gahitaṃ nāmaṃ, “sāriputto”ti mātuvasena, “dhammasenāpatī”ti pana ariyabhāvappatte sammāsambuddhena gahitaṃ nāmaṃ. Kusaladhammāvudhehi kāmādikā akusaladhammasenā jitā yesaṃ dhammasenā, anekakoṭisatasahassasaṅkhyā bhagavato sāvakasaṅghā, tesaṃ pati nāyakaṭṭhena dhammasenāpati.

There are three terms for the General of the Dhamma. The brahmin woman's name was Sārī, and her son was Sāriputta. Because they are pleased (tussanti) in him due to the accomplishment of his purpose (atthasiddhito), he is called Tissa; from the root tus with the suffix sa. The revered Tissa is Upatissa. Alternatively, ‘Tissa,’ ‘Phussa,’ or ‘Upatissa’ was the name arbitrarily given by his parents in childhood. He was called ‘Sāriputta’ on account of his mother, while ‘Dhammasenāpati’ was the name given by the Perfectly Enlightened One upon his attainment of noble status. The army of the Dhamma (dhammasenā) are those by whom the army of unwholesome states, such as sensual desires, has been conquered with the weapons of wholesome states—this is the Blessed One's community of disciples, numbering many hundreds of thousands of crores. He is the leader (pati) of them in the sense of being a guide (nāyakaṭṭhena), hence Dhammasenāpati.

435. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0300] bhagavato vāmapassaṭṭhe mahāmoggallāne. Kule jāyatīti koliko, so eva kolito. Moggallibrāhmaṇiyā apaccaṃ moggallāno, ṇāno. Dvayaṃ ariyasāmaññe. Kilesārayo hanatīti araho, so eva ariyo, ara gamane vā, arati adhigacchati maggaphaladhammeti ariyo, ṇyo. Adhigacchitthāti adhigato, to.

435. There are two terms for Mahāmoggallāna, who stood on the left side of the Blessed One. He is called Kolika because he was born in a clan (kule); he is also Kolita. He is called Moggallāna as the offspring (apaccaṃ) of the brahmin woman Moggallī, with the suffix ṇāna. There are two terms in the general sense of ‘noble one’ (ariya). He is called araha because he destroys (hanati) the enemies (ari) that are the defilements (kilesa); he is also ariyo. Or, from the root ara in the sense of ‘to go,’ he is called ariyo because he goes to and attains (arati adhigacchati) the Dhamma of the path and fruit, with the suffix ṇya. He is called adhigato because he has attained (adhigacchittha), with the suffix to.

Asekkhassa gahitattā “sotāpannādikā”ti etthādinā chaḷeva puggalā saṅgahitā, tena sotāpattimaggaṭṭhādayo satta sekkhā, eko arahā asekkhāti siddhaṃ. Tīhi sikkhāhi yuttatāya sekkhā, kakāralopena “sekhā, asekhā”tipyatthi. Dvayaṃ anadhigate. Ariyehi puthu visuṃbhūto jano puthujjano, puthu vā nānākilese janetīti puthujjano.

Because the non-learner (asekkha) is included, by the phrase 'stream-enterer and so on,' only six persons are encompassed. Thus, it is established that the seven learners (sekkhā) are the one on the path to stream-entry and the others, while the one Arahant is the non-learner (asekkha). They are called learners (sekkhā) because they are endowed with the three trainings (sikkhā); by the elision of the letter 'ka', the forms sekhā and asekhā also exist. There are two terms for one who has not attained. An ordinary person (puthujjana) is a person (jano) who is separate (puthu) and distinct from the noble ones. Or, an ordinary person (puthujjana) is so called because they generate (janeti) various (puthu) defilements.

436. Dvayaṃ aggaphale. Paṭhamamaggādīhi diṭṭhamariyādamanatikkamitvā jānitthāti aññā, rasso, rūparāgādīnaṃ vā pañcuddhambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ odhivasena māraṇato aññā, mariyādattho cettha ākāro, ñā māraṇatosananisānesu, itthiyamati a. Arahato bhāvo arahattaṃ, bhāve tto, bhāvotra abhidhānabuddhīnaṃ pavattiyā nimittaṃ[M 0.0301], tañca duvidhaṃ byuppattipavattinimittavasena. Tatra visesehi kriyāpakatipaccayādīhi uppajjatīti byuppatti, goādisaddasarūpaṃ, tassā nimittaṃ byuppattinimittaṃ, kriyāpakatipaccayādayo, vividhaṃ vā goādisaddasarūpaṃ uppādetīti byuppatti, sā eva nimittaṃ, yathāvuttā kriyādayoyeva. Pavattayati tattha tattha atthe payojayatīti pavatti, goādiko saddo, tassa nimittaṃ pavattinimittaṃ, jātikriyāguṇadabbanāmāni. Tatra byuppattinimittaṃ saddasarūpuppattiyā kāraṇaṃ, pavattinimittaṃ pana saddappayojanassa kāraṇanti ayametesaṃ saṅkhepato lakkhaṇaviseso.

436. There are two terms for the supreme fruit. It is called aññā (final knowledge), with a short vowel, because it is known without transgressing the boundary (mariyāda) seen by the first path and so on. Or, it is aññā because it kills (māraṇato) the five higher fetters, such as attachment to form, by way of a boundary (odhivasena). Here, the ā has the meaning of 'boundary'. The root ñā is in the senses of killing, sharpening, and polishing. It is feminine, with the suffix a. The state (bhāvo) of an Arahant is arahattaṃ (Arahantship); the suffix tta is in the sense of 'state' (bhāve). Here, 'state' (bhāva) is the cause for the functioning of expression and understanding, and it is twofold: in terms of the cause of derivation (byuppattinimitta) and the cause of application (pavattinimitta). Among these, derivation (byuppatti) is what arises from specifics such as action, root, suffix, etc., for example, the form of words like 'go' (cow). Its cause is the 'cause of derivation,' which includes action, root, suffix, etc. Or, derivation (byuppatti) is that which produces various word-forms like 'go', and that very production is the cause, consisting of actions, etc., as previously described. Application (pavatti) refers to employing a word, such as 'go', for its meaning in various contexts. Its cause is the 'cause of application,' which includes categories such as genus, action, quality, substance, and proper name. Here, the 'cause of derivation' is the cause for the production of word-forms, while the 'cause of application' is the cause for the employment of the word. This, in brief, is the distinguishing characteristic between them.

Dvayaṃ cetiye. Thu abhitthave, po, dīghādi. Cita pūjāyaṃ, cetitabbaṃ pūjetabbanti, ṇyo, cetiyaṃ. Ettha ca thūpasaddo samukhepi, cetiyasaddo pana mukharahiteyeva vattati. “Cetiyamāyatane buddha-bimbe coddissapādape”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 12.7 byākhyāsudhā 2.2.7 ruddo.

There are two terms for a shrine (cetiya). From the root thu in the sense of 'praise' (abhitthave), with the suffix po, and lengthening of the vowel, etc., comes thūpa. From the root cita in the sense of 'veneration' (pūjāyaṃ), that which should be venerated (cetitabbaṃ pūjetabbaṃ) is cetiyaṃ, with the suffix ṇya. Here, the word thūpa applies also to that which has a front (samukhe), but the word cetiya applies only to that which is without a front (mukharahite). Rudda says: 'Cetiya is used for a shrine, a Buddha image, and a dedicatory tree.'

Dvayaṃ ānande. Dhammo pariyatti, sova bhaṇḍaṃ dhanaṃ sukhadāyakato, tassa agāraṃ ṭhapanaṭṭhānaṃ gehaṃ, tabbhāve tiṭṭhatīti dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko, iko. Nanda samiddhiyaṃ. Ime dve saddā samā samānatthā.

There are two terms for Ānanda. The Dhamma is the teaching (pariyatti). It is a treasure (bhaṇḍaṃ) and wealth (dhanaṃ) because it gives happiness. Its repository (agāraṃ), the place where it is stored (ṭhapanaṭṭhānaṃ), is a house (gehaṃ). One who stands in that state is a treasurer of the Dhamma (dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko), with the suffix iko. The root nanda is in the sense of 'prosperity' (samiddhiyaṃ). These two words are equivalent, having the same referent.

437. Dvayaṃ visākhāyaṃ seṭṭhidhītari. Vividhā bahukā puttanattapanattādikā sākhā yassā sā visākhā. Migārassa seṭṭhino mātuṭṭhāniyattā migāramātā.

437. There are two terms for Visākhā, the merchant’s daughter. She is called Visākhā because she has many (vividhā) and numerous (bahukā) branches (sākhā), such as sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and so on. She is called Migāramātā (Migāra's mother) because she held the position of a mother to Migāra the merchant.

Dvayaṃ anāthapiṇḍikaseṭṭhimhi. Sundaro attā yassa sudatto, sundaraṃ dattaṃ dānamassa vā sudatto, idamassa daharakāle [M 0.0302] pavattaṃ nāmaṃ. Anāthānaṃ piṇḍaṃ dadātīti anāthapiṇḍiko, idamassa kriyānāmaṃ.

There are two terms for Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant. He whose self (attā) is beautiful (sundaro) is Sudatta; or, he whose giving (dattaṃ dānaṃ) is beautiful is Sudatta. This was his name in his youth. He is called Anāthapiṇḍika because he gives (dadāti) alms (piṇḍaṃ) to the destitute (anāthānaṃ). This is his name based on his actions.

438-439. Bhikkhuādayo ete pañca sahadhammikā. Saha ekato dhammaṃ carantīti sahadhammikā.

438-439. These five, beginning with monks, are co-practitioners of the Dhamma (sahadhammikā). They are called sahadhammikā because they practice (caranti) the Dhamma together (saha ekato).

Pattādayo aṭṭha parikkhārā ukkaṭṭhavasena vuttā, majjhimavasena pana kattaradaṇḍopi telanāḷipīti dasa parikkhārā vattabbā, omakavasena chattampi upāhanāpīti dvādasa parikkhārā ca vattabbā.

The eight requisites, beginning with the bowl, are stated in the highest sense. In the intermediate sense, however, ten requisites should be stated, including a staff with a blade and an oil-tube. And in the lowest sense, twelve requisites should be stated, including an umbrella and sandals.

440. Dvayaṃ sāmaṇere. Samaṇassāpaccaṃ sāmaṇero. Samaṇaliṅgācārattā “samaṇoya”nti uddisitabboti samaṇuddeso. Disī uccāraṇe.

440. There are two terms for a novice (sāmaṇera). A sāmaṇera is the offspring (apaccaṃ) of a recluse (samaṇa). One who should be designated (uddisitabbo) as 'this is a recluse' (samaṇo yaṃ) on account of having the appearance and conduct of a recluse is a samaṇuddesa. The root disī is in the sense of 'utterance'.

Tikaṃ acelake. Disā eva ambaraṃ vatthaṃ, na pakativatthametassa digambaro, sassa go. Natthi celaṃ vatthametassa, samāsante ko. Catūhi ganthehi bandhanīyattā nigantho, nisaddo [M 0.0303] bandhane. Dvayaṃ jaṭāvati. Jaṭaṃ yassatthi jaṭilo, ilo. Jaṭaṃ dhāretīti jaṭādharo.

There are three terms for a naked ascetic (acelaka). One whose garment (ambaraṃ) is the directions (disā), who has no ordinary cloth, is a digambara; the 's' becomes 'g'. One who has no cloth (celaṃ) is an acelaka; 'ka' is at the end of the compound. One who is bound by the four knots is a nigaṇṭha; the particle ni is in the sense of 'binding'. There are two terms for one with matted hair (jaṭāvati). One who has matted hair (jaṭaṃ) is a jaṭila, with the suffix ila. One who wears (dhāreti) matted hair is a jaṭādhara.

441. Kuṭisakādikā catuttiṃsa laddhiyo parasamayānamāgamato gahetabbā, tathā dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhiyo brahmajālasuttantato. Itīti parisamāpanattho. Eteti nidassanattho. Ete channavutiladdhiyo taṇhāpāsaṃ, diṭṭhipāsañca ḍenti pavattentīti pāsaṇḍāti sampakāsitā kathitā. “Iti channavuti etā”tipi pāṭho.

441. The thirty-four doctrines (laddhiyo), such as that of the Kuṭisakas, are to be understood from the scriptures of other schools. Similarly, the sixty-two views (diṭṭhiyo) are from the Brahmajāla Sutta. 'Iti' is in the sense of 'conclusion.' 'Ete' is in the sense of 'illustration.' These ninety-six doctrines are declared and spoken of as pāsaṇḍa because they spread (ḍenti) and propagate (pavattenti) the snare of craving (taṇhāpāsaṃ) and the snare of views (diṭṭhipāsaṃ). The reading 'iti channavuti etā' (thus these ninety-six) is also found.

442. Tikaṃ sucimhi. Pu pavane, to. Dvittādi. Yata payatane, to. Dīghādi. Dvayaṃ cammani. Caritaṃ tanti cammaṃ, caratimhā mana, camu adane vā, mana. Aja gamane, yu, ino vā.

442. There are three terms for what is pure (suci). From the root pu in the sense of 'purifying' (pavane), with the suffix to, doubling, etc., comes pūta. From the root yata in the sense of 'effort' (payatane), with the suffix to, lengthening, etc., comes yāta. There are two terms for leather (camma). That which is walked upon (carīyati) is cammaṃ, from the root car with the suffix man; or from the root camu in the sense of 'eating,' with the suffix man. From the root aja in the sense of 'going' (gamane), with the suffix yu or ina, comes ajina.

Dvayaṃ dantakaṭṭhe. Dante punāti sodheti yenāti dantapono, yu. Dantapoṇopi. Dantasodhanatthaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ. Dvayaṃ rukkhattace. Vakka tace, alo. Tara taraṇe, ito, sakatthe ko.

There are two terms for a tooth-stick (dantakaṭṭha). That by which one cleanses (punāti) and purifies (sodheti) the teeth is a dantapona, from the suffix yu. Also dantapoṇa. Wood (kaṭṭhaṃ) for cleaning (sodhana) the teeth (danta) is a dantakaṭṭha. There are two terms for tree bark (rukkhattaca). From the root vakka in the sense of 'bark' (tace), with the suffix ala, comes vakkala. From the root tara in the sense of 'crossing' (taraṇe), with the suffix ita, and ka in its own sense.

443. Dvayaṃ bhājanasāmaññe. Patati yattha so patto, pata gatiyaṃ, to. Pā rakkhaṇe,ti.

443. There are two terms in the general sense of 'vessel' (bhājana). That into which things fall (patati yattha) is a patto (bowl), from the root pata in the sense of 'to go,' with the suffix to. From the root pā in the sense of 'protecting' (rakkhaṇe), with the suffix ti, comes pāti.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0304] kuṇḍikāyaṃ. Kassa jalassa maṇḍo pasannabhāvo kamaṇḍo, taṃ lātīti kamaṇḍalu, u. Kuḍi rakkhaṇe, sakatthe ko. Kattarassa jiṇṇassa ālambanayaṭṭhi.

Two terms for a water-pot. The clear and settled portion of water is 'kamaṇḍo'; that which holds it is 'kamaṇḍalu,' with the suffix 'u.' The root 'kuḍi' is in the sense of 'protecting,' with the suffix 'ko' in its own sense. The walking stick of an aged person.

444. Yaṃ “pāṇātipātā veramaṇī”tiādi brahmacariyakammaṃ niccaṃ yāvajīvamavassambhāvena, taṃ dehasādhanāpekkhaṃ sarīreneva sādhanamapekkhate, na bāhirena sādhanaṃ, ayaṃ yamo nāma, yamu uparame.

444. That practice of the holy life, such as abstaining from killing living beings and so on, which is constant, lifelong, and unfailing, is dependent on the body for its accomplishment; it expects accomplishment through the body itself, not through external means. This is called 'yama' (restraint). The root 'yamu' is in the sense of 'cessation'.

“Sarīrasādhanāpekkha-niccakammamaye yame;

Saṃyame yamarāje ca, yamake tu yamaṃ tisū”ti amara 17.38.

The word 'yama' is used in the three genders in the senses of: 'yama' which consists of constant action dependent on bodily accomplishment; 'saṃyama' (self-restraint); 'Yamarāja' (King of Death); and 'yamaka' (a twin).

Ruddo.

Thus Rudda.

Yaṃ panāgantunā sukkapakkhādivasena aniccaṃ niyamitakālamupavāsādikaṃ kammaṃ, ayaṃ niyamo, kālādivasena niyamitabboti niyamo, yamu uparame. “Mantanāyaṃ paṭiññāyaṃ, niyamo nicchaye vate”ti ruddo.

Now, whatever action, such as fasting, is undertaken by a visitor on account of the bright fortnight and so forth, which is impermanent and for a fixed time—this is 'niyama' (observance). It is 'niyama' because it is to be regulated by time and so forth. The root 'yamu' is in the sense of 'cessation.' Thus Rudda: 'Niyama' is used in the sense of counsel, promise, determination, and vow.

Brāhmaṇavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Brahmin Chapter is concluded.

445. Dvayaṃ vesse. Visa pavesane, so. Iyānapaccaye vesiyāno. Ūrujo, ariyopyatra.

445. Two terms for a Vaiśya. The root 'visa' is in the sense of 'entering,' with the suffix 'so.' With the suffix 'iyāna,' it becomes 'vesiyāno.' Also 'ūrujo' (thigh-born). 'Ariya' (noble) is also used here.

Pañcakaṃ [M 0.0305] kasiādijīvikāyaṃ. Jīva pāṇadhāraṇe, yu. Sabbatra bhāve paccayo, karaṇetyeke. Vata vattane,ti, assu, ṇvumhi jīvikā. Vuttīnaṃ sarūpappakāre dasseti. Dvayaṃ kasikamme. Kasanaṃ kasi, sā eva kammaṃ kasikammaṃ. Kasa vilekhane, i, kasi.

A pentad of terms for livelihood beginning with agriculture. The root 'jīva' is in the sense of 'sustaining life,' with the suffix 'yu.' Everywhere the suffix is in the sense of 'state,' or according to some, 'instrument.' The root 'vata' is in the sense of 'to exist'; with 'ti,' 'assu,' and with 'ṇvu,' 'jīvikā' is formed. It shows the nature and types of livelihoods. Two terms for agricultural work. Ploughing is 'kasi'; that work itself is 'kasikammaṃ.' The root 'kasa' is in the sense of 'to scratch'; with the suffix 'i,' it forms 'kasi'.

446. Dvayaṃ vāṇijje. Vaṇijānaṃ kammaṃ vāṇijjaṃ, vaṇijjā ca. Dvayaṃ pasuposane. Gunnaṃ rakkhā gorakkhā. Pasūnaṃ gomahiṃsādikānaṃ pālanaṃ posanaṃ cikicchādi pasupālanaṃ vuttaṃ sarūpaṃ, vuttappakārā ca iti vessassa vuttiyo vuttikāraṇā tisso bhavanti kasikammādippakārena.

446. Two terms for trade. The work of merchants is 'vāṇijja,' and also 'vaṇijjā.' Two terms for animal husbandry. The protection of cattle is 'gorakkhā.' The protection, nourishment, medical treatment, and so forth, of animals such as cattle and buffaloes is called 'pasupālana'; its nature and manner have been stated. Thus, the livelihoods of a Vaiśya, which are the means of subsistence, become threefold: agriculture and so forth.

Tikaṃ gihimhi. Gahe gehe, pañcakāmaguṇe vā bhavavasena tiṭṭhatīti gahaṭṭho. Agāre gehe vasatīti agāriko, gahametassatthīti gihi, assi, rasso ca.

A triad of terms for a householder. One who stands in a house, or who abides through the state of being in the five strands of sensual pleasure, is a 'gahaṭṭho.' One who lives in a house is an 'agāriko.' One who has a house is a 'gihi'; this is formed with the suffix 'assi' and shortening of the vowel.

447. Dvayaṃ kasibale. Khettenājīvati. Kasatīti kassako, ṇvu. Dvayaṃ khette. Bījāni khipantyasminti khettaṃ, khipa peraṇe, to, khittaṃ tāyatītipi khettaṃ, khi nivāsagatīsu vā, ta, traṇa, khettaṃ, khetraṃ. Kleda, klida allabhāve, lalopo, kledīyatīti kedāraṃ, ke jale sati dāro vidāraṇamassāti vā kedāraṃ, saññāsaddattā sattamiyā na lopo, vāpopyatra, vappate yasminti vāpo, ṇo.

447. Two terms for a farmer. He lives by the field. He ploughs, therefore he is a 'kassako,' with the suffix 'ṇvu.' Two terms for a field. 'Khetta' is that wherein seeds are cast; from the root 'khipa' in the sense of 'to cast,' with the suffix 'to.' Or, 'khetta' is that which protects what is cast. Alternatively, from the root 'khi' in the sense of 'dwelling' or 'going,' with the suffixes 'ta' and 'traṇa,' it becomes 'khettaṃ' or 'khetraṃ.' From the roots 'kleda' or 'klida' in the sense of 'wetness,' with the elision of 'la,' 'kedāraṃ' is that which is moistened. Or, 'kedāraṃ' is that which has a splitting when there is water. Because it is a conventional noun, there is no elision of the locative case ending. 'Vāpo' is also used here: 'vāpo' is that wherein sowing occurs, with the suffix 'ṇo'.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0306] mattikākhaṇḍe. Leḍḍa saṅghāte, u, leḍḍu. Pume utto kathito. “Leḍḍavo pume”tya amara 19.12 marakose. Dvayaṃ khaṇittiyaṃ. Khaññate yāya, sā khaṇitti, khanu avadāraṇe,ti, ṇattaṃ, ussi. Avadārīyate yena avadāraṇaṃ, dara vidāraṇe, yu.

Two terms for a clod of earth. From the root 'leḍḍa' in the sense of 'to lump together,' with the suffix 'u,' comes 'leḍḍu.' It is said to be masculine. 'Leḍḍavo is masculine' is in the Amarakośa. Two terms for a digging tool. That by which one digs is 'khaṇitti'; from the root 'khanu' in the sense of 'to split,' with the suffix 'ti,' cerebralization, and the suffix 'ussi.' That by which one splits is 'avadāraṇa'; from the root 'dara' in the sense of 'to split,' with the suffix 'yu'.

448. Tikaṃ dātte. Danti lunantyanenāti dāttaṃ, dā lavane, to. Dātrampi. Lū chedane, lavittaṃ, asu khepane. Asitaṃ, sabbatra karaṇe paccayo.

448. A triad of terms for a sickle. 'Dātta' is that by which they cut; from the root 'dā' in the sense of 'to cut,' with the suffix 'to.' Also 'dātra.' From the root 'lū' in the sense of 'to cut,' comes 'lavittaṃ.' From the root 'asu' in the sense of 'to throw,' comes 'asitaṃ.' In all cases, the suffix is in the instrumental sense.

Tikaṃ pājanadaṇḍe. Tuda byathane, ṇo, patodo. Tapaccaye tuttaṃ. Aja khepane, gatimhi ca, karaṇe yu, pājanaṃ. Vaṇṇavikāre pācanaṃ. Todanaṃpyatra.

A triad of terms for a goad-stick. From the root 'tuda' in the sense of 'to hurt,' with the suffix 'ṇo,' comes 'patodo.' With the suffix 'ta,' 'tuttaṃ' is formed. From the root 'aja' in the sense of 'to throw' and 'to go,' with the instrumental suffix 'yu,' comes 'pājanaṃ.' With a vowel change, it becomes 'pācanaṃ.' 'Todanaṃ' is also used here.

Tikaṃ rajjuyaṃ. Yuja yoge, to, yottaṃ. Rudha āvaraṇe, ju, ussattaṃ, pararūpattañca, rajju thiyaṃ. Rasa assādane, mi, ābandhopyatra.

A triad of terms for a rope. From the root 'yuja' in the sense of 'to join,' with the suffix 'to,' comes 'yottaṃ.' From the root 'rudha' in the sense of 'to obstruct,' with the suffix 'ju,' vowel raising, and assimilation, comes 'rajju,' which is feminine. From the root 'rasa' in the sense of 'to taste,' with the suffix 'mi,' comes 'rasmi.' 'Ābandha' is also used here.

Dvayaṃ phāle. Phālayati pāṭayati bhūmi yena phālo, ṇo. Kasa vilekhane, ṇvu, kasako. “Phālakasakā”ti byākhyāsudhā 2.9.13 ruddo. Nirīsaṃ, kūṭakaṃ, halampi. Īsāya niggataṃ nirīsaṃ. Kuṭa chedane, sakatthe ko, kūṭakaṃ, dīghādi. Hala vilekhane.

Two terms for a ploughshare. 'Phālo' is that by which one splits or breaks up the earth, with the suffix 'ṇo.' From the root 'kasa' in the sense of 'to scratch,' with the suffix 'ṇvu,' comes 'kasako.' 'Phālakasakā' is from Rudda. Also 'nirīsaṃ,' 'kūṭakaṃ,' and 'hala.' 'Nirīsaṃ' is that which is without a pole. From the root 'kuṭa' in the sense of 'to cut,' with the suffix 'ko' in its own sense, comes 'kūṭakaṃ,' with lengthening and so forth. The root 'hala' is in the sense of 'to scratch'.

449. Tikaṃ naṅgale. Bhūmīnaṅga’manaṅgaṃ karonto lunātīti naṅgalaṃ. Sī bandhane, ro, sīro. “Sīro tikkhakare hale”ti nānatthasaṅgahe. [M 0.0307] Godāraṇaṃpyatra. Naṅgalassa daṇḍake īsā, īsa issariye, īsā nārī. “Pabhumhi saṅkare īso, thiyaṃ naṅgaladaṇḍake”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 19.13-4 byākhyāsudhā 2.9.14 rabhaso.

449. A triad of terms for a plough. 'Naṅgala' is that which cuts, making the surface of the earth uneven. From the root 'sī' in the sense of 'to bind,' with the suffix 'ro,' comes 'sīro.' 'Sīro means a sharp-edged plough' is in the Nānatthasaṅgaha. 'Godāraṇaṃ' is also used here. The pole of the plough is 'īsā.' The root 'īsa' is in the sense of 'to rule'; 'īsā' is feminine. Thus Rabhasa: 'Īso means a lord or Śaṅkara; in the feminine, it means the plough-pole.'

Yugakīlake sammāsaddo, samanti yāya sammā, samu samane. Halapaddhati naṅgalalekhā sītā nāma. “Sītā naṅgalalekhā ca, divagaṅgā ca jānakī”ti tikaṇḍasesa 3.3.191 tikaṇḍasese. Sī saye, to, sītā nārī.

The word 'sammā' is used for a yoke-pin. 'Sammā' is that by which things are calmed; from the root 'samu' in the sense of 'to be calm.' 'Halapaddhati' (plough-path) and 'naṅgalalekhā' (plough-line) are called 'sītā' (furrow). 'Sītā means a plough-line, the celestial Gaṅgā, and Jānakī' is in the Tikaṇḍaśeṣa. From the root 'sī' in the sense of 'to lie,' with the suffix 'to,' comes 'sītā,' which is feminine.

450-451. Muggādike dhaññavisese aparannasaddo, pubbannato aparabhāge pavattaṃ annaṃ aparannaṃ, aparaṇṇañca. Sāliādike pubbannasaddo, aparannassa pubbe pavattaṃ annaṃ pubbannaṃ, pubbaṇṇañca. Pubbāparattañca nesaṃ ādikappe sambhavāsambhavavasena daṭṭhabbaṃ.

450-451. The word 'aparanna' is used for types of grain such as mung beans and so forth. 'Aparanna' is food that occurs later than 'pubbanna'; it is also spelled 'aparaṇṇa.' The word 'pubbanna' is used for grains such as rice and so forth. 'Pubbanna' is food that occurs before 'aparanna'; it is also spelled 'pubbaṇṇa.' Their being earlier and later should be understood according to their arising or non-arising in the primordial aeon.

Sālyādayo satta dhaññāni. Dhānaṃ posanaṃ, tatra sādhūni dhaññāni, yo, rasso. Kalamā rattasāli mahāsālisaṭṭhikappabhutayo sūkadhaññavisesā sālayo nāma. Saṭṭhidināni paripākamassa saṭṭhiko. Sāla silāghāyaṃ, i, sāli. Vahati, brūheti vā sattānaṃ jīvitanti vīhi, vaha pāpuṇe, brūha vuḍḍhiyañca, i, assī, pakkhe ralopo, vīhi[M 0.0308]. Koraṃ rudhiraṃ dūsatīti kudrūso, govaḍḍhano, a. Vaṇṇavipariyayo, ossu ca. Gudha parivedhane, umo. Godhumo. “Godhūmasumano milakkha, bhojanaṃ pāvaṭo yavo”ti rabhaso. Vara varaṇasambhattīsu, ṇvu, varako. Yu missane, a, yavo. Kaṅgu atisukhumasasse dhaññavisese, sobhanasīsattā kamanīyabhāvaṃ gacchatīti kaṅgu, u. “Sāmā piyaṅgu kaṅgu dve”ti ruddo. Tabbhedā tesaṃ dhaññānaṃ bhedā visesā nīvārādayo vuccante. Nīvārāni tiṇadhaññāni, ādinā sāmākādayo.

The seven grains, beginning with rice. 'Dhāna' means nourishment; good for that are 'dhaññāni,' formed with the suffix 'yo' and shortening. Kalamā, red rice, great rice, sixty-day rice, and so forth, are types of awned grain called 'sālayo.' 'Saṭṭhiko' is that which ripens in sixty days. From the root 'sāla' in the sense of 'to praise,' with the suffix 'i,' comes 'sāli.' 'Vīhi' is so called because it sustains or increases the life of beings; from the root 'vaha' in the sense of 'to carry,' or 'brūha' in the sense of 'to increase,' with the suffix 'i,' vowel change, and optional elision of 'r.' 'Kudrūso' is so called because it spoils the blood; it is also called 'govaḍḍhano'; with the suffix 'a.' With metathesis and vowel change. From the root 'gudha' in the sense of 'to wrap,' with the suffix 'umo,' comes 'godhumo' (wheat). Thus Rabhasa: 'Wheat, sumana, and barley are the food of barbarians.' From the root 'vara' in the sense of 'to choose' or 'to serve,' with the suffix 'ṇvu,' comes 'varako.' From the root 'yu' in the sense of 'to mix,' with the suffix 'a,' comes 'yavo' (barley). 'Kaṅgu' is a type of very fine grain; it is 'kaṅgu' because, having a beautiful head, it becomes desirable; with the suffix 'u.' Thus Rudda: 'Sāmā, piyaṅgu, kaṅgu are two.' Their varieties, the distinctions of these grains, such as 'nīvāra' and so forth, are mentioned. 'Nīvāra' is grass-grain; by 'and so forth' is meant 'sāmāka' and others.

Dvayaṃ kaḷāye. Caṇa dāne, ṇvu, caṇako, harimanthakepi. Kaṃ vātaṃ lātīti kaḷāyo, ḷattaṃ, kalāyampi. Dvayaṃ sāsapasāmaññe. “Sāsapo tu sarisapo, kaṭusneho ca tantubho”ti tikaṇḍaseso 2.8.3. “Pume suddhodanasute, siddhattho setasāsape”ti rabhaso. Siddhā atthā asminti siddhattho. Sāsa anusiṭṭhiyaṃ, apo. Sāsapassāpi vīhibhedattā idha gahaṇaṃ.

Two terms for pea. From the root 'caṇa' in the sense of 'to give,' with the suffix 'ṇvu,' comes 'caṇako' (chickpea); also 'harimanthaka.' 'Kaḷāyo' is so called because it takes water and wind; with retroflexion of 'l,' it is also 'kalāya.' Two terms for mustard in general. 'Sāsapo is sarisapo, kaṭusneho, and tantubho' is in the Tikaṇḍaśeṣa. Thus Rabhasa: 'In the masculine, "siddhattho" means the son of Suddhodana, and it also means white mustard.' 'Siddhattho' is that in which purposes are accomplished. From the root 'sāsa' in the sense of 'to instruct,' with the suffix 'apo.' Mustard is included here because it is also a variety of grain.

452. Dvayaṃ kaṅguyaṃ. Piyabhāvaṃ aṅgatīti piyaṅgu. Dvayaṃ atasiyaṃ. Ava rakkhaṇe, mo, avassu, dvittaṃ, ummā. Ata sātaccagamane, aso, nadādi. Khumāpyatra.

452. Two terms for millet. 'Piyaṅgu' is so called because it attains a state of being dear. Two terms for flax. From the root 'ava' in the sense of 'to protect,' with the suffix 'mo,' comes 'avassu'; with doubling, it becomes 'ummā.' From the root 'ata' in the sense of 'continuous going,' with the suffix 'aso,' from the nadādi group, comes 'atasi.' 'Khumā' is also used here.

Catukkaṃ sasse. Kiṭa gatiyaṃ, ṭho, kasito sambhūtaṃ vā kiṭṭhaṃ, kiṭṭhaṭṭhāne uppannasassañhi “kiṭṭha”nti vuccati ṭhānūpacārena, ṭho, silopo, assi. Sasa gatihiṃsāpāpuṇanesu, so. Thambo gumbo, taṃ karotīti thambakari, i. Dhaññaṃpyatra. “Dhaññaṃ vīhīsu dhaññake, dhañño puññavatīrito. Dhaññā vātāmalakīsū”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe.

A tetrad of terms for a crop. From the root 'kiṭa' in the sense of 'to go,' with the suffix 'ṭho.' Or, 'kiṭṭha' is that which is produced from ploughing. Indeed, a crop that arises in a weed-infested place is called 'kiṭṭha' by transference of epithet; with the suffix 'ṭho,' elision of 's,' and 'assi.' From the root 'sasa' in the senses of 'to go,' 'to harm,' or 'to attain,' with the suffix 'so.' 'Thambo' (stalk) or 'gumbo' (bush); that which makes it is 'thambakari,' with the suffix 'i.' 'Dhañña' is also used here. Indeed, in the Nānatthasaṅgaha it is said: ''Dhaññaṃ' is used for grain among rice plants and for coriander; 'dhañño' is said of a meritorious person; 'dhaññā' is used for wind and myrobalan.'

453. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0309] sassādīnaṃ kaṇḍamatte. Kaṇa sadde, ḍo. Nala ganthe, ṇo, nālaṃ. Nāḷipi. So eva sassādikaṇḍo nipphalo ce, palālamuccate. Pala lavanapavanesu, alo, palālopi.

453. Two terms for the stalk of grains and so forth. Kaṇḍa is from the root kaṇa in the sense of 'to sound,' with the suffix ḍo. Nāḷaṃ is from the root nala in the sense of 'to bind,' with the suffix ṇo. Nāḷi is also a form. If that very stalk of grains and so forth is fruitless, it is called palāla, straw. Palāla is from the root pala in the sense of 'to cut' and 'to winnow,' with the suffix alo; palālo is also a form.

Dvayaṃ asāre tucchadhaññe. Bhasa bhasmīkaraṇe, assu, bhusaṃ atisayepi. Thusampi. Tusa ussagge. Kena vātena iṅgatīti kaliṅgaro, lāgamo, aro ca. Dhaññānameva tace vakkale thuso, tusa tuṭṭhimhi, tassa tho, thuso pume. “Dhaññattace pumā thuso” amara 19.22 tyamarakose.

Two terms for worthless, empty grain. Bhusaṃ is from the root bhasa in the sense of 'to reduce to ashes,' with the suffix assu; it also means 'excess.' Thusa is also a synonym, from the root tusa in the sense of 'to discard.' Kaliṅgaro is so called because it moves (iṅgati) by the wind (kena vātena), with the insertion of l and the suffix aro. Thuso is the husk or bark of grains; it is from the root tusa in the sense of 'to be content,' with the suffix tha, and is masculine. As stated in the Amarakośa: “Thuso, meaning the husk of grain, is masculine.”

454. Dvayaṃ sassaroge. Setavaṇṇakaraṇavasena aṭati hiṃsatīti setaṭṭikā, sā eva setaṭṭhikā. Dvayaṃ taṇḍulakaṇe. Kaṇa nimīlane, kaṇa nimīlanasaddagatīsu vā, a, kaṇo. Kuṇḍa dāhe, sakatthe ko. Dvayaṃ dhaññamaddanabhūmiyaṃ. Khala soceyye, dhaññāni karonti maddanti asmiṃ dhaññakaraṇaṃ. Tiṇādīnaṃ, sassānañca thambo gumbo nāma, thamba vekalye, thamba paṭibandhe vā. Guha saṃvaraṇe, bo, hassa mo.

454. Two terms for grain disease. Setaṭṭikā is so called because it spreads (aṭati) and harms (hiṃsati) by causing a white color; that itself is setaṭṭhikā. Two terms for a rice grain or fragment. Kaṇo is from the root kaṇa in the sense of 'to close,' or from the root kaṇa in the sense of 'to close,' 'to sound,' or 'to go,' with the suffix a. Kuṇḍaka is from the root kuṇḍa in the sense of 'to burn,' with the suffix ko in its own sense. Two terms for a grain-threshing ground. Khala is from the root khala in the sense of 'to purify.' Dhaññakaraṇaṃ is a place where they process and thresh grains. The stem or bush of grass and so forth, and of crops, is called thambo or gumbo. Thambo is from the root thamba in the sense of 'to be unsteady,' or 'to obstruct.' Gumbo is from the root guha in the sense of 'to cover,' with the suffix bo, and the change of h to m.

455. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0310] musale. Ayo aggekoṭiyaṃ yassāti ayoggaṃ. Musa khaṇḍane, alo. Dvayaṃ suppe. Kucchitaṃ lunātyapanetīti kullo. Supa māne, a, saratyaneneti vā suppaṃ, po, assu. Papphoṭanaṃpyatra.

455. Two terms for a pestle. Ayoggaṃ is that which has iron (ayo) at its tip (aggekoṭiyaṃ). Musala is from the root musa in the sense of 'to break,' with the suffix alo. Two terms for a winnowing basket. Kullo is so called because it cuts off (lunāti) and removes (apaneti) what is bad (kucchitaṃ). Suppaṃ is from the root supa in the sense of 'to measure,' with the suffix a. Or, suppaṃ is so called because one scatters (sarati) with it, with the suffix po and a vowel change. Papphoṭana is also a term here.

Dvayaṃ uddhane. Upari dhīyate thālyādikamasminti uddhanaṃ, uddhānampi, yu. Culla hāvakaraṇe, i, īmhi cullī. Adhisayanī, antikāpyatra. Ati adi bandhane, antyate bhikkhādikamassanti antikā, ṇvu. “Santike sannidhāne ca, uddhane cāpi antikā”tyajayo.

Two terms for a hearth. Uddhanaṃ is that upon which a cooking pot and so forth is placed (upari dhīyate); uddhāna is also a form; the suffix is yu. Cullī is from the root culla in the sense of 'to cook,' with the suffix i; with the feminine suffix ī, it is cullī. Adhisayanī and antikā are also terms here. Antikā is from the root ati or adi in the sense of 'to bind.' Antikā is so called because alms-food and so forth is bound or kept (antyate) at it; the suffix is ṇvu. As stated by Ajaya: “Antikā means near, in the presence, and also a hearth.”

Kāsādiracito kaṭo yena marāvo bandhīyate. Marāvo ca vīhyagāraṃ, “kusūlo vīhyagārañca, kantaro ca marāvako”ti rabhaso. Keci marāvameva kaṭamāhu, taṃ na, “kusūlo ca marāvo ca, kilañjo ca kaṭo bhave”ti amaramālāyaṃ pādanāmapakaraṇe bhedena pāṭhā. Kila bandhane, kilanaṃ kilo, tadatthaṃ jāyatīti kilañjo, niggahītāgamo. Kaṭa gatiyaṃ, a.

Kaṭo, a mat, is woven from reeds and so forth, by which the granary, marāvo, is bound. Marāvo is also a grain-store. As stated by Rabhasa: “Kusūlo, vīhyagāra, and kantaro are synonyms for marāvako.” Some say that marāva itself is a kaṭa, but that is not so, for in the Amaramālā, in the section on names of feet, there is a distinct reading: “Kusūlo, marāvo, kilañjo, and kaṭo exist.” Kilañjo is from the root kila in the sense of 'to bind'; the act of binding is kilo, and kilañjo is so called because it arises for that purpose, with the insertion of a niggahīta. Kaṭa is from the root kaṭa in the sense of 'to go,' with the suffix a.

456. Aṭṭhakaṃ thāliyaṃ. Kāmīyatīti kumbhī, kamu icchāyaṃ, bho, assu, ī ca, kuyā pathaviyā bhavatīti vā kumbhī, kena agginā bhaṇatīti vā kumbhī, bhaṇa sadde, ṇalopo, kena [M 0.0311] jalena umbhīyati pūrīyatīti vā kumbhī, ubha ubbha umbha pūraṇe, sabbatra nadādi. Piṭha hiṃsāsaṃkilesesu, aro. Kuṇḍa dāhe. Khala soceyye, ḷattaṃ. Ukha gamane, alo, nadādi, rasso. Apaccaye ukhā. Thala ṭhāne, i, thāli, īmhi thālī. Kena agginā lapatīti kolambo, assottaṃ, niggahītāgamo, battañca, ke aggimhi olambatīti vā kolambo. Labi avasaṃsane.

456. Eight terms for a pot. Kumbhī is so called because it is desired (kāmīyati), from the root kamu in the sense of 'to desire,' with the suffixes bho, assu, and ī. Or, kumbhī is so called because it comes from the earth (kuyā). Or, kumbhī is so called because it sounds (bhaṇati) with fire, from the root bhaṇa in the sense of 'to sound,' with the elision of ṇa. Or, kumbhī is so called because it is filled (umbhīyati) with water, from the roots ubha, ubbha, and umbha in the sense of 'to fill'; in all cases, it is like the nadādi class of nouns. Piṭhara is from the root piṭha in the sense of 'to harm' and 'to defile,' with the suffix aro. Kuṇḍa is from the root kuṇḍa in the sense of 'to burn.' Khaḷa is from the root khala in the sense of 'to purify,' with l becoming ḷ. Ukhali is from the root ukha in the sense of 'to go,' with the suffix alo, is like the nadādi class, and is shortened; without a suffix, it forms ukhā. Thāli is from the root thala in the sense of 'to stand,' with the suffix i; with the feminine suffix ī, it forms thālī. Kolambo is so called because it sounds or burns (lapati) with fire, with the vowel a becoming o, the insertion of a niggahīta, and p becoming b; or, kolambo is so called because it hangs (olambati) in the fire, from the root labi in the sense of 'to hang down.'

Tikaṃ maṇike. Mana ñāṇe, i, ṇattaṃ, maṇiyeva maṇikaṃ. Bhaṇa sadde, ṇvu, araṃ sīghaṃ jaro assa arañjaro.

Three terms for a large water pot. Maṇikaṃ is from the root mana in the sense of 'to know,' with the suffix i, and n becoming ṇ; maṇikaṃ is indeed a maṇi. Bhaṇaka is from the root bhaṇa in the sense of 'to sound,' with the suffix ṇvu. Arañjaro is so called because decay (jaro) comes swiftly (araṃ sīghaṃ) to it (assa).

457. Dvipādaṃ ghaṭe. Ghaṭa calane, a, nadādimhi ghaṭī, kuṭa koṭilye. Kena jalena lasati silissatīti kalaso, lisa silesane, a, issattaṃ, kalaso tīsu. Vara vāraṇasambhattīsu, ṇvu. Kalasasahacaraṇato vārakopi tīsu. “Kalaso tu tīsū”tyamarakose amara 19.31.

457. Two couplets for a water pot. Ghaṭa is from the root ghaṭa in the sense of 'to move,' with the suffix a; in the feminine, like the nadādi class, it is ghaṭī. Kuṭa is from the root kuṭa in the sense of 'to be crooked.' Kalaso is so called because it shines (lasati) or adheres (silissati) to water (kena jalena); or from the root lisa in the sense of 'to adhere,' with the suffix a, and the vowel becoming i; kalaso is in three genders. Vāraka is from the root vara in the sense of 'to ward off' or 'to partake,' with the suffix ṇvu. Due to its association with kalasa, vāraka is also in three genders. As stated in the Amarakośa: 'Kalaso is indeed in three genders.'

Bhuñjitabbanti bhuñjanaṃ, annādi, tassa patto bhājanaṃ suvaṇṇarajatādinimmitampi kaṃso nāma.

That which is to be eaten (bhuñjitabbaṃ) is bhuñjanaṃ, food, such as rice; its bowl or vessel, even one made of gold, silver, or the like, is called kaṃsa.

“Kaṃso racchantare māne, tejasepi bhave tathā;

Pānapatte ca kaṃsye ca, sobhikkhāsu ca kittisū”. –

“Kaṃsa is used in crafting, in measure, and likewise in brilliance; and in drinking vessels, in bronze, in good alms, and in fame.”

Tyajayena vuttattā pānapattepi kaṃso. Kana dittigatikantīsu, so, kaṃso. Anitthī. Tikaṃ bhājanasāmaññe. Ama gatiyaṃ, atto, amattaṃ. Bhāja puthakammani, curādi, yu.

As stated by Ajaya, kaṃsa is also used for a drinking bowl. Kaṃso is from the root kana in the sense of 'to shine,' 'to go,' and 'to be lovely,' with the suffix so. It is not feminine. Three terms in the general sense of a vessel. Amattaṃ is from the root ama in the sense of 'to go,' with the suffix atto. Bhājanaṃ is from the root bhāja of the curādi class, in the sense of 'to divide,' with the suffix yu.

458. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0312] bhājanādīnamādhāre. Antaṃ samīpamādheyyassa upagacchatīti aṇḍupakaṃ, ntassaṇḍo, gassa ca ko. Cumba vadanasaṃyoge, aṭo, assu, sakatthe ko. Dvayaṃ sarāve, sarati vuḍḍhiṃ gacchatīti sarāvo, avo. Malla dhāraṇe. Ṇvu. Vaḍḍhamānakopyatra, vaḍḍhati vitthiṇṇī bhavatīti vaḍḍhamānako, sakatthe ko.

458. Two terms for a support for bowls and so forth. Aṇḍupakaṃ is so called because it approaches (upagacchati) the proximity (antaṃ samīpaṃ) of what is to be placed (ādheyyassa); nta becomes ṇḍa, and ga becomes ka. Cumbatakaṃ is from the root cumba in the sense of 'to join the mouth,' with the suffix aṭo, a vowel change, and the suffix ko in its own sense. Two terms for a dish or bowl. Sarāvo is so called because it goes (sarati) to growth (vuḍḍhiṃ gacchati), with the suffix avo. Mallaka is from the root malla in the sense of 'to hold,' with the suffix ṇvu. Vaḍḍhamānako is also a term here; it is so called because it grows (vaḍḍhati) and becomes wide (vitthiṇṇī bhavati), with the suffix ko in its own sense.

Dvayaṃ bhelabyañjanādighaṭṭanopayuttabhaṇḍe. Kaṭa gatiyaṃ, chu, dvittādi. Du gatiyaṃ, bo, nadādi, dabbī, rasse dabbi. Khajākāpi, khaja manthane, ako, khajākā thiyaṃ. Dvayaṃ dhaññādinilaye. Kusa silesane, ūlo. Kusa akkose, ṭho. Dvepi punnapuṃsake.

Two terms for utensils used for grinding condiments and so forth. Kaṭacchu, a ladle, is from the root kaṭa in the sense of 'to go,' with the suffix chu, doubling, and so forth. Dabbī, a spoon, is from the root du in the sense of 'to go,' with the suffix bo; it is like the nadādi class, and when shortened, is dabbi. Khajākā is also a term; it is from the root khaja in the sense of 'to churn,' with the suffix ako; khajākā is feminine. Two terms for a place for storing grain and so forth. Kusūla is from the root kusa in the sense of 'to join,' with the suffix ūlo. Kuṭṭha is from the root kusa in the sense of 'to revile,' with the suffix ṭho. Both are masculine and neuter.

459. Dvayaṃ māsādisākamatte, sā tanukaraṇe, ṇvu. Ḍaṃsa khādane, ṇvu. Salopo, siggu, haritakampi. Haritā sakatthe ko. “Pulliṅgo sākamattasmiṃ, siggu sobhañjanepi ce”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 19.34 rabhaso. Dvayaṃ addake. Āddāyaṃ jātaṃ addakaṃ, rasso. Siṅgamiva veraṃ vapu yassa tameva siṅgiveraṃ.

459. Two terms for vegetables and pulses. Sāka is from the root sā in the sense of 'to make thin,' with the suffix ṇvu. From the root ḍaṃsa in the sense of 'to bite,' with the suffix ṇvu and elision of sa, is formed siggu. Haritaka is also a term. Haritaka is from the root haritā in its own sense, with the suffix ko. As Rabhasa says, 'siggu is masculine in the sense of vegetable matter, and also for the sobhañjana tree.' Two terms for ginger. Addakaṃ is so called because it is born (jātaṃ) in moisture (āddāyaṃ), with shortening of the vowel. Siṅgiveraṃ is that which has a body (vapu) like a horn (siṅga).

Yadā sukkhaṃ, tadā mahosadhādhyaṃ, tikkharasattā mahantaṃ osadhaṃ. Suṇṭhī, nāgaraṃ, visaṃ, visabhesajjampi. Suṭhi sosane, i, suṇṭhi, īpaccaye suṇṭhī.

When it is dry, then it is called a great medicine; due to its pungent taste, it is a great medicine. Suṇṭhī, nāgaraṃ, visaṃ, and visabhesajja are synonyms. Suṇṭhi is from the root suṭhi in the sense of 'to dry,' with the suffix i; with the suffix ī, it is suṇṭhī.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0313] marīce. Mara pāṇacāge, co. Kula saṅkhyāne, ṇvu. “Marīcaṃ kolakaṃ kaṇhaṃ, usanaṃ dhammapattana”ntyamarasīho.

Two terms for pepper. Marīca is from the root mara in the sense of 'to abandon life,' with the suffix co. Kolaka is from the root kula in the sense of 'to count,' with the suffix ṇvu. As Amarasimha says: 'Marīcaṃ, kolakaṃ, kaṇhaṃ, usanaṃ, dhammapattana are synonyms.'

460. Tipādaṃ kañjike. Suvīraraṭṭhe bhavaṃ sovīraṃ. Kena jalena añjiyamabhibyattaṃ assa kañjiyaṃ. Ārānaṃ bhūmyakkajānaṃ vāresu gahitena nārena jalena jātaṃ āranāḷaṃ, “āro kkhiti sute’kkaje, nāro taṇḍulanīresū”ti hi vuttaṃ, rassa ḷo. Thusato jātamudakaṃ thusodakaṃ, thusodakato vā jātaṃ thusodakaṃ. Dhaññato vīhito jātaṃ ambilaṃ dhaññambilaṃ. Vātaṃ laṅkati hīnaṃ karotīti bilaṅko, vātassa bi, visesena laṅkatīti vā bilaṅko. Kummāso, abhisutaṃ, avantisomaṃ, kuñjalaṃ, kañjikaṃ, maṇḍo, jeṭṭhambu, khadikāpyatra.

460. A triplet of terms for sour gruel. Sovīraṃ is so called because it originates in the Suvīra country. Kañjiyaṃ is so called because it is manifested (añjiyamabhibyattaṃ) by water (kena jalena). Āranāḷaṃ is so called because it is born from water (nārena jalena) taken at turns (vāresu) from hollows (ārānaṃ) or crevices in the earth (bhūmyakkajānaṃ). For it is said: 'āro means a hole in the earth or a crevice; nāro means rice-water'; with ra becoming ḷa. Thusodakaṃ is water born from husks, or that which is born from husk-water. Dhaññambilaṃ is a sour liquid (ambilaṃ) born from grain or paddy. Bilaṅko is so called because it diminishes (laṅkati) or makes inferior (hīnaṃ karoti) the wind element (vātaṃ), with bi as a substitute for vāta; or, bilaṅko is so called because it especially diminishes (visesena laṅkati). Kummāso, abhisutaṃ, avantisomaṃ, kuñjalaṃ, kañjikaṃ, maṇḍo, jeṭṭhambu, and khadikā are also terms here.

Dvayaṃ lavaṇamatte. Lū chedane, yu, ossā’navādese loṇaṃ.

Two terms for salt. Loṇaṃ is from the root lū in the sense of 'to cut,' with the suffix yu; the form is according to the grammatical rule 'ossā’navādese'.

461. Sāmuddādayo ete pañca lavaṇassa pabhedā visesā. Samuddabhūmiyamavaṭṭhitaṃ laddhaṃ loṇodakaṃ sukkhasantanaṃ sitaṃ yaṃ bhavati, taṃ sāmuddalavaṇaṃ. Akkhivaṃ, vasirampi. Vasu thambhe, iro. Sindhudese bhavo sindhavo, ṇo. Sitasivaṃ sītasivaṃ (sakkate), māṇimanthaṃ, sindhujampi. Sitaṃ dhavalaṃ, sivaṃ kalyāṇaṃ, kammadhārayasamāso[M 0.0314]. Sitasivanti vā bandhanaṃ. Maṇimantho pabbato, tatra bhavo, ṇo. Kāḷaloṇo nāma sovaccalavaṇānaṃ majjhe kāḷavaṇṇaṃ lavaṇaṃ tīṇi madhuralavaṇassalavaṇabhedassa (amarakosa, mahesvaraṭīkā), “tilakaṃ tatra mecake”ti madaṃ sandate pisodarādi (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 19.43) madaṃ mudaṃ vā sandate… visodarādi (byākhyāsudhāṭīkā) vuttattā tilakampi. Ubbhidaṃ nāma romakalavaṇaṃ, sambharidese kira rumā nāma lavaṇākaro. Tatra paviṭṭhaṃ kaṭṭhampi acirena vilīya lavaṇaṃ bhavati, tabbhavaṃ romalavaṇaṃ. Vasukampi. Kaṭṭhādīnaṃ sayaṃ sabhāvavijahanakarattā bhindituṃ sakkotīti ubbhidaṃ, sakyatthe usaddo. Bilālaṃ nāma samuddatīrāsannadesabhavaṃ mattikaṃ pācayitvā nipphāditalavaṇaṃ. Samuddavelāsannadese jātaṃ bilālaṃ, essittaṃ, lo, atha vā ubbhidaṃ nāma yattha katthaci padese bhūmito uggataṃ lavaṇamattikaṃ pācayitvā nipphāditalavaṇaṃ. Bilālaṃ nāma lavaṇabhūmiṃ vidārayitvā nipphāditalavaṇaṃ. Vipubbo dala vidāraṇe. Dassa lo. Atha vā ubbhidaṃ nāma pākyaṃ lavaṇaṃ. Bilālaṃ nāma vaccagandhaṃ kāḷalavaṇaṃ.

461. These five, sea salt and others, are the distinctions and varieties of salt. That which is obtained from seawater settled on the ground, dried, and whitened, is 'sāmuddalavaṇa'. Also 'akkhivaṃ' and 'vasiraṃ'. The root 'vasu' is in the sense of a pillar; 'iro' is the suffix. That which is from the Sindhu region is 'sindhavo'; 'ṇo' is the suffix. Also 'sitasivaṃ', 'māṇimanthaṃ', and 'sindhujaṃ'. 'Sitaṃ' means white, 'sivaṃ' means auspicious; it is a determinative compound. Alternatively, 'sitasiva' means binding. 'Maṇimantha' is a mountain; that which is from there is formed with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Kāḷaloṇa' is a black-colored salt among the 'sovaccalavaṇa' salts; it is also called 'tilaka' because it is said, 'there is a black spot there'. 'Ubbhidaṃ' is 'romakalavaṇa'; in the Sambhara region, there is said to be a salt mine called Rumā. There, even wood that has entered quickly dissolves and becomes salt; that which is from there is 'romalavaṇa'. Also 'vasukaṃ'. Because it can break the natural state of wood and other things, it is called 'ubbhidam'; the prefix 'u' is in the sense of capability. 'Bilālaṃ' is salt produced by baking clay found in a region near the seashore. 'Bilālaṃ' is that which is produced near the sea coast; with the vowel change 'e' and the suffix 'lo'. Alternatively, 'ubbhidam' is salt produced by baking salty clay that has risen from the ground in any place whatsoever. 'Bilālaṃ' is salt produced by splitting salty ground. From the root 'dala' (to split) with the prefix 'vi'; 'da' becomes 'lo'. Alternatively, 'ubbhidam' is cooked salt. 'Bilālaṃ' is black salt with a smell like feces.

462. Guḷādayo pañca ucchuno vikārā. Guḷa rakkhāyaṃ, guḷo pakkaraso. Phāṇa gatiyaṃ, to, phāṇitaṃ guḷato kiñci thaddhaṃ. Khaṇḍa manthe, khaṇḍo phāṇitatopi thaddho. Ucchuvisesassa rasapāke khaṇḍayogyasārabhūte yā guḷikākārā jāyate, sā macchaṇḍī khaṇḍasālūkaṃ. “Macchaṇḍī tu [M 0.0315] pupphaguḷā, thaddhapattantu phāṇita”nti rabhaso, khaṇḍakakkaṃ phāṇitamiccaññe. Sara hiṃsāyaṃ, kharapaccayo, sakkharā, yā “sitā”tipi vuccati, sinoti bandhati taṇhaṃ sitā. Sitasakkharetyatra tu sito dhavalattho, sakkharāpamāṇasaṇṭhānattā vā sakkharā. Ime ca guḷādayo yathākkamaṃ thaddhatarā. Ettha ca macchaṇḍī phāṇitā khaṇḍavikārāpi. Dvayaṃ guḷe. Rogādhikesu vināsakarattā visañca taṃ kaṇṭakañca.

462. These five, jaggery and others, are derivatives of sugarcane. The root 'guḷa' is in the sense of preserving; 'guḷo' is ripened juice. The root 'phāṇa' is in the sense of motion, with the suffix 'to'; 'phāṇitaṃ' is somewhat harder than jaggery. The root 'khaṇḍa' is in the sense of churning; 'khaṇḍo' is harder than 'phāṇita'. When the juice of a special sugarcane is boiled, that which is produced in the form of a lump with an essence suitable for candy is 'macchaṇḍī' or 'khaṇḍasālūkaṃ'. As Rabhasa says, 'macchaṇḍī is a flower-lump, and phāṇita is a hardened leaf'; others say 'khaṇḍakakkaṃ' is 'phāṇita'. The root 'sara' is in the sense of harming, with the suffix 'khara', forming 'sakkharā', which is also called 'sitā'; 'sitā' binds craving. Here, in 'sitasakkhara', however, 'sita' has the meaning of white; or it is 'sakkharā' because of its granular form and measure. And these, jaggery and others, are progressively harder. Here, 'macchaṇḍī' and 'phāṇita' are also derivatives of 'khaṇḍa'. Two terms for jaggery: because it causes destruction in excessive diseases, it is both poison and a thorn.

463. Dvayaṃ bhaṭṭhadhaññe. Lāja bhassane, bhassanaṃ bhajjanaṃ, a. Na khataṃ akkhataṃ. “Tatiyā pakati lājesvakkhataṃ tīsva’hiṃsite”ti ruddo.

463. Two terms for parched grain. The root 'lāja' is in the sense of parching; 'bhassanaṃ' means 'bhajjanaṃ' (roasting); the suffix is 'a'. Not injured is 'akkhataṃ'. As Rudda says: 'The third word, akkhata, is used for parched grains (lājesu) and for that which is uninjured (ahiṃsite) in the three genders.'

Bhaṭṭhayave dhānāsaddo siyā, “bahumhi bhaṭṭhayave dhānā, thiyaṃ abhinavo’bbhide”ti rabhaso. Dhā dhāraṇe, yu.

For parched barley, the word 'dhānā' may be used; as Rabhasa says: 'Dhānā is used for much parched barley, and, in the feminine gender, for a new sprout.' The root 'dhā' is in the sense of holding; the suffix is 'yu'.

Dvayaṃ yavādicuṇṇe. Saca samavāye, saca secane vā, tu. Mantha viloḷane. Tikaṃ samaṃ. Pūretīti pūpo, po. Akārayutte apūpo, yathā “lābu, alābū”ti. Taṇḍulādīnaṃ piṭṭhānaṃ vikāro piṭṭhako, saññāyaṃ ko.

Two terms for flour of barley and other grains. From the root 'saca' (to combine), or 'saca' (to moisten), with the suffix 'tu'. From the root 'mantha' (to churn). Three terms are equivalent. Because it fills (pūreti), it is called 'pūpo'; the suffix is 'po'. When joined with the letter 'a', it is 'apūpo', just as 'lābu' and 'alābū'. A derivative of the flour of rice and other grains is 'piṭṭhako'; 'ko' is a suffix used for a designation.

464. Chakkaṃ sūde. Bhattaṃ, sūpañca karoti akāsi karissatīti bhattakāro, sūpakāro ca. Su paggharaṇe. Savati rasaṃ paggharāpetīti sūdo, do, dīghādi. Sūda paggharaṇe [M 0.0316] vā, a. Aḷāro nāma sūpādivikati, taṃ karotīti āḷāriko. Odanaṃ pacatīti odaniko. Rasaṃ karotīti rasako.

464. Six terms for a cook. One who makes, made, or will make cooked rice and soup is a 'bhattakāra' and 'sūpakāra'. The root 'su' is in the sense of flowing. Because one causes the essence to flow, one is a 'sūda'; the suffix is 'do', with lengthening and so forth. Alternatively, from the root 'sūda' (to flow), with the suffix 'a'. 'Aḷāro' is a preparation such as soup; one who makes that is an 'āḷāriko'. One who cooks boiled rice is an 'odaniko'. One who makes sauces is a 'rasako'.

Dvayaṃ sūpe. Sukhatthāya pātabbattā sūpo, dīghādi. Visesato bhattaṃ añjati anto gacchati yena, taṃ byañjanaṃ, añja gatiyaṃ, yu.

Two terms for soup or curry. Because it is to be drunk for comfort, it is called 'sūpo'; with lengthening and so forth. That by which rice especially goes inside is 'byañjanaṃ'; from the root 'añja' (to go), with the suffix 'yu'.

465. Pañcakaṃ tipādaṃ (ka.) bhatte. Udi savanakledanesu, yu. Vākāro odanasaddassa napuṃsakattaṃ samuccinoti. Kura sadde, kara karaṇe vā, karoti balanti kuraṃ, assu, kira vikkhipane vā, kirati bubhukkhanti kuraṃ, issu, kara hiṃsāyaṃ vā, ku sadde vā, rapaccayo. Bhajati yena, bhuñjitabbanti vā bhattaṃ, bhaja sevāyaṃ, to. Bhakkhitabbāti bhikkhā, bhakkha adane, assi, bhikkha yācane vā, bhikkhā nārī. Ada bhakkhane, to. Bhidādittā annādeso, dalopo.

465. Five terms for cooked rice. From the root 'udi' (to flow, to be moist), with the suffix 'yu'. The particle 'va' indicates the neuter gender of the word 'odana'. From the root 'kura' (to make a sound); or from 'kara' (to make), meaning 'it makes strength', with the suffix 'assu'; or from 'kira' (to scatter), meaning 'it scatters hunger', with the suffix 'issu'; or from 'kara' (to harm); or from 'ku' (to make a sound), with the suffix 'ra'. That by which one partakes, or that which is to be eaten, is 'bhattaṃ'; from the root 'bhaja' (to serve), with the suffix 'to'. That which is to be eaten is 'bhikkhā'; from the root 'bhakkha' (to eat), with the suffix 'assi'; or from 'bhikkha' (to beg); 'bhikkhā' is feminine. From the root 'ada' (to eat), with the suffix 'to'; 'anna' is the substitute form due to the 'bhidādi' class, with elision of 'da'.

Catukkaṃ bhojane, asa bhakkhane, kamme yu. Hara haraṇe. Āharati balāyūnīti āhāro, ṇo. Bhujadhātumhā yu, bhojanaṃ. Ghasa adane, ṇo. Andhopyatra, adadhātumhā tapaccayassa andhādeso nipātanā.

Four terms for food. From the root 'asa' (to consume), in the objective sense, with the suffix 'yu'. From the root 'hara' (to carry). That which brings strength and vitality is 'āhāro', with the suffix 'ṇo'. From the root 'bhuj', with the suffix 'yu', comes 'bhojanaṃ'. From the root 'ghasa' (to eat), with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Andha' is also used here; from the root 'ada', the suffix 'ta' becomes 'andha' by irregular formation.

Dvayaṃ yāguyaṃ. Tara plavanataraṇesu. Tarati plavati byāpībhavatīti taraṇaṃ, yu. Taralaṃ, taralāpi. Yā pāpuṇe, gu, yu missane vā, gu, ussā. Uṇhikā, sāṇā, vilepī ca yāgunāmāni. Sā pāke, yu, sāṇā.

Two terms for gruel. The root 'tara' is in the sense of floating and crossing. That which crosses, floats, or pervades is 'taraṇaṃ', with the suffix 'yu'. Also 'taralaṃ' and 'taralā'. From the root 'yā' (to reach), with the suffix 'gu'; or from 'yu' (to mix), with the suffix 'gu'. Also 'ussā'. 'Uṇhikā', 'sāṇā', and 'vilepī' are also names for gruel. From the root 'sā' (to cook), with the suffix 'yu', comes 'sāṇā'.

466. Khajjādayo [M 0.0317] cattāro asanabhedā. Khāda bhakkhane, kamme to, bhujādi. Khajjaṃ maṃsādi. Bhojjaṃ annādi. Liha assādane, ṇyo, hassa yo. Leyyaṃ madhvādi. Pātabbanti peyyaṃ, pā pāne, ṇyo, āsse, peyyaṃ sūpādi.

466. 'Khajja' and so forth are the four kinds of food. From the root 'khāda' (to eat), in the objective sense, with the suffix 'to', as in the 'bhujādi' class. 'Khajjaṃ' refers to meat and other hard foods. 'Bhojjaṃ' refers to cooked rice and other soft foods. From the root 'liha' (to taste), with the suffix 'ṇyo', and 'ha' becomes 'ya'. 'Leyyaṃ' refers to honey and other lickable foods. That which is to be drunk is 'peyyaṃ'; from the root 'pā' (to drink), with the suffix 'ṇyo', and 'ā' becomes 'e'. 'Peyyaṃ' refers to soup and other drinkable foods.

Dvayaṃ bhattamaṇḍe. Su savane, visarujapadādito ṇa. Camu adane, āpubbattā pāne, kamme ṇo. Māsaropyatra, masi parimāṇe, aro. Dvayaṃ ālope. Lupa chedane, āpubbo sampiṇḍane, ku sadde. Kabi vaṇṇe vā, alo, ḷattaṃ, kena toyena balamassāti vā kabaḷo, pume, gāsopi.

Two terms for rice-scum. From the root 'su' (to flow), with the suffix 'ṇa', according to the rule for 'visaruja' and other words. From the root 'camu' (to eat); when prefixed with 'ā', it means to drink; in the objective sense, with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Māsara' is also used here; from the root 'masi' (to measure), with the suffix 'aro'. Two terms for a morsel. From the root 'lupa' (to cut); when prefixed with 'ā', it means to gather into a ball. From the root 'ku' (to make a sound), or 'kabi' (to color), with the suffix 'alo', and the change of 'l' to 'ḷ'. Alternatively, 'kabaḷo' means that by which strength is gained through water ('kena toyena balam'); it is masculine. Also 'gāso'.

467. Rasānaṃ sabbarasānaṃ aggamhi rase maṇḍasaddo, maṇḍa bhūsāyaṃ, “sabbarasagge maṇḍamanitthiya”ntyamarasīho amara 19.49. Dvayaṃ bhuttato sese. Virūpo, kucchito vā ghāso vighāso. Bhuttato seso bhuttaseso, sova bhuttasesako, sakatthe ko.

467. Among all flavors, the word 'maṇḍa' refers to the best flavor; the root 'maṇḍa' is in the sense of adorning. As Amarasīha says: 'Maṇḍa is the best of all flavors, and is not feminine.' Two terms for what remains after eating. Deformed or contemptible food is 'vighāso'. What remains after eating is 'bhuttaseso'; this is also 'bhuttasesako', with 'ka' used in a reflexive sense.

Dvayaṃ vighāsāde. Vighāsaṃ adatīti, a, damu damane, ṇvu. Dvayaṃ pipāsāyaṃ. Pātuṃ icchā pipāsā, pā pāne, so, dvittādi. Tasa pipāsāyaṃ, yu.

Two terms for one who eats leftovers. 'Vighāsāda' is one who eats leftovers ('vighāsaṃ adati'), from the root 'ada' with the suffix 'a'. The second term is derived from the root 'damu' (to tame), with the suffix 'ṇvu'. Two terms for thirst. The desire to drink ('pātuṃ icchā') is 'pipāsā', from the root 'pā' (to drink), with the suffix 'so', reduplication, and so forth. From the root 'tasa' (to be thirsty), with the suffix 'yu'.

468. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0318] bhuttumicchāyaṃ. Khuda bubhukkhāyaṃ, do. Ghasitumicchā jighacchā, ghasa adane, icchatthe cho, dvittādi. Maṃsassa raso paṭicchādanīyamuccate. Chanda icchāyaṃ. Paṭicchādetīti paṭicchādanīyaṃ, anīyo, chada saṃvaraṇe vā, maṃsena paṭicchādetabbattā paṭicchādanīyaṃ.

468. Two terms for the desire to eat. From the root 'khuda' (to be hungry), with the suffix 'do'. The wish to devour ('ghasitum icchā') is 'jighacchā', from the root 'ghasa' (to eat), with 'cha' in the sense of desire, reduplication, and so forth. A meat preparation is called 'paṭicchādanīya'. It is so called because it is desirable, from 'chanda' (desire). Alternatively, because it covers ('paṭicchādeti'), from the root 'chada' (to cover), with the suffix 'anīya'. Or, because it is to be covered with meat, it is 'paṭicchādanīya'.

Dvayaṃ uggāre, deki saddossāhesu, uddhaṃ dekati gantumussahatīti udreko, ekassa dakārassa ro. Uddekopi. Gira niggiraṇe, issā, uggāro. Pādo tittiyaṃ. Suhito titto, tassa bhāvo sohiccaṃ. Tipi pīṇane,ti, bhujādi. Yupaccaye, issatte ca tappanaṃ.

Two terms for belching. From the root 'deki' (to sound, to strive); 'udreko' is that which strives to go upwards, with 'ro' substituted for one 'da'. Also 'uddeko'. From the root 'gira' (to swallow), with the suffix 'issā', comes 'uggāro'. Three terms for satisfaction. 'Suhito' means well-fed, content; the state of that is 'sohiccaṃ'. From the root 'tipi' (to satisfy), with the suffix 'ti', as in the 'bhujādi' class. With the suffix 'yu', and in the sense of 'issatta', comes 'tappanaṃ'.

469. Yathicchitantaṃ yathicchite. Kriyāvisesanatāya cete napuṃsake, kriyābyayānañhi satipyekatte tabbisesanāni napuṃsake bhavanti ekattepi, tathā hi kriyānamabyayānañca sattābhūtattā liṅgasaṅkhyāvisesopādānaṃ natthīti tabbisesanānampi sāmaññaliṅgā napuṃsakattaṃ, sāmaññasaṅkhyā cekattaṃ yuttanti, taṃ yathā – muduṃ pacanti, sāduṃ pacanti. Bahuvacanantepi kriyāsadde tabbisesanassekattameva kriyāvisesanānaṃ kammani dutiyā, sabbo hi dhātvattho karotyatthena byāpito, muduṃ pacanti muduṃ pacanaṃ kubbantītyattho, tena mudādīnañca tabbisesanānaṃ kammattaṃ. Añño panāha [M 0.0319] “sabbe dhātvatthā bhavatyatthānugatā, bhavatikriyā katvatthamanubhavantītyattho. ‘Pacati devadatto’ti devadattapayutto pāko bhavati, gacchati gamanaṃ bhavati, paṭhati pāṭho bhavatī”ti, tammatena paṭhamā, mudupacanaṃ yathā bhavati, tathā pacatītyattho. Ramaṇīyaṃ pāto, vimalaṃ pāto, idamupakumbhaṃ. Kamu kantiyaṃ, kammani ṇo, kāmaṃ, nikāmañca. Isu icchāyaṃ, to, “sādisantapucche”tyādinā antena saha tassa ṭṭho, iṭṭhaṃ. Paripubbo āpa pāpuṇane, to, bhujādi, rasso, yāgamo ca. “Sattyaṃ nivāraṇe tittiyaṃ, pariyattaṃ yathicchite”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 19.57 rabhaso. Icchitassa anatikkamo yathicchitaṃ, yathātthe abyayībhāvo. Pakāmaṃpyatra.

469. The word `yathicchitaṃ` is used in the sense of 'as desired'. These are in the neuter gender due to being adverbs of action. For even when actions and indeclinables are singular, their qualifiers become neuter, even in the singular. Thus, because actions and indeclinables are not substances, there is no specific assignment of gender or number; therefore, their qualifiers also take the common neuter gender, and a common singular number is appropriate. For example: 'they cook softly', 'they cook deliciously'. Even when the word for action is plural, its qualifier is singular. For adverbs of action, the accusative case is used in the sense of object. Indeed, the entire meaning of the verbal root is pervaded by the sense of 'doing'. 'They cook softly' means 'they perform a soft cooking'. Therefore, 'soft' and so forth, being their qualifiers, are objects. Another, however, says: 'All verbal root meanings are accompanied by the sense of 'being'; the action of 'being' partakes of the meaning of the agent.' For example, 'Devadatta cooks' means 'cooking connected with Devadatta occurs'; 'he goes' means 'going occurs'; 'he recites' means 'recitation occurs.' According to this view, the nominative case is used. The meaning is: 'he cooks in such a way that the cooking is soft.' A pleasant morning, a clear morning, this is near the pot. From the root `kamu` in the sense of desiring, in the sense of action, with the suffix `ṇo`, `kāmaṃ` and `nikāmañca` are formed. From the root `isu` in the sense of desiring, with the suffix `ta`; by the rule beginning `sādisantapucche`, `ṭṭha` replaces the final `s` along with the `t` suffix, forming `iṭṭhaṃ`. From the root `āpa` 'to reach', preceded by `pari`, with the suffix `ta`, like `bhuj` etc., with shortening of the vowel and the augment `y`. '`Sattyaṃ` is in the sense of preventing, `tittiyaṃ` in satisfaction, `pariyattaṃ` in the sense of 'as desired',' says Rabhasa. The non-transgression of what is desired is `yathicchitaṃ`; in the sense of `yathā`, it is an indeclinable compound. Also `pakāmaṃ` here.

Dvipādaṃ vaṇijake. Kayavikkayehi jīvatīti, iko. Satthaṃ vāṇijjopajīvīnaṃ saṅghātaṃ vahati desantaraṃ pāpayatīti, kammādimhi ṇo. Satthavāho vaṇijanāyako, taṃyogā satthavāho, ṇo. Āpaṇo kayavikkayavohāro, taṃyogā āpaṇiko, ṇiko. Vaṇa sadde, ijo. Vedahako, negamo, paṇyājīvo, vaṇijopyatra.

Two terms for a merchant. One who lives by buying and selling is a `vaṇijaka`, with the suffix `ika`. One who leads a caravan (`sattha`), which is a group of those who live by trade, and makes them reach another country, is a `satthavāha`, with the suffix `ṇa` in the sense of agent and so forth. A `satthavāha` is a leader of merchants; due to that connection, `satthavāha` is formed, with the suffix `ṇa`. An `āpaṇa` is the business of buying and selling; due to connection with that, `āpaṇika` is formed, with the suffix `ṇika`. From the root `vaṇa` 'to trade', with the suffix `ija`, `vaṇija` is formed. `Vedahako`, `negamo`, `paṇyājīvo`, and `vaṇijo` are also here.

470. Vikkayo nāma pubbameva attano dhanassa parassa dānaṃ. Kī dabbavinimaye, tatra niyutto vikkayiko. Vikkiṇātīti vikketā, ritu. Kayo nāma parassa dhanaṃ gahetvā attano dhanassa dānaṃ. Kayena jīvatīti kayiko. Kinātīti, ṇvu.

470. Selling, indeed, is the giving of one's own wealth to another beforehand. From the root `kī` in the sense of exchanging goods; one engaged therein is a `vikkayika`. One who sells is a `vikketā`, with the suffix `ritu`. Buying, indeed, is the taking of another's wealth and the giving of one's own wealth. One who lives by buying is a `kayika`. One who buys is a `kāyaka`, from the suffix `ṇvu`.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0320] dhanappayottari. Iṇe uttamo uttamaṇṇo, abhidhānā pubbanipāto, issattaṃ, dvittañca. Dhanaṃ vuḍḍhatthaṃ payojetīti dhaniko. Dvayaṃ dhanagāhake. Iṇe adhamo adhamaṇṇo. Iṇaṃ gaṇhātīti iṇāyiko, āyiko. Iṇaṃ āyati pavattetīti vā iṇāyako, ṇvu.

Two terms for a lender of money. In debt, the superior one is an `uttamaṇṇa`; by convention, there is fronting of the first member of the compound, the change of `u` to `i`, and doubling. One who employs money for the purpose of increase is a `dhanika`. Two terms for a taker of money. In debt, the inferior one is an `adhamaṇṇa`. One who takes a debt is an `iṇāyika`, with the suffix `āyika`. Or, one who causes a debt to proceed into the future is an `iṇāyaka`, with the suffix `ṇvu`.

471-472. Dvayaṃ iṇe. Uddharīyate gayhateti uddhāro, upubbo dharati gahaṇe, ṇo. Eti vuḍḍhiṃ gacchatīti iṇaṃ, yu, ṇattaṃ. Pariyudañcanampi, parito udañjhate gayhateti, yu. Vuttanti kriyāpadaṃ. Yattakena dhanena lābho labbhate, tatra mūladhane mūlādidvayaṃ. Mūla patiṭṭhāyaṃ. Paṭhamameva ābhataṃ pābhataṃ.

471-472. Two terms for debt. That which is taken up or taken is an `uddhāra`; from the root `dharati` preceded by `ud`, in the sense of taking, with the suffix `ṇa`. That which goes to increase is `iṇaṃ`, with the suffix `yu`, and nasalization. Also `pariyudañcanaṃ`; that which is drawn up or taken from all sides, with the suffix `yu`. This has been said. The two terms `mūla` etc. refer to the principal capital, that money by which profit is obtained. The root `mūla` is in the sense of foundation. What is brought first is `pābhataṃ`.

Dvayaṃ paṭipāde. “Avassamassidaṃ kayitabba”miti saccassākhyāpanaṃ, karaṇaṃ vā saccāpanaṃ, saccassa karañcittabharaṇamiccattho, saccasaddā dhāturūpā yu, majjhe apāgamo, saccassa vā āpuṇanaṃ saccāpanaṃ, apadhātumhā yu. “Saccāpanā saccākati”riti tikaṇḍasese thīkaṇḍe (?) vopālito. Saccaṃ karoti, saccassa vā karaṇaṃ saccakāro. Saccaṃkāropi. “Klive saccāpanaṃ sacca-ṅkāro saccākatitthiya”ntyamarakose amara 19.82. Dvayaṃ vikkanīyadabbe. Vikkinitabbanti vikkeyyaṃ, ṇyo. Paṇa byavahāre, ṇyo, dvepi tīsu.

Two terms for an earnest payment. `Saccāpanaṃ` is the declaration of truth that 'this must certainly be bought', or the making of a truth; the meaning is the fulfillment of the intention to make it true. It is formed from the word `sacca` in a root-like form, with the suffix `yu`, and the augment `āpa` in the middle. Or `saccāpanaṃ` is the attaining of truth, from the root `āpa` with the suffix `yu`. '`Saccāpanā` and `saccākati`' are mentioned in the Tikaṇḍasesa by Vopālita. One who makes a truth, or the making of a truth, is `saccakāra`. Also `saccaṃkāra`. '`Saccāpanaṃ`, `saccaṅkāra`, and `saccākati` are neuter,' according to the Amarakośa. Two terms for merchandise. What is to be sold is `vikkeyyaṃ`, with the suffix `ṇya`. From the root `paṇa` 'to trade', with the suffix `ṇya`, `paṇya` is formed; both terms are in the three genders.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0321] nyāsassappane nyāsampanne (ka.). Nyāsassa appanaṃ sampannaṃ (ka.) paṭidānaṃ. Patipubbo dadāti nyāsasampannattho, tathā paripubbo vattati. Paridānaṃpyatra.

Two terms for the return of a deposit. The giving back of a deposit is `paṭidānaṃ`. The root `dadāti` preceded by `pati` has the meaning of handing over a deposit; similarly when preceded by `pari`. Also `paridānaṃ` here.

Dvayaṃ nyāse. Asu khepane. Nyassate nikkhipīyateti, ṇo. Upanidhiyyateti upanidhi, i, upanidhi pume. “Pume upanidhinyāso”ti amara 19.81 amarakose.

Two terms for a deposit. From the root `asu` 'to throw'. That which is thrown down or deposited is `nyāsa`, with the suffix `ṇa`. That which is deposited near is `upanidhi`, with the suffix `i`; `upanidhi` is masculine. '`Upanidhi` and `nyāsa` are masculine,' according to the Amarakośa.

473. Ekādayo aṭṭhārasapariyantā saṅkhyāsaddā saṅkhyeyye dabbe vattanti tīsu ca liṅgesu. Saṅkhyeyyekatte ca “eko brāhmaṇo, aṭṭhārasa brāhmaṇā”ti samānādhikaraṇaṃ bhavati, na tu bhinnādhikaraṇaṃ “brāhmaṇānaṃ ekādasa ce”ti. Tīsūtyanena “na kevalaṃ ekasaddova saliṅgo, atha kho aṭṭhārasapariyantāpī”ti dasseti, tena katthaci tesaṃ aliṅgatāvacanaṃ liṅgavisesābhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ, na pana sāmaññaliṅgābhāvanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Iminā nayena “atiliṅgaṃ dvivacanaṃ, tadākhyātanti vuccatī”tyādīsupi daṭṭhabbaṃ, tena “puriso gacchati, itthī gacchati, cittaṃ gacchatī”tyādīsu gacchatisaddassa taṃtaṃliṅgavisesavacanatā, “gacchatī”tyādīsu sāmaññaliṅgavacanatā ca daṭṭhabbā. Vīsatyādayo saṅkhyāsaddā saṅkhyāne, saṅkhyeyye ca vattanti “vīsati gāvo, gavaṃ vīsatī”ti. Ekatteti yadā panetā saṅkhyeyye ekattavisiṭṭhameva vaggattaṃ sabhāvato paṭipādayanti. Tadā bhinnasaṅkhyenāpi samānādhikaraṇe ekavacaneyeva sabbakālaṃ vattate “vīsati gāvo”ti. Yadyekatte, kathaṃ? Dvevīsatiyo, tisso vīsatiyo, pañcasatāniccādayo payogā iccāha “vaggabhede bahuttepī”ti[M 0.0322]. Vīsatyādīnaṃ vaggānaṃ bhede vattumicchite sati bahuttepi bahuvacanepi bhavanti. Amarakose pana “saṅkhyantarassatthe abhidheyyevīsatyādayo taṃsamānādhikaraṇato bahuvacanānipi bhavantī”ti amara 19.83-4 vuttaṃ, saṅkhyantaramiha vaggabhedo, tena dvinnampi vohāramattanānattaṃ, na atthanānattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ānavuti navutisaddamabhibyāpetvā tā vīsatyādayo bhinnaliṅgenāpi samānādhikaraṇe nāriyaṃ itthiyaṃ, yathā vīsati kuṇḍāni. Vīsatyādayo vikatasamāhāradvandā. Liṅgassa lokāsayattā dvandekattanti napuṃsakattanti vīsatyādayo abyuppannā paramatena, kaccāyanamatena pana byuppannā.

473. The numerals from one up to eighteen are used for countable things and in the three genders. When the countable is one, there is agreement, as in 'one brahmin, eighteen brahmins', but not non-agreement, as in 'eleven of the brahmins'. By 'in the three genders', it is shown that 'not only the word 'one' has gender, but also those up to eighteen'. Therefore, when their genderlessness is mentioned somewhere, it should be understood that this is said with reference to the absence of a specific gender, not the absence of a common gender. In this way, it should also be understood in cases like 'the dual is beyond gender, and so is the verb that expresses it'. Therefore, in 'a man goes, a woman goes, the mind goes', the word `gacchati` expresses the specific gender of each, whereas in `gacchati` etc. by itself, it expresses the common gender. The numerals from twenty onwards are used for the number and for the numbered, as in 'twenty cows' and 'a twenty of cows'. Regarding the singular: when these numerals, by their nature, express the quality of being a group characterized by singularity, then they are always in the singular, even when in agreement with a noun of a different number, as in 'twenty cows'. If they are in the singular, how are usages like 'two twenties, three twenties, five hundreds' etc. explained? He says: 'even in the plural when there is a division of groups'. When it is desired to express a division of the groups of twenty etc., they can also be in the plural. In the Amarakośa, however, it is said: 'When numerals from twenty onwards have the sense of another number as their meaning, they can also be plural by being in agreement with it'. Here, 'another number' is the division of a group. Therefore, it should be understood that for both, the difference is only a matter of usage, not a difference in meaning. Up to ninety, including the word ninety, those numerals from twenty onwards, even when in agreement with a noun of a different gender, are in the feminine gender, for example, `vīsati kuṇḍāni` (twenty pots). Numerals from twenty onwards are irregular collective dvanda compounds. Because gender is based on worldly usage, the rules of singularity and neuter gender for dvanda compounds do not apply. According to another's opinion, numerals from twenty onwards are underived. But according to Kaccāyana's opinion, they are derived.

474-476. Satādīni asaṅkhyeyyapariyantāni catuvīsati ṭhānāni gaṇanabhedāni. Tattha dasadasasaddehi nipphādito satasaddo, tathā satadasasaddehi sahassasaddo. Yuja yoge, niyutaṃ, ayutampi. Yu missane vā, to. Lakkha dassanaṅkesu, lakkhaṃ, satasahassampi. Kuṭa chedane, dasaguṇaṃ kuṭatīti koṭi. Upasaggena visesetvā eko gaṇanaviseso pakoṭīti vuccati, dvepi missetvā eko koṭipakoṭīti. Naha bandhane, to. Āgamassu. Vida lābhe, u, niggahītāgamo. Aba hiṃsāyaṃ, gatimhi ca, do, āgamassu. Ahi gatimhi, hapaccayo. Ava rakkhaṇe, vo[M 0.0323]. Aṭa gamane, ṭo. Sogandhikanti kamalavisesanāmena eko gaṇanaviseso vuccati, tathoppalādināmehi ekeko gaṇanaviseso. Katha vākyappabandhe, yu, saṅkhyātumasakkuṇeyyatāya asaṅkhyeyyaṃ.

474-476. The twenty-four places, which are distinctions of counting, begin with 'sata' and end with 'asaṅkhyeyya'. Therein, the word 'sata' (hundred) is formed from the words 'dasa' (ten) and 'dasa'. Similarly, the word 'sahassa' (thousand) is formed from the words 'sata' and 'dasa'. From the root 'yuj' in the sense of 'yoking', come 'niyutaṃ' and also 'ayutaṃ'. Or from 'yu' in the sense of 'mixing', with the suffix 'to'. From 'lakkha' in the sense of 'seeing' or 'marking', comes 'lakkhaṃ', which is also a hundred thousand. From 'kuṭa' in the sense of 'cutting'; because it cuts tenfold, it is 'koṭi'. Having been distinguished by a prefix, one specific number is called 'pakoṭi'; having mixed both, one is 'koṭipakoṭi'. From 'naha' in the sense of 'binding', with the suffix 'to', and an augment is added. From 'vida' in the sense of 'gaining', with the suffix 'u', and the insertion of a niggahīta. From 'aba' in the sense of 'harming' and 'moving', with the suffix 'do', and an augment is added. From 'ahi' in the sense of 'moving', with the suffix 'ha'. From 'ava' in the sense of 'protecting', with the suffix 'vo'. From 'aṭa' in the sense of 'going', with the suffix 'ṭo'. A specific number is called 'sogandhika' by the name of a particular lotus; similarly, by the names of 'uppala' and so on, each is a specific number. From 'katha' in the sense of 'a composition of sentences', with the suffix 'yu'; because of its uncountability, it is 'asaṅkhyeyya' (innumerable).

Nanu saṅkhyātumasakkuṇeyyatte sati ekena bhavitabbaṃ, atha kathameko asaṅkhyeyyo, dve asaṅkhyeyyāniccādīni bhedāni vuttānīti? Nāyaṃ doso, tesaṃ kāladesādivasena bhinnānampi sambhavato. Etāsu saṅkhyāsu kamā kamena satādilakkhapariyantaṃ dasaguṇaṃ dasahi guṇitaṃ bhavati. Koṭyādikaṃ asaṅkhyeyyapariyantaṃ satalakkhaguṇaṃ satalakkhehi guṇitaṃ bhavati, tasmā ekā lekhā dvisuññasahitā sataṃ bhavati, tathā tisuññasahitā sahassaṃ, catusuññasahitā niyutaṃ, pañcasuññasahitā ekā lekhā lakkhaṃ bhavati, ekā pana lekhā sattasuññasahitā koṭi, tathā cuddasasuññasahitā pakoṭi, iminā nayena yāvāsaṅkhyeyyaṃ netabbaṃ, ayamekaccānamācariyānaṃ mati.

Surely, if it is uncountable, should it not be one? Then how are distinctions such as 'one asaṅkhyeyya, two asaṅkhyeyyas' spoken of? This is not a fault, for their existence is possible even when they are differentiated by way of time, place, and so on. Among these numbers, successively, from 'sata' up to 'lakkha', each is multiplied by ten. From 'koṭi' onwards up to 'asaṅkhyeyya', each is multiplied by a hundred thousand. Therefore, one figure accompanied by two zeros becomes a hundred; similarly, with three zeros, a thousand; with four zeros, a niyuta; one figure with five zeros becomes a lakkha; but one figure with seven zeros becomes a koṭi; similarly, with fourteen zeros, a pakoṭi. By this method, one should proceed up to the asaṅkhyeyya. This is the opinion of certain teachers.

Atha vā satādayo asaṅkhyeyyapariyantā sabbepi dasaguṇitā kātabbā, ayaṃ kaccāyanassa mati, tena hi “yāva taduttari dasaguṇitañce”ti suttamāha. Atha vā satādayo lakkhantā dasadasaguṇitā, tena ekā lekhā dvibindusahitā sataṃ bhavati, tathā catupañcādibindusahitā sahassādikaṃ bhavati, ekā lekhā pana dvādasabindusahitā koṭi, tathā ekūnavīsatibindusahitā pakoṭīti yāva asaṅkhyeyyā ekekasmiṃ satta satta bindūni katvā gaṇanā kātabbā, tasmā asaṅkhyeyyagaṇanavisese pañcacattālīsādhikāni satabindūni bhavanti, ayamamhākaṃ mati.

Alternatively, all numbers from 'sata' up to 'asaṅkhyeyya' should be multiplied by ten. This is the opinion of Kaccāyana, for he has stated the sutta: 'and as far as that, further multiplied by ten.' Alternatively, the numbers from 'sata' up to 'lakkha' are multiplied by ten. Thus, one figure accompanied by two zeros becomes a hundred; similarly, accompanied by four, five, and so on zeros, it becomes a thousand and so on. But one figure accompanied by twelve zeros becomes a koṭi; similarly, accompanied by nineteen zeros, a pakoṭi. Up to 'asaṅkhyeyya', the calculation should be made by adding seven zeros for each one. Therefore, in the specific calculation of 'asaṅkhyeyya', there are one hundred and forty-five zeros. This is our opinion.

Amarakose amara 19.84 pana “pantyā satasahassādi, kamā dasaguṇottara”mityuttaṃ, tassattho – dasasaṅkhyā pantītyuccate[M 0.0324], tato ārabbha dasaguṇottaraṃ satasahassādikaṃ kamā viññeyyaṃ, taṃ yathā – dasasaṅkhyāya dasaguṇottaraṃ sataṃ, satā dasaguṇottaraṃ sahassaṃ, sahassā dasaguṇottaraṃ ayutaṃ, ayutā dasaguṇottaraṃ lakkhaṃ, lakkhā dasaguṇottaraṃ payutaṃ, payutā dasaguṇottaraṃ koṭi, evaṃ koṭiyā abbudaṃ, abbudā padumaṃ, padumā khabbo, khabbā mahākatho, tatopi mahāpadumaṃ, tatopi saṅku, saṅkuto samuddo, tato antyaṃ, antyā majjhaṃ, majjhā paraddhaṃ, paraddhā amataṃ, amatā dasaguṇottaraṃ saṅkhyaṃ, saṅkhyañca vīsatimaṃ ṭhānaṃ, asaṅkhyeyyamito paranti.
