Sabbapārisadattā hi byākaraṇassa sabbesaṃpyatra vādā dassitā.

Moreover, in the Amarakośa it is said: 'From panti, hundred, thousand, and so on are successively tenfold.' Its meaning is this: the number ten is called panti. Starting from that, hundred, thousand, and so on should be understood in sequence as successively tenfold, as follows: ten times ten is a hundred; ten times a hundred is a thousand; ten times a thousand is an ayuta; ten times an ayuta is a lakkha; ten times a lakkha is a payuta; ten times a payuta is a koṭi. Likewise, ten times a koṭi is an abbuda; ten times an abbuda is a paduma; ten times a paduma is a khabbo; ten times a khabbo is a mahākatho; ten times a mahākatho is a mahāpaduma; ten times a mahāpaduma is a saṅku; ten times a saṅku is a samuddo; ten times a samuddo is an antya; ten times an antya is a majjha; ten times a majjha is a paraddha; ten times a paraddha is an amata; ten times an amata is a saṅkhya. And saṅkhya is the twentieth place; beyond this is asaṅkhyeyya. Indeed, because grammar is for all assemblies, the views of all have been presented here.

477-478. Sādhikena dvepādena “aḍḍhena catuttho aḍḍhuḍḍho, aḍḍhena tatiyo aḍḍhatiyo, aḍḍhateyyo cā”ti imaṃ vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Aḍḍhūpapadena saha catutthādisaddānaṃ aḍḍhuḍḍhādyādeso. Sādhikapādena “aḍḍhena dutiyo diyaḍḍho, divaḍḍho cā”ti imaṃ vacanatthaṃ dasseti. Antaritassāpi aḍḍhenasaddassa idhānuvattanatā adhippetā abhidhānantarābhāvā, sabbatrevaṃ.

477-478. With two additional pādas, it shows the meaning of this statement: 'a fourth with a half is aḍḍhuḍḍho; a third with a half is aḍḍhatiyo and also aḍḍhateyyo.' There is the substitution of aḍḍhuḍḍha, etc., for the words 'fourth', etc., when accompanied by the prefix 'aḍḍha'. With an additional pāda, it shows the meaning of this statement: 'a second with a half is diyaḍḍho and also divaḍḍho.' Here, the continuation of the word 'aḍḍhena', even though it is separated, is intended, due to the absence of another expression; it is so in all cases.

479-480. Mīyate paricchindīyate yena, taṃ mānaṃ. Tañca tulāpatthaṅgulivasā tidhā māniyadabbassa bhavati. Tula ummāne[M 0.0325], curādi, tulā itthī. Pada gatiyaṃ, tho. Aṅga gamane, ulo, aṅgulaṃ, “aṅgulī”tipi pāṭho, karasākhā.

479-480. That by which one measures or determines is called 'māna' (measure). And that measure for measurable substances is threefold: by balance, by capacity ('pattha'), and by finger-breadth. From the root 'tul' in the sense of 'weighing', of the curādi group; 'tulā' is feminine. From 'pada' in the sense of 'going', with the suffix 'tho'. From 'aṅga' in the sense of 'going', with the suffix 'ulo', comes 'aṅgulaṃ' (a finger-breadth); there is also the reading 'aṅgulī' (a finger), meaning a branch of the hand.

Cattāro vīhayo sampiṇḍitā ekāva guñjā samagarukā, tathā dve guñjā ekova māsako samagarukoti sabbatra nayo netabbo. Dve māsakā akkho nāma, vibhīṭakoti vutto, akkhaphalasamānagarukattā vā akkho. Karisopyatra, kasa vilekhane, a, rimajjho, anitthī. Akkhānaṃ pañca dharaṇaṃ nāma, dharatidhātuyā yu. Akkhānamaṭṭhakaṃ suvaṇṇo nāma. Pañcadharaṇaṃ nikkhaṃ nāma. Te nikkhā pañca pādo nāma. So pādo catutthe bhāge vattatītyekaccānaṃ mati. Yathāvuttāyeva cattāro vīhayo guñjā nāma. Dve guñjā māsako nāma. Dve pañcamāsakā dasamāsakā akkho nāma. Akkhānaṃ aṭṭhakaṃ dharaṇaṃ nāma. Pañcadharaṇaṃ suvaṇṇo nāma. Te pañcasuvaṇṇā nikkhaṃ nāmātyamhākaṃ mati. Kana dittigatikantīsu, nipubbo, nassa kho, nikkho, suvaṇṇavikārepi. Yassa kassaci vatthuno catutthe bhāge pādo. Dasa dharaṇāni palaṃ nāma, pala pathe ca gatimhi.

Four vīhi grains, when gathered together, are equal in weight to one guñjā, and likewise two guñjās are equal in weight to one māsaka—this principle should be applied universally. Two māsakas are called an akkha, also referred to as vibhīṭaka, or an akkha because it is equal in weight to the akkha fruit. Here, karisa is also mentioned; from 'kasa' in the sense of 'furrowing', with 'a', 'ri' in the middle, and it is not feminine. Five akkhas are called a dharaṇa, derived from the root 'dharati' (to hold) with the suffix 'yu'. Eight akkhas are called a suvaṇṇa. Five dharaṇas are called a nikkha. Five of those nikkhas are called a pāda. That this pāda refers to a fourth part is the opinion of some. As has been said, four vīhi grains are called a guñjā. Two guñjās are called a māsaka. Two five-māsakas, that is, ten māsakas, are called an akkha. Eight akkhas are called a dharaṇa. Five dharaṇas are called a suvaṇṇa. That five of those suvaṇṇas are called a nikkha is our opinion. From 'kana' in the senses of 'shining', 'going', and 'desiring', with the prefix 'ni', 'n' becomes 'kh', thus 'nikkho', also in the sense of a modification of gold. A pāda is the fourth part of any object. Ten dharaṇas are called a pala; 'pala' is also in the sense of 'path' and 'going'.

481. Yassa kassaci vatthuno palasataṃ tulā. Tula ummāne, tulā nārī.

481. For any object, a hundred palas is a tulā. From the root 'tul' in the sense of 'weighing'; 'tulā' is feminine.

Gehānaṃ dārubandhāya, piṭhikāyaṃ tulā thiyaṃ;

Mānabhaṇḍe ca sādise, rāsipalasatesu ca.

The feminine word 'tulā' is used for the timber-binding of houses, for a carrying frame, for a measuring vessel, for similarity, for a heap, and for a hundred palas.

Tā [M 0.0326] tulā vīsati bhāro nāma. Bhara dhāraṇaposanesu, ṇo. “Bhāro tu dvisahassesu, palānamapi vivadhe”tyajayo byākhyāsudhāṭīkāyampi. Vivadho bhārabhedo.

Twenty of those tulās are called a bhāra. From the root 'bhar' in the senses of 'bearing' and 'nourishing', with the suffix 'ṇo'. Ajaya says: 'A bhāra is indeed two thousand palas, also in a vivadha.' A vivadha is a type of load.

Rūpiyassa karisena kato saṃvohārapadattho kahāpaṇo nāma. Karisappamāṇena rūpiyena kato paṇo paṇiyo dabbabhedo kahāpaṇo. Risassa hādeso. Ahādese karisāpaṇo, ete dve rūpavikāro, aññatrūpacārā. Iti tulāmānaṃ vuttaṃ.

A kahāpaṇa is so called, being made from a karisa of silver for the purpose of transaction. A kahāpaṇa is a paṇa, a type of commodity to be traded, made from a quantity of silver equal to a karisa. There is an elision of 'risa'. When there is no elision, it is a karisāpaṇa. These two are modifications of silver, used metaphorically elsewhere. Thus the measure by weight has been stated.

482. Patthamānaṃ dassetumāha “kuḍuvo”ccādi. Eko pasato kuḍuvo nāma. Sara gatiyaṃ, to, ralopo, kaḍi bhede, vo, kaḍissa kuḍu, te kuḍuvā cattāro pattho. Catupatthā āḷhako, aha pūjāyaṃ, ṇvu, ḷattādi dasaṅgulaṃ, dvādasaṅgulaṃ vāsabbato mānampi āḷhako. Caturo āḷhakā doṇaṃ nāma, “caturāḷhaka”ntipi pāṭho, du gamane, ṇo, duṇa gatiyaṃ, hiṃsāyañca vā, doṇaṃ. Vākārena doṇo.

482. To show the measure of capacity, he says: 'kuḍuvo' and so on. One pasata is called a kuḍuva. The word 'pasata' is derived from 'sara' (to move), with the suffix 'to' and elision of 'ra'. The word 'kuḍuva' is from 'kaḍi' (to divide), with the suffix 'vo', where 'kaḍi' becomes 'kuḍu'. Four of those kuḍuvas make a pattha. Four patthas make an āḷhaka. The word 'āḷhaka' is from 'aha' (to honor), with the suffix 'ṇvu', and the change to 'ḷa'. An āḷhaka is also a measure of ten or twelve aṅgulas according to the Vāsabba system. Four āḷhakas make a doṇa; the reading 'caturāḷhaka' is also found. The word 'doṇaṃ' is from 'du' (to move), with the suffix 'ṇo'; or from 'duṇa' (to move or to harm). In the masculine gender, it is 'doṇo'.

483. Caturo doṇā mānikā, māna pūjāyaṃ, sakatthe ko, assi. Catumānikaṃ catassannaṃ mānikānaṃ samūho catumānikaṃ [M 0.0327] khārī nāma, khara vināse, ṇo, nadādi. Dasambaṇaṃ dasādhikasatadoṇamattaṃ kumbhoti ghaṭanāmena eko patthamānaviseso dassito, “ambaṇa”ntipi pāṭho.

483. Four doṇas are a mānikā. From the root `māna` in the sense of 'to honor', with the suffix `ko` in its own sense. A `catumānika` is the aggregate of four mānikās; a `catumānika` is called a `khārī`. From the root `khara` in the sense of 'to destroy', with the suffix `ṇo`, of the `nadādi` group. A `dasambaṇa`, a measure of one hundred and ten doṇas, is called a `kumbha`; by the name `ghaṭa`, a particular measure is indicated. The reading `ambaṇa` is also found.

484. Patthamānavisesānaṃ labbhamānapariyāye dassetumāha “āḷhako”ccādi. Tumba kampane, a. Dvayaṃ patthe. Patthasaddoyaṃ sāmaññabhedamānesu pavattati, idha pana visesamānavācako adhippeto. Nala ganthe, iṇa.

484. To show the obtainable varieties of particular measures, he said, 'āḷhako' and so on. From the root `tumba` in the sense of 'to shake', with the suffix `a`. A pair of terms for `pattha`. This word `pattha` is used for both general and specific measures, but here it is intended to denote a specific measure. From the root `nala` in the sense of 'to tie', with the suffix `iṇa`.

Dvayaṃ vāhe. Vahatīti vāho, vaha pāpuṇane, ṇo.

A pair of terms for `vāha`. That which carries is a `vāha`. From the root `vaha` in the sense of 'to attain', with the suffix `ṇo`.

Ambaṇamānaṃ, pariyāyaṃ vā dassetumāha “ekādasa doṇe”ccādi. Amba gamane, yu, amba sadde vā, iti patthamānaṃ vuttaṃ, aṅgulamānaṃ pana aṇvādyābhidhānāvasare bhūmivagge abhihitaṃ.

To show the measure `ambaṇa`, or its synonym, he said, 'eleven doṇas' and so on. From the root `amba` in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix `yu`; or from `amba` in the sense of 'to sound'. Thus, the measures have been stated. The `aṅgula` measure, however, was stated in the Bhūmivagga on the occasion of defining `aṇu` and so forth.

485. Catukkaṃ bhāge. Visa pavesane, dīghādi, koṭṭhaṃ vuccati sarīraṃ, tattha setīti koṭṭhāso. Āttaṃ. Ana pāṇane, ama gamane vā, so. Bhajīyate sevīyateti bhāgo. Ṇo. Vaṇṭakopyatra. Vaṭi vibhājane, ṇvu, ṇantā vā sakatthe ko.

485. A set of four terms for 'part'. From the root `visa` in the sense of 'to enter', with lengthening and so on. `Koṭṭha` is said to be the body; that which lies therein is `koṭṭhāso`. `Āttaṃ`. From the root `ana` in the sense of 'to breathe' or `ama` in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix `so`. That which is divided or served is `bhāgo`, with the suffix `ṇo`. `Vaṇṭako` is also here. From the root `vaṭi` in the sense of 'to divide', with the suffix `ṇvu`; or from a stem ending in `ṇa`, with `ko` in its own sense.

Vibhavantaṃ dhane. Dhana dhaññe, a. Sassa attano ayaṃ so, sampi. Duiva dabbaṃ, sāramiccattho, ivatthe vo, vida lābhe, to[M 0.0328]. Sassa dhanassa pati sapati, tasmiṃ sādhu sāpateyyaṃ, ṇeyyo. Vasa nivāse, u. Ara gamane, tho. Rassa to. Vibhavanti pabhavantyanenāti vibhavo, a. Hiraññaṃ, kosopyatra.

The section ending with `vibhava` concerns wealth. From the root `dhana` in the sense of 'grain', with the suffix `a`. From `sa`, meaning 'one's own', with the suffix `so`. `Du iva dabbaṃ` (substance is like a tree), meaning 'essence'; `vo` is in the sense of `iva`. From the root `vida` in the sense of 'to gain', with the suffix `to`. The master of one's own wealth is `sāpati`; that which is suitable for him is `sāpateyyaṃ`, with the suffix `ṇeyyo`. From the root `vasa` in the sense of 'to dwell', with the suffix `u`. From the root `ara` in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix `tho`; `ra` becomes `ta`. That by which they become powerful or flourish is `vibhavo`, with the suffix `a`. `Hirañña` and `kosa` are also here.

486. Katākataṃ kañcanaṃ, rūpiyañca missitaṃ militaṃ (ka.), militaṃ paccekañca (amara khīrasvādhīṭīkā) kosādidvayavāccaṃ, tatra piṇḍīkataṃ ābharaṇīkataṃ, kammībhāvamāpāditaṃ vā kataṃ. Ākarotthaṃ ajātakammaṃ cuṇṇādirūpaṃ akataṃ, tadaññaṃ tehi kañcanarūpiyehi aññaṃ tejasaṃ dabbaṃ tambaṃ. Ādinā kaṃsarītisīsakādi, yañcātejasaṃ rājapaṭṭadāruvisādika’masāraṃ dabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ kuppaṃ, gupa rakkhaṇe, guppateti, po, kattañca gassa.

486. Wrought and unwrought gold and silver, mixed, are denoted by the pair of terms beginning with `kosa`. Therein, that which is formed into lumps, made into ornaments, or brought into a worked state is called `kata`. That which is from the mine, unworked, in the form of dust and so on, is `akata`. Other than these, any other metallic substance apart from that gold and silver, such as copper—and by 'and so on' is meant bronze, brass, lead, etc.—and any non-metallic, insubstantial substance like royal cloth, wood, poison, etc., all that is `kuppa`. From the root `gupa` in the sense of 'to protect', it is protected, with the suffix `po`, and `g` becomes `k`.

Dvayaṃ kañcanaṃ rūpiyañcāhatamuṭṭhāpitahayavarāhapurisādi rūpaṃ nigghātikāya tāḷitaṃ dīnārādikaṃ rūpiyākhyaṃ. Assādirūpamassāhatamatthīti rūpiyaṃ. Rūpa āhatapasaṃsāsu, iyo.

A pair of terms for struck gold and silver. That which has forms of horses, boars, men, and so on, raised upon it, struck with a hammer, such as dīnāras and the like, is called `rūpiya`. Because it has forms of horses and so on struck upon it, it is `rūpiya`. From the root `rūpa` in the senses of 'to strike' and 'to praise', with the suffix `iyo`.

487-488. Hiraññantaṃ suvaṇṇe. Sobhano vaṇṇo yassa suvaṇṇaṃ. Kana dittiyaṃ, ṇvu, jananaṃ jātaṃ, pakaṭṭhaṃ jātaṃ jātarūpaṃ, [M 0.0329] pakaṭṭhatthe rūpapaccayo pasaṃsāyaṃ rūpapaccayo iti subhū (cintāmaṇiṭīkā) pasaṃsāyaṃ rūpaṃ (pāṇini 5.3.66). Jātaṃ rūpamassāti vā jātarūpaṃ. Iṇa gatiyaṃ, dittiyañca anekatthattā. Suṭṭhu dippate dittiyā yujjateti soṇṇaṃ, usso, “vā paro asarūpā”ti ilopo, dvittaṃ. Kañca dittiyaṃ, yu. Satthu vaṇṇo viya vaṇṇo yassa. Cittamattānaṃ haratīti hari. I, kamu icchāyaṃ, bu. Carati ettha cittaṃ cāru, ṇu. Hi gatiyaṃ, mo. Haṭa dittiyaṃ, ṇvu. Tapanaṃ dāhamarahatīti tapaniyo, iyo. Hara haraṇe, añño, assi. Hā cāge, hā gatiyaṃ vā, añño, hirādeso ca.

487-488. The section ending with `hirañña` concerns gold. That which has a splendid color is `suvaṇṇa`. From the root `kana` in the sense of 'to shine', with the suffix `ṇvu`. `Jananaṃ` means `jātaṃ` (born); that which is excellently born is `jātarūpa`; the suffix `rūpa` is in the sense of excellence. Or, that which has a born form is `jātarūpa`. From the root `iṇa` in the sense of 'to go' and 'to shine', due to its multiple meanings. It shines well and is endowed with brightness, hence `soṇṇa`; with the suffix `usso`, and by the rule `vā paro asarūpā`, the `i` is elided, and there is doubling of the consonant. From the root `kañca` in the sense of 'to shine', with the suffix `yu`. That whose color is like the Teacher's color. That which captivates one's mind is `hari`. From the root `i`. From the root `kamu` in the sense of 'to desire', with the suffix `bu`. The mind moves delightfully in it, hence `cāru`, with the suffix `ṇu`. From the root `hi` in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix `mo`. From the root `haṭa` in the sense of 'to shine', with the suffix `ṇvu`. That which is worthy of being heated or burnt is `tapaniyo`, with the suffix `iyo`. From the root `hara` in the sense of 'to seize', with the suffix `añño`, and `a` becomes `i`. From the root `hā` in the sense of 'to abandon' or `hā` in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix `añño`, and also the substitution of `hira`.

Cāmīkarādayo cattāro tabbhedā tassa suvaṇṇassa visesā. Cāmī nāma ekā pupphajāti, taṃkarattā cāmīkaro, atha vā cāmī nāma aggi. Camu adane, ṇī, takkarattā cāmīkaro. Satakumbhaṃ paddhakesaravaṇṇaṃ, tabbaṇṇasadisattā sātakumbhaṃ. Devarukkhabhūtāya mahājambuyā patiṭṭhitaṭṭhāne nadī jambunadī, tassaṃ patitehi mahāgajappamāṇānaṃ, kumbhappamāṇānaṃ vā phalānaṃ bījehi jātaṃ suvaṇṇaṃ jambunadaṃ, idaṃ pana suvaṇṇaṃ analappabhaṃ devālaṅkāramatulaṃ jāyate. Taṃ panānalamiti visesatthepi amarasīho suvaṇṇasāmaññeva paṭhati. Siṅgī nāma ekā macchajāti, tabbaṇṇatāya. Khaṇiyaṃ vā taṃsaṇṭhānasilākhaṇḍehi jātatāya siṅgī, amarakose pana cāmīkarādīnipi suvaṇṇasāmaññe paṭhati, siṅgī pana visese. Vuttañhi tattha “alaṅkārasuvaṇṇaṃ yaṃ, siṅgīkanakamiccaya”nti amara 19.96. Tassattho – kaṭakakuṇḍalādino alaṅkārasuvaṇṇassa “siṅgī”ti nāmanti. “Siṅgīmaṇḍanasoṇṇa”nti [M 0.0330] ratanakoso. Suvaṇṇatāya siṅgī “kanaka”mityuccate.

`Cāmīkara` and the other three are its varieties, specific types of that gold. `Cāmī` is a type of flower; because it is made from it, it is `cāmīkara`. Alternatively, `cāmī` is fire; from the root `camu` in the sense of 'to eat', with the suffix `ṇī`, because it does that, it is `cāmīkara`. `Satakumbha` is the color of the `paddhakesara` flower; because it resembles that color, it is `sātakumbha`. The river at the place where the great Jambu tree, a divine tree, stands is the Jambunadī. Gold born from the seeds of fruits—the size of great elephants or pots—that have fallen into that river is `jambunada`. This gold is born with the radiance of fire, peerless, for divine ornaments. Although this is described as 'fire-like' in a specific sense, Amarasīha reads it as a general synonym for gold. `Siṅgī` is a type of fish, so named because of its color. Or, it is `siṅgī` because it is born from fragments of rock of that shape from a mine. In the Amarakośa, however, `cāmīkara` and others are also read in the general sense of gold, but `siṅgī` in a specific sense. For it is stated there: 'Ornamental gold is called `siṅgīkanaka`.' Its meaning is that ornamental gold, such as bracelets and earrings, is called `siṅgī`. The Ratnakosa states: '`siṅgīmaṇḍanasoṇṇa`'. Because it is gold, `siṅgī` is also called `kanaka`.

489. Pañcakaṃ rajate. Rūpayuttatāya rūpiyaṃ. Rañja rāge, ato. Sañja saṅge, jhu, ñalopo, sajjhu. Rūpayuttatāya rūpī, sañja saṅge, jho, ñalopo, sajjhaṃ, “rūpiyajjha”ntipi pāṭho. Tadā iyajjhapaccayena siddhaṃ. Dubbaṇṇaṃ, khajjūraṃ, setampi.

489. A set of five terms for silver. Because it is endowed with form, it is `rūpiya`. From the root `rañja` in the sense of 'to color', with the suffix `ato`. From the root `sañja` in the sense of 'to attach', with the suffix `jhu`, and elision of `ñ`, it becomes `sajjhu`. Because it is endowed with form, it is `rūpī`. From the root `sañja` in the sense of 'to attach', with the suffix `jho`, and elision of `ñ`, it becomes `sajjhaṃ`. The reading `rūpiyajjha` is also found; in that case, it is formed with the suffix `iyajjha`. `Dubbaṇṇa`, `khajjūra`, and `seta` are also included.

Āhatasoṇṇarajate, rajate rūpiyaṃ mataṃ;

Rajate ca khaleklivaṃ, khajjūro pādapantare;

Setā ca bhatikāyaṃ tha, klivaṃ sajjhe site tisu.

In the context of struck gold and silver, `rūpiya` is considered silver. `Rajata` and `khala` are neuter. `Khajjūro` is a type of tree. `Setā` means wages. `Sajjha` is neuter; `sita` is in all three genders.

Asmajātiyaṃ puppharāgādimhi, muttāvajirādimhi ca vasvādittayaṃ. Vasa nivāse, u. Ratiṃ tanotīti ratanaṃ, kammādimhi ṇo, tilopo. “Ratnaṃ sajātiseṭṭhepī”tyamarakose amara 23.126, tena gajaseṭṭho gajaratanaṃ, itthiseṭṭho itthiratananti. Manasaddato i, īpaccaye maṇī ca. Puppharāgādayo vakkhamānā tabbhidā tassa maṇino visesā. Bhāsanto rañjetīti puppharāgo, bhāsassa puppho.

In the category of stones, regarding gems like `puppharāga` and so on, and pearls, diamonds, and so forth, there is a set of three terms beginning with `vasu`. From the root `vasa` in the sense of 'to dwell', with the suffix `u`. That which extends delight is `ratana`, with the suffix `ṇo` in formations like `kamma`, and elision of `ti`. In the Amarakośa, it is stated: 'A `ratna` is also the best of its kind.' Therefore, the best elephant is an elephant-`ratana`, and the best woman is a woman-`ratana`. From the word `maṇa`, with the suffixes `i` and `ī`, it becomes `maṇi` and `maṇī`. `Puppharāga` and others, which will be explained, are its varieties, specific types of that gem. It delights while shining, hence `puppharāgo`; `bhāsa` becomes `puppha`.

490. Suvaṇṇādayo ime satta ratanānyāhu. Maṇi rattamaṇi.

490. These seven, beginning with gold, are called gems. `Maṇi` refers to a ruby.

491. Sattaratanānaṃ labbhamānapariyāye dassetumāha “lohitaṅgo”ccādi. Lohitaṅgādittayaṃ rattamaṇiyaṃ[M 0.0331]. Lohitavaṇṇena aṅgīyateti lohitaṅgo, lohitaṃ aṅgaṃ sarīrametassa vā lohitaṅgo. Padumañcātra kokanadaṃ, tabbaṇṇasadiso maṇi padumarāgo. Soṇaratanaṃ, lohitakopyatra.

491. To show the obtainable varieties of the seven gems, he said, 'lohitaṅgo' and so on. The three terms beginning with `lohitaṅga` refer to the ruby. It is called `lohitaṅgo` because it is marked by a red color, or because its body is red. Here, `paduma` is the red lotus. A gem resembling that color is `padumarāgo`. `Soṇaratana` and `lohitako` are also included here.

Dvayaṃ veḷuriye. Vaṃso tacasāro, tabbaṇṇo maṇi vaṃsavaṇṇo. Veḷu viya dissatīti veḷuriyo, ivatthe iyo, rāgamo ca. Dvayaṃ pavāḷe. Vala saṃvaraṇe, ṇo, ḷattaṃ, vākārena pavāḷopi. Du gamane, du upatāpe vā, mo, dvittaṃ.

A pair of terms for `veḷuriya`. Bamboo is the essence of bark; a gem of that color is `vaṃsavaṇṇo`. It appears like bamboo, hence `veḷuriyo`, with the suffix `iyo` in the sense of 'like', and the insertion of `r`. A pair of terms for `pavāḷa`. From the root `vala` in the sense of 'to cover', with the suffix `ṇo`, and `l` becomes `ḷ`; with the letter `va`, it is also `pavāḷo`. From the root `du` in the sense of 'to go' or 'to afflict', with the suffix `mo`, and doubling.

492. Dvayaṃ kabaramaṇimhi. Masāragirimhi jātaṃ masāragallaṃ, lo, rassa lo. Kabaro sabalo maṇi. Dvayaṃ muttāyaṃ. Muca mocane, tho, muttā eva muttikaṃ, sakatthe iko. Satthikā pakatito liṅgavacanānyativattanteti napuṃsakattaṃ. Ettha ca ratanapariyāyānaṃ uppaṭipāṭiyā kathanaṃ sattannaṃ ratanānaṃ uppattikkamapaṇītakkamādino abhāvadīpanatthaṃ.

492. A pair of terms for `kabaramaṇi` (variegated gem). `Masāragalla` is that which is born on Mount Masāra; `r` becomes `l`. `Kabaro` is a variegated gem. A pair of terms for `muttā` (pearl). From the root `muca` in the sense of 'to release', with the suffix `tho`. `Muttikaṃ` is `muttā` itself, with the suffix `iko` in its own sense. By the rule `satthikā`, words by nature sometimes transcend their gender and number; hence the neuter gender. And here, the statement of the gem synonyms in reverse order is for the purpose of showing the absence of a sequence of origin, a sequence of excellence, and so on, among the seven gems.

Dvayaṃ pittale. Rī gamane, ri. Rītipi. “Rīti pacāre sande ca, lohakiṭṭārakūṭesū”ti ruddo. Ārasseva kūṭo, yassa. Dabbasaddopyatra. Dvayaṃ abbhake. Ama gamane, alo. Abbhaṃ ākāso, megho ca, taṃsaññakattā abbhakaṃ, saññāyaṃ ko. “Meghambarābhidhānañca, gori bījañca abbhaka”nti hi vuttaṃ. Girijatu, silājatupyatra.

Two terms for brass. From the root 'rī' in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix 'ri'. Also 'rīti'. Rudra states: 'Rīti is used for movement, doubt, and heaps of metal dross.' A heap of dross. The word 'dabba' is also here. Two terms for mica. From the root 'ama' in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix 'alo'. 'Abbha' means sky and cloud; because it is designated as such, it is 'abbhakaṃ', with the suffix 'ko' in the sense of designation. Indeed, it is said: 'Abbhaka is also named meghambara and gori bīja.' Girijatu and silājatu are also here.

493. Tikaṃ [M 0.0332] lohe. Lū chedane, ho. Aya gamane, manogaṇādi. Kāḷañca taṃ ayasañceti kāḷāyasaṃ. Satthakaṃ, tikkhaṇaṃ, piṇḍaṃ, ayasaṃ, asmasāropyatra. “Satthamāyudhalohesū”ti anekattho. “Sāmuddalavaṇetikkhaṃ, visalohājimukkake”ti rabhaso. Paṇḍa gamane, a. Asmassa sāro. “Kāḷāyasa’mayo lohaṃ, asmasārañca satthaka”nti tvamaramālāyaṃ klīvakaṇḍaṃ.

493. Three terms for metal. From the root 'lū' in the sense of 'to cut', with the suffix 'ho'. From the root 'aya' in the sense of 'to go', of the manogaṇa group, etc. That which is black and is iron is 'kāḷāyasa'. Satthaka, tikkhaṇa, piṇḍa, ayasa, and asmasāra are also here. The Anekārthasaṅgraha states: 'Sattha is used for a weapon and for metal.' Rabhasa states: 'Tikkha is used for sea salt, poison, metal, and the beginning of a battle.' From the root 'paṇḍa' in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix 'a'. The essence of stone. In the neuter section of the Amaramālā it is stated: 'Kāḷāyasa, ayo, loha, asmasāra, and satthaka.'

Dvayaṃ capale. Pāra sāmatthiye, do, pārayati sakkoti sabbalohaṃ kañcanaṃ kātunti pārado. Rasa sadde, aggimhi pakkhitte rasatīti raso, madhurādīsu ca raso. Capalo, sūtopyatra.

Two terms for mercury. From the root 'pāra' in the sense of 'ability', with the suffix 'do'; 'pārada' is so called because it is able to transmute all metals into gold. From the root 'rasa' in the sense of 'to sound'; 'rasa' is so called because it makes a sound when put into fire; 'rasa' also refers to taste, sweetness, etc. Capala and sūta are also here.

“Cañcalādimhi capalo”.

'Capala' is used for 'fickle', etc.

“Sārathimhi rase sūto, pasūte perite tisu”;

“Rasendo pārado vutto, pāratopi nigadyate”ti. –

'Sūta' is used for a charioteer and for rasa; in the three genders, for 'produced' and 'impelled'. 'Rasenda' is said to be 'pārada'; it is also called 'pārata'.

Tārapālo.

— Tārapāla.

“Pārado siddhadhātu ca, varabījañca sūtaka”nti. –

'Pārada' is also 'siddhadhātu', 'varabīja', and 'sūtaka'.

Tikaṇḍaseso tikaṇḍasesa 2.9.34.

— Tikaṇḍasesa.

Tikaṃ nāge. Tipu pīḷane, u. Tipusaddassa setepi pavattanato kāḷasaddena visesetvā kāḷatipūti vutto, tena tipusaddassadvinnampi vācakatādaṭṭhabbātyeke, taṃ “nāgo sīsakayogiṭṭha-vappāṇi tipu piccaṭa”nti amara 19.105 amarakose, “tipu [M 0.0333] sīsakaraṅgesū”ti ca tikaṇḍasesa nānatthasaṅgahādīsu vuttattā na gahetabbaṃ, tena kāḷo ca tipu cāti dveyevatthābhidhānāni. Kāḷavaṇṇatāya kāḷo. Tipu yathāvuttatthova. Tapa santāpe vā, u, assittaṃ. Sī saye, si bandhane vā, so. “Seṭṭhabhakaddujo nāgo, klivaṃ sīsakaraṅgesū”ti rabhaso. “Yogiṭṭha”mityekaṃ nāmaṃ sīsassa. “Vappo so sīsamattaka”nti tvamaramālā.

Three terms for 'nāga' (lead). From the root 'tipu' in the sense of 'to press', with the suffix 'u'. Because the word 'tipu' also occurs with 'white', it is specified as 'kāḷatipu' by the word 'kāḷa'. Therefore, some say that the word 'tipu' should be understood as denoting both. That should not be accepted, because in the Amarakosa it is stated: 'nāga, sīsa, yogiṭṭha, vappa, tipu, piccaṭa', and in the Tikaṇḍasesa, Nānārthasaṅgraha, etc., it is stated: 'tipu for lead and tin'. Therefore, only two meanings are indicated: 'kāḷa' and 'tipu'. 'Kāḷa' is so called from its black color. 'Tipu' has the meaning as stated before. Or, from the root 'tap' in the sense of 'to heat', with the suffix 'u'; it is poured. Or from the root 'sī' in the sense of 'to lie', or 'si' in the sense of 'to bind', with the suffix 'so'. Rabhasa states: ''Nāga' is used for the best of elephants and for the son of Kadrū; in the neuter, for lead and tin.' 'Yogiṭṭha' is one name for lead. The Amaramālā states: 'Vappa is only lead.'

“Ārakūṭosī rīti ca, sīsakaṃ tipu vaddhakaṃ;

Nāgaṃ mahāmalañceva, yogiṭṭhaka”nti. –

'Ārakūṭa, rīti, sīsaka, tipu, vaddhaka, nāga, mahāmala, and yogiṭṭhaka.'

Byāḍi.

— Byāḍi.

“Sīsamattaṃ bahumalaṃ, yogiṭṭhaṃ piṭṭhapiccaṭā;

Suvaṇṇādisamāluka-mapi sindūrasambhava”nti. –

'Sīsamatta, bahumala, yogiṭṭha, piṭṭha, piccaṭa; also that which resembles gold etc., and that which is produced from vermilion.'

Tantātantaraṃ.

— Tantāntara.

Sete tu raṅgavaṅgā, te gatyatthā.

But for white metal, there are raṅga and vaṅga; they are from roots meaning 'to go'.

“Raṅgaṃsurebhaṃ mudaṅgaṃ, kusumbhaṃ gāmyakuṅkuma”nti. –

'Raṅga is used for tin, a stage, a type of drum, safflower, and village saffron.'

Tikaṇḍaseso tikaṇḍasesa 2.9.34.

— Tikaṇḍasesa.

Dvayaṃ haritāle. Haritavaṇṇaṃ alaṃ haritālaṃ, byuppattimattametaṃ. Rūḷhīsaddo tvayaṃ. Pītiṃ netīti pītanaṃ. “Piñjaraṃ pītanaṃ tāla-mālañca haritālake”tyamarasīho amara 19.103 . Piñja vaṇṇe, aro. Ala bhūsane, alantyaneneti, ṇo, “haritālamalaṃ tāla-vaṇṇakaṃ naṭabhūsana”nti tu mādhavo. “Haritāle tu kappūraṃ, godanto naṭasaññako”ti tikaṇḍaseso tikaṇḍasesa 2.9.35.

Two terms for orpiment. Sufficiently green in color is 'haritāla'; this is merely an etymology. This word is conventional. It leads to yellow, hence 'pītana'. Amarasīha states: 'Piñjara, pītana, tāla, and māla are used for haritālaka.' From the root 'piñj' in the sense of 'to color', with the suffix 'aro'. From the root 'al' in the sense of 'to adorn', meaning 'that by which one is adorned', with the suffix 'ṇo'. Mādhava, however, states: 'Haritāla is an ornament, the color of the palm, an actor’s ornament.' The Tikaṇḍasesa states: 'For haritāla, there are also kappūra, godanta, and naṭasaññaka.'

494. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0334] sindūre. Piṭṭhena nāgena jātaṃ piṭṭhaṃ. Cīnadesappavattaṃ piṭṭhaṃ cīnapiṭṭhanti pubbapade uttarapadalopo. Sanda savane, ūro, assi. “Sindūraṃ nāgasambhava”ntyamarasīho amara 19.105. Vasantassavo, rattacuṇṇaṃ, rattavālukaṃpyatra. Dvayaṃ tūle. Tula nikase, a. Picu maddane, u. Picu tuloti samuditañcassa nāmaṃ. “Tūlo picu picutūlo, makkaṭisuttaṃ takkoṭī”ti hi rabhaso.

494. Two terms for vermilion. 'Piṭṭha' is that which is produced from ground lead. Piṭṭha originating from the country of China is 'cīnapiṭṭha', with elision of the latter part of the first member of the compound. From the root 'sand' in the sense of 'to flow', with the suffix 'ūro', and the augment 'si'. Amarasīha states: 'Sindūra is produced from lead.' Vasantāsava, rattacuṇṇa, and rattavāluka are also here. Two terms for cotton. From the root 'tul' in the sense of 'to weigh', with the suffix 'a'. From the root 'picu' in the sense of 'to press', with the suffix 'u'. 'Picutūla' is its combined name. Indeed, Rabhasa states: 'Tūla, picu, picutūla, makkaṭisutta, and takkoṭī.'

Madhusaddena khuddajantu, khuddañcoccate. Khuddajantavo bhamarādayo. Tatra bhamarakataṃ khuddaṃ bhāmaraṃ, makkhikākataṃ makkhikaṃ, saraghañcoccate. Varaṭā kataṃ vāraṭaṃ. Puttikā kataṃ puttikanti sabbatraññatthe ṇo. Madhu unde, u. Khu sadde, do, khuda pipāsāyaṃ vā, do.

By the word 'madhu', small creatures and honey are denoted. Small creatures are bees and the like. Among them, honey made by bees is 'bhāmara'; that made by flies is 'makkhika', and it is also called 'saragha'. That made by wasps is 'vāraṭa'. That made by termites is 'puttika'. In all these cases, the suffix 'ṇa' is used in the sense of 'product of another'. From the root 'madhu' in the sense of 'to be moist', with the suffix 'u'. From the root 'khu' in the sense of 'to sound', with the suffix 'do'; or from 'khud' in the sense of 'to be thirsty', with the suffix 'do'.

Dvayaṃ sitthe. Madhūhi khuddajantūhi ucchiṭṭhaṃ sajjitanti madhucchiṭṭhaṃ. Sajja visajjanāliṅgananimmānesu. Nimmānaṃ sampiṇḍīkaraṇaṃ, to, jatānaṃ ṭhādeso, sassa cho, dvittaṃ, ittañca. Sica paggharaṇe, tho. Sitthameva sitthakaṃ. Madanopyatra.

Two terms for beeswax. 'Madhucchiṭṭha' is that which is left over and prepared by bees and small creatures. The root 'sajja' is used in the senses of releasing, embracing, and creating. 'Creation' here means 'compacting'. From the root 'sic' in the sense of 'to sprinkle', with the suffix 'tho'. 'Sitthaka' is the same as 'sittha'. 'Madana' is also here.

495. Tikaṃ gopāle. Gāvo pāleti, pāti cāti gopālo, gopo ca, kammani ṇo. Gāvo saṅkhyāyatīti gosaṅkhyo, saṃpubbo khyā gaṇane. Goduho, ābhiro, vallavopyatra. Dvayaṃ gomike. Gāvo assa santīti gomā, mantu. Ikapaccaye, māgame ca gomiko.

495. Three terms for cowherd. One who protects or tends cows is a 'gopāla' or 'gopa'; the suffix 'ṇo' is in the agent sense. One who counts cows is a 'gosaṅkhya'; from the root 'khyā' in the sense of 'to count', with the prefix 'saṃ'. 'Goduha', 'ābhira', and 'vallava' are also here. Two terms for cow-owner. One who has cows is 'gomā', from the suffix 'mantu'. With the suffix 'ika' and the augment 'ma', it becomes 'gomiko'.

Dvipādaṃ [M 0.0335] balībadde. Usa dāhe, abho. Balaṃ vaddhayatīti balībaddo, nipātanā. Gacchatīti goṇo, yu, malopo, asso, ṇattaṃ. Gacchatīti go, gamu gamane, ro.

Two terms for ox. From the root 'us' in the sense of 'to burn', with the suffix 'abho'. One who increases strength is 'balībadda', by irregular formation. One who goes is 'goṇa'; from the root 'gam' with the suffix 'yu', with elision of 'm' and change to 'ṇ'. One who goes is 'go'; from the root 'gam' in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix 'ro'.

“Sagge kare ca vajire, balībadde ca go pumā;

Thī sorabheyyinettambu-disāvacanabhūmisū”ti. –

In the masculine, 'go' is used for heaven, a ray, a thunderbolt, and an ox; in the feminine, for a cow, the eye, water, direction, speech, and the earth.

Ruddo. Vasa nivāse, abho. Vassatīti vuso, vassa secane, ṇo, assu, saṃyogalopo ca. Ukkho, bhaddo, anavāho, sorabheyyopyatra. Ukkha secane. Anaṃ sakaṭaṃ vahatīti anavāho, ṇo. Surabhi go, tassāpaccaṃ sorabheyyo, ṇeyyo.

— Rudra. From the root 'vas' in the sense of 'to dwell', with the suffix 'abho'. One who sprinkles is 'vuso'; from the root 'vass' in the sense of 'to sprinkle', with the suffix 'ṇo', the augment 'u', and elision of the conjunct consonant. 'Ukkha', 'bhadda', 'anavāha', and 'sorabheyya' are also here. From the root 'ukkh' in the sense of 'to sprinkle'. One who pulls a cart is 'anavāha', with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Surabhi' is a cow; her offspring is 'sorabheyya', with the suffix 'ṇeyya'.

496. So go vuddho jaraggavo nāma. Jaraṃ patto go jaraggavo, simhi ossa avo. Dvayaṃ misabālyayutte kiñciphuṭṭhatāruññe asampattabalībaddabhāve vacche. “Vaccho vuddho vacchataro”ti nāmamālā. Damanāraho dammo, mo. Vasa nivāse, cho, vacchassāyeva gāviyā tanutthe nipātanā taro pāṇini 5.3.91 suttaṃ passitabbaṃ. Samāti ete dve tulyatthā.

496. That ox, when old, is named 'jaraggava'. An ox that has reached old age is 'jaraggava'; in the nominative singular, 'o' becomes 'ava'. Two terms for a calf that is past childhood, slightly touched by youth, but has not yet reached the state of a bullock. The Nāmamālā states: 'Vaccha, vuddha, vacchatara'. One fit for taming is 'damma', with the suffix 'mo'. From the root 'vas' in the sense of 'to dwell', with the suffix 'cho'. 'Taro' is an irregular formation from 'vaccha' itself, in the sense of a young cow. These two are equal in meaning.

Dvayaṃ dhuravāhe. Dhuraṃ vahati sīlenāti dhuravāhī, ṇī. Dhuraṃ vahitumarahatīti dhorayho, ṇo, vassa yo.

Two terms for a beast of burden. One who by nature bears a yoke is 'dhuravāhī', with the suffix 'ṇī'. One who is fit to bear a yoke is 'dhorayha', with the suffix 'ṇo', and 'ya' replacing 'va'.

Gavaṃ gunnaṃ adhikato jano govindo, gavaṃ indo govindo, gavaṃ vindatīti vā govindo.

A person who is chief among cowherds is 'govinda'; or the lord of cows is 'govinda'; or one who obtains cows is 'govinda'.

497. Vahatyanena [M 0.0336] vaho, a. Kuka ādāne, udo, ussattaṃ, dassa dho vā, kakudo, kakudho ca. Dvayaṃ siṅge. Visa pavesane, yu. Sī saye, go, niggahītāgamo, rassattañca. Lohitavaṇṇatāya rohiṇī, tassa ṇo, nadādi.

497. That by which one carries is 'vaha', with the suffix 'a'. From the root 'kuk' in the sense of 'to take', with the suffix 'uda', with the vowel becoming 'u', and 'd' optionally becoming 'dh'; hence 'kakuda' and 'kakudha'. Two terms for horn. From the root 'vis' in the sense of 'to enter', with the suffix 'yu'. From the root 'sī' in the sense of 'to lie', with the suffix 'ga', the augment 'ṃ', and shortening of the vowel. Because of its red color, it is 'rohiṇī'; the suffix is 'ṇa', as in the nadādi group.

498. Tikaṃ gāvīsāmaññe. Pumepi gāvī, tadā yossa ī. Siṅgayuttatāya siṅginī, taddhitantā inī. Dvayaṃ aputtikāyaṃ. Hanatismā itthiyaṃ a, hanatissa vadho, niggahītāgamo, dhassa jho ca, bandha bandhane vā, vañjhā. Vasa kantiyaṃ, a.

498. Three terms for cow in general. 'Gāvī' is also used in the masculine; then 'ī' replaces 'ya'. Because it has horns, it is 'siṅginī'; the taddhita suffix is 'inī'. Two terms for a barren cow. From 'han' (to kill), in the feminine, with the suffix 'a'; 'han' has the sense of 'to destroy'; with the augment 'ṃ', and 'dh' becomes 'jh'. Or from the root 'bandh' in the sense of 'to bind', it becomes 'vañjhā'. From the root 'vas' in the sense of 'to desire', with the suffix 'a'.

Navappasūtikā paccagghapasūtā go dhenu nāma, dhe pāne, nu. Dvayaṃ piyaputtāyaṃ. Vacchaṃ kāmayatīti vacchakāmā. Vacchaṃ lātīti vacchalā. Savacchakāyamapi dvayamidaṃ vadanti.

A cow that has newly given birth, one that has recently calved, is named 'dhenu'; from the root 'dhe' in the sense of 'to drink', with the suffix 'nu'. Two terms for a cow fond of its calf. One that desires its calf is 'vacchakāmā'. One that takes up its calf is 'vacchalā'. They also say these two terms refer to a cow with its calf.

499. Dvayaṃ manthanakumbhikāyaṃ. “Gagga”nti saddaṃrātīti gaggarī, nadādi. Manthati yassa manthanī. Mantha viloḷane, yu, nadādi, dvepi itthī. Yatrekasmiṃ bahupaggahayutte aneke bandhīyante, tatra [M 0.0337] sandānādidvayaṃ. Saṃpubbo dā dāne saṃyamanattho, karaṇe yu. Dā dāne, mo, dāmaṃ.

499. Two terms for a churning pot. That which makes the sound ‘gagga’ is a ‘gaggarī’, like those in the nadādi group. That by which one churns is a ‘manthanī’. The root ‘manth’ is in the sense of churning, with the suffix ‘yu’, like those in the nadādi group; both are feminine. Where many are bound together in one place with many tethers, there are two terms such as ‘sandāna’. ‘Sandāna’ is from the root ‘dā’, to give, preceded by ‘saṃ’, in the sense of restraining, with the suffix ‘yu’ in the instrumental sense. ‘Dāma’ is from the root ‘dā’, to give, with the suffix ‘mo’.

Dvayaṃ govacce. Miha secane, lo. Gavaṃ mīḷho vacco gomīḷho. Goto nibbatto gomayo, dvepyanitthī. Dvayaṃ ghate. Sappa gamane, i, sappi napuṃsake. Ghara secane, to. Havipyatra.

Two terms for cow excrement. ‘Mīḷha’ is from the root ‘mih’, to secrete, with the suffix ‘lo’. The urine of a cow is ‘gomīḷha’. That which is produced from a cow is ‘gomaya’; both are not feminine. Two terms for ghee. ‘Sappi’ is from the root ‘sapp’, to move, with the suffix ‘i’; ‘sappi’ is neuter. ‘Ghata’ is from the root ‘ghar’, to sprinkle, with the suffix ‘to’. ‘Havi’ is also used here.

500. Taṃdivasiyā dadhito, duddhā vā samubbhataṃ ghataṃ tappakati ca navanītaṃ. Navadadhyādīhi nītaṃ pavattaṃ nonītaṃ, vasso. Navanītampi. Dvayaṃ dadhisāre. Dadhino maṇḍaṃ sāro dadhimaṇḍaṃ. Masa parimāṇe, thu, sassa to, matthu napuṃsake.

500. Ghee extracted on that very day from curds or milk, and its precursor, is called ‘navanīta’. That which is produced from fresh curds and so forth is ‘nonīta’; also ‘vassa’ and ‘navanīta’. Two terms for the essence of curds. The cream, which is the essence of curds, is ‘dadhimaṇḍa’. ‘Matthu’ is from the root ‘mas’, to measure, with the suffix ‘thu’, where ‘s’ becomes ‘t’; ‘matthu’ is neuter.

Catukkaṃ khīre, khi khaye, īro. Duhyateti duddhaṃ, duha papūraṇe, to. Pā pāne, pātabbanti payo, ṇyo, āssattaṃ. Thanato sambhūtaṃ thaññaṃ.

Four terms for milk. ‘Khīra’ is from the root ‘khi’, to diminish, with the suffix ‘īra’. That which is milked is ‘duddha’, from the root ‘duh’, to milk, with the suffix ‘to’. That which is to be drunk is ‘payo’, from the root ‘pā’, to drink, with the suffix ‘ṇya’, and ‘ā’ becomes ‘a’. That which is produced from the breast is ‘thañña’.

Dvayaṃ takke. Tīṇi kāni jalabhāgāni ettha santīti takkaṃ, issattaṃ, dvittañca. Matha viloḷane, to, “yathāgamamikāro”ti ikārāgamo, aññatra pana –

Two terms for buttermilk. ‘Takka’ is so called because it contains three parts water, with the vowel becoming short and the consonant doubled. ‘Mathita’ is from the root ‘math’, to churn, with the suffix ‘to’; the augment ‘i’ is added according to the rule, but elsewhere—

“Addhodakasamāyuttaṃ, udassitamudīritaṃ;

Takkaṃ tibhāgasaṃyuttaṃ, mathitanti gatodaka”nti. –

‘Udassita’ is said to be that which is mixed with half water; ‘takka’ is that which is mixed with a third part of water, and ‘mathita’ is that from which the water has been removed.

Takkamathitā bhedenuttā, gatodakamiti nijjalaṃ.

‘Takka’ and ‘mathita’ are stated with a distinction. ‘Gatodaka’ means waterless.

“Nijjalaṃ mathitaṃ siniddhaṃ, takkantu jalapādikaṃ;

Udassitaṃ jaladdhañca, sotakhyantu samodaka”nti. –

‘Mathita’ is waterless and creamy. ‘Takka’, however, has a quarter part water. ‘Udassita’ has half water, and ‘sotakhya’ is with water.

Ratanamālā.

Ratanamālā.

501. Khīrādayo [M 0.0338] pañca goto sañjātarasā. Khīraṃ navaṃ, dadhi khīrato jātaṃ. “Khīrajaṃ dadhimaṅgala”nti hi ratanāmālā. Dhā dhāraṇe. I, dvittaṃ, nipātanā. Dadhito vā ghataṃ, nonītañca. Sabbaseso takkaṃ, khīratoyeva vā.

501. The five products beginning with milk are essences born from the cow. Milk is fresh; curds are born from milk. Indeed, the Ratanamālā states: ‘Curds born of milk are auspicious’. ‘Dadhi’ is from the root ‘dhā’, to hold, with the suffix ‘i’, with doubling, by irregular formation. Ghee and fresh butter are from curds. Buttermilk is the remainder of all, or it is from milk itself.

Chakkaṃ eḷake. Bādhiyamānopi na ravatīti urabbho. Ru sadde, bho. Meṇḍa kuṭilatthe, ko. Misati paddhate aññamaññaṃ meso. “Saṃhasane meso, paddhāya’masamunnatī”ti nānatthasaṅgahe. Na raṇatīti uraṇo, raṇa sadde. Ava rakkhaṇe, i. Avi, “avayo selamesakkā”tyamarasīho amara 23.207. “Ajī”tipi pāṭho. Ila gatiyaṃ, ṇvu. Uṇṇāyupyatra, uṇṇāyogā uṇṇāyu, yu, luhu ubhe ulomasasaddā ca rabhasena vuttā.

Six terms for the ram. Though being oppressed, it does not cry out, hence ‘urabbha’. From the root ‘ru’, in the sense of sound, with the suffix ‘bha’. The root ‘meṇḍa’ is in the sense of crookedness, with the suffix ‘ka’. They mingle and butt each other, hence ‘mesa’. In the Nānatthasaṅgaha it is said: “In jesting, the ram, by butting, is not elevated”. It does not make a sound, hence ‘uraṇa’; from the root ‘raṇa’, in the sense of sound. From the root ‘ava’, to protect, with the suffix ‘i’, is ‘avi’. Amarasīha says: “avayo selamesakkā”. ‘Ajī’ is also a reading. From the root ‘ila’, to go, with the suffix ‘ṇvu’. ‘Uṇṇāyu’ is also used here; from its association with wool, it is ‘uṇṇāyu’, with the suffix ‘yu’. The words ‘luhu’ and ‘uloma’ are also spoken with force.

502. Tikaṃ aje. Vasa nivāse. To, vasto, vattopi. Aññe tu “vasa gandhaadane”ti curādimāhu, aja gamane, na jāyatīti vā ajo. Chindanto gacchatīti chagalako, cho chedane, gamu gamane, ṇo, massa lo, ossattaṃ, sakatthe ko, chakalakopi. Chāgopyatra. Dvayaṃ karabhe. Vasa kantimhi, to, vassottaṃ, usa [M 0.0339] dāhe vā, ottādi, oṭṭho, dantacchadepi. Kara karaṇe, abho. “Kharabho”tyeke paṭhanti. Kamelako, mayo, mahāṅgopyatra.

502. Three terms for the goat. From the root ‘vasa’, to dwell, with the suffix ‘to’, is ‘vasto’; also ‘vatto’. Others, however, say the root ‘vasa’ is in the sense of taking scent, from the curādi class. ‘Aja’ is from the root ‘aja’, to go, or it means ‘not born’. It goes while cutting, hence ‘chagalaka’; from the root ‘cho’, to cut, and ‘gamu’, to go, with the suffix ‘ṇo’, where ‘m’ becomes ‘l’, and a vowel change occurs, with the suffix ‘ko’ in its own sense; also ‘chakalaka’. ‘Chāgo’ is also used here. Two terms for the camel. From the root ‘vasa’, in the sense of beauty, with the suffix ‘to’. Or from the root ‘usa’, to burn, with the suffix ‘oṭṭha’, is ‘oṭṭho’, which also means lip. From the root ‘kara’, to do, with the suffix ‘abho’, is ‘karabho’. Some read ‘kharabho’. ‘Kamelaka’, ‘maya’, and ‘mahāṅga’ are also used here.

Dvayaṃ gadrabhe. Gadatismā rabho, gadrabho. Khaṃ kaṇṭhavivaraṃ mahantamassatthīti kharo, ro. Cakkavā, bāleyyo, rāsabhopyatra. Cakkayogā, vantu. Balayuttattā bāleyyo. Rasa sadde, abho. Dvayaṃ aviyaṃ. Uraṇassa ayaṃ uraṇī. Avino esā avī. Ajāsaddo eko chāgiyaṃ. Aññe tu “uraṇī tu ajī ajā”tipi pāṭhaṃ vatvā tiṇṇampi uraṇīpariyāyattaṃ vadanti, tesaṃ mate ajīajāsaddāpi uraṇīpariyāyā atthīti daṭṭhabbā. Atha vā tikaṃ ajiyaṃ. Uraṇasaddassāpi ajapariyāyassa sambhavato “uraṇī tu ajī ajā”ti vuttaṃ, vakkhati hi anekatthavagge “ummāre eḷako aje”ti abhidhāna 1124 gāthā, uraṇapariyāyo hettha eḷako.

Two terms for the donkey. From ‘gadati’ and ‘rabha’ comes ‘gadrabha’. Because it has a large throat-opening, it is called ‘khara’, with the suffix ‘ra’. ‘Cakkavā’, ‘bāleyya’, and ‘rāsabha’ are also used here. From being yoked to a wheel is ‘cakkavā’, with the suffix ‘vantu’. Because it is yoked with strength, it is called ‘bāleyya’. From the root ‘ras’, in the sense of sound, with the suffix ‘abha’, is ‘rāsabha’. Two terms for the ewe. The female of the ‘uraṇa’ is ‘uraṇī’. The female of the ‘avi’ is ‘avī’. The word ‘ajā’ is one term for the she-goat. Others, however, having stated the reading “uraṇī, ajī, ajā,” say that all three are synonyms for ‘uraṇī’. According to their view, the words ‘ajī’ and ‘ajā’ are also to be understood as synonyms for ‘uraṇī’. Alternatively, there are three terms for the she-goat. Since the word ‘uraṇa’ can also be a synonym for ‘aja’, it is said, “uraṇī, ajī, ajā.” For it will be stated in the Anekatthavagga: “eḷako for ummāra and aja”; here, ‘eḷaka’ is a synonym for ‘uraṇa’.

Vessavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Vessavagga is concluded.

503. Tikaṃ sudde. Sada assādane, do, assu. Antavaṇṇo lāmakavaṇṇo. Vasa secane, vasetabbo asucitattā vasalo, alo. Yatra yatra vā muttaṃ karīsaṃ siñcatīti vasalo, alo, jaghaññajopyatra. Brahmuno jaghaññaṅge pāde jāto jaghaññajo.

503. Three terms for a Sudda. From the root ‘sad’, in the sense of tasting, with the suffix ‘da’, is ‘sudda’. ‘Antavaṇṇa’ means the lowest caste. From the root ‘vas’, to sprinkle; one to be settled due to impurity is a ‘vasala’, with the suffix ‘ala’. Or, one who sprinkles urine and feces everywhere is a ‘vasala’, with the suffix ‘ala’. ‘Jaghaññaja’ is also used here. Born from the lowest limb of Brahmā, the foot, is a ‘jaghaññaja’.

Māgadhādayo [M 0.0340] sūtapariyantā vijātiyamātāpitikattā ubhayavaṇṇoppattiyā saṃkiṇṇajātiyo iccattho, bhinnajātisaṃsaggo eva hi saṅkaro. Suddena sambandhāya khattāya jāto putto māgadho. Thutikriyāvutti. Suddāya sambandhena khattiyena jāto uggo, uca samavāye, ṇo.

The Māgadhas and others, up to the Sūtas, are of mixed birth, due to being born from parents of different castes, thus having arisen from two castes; this is the meaning. For the mixing of different castes is indeed intermingling. The son born from a Sudda man and a Khattiya woman is a Māgadha. His profession is praise. The one born from a Khattiya man and a Sudda woman is an Ugga; from the root ‘uca’, in the sense of assembling, with the suffix ‘ṇo’.

504. Brāhmaṇiyā sambandhena khattiyena jāto sūto, su abhibhave, to, dīghādi.

504. The one born from a Khattiya man and a Brāhmaṇī woman is a Sūta; from the root ‘su’, in the sense of overcoming, with the suffix ‘to’, and lengthening of the vowel, etc.

Suddāvessahi karaṇo-mbaṭṭho vessādvijātihi. Māhiṃso vessākhattajo, khattā khattāya suddajo.

The Karaṇa is born from a Vessa man and a Sudda woman; the Ambaṭṭha from a twice-born man and a Vessa woman. The Māhiṃsa is born from a Vessa man and a Khattiya woman; the Khattā from a Khattiya man and a Sudda woman.

Brāhmaṇīkhattajo sūto,

Tassaṃ vedehako vesse;

Rathakāro tu māhiṃsā,

Karaṇyaṃ yassa sambhavo;

Caṇḍālo nāma janito,

Brāhmaṇīvasalehi yo.

The Sūta is born from a Khattiya man and a Brāhmaṇī woman. The Vedehaka is born from a Vessa man and that same Brāhmaṇī woman. The Rathakāra, however, is one whose origin is from a Māhiṃsa man and a Karaṇī woman. The one who is born from a Vasala man and a Brāhmaṇī woman is named Caṇḍāla.

Tatra karaṇo lipilekhanavutti, ambaṭṭho vicikicchāvutti.

Among them, the profession of a Karaṇa is that of a scribe, and the profession of an Ambaṭṭha is that of a physician.

Dvayaṃ sippini. Karoti nimmināti citralepyādikanti kāru, ṇu. Sippamassatthīti sippiko. Sajātīnaṃ tesaṃ sippīnaṃ saṅghāto “seṇī”tyuccate. Si sevāyaṃ, ṇi.

Two terms for the artisan. One who makes and fashions things like paintings and plasterwork is a ‘kāru’, with the suffix ‘ṇu’. Because he possesses a craft, he is a ‘sippika’. A guild of such artisans of the same kind is called a ‘seṇī’; from the root ‘si’, in the sense of service, with the suffix ‘ṇi’.

505. Tacchakādayo [M 0.0341] ime pañca kāravo sippino nāma siyuṃ. Vuttañca –

505. These five, the carpenter and so on, may be called craftsmen and artisans. And it is said:

“Tacchako tantavāyo ca, rajako ca nahāpito;

Pañcamo cammakāro ca, kāravo sippino matā”ti.

The carpenter, the weaver, the dyer, the barber, and the fifth, the leatherworker—these are considered craftsmen and artisans.

506. Pañcakaṃ tacchake. Taccha tanukaraṇe. Tacchati tanuṃ karotīti tacchako, ṇvu, vaddhayati chindatīti vaddhakī, vaddha chedane, curādi, “chedane cāpi vaddhana”nti ratanamālā, ṇvu. Sakatthe ī, vaddhakī, vaḍḍhakīpi. Palādyummānappakārena gaṇḍati chindatīti palagaṇḍo. Gaṇḍa chedanopalepanasannicayavadanekadesesu. Palagaṇḍo sudhājīvinyapi. Ṭhā gatinivattiyaṃ,ti, pakāravaṇṇāgamo. Ṭhātissa thopi. Rathaṃ karotīti, kammani ṇo, rathakāro, cammakārepi. Dvayaṃ suvaṇṇakāre. Nāḷiṃ dhamati mukhe vināsayitvā mukhavāyunā aggidīpanatthaṃ nāḷiṃ saddāpayatīti nāḷidhamo.

506. Five terms for the carpenter. The root ‘taccha’ is in the sense of making thin. One who makes thin is a ‘tacchaka’, with the suffix ‘ṇvu’. One who increases or cuts is a ‘vaddhakī’; from the root ‘vaddha’, in the sense of cutting, of the curādi class. The Ratanamālā says: “vaddhana is also in the sense of cutting”. The suffix is ‘ṇvu’, and ‘ī’ in its own sense, hence ‘vaddhakī’; also ‘vaḍḍhakī’. One who cuts according to measures such as the pala is a ‘palagaṇḍa’. The root ‘gaṇḍa’ is in the senses of cutting, smearing, accumulating, speaking, and parts. ‘Palagaṇḍa’ also refers to a plasterer. From the root ‘ṭhā’, in the sense of standing, with the suffix ‘ti’, and the addition of the letter ‘pa’, is ‘thapati’. One who makes chariots is a ‘rathakāra’, with the suffix ‘ṇo’ in the accusative sense; this term also applies to a leatherworker. Two terms for the goldsmith. One who blows a tube with the breath of his mouth to kindle a fire is a ‘nāḷidhamo’.

507. Athoparaṃ pukkusaṃyāvapādena nāmaṃ. Ve tantasantāne, tantaṃ vāyatīti, ṇo. Pesa peraṇapayatanagatīsu. Pesanaṃ peso, taṃ karotīti, ṇo. Kuvindopyatra[M 0.0342], kucchitaṃ vindatīti kuvindo. Mālāsippayogā, mālāpanayogā vā māliko, iko.

507. Furthermore, the names up to Pukkusa are given in this section. From the root ‘ve’, in the sense of weaving threads; one who weaves thread is a ‘tantavāya’, with the suffix ‘ṇo’. The root ‘pesa’ is in the senses of sending, striving, and going. Sending is ‘pesa’; one who does this is a ‘pesakāra’, with the suffix ‘ṇo’. ‘Kuvinda’ is also used here; one who finds what is contemptible is a ‘kuvinda’. From connection with the craft of garlands, or from connection with making garlands, is ‘mālika’, with the suffix ‘ika’.

Kuṃ lalayati icchatīti kulālo, lala icchāyaṃ, ṇo. Dvayaṃ sūcikammopajīvini. Sūcivānakammaṃ duvidhaṃ sūcanaṃ, tunnañcāti, tatra tunnavānakammena pavattinimittena tunnavāyo, sūcivānasippayogā sociko.

One who desires to fashion the earth is a ‘kulāla’; from the root ‘lala’, in the sense of desiring, with the suffix ‘ṇo’. Two terms for one who lives by needlework. Needlework is of two kinds: piercing and sewing. Among these, a ‘tunnavāya’ is so called by reason of his occupation of sewing. A ‘socika’ is so called from his connection with the craft of needlework.

508. Cammaṃ karoti vikāramāpādayatīti, kammani ṇo. Pādukaropyatra. Kappa chedane, ṇvu. Naha soceyye, divādito nipātanā pakārāgamādi, na hāpetīti vā nahāpito, hā parihāne, ṇāpe paccayo, to, essittaṃ, saññāsaddattā nassapakati. Khurī, muṇḍī, divākittipyatra. Khuravā khurī, muṇḍavā muṇḍī, muṇḍo, muṇḍī, muṇḍakoti pasiddhi. Divā divase kitti byāpāro assa divākitti. “Caṇḍāle tu divākitti, nahāpito”ti ruddo.

508. One who works with leather and brings about a change is a `cammakāra`, with the suffix `ṇo` in the sense of action. `Pādukara` (shoemaker) is also included here. `Kappa` is in the sense of cutting, with the suffix `ṇvu`. From `naha` in the sense of purity, by irregular derivation from the `divādi` class, with the addition of `pa`, etc. Or, one who does not cause to diminish is a `nahāpito`; from the root `hā` in the sense of diminishing, with the suffix `ṇāpe` and `to`, and the elision of `e`. Because it is a proper noun, it is not in its natural form. `Khurī`, `muṇḍī`, and `divākitti` are also included here. One with a razor (`khuravā`) is a `khurī`; one who shaves (`muṇḍavā`) is a `muṇḍī`. `Muṇḍo`, `muṇḍī`, and `muṇḍako` are well-known. One whose activity (`kitti`) is during the day (`divā`) is a `divākitti`. Rudda says: "A `caṇḍāla` is a `divākitti`, and a barber is a `nahāpito`."

Rañjate suttaṃ rattamāpajjate yasmiṃ, sa raṅgo. Haritālamanosilādi, tamājīvatīti, kammani ṇo.

That in which thread is dyed or becomes colored is `raṅgo` (dye). Orpiment, realgar, and the like are used. One who lives by that is a `rajaka`, with the suffix `ṇo` in the sense of action.

Puñjaṃ kasatīti pukkuso, nipātanā, atha vā “pu”iti purisassa nāmaṃ, taṃ kuseti apanetīti pukkuso. Pupphaṃ vuccati karīsaṃ, kusumaṃ vā, taṃ chaḍḍetīti, ṇvu. Chaḍḍa apanayane.

One who scrapes a heap is a `pukkuso`, by irregular derivation. Or else, `pu` is a name for a person; one who reviles or removes that person is a `pukkuso`. `Puppha` is said to mean feces, or a flower; one who discards that is a `pupphachaḍḍaka`, with the suffix `ṇvu`. `Chaḍḍa` is in the sense of removing.

509. Venādayo [M 0.0343] tayo samā tulyatthā. Veṇunā jīvatīti veno. Ṇassa nattaṃ. Veṇopi. Veṇuvettādīnaṃ vikati vilīvā, tehi vilīvaṃ karotīti vilīvakāro. Naḷopi veṇuvettādīnaṃyeva vikati, taṃ karotīti, kammani ṇo. Naḷehi vā vilīvaṃ karotīti naḷakāro.

509. The three terms beginning with `vena` are synonymous. One who lives by bamboo (`veṇu`) is a `veno`; the `ṇ` becomes `n`. `Veṇo` is also a term. The product of bamboo, rattan, and so forth, is `vilīvā` (plaiting); one who makes `vilīva` from them is a `vilīvakāro`. `Naḷa` (reed) is also a product of bamboo, rattan, and so forth; one who makes it is a `naḷakāro`, with the suffix `ṇo` in the sense of action. Or, one who makes `vilīva` from reeds is a `naḷakāro`.

Ito paraṃ soṇḍikaṃ yāva pādena nāmaṃ. Cunda chedane, sañcodane ca. Cunda nisāmane vā. Bhamu anavaṭṭhāne, taṃ karotīti bhamakāro. Kara karaṇe, māro, kammāro, kammani ṇvu. Lohakārako. Ākaroṭṭhitaṃ āṭavoṭṭhitaṃ (ka.) yo lohaṃ dhamitvā saṅkharoti, tatrāpi lohakārako.

From here onwards, up to `soṇḍika`, are the names by the verse-foot. `Cunda` is in the sense of cutting, and also urging. Or `cunda` is in the sense of observing. `Bhamu` is in the sense of not standing still; one who does that is a `bhamakāro`. `Kara` is in the sense of doing; `kammāro` (blacksmith) is formed with the suffix `ṇvu` in the sense of action. `Lohakārako` (metalworker) is also a term. One who, having smelted metal extracted from a mine, fashions it—he too is a `lohakārako`.

510. Rajakassa dve kammāni celadhovanaṃ, rajanañca. Tatra celadhovano ninnejako, ṇvu, niji suddhiyaṃ, niji soceyyasocanesu vā. Vattharañjanā rajako. Ranja raṅge, ṇvu. Netīti nettiko. Sakatthe ko, nettiyaṃ udakanayena niyuttoti vā nettiko, nettiyā mātikāya netīti vā nettiko, iko. Udakaṃ hāretīti udahārako. Kalopo, ṇvu.

510. A dyer has two tasks: washing clothes and dyeing. Among these, the one who washes clothes is a `ninnejako`, with the suffix `ṇvu`, from the root `niji` in the sense of purity, or `niji` in the senses of cleanliness and purification. From dyeing cloth, he is a `rajako`; from the root `ranja` in the sense of coloring, with the suffix `ṇvu`. One who leads is a `nettiko`. The suffix `ko` is in its own sense. Or, one who is appointed to lead water by means of a water-channel is a `nettiko`. Or, one who leads by means of a water-course is a `nettiko`, with the suffix `iko`. One who carries water is an `udahārako`. From `kalopa`, with the suffix `ṇvu`.

Vīṇāvādanasīlattā vīṇāvādi. Vīṇāvādanasippayogā veṇiko. Usumhi, usukāro vā vaḍḍhakī usuvaḍḍhakī, [M 0.0344] etena vaḍḍhakīsaddassa sabbesampi sippikānaṃ vācakatā dīpitā, tena suvaṇṇavaḍḍhakī, tantavaḍḍhakītyādayopi yojjā.

Due to the habit of playing the lute, he is a `vīṇāvādi` (lute-player). From connection with the craft of lute-playing comes `veṇiko`. In the case of an arrow (`usu`), an arrow-maker (`usukāro`) or a carpenter (`vaḍḍhakī`) is an `usuvaḍḍhakī` (arrow-fletcher). By this, the applicability of the word `vaḍḍhakī` to all artisans is shown. Therefore, `suvaṇṇavaḍḍhakī` (gold-worker), `tantavaḍḍhakī` (weaver), and so forth should also be applied.

511. Veṇuṃ vaṃsaṃ dhamatīti veṇudhamo. Veṇuvādanasippayogā veṇaviko, ṇiko. Yo pāṇineva pāṇantare murajādisaddaṃ uṭṭhāpayati, so pāṇivādo. Pāṇiṃ hantīti pāṇigho. Pāṇiyopi. Pāṇivādanasippayogā pāṇiyo, yo.

511. One who blows a bamboo flute is a `veṇudhamo`. From connection with the craft of flute-playing comes `veṇaviko`, with the suffix `ṇiko`. One who produces sounds like drums and so forth by striking one hand against the other is a `pāṇivādo`. One who strikes with the hand is a `pāṇigho`. `Pāṇiyo` is also a term. From connection with the craft of playing with the hands comes `pāṇiyo`, with the suffix `yo`.

Pūpena jīvatīti pūpiyo, pūpo paṇiyo vikkeyyo yassa. Pānāgāraṃ suṇḍā, taṭṭhattā surā soṇḍā, taṃ vikkiṇātīti soṇḍiko, “nenaniddiṭṭhamanicca”nti kātanta 1.2.18 naghaṭītaṃ aniccaṃ (paribhāsendusekhara 97) paribhāsato vuddhi. Majjaṃ vikkiṇāti sīlena. Maṇḍahāropyatra, maṇḍaṃ surāsambandhamaggabhāgaṃ harati uddharatīti maṇḍahāro.

One who lives by cakes is a `pūpiyo`; one whose salable commodity is cake. A liquor-shop is a `suṇḍā`. Because it is located there, liquor is `soṇḍā`. One who sells that is a `soṇḍiko`. By the grammatical rule `nenaniddiṭṭhamaniccam`, there is `vuddhi` (vowel strengthening). He sells liquor by habit. `Maṇḍahāro` is also included here. One who carries away or removes the scum (`maṇḍa`), the upper part connected to liquor, is a `maṇḍahāro`.

512. Dvayaṃ indacālakhye kapaṭe. Mayena asurena sure vañcayituṃ calayituṃ (ka.) payuttattā mayassa ayaṃ māyā, mayo eva sambaro, tassāyaṃ sambarī, ṇī, nadādi. Dvayaṃ māyākāre. Indajāle niyutto indajāliko. Pāṭihārakopi. Paṭiharati nayanamanenāti pāṭihārako, ṇvu.

512. Two terms for deception, known as `indacāla`. Because this illusion (`māyā`) was employed by the Asura Maya to deceive the gods, it is Maya's illusion. Maya himself is Sambara. This illusion belongs to him, hence `sambarī`, with the suffix `ṇī`, like `nadī`, etc. Two terms for the illusionist. One engaged in `indacāla` is an `indajāliko`. `Pāṭihārako` (conjurer) is also a term. Because one diverts the eye by this, he is called a `pāṭihārako`, with the suffix `ṇvu`.

513. Ariyāsāmaññaṃ [M 0.0345] orabbhikādīnaṃ catunnamatthe. Ye urabbhaṃ eḷakaṃ hantvā jīvantīti orabbhikā. Sūkare hantvā jīvanti sūkarikā, tathā magaṃ hantvā jīvanti māgavikā. Sakuṇe pakkhino hantvā jīvanti sākuṇikā, iti kamato bhavanti.

513. A common term for the four beginning with `orabbhika`. Those who live by killing sheep (`urabbha`, `eḷaka`) are called `orabbhikā`. Those who live by killing pigs are `sūkarikā`; similarly, those who live by killing deer are `māgavikā`. Those who live by killing birds (`sakuṇa`, `pakkhī`) are `sākuṇikā`. Thus they are, in order.

514. Dvayaṃ jālike. Vāgurā migabandhanajālaṃ, tāya caratīti vāguriko, vākarikopi. Vaka ādāne, aro, ā, vākarā, tāya caratīti vākariko, pubbapakkhe kassa go, assu ca, vāguriko. Dvayaṃ bhāravāhe. Bhāraṃ vahatīti, kammani ṇo. Bhāraṃ vahatīti bhāriko.

514. Two terms for a net-user. A `vāgurā` is a net for trapping animals; one who goes about with it is a `vāguriko`, also `vākariko`. `Vaka` is the root in the sense of seizing; with the suffixes `aro` and `ā`, it forms `vākarā`; one who goes about with it is a `vākariko`. In the former case, `ka` becomes `ga`, and there is `u`, thus forming `vāguriko`. Two terms for a burden-bearer. One who carries a burden is a `bhāravāha`, formed with the suffix `ṇo` in the agentive sense. One who carries a burden is also called `bhāriko`.

Tikaṃ vetanopajīvini kiṅkare. Vetanena jīvatīti vetaniko. Bhato vetanena kīto, so eva bhatako, saññāyaṃ vā ko. Bhatiṃ vetanaṃ bhuñjatīti vā bhatako, ko, issattaṃ. Kammaṃ karotīti kammakaro, kammakāropi.

Three terms for a wage-earner or servant. One who lives by wages is a `vetaniko`. One who is supported or bought with wages is a `bhataka`; or the `ko` is in the sense of a designation. Or, one who enjoys wages is a `bhatako`, with the suffix `ko`, implying ownership. One who performs work is a `kammakaro`, also `kammakāro`.

Chakkaṃ [M 0.0346] dāse. Kiñci karotīti kiṅkaro, “ahamajja kiṃ karissāmī”ti bhattu kattabbakiccayācanattā vā kiṅkaro. Dāsa dāhe. Dāsantetassāti dāso, a. Ciṭa pesanīye, pesīyate sāmināti ceṭo, ṇo, sakatthe ko, ceṭako. Pisa pesanīye, ṇo, sassa dvittaṃ. Bhara dhāraṇaposanesu, bharīyatīti bhacco, “riccā”tiyogavibhāgena bharāditopi riccapaccayo, “ramhi ranto rādino”ti ralopo ca, bhacco. Paricarati sāmīnanti paricāriko. Dāsero, dāseyyo, goppako, niyojjo, abhujissopyatra.

Six terms for a slave. One who does something is a `kiṅkaro`; or a `kiṅkaro` because he asks his master, 'What shall I do today?' regarding the duty to be performed. `Dāsa` is the root in the sense of burning. One who is bound is a `dāso`, with the suffix `a`. `Ciṭa` is the root in the sense of sending; one who is sent by his master is a `ceṭo`, with the suffix `ṇo`; or `ceṭako`, with `ko` in the same sense. `Pisa` is the root in the sense of sending; with the suffix `ṇo`, and the doubling of `s`, it forms `pisso`. `Bhara` is the root in the sense of bearing and sustaining; one who is maintained is a `bhacco`. By a division of the rule `riccā`, the `ricca` suffix also comes from `bhara`, etc., and there is elision of `ra` according to `ramhi ranto rādino`, hence `bhacco`. One who serves his masters is a `paricāriko`. Other terms include `dāsero`, `dāseyyo`, `goppako`, `niyojjo`, and `abhujisso` (an unfree person).

515. Te ca dāsā antojātādivasena catudhā siyuṃ. Antogehe dāsiyā kucchimhi jāto antojāto, dhanena kīto dhanaṃ datvā dāsabhāvaṃ gato dhanakkīto, sayameva dāsabyopagato bhayanivāraṇādyatthaṃ dāsabhāvamupagato ca karamarabhāvena ānīto karamarānīto ca, iccevaṃ te dāsā catudhā siyunti pakataṃ.

515. And those slaves are of four types, beginning with the house-born. One born in the house in the womb of a female slave is an `antojāto` (house-born). One bought with money, or one who has entered into servitude by giving money, is a `dhanakkīto` (purchased). One who has voluntarily undertaken slavery (`dāsabyopagato`) for the purpose of avoiding fear and so forth. And one brought as a captive (`karamarānīto`). Thus, it is stated that those slaves are of four types.

516. Dvayaṃ bhujisse. Bhuja pālanajjhohāresu, iso, dvittaṃ. Tikaṃ nīce. Nihīnaṃ cinotīti nīco, ṇo, rassassa dīghatā. Jama adane, mo. Nicchayena hāniṃ gacchatīti [M 0.0347] nihīnako, hā parihāne, i gatiyaṃ, yu, sakatthe ko.

516. Two terms for a freedman. From the root `bhuja` in the senses of protecting and eating, with the suffix `iso`, and doubling of the consonant. Three terms for a low person. One who accumulates what is low is a `nīco`, with the suffix `ṇo`, and lengthening of the short vowel. From the root `jama` in the sense of eating, with the suffix `mo`. One who certainly goes to ruin is a `nihīnako`; from the root `hā` in the sense of diminishing, and `i` in the sense of going, with the suffix `yu`, and `ko` in its own sense.

“Vivaṇṇo pāparo nīco, pākito ca puthujjano;

Nihīno’pasado jammo, khullako itaro ca so”. –

"Of low caste, wicked, base, common, and a worldling; degraded, contemptible, low-born, petty, and the other."

Tyamarakose amara 20.16. Vigato vaṇṇo assamo yassa vivaṇṇo. “Assamo brahmacāriyādi, catukkepi maṭhepi ce”ti nānatthasaṅgahe. Pāpaṃ rātīti pāparo. Pakatiyaṃ yathājātabhāve bhavo vijjamāno, na tu byāpāroti pākito, ṇo. Sajjanehi puthubhūto jano puthujjano. Apakaṭṭhaṃ sadati gacchatīti apasado. Khudaṃ lātīti khullo, dassa lo, khullo eva khullako. Itaṃ kampitaṃ rātīti itaro.

In the Amarakośa. One whose caste (`vaṇṇa`) or stage of life (`assama`) is gone is `vivaṇṇo`. As stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: '`Assamo` means celibacy, etc., and also in the fourfold division or in a monastery.' One who takes up evil is `pāparo`. One existing by nature in their original state, not by action, is `pākito`, with the suffix `ṇo`. A person separate from the virtuous is a `puthujjano`. One who goes to a low state is an `apasado`. One who takes what is small is `khullo`, with `la` for `da`; `khullako` is simply `khullo`. One who takes up what is gone or shaken is `itaro`.

Dvayaṃ anālase. Kusītassa bhāvo kosajjaṃ, taṃ yassa natthīti nikkosajjo. Lasa kantiyaṃ, appaṃ lasatīti kilāsu, ṇu, na kilāsu akilāsu. Manda supane, a. Na lasati kīḷatīti alaso.

Two terms for the diligent. The state of a lazy person is `kosajja`; one who does not have that is `nikkosajjo`. `Lasa` is the root in the sense of shining; one who shines little is `kilāsu`, with the suffix `ṇu`; one who is not `kilāsu` is `akilāsu`. `Manda` is the root in the sense of sleeping, with the suffix `a`. One who does not shine or play is `alaso`.

517. Catukkaṃ caṇḍāle. Saṃ sunakhaṃ pacatīti sapāko. Caṇḍa caṇḍikke, ālo. Mataṅgassa apaccaṃ mātaṅgo. Cu cavane, ṇvu, cavako. “Plavako”tipi pāṭho, plava gatiyaṃ, ṇvu.

517. Four terms for a `caṇḍāla`. One who cooks a dog is a `sapāko`. `Caṇḍa` is the root in the sense of fierceness, with the suffix `ālo`. The descendant of Mataṅga is a `mātaṅgo`. `Cu` is the root in the sense of moving; with the suffix `ṇvu`, it forms `cavako`. The reading `plavako` also exists, derived from `plava` in the sense of movement, with the suffix `ṇvu`.

“Caṇḍālaplavamātaṅgā[M 0.0348], divākittijanaṅgamā;

Nisādasapacāante-vāsī caṇḍālapukkusā”. –

"Caṇḍālas, plavakas, mātaṅgas, divākittis, janaṅgamas; Nisādas, sapacas, antevāsīs, caṇḍālas, and pukkusas."

Tyamarakose amara 20.19-20.

In the Amarakośa.

Milakkhajātyādayo mahāraññanivāsino tabbhedā tassa caṇḍālassa visesā.

The Milakkha caste and others, dwelling in the great forest, are divisions and particular types of that `caṇḍāla`.

Gomaṃsabhakkhako yo tu,

Lokabāhyañca bhāsate;

Sabbācāravihīno’yaṃ,

Milakkhajāti vuccate cintāmaṇiṭīkā 20.20.

One who eats the flesh of cattle, and speaks what is contrary to worldly custom; this one, devoid of all good conduct, is said to be of the milakkha race.

Milakkha abyattasadde. Milakkhante abyattaṃ bhāsanteti milakkhā, tesaṃ jāti yoni milakkhajāti. Mayūrapiñchādiparidhāno kirāto, kira vikiraṇe, ato, kiratīti kirāto. Kiratopi. Pattaparidhāno savaro. Sava gatiyaṃ, aro. Ādinā pulindo, pula mahatthe, do, pulindo, sabhāsā byavahārī desantarabhāsānabhiñño, pulindo savarapariyāyoti keci.

Milakkha is used in the sense of indistinct sound. Those who speak indistinctly are milakkhā; their birth or origin is milakkhajāti. A kirāto is one adorned with peacock feathers, etc.; derived from the root kira in the sense of scattering, with the suffix ato; one who scatters is a kirāto. Also kirato. A savaro is one clad in leaves; derived from the root sava in the sense of movement, with the suffix aro. Furthermore, pulindo, derived from the root pula in the sense of greatness, with the suffix do, forms pulindo; one who uses a local language, unskilled in foreign languages. Some say pulindo is a synonym for savaro.

518-519. Tikaṃ luddamatte, ayampi milakkhappakāro. Migamacchādīnaṃ nisādanato māraṇato nesādo. Ludha upaghāte[M 0.0349], do, dhassa do, lū chedane vā, do, ubhayatrāpi sakatthe ko. Vijjhatīti byādho, rassassa dīghatā. Dvayaṃ migaludde. Mige hantīti migavo, vo. Mige vijjhatīti migabyadho.

Three terms for a hunter; this too is a type of milakkha. A nesādo is one who kills deer, fish, and so forth, by lying in wait. Ludha is the root in the sense of harming; with the suffix do, 'dh' becomes 'd'. Or lū is the root in the sense of cutting, with the suffix do; in both cases, 'ko' is in its own sense. One who pierces is a byādho, with elongation of the short vowel. Two terms for a deer-hunter. One who kills deer is a migavo, with the suffix vo. One who pierces deer is a migabyadho.

Siloko sunakhe. Saramā sunī, tassāpaccaṃ sārameyyo, ṇeyyo. Sundaraṃ nakhametassa sunakho, sunassa vā pāṭipadikassa unakho, suna gatiyaṃ vā, kho, evaṃ sabbatra pāṭipadikavasena vā dhātuvasena vā rūpasiddhi veditabbā. Suna gatiyaṃ, sunassa vā uno. Soṇa vaṇṇagatīsu, suna gatiyaṃ vā, ṇo, ṇattaṃ, sunassa vā oṇo. Kuka ādāne, uro, kukkuro. Suna gatiyaṃ, ussa vādese svāno, uvādese suvāno. Mige sarati hiṃsatīti sāḷūro, ūro, rassa ḷo. Dīghādimhi sūno. Ussātte sāno. Nalope ussātte sā, ayaṃ pume, koleyyo, migadaṃsako, bhasakopyatra, kule gehe bhavo koleyyo. Migaṃ daṃsatīti migadaṃsako. Bhasati bukkatīti bhasako, bhasa bhaṇane.

A section on the dog. Saramā is a female dog; her offspring is sārameyyo, with the suffix ṇeyyo. One whose claws are beautiful is a sunakho; or unakho is derived from the nominal stem suna; or from the root suna in the sense of movement, with the suffix kho. Thus, in all instances, the word formation should be understood based on either the nominal stem or the root. From the root suna in the sense of movement, or uno from suna. From the root soṇa in the sense of color and movement; or from the root suna in the sense of movement, with the suffix ṇo, and cerebralization; or oṇo from suna. From the root kuka in the sense of taking, with the suffix uro, forms kukkuro. From the root suna in the sense of movement; with 'v' as a substitute for 'u', it forms svāno; with the substitution of 'uva', it forms suvāno. One who pursues or harms deer is a sāḷūro, with the suffix ūro, and 'ḷ' for 'r'. With an initial long vowel, it is sūno. Sāno is formed with 'ussātta'. With the elision of 'na' and with 'ussātta', it forms sā; this is masculine. Koleyyo, migadaṃsako, and bhasako are also here. Koleyyo means born in a family or house. Migadaṃsako means one who bites deer. Bhasako means one who barks or growls; from the root bhasa in the sense of speaking.

Bhesajjādiyogena, nissaggena vā ummattādibhāvamāpanno sunakho “aḷakko, atisuno”ti ca vuccate. Ala nivāraṇe, kammani ṇvu, dvittaḷattāni, aḷakko. Alakkopi. Pakatiṃ atikkanto suno atisuno.

A dog that has become mad and so forth, either by the application of medicine or naturally, is also called 'aḷakko' and 'atisuno'. Ala is the root in the sense of prevention; with the suffix ṇvu in the objective sense, and the doubling of 'ḷ', it forms aḷakko. Also alakko. A dog that has exceeded its natural state is atisuno.

520. Sādibandhanaṃ sunakhādibandhanaṃ rajjādi gaddūlo nāma. Gadda sadde, ulo, dīgho. Dvayaṃ dīpake. Dīpa dittiyaṃ, ṇvu, ciṭa pesanīye, luddena ciṭyateti ceṭako, ṇo, sakatthe ko, ṇvupaccayena vā siddhaṃ.

520. A leash for dogs and other animals, such as a rope, is called gaddūlo. It is derived from the root gadda in the sense of sound, with the suffix ulo, and elongation of the vowel. Two terms for a cheetah. Dīpa is the root in the sense of shining, with the suffix ṇvu. Ciṭa is the root in the sense of sending; one who is sent by a hunter is a ceṭako, with the suffix ṇo, or ko in its own sense; or it is formed with the suffix ṇvu.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0350] pāse. Bandha bandhane, kattari yu. Gantha ganthane, gantha koṭilye vā, nthassa ṇṭho. Pasa bādhanaphusanesu, kattari ṇo. Dvayaṃ vākarāyaṃ, yā sāṇatacādīhi migādīnaṃ bandhanatthaṃ katā. Vaka ādāne, aro, itthiyamato ā. Mige ganthati bandhatīti migaganthanī, “migabandhanī”tipi pāṭho.

Three terms for a snare. Bandha is the root in the sense of binding, with the suffix yu in the agentive sense. Gantha is the root in the sense of knotting, or gantha in the sense of crookedness; 'nth' becomes 'ṇṭh'. Pasa is the root in the senses of obstructing or touching, with the suffix ṇo in the agentive sense. Two terms for a net, which is made with hemp, bark, and so forth, for the purpose of binding deer and other animals. Vaka is the root in the sense of taking, with the suffix aro; 'ā' is added in the feminine sense. One that knots or binds deer is a migaganthanī; 'migabandhanī' is also a reading.

521. Dvayaṃ kumīne. Yatra macchā pavisanteva, na nissaranti, kucchitā veṇī assā kuveṇī, nadādi. Vajjhappattatāya kucchitā mīnā yasmiṃ kumīnaṃ, kamu padavikkhepe vā, ino, macchādhānīpyatra, macchā ādhīyante yassaṃ macchādhānī, yu, nadādi. Dvayaṃ jāle. Ānīyantenenāti ānayo, ṇo, īsse, e aya. Jale hitaṃ jālaṃ, ṇa.

521. Two terms for a fish trap. Where fish enter but do not escape; a kuveṇī is that which has a foul braid, formed like words in the nadī group. A kumīnaṃ is that in which fish are contemptible due to being caught for slaughter; or it is derived from the root kamu in the sense of stepping, with the suffix ino. Macchādhānī, a fish container, is also used here; that in which fish are placed is a macchādhānī, with the suffix yu, formed like words in the nadī group. Two terms for a net. That by which fish are brought is an ānayo, with the suffix ṇo; 'ī' becomes 'e', and then 'ay'. That which is placed in water is a jālaṃ, with the suffix ṇa.

Dvayaṃ vadhaṭṭhāne. Āgantvā hananti yasmiṃ āghātanaṃ, yu, hanassa ghāto. Vadhassa māraṇassa ṭhānaṃ vadhaṭṭhānaṃ. Dvayaṃ adhikoṭṭane. Sadā ākoṭṭanattā saha ūnenāti sūnā, suna gatiyaṃ vā, itthiyamati a, dīghādi. Kuṭa chedane, adhikoṭenti yasmiṃ adhikoṭṭanaṃ.

Two terms for a slaughterhouse. That in which they come and kill is an āghātanaṃ, with the suffix yu, and 'han' becomes 'ghāta'. The place of killing or slaughter is a vadhaṭṭhānaṃ. Two terms for a slaughtering block. Sūnā is so called because of constant beating; or it is derived from the root suna in the sense of movement, with the suffix 'a' in the feminine sense, and an initial long vowel, and so forth. Kuṭa is the root in the sense of cutting; that on which they beat excessively is an adhikoṭṭanaṃ.

522. Dvipādaṃ core. Taṃ karotīti takkaro, theyyatthaṃ vā takkayatīti takkaro. Takka vitakke, aro. Musa [M 0.0351] theyye, kattari ṇvu. Cura theyye, ṇo, curā theyyasīlamasseti vā coro, ṇo. Thena coriye, curādi, a. Ekaṃ asahāyaṃ agāraṃ gehaṃ ekāgāraṃ, taṃ payojanaṃ yassa ekāgāriko, iko. Mosatthino hyekāgāraṃ payojanaṃ. Samāti tulyatthā. Dassupyatra. Daṃsa daṃsane, su, niggahītalopo.

522. Two terms for a thief. One who does that is a takkaro, or one who speculates for the purpose of theft is a takkaro; from the root takka in the sense of speculation, with the suffix aro. From the root musa in the sense of theft, with the suffix ṇvu in the agentive sense. From the root cura in the sense of theft, with the suffix ṇo; or one whose nature is thievery is a coro, with the suffix ṇo. From the root thena in the sense of thievery, of the curādi group, with the suffix a. A single, solitary house is an ekāgāraṃ; one whose purpose is that is an ekāgāriko, with the suffix iko. Indeed, for thieves, a solitary dwelling is the purpose. These have the same meaning. Dassu is also used. From the root daṃsa in the sense of biting, with the suffix su, and elision of the niggahīta.

Tikaṃ theyyakriyāyaṃ. Thenassa kammaṃ theyyaṃ, corassa kammaṃ corikā. Musanaṃ moso, bhāve ṇo. Ve tantasantāne, vemo, anitthī. Vāyanattho daṇḍako vāyanadaṇḍako, vāsaradaṇḍakopi.

Three terms for the act of theft. The act of a thief is theyyaṃ; the act of a robber is corikā. The act of stealing is moso, with the suffix ṇo in the sense of the action itself. The root ve is in the sense of weaving threads; it forms vemo, which is not feminine. A stick for weaving is a vāyanadaṇḍako; also vāsaradaṇḍako.

523. Tikaṃ sutte. Suca gatiyaṃ, to. Tanu vitthāre, tu, tantu pume, tantapayojanattā tantaṃ. Lepyādikammani lepanādikriyāyaṃ potthasaddo vattati. Ādinā potthalikādilikhanakammaṃ gayhate, pusa snehasecanapūraṇesu, bhāve tho. Atha vā lepyādikammani kammakārakabhūte lepitabbādimhi potthasaddo, tadā kammani tho, potthaṃ.

523. Three terms for thread. From the root suca in the sense of movement, with the suffix to. From the root tanu in the sense of spreading, with the suffix tu; tantu is masculine, and tantaṃ means thread because it serves the purpose of weaving. The word pottha is used for the action of smearing, such as plastering and so forth. By 'and so forth,' the act of writing on a potthalikā and the like is included. From the root pusa in the senses of anointing, sprinkling, or filling, with the suffix tho in the sense of the action itself. Alternatively, the word pottha is used for the object of an action like smearing, such as the thing to be smeared; in that case, it is formed with the suffix tho in the objective sense, becoming potthaṃ.

Vatthadantakaṭṭhasiṅgādipotthalikāyaṃ pañcālikādidvayaṃ. Pañcaṅgāni yassā santi sajīvassevāti pañcālikā, iko. Majjhe lakārāgamo. Potthena vatthena alaṅkariyattā potthalikā. Ala bhūsane, ṇvu. “Caturo janā potthakamaggahesu”nti ettha potthakasaddena vatthaṃ vuttaṃ, potthasaddoyeva hi sakatthe kapaccayena “potthako”ti vutto. “Puttalikā”tipi pāṭho, putto viya alaṅkarīyateti puttalikā, puttikāpyatra.

Two terms, pañcālikā and so forth, are used for a doll made of cloth, ivory, wood, horn, and other materials. A pañcālikā is that which has five limbs, as if it were alive; it is formed with the suffix iko. A medial 'l' is inserted. A potthalikā is so called because it is adorned with pottha, that is, cloth; from the root ala in the sense of adorning, with the suffix ṇvu. In the phrase 'Four people grasped the potthaka,' the word potthaka means cloth, for the word pottha itself, with the suffix ka in its own sense, is called potthako. Puttalikā is also a reading; it is so called because it is adorned like a child (putta); puttikā is also used here.

524. Yaṃ [M 0.0352] kūpato āvāṭato ambuno jalassa ubbāhanaṃ uddhāraṇaṃ bhave, taṃ “ugghāṭanaṃ, ghaṭīyanta”miti coccate. Uddhaṃ ghaṭīyati udakanti ugghāṭanaṃ, yu. Ghaṭa cetāyaṃ, ghaṭīyeva uddhādhogamanavasena gamanato ghaṭīyantaṃ, yā gatipāpuṇanesu, anto, to vā.

524. The drawing up or lifting of water from a well or pit is called ugghāṭanaṃ and ghaṭīyantaṃ. Ugghāṭanaṃ means water is drawn up, formed with the suffix yu. From the root ghaṭa, in this context; ghaṭīyantaṃ is so called from its movement, going up and down like a bucket. It is derived from the root yā in the senses of going and reaching, with the suffix anta or ta.

Dvayaṃ mañjusāyaṃ, yā kaṭṭhehi karīyati. Mana ñāṇe, so, jumajjho manissa jūka (ṇvādi 215) uṇādivuttiyaṃ 4.77 sutte ca passitabbaṃ, pela gatiyaṃ, pe pālane vā, lo, ḷattaṃ, peḷā, pala rakkhaṇe vā, kattari a, asse, peḷā. Tikaṃ pacchiyaṃ. Piṭa saṅghāte, ṇvu, piṭako, vuddhimhi peṭako. Pasa pālane, chi, pacchi, itthiyaṃ.

Two terms for a casket, which is made of wood. From the root mana in the sense of knowledge, with the suffix so, and 'ju' inserted in the middle. From the root pela in the sense of movement, or pā in the sense of protection, with the suffix lo, and 'l' becomes 'ḷ', forming peḷā. Or from the root pala in the sense of protection, with the agentive suffix a, and the vowel 'a' becomes 'e', forming peḷā. Three terms for a basket. From the root piṭa in the sense of collection, with the suffix ṇvu, forming piṭako; with vowel gradation, it becomes peṭako. From the root pasa in the sense of protection, with the suffix chi, forming pacchi, which is feminine.

525. Dvayaṃ kāje. Vividhaṃ bhāramābhañjanti olambanti yassaṃ byābhaṅgī. Kajja byadhane, kattari ṇo, ekassa jassa lopo, kaca bandhane vā, adhikaraṇe ṇo, cassa jo, kājo, kācopi. Atra kāje avalambanaṃ vettādivikati sikkā nāma. Saka sattiyaṃ, kattari ko, upāntassi, sikkā, kājopi.

525. Two terms for a carrying pole. That on which various burdens are hung is a byābhaṅgī. From the root kajja in the sense of hurting, with the agentive suffix ṇo, and the elision of one 'j'. Or from the root kaca in the sense of binding, with the locative suffix ṇo, and 'c' becomes 'j', forming kājo; also kāco. In this context, the hanging sling made of cane and so forth is called a sikkā. From the root saka in the sense of ability, with the agentive suffix ko, and the penultimate vowel becoming 'i', forming sikkā; this is also a term for a carrying pole.

Dvayaṃ upāhane. Upanayhate bandhīyateti upāhano, vaṇṇavipariyayo, rassassa dīghatā, vākārena upāhanaṃ. Pajjate [M 0.0353] yāya pādu, u, pādu itthī, “pannaddhī pādukā pāṇihitā padarathī”tipi tikaṇḍaseso tikaṇḍasesa 2.10.13 . Tabbhedā tassupāhanassa bhedā visesā pādukā nāma, pada gamane, ṇuko, pādukā, bahupaṭalā cammamayā kaṭṭhamayātyeke.
