Two terms for footwear. That which is brought near or tied is upāhano; the form upāhanaṃ is derived by transposition of letters, lengthening of a short vowel, and with the letter 'v'. That by which one walks is a pādu, with the suffix u; pādu is feminine. Pannaddhī, pādukā, pāṇihitā, and padarathī are also synonyms, according to the Tikaṇḍasesa. The specific types or variations of that footwear are called pādukā. From the root pada in the sense of going, with the suffix ṇuka, it forms pādukā. Some say it is multi-layered, made of leather or wood.

526. Tikaṃ cammarajjuyaṃ. Vara icchāyaṃ, vara saṃvaraṇe vā, chadādīhi tatraṇa. Varattā, varattaṃ, varatrā, varatrampi. Vaddha vaddhiyaṃ, sakatthe ko, vaddhikā. Nayhate bandhīyate yāya naddhī, naha bandhane, to, nadādi.

526. Three terms for a leather strap. 'Vara' is in the sense of 'wishing,' or 'vara' in the sense of 'restraining'; for protection by means of the chadādi group. 'Varattā,' 'varattaṃ,' 'varatrā,' and also 'varatraṃ' are terms. From 'vaddha' in the sense of 'growth,' with the suffix '-ka' in its own sense, comes 'vaddhikā.' That by which one ties or binds is 'naddhī,' from the root 'naha' in the sense of 'binding,' with the suffix '-ti,' belonging to the nadādi group.

Dvayaṃ aggidīpane. Bhasa bhāsadittīsu, dibbate aggi yāya bhastā, to, traṇamhi bhastrā, nadādino ākatigaṇattā īpaccayābhāvo. Cammamayaṃ pasibbakaṃ cammapasibbakaṃ, cammapasibbakāpi.

Two terms for a fire-kindler, or bellows. From the root 'bhasa' in the senses of 'shining' and 'light'; that by which fire is kindled is 'bhastā,' with the suffix '-ti.' In the sense of 'protection,' it is 'bhastrā'; due to being an ākatigaṇa of the nadādi group, there is an absence of the '-ī' suffix. A bag made of leather is a 'cammapasibbakaṃ'; also 'cammapasibbakā.'

Tejase suvaṇṇādike āvatyate yatra, sā soṇṇādyāvattanī mūsā nāma, musa theyye, a, mūsā, dīghādi. Kalādikaṃ yāva pādena nāmaṃ. Kuṭa chedane, karaṇasādhanaṃ, kūṭaṃ, dīghādi, vākārena kūṭo. Ayaso, ayomayo vā ghano ayoghano.

That wherein gold and so forth is melted for brilliance is named 'soṇṇādyāvattanī' or 'mūsā' (a crucible). 'Mūsā' is from the root 'musa' in the sense of 'stealing,' with the suffix '-a,' hence 'mūsā,' with a long vowel, etc. The name for the kalādika extends up to the pāda. From the root 'kuṭa' in the sense of 'cutting,' as an instrument, it is 'kūṭaṃ,' with a long vowel, etc.; by the vākāra rule, it becomes 'kūṭo.' An iron, or iron-made, solid block is an 'ayoghano.'

527. Kammārānaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ kammārabhaṇḍaṃ. Saṅgamma ḍaṃsatīti saṇḍāso, ṇo, niggahītalopo, saṇḍāso, yenādittalohādi [M 0.0354] gayhate. Dvayaṃ adhobhāgaṭṭhe ayoghane. Muda saṃsagge, thi, muṭṭhi, itthī. Adhikaroti yassaṃ adhikaraṇī, yu, nadādi.

527. The equipment of blacksmiths is 'kammārabhaṇḍaṃ.' Because it bites when brought together, it is a 'saṇḍāso' (pincers), with the suffix '-ṇa' and elision of the niggahīta; 'saṇḍāso' is that by which heated metal and so forth is grasped. Two terms for the lower part of the iron block, or anvil. From the root 'muda' in the sense of 'contact,' with the suffix '-ti,' comes 'muṭṭhi,' which is feminine. That upon which one places it is 'adhikaraṇī,' with the suffix '-yu,' belonging to the nadādi group.

Tabbhastā tesaṃ kammārānaṃ bhastā aggidīpanī gaggarī nāma, yā “ukkā”tipi vuccati, sā ca nārī, “gagga”iti saddaṃ rātīti gaggarī, manthaniyampi. Dvayaṃ khuddakasatthe. Sasa hiṃsāyaṃ, tho. Piyampi phāletīti pipphalaṃ, phala vidāraṇe.

Their bellows, the fire-kindling bellows of those blacksmiths, is named 'gaggarī,' which is also called 'ukkā'; and it is feminine. Because it gives the sound 'gagga,' it is 'gaggarī'; it is also 'manthanī.' Two terms for a small knife. From the root 'sasa' in the sense of 'harming,' with the suffix '-tha.' Because it splits even a dear thing, it is 'pipphalaṃ,' from the root 'phala' in the sense of 'splitting.'

528. Dvayaṃ nikase. Sā tanukaraṇe, yu, ṇattaṃ, nikasate parikkhyate suvaṇṇanti nikaso. Kasopi. Sūciyā nāsāvijjhanaṃ ārā, ara gamane, ā, ārā, cammakārānaṃ cammavedhanepi ārā, “tikaṃ sūciya”nti keci.

528. Two terms for a touchstone. From the root 'sā' in the sense of 'thinning,' with the suffix '-yu,' and nasalization; that by which gold is tested or examined is 'nikaso.' Also 'kaso.' The needle for piercing the nose is an 'ārā'; from the root 'ara' in the sense of 'going,' with the suffix '-ā,' hence 'ārā.' An 'ārā' is also for the piercing of leather by leatherworkers. Some say, 'Three terms for a needle.'

Dvayaṃ kharapatte. Kharasamphassatāya kharo. “Ka”iti kacati pāṭayati kakaco, anitthī, “kakacaṃ kharapattañce”tyamaramālāyaṃ napuṃsakakaṇḍaṃ. Vacchāyanasatthe vuttā gītavajjādikā vijjā catusaṭṭhikriyā, tathā āliṅganacumbanādikā ca abbhantarā catusaṭṭhikriyā kalāsaddenoccate. Ādinā yaṃ tatra vuttaṃ kārukammaṃ, taṃ gayhate, taṃ sabbampi kalādikaṃ kammaṃ kriyā sippaṃ nāma, sī saye, po, sappa gamane vā, upāntassi, sippaṃ.

Two terms for a saw. Because of its rough contact, it is 'kharo.' Because it sounds 'ka,' cuts, or splits, it is 'kakaco'; it is not feminine. 'Kakacaṃ' and 'kharapattaṃ' are in the neuter section of the Amaramālā. The sixty-four activities, the sciences such as singing, playing instruments, etc., mentioned in the Vātsyāyanaśāstra, and likewise the sixty-four internal activities such as embracing, kissing, etc., are called by the word 'kalā.' By 'ādi' (etc.), whatever handicraft is mentioned there is included; all such art, etc., is named 'kammaṃ,' 'kriyā,' or 'sippaṃ.' 'Sippaṃ' is from the root 'sī' in the sense of 'lying,' with the suffix '-pa'; or from 'sappa' in the sense of 'going,' with the penultimate vowel becoming 'i,' hence 'sippaṃ.'

529-530. Patisadisaṃ [M 0.0355] yaṃ silādinā patirūpakaṃ karīyate, tatra paṭimādicatukkaṃ. Mā māne, mānamatra sadisīkaraṇaṃ, kattari, karaṇe vā a, paṭimā, nārī. Vamu uggiraṇe, bo, ittaṃ, paṭibimbaṃ. Dhā dhāraṇe, i, paṭinidhi, dvīsu. Paṭimānaṃ, paṭiyātanā, paṭicchāyā, paṭikatipyatra.

529-530. For that likeness which is made similar with stone and so forth, there is a quartet of terms beginning with 'paṭimā.' From the root 'mā' in the sense of 'measuring'; here 'māna' means 'making similar'; with the suffix '-a' in the agentive or instrumental sense, it becomes 'paṭimā,' which is feminine. From the root 'vamu' in the sense of 'emitting,' comes 'paṭibimbaṃ.' From the root 'dhā' in the sense of 'holding,' with the suffix '-i,' comes 'paṭinidhi,' which is in two genders. 'Paṭimānaṃ,' 'paṭiyātanā,' 'paṭicchāyā,' and also 'paṭikati' are terms here.

Pajjaṃ sadise, tatra samādayo kevalā api tīsu, sadisatthe ca vattanti, sannikāso, pana ante tayo ca uttarapadībhūtā, taṃ yathā – tena samo’yaṃ taṃsamo’yaṃ (?), taṃsamamidaṃ, taṃsannikāso iccādi amū nibhādayo uttarapadaṭṭhā eva sadisavacanā vāccaliṅgā siyuṃ yathā “pitunibho putto, mātunibhā kaññā, devanibhama- pacca”miti, byākhyāsudhā 2.10.37. Sama velambe, a. Patirūpakaṃ bhajatīti paṭibhāgo, ṇo, kāsa dittiyaṃ, a, sannikāso. Samānamiva naṃ dissatīti sarikkhako, samānassa so, dissa ri, sassa kkho, sakatthe ko, sarikkhako. Sama velambe, yu, samāno, saha mānenāti vā samāno. Samānaṃ katvā naṃ passatīti sadiso, samānassa so. Paricchedasadhammā tulyādhiṭṭhitāya sammito paricchinno tulyo, sammitatthe yo, apaccaye tulopi. Bhā dittiyaṃ[M 0.0356], sannibho, nibho ca. Bhūta rūpādayopyatra, yathā pitubhūto, māturūpo.

A verse on 'similar.' Therein, 'sama' and so forth, even when standing alone, are in three genders and are used in the sense of 'similar.' But 'sannikāsa' and the three at the end can also be the final member of a compound, for example: 'tena samo’yaṃ' (this is equal to that), 'taṃsamamidaṃ' (this is equal to that), 'taṃsannikāso' (similar to that), etc. From the root 'sama' in the sense of 'being level,' with the suffix '-a.' Because it partakes of a likeness, it is 'paṭibhāgo,' with the suffix '-ṇa.' From the root 'kāsa' in the sense of 'shining,' with the suffix '-a,' comes 'sannikāso.' Because it appears like something similar, it is 'sarikkhako'; from 'samāna' comes 'sa,' from 'dis' comes 'ri,' 'sa' becomes 'kkha,' with the suffix '-ka' in its own sense, hence 'sarikkhako.' From the root 'sama' in the sense of 'being level,' with the suffix '-yu,' comes 'samāno'; or, 'with measure,' hence 'samāno.' Because one sees it having made it similar, it is 'sadiso'; 'sa' comes from 'samāna.' Having the same quality of measurement, established in equality, it is 'sammito,' 'paricchinno,' or 'tulyo.' 'Tulya' is formed with the suffix '-ya' in the sense of 'sammito'; 'tulo' also occurs, without a suffix. From the root 'bhā' in the sense of 'shining,' come 'sannibho' and 'nibho.' 'Bhūta,' 'rūpa,' and so forth are also used here, as in 'pitubhūto' (like a father) and 'māturūpo' (like a mother).

Tikaṃ upamāne. Upamīyate yena opammaṃ, mana, upapubbo mā māne, yupaccaye upamānaṃ, itthiyamati a, upamā, upamānopameyyānaṃ sadhammattepyayaṃ, vuttañca “upamānopameyyānaṃ, sadhammattaṃ siyopamā”ti subodhālaṅkāra 176 gāthā. “Yenopamīyate, yā copamīyate, tesvapi opammādittaya”ntyamarasīho byākhyāsudhā 2.10.36.

Three terms for a simile. That by which something is compared is 'opammaṃ.' From the root 'mā' in the sense of 'measuring,' preceded by 'upa,' with the suffix '-yu,' it becomes 'upamānaṃ.' In the feminine, with the suffix '-a,' it is 'upamā.' This term is also used for the common property of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison. And it is said: 'The common property of the upamāna and the upameyya may be an upamā.' Amarasiṃha states: 'That by which one compares, and that which is compared—for these also, the three terms beginning with opamma are used.'

531. Catukkaṃ vetane. Bharati kammakare yāya, sā bhati,ti. Visa peraṇe, peraṇaṃ gamanādīsu niyojanaṃ, karaṇe ṇo, nibbeso, nivesopi. Vī gamane, tano. Mūlena samitaṃ mūlyaṃ, mūla patiṭṭhāyaṃ vā, karaṇe yo.

531. Four terms for wages. That by which one supports workers is 'bhati,' with the suffix '-ti.' From the root 'visa' in the sense of 'sending'; 'peraṇaṃ' is employing in going, etc.; in the instrumental sense, with the suffix '-ṇa,' it becomes 'nibbeso,' also 'niveso.' From the root 'vī' in the sense of 'going,' with the suffix '-tana.' That which is equivalent to the price is 'mūlyaṃ'; or from the root 'mūla' in the sense of 'foundation,' in the instrumental sense, with the suffix '-ya.'

“Kammaññā tu vidhā bhaccā, bhatayo bhammavetanaṃ;

Bharaṇyaṃ bharaṇaṃ mūlyaṃ, nibbeso paṇamiccapī”. –

Terms for wages are: 'Kammaññā, vidhā, bhaccā, bhatayo, bhammavetanaṃ; bharaṇyaṃ, bharaṇaṃ, mūlyaṃ, nibbeso, and also paṇa.'

Tyamarasīho amara 20.38-9.

Thus says Amarasiṃha.

Dvayaṃ jūte. Ju gatijavanesu, to, dīghādi, jūtaṃ, juta dittiyaṃ vā, karaṇe a. Kitavassa jūtakārassa kammaṃ ketavaṃ, ṇo. Akkhavatī, paṇopyatra. Akkhā pāsakā upāyatthena assaṃ santīti, vantu, sabhāvato itthittaṃ. Paṇo aṭṭo, taṃyogā paṇo.

Two terms for gambling. From the root 'ju' in the senses of 'going' and 'speed,' with the suffix '-ta,' and a long vowel, etc., hence 'jūtaṃ'; or from the root 'juta' in the sense of 'shining,' in the instrumental sense, with the suffix '-a.' The work of a gambler is 'ketavaṃ,' with the suffix '-ṇa.' 'Akkhavatī' and also 'paṇo' are terms here. 'Akkhā' are dice; because they exist in it as a means, the suffix '-vantu' is used; by its nature, it is feminine. 'Paṇo' is a stake; from connection with that, it is 'paṇo.'

Pañcakaṃ [M 0.0357] jūtakāre. Dhāvantī atti dhutti, nipātanā, taṃyogā dhutto, ṇo, dhū kampane vā, to, rasso, dhutto, sabbakīḷādipasutepyayaṃ. Akkhesu dhutto akkhadhutto. Mariyādamatikkamma kīḷādipasuto hi “dhutto”ti vuccati. Kitavaṃ assatthīti kitavo, nipātanā, kita nivāse vā, avo. Akkhehi jūtehi dibbatīti akkhadevī, ṇī.

Five terms for a gambler. Because a running person takes, it is 'dhutti,' by irregular formation; from connection with that, 'dhutto,' with the suffix '-ṇa.' Or from the root 'dhū' in the sense of 'shaking,' with the suffix '-ta,' and a short vowel, hence 'dhutto.' This term is also for one devoted to all games, etc. One who is a rogue at dice is an 'akkhadhutto.' Indeed, one who, having transgressed the boundary, is devoted to games, etc., is called a 'dhutto.' Because there is a trick for him, he is a 'kitavo,' by irregular formation; or from the root 'kita' in the sense of 'dwelling,' with the suffix '-ava.' Because one plays with dice in gambling, one is an 'akkhadevī,' with the suffix '-ṇī.'

532. Dvayaṃ pāṭibhoge, paṭibhuñjati pālayatīti pāṭibhogo, bhuja pālane, ṇo. Paṭibhavatīti paṭibhū. Dvayaṃ catuvīsatipāsake, yena jūtakārā dibbanti. Aka kuṭilāyaṃ gatiyaṃ, kho, akkho. Pasa bādhanaphusanesu, ṇvu. Devanopyatra. Dibbanti yena devano, divu kīḷāyaṃ, yu.

532. Two terms for a guarantor. Because one undertakes or protects, one is a 'pāṭibhogo,' from the root 'bhuja' in the sense of 'protecting,' with the suffix '-ṇa.' Because one becomes responsible for, one is a 'paṭibhū.' Two terms for the twenty-four dice, by which gamblers play. From the root 'aka' in the sense of 'crooked movement,' with the suffix '-kha,' comes 'akkho.' From the root 'pasa' in the senses of 'hindering' and 'touching,' with the suffix '-ṇvu.' 'Devano' is also a term here. That by which they play is 'devano,' from the root 'divu' in the sense of 'playing,' with the suffix '-yu.'

Sāraphalake aṭṭhāpadaṃ, pume, napuṃsake vā, aṭṭhapadānyassa aṭṭhāpadaṃ. Desantare hi caturaṅgasseva paṭṭikāyaṃ pāsakajūtampi vattate, saññāyaṃ aṭṭhasaddassa uttarapade rassassa dīghatā pāṇini 6.3.125. Aṭṭhapadampi. Paṭṭe ito cito ca saranti parivattantīti sārino, tesaṃ phalakaṃ sāriphalakaṃ, sakatthe ko.

For the game board, 'aṭṭhāpadaṃ,' in the masculine or neuter. That which has eight squares is 'aṭṭhāpadaṃ.' Indeed, in other regions, the dice game also proceeds on a board like that of chess. In this technical term, there is a lengthening of the short vowel of the word 'aṭṭha' in the latter part of the compound. Also 'aṭṭhapadaṃ.' Because they move and turn here and there on the board, they are 'sārino' (pieces). Their board is 'sāriphalakaṃ,' with the suffix '-ka' in its own sense.

Dvayaṃ abbhute, yena satādilābhajānivasena jūtakārādīnaṃ jayaparājayā honti. Paṇa byavahāre, a, paṇo, panopi. Abbha gamane, to, abhi sadde vā, to, asarūpadvittaṃ, abbhatopi.

Two terms for a wager, by which victory and defeat come to gamblers and others through the gain and loss of hundreds, etc. From the root 'paṇa' in the sense of 'transacting,' with the suffix '-a,' comes 'paṇo'; also 'pano.' From the root 'abbha' in the sense of 'going,' with the suffix '-ta'; or from 'abhi' in the sense of 'sound,' with the suffix '-ta,' and dissimilar reduplication, comes also 'abbhuta.'

533. Nānādabbakate [M 0.0358] madirābīje surābīje kiṇṇā, kiranti nānādabbāni missībhavantyassaṃ kiṇṇā, to. Madhvāsave madhukapupphakate majje madhu mataṃ, madhukapupphaṃ madhu, tappakatattā madhu, madhukatepi majje madhu madhvāsavā vuttā, mādhavako, mādhvikampi, advīsvidaṃ.

533. For the 'seed' of liquor or spirits, made of various substances, the term is 'kiṇṇā.' Because various substances are scattered and become mixed in it, it is 'kiṇṇā,' with the suffix '-ta.' For honey-liquor, that is, liquor made from madhuka flowers, the term is 'madhu.' The madhuka flower is 'madhu'; because the liquor is made from that, it is 'madhu.' Even for liquor made from honey, the terms 'madhu' and 'madhvāsavā' are used. 'Mādhavako' and also 'mādhvikaṃ' are terms; this is not in two genders.

Surāntaṃ majje. Mada ummāde, karaṇe iro. Varuṇo nāma eko jano, teneva paṭhamaṃ diṭṭhattā varuṇato jāyatīti vāruṇī, ṇī, vara patthanāyaṃ vā, kamme yu, assu, nadādi. Majjante yena majjaṃ, vajādinā yo, dyassa jjo ca. Su abhisave, ro, su savane vā, surā. Halippiyā, hālā, gandhottamā, pasannā, irā, kādambarīpyatra. Halino balabhaddassa piyā ruccā halippiyā. Hala vilekhane, ṇo, hālā. I gamane, ro, irā. Paṭhama’mayaṃ gomantha pabbate kadambakoṭare bhavā kādambarī, tathā cāgamo “kadambakoṭare jātā, tena kādambarī matā”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 20.39.

The synonyms for 'surā' are included under 'majja' (intoxicant). 'Mada' is from the root 'mad' (to be intoxicated); 'iro' is the suffix in the sense of instrument. A person named Varuṇa, because it was first seen by him, it is called 'vāruṇī', being born from Varuṇa, with the suffix 'ṇī'. Alternatively, it is from the root 'vara' (to desire) with the suffix 'yu' in the sense of action, or from 'assu' (tears), or from words like 'nada' (river), and so forth. That by which one becomes intoxicated is 'majja', from the root 'mad' with the suffix 'ya' according to the 'vajādi' group, and 'dya' becomes 'jja'. From the root 'su' (to press out), with the suffix 'ra'; or from the root 'su' (to hear), it is 'surā'. 'Halippiyā', 'hālā', 'gandhottamā', 'pasannā', 'irā', and 'kādambarī' are also synonyms. 'Halippiyā' is that which is dear and pleasing to Halin, that is, Balabhadra. From the root 'hala' (to plough), with the suffix 'ṇa', it is 'hālā'. From the root 'i' (to go), with the suffix 'ra', it is 'irā'. This 'kādambarī' first arose in the hollow of a kadamba tree on Gomantha mountain. Thus, there is also the traditional saying: 'Born in the kadamba hollow, hence it is considered kādambarī.'

Dvayaṃ tālādirasaje. Āsavanti mānapurisamadādayo yenāti āsavo. Madaṃ janetīti merayaṃ, ṇeyyo, asse, dassa ro ca. Sīdhupyatra. Majjavisesepi tayamidaṃ vadanti, vuttañca –

Two terms refer to that which is produced from the juice of the palm tree and so forth. That by which pride, intoxication, and so forth flow is 'āsava'. That which generates intoxication is 'meraya'; the suffix is 'ṇeyya', 'a' becomes 'e', and 'd' becomes 'r'. 'Sīdhu' is also a term here. These three are also spoken of as specific types of intoxicants, and it has been said:

“Sīdhuucchurase pakke, apakke āsavo bhave;

Merayaṃ dhātakīpuppha-guḷadhaññambiloṭṭhita”nti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 20.42 byākhyāsudhā 2.10.41.

'Sīdhu' is from cooked sugarcane juice; 'āsava' would be from uncooked juice. 'Meraya' is a mixture of dhātakī flowers, jaggery, grains, and sour fruit.

534. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0359] pānapatte. Sara gatiyaṃ, ṇvu. Sara gatihiṃsācintāsu vā. Casa bhakkhane, ṇvu, dvayaṃpyanitthī. Sīdhumhi ca sarako.

534. Two terms refer to a drinking vessel. 'Saraka' is from the root 'sar' (to move), with the suffix 'ṇvu'. Alternatively, from the root 'sar' in the senses of moving, harming, or thinking. 'Casaka' is from the root 'cas' (to eat), with the suffix 'ṇvu'; both terms are non-feminine. And 'saraka' also means 'sīdhu'.

Dvayaṃ pānamaṇḍale. Āpivanti saṃbhūya pivantyasmiṃ āpānaṃ, yu. Pānassa maṇḍalaṃ koṭṭhaṃ pānamaṇḍalaṃ.

Two terms refer to a drinking circle. 'Āpāna' is where people gather and drink together; the suffix is 'yu'. A 'pānamaṇḍala' is a circle or enclosure for drinking.

535. Samattaliṅgāsaṅgahato asampuṇṇataṃ pariharati. Atra asmiṃ vagge ye yogikā saddāveṇikamāyākāracoraakkhadevippabhutayo pume bhūrippayogattā pacurappayogadassanato ekasmiṃ liṅge pume īritā kathitā, te taddhammattā taṃyogavasā ekakriyākārittā aññavuttiyaṃ tato aññatra itthādīsu vuttiyaṃ satyaṃ liṅgantarepi itthiliṅgādopi neyyā upanīyā, taṃ yathā – māyākārī itthī, māyākāramidaṃ kulamiccādi. Ye tvayogikā māgadhamālikakumbhakārādayo, te jātivacanattā suddādayo viya dvīsūti.

535. He avoids incompleteness by including all genders. Here in this chapter, those 'yogika' words (words derived from a root), such as lute player, magician, thief, dice-player, and so forth, are stated in one gender, the masculine, due to their frequent and abundant usage being seen in that gender. They, because of having that nature, because of their connection to that action, and because of being the agent of a single action, when used in another context—that is, in other genders such as the feminine—can be inferred and applied. For example: 'māyākārī' is a female magician; 'māyākāraṃ idaṃ kulaṃ' means this is a family of magicians, and so forth. However, those words that are 'ayogika' (not derived from a root), such as a person from Magadha, a garland-maker, a potter, and so forth, because they are words denoting a class, are like 'sudda' and so forth, used in two genders.

Suddavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Suddavagga is finished.

Catubbaṇṇavaggavaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the Catubbaṇṇavagga is complete.

5. Araññavaggavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Forest Chapter

536. Sattakaṃ [M 0.0360] vane. Ara gamane, añño, araññaṃ. Kena jalena ananaṃ pāṇamanassa kānanaṃ, dā avakhaṇḍane, dā chedane vā. Adhikaraṇe ṇo, “ākārantānamāyo”ti āyo. Daya dānagatihiṃ sādānesu vā, ṇo, gaha upādāne gāhū viloḷane (?), adhikaraṇe yu. Vapa bījanikkhepe, ino, assittaṃ. Vana sambhattisaddesu, kattari a, vanaṃ. Aṭā avayavo selā atreti aṭavi, i, īmhi aṭavī.

536. A set of seven terms for forest. 'Arañña' is from the root 'ar' (to go), with the suffix 'añña'. 'Kānana' is where there is movement of life with little water. 'Dāya' is from the root 'dā' (to cut) or 'dā' (to divide), with the suffix 'ṇo' in the locative sense. 'Gahaṇa' is from the root 'gah' (to take), with the suffix 'yu' in the locative sense. 'Vipina' is from the root 'vap' (to sow seeds), with the suffix 'ina'; it is unsown. 'Vana' is from the root 'van' (to serve or to sound), with the suffix 'a' in the agent sense. 'Aṭavi' is from the root 'aṭ' (to wander); here there are parts and rocks, hence 'aṭavi', with the suffix 'i'; in the feminine it is 'aṭavī'.

Mahāpadumalatāvanaṃ mahāraññaṃ, nadādi, ananto ca, araññānī.

A great forest is 'mahārañña'. Also included are words from the 'nadādi' group, and 'ananta' (endless), and 'araññānī' (a large forest).

537. Nagarato nātidūrasmiṃ ṭhāne santehi abhiropito tarusaṇḍo pūgapanasāditarusamūho atthi, so “upavana”nti coccate, kittimavanametaṃ. Āramantyasminti ārāmo, ṇo. Upagataṃ, uparopitaṃ vā vanaṃ upavanaṃ.

537. A grove of trees, a collection of trees such as areca palms and jackfruit, planted by good people in a place not too far from the city, is called an 'upavana'; this is an artificial forest. 'Ārāma' is so called because people delight in it; the suffix is 'ṇo'. An 'upavana' is a forest that is near or has been planted.

538. Sabbasādhāraṇaṃ sabbalokehi sādhāraṇopabhogaṃ raññaṃ rājūnaṃ araññaṃ “upavanaṃ, uyyāna”mityuccate, ullokentā [M 0.0361] yanti janā etasminti uyyānaṃ, yu. Ākīḷopyatra.

538. A forest belonging to kings, which is common to all and for the common enjoyment of all people, is called an 'upavana' or 'uyyāna'. 'Uyyāna' is so called because people go forth into it looking about; the suffix is 'yu'. 'Ākīḷa' is also a term here.

Tadeva rājopavanameva upakārikāsannihitaṃ, purasannihitaṃ vā antepurācitaṃ pamadavanākhyaṃ. Yatra antepurasahito eva rājā viharati, nāññajanappaveso. Pamadānaṃ itthīnaṃ vanaṃ pamadavanaṃ, rasso.

That very royal park, situated near the royal attendants or near the city, and surrounded by the inner apartments, is known as a 'pamadavana'. It is where only the king dwells, accompanied by the women of the inner palace; no other person is allowed to enter. 'Pamadavana' is the grove of women ('pamadā'); the vowel is short.

539-540. Sāntarāḷā panti, yathā – tarupanti, pāsādapanti, nirantarāḷā tu rājīti. Tatra pañcakaṃ pantiyaṃ. Pana byavahāre, thutimhi ca, panti. Vī gamane, thi, vīthi. Vala saṃvaraṇe, i, āvali. Ālipi, aladhātumhā i. Si sevāyaṃ, ṇi, seṇi. Pā rakkhaṇe, ḷi, pāḷi, sogatepi. Dve samā. Likha lekhane, a. Rāja dittiyaṃ, i.

539-540. A 'panti' is a row with intervals, for example, a row of trees or a row of palaces; but a 'rājī' is a row without intervals. Therein, a set of five terms for 'panti'. 'Panti' is from the root 'pan' (to transact or to praise). 'Vīthi' is from the root 'vī' (to go), with the suffix 'thi'. 'Āvali' is from the root 'val' (to cover), with the suffix 'i'. 'Āli' is also from the root 'al', with the suffix 'i'. 'Seṇi' is from the root 'si' (to serve), with the suffix 'ṇi'. 'Pāḷi' is from the root 'pā' (to protect), with the suffix 'ḷi'; it is also used in the teaching of the Sugata. Two terms are for a continuous line. 'Lekhā' is from the root 'likh' (to write), with the suffix 'a'. 'Rājī' is from the root 'rāj' (to shine), with the suffix 'i'.

Tipādaṃ rukkhamatte. Pādena mūlena pivatīti pādapo, ṇo. Viṭapayogā viṭapī. Rukkha varaṇe, a, ruha janane vā, kho, hassa ko. Na gacchatīti ago. Sala gamane, ṇo, sāravantatāya vā sāro, so eva sālo, aññatropacārā. Mahiyaṃ ruhatīti, a. Du gatiyaṃ, mo. Tara taraṇe, u. Kuto bhūmito jāyatīti kujo, aṅgārepi. Sākhāyogato sākhī.

A stanza of three lines on the subject of 'tree'. 'Pādapa' is so called because it drinks with its foot, that is, its root; the suffix is 'ṇo'. 'Viṭapin' is so called because of its connection with branches. 'Rukkha' is from the root 'rukkha' (to cover), with the suffix 'a'; or from the root 'ruh' (to be born), with the suffix 'kha', where 'h' becomes 'k'. 'Aga' is so called because it does not go. 'Sāla' is from the root 'sal' (to move), with the suffix 'ṇo'; or it is 'sāra' because of having essence, and that itself is 'sāla', used metaphorically elsewhere. 'Mahīruha' is so called because it grows on the earth; the suffix is 'a'. 'Duma' is from the root 'du' (to go), with the suffix 'ma'. 'Taru' is from the root 'tar' (to cross), with the suffix 'u'. 'Kuja' is so called because it is born from the earth; it also means charcoal. 'Sākhin' is so called because of its connection with branches.

Gamu [M 0.0362] gamane, ṇo, “gamissanto ccho vā sabbāsū”ti ccho. Khuddo avuḍḍhippatto pādapo khuddapādapo. Ye rukkhā pupphaṃ vinā apupphakā phalanti, te assatthodumbarapanasādayo “vanappatī”ti vuccanti, vanānaṃ pati vanappati. Pupphato jātaphalā pana ambakhajjūrādayo vānappatayo. Vanappatimhi bhavā vānappatayo.

'Gaccha' is from the root 'gam' (to go), with the suffix 'ṇa'; or it becomes 'ccha' from the rule 'gamissanto ccho vā sabbāsū'. A 'khuddapādapa' is a small tree that has not attained its full growth. Those trees that bear fruit without flowers, such as the assattha, udumbara, and panasa, are called 'vanappati', meaning lord of the forests. But those whose fruit is born from a flower, such as the mango and date palm, are 'vānappataya'. 'Vānappataya' are those that are in the 'vanappati' class.

541. Yo phalapākāvasāne marati, so kadalīdhaññādiko osadhi nāma bhave, oso dhīyate yassaṃ oso gloso dittibbā dhīyate’tra byākhyāsudhā 2.4.6, sā osadhi, i. Sāsaddo osadhisaddassa itthiliṅgattadīpako.

541. That which dies at the end of the ripening of its fruit, such as the plantain, grain, and so forth, is called an 'osadhi'. 'Osadhi' is that in which essence is placed; the suffix is 'i'. The word 'sā' indicates that the word 'osadhi' is of the feminine gender.

Dvayaṃ utuppattepi phalahīne. Vana yācane, jho, vañjhā, vadhati phalanti vā vañjhā, vajādinā yo, jhassa jho, niggahītāgamo ca. Na vijjati phalametissāti aphalā, dve tīsu. Tikaṃ vattamānaphale rukkhādo. Phalayogā, ino, vantu, ī ca.

Two terms refer to that which is fruitless even when the season has arrived. 'Vañjhā' is from the root 'van' (to ask), with the suffix 'jha'. Alternatively, 'vañjhā' is that which kills fruit, from the root 'vadh' with the suffix 'ya' according to the 'vajādi' group, where 'dh' becomes 'jh', and with the insertion of a niggahīta. 'Aphalā' is that for which there is no fruit; these two terms are used in three genders. A set of three terms refers to a tree and so forth with present fruit. Because of its connection with fruit, the words are formed with the suffixes 'in', 'vantu', and 'ī'.

542. Catukkaṃ vikasite. Phulla vikasane, kattari to, sañjātatthe vā ito, phala visaraṇe vā, visaraṇaṃ vikāso, assu. Kaca bandhane, vipubbo vikasane, kattari a[M 0.0363]. Vikacate vidalati visiliṭṭhadalo bhavatīti vā vikaco, a, visaddo visilesajotako. Kasa gamane, to. Dalānaṃ aññamaññaṃ visilesato samudāyo “vikasito”tyuccate. Phuṭopyatra. Phuṭa vikasane.

542. A set of four terms for that which is bloomed. 'Phulla' is from the root 'phull' (to bloom), with the suffix 'ta' in the agent sense, or 'ita' in the sense of 'having become'; or from the root 'phal' (to split open), where splitting open means blooming, with the suffix 'a'. 'Vikaca' is from the root 'kac' (to bind), which with the prefix 'vi' means to bloom, with the suffix 'a' in the agent sense. Or 'vikaca' is so called because it splits open, its petals become separated; the suffix is 'a', and the prefix 'vi' indicates separation. 'Vikasita' is from the root 'kas' (to go), with the suffix 'ta'. The state of petals being separated from each other is called 'vikasita'. 'Phuṭa' is also a term here, from the root 'phuṭ' (to bloom).

Pādo rukkhagge. “Na nā’ggaṃ sikharaṃ siro”ti vopālitavacanato “siraso agga”nti na chaṭṭhīsamāso. Siro vutto. Aja gamane, go, aggaṃ, seṭṭhe tīsu. Sī saye, kharo, sikhā vā cūḷā, sā viya jāyatīti sikharo. Dvayaṃ sākhāyaṃ. Sākha byāpane, a. “Latā vallī samākhyātā, latā sākhā ca sākhina”nti latā nānatthā. Lā ādāne, to, rasso.

A line of verse on the top of a tree. 'Sira' has been explained. 'Agga' is from the root 'aj' (to go), with the suffix 'ga'; it means 'best' in three genders. 'Sikhara' is from the root 'sī' (to lie), with the suffix 'khara'; or it is born like a 'sikhā' (crest) or 'cūḷā' (topknot), hence 'sikhara'. Two terms for a branch. 'Sākhā' is from the root 'sākh' (to pervade), with the suffix 'a'. The word 'latā' has various meanings, as stated: 'A latā is known as a creeper, and a latā is also a branch of a tree'. 'Latā' is from the root 'lā' (to take), with the suffix 'ta', and the vowel is short.

543. Chakkaṃ patte. Dalati vikasatīti dalaṃ, a. Lasa kantiyaṃ, pakārena lasatīti palāso, ṇo. Chada saṃvaraṇe, chādīyate yena chadanaṃ, yu. Pūrayatīti paṇṇaṃ, nipātanā, pata adhogamane vā, patatyacirena paṇṇaṃ, pattañca, to, pume. Saññāyaṃ ṇamhi chado.

543. A set of six terms for a leaf. 'Dala' is so called because it splits or opens; the suffix is 'a'. 'Palāsa' is from the root 'las' (to shine); it shines in a special way; the suffix is 'ṇa'. 'Chadana' is from the root 'chad' (to cover); that by which one is covered; the suffix is 'yu'. 'Paṇṇa' is so called because it fills, which is an irregular formation; or from the root 'pat' (to go downwards), 'paṇṇa' is that which falls quickly; and 'patta', with the suffix 'ta', is masculine. 'Chada' is formed with the suffix 'ṇa' in the sense of a name.

Dvayaṃ pattādisaṅghātavati sākhāya pabbe. Palla gamane, avo. Kisa gamane, yo, lāgamo majjhe. Dvayaṃ aṅkure. Navo eva ubbhito uggato navubbhinno. Aṅka lakkhaṇe, uro.

Two terms refer to the node of a branch having a cluster of leaves and so forth. 'Pallava' is from the root 'pall' (to go), with the suffix 'ava'. 'Kisalaya' is from the root 'kis' (to go), with the suffix 'ya', and the insertion of 'la' in the middle. Two terms refer to a sprout. 'Navubbhina' is that which has newly sprung up or arisen. 'Aṅkura' is from the root 'aṅk' (to mark), with the suffix 'ura'.

544. Pakkaṃ yāva pādena nāmaṃ. Vikāso mukhapabuddhakalikāyaṃ makuḷādidvayaṃ. Muca mocane, ulo, ussattaṃ, cassa ko, makuḷaṃ, makuḷo vā. Kuṭa chedane, malo, assu, kuṭumalo, kutumalopi. Pupphassa ca phalassa ca pakatibhūte [M 0.0364] jālapatte khārakādidvayaṃ. Khura vināse. Ṇvu. Jala dhaññe, sakatthe ko. Jālakaṃ napuṃsake. Dvayaṃ jālakato pavuddhe pupphe, phale ca. Kala saṅkhyāne, ṇvu, kura sadde, ṇvu.

544. The name for a ripe thing is 'phala' (fruit). Blooming (vikāsa) is the opening of a bud's mouth; the pair beginning with 'makuḷa' are names for a bud. 'Makuḷa' or 'makuḷo' is from the root 'muc' (to release), with the suffix 'ula', and 'c' becoming 'k'. 'Kuṭumala' or 'kutumala' is from the root 'kuṭ' (to cut), with the suffix 'mala' and the insertion of 'u'. The pair beginning with 'khāraka' refers to the calyx, which is the natural state of a flower and fruit. 'Khāraka' is from the root 'khur' (to destroy), with the suffix 'ṇvu'. 'Jālaka' is from the root 'jal' (to shine), with the suffix 'ko' in its own meaning; 'jālaka' is neuter. The two terms refer to a flower and fruit developed from the calyx. [These are derived as follows:] from the root 'kal' (to count), with the suffix 'ṇvu'; from the root 'kur' (to sound), with the suffix 'ṇvu'.

Pupphādibandhanaṃ pupphaphalānaṃ bandhanaṃ vaṇṭaṃ nāma. Bandhīyate yena vaṇṭaṃ, vajādi.

The stalk that binds flowers, fruits, and so forth is called 'vaṇṭa'. That by which they are bound is 'vaṇṭa', derived according to the 'vajādi' group of rules.

545. Tikaṃ pupphe. Pasu pāṇigabbhavimocane, ṇo. Khapaṇakabhāsāya rukkhopi pāṇi, vuddhādi, pasavo. Kusa akkose, umo, kasa gamane vā, kāsa dittiyaṃ vā, umo, rasso. Puppha vikasane, pupphatīti, a. Pupphajo rajo pupphadhūlī parāgo nāma, ranja raṅge, ṇo.

545. Three terms refer to a flower. 'Pasava' is from the root 'pasū' (to bring forth), with the suffix 'ṇa'. In the language of ascetics, a tree is also a living being; from its growth and so forth, it is called 'pasava'. 'Kusuma' is from the root 'kus' (to scold), with the suffix 'uma'; or from 'kas' (to go), or from 'kās' (to shine), with the suffix 'uma', and the vowel is shortened. 'Puppha' is from the root 'pupph' (to bloom); that which blooms is 'puppha', with the suffix 'a'. The dust produced from a flower, flower-dust, is called 'parāga', from the root 'rañj' (to color), with the suffix 'ṇa'.

Madhurapuppharaso makarando nāmāti mataṃ. Makkhikā ramanti yasmiṃ makarando, vajādi. Dvayaṃ kalikābhi ākiṇṇe pariṇāyavati. Thu abhitthave, ṇvu, thavako. Gudha parivedhane, ṇvu, dhassa cho, gocchako.

The sweet juice of a flower is called 'makaranda', so it is thought. That in which bees delight is 'makaranda', derived according to the 'vajādi' group of rules. Two terms are for that which is crowded with buds and is maturing. 'Thavaka' (cluster) is from the root 'thu' (to praise), with the suffix 'ṇvu'. 'Gocchaka' (cluster) is from the root 'gudh' (to encompass), with the suffix 'ṇvu', and 'dh' becoming 'ch'.

546-547. Āme apakke phale salāṭu utto, salāṭa bālyaparibhāsanesu, u, vijjamānabālyatāya salāṭu[M 0.0365]. Pakkantu phalaṃ nippariyāyena “phala”mityuccate, tena “āmasmiṃ phalavohāro rūḷhiyā pavattatī”ti ñātabbo, phala nipphattiyaṃ, nipphatti cātra supakkattaṃ, sukkhe tu phale vāno. Tatra salāṭu vānā tīsu, yathā salāṭu jambū, salāṭavo māsā, salāṭūni kumbhaṇḍāni, vānā harīṭakī, vāno muggo, vānamambaṃ.

546-547. For an unripe fruit, 'salāṭu' is said; the root 'salāṭa' is used in expressions of immaturity, and with the suffix 'u', 'salāṭu' is used due to the presence of immaturity. But a ripe fruit is unequivocally called 'phala'. Therefore, it should be understood that the use of the term 'phala' for an unripe fruit occurs by convention. The root 'phal' is in the sense of attainment; and here attainment means full ripeness. But for a dried fruit, 'vāna' is used. Therein, 'salāṭu' and 'vāna' are used in the three genders, for example: 'salāṭu jambū' (unripe rose apple), 'salāṭavo māsā' (unripe beans), 'salāṭūni kumbhaṇḍāni' (unripe gourds); and 'vānā harīṭakī' (dried yellow myrobalan), 'vāno muggo' (dried mung bean), 'vānamambaṃ' (dried mango).

Campakādi campakaṃ karavīraṃ kadambakaṃ asokaṃ kaṇṇikāraṃ campakādīnaṃ pupphaṃ vikāro, avayavo ceti aññatthe ṇo na bhavati, tadantato pupphassuppatitato, evaṃ campakādīni kusumanāmāni napuṃsake vattanti, ambādi dāḷimaṃ nāraṅgaṃ āmalakaṃ kuvalaṃ badaranti pakatyantarameva phale vattate, āmalakiyā kuvaliyā badariyā phalaṃ vikāro, avayavo ceti aññatthe taddhitopi noppajjate, tadantato phalassuppatitato, evaṃ ambādīni phalanāmāni napuṃsake vattanti. Mallikādayo kusumepi vattamānā saliṅgā pakatiliṅgāabhedopacārena pavattiyā, yathā – mallikā jāti, vanamallikā iccādi. Vīhayopyabhedopacārena phalepi saliṅgā, yathā māsassa phalaṃ māso, muggassa phalaṃ muggo, evaṃ yavo, tilo, atasī, kaṅgu, dhaññaṃ.

For the campaka and others—campaka, karavīra, kadamba, asoka, kaṇṇikāra—when referring to the flower as a modification or a part, the suffix 'ṇa' does not occur in another sense, because it originates from that which ends in the name of the flower. Thus, campaka and others, as names for flowers, are used in the neuter gender. The mango and others—pomegranate, orange, emblic myrobalan, jujube—are used for the fruit as a distinct natural entity. For āmalakī, kuvalī, badarī, when referring to the fruit as a modification or a part, a taddhita suffix also does not arise in another sense, because it originates from that which ends in the name of the fruit. Thus, mango and others, as names for fruits, are used in the neuter gender. The jasmine and others, though used in relation to flowers, retain their own gender due to their usage by way of non-distinction from their natural gender, such as mallikā, jāti, vanamallikā, etc. Similarly, grains, by way of non-distinction, retain their own gender even when referring to the fruit, such as: the fruit of māsa is māsa, the fruit of mugga is mugga; likewise yava (barley), tila (sesame), atasī (linseed), kaṅgu (millet), dhañña (grain).

Tikaṃ jambuyā phale. Tatra yadā lokato phale vutti, tadā jambusaddo pakatyantarameva phale vattate, yadā na phalavutti, tadā vikāre avayave vāno, jama adane, bū, jambū, pakatyantarāphale vutti. Jambuyā phalaṃ jambuvaṃ. Jambu ca. Lokato eva phalepi vattamānā harīṭakyādayo sabhāvato itthiyaṃ bhavanti amara 14.18-20. Harīṭakiyā phalaṃ harīṭakī, evaṃ kosātakī, sallakī, dakkhā, kaṇḍakārikā, sephālikā iccādi, pubbe viya vikārāvayavatthesu paccayābhāvo, assatthādikaṃ chakkameva taddhitantaṃ assatthādīnaṃ [M 0.0366] phale vattamānānaṃ napuṃsakaṃ siyā rūpabhedo, yathā – assatthassa phalaṃ assatthaṃ, veṇuno phalaṃ veṇavaṃ, pilakkhassa phalaṃ pilakkhaṃ, nigrodhassa phalaṃ nigrodhaṃ, iṅgudiyā phalaṃ iṅgudaṃ, brahatiyā phalaṃ brāhataṃ, vidārī aṃsumatī gambhariyādayo mūle, pupphepi saliṅgā amara 14.18-20. Pāṭalāsaddo pana abhedavatticchāyaṃ mūle pupphepi vattamāno sabhāvato itthiliṅgo, bhedavatticchāyaṃ vikāre avayave vā ṇamhi pāṭalaṃ amara 14.18-20. Dvayaṃ sākhāpallavādisamudāyalakkhaṇe ābhoge, viṭa vedhane, viṭa akkose vā, apo, passa bhatte viṭabhī, nadādi.

Three terms for the fruit of the jambu. There, when 'jambu' is commonly used for the fruit, then the word 'jambu' is used for the fruit as a distinct natural entity. When it is not used for the fruit, then for a modification or a part, the suffix 'ṇa' is used. From the root 'jam' (to eat), with the suffix 'bū', comes 'jambū', which is used for the fruit as a distinct natural entity. The fruit of the jambu is 'jambavaṃ', and also 'jambu'. Even when commonly used for fruits, harīṭakī and others are inherently feminine. The fruit of harīṭakī is 'harīṭakī'; similarly 'kosātakī', 'sallakī', 'dakkhā', 'kaṇḍakārikā', 'sephālikā', etc. As before, in the sense of modification or part, there is no suffix. The six terms beginning with assattha, when used for the fruit of assattha and others, become neuter with a taddhita suffix, differing in form. For example: the fruit of the assattha is 'assatthaṃ', the fruit of the bamboo is 'veṇavaṃ', the fruit of the pilakkha is 'pilakkhaṃ', the fruit of the nigrodha is 'nigrodhaṃ', the fruit of the iṅgudī is 'iṅgudaṃ', the fruit of the brahatī is 'brāhataṃ'. Vidārī, aṃsumatī, gambhariyā and others, when referring to the root or flower, retain their own gender. However, the word 'pāṭalā', when used for the root or flower with the intention of non-distinction, is inherently feminine. When used with the intention of distinction as a modification or part, with the suffix 'ṇa', it becomes 'pāṭalaṃ'. Two terms are used for the expanse characterized by an aggregate of branches, shoots, etc. 'Viṭapa' is from the root 'viṭ' (to pierce) or 'viṭ' (to abuse), with the suffix 'apa'. 'Viṭabhī' is also a form, belonging to the 'nadādi' group.

548. Mūlamārabbha mūlato paṭṭhāya sākhanto sākhāvadhi tarussa bhāgo khandho nāma, yo “pakaṇḍo”tipi vuccati, khanu avadāraṇe, dho, khandho, khāda bhakkhane vā, ko, “khādāmagamānaṃ khandhandhagandhā”ti khandhādeso, kalopo.

548. Beginning from the root, starting from the base up to the limit of the branches, that part of the tree is called the trunk (khandha), which is also called 'pakaṇḍa'. 'Khandha' is from the root 'khanu' (to split), with the suffix 'dha'. Or, it is from the root 'khād' (to eat), with the suffix 'ka'; according to the grammatical rule 'khādāmagamānaṃ...', 'khandha' is the substitute form, with elision.

Rukkhacchidde rukkhādīnaṃ vivare koṭaro. Kuṭa chedane, aro, koṭaro, nikkuhopi. Dve samā. Kāsa dittiyaṃ, kāsate agginā dippateti kaṭṭhaṃ, to, tassa ṭṭho, rasso ca, kasa gamane vā, to, kaṭṭhaṃ. Dara vidāraṇe, ṇu.

A hollow in a tree, an opening in a tree or the like, is a 'koṭara'. 'Koṭara' is from the root 'kuṭ' (to cut), with the suffix 'ara'. 'Nikkuha' is also a synonym. Two terms are synonymous for wood. 'Kaṭṭha' (wood) is from the root 'kās' (to shine); because it shines or blazes with fire, it is called 'kaṭṭha'. It is formed with the suffix 'ta', which is substituted by 'ṭṭha', and the vowel is shortened. Or, it is from the root 'kas' (to go), with the suffix 'ta'. [The second term, 'dāru', is] from the root 'dar' (to split), with the suffix 'ṇu'.

549. Tikaṃ mūle. Vu saṃvaraṇe, do, niggahītāgamo, budha gamane vā, a, dhassa do. Mūla patiṭṭhāyaṃ, ṇo, pādasaddena [M 0.0367] tappariyāyā caraṇatthā sabbe saṅgahitā, pādasadisattā pādo, dvayaṃ chinnassa tarukkhandhassa bhūmiṭṭhabhāge. Saṅka saṅkāyaṃ, u, saka sattiyaṃ vā, niggahītāgamo. Khanu avadāraṇe, ṇu, khāṇu. Dhuvopi, dhuvati thirāyateti dhuvo, dhu gatitheriyesu, a, uvādeso.

549. Three terms for the root. ['Bundha' is] from the root 'vu' (to cover), with the suffix 'da' and the augment 'niggahīta' (ṃ); or from the root 'budh' (to go), with the suffix 'a', and 'dh' becoming 'd'. 'Mūla' is from the root 'mūl' (to be established), with the suffix 'ṇa'. By the word 'pāda', all its synonyms meaning 'foot' are included; it is called 'pāda' due to its similarity to a foot. Two terms refer to the part of a severed tree trunk remaining in the ground. ['Saṅku' is] from the root 'saṅk' (to doubt), with the suffix 'u'; or from the root 'sak' (to be able), with the augment 'niggahīta'. 'Khāṇu' is from the root 'khanu' (to split), with the suffix 'ṇu'. 'Dhuva' is also a synonym; because it is firm and stable, it is 'dhuva'. It is from the root 'dhu' (in the sense of going and stability), with the suffix 'a' and the substitution of 'uva'.

Dvayaṃ vidāriyādīnaṃ kande. Kuyaṃ pathaviyaṃ ruhatīti kuruhāṭaṃ, aṭo, kanda avhāne, rodane ca, “karahāṭo’mbujakande, puppharukkhabhītesu ce”ti nānatthasaṅgahe. Dvayaṃ halādīnaṃ kalīre. Kala saṅkhyāne, īro. Masa āmasane, thako, matthake sīse vā jāto matthako.

Two terms for the bulbous root of vidārī and others. Because it grows on the earth, it is called 'kuruhāṭa'; with the suffix 'aṭa'. The root 'kand' is in the sense of calling and weeping. In the Nānatthasaṅgaha it is said: 'karahāṭa' is used for a lotus root, and for flowers and trees when frightened. Two terms for the shoot of hala and others. ['Kalīra' is] from the root 'kal' (to count), with the suffix 'īra'. ['Matthaka' is] from the root 'mas' (to touch), with the suffix 'thaka'; that which is born on the top or head is 'matthaka'.

550. Dve samā. Abhinavaniggatā āyatā sakusumā, kusumasuññā ca mañjarī, vallarī tu tadaññāpi, yathā tālavallarī, vala, valla saṃvaraṇe, aro, nadādi. Muñjayogato mañjarī, ro, nadādi, ussattañca, dvepi nārī. Dvayaṃ latāyaṃ. Valla saṃvaraṇe, nadādi. Latā vuttā, “latā patāninī vallī matakīthā”ti halāyudho.

550. Two terms are synonymous. A 'mañjarī' is newly emerged, elongated, with or without flowers. A 'vallarī', however, is also something else, for example, a palm-shoot. ['Vallarī' is] from the root 'val' or 'vall' (to cover), with the suffix 'ara', belonging to the 'nadādi' group. 'Mañjarī' is from its connection with muñja grass, with the suffix 'ra', belonging to the 'nadādi' group; and also 'ussatta'. Both terms are feminine. Two terms for a creeper. ['Vallī' is] from the root 'vall' (to cover), belonging to the 'nadādi' group. 'Latā' is mentioned; Halāyudha states: 'latā, patāninī, vallī, matakīthā'.

Akkhandho appakkhaṇḍo, bahupattatacadaṇḍikādi. Yo vā tanupakaṇḍo vaṃsanaḷādi, so “thambo, gumbo”ti coccate, thaka saṃvaraṇe, bo, kassa mo. Gupa rakkhaṇe, bo, passa mo. Patāno sākhāpattacayo, tena yuttā gorakkhā [M 0.0368] tambūli dhivusajīmūta gaḷojhādikā latā, sā vīru nāma, vividhehi ruhatīti katvā, kvi, vīru, dīghādi, gumbinīpi.

That which has no trunk, or a small trunk, or has many leaves, bark, stalks, etc. Or that which has a slender stem, like bamboo or reeds, is called 'thamba' or 'gumba'. ['Thamba' is] from the root 'thak' (to cover), with the suffix 'ba', and 'k' becoming 'm'. ['Gumba' is] from the root 'gup' (to protect), with the suffix 'ba', and 'p' becoming 'm'. 'Patāna' is a mass of branches and leaves. A creeper endowed with that, such as gorakkhā, tambūlī, dhivusajīmūta, gaḷojhā, etc., is called 'vīru'. Because it grows in various ways, with the suffix 'kvi', it becomes 'vīru', with lengthening of the vowel, etc. 'Gumbinī' is also a synonym.

551. Pajje pādena nāmaṃ. Yatra dvayaṃ “bodhirukkho”ti saññite buddhassa bhagavato sabbaññutaññāṇappaṭilābhaṭṭhānabhūte dumarāje, aññatra tūpacārā. Assaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhati etthāti assattho, ṭhassa tho, dvittaṃ, māravijayasabbaññutaññāṇappaṭilābhādikehi bhagavantaṃ assāsetīti vā assattho, āpubbo sāsa anusiṭṭhiyaṃ, tosane ca vattati, to, rasso. Sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ bujjhati etthāti bodhi, budha avagamane, i, bodhi, dvīsu. Caladalo, pippalo, kuñjarāsanopi. Dvayaṃ bahupāde. Adhobhāgaṃ rundhatīti nigrodho, usso, gāgamo ca. Vaṭa vedhane, vaṭatīti, a.

551. The name is formed by the foot (pāda), as in 'pajje'. Wherein the two terms designated 'bodhirukkho' refer to the king of trees, the place where the Blessed One, the Buddha, attained the knowledge of omniscience; elsewhere, it is by convention. Herein omniscience abides, hence 'assattha'; the 'ṭh' becomes 'th', with doubling. Or, it consoles the Blessed One through the conquest of Māra, the attainment of the knowledge of omniscience, and so forth, hence 'assattha'; from the root 'sāsa' with the prefix 'ā', which is used in the sense of teaching and also of satisfying, with the suffix 'to' and shortening of the vowel. Herein the knowledge of omniscience is awakened, hence 'bodhi'; from the root 'budha' in the sense of understanding, with the suffix 'i', forming 'bodhi', used in two genders. 'Caladala', 'pippala', and 'kuñjarāsana' are also synonyms. The two terms are for 'bahupāda'. That which obstructs the lower part is 'nigrodha', with the suffix 'usso' and the augment 'ga'. From the root 'vaṭa' in the sense of surrounding; that which surrounds is 'vaṭati', with the suffix 'a'.

Dvayaṃ kabiṭṭhe. Kavimhi vānare tiṭṭhatīti kabiṭṭho pāyena kapayo tiṭṭhanti atra kapittho (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.21) “vānare paṇḍite kavī”ti vopālito, tathā kapittho, to, ṭhassa tho ca. Dadhittho, ambilaphalopi. Dvayaṃ udumbare. Yaññakammānamaṅgo ekaṅgattā yaññaṅgo, dubbī hiṃsāyaṃ, aro, niggahītāgamo, ekassa bassa lopo ca. Jantuphalo hemaduddhopi.

The two terms are for 'kabiṭṭha'. That which stands on the monkey-poet is 'kabiṭṭho', for Vopālita states: 'kavi is used for a monkey or a wise person'. Similarly 'kapittho', with the suffix 'to', and 'ṭh' becomes 'th'. 'Dadhittha' and 'ambilaphala' are also synonyms. The two terms are for 'udumbara'. It is a component of sacrificial acts, being a single part, hence 'yaññaṅga'. From the root 'dubbī' in the sense of harming, with the suffix 'aro', the augment of the nasal, and the elision of one 'b'. 'Jantuphala' and 'hemaduddha' are also synonyms.

552. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0369] koviḷāre.

552. The two terms are for 'koviḷāra'.

“Sukapadāccharo campo,

Koviḷāro tu kañcano;

Pubbo sito paro ratto,

Yugapattā ubhopite”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.22.

The Campa is like a parrot's foot, but the Koviḷāra is golden; the former is white, the latter is red, and both have paired leaves.

Hi ratanakoso, kañjanālakopyatra. Yugaṃ yamakaṃ pattamassa.

Indeed, 'ratanakosa' and 'kañjanālaka' are also synonyms here. Its leaf is a pair, a twin.

Tipādaṃ uddāle. Vātaṃ uddālatīti uddālo. Siṅgārādīnaṃ saññāvasena rukkhānaṃ rājā rājarukkho, vātarogahanane rājabhūto rukkho vā rājarukkho. Katā mālā assa pupphehīti katamālo, siṅgārappakāso. Indati paramissariyaṃ karoti vātahananeti indīvaro, īvaro, indiyā sakkassa bhariyāya icchitabbattā vā indīvaro. Caturaṅgulo, ārevato, suvaṇṇakopi.

Three terms for 'uddāla'. It removes wind diseases, hence 'uddālo'. The king of trees by way of the designation of adornment and so forth is 'rājarukkho'; or, the tree that is a king in destroying wind-diseases is 'rājarukkho'. A garland is made from its flowers, hence 'katamālo', a manifestation of adornment. It exercises supreme lordship in destroying wind-diseases, hence 'indīvaro'; also 'īvaro'. Or, it is 'indīvaro' because it is desirable to Indī, Sakka's wife. 'Caturaṅgula', 'ārevata', and 'suvaṇṇaka' are also synonyms.

553. Dvayaṃ jambhīre, yassa phalamambilaṃ hoti. Ambilattā dantassa saṭho dantasaṭho. Saṭha ketavahiṃsāsaṃkilesesu, a. Jamu adane, īro, bhanto ca, jambha gattavināme vā, jambho, jambhalo, jambīropi. Dvayaṃ varaṇe. Vara icchāyaṃ[M 0.0370], yu. Kala saṅkhyāne, iro, nadādi, rassanto. Varuṇo, tittasākopi.

553. The two terms are for 'jambhīra', whose fruit is sour. Because of its sourness, it deceives the teeth, hence 'dantasaṭho'. The root 'saṭha' is in the senses of deceit, harming, and defilement, with the suffix 'a'. From the root 'jamu' in the sense of eating, with the suffix 'īro', and also 'bhanta'. Or from the root 'jambha' in the sense of bending the limbs; 'jambho', 'jambhalo', and 'jambhīro' are also synonyms. The two terms are for 'varaṇa'. From the root 'vara' in the sense of desiring, with the suffix 'yu'. From the root 'kala' in the sense of counting, with the suffix 'iro'; it is of the nadādi group, with a short final vowel. 'Varuṇa' and 'tittasāka' are also synonyms.

Dvayaṃ phalahare. “Ko ayaṃ, suko”ti vimatuppattikarapattakusumatāya kiṃsuko. Pāri samuddo, tatra bhaddo pāribhaddo, so eva pāḷibhaddo, koviḷāro, taṃsaṇṭhānapattakusumatāya pāḷibhaddo. Dvayaṃ vidule, yo abbhasamaye pupphati. Vaja gamane, ulo. Vī pajane, aso, tonto ca, vipubbo ata sātaccagamane vā, aso. Vānīropi.

The two terms are for 'phalahara'. It is 'kiṃsuko' because its leaves and flowers cause the arising of doubt, as in, 'What is this? A parrot?'. 'Pāri' is the ocean; that which is auspicious there is 'pāribhaddo'. That same one is 'pāḷibhaddo'. The 'koviḷāra' is called 'pāḷibhaddo' because its leaves and flowers have a similar shape. The two terms are for 'vidula', which blooms in the cloudy season. From the root 'vaja' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'ulo'. From the root 'vī' in the sense of producing, with the suffix 'aso', and also 'tonta'. Or from the root 'ata' with the prefix 'vi', in the sense of continuous going, with the suffix 'aso'. 'Vānīro' is also a synonym.

554. Dvayaṃ pītane, yassa pattaphalāni ambilāni, pūgaphalappamāṇañca phalaṃ, sallakīrukkhasaṇṭhāno ca, so rukkho. Amba sadde, aṭo, sakatthe ko. Pī tappanakantīsu, tano, pītiṃ vā tanotīti pītano, sakatthe ko. Dvayaṃ guḷapupphe. Mana ñāṇe, ko, madhvādeso ca. Madhunāmo dumo madhuddumo. Dvayaṃ “lambū”ti khyāte. Guḷo viya sātena phalamassa guḷaphalo. Pīla patitthambhe, u. Dvayaṃ tikkhagandhe. Sobhaṃ janetīti sobhañjano, sobhaṃ visañjanametena hetubhūtenāti vā sobhañjano. Vuttañca –

554. The two terms are for 'pītana', the tree whose leaves and fruits are sour, whose fruit is the size of a betel nut, and which has the shape of a sallakī tree. From the root 'amba' in the sense of sound, with the suffix 'aṭo', and 'ko' in its own sense. From the root 'pī' in the senses of delight and loveliness, with the suffix 'tano'; or, it extends delight, hence 'pītano', with 'ko' in its own sense. The two terms are for 'guḷapuppha'. From the root 'mana' in the sense of knowledge, with the suffix 'ko', and the substitution of 'madhu'. The tree named 'madhu' is 'madhuddumo'. The two terms are for that known as 'lambū'. Its fruit is like jaggery in sweetness, hence 'guḷaphalo'. From the root 'pīla' in the sense of supporting, with the suffix 'u'. The two terms are for that with a sharp fragrance. It produces beauty, hence 'sobhañjano'; or, beauty is destroyed by it as a cause, hence 'sobhañjano'. And it is said:

“Sirīsapupphassa rasena bhāvitaṃ,

Sahassavāraṃ marīcaṃ sitavhayaṃ;

Etena samanti visāhi sambhavā,

Katañjanasnehanapādanatthuto”ti.

White pepper, imbued a thousand times with the juice of the sirīsa flower; by this, poisons and their effects are pacified. It is made as an ointment, a liniment, a foot-salve, and a nasal application.

Si sevāyaṃ, viddhavināsanatthaṃ sevīteti siggu, gu, thī. Cittahārī, pabhañjano, viddhavināsanopi.

From the root 'si' in the sense of serving; it is served for the purpose of destroying enemies, hence 'siggu', with the suffixes 'gu' and 'thī'. 'Cittahārī', 'pabhañjano', and 'viddhavināsano' are also synonyms.

555. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0371] visālatace, yo sarade pupphati pupphaṃ. Sattapaṇṇānyassa sattapaṇṇī pume. Chattamiva paṇṇamassa chattapaṇṇo. Visamacchadopi, sattapaṇṇattā visamacchado. Dvayaṃ rathaddume. Rathaṃ tanoti yena tiniso, iso. Atipamuccati dāhapittamaneneti atimuttako. Cittakipi.

555. The two terms are for that with broad bark, which blooms in autumn. It has seven leaves, hence 'sattapaṇṇī', in the masculine. Its leaf is like a parasol, hence 'chattapaṇṇo'. Also 'visamacchado'; because it has seven leaves, it has an uneven covering. The two terms are for 'rathadduma'. That by which one makes a chariot is 'tiniso', with the suffix 'iso'. Burning and bile are greatly released by this, hence 'atimuttako'. 'Cittaki' is also a synonym.

Dvayaṃ vātapothe, paṃ vātaṃ lunātīti palāso, aso. “Patte palāsaṃ so rukkhe, pītaharitakiṃ suke”ti hi ruddo. Vātapothopi, vātassa potho vātapotho, putha hiṃsāyaṃ.

The two terms are for 'vātapotha'. It cuts the wind, hence 'palāso', with the suffix 'aso'. For Rudda says: '`palāsa` is used for a leaf on a tree, and `pītaharitaki` for a parrot'. Also 'vātapotha'; the striking of the wind is 'vātapotha', from the root 'putha' in the sense of harming.

Dvayaṃ “putīti” khyāte. Hatajantupamohasaṅkhātāriphalatāya ariṭṭho, nipātanā hantissa ṭṭho, taṃrogārivantajanehi icchitabbaphalattā vā ariṭṭho, isu icchāyaṃ. Phaṇa gatiyaṃ, ilo, asse.

The two terms are for that known as 'putīti'. It is 'ariṭṭho' because its fruit is an enemy characterized as delusion, which is like a slain creature; by irregular formation, 'hanti' becomes 'ṭṭho'. Or, it is 'ariṭṭho' because its fruit is desirable to people afflicted by disease and enemies, from the root 'isu' in the sense of desiring. From the root 'phaṇa' in the sense of movement, with the suffixes 'ilo' and 'asse'.

556. Tikaṃ siriphale. Mala dhāraṇe, ūro. Bila bhedane, ṇuvo, beluvo. Lapaccaye billo. Saṇḍilyo, selusopi. “Munippabhede mālūre, saṇḍilyo pādapantare, naṭe bille ca seluso”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.32 rabhaso.

556. The three terms are for 'siriphala'. From the root 'mala' in the sense of holding, with the suffix 'ūro'. From the root 'bila' in the sense of breaking, with the suffix 'ṇuvo', it becomes 'beluvo'. With the suffix 'la', it becomes 'billo'. 'Saṇḍilyo' and 'seluso' are also synonyms. For Rabhasa says: '`mālūra` is used for a type of sage, `saṇḍilyo` for a kind of tree, and `seluso` for a dancer and for the bilva tree'.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0372] tuṅge. Pumanāmo nāgo rukkho punnāgo. “Punnāge puriso tuṅgo, kesaro devavallabho”ti amara 14.25 hyamarasīho, dīgho, “pumassa liṅgādīsu samāsesū”ti akāralopo ca. Atisayapupphakesaravantatāya kesaro, kisa tanukaraṇe vā, aro, pupphakesayuttatāya vā kesaro, ro.

The two terms are for 'tuṅga'. The tree 'nāga', with the name 'puma', is 'punnāga'. For Amarasīha says: '`punnāga`, `puriso`, `tuṅgo`, `kesaro`, `devavallabho`'. There is lengthening, and the elision of the vowel 'a' of 'puma' in compounds related to gender and so forth. It is 'kesaro' because it possesses an abundance of flower filaments; or from the root 'kisa' in the sense of making thin, with the suffix 'aro'; or it is 'kesaro' because it is endowed with flower filaments, with the suffix 'ro'.

Dvayaṃ loddamatte. Sala gamanattho, avo. Rattakaphapittasote lunātīti loddo, ddo. Tiriṭo, sāvaropi. “Sāvaro aparādhe ca, lodde pāpe ca kathyate” cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.33 tyajayo. Dvayaṃ dhanupaṭṭe phalini. Pī pāne, alo, īssa iyādeso. Sannakā tāpasā, tesaṃ du dumo sannakaddu, “sannakaddu cāpapaṭā, varaṇo tāpasappiyo”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.35 hi kosantare.

The two terms are for 'loddamatta'. From the root 'sala' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'avo'. It cuts the flow of blood, phlegm, and bile, hence 'loddo', with the suffix 'ddo'. 'Tiriṭo' and 'sāvaro' are also synonyms. For Ajaya says: '`sāvaro` is spoken of in the sense of offense, and `loddo` in the sense of evil'. The two terms are for the fruit-bearing tree used for bowstrings. From the root 'pī' in the sense of drinking, with the suffix 'alo', and the substitution of 'iya' for 'ī'. 'Sannakā' are ascetics; their tree is 'sannakaddu'. For in another lexicon it is said: '`sannakaddu` and `cāpapaṭā`; `varaṇo` and `tāpasappiyo`'.

557. Dvayaṃ “mhanakū”iti khyāte. Likuco nāma ḍahurukkho, tagguṇattā likocako, saññāyaṃ ko. Aṅka lakkhaṇe, olo, aṅkolo. Dvayaṃ kumbhe. Rogaharaṇe garunopi vejjassa garu guggulu, nipātanā. Kusa chedane, ṇvu. Kumbho, puropi.

557. The two terms are for that known as 'mhanakū'. 'Likuco' is the name of the ḍahu tree; because of its qualities, it is 'likocako', with 'ko' as a suffix of designation. From the root 'aṅka' in the sense of marking, with the suffix 'olo', hence 'aṅkolo'. The two terms are for 'kumbha'. In removing diseases, though heavy, it is important to a physician, hence 'guggulu', by irregular formation. From the root 'kusa' in the sense of cutting, with the suffix 'ṇvu'. 'Kumbho' and 'puro' are also synonyms.

“Rāsibhede gajamuddhaṃse,

Kumbhakaṇṇasuke ghaṭe;

Kāmuke vāranāriyañca,

Kumbho klīvantu vaggulumhī”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.34.

The word 'kumbha' is used for a heap, a type, and an elephant's frontal globe; for Kumbhakaṇṇa, a parrot, and a pot; for a lustful person and a female elephant. But 'kumbha' is neuter in the sense of bdellium.

Rabhaso. Pura aggagamane, ṇo, puro.

Thus Rabhasa. From the root 'pura' in the sense of going foremost, with the suffix 'ṇo', hence 'puro'.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0373] ambe. Ama gatiyaṃ, bo, amba sadde vā, a. Cuti āsecane, rakkhaṇe ca, a, cu cavane vā, to, dīghādi. Rasālopi, rasaṃ lātīti rasālo, dīgho. Eso ambo sugandhavā atisayagandhayutto samāno “saho, sahakāro”ti coccate. Saha sattiyaṃ, sugandhaṃ kattuṃ sahatīti saho, a. Sahanaṃ saho, taṃ karotīti sahakāro, hā vā pamudā, tāya saha vattatīti saho, sahaṃ samudaṃ karotīti sahakāro.

The two terms are for 'amba'. From the root 'ama' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'bo'; or from 'amba' in the sense of sound, with the suffix 'a'. From the root 'cuti' in the senses of sprinkling and protecting, with the suffix 'a'; or from 'cu' in the sense of falling, with the suffix 'to', with lengthening and so forth. Also 'rasālo'; it takes juice, hence 'rasālo', with lengthening. This mango, being fragrant and possessing an excellent fragrance, is also called 'saho' and 'sahakāro'. From the root 'saha' in the sense of being able; it is able to produce a good fragrance, hence 'saho', with the suffix 'a'. 'Sahana' is 'saho'; it makes that, hence 'sahakāro'. Or, 'hā' means joy; it exists with that, hence 'saho'; it produces joy, hence 'sahakāro'.

558. Dvayaṃ setambe. Puṇḍa puṇḍane. Puṇḍa khaṇḍanetyeke, ṇvu, assī, arāgamo ca. Setavaṇṇo ambo setambo. Dvayaṃ bahuvārake, yassa phalāni atipicchilāni. Si bandhane, lu, sala gamanattho vā, u, asse. Picchilattā bahūni vārīni yasmiṃ bahuvārako, saññāyaṃ ko. Sīto, uddālo, kaphalopi.

558. Two for setamba. From the root 'puṇḍ' in the sense of pulverizing. Some say from the root 'puṇḍ' in the sense of breaking, with the suffixes 'ṇvu', 'assī', and the augment 'ara'. A white-colored amba is a setamba. Two for bahuvāraka, whose fruits are very sticky. From the root 'si' in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'lu'; or from 'sal' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'u' and 'asse'. Because of its stickiness, it has many layers, hence bahuvārako, with 'ko' as a suffix in the designation. Also sīta, uddāla, and kaphala.

Dvayaṃ kāsmariyaṃ. Sirimantāni paṇṇāni yassā sepaṇṇī, nadādi, sirīsaddassa se. Kasmīradesajattā kāsmarī, kāsa dittiyaṃ vā, maro, nadādi. Madhupaṇṇī, bhaddapaṇṇīpi. Dvayaṃ sakaṇṭakambilaphalarukkhe. Sakaṇṭakattā kucchitaṃ lātīti kolī, nadādi. Vada theriye, aro, nadādi. Kuvalī, kakkandhūpi.

Two for kāsmariya. It has glorious leaves, hence sepaṇṇī; it is of the nadādi class, with 'se' from the word 'sirīsa'. Because it originates from the country of Kashmir, it is kāsmarī; or it is derived from the root 'kāsa' in the sense of shining, with the suffix 'maro', and is of the nadādi class. Also madhupaṇṇī and bhaddapaṇṇī. Two for the thorny tree with sour fruit. Because it is thorny, it takes what is despised, hence kolī; it is of the nadādi class. From the root 'vada' in the sense of old age, with the suffix 'aro', and it is of the nadādi class. Also kuvalī and kakkandhū.

559. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0374] tassā koliyā phale. Koliyā phalaṃ kolaṃ. Badariyā ayaṃ avayavo badaro. Kuvalaṃ, phenilaṃ, sovīrampi. “Sotañjane tu sovīraṃ, kañjike badarepi ce”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.36 rabhaso. Dvayaṃ assatthakulasambhūte rukkhapāsāṇādīsu sañjātarukkhe. Pilaṃ paraṃ nissayabhūtaṃ kasatīti pilakkho, kasa vilekhane, sassa khattādi nipātanā. Akhādanīyaphalatāya virūpaṃ phalamassatthīti pipphalī, ī, nadādi, vissapi ca.

559. Two for the fruit of that kolī tree. The fruit of the kolī is kola. This part of the badarī is badara. Also kuvala, phenila, and sovīra. For it is said by Rabhasa: 'Sovīra is used for sotañjana, and also for kañjika and badara.' Two for a tree born from the assattha family, a tree growing on rocks and so forth. It scrapes that which is a support for others, hence pilakkho; from the root 'kasa' in the sense of scraping, with 'sa' becoming 'kha', etc., by irregular formation. Because its fruit is inedible and unsightly, it is pipphalī, with the suffix 'ī', of the nadādi class, and also 'vissa'.

Dvayaṃ toyādivāpiniyaṃ, yassā mūlaṃ mahāpañcamūle paviṭṭhaṃ. Paṭa gamane, alo, nadādi, pāṭalī, pāṭalāpi. Kaṇhaṃ pupphavaṇṭaṃ yassā sā kaṇhavaṇṭā, kāsmariyampi. Alippiyaṃ, tambapupphipyatra. Dvayaṃ gandhile. Sāduphalatāya sādu ca so kaṇṭasahitatāya kaṇṭo ceti sādukaṇṭo. Sakaṇṭakatāya attānaṃ virūpaṃ karotīti vikaṅkato, dvittaṃ, niggahītāgamo ca.

Two for toyādivāpinī, whose root is included among the great five roots. From the root 'paṭa' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'alo', of the nadādi class; also pāṭalī and pāṭalā. It has a dark flower stalk, hence kaṇhavaṇṭā; also kāsmariya. Here also are alippiya and tambapupphi. Two for the fragrant tree. Because its fruit is sweet, it is sādu, and because it has thorns, it is kaṇṭa, hence sādukaṇṭo. Because it makes itself unsightly with thorns, it is vikaṅkato, with doubling and the augment niggahīta.

560. Catukkaṃ tinduke. Tanu vitthāre, uko, danto ca. Tidi hiṃsāyaṃ vā, u, saññāyaṃ ko. Kāḷo khandho pakaṇḍo yassāti. Tima addabhāve, ūso, sakatthe ko, varanto ca. Upaccaye timbaru.

560. Four for tinduka. From the root 'tanu' in the sense of spreading, with the suffixes 'uko' and 'danto'. Or from the root 'tidi' in the sense of harming, with the suffix 'u', and 'ko' in the designation. It has a black trunk, hence pakaṇḍo. From the root 'tima' in the sense of being moist, with the suffix 'ūso', 'ko' in its own sense, and 'varanto'. In growth, it is timbaru.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0375] tambaphale. Irāvatī nadī, paṭhamakāle tassā tīre jāto erāvato. Nāraṃ vuccati nīraṃ, taṃ gacchatīti nāraṅgo. Dvayaṃ makkaṭatinduke. Kula saṅkhyāne, ṇvu. Kākendu, kākalukopi.

Two for tambaphala. The Irāvatī is a river; erāvato was born on its bank in a former time. Water is called nāra; it goes to that, hence nāraṅgo. Two for makkaṭatinduka. From the root 'kula' in the sense of counting, with the suffix 'ṇvu'. Also kākendu and kākaluko.

561. Tikaṃ kadambe. Kaṃ vātaṃ dametīti kadambo, bo. Pinetīti piyako, ṇvu, iyādeso. Nayati mudaṃ nīpo, po. Dvayaṃ, vidarukkhe, yassa niyyāsena peḷādayo limpanti. Bhala, bhalla paribhāsanahiṃsādānesu, nadādi, aññatra to, kanto ca, bhallātako, tīsvayaṃ. Arukaro, aggimukhopi.

561. Three for kadamba. It subdues the wind, hence kadambo, with the suffix 'bo'. It delights, hence piyako, with the suffix 'ṇvu' and the 'iya' substitution. It brings joy, hence nīpo, with the suffix 'po'. Two for the vida tree, whose sap is used to smear boxes and so forth. The roots bhala and bhalla are in the senses of reviling, harming, and taking; it is of the nadādi class, except for 'to' and 'kanto'; this bhallātako is in the three genders. Also arukaro and aggimukho.

Dvayaṃ “pāvusā”iti khyāte. Jhapa dāhe, ṇvu. Passa vo. Paca pāke, ulo. Dvayaṃ sirimati, yassa phalāni marīcappamāṇāni, ambilāni ca. Tila gamane, ṇvu. Khura chedane, ṇvu.

Two for the tree known as 'pāvusā'. From the root 'jhapa' in the sense of burning, with the suffix 'ṇvu'. See, you. From the root 'paca' in the sense of cooking, with the suffix 'ulo'. Two for sirimatī, whose fruits are the size of peppers and are sour. From the root 'tila' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'ṇvu'. From the root 'khura' in the sense of cutting, with the suffix 'ṇvu'.

562. Dvayaṃ ambilikāyaṃ. Ci cayane, co, cica ādānasaṃvaraṇesu vā. Tanu vitthāre, ambilarasaṃ tanotīti tintiṇī, dvittamittaṃ, ṇattañca, nadādi. Dvayaṃ ambilaṅkuraphale setarukkhe. Gadrabhaṇḍappamāṇaphalattā gaddabhaṇḍo, ralopo. Kapi calane, tano, dīgho āgamassa. Kandarālo, pilakkhopi.

562. Two for ambilikā. From the root 'ci' in the sense of collecting, with the suffix 'co'; or from 'cica' in the senses of taking and restraining. From the root 'tanu' in the sense of spreading; it extends the sour taste, hence tintiṇī, with doubling, the letter 'i', the state of being 'ṇ', and of the nadādi class. Two for the white tree with sour sprout-like fruits. Because its fruit is the size of a donkey's testicle, it is gaddabhaṇḍo, with elision of 'ra'. From the root 'kapi' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'tano', and lengthening of the augment. Also kandarālo and pilakkho.

Tikaṃ [M 0.0376] sālarukkhe. Sala gamane, ṇo, sāravantatāya vā sālo. Assakaṇṇasadisapaṇṇatāya assakaṇṇo. Sanja saṅge, a, sajja adane vā, a. Dvayaṃ nadīsajje. Ajja ajjane, uno. Kaka lolye, udho. Vīrataru, indadumopi.

Three for the sāla tree. From the root 'sala' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'ṇo'; or it is sālo because it possesses essence. Because its leaves resemble a horse's ear, it is assakaṇṇo. From the root 'sañja' in the sense of joining, with the suffix 'a'; or from 'sajja' in the sense of eating, with the suffix 'a'. Two for nadīsajja. From the root 'ajja' in the sense of acquiring, with the suffix 'uno'. From the root 'kaka' in the sense of unsteadiness, with the suffix 'udho'. Also vīrataru and indadumo.

563. Tikaṃ mucalinde. Cula nimujjane. Mucala saṅgāte, indo. Nīpo kadambepi. Tikaṃ pītasāle. Piyako kadambepi. Asa bhakkhane, yu, pītapuppho sālo rukkho pītasālo. Bandhūkapuppho, jīvakopi.

563. Three for mucalinda. From the root 'cula' in the sense of immersion. From the root 'mucala' in the sense of meeting, with the suffix 'indo'. Nīpo is also a kadamba. Three for pītasāla. Piyako is also a kadamba. From the root 'asa' in the sense of eating, with the suffix 'yu'; a sāla tree with yellow flowers is pītasālo. Also bandhūkapuppho and jīvako.

Dvayaṃ jhāṭaliyaṃ. Gāvo lihantīti golīso, hassa so. Jhaṭa saṅghāte, alo. Jhāṭalo, pāṭalipupphākāro dīghaphalo rukkho. Pamokkhopi.

Two for jhāṭaliya. Cows lick it, hence golīso, with 'h' becoming 's'. From the root 'jhaṭa' in the sense of gathering, with the suffix 'alo'. Jhāṭalo is a tree with pāṭali-like flowers and long fruits. Also pamokkho.

564. Dvayaṃ rājāyatane, khīravantatāya khīrikā. Devarājassa nivāsanaṭṭhānabhūtattā rājāyatanaṃ, piyālepi. Dvayaṃ kapphale. Kucchitena phalena umbhati pūratīti kumbho. Kucchitena modatīti kumudikā, ṇvu.

564. Two for rājāyatana; because it possesses milky sap, it is khīrikā. Because it was the dwelling place of the king of gods, it is rājāyatanaṃ; also piyāla. Two for kapphala. It swells or fills with bad fruit, hence kumbho. It delights unpleasantly, hence kumudikā, with the suffix 'ṇvu'.

Dvayaṃ guvākarukkhe, yassa phalena tambūlanāmaṃ jāyati. Pūja pūjāyaṃ, ṇo, jassa go. Kamu icchāyaṃ, hetukattari ṇvu. Khapuropi. Dvayaṃ lohitalodde. Paṭṭiityākhyā yassa paṭṭi[M 0.0377]. “Paddhī”tipi pāṭho. Asmiṃ pakkhitte lākhā rattā bhavatīti lākhāpasādano. Kamukopi.

Two for the guvāka tree, from whose fruit the name 'tambūla' arises. From the root 'pūja' in the sense of worship, with the suffix 'ṇo', and 'ja' becomes 'go'. From the root 'kamu' in the sense of desire, with the agentive suffix 'ṇvu'. Also khapuro. Two for the lohitalodda. Its bark is called paṭṭi. 'Paddhī' is also a reading. Because when this is applied, lac becomes red, it is called lākhāpasādano. Also kamuko.

565. Dvayaṃ iṅgudiyaṃ, ayañca kaṇṭakī bāhulyena majjhimadese jāyate. Iṅga gamanattho, ido, issu, nadādi. Tāpaso payujjamānaphalakatāya tāpasataru. Dvayaṃ “bhujapatto”itikhyāte sundaratace rukkhe, yassa tace mantakkharāni likhanti. Bhujo pāṇi, taṃsadisapattatāya bhujapatto. Mantalekhakehi ābhujitatacavantatāya ābhujī. Bhūjo, cammī, muduttacopi.

565. Two for iṅgudiya; and this thorny plant grows abundantly in the middle country. From the root 'iṅga' in the sense of going, with the suffixes 'ido', 'issu', and of the nadādi class. Because its fruit is used by ascetics, it is tāpasataru. Two for the tree with beautiful bark known as 'bhujapatto', on whose bark mantra syllables are written. 'Bhujo' means hand; because its leaves resemble it, it is bhujapatto. Because its bark is used by mantra-writers, it is ābhujī. Also bhūjo, cammī, and muduttaco.

Dvayaṃ simbaliyaṃ. Picchāyogā picchilā, ilo. Samba maṇḍale, ali, assi. “Picchilā pūraṇī mocā, thirāyu simbalī dvisū”ti amara 14.46 amarakoso. Dvayaṃ picchilākāre kaṇṭakasahite rukkhe. Ruca dittiyaṃ, hetukattari yu, kuṭa koṭilye, kattari ṇo, koṭo asimbali samānopi simbalisadisākāradassanato koṭasimbali, pume. Kasambalopi.

Two for simbalī. Due to its resinous nature, it is picchilā, with the suffix 'ilo'. From the root 'samba' in the sense of a circle, with the suffixes 'ali' and 'assi'. The Amarakosa states: 'Picchilā, pūraṇī, mocā, and thirāyu are synonyms for simbalī in two genders.' Two for a sticky-shaped tree with thorns. From the root 'ruca' in the sense of shining, with the agentive suffix 'yu'; from the root 'kuṭa' in the sense of crookedness, with the agentive suffix 'ṇo'; although koṭo is not a simbalī, because it shows an appearance similar to a simbalī, it is koṭasimbali, in the masculine. Also kasambalo.

566. Dvayaṃ “kaṇṭakarañja”iti khyāte kaṇṭakini karañjagumbe, yaṃ loke “kalino”ti vuccati. Kara hiṃsāyaṃ, karato [M 0.0378] ririyā. Pū pavane, iko, tonto ca. Pūtikarajo, kalimārakopi, kalino. Dvayaṃ dālimapupphākāre pītanāsakarukkhe. Ruha janane, ṇī. Lohitapupphatāya rohitako.

566. Two for the thorny karañja shrub known as 'kaṇṭakarañja', which is called 'kalino' in the world. From the root 'kara' in the sense of harming; from 'karato' with 'ririyā'. From the root 'pū' in the sense of cleansing, with the suffixes 'iko' and 'tonto'. Pūtikarajo, also kalimārako, and kalino. Two for the tree with yellow-tipped flowers resembling pomegranate flowers. From the root 'ruha' in the sense of generating, with the suffix 'ṇī'. Because it has red flowers, it is rohitako.

Dvayaṃ eraṇḍe. Eraḍi hiṃsāyaṃ. Vātaṃ eraṇḍatīti eraṇḍo, ṇo. Maṇḍa bhūsane, īsaṃpasannatelatāya vā āmaṇḍo, āmaṃ vā vātaṃ, taṃ dāyatīti āmaṇḍo. Dā avakhaṇḍane, dāssa ḍo. Cittako, cañcupi.

Two for eraṇḍa. From the root 'eraḍi' in the sense of harming. Because it harms the wind, it is eraṇḍo, with the suffix 'ṇo'. From the root 'maṇḍa' in the sense of ornament; or it is āmaṇḍo because of its slightly clarified oil; or because it cuts raw wind, it is āmaṇḍo. From the root 'dā' in the sense of cutting; 'dā' becomes 'ḍo'. Cittako, also cañcu.

“Aggisaññepi cittako, pume eraṇḍake cañcu.

Cittako is also a name for fire; cañcu is used in the masculine for eraṇḍaka.

Pakkhituṇḍe thiyaṃ mato”.

It is considered feminine for a bird's beak.

Dvayaṃ sivārukkhe. Sattuyuttaphalatāya sattuphalā. Gaṇḍaṃ sametīti samī, a, nadādi, pāribhaddakepi. Garudāru, pūtikaṭṭhampi.

Two for the sivāru tree. Because its fruit is suitable for flour, it is sattuphalā. Because it alleviates tumors, it is samī, with the suffix 'a', of the nadādi class; also pāribhaddaka. Also garudāru and pūtikaṭṭha.

567. Dvayaṃ karañje. Nattaṃ rattā mālā yassa. Kaṃ rañjayatīti karañjo, ṇo. Cillavillo, karajopi. Dvayaṃ khadire. Khada hiṃsāyaṃ, theriye ca. Khadanti dantā yenāti khadiro, iro. Dantā dhāvanti yena nirogattāti dantadhāvano, yu, dhāva gatisuddhiyaṃ. Gāyattī, bālatanayopi. “Gāyattī khadire itthī, chandasipi chaḷakkhare”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.49 byākhyāsudhā 2.4.50 rabhaso. Bālo sukhumo pattasaññito tanayo yassa bālatanayo. Dvayaṃ pītasāre khadire. Khadirādikantu pītasāre. Setavaṇṇatāya [M 0.0379] somo kappūrasadiso vakko vakkalametassa somavakko. “Somo kuvere pitudevatāyaṃ, vasuppabhede vasudhākare ca. Dibbosadhī somalatā samīraṇe, kappūranīresu ca vānare cā”ti nānatthasaṅgaho. Īsaṃ khuddakaṃ dalametassa kadaro, lassa ro. Dvayaṃ piṇḍītake. Sala gamane, lo. Mada ummāde, yu. “Piṇḍītako maravako, sasano karahāṭako”tyamarakose amara 14.52.

567. Two words for karañja. That whose garland is not red. Because it delights someone, it is called karañja, with the suffix ṇa. Cillavilla, also karaja. Two words for khadira. The root 'khad' is in the sense of harming and also stability. Because teeth bite with it, it is called khadira, with the suffix ira. Because teeth are cleansed by it, resulting in freedom from disease, it is called dantadhāvana, with the suffix yu; the root 'dhāv' is in the sense of movement and purity. Gāyattī, also bālatanaya. Rabhasa states: 'Gāyattī is a feminine word for khadira, and also a meter with six syllables in prosody.' That whose delicate offspring is known as a leaf is called bālatanaya. Two words for pītasāra khadira, the yellow-wood acacia. Khadira and the like are for pītasāra. Because of its white color, it is Soma, like camphor; its bark is crooked, hence Somavakka. The Nānatthasaṅgaho states: 'Soma is used for Kuvera, for a paternal deity, for a type of Vasu, and for a wealth-maker. It is also used for a divine herb, the Soma creeper, for wind, for camphor, for water, and for a monkey.' That whose leaf is slightly small is called kadara, with 'l' changing to 'r'. Two words for piṇḍītaka. The root 'sal' is in the sense of going, with the suffix la. The root 'mad' is in the sense of intoxication, with the suffix yu. The Amarakośa states: 'Piṇḍītaka, maravaka, sasana, and karahāṭaka are synonyms.'

568. Tikaṃ indasāle. Sālānaṃ rukkhānaṃ indo rājā indasālo, dāsādīsu sirivaḍḍhakādisaddo viya adhivacanamattamidaṃ. Indassa sakkassa sālotipi indasālo. Sallato ṇvu, nadādi, sallakī. Khara chedanavināsanesu, ṇvu.

568. Three words for indasāla. The lord, the king of the sāl trees, is indasāla; this is merely a designation, like the term sirivaḍḍhaka and so forth among servants and others. The sāl tree of Indra, Sakka, is also indasāla. From the root 'sall', with the suffix ṇvu, and being a nadādi word, comes sallakī. The root 'khar' is in the sense of cutting and destroying, with the suffix ṇvu.

Dvayaṃ devadārumhi. Devānaṃ dāru. Bhaddattā bhaddadāru. Sakkapādapo, pāribhaddako, pītadāru, dāru, pūtikaṭṭhampi. Dvayaṃ hemapupphake. Paṭhamakāle campānagare jāto campeyyo, ṇeyyo. Kapaccaye campako.

Two words for devadāru. The wood of the devas. Because of its auspiciousness, it is called bhaddadāru. Sakkapādapa, pāribhaddaka, pītadāru, dāru, and also pūtikaṭṭha. Two words for hemapupphaka. Because it was born in the city of Campā in ancient times, it is called campeyya, with the suffix ṇeyya. With the suffix ka, it is campaka.

569. Dvayaṃ panase. Pana byavahāre, thutimhi ca, aso. Kaṇṭakayuttaṃ phalamassa kaṇṭakiphalo. Dvayaṃ sivāyaṃ. Na vijjate [M 0.0380] rogabhayaṃ, rogabyatho copayujjamānāyamassanti abhayā. Rogabhayaṃ harati apanetīti harītakī, to, sakatthe ko, nadādi. Harittakīpi. Abyathā, putanā, amatā, hemavatī, cetakī, sivāpi.

569. Two words for panasa, the jackfruit. The root 'pan' is in the sense of transaction and also praise, with the suffix asa. That whose fruit is thorny is called kaṇṭakiphala. Two words for sivā. Because fear of disease and suffering do not exist when it is used, it is called abhayā. Because it removes the fear of disease, it is called harītakī, with the suffix ta, and ka in its own sense, and it is a nadādi word. Also harittakī, abyathā, putanā, amatā, hemavatī, cetakī, and sivā.

Dvayaṃ karisaphale. Rogaṃ asati bhakkhatīti akkho, kho, sassa ko. Rogaṃ vibhūtaṃ karotīti vibhītako, vibhīṭakopi. Bhūtāvāso, kaliddumopi, kalissa āsayabhūto dumo kaliddumo. Dvayaṃ pussaphale. Natthi matametissaṃ hetubhūtāyaṃ amatā. Mala dhāraṇe, ṇvu, nadādi, āmalakī. Vayaṭṭhāpi. Vayo tiṭṭhati thirībhavatyetāyāti vayaṭṭhā.

Two words for karisaphala. Because it eats disease, it is called akkha, with the suffix kha, and the 's' of the root becomes 'k'. Because it makes disease disappear, it is called vibhītaka, also vibhīṭaka. Bhūtāvāsa, also kalidduma; the tree that is the abode of Kali is kalidduma. Two words for pussaphala. Because it is the cause of no death, it is called amatā. The root 'mal' is in the sense of holding, with the suffix ṇvu, and it is a nadādi word, hence āmalakī. Also vayaṭṭhā. Because age stands firm and becomes stable through it, it is called vayaṭṭhā.

570. Dvayaṃ ḍahurukkhe. Labunāmake pabbate jāyatīti labujo. Khuddakattā līnaṃ apākaṭaṃ kucasaṅkhātaṃ phalametassa likuco, nipātanā. Dvayaṃ pītapupphe. Agandhapupphatāya attānaṃ kaṇiṭṭhaṃ karotīti kaṇikāro, ṭṭhalopo, padumappamāṇapupphadumatāya dumuppalo.

570. Two words for the ḍahuru tree. Because it grows on the mountain named Labunā, it is called labuja. Because its fruit, known as kuca, is small, hidden, and inconspicuous, it is called likuca, by irregular formation. Two words for pītapuppha, the yellow-flowered tree. Because its flowers lack fragrance, it makes itself inferior, hence it is called kaṇikāra, with elision of 'ṭṭha'; and because its flowering tree has flowers the size of a lotus, it is called dumuppala.

Tikaṃ hiṅguniyyāse. Nī naye, bo, monto ca. Tittarasattā aribhāve tiṭṭhatīti ariṭṭho. Puciṃ kuṭṭhaṃ maddatīti pucimando, ittaṃ, bindāgamo. Dhammaseno, mālakopi. Malate rogaṃ mālako, ṇvu. Dvayaṃ rattapupphe. Karotismā ṇvu. Dala vidāraṇe, mo, ikārāgamo. Dāḷimopi.

Three words for hiṅgu resin. The root 'nī' is in the sense of leading, with the suffixes ba and manta. Because of its bitter taste, it stands as an enemy to disease, hence ariṭṭha. Because it crushes the kuṭṭha disease, it is called pucimanda, with the suffix itta and the addition of a bindu. Dhammasena, also mālaka. Because it removes disease, it is called mālaka, with the suffix ṇvu. Two words for rattapuppha, the red-flowered tree. From 'karoti', with the suffix ṇvu. The root 'dal' is in the sense of splitting, with the suffix ma and the addition of the vowel 'i'. Also dāḷima, the pomegranate.

571. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0381] pītaddume. Sarati kālantaraṃ saralo, alo. Pūtiyeva kaṭṭhaṃ pūtikaṭṭhaṃ, pūtimuttanti yathā. Dvayaṃ picchilāyaṃ. Kapi calane, ilo. Sāsa anusiṭṭhiyaṃ, sisa icchāyaṃ vā, apo, niggahītāgamo, siṃsapā. Agurupi.

571. Two words for the pīta tree. Because it extends over time, it is called sarala, with the suffix ala. Wood that is simply rotten is pūtikaṭṭha, just as in pūtimutta.
