Two words for picchilā, the slippery or resinous tree. The root 'kap' is in the sense of moving, with the suffix ila. The root 'sās' is in the sense of instruction, or 'sis' is in the sense of desire, with the suffix apa and the addition of a niggahīta, hence siṃsapā. Also aguru.

Tikaṃ phaliniyaṃ. Sā tanukaraṇe, mo. Piyabhāvaṃ gacchatīti piyaṅgu, u. Kamanīyabhāvaṃ gacchatīti kaṅgu, u, nipātanā. Mahilāvhayā, latā, gundā, gandhaphalī, kārambhāpi. Dvayaṃ sirīse. Sarati rogaṃ hiṃsatīti sirīso. Īso, assi. Bhaṇḍa paribhāsane, ilo. Kapītanopi. Ambāṭake, gaddabhaṇḍe ca kapītano.

Three words for phalinī. The root 'sā' is in the sense of thinning, with the suffix ma. Because it attains a beloved state, it is called piyaṅgu, with the suffix u. Because it attains a desirable state, it is called kaṅgu, with the suffix u, by irregular formation. Mahilāvhayā, latā, gundā, gandhaphalī, and also kārambhā. Two words for sirīsa. Because it goes and harms disease, it is called sirīsa, with the suffix īsa or assi. The root 'bhaṇḍ' is in the sense of reviling, with the suffix ila. Also kapītana. Kapītana is also used for ambāṭaka and gaddabhaṇḍa.

572. Dvayaṃ maṇḍūkapaṇṇe. Suṇa gatiyaṃ, ṇvu, dīghaṃ phalavaṇṭaṃ yassa. Naṭo kuṭannaṭāpi. Dvayaṃ bakule. Vaka ādāne, ulo. Kesarayuttapupphatāya kesaro.

572. Two words for maṇḍūkapaṇṇa, the frog-leaf plant. The root 'suṇ' is in the sense of movement, with the suffix ṇvu; that whose fruit-stalk is long. Naṭa, also kuṭannaṭa. Two words for bakula. The root 'vak' is in the sense of taking, with the suffix ula. Because its flower has filaments, it is called kesara.

Dvayaṃ malapupphasmiṃ. Kākānaṃ udumbaro kākodumbaro, so eva kākodumbarikā, sakatthe iko. Phala nipphattiyaṃ, gu, lassa go. Dvayaṃ nāgarukkhe. Na gacchatīti nāgo, dīghādi. Nāgānaṃ mālā, sā sañjātā yatra nāgamālikā.

Two words for malapuppha. The udumbara of crows is kākodumbara; that same is called kākodumbarikā, with the suffix ika in its own sense. The root 'phal' is in the sense of production, with the suffix gu, and 'l' becomes 'g'. Two words for the nāga tree. Because it does not move, it is called nāga, with lengthening and so forth. The garland of nāgas; that which is produced there is called nāgamālikā.

573. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0382] asoke. Natthi soko yena. Vaja gamane, ulo. Dvayaṃ jayāyaṃ. Taṃtaṃrogajayādikaṃ karotīti takkārī, ṇī. Visesena jayatīti vejayantikā, anto, nadādi, sakatthe ko. “Jayā jayantī takkārī, nādeyī vejayantikā”tyamarakoso amara 14.65.

573. Two words for asoka. That by which there is no sorrow. The root 'vaj' is in the sense of going, with the suffix ula. Two words for jayā. Because it causes the overcoming of various diseases and so forth, it is called takkārī, with the suffix ṇī. Because it conquers especially, it is called vejayantikā, with the suffix anta, and it is a nadādi word, with ka in its own sense. The Amarakośa states: 'Jayā, jayantī, takkārī, nādeyī, and vejayantikā are synonyms.'

Dvayaṃ samuddasamīpadesaje sāmadale tamālanāme tarumhi. Tāpiyaṃ jāyatīti tāpiñcho, aññatthe cho, bindāgamo, “tāpī tu saritāntare”ti hi nānatthasaṅgaho. Tamu kaṅkhāyaṃ, alo. Dvayaṃ kuṭaje. Rogaṃ chindatīti kuṭajo, jo. Girimhi jātā mallikā girimallikā, sakkapariyāyopyatra.

Two words for the tamāla tree, which has dark leaves and grows in regions near the ocean. Because it grows on the Tāpī river, it is called tāpiñcha, with the suffix cha in a different sense, and the addition of a bindu. Indeed, the Nānatthasaṅgaho states: 'Tāpī is a river.' The root 'tam' is in the sense of longing, with the suffix ala. Two words for kuṭaja. Because it cuts diseases, it is called kuṭaja, with the suffix ja. The jasmine born on the mountain is girimallikā; a synonym for Sakka is also used here.

574. Tassa kuṭajassa phale indayavo. Indassa sakkassa yavo dhaññaviseso indayavo. Kaliṅgaṃ, kaddayavampi.

574. Indayava is found in the fruit of that kuṭaja. Indayava is the barley of Indra, Sakka, a special type of grain. Kaliṅga, also kaddayava.

“Pūtikarañja dhūmyāṭe, desabhede pumā bhave;

Kuṭajassa phale klīvaṃ, kaliṅgaṃ thī tu nāriya”nti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.67. –

'Pūtikarañja and Dhūmyāṭa are masculine in a specific region; the fruit of Kuṭaja is neuter; but Kaliṅga is feminine when meaning a woman.'

Rabhaso. Amaramālāyantu “kaliṅge’ndayavo pumā”ti itthikaṇḍe pāṭho. Tassattho kaliṅgā itthī, indayavo pumā[M 0.0383]. Dvayaṃ kaṇikārikāyaṃ. Aggi anena manthyate aggimantho, ṇo. Taṃ kaṭṭhehi ghaṃsiyamāne aggi uṭṭhahati. Kaṇa gatiyaṃ, ṇvu. Jayāpyatra. “Vijaye so jayā duggā, jayantī gaṇikārike”ti jayā nānātthā.

This is from Rabhasa. However, in the Amaramālā, in the section on women, the reading is: 'In Kaliṅga, indayava is masculine.' Its meaning is: Kaliṅgā is feminine, indayava is masculine. Two words for kaṇikārikā. Because fire is churned with this, it is called aggimantha, with the suffix ṇa. When it is rubbed with sticks, fire arises. The root 'kaṇ' is in the sense of movement, with the suffix ṇvu. Jayā is also a synonym here. 'Jayā' has various meanings, as in the quote: 'In victory, it is Jayā; Durgā is Jayantī; and it is a synonym for gaṇikārikā.'

Dvayaṃ nigguṇḍiyaṃ. Natthi guṇḍaṃ gabbhabandhanametāyāti nigguṇḍī. Si bandhane, du, sinduṃ gabbhabandhanaṃ vāretīti sinduvāro. Indānīpyatra. Indānīkaraṇe thīnaṃ, sinduvārendanārisu. Dvayaṃ mallikāyaṃ. Tiṇāni sūlanti yasminti tiṇasūlaṃ, sūla rujāyaṃ. Yatra taṃ jāyati, tatra tiṇāni rogīni bhavantītyattho. “Tiṇasūlaṃ mallikāyaṃ, paṇḍakaṃ ketakīphale”. Mallate dhārīyate sabbehīti mallikā, malla dhāraṇe, i, sakatthe ko. Bhūpadī, sītabhīru ca.

Two words for nigguṇḍī. Because it has no protuberance or womb-binding, it is called nigguṇḍī. The root 'si' is in the sense of binding, with the suffix du; it prevents womb-binding, hence sinduvāra. Indānī is also a synonym here. 'In the making of Indānī among women, in sinduvāra and indanārī.' Two words for mallikā. Because grass is pained by it, it is tiṇasūla; the root 'sūl' is in the sense of pain. The meaning is that where it grows, the grass becomes diseased. 'Tiṇasūla is for mallikā, paṇḍaka for the ketakī fruit.' Because it is worn or borne by all, it is mallikā; from the root 'mall' in the sense of bearing, with the suffix i, and ka in its own sense. Also bhūpadī and sītabhīru.

575. Dvayaṃ kaṇhapupphasephālikāyaṃ. Siphā jaṭā yassatthi sephālikā, iko, lamajjho. Nīlapupphatāya nīlikā. Suvahā, nigguṇḍīpi. “Sinduvārepi nigguṇḍī, nīlasephālikāya ce”ti ruddo. Dvayaṃ vanamallikāyaṃ. Phuṭa vikasane, ā bhuso phuṭatīti apphoṭā, rassādi.

575. Two words for the black-flowered sephālikā. That which has fibrous roots, meaning matted roots, is sephālikā, with the suffix ika and an 'l' in the middle. Due to having blue flowers, it is called nīlikā. Also suvahā and nigguṇḍī. Rudda says: 'Nigguṇḍī is also for sinduvāra, and for nīlasephālikā.' Two words for vanamallikā, the forest jasmine. The root 'phuṭ' is in the sense of blooming; because it blooms greatly, it is apphoṭā, with shortening and so forth.

Catukkaṃ rattapupphe. Bandha bandhane, u, sakatthe ko. Jayatthaṃ sumanaṃ jayasumanaṃ. Bhaṇḍatismā iko, bhaṇḍiko. Jīvatīti jīvako, jīva pāṇadhāraṇe, ṇvu. Jīvakasaddassa pītasālādīsvapi pavattanato bandhu eva jīvako bandhujīvakoti bandhusaddena visesetvā vuttaṃ, samuditena vā nāmamidamekassa. “Bandhu bandhukapupphe ca, bandhubhātari bandhave”ti vacanato,

Four [terms] for the red flower. 'Bandha' is used in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'u', and 'ko' in its own sense. For victory, 'sumanaṃ' is 'jayasumanaṃ.' From 'bhaṇḍa', with the suffix 'iko', it becomes 'bhaṇḍiko.' It lives, hence 'jīvako'; 'jīva' is used in the sense of sustaining life, with the suffix 'ṇvu.' Since the term 'jīvaka' also applies to things like the pītasāla tree, it is stated as 'bandhujīvaka', having been specified by the term 'bandhu'; or this is a collective name for one thing. According to the saying: "'Bandhu' is used for the bandhuka flower, and for a kinsman-brother, and for a kinsman,"

“Jīvako [M 0.0384] pītasāle ca, khepane vuddhijīvini;

Sevini pāṇake phāti-kuṇḍike pādapantare”ti. –

"'Jīvaka' is used for pītasāla, khepana, vuddhijīvinī, sevinī, pāṇaka, phātikuṇḍika, and pādapantara."

Vacanato ca “bandhujīvako”ti ettha dve nāmānipi daṭṭhabbāni.

And from the saying, in the phrase "bandhujīvaka," two names should also be understood.

576. Pañcakaṃ sumanāyaṃ. Sundaraṃ mano yassaṃ. Sugandhattā jātisumanāti samuditanāmaṃ. Mala dhāraṇe, to, nadādi. Jana janane,ti. Vassakālasañjātapupphatāya vassikī. Iko, nadādi.

576. Five [terms] for sumanā. That in which the mind is beautiful. Because of its fragrance, 'jātisumanā' is a collective name. 'Mala' is used in the sense of bearing, with the suffix 'to', and it belongs to the nadādi group. 'Jana' is used in the sense of giving birth, with the suffix 'ti.' Because its flowers arise in the rainy season, it is called 'vassikī.' With the suffix 'ika', it belongs to the nadādi group.

Dvayaṃ “campeyya”iti khyāte. Yutha hiṃsāyaṃ, i, sakatthe ko, dīghādi. Magadhe bhavā māgadhī. Gaṇikā, ambaṭṭhāpi. Dvayaṃ “devāli”iti khyātāyaṃ. Sundaraṃ dalametissā sattalā, dassa to, satta dalāni yassā vā sattalā. Navā nūtanā mallikā navamallikā. Navamālikāpi.

Two [terms] for that known as 'campeyya.' 'Yutha' is used in the sense of harming, with the suffix 'i', 'ko' in its own sense, and with lengthening, etc. That which originates in Magadha is 'māgadhī.' Also gaṇikā and ambaṭṭhā. Two [terms] for that known as 'devāli.' It has beautiful petals, hence 'sattalā'; 'dassa' is replaced by 'to'; or that which has seven petals is 'sattalā.' New, fresh mallikā is 'navamallikā.' Also 'navamālikā'.

577. Dvayaṃ puṇḍake “laṃsvaṇa”iti khyāte. Vasante pupphati vāsantī. Atimudaṃ tanotīti atimutto, nipātanā. Mādhavī, latāpi. Madhumhi citte, vesākhe vā pupphatīti mādhavī.

577. Two [terms] for puṇḍaka, known as 'laṃsvaṇa.' It blooms in spring, hence 'vāsantī.' It extends extreme joy, hence 'atimutto'; this is by irregular formation. Also mādhavī and latā. It blooms in the month of Madhu, that is, Citta, or in Vesākha, hence 'mādhavī'.

“Latā jotimatīpakka-sākhāvallīpiyaṅgusu;

Latā katthūrikāyañca, sā dubbāmādhavīsu cā”ti.

'Latā' is used for jotimatī, a ripe branch, a tendril, and piyaṅgu; and 'latā' is used for katthūrikā, and it is also among dubbā and mādhavī.

Latā [M 0.0385] anekatthā. Dvayaṃ karavīre. Kucchitaṃ ravanti assā yena karavīro, īro. Asse māretīti assamārako. Paṭihāsopi.

The term 'latā' has many meanings. Two [terms] for karavīra. Because horses cry out wretchedly due to it, it is 'karavīro'; with the suffix 'īro.' It kills horses, hence 'assamārako.' Also paṭihāsa.

Dvayaṃ mātuluṅge. Matto lujjati yena mātuluṅgo, luja vināse. Paripuṇṇabījatāya bījapūro. Rucakopi, ruca dittiyaṃ, ṇvu. Dvayaṃ dhutture. Uggaṃ majjati yena ummatto, mada ummāde. Māretīti mātulo, ulo, rassa to. “Ummatto kitavo dhutto, dhattūro kanakāvhayo, mātulo madano”tyamarakoso amara 14.77.

Two [terms] for mātuluṅga. That by which one is intoxicated and destroyed is 'mātuluṅgo'; 'luja' is used in the sense of destruction. Because it is full of seeds, it is 'bījapūro.' Also rucaka; 'ruca' is used in the sense of shining, with the suffix 'ṇvu.' Two [terms] for dhuttura. That by which one is intensely intoxicated is 'ummatto'; 'mada' is used in the sense of madness. It kills, hence 'mātulo'; with the suffix 'ulo', and shortening of 'to.' The Amarakosa states: "Ummatto, kitavo, dhutto, dhattūro, kanakāvhayo, mātulo, madano."

578. Dvayaṃ kaṇhapākaphale. Karaṃ hatthaṃ maddati kaṇṭakena karamando. Karamaddopi. Suṭṭhu sinotīti suseno, si bandhane, yu. Dvayaṃ kunde. Kuṇa saṅkocane, do, nattaṃ, kuṇa saddopakaraṇesu vā. Māghe bhavaṃ māghyaṃ, yo, tasmiṃ kāle hi pupphādisamiddhi bhavatīti tabbhavattena byapadeso.

578. Two [terms] for kaṇhapākaphala. It crushes the hand with a thorn, hence 'karamando.' Also karamaddo. It binds well, hence 'suseno'; 'si' is used in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'yu.' Two [terms] for kunda. 'Kuṇa' is used in the sense of contracting, with the suffix 'do', and cerebralization is applied; or 'kuṇa' is used in the sense of sounds or instruments. That which originates in Māgha is 'māghyaṃ', with the suffix 'yo'; for at that time, indeed, there is an abundance of flowers and so forth, hence the designation by its origin.

Dvayaṃ devatāse. Devatā āsanti yaṃ devatāso. Jīmūtakāle sañjātattā jīmūto, mhanalā. Dvayaṃ sanāmapasiddhe pupphaviṭape. Pupphamāsuṃ na milātamassa bhavatīti amilāto. Mahantampi kālaṃ sahatīti mahāsahā.

Two [terms] for devatāsa. That which deities sit upon is 'devatāso.' Because it arises in the time of jīmūta, it is 'jīmūto'; with the suffix 'mhanalā.' Two [terms] for the flower-tree famous by its name. Because its flower does not wither quickly, it is 'amilāto.' Because it endures for a long time, it is 'mahāsahā'.

579. Catukkaṃ [M 0.0386] jhiṇḍisāmaññe. Sirī vattati yena sereyyako, ṇeyyako. Dāsanāmakattā dāsī. Kira vikkiraṇe, āto, dvittaṃ. Kura sadde, ḍo, sakatthe ko.

579. Four [terms] in the general sense of jhiṇḍi. That by which beauty exists is 'sereyyako'; with the suffix 'ṇeyyako.' Because of having the name 'dāsī', it is 'dāsī.' 'Kira' is used in the sense of scattering, with the suffix 'āto', and doubling of the consonant. 'Kura' is used in the sense of sound, with the suffix 'ḍo', and 'ko' in its own sense.

Dvayaṃ kaṇṭena, patrena ca site paṇṇāse. Aja gamane, uko. Sito sukko paṇṇāso sitapaṇṇāso. Dvayaṃ appapatte paṇṇāse. Īra kampane, yu. Phaṇiṃ jayati phaṇijjako, yassa ko.

Two [terms] for the paṇṇāsa which is white with thorns and leaves. 'Aja' is used in the sense of going, with the suffix 'uko.' White, bright paṇṇāsa is 'sitapaṇṇāso.' Two [terms] for the paṇṇāsa with few leaves. 'Īra' is used in the sense of trembling, with the suffix 'yu.' It conquers the serpent, hence 'phaṇijjako'; 'ya' becomes 'ko'.

580. Dvayaṃ japākusume. Japati yāya japā, ju javane vā, po, ussattaṃ. Marudesaje kaṇṭakini karabhappiye taruvisese karīrādidvayaṃ. Karotismā īro. Kaca bandhane, dvittaṃ, kakaco, ganthilopi.

580. Two [terms] for japākusuma. That by which one recites is 'japā'; or 'ju' is used in the sense of swiftness, with the suffix 'po', and prominence. Two [terms], karīra and so forth, for a special type of tree in the Marudesa region that is thorny and dear to camels. From 'karoti' comes the suffix 'īro.' 'Kaca' is used in the sense of binding, with doubling of the consonant, resulting in 'kakaco'; also 'ganthilo'.

Dvayaṃ rukkhoparijāte vijātiye pallave. Rukkhe jāyamānā taṃ addati hiṃsatīti rukkhādanī, adda hiṃsāyaṃ, yu, nadādi, dalopo. Vanda abhivādanathutīsu, a, itthiyaṃ, sakatthe ko, assa dīgho. Rukkharuhā, jīvantikāpi. Dvayaṃ cittake. Citi hiṃsāyaṃ, gandhe ca, ṇvu. Aggisaññitoti aggipariyāyanāmako. Pāṭhīpi, pume’yaṃ.

Two [terms] for a parasitic sprout growing on a tree. Being born on a tree, it consumes and harms it, hence 'rukkhādanī'; 'adda' is used in the sense of harming, with the suffix 'yu', it belongs to the nadādi group, and there is elision of 'da.' 'Vanda' is used in the sense of saluting and praising, with the suffix 'a', in the feminine gender, 'ko' in its own sense, and lengthening of 'a.' Also rukkharuhā and jīvantikā. Two [terms] for cittaka. 'Citi' is used in the sense of harming and fragrance, with the suffix 'ṇvu.' Because it is called 'fire', it has a name synonymous with fire. Also pāṭhī; this term is masculine.

581. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0387] gaṇarūpe. Akko sūriyo, tappariyāyanāmakattā akko. Vikarotīti vikiraṇo, yu. Assi. Akkavho, vasuko, apphoṭo, mandāro, akkapaṇṇopi. “Pume akkavho apphoṭo, vanamālyaparājite”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.80 ruddo. Mandāro devadumamhi pāribhaddakepi. Tasmiṃ akke yo setapupphako, tasmiṃ aḷakko. Setapupphatāya alaṃbhūto akko aḷakko, ala bhūsane, ḷattaṃ. Patāpasopi. Dvayaṃ chinnaruhāyaṃ. Tittarasattā pūtibhūtā latā pūtilatā, pū pavane vā,ti. Rogamalaṃ punātīti pūti, sā eva latā pūtilatā. Guḷa rakkhaṇe, co, nadādi. Gara secane vā. Amatā, madhupaṇṇīpi. Madhu iva paṇṇamassā madhupaṇṇī. Dvayaṃ dhanuseniyaṃ, yā pattehi vacāsadisī, tattaco tantadhanuguṇopayutto. Mubbāvikāratāyeva dhanujiyā “mubbī”tyuccate, mubba bandhane, a, mubbā. Madhurasattā madhurasā. Devī, moraṭāpi. Mura pavedhane, aṭo, moraṭā.

581. Two [terms] for the plant with a clustered form. Akka is the sun; because it has a name synonymous with it, it is 'akka.' It scatters, hence 'vikiraṇo'; with the suffix 'yu.' Also assi, akkavho, vasuko, apphoṭo, mandāro, and akkapaṇṇo. Rudda says: "In the masculine, akkavho and apphoṭo are used for vanamālya and aparājita." Mandāro is used for the divine tree, and also for pāribhaddaka. For that variety of akka which has white flowers, the name is 'aḷakko.' Because it is adorned with white flowers, the akka is 'aḷakko'; 'ala' is used in the sense of ornamenting, and 'ḷattaṃ' is applied. Also patāpaso. Two [terms] for chinnaruhā. A creeper that is bitter and foul-smelling is 'pūtilatā'; or 'pū' is used in the sense of purifying, with the suffix 'ti.' It purifies disease and impurity, hence 'pūti'; that very creeper is 'pūtilatā.' 'Guḷa' is used in the sense of protecting, with the suffix 'co', and it belongs to the nadādi group. Or 'gara' is used in the sense of sprinkling. Also amatā and madhupaṇṇī. Its leaves are like honey, hence 'madhupaṇṇī.' Two [terms] for dhanuseni, which resembles the vacā plant in its leaves, and whose bark is used for bowstrings. Precisely because the bowstring is a product of the mubbā plant, it is called 'mubbī'; 'mubba' is used in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'a', resulting in 'mubbā.' Because of its sweet essence, it is 'madhurasā.' Also devī and moraṭā. 'Mura' is used in the sense of shaking, with the suffix 'aṭo', resulting in 'moraṭā'.

582. Dvayaṃ makkaṭiyaṃ. Kapīnaṃ vānarānaṃ kacchuṃ janetīti kapikacchu. Kapikaccupi. Dukkhasamphassatāya duphasso. Attaguttā, jaḍā, abyaṇḍā, kaṇḍūrā, pāvusāyinī, sūkasimbipi. “Ayaṃ [M 0.0388] phassena kaṇḍuṃ janayatī”ti yā lokehi pariharīyate, tato ayaṃ attanā guttā rakkhitā attaguttā. Pāvusāyaṃ utuyaṃ eti jāyate, ṇo, inī. Sūkasahitā simbi assā sūkasimbi, rassanto. Dvayaṃ maṇḍūkapaṇṇiyaṃ. Maja suddhiyaṃ, ṭho. Kāsa dittiyaṃ, karaṇe a, rasso. Samaṅgā, yojanavallīpi. Samaṅgatīti samaṅgā, a. Yojanaṃ vallī yassā yojanavallī.

582. Two [terms] for makkaṭī. It causes itching in monkeys, hence 'kapikacchu.' Also kapikaccu. Because of its painful contact, it is 'duphasso.' Also attaguttā, jaḍā, abyaṇḍā, kaṇḍūrā, pāvusāyinī, and sūkasimbi. Because it causes itching by contact, it is avoided by people; therefore, it is self-protected and guarded, hence 'attaguttā.' It arises in the rainy season, with the suffixes 'ṇo' and 'inī.' Its pod has bristles, hence 'sūkasimbi', with shortening of the final vowel. Two [terms] for maṇḍūkapaṇṇī. 'Maja' is used in the sense of cleansing, with the suffix 'ṭho.' 'Kāsa' is used in the sense of shining, with the suffix 'a' in the sense of an instrument, and shortening of the vowel. Also samaṅgā and yojanavallī. It is well-matched, hence 'samaṅgā', with the suffix 'a.' Its creeper is a yojana long, hence 'yojanavallī'.

Dvayaṃ vanatittikāyaṃ. Amba sadde, ṭho, ava rakkhaṇe vā, niggahītāgamo. Pā rakkhaṇe, ṭho. Setā, pāpacelīpi. Setarasena yujjateti, a. Dvayaṃ kaṭukarohiṇiyaṃ. Kaṭa vassāvaraṇagatīsu. U, kaṭu, nārī. Kaṭukarasā hutvā ruhatīti kaṭukarohiṇī, ruha janane, yu, nadādi. “Kaṭukarohiṇī”ti samuditena nāmamidaṃ. Kaṭurohiṇīpi.

Two [terms] for vanatittikā. 'Amba' is used in the sense of sound, with the suffix 'ṭho'; or 'ava' is used in the sense of protecting, with the addition of niggahīta. 'Pā' is used in the sense of protecting, with the suffix 'ṭho.' Also setā and pāpacelī. It is joined with white essence, with the suffix 'a.' Two [terms] for kaṭukarohiṇī. 'Kaṭa' is used in the senses of rain, covering, and going. With the suffix 'u', it becomes 'kaṭu', in the feminine. Because it grows having a bitter taste, it is 'kaṭukarohiṇī'; 'ruha' is used in the sense of producing, with the suffix 'yu', and it belongs to the nadādi group. This is a collective name, 'kaṭukarohiṇī.' Also kaṭurohiṇī.

583. Dvayaṃ kharamañjariyaṃ “cacasima”iti khyātāyaṃ. Apamajjanti vatthādika’maneneti apāmaggo, dīgho upasaggassa. Sikharamassāti sekhariko. Dhāmaggavo, vimukhapupphīpi. “Ghosake kharamañjariyaṃ, dhāmaggavo pume mato”. Vimukhaṃ pupphamassā. Dvayaṃ kaṇāyaṃ. Pittaṃ phalati kuppati yāya pipphalī, nadādi. Magadhe bhavā māgadhī, magadhānaṃ ayaṃ vā māgadhī, tatra paṭhamuppannattā, bāhulyena vā tatra jāyamānattā taṃsamaññāya byapadissate. Vedehī, kaṇā, kolāpi. Vedehānamayaṃ vedehī. Kaṇā nānatthā, vuttañca “kaṇā pipphali’jājī ce”ti.

583. Two terms for kharamañjarī, which is known as 'cacasima.' Because one cleanses clothes and so forth with it, it is 'apāmaggo,' with lengthening of the prefix. It has a crest, hence 'sekhariko.' Also dhāmaggavo and vimukhapupphī. In the Ghosaka it is said: 'Kharamañjarī, and dhāmaggavo is considered masculine.' Its flower is turned away. Two terms for kaṇā. That by which bile ripens or is agitated is 'pipphalī'; it belongs to the nadādi group. That which is from Magadha is 'māgadhī'; or this belongs to the Magadhans, 'māgadhī,' because it first arose there, or because it commonly grows there, it is designated by that name. Also vedehī, kaṇā, and kolā. This belongs to the Videhans, hence 'vedehī.' Kaṇā has various meanings, and it is stated: 'Kaṇā is for pipphalī and ajājī.'

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0389] tikaṇṭake. Gavaṃ kaṇṭako gokaṇṭako, pathaviyaṃ vā laggo kaṇṭako gokaṇṭako. Siṅgha ghāyane, āṭo. Palaṅkasā, sādukaṇṭopi. Yuttarāsnāyaṃ palāse ca palaṅkasā thiyaṃ. Sādukaṇṭo vikaṅkatepi. Dvayaṃ hatthipipphaliyaṃ. Kolākārā, taṃnāmikā vā vallī kolavalli, rasso. Ibhānaṃ hatthīnaṃ pipphalī ibhapipphalī. Kapivallī, vasiropi. Vasiro nānattho. Vasiro apāmaggo sāmuddalavaṇaṃ hatthipipphali ceti. Pume’yaṃ.

Two terms for tikaṇṭaka. The thorn of cattle is 'gokaṇṭaka,' or a thorn attached to the earth is 'gokaṇṭaka.' The root 'siṅgh' is in the sense of smelling; also āṭo. Also palaṅkasā and sādukaṇṭa. Palaṅkasā, in the feminine, is also for yuttarāsnā and palāsa. Sādukaṇṭa is also for vikaṅkata. Two terms for hatthipipphalī. A vine shaped like a kola fruit, or a vine of that name, is 'kolavalli,' with a short vowel. The pipphalī of elephants (ibha, hatthī) is 'ibhapipphalī.' Also kapivallī and vasiro. Vasiro has various meanings. Vasiro is apāmaggo, sea salt, and hatthipipphalī. This word is masculine.

584. Dvayaṃ chaganthāyaṃ, yā “uggagandhā”tipyuccate. Gunnaṃ lomasampātanaṭṭhāne jātā golomī, vaca viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, karaṇe a, satapabbikāpi. Vacā sukkalohitamūlabhedena duvidhā, tatrasukkā “hemavatī”tyuccate amarakose amara 14.102-3. Dvayaṃ apphoṭāyaṃ. Kaṇṇasaṇṭhānapupphatāya kaṇṇī. Girimhi jātā kaṇṇī girikaṇṇī. Rogādijitattā aparājitā.

584. Two terms for chaganthā, which is also called 'uggagandhā.' 'Golomī' is so named because it is born in the place where the hair of cattle falls. From the root 'vac' in the sense of clear speech, with the suffix 'a' in the instrumental sense, comes 'vacā'; also satapabbikā. Vacā is of two kinds, distinguished by its white and red root; of these, the white one is called 'hemavatī' in the Amarakośa. Two terms for apphoṭā. Because it has ear-shaped flowers, it is 'kaṇṇī.' The kaṇṇī born on a mountain is 'girikaṇṇī.' Because it conquers diseases and so forth, it is 'aparājitā.'

Dvayaṃ kalasiyaṃ. Sīhapucchākārakusumamañjaritāya sīhapucchi. Pañhi appatanu vuccate. Pañhi paṇṇaṃ yassā pañhipaṇṇī. Puthupaṇṇī, guhāpi, puthu asiliṭṭhaṃ paṇṇamassā puthupaṇṇī. Gahvare sīhapucchañca, thiyaṃ chamātuke guho cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.93. Dvayaṃ sālapaṇṇiyaṃ. Sālapaṇṇasadisaviṭatāya sālapaṇṇī. Sālaṃ sobhanayuttaṃ paṇṇamassā vā sālapaṇṇī. Thu gatitheriyesu, iro, thiro.

Two terms for kalasī. Because it has flower clusters shaped like a lion's tail, it is 'sīhapucchī.' 'Pañhi' is said to be 'not very thin.' That whose leaf is 'pañhi' is 'pañhipaṇṇī.' Also puthupaṇṇī and guhā. 'Puthupaṇṇī' is so called because its leaf is broad and separate. 'In a cave, sīhapuccha; and guhā, in the feminine, for chamātuka.' Two terms for sālapaṇṇī. Because it is spread out like a sāla leaf, it is 'sālapaṇṇī.' Or, 'sālapaṇṇī' is so called because its leaf is excellent and endowed with beauty. The root 'thu' is in the senses of movement and stability; from it, with the suffix 'iro', comes 'thiro'.

585. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0390] kaṇṭakārikāyaṃ. Niddahati kaṇṭakamuṭṭheti nididdhikā, ṇvu. Bhayakaraṇavasena byagghasadisatāya byagghī, brahatī, khuddāpi. Dvayaṃ nīlirukkhe. Nīla vaṇṇe. Nīlavaṇṇatāya nīlī, nadādi, inī, nīlinī, kāḷā, tutthāpi.

585. Two terms for kaṇṭakārikā. Because it removes thorns, it is 'nididdhikā,' formed with the suffix ṇvu. Because it is like a tiger in causing fear, it is 'byagghī'; also brahatī and khuddā. Two terms for the nīli tree. The root 'nīl' is in the sense of color. Because of its blue color, it is 'nīlī,' which belongs to the nadādi group; with the suffix 'inī', it becomes 'nīlinī'; also kāḷā and tutthā.

Kāḷā kaṇhativutāyaṃ, nīlī yojanavallisu;

Paṇḍe rasañjane tutthā, sukhumelāya nīliyaṃ cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.94-5.

'Kāḷā' is used for kaṇhativutā, and nīlī for yojanavallī. 'Tutthā' is used for paṇḍa and rasañjana, and 'nīlī' also for sukhumelā.

Dvayaṃ guñjāyaṃ. Jañja yuddhe, uko, assi, guja sadde, a, bindāgamo. Nāmantarāni cassa –

Two terms for guñjā. The root 'jañj' is in the sense of battle; 'uko' and 'assi' are suffixes. The root 'guj' is in the sense of sound; with the suffix 'a' and the addition of a bindu. And its other names are:

Dume sā rattikā ratta-dalā cūḷāmaṇī ca sā;

Kākaciñcī tulābījaṃ, kaṇhalā ca sikhaṇḍinī.

On the tree, it is rattikā, rattadalā, and cūḷāmaṇī; also kākaciñcī, tulābījaṃ, kaṇhalā, and sikhaṇḍinī.

Dvaya’maheruyaṃ. Ayamaheruicceva khyātakaṇṭakavatī bhavati. Sataṃ mūlāni yassa satamūlī. Sataṃ roge āvaratīti satāvarī, vara āvaraṇicchāsu, atha vā “satā”ti ca “āvarī”ti ca dve nāmāni tassā. “Satamūlī bahusutā-bhīru indīvarī varī”ti amara 14.100 hi vuttaṃ.

Two terms for aheru. This plant, known as aheru, is thorny. That which has a hundred roots is 'satamūlī.' Because it wards off a hundred diseases, it is 'satāvarī,' from the root 'var' in the senses of covering and desiring; or alternatively, it has two names: 'satā' and 'āvarī.' Indeed, it is said: 'Satamūlī, bahusutā, bhīru, indīvarī, varī'.

586. Dvayaṃ ativisāyaṃ. Mahāvīriyaṃ osadhaṃ mahosadhaṃ. “Lasuṇe tivisāyañca, suṇṭhiyampi mahosadha”nti ruddo[M 0.0391]. Atīva visati bhesajjapayogesūti ativisā, visā, aruṇā, siṅgīpi.

586. Two terms for ativisā. A medicine of great potency is 'mahosadha.' Rudda says: 'Mahosadha is also for lasuṇa, tivisā, and suṇṭhi.' Because it enters greatly into medicinal applications, it is 'ativisā'; also visā, aruṇā, and siṅgī.

“Aruṇo kiñcirattakke, sañjhārāge anūruke;

Nisadde kapile kuṭṭhe, dabbeva vāccaliṅgiko”.

'Aruṇa' is used for that which is somewhat reddish, for the evening glow, for Anūru; for that which is silent, tawny, or kuṭṭha; and like 'dabba,' it is adjectival.

“Aruṇātivisāsāmā, mañjaṭṭhātivutāsu ca;

Usīretivisāyañca, siṅgimagguravallabhā”ti.

'Aruṇā' is used for ativisā, sāmā, mañjaṭṭhā, and ativutā; and 'siṅgī' for usīra, ativisā, maggura, and vallabhā.

Dvayaṃ somarājiyaṃ. Vaka ādāne, aco, somasamatāya kāritā vallikā somavallikā, sakatthe ko, kaṇhaphalā, pūtiphalāpi.

Two terms for somarājī. The root 'vak' is in the sense of taking; 'aco' is a suffix. The creeper called such due to its similarity to Soma is 'somavallikā,' with the suffix 'ka' used in its own sense; also kaṇhaphalā and pūtiphalā.

Dvayaṃ dāruhaliddārukkhe. Dara vidāraṇe, bo, rassa bo, dābbī, dīghādi, nadādi. Haliddavaṇṇadārutāya dāruhaliddā, haliddāpi. Dvayaṃ biḷaṅge. Aṅga, raṅga, laṅga, gatyatthā daṇḍakā dhātū, a, ḷattaṃ, biḷaṅgaṃ. Citrāni taṇḍulāni yassā, taṇḍulo, kimisattupi.

Two terms for the dāruhaliddā tree. From the root 'dar' in the sense of splitting, with the suffix 'bo.' A name is 'dābbī,' with a long initial vowel, belonging to the nadādi group. Because its wood is the color of turmeric, it is 'dāruhaliddā'; also haliddā. Two terms for biḷaṅga. The daṇḍaka roots 'aṅg', 'raṅg', and 'laṅg' have the meaning of movement; with the suffix 'a' and the change to 'ḷ', it becomes 'biḷaṅga.' That which has variegated grains is 'taṇḍulo'; also kimisattu (enemy of worms).

587. Dvayaṃ samantaduddhāyaṃ, nuha uggiraṇe, nadādi, mahantaṃ nāmamassa. Sīhuṇḍo, vajiradumo, guḷāpi. Dvayaṃ dakkhāyaṃ. Muduguṇayogā muddikā, madhuraso sādu, tena vuttaṃ vejjaganthe “sādu lavaṇatittambilakaṭukasāyakā”iti, taṃyogā madhurasā. Gotthanī, dakkhāpi. Tikaṃ yaṭṭhimadhukāyaṃ. Madhurasatāya madhukaṃ, upamāne ko. Daṇḍākārattā yaṭṭhi ca sā madhurasattā madhukā ceti yaṭṭhimadhukā. Madhurasabhāve tiṭṭhatīti madhulaṭṭhikā, rassa lo, sakatthe ko ca. “Madhuyaṭṭhikā”tipi pāṭho, vuttañca “madhukaṃ klītakaṃ yaṭṭhi-madhukaṃ madhuyaṭṭhikā”ti amara 14.109.

587. Two terms for samantaduddhā. From the root 'snuh' in the sense of ejecting; it belongs to the nadādi group; it has a great name. Also sīhuṇḍo, vajiradumo, and guḷā. Two terms for dakkhā. Due to its connection with the quality of softness, it is 'muddikā.' Its taste is sweet (madhurasa); for it is said in a medical text: 'sweet, salty, bitter, sour, pungent, astringent'; due to its connection with that sweet taste, it is 'madhurasā.' Also gotthanī and dakkhā. Three terms for yaṭṭhimadhukā. Because of its sweetness, it is 'madhuka,' with the suffix 'ka' in the sense of comparison. Because it is a staff (yaṭṭhi) and it is sweet (madhukā), it is 'yaṭṭhimadhukā.' Because it abides in a sweet nature, it is 'madhulaṭṭhikā,' with 'r' becoming 'l', and with the suffix 'ka' in its own sense. 'Madhuyaṭṭhikā' is also a reading, and it is said: 'madhuka, klītaka, yaṭṭhimadhuka, madhuyaṭṭhikā.'

588. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0392] vātiṅgaṇe. Vātaharattena gaṇīyateti vātiṅgaṇo, bhaṇḍa paribhāsane, ṇvu, nadādi. Ṭakārakaraṇe bhaṇṭākīpi, brahatiyampi ayaṃ.

588. Two terms for vātiṅgaṇa. Because it is reckoned as a remover of vāta (wind), it is 'vātiṅgaṇa.' From the root 'bhaṇḍ' in the sense of designation, with the suffix ṇvu, it belongs to the nadādi group. When the sound 'ṭ' is used, it is also 'bhaṇṭākī'; this name is also for brahatī.

“Vātiṅgaṇo tu vāttāku,

Vāttāko sākaveḷu ca;

Bhaṇḍākī rājakumbhaṇḍo,

Vāttākī duppahāsinī”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.114.

Vātiṅgaṇa is vāttāku; vāttāko is also sākaveḷu; bhaṇḍākī, rājakumbhaṇḍa, vāttākī, and duppahāsinī.

Rabhaso. Dvayaṃ brahatiyaṃ. Vāttaṃ nirāmayaṃ karotīti vāttākī, vātiṅgaṇepi. Braha vuttiyaṃ, to, nadādi.

Rabhaso. Two terms for brahatī. Because it makes the vāta (wind) free from sickness, it is 'vāttākī'; this is also used for vātiṅgaṇa. From the root 'brah' in the sense of growth, with the suffix 'to'; it belongs to the nadādi group.

Dvayaṃ gorakkhataṇḍule, vuttañca tantantare “gaṅgerukī nāgabalā, tathā gorakkhataṇḍulā”ti. Nāgassa balamiva balametissā rogaharaṇattā nāgabalā, jhasa hiṃsattho, a. Dvayaṃ aggisikhāyaṃ. Naṅgalasadisamūlatāya lāṅgalī, nassa lo, dīgho ca. “Naṅgalī”tipi pāṭho, saradakāle sañjātattā sāradī.

Two terms for gorakkhataṇḍula; and it is said in another text: 'gaṅgerukī, nāgabalā, and also gorakkhataṇḍulā.' Because its strength in removing diseases is like the strength of a nāga, it is 'nāgabalā.' The root 'jhas' is in the sense of harming; 'a' is a suffix. Two terms for aggisikhā. Because its root is like a plowshare (naṅgala), it is 'lāṅgalī,' with 'n' becoming 'l' and lengthening of the vowel. 'Naṅgalī' is also a reading. Because it is born in the autumn season, it is 'sāradī.'

589. Tikaṃ kadaliyaṃ. Ramanti yassaṃ rambhā, bho. Kada māraṇe, alo, nadādi. Muca mocane, ṇo. Dvayaṃ kappāsiyaṃ[M 0.0393], yassā phalaṃ kappāsaṃ karoti lokānamupakāranti kappāsī, karotismā pāso, nadādi. Vada theriye, aro, samuddantāpi.

589. Three terms for kadalī. That in which they delight is 'rambhā,' bho. From the root 'kad' in the sense of killing, with the suffix 'alo'; it belongs to the nadādi group. From the root 'muc' in the sense of freeing, with the suffix 'ṇo'. Two terms for kappāsī. Because its fruit produces cotton (kappāsa) for the benefit of the world, it is 'kappāsī'; from 'karoti' with the suffix 'pāso'; it belongs to the nadādi group. From the root 'vad' in the sense of firmness, with the suffix 'aro'; also samuddantā.

Samuddantā tu kappāsī, sikkādurālabhāsu ca;

Kappāsī vanasambhavā ce, bhāradvājīti vuccati.

'Samuddantā' is used for kappāsī, and also for sikkā and durālabhā. If kappāsī is forest-born, it is called 'bhāradvājī.'

Dvayaṃ paṇṇalatāyaṃ. Nāgaloke jātā latā nāgalatā. Tambavaṇṇaṃ lātīti tambūlī, assū, nadādi. Tambūlassa ayaṃ vā tambūlī. Tambūlavallī, nāgavallīpi, tambūlaṃ nāma phalapattacuṇṇādiyogasamūhānaṃ nāmaṃ, tadatthā vallī tambūlavallī, nāgalokassa vallī. Dvayaṃ dhātakiyaṃ, ayaṃ tambapupphī, majjopayuttā. Pupphā sugandhikā dhātakicceva khyātā. Aggijālasamānapupphatāya aggijālā. Atisayaṃ ṭhitiṃ karotīti dhātakī, nadādi.

Two terms for paṇṇalatā. The creeper born in the nāga world is 'nāgalatā.' Because it takes on a copper color, it is 'tambūlī,' with the suffix 'assū'; it belongs to the nadādi group. Or, this is the 'tambūlī' for tambūla. Also tambūlavallī and nāgavallī. 'Tambūla' is the name for a collection of combinations of fruit, leaf, powder, and so forth; the creeper for that purpose is 'tambūlavallī'; the creeper of the nāga world is 'nāgavallī.' Two terms for dhātaki. This is 'tambapupphī,' used in intoxicants. Its fragrant flowers are known as 'dhātaki.' Because its flowers are like a flame of fire, it is 'aggijālā.' Because it creates excellent stability, it is 'dhātakī'; it belongs to the nadādi group.

590. Dvayaṃ sukkativutāyaṃ. Tisso vutā tacarājiyo yassā tivutā. Tisso puṭā tacarājiyo yassā tipuṭā. Saralā, tibhaṇḍī, rocanīpi devanīpi (ka.). Dvayaṃ kaṇhativutāyaṃ. Sā tanukaraṇe, virecanakaraṇena kāyaṃ, rogañca sāyatīti sāmā.

590. Two (names) for sukkativutā. That which has three layers of bark is called 'tivutā.' That which has three folds of bark is called 'tipuṭā.' 'Saralā,' 'tibhaṇḍī,' and 'rocanī' are also (names). Two (names) for kaṇhativutā. Because it thins the body by inducing purging, and alleviates illness, it is 'sāmā'.

“Sāmā tu mecake vuddha-dārake harite nadi;

Tikaṇhativutā gundā, sārivāyaminīsu ce”ti. –

‘Sāmā’ is used for ‘mecaka’ (dark), ‘vuddha-dāraka’ (an old child), ‘harita’ (green), and ‘nadī’ (a river); and also for ‘tikaṇhativutā’, ‘gundā’, ‘sārivā’, and ‘yaminī’.

Rabhaso, kala [M 0.0394] saṅkhyāne, kara karaṇe vā, a, kāḷā. Thī kāḷā kaṇhativutāyaṃ, nīlīyojanavallisu. Masūravidalā, addhacandā, kāḷamesikāpi.

'Rabhaso' (is a name). 'Kala' (is used) in the sense of 'counting,' or 'kara' (is used) in the sense of 'doing'; 'a' (is a suffix); hence 'kāḷā.' The feminine 'kāḷā' is used for 'kaṇhativutā,' and for 'nīlīyojanavallī.' 'Masūravidalā,' 'addhacandā,' and 'kāḷamesikā' are also (names).

Dvayaṃ kukkuṭasiṅgāyaṃ. Siṅgasadisapupphatāya siṅgī, kuḷīrasiṅgī, vakkaṅgīpi. Dvayaṃ reṇukākhye gandhadabbe, ayaṃ reṇuketyeva vāṇijādīnaṃ khyātā. Assā ca marīcākati phalaṃ. Reṇu gatisaddesu, ṇu, kapilā vuttā. Dvijā, hareṇū, kontī, bhasmagandhanīpi. “Hareṇu so kalāyepi, reṇukāyaṃ thiyaṃ bhave”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.120 ruddo.

Two (names) for kukkuṭasiṅgā. Because its flowers are horn-shaped, (it is called) 'siṅgī'; (also) 'kuḷīrasiṅgī,' and 'vakkaṅgī.' Two (names) for the fragrant substance called reṇukā. This (substance) is known as 'reṇukā' among traders and others. And its fruit is like pepper. 'Reṇu' (is used) in the sense of 'movement' and 'sound'; 'ṇu' (is a suffix); 'kapilā' is said (to be a name for it). 'Dvijā,' 'hareṇū,' 'kontī,' and 'bhasmagandhanī' are also (names). Rudda says: 'Hareṇu' is also used for 'kalāya' (pea); when it means 'reṇukā', it would be feminine.

591. Dvayaṃ phālake. Hirīnāmikāya devadhītāya sarīrato sañjātattā hiriveraṃ. Vāretīti vāraṃ, vārināmakattā vā vāraṃ, latte vālaṃ. Udījhaṃ. Kesambunāmampi, udīcīdese bhavaṃ udījhaṃ, kesassa ambuno ca yāni nāmāni, tāni sabbānyassāti kesambunāmaṃ. Dvayaṃ bimbikāyaṃ. Rattaṃ pakkaphalamassā. Oṭṭhavaṇṇasamānaphalatāya bimbikā, assā eva hi phalenoṭṭho upamīyate. Tuṇḍikerī, pilupaṇṇīpi.

591. Two (names) for phālaka. Because it arose from the body of the goddess named Hirī, (it is called) 'hiriveraṃ.' Because it prevents, (it is called) 'vāraṃ'; or because it has the name 'vāri' (water), it is 'vāraṃ'; (or) 'vālaṃ' (is used) in the sense of 'hair.' 'Udījhaṃ' (is a name). 'Kesambunāmaṃ' is also a name. 'Udījhaṃ' (is so called because) it exists in the northern region; 'kesambunāmaṃ' means it has all the names of 'kesa' (hair) and 'ambu' (water). Two (names) for bimbikā. Its ripe fruit is red. Because its fruit resembles the color of lips, (it is called) 'bimbikā'; indeed, lips are compared to its fruit. 'Tuṇḍikerī' and 'pilupaṇṇī' are also (names).

Dvayaṃ seleyye, tañca pāsāṇabhavaṃ sugandharasadabbaṃ selajanti khyātaṃ. Silāyaṃ pāsāṇe bhavaṃ seleyyaṃ, ṇeyyo. Asmano, asmassa vā pupphaṃ asmapupphaṃ, kāḷānusāriyampi. Dvayaṃ elāyaṃ “phālā”ti khyātāyaṃ. Ila gamane, a, isse. Bahavo atthe lātīti bahulā, bahuroge vā lunātīti bahulā, candavālāpi.

Two (names) for seleyya. And that fragrant and tasty substance born from stone is known as 'selaja.' 'Seleyya' (is so called because it is) born on a rock or stone; 'ṇeyyo' (is a suffix). The flower of a stone, 'asmapupphaṃ', and also 'kāḷānusāriyaṃ' (are names). Two (names) for elā, which is known as 'phālā.' 'Ila' (is used) in the sense of 'going'; 'a' (is a suffix), 'isse' (is a grammatical form). Because it carries many meanings, (it is called) 'bahulā'; or because it cuts many diseases, (it is called) 'bahulā'; (also) 'candavālā'.

592. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0395] “kuṭṭha”iti khyāte sugandhadabbe. Kuṭa cedane, ṭho. Kuyaṃ pathaviyaṃ tiṭṭhatīti vā kuṭṭhaṃ. Byādhināmakattā byādhi, tathā ca “koveraṃ bhāsuraṃ kuṭṭhaṃ, pāribhābyaṃ gadāhvaya”nti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.126 rabhaso. Pākalaṃ, uppalampi. Dvayaṃ kevattīmutthake. Vuttañca –

592. Two (names) for the fragrant substance known as 'kuṭṭha'. 'Kuṭa' (is from the root) 'cedane' (to cut), with the suffix 'ṭho'. Or, 'ku' (means) on the earth, it stands, thus 'kuṭṭhaṃ'. Because it has the name of a disease, (it is called) 'byādhi'. And as Rabhasa said: 'Koveraṃ, bhāsuraṃ, kuṭṭhaṃ, pāribhābyaṃ, gadāhvaya' (are synonyms). 'Pākalaṃ' and 'uppalaṃ' are also (names). Two (names are also used) for kevattīmutthaka. And it is said:

“Paripelavaṃ plavaṃ vanyaṃ, taṃ kuṭannaṭasaññakaṃ;

Jāyate maṇḍūkākāraṃ, sevāladalasañcaye”ti.

"A swaying, floating, forest (plant), that which is called 'kuṭannaṭa'; it arises in the shape of a frog, in a heap of moss and leaves."

Vane pānīye jātaṃ vāneyyaṃ, ṇeyyo, kevattīmutthake paṇḍo, soṇakoso kuṭannaṭo. Kuṭa chedane, naṭa avabandhane, naṭa naṭṭane vā, kuṭannaṭanti samuditanāmaṃ. Niggahītāgamo. Dāsapurampi.

Born in the forest water, (it is) 'vāneyyaṃ', (with the suffix) ṇeyyo. 'Paṇḍo', 'soṇakoso', (and) 'kuṭannaṭo' (are names) for kevattīmutthaka. 'Kuṭa' (is from the root) 'chedane' (to cut), 'naṭa' (is from the root) 'avabandhane' (to bind), or 'naṭa' (is from the root) 'naṭṭane' (to dance); thus 'kuṭannaṭa' is a compound name. There is an augment of niggahīta. 'Dāsapuraṃ' is also (a name).

Phalapākantalatādi jātimattameva osadhi nāma, na tu tiphalakakkolādi, ipaccayo, bahuvacanantu atthabahulattā eva, ekavacanantopi dissate, osadhi itthiyameva. Osadhaṃ sabbamajātiyaṃ. Phalapākantattā jātito aññaṃ yaṃ kiñci rogāpanayanakaraṃ, tadosadhamuccate. Osadhijātisambandhidabbampi jātivatticchāyaṃ rogapahīnakriyāhetuttā osadhasaddavāccanti paṭipādanatthaṃ sabbaggahaṇaṃ. Osadhasaddato jātiyaṃ ṇo. Keci pana “osadhijātimattamosadhaṃ sabbamajātiya”nti pāṭhamavatvā “osadhijātimattaṃ bhesajjaṃ sabbamajātiya”nti paṭhanti. Tamidha osadhiosadhasaddānameva ekadesavikativasena vuttānaṃ saṃsayāpagamanatthaṃ visesassa vuttattā na [M 0.0396] gahetabbaṃ, amarakosepi vuttaṃ “osadhyo jātimattesu, ajātyaṃ sabbamosadha”nti amara 14.135. Tattha sakavādīpakkhe eko makāro āgamavasena vutto.

The term 'osadhi' refers only to plants that perish after ripening their fruit, such as annuals, and not to (plants like) tiphalā or kakkola. The suffix is 'i'. The plural form is due to the abundance of meanings, but the singular form is also seen. 'Osadhi' is only in the feminine gender. 'Osadhaṃ' refers to everything that is not of that specific species. Anything that removes disease, other than a species that perishes after ripening its fruit, is called 'osadhaṃ.' Even a substance related to the species 'osadhi' is denoted by the word 'osadha' because it is the cause for the action of eliminating disease, by extension of the term for the species; the inclusion of 'sabba' (all) is to establish this. From the word 'osadha', the suffix 'ṇo' is applied in the sense of 'species'. Some, however, having read the passage as: "Only the species 'osadhi' is 'osadha', and everything else is not a species," read it further as: "Only the species 'osadhi' is 'bhesajja', and everything else is not a species." This reading should not be accepted here, because the distinction is stated for the purpose of removing doubt regarding the words 'osadhi' and 'osadha', which are used in a partial and altered sense. And it is also stated in the Amarakosha: "'Osadhyo' is used for those that are specific species, and 'osadha' is used for everything that is not a species." In that context, according to the Sakavādin's view, one 'm' is stated as an augment.

593. Mūlādikaṃ dasavidhaṃ sākanti mataṃ, sakkoti yenāti katvā. Tatra mūlaṃ mūlakādīnaṃ, pattaṃ bākucādīnaṃ, kalīraṃ vaṃsādīnaṃ, aggaṃ vettādīnaṃ, kandaṃ nīluppalādīnaṃ, miñjaṃ tālādīnaṃ, phalaṃ kumbhaṇḍādīnaṃ, taco mātuluṅgādīnaṃ, pupphaṃ vaṅgasusenādīnaṃ, chattaṃ ahichattādīnaṃ.

593. The tenfold classification of greens, starting with roots, is considered 'sāka', because it is that by which one is able to sustain oneself. Therein, the root is of plants like radish; the leaf, of plants like bākucī; the shoot, of plants like bamboo; the tip, of plants like rattan; the bulb, of plants like the blue lotus; the pith, of plants like the palmyra palm; the fruit, of plants like the pumpkin; the bark, of plants like the citron; the flower, of plants like vaṅgasusena; and the umbrella-like part, of plants like ahichatta.

594. Dvayaṃ eḷagale. Pakārena dadduṃ punātīti papunnāṭo. Pu pavane, kiyādi, aṭo, niggahītāgamo. Eḷagaṃ dadduṃ lunātīti eḷagalo. Daddugho, cakkamaddako, uraṇākhyopi, dadduṃ hantīti daddugho, hanassa gho. Cakkākāratāya cakkaṃ, daddu, taṃ maddayatīti cakkamaddako. Uraṇākhyo mesākhyo. Mārisākatiappapattako bhūmilaggapatto taṇḍuleyyo appamāriso ca nāma, taṇḍulato jāyatīti taṇḍuleyyo, ṇeyyo. Appapattatāya appo ca so mārisākatittā māriso ceti appamāriso.

594. Two (names are used) for eḷagala. Because it purifies the itch by means of the prefix 'pa', it is called 'papunnāṭo'. 'Pu' (is from the root) 'pavane' (to purify), (it is) kiyādi (root class), with the suffix 'aṭo', and a niggahīta augment. Because it cuts the eḷaga itch, it is called 'eḷagalo'. 'Daddugho', 'cakkamaddako', and also 'uraṇākhyo' (are names). Because it destroys the itch, it is 'daddugho'; 'gha' (is derived) from 'han' (to destroy). Because of its wheel-like shape, (it is) 'cakka' (wheel), and it crushes the itch, thus 'cakkamaddako'. 'Uraṇākhyo' is also 'mesākhyo' (sheep-like). A plant with small leaves like mārisa greens, whose leaves cling to the ground, is named 'taṇḍuleyyo' and 'appamāriso'. Because it is born from rice (taṇḍula), it is 'taṇḍuleyyo', (with the suffix) ṇeyyo. Because of its small leaves, it is 'appa', and because it has the appearance of mārisa greens, it is 'mārisa', thus 'appamāriso'.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0397] jīvantiyaṃ, ayaṃ rattaṅgamārisākati, jīvato anto, nadādi. Itarato yu, nadādi. Jīvā, jīvanīyā, madhupi. “Heṃ nu nve nī”. Dvayaṃ jīvake, ayaṃ aṭṭhavaggapaviṭṭho. Aneneva nāmena vāṇijānaṃ pasiddho. Madhurasatāya madhurako, jīvāpetīti jīvako, ṇvu.

Two (names are used) for jīvantī. This plant has the appearance of red mārisa greens. (It is derived from) 'jīvato anto' (end of life), (from the root class) nadādi. From the other (root), with the suffix 'yu', (it is also from the root class) nadādi. 'Jīvā', 'jīvanīyā', and 'madhupi' are also (names). 'Heṃ nu nve nī'. Two (names are used) for jīvaka. This is included in the Aṭṭhavagga. It is well-known among merchants by this very name. Because of its sweet taste, (it is) 'madhurako'. Because it enlivens, it is 'jīvako', (with the suffix) ṇvu.

“Jīvako siṅgako seko,

Dīghāyu kuccasīsako;

Rassaṅgo madhuro sādu,

Pāṇako cirajīvinī”ti.

"Jīvako, siṅgako, seko, dīghāyu, kuccasīsako; rassaṅgo, madhuro, sādu, pāṇako, cirajīvinī."

Tantantaraṃ amarakosugghāṭanaṭīkāyampi aparāddhaṃ cintāmaṇiṭīkāyampi.

Another treatise.

595. Dvayaṃ lasuṇe. Yassa mūlaṃ setavaṇṇaṃ. Palaṇḍukandato mahantakandatāya mahākando. Ambilenekena rasena ūnatāya lasuṇaṃ, lattaṃ, rassattaṃ, ṇattañca, lasa kantiyaṃ vā, yu, assu, ṇattaṃ. Mahosadhaṃ, ariṭṭhaṃ, rasonopi. Dvayaṃ rattamūle, harite ca. Palaḍi gandhane, u, sundaro kando yassa sukandako. Kraṇasvananī.

595. Two (names are used) for garlic, whose root is white in color. Because its bulb is larger than an onion bulb, it is 'mahākando' (large-bulbed). Because it is deficient in one taste, the sour (taste), it is 'lasuṇaṃ'; (this involves) the change of 'ra' to 'la', shortening, and the change to 'ṇ'. Or, (it is 'lasuṇaṃ') from 'lasa' (to shine) in the sense of 'kanti' (lustre), with the suffix 'yu', the augment 'assu', and the change to 'ṇ'. 'Mahosadhaṃ', 'ariṭṭhaṃ', and also 'rasono' (are names). Two (names are used) for red-rooted and green (plants). 'Palaḍi' (is from the root) 'gandhane' (to smell/be fragrant), with the suffix 'u'. (It is) 'sukandako' (good-bulbed) because its bulb is beautiful. 'Kraṇasvananī' (is also a name).

Dvayaṃ paṭole. Paṭa gamane, olo, paṭuṃ rasaṃ lātīti vā paṭolo, usso, tittarasatāya tittako. Sakatthe ko. Kulakaṃ, paṭupi. Dvayaṃ “bhiṅgarāja”iti khyāte kesarañjane. Bhiṅgo vuccati bhamaro, tabbaṇṇaṃ katvā tesaṃ rañjetīti bhiṅgarājo. Muca mocane, avo, ussā, mākkavo.

Two (names are used) for paṭola. 'Paṭa' (is from the root) 'gamane' (to go), with the suffix 'olo'. Or, because it takes a pungent juice, it is 'paṭolo', with the augment 'usso'. Because of its bitter taste, (it is) 'tittako'. The suffix 'ko' is used in its own sense. 'Kulakaṃ' and also 'paṭu' (are names). Two (names are used) for the hair-dye known as 'bhiṅgarāja'. 'Bhiṅgo' is called a bee; because it dyes hair that color, it is 'bhiṅgarājo'. 'Muca' (is from the root) 'mocane' (to free), with the suffix 'avo' and the augment 'ussā'; (hence) 'mākkavo'.

596. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0398] punannavāyaṃ, vuddhopi puna navo bhavati yāya yogitāyāti punannavā. Sothaṃ hantīti sothaghātaṃ, hanassa ghāto. Dvayaṃ anūpaje sāke. Tuda byathane, bhāve to. Vigataṃ tunnametassa khādane vitunnaṃ. Sada visaraṇagatyāvasānesu, to, annādeso, sakatthe ko.

596. Two (names are used) for punannavā. Because by its efficacy even an old person becomes new again, it is 'punannavā'. Because it destroys edema, it is 'sothaghātaṃ'; 'ghāta' (is derived) from 'han' (to destroy). Two (names are used) for anūpaja sāka (marshy greens). 'Tuda' (is from the root) 'byathane' (to afflict), with the suffix 'to' in the sense of 'bhāve' (state/action). It is 'vitunnaṃ' because its piercing quality is gone when eaten. 'Sada' (is from the root) 'visaraṇagatyāvasānesu' (in spreading, going, and ending), with the suffix 'to', and the substitution 'anna'; the suffix 'ko' is used in its own sense.

Dvayaṃ kāravellake. Tittarasatāya kucchitākārena lambatīti kāravello. Ussāttaṃ, rattaṃ, illo, kupubbo lavi avasaṃsane. Sasu hiṃsāyaṃ, avo, nadādi, assu. “He khā le-khyā”. Tikaṃ lābuyaṃ. Tumba adane, tumbati hiṃsati pittanti tumbī, nadādi. Napubbo lamba avasaṃsane, u, malopo, nassa attaṃ, alābu, pāṇiniyānaṃ uṇādi 1.87, āpubbo lamba avasaṃsane, ālābu. Kātantikānaṃ, candānañcevaṃ, asmākantu rassaṃ katvā alābu, alope lābu, abhedopacārena tīṇipi phalepi itthiliṅgāni, sāsaddo itthi liṅgatthajotako.

Two for the bitter gourd. Because it hangs down in a wretched shape due to its bitter taste, it is kāravella. [The derivation involves] lengthening of 'u', lengthening of 'a', the suffix 'illa'; and from the root 'lav' in the sense of hanging down, preceded by 'ku'. From the root 'sas' in the sense of harming, with the suffix 'ava', of the nadādi class, with the augment 'assu'. “He khā le-khyā.” Three for the bottle gourd. From the root 'tumb' in the sense of destroying; because it harms or destroys bile, it is tumbī, of the nadādi class. From the root 'lamb' in the sense of hanging down, preceded by 'na', with the suffix 'u', the elision of 'm', and the change of 'n' to 'a', it becomes alābu, according to the Pāṇinians. From the root 'lamb' in the sense of hanging down, preceded by 'ā', it becomes ālābu. According to the followers of Kātantra and Candra, it is thus. But for us, by shortening the vowel, it is alābu; by elision of 'a', it is lābu. By metaphorical application, all three, even when referring to the fruit, are of the feminine gender; the word 'sā' indicates the feminine gender.

597. Dvayaṃ sampuse. Iraṃ vāriṃ lāti tabbāhulyatoti eḷālukaṃ. “Irā vārisurā bhūmi-bhāratīsu payujjate”ti hi [M 0.0399] nānatthasaṅgaho. Thiyaṃ, u, sakatthe ko. Kuka ādāne, aro, nadādi, ussattaṃ, kaṃ vātaṃ, kaphañca karotīti kakkarī, aparatra phalopo. Kakaḷipi. Dvayaṃ kumbhaṇḍe. Kumbhappamāṇaphalatāya kumbhaṇḍo, aññatthe ṇḍo, kumbho viya ḍetīti vā kumbhaṇḍo, bindāgamo, kusa chedane vā, aṇḍo, sassa bho, bindāgamo, kaṃ vātaṃ umbhetīti vā kumbhaṇḍo, aṇḍo. Valla saṃvaraṇe, ibho, mahāphalatāya sabbāsaṃ vallijātīnaṃ bhāti dibbatīti vā vallibho, kakkārūpi.

597. Two for the cucumber. Because it takes water in abundance, it is eḷāluka. For the Nānārthasaṅgraha states: 'Irā is used for water, liquor, earth, and speech.' In the feminine, with the suffix 'u', and 'ka' in its own sense. From the root 'kuk' in the sense of taking, with the suffix 'ara', of the nadādi class, with lengthening of 'u'. Because it produces wind and phlegm, it is kakkarī. Elsewhere, there is elision of a syllable. Also kakaḷi. Two for the pumpkin. Because its fruit is the size of a pot, it is kumbhaṇḍa. Elsewhere, with the suffix 'ṇḍa'. Or, because it swells like a pot, it is kumbhaṇḍa, with the insertion of a bindu. Or, from the root 'kus' in the sense of cutting, with the suffix 'aṇḍa', the change of 's' to 'bh', and the insertion of a bindu. Or, because it fills [the body] with wind, it is kumbhaṇḍa, with the suffix 'aṇḍa'. From the root 'vall' in the sense of covering, with the suffix 'ibha'. Or, because it shines or thrives among all species of creepers due to its large fruit, it is vallibha. Also kakkārū.

Dvayaṃ gorakkhakakkariyaṃ. Indassa sakkassa vāruṇī surā indavāruṇī. Visesena sarati hiṃsati kaphapittādayoti visālā. “Sarameho kuṭṭhahari, visālā kaphapittaghā”ti hi dabbaguṇe. Visarati virecati etāyāti vā visālā. Dvayaṃ anupasāke. Vasati yasmiṃ khāraguṇo vatthu. Vasa nivāse, ratthu, vasa hiṃsāyaṃ vā, vasati kaphavātapitteti vatthu. Vatthuleyyakoti samuditanāmaṃ. Laya sāyye, layāpeti sabbadoseti leyyako, ṇvu, asse, vatthu ca so leyyako cāti vatthuleyyako. “Mौṃ-heṃ”.

Two for the gorakkhakakkari. Indavāruṇī is the liquor of Indra Sakka. Because it especially moves against and harms phlegm, bile, and so forth, it is visālā. For in the Dravyaguṇa it is said: 'It removes diabetes and leprosy; visālā destroys phlegm and bile.' Or, because one purges or it spreads by means of it, it is visālā. Two for the anupasāka. Vatthu is that in which the alkaline quality resides. From the root 'vas' in the sense of dwelling, with the suffix 'tthu'. Or from 'vas' in the sense of harming; because it harms phlegm, wind, and bile, it is vatthu. Vatthuleyyaka is a compound name. From the root 'lay' in the sense of dissolving; because it causes all the bodily humors (doṣas) to dissolve, it is leyyaka, with the suffix 'ṇvu' and the augment 'assa'. And it is vatthu and it is that leyyaka, thus it is vatthuleyyaka. “Mौṃ-heṃ”.

598. Dvayaṃ mūlake. Ṇvumhi mūlako. Cacca paribhāsanatajjanesu, u, assu, muṃlāpaṅa. Dvayaṃ kalambuke. Tamu kaṅkhāyaṃ, ṇvu, banto ca, ke jale lambatīti kalambuko, ṇvu, assu. Upodikāpi, udakaṃ apagatā upodikā.

598. Two for the radish. With the suffix 'ṇvu', it is mūlaka. From the root 'cacc' in the senses of scolding and threatening, with the suffix 'u', the augment 'assu', and the change 'muṃlāpaṅa'. Two for the kalambuka (water spinach). From the root 'tam' in the sense of desiring, with the suffix 'ṇvu', and the augment 'banta'. Or, because it hangs in water, it is kalambuka, with the suffix 'ṇvu' and the augment 'assu'. Also upodikā. That from which water has gone away is upodikā.

Kāsamaddajhajjharīmaggavādayo [M 0.0400] sākabhedā sākavisesā. Kāsaṃ maddatīti kāsamaddo. Kaco, jhajjha paribhāsanatajjanesu, aro, nadādi, jhajjharī. Kanakalā. Phaṃ vātaṃ gaṇhātīti phaggavo, hassa vo, phaggavo, “pै-teṃ-khā”.

Kāsamadda, jhajjharī, maggava, and so forth are kinds of greens and specific greens. Because it suppresses cough, it is kāsamadda. From the root 'kac'. From the root 'jhajjh' in the senses of scolding and threatening, with the suffix 'ara', of the nadādi class, it is jhajjharī. Kanakalā. Because it seizes phlegm and wind, it is phaggava; with the change of 'h' to 'v', it is phaggava. “pै-teṃ-khā”.

599-600. Dvayaṃ dubbāyaṃ. Sundaraṃ dalaṃ pattametassa maṅgalapāṭheti saddalo, saddaṃ maṅgalasaddaṃ lānti bhāsanti paṭhanti brāhmaṇā yenāti vā saddalo. Dubbī hiṃsāyaṃ, a, avamaṅgalaṃ dubbatīti dubbā, dunnimittādayo vārenti yāyāti vādubbā, nerutto. Satapabbikā, bhaggavī, anantā, ruhāpi. Sā dubbā sitā sukkā ce, golomī nāma, golomajattā golomī. Satavīriyā, gaṇḍālī, sakulākkhakopi.

599-600. Two for dubbā (dūrvā grass). Because its beautiful leaf is for auspicious recitation, it is saddala. Or, because brahmins take, speak, and recite the auspicious sound by means of it, it is saddala. From the root 'dubb' in the sense of harming, with the suffix 'a'. Because it harms the inauspicious, it is dubbā. Or, because bad omens and so forth are warded off by it, it is dubbā; this is an etymological explanation. Also satapabbikā, bhaggavī, anantā, and ruhā. If that dubbā is white or dried, it is named golomī. Because it has the nature of cow's hair, it is golomī. Also satavīriyā, gaṇḍālī, and sakulākkhaka.

Dvayaṃ bhaddamutte. Gu sadde, do. Muca mocane, to, rogaharaṇattā bhaddañca taṃ muttañceti bhaddamuttaṃ, “nvā-mye-yeṃ-jī”. Dvayaṃ ucchumhi. Rasaṃ lātīti rasālo, dīgho. Isu icchāyaṃ, u, usa dāhe vā, u, sassa cho, pubbatra issu, asarūpadvittaṃ, ucchu, pume.

Two for bhaddamutta. From the root 'gu' in the sense of sounding, with the suffix 'da'. From the root 'muc' in the sense of freeing, with the suffix 'ta'. And because it is auspicious and freeing due to its removal of disease, it is bhaddamutta. “nvā-mye-yeṃ-jī.” Two for sugarcane. Because it gives juice, it is rasāla, with a long vowel. From the root 'is' in the sense of desiring, with the suffix 'u'. Or from 'us' in the sense of burning, with the suffix 'u'. 's' becomes 'ch'. Previously 'issu'. With dissimilar doubling, it becomes ucchu, in the masculine gender.

Catukkaṃ [M 0.0401] vaṃse. Vī gamane, ḷu, tacova sāro yassa. Vī gamane, u, nāgamo, ṇattaṃ, vanati sambhatīti vaṃso. Vana sambhattiyaṃ, so, vasa nivāse vā, karaṇe a, niggahītāgamo. Satapabbo, yavaphalo, makkaro, tejanopi, makkaroti paṭisevati yena makkaro, saññāyaṃ a. Tikaṃ pabbe. Pabba pūraṇe, pabbaṃ. Phala visaraṇe, u, ḷattaṃ. Gantha ganthane, i, vaṇṇavikāre gaṇṭhi, so pumā.

A group of four for vaṃsa (bamboo). From the root 'vī' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'ḷu'; that of which the bark is the essence. From the root 'vī' in the sense of going, with the suffix 'u', the insertion of 'na', and cerebralization. Because it is desired and used, it is vaṃsa. From the root 'van' in the sense of serving, with the suffix 'sa'. Or from 'vas' in the sense of dwelling, with the suffix 'a' in the instrumental sense, and the insertion of a niggahīta. Also satapabba, yavaphala, makkara, and tejana. Because one frequents it, it is makkara; the suffix 'a' is for designation. A triad for pabba (joint). From the root 'pabb' in the sense of filling, it is pabba. From the root 'phal' in the sense of splitting, with the suffix 'u', and the change to 'ḷ'. From the root 'ganth' in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'i'; with a change in the vowel, it is gaṇṭhi, which is masculine.

Aniladdhutā anilena kampitā ye veṇū kīṭādibhi katarandhatāya nadanti, te kīcakā nāma siyuṃ, cakī āmasane, ṇvu, pubbāparabyañjanānaṃ vipariyayo, kīcakā.

Those bamboos which, being shaken by the wind, make a sound because they have been hollowed out by insects and so forth, are called kīcakā. From the root 'cak' in the sense of touching or trembling, with the suffix 'ṇvu', and a reversal of the preceding and following consonants, it becomes kīcaka.

601. Dvayaṃ naḷe. Nī naye, alo, ḷattaṃ, dhama saddaggisaṃyogesu, yu, poṭagalopyatra. Dvayaṃ kāse. Puṭaṃ aññamaññaṃ saṃsaggaṃ gacchatīti poṭagalo, massa lo. Kāsa dittiyaṃ, a, ayamanitthī.

601. Two for naḷa (reed). From the root 'nī' in the sense of leading, with the suffix 'ala', and the change to 'ḷ'. From the root 'dham' in the senses of sounding and combining with fire, with the suffix 'yu'. Poṭagala is also [a name] here. Two for kāsa (grass). Because it goes into mutual contact in a bundle, it is poṭagala; 'm' becomes 'l'. From the root 'kās' in the sense of shining, with the suffix 'a'; this is not feminine.

Dvayaṃ sare. Tija nisāne, yu. Sarantyaneneti saro. Pume saññāyaṃ a, sara hiṃsāyaṃ vā. Gundopyatra. Bīraṇassa setakusumassa tiṇavisesassa mūlaṃ usīraṃ nāma, vasa kantiyaṃ, usa dāhe vā, īro, pubbasmiṃ vassu, abhayaṃ, naladaṃ, sebyaṃ, jalāsayaṃ, amaṇālaṃ, lāmajjakampi.

Two for sara (arrow-grass). From the root 'tij' in the sense of sharpening, with the suffix 'yu'. That by which they go is sara. In the masculine, the suffix 'a' is for designation. Or from the root 'sar' in the sense of harming. Gunda is also [a name] here. The root of bīraṇa, a specific type of grass with white flowers, is named usīra. It is derived from the root 'vas' in the sense of desiring, or from 'us' in the sense of burning, with the suffix 'īra'; in the former case, 'vas' becomes 'u'. Other synonyms are abhaya, nalada, sebya, jalāsaya, amaṇāla, and lāmajjaka.

Haritakyābhayā paṇḍo, usīre nibbhaye tisu.

The word abhayā is a name for haritakī; the word abhaya is a name for usīra and also means 'fearless', an adjective used in all three genders.

Jalāsayo jalādhāre, usīre tu jalāsayaṃ.

Jalāsaya, in the masculine, means a water receptacle; but jalāsayaṃ, in the neuter, is a name for usīra.

Sebyā sevārahe siyā.

The word sebyā is used for that which is worthy of being served.

602. Tikaṃ [M 0.0402] kuse, kusa chedane, a, varaha pādhānye, paribhāsanahiṃ sādānesu ca, iso, du paritāpe, abbho, dabbho, kutho, pavitrampi.

602. A triad for kusa grass. The word kusa is from the root 'kus' in the sense of cutting, with the suffix 'a'. Other synonyms are dabbha, kutha, and also pavitra. [The text also lists the following unrelated terms:] from the root 'varah' in the sense of pre-eminence; from 'paribhās' in the senses of reproach, harming, and taking; from 'iṣ' [comes] 'iso' (arrow); from 'du' in the sense of tormenting [comes] 'abbha' (cloud).

Dvayaṃ “gandhakheḍa”iti khyāte tiṇe, vuttañca “bhūtinaṃ gandhakheḍañca, sugandhaṃ gomayappiya”nti. Atha rāmakappūrato ko assa bhedo. Rāmakappūraṃ bahupakaṇḍaṃ kappūrasugandhaṃ. Gandhakheḍantu ikaḍasamānapattaṃ sākhāsabhāvaṃ bhūmilaggaṃ, atoyeva bhūtinakamuccate, bhūmiyaṃ laggaṃ tiṇaṃ bhūtinakaṃ, nattaṃ, sakatthe ko.

Two for the grass known as 'gandhakheḍa'. And it is said: 'Bhūtina and gandhakheḍa are fragrant and beloved of cow-dung.' Now, what is its difference from rāmakappūra? Rāmakappūra has many stalks and a camphor-like fragrance. Gandhakheḍa, however, has leaves similar to the ikaḍa plant, has a branching nature, and clings to the ground. Therefore it is called bhūtinaka; bhūtinaka is the grass that clings to the earth. The suffix 'na', and 'ka' in its own sense.

Dvayaṃ gavādīnaṃ madanīye tiṇe, ghasa adane, ṇo, yu missane, aso. Dvayaṃ pūgarukkhe. Pūja pūjāyaṃ, ṇo, pūgo. Kamu icchāyaṃ, ṇvu. Ghoṇṭāpi, “ghoṇṭā badarapūgesū”ti ruddo.

Two for the grass that intoxicates cattle and other animals. From the root 'ghas' in the sense of eating, with the suffix 'ṇa'. From 'yu' in the sense of mixing, with the suffix 'asa'. Two for the pūga tree (areca nut). From the root 'pūj' in the sense of honoring, with the suffix 'ṇa', it is pūga. From the root 'kam' in the sense of desiring, with the suffix 'ṇvu'. Also ghoṇṭā. Rudra says: 'Ghoṇṭā is used for the badara and pūga trees'.

603. Dvayaṃ tāle. Tala patiṭṭhāyaṃ, curādi, a. Vātādayo vibhindatīti vibhedikā.

603. Two for the tāla (palmyra palm). From the root 'tal' in the sense of establishing, of the curādi class, with the suffix 'a'. Because it splits wind and so forth, it is vibhedikā.

“Vātagho brūhano cāpi, kimihā kuṭṭhanāsano;

Rattapittaharo sādu, tālo sattaguṇo mato”ti.

The tāla is considered to possess seven qualities: it is wind-destroying, nourishing, worm-destroying, a cure for skin diseases, a remover of blood-bile disorders, and sweet.

Hi dabbaguṇo. Tiṇarājāpi. Dvayaṃ khajjūriyaṃ. Khajja khajjane, byathane ca, ūro, nadādi. Sida mocane, snehane ca, i, sanda savane vā, i, upāntassi ca, sindi.

Indeed, this is from the Dravyaguṇa. It is also the king of grasses. Two for the khajjūrī (date palm). From the root 'khajj' in the senses of eating and tormenting, with the suffix 'ūra', of the nadādi class. The word sindi is from the root 'sid' in the senses of releasing and anointing, with the suffix 'i'; or from 'sand' in the sense of flowing, with the suffix 'i', and a change to the penultimate vowel.

604. Hintālādayo [M 0.0403] satta nissāratāya tiṇāni ca tāni mūlena jalapānasāmaññato pādapā ceti tiṇapādapā vuccanti, tiṇa adane, pamāṇato tālato hīno hintālo, padavipariyayo, rasso ca. Nāḷi viya jāyatīti nāḷikero. Aññatthe iro, konto ca, nāḷikero. Lāṅgalīpi. “Lāṅgalī nāḷikere ca, sirapāṇimhi lāṅgalī”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 14.168 rabhaso. Saṇṭhānato tālasadisatāya tāḷī, ḷattaṃ, upamāne ī, taḷa āghāte vā, curādi, nadādi, tāḷī. Kita nivāse, rogāpanayane ca, ṇvu, nadādittā ī, ketakī, ayaṃ nārī.

604. The seven types of plants, starting with hintāla, are called tiṇapādapā (grass-trees) because they are grasses due to their lack of essence, and also trees due to their commonality of drinking water through their roots. The root `tiṇa` is in the sense of eating; hintāla is inferior in size to tāla; there is a reversal of syllables and shortening. That which grows like a reed is called nāḷikera. In another sense, `iro` and `konto` are also used for nāḷikera. Lāṅgalī is also a synonym. Rabhasa says: 'Lāṅgalī is used for nāḷikera, and lāṅgalī also for sirapāṇi (one with a plough in hand).' Due to its resemblance to tāla in shape, it is called tāḷī; with the change to `ḷ`, and `ī` in the sense of comparison; or from the root `taḷa` (to strike), of the curādi and nadādi groups, it is called tāḷī. The word `ketakī` is derived from the root `kita` (to dwell, and to remove disease), with the suffix `ṇvu`, and `ī` due to being in the nadādi group; this word is feminine.

Araññavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Araññavagga is concluded.

6. Araññādivaggavaṇṇanā

6. The Explanation of the Araññādi-vagga.

605. Nava pabbatassa nāmāni. Pabba pūraṇe, to. Gira niggiraṇe, osadhādayo niggiratīti giri, i. Silānaṃ rāsi selo, [M 0.0404] silā pacurā santyasmiṃ vā selo, sela gatiyaṃ vā, a. Adda gatimhi yācane ca, bhūvādi, i, adda hiṃsāyaṃ vā, curādi. Na gacchatīti nago. Na calatīti acalo. Silānamuccayo ubbedho, thūpo vā siluccayo. Sikharayogā sikharī, ī, tilakībhūto. Bhuṃ bhūmiṃ dharatīti bhūdharo, bhuyā dharīyatīti vā bhūdharo, bāhulyena a, bhūdharo. Ahāriyo, gottopi, desantaraṃ netumasakyattā ahāriyo, gavaṃ bhūmiṃ dhāraṇena tāyate gotto.

605. There are nine names for a mountain. The word `pabbata` is from the root `pabba` (to fill), with the suffix `to`. The word `giri` is from the root `gira` (to swallow); it is called `giri` because it swallows herbs and so forth, with the suffix `i`. A mass of rocks is `selo`, or where rocks are abundant is `selo`; or it is from the root `sela` (to move), with the suffix `a`. The word `addri` is from the root `adda` (to go, and to beg), of the bhūvādi group, with the suffix `i`; or from `adda` (to harm), of the curādi group. That which does not go is `nago`. That which does not move is `acalo`. An accumulation of rocks is a `siluccayo`, that is, a height or a heap. Due to its connection with peaks, it is called `sikharī`, with the suffix `ī`, becoming like a tilaka. That which bears the earth is `bhūdharo`, or because the earth is borne by it, it is `bhūdharo`; mostly with the suffix `a`, it is `bhūdharo`. `Ahāriyo` (immovable), and also `gotto`; `ahāriyo` because it cannot be taken to another country; `gotto` is so called because it protects the land for cows by bearing it.

Pañcakaṃ silāyaṃ. Ama gatiyaṃ, bho. Vana, sana sambhattiyaṃ, pasanati byāpetīti pāsāṇo, nipātanā, pasa bandhane vā, yu. Asu khepane, mo, asmā, rājādi, asu byāpane vā. Pala rakkhaṇe, upalo, upa dehe vā, alapaccayo nipāto. Sila ucce, a. Silā, nārī.

There are five synonyms for silā (stone). A word is derived from the root `ama` (to go), with the suffix `bho`. The word `pāsāṇa` is from `vana` or `sana` (to serve), it is called `pāsāṇa` because it spreads; by special derivation; or from `pasa` (to bind), with the suffix `yu`. The word `asmā` is from `asu` (to throw), with the suffix `mo`, a root in the `rājādi` group; or from `asu` (to pervade). The word `upala` is from `pala` (to protect); or from `upa` (near) and `deha` (body), with the suffix `ala` by special derivation. The word `silā` is from `sila` (to be high), with the suffix `a`. Silā is feminine.

606. Gijjhakūṭādayo tikūṭantā “vaṅkādī”ti ettha ādinā malayadaddurādayo ca nagā nagavisesā. Gijjhā sakuṇavisesā assa kūṭe vasanti, gijjhasadisakūṭayuttatāya vā gijjhakūṭo. Visesena bhātīti vebhāro, aro. Pula mahatte, visesena pulatīti vepullo. Isayo gilatīti isigili, i. Ādiccagamanavirodhena viruddhaṃ jhāyatīti viñjho. Paṇḍuvaṇṇatāya paṇḍavo[M 0.0405], paṇḍa gatiyaṃ vā, avo. Kuṭilatāya vaṅko. Dvayaṃ udayagirimhi. Aparaselāpekkhāya pubbaselo. Udayantyasmā sūriyādayoti udayo, sūriyādīnamudayayogato vā udayo.

606. Gijjhakūṭa and others up to Tikūṭa, referred to as 'Vaṅkādi,' where 'ādi' (etc.) includes mountains like Malayadaddara and other specific types of mountains. Vultures, a specific type of bird, dwell on its peak; or it is called Gijjhakūṭa because it has a peak like a vulture's. That which shines especially is `vebhāro`, with the suffix `aro`. From `pula` (to be great); that which is especially great is `vepullo`. It swallows sages, hence it is called `isigili`, with the suffix `i`. That which burns in opposition to the movement of the sun is called `viñjho`. Due to its pale color, it is called `paṇḍavo`; or from `paṇḍa` (to go), with the suffix `avo`. Due to its crookedness, it is called `vaṅko`. There are two synonyms for Udayagiri. In comparison to Aparasela, it is Pubbasela. From this, the sun and others rise, hence it is called `udayo`; or because of its connection with the rising of the sun and others, it is called `udayo`.

Tikaṃ atthagirimhi. Mandayati sūriyo yasmiṃ mandaro. Mandappabho vā arati yasmiṃ sūriyoti mandaro, atthaṃ anupaladdhiṃ gahanakkhattānaṃ karotītyattho, nāmadhātukāritantā a. Dvayaṃ himavati pabbate. Himappacuratāya himavā, himaṃ vā vamatīti himavā, kvi, rājādipakkhepattā sissā. Himayutto acalo himācalo.

There is a triad of synonyms for Atthagiri (the setting mountain). That on which the sun becomes dim is `mandara`. Or, that on which the sun with dim light sets is `mandara`; the meaning is that it causes the non-perception of planets and constellations. This is derived from a denominative causal with the suffix `a`. There is a pair of synonyms for the Himavat mountain. Due to the abundance of snow, it is `himavā`; or because it emits snow, it is `himavā`, with the suffix `kvi`; its formation is accomplished due to its inclusion in the `rājādi` group. A mountain connected with snow is `himācalo`.

607. Attani sañjātagandhadabbānaṃ gandhehi loke madayati, modayatīti vā gandhamādano, yu. Kelāso vutto. Vicittakūṭayuttatāya cittakūṭo. Sukhaṃ dassanaṃ yassa, yasmiṃ vā sudassano, kāḷavaṇṇakūṭatāya kāḷakūṭo. Tīṇi kūṭānyassa tikūṭo, chaḷetepi pabbatavisesā. Assa yathāvuttassa pabbatassa pattho samo bhūmibhāgo sānu nāma, assa vā pabbatassa samāya bhūmiyaṃ pattho sānu ca bhavantīti ajjhāharitabbaṃ. Patiṭṭhate asminti pattho, ṭhassa tho. Sana sambhattiyaṃ, ṇu, sambhajīyate sevīyateti sānu, dvepyanitthiyaṃ.

607. That which intoxicates or delights the world with the scents of fragrant substances born within itself is `gandhamādano`, with the suffix `yu`. Kelāsa is mentioned. Due to being endowed with variegated peaks, it is called `cittakūṭo`. That whose sight is pleasant, or on which there is pleasant sight, is `sudassano`. Due to its dark-colored peak, it is called `kāḷakūṭo`. Having three peaks, it is `tikūṭo`; these six are specific types of mountains. The level ground of that aforementioned mountain is called `sānu`; or it should be supplied that the level ground of that mountain is `pattho` and `sānu`. That on which one stands is `pattho`; `ṭha` becomes `tha`. The word `sānu` is from `sana` (to serve), with the suffix `ṇu`; that which is frequented or served is `sānu`; both words are not feminine.

608. Tikaṃ [M 0.0406] siṅgassa nāmaṃ. Kuṭa dāhe, kammani ṇo, vākārena kūṭampi. Sikhaṃ ruhatīti sikharaṃ. Nerutto. Sikhaṃ gacchatīti siṅgaṃ, iṅga gamanattho, khalopo. Dvayaṃ pabbatādīnaṃ papatanaṭṭhānassa nāmaṃ. Papatantyasmā, ṇo. Pata adhogamane, papāto. Taṭa samussaye, taṭo.

608. There are three names for a peak. The word `kūṭa` is from `kuṭa` (to burn), with the suffix `ṇo` in the objective sense; `kūṭa` is also formed by vowel modification. That which rises to a crest is `sikharaṃ`. This is an etymological explanation. That which goes to the crest is `siṅgaṃ`; `iṅga` has the meaning of going, with the elision of `kha`. Two names for the place of falling from mountains and so forth. That from which one falls, with the suffix `ṇo`, is `papāto`. From `pata` (to go downwards), `papāto`. From `taṭa` (to heap up), `taṭo`.

Dvayaṃ pabbatanitambe. Nitambo jaghanepi, kaṭa vassāvaraṇesu, ṇvu. Pabbate pāsāṇādīsu ambuno jalassa pasavo pasavanaṃ nijjharo nāma, nissaraṇaṃ nijjharo, sassa jho, asarūpadvittaṃ. Jharopi.

There are two synonyms for the slope of a mountain. `Nitamba` is also used for the hip; `kaṭaka` is from `kaṭa` (to cover, to ward off rain), with the suffix `ṇvu`. On a mountain, the flowing or gushing forth of water from rocks and so forth is called `nijjharo`; the outflow is `nijjharo`; `sa` becomes `jha`, and there is reduplication of a dissimilar consonant. `Jhara` is also a synonym.

609. Dvayaṃ kittime akittime, sajale nijjale vā kandare. Dara vidāraṇe, a, ī, darī. Kaṃ jalavācakamabyayaṃ, kena darīyate kandaro, ā, kandarā. Tikaṃ devakhātabile. Nilīyantyasmiṃ leṇaṃ, lī silesane, yu. Gatiṃ hvayati kuṭilayatīti gabbharaṃ, nipātanā. Gabbha dhāraṇe vā, aro. Guhū saṃvaraṇe, a, guhā.

609. There are two synonyms for a ravine, whether artificial or natural, with or without water. The word `darī` is from `dara` (to split), with the suffix `a` or `ī`. `Kaṃ` is an indeclinable denoting water; that which is split by water is `kandaro`, or `kandarā`. There is a triad of synonyms for a cave dug by deities. That in which one hides is `leṇaṃ`; from `lī` (to adhere), with the suffix `yu`. That which bends or makes movement crooked is `gabbharaṃ`, by special derivation. Or from `gabbha` (to hold), with the suffix `aro`. From `guhū` (to conceal), with the suffix `a`, `guhā`.

Dvayaṃ silāmayapokkharaṇiyaṃ. Soḍi gabbhe, ī. Soṇa vaṇṇagatisaṅghātesu vā, ḍo, ī. Dvayaṃ pabbatādīnaṃ gabbharadese latāpallavatiṇādīhi pihitodare gabbhare. Kuñja abyattasadde, karaṇe, ṇo, nikuñjaṃ nipubbo. Dvayaṃpyanitthiyaṃ. Nikuñjavacanaṃ pakuñjādinivattanatthaṃ.

There are two synonyms for a rocky pond. The word `soṇḍī` is from `soḍi` (in a cave), with the suffix `ī`; or from `soṇa` (to color, to go, to aggregate), with the suffix `ḍo` and `ī`. There are two synonyms for a cave in the hollow part of mountains and so forth, whose interior is covered with creepers, leaves, grass, and other things. The word `nikuñjaṃ` is from `kuñja` (to make an indistinct sound), with the suffix `ṇo` in the instrumental sense, and the prefix `ni`. Both words are not feminine. The word `nikuñja` is used to exclude `pakuñja` and so forth.

610. Selassa [M 0.0407] pabbatassa uddhaṃbhūmi adhiccakā nāma. Selassādhobhāgāsannabhūmi upaccakā nāma. Atra tehi upādisaddehi ccako yadādinā pāṇini 5.2.34.

610. The upper ground of a rock or mountain is called `adhiccakā`. The ground near the lower part of a rock is called `upaccakā`. Here, with these prefixes such as `upa`, the suffix `ccaka` is formed by the rule beginning with `ya`, and so on.

Mūlapabbatassante parivāretvā ṭhitā khuddapabbatā pādā nāma. Tatra pādādidvayaṃ. Pajjate gamyateti, ṇo. Selassa upanto samīpe pabbato upantaselo.

Small mountains standing surrounding the base of a main mountain are called `pādā`. There, the pair of synonyms begins with `pāda`. That which is gone to is `pāda`, with the suffix `ṇo`. A mountain near the edge of a rock is `upantaselo`.

Gerikamanosilāharitālakaṭṭhinyādikosabbo eva silāvikāro “dhātū”tyutto, dhara dhāraṇe, tu, dhātu.

Every modification of rock, such as red ochre, red arsenic, yellow orpiment, chalk, and so forth, is called `dhātu`. The word `dhātu` is from `dhara` (to hold), with the suffix `tu`.

Selavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Selavagga is concluded.

611. Tikaṃ sīhe. Kesaro jaṭā, taṃyogā, ī, kesarī. Mige hiṃsatīti sīho, nipātanā vaṇṇavipariyayo, mige hantuṃ saṃvijjamānā īhā assāti vā sīho, sahatīti vā sīho. Pañcasso, haripi. Mukhamiva caraṇāpyassa karikumbhadāraṇasamatthāti tehi saha pañcassāni [M 0.0408] yassa. Harati migeti hari, i. Mahākukkurappamāṇo kukkurākati kaṇhalekhācittasarīro gomanussādihiṃsakkhamo rassamukho taraccho nāma, so “sunakhabyaggho”ti vuccati. Tara taraṇe, cho, mige adatīti migādano, nandādīhi yu.

611. There is a triad of synonyms for the lion. `Kesaro` means mane; due to its connection, with `ī`, it is `kesarī`. One who harms beasts is `sīho`, by irregular formation with transposition of letters; or one who has the existing will to harm beasts is `sīho`; or one who overcomes is `sīho`. `Pañcasso` and `hari` are also synonyms. Its feet are like its face, capable of tearing apart an elephant's temples; hence, it has five faces (`pañcāsyāni`) including these. It seizes beasts, hence `hari`, with the suffix `i`. A creature the size of a large dog, with the shape of a dog, a body marked with black stripes, capable of harming cattle and humans, and with a short snout, is called `taraccho`; it is also called `sunakhabyaggho` (dog-tiger). From `tara` (to cross), with the suffix `cho`; one who eats beasts is `migādano`, with the suffix `yu` from the `nandādi` group.

Dvayaṃ byagghe. Vinihantvā āghāyatīti byaggho, ghā gandhopādāne, byaggho dīpinipi. Puṃ pumāno dāletīti puṇḍarīko, dala vidāraṇe, ṇvu. Dassa ḍo, lassa ro, assī, puṇḍarīko.

There is a pair of synonyms for the tiger. One who, having struck, smells its prey is `byaggho`, from `ghā` in the sense of taking scent; `byaggho` is also a leopard. One who cleaves a male is `puṇḍarīko`, from `dala` (to split), with the suffix `ṇvu`. `D` becomes `ḍ`, `l` becomes `r`, and `assī` is a phonetic change; hence `puṇḍarīko`.

“Puṇḍarīkaṃ sitamboje,

Sitacchatre ca bhesajje;

Kosakārantare byagghe,

So disāvāraṇaggisū”ti. –

"Puṇḍarīka is a white lotus, a white umbrella, and medicine; a tiger in the interior of a sheath; it is in a direction, an enclosure, fire, and the sun."

Nānatthasaṅgahe. Vagghopi. Dīpinivisaye saddūlo īrito, saratīti saddūlo, ūlo, do canto, saddena ulati gacchatīti vā saddūlo. Dīpaṃ taccammaṃ, taṃyogā dīpī, tasmiṃ dīpini.

In the Nānatthasaṅgaha. Also `vaggho`. In the context of the leopard, `saddūlo` is stated; it is called `saddūlo` because it goes (`sarati`), with the suffix `ūlo`, and `da` at the end; or because it goes (`ulati`, `gacchati`) with a sound (`saddena`), hence `saddūlo`. `Dīpaṃ` refers to its hide, and `dīpī` is connected to that; hence, `dīpinī` for the leopard.

612. Pañcakaṃ acche. Asu khepane, cho. Ica thutiyaṃ, a, ikko. Bhallukopi, bhala, bhalla paribhāsanahiṃsādānesu, ṇvu, assu, īsa gatihiṃsādānesu, so, rassādi. Apaccaye iso.

612. The fivefold group is for the bear (`accha`). The root `asu` is in the sense of throwing; `cho` is the suffix. The root `ica` is in the sense of praise; `a` and `ikko` are suffixes. Also `bhalluka`; the roots `bhala` and `bhalla` are in the senses of reviling, harming, and giving; `ṇvu` is the suffix. Also `assu`. The root `īsa` is in the senses of going, harming, and giving; `so` is the suffix, with shortening and so forth. In the absence of a derivative suffix, `iso`.

Dvayaṃ rohite. Lohitavaṇṇatāya rohiso, lohito ca, pubbatra tassa so. Tikaṃ gokaṇṇe. Gavassa [M 0.0409] kaṇṇo viya yassa kaṇṇoti gokaṇṇo. Gaṇayuttatāya gaṇī ca so kaṇṭakasadisasiṅgatāya kaṇṭako ceti gaṇikaṇṭako, samuditanāmampi vadanti. Gaṇi ca kaṇṭako ca gaṇikaṇṭakāti dve nāmānipi daṭṭhabbāni, teneva hi “gaṇikaṇṭakā”ti bahuvacananiddeso kato.

The pair is for the `rohita`. Because of its red color, it is `rohisa`, and also `lohita`; in the former case, `so` is its suffix. The triad is for the `gokaṇṇa`. `Gokaṇṇa` is one whose ear is like the ear of a cow. Because it is associated with a herd, it is `gaṇī`, and because it has a horn like a thorn, it is `kaṇṭaka`; hence `gaṇikaṇṭaka`. They also call it a compound name. `Gaṇikaṇṭaka` is also to be understood as two names, `gaṇī` and `kaṇṭaka`; for this very reason, the plural designation `gaṇikaṇṭakā` is used.

613-614. Catukkaṃ khagge. Siṅgañca khaggākhyaṃ, taṃyogā khaggo. “Khaggo gaṇḍakasiṅgāsi-vuddhabhedesu gaṇḍake”ti byākhyāsudhā 2.5.4 hi nānatthasaṅgahe. Khaggasadisaṃ visāṇamassa saṇṭhānatoti khaggavisāṇo, ṇo. Ettha khaggasaddo asipariyāyo. Palāsamadatīti palāsādo. Gaṇḍa vadanekadese, ṇvu, gaṇḍako.

613-614. The tetrad is for the rhinoceros (`khagga`). The horn (`siṅga`) is also called `khagga`; from its connection with that, the animal is `khaggo`. For in the Nānārthasaṅgaha it is said: 'The word `khagga` is used in the distinct senses of rhinoceros (`gaṇḍaka`), horn (`siṅga`), sword (`āsi`), and a wise person (`buddha`).' `Khaggavisāṇa` is so called because its horn has a shape like a sword; `ṇo` is the suffix. Here, the word `khagga` is a synonym for sword. `Palāsādo` is so called because it eats palāsa leaves. The root `gaṇḍa` is in the sense of 'a part of the face'; `ṇvu` is the suffix, hence `gaṇḍako`.

Byagghādiko sabbopi migabhedo “vāḷamigo, sāpado”ti coccate. Byagghassātisayena manussādīnaṃ hiṃsanato duṭṭhatā pākaṭāti tappamukhatā vuttā. Vala saṃvaraṇe, valantyattānamasmāti vāḷo, ṇo, vāḷo ca so migo ceti vāḷamigo, duṭṭhamigotyattho. “Byaggho taṃ khādatū”tyādinā sapanti yenāti sāpado, sapa akkose, do, dīghādi.

Every kind of beast of prey, beginning with the tiger, is also called `vāḷamiga` and `sāpado`. Because the tiger's wickedness in exceedingly harming humans and others is manifest, its preeminence is stated.
