The root `vala` is in the sense of enclosing; `vāḷo` is so called because they enclose themselves in it; `ṇo` is the suffix. `Vāḷo ca so migo ceti vāḷamigo` means a `vāḷamiga`, which has the meaning 'a vicious beast'. `Sāpado` is so called because one curses with it, saying 'May a tiger eat you!' and so on; the root `sapa` is in the sense of cursing; `do` is the suffix, with lengthening and so forth.

Plavaṅgantaṃ [M 0.0410] makkaṭe. Plavo gatibhedo, tena gacchatīti plavaṅgamo, plavaṅgo ca. Mara pāṇacāge, aṭo, ko canto, makkaṭo. Naro iva vānaro, vāsaddo ivatthe, nāmānaṃ yuttatthattā samāso. Sākhāyaṃ pasuto migo sākhāmigo. Gatyatthatāya kriyāya payogā. Kapi calane, i, kapi. Valī sithilaṃ cammaṃ mukhe assa valīmukho. Kiso, vanokopi, kucchitenākārena setīti kiso, ussi. Vanamokamāsayo assa vanoko. So makkaṭo ce kaṇhatuṇḍo kāḷamukho siyā, tadā “gonaṅgalo”ti mato, gunnaṃ naṅgalasadisatāya gonaṅgalo.

The group of terms ending with `plavaṅga` is for the monkey (`makkaṭa`). `Plava` is a type of movement; one that goes by that is a `plavaṅgama`, and also `plavaṅga`. The root `mara` is in the sense of abandoning life, with the suffix `aṭo` and the ending `ko`, hence `makkaṭo`. `Vānara` is 'like a man' (`naro iva`); the word `vā` is in the sense of 'like'; the compound is formed because the meanings of the words are suitable. `Sākhāmiga` is a beast devoted to branches. This is a usage of the verb due to the meaning of movement. The root `kapi` is in the sense of moving, with `i` as the suffix, hence `kapi`. `Valīmukha` is one who has wrinkled, loose skin on his face. Also `kiso` and `vanoko`; `kiso` is so called because it lies in an ugly manner, with `ussi` as the suffix. `Vanoko` is one whose dwelling and abode is the forest. If that monkey has a black snout or a black face, then it is considered a `gonaṅgala`; `gonaṅgala` is so called from its resemblance to the plow of oxen.

615. Pajjaddhaṃ siṅgālassa nāmaṃ. Sara gatihiṃsācintāsu, alo. Saratissa siṅgo. Jamu adane, ṇvu, bo canto, assu. Kusa akkose, tu, thu vā. Bheravayuttatāya bheravo, “bhe”iti ravatīti vā bheravo. Samu upasame, ivo, sivā, nārī, si sevāyaṃ vā, vo. Migadhutto, vañcakopi, migesu vanapasūsu dhutto. Brāhmaṇaṃ vañcetīti vañcako.

615. Half a verse of names for the jackal. The root `sara` is in the senses of going, harming, and thinking; `alo` is the suffix. Of `sarati`, `siṅgo`. The root `jamu` is in the sense of eating; `ṇvu` is the suffix, `bo` is the ending. Also `assu`. The root `kusa` is in the sense of crying out; `tu` or `thu` is the suffix. Because of its association with terror, it is `bheravo`; or because it howls 'bhe', it is `bheravo`. The root `samu` is in the sense of calming, with the suffix `ivo`, giving `sivā`, a feminine form; or the root `si` is in the sense of serving, with `vo` as the suffix. `Migadhutto`, also `vañcako`; a cheat among the wild animals, the beasts of the forest. It deceives a brahmin, hence `vañcako`.

Tikaṃ biḷāre. Bila bhedane, aro, ḷattaṃ. Babba gatiyaṃ, u. Maja suddhiyaṃ, āro, niggahītāgamo. Otu, ākhubhujopi. Dvayaṃ koke, ayaṃ kukkurappamāṇo kapilo hariṇo. Kuka, vaka ādāne. Īhāmigopi, mige īhati kaṅkhatīti, kammani ṇo.

The triad is for the cat (`biḷāra`). The root `bila` is in the sense of splitting, with `aro` as the suffix, and the change to `ḷ`. The root `babba` is in the sense of going, with `u` as the suffix. The root `maja` is in the sense of cleansing, with `āro` as the suffix, and the insertion of a nasal. Also `otu` and `ākhubhujo`. The pair is for the wolf (`koka`); this is a tawny deer the size of a dog. The roots `kuka` and `vaka` are in the sense of taking. Also `īhāmiga`; it desires and longs for deer; `ṇo` is the suffix in the sense of object.

616. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0411] mahiṃse. Mahiyaṃ setīti mahiṃso, rasso, niggahītāgamo ca. Lala icchāyaṃ, udakaṃ lalatīti lulāyo, nipātanā, ayo, assu ca. Go viya vajati jāyatīti gavajo. Go viya ayatīti gavayo, samā dve tulyatthā.

616. The pair is for the buffalo (`mahiṃsa`). `Mahiṃso` is so called because it lies on the earth, with shortening and the insertion of a nasal. The root `lala` is in the sense of desire; `lulāyo` is so called because it desires water, by irregular formation; `ayo` is the suffix. Also `assu`. `Gavajo` is so called because it goes and is born like a cow. `Gavayo` is so called because it goes like a cow; the two are the same, with equivalent meaning.

Dvayaṃ salle. Salla āsugatiyaṃ, a, sallo, sakatthe ko, sallako attano sarīrajātena sallena sunakhaṃ salati hiṃsatīti vā sallo, sallako ca, ayaṃ sūkarasaṇṭhāno, salākāpāyo ca. Assa sallassa lomamhi salalaṃ, salañca bhave. Pala, sala, patha gatiyaṃ, alo, nadāditte salalī, thittābhāve salalaṃ, amhi salaṃ.

The pair is for the porcupine (`salla`). The root `salla` is in the sense of swift movement, with `a` as the suffix, giving `sallo`; with `ko` in its own sense, `sallako`. Or, `sallo` and `sallako` are so called because it pierces and harms a dog with a quill born from its own body. This one has the shape of a boar and resembles a ticket. In the quill of this porcupine, there may be `salalaṃ` and `salaṃ`. The roots `pala`, `sala`, and `patha` are in the sense of going, with `alo` as the suffix. In the sense of a river, etc., `salalī`. In the absence of firmness, `salalaṃ`. In the locative singular, `salaṃ`.

617. Pañcakaṃ mige, harantyanena hariṇo, hara haraṇe yu. Ṇattamittañca. Mara pāṇacāge, a, rassa go, ittañca. Sena sunakhena raṅgati gacchati palāyatīti sāraṅgo. Dīghādi, mago, migo ca ete dve migamattepi. Ajinassopayujjamānassa yoni, tena bhūtassājinassuppattikāraṇattā vā ajinayoni. Ayampi migamattepi. Kuraṅgo, vātāyupi. Kuyaṃ pathaviyaṃ raṅgatīti kuraṅgo. Vātamayatīti vātāyu, u.

617. The fivefold group is for the deer (`miga`). `Hariṇo` is so called because it captivates; the root `hara` is in the sense of carrying away, with `yu` as the suffix. And `ṇattamitta`. The root `mara` is in the sense of abandoning life, with `a` as the suffix, `ga` as a substitute for `ra`, and `itta` as a suffix. `Sāraṅgo` is so called because it goes and flees from a dog. With lengthening and so forth, `mago` and `migo`; these two are also just general terms for deer. `Ajinayoni` is the source of the hide that is used, or because it is the cause for the arising of the hide of that being. This too is just a general term for deer. Also `kuraṅgo` and `vātāyu`. `Kuraṅgo` is so called because it roams on the earth. `Vātāyu` is so called because it goes like the wind, with `u` as the suffix.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0412] sūkare. Sundaraṃ phalaṃ karotīti sūkaro. Vuttañca dabbaguṇe –

The pair is for the pig (`sūkara`). `Sūkaro` is so called because it produces a beautiful result. And it is said in the Dabbaguṇa:

“Snehanaṃ brūhanaṃ vassaṃ, tathā vātasamāpahaṃ;

Vārāhaṃ pisitaṃ bālyaṃ, rocanaṃ sedanaṃ garū”ti dabbaguṇasaṅgaha 2.11-2.

"Emollient, nourishing, virilific, and also pacifying of the wind humor; the flesh of the boar is strength-giving, appetizing, sweat-inducing, and heavy."

Sukhaṃ karotīti vā sūkaro. Sundaro karo yassa vā sūkaro. Vare āhantīti varāho, vare sati āhantabboti vā varāho, kolo, thaddhalomo, bhūdāropi. Dvayaṃ sase. Pela gatiyaṃ, ṇvu. Sasa plutagatiyaṃ, a.

Or `sūkaro` is so called because it makes happiness. Or `sūkaro` is one that has a beautiful snout. `Varāho` is so called because it strikes at the best things; or because it should be struck when there is an opportunity. Also `kolo`, `thaddhalomo` (stiff-haired), and `bhūdāro` (earth-splitter). The pair is for the hare (`sasa`). The root `pela` is in the sense of going, with the suffix `ṇvu`. The root `sasa` is in the sense of leaping motion, with the suffix `a`.

618. Dvayaṃ eṇīmige. Eṇiyā migiyā, eṇassa vā apaccaṃ eṇeyyo, ayaṃ cammādīsupi “eṇassa, eṇiyā vā cammādiko eṇeyyo”ti vacanatthaṃ katvā. Eṇiyā itthiyā putto migo eṇīmigo, i gatiyaṃ, yu, nadādi, anadāditte eṇo, evametepyuppāditā. Dvayaṃ pampaṭake. Paṭa gamane, ṇvu, upasaggante bindāgamo ca. Pabba gatiyaṃ, ṇvu, bindāgamo, balopo ca.

618. The pair is for the `eṇīmiga`. `Eṇeyyo` is the offspring of a female deer or a male deer; this is also applied to hides and so forth, by constructing the meaning thus: 'A hide, etc., from a male or female deer is `eṇeyyo`.' `Eṇīmigo` is a deer that is the son of a female deer. The root `i` is in the sense of going, with the suffix `yu`, forming a word of the `nadādi` class (`eṇī`); in the absence of the `nadādi` class, it is `eṇo`. Thus are these derived. The pair is for the `pampaṭaka`. The root `paṭa` is in the sense of going, with `ṇvu` as the suffix, and when at the end of a prefix, there is the insertion of a nasal. The root `pabba` is in the sense of going, with `ṇvu` as the suffix, with insertion of a nasal and elision of `ba`.

Dvayaṃ vātamige. Gamanena vātasamo migo vātamigo. Calatismā yu, nadādi. Tikaṃ mūsike. Musa theyye, ṇvu, ittañca. Āpubbo khanu avadāraṇe, u, nalopo. Unda pasavanakledanesu, ūro.

The pair is for the `vātamiga`. `Vātamigo` is a deer equal to the wind in its movement. From `calati`, with the suffix `yu`, of the `nadādi` class. The triad is for the mouse (`mūsika`). The root `musa` is in the sense of stealing, with the suffix `ṇvu`, and also `itta`. The root `khanu`, preceded by `ā`, is in the sense of digging up, with `u` as the suffix and elision of `na`. The root `unda` is in the senses of bringing forth and moistening, with `ūro` as the suffix.

619. Camarādayo[M 0.0413], sarabhādayo ca migantarā migavisesā. Camaro uttarāpathe khyāto, yassa pucchaṃ cāmaraṃ, camu adane, aro, camaro, thiyaṃ camarī. Pasado cittalomī, pasa bandhane, ado. Kuyaṃ raṅgatīti kuruṅgo, assu, uttābhāve kuraṅgo. Sabbesampi migānaṃ mātuṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti migamātukā, upamāne ko. Ru sadde, ru. Ruṇaṃ karotīti raṅku, u, ṇassa lopo rakārassa, ussa ca. Attānaṃ nīcaṃ karotīti nīko. Saratismā abho, sarabho. Aṭṭhāpado uddhaṃnayano sīhassāpi hantā, tassa ca pādacatukkaṃ uddhaṃ bhavatīti.

619. The `camara` and others, and the `sarabha` and others, are other types of deer, special deer. The `camara` is famous in the northern region; its tail is the `cāmara`. The root `camu` is in the sense of eating; `aro` is the suffix, hence `camaro`; in the feminine, `camarī`. `Pasado` has spotted fur; the root `pasa` is in the sense of binding; `ado` is the suffix. `Kuruṅgo` is so called because it roams on the earth; `assu` is the suffix; in the absence of `utta`, it is `kuraṅgo`. `Migamātukā` is so called because it stands in the place of a mother to all deer; `ko` is the suffix in the sense of comparison. The root `ru` is in the sense of sound, hence `ru`. `Raṅku` is so called because it makes a sound; `u` is the suffix, with elision of `ṇa`, of the letter `ra`, and of `u`. `Nīko` is so called because it makes itself low. From `sarati`, with `abho` as the suffix, hence `sarabho`. The `aṭṭhāpada` has upward-facing eyes, is a killer even of a lion, and its four feet are upwards.

620. Piyakādayo tayo, ādinā kandalīcīnasamūruādayo ca cammayonayo, tena bhūtassa cammassa uppattikāraṇattā, ete ca citratanuruhādayo kambojādimhi, uttarāpathe ca jāyanti, tatreva sanāmakhyātā. Yathā migasaddo vanyapasusāmaññe, visese ca kuraṅgākhye vattati, yathā ca lohasaddo suvaṇṇādike tejasasāmaññe, visese ca, tathā cammayoniajinayonisaddāpi migasāmaññe, migavisese ceti tathā vuttā.

620. The three beginning with `piyaka`, and by `ādi` others like `kandalī`, `cīna`, `samūru`, etc., are `cammayoni` (hide-source), because they are the cause of the arising of the hide of that being. And these, `citra`, `tanuruha`, etc., are born in Kamboja and other places, and in the northern region, and are known there by those very names. Just as the word `miga` applies generally to forest animals, and specifically to the one called `kuraṅga`; and just as the word `loha` applies generally to metals like gold, etc., and specifically to iron; so too the words `cammayoni` and `ajinayoni` apply generally to deer, and to specific types of deer. Thus it is said.

Pī tappanakantīsu, ṇvu, iyādeso. Ūrumhi atisayacammayuttatāya camūru, ekassa massa lopo. Kadi avhāne, alo, ī, kadalī ca so migo ceti kadalīmigo.

The root `pī` is in the senses of satisfying and pleasing, with `ṇvu` as the suffix and `iya` as a substitute. `Camūru` is so called because of being endowed with an excessive amount of hide on its thigh, with the elision of one `ma`. The root `kadi` is in the sense of calling, with `alo` and `ī` as suffixes; `kadalīmigo` is so called because it is a `kadalī` and that deer.

Sīhādayo [M 0.0414] yathāvuttā, avuttā ca sabbe catuppadā sattā “migā, pasavo”ti coccante. Pasavantīti pasavo, su abhisave, pasa bandhane vā, u.

Lions and others, both those mentioned and those unmentioned, all four-footed beings, are called 'migā' and 'pasavo'. They are called 'pasavo' because they procreate (pasavanti); from the root 'su' in the sense of pressing out, or 'pasa' in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'u'.

621. Catukkaṃ lūtāyaṃ. Lū chedane, to, lūtā, sakatthe iko, lūtikā, dve nāriyaṃ. Uṇṇāpāyo tantu uṇṇā, sā nābhiyaṃ assa uṇṇanābhi, rasso. Makkaṭo viya sākhāyaṃ attano tantumhi gacchatīti makkaṭako.

621. There are four terms for spider. From the root 'lū' in the sense of cutting, with the suffix 'to', comes 'lūtā'. With the suffix 'iko' in its own sense, it becomes 'lūtikā'. These two are feminine. The thread of a spider is 'uṇṇā'. That which has this 'uṇṇā' at its navel is 'uṇṇanābhi'; the vowel is shortened. Because it moves on its own thread on a branch like a monkey, it is called 'makkaṭako'.

Dvayaṃ gomayajavicchike. Viccha gamane, ṇvu, vicchiko, satapadiyampi, āḷaṃ vicchikanaṅgulaṃ, taṃyogā āḷi. Dvayaṃ gharagodhāyaṃ. Saratismā ū, avo canto. Gharaṃ nissitā godhā gharagoḷikā, dhassa ḷo, sakatthe ko.

There are two terms for the cow-dung scorpion. From the root 'viccha' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'ṇvu', comes 'vicchiko'. It is also called 'satapadī'. 'Āḷaṃ' is the scorpion's sting; from its association comes 'āḷi'. There are two terms for the house-lizard. From 'sarati' (it moves), with the suffix 'ū', and 'avo' at the end. A lizard that depends on the house is 'gharagoḷikā'; 'dh' becomes 'ḷ', and 'ko' is a suffix in its own sense.

622. Dvayaṃ godhāyaṃ. Gudha rose, a, godhā, nārī. Kuṇḍa dāhe, a, kuṇḍo. Dvayaṃ rattapāyaṃ. Kaṇṇassa jalūkā rattapā kaṇṇajalūkā. Sataṃ padā yassā satapadī, padasaddo pādattho.

622. There are two terms for lizard. From the root 'gudha' in the sense of being angry, with the suffix 'a', comes 'godhā', which is feminine. From the root 'kuṇḍa' in the sense of burning, with the suffix 'a', comes 'kuṇḍo'. There are two terms for blood-drinker. The ear-leech is called 'rattapā' and 'kaṇṇajalūkā'. That which has a hundred feet is 'satapadī'; the word 'pada' has the meaning of 'foot'.

Dvayaṃ kalandake. Kanda avhāne, rodane ca, kandatīti kalandako, lamajjho, ṇvu. Kāḷavaṇṇatāya kāḷakā, nāriyaṃ. Dvayaṃ nakule, natthi kulaṃ etassa sappesu nakulo, arisappopi. Nakka nāsane vā, ulo, kalopo, sappe nāsetīti [M 0.0415] nakulo. Maṅga gatyattho daṇḍako dhātu, uso.

There are two terms for squirrel. From the root 'kanda' in the sense of calling or weeping, because it calls, it is 'kalandako'; 'la' is inserted in the middle, with the suffix 'ṇvu'. Due to its black color, it is 'kāḷakā', which is feminine. There are two terms for mongoose. Because it has no family among snakes, it is 'nakulo'; it is also called 'arisappo'. Or, from the root 'nakka' in the sense of destroying, with the suffix 'ulo' and elision of 'ka', because it destroys snakes, it is 'nakulo'. From the root 'maṅga' meaning 'to move', with the suffix 'uso', comes 'maṅguso'.

623. Dvayaṃ kakaṇṭake. Kucchito kaṇṭako assa, ussattaṃ. Sarati dhāvatīti saraṭo, aṭo.

623. There are two terms for chameleon. Because it has a despised spine (kucchito kaṇṭako), it is 'kakaṇṭaka'; the 'ku' is substituted. Because it moves or runs (sarati, dhāvati), it is 'saraṭo', with the suffix 'aṭo'.

Catukkaṃ kīṭe. Kīṭa bandhane, a, kīṭa gamane vā, dīghādi. Pula mahatthe, avo, ḷattaṃ. Kucchitaṃ amati gacchatīti kimi, i, assittaṃ. Pakārena anatīti pāṇako, ṇvu, ṇattaṃ.

There are four terms for insect. From the root 'kīṭa' in the sense of binding, with the suffix 'a', or from 'kīṭa' in the sense of moving, with lengthening of the initial vowel, etc. From the root 'pula' in the sense of being great, with the suffix 'avo', and 'l' becoming 'ḷ', giving 'puḷavo'. Because it moves badly (kucchitaṃ amati/gacchati), it is 'kimi', with the suffix 'i', and the 'a' becomes 'i'. Because it lives in a particular way (pakārena anati), it is 'pāṇako', with the suffix 'ṇvu', and 'n' becomes 'ṇ'.

Dvayaṃ kaṇṭalomakīṭe. Uccaṃ ṭhānaṃ āliṅgatīti uccāliṅgo. Bahulomayutto pāṇako lomasapāṇako.

There are two terms for the hairy caterpillar. Because it clings to a high place (uccaṃ ṭhānaṃ āliṅgati), it is 'uccāliṅgo'. A creature endowed with much hair is 'lomasapāṇako'.

624-625. Sāddhapajjena sakuṇassa nāmāni. Vihe ākāse gacchatīti vihaṅgo, vihaṅgamo ca, ākāsapariyāyo cettha vihasaddo, vehāsassa vā vihādeso. Pakkhayuttatāya [M 0.0416] pakkhī. Khena, khasmiṃ vā gacchatīti khago. Aṇḍato jāto. Sakkoti uddhaṃ gantunti sakuṇo, sakunto, sakuṇī ca, saka sattiyaṃ, uṇo, unto, uṇī ca. Patanto ḍento, pattena vā gacchatīti pataṅgo, aparatra talopo. Mātukucchito, aṇḍato cāti dvikkhattuṃ jāyatīti dvijo. Uḍḍanādīsu vakkaṃ kuṭilaṃ aṅgaṃ gīvādikaṃ etassa, vakkena gamanena aṅgatīti vā vakkaṅgo. Pattena yāti, taṃ vā yānaṃ etassa. Patati patanto viya ākāsato hotīti patanto. Nīḷe kulāvake jāyatīti nīḷajo.

624-625. The names for a bird are in one and a half verses. Because it goes in the sky (vihe ākāse), it is 'vihaṅgo' and 'vihaṅgamo'; here the word 'viha' is a synonym for sky, or 'vihā' is a substitute for 'vehāsa'. Because it possesses wings, it is 'pakkhī'. Because it goes in the sky (khena or khasmiṃ), it is 'khago'. It is 'aṇḍaja' because it is born from an egg. Because it is able to go upwards, it is 'sakuṇo', 'sakunto', and 'sakuṇī'; from the root 'saka' in the sense of being able, with the suffixes 'uṇo', 'unto', and 'uṇī'. Because it flies or goes by wing, it is 'pataṅgo'; elsewhere, 'ta' is elided. Because it is born twice, from its mother's womb and from an egg, it is 'dvijo'. Because its limbs, such as its neck, are crooked when flying, or because it moves with a crooked gait, it is 'vakkaṅgo'. It is 'pattayāna' because it goes by wing, or that is its vehicle. Because it appears as if falling from the sky, it is 'patanto'. Because it is born in a nest, it is 'nīḷajo'.

Vaṭṭakādayo, pokkharasātakādayo ca tabbhedā tesaṃ sakuṇānaṃ visesā. Vaṭṭa vaṭṭane, ṇvu, vaṭṭakā nārī. Mayūrappamāṇo tadākaticittapakkho jīvañjīvo dakkhiṇapathādīsu jāyate, “jīvajīvā”ti saddaṃ karotīti jīvañjīvo. “Jīvajīvo”ti nirānunāsikāpi. Candikāyuttarattippiyo pakkhī cakoro, caka paritakkane, uro, usso, caṅkoropi. Taratismā iro, dvittamittañca, tittiro.

Quails and others, and 'pokkharasātaka' birds and others, are specific varieties of those birds. From the root 'vaṭṭa' in the sense of turning, with the suffix 'ṇvu', comes 'vaṭṭakā', which is feminine. The 'jīvañjīvo', which is the size of a peacock with variegated wings, is born in the southern regions and is so called because it makes the sound 'jīvajīvā'. The form 'jīvajīvo', without the nasal, also exists. The 'cakoro' is a bird fond of the moonlit night; from the root 'caka' in the sense of reflecting, with the suffixes 'uro' or 'usso'; it is also 'caṅkoro'. From 'tarati', with the suffix 'iro' and duplication of the initial syllable, comes 'tittiro' (partridge).

626. Sala gatiyaṃ, ṇiko, ḷattaṃ, sāḷikā, nārī. Kalaṃ ravatīti karavīko, īko, lalopo. Karavīko, yassa saro bhagavato sarena upamīyate, so vuccati “karavīko”ti. Javena ravinā sadiso haṃso ravihaṃso. Kusa sadde, thako, dvittaṃ, kusassa sassa to, kukutthako[M 0.0417]. Karaṇḍa bhājanatthe, avo, karaṇḍavo, jalacaro pakkhī. Bilu patitthambhe, a, avādeso, bilavo, “gaṇḍaplavo”ti khyāto rattapakkho mahāpakkhī pokkharasātako, pokkharassa saññā yassa pokkharasātako, ññassa to, dīgho ca, samuditanāmameva vā tassa, tadā sāda assādane, ṇvu, dassa to, pokkharasātako.

626. From the root 'sala' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'ṇiko', and 'l' becoming 'ḷ', comes 'sāḷikā', which is feminine. Because it makes a sweet sound (kalaṃ ravati), it is 'karavīko', with the suffix 'īko' and elision of 'la'. The 'karavīko' is the one whose voice is compared to the voice of the Blessed One. A 'haṃsa' similar to the sun in swiftness is a 'ravihaṃso'. From the root 'kusa' in the sense of sounding, with the suffix 'thako', with duplication, and the 'sa' of 'kusa' becoming 'ta', comes 'kukutthako'. From 'karaṇḍa' in the sense of a vessel, with the suffix 'avo', comes 'karaṇḍavo', an aquatic bird. From the root 'bilu' in the sense of supporting, with the suffix 'a' and the substitution of 'ava', comes 'bilavo'. The 'pokkharasātako' is a large, red-winged bird known as 'gaṇḍaplavo'; it is called 'pokkharasātako' because it has the mark of a lotus, where 'ññ' becomes 't' and the vowel is lengthened; or it is simply its composite name; alternatively, from 'sāda' in the sense of tasting, with the suffix 'ṇvu', and 'da' becoming 'ta', comes 'pokkharasātako'.

627. Sattakaṃ pakkhe. Patanti anenāti patattaṃ, yadādinā to, dvittaṃ. Ukha gatiyaṃ, yu, usse, assu, pekhuṇaṃ, ṇattaṃ. Pata gamane, to, pātato tāyatīti vā pattaṃ. Pata gamane, kho, tassa ko, pakkho. Patituṃ icchati yena piñchaṃ, nerutto, pata gamane vā, cho, talopo, bindāgamo, assi. Chādyate anena chado. Gira niggiraṇe, u, issattaṃ, gamu gamane vā, u, massa ro.

627. There are seven terms for wing. That by which they fly is 'patattaṃ', with the suffix 'ta' and duplication. From the root 'ukha' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'yu', come 'ussa', 'assu', and 'pekhuṇaṃ'; in the last, 'n' becomes 'ṇ'. From the root 'pata' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'ta', comes 'pattaṃ'; or because it protects from a fall, it is 'pattaṃ'. From the root 'pata' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'kho' which becomes 'ko', comes 'pakkho'. That by which one desires to fly is 'piñchaṃ', an irregular formation; or from the root 'pata' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'cho', elision of 'ta', and insertion of a nasal, comes 'aṃsi'. That by which one is covered is 'chado'. From the root 'gira' in the sense of swallowing, with the suffix 'u' and substitution of 'i', or from the root 'gamu' in the sense of moving, with the suffix 'u' and 'm' becoming 'r', comes 'garu'.

Pakkhīnaṃ bīje “au”iti khyāte aṇḍaṃ, kacchapādīnaṃ bījepi, “aṇḍaṃ khagādikose cā”ti nānatthasaṅgahe. Aḍi aṇḍatthe, ṇo, pesi, kosopi, pisa avayave, i, pesi, “pesiyaṃ pattabhede ca, koso pumeva icchito”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 15.37 ruddo. Dvayaṃ pakkhigehe. Nīla vaṇṇe, a, ḷattaṃ, nī naye vā, ilo. Kucchitaṃ aṇḍavināsanādikaṃ lunātīti kulāvakaṃ, ṇvu.

The seed of birds, known as 'au', is 'aṇḍaṃ' (egg); it is also the seed of turtles and others, as stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: 'and also in the sheath of birds, etc.'. From the root 'aḍi' in the sense of egg, with the suffix 'ṇo', come 'pesi' (embryo) and 'koso' (sheath). From the root 'pisa' in the sense of a part, with the suffix 'i', comes 'pesi'. Rudra states: 'pesi also refers to a type of leaf, and kosa is considered masculine'. There are two terms for a bird's nest. From 'nīla' in the sense of color, with the suffix 'a' and 'l' becoming 'ḷ', comes 'nīḷa'; or from the root 'nī' in the sense of leading, with the suffix 'ilo'. Because it prevents the wretched destruction of eggs and the like, it is 'kulāvakaṃ', with the suffix 'ṇvu'.

628. Dvayaṃ garuḷānaṃ mātari. Vino pakkhino namanti yaṃ vinatā. Thīpumadvayaṃ itthipurisānaṃ dvayaṃ mithunaṃ nāma, saṅkhyānassa [M 0.0418] saṅkhyeyyanissitatāya itthipurisāyeva mithunaṃ, mitha saṅgame, uno.

628. There are two terms for the mother of the Garuḍas. She to whom the birds bow is 'Vinatā'. The pair of a female and a male, the couple of a woman and a man, is called 'mithuna'. Because a number depends on that which is numbered, the man and woman themselves are the 'mithuna'. From the root 'mitha' in the sense of uniting, with the suffix 'uno'.

Chakkaṃ yugaḷamatte. Yuja yoge, a, yugaṃ, alapaccaye yugaḷaṃ, ḷattaṃ, yugalampi. Ubha pūraṇe, ṇo, dvandādeso ca, dvandaṃ, yamu uparame, ṇvu, alo ca, yamakaṃ, yamalañca, apaccaye yamaṃ.

There are six terms for a pair. From the root 'yuja' in the sense of joining, with the suffix 'a', comes 'yugaṃ'; with the suffix 'ala', it becomes 'yugaḷaṃ', with 'l' becoming 'ḷ'; it is also 'yugalaṃ'. From the root 'ubha' in the sense of filling, with the suffix 'ṇa', and with the substitution of 'dvanda', comes 'dvandaṃ'. From the root 'yamu' in the sense of restraining, with the suffixes 'ṇvu' and 'ala', come 'yamakaṃ' and 'yamalaṃ'; and with the suffix 'a', comes 'yamaṃ'.

629-631. Maṇḍalantaṃ samūhe. Sammā, visesena ca ūhate puñjībhūtattāti samūho, ṇo, samaṃ saha avayavena ūhati tiṭṭhatīti vā samūho. Gaṇa saṅkhyāne, gaṇīyati avayavena sahāti gaṇo. Saha avayavena gacchatīti saṅghāto, hana gamane, ṇo, saha avayavena udayatīti samudāyo, dāgamo, majjhe dīgho. Sañcinoti avayavanti sañcayo, ci caye. Saha avayavena duhayatīti sandoho, duha papūraṇe. Nissesato vahati avayavanti nivaho. Avayavaṃ katvā byapiyati gacchatīti ogho ucyate ogho uca samavāye ghau nipātanā cassa gho (cintāmaṇiṭīkā 15.39). Visanti avayavā yasminti visaro, [M 0.0419] aro. Avayavaṃ samīpe karotīti nikaro. Ekekāpekkhāya appatthena kasaṅkhātā avayavā āyanti yasmiṃ kāyo, atha vā kucchitānaṃ kesādīnaṃ āyoti kāyo, so viya avayavānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānaṃ kāyoti idha samūho vutto. Antatthena khaṃsaṅkhātaṃ avayavaṃ dhāretīti khandho, khādati avayaveti vā khandho, amajjhadīghe samudayo. Ghaṭa ghaṭane. Ghaṭanaṃ rāsibhavanaṃ, ghaṭenti assaṃ avayavāti ghaṭā. Saha avayavena etīti samiti,ti. Saha avayavena gacchatīti saṃhati, hana gatiyaṃ,ti, nalopo. Rasa assādane, iṇa. Puñja kucchāyaṃ. Saha avayavena byāpetvā ayatīti samavāyo. Pūgo tambūlepi. Janeti avayaveti jātaṃ, to. Kaṃ attānaṃ detīti kado, cakkhādiko sarīrāvayavo. Kado viya kado, avayavo, taṃ vakati ādadātīti kadambakaṃ. Visesena ūhantyasmiṃ avayavā byūho. Vitanoti avayaveti vitānaṃ, ṇo. Gupa rakkhaṇe, bo, passa mo, gumbo, gumbampi. Kalaṃ avayavabhāvaṃ pāti rakkhatīti kalāpo, “kalā soḷasamo bhāgo”ti hi vuttattā kalāsaddo bhāgatthopyatthīti ñāyati. Jala dittiyaṃ. Jalati avayavenāti jālaṃ. Avayavena maṇḍatīti maṇḍalaṃ, maṇḍa vibhūsāyaṃ, alo.

629-631. The terms up to 'maṇḍala' refer to a collection. A 'samūha' (collection) is so called because it is gathered well and in particular, being heaped up; with the suffix 'ṇo'. Or, 'samūha' is so called because it stands together equally with its parts. From the root 'gaṇa' (to count); 'gaṇo' (group) is so called because it is counted together with its parts. Because it goes together with its parts, it is 'saṅghāto'; from the root 'hana' (to go), with the suffix 'ṇo'. Because it arises together with its parts, it is 'samudāyo'; 'dā' is inserted, and the middle vowel is lengthened. Because it accumulates parts, it is 'sañcayo'; from the root 'ci' (to collect). Because it is filled together with its parts, it is 'sandoho'; from the root 'duha' (to fill). Because it carries parts completely, it is 'nivaho'. Because having formed a part, it pervades and goes, it is 'ogho'. Because parts enter into it, it is 'visaro'; with the suffix 'aro'. Because it brings parts near, it is 'nikaro'. A 'kāya' (body or collection) is so called because parts, designated as 'ka' due to their individual insignificance, come to it; or because it is the coming of contemptible things like hair. Here, 'kāya' is said to mean a collection, like the place of origin for parts. A 'khandho' (aggregate) is so called because it holds a part designated as 'kha' in the ultimate sense; or because it consumes parts. The word 'samudayo' is without a long vowel in the middle. From the root 'ghaṭa' (to join). 'Ghaṭana' is becoming a heap; 'ghaṭā' (a dense mass) is that in which parts are joined. Because it comes together with its parts, it is 'samiti'; with the suffix 'ti'. Because it goes together with its parts, it is 'saṃhati'; from the root 'hana' (to go), with the suffix 'ti', and the elision of 'n'. From the root 'rasa' (to taste), with the suffix 'iṇa'. The root 'puñj' is in the sense of despising. Because having pervaded, it comes together with its parts, it is 'samavāyo'. 'Pūga' (multitude) is also used for betel. Because it generates parts, it is 'jātaṃ'; with the suffix 'to'. Because it gives the head or self, it is 'kado', a bodily part such as the eye. Like 'kado', it is a part; because it takes that, it is 'kadambakaṃ'. Because parts are especially gathered in it, it is 'byūho'. Because it spreads out parts, it is 'vitānaṃ'; with the suffix 'ṇo'. From the root 'gup' (to protect), with the suffix 'bo', and 'p' becomes 'm', forming 'gumbo'; also 'gumba'. Because it protects the state of being a part, it is 'kalāpo'; for since it is said, “a kalā is the sixteenth part,” it is understood that the word 'kalā' also has the meaning of 'part'. From the root 'jala' (to shine). Because it shines with its parts, it is 'jālaṃ'. Because it is adorned with parts, it is 'maṇḍalaṃ'; from the root 'maṇḍa' (to adorn), with the suffix 'alo'.

632. Sāddhapajjena gaṇabhedā vuccante. Tatra jātyādīhi samānānaṃ pāṇīnaṃ, apāṇīnañca gaṇo vaggo nāma, yathā [M 0.0420] “bandhuvaggo, kavaggo”ccādayo, vajja vajjane, vajjeti asamānajātyādayoti vaggo, ṇo, jjassa ggo. Jantūnaṃ samānajātiyānaṃ, vijātiyānañca gaṇo “saṅgho, sattho”ti coccate, yathā “bhikkhusaṅgho, vāṇijasattho”ccādayo. Saṃhaññante nibbisesena ñāyante avayavā tasminti saṅgho, ro. Saranti vattanti avayavā yasminti sattho, tho, rassa to.

632. The types of groups are explained in this half-stanza. Among these, a group of beings and non-beings that are similar by birth, etc., is called a 'vagga', as in 'bandhuvaggo' (group of relatives) and 'kavaggo' (the k-group of consonants), etc. From the root 'vajja' (to reject); 'vaggo' is so called because it rejects those not of the same birth, etc.; with the suffix 'ṇo', and 'jj' becomes 'gg'. A group of beings, both of the same species and different species, is called 'saṅgho' or 'sattho', as in 'bhikkhusaṅgho' (community of monks) and 'vāṇijasattho' (caravan of merchants), etc. 'Saṅgho' is so called because its members are compacted without distinction; with the suffix 'ro'. 'Sattho' is so called because its members move or proceed together; with the suffix 'tho', and 'r' becomes 't'.

Sajātikānaṃ samānajātikānaṃ jantūnameva gaṇo kulaṃ nāma, yathā “khattiyakulaṃ, gokula”miccādayo. Kula saṅkhyāne, bandhumhi ca, a, kulaṃ. Sadhammīnaṃ samānadhammānameva jantūnaṃ gaṇo nikāyo nāma, yathā “bhikkhunikāyo”ti. Ci caye, ṇo, nibbisesena cinoti avayaveti nikāyo.

A group of beings of the same kind or species is called a 'kula' (family), as in 'khattiyakulaṃ' (khattiya family) and 'gokulaṃ' (herd of cattle), etc. From the root 'kula' (to count, and in the sense of a relative), with the suffix 'a', comes 'kulaṃ'. A group of beings sharing the same principles is called a 'nikāyo', as in 'bhikkhunikāyo' (community of bhikkhunis). From the root 'ci' (to collect), with the suffix 'ṇo'; 'nikāyo' is so called because it collects parts without distinction.

Sajātiyatiracchānānaṃyeva gaṇo “yūtho”tyuccate, so cānitthī, yathā “hatthiyūtho, migayūtha”miccādayo, yu missane, tho, dīghādi, yūtho, “gaṇo pasūnaṃ samajo, samājoññesa’muccate”ti amara 15.42 gāthāyaṃ passitabbaṃ idhānāgatavacanampi ñātabbaṃ.

A group of animals of the same species is called a 'yūtha' (herd), and it is not feminine in gender, as in 'hatthiyūtho' (elephant herd), 'migayūtho' (deer herd), and so on. From the root 'yu' (to mix), with the suffix 'tho,' and the initial vowel lengthened, comes 'yūtha.' The statement 'a group of beasts is called a 'samaja,' while 'samāja' is said of others' is also to be understood, though not found here.

633. Catukkaṃ garuḷe. Kanakarucirattā sobhano paṇṇo pakkho yassa supaṇṇo. Vinabhāya nāma mātuyā apaccaṃ venateyyo, ṇeyyo. Garaṃ visadharaṃ hantīti garuḷo, ṇo, rantassu, hassa ca ḷattaṃ, vaṇṇavikāro, garuḍo. [M 0.0421] Pakkhisīho, uḷūtīso, vajiratuṇḍo, sudhāharo, suvaṇṇapakkho, bhujagāsanopi tikaṇḍasesa 1.1.42.

633. Four names for Garuḷa. Because of his golden radiance, he has beautiful feathers and wings, hence 'Supaṇṇa.' He is 'Venateyya' because he is the offspring of the mother named Vinatā; with the suffix 'ṇeyya.' He is 'Garuḷa' because he destroys poison-bearers; with the suffix 'ṇo,' the final 'r' becomes 'u', and 'h' becomes 'ḷ'; by a change of sound, it is also 'Garuḍa.' Also 'Pakkhisīha' (lion among birds), 'Uḷūtīsa' (chief of owls), 'Vajiratuṇḍa' (thunderbolt-beaked), 'Sudhāhara' (nectar-bearer), 'Suvaṇṇapakkha' (golden-winged), and 'Bhujagāsana' (serpent-eater).

Pikantaṃ kokile. Parena vijātiyena kākena positoti parapuṭṭho, pusa posane, to. Parena bhato puṭṭho parabhato, bhara dhāraṇaposanesu, to. Kuṇa saddopakaraṇesu, alo. Kuka, vaka ādāne, ilo, kokilo. Apihito kāyatīti piko, api antaradhāne, vaṇṇanāso, apissākāralopo.

The terms up to 'pika' are for the cuckoo. It is called 'parapuṭṭha' because it is nourished by another species, the crow; from the root 'pusa' (to nourish), with the suffix 'to.' It is called 'parabhata' because it is fed and nourished by another; from the root 'bhara' (to bear, to nourish), with the suffix 'to.' From the root 'kuṇa' (to make sound), with the suffix 'alo.' From the roots 'kuka' and 'vaka' (to take), with the suffix 'ilo,' comes 'kokila.' It is called 'pika' because it sings while hidden; the prefix 'api' is in the sense of 'to disappear,' with loss of a letter, and elision of the 'a' of 'api'.

634. Aṭṭhakaṃ more. Mura saṃvaraṇe, ṇo. Maya gatiyaṃ, ūro, mahiyaṃ ravatīti vā mayūro, dhātussa atthātisayena yogoti nerutto. Varahaṃ sikhaṇḍo, taṃyogā varahī. Nīlā gīvā kaṇṭho yassa, bhujaṅgabhujopi.

634. Eight names for the peacock. From the root 'mura' (to enclose), with the suffix 'ṇo', comes 'mora'. From the root 'maya' (to go), with the suffix 'ūro,' or because it cries on the earth, hence 'mayūra'; thus, the etymologist explains it as a connection with an excess of the root's meaning. 'Varaha' is its crest; due to association with that, it is 'varahī'. 'Nīlagīva' is one whose neck is blue. Also 'Bhujaṅgabhuja' (snake-eater).

Dvayaṃ mayūramatthakasikhāyaṃ. Sikhā aggijālāyañca, pubbe vuttā.

Two names for the peacock's head-crest. The word 'sikhā' is also used for a flame, as stated previously.

635-636. Catukkaṃ mayūrakalāpe. Sikhaṇḍino ayaṃ sikhaṇḍo, varaha pādhānye, paribhāsanahiṃsādānesu ca, karaṇe [M 0.0422] a. Ko mayūro lasati yena kalāpo, ṇo, sassa po. Pī tappanakantīsu, cho, niggahītāgamo, rasso ca. Dvayaṃ morassa piñchaṭṭhe akkhisaṇṭhāne. Cadi hilādane, dittiyañca, ṇvu. Mecako kaṇhavaṇṇepi vutto.

635-636. Four names for the peacock's tail-feathers. This 'sikhaṇḍa' belongs to the 'sikhaṇḍī' (peacock). The root 'varaha' is in the sense of pre-eminence, and also in rebuking, harming, and giving, with the instrumental suffix 'a.' 'Kalāpa' is that by which the peacock ('ko') shines ('lasati'); with the suffix 'ṇo,' and 's' becomes 'p.' From the root 'pī' (to satisfy, to shine), with the suffix 'cha,' with the insertion of a nasal consonant, and shortening of the vowel. Two names for the eye-like mark on the peacock's tail-feather. From the root 'cadi' (to delight, to shine), with the suffix 'ṇvu.' 'Mecaka' is also said to mean dark-colored.

Aḷyantaṃ bhamare, cha padāni assa. Madhuṃ vatayati bhuñjate madhubbato, vata bhojane. Bhama anavaṭṭhāne, pupphamatthake bhamatīti bhamaro, aro. Ara gamane, i, ḷattaṃ.

The terms up to 'aḷi' are for the bee; it has six feet. It is 'madhubbata' because it consumes honey; from the root 'vata' (to eat). From the root 'bhama' (to be unsteady); it is 'bhamara' because it hovers over the flower's top; with the suffix 'aro.' From the root 'ara' (to go), with the suffix 'i', and 'r' becomes 'ḷ'.

Catukkaṃ gehavanakapotesu. Pārena sabalena āpatatīti pārāpato, pāravatopi. Kapa acchādane, kampa calane vā. Oto, parapakkhe malopo. Kuka ādāne, aṭo, ussattamassuttañca. Pakārena ravatīti pārevaṭo, ru sadde, aṭo, upasaggassa dīgho, asse, pārevaṭo, parevaṭopi.

Four names for domestic and wild pigeons. It is 'pārāpata' because it flies with strength; also 'pāravata.' From the root 'kapa' (to cover), or 'kampa' (to shake), with the suffix 'ota,' and in the latter case, elision of 'm'. From the root 'kuka' (to take), with the suffix 'aṭo,' and 'u' becomes 'o' and 'a' becomes 'u'. It is 'pārevaṭa' because it cries in a particular way; from the root 'ru' (to sound), with the suffix 'aṭo,' with lengthening of the prefix, and 'a' becomes 'e'; hence 'pārevaṭa,' also 'parevaṭa'.

“Pārāvato ca chejjo ca,

Kapoto rattalocano;

Pārāpato kalaravo,

Pattī seno sasādano”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 15.14. –

The rock pigeon and the chejja, the red-eyed dove; the sweet-sounding pārāpata, the winged one, the hawk, and the sasādana.

Rabhaso.

From the Rabhasa lexicon.

637. Dvayaṃ gijjhe. Gidha abhikaṅkhāyaṃ, yo, jhassa jho, asarūpadvittaṃ, jhapaccayena vā siddhaṃ, tathā dhassa jo. Gidhatismā a, niggahītāgamo, issattaṃ, gandho. Tikaṃ senasāmaññe. Kukkuṭādīnaṃ kulaṃ lunāti chindatīti kulalo, kula santāne [M 0.0423] vā, alo. Se gamane, no. Sattānaṃ hiṃsanato byaggho viya byagghi, satte nāsetīti nāso. Byagghi eva nāsoti samuditanāmaṃ.

637. Two names for the vulture. From the root 'gidha' (to crave), with the suffix 'ya,' 'dh' becomes 'jh', and there is doubling of the dissimilar consonant; or it is formed with the suffix 'jha', and similarly 'dh' becomes 'j'. From the root 'gidha', with the suffix 'a', insertion of a nasal, and the vowel becoming 'i', is 'gandha'. Three names for the hawk in general. It is 'kulala' because it cuts or destroys the lineage of chickens and so on; or from 'kula' (lineage), with the suffix 'alo'. From the root 'se' (to go), with the suffix 'no'. From harming beings, like a tiger ('byaggha'), it is 'byagghi'; it destroys ('nāseti') beings, hence 'nāso'. 'Byagghināso' is the combined name.

Sakuṇagghādayo tayo tabbhedā tassa senassa visesā. Sakuṇaṃ hantīti sakuṇagghi, sina?. Aṭa gamane, ṇo. Āṭo. Dabbisadisaṃ tuṇḍaṃ yassa dvijassa so dabbimukhadvijo. “Dabbimukhadvijo āṭo nāmā”tipyeko attho, tadā dveyeva senabhedā.

Sakuṇagghi and others are three specific types of that hawk. It is 'sakuṇagghi' because it kills birds; from the root 'han' (to kill). From the root 'aṭa' (to go), with the suffix 'ṇo,' comes 'āṭa.' The bird whose beak resembles a spoon is 'dabbimukhadvija.' According to one meaning, 'The dabbimukhadvija is named āṭa,' in which case there are only two types of hawk.

638. Catukkaṃ ulūke. “Uhu”nti saddaṃ karotīti uhuṅkāro. “Uddhaṃ kaṇṇā yassa uddhaṃkaṇṇo”ti sampatte niruttinayena ulūko ulabhinettethi dahatyulūko, uddholokanā iti niruttama (amarakosugghāṭanaṭīkā 15.15), ucati samaveti koṭaranti vā nipātanā. Kusa akkose, yassa amanāpatāya saddena lokā kosanti, so kosiyo, kositabboti katvā, koṭare vasatīti vā kosiyo, nerutto, vāyasānaṃ kākānaṃ ari sattu, sakkahvayo, divāndho vakkanāsiko, harinetto, divābhīto, kākabhīrū, ratticārīpi.

638. Four names for the owl. It is 'uhuṅkāra' because it makes the sound 'uhu.' It is 'ulūka' by etymological method, from having raised ears ('uddhaṃkaṇṇa'); or, by derivation, because it enters or dwells in a hollow ('koṭaraṃ ucati samaveti'). From the root 'kus' (to scold); it is 'kosiya' because people scold it due to its unpleasant sound, or because it is to be scolded, or because it dwells in a hollow; thus says the etymologist. Also: 'enemy of crows,' 'named Sakka,' 'blind by day,' 'crooked-nosed,' 'tawny-eyed,' 'fearful by day,' 'afraid of crows,' and 'night-wanderer'.

Vāyasantaṃ kāke. “Kā”iti saddaṃ kāyatīti kāko. Riṭṭhaṃ maraṇalakkhaṇaṃ, tadassa natthi ariṭṭho. Dhaṅka ghoravāsite, a. Balinā puṭṭho bhato. Vaya gamane, vayo eva vāyaso, sakatthe so, sakiṃpajo, attaghoso, parabharo, balibhujo, guḷhamethunopi. Sakiṃ ekavāraṃpajā [M 0.0424] pasūti yassa. “Kāka”iccattānaṃ ghosayati. Vijātiyaṃ kokilaṃ bharati.

Names for the crow, such as vāyasa. It is 'kāka' because it makes the sound 'kā.' It is 'ariṭṭha' because it has no sign of death. From the root 'dhaṅk' (to make a terrible sound), with the suffix 'a,' comes 'dhaṅka.' It is 'balipuṭṭha' because it is nourished and fed by offerings. From the root 'vay' (to go); 'vaya' itself is 'vāyasa,' with the suffix 'so' used in its own sense. Also: 'sakiṃpaja' (born once), 'attaghosa' (self-sounding), 'parabhara' (supported by others), 'balibhuja' (eater of offerings), and 'guḷhamethuna' (hidden in mating). 'Sakiṃpaja' is one whose offspring are born only once. 'Attaghosa' is one that proclaims itself as 'kāka.' 'Parabhara' is one that supports the cuckoo of another species.

639. Kāko viya ulati gacchatīti kākoḷo, ḷattaṃ. Doṇakāko, daddhakākopi. Dvayaṃ “bī-lौṃ”iti khyāte sakuṇe. Lū chedane, ṇo, vassa po, lāpo, lāvopi. Leḍḍu viya akatīti laṭukikā leḍḍukikā (ka.), ṇvu.

639. It is 'kākoḷa' because it moves about like a crow ('kāko viya ulati'); with the change to 'ḷa.' Also 'doṇakāka' (trough-crow) and 'daddhakāka' (burnt crow). Two names for the bird known as 'bīlāuṃ.' From the root 'lū' (to cut), with the suffix 'ṇo,' comes 'lāva'; with 'va' becoming 'pa,' it is also 'lāpa.' It is 'laṭukikā' because it moves like a clod of earth ('leḍḍu viya akati'); with the suffix 'ṇvu'.

Tikaṃ hatthiliṅgasakuṇe. Vāraṇasadisattā vāraṇo. Hatthino liṅgaṃ ñāpakaṃ soṇḍaṃ yasmiṃ vijjatīti hatthiliṅgo. Hatthisoṇḍaṃ yasmiṃ vijjati, so hatthisoṇḍo ca vihaṅgamo ceti hatthisoṇḍavihaṅgamo.

Three names for the elephant-marked bird. It is 'vāraṇa' because it resembles an elephant. It is 'hatthiliṅga' because it possesses a trunk, which is the distinguishing mark ('liṅga') of an elephant. It is 'hatthisoṇḍavihaṅgama' because it has an elephant's trunk ('hatthisoṇḍa') and is a bird ('vihaṅgama').

640. Dvayaṃ ukkuse. Uccaṃ kosatīti ukkuso, kusa sadde, a. Kura sadde, aro, thiyaṃ kurarī. Kolaṭṭhipakkhimhi “ubhuta”iti khyāte pakkhimhi kukkuho. Kolaṭṭhiajjhohārako pakkhī kolaṭṭhipakkhī. “Kukku”iti saddāyatīti kukkuho, ho, kuka avhāne vā, uho.

640. Two names for the osprey. It is 'ukkusa' because it cries loudly ('uccaṃ kosati'); from the root 'kus' (to sound), with the suffix 'a.' From the root 'kur' (to sound), with the suffix 'aro,' comes 'kurara'; in the feminine, it is 'kurarī.' For the bird known as 'ubhuta,' which is the 'kolaṭṭhipakkhī,' the name is 'kukkuha.' The bird that eats 'kolaṭṭhi' berries is the 'kolaṭṭhipakkhī.' It is 'kukkuha' because it makes the sound 'kukku,' with the suffix 'ho'; or from the root 'kuk' (to call), with the suffix 'uho'.

Tikaṃ suve. Su savane. Manussasaddampi suṇātīti suvo, a, uvādeso. “Kī”iti saddaṃ karotīti kīro. Karoti manussasaddanti vā kīro. A, assī. Suka gatiyaṃ, sundaraṃ[M 0.0425], suṭṭhu vā manussasaddaṃ kāyatīti suko. Dvayaṃ kukkuṭamatte. Tambā cūḷā yassa. Kukkuṭatīti kukkuṭo, kuka, vaka ādāne vā, aṭo.

Three names for the parrot. From the root 'su' (to hear); it is 'suva' because it hears human sounds, with the suffix 'a' and the substitution of 'uva' for 'u.' It is 'kīra' because it makes the sound 'kī'; or it is 'kīra' because it produces human sounds, with the suffix 'a' which becomes 'ī.' From the root 'suk' (to go); it is 'suka' because it sings human sounds beautifully or well. Two names for the rooster. 'Tambacūḷa' is one whose crest is red. It is 'kukkuṭa' because it crows ('kukkuṭati'); or from the root 'kuk' or 'vak' (to take), with the suffix 'aṭo'.

641. Dvayaṃ nijjivhe. Natthi jivhā yassa nijjivho. Dvayaṃ koñcāsakuṇe. Itthiliṅgena mithunānaṃ nāmāni. Koñca koṭilyappībhāvesu, a, koñcā. Kanta chedane, yu, nadādi, assu. Kuṇḍanīpi, kuṇḍa dāhe.

641. Two names for the tongueless creature. 'Nijjivha' is one who has no tongue. Two names for the curlew. These are feminine gender names for the pairs. From the root 'koñc' (in the sense of crookedness and bending), with the suffix 'a,' comes 'koñcā.' From the root 'kant' (to cut), with the suffix 'yu' of the 'nadādi' class, comes 'assu.' Also 'kuṇḍanī,' from the root 'kuṇḍ' (to burn).

Dvayaṃ cakkavāke. Cakkena cakkasaddena uccate cakkavāko, ṇo. Vaca viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, cakkamiccāvhā yassa, rathaṅgāvhayanāmakopi, rathaṅgaṃ cakkaṃ, tassa avhayo rathaṅgāvhayo, so nāmaṃ assa rathaṅgāvhayanāmako, tena rathaṅganāmo rathacaraṇasamāno avhayo coccate.

Two names for the ruddy goose. It is called 'cakkavāka' because it is named for the sound of a wheel ('cakkasaddena'), with the suffix 'ṇo.' From the root 'vac' (to speak distinctly); it is also 'rathaṅgāvhayanāmaka' (named with the call of a chariot-part), because its call ('āvhā') is 'cakka.' 'Rathaṅga' is a wheel; its call is 'rathaṅgāvhaya'; that is its name, 'rathaṅgāvhayanāmaka.' By this, it is called 'rathaṅganāma,' having a call similar to a chariot wheel.

Lakkhitalakkhaṇā cātra, lakkhaṇopacaritavuttiyā, goṇamukhyāya vā vuttiyā lakkhitena atthena yatra atthantaraṃ lakkhyate, sā lakkhitalakkhaṇā. Yathā “rathāvayavāyudho” iccatra rathāvayavasaddena cakkaṃ lakkhyate, na tadākati tannāmo cāyudhaviseso. “Pantiratho”iccatra pantisaddena dasakkharaṃ chando lakkhyate, na dasasaddo, tehi tu āyudharathasaddasanniveso “cakkāvayavāyudho, dasaratho” iti devaviseso, rājaviseso ca lakkhyate, tathātrāpi “rathaṅga”ntyanena rathekadeso lakkhīyate, “avhāyate”iccanena ca paribhāsanaṃ, na tenāpi vākasaddo. Tehi ca aññamaññasanniveso cakkavākoti pakkhiviseso [M 0.0426] lakkhīyateti guṇato sukkādīhi evaṃgatā goṇī vutti.

And here there is 'lakkhitalakkhaṇā' (implication of the implied). 'Lakkhitalakkhaṇā' is where another meaning is implied by a meaning that is itself indicated through figurative usage ('lakkhaṇā') or secondary usage ('goṇī vutti'). For example, in 'rathāvayavāyudha,' by the word 'rathāvayava' (chariot-part), the wheel is implied, not its shape, its name, or a specific weapon. In 'pantiratha,' by the word 'panti' (row), the ten-syllable meter is implied, not the word 'dasa' (ten). By the combination of these words with 'āyudha' (weapon) and 'ratha' (chariot), a specific deity, 'cakkāvayavāyudha,' and a specific king, 'Dasaratha,' are implied. Similarly here, by 'rathaṅga,' a part of the chariot is implied, and by 'āvhāyate' (is called), a designation is implied, not the word 'vāka.' And by their mutual combination, 'cakkavāka,' a specific bird, is implied. This is a secondary usage ('goṇī vutti') based on qualities such as whiteness and so forth.

Dvayaṃ cātake. Ayaṃ meghajalapāyī, sara hiṃsāyaṃ, saraṇaṃ sāro, taṃ gacchatīti sāraṅgo. “Cātake hariṇe pume, sāraṅgo sabale tisū”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 23.23 rabhaso. Cata yācane, ṇvu, thokakopi, thokaṃ kaṃ jalaṃ īhanīyaṭṭhena assatthi thokako.

Two names for the cātaka bird. This one drinks rainwater. From the root 'sar' (to go); 'sāra' is water; it goes to that ('taṃ gacchati'), hence 'sāraṅga.' The Rabhasa lexicon states: ''Sāraṅga' is masculine for the cātaka and the deer; it is used in all three genders for that which is variegated.' From the root 'cat' (to beg), with the suffix 'ṇvu,' comes 'cātaka.' Also 'thokaka'; it is 'thokaka' because it desires a little water ('thokaṃ kaṃ').

642. Dvayaṃ pakkhibiḷāle. Tula ummāne, iyo. Pakkhayutto biḷālo, “sū”.

642. Two names for the winged cat. From the root 'tul' (to weigh), with the suffix 'iyo,' comes 'tuliya.' A cat endowed with wings is a 'pakkhibiḷāla.' Also 'sū'.

Dvayaṃ rukkhakīṭakhādake. Sataṃ pattāni assa. Sarati kīṭeti sāraso, so, “khāva sā”.

Two names for the tree-insect eater. 'Satapatta' is one that has a hundred feathers. It is 'sārasa' because it moves ('sarati') and eats insects ('kīṭe ati'); with the suffix 'so.' Also 'khāva sā'.

Dvayaṃ kākehi saddhiṃ nīḷaṃ katvā vasanake sukkasakuṇe. Vaka ādāne, a. Setavaṇṇatāya sukko ca so kākehi saddhiṃ nivāsanato, kākasaṇṭhānattā vā kāko ceti sukkakāko.

Two names for the white bird that makes its nest and lives with crows. From the root 'vak' (to take), with the suffix 'a,' comes 'vaka.' It is 'sukkakāka' because it is white ('sukka') due to its white color, and it is a 'kāka' because it lives with crows, or because it has the shape of a crow.

Dvayaṃ visakaṇṭhikāyaṃ. Bala pāṇane, ṇvu, dīgho, āko vā. Visasadiso kāḷavaṇṇo kaṇṭho yassā sā visakaṇṭhikā, etissā pumo nāma na vijjati. Vuttañca apadāne –

Two names for the visakaṇṭhikā bird. From the root 'bal' (to live), with the suffix 'ṇvu' and lengthening of the vowel, or with the suffix 'āka,' comes 'balākā.' It is 'visakaṇṭhikā' because its throat is black like poison. For this bird, a male name does not exist. And it is said in the Apadāna:

“Yathā balākayonimhi, na vijjati pumo sadā;

Meghesu gajjamānesu, gabbhaṃ gaṇhanti tā tadā”ti apa. thera. 1.1.511.

Just as in the species of the crane, a male is never found; when the clouds rumble, they then conceive.

643. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0427] kaṅke. Lohasadiso piṭṭhi yassa lohapiṭṭho. Kaṅka lolye, a, kaṅko.

643. Two names for the heron. 'Lohapiṭṭha' is one whose back is like metal. From the root 'kaṅk' (to be unsteady), with the suffix 'a,' comes 'kaṅka'.

Dvayaṃ pattakaṇṭhe. Khañjo viya caratīti khañjarīṭo, īṭo. Passantānaṃ khaṃ sukhaṃ janetīti khañjano. Khañja gativekalye vā, yu.

Two names for the wagtail ('pattakaṇṭha'). It is 'khañjarīṭa' because it moves as if lame ('khañjo viya carati'), with the suffix 'īṭa.' It is 'khañjana' because it brings joy ('sukhaṃ janeti') to those who see it. Or, from the root 'khañj' (impaired movement), with the suffix 'yu'.

Dvayaṃ gāmacāṭake, cāṭakamatte vā. Kalahaṃ ravatīti kalaviṅko, yadādi. Kaṃ sukhaṃ lunātīti vā kalaviṅko, iko, niggahītāgamo ca. Caṭa bhede, ṇvu, cāṭako.

Two names for the village sparrow, or for a sparrow in general. It is 'kalaviṅka' because it cries out in quarrel ('kalahaṃ ravati'), with a 'yadādi' suffix. Or, it is 'kalaviṅka' because it cuts off happiness ('kaṃ sukhaṃ lunāti'), with the suffix 'ika' and the insertion of a niggahīta. From the root 'caṭ' (to break), with the suffix 'ṇvu,' comes 'cāṭaka'.

Dvayaṃ veḷuriyacchavilome citrapakkhe “suvaṇṇacūḷe”ti khyāte. Dibha santhambhe, dvittaṃ, bindāgamo ca. “Ki”iti saddaṃ karotīti kikī, ṇī, cāso, divipi cāso kikīdivi (amara 15.16).

Two names for the bird with beryl-like plumage and colorful wings, known as 'suvaṇṇacūḷa' (golden-crested). From the root 'jīv' (to live), with reduplication and the insertion of a bindu, comes 'jīvañjīva.' It is 'kikī' because it makes the sound 'ki,' with the suffix 'ṇī.' Also 'cāsa' and 'divi'.

644. Dvayaṃ meghasāme “ṭī-ṭौ”iti khyāte. Kadambayogā kādambo. Kāḷavaṇṇo haṃso kāḷahaṃso, kālahaṃsopi.

644. Two names for the bird dark as a cloud, known as 'ṭī-ṭau.' It is 'kādamba' due to its association with the Kadamba tree. A black-colored goose is a 'kāḷahaṃsa'; also 'kalahaṃsa'.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0428] “ṅahe-ḍo”iti khyāte sakuṇe. Sakunto vutto, “sakunto pakkhibhedasmiṃ, bhāsapakkhīkhagesu ce”ti nānatthasaṅgahe. Sundarākārena pakkhena yutto sakuṇo bhāsapakkhī, “bhāsanto sundarākāre, bhāsanto bhāsapakkhinī”ti hi nānatthasaṅgahe.

Two names for the bird known as 'ṅahe-ḍo.' 'Sakuṇo' is stated in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: ''Sakunta' refers to a species of bird, the Bhāsa bird, and birds in general.' A 'bhāsapakkhī' is a bird endowed with beautifully shaped wings. For it is said in the Nānatthasaṅgaha: ''Bhāsanta' means having a beautiful form; 'bhāsanta' also refers to the Bhāsa bird.'

Dvayaṃ “nvā-mī-sve”iti khyāte nīlapakkhini. Dhūmyaṃ dhūmaṃ aṭati sahatīti dhūmyāṭo, ṇo. Kāḷavaṇṇatāya kucchitaṃ liṅgaṃ yassa. Bhiṅgopi.

Two names for the blue-winged bird known as 'nvā-mī-sve.' It is 'dhūmyāṭa' because it wanders in or endures smoke ('dhūmaṃ aṭati sahati'), with the suffix 'ṇo.' 'Bhiṅga' is one whose form is despised due to its black color.

Dvayaṃ jalakukkuṭe. Dā lavane,ti, dāti ūhati ussahatīti dātyūho, khaṇḍitaddhaniiccattho. Kāle sassamutumhi kaṇṭho kaṇḍaddhani yassa kāḷakaṇṭhako, samāsante ko.

Two names for the watercock. From the root 'dā' (to cut), with the suffix 'ti'; it is 'dātyūha' because it strives ('ūhati ussahati') to cut ('dāti'); the meaning is 'one with a broken neck.' It is 'kāḷakaṇṭhaka' because at the time of the harvest season, its throat has a dark mark; with 'ka' at the end of the compound.

645. Khuddādi madhucchiṭṭhakarādiko kammabhūto “makkhikābhedo”tyuccate, makkhi saṅghāte, ṇvu, makkhikā, tāsaṃ bhedo makkhikābhedo. Piṅgalamakkhikāyaṃ “mhaṇa”iti khyātāyaṃ dvayaṃ. Ḍaṃsa ḍaṃsane, ḍaṃso. Daṃsopi, ḍaṃsa khādane vā, piṅgalamakkhikātivaṇṇanāmaṃ.

645. Small creatures and the like, such as those that make beeswax, born from kamma, are called 'a type of fly' ('makkhikābheda'). From the root 'makkh' (to swarm), with the suffix 'ṇvu,' comes 'makkhikā' (fly); a type of these is 'makkhikābheda.' Two names for the tawny fly known as 'mhaṇa.' From the root 'ḍaṃs' (to bite), comes 'ḍaṃsa.' Also 'daṃsa.' Or from the root 'ḍaṃs' (to eat). It is a name for the tawny fly.

Makkhikāya aṇḍaṃ āsāṭikā nāma, saṭa avayave, ṇvu. Dvayaṃ “nhaṃ”iti khyāte. Paṭaṃ gacchatīti paṭaṅgo, pataṅgopi, sarati hiṃsatīti salabho, abho, lattaṃ, sala gamane vā.

The egg of a fly is called āsāṭikā, from the root saṭ meaning to divide into parts, with the suffix ṇvu. These two terms are for the creature known as 'nhaṃ'. That which goes to a cloth is a paṭaṅga, also pataṅga. That which moves while harming is a salabha, from the suffix abha, with the change to la; or from the root sal meaning to move.

646. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0429] “cheṃ”iti khyāte, maka pāṇe, aso, makaso. Dvayaṃ nidāghe nuhādīsu varaṇakamakkhikāyaṃ. “Cīrī”ti saddāyatīti cīrī, ciri hiṃsāyaṃ vā, nadādi, dīghādi. Jhalla sadde, ṇvu, jhallikā.

646. These two terms are for the creature known as 'cheṃ'; from the root mak meaning to live, with the suffix asa, forming makasa (a mosquito). These two terms are for the varaṇaka fly, found in the hot season and in bathing places and so forth. It is called a cīrī because it makes the sound 'cīrī'; or from the root cir meaning to harm, belonging to the nadādi group, with lengthening of the initial vowel. From the root jhall meaning to make a sound, with the suffix ṇvu, forming jhallikā (a cricket).

Dvayaṃ tālapattādyantaresu nilīnāyaṃ cammapattāyaṃ. Jatu viya jatukā, upamāne ko, “rāmaṭhe jatukaṃ camma-pattajatukaresu thī”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 19.40 hi rabhaso. Ajinaṃ cammaṃ pattaṃ yassā ajinapattā. Dvayaṃ haṃsasāmaññe. Hanti addhānaṃ haṃso. Seto chado pattaṃ yassa. Yathākathañci byuppattīti vuttattā asetacchadepi, cakkaṅgo, mānasokopi, cakkassa cakkavākasseva aṅgāni yassa. Mānasaṃ saro oko yassa.

These two terms are for the bat (cammapattā), which hides between palm leaves and the like. It is like lac (jatu), hence jatukā; the suffix ka is used in the sense of comparison. For it is said in the Rabhasa: 'The word jatuka is feminine when it means asafoetida, a bat, or a lac-worker.' That which has wings (patta) of hide (ajinaṃ cammaṃ) is an ajinapattā. These two terms are for a swan in general. A swan (haṃsa) is so called because it travels a long distance. It is one that has white wings (seta-chada). Because it is said that the etymology may be derived in any way, this can also apply to one without white wings. Also cakkaṅga and mānasoka; the former is so called because its limbs are like those of a cakkavāka (ruddy shelduck). The latter is so called because Lake Mānasa is its dwelling (oka).

647. Ye rattehi lohitehi pādatuṇḍehi caraṇacañcūhi visiṭṭhā sitā ca sarīre, te rājahaṃsā nāma, haṃsānaṃ rājāno rājahaṃsā.

647. Those which are distinguished by red feet and beaks, and are white in body, are called rājahaṃsā (royal swans); they are the kings of swans, hence rājahaṃsā.

Malīnehi pādatuṇḍehi visiṭṭhā ye te mallikākhyā, mala, malla dhāraṇe, i, saññāyaṃ ko, “malliko haṃsabhede ca, tiṇasūle ca mallike”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 15.24 ruddo. Ākhyāsaddena bahubbīhi. Asitehi kaṇhehi pādatuṇḍehi visiṭṭhā ye, te dhataraṭṭhā, dhataraṭṭhānaṃ apaccāni dhataraṭṭhāti, ṇo.

Those which are distinguished by soiled feet and beaks are called mallikā; from mala (dirt), or the root mall meaning to hold, with the suffix i, and ka in the sense of a name. For it is said in the Rudda: 'Mallika refers to a type of swan and also a grass spike.' The word ākhyā indicates a bahubbīhi compound. Those which are distinguished by black feet and beaks are dhataraṭṭhā; the offspring of Dhataraṭṭha are called dhataraṭṭhā, formed with the suffix ṇa.

648. Tikaṃ [M 0.0430] tiracchāne. Tiriyaṃ añcayatīti tiraccho, tiriyassa tiro, añcatissa ccho. Yumhi tiracchāno, tiracchānoyeva tiracchānagataṃ, tabbhāvaṃ vā gataṃ pattaṃ, tesu vā gataṃ antogadhanti tiracchānagataṃ, siyāti pakatyānapekkhakriyāpadaṃ, bhavatyattho vā hi karotyattho vā kadāci pakatyānapekkho bhavati, na pana vikatyānapekkho. Tathā kadāci ubhayāpekkhopi bhavati, na panubhayānapekkhoti sabbatrevaṃ. Sīhādivaggo.

648. These three terms are for an animal. That which moves horizontally is a tiraccha; tiriya becomes tiro, and añcati becomes ccha. With the suffix yu, it forms tiracchāna. Tiracchānagata means an animal itself, or one that has attained that state, or one that has gone among them and is included therein. The word siyā is a verb that is independent of the original form. For the meaning 'to be' or 'to do' is sometimes independent of the original form, but not of the modified form. Similarly, it is sometimes dependent on both, but not independent of both. Thus it is in all cases. The Section on Lions, etc.

Araññādivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the chapter beginning with 'Forest' is finished.

7. Pātālavaggavaṇṇanā

7. The Explanation of the Pātāla Chapter

649-650. Catukkaṃ pātāle. Adharaṃ bhuvanaṃ adhobhuvanaṃ. Patanti asmiṃ pātālaṃ, alo, majjhe dīgho. Nāgānaṃ loko. Rasāya talaṃ rasātalaṃ.

649-650. These four terms are for the nether region. The lower world is adhobhuvana. Beings fall into this, hence it is pātāla, from the suffix ala, with the middle vowel lengthened. It is the world of the Nāgas. The bottom level of the earth is rasātala.

Sobbhantaṃ [M 0.0431] chiddamatte. Raṇa sadde, dho, nattaṃ, yadādi. Vara dittiyaṃ. Vigato varo vāraṇaṃ assa vivaraṃ, chidi dvidhākaraṇe, do. Kuha vimhayane, aro. Susa sosane, iro. Bila bhedane, a. Susato i, susi. Chinditvā gacchatīti chiggalaṃ, yadādi. Suṭṭhu abbhaṃ ākāsaṃ asmiṃ sobbhaṃ.

The term sobbha and others mean merely a hole. From the root raṇ meaning to sound, with the suffix dha, and the change to na, from the yadādi group. From the root var meaning to shine. That from which the covering is gone is a vivara (an opening). From the root chid meaning to split in two, with the suffix da. From the root kuh meaning to astonish, with the suffix ara. From the root sus meaning to dry, with the suffix ira. From the root bil meaning to split, with the suffix a. From susa with the suffix i, forms susi. That which is formed by cutting a path is a chiggala, from the yadādi group. That in which there is much space is a sobbha.

“Susira”nti chiddasāmaññe yaṃ napuṃsakavacanaṃ, taṃ sacchidde chiddavati dabbe tīsu, yathā “susiro rukkho, susirā ciñcā, susiraṃ kaṭṭha”nti.

The word 'susira', which is a neuter noun in the general sense of a hole, is used in all three genders when referring to a substance that has a hole, for example: 'a hollow tree' (susiro rukkho), 'a hollow tamarind' (susirā ciñcā), and 'hollow wood' (susiraṃ kaṭṭha).

Dvayaṃ bhūmichidde. Kāsa dittiyaṃ, u. Ava rakkhaṇe, aṭo, āvāṭo, avāṭopi. Dvayaṃ sappānaṃ rājini. Vasu ratanaṃ yassatthīti vāsukī.

These two terms are for a hole in the ground. From the root kās meaning to shine, with the suffix u. From the root av meaning to protect, with the suffix aṭa, forming āvāṭa, also avāṭa (a pit). These two terms are for the king of serpents. One who possesses the jewel (vasu) is Vāsukī.

651. Dvayaṃ nāgānaṃ rājini. Devehipyassanto nopaladdhoti ananto, sesopi, sisa hiṃsāyaṃ, sisati kappanteti seso, a.

651. These two terms are for the king of Nāgas. He is called Ananta because his end is not found even by the gods. Also Sesa; from the root sis meaning to be left over; that which remains at the end of the aeon is Sesa, with the suffix a.

Dvayaṃ ajagare. Vahatismā aso, vāhaso. Ajaṃ chāgaṃ gilatīti ajagaro, a, issattaṃ, lassa rattañca. Sayīpi, sayanasīlo sayī.

These two terms are for the python. From the root vah, with the suffix asa, it forms vāhasa. It swallows goats, hence ajagara, with the suffix a; the vowel of the root gil becomes i, and l becomes r. Also sayī; one who is accustomed to sleeping (sayanasīla) is a sayī.

Dvayaṃ gonasasappe “ṅā-cve”iti khyāte. Gavasseva nāsā assāti gonaso, saññāyaṃ nāsasaddassa naso kato pāṇini 5.4.119. Tilaṃ icchatīti tiliccho, tiriyaṃ añcatīti vā tiliccho, yadādi.

These two terms are for the gonasa serpent, known as 'ṅā-cve'. It has a nose like a bull's, hence gonasa; in this designation, the word nāsā becomes nasa. It desires sesame, hence tiliccha; or it moves sideways, hence tiliccha, from the yadādi group.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0432] deḍḍubhe, yo “jalasappo”ti vuccati. Deḍḍunā rājiyā ubhatīti deḍḍubho. Piṭṭhe rājiyogā rājulo, ulo, badhirasappepyete.

These two terms are for the deḍḍubha, which is called the 'water serpent'. It is marked with a stripe like a deḍḍu, hence deḍḍubha. Due to the presence of a stripe on its back, it is a rājula, with the suffix ula. These are also names for the deaf serpent.

652. Kambalo ca assataro cāti ime dve nāgakulā merupāde vasanti.

652. Kambala and Assatara—these two Nāga clans dwell at the foot of Mount Meru.

Dvayaṃ vesmanivuṭṭhasappe. “Vammanī”tipi pāṭho. “Asuddo gharasappo”ti vuttattā nibbisatāya amāritattā sīlayuttaṃ attā mano yasmiṃ silutto, assu, rassādi.

These two terms are for a house-dwelling serpent. There is also the reading 'Vammanī'. Because it is said, 'a non-venomous house serpent', and because it is not killed due to its non-venomous nature, it is called a silutta, one in whom the self and mind are endowed with virtue; from the root assu, with shortening of the vowel, etc.

Dvayaṃ rukkhaggādīsu nivuṭṭhasappe. Nīlo harito sappoti nīlasappo. “Nīlo kaṇhamhi harite”ti hi tārapālo. Paṭhamakāle silāyaṃ bhavatīti silābhu.

These two terms are for serpents dwelling in treetops and the like. A serpent that is blue or green is a nīlasappa. For it is said in the Tārapāla: 'The word nīla can mean black or green.' It arises on a rock in the first instance, hence it is a silābhu.

653-654. Visadharantaṃ sappamatte. Āsiyaṃ visaṃ etassa āsīviso, āsī sappadāṭhā. Bhuja koṭilye, kuṭilāyamāno gacchatīti bhujaṅgo, evaṃ bhujago, bhujaṅgamo ca. Ahi gamane, i. Saranto sappati gacchatīti sarīsapo, assī, saṃyogalopo, aluttasamāsoyaṃ, bhujaṅgabhujaṅgamāpi, sabbadharakate pana “bhusaṃ, punappunaṃ vā kuṭilaṃ sappatīti [M 0.0433] sarīsapo”ti vuttaṃ. Phaṇayogā, ī, phaṇī. Sappatismā a, bhūmiphuṭṭhena gattena gati sappanaṃ. Araṃ sīghaṃ gacchatīti alagaddo, massa do, rassa lattañca, alagaddo, jalasappepyayaṃ, “alagaddo jalavāḷo”ti amara 8.5 hi amarasīho. Bhogo phaṇikāyo, taṃyogā bhogī. Pannaṃ gacchatīti pannago, pādehi vā na gacchatīti pannago. Dve jivhā assa. Urasā gacchatīti urago. Visesena ālāti gaṇhāti āyunti vāḷo, lassa ḷattaṃ, vā gamane vā, alo. Dīghasarīratāya dīgho. Dīghā piṭṭhi yassa, samāse ko. Udarameva pādo yassa. Visaṃ dharati. Cakkī, kuṇḍalī, gūḷhapādo, cakkhussavo, kākodaro, dabbīkaro, bilesayo, jimhago, pavanāsanopi. Sirasi cakkayogā cakkī. Kuṇḍalamiva vapu assatthīti taṃyogā kuṇḍalī. Cakkhunā suṇotīti cakkhussavo. Kākodaramiva udaraṃ assa. Dabbigatikattā phaṇā dabbī, taṃ karoti bandhatīti dabbīkaro. Sāmaññaniddesepi kaṇhasappādiyeva dabbīkaro. Jimhaṃ kuṭilaṃ gacchatīti. Pavanāsano vātabhojī.

653-654. The terms ending with visadhara are for a snake in general. That which has poison in its fang is an āsīvisa; āsī is a snake's fang. From the root bhuj meaning to be crooked; that which goes crookedly is a bhujaṅga, and similarly bhujaga and bhujaṅgama. From the root ah meaning to go, with the suffix i. That which moves by creeping is a sarīsapa; from the root sṛ, with elision of the conjunct consonant; this is an indeclinable compound. Bhujaṅga and bhujaṅgama are also used. In the Sabbadharakata, however, it is said: 'It moves very much, or repeatedly, in a crooked manner, hence sarīsapa.' Due to having a hood, with the suffix ī, it is called a phaṇī. From sappati, with the suffix a; sappana is movement with the body touching the ground. That which goes swiftly (araṃ) is an alagadda; ma becomes da, and ra becomes la. This term is also for a water snake; for it is said in the Amarasiṃha: 'Alagadda is a water snake (jalavāḷa)'. Bhoga is the coiled body; due to possessing this, it is called a bhogī. That which goes spread out is a pannaga; or that which does not go by means of feet is a pannaga. It has two tongues. That which goes on its chest is an uraga. That which especially seizes is a vāḷa; la becomes ḷa; or from the root vā meaning to go, with the suffix ala. Due to its long body, it is dīgha. That which has a long back, with the suffix ka in a compound. That whose belly is its foot. It bears poison. Also cakkī, kuṇḍalī, gūḷhapāda, cakkhussava, kākodara, dabbīkara, bilasaya, jimhaga, and pavanāsana. Due to having a wheel-like mark on its head, it is a cakkī. That which has a body like an earring (kuṇḍala), due to that connection, is a kuṇḍalī. That which hears with its eyes is a cakkhussava. Its belly is like a crow's, hence kākodara. Because its hood is like a ladle (dabbī), one that makes it is a dabbīkara. Although a general term, dabbīkara refers specifically to the black snake and others. That which goes crookedly is a jimhaga. Pavanāsana means wind-eater.

Phaṇino sappassa tanu kāyo bhogo nāma. Bhujatīti bhogo, bhuja koṭilye, ṇo.

The body of a hooded snake is called bhoga. It is called bhoga because it bends; from the root bhuj meaning to be crooked, with the suffix ṇa.

655-656. Dvayaṃ sappassa dāṭhāyaṃ. Asati yena asaṃ, mukhaṃ, tasmiṃ bhavā āsī, sappassa dāṭhā dantuttamā. Dvayaṃ sappassa jiṇṇatace[M 0.0434], nimuccate yasmā sappoti, ṇo. Kañcukasadisattā kañcuko. Samā tulyatthā.

655-656. These two terms are for a snake's fang. That which is in the mouth, by which one eats, is an āsī; the snake's fang is the foremost tooth. These two terms are for a snake's old skin. Because it is shed, it is called nimutta. Due to being like armor, it is a kañcuka. Samā means they are synonyms.

Dvayaṃ visamatte. Soṇipathagataṃ visati dehanti visaṃ, visa pavesane. Giratīti garaḷaṃ, aḷo.

These two terms are for poison in general. That which enters the body via the bloodstream is visa, from the root vis meaning to enter. That which is swallowed is garaḷa, with the suffix aḷa.

Halāhalo, kāḷakūṭo, ādinā kākolādayo ca sattāti ime nava tabbhedā tassa visassa bhedā. Vuttañca –

Halāhala, Kāḷakūṭa, and the seven others beginning with Kākoḷa—these nine are the varieties of that poison. And it is said:

“Pume paṇḍe ca kākola-kāḷakūṭahalāhalā;

Soraṭṭhiko sukkikeyyo, brahmaputto padīpano;

Dārado vacchanābho ca, visabhedā ime navā”ti amara 8.10-11.

'Kākoḷa, Kāḷakūṭa, and Halāhala are masculine and neuter; Soraṭṭhika, Sukkikeyya, Brahmaputta, Padīpana; Dārada and Vacchanābha—these are the nine kinds of poison.'

Tatra halāhalo pume, vākārena napuṃsakepi, “hālāhala”nti hi tikaṇḍasese tikaṇḍasesa 1.8.5 dīghādipi. Tālapatrasaṇṭhāno nīlapatro gothanākatiphalo gaccho halāhalo. Assa ca samīpe rukkhādayo ḍayhante. Himavati, kikkindāyaṃ, koṅkaṇesu, dakkhiṇasamudde ca jāyate, hanatīti halo, a, nassa lo, halānampi halo halāhalo, majjhadīgho. Tiriyalekhāya citaṃ dvijapadehi yuttaṃ, tathā gaṇṭhibhi byāpitaṃ bindubhideva yaṃ ghanatarehi, taṃ kāḷakūṭaṃ. Idañca puthumālināmassāsurassa soṇitamhā eva asurasamaye devāsuraraṇe (?) samuppannassa assattharukkhasadisassa rukkhassa niyyāso, ahicchattamalayakoṅkaṇasiṅgaverapabbatādīsu coppajjate. Vaṇṇena kāḷañca taṃ sattānaṃ jīvitaharaṇato lohamuggarasadisatāya kūṭañceti kāḷakūṭaṃ.

Therein, halāhala is masculine, but optionally also neuter, for 'hālāhala' is found with a long initial vowel in the Tikaṇḍasesa. The halāhala is a shrub with blue leaves shaped like palm leaves and bearing fruit like a cow's udder. Nearby trees and the like are burned by it. It grows in the Himalayas, in Kikkindā, in the Koṅkaṇa regions, and in the southern ocean. It kills (hanati), hence hala, with the suffix 'a' and the elision of 'n'; it is a killer (hala) even of killers (halānaṃ), hence halāhala, with a long middle vowel. That which is marked with horizontal lines, furnished with bird-foot markings, and pervaded by knots, as if thickly dotted with points—that is kāḷakūṭa. This is the sap of a tree resembling the assattha tree, which arose from the blood of the asura named Puthumālin during the time of the asuras. It also arises on the Ahicchattā, Malayaka, Koṅkaṇa, and Siṅgavera mountains, among others. Because it is black in color and, by taking the lives of beings, resembles an iron hammer, it is called kāḷakūṭa.

Brahmaputto tu kapilo, malayaddibhavo kharo;

Padīpano tu dahano, rattavaṇṇo’ñjanaddijo cintāmaṇiṭīkā 8.10-11.

The son of Brahmā is Kapila, fierce, born of the Malayādri mountain; Padīpana is burning, red in color, born of the Añjanāddi mountain.

Darade [M 0.0435] bhavo dārado, suppabhanāmako taṃdesapasiddho ca. Vacchanābho sinduvārapattasadiso ca taṃsamīpe rukkho na vaddhate, taṃsamphassavāyu ca jarayati, viñjhāyaṃ, kikkindāyañca jāyate, evaṃ visantarānampi sarūpaṃ āgamato viññeyyaṃ.

The Dārada is that which is born in Darada, and it is well-known in that region by the name Suppabha. The Vacchanābha is similar to the leaf of the Sinduvāra; near it, a tree does not grow, and the wind that touches it causes decay. It is born in the Vindhya mountains and in Kikkindā. Thus, the nature of other poisons should also be understood from the traditional texts.

Dvayaṃ dhanatthaṃ sappaggāhe. Vāḷaṃ sappaṃ gaṇhanasīlatāya vāḷagāhī. Ahino tuṇḍena mukhena dibbatīti ahituṇḍiko, ṇiko, “vāḷaggāho’hituṇḍiko”ti amarakose 8.11-gāthāyampi amaramālā.

Two terms for a snake-catcher who works for wealth. One who is in the habit of seizing a vicious snake (vāḷaṃ sappaṃ) is a vāḷagāhī. One who plays with a snake's (ahino) snout or mouth (tuṇḍena mukhena) is an ahituṇḍika, with the suffix ṇika. As stated in the Amaramālā: 'vāḷaggāho' and 'ahituṇḍiko'.

657. Tikaṃ niraye. Ayo iṭṭhaphalaṃ, so niggato asmāti nirayo, nindito rayo gamanaṃ etthāti vā nirayo. Duṭṭhā gati duggati. Apuññe netīti narako, ṇvu, ranto ca, narako.

657. Three terms for hell. Because desirable fortune (ayo) has departed (niggato) from it, it is called niraya; or, because going (rayo) therein is censured (nindito), it is niraya. A bad destination (duṭṭhā gati) is a duggati. Because it leads (neti) to demerit (apuñña), it is a naraka, formed with the suffix ṇvu and the infix 'ra'.

Tesu nirayesu yo “mahānirayo”ti vutto, so aṭṭhadhā hotīti taṃ dasseti “sañjīvo”ccādinā silokena. Marantāpi kammaphalānubhavanatthaṃ punappunaṃ jīvanti asmiṃ sañjīvo. Yattha niraye nerayikānaṃ sarīrāni vaḍḍhakīnaṃ kāḷasuttena saññāṇaṃ katvā vāsiyā tacchanti, so kāḷasutto. Bhusaṃ, punappunaṃ vā dukkhitasaddena ravanti asmiṃ roruvo, mahanto ca so roruvo cāti mahāroruvo. Puna “roruvo”ti cūḷaroruvo vutto. Bhusaṃ patanti [M 0.0436] asmiṃ patāpano, “vīci taraṅge appe cā”ti ruddo, natthi sukhassa vīci lesopi atrāti avīci, “vīci sukhataraṅgesū”ti tikaṇḍaseso tikaṇḍasesa 3.3.78, tasmā natthi vīci sukhaṃ etthāti avīci. Samantato āgatehi pabbatehi haññanti atrāti saṅghāto. Tapanti atra tāpano, itisaddo aṭṭhannaṃ parisamāpanattho.

Among these hells, that which is called the 'Great Hell' is eightfold, as shown by the verse beginning with 'Sañjīva.' In the Sañjīva, even while dying, beings live again and again to experience the fruit of their karma. The Kāḷasutta is that hell wherein the bodies of hell-beings are marked with a black thread by carpenters and then hewn with an adze. In the Roruva, they scream loudly or repeatedly with sounds of suffering; and that Roruva is vast, hence it is Mahāroruva. Again, 'Roruva' by itself refers to the Cūḷaroruva. In the Patāpana, they fall violently. According to Rudda, 'vīci' means 'wave' and also 'a little'; in the Avīci, there is not even a little trace of happiness. According to the Tikaṇḍasesa, 'vīci' means 'waves of happiness'; therefore, in the Avīci, there is no wave of happiness. In the Saṅghāta, they are crushed by mountains approaching from all sides. In the Tāpana, they are tormented by heat. The word 'iti' is for the purpose of concluding the list of the eight.

658. Tattha nirayesu vetaraṇī ca lohakumbhī cāti ime dve nirayā jalāsayā jalādhārā, te ca thiyaṃ, taraṇī nāvā, sā natthi yassaṃ vetaraṇī. Lohamayā kumbhī lohakumbhī.

658. Among those hells, Vetaraṇī and Lohakumbhī are two hells that are reservoirs and receptacles of water, and these two are feminine nouns. A taraṇī is a boat; that river in which there is no boat is the Vetaraṇī. A pot made of iron (lohamayā kumbhī) is a Lohakumbhī.

Dvayaṃ nirayapāle. Kāraṇā yātanā, sā ca tibbavedanā, taṃ karotīti kāraṇiko. Nirayagatasatte pātīti nirayapo.

Two terms for a hell-warden. Kāraṇā means torment, which is intense suffering; one who inflicts that is a kāraṇika. One who guards the beings who have gone to hell is a nirayapa.

Dvayaṃ nirayagatasatte. Nirayaṃ gacchatīti nerayiko. Narakaṃ gacchatīti nārako.

Two terms for a being who has gone to hell. One who goes to Niraya is a nerayika. One who goes to Naraka is a nāraka.

659. Udadhi pariyantaṃ samuddassa nāmaṃ. Aṇṇo jalaṃ, so vāti gacchati yasmiṃ aṇṇavo, aṇṇo yasmiṃ vijjatīti vā aṇṇavo, assatthyatthe vo. Sagarehi rājakumārehi khato [M 0.0437] sāgaro, sānaṃ dhanānaṃ ākaroti vā sāgaro, kassa go, sāga saṃvaraṇe vā, aro. Sandateti sindhu, sanda savane, yadādi. Udi kledane, sammā klidanti candodaye asmā āpānīti samuddo. Jalāni, udakāni ca nidhīyante, dhīyante cātrāti jalanidhi, udadhi ca, udakassa udādeso.

659. The following are names for the ocean. Aṇṇa means water; that wherein it flows (vāti) is the aṇṇava; or, that wherein water (aṇṇa) is found is the aṇṇava, with the suffix 'va' in the sense of 'possessing'. Because it was dug (khato) by the Sagara princes, it is the sāgara; or, it is a mine (ākara) of their (sa) treasures. It flows (sandati), hence it is sindhu, from the root sand, 'to flow'. Because the waters in it swell up (sam-ud) at the rising of the moon, it is the samudda. Because waters (jalāni, udakāni) are placed (nidhīyante) and held (dhīyante) therein, it is a jalanidhi and an udadhi, with 'uda' being a substitute for 'udaka'.

Tassa samuddassa khīraṇṇavo, ādinā lavaṇodo, dadhyudo, ghatodo, ucchurasodo, madirodo, sādudako cāti ime satta mahaṇṇavavisesā bhavanti byākhyāsudhā 1.10.2. Khīravaṇṇo aṇṇavo khīraṇṇavo.

Of that ocean, there are these seven types of great oceans, beginning with the Milk Ocean: the Salt-Water Ocean, the Curd-Water Ocean, the Ghee-Water Ocean, the Sugarcane-Juice Ocean, the Liquor Ocean, and the Fresh-Water Ocean. The Milk Ocean (khīraṇṇava) is the ocean that is the color of milk.

660. Assa samuddassa kūladeso tīradeso velā nāma, vigacchanti irā yassaṃ velā, lattaṃ. Cakkamiva salilānaṃ jalānaṃ bhamo bhamanaṃ āvaṭṭo nāma, āvaṭṭanti jalāni atrāti āvaṭṭo.

660. The shore region or bank region of this ocean is called the velā. The velā is that from which the waters (irā) recede (vigacchanti). A whirl (bhamo) or whirling (bhamanaṃ) of the waters, like a wheel (cakka), is called an āvaṭṭa; it is an āvaṭṭa because the waters whirl (āvaṭṭanti) therein.

Tikaṃ bindumhi. Thu abhitthave, vo, usse. Vidi avayave, u, bindu. Phusa phusane, to, phusitaṃ. Pākāre, gehāditittiyañca jalaniggamo bhamo nāma, bhamu anavaṭṭhāne.

Three terms for a drop. From the root thu, 'to praise', with the suffix 'va', comes ussāva. From the root vid, 'to divide into parts', with the suffix 'u', comes bindu. From the root phus, 'to touch', with the suffix 'ta', comes phusita. The outflow of water from a wall or the eaves of a house is called a bhama; this is from the root bham, 'to be unsteady'.

661. Siloko udake. Āpa byāpane, appoti sabbatrāti āpo. Pātabbanti payo, pā pāne, ṇyo. Rasso[M 0.0438], payo. Jala dhaññe, a. Vārayati ninnonatanti vāri, vara nisedhe, ṇi, vārayati pipāsanti vā vāri. Pīyateti pānīyaṃ, anīyo. Salatīti salilaṃ, sala gatiyaṃ, ilo. Udi kledane, ṇvu, ulopo, dakaṃ pipāsacchedaṃ karotīti vā dakaṃ, “dā dānacchedadhātū”ti ekakkharakosa 20 gāthā hi ekakkharakose, rasso. Ana sadde, a, dvittaṃ, ara gamane vā, to, annādeso, ṇattaṃ. Nī naye, īro. Vana sambhattiyaṃ. Vanīyate pipāsehīti vanaṃ. Vā gamane, alo. Tāyate pālayateti toyaṃ, tā pālane, curādi, yo, ākārassottaṃ. Amba sadde, u, ambu. Udi pasavanakledanesu, ṇvu, udakaṃ. Kara karaṇe, kvi, kaṃ. Kamalaṃ, khīrampi, kamu icchākantīsu, alo. Khanu hiṃsāyaṃ, īro, nalopo, khī khaye vā, khīraṃ.

661. A collection of terms for water. From the root āp, 'to pervade', since it pervades (āpnoti) everywhere, comes āpa. That which is to be drunk (pātabbaṃ) is paya; from the root pā, 'to drink', with the suffix ṇya and shortening. From the root jal, in the sense of 'grain', with the suffix 'a', comes jala. It covers (vārayati) the low and the high, hence vāri; from the root var, 'to prevent', with the suffix 'ṇi'; or it prevents (vārayati) thirst. That which is to be drunk is pānīya, with the suffix 'anīya'. It moves (salati), hence salila; from the root sal, 'to move', with the suffix 'ila'. From the root ud, 'to moisten', with the suffix 'ka' and elision of 'u', comes daka; or, it makes (karoti) a cutting (chedaṃ) of thirst (pipāsā), hence daka, as the root dā means 'to cut' according to the Ekakkharakosa, with shortening. From the root an, 'to sound', with the suffix 'a' and doubling, comes aṇṇa; or from the root ar, 'to go', with the suffix 'ta', by substitution of 'aṇṇa' and cerebralization. From the root nī, 'to lead', with the suffix 'īra', comes nīra. From the root van, 'to serve', as it is sought (vanīyate) by the thirsty, comes vana. From the root vā, 'to go', with the suffix 'ala', comes vāla. It protects (tāyate), hence toya; from the root tā, 'to protect' (curādi group), with the suffix 'ya' and the change of 'ā' to 'o'. From the root amb, 'to sound', with the suffix 'u', comes ambu. From the root ud, 'to flow' and 'to moisten', with the suffix 'ka', comes udaka. From the root kar, 'to do', with the suffix 'kvi', comes ka. Kamala and also khīra are terms for water. Kamala is from the root kam, 'to desire', with the suffix 'ala'. Khīra is from the root khanu, 'to harm', with the suffix 'īra' and elision of 'n'; or from the root khī, 'to waste away'.

662. Catukkaṃ taraṅge. Taranto gacchati, tīraṃ vā gacchatīti taraṅgo, aluttasamāso, paratra īssattaṃ. Sayameva bhijjateti bhaṅgo, a. Ūha vitakke, mi, halopo, ūmi, ara gamane vā, mi, assū, ralopo. Vimhayaṃ vicittaṃ cinotīti vīci, i, upasaggassa dīgho, ete dve pumitthiyaṃ.

662. Four terms for a wave. Because it goes while crossing (taranto gacchati), or because it goes to the shore (tīraṃ gacchati), it is a taraṅga; this is an alutta-samāsa. Because it breaks (bhijjati) by itself, it is a bhaṅga, with the suffix 'a'. From the root ūh, 'to reason', with the suffix 'mi' and elision of 'h', comes ūmi; or from the root ar, 'to go', with the suffix 'mi', the change of 'ar' to 'ū', and the elision of 'r'. Because it collects (cinoti) the wonderful (vimhayaṃ) and the varied (vicittaṃ), it is a vīci, with the suffix 'i' and the lengthening of the prefix. These two, ūmi and vīci, are of both masculine and feminine gender.

Ullolo, kallolo cāti idaṃ dvayaṃ mahāvīcīsu kathyate, lola ummādane, ullolayatīti ullolo, ṇo, ula gamane vā, olo, dvittaṃ. Kalla sadde, olo, kallolo.

Ullola and kallola—these two terms are used for great waves. From the root lul, 'to agitate', because it agitates (ullolayati), comes ullola, with the suffix 'ṇa'; or from the root ul, 'to go', with the suffix 'ola' and doubling.
