From the root kall, 'to sound', with the suffix 'ola', comes kallola.

663. Silokaddhaṃ [M 0.0439] kaddame. Jalaṃ balate jambālo, kammani ṇo, makāro vaṇṇavikāro. Kala saṅkhyāne, alo. Paca vitthāravacane, kammani ṇo. Cikkha vacane, alo, dvittaṃ. Kada madde, amo, dvittaṃ.

663. Half a verse on terms for mud. Because water is held fast in it, it is jambāla; with the suffix 'ṇa' in the objective sense, and the letter 'm' is a phonetic modification. From the root kal, 'to count', with the suffix 'ala', comes kalala. From the root pac, 'to spread out', with the suffix 'a' in the objective sense, comes paṅka. From the root cikkh, 'to speak', with the suffix 'alla' and doubling, comes cikkhalla. From the root kad, 'to crush', with the suffix 'ama' and doubling, comes kaddama.

Chakkaṃ vālukāyaṃ. Pula mahatthe, ino, ḷattaṃ. Vala saṃvaraṇe, ṇvu, assu, vālukā, thī. Vaṇṇa sadde, vaṇṇo. Mara pāṇacāge, u, maru, devepi. Ara gamane, u, assu, uru, mahantepi, vaṇṇo ca maru ca uru ca vaṇṇamarūru. Sica paggharaṇe, to, sikatā, thī.

Six terms for sand. From the root pul, 'to be great', with the suffix 'ina' and the change of 'l' to 'ḷ', comes pulina. From the root val, 'to cover', with the suffix 'uka', comes vālukā, which is feminine. From the root vaṇṇ, 'to describe', comes vaṇṇa. From the root mar, 'to die', with the suffix 'u', comes maru, which also means a desert or a god. From the root ar, 'to go', with the suffix 'u', comes uru, which also means 'great'. The terms are vaṇṇa, maru, and uru. From the root sic, 'to sprinkle', with the suffix 'tā', comes sikatā, which is feminine.

664. Jalamajjhagataṃ talaṃ kammabhūtaṃ “antarīpaṃ, dīpo”ti coccate. Dvidhāgatānaṃ āpānaṃ antaragataṃ antarīpaṃ, ākārassī. “Antarīya”nti vā pāṭho, tadā dvidhāgatānaṃ āpānaṃ antare bhavaṃ antarīyanti viggaho, akārassī. Dvidhāgatāni āpāni asmiṃ hetubhūteti dīpo. Vakāraākārānaṃ lopo, issī ca, dīpo, vākārena dīpampi.

664. A land situated in the middle of water, a place of activity, is called 'antarīpa' or 'dīpa'. That which is situated between waters coming from two directions is 'antarīpa', with the lengthening of 'ā'. Alternatively, the reading is 'antarīya'; then the analysis is: 'antarīya' is that which exists between waters coming from two directions, with the lengthening of 'a'. 'Dīpo' is so called because waters coming from two directions are a causal factor in it. There is elision of the letter 'va' and the letter 'ā', and lengthening to 'ī', thus 'dīpo'; or by the letter 'va', also 'dīpaṃ'.

Pañcakaṃ tīrassa nāmaṃ. Pāra tīra kammasampattiyaṃ, curādi, a. Kūla āvaraṇe, ṇo. Rudha āvaraṇe, rodhaṃ. Aññapārādinivattanatthaṃ “patīra”nti vuttaṃ. Taṭa ussaye, a, thiyaṃ, taṭī.

A group of five are names for the shore. 'Pāra' is from the root `pār`, meaning 'to cross over' or 'accomplishment of action', of the `curādi` group, with the suffix 'a'. 'Kūla' is from the root `kūl`, meaning 'enclosing', with the suffix 'ṇo'. 'Rodhaṃ' is from the root `rudh`, meaning 'enclosing'. The word 'patīra' is stated for the purpose of turning back from the other shore and so forth. 'Taṭa' is from the root `taṭ`, meaning 'height', with the suffix 'a'; in the feminine, it is 'taṭī'.

665. Paramhi [M 0.0440] tīrasmiṃ pārasaddo, so ca napuṃsake, pāra tīra kammasampattiyaṃ, pāra sāmatthiye vā, pārayati taraṅgādayo vāretunti pāraṃ. Orantutīraṃ “apāra”ntyuccate, avare tīradese bhavaṃ oraṃ, ṇo. Pārato aññaṃ tīraṃ apāraṃ.

665. The word 'pāra' is used for the far shore, and it is neuter. 'Pāra' is from the root `pār`, meaning 'to cross over' or 'accomplishment of action', or `pār`, meaning 'ability'; it brings to an end or wards off waves and so forth, thus it is 'pāraṃ'. The near shore is called 'apāra'; 'oraṃ' is that which exists in the near shore-region, with the suffix 'ṇo'. The shore other than the far shore is 'apāra'.

Pañcakaṃ uḷumpe. Uḷuto dakato pāti rakkhati uḷupo, soyeva niggahītāgamavasena uḷumpo. Plavati, plavanti anenāti vā plavo, plava gamane, gamanaṃ atra jalagamanaṃ. Kula santāne, a, ke ulati gacchatīti vā kullo, a, dvittaṃ. Taranti anena taro, tara plavataraṇesu. Gamanāgamanavasena punappunaṃ jale aranti yāya, sā paccarī, a, nadādi.

A group of five are terms for 'uḷumpa'. 'Uḷupo' protects from water; that very word becomes 'uḷumpo' by means of the niggahīta augment. 'Plavo' is that which floats, or that by which one floats, from the root `plu`, meaning 'to go'; here, 'going' means going on water. 'Kullo' is from the root `kul`, meaning 'lineage', with the suffix 'a'; or that which goes in water, with the suffix 'a' and doubling. 'Taro' is that by which one crosses, from the root `tar`, meaning 'to float' or 'to cross'. 'Paccarī' is that by which one repeatedly moves on the water by means of going and coming; it is formed with the suffix 'a' and belongs to the `nadādi` group.

666. Tikaṃ nāvāyaṃ. Taranti yāya taraṇī, yu, nadādi, ipaccaye tari, īmhi tu tarī. Nu thutiyaṃ, a, vuḍḍhāvādesā, nāvā. Dvayaṃ laṅkārathambhe. Kūpa gamane, ṇvu, kūpako, apaccayo vā, tadā sakatthe ko. Kamu icchāyaṃ, bho, sakatthe ko, assu ca, kumbhakaṃ.

666. A group of three are terms for a ship. 'Taraṇī' is that by which one crosses, formed with the 'yu' suffix, belonging to the `nadādi` group; with the 'i' suffix, it is 'tari'; and with 'ī', it is 'tarī'. 'Nāvā' is from the root `nu`, meaning 'to praise', with the 'a' suffix, and with vowel gradation and substitution. A group of two are terms for a ship's mast. 'Kūpako' is from the root `kūp`, meaning 'to go', with the 'ṇvu' suffix; or with the 'a' suffix, in which case 'ka' is pleonastic. 'Kumbhakaṃ' is from the root `kam`, meaning 'to desire', with the 'bha' suffix, the 'ka' suffix being pleonastic, and with 'u' substituting for 'a'.

Dvayaṃ “pe seṃ”iti khyāte. Tarassa pacchābhāge bandhitabboti pacchābandho. Ga’micchitadisaṃ aṭati yena goṭaviso, iso, avanto ca assottañca, goṭaviso. Dvayaṃ “pe tamā”iti [M 0.0441] khyāte. Nāvāya kaṇṇo viya kaṇṇo, mahanto kenipāto, tena pavahaṇapatisavanato, taṃ dharatīti, kammani ṇo. Nāvāya yutto nāviko.

A group of two are terms known as 'pe seṃ'. 'Pacchābandho' is that which should be tied at the rear part of the raft. 'Goṭaviso' is that by which one moves in the desired direction of going; also 'iso', 'avanto', and 'assotta' are 'goṭaviso'. A group of two are terms known as 'pe tamā'. 'Kaṇṇo' is like the ear of a boat, a large oar; because the vessel flows on account of it, and because it holds it, it is so called, with the suffix 'ṇo' in the sense of object. 'Nāviko' is one yoked to a boat.

667. Dvayaṃ nāvāya gamanopāye. Arati yenāti arittaṃ, chadādīhi tatraṇa, ikārāgamo, dvittañca. Ke jale nipātiyate kenipāto, aluttasamāsoyaṃ.

667. A group of two are terms for the means of a ship's movement. 'Arittaṃ' is that by which one moves; it is formed from a root of the `chadādi` group with the 'tra' suffix, the 'i' augment, and doubling. 'Kenipāto' is that which is cast down into the water; this is an `aluttasamāsa` (a compound with unelided case ending).

Dvayaṃ niyāmake. Poto pavahanaṃ, taṃ vāhayatīti potavāho. Niyacchati potanti niyāmako, yamu uparame, nipubbo gamane, ṇvu, niyāmako, curādi. Niyāmakepi.

A group of two are terms for a pilot. 'Potavāho' is so called because a 'pota' is a vessel, and he is one who drives it. 'Niyāmako' is one who controls the boat; it is from the root `yam`, meaning 'to restrain', with the prefix 'ni-' meaning 'to go', with the 'ṇvu' suffix, from the `curādi` group. The same applies to 'niyāmaka'.

Ye vāṇijā nāvāya vāṇijakammaṃ ācaranti, te saṃyattikā nāma, saṃyānaṃ saṃyātrā, dīpantaragamanaṃ, traṇa, sā payojanametesaṃ saṃyattikā, ṇiko, ralopo, rasso ca. Tapaccayena vā siddhaṃ. Potavāṇijāpi, poto pavahanaṃ, tassa vāṇijā.

Those merchants who conduct the business of trade by boat are called 'saṃyattikā'. 'Saṃyāna' is a voyage, a journey to other islands, formed with the 'tra' suffix. That voyage is their purpose, hence 'saṃyattikā', formed with the 'ṇika' suffix, with elision of 'ra' and shortening of the vowel. Alternatively, it is formed with the 'ta' suffix. Also 'potavāṇijā': a 'pota' is a vessel, and they are its merchants.

668. Laṅkārādayo, phiyādayo ca nāvāya aṅgā avayavā. Lo indo, tassa kāraṇaṃ laṅkāro. Vaṭo vuccati sivaṭo, tadākāratāya vaṭākāro. “Vaṭo kamadde [M 0.0442] nigrodhe”ti hi nānatthasaṅgaho. Phā vuḍḍhiyaṃ, iyo, phiyo.

668. 'Laṅkāra' and others, and 'phiya' and others, are limbs and parts of a ship. 'Laṅkāro' is the cause of 'lo', which means Indra. 'Vaṭo' is called 'sivaṭo'; because of its shape, it is 'vaṭākāro'. For the Nānārthasaṅgaho says, 'Vaṭo means kammadde and nigrodhe'. 'Phiyo' is from the root `phā`, meaning 'to increase', with the 'iya' suffix.

Dvayaṃ “talaka”iti khyāte. Pū pavane, to, vuḍḍhi, pavahati niyāmaketi pavahanaṃ. Vuttanti kriyāpadaṃ. Dvayaṃ kaṭṭhambuvāhiniyaṃ, duṇa gatihiṃsāsu, a, nadādi, vuḍḍhi, doṇī. Ambuṃ neti yena ambaṇaṃ, ussattaṃ, ṇattañca, amba sadde vā, yu.

A group of two are terms known as 'talaka'. 'Pavahanaṃ' is from the root `pū`, meaning 'to purify', with the 'ta' suffix and vowel gradation; it is so called because it carries the pilot. 'Vuttaṃ' is a verb. A group of two are terms for a wooden water-carrier. 'Doṇī' is from the root `duṇ`, meaning 'to go' or 'to harm', with the 'a' suffix, belonging to the `nadādi` group, with vowel gradation. 'Ambaṇaṃ' is that by which one leads water; the derivation involves `ussatta` and `ṇatta`; or it is from the root `amb`, meaning 'to sound', with the 'yu' suffix.

669. Tikaṃ gambhīre. Gamu gamane, īro, bhonto ca malopo ca, gabhīro. Mālope tu gambhīro, gacchantā bhāyanti asminti vā gabhīro, gambhīro ca. Nipubbo mana abhyāse, ṇo, massa no. Tabbipakkhato gambhīraviparītato uttānaṃ nāma, uggataṃ tānaṃ pamāṇaṃ assa uttānaṃ, agambhīraṃ.

669. A group of three are terms for 'deep'. 'Gabhīro' is from the root `gam`, meaning 'to go', with the 'īra' suffix, the augment 'bha', and elision of 'ma'. Without the elision of 'ma', however, it is 'gambhīro'. Alternatively, because those who go are afraid in it, it is 'gabhīro' or 'gambhīro'. With the prefix 'ni-', from the root `man`, meaning 'to practice', with the 'ṇa' suffix, and with 'ma' becoming 'na', the word is 'nimna'. Opposite to that, contrary to 'deep', is the term 'uttāna'. 'Uttāna' is that whose measure is a raised expanse; it means not deep.

Dvayaṃ agādhe. Gādha patiṭṭhākaṅkhāsu, ganthe ca, natthi gādhaṃ yatra agādhaṃ. Na heṭṭhimatalaṃ phusati yatra atalamphassaṃ.

A group of two are terms for 'unfathomable'. 'Agādhaṃ' is where there is no foothold, from the root `gādh`, meaning 'to seek a firm standing' or 'to bind'. 'Atalamphassaṃ' is where one does not touch the bottom surface.

Tikaṃ appasanne. Natthi acchabhāvo atra anaccho. Kalusaṃ pāpepi vuttaṃ. Vila bhedane, ṇo, āvilo. Ava rakkhaṇe vā, ilo.

A group of three are terms for 'turbid'. 'Anaccho' is where there is no state of clarity. 'Kalusaṃ' is also used in the sense of 'evil'. 'Āvilo' is from the root `vil`, meaning 'to split', with the 'ṇa' suffix; or from the root `av`, meaning 'to protect', with the 'ila' suffix.

670. Tikaṃ nimmale. Cho chedane, na chindati dassananti accho, ṇo, sacchopi, sara visaraṇe, to, annādeso. Natthi malaṃ etasmiṃ vimalo. Gabhīrappabhutī gabhīrādayo vimalantā tīsu liṅgesu.

670. A group of three are terms for 'pure'. 'Accho' is from the root `cho`, meaning 'to cut'; it is so called because it does not obstruct the sight, with the 'ṇa' suffix. Also 'saccho', from the root `sar`, meaning 'to spread', with the 'ta' suffix and the substitution of 'anna'. 'Vimalo' is that in which there is no stain. The words beginning with 'gabhīra' up to 'vimala' are in the three genders.

Pañcakaṃ [M 0.0443] kevaṭṭe. Dhā dhāraṇe, īvaro. Macche hantvā jīvatīti macchiko, iko. Macche bandhati jālenāti macchabandho, macche vadhatīti vā macchabandho, niggahītāgamo, kaṃ jalaṃ, tassa īlakkhī, tāya vaṭṭo vaṭṭanaṃ assatthīti kevaṭṭo. Kevattopi, ṇo. Jāle niyutto, jālena hantīti vā jāliko, dāsopyatra, dāsa dāne, a, “dāso kevaṭṭabhaccesū”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 10.15 ruddo.

A group of five are terms for a fisherman. 'Dhīvaro' is from the root `dhā`, meaning 'to hold', with the 'īvara' suffix. 'Macchiko' is one who lives by killing fish, with the 'ika' suffix. 'Macchabandho' is one who binds fish with a net, or one who kills fish, with the niggahīta augment. 'Kevaṭṭo' is derived thus: 'kaṃ' means water; he is one for whom there is the act of encircling by means of that. Also 'kevatto', with the 'ṇa' suffix. 'Jāliko' is one employed with a net, or one who kills with a net. Here also 'dāso', from the root `dās`, meaning 'to give', with the 'a' suffix; as Rudda says, 'dāso is used for fishermen and servants'.

671-672. Jhasāntaṃ macche. Masa āmasane, cho, maradhātuvasena vā siddho, mara pāṇacāge, ino, ralopo. Mukhappadese puthūni lomāni assa puthulomo. Pāṭhīnādīnaṃ macchattā visesato alomakepyassa vutti. Jhasa hiṃsattho daṇḍako dhātu, a, jhaso. Aṇḍajo, visāro, sakalīpi, vicitraṃ sarati anena visāro, ṇo. Rohitādīnaṃ vakkalappāyo battalappāyo (ka.) taco sakalaṃ. Taṃyogā, ī, sakalī.

671-672. Terms ending with 'jhasa' refer to fish. 'Maccho' is from the root `mas`, meaning 'to touch', with the 'cha' suffix; or it is formed by means of the root `mar`, meaning 'to give up life', with the 'ina' suffix and elision of 'ra'. 'Puthulomo' is that which has thick hairs on the mouth region. Although Pāṭhīna and other fish are hairless, this term is used for them specifically because they are fish. 'Jhaso' is from the `daṇḍaka` root `jhas`, meaning 'to harm', with the 'a' suffix. 'Aṇḍajo', 'visāro', and also 'sakalī' are terms for fish. 'Visāro' is that by which one moves variously, with the 'ṇa' suffix. The skin of Rohita and other fish, which is like bark, is called 'sakalaṃ'. Due to its connection with that, with the 'ī' suffix, it becomes 'sakalī'.

Rohitādayo, makarādayo ca macchappabhedā. Ruha janane, to, rohito. Vipāke madhurasattā magguro, vaṇṇavikāro, majjatīti vā magguro, ūro, majja suddhiyaṃ, jjassa ggattaṃ, rasso ca, magguro, “ṅā khū”. Siṅgayuttatāya siṅgī, ṇo, nadādi, saṅgupi, sarati vātanti vā siṅgī, sara hiṃsāyaṃ, a, rassa go, assi, niggahītāgamo, nadādi, siṅgī, “ṅa cve”. Bala [M 0.0444] saṃvaraṇe, alo, lassa jo, balajo,”ṅa pā”. Muñja saddattho, muñjo. Pū pavane, uso, vuddhyāvādesā, pāvuso, mahāmukhamaccho, “ṅa ṭā”.

Rohita and others, and Makara and others, are varieties of fish. 'Rohito' is from the root `ruh`, meaning 'to generate', with the 'ta' suffix. 'Magguro' is so called from its sweet taste when cooked, or its change of color; or because it immerses, with the 'ūra' suffix; from the root `majj`, meaning 'to purify', 'jj' becomes 'gg', and the vowel is shortened, thus 'magguro'. 'Siṅgī' is so called from its association with a horn, with the 'ṇa' suffix, of the `nadādi` group; also 'saṅgupi'. Alternatively, 'siṅgī' is from the root `sar`, meaning 'to harm', with the 'a' suffix, 'r' becoming 'g', 'a' becoming 'i', with the niggahīta augment, of the `nadādi` group. 'Balajo' is from the root `bal`, meaning 'to restrain', with the 'ala' suffix, and 'l' becomes 'j'. 'Muñjo' is from the root `muñj`, meaning 'to sound'. 'Pāvuso' is from the root `pū`, meaning 'to purify', with the 'usa' suffix, and with vowel gradation and substitution; it is a large-mouthed fish.

Sattakkhattuṃ vaṅkatīti sattavaṅko, “ṅa se”. Saha vaṅkena, saṃvijjamāno vā vaṅko yassa savaṅko, “ṅa mve”. Naḷasaṇṭhāno mīno naḷamīno, “ṅa phौ-yo”. Kaḍi sannicayavadanekadesesu, ṇvu, gaṇḍako, “ṅa mā”. Sasu hiṃsāyaṃ, u, assu, susukā, sakattheko, “ṅa-pौ-ṭaye”. Sayanato passena pharatīti sapharī, nadādi, phara pharaṇe, sapharī dvīsu, “ṅa khū-mā”. Pāṇiggahaṇe mukhaṃ kiratīti makaro, yadādi.

'Sattavaṅko' is that which bends seven times. 'Savaṅko' is that which is with a bend, or for which there is an existing bend. 'Naḷamīno' is a fish shaped like a reed. 'Gaṇḍako' is from the root `kaḍ`, meaning 'to accumulate' or 'parts of the face', with the 'ṇvu' suffix. 'Susukā' is from the root `sas`, meaning 'to harm', with the 'u' suffix, 'a' becoming 'u', and a pleonastic 'ka'. 'Sapharī' is that which spreads out with its side from lying down, of the `nadādi` group; it is from the root `phar`, meaning 'to spread'; 'sapharī' is used in two genders. 'Makaro' is that which scatters with its mouth when seizing with its jaw, from the `yadādi` group.

673. Timiādayo satta mahāmacchā nāma. Tima addabhāve, timatīti timi, i, timi macchamattepi. Gira niggiraṇe, ṇo, lattaṃ, issattaṃ. Timino galo timiṅgalo, niggahītāgamo. Vaṇṇena piṅgalatimirasadisatāya timirapiṅgalo. Ā bhuso nandatīti ānando, nanda samiddhiyaṃ. Timino macche nandayatīti timinando. “Timindo”tipi pāṭho, timīnaṃ macchānaṃ indo timindo. Adhiko āroho yassa ajjhāroho. Mahanto timi maccho mahātimi.

673. The seven great fishes, beginning with Timi, are named. ‘Timi’ is from the root ‘tim’ in the sense of being wet; ‘timati’ means it is wet, hence ‘timi’, with the ‘i’ suffix; ‘timi’ can also refer to a mere fish. ‘Timiṅgalo’ is from the root ‘gira’ in the sense of swallowing, with the ‘ṇo’ suffix, and the states of ‘la’ and ‘issa’; it is the throat of the Timi, with the insertion of a niggahīta. ‘Timirapiṅgalo’ is so called because its color resembles that of tawny darkness. ‘Ānando’ is that which greatly delights, from the root ‘nanda’ in the sense of prospering. ‘Timinando’ is that which delights the Timi fish. There is also the reading ‘timindo’, meaning the lord of the Timi fishes. ‘Ajjhāroho’ is that which has an excessive ascent. ‘Mahātimi’ is a great Timi fish.

674. Dvayaṃ “ṅa phe”iti khyāte. Pāsāṇasadisasaṇṭhāno maccho pāsāṇamaccho. Paṭha viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, ino[M 0.0445], ubhayatra dīgho, pāṭhīno, “ṅa-pौ”ti ca vadanti. Dvayaṃ baḷise. Vaṅkatīti vaṅko, vaṅka koṭilye. Bala saṃvaraṇe, iso, ḷattaṃ. Macchavedhanampi, vidha vidhāne, bhedane ca, anekatthattā, yu.

674. A pair of terms for the fish known as ‘ṅa phe’: ‘Pāsāṇamaccho’ is a fish with a form resembling a stone. ‘Pāṭhīno’ is from the root ‘paṭha’ in the sense of clear speech, with the ‘ino’ suffix and lengthening in both syllables; they also call it ‘ṅa-pau’. A pair of terms for a fishhook: ‘Vaṅko’ is so called because it is bent, from the root ‘vaṅka’ in the sense of crookedness. ‘Baḷiso’ is from the root ‘bala’ in the sense of restraining, with the ‘iso’ suffix, and the change of the consonant to ‘ḷa’. Also, the term ‘macchavedhanaṃ’ (fish-spearing) is from the root ‘vidha’ in the sense of arranging and also piercing, due to its multiple meanings, with the ‘yu’ suffix.

Tikaṃ kumbhīle. “Suṃsumāro”ti samuditanāmaṃ, sasatīti susu. Susu eva suṃsu, māretīti māro, suṃsu eva māro suṃsumāro. Kena ubhati pūretīti kumbho, jalāsayo, tatra ulati gacchatīti kumbhīlo, kumbhī vā ghaṭo, taṃ lātīti kumbhīlo. Na kamatīti nakko, kvi, saññāsaddattā nassa pakati, nakka nāsane vā, curādi.

A group of three terms for a crocodile: ‘Suṃsumāro’ is a compound name: from ‘sasati’ (it moves swiftly) comes ‘susu’; ‘susu’ becomes ‘suṃsu’; from ‘māreti’ (it kills) comes ‘māro’; ‘suṃsu’ and ‘māro’ together form ‘suṃsumāro’. ‘Kumbhīlo’: ‘kumbho’ means a water reservoir, from ‘kena ubhati pūreti’ (it fills with water); ‘kumbhīlo’ is so called because it goes (‘ulati’) there (‘tatra’); or, ‘kumbhī’ is a pot, and it takes (‘lāti’) that, hence ‘kumbhīlo’. ‘Nakko’ is so called because it does not move (‘na kamati’), with the ‘kvi’ suffix; because it is a proper noun, the ‘na’ remains in its natural form; or, it is from the root ‘nakka’ in the sense of destroying, of the curādi class.

Dvayaṃ kacchape. Kucchito ūmi vego assa kummo, “pakāse vegabhaṅgesu, taraṅge ūmi puṃthiya”nti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 10.21 rabhaso, “vege bhaṅgappakāsesu, bilāyaṃ ūmi vīciya”nti nānatthasaṅgaho. Kacchena pivatīti kacchapo, ṇo, kamaṭhopyatra, kamu icchāyaṃ, aṭho.

A pair of terms for a tortoise: ‘Kummo’ is one whose impulse and speed are contemptible. Rabhasa states: ‘ūmi’ is used in the senses of display, breaking of speed, and wave. The Nānatthasaṅgaha states: ‘ūmi’ is used in the senses of speed, breaking, display, and ripple in a cave. ‘Kacchapo’ is one who drinks with its side, with the ‘ṇo’ suffix. Here also is the term ‘kamaṭho’, from the root ‘kamu’ in the sense of desiring, with the ‘aṭho’ suffix.

675. Dvayaṃ kakkaṭe. Kakatīti kakkaṭako. Sakatthe ko, kuka ādāne vā, aṭo, ussattaṃ. Kula santāne, bandhumhi ca, īro, kuṃ vā pathaviṃ lunātīti kuḷīro, īro. Dvayaṃ rattape. Jalassa ūkā kimiviseso jalūkā, jalaṃ okaṃ gehaṃ etissāti vā jalūkā, ossū, uca samavāye, ṇo, okaṃ. Rattaṃ rudhiraṃ pivatīti rattapā.

675. A pair of terms for a crab: ‘Kakkaṭako’ is so called because it moves crookedly (‘kakatī’); the ‘ka’ suffix is in its own sense. Or, it is from the root ‘kuka’ in the sense of taking, with the ‘aṭo’ suffix, and the state of being ‘ussa’. ‘Kuḷīro’ is from the root ‘kula’ in the sense of lineage and also kinship, with the ‘īro’ suffix; or, it cuts the earth (‘kuṃ’ or ‘pathaviṃ’), hence ‘kuḷīro’, with the ‘īro’ suffix. A pair of terms for a blood-drinker: ‘Jalūkā’ is a type of insect, a water-louse (‘jalassa ūkā’); or, ‘jalūkā’ is that which has water as its home (‘okaṃ’); ‘okaṃ’ is from the root ‘uca’ in the sense of collecting, with the ‘ṇo’ suffix. ‘Rattapā’ is one who drinks blood (‘rattaṃ’).

Tikaṃ [M 0.0446] maṇḍūke. Maṇḍa bhūsane, uko, dīgho. Dada dāne, uro, dvittaṃ. Bhī bhaye, sappato bhāyatīti bheko, iko, īsse. Vassābhū, sāluro, plavopi. Dvayaṃ “tī”iti khyāte. Gaṇḍaṃ vaccasannicayaṃ uppādetīti gaṇḍuppādo. Mahiyā latā mahīlatā, kiñculukopi. Kiñca culatīti kiñculuko, uko.

A group of three terms for a frog: ‘Maṇḍūko’ is from the root ‘maṇḍa’ in the sense of adorning, with the ‘uko’ suffix and lengthening of the vowel. ‘Daddura’ is from the root ‘dada’ in the sense of giving, with the ‘uro’ suffix and doubling of the consonant. ‘Bheko’ is from the root ‘bhī’ in the sense of fear, meaning it fears snakes, with the ‘iko’ suffix and the state of ‘īssa’. Also ‘vassābhū’ (rain-born), ‘sāluro’, and ‘plavo’ (floater). A pair of terms for the creature known as ‘tī’: ‘Gaṇḍuppādo’ is that which produces a lump, an accumulation of excrement. ‘Mahīlatā’ is a creeper of the earth. Also ‘kiñculuko’, from ‘kiñca culati’ (it moves somewhat), with the ‘uko’ suffix.

676. Dvayaṃ muttāphoṭe. Sappa gamane, i, assi, sippi, thī. Su abhisave, tti, sutti. Dvayaṃ saṅkhe. Khanu avadāraṇe, kvi, saṅkho. Samu upasame vā, kho, saṅkho. Kaṃ vāti gacchatīti kumbu, u, dvepyanitthiyaṃ.

676. A pair of terms for a pearl-oyster: ‘Sippi’ is from the root ‘sappa’ in the sense of moving, with the ‘i’ suffix, becoming ‘assi’, then ‘sippi’; it is feminine. ‘Sutti’ is from the root ‘su’ in the sense of extracting, with the ‘tti’ suffix. A pair of terms for a conch shell: ‘Saṅkho’ is from the root ‘khanu’ in the sense of digging, with the ‘kvi’ suffix. Or, ‘saṅkho’ is from the root ‘samu’ in the sense of calming, with the ‘kho’ suffix. ‘Kumbu’ is from ‘kaṃ vāti’ (it goes in the water), with the ‘u’ suffix. Both terms are non-feminine.

Dvayaṃ khuddasaṅkhajātiyaṃ. Saṅkhassa nakho iva saṅkhanakho. Dvayaṃ “kharu”iti khyāte. Jale savatīti jalasutti, su pasave, tti. Samatīti sambuko, uko, bonto ca, “sambuko jalasutti’tthī”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 10.23 puṃkaṇḍe vopālito.

A pair of terms for a species of small conch: ‘Saṅkhanakho’ is so called as it is like the nail of a conch. A pair of terms for the creature known as ‘kharu’: ‘Jalasutti’ is so called because it is produced (‘savati’) in water, from the root ‘su’ in the sense of producing, with the ‘tti’ suffix. ‘Sambuko’ is so called because it is calm (‘samati’), with the ‘uko’ suffix and the insertion of ‘b’. In the masculine section, Vopālita states: “sambuko, jalasutti are feminine”.

677. Dvayaṃ jalāsaye. Jalānaṃ āsayo patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ jalāsayo. Tesu jalāsayesu majjhe yo gambhīro [M 0.0447] agādho, so rahadākhyo, hara haraṇe, bhūvādi, do, vaṇṇavipariyayo, rahado.

677. A pair of terms for a water reservoir. A ‘jalāsaya’ is a repository for water, an established place. Among these water reservoirs, that which is deep and unfathomable is called a ‘rahada’. ‘Rahado’ is derived from the root ‘hara’ in the sense of carrying, of the bhūvādi class, with the ‘do’ suffix and a transposition of letters.

Dvayaṃ udapāne. Udakaṃ pivanti asmiṃ, yu, kalopo. Pivanti asmiṃ pāno, so eva kūpo pānakūpo, ku sadde, po, dīghādi, kūpo, kena ubhatīti vā kūpo, bhassa po. Andhupi, andha dassanupasaṅghāte, curādi, u. Dvayaṃ samacaturassapokkharaṇiyaṃ. Khanu avadāraṇe, kamme to, nalopo, dīghādi. Pokkharaṃ jalaṃ, taṃyogā ano, nadādi, pokkharaṇī.

A pair of terms for a well: ‘Udapāna’ is so called because they drink water in it, with the ‘yu’ suffix and elision. ‘Kūpo’ is from the root ‘ku’ in the sense of sounding, with the ‘po’ suffix, lengthening, and so on; a drinking well is a ‘pānakūpo’. Or, ‘kūpo’ is from ‘kena ubhati’ (it is drawn up by something), with ‘bha’ becoming ‘pa’. Also the term ‘andhu’, from the root ‘andha’ in the sense of obstructing sight, of the curādi class, with the ‘u’ suffix. A pair of terms for a square pond: ‘Khātā’ is from the root ‘khanu’ in the sense of digging, in the passive voice, with the ‘ta’ suffix, elision of ‘n’, and lengthening. ‘Pokkharaṇī’: ‘pokkhara’ means water; from its association with that, with the ‘ana’ suffix, of the nadādi class, comes ‘pokkharaṇī’.

678. Tipādena mahato sadā agādhajalassa padmaṭṭhānassa ca padmasuññassa ca yogyatāya nāmaṃ amara 10.28 gāthāyaṃ passitabbaṃ. Taḷa āghāte, tala patiṭṭhāyaṃ vā, āko, aparapakkhe ḷattaṃ. Sara gamane, a, saro. Vapa bījanikkhepe, vapanti yāya vāpī, āyatacaturassāyampi. Saratismā aso, nadādi, sarasī. Daha bhasmīkaraṇe, a, dadha dhāraṇe vā, dhassa ho. Ambujānaṃ paddhānaṃ ākaro uppattiṭṭhānaṃ.

678. By three quarters of a verse, names are given to a large body of water that is always deep, suitable for being both a place with lotuses and one devoid of lotuses. ‘Taḷāko’ is from the root ‘taḷa’ in the sense of striking, or ‘tala’ in the sense of establishing, with the ‘āka’ suffix; in the alternative form, there is the change to ‘ḷa’. ‘Saro’ is from the root ‘sara’ in the sense of moving, with the ‘a’ suffix. ‘Vāpī’ is from the root ‘vapa’ in the sense of sowing seeds; it is that by which one sows; it is also used for an oblong pond. ‘Sarasī’ is from the root ‘sara’, with the ‘asa’ suffix, of the nadādi class. ‘Daho’ is from the root ‘daha’ in the sense of burning, with the ‘a’ suffix; or from ‘dadha’ in the sense of holding, with ‘dha’ becoming ‘ha’. ‘Ākaro’ is a mine, a place of origin, for lotuses.

Khuddako saro “pallala”ntyuccate. Yatra vassāsu adhikaṃ jalaṃ, gimhesu jāṇumattaṃ, sukkhatyeva vā, palla rakkhaṇe, curādi, alo, pallalaṃ.

A small lake is called a ‘pallala’. It is a place where there is much water in the rainy season, while in the hot season it is knee-deep, or it dries up completely. The term ‘pallalaṃ’ is from the root ‘palla’ in the sense of protecting, of the curādi class, with the ‘ala’ suffix.

679-680. Anotattādayo [M 0.0448] ete satta mahāsarā nāma. Tatra sūriyaraṃsisamphuṭṭhābhāvena na avatapati udakametthāti anotatto. Kaṇṇamuṇḍapabbatasamīpattā kaṇṇamuṇḍo. Rathaṃ karotīti rathakārako, yathākathañci ayaṃ byuppatti nāma, saññā pana lokatoyevāvagantabbā. Chabbaṇṇadantavantatāya chaddanto, nāgarājā, tassa nivāsanaṭṭhānasamīpattā chaddanto, saro. Kuṇālasakuṇā bahavo yattha santi kuṇālo. Mandākinī ākāsagaṅgāyampi vuttā. Bahavo sīhā papatanti asmiṃ sīhappapāto.

679-680. These seven, beginning with Anotatta, are the names of the great lakes. Therein, ‘Anotatta’ is so called because the water is not heated, due to the absence of contact with the sun's rays. ‘Kaṇṇamuṇḍo’ is so called because of its proximity to Mount Kaṇṇamuṇḍa. ‘Rathakārako’ has the etymology ‘he who makes a chariot’; however, this derivation is somewhat forced, and the name should be understood from worldly convention. ‘Chaddanto’ is the name of the Nāga king, so called because he possesses tusks of six colors; the lake is named ‘Chaddanto’ due to its proximity to his dwelling place. ‘Kuṇālo’ is where there are many kuṇāla birds. ‘Mandākinī’ is also a name for the celestial Ganges. ‘Sīhappapāto’ is so called because many lions fall into it.

Dvayaṃ jalappāye dese kūpanikaṭe pasupānatthaṃ patthārādiracite jalāsaye. Āhūyante pasavo atra pānāyāti āhāvo, ṇo, vuḍḍhāvādeso. Nipivanti asmiṃ nipānaṃ, yu. Dvayaṃ surakhāte, aporise devanimmiteti bhāvo, soṇḍeiccaññe. “Akhāto devakhātako”ti amara 10.27 hi amaramālāyaṃ puṃsakaṇḍaṃ.

A pair of terms for a reservoir constructed with stone slabs and the like, near a well in a water-scarce region, for animals to drink from. ‘Āhāvo’ is so called because animals are called here to drink, with the ‘ṇa’ suffix and vṛddhi substitution. ‘Nipānaṃ’ is so called because they drink down in it, with the ‘yu’ suffix. A pair of terms for a pond dug by the gods, meaning not made by humans but created by gods; others say it is a natural pond. Indeed, in the masculine section of the Amaramālā it is stated: “That which is not dug by man is dug by the gods”.

681. Nadyantaṃ [M 0.0449] nadīyaṃ. Savatīti, anto, nadādi, savantī. Ninnaṭṭhānaṃ gacchatīti ninnagā, kvi. Sanda pasavane, u, assittaṃ, vaṇṇavikāro, sindhu. Sara gamane, to, ikārāgamo, saritā. Āpānaṃ nivāso āpo, samuddo, ṇo, taṃ gacchatīti āpagā. Nada abyattasadde, nadatīti nadī, nadādi, taraṅganīpyatra.

681. Synonyms for river: ‘Savantī’ is so called because it flows, with the ‘anta’ suffix, of the nadādi class. ‘Ninnagā’ is so called because it goes to a low place, with the ‘kvi’ suffix. ‘Sindhu’ is from the root ‘sanda’ in the sense of flowing, with the ‘u’ suffix, the state of being ‘assi’, and a vowel change. ‘Saritā’ is from the root ‘sara’ in the sense of moving, with the ‘ta’ suffix and the insertion of an ‘i’. ‘Āpagā’ is so called because it goes to the waters, that is, the ocean, their abode, with the ‘ṇa’ suffix. ‘Nadī’ is from the root ‘nada’ in the sense of making an indistinct sound; it sounds, hence ‘nadī’, of the nadādi class. Also here is the term ‘taraṅginī’.

Dvayaṃ gaṅgāyaṃ. Bhagīrathena raññā nibbattitā bhāgīrathīti lokiyā, asmākantu matena nāmamattamevetaṃ tassāti sanniṭṭhānaṃ, evaṃ sabbatra. Gacchatīti gaṅgā, gamito go, tipathagatāpi, tayo saggamaccapātālapathe gatā tipathagatā. Sindhūnaṃ nadīnaṃ saṅgamo melako sambhedo. Sammā bhijjanti asmiṃ sambhedo, saṃpubbo bhidi melane, ṇo.

A pair of terms for the Ganges. According to worldly tradition, she is called ‘Bhāgīrathī’ because she was brought forth by King Bhagīratha; in our opinion, however, this is merely its name. Such is our conclusion, and so it is in all cases. ‘Gaṅgā’ is so called because it goes (‘gacchati’); from the root ‘gam’ comes ‘ga’. It is also called ‘Tipathagā’, meaning one who has gone on the three paths of heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld. The confluence of rivers is a meeting, a junction, a ‘sambhedo’. ‘Sambhedo’ is so called because they meet together there; it is from the root ‘bhid’ in the sense of meeting, preceded by ‘saṃ’, with the ‘ṇa’ suffix.

682. Gaṅgādikā imā pañca nadiyo mahānadī nāma. Aciraṃ sīghagamanaṃ etissamatthīti aciravatī. Yamu uparame, uno, yamassa bhaginī vā yamunā, bhaginyatthe uno. Sarāni bhavanti yāya avadhibhūtāyāti sarabhū, sara gatihiṃsācintāsu vā, ū, abhonto ca, sarabhū. Maha pūjāyaṃ, a, nadādi.

682. These five rivers, beginning with the Ganges, are called the great rivers. ‘Aciravatī’ is so called because it has swift, not slow, movement. ‘Yamunā’ is from the root ‘yamu’ in the sense of restraining, with the ‘una’ suffix; or, she is the sister of Yama, with ‘una’ used in the sense of sister. ‘Sarabhū’ is so called because arrows are made from it, it being the source material; or, it is from the root ‘sara’ in the senses of going, harming, or thinking, with the ‘ū’ suffix and the insertion of ‘bh’. ‘Mahī’ is from the root ‘maha’ in the sense of worshipping, with the ‘a’ suffix, of the nadādi class.

Candabhāgādikā [M 0.0450] ninnagā pañca mahānadito aññāsaṃ nadīnaṃ bhedā. Candabhāgo nāma pabbato, tato pabhavatīti candabhāgā. Sarayogā vantu, majjhe sakārāgamo, nadādi, sarasvatī. Vanturatrātisaye.

The five rivers, beginning with the Candabhāgā, are varieties of rivers other than the great rivers. Candabhāga is the name of a mountain; because it originates from there, it is called Candabhāgā. From `sara` with the suffix `vantu`, with the insertion of `sa` in the middle, belonging to the `nadādi` class, thus Sarasvatī. The suffix `vantu` is here used in the sense of abundance.

683. Niddosaṃ jalaṃ assaṃ nerañjarā, yadādi, atha vā nerañjarā nāma tūriyaviseso, taṃsamānasaddatāya ayaṃ nadī nerañjarā nāma. Nānāgāhākulībhūtatāya kucchitaṃ veraṃ assā kāverī, nadādi. Nammaṃ sukhaṃ dadātīti nammadā, ṇo. Ādinā sarāvatī vettavatī kaṇṭakī kosikīādikā anekā nadībhedā saṅgahitā.

683. Its water is faultless, hence Nerañjarā; with `yadādi`. Alternatively, Nerañjarā is the name of a particular musical instrument, and because its sound is similar, this river is called Nerañjarā. Because it is infested with various crocodiles, its current is foul, hence Kāverī; of the `nadādi` class. It gives pleasure and happiness, hence Nammadā; with `ṇo`. By 'and others,' many varieties of rivers such as Sarāvatī, Vettavatī, Kaṇṭakī, Kosikī, and so forth, are included.

Dvayaṃ hammiyadevālayādīsu jalamagge. Vārino nikkhamanamaggo vārimaggo. Nala gandhe, a, nadādi, ḷattaṃ, panāḷi, ayaṃ itthiyaṃ, pume ca.

Two terms for a watercourse in mansions, temples, and so forth. The path for the outflow of water is a `vārimagga`. From the root `nala` (in the sense of fragrance), with the suffix `a`, belonging to the `nadādi` class, with the substitution of `ḷa`, thus `panāḷi`; this word is both feminine and masculine.

Tikaṃ gāmadvāramhi asucipūtipaṅkasampuṇṇāyaṃ kāsuyaṃ. Cittaṃ dunotīti candanikā, yadādi.

Three terms for a pit at the village gate filled with impure, putrid mud. It distresses the mind, hence `candanikā`; with `yadādi`.

684-685. Jamu adane, alo, nadādi, bonto ca, ḷattaṃ, jambāḷī. Avalagganti asmiṃ oḷigallo, lagga saṅge, alo, ḷattaṃ, assi, galopo, dvittañca. Sāddhapajjena padumassa nāmaṃ. Sarasi ruhatīti saroruhaṃ, ro. Sataṃ pattāni [M 0.0451] assa, padmavisesatthepyassa padmattā visesato abhedo. Araṃ vindatīti aravindaṃ. Pada gamane, umo. Padumaṃ, anitthī. Paṅke kaddame ruhatīti paṅkeruhaṃ, aluttasamāsoyaṃ. Nala gandhe, ino, ḷattaṃ. Pusa vuḍḍhimhi, kharo, vuḍḍhi, sassa ko, pokkhare jale jātanti vā pokkharaṃ. Muḷālatopi uggantvā pupphati muḷālapupphaṃ. Kaṃ jalaṃ alayati bhūsayatīti kamalaṃ, ala bhūsane. Bhisatopi uggantvā pupphatīti bhisapupphaṃ. Kuse jale seti tiṭṭhatīti kusesayaṃ, ro, aluttasamāso. Tāmarasampi, tāmaraṃ jalaṃ, “tāmaraṃ ghatamaṇṇo ce”ti tantatantaraṃ, tatra seti tiṭṭhatīti tāmarasaṃ, ro.

684-685. From the root `jamu` (to eat), with `alo`, of the `nadādi` class, and `bonta`, and with the substitution of `ḷa`, thus `jambāḷī`. They stick in it, hence `oḷigallo`; from the root `lagga` (to stick), with `alo`, the substitution of `ḷa`, `assi`, the elision of `ga`, and doubling. By the half-stanza, the names of the lotus. It grows in a pond, hence `saroruhaṃ`; with `ro`. It has a hundred petals; even when meaning a specific type of lotus, because it is a lotus, there is fundamentally no difference. It finds the spokes, hence `aravindaṃ`. From the root `pada` (to go), with `umo`, thus `padumaṃ`; it is not feminine. It grows in mud, hence `paṅkeruhaṃ`; this is an unelided compound. From the root `nala` (in the sense of fragrance), with `ino`, and the substitution of `ḷa`, thus `naḷina`. From the root `pusa` (to grow), with `kharo`, vowel gradation, and `sa` becoming `ka`; or, because it is born in `pokkhara` water, it is called `pokkharaṃ`. It blooms having sprung from the lotus root, hence `muḷālapupphaṃ`. It beautifies the water, hence `kamalaṃ`; from the root `ala` (to beautify). It blooms having sprung from the lotus stalk, hence `bhisapupphaṃ`. It rests or stands in the `kusa` water, hence `kusesayaṃ`; with `ro`, an unelided compound. Also `tāmarasa`; `tāmaraṃ` is water—another text states: '`tāmara` also means ghee and jewel'—and because it rests or stands therein, it is called `tāmarasa`; with `ro`.

686. Sitaṃ setaṃ kamalaṃ “puṇḍarīka”ntyuccate, puḍi khaṇḍane, muḍirityeke, iko, arāgamo ca, massa po, issīkāro ca, puṇḍarīkaṃ. Rattaṃ tu kamalaṃ “kokanadaṃ, kokāsako”ti coccate. Koke nādayatīti kokanādaṃ, ṇo. Rattuppale ca, “kokanadaṃ, kokanuda”ntipi pāṭho, ke kanati dibbatīti vā kokanadaṃ, bhūvādi, do, asso. Kana dittikantigatīsu, ke kāsatīti kokāsako, ṇvu, kāsa dittiyaṃ.

686. A white lotus is called `puṇḍarīka`. From the root `puḍi` (to break)—some say `muḍi`—with the suffix `ika`, the insertion of `ara`, `ma` becoming `pa`, and the vowel `ī`, thus `puṇḍarīka`. A red lotus, however, is called `kokanada` or `kokāsaka`. It makes the `koka` bird cry out, hence `kokanādaṃ`; with `ṇo`. For the red water-lily, the readings `kokanada` and `kokanuda` also exist. Alternatively, because it shines in the water, it is called `kokanada`; from the `bhūvādi` class, with `da`, and `assa`. From the root `kana` (in the senses of shining, desiring, and moving); because it shines in the water, it is `kokāsako`; with `ṇvu`; from the root `kāsa` (in the sense of shining).

Dvayaṃ kesare, ke jāyatīti ki, kamalādi, tasmiṃ jāyati, jalatīti vā kiñjakkho, kho, nassa, lassa vā ko, niggahītāgamo, ke saratīti, a, sattamiyā alopo, dvayamanitthī. Dvayaṃ padmādidaṇḍe. Daṇḍasadisatāya daṇḍo. Nala gandhe, ṇo.

Two terms for the filament. For `kiñjakkha`: what is born in water is `ki`; what is born or shines in that lotus, etc., is `kiñjakkha`; with the suffix `kha`, `na` or `la` becoming `ka`, and the insertion of a `niggahīta`. For `kesara`: it moves in the water, hence `kesara`; with the suffix `a`, and elision of the seventh case ending. Both terms are not feminine. Two terms for the stalk of a lotus and so forth. Due to its resemblance to a stick, it is called a `daṇḍa`. From the root `nala` (in the sense of fragrance), with `ṇo`, thus `nāḷa`.

687. Dvayaṃ [M 0.0452] muḷāle. Visa peraṇe, vassa bho, bhisaṃ, bhāsa dittiyaṃ vā, ākārassi. Mūle jāyatīti muḷālo, aññatthe alo, rassādi, ḷattañca, mūla patiṭṭhāyaṃ vā, alo, sesaṃ pubbasadisaṃ, dvayaṃpyanitthī.

687. Two terms for the lotus root. From the root `visa` (to spread), with `va` becoming `bha`, thus `bhisa`. Alternatively, from the root `bhāsa` (to shine), with the long `ā` becoming `i`. It is born from the root, hence `muḷāla`; from the root `mūla` with the suffix `ala`, shortening of the vowel, and the substitution of `ḷa`. Alternatively, from the root `mūla` (to be established), with `ala`; the rest is as before. Both terms are not feminine.

Dvayaṃ kaṇṇikāyaṃ. Bījassa koso ākaro bījakoso. Kaṇṇe karīyatīti kaṇṇikā, kaṇṇālaṅkāro, taṃsadisasaṇṭhānatāya kaṇṇikā, padumādīnaṃ samūhe gahane vanetyattho. Saṇa dāne, ḍo, saṇḍaṃ, “saṇḍaṃ paddhādisaṅghāte, gopatimhi pume bhave”ti nānatthasaṅgaho.

Two terms for the pericarp. The container or source of seeds is `bījakosa`. It is made for the ear, hence `kaṇṇikā`, an ear ornament; it is called `kaṇṇikā` due to its resemblance in shape. A dense group or thicket of lotuses and so forth is a `vana`. From the root `saṇa` (to give), with `ḍo`, thus `saṇḍa`. '`Saṇḍa` is used for a collection, such as a herd, and in the masculine for a bull'—thus in the `Nānārthasaṅgaha`.

688. Dvayaṃ padmakumudādisāmaññe, tathā hi padmaṃ mahoppalaṃ sitoppalamuccate, “kuvalayaṃ uppalañca, nīlamindīvaranti hi”iti byāḍi, “uppalañca kuvalayaṃ, nīlamindīvaraṃ mata”nti bhāguri ca, “romo siti ca nīlo, kuvalayamindīvarañca nīlambuja”nti tu vararuci. “Kuvalayadalasāmopyaṅgadadhiti paridhū sara”nti māladhi, mādhavo ca, tatra pubbakamatamiha nissīyate. Yadyevaṃ kathamuppalasaddena nīluppalādīsveva buddhi, na pana mahoppalādimhīti? Vuccate – sāmaññepi dhaññatte yathā dhaññasaddena kalamādīsveva buddhi, na pana muggādīsu, evamihāpi. Upubbo [M 0.0453] pā pāne, alo, dvittaṃ, udake plavatīti vā uppalaṃ, yadādi. Kuyā pathaviyā valayaṃ iva sobhākarattā kuvalayaṃ.

688. Two terms are used in the general sense for the lotus, water-lily, and so forth. For indeed, the `padma` is called `mahoppala` and `sitoppala`. As Vyāḍi states: '`Kuvalaya`, `uppala`, and `nīlamindīvara`.' And Bhāguri says: '`Uppala`, `kuvalaya`, and `nīlamindīvara` are considered.' But Vararuci says: '`Roma`, `siti`, and `nīla`, as well as `kuvalaya`, `indīvara`, and `nīlambuja`.' Māladhi and Mādhava cite: '`Kuvalayadalasāmopyaṅgadadhiti paridhū sara`.' Here, the earlier opinion is followed. If this is so, why is the term `uppala` understood to refer only to the blue water-lily and the like, and not to the great lotus and the like? It is said: Although `dhañña` is a general term for grain, it is understood to refer only to rice and the like, not to mung beans and the like; so too here. `Uppala` is derived from the root `pā` (to drink) with the prefix `u`, with the suffix `ala` and doubling of the consonant; or, because it floats on the water, it is called `uppala`; with `yadādi`. `Kuvalaya` is so called because it beautifies the earth like a bracelet.

Dvayaṃ nīluppale. Nīlavaṇṇe, a, nīlaṃ, indatīti indī, nadādi, indī lakkhī, tassā varaṃ indīvaraṃ, inda paramissariye vā, īro.

Two terms for the blue water-lily. `Nīla` is from `nīlavaṇṇa` (blue color), with the suffix `a`. `Indīvara`: from the root `ind` (to be powerful), thus `indī`, of the `nadādi` class. `Indī` is Lakkhmī, and her choice is `indīvara`. Alternatively, from the root `inda` (in the sense of supreme lordship), with the suffix `īra`.

Asmiṃ nīluppale sete kumudaṃ nāma. Kuyaṃ modate kumudaṃ, ṇo. Assa padumādino kando sālūkamuccate. Kaṃ sukhaṃ dadātīti kando, kanda avhāne vā rodane ca. Sala gamanattho daṇḍako dhātu, uko, dīgho, sālūkaṃ.

Among these water-lilies, the white one is called `kumuda`. It delights in the earth, hence `kumuda`; with the suffix `ṇa`. Its bulb, and that of the lotus and so forth, is called `sālūka`. `Kanda`: it gives happiness, hence `kanda`; or from the root `kanda` (in the sense of calling or weeping). `Sālūka`: from the `daṇḍaka` root `sala` (meaning to go), with the suffix `uka` and lengthening of the vowel, thus `sālūka`.

689. Tikaṃ rattārattasāmaññe. Kamalato aññatarasmiṃ jalakusume, na tu ratteyeva, sugandhena yuttaṃ sogandhikaṃ. Kassa hāraṃ iva sobhākarattā kallahāraṃ, lāgamo, dvittañca. Dakaṃ sītalaṃ karotīti dakasītalikaṃ.

689. Three terms for the general category of red and non-red water-lilies. `Sogandhika`: a certain water flower other than the lotus, not necessarily red, which is endowed with fragrance. `Kallahāra`: because it is beautiful like a garland on the water, hence `kallahāra`; with the insertion and doubling of `la`. `Dakasītalika`: it makes the water cool.

Dvayaṃ sevāle. Udakaṃ sevatīti sevālo, alo, vakārāgamo, isse ca. Nīlatīti nīlikā, nīla vaṇṇe, iko, nīlavaṇṇayogato vā nīlikā, sevalopi, dvayaṃ padmayutte dese, padmasamūhe ca. Naḷinī ca paṅkajinī visinī ca sarojinī padminīti pariyāyā. “Padmasaṇḍaṃ tadākare”ti hi pariyāyaṃ ratanamālāyaṃ mādhavo, visaṃ samaṃ, tabbantatāya visinī, ino, nadādi. Ambujayogato, ambujānaṃ samūhato vā ambujinī.

Two terms for moss or algae. `Sevāla`: because it frequents water, with the suffix `ala`, the insertion of `va`, and `i` becoming `e`. `Nīlikā`: from the root `nīl` (to be blue), with the suffix `ika`; or `nīlikā` from its association with the color blue. Also `sevala`. Two terms for a place abounding in lotuses, or a cluster of lotuses. `Naḷinī`, `paṅkajinī`, `visinī`, `sarojinī`, and `padminī` are synonyms. As Mādhava states in the `Ratanamālā`, '`Padmasaṇḍa` is a synonym for their source.' `Visinī`: because it possesses lotus stalks (`visa`), with the suffix `inī`, of the `nadādi` class. `Ambujinī`: from its association with lotuses, or from being a cluster of lotuses.

690. Tilabījādayo [M 0.0454] sevālo nāma. Tatra tilabījappamāṇaṃ jalasaṇṭhitaṃ nīlādivaṇṇayuttaṃ tilabījaṃ nāma. Saṅkho nāma sapatto appakaṇḍo ukhāpidhānādippamāṇo samūlo eko sevālaviseso. Paṇako nāma bhamarasaṇṭhāno nīlavaṇṇo eko sevālaviseso, paṇa saṅkhāte, ṇvu, paṇako.

690. `Tilabīja` and others are types of algae. Among them, `tilabīja` is an aquatic formation the size of a sesame seed, possessing a blue or other such color. `Saṅkha` is a particular type of algae with leaves, a small stem, roots, and the size of a pot lid or the like. `Paṇaka` is another type of algae, shaped like a bee and blue in color. `Paṇaka` is derived from the root `paṇa` (in the sense of transacting), with the suffix `ṇvu`.

Pātālavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the Pātālavagga is concluded.

Iti sakalabyākaraṇamahāvanāsaṅgañāṇacārinā kavikuñjarakesarinā dhīmatā sirimahācaturaṅgabalena mahāmaccena viracitāyaṃ abhidhānappadīpikāvaṇṇanāyaṃ bhūkaṇḍavaṇṇanā samattā.

Thus concludes the explanation of the Earth Section in the commentary on the Abhidhānappadīpikā, composed by the wise great minister Sirimahācaturaṅgabala, a lion to poet-elephants, who wanders with knowledge unattached in the great forest of all grammar.

3. Sāmaññakaṇḍa

3. The Section on General Terms

1. Visesyādhīnavaggavaṇṇanā

1. Explanation of the Section on Dependence on the Qualified Noun

691. Iha vakkhamāne sāmaññakaṇḍe sāṅgopāṅgehi aṅgaupāṅgadvayasahitehi visesyādhīnehi visesyāyattehi visesanasaddehi sobhanādīhi saṃkiṇṇehi aññamaññavijātiyatthehi dabbakriyāguṇādīhi anekatthehi samayavaṇṇādīhi abyayehi cirassamādīhi ca kamā kamato vaggā kathyante, te ca pubbavaggasannissayā, tathā hi sobhanādayo [M 0.0455] devamanussādīsu visesanabhāvena sambandhā, kriyādayo tu tadādhāratāya, samayādayo vācakatāya, cirassamādayo taṃkriyāvisesanabhāvena, tatoyeva sādhāraṇattā sāmaññakaṇḍamidaṃ.

691. Here, in the forthcoming section on general terms (Sāmaññakaṇḍa), the groups (vaggas) are explained in due order, complete with their main and subsidiary parts, dependent on and subject to the qualified noun, intermingled with qualifying words like 'sobhana' and others, with words of various meanings from different classes such as substance, action, and quality, with indeclinables of various meanings such as 'samaya' and 'vaṇṇa', and with those like 'cirassam'. And these groups are dependent on the preceding group. Thus, 'sobhana' and others are related as qualifiers to gods, humans, and so on; actions and others, however, by being their basis; 'samaya' and others, by being expressive thereof; 'cirassam' and others, by being qualifiers of that action. Therefore, because of this common applicability, this is the Sāmaññakaṇḍa.

692. Iha satthe bhiyyo rūpantarā liṅgavinicchayo, so atrāpi vagge bhiyyo rūpantarāyevāti vippaṭipattinirāsatthaṃ byāpakanyāyamāha “guṇi”ccādinā. Tassattho – visesanabhūtā sabbe guṇasaddā, dabbasaddā, kriyāsaddā ca visesyādhīnabhāvena hetunāyeva, na bhiyyo rūpantarāpi visesanasaddena samaliṅgino siyunti, yathā – sobhanā itthī, sobhano puriso, sobhanaṃ cittaṃ.

692. Here in this treatise, the determination of gender is largely based on difference in form. Therefore, to dispel the misunderstanding that in this section also it is based on difference in form, he states a general rule with 'guṇi', etc. Its meaning is: all words denoting qualities, words denoting substances, and words denoting actions, in their capacity as qualifiers, become of the same gender as the qualified noun solely by reason of their dependence on it, and not due to any difference in their own form. For example: 'sobhanā itthī' (a beautiful woman), 'sobhano puriso' (a handsome man), 'sobhanaṃ cittaṃ' (a beautiful mind).

693-696. Subhantaṃ sobhane. Subha sobhane, yu. Ruca dittiyaṃ, iro. Sādha saṃsiddhiyaṃ, u. Manaṃ tosetīti manuññaṃ. Ñā parimāṇatosananisāmanesu, antassukāro, manaṃ ā bhuso tosetīti vā manuññaṃ, tadā “mano añña”nti chedo, ālopo. Cara gatibhakkhanesu, ṇvu, carati cittametthāti cāru. Suṭṭhu darīyate sundaraṃ, dara dāraṇe[M 0.0456]. Vagga gamane, u, vaggu. Mano ramati asmiṃ. Kamu icchāyaṃ, to. Harati cittaṃ hārī, ṇī. Mana ñāṇe, ju, mano javati yasmiṃ vā mañju, nalopo. Piyasīlayuttatāya pesalaṃ, piyassa pe, īssattaṃ. Bhadi kalyāṇe, do. Vā gatiyaṃ, mo. Kala saṅkhyāne, yāṇo. Manaṃ appeti vaḍḍhetīti manāpaṃ, mano appoti yasminti vā manāpaṃ, āpa pāpuṇane, apādipubbo ca. Labhitabbanti laddhaṃ, to, sakatthe ko. Subhatīti subhaṃ, sundarena sabhāvena bhavatīti vā subhaṃ.

693-696. The word 'subha' and its synonyms are in the sense of 'beautiful'. 'Subha' is from the root 'subh' (to shine), with the suffix 'yu'. 'Rucira' is from 'ruc' (to shine), with 'ira'. 'Sādhu' is from 'sādh' (to accomplish), with 'u'. 'Manuñña' is so called because it pleases the mind (manaṃ toseti); it is from 'ñā' (to measure, satisfy, observe), where the final vowel becomes 'u'. Or, 'manuñña' is so called because it greatly pleases the mind (manaṃ ā bhuso toseti); in that case, the analysis is 'mano añña', with elision of 'o'. 'Cāru' is from 'car' (to go, eat), with 'ṇvu'; or, because the mind moves in it (carati cittamettha). 'Sundara' is so called because it is well-split (suṭṭhu darīyate), from 'dar' (to split). 'Vaggu' is from 'vagg' (to go), with 'u'. 'Manorama' is so called because the mind delights in it (mano ramati asmiṃ). 'Kanta' is from 'kam' (to wish), with the suffix 'ta'. 'Hārī' is so called because it captivates the mind (harati cittaṃ), with 'ṇī'. 'Mañju' is from 'man' (to know), with 'ju'; or, because the mind is swift in it (mano javati yasmiṃ), with elision of 'na'. 'Pesala' is so called because it is endowed with beloved virtues (piyasīlayuttatāya), with 'piya' becoming 'pe', and the lengthening of 'i'. 'Bhadda' is from 'bhad' (to be auspicious), with the suffix 'ra'. 'Vāma' is from 'vā' (to go), with 'ma'. 'Kalyāṇa' is from 'kal' (to count), with 'yāṇa'. 'Manāpa' is so called because it pleases and increases the mind (manaṃ appeti vaḍḍheti); or, because the mind attains it (mano appoti yasminti), from 'āp' (to attain), with 'apa' etc. as prefix. 'Laddha' is so called because it is fit to be obtained (labhitabbaṃ), with the suffix 'ta', and 'ka' in its own sense. 'Subha' is so called because it shines (subhati); or, because it exists with a beautiful nature (sundarena sabhāvena bhavati).

Puṅgavantaṃ uttame, ubbhuto atyatthaṃ uttamo, ubhasaddato ubbhutatthato visesatthe tamo, uggatatamattā vā uttamo. Vara patthanāyaṃ, pavaro. Iṭṭhapaccaye vuḍḍhassa jādeso, jeṭṭho. Pakaṭṭhaṃ mukhaṃ ārambho assa pamukho. Natthi uttaro uttamo yasmā anuttaro. Pamukho ca anuttaro cāti dvando. Apādipubbe varo. Mukhamiva mukhyo, ivatthe yo. Padadhātīti padhānaṃ, yu. Pamukhabhāve tiṭṭhatīti pāmokkho, ubhayatrāpi vuḍḍhi. Pakaṭṭhaṃ rātīti paraṃ, ṇo. “Agga”nti jānitabbanti aggaññaṃ, “agga”nti pamānitabbanti vā aggaññaṃ. Uttaro uttamasadiso. Padhānabhāvaṃ nītaṃ paṇītaṃ, nī naye, kammani ṇo. Paraṃ paccanīkaṃ māretīti paramaṃ, pakaṭṭhabhāve ramatītivā paramaṃ, ṇo. Iyiṭṭhesu pasatthassa, vuḍḍhassa ca so, seyyo, seṭṭho ca, “kvacāsavaṇṇaṃ lutte”ti isse. Gāmaṃ netīti gāmaṇi, “tassīlādīsu ṇī tvāvī cā”ti ṇī, rasso, gāmaṇi. Santatamatāya sattamo, santato tamo, santassa ca so. Visesīyateti visiṭṭho, sisa visesane, to. Ara gamane, ṇyo, ikārāgamo, ariyo. Natthi aggo yasmā nāgo, dīghādi, galopo ca. I gatiyaṃ, ṇvu, isse, alopo ca, eko, sadisarahitatāya vā ekībhāve tiṭṭhatīti eko, ko. Ussāpeti paccanīketi usabho, usa dāhe, abho[M 0.0457]. Aja gamane, a, jassa go, dvittaṃ, aggo. Muca mocane, hīnamajjhimabhāvehi muccatīti mokkho, to, tassa kho. Mokkha mocane vā, a. Padhānabhāvaṃ gacchatīti puṅgavo, yadādi, pukkhalopyatra, pusa vuḍḍhimhi, alo, sassa kho, asarūpadvittaṃ. Ete cuttamādayo samāsagāpi asamāsagāpi uttamatthavācakā. Amarakose pana nāgosabhapuṅgavānaṃ samāsagatteyeva uttamatthavācakatā vuttā, vuttañca –

The word 'puṅgava' and its synonyms are used in the sense of 'supreme'. 'Uttama' is so called because one is exceedingly exalted (ubbhuto atyatthaṃ); or from the word 'ubha' in the sense of 'exalted', with the suffix 'tama' in a special sense; or from being in the most elevated state (uggatatamattā). 'Pavara' is from 'var' (to wish), with the prefix 'pa'. 'Jeṭṭha' is formed from the base 'vuḍḍha' with the superlative suffix '-iṭṭha', where 'vuḍḍha' is replaced by 'ja'. 'Pamukha' is one whose face (mukha) or beginning (ārambho) is prominent (pakaṭṭhaṃ). 'Anuttara' is one than whom there is no higher (uttaro) or more supreme (uttamo). 'Pamukho ca anuttaro ca' is a dvanda compound. 'Avara' is from 'vara' with the prefix 'apa'. 'Mukkhya' is so called because one is like the face (mukhamiva), with the suffix 'ya' in the sense of 'like'. 'Padhāna' is so called because it sets forth (padadhāti), with the suffix 'yu'. 'Pāmokkha' is so called because one stands in the position of being foremost (pamukhabhāve tiṭṭhati); in both ('pamukha' and 'pāmokkha'), there is vowel strengthening (vuḍḍhi). 'Para' is so called because it gives prominence (pakaṭṭhaṃ rāti), with the suffix 'ṇa'. 'Aggañña' is so called because 'agga' (foremost) is to be known (jānitabbaṃ); or because 'agga' is to be esteemed (pamānitabbaṃ). 'Uttara' is similar to 'uttama'. 'Paṇīta' is so called because it is led (nītaṃ) to a prominent state (padhānabhāvaṃ), from 'nī' (to lead), with the suffix 'ṇa' in the passive sense. 'Parama' is so called because it destroys (māreti) the opposing force (paraṃ paccanīkaṃ); or because it delights (ramati) in a prominent state (pakaṭṭhabhāve), with the suffix 'ṇa'. For the bases 'pasattha' (praised) and 'vuḍḍha' (old), with the suffixes '-iya' and '-iṭṭha', 'sa' is the substitute, yielding 'seyya' and 'seṭṭha'. 'Gāmaṇi' is so called because he leads the village (gāmaṃ neti), with the suffix 'ṇī' according to the rule 'tassīlādīsu...', and shortening of the vowel. 'Sattama' is from 'santata' (continuous) with the suffix 'tama'; or from 'santa' (peaceful), with 'sa' as a substitute. 'Visiṭṭha' is so called because it is distinguished (visesīyate), from 'sis' (to distinguish), with the suffix 'ta'. 'Ariya' is from 'ar' (to go), with the suffix 'ṇya', and the insertion of 'i'. 'Nāga' is so called because there is no superior (na aggo) to it, with lengthening of the initial vowel and elision of 'ga'. 'Eka' is from 'i' (to go), with the suffix 'ṇvu' ('aka'), elision of 'a', and substitution; or because it stands in a state of oneness (ekībhāve tiṭṭhati) due to being without an equal, with the suffix 'ka'. 'Usabha' is so called because it raises up (ussāpeti) and opposes (paccanīketi), from 'us' (to burn), with the suffix 'abha'. 'Agga' is from 'aj' (to go), with the suffix 'a', 'j' becoming 'g', and doubling. 'Mokkha' is from 'muc' (to release); or because one is released (muccati) from lower and middling states, with the suffix 'ta' which becomes 'kha'. Or it is from 'mokkh' (to release), with 'a'. 'Puṅgava' is so called because it goes (gacchati) to a prominent state (padhānabhāvaṃ), with complex derivation. These words from 'uttama' onwards signify 'supreme', whether they are compounded or not. In the Amarakośa, however, it is said that 'nāga', 'usabha', and 'puṅgava' signify 'supreme' only when compounded. And it is said:

“Uttarasmiṃ pade byaggha-puṅgavo’sabhakuñjarā;

Sīhasaddūlanāgādyā, pume seṭṭhatthagocarā”ti amara 21.59.

“When in the latter part of a compound, the words 'byaggha', 'puṅgava', 'usabha', 'kuñjara', 'sīha', 'saddūla', 'nāga', and others, being masculine, convey the meaning of 'foremost'.”

Tassattho – byagghādayo kammadhārayasamāse sati uttarapadībhūtā seṭṭhatthavisayā pubbapadassa seṭṭhatthavācakā pulliṅgā ca bhavanti, yathā “purisabyaggho, munipuṅgavo”iccādi. Sīhādayo, ādinā varāhapuṇḍarīkadhorayhasovīrādayo ca samāsagā kammadhārayasamāse uttarapadabhūtā seṭṭhatthavācakā pumeva bhavanti, yathā “sakyasīho, kavikuñjaro, purisasaddūlo, purisavarāho”iccādi.

Its meaning is: When words like 'byaggha' and others become the latter term in a karmadhāraya compound, they, being masculine, express the meaning of 'foremost' for the former term, as in 'purisabyaggho' (a man-tiger, i.e., foremost among men), 'munipuṅgavo' (a sage-bull, i.e., foremost among sages), and so on. Words like 'sīha' and others—including 'varāha', 'puṇḍarīka', 'dhorayha', 'sovīra', etc.—when compounded and becoming the latter term in a karmadhāraya compound, are masculine and express the meaning of 'foremost', as in 'sakyasīho' (a Sakyan lion, i.e., foremost among Sakyans), 'kavikuñjaro' (a poet-elephant, i.e., foremost among poets), 'purisasaddūlo' (a man-leopard, i.e., foremost among men), 'purisavarāho' (a man-boar, i.e., foremost among men), and so on.

697. Cittassa, akkhino ca pītijanakaṃ vatthu abyāsekaṃ, asecanañca nāma, na byāsiñcanti nakkharanti nayanamanāni yasmāti abyāsekaṃ, asecanañca, na byāsiñcanti ca yasmiṃ āgantukabhūtāni aññarasānīti vā abyāsekaṃ, asecanañca. Ṇo, yu ca.

697. An object that generates delight for the mind and the eye is called 'abyāseka' and 'asecana'. They are so called because the eyes and mind are not scattered or distracted from it. Or, they are so called because other, adventitious flavors do not pervade it. The suffixes are 'ṇa' and 'yu' respectively.

Chakkaṃ iṭṭhe vatthumhi. Icchitabbaṃ, esitabbanti vā iṭṭhaṃ, isu icchāyaṃ, isa gavesane ca, to. Subhattaṃ gacchatīti subhagaṃ, kvi. Hadaye sādhu, hadayassa vā piyanti hajjaṃ, ṇo, dantassa lopo, dyassa jjo. Dayitabbaṃ ādātabbanti dayitaṃ, [M 0.0458] to. Valla saṃvaraṇe, kammani abho. Piyāyitabbanti piyaṃ,pī tappanakantīsu, ṇyo, rassādi.

A group of six terms for a desirable object. 'Iṭṭha' is that which is to be desired (icchitabbaṃ) or sought (esitabbaṃ), from 'isu' (to desire) and 'isa' (to seek), with the suffix 'ta'. 'Subhaga' is that which attains (gacchati) a beautiful state (subhattaṃ), with the suffix 'kvi'. 'Hajja' is that which is good for the heart (hadaye sādhu) or dear to the heart (hadayassa piyaṃ), with the suffix 'ṇa', elision of the final 'da' of 'hadaya', and 'dy' becoming 'jja'. 'Dayita' is that which is to be given (dayitabbaṃ) or taken (ādātabbaṃ), with the suffix 'ta'. 'Vallabha' is from 'valla' (to cover), with the suffix 'abha' in the passive sense. 'Piya' is that which is to be cherished (piyāyitabbaṃ), from 'pī' (to delight, to please), with the suffix 'ṇya', shortening, etc.

698. Tikaṃ tucche. Tuca vināse, cho. Rica viyojanasambajjhanesu, sambajjhanaṃ missanaṃ, to, sakatthe ko. Sunassa hitaṃ suññaṃ, yo, nyassa ñño, suna gatiyaṃ vā, yo. Dvayaṃ asāre. Phala nipphattiyaṃ, u, gu vā. Pubbatra gonto, asse, pheggu.

698. A group of three terms for the worthless. 'Tuccha' is from 'tuc' (to destroy), with the suffix 'cha'. 'Ritta' is from 'ric' (to separate, to join; joining means mixing), with the suffix 'ta', and 'ka' in its own sense. 'Suñña' is that which is fit for a dog (sunassa hitaṃ), with the suffix 'ya', where 'ny' becomes 'ñña'; or it is from 'suna' (to go), with 'ya'. A group of two terms for the sapless. From 'phal' (to produce), with the suffix 'u' or 'gu', giving 'pheggu'.

Tikaṃ pavitte. Medha hiṃsāsaṅgamesu, medhīyate saṅgamīyate mejjhaṃ, ṇyo, jhassa jho, asarūpadvittaṃ. Pu pavane, to, dīghādi. Vuḍḍhāvādeso, ikārāgamo ca. Dvayaṃ aviraddhe. Na virajjhatīti aviraddho, radha hiṃsāparādhāpagamanesu, to. “Dhaḍhabhahehi dhaḍhā ce”ti tassa dho. Paṇa byavahārathutīsu, ṇvu, viraddhavohārena na paṇāmetīti apaṇṇako.

A group of three terms for the pure. 'Mejjha' is from 'medh' (to harm, to engage); it is that which is engaged with (medhīyate, saṅgamīyate), with the suffix 'ṇya', where 'dh' becomes 'jjh' through doubling. 'Pūta' is from 'pu' (to purify), with the suffix 'ta' and lengthening of the vowel. 'Pavitra' is also from 'pu', with vṛddhi substitution and the insertion of 'i'. A group of two terms for the unfailing. 'Aviraddha' is that which does not fail (na virajjhati), from 'radh' (to harm, offend, fail), with the suffix 'ta', which becomes 'dha' according to the rule 'dhaḍhabhahehi...'. 'Apaṇṇaka' is from 'paṇ' (to transact, praise), with the suffix 'ṇvu'; it is one who does not set aside something through a failed transaction (viraddhavohārena na paṇāmeti).

699-701. Dvayaṃ jātyācārādinā anindite. Upubbo, papubbo ca kasa vilekhane, hiṃsāyañca, to, “sādisantapucchabhanjahaṃsādīhi ṭṭho”ti sahādibyañjanena tassa ṭṭho.

699-701. A group of two terms for that which is blameless by birth, conduct, etc. From the root 'kas' (to plow, to harm), preceded by 'u' and 'pa', with the suffix 'ta'. According to the rule 'sādisantapucchabhanjahaṃsādīhi ṭṭho', the 's' of the root is elided and the 't' of the suffix becomes 'ṭṭha', yielding 'ukkaṭṭha' and 'pakkaṭṭha'.

Gārayhantaṃ [M 0.0459] jātyācārādinā nindite. Nihīyateti nihīno, hā cāge, ino, dīgho. Apādipubbe hīno. Lama nindāyaṃ, ṇvu, lāmako. Kiṭa gatiyaṃ, pati nipubbo tu nindāyaṃ, ṭho, patikiṭṭhaṃ, nikiṭṭhañca. Ittarasaddo lāmakatthavācako pāṭipadiko, “jātyācārādīhi nihīnoya”nti avaditabboti avajjo, tabbhāvattho cettha akāro. Vada viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, ṇyo, dyassa jjo. Kucchā sañjātā assa kucchito. Adhobhāge jāto adhamo, ossattaṃ. Uma nindāyaṃ, kamme a, sakatthe ko, usso, omako. Garahitabboti gārayho, garaha nindāyaṃ, ṇyo, vaṇṇavipariyayo.

Terms ending in `gārayha` for that which is censured by birth, conduct, etc. That which is abandoned is `nihīno`, from the root `hā` in the sense of abandoning, with the suffix `ino` and vowel lengthening. `Hīno` has prefixes such as `apa`. `Lāmako` is from the root `lama` in the sense of blaming, with the suffix `ṇvu`. `Patikiṭṭhaṃ` and `nikiṭṭhaṃ` are from the root `kiṭa` in the sense of going, but with the prefixes `pati` and `ni` respectively, it is in the sense of blame; the suffix is `ṭha`. The word `ittara` is a nominal stem denoting something of little worth. `Avajjo` is so called because it is not to be spoken of, as in 'This one is inferior due to birth, conduct, etc.'; here the `a` is in the sense of that state. `Avajjo` is from the root `vada` in the sense of articulate speech, with the suffix `ṇya`, and `dy` becomes `jj`. One for whom disgust has arisen is `kucchito`. `Adhamo` is one born in a lower part; it means inferior. `Omako` is from the root `uma` in the sense of blaming, with the suffix `a` in the sense of object, `ko` in its own sense, and `o` for `u`. `Gārayho` is that which is to be censured, from the root `garaha` in the sense of blaming, with the suffix `ṇya`, and a metathesis of letters.

Dvayaṃ malayutte. Malayuttatāya malīno, ino, dīgho. Assatthyatthe ī, masapaccaye malīmaso, kaccaraṃ, maladūsitampi, kucchitaṃ caratīti kaccaraṃ.

Two terms for that which is joined with stain. `Malīno` is so called because of being joined with stain, with the suffix `ino` and vowel lengthening. In the possessive sense, with the suffixes `ī` and `masa`, it becomes `malīmaso`. `Kaccaraṃ` also means defiled by stain. Alternatively, `kaccaraṃ` is that which behaves in a repulsive way.

Tipādaṃ vipule. Braha vuddhiyaṃ, rājādi, brahā. Maha pūjāyaṃ, anto. Pula mahatte, vipulaṃ. Sala gamane, visālaṃ, ṇo. Patha saṅkhyāne, ulo, assu, puthulaṃ, umhi puthu. Gara secane, u, garu. Ara gamane, u, assu, uru. Tanu vitthāre, to, iṇṇādeso, tassa tho, assi, asarūpadvittaṃ, vitthiṇṇaṃ.

A three-line stanza on 'broad' or 'extensive'. `Brahā` is from the root `braha` in the sense of growing; it is in the `rājādi` group. `Maha` is from the root `maha` in the sense of honoring, with the suffix `anta`. `Vipulaṃ` is from the root `pula` in the sense of greatness. `Visālaṃ` is from the root `sala` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ṇa`. `Puthulaṃ` is from the root `patha` in the sense of counting, with the suffix `ula`, and `a` becomes `u`; it is `puthu` in the locative singular. `Garu` is from the root `gara` in the sense of sprinkling, with the suffix `u`. `Uru` is from the root `ara` in the sense of going, with the suffix `u`, and `a` becomes `u`. `Vitthiṇṇaṃ` is from the root `tanu` in the sense of spreading, with the suffix `ta`; `iṇṇa` is substituted, `t` becomes `th`, `a` becomes `i`, and there is non-homorganic gemination.

Vaṭharantaṃ thūle. Pī tappanakantīsu, ino. Thūla paribrūhane, a. Pīdhātuto īvaro, pīvaraṃ. Lapaccaye thullaṃ, rassādi. Vada viyattiyaṃ vācāyaṃ, vadatīti vaṭharaṃ, aro, dassa ṭho. Thūlamupacitamaṃsavipulāyatamaṃsādi.

Terms ending in `vaṭhara` for 'thick' or 'stout'. `Pīno` is from the root `pī` in the senses of satisfying and pleasing, with the suffix `ino`. `Thūla` is from the root `thūla` in the sense of making thick, with the suffix `a`. `Pīvaraṃ` is from the root `pī` with the suffix `īvara`. With the suffix `la`, it becomes `thullaṃ`, with shortening, etc. `Vaṭharaṃ` is that which speaks, from the root `vada` in the sense of articulate speech, with the suffix `ara`, and `d` becomes `ṭh`. 'Thick' means having accumulated flesh, broad and extensive flesh, and so on.

Dvayaṃ sannicite. Ānipubbo ci caye, kamme to, ācitaṃ, nicitañca.

Two terms for 'amassed'. `Ācitaṃ` and `nicitaṃ` are from the root `ci` in the sense of accumulating, with the prefixes `ā` and `ni` respectively, and the suffix `ta` in the sense of object.

702. Siloko [M 0.0460] sabbasmiṃ. Saratīti sabbaṃ, vo, rassa ca vo. Saṃpubbo asu khepane, to, samattaṃ, atha vā sama tima vekallabye, to, samattaṃ. Na khiyatīti akhilaṃ, lo, akhilaṃ, nikhilañca tathā. Saka sattiyaṃ, alo, kalābhi avayavehi saha vattateti vā sakalaṃ. Sesato avasiṭṭhato niggataṃ nissesaṃ. Kasa gamane, ino, ṇattaṃ, kasiṇaṃ. Na sesaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ asesaṃ. Aggena sikharena saṅgataṃ samaggaṃ. Kate samāse pubbanipāto abhidhānā. Ūna parihāne, na ūnaṃ asmiṃ anūnakaṃ, ko.

702. A verse on 'all'. `Sabbaṃ` is that which moves, from the root `sara`, with the suffix `va`, and `r` also becomes `v`. `Samattaṃ` is from the root `asu` in the sense of throwing, with the prefix `saṃ`, and the suffix `ta`; alternatively, `samattaṃ` is from the root `sama` or `tima` in the sense of being incomplete, with the suffix `ta`. `Akhilaṃ` is that which is not diminished, with the suffix `la`; `nikhilaṃ` is likewise. `Sakalaṃ` is from the root `saka` in the sense of being able, with the suffix `ala`; or, it is that which exists together with its parts and limbs. `Nissesaṃ` is that which has gone out from the remainder. `Kasiṇaṃ` is from the root `kasa` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ina`, and `n` becomes `ṇ`. `Asesaṃ` is that which has no remainder. `Samaggaṃ` is that which is joined with the top or peak. When a compound is formed, the placement of the prior member is by convention. `Anūnakaṃ` is that in which there is no deficiency, from the root `ūna` in the sense of diminishing, with the suffix `ka`.

703. Bahulantaṃ bahutte, bhāveti vaḍḍhetīti bhūri, bhū sattāyaṃ, ri, bhūri, dīghādi, rassanto, īmhi bhūrī, medhā. Pahu sattiyaṃ, to, ukārāgamo, papubbo hū sattāyaṃ vā, rasso. Paci vitthāre, uro, pacuraṃ. Bhī bhaye, bhāyati yasmāti bhiyyo, dvittaṃ. Sampahotīti sampahulaṃ, lo. Baha vuḍḍhiyaṃ, u, bahu. Yebhuyyasaddo bahulatthavācako pāṭipadiko. Bahū atthe lābhīti bahulaṃ.

703. Terms ending in `bahula` for 'much' or 'abundance'. `Bhūri` is that which causes to be or increases, from the root `bhū` in the sense of being, with the suffix `ri`; `bhūri` has a long initial vowel but ends in a short vowel; in the feminine, `bhūrī` means wisdom. `Pahu` is from the root `pahu` in the sense of being able, with the suffix `ta` and the insertion of `u`; or, it is from the root `hū` in the sense of being, with the prefix `pa`, and shortening. `Pacuraṃ` is from the root `paci` in the sense of spreading, with the suffix `ura`. `Bhiyyo` is from the root `bhī` in the sense of fear, because one fears it; with gemination. `Sampahulaṃ` is that which is very able, with the suffix `la`. `Bahu` is from the root `baha` in the sense of growing, with the suffix `u`. The word `yebhuyya` is a nominal stem denoting abundance. `Bahulaṃ` is that which obtains many things.

Dvayaṃ bahigate. Bahi jātaṃ bāhiraṃ, iraṇa.

Two terms for 'external' or 'gone outside'. `Bāhiraṃ` is that which is born outside, with the suffix `iraṇa`.

704-706. Yesaṃ [M 0.0461] padatthānaṃ mattaṃ pamāṇaṃ satādito paraṃ adhikaṃ bhavati, te parosatādī. Ādinā parosahassādi. Satato paro parosataṃ. Sahassato paro parosahassaṃ, parassa pubbanipāto abhidhānā parasaddā okārāgamo. Pajjaṃ appe. Parito attaṃ khaṇḍitaṃ parittaṃ. Sukha takriyāyaṃ, takriyā sukhanaṃ, umo. Suca socane vā. Khuda pipāsāyaṃ, do, khuddaṃ. Thuca pasāde, ṇo. Ala bhūsanapariyattinivāraṇesu, po, lassa po, appaṃ. Kisa tanukaraṇe, ṇo. Tanu vitthāre. Ci caye, ulo, dvittaṃ, cullaṃ, nīce pana cullo. Mā māne, chadādīhi to. Rassādi, mattā, itthiyaṃ. Lisa appībhāve, a. Lū chedane, luyateti lavo, a. Aṇa gatyattho, u. Kaṇa sadde, a, kaṇo. Lavādīhi saha kaṇo pume, vuttañca amarakose “pume lavalesakaṇāṇavo”ti amara 21.62.

704-706. Those terms whose measure or quantity is more than or beyond a hundred, etc., are `parosatādī`. By `ādi` (etc.), `parosahassādi` (beyond a thousand, etc.) is included. `Parosataṃ` is beyond a hundred. `Parosahassaṃ` is beyond a thousand; the prior placement of `para` is by convention, and there is an insertion of the vowel `o` for the word `para`. A verse on 'little'. `Parittaṃ` is that which is taken or cut all around. `Sukhumaṃ` is from `sukha` in the sense of doing; the action is making happy, with the suffix `uma`. Or it is from `suca` in the sense of purifying. `Khuddaṃ` is from the root `khuda` in the sense of hunger, with the suffix `da`. `Thokaṃ` is from `thuca` in the sense of clearness, with the suffix `ṇa`. `Appaṃ` is from the root `ala` in the senses of adorning, being sufficient, and preventing, with the suffix `pa`, and `l` becomes `p`. `Kisa` is from the root `kisa` in the sense of making thin, with the suffix `ṇa`. `Tanu` is from the root `tanu` in the sense of spreading. `Cullaṃ` is from the root `ci` in the sense of accumulating, with the suffix `ula` and gemination; but `cullo` means 'low'. `Mattā` is from the root `mā` in the sense of measuring, with the suffix `ta` from the `chadādi` group; with shortening, etc., it is feminine. `Lesa` is from the root `lisa` in the sense of becoming small, with the suffix `a`. `Lavo` is from the root `lū` in the sense of cutting, meaning 'it is cut', with the suffix `a`. `Aṇu` is from the root `aṇa` which has the sense of going, with the suffix `u`. `Kaṇo` is from the root `kaṇa` in the sense of sounding, with the suffix `a`. `Kaṇo` along with `lava`, etc., is masculine, and it is said in the Amarakośa: '`lava`, `lesa`, `kaṇa`, and `aṇu` are masculine'.

Ñattantaṃ [M 0.0462] samīpe. Saṅgatā āpo yasmiṃ samīpaṃ, āssī. Pādito yadādinā kaṭo, nikaṭo, natthi kaṭo āvaraṇaṃ etassāti vā nikaṭo. Sadasmā to, āsanno. Kaṇṭhaṃ samīpaṃ upagataṃ upakaṭṭho. “Kaṇṭho gale sanniṭṭhāne, sadde madanapādape”ti hi nānatthasaṅgaho, idha pana kaṇṭhassa kaṭṭhādeso, ṇalopo vā. Abhyāsīdatīti abhyāso. “Abhyāso tu samīpamhi, pumā abhyasanepi ce”ti cintāmaṇiṭīkā 21.67 rabhaso. Saha antena santikaṃ, sakatthe iko. Vidūrapaṭipakkhattā avidūraṃ. Saṅgataṃ antaṃ sāmantaṃ, sasaddassa dīgho, niggahītassa mo, saṃ nipubbopi kaṭṭhasaddo samīpatthoyevāti dassanatthaṃ udāhaṭaṃ, kasa vilekhane vā, to, sannikaṭṭhaṃ. Antikabhāvaṃ upagataṃ upantikaṃ. Saha kāsena vattate sakāsaṃ, kāsa dittiyaṃ. Antayogā antikaṃ, iko. Ñāyateti ñattaṃ, to, sakāsasaddena saniḍasadesasavidhasamariyādasavesāpi gayhanti. Saha niḍena, saha desena, saha vidhāya, saha mariyādāya, saha vesena vattateti viggaho, byuppattinimittaṃ, rūḷhīsaddā pana ete.

Terms ending in `ñatta` for 'nearness'. `Samīpaṃ` is where waters come together; `ā` becomes `ī`. `Nikaṭo` is from `kaṭa` with `yadādi` from `pāda`; or, `nikaṭo` is that for which there is no covering. `Āsanno` is from the root `sad`, with the suffix `ta`. `Upakaṭṭho` is that which has approached near the throat. Indeed, from the Nānatthasaṅgaha: '`Kaṇṭha` means throat, proximity, sound, and the madana tree'; here, however, `kaṭṭha` is a substitute for `kaṇṭha`, or there is elision of `ṇa`. `Abhyāso` is that which sits near. According to Rabhasa: '`Abhyāso` means nearness, and in the masculine, also practice'. `Santikaṃ` is 'with the end', with the suffix `ika` in its own sense. `Avidūraṃ` is so called because it is the opposite of `vidūra` (far). `Sāmantaṃ` is a conjoined end; the vowel of `sa` is lengthened, and the `niggahīta` becomes `m`. The example is given to show that the word `kaṭṭha` with the prefixes `saṃ` and `ni` also has the meaning of nearness; or, `sannikaṭṭhaṃ` is from the root `kasa` in the sense of scratching, with the suffix `ta`. `Upantikaṃ` is that which has approached a state of nearness. `Sakāsaṃ` is that which exists with visibility, from the root `kāsa` in the sense of shining. `Antikaṃ` is from connection with the end, with the suffix `ika`. `Ñattaṃ` is that which is known, with the suffix `ta`. By the word `sakāsa`, `saniḍa`, `sadesa`, `savidha`, `samariyāda`, and `savesa` are also included. The analysis is: 'existing with a nest', 'with a place', 'with a manner', 'with a boundary', 'with an appearance'. This is the etymological reason, but these are conventional words.

Dvayaṃ dūramatte. Dukkhena arati yaṃ dūraṃ. Vipapubbo kaṭṭhasaddo dūre, sakatthe ko, vippakaṭṭhakaṃ.

Two terms for 'distance'. `Dūraṃ` is that to which one goes with difficulty. `Vippakaṭṭhakaṃ` is the word `kaṭṭha` with the prefix `vippa`, in the sense of distance, with the suffix `ka` in its own sense.

707. Tikaṃ ghane, natthi antaraṃ chiddaṃ yassa. Hanatismā a, hassa gho ca, ghanaṃ. Samu upasame, do, sandaṃ. Pādo viraḷe. Viramatīti viraḷaṃ, a, vaṇṇavikāro. Piyo lavo appo yasmiṃ pelavaṃ, piyassa pe, pili gamane vā, avo. Tanu appādīsupi.

707. Three terms for 'dense', which is that which has no interval or gap. `Ghanaṃ` is from the root `han`, with the suffix `a`, and `h` becomes `gh`. `Sandaṃ` is from the root `samu` in the sense of being calm, with the suffix `da`. A line on 'sparse'. `Viraḷaṃ` is that which ceases, with the suffix `a` and a letter modification. `Pelavaṃ` is that in which what is dear or what is cut is small; `piya` becomes `pe`. Alternatively, it is from the root `pili` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ava`. `Tanu` is also in the senses of 'little', etc.

Dvayaṃ [M 0.0463] dīghe. Yata āyatane, āyataṃ. I gamane vā, to, bhūvādi, isse, e aya, dīghādi. Di khaye, gho, dīghādi. Tikaṃ vaṭṭale. Niggataṃ talaṃ asmāti nittalaṃ. Vaṭṭa vaṭṭane, vaṭṭaṃ, latādi. Ulapaccaye vaṭṭulaṃ.

Two terms for 'long'. `Āyataṃ` is from the root `yata` in the sense of extending. `Dīghaṃ` is from the root `i` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ta`, from the `bhūvādi` group; `i` becomes `e`, then `aya`, with lengthening, etc. Alternatively, it is from the root `di` in the sense of wasting away, with the suffix `gha`, and lengthening, etc. Three terms for 'round'. `Nittalaṃ` is that from which the surface has gone out. `Vaṭṭaṃ` is from the root `vaṭṭa` in the sense of turning, like `latā`, etc. `Vaṭṭulaṃ` is formed with the suffix `ula`.

708. Ucchitantaṃ unnate. Ci caye, uccinotīti ucco, a. Unnamatīti unnato. Tuja hiṃsāyaṃ, phalane ca, a, tuṅgo. Uggataṃ aggaṃ assa udaggo. Uddhaṃ sito ucchito, si sevāyaṃ, to, sassa cho, asarūpadvittaṃ, ucchito. Paṃsupi, pakaṭṭho aṃsu ditti yassa paṃsu.

708. Terms ending in `ucchita` for 'elevated' or 'high'. `Ucco` is that which accumulates, from the root `ci` in the sense of accumulating, with the suffix `a`. `Unnato` is that which rises up. `Tuṅgo` is from the root `tuja` in the senses of harming and bursting forth, with the suffix `a`. `Udaggo` is that whose summit has gone up. `Ucchito` is that which is attached above, from the root `si` in the sense of resorting to, with the suffix `ta`; `s` becomes `ch`, with non-homorganic gemination. `Paṃsu` is also a term; it is that whose prominent ray is its radiance.

Tikaṃ vāmane. Uddhaṃ na añcatīti nīco, añca gamane, ṇo, akārañakārānaṃ lopo, nisaddo atra nisedhe. Rasa sadde, so, rasso. Vā gamane, mano, vāmano.

Three terms for 'dwarf' or 'short'. `Nīco` is that which does not go upwards, from the root `añca` in the sense of going, with the suffix `ṇa`, and elision of `a` and `ñ`; here the word `ni` is in the sense of negation. `Rasso` is from the root `rasa` in the sense of sounding, with the suffix `sa`. `Vāmano` is from the root `vā` in the sense of going, with the suffix `mana`.

Tikaṃ ujumhi. Na jimhaṃ kuṭilaṃ ajimhaṃ. Tasmiṃ avaṅkatāya pakaṭṭho guṇo yassa paguṇo. Aja gamane, u, assu, uju.

Three terms for 'straight'. `Ajimhaṃ` is that which is not crooked or bent. `Paguṇo` is that whose prominent quality is its straightness. `Uju` is from the root `aja` in the sense of going, with the suffix `u`, and `a` becomes `u`.

709. Chakkaṃ vaṅke. Aladhātumhā aro, ḷattaṃ. Vela gamane, to, dvittādi, virūpena ilayatīti vā vellitaṃ, to, ila gamane. Vaṅka koṭilye, a. Kuṭa chedane, ilo, kuṭa koṭilye vā. Hā cāge, kattari mo, dvittaṃ, vaṇṇavipariyayādi, jimhaṃ. Kuñca koṭilye, to. Vakkampi, vakka gamane.

709. Six [terms] for 'crooked'. From the root ala, with the suffix aro, and the change to ḷ. From the root vela in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix to, doubling [of consonants], etc.; or, 'it bends with distortion', thus vellitaṃ; from the root ila in the sense of 'to go', with the suffix to. From the root vaṅka in the sense of 'crookedness', with the suffix a. From the root kuṭa in the sense of 'to cut', with the suffix ilo; or from kuṭa in the sense of 'crookedness'. From the root hā in the sense of 'to abandon', with the suffix mo in the agentive sense, with doubling [of consonants], reversal of letters, etc., [resulting in] jimhaṃ. From the root kuñca in the sense of 'crookedness', with the suffix to. Also vakkaṃ, from the root vakka in the sense of 'to go'.

Pañcakaṃ [M 0.0464] dhuve. Dhu gatitheriyesu, a, uvādeso. Sassate nicce bhavo sassato. Nicco vutto abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkā. Sadā kāle bhavo sadātano. Sanasaddo niccattho sattamyanto nipāto, sanaṃsaddo vā abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkā, tatra bhavo sanantano, ubhayatrāpi bhavatthe tano, pubbe niggahītāgamo.

Five [terms] for 'stable'. From the root dhu in the sense of 'to go' and 'to be stable', with the suffix a, and the substitution of uva. That which exists eternally and constantly is sassato. Nicco has been explained. That which exists always in time is sadātano. The word sana, a particle ending in the seventh case, has the meaning of 'eternal'; or the word is sanaṃ; that which exists therein is sanantano. In both cases, the suffix tano is in the sense of 'being', and there is a preceding niggahīta augment.

710. Ekeneva bhāvādirūpena kālassa byāpako nibbānākāsādikūṭaṭṭhoti pakāsito. Māyāniccalayantādīsu kūṭaṃ vakkhati abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkā. Niccalo tiṭṭhatīti kūṭaṭṭho, pabbato, kūṭaṭṭho viya sadā tiṭṭhatīti kūṭaṭṭho.

710. By a single nature, such as being, it pervades time; thus it is explained as kūṭaṭṭha, like Nibbāna, space, and so on. The term kūṭa will be explained in the context of illusion, impermanence, dissolution, and so on. That which stands unmoving is kūṭaṭṭho, for example, a mountain. That which always stands like a peak is kūṭaṭṭho.

Dvayaṃ lahuke. Laṅgha gati sosanesu, u, ghassa hattaṃ, niggahītalopo, lahu, laghupi. Saṃpubbe, satthikakapaccaye ca sallahukaṃ. Tikaṃ saṅkhyāte. Khyā kathane. Gaṇa saṅkhyāne. Mā parimāṇe, sabbatra to.

Two [terms] for 'light'. From the root laṅgh in the sense of 'to go' and 'to dry', with the suffix u, the change of gh to h, and the elision of the niggahīta, [resulting in] lahu, also laghu. With the prefix saṃ, and with the suffix ka in its own sense, it becomes sallahukaṃ. Three [terms] for 'counted'. From the root khyā in the sense of 'to speak'. From the root gaṇa in the sense of 'to count'. From the root mā in the sense of 'to measure'; in all cases with the suffix to.

711. Tikaṃ tikhiṇe. Tija nisāne, ho, vaṇṇavikāro, tiṇhaṃ. Tija nisāne, ino, jassa kho, ṇattaṃ, tikhiṇaṃ. Tijatoyeva vo, jassa vo, battaṃ, tibbaṃ. Tikaṃ caṇḍe. Caṇḍa kope, caṇḍaṃ. Ujja balapālanesu, a, jjassa ggo, uggaṃ. Khara vināse, a, kharaṃ.

711. Three [terms] for 'sharp'. From the root tij in the sense of 'to sharpen', with the suffix ha and a change of letter, [resulting in] tiṇhaṃ.
