Tatra āhosaddo dīghādi. “Diṭṭho āho udāhu ca, vikappatthe vibhāvane”ti hi bhāguri. Khāṇurayamāho puriso. Ruddo tu rassādimāha “issarepyadhikepi ca, vikappevimhayepyaho”ti. Kimusaddo rassanto. Kimāyaṃ khāṇu, kimu puriso. Udasaddo rassādi. Dhūmoyamoda kāpotaṃ, samūhatthe ṇo. Kiñcasaddopi vikappe. Kimutasaddo atisayeti vutto.

1138. The six terms, `balavaṃ`, `suṭṭhu`, `atīva`, `kimuta`, `su`, and `ati`, are in the sense of excess. `Suṭṭhu` is also in the sense of praise. `Kimuta` is also in the sense of a question. The six terms, `āho`, `kiṃ`, `kimu`, `udāhu`, `kimuta`, and `uda`, are in the sense of alternatives or deliberation. Among these, the word `āho` has a long initial vowel. For Bhāguri says: “`Diṭṭho`, `āho`, or `udāhu`, in the sense of alternatives, in specification.” For example: “Is this a stump, or a man?” Rudra, however, says that `aho` with a short initial vowel is used “in lordship, also in excess, also in alternatives, also in wonder.” The word `kimu` ends in a short vowel. For example: “Is this a stump, or a man?” The word `uda` has a short initial vowel. For example: “Is this smoke, or a pigeon?” The particle `ṇo` is used in the sense of collection. The particle `kiñca` is also in the sense of alternatives. The word `kimuta` has been stated to be in the sense of excess.

1139. Bho are ambho hambho re je aṅga āvuso he hare ete dasa avhāne. Haṃ hosaddāpyatra. Kathaṃ kiṃsu nanu kacci nu kiṃ ete cha samā samānatthā.

1139. 'Bho,' 'are,' 'ambho,' 'hambho,' 're,' 'je,' 'aṅga,' 'āvuso,' 'he,' 'hare'—these ten are in the sense of calling. The words 'haṃ' and 'ho' are also included here. 'Kathaṃ,' 'kiṃsu,' 'nanu,' 'kacci,' 'nu,' 'kiṃ'—these six are similar, having the same meaning.

1140. Adhunā, etarahi, idāni, sampati cāti cattāro idānītyatthe. Aññadatthu taggha sasakkaṃ addhā kāmaṃ jātu ve have ete aṭṭha ekaṃse ekaṃsatthe.

1140. 'Adhunā,' 'etarahi,' 'idāni,' and 'sampati'—these four are in the sense of 'now.' 'Aññadatthu,' 'taggha,' 'sasakkaṃ,' 'addhā,' 'kāmaṃ,' 'jātu,' 've,' 'have'—these eight are in the sense of certainty.

1141. Yāvatādayo [M 0.0599] satta paricchedavācakā. Tatra yāvatā, yāvāti dve aniyamaparicchedatthavācakā. Tāvatā, tāva, ettāvatāti niyamaparicchedatthavācakā. Kittāvatā, kīveti paricchedapucchanatthavācakā.

1141. The seven terms beginning with 'yāvatā' are expressive of limitation. Among them, 'yāvatā' and 'yāva' are two terms expressive of indefinite limitation. 'Tāvatā,' 'tāva,' and 'ettāvatā' are expressive of definite limitation. 'Kittāvatā' and 'kīva' are expressive of questioning about limitation.

1142-1143. Yathā tathā yatheva evaṃ yathānāma yathāhi seyyathāpi evamevaṃ vā tatheva yathāpi evampi seyyathāpi nāma yathariva yathā ca viya tathariva iccete sattarasa paṭibhāgatthe sadisatthe bhavanti.

1142-1143. 'Yathā,' 'tathā,' 'yatheva,' 'evaṃ,' 'yathānāma,' 'yathāhi,' 'seyyathāpi,' 'evamevaṃ,' 'vā,' 'tatheva,' 'yathāpi,' 'evampi,' 'seyyathāpi nāma,' 'yathariva,' 'yathā,' 'viya,' 'tathariva'—these seventeen terms are in the sense of comparison and similarity.

1144. Saṃ, sāmaṃ, sayañceti tayo sayamiccatthe. Āma sāhu lahu opāyikaṃ patirūpaṃ sādhu evaṃ ete satta sampaṭicchanatthe. Āmantāpyatra.

1144. 'Saṃ,' 'sāmaṃ,' and 'sayaṃ'—these three are in the sense of 'self.' 'Āma,' 'sāhu,' 'lahu,' 'opāyikaṃ,' 'patirūpaṃ,' 'sādhu,' 'evaṃ'—these seven are in the sense of acceptance. 'Āmantā' is also included here.

1145. Yamādayo [M 0.0600] cha kāraṇatthesiyuṃ. Canasaddo, cisaddo cāti dve asākalye asakalatthe. Kadācanaṃ, kadācītyādi payogo. Mudhāsaddo nipphale phalarahite, nippayojanetyattho. Amūlepi ca mudhā.

1145. The six terms beginning with 'yaṃ' are in the sense of cause. The word 'cana' and the word 'ci' are two terms in the sense of incompleteness or non-totality. Usage is such as 'kadācanaṃ' and 'kadāci.' The word 'mudhā' is in the sense of fruitless, devoid of fruit, or without purpose. And 'mudhā' is also in the sense of baseless.

1146. Jātusaddo ekaṃsepi. Sabbato, samantato, parito, samantā cāti cattāro tulyatthā.

1146. The word 'jātu' is also in the sense of certainty. 'Sabbato,' 'samantato,' 'parito,' and 'samantā'—these four have an equivalent meaning.

1147. Na a no mā alaṃ nahi iccete cha nisedhe. Ce, sace, yadīti tayo yadyatthe. Saddhaṃsaddo anukūlatthe. Nattaṃ doso ca rajanīyamiccatthe. Divāsaddo ahe ahanītyatthe.

1147. 'Na,' 'a,' 'no,' 'mā,' 'alaṃ,' and 'nahi'—these six are in the sense of negation. 'Ce,' 'sace,' and 'yadi'—these three are in the sense of 'if.' The word 'saddhaṃ' is in the sense of 'favorable.' 'Nattaṃ,' 'doso,' and 'rajanīyaṃ' are in the sense of night. The word 'divā' is in the sense of day.

1148. Īsaṃ[M 0.0601], kiñci, manaṃ iccete appatthe. Atakkite avitakkite. Balakkāre tu sāhasaṃ. Aggato, purato ca pureiccatthe. Pecca amutrasaddā bhavantare.

1148. 'Īsaṃ,' 'kiñci,' and 'manaṃ' are in the sense of smallness. 'Atakkite' and 'avitakkite' mean unreasoned and unconsidered. 'Sāhasaṃ', however, is in the sense of force. 'Aggato' and 'purato' are in the sense of 'in front.' The words 'pecca' and 'amutra' are in the sense of another existence.

1149. Aho ca hi cāti ete vimhaye. Vikappepi aho. Sammodepi hi. Tuṇhīsaddo mone abhāsane. Āvi, pātu ca pākaṭatthe. Sajju sapadisaddā taṅkhaṇetyatthe.

1149. 'Aho' and 'hi' are in the sense of wonder. 'Aho' is also in the sense of deliberation. 'Hi' is also in the sense of agreement. The word 'tuṇhī' is in the sense of silence, not speaking. 'Āvi' and 'pātu' are in the sense of manifest. The words 'sajju' and 'sapadi' are in the sense of 'at that very instant'.

1150. Sudaṃ kho assu yagghe ve hādayo hakārādayo ca padapūraṇe siyuṃ. Antarena, antarā, anto cāti ete abbhantareiccatthe. Avassaṃ, nūna ca nicchayatthe.

1150. 'Sudaṃ,' 'kho,' 'assu,' 'yagghe,' 've,' and terms beginning with 'ha' may be used as expletives. 'Antarena,' 'antarā,' and 'anto'—these are in the sense of 'inside.' 'Avassaṃ' and 'nūna' are in the sense of certainty.

1151. Saṃsaddo diṭṭhāsaddo ānandatthe. Samupajo, saṃpyatra. Kāmappavedane icchāya akkhāne kacci jīvati te mātā[M 0.0602], mamedamabhimatamiccatthe. Usūyopagame usūyāpubbake upagame.

1151. The word 'saṃ' and the word 'diṭṭhā' are in the sense of delight. 'Samupajo' and 'saṃ' are also included here. In expressing desire, in stating a wish, as in 'Does your mother still live?' (kacci jīvati te mātā), it is in the sense of 'This is what is agreeable to me' (mama idam abhimataṃ). 'Usūyopagame' means in an approach preceded by envy.

“Kāmānumatiyaṃ kāmo,

“The word 'kāma' is used in the sense of approval of desire,

Usūyopagamepi cā”ti ruddo.

and also in the approach of envy,” so says Rudra.

Usūyopagamānuññāṇepicāyaṃ attho dissate.

This meaning is also seen in the sense of permission regarding the approach of envy.

1152-1153. Yathāttanti saccaṃ. Tathassa anatikkamo yathātathaṃ, yathātthe abyayībhāvo. Tathasaddoyaṃ bhūtapariyāyo. Sadāsaddo, sanaṃsaddo cāti nicce. Sanasaddopyatra. Pāyo, bāhulyañca samā. Pañcakaṃ bāhye. Saṇikaṃsaddo asīghe.

1152-1153. 'Yathāttaṃ' means true. 'Yathātathaṃ' means no transgression of that, and in the sense of 'yathā' it is an indeclinable compound. This word 'tatha' is a synonym for 'bhūta.' The word 'sadā' and the word 'sanaṃ' are in the sense of eternal. The word 'sana' is also included here. 'Pāyo' and 'bāhulya' are synonymous. 'Pañcakaṃ' is in the sense of external. The word 'saṇikaṃ' is in the sense of not swift.

1154. Sammā, suṭṭhūti dve abhidhānāni.

1154. 'Sammā' and 'suṭṭhu' are two designations.

1155. Sāyaṃ sāye [M 0.0603] sāyanhe. Atrāheti imasmiṃ ahani ajjasaddo.

1155. 'Sāyaṃ,' 'sāye,' and 'sāyanhe' mean evening. The word 'ajja' is used in the sense of 'on this day'.

1156. Yatthādayo tayo aniyamaṭṭhānādivācakā. Tatthādayo niyamaṭṭhānādivācakā.

1156. The three terms beginning with 'yattha' are expressive of indefinite locations, etc. The terms beginning with 'tattha' are expressive of definite locations, etc.

1157. Sammukhā, āvi, pātu ca samānatthā.

1157. 'Sammukhā,' 'āvi,' and 'pātu' have the same meaning.

1158. Appevādayo tayo saṃsayatthamhi. Iti itthaṃ evaṃsaddā nidassane vattanti. Kathañcisaddo kicchatthe.

1158. The three terms beginning with 'appeva' are in the sense of doubt. The words 'iti,' 'itthaṃ,' and 'evaṃ' are used in the sense of exemplification. The word 'kathañci' is in the sense of difficulty.

1159. Khedo [M 0.0604] khinnatā. Paccakkhe sacchisaddo. Thire, avadhāraṇe ca dhuvaṃ. Tiro tiriyaṃsaddā samā. Duṭṭhukusaddā kucchāyaṃ.

1159. 'Khedo' means weariness. The word 'sacchī' is in the sense of direct perception. 'Dhuvaṃ' is in the sense of firmness and ascertainment. The words 'tiro' and 'tiriyaṃ' are synonymous. The words 'duṭṭhu' and 'ku' are in the sense of disparagement.

1160. Āsiṭṭhatthamhi suvatthi. Dhisaddo nindāyaṃ. Kuhiñcanādayo satta ṭhānādipucchanatthā.

1160. 'Suvatthi' is in the sense of a wish. The word 'dhi' is in the sense of blame. The seven terms beginning with 'kuhiñcana' are in the sense of asking about place, etc.

1161. Iha idha atra ettha attha ete okāsatthādivācakā. Sabbasmiṃ kālādike sabbatrādidvayaṃ. Kismiṃ kāle kadā. Kasmiṃ kāle kudācanaṃ.

1161. 'Iha,' 'idha,' 'atra,' 'ettha,' and 'attha'—these are expressive of location, etc. In the sense of 'all' regarding time and so forth, the two terms beginning with 'sabbatra' are used. 'Kadā' means 'at what time.' 'Kudācanaṃ' means 'at what time.'

1162-1163. Vibhatyantanāmasarākhyātapatirūpake abyaye dassetvā tadaññabhāve abyaye dassetumāha “ādikamme”iccādi. Tatra vibhatyantapatirūpakaṃ yathā – “cirassaṃ, ciraṃ[M 0.0605], cireni”ccādi. Nāmapatirūpakaṃ yathā – “āma, sāhu, lahu, opāyika”miccādi. Sarapatirūpakaṃ yathā – “a”-iccādi. Ākhyātapatirūpakaṃ yathā – “atthi”iccādi.

1162-1163. After showing indeclinables that resemble case endings, nouns, vowels, and verbs, it is said, 'ādikamme,' etc., to indicate indeclinables in other senses. Among these, those resembling case endings are like 'cirassaṃ,' 'ciraṃ,' 'cirena,' etc. Those resembling nouns are like 'āma,' 'sāhu,' 'lahu,' 'opāyika,' etc. Those resembling vowels are like 'a,' etc. Those resembling verbs are like 'atthi,' etc.

Sambhavo pabhavo. Udiṇṇe pavuddhe vaḍḍhane. Tisa pīṇane,ti, titti. Niyoge niyojane. Agge uttame. Tappare tappadhāne. Saṅge laggane. Pakāre sadise, bhede vā. Antobhāve pakkhitte. Viyoge pavāse. Avayave padese. Dhitiyaṃ vīriye padhāne. Ete catthā dhātusaṃyogatthā vā nāmasaṃyogatthā vā bhavanti. Asaṃyogassa pana nāmapadassa attho “po siyā paramatthasmiṃ, pātu vātesu pā bhave”ti ekakkharakose ekakkharakosa 73 gāthā vutto.

'Sambhavo' and 'pabhavo' mean origin or source. 'Udiṇṇe,' 'pavuddhe,' and 'vaḍḍhane' denote increase. 'Tisa' is in the sense of satisfaction; 'ti' also means satisfaction ('titti'). 'Niyoge' and 'niyojane' mean appointment. 'Agge' and 'uttame' indicate excellence. 'Tappare' and 'tappadhāne' refer to adherence. 'Saṅge' and 'laggane' mean attachment. 'Pakāre' means in similarity, or in difference. 'Antobhāve' and 'pakkhitte' mean inclusion. 'Viyoge' and 'pavāse' indicate separation. 'Avayave' and 'padese' refer to parts. 'Dhitiyaṃ,' 'vīriye,' and 'padhāne' signify effort. These four meanings arise from combinations with roots or combinations with nouns. But the meaning of a non-compound nominal word is stated in the single-syllable dictionary: “'Po' may be in the highest sense; 'pā' may be in the sense of winds.”

1164. Vikkamo padhānaṃ.

1164. 'Vikkamo' means exertion or pre-eminence.

1165-1167. Sanyāse nikkhitte. Mokkho nibbānaṃ. Rāsi nikaro. Gehe nilaye. Ādeso ācikkhanaṃ. Upamāya sannibhe. Accayo atikkamo. Sāmīpye samīpabhāve[M 0.0606]. Uparati upasamo. Nīharaṇaṃ apanayanaṃ. Āvaraṇaṃ nīvaraṇaṃ āharaṇaṃ gahaṇaṃ (ka.).

1165-1167. 'Sanyāse' and 'nikkhitte' denote abandonment. 'Mokkho' is Nibbāna. 'Rāsi' and 'nikaro' mean a heap. 'Gehe' and 'nilaye' refer to a dwelling. 'Ādeso' and 'ācikkhanaṃ' mean instruction. 'Upamāya' and 'sannibhe' indicate likeness. 'Accayo' and 'atikkamo' mean transgression. 'Sāmīpye' and 'samīpabhāve' denote proximity. 'Uparati' and 'upasamo' signify cessation. 'Nīharaṇaṃ' and 'apanayanaṃ' mean removal. 'Āvaraṇaṃ' and 'nīvaraṇaṃ' denote obstruction.

1168. Uddhakamme uyyāne. Viyoge uppāsite. Atthalābho uppatti. Pabalatte mahābahalatte. Dakkhaggatāsūti dakkhabhāve, aggabhāve ca. Sattiyaṃ, mokkhe nibbāne ca.

1168. 'Uddhakamme' means in an upward act; 'uyyāne' means in an effort. 'Viyoge' means in separation; 'uppāsite' means in uprooting. 'Atthalābho' means gain of purpose; 'uppatti' means origin. 'Pabalatte' means in great strength; 'mahābahalatte' means in great abundance. 'Dakkhaggatāsu' means in the state of skill and in the state of excellence. 'Sattiyaṃ' means in power; 'mokkhe' and 'nibbāne' mean in liberation.

1169. Du ca abhāve dussīlo, duppañño. Asamiddhiyaṃ dubbhikkhaṃ. Anandanaṃ amodanaṃ.

1169. 'Du' is used in the sense of badness, as in 'dussīlo' (immoral) and 'duppañño' (unwise). 'Asamiddhiyaṃ' means in lack of prosperity, as in 'dubbhikkhaṃ' (famine). 'Anandanaṃ' and 'amodanaṃ' mean displeasure or lack of delight.

1170. Samantattasamiddhīsūti samantabhāve, samiddhiyañca. Saṅgate sahite. Vidhāne karaṇe. Pabhavo sambhavo. Punappunakriyā punappunakaraṇaṃ.

1170. 'Samantattasamiddhīsu' means in the state of being all-around and in prosperity. 'Saṅgate' and 'sahite' mean joined or united. 'Vidhāne' and 'karaṇe' mean in arrangement or in doing. 'Pabhavo' and 'sambhavo' mean origin. 'Punappunakriyā' and 'punappunakaraṇaṃ' denote repeated action.

1171-1172. Atisayo atra adhimattaṃ. Bhusattho samantattho, tena samanta pariyāyopi bhusasaddo atthīti veditabbo. Issariyo pabhūti. Accaye atikkame. Kalahe [M 0.0607] viggahe. Bhāse kathane, “bhāsāyā”tipi pāṭho. Kucchane kucchāyaṃ. Anabhimukhatthe vimukho. Moho vimati. Padhāne visiṭṭhe. Dakkhatā chekatā. Khede parissame.

1171-1172. 'Atisayo' here means 'adhimattaṃ' (exceedingly). 'Bhusattho' means 'samantattho' (having an all-around meaning); therefore, it should be understood that the word 'bhusa' is also a synonym for 'samanta.' 'Issariyo' and 'pabhūti' mean lordship or power. 'Accaye' and 'atikkame' mean transgression. 'Kalahe' and 'viggahe' mean quarrel or strife. 'Bhāse' and 'kathane' mean in speaking; there is also the reading 'bhāsāyaṃ.' 'Kucchane' and 'kucchāyaṃ' mean disparagement or contempt. 'Anabhimukhatthe' means in disinclination, as in 'vimukho' (averse). 'Moho' and 'vimati' mean delusion or doubt. 'Padhāne' and 'visiṭṭhe' mean distinguished or pre-eminent. 'Dakkhatā' and 'chekatā' mean cleverness or skill. 'Khede' and 'parissame' mean weariness or fatigue.

1173. Jānane avagate. Adhobhāge avaṃsire. Anicchaye aniṇṇaye. Paribhave avaññāte. Deso ca byāpanañca hāni cāti dvando. Vacokriyāya vacanakriyāyaṃ. Theyye coriye. Aññāṇe ca pattiādike ca.

1173. 'Jānane' and 'avagate' mean in knowing. 'Adhobhāge' and 'avaṃsire' mean in the lower part. 'Anicchaye' and 'aniṇṇaye' mean in unwillingness or indecision. 'Paribhave' and 'avaññāte' mean in contempt. 'Deso ca byāpanañca hāni ca' is a dvanda compound. 'Vacokriyāya' and 'vacanakriyāyaṃ' mean in verbal action. 'Theyye' and 'coriye' mean in theft. And in ignorance ('aññāṇe') and in attainments, etc. ('pattiādike').

1174. Pacchātthe anucaro. Bhusatthe anuggato. Sadise anurūpo. Anuvattiyaṃ anveti. Hīne anu sāriputtaṃ paññavanto. Tatiyatthe nadimanvavasitā bārāṇasī. Dese, lakkhaṇe, vicchāyaṃ, itthambhūte, bhāgādike ca anu. Lakkhaṇe rukkha’manu vijjotate cando. Vicchāyaṃ rukkhaṃ rukkhamanu tiṭṭhati. Itthambhūte sādhu devadatto mātara’manu. Bhāge yadettha maṃ anu siyā.

1174. In the sense of 'after' ('pacchātthe'), as in 'anucaro' (a follower). In the sense of 'exceedingly' ('bhusatthe'), as in 'anuggato' (deeply entered). In the sense of 'similar' ('sadise'), as in 'anurūpo' (corresponding). In the sense of 'following' ('anuvattiyaṃ'), as in 'anveti' (he follows). In the sense of 'inferior' ('hīne'), as in 'anu sāriputtaṃ paññavanto' (wise ones are inferior to Sāriputta). In the sense of the third case ending ('tatiyatthe'), as in 'nadimanvavasitā bārāṇasī' (Bārāṇasī was settled along the river). The prefix 'anu' is also used in the senses of place, characteristic, distribution, suchness, and part, etc. In the sense of characteristic ('lakkhaṇe'): 'rukkhaṃ anu vijjotate cando' (the moon shines towards the tree). In the sense of distribution ('vicchāyaṃ'): 'rukkhaṃ rukkhamanu tiṭṭhati' (he stands by every tree). In the sense of suchness ('itthambhūte'): 'sādhu devadatto mātaraṃ anu' (Devadatta is good, like his mother). In the sense of part ('bhāge'): 'yadettha maṃ anu siyā' (whatever portion of this should be for me).

1175. Āliṅgane [M 0.0608] parissajati. Dosakkhāne paribhāsetvā. Nivāsane vatthaṃ paridahitvā. Avañño paribhavo. Ādhāre bhojane soke byāpane. Tatve sabhāve. Lakkhaṇādo lakkhaṇavicchāitthambhūtabhāge.

1175. In embracing ('āliṅgane'), as in 'parissajati' (he embraces). In pointing out faults ('dosakkhāne'), as in 'paribhāsetvā' (having reproached). In dressing ('nivāsane'), as in 'vatthaṃ paridahitvā' (having put on a cloth). 'Avaññā' and 'paribhavo' mean disrespect or contempt. In support ('ādhāre'), in food ('bhojane'), in sorrow ('soke'), and in pervasion ('byāpane'). 'Tatve' and 'sabhāve' mean in reality or in nature. 'Lakkhaṇādo' means in characteristic, distribution, suchness, and part.

1176. Visiṭṭhe abhidhammo. Uddhakamme sāruppe vuddhiyaṃ pūjāyaṃ adhike. Kule abhijano. Asacce lakkhaṇādimhi catubbidhe ‘abhirabhāge (pā.1.4.91)’ ti abhissa bhāgavajjitesu lakkhaṇādīsu kammappavacanīyasaññā vuttā (rūpasiddhi-kārakataṇḍe).

1176. In the sense of 'distinguished' ('visiṭṭhe'), as in 'abhidhammo'. In upward action ('uddhakamme'), in suitability ('sāruppe'), in growth ('vuddhiyaṃ'), in veneration ('pūjāyaṃ'), and in excess ('adhike'). In lineage ('kule'), as in 'abhijano' (noble birth). In untruth ('asacce'), and in the fourfold division beginning with characteristic, etc. ('lakkhaṇādimhi catubbidhe').

1177. Adhike issare pāṭhe uccāraṇe, adhiṭṭhāne pāpuṇane nicchaye uparibhāgādike bhaṭane bhattiyaṃ visesane ca adhi.

1177. The prefix 'adhi' is used in the senses of superior ('adhike'), lordship ('issare'), recitation ('pāṭhe'), utterance ('uccāraṇe'), resolution ('adhiṭṭhāne'), attainment ('pāpuṇane'), certainty ('nicchaye'), the upper part, etc. ('uparibhāgādike'), support ('bhaṭane'), devotion ('bhattiyaṃ'), and distinction ('visesane').

1178-1179. Vāmādāne [M 0.0609] iti pāṭhe vāme paṭilome, ādāne gahaṇe. Vācādāne paccassosi. Paṭinidhimhi mukhyasadise buddhasmā pati. Paṭibādhe nivattane. Paṭiccatthe “paṭiccā”ti padassa atthe. Lakkhaṇādike catubbidhe.

1178-1179. With the reading 'vāmādāne,' 'vāme' means 'reverse' ('paṭilome'), and 'ādāne' means 'taking' ('gahaṇe'). In the sense of responding ('vācādāne'), as in 'paccassosi' (he responded). 'Paṭinidhimhi' means 'in a substitute'; 'mukhyasadise' means 'like the chief'; an example is the phrase `buddhasmā pati`. 'Paṭibādhe' and 'nivattane' mean 'in hindering' or 'in turning back.' 'Paṭiccatthe' means 'in the sense of the word 'paṭicca'.' 'Lakkhaṇādike catubbidhe' means 'in the fourfold division beginning with characteristic.'

1180-1181. Samīpe ādikammani mariyāde uddhakammani icchāyaṃ bandhane abhividhimhi ca ā. Kicche īsatthe nivattiyañca appasāde āsīsane saraṇe vākyasaraṇe ā evaṃ anussaraṃ. Patiṭṭhāyaṃ, vimhayādīsu ca ā.

1180-1181. The prefix 'ā' is used in the senses of near ('samīpe'), the beginning of action ('ādikammani'), a limit ('mariyāde'), superior action ('uddhakammani'), desire ('icchāyaṃ'), binding ('bandhane'), and pervasion ('abhividhimhi'). Also in difficulty ('kicche'), in a slight sense ('īsatthe'), in turning back ('nivattiyaṃ'), in displeasure ('appasāde'), in blessing ('āsīsane'), in remembering ('saraṇe'), and in recalling speech ('vākyasaraṇe'), as in 'anussaraṃ' (recollecting). Also in establishment ('patiṭṭhāyaṃ'), and in astonishment, etc. ('vimhayādīsu').

1182. Bhūtabhāve [M 0.0610] atīto.

1182. In the sense of 'having been' ('bhūtabhāve'), as in 'atīto' (past).

1183. Sambhāvane api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati dha. pa. 187. Sambhāvanamadhikatthavacanena aññatra sattiyā avighāto. Saṃvaraṇe apidhānaṃ.

1183. In the sense of possibility ('sambhāvane'), as in 'api dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati' (even in divine pleasures, he does not attain delight). 'Sambhāvanamadhikatthavacanena' means 'by a statement of an additional matter'; 'aññatra sattiyā avighāto' means 'non-obstruction except by a weapon.' In the sense of covering ('saṃvaraṇe'), as in 'apidhānaṃ' (a lid).

1184-1185. Apagato apeto. Upapattiyaṃ yuttiyaṃ upekkhā. Ādhikye upakhāriyaṃ doṇo. Pubbakammani buddhopakkamaṃ kilesacchedo. Gayhākāre paccupaṭṭhānaṃ. Uparitte uparibhāve upapanno. Anasane upavāso.

1184-1185. 'Apagato' means 'gone away'; 'apeto' means 'departed.' 'Upapattiyaṃ' means 'in arising'; 'yuttiyaṃ' means 'in suitability'; 'upekkhā' means 'equanimity.' In the sense of excess ('ādhikye'), as in 'upakhāriyaṃ doṇo' (a doṇa measure over a khāri). In the sense of a prior action ('pubbakammani'), as in 'buddhopakkamaṃ kilesacchedo' (the Buddha's undertaking which is the cutting off of defilements). In the manner of being graspable ('gayhākāre'), as in 'paccupaṭṭhānaṃ' (presence). 'Uparitte' and 'uparibhāve' mean 'in a higher state' or 'in a superior condition,' as in 'upapanno' (arisen). In the sense of not eating ('anasane'), as in 'upavāso' (fasting).

1186. Upadese [M 0.0611] evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabbaṃ. Vacanapaṭiggāhe evaṃ hotu. Idamatthe idaṃsaddassa atthe.

1186. In instruction ('upadese'), as in 'evaṃ te abhikkamitabbaṃ, evaṃ te paṭikkamitabbaṃ' (Thus you should go forward, thus you should return). In accepting words ('vacanapaṭiggāhe'), as in 'evaṃ hotu' (Let it be thus). 'Idamatthe' means 'in this sense,' that is, in the meaning of the word 'idaṃ'.

1187. Samuccaye kevalasamuccaye –

1187. In conjunction ('samuccaye'), in simple conjunction ('kevalasamuccaye')—

Cīvaraṃ piṇḍapātañca, paccayaṃ sayanāsanaṃ;

Adāsi ujubhūtesu, vippasannena cetasā jā. 2.22.551.

Robes and almsfood, requisites, lodging; he gave to the upright ones, with a serene mind.

Samāhāre cakkhu ca sotañca cakkhusotaṃ. Anvācayo ekaṃ padhānabhāvena vatvā itarassa appadhānabhāvena vacanaṃ, tasmiṃ. Sīlaṃ rakkhāhi, dānañca dehi. Itarītare samaṇo ca brāhmaṇo ca samaṇabrāhmaṇā. Tatra kevalasamuccayo ca anvācayo ca samāse natthi, itaradvayaṃ samāseyeva.

In aggregation ('samāhāre'), as in 'cakkhu ca sotañca' becomes 'cakkhusotaṃ' (the eye and ear). 'Anvācayo' is subsequent collection, which is stating one thing with prominence and another with non-prominence. For instance: 'Sīlaṃ rakkhāhi, dānañca dehi' (Protect morality, and give alms). In mutual connection ('itarītare'), as in 'samaṇo ca brāhmaṇo ca' becomes 'samaṇabrāhmaṇā' (ascetics and brahmins). Among these, simple conjunction and subsequent collection do not occur in compounds; the other two types only occur in compounds.

1188. Pakāro tulyo, bhedo ca. Padatthassa vipallāse goti ayamāheti. Samāpane icchitassa padassa pariniṭṭhāpane.

1188. 'Pakāro' means similarity ('tulyo') and difference ('bhedo'). In the reversal of a word's meaning ('padatthassa vipallāse'), as in 'goti' which means 'ayam āha' (this one says). In completion ('samāpane'), which is the finishing of the desired word ('icchitassa padassa pariniṭṭhāpane').

1189. Pajjaṃ [M 0.0612] vāsaddassatthe. Vavatthitavibhāsāyaṃ vā paro asarūpā. Viavapubbo ṭhā gatinivattiyaṃ, to, ṭhātissa tho, asarūpadvittañca. Vavatthitā niyamitā vibhāsā vavatthitavibhāsā. Avassaggeti avapubbo saja vissajjanāliṅgananimmānesu.

1189. 'Pajjaṃ' is in the sense of the word 'vā'. In a defined option ('vavatthitavibhāsāyaṃ'), 'vā' is used when a dissimilar form follows. When the root 'ṭhā' is preceded by 'vi' or 'ava,' it is in the sense of stopping motion; 'to' is the suffix, 'tho' replaces 'ṭhā,' and there is doubling of a dissimilar consonant. 'Vavatthitā' means defined, 'vibhāsā' means option; thus 'vavatthitavibhāsā' is a defined option. 'Avassagga' is formed from the root 'saj' preceded by 'ava,' in the senses of dismissing, embracing, and creating.

1190. Bhūsane alaṅkāre. Vāraṇe nivāraṇe. Pariyatti pariyāpuṇanatā, yuttatthepi alaṃ. Atho athasaddā anantarādīsu catūsu atthesu siyuṃ.

1190. 'Bhūsane' and 'alaṅkāre' mean in ornamentation. 'Vāraṇe' and 'nivāraṇe' mean in warding off or prevention. 'Pariyatti' means 'pariyāpuṇanatā' (mastery); the word 'alaṃ' is also used in the sense of suitability ('yuttatthepi'). 'Atho' and the word 'atha' may occur in four senses, beginning with immediate succession.

1191. Pasaṃsādīsu tīsu. Svīkāre paṭiññāṇe. Ādinā pakāsatthasambhābyākodhādike catthe nāmasaddo. Avadhāraṇamevattho.

1191. The word 'nāma' is used in three senses, beginning with praise. 'Svīkāre' and 'paṭiññāṇe' mean in acceptance or avowal. With 'ādi' (etc.), the word 'nāma' is used in four senses, such as declaring, possibility, anger, etc. The meaning is precisely determination ('avadhāraṇa').

1192. Anuññā anumati. Santānaṃ anunayo. Ālapanaṃ sambodhanaṃ. Vatasaddo ekaṃse dayāyaṃ karuṇāyaṃ hāse [M 0.0613] pahāse khede parissame ālapane vimhaye acchariye ca siyā.

1192. 'Anuññā' and 'anumati' mean permission or consent. 'Sāntvanaṃ' and 'anunayo' mean consolation or conciliation. 'Ālapanaṃ' and 'sambodhanaṃ' mean addressing. The particle 'vata' may occur in these senses: certainty, sympathy, compassion, mirth, derision, sorrow, weariness, calling, amazement, and wonder.

1193. Vākyārambhe “handa vadāmi te”ti. Visāde khede. Yāva tāva tūti yāvatāvasaddā sākalye niravasese. Yāvadatthaṃ tāva gahitaṃ. Māne pamāṇe. “Yāva pamāṇamariyādā-vadhāraṇatthakaṃ mata”miti bhāguri. Avadhimhi paricchinne.

1193. In commencing speech ('vākyārambhe'), as in 'handa vadāmi te' (Come, I will speak to you). 'Visāde' and 'khede' mean in dejection or sorrow. The words 'yāva' and 'tāva' are used in the sense of totality ('sākalye') and without remainder ('niravasese'). As in: 'Yāvadatthaṃ tāva gahitaṃ' (As much as was needed, so much was taken). 'Māne' and 'pamāṇe' mean in measure. According to Bhāguri: “'Yāva' is held to have the meanings of measure, limit, and determination.” 'Avadhimhi' and 'paricchinne' mean in a limit or defined.

1194. Puratthāsaddo pāciyaṃ disāyaṃ iccatthe, puratthe vakkhamāne, aggato samuddhe iccatthe ca paṭhamepi ādimhi vattati. Pabandhe vākyaracanāyaṃ vākyapabandhe purāṇādike. Cirantare atītabhūte. Nikaṭe sannihite. Āgāmike anāgate.

1194. The word 'puratthā' is used in the sense of 'eastern direction' ('pāciyaṃ disāyaṃ'), 'in front' ('puratthe'), 'in what is about to be said' ('vakkhamāne'), 'at the top' ('aggato'), 'in the ocean' ('samuddhe'), and also 'at first' ('paṭhamepi') or 'at the beginning' ('ādimhi'). 'Pabandhe,' 'vākyaracanāyaṃ,' and 'vākyapabandhe' mean in composition or sentence construction; 'purāṇādike' means in ancient texts, etc. 'Cirantare' and 'atītabhūte' mean in the distant past or in the past. 'Nikaṭe' and 'sannihite' mean near or in proximity. 'Āgāmike' and 'anāgate' mean in the future.

1195. Khalusaddo nisedhe vākyālaṅkāre vākyabhūsāyaṃ avadhāraṇe evatthe, pasiddhiyañca vattati. Abhitosaddo āsanne abhimukhe ubhayato iccatthe[M 0.0614], ādinā sīghe, sākalye ca atthe vattati. Āsanne abhitoyaṃ nadī. Abhimukhe abhitova tātā. Ubhayatoiccatthe abhito maggassa. Sīghe abhito adhīyitvā. Sākalye abhito vanaṃ daḍḍhaṃ.

1195. The word 'khalu' is used in the sense of prohibition, in the ornamentation of speech, in the embellishment of a statement, in emphasis, and in well-known fact. The word 'abhito' is used in the sense of nearness, facing, and on both sides; and by extension, also in the sense of 'quickly' and 'completely.' For nearness, as in: 'The river is near.' For facing, as in: 'Father is in front.' For on both sides, as in: 'On both sides of the road.' For quickly, as in: 'Having quickly studied.' For completely, as in: 'The whole forest was burned.'

1196. Yadyapisaddatthe anuggahaṇagarahatthe. Ekaṃsatthe avitathatthe. Atho panasaddo visesasmiṃ atthe, padapūraṇatthe ca siyā.

1196. The word 'yadyapi' is used in the sense of approval and disapproval, as well as in the sense of certainty and truthfulness. The words 'atho' and 'pana' may occur in the sense of specification and also to fill a metrical line.

1197. Hisaddo kāraṇādīsu catūsu atthesu vattati. Tusaddo pana tattha catūsu atthesu majjhe hetuvajje tike atthe vattati. Kusaddo pāpe īsatthe kucchane jigucchāyañca.

1197. The word 'hi' is used in four senses, beginning with 'cause.' The word 'tu,' however, is used in three of those four senses, excluding 'cause.' The word 'ku' is used in the sense of evil, slightness, reviling, and loathing.

1198. Nukāro saṃsaye, pañhe ca. Nānāsaddo anekatthe, vajjane ca. Kiṃsaddo pucchāyaṃ, jigucchāyañca, abyayo. Tiliṅgo ca, niyame tu tiliṅgova. Vārimhi udake. Muddhani sīse ca, kaṃ sukhepi, vuttañca nānatthasaṅgahe –

1198. The particle 'nu' is used in the sense of doubt and in questions. The word 'nānā' is used in the sense of 'various' and 'in avoidance.' The word 'kiṃ' is used in questions and in disgust, and is an indeclinable. It is also three-gendered, and as a rule, it is indeed three-gendered. 'Vārimhi' means 'in water,' as does 'udake.' 'Muddhani' means 'on the head,' as does 'sīse.' 'Kaṃ' is used even in the sense of 'happiness,' and it is stated in the Nānārthasaṅgraha—

“Ko [M 0.0615] brahmattānīlakkesu, samāne sabbanāmike;

Pāvake ca mayūre ca, sukhasīsajalesu ka”nti.

The word 'ko' is used in the sense of Brahma, self, wind, and sun; of 'similar' and as a pronoun; of fire and of peacocks. The word 'kaṃ' is used in the sense of happiness, head, and water.

1199. Amāsaddo sahatthe, samīpatthe ca, amāvāsī, amāgato ca. Punasaddo bhede visese. Apaṭhame puna dadāti. Kirasaddo anussave anukkamena savane, aruciyañca. Udasaddo apyatthe pañhe. Vikappane atthantarassa vikappane ca.

1199. The word 'amā' is used in the sense of 'together' and 'in proximity,' as in 'amāvāsī' and 'amāgato.' The word 'puna' is used in the sense of 'difference' and 'distinction,' as in: 'He gives again, not for the first time.' The word 'kira' is used in the sense of hearsay, sequential hearing, and displeasure. The word 'uda' is used in the sense of 'also' and in questions, and also for alternatives and for the alteration of meaning.

1200. Pacchāsaddo patīciyaṃ disāyaṃ. Carime anāgate kāle. Sāmisaddo tu addhe bhāge, jigucchane nindāyañca. Addhe bhāge sāmi vuttaṃ, jigucchanepi tadeva. Pātu pakāse pakāsanīye, sambhave uppattiyañca. Mithosaddo aññoññeiccatthe, rahoiccatthe ca.

1200. The word 'paccha' means 'in the western direction,' and also 'in the last' and 'in future time.' The word 'sāmi,' however, is used in the sense of a half portion, in disgust, and in blame. It is said that 'sāmi' means 'a half portion,' and the same is used in disgust. 'Pātu' means 'in manifestation,' 'what should be manifested,' 'in possibility,' and 'in origin.' The word 'mitho' means 'in the sense of mutually' and 'in the sense of secretly.'

1201. Hāsaddo khede, soke, dukkhe ca. Ahahasaddo khede, vimhaye abbhute ca. Dhisaddo hiṃsāpane, nindāyañca. Tiriyaṃ tirosaddā pidhāne vattanti. Tiriyaṃ katvā kaṇḍaṅgato, tirokatvā vā.

1201. The word 'hā' is used in the sense of weariness, sorrow, and suffering. The word 'ahaha' is used in the sense of weariness, astonishment, and wonder. The word 'dhi' is used in the sense of injuring and censure. The words 'tiriyaṃ' and 'tiro' are used in the sense of concealment. As in: 'Having made it sideways, he went into the thicket,' or 'having concealed it.'

1202-1203. Saṅkhyātāsaṅkhyātatthānaṃ [M 0.0616] upasagganipātasaṅkhyātānaṃ abyayānaṃ pasiddhe pacurappayoge ekacce vā dassetvā tadaññepi saṅkhepanayena dassetumāha “tuni”ccādi. Ettha ca tunādisaddehi jjupariyantehi tadantāva gahitā, na hi kevalānaṃ etesaṃ abyayabhāvo sambhavati. Tassattho – tunapaccayanto ca tathā tvāna tave tvā tuṃ dhā so thā kkhattuṃ to tha tra hiñcanaṃ hiṃ haṃ dhi ha yakārato hiṃdha dhunā rahi dāni, kiṃsmā vo dācanaṃ dājjathaṃ thattaṃ jjhajjupaccayanto ca abyayībhāvasamāso ca tunādīnaṃ yādesanto ca abyayaṃ nāma bhaveti. Payogo yathā – “kātuna, katvāna, kātave, katvā, kātuṃ, sabbadhā, sabbaso, sabbathā, catukkhattuṃ, sabbato, sabbattha, sabbatra, kuhiñcanaṃ, kuhiṃ, kuhaṃ, sabbadhi, iha, yahiṃ, idha, adhunā, etarahi, idāni, kva, kudācanaṃ, kadā, ajja, kathaṃ, aññathattaṃ, ekajjhaṃ, sajju, upanagaraṃ, antopāsādaṃ, abhivandiya”iccādi. Idaṃ pana sabbesampi abyayānaṃ saṅkhepalakkhaṇaṃ.

1202-1203. Having shown some of the well-known and frequently used indeclinables—which are counted as prefixes and particles and have both definite and indefinite meanings—the text states 'tuna,' etc., to briefly show others as well. Here, by the words beginning with 'tuna' and ending with 'jju', those words that end in these suffixes are to be understood, for these suffixes alone cannot be indeclinables. Its meaning is: words ending with the 'tuna' suffix, and similarly 'tvāna,' 'tave,' 'tvā,' 'tuṃ,' 'dhā,' 'so,' 'thā,' 'kkhattuṃ,' 'to,' 'tha,' 'tra,' 'hiñcanaṃ,' 'hiṃ,' 'haṃ,' 'dhi,' 'ha'; those formed from 'ya'; 'hiṃdha,' 'dhunā,' 'rahi,' 'dāni,' 'kiṃsmā,' 'vo,' 'dācanaṃ,' 'dā,' 'ajja,' 'thaṃ,' 'thattaṃ'; those ending in the suffixes 'jjha' and 'jju'; avyayībhāva compounds; and those derived from roots with prefixes ending in 'ya'—these are called indeclinables. Examples of usage are: 'kātuna,' 'katvāna,' 'kātave,' 'katvā,' 'kātuṃ,' 'sabbadhā,' 'sabbaso,' 'sabbathā,' 'catukkhattuṃ,' 'sabbato,' 'sabbattha,' 'sabbatra,' 'kuhiñcanaṃ,' 'kuhiṃ,' 'kuhaṃ,' 'sabbadhi,' 'iha,' 'yahiṃ,' 'idha,' 'adhunā,' 'etarahi,' 'idāni,' 'kva,' 'kudācanaṃ,' 'kadā,' 'ajja,' 'kathaṃ,' 'aññathattaṃ,' 'ekajjhaṃ,' 'sajju,' 'upanagaraṃ,' 'antopāsādaṃ,' 'abhivandiya,' etc. This, however, is a concise definition of all indeclinables.

“Sadisaṃ [M 0.0617] tīsu liṅgesu, sabbāsu ca vibhattisu;

Vacanesu ca sabbesu, yaṃ na byeti tadabyaya”nti.

That which is the same in all three genders, in all cases, and in all numbers, that which does not change, is an indeclinable.

Abyayavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Chapter on Indeclinables is concluded.

Iti sakalabyākaraṇamahāvanāsaṅgañāṇacārinā kavikuñjarakesarinā dhīmatā sirimahācaturaṅgabalena mahāmaccena viracitāyaṃ abhidhānappadīpikāvaṇṇanāyaṃ sāmaññakaṇḍavaṇṇanā samattā.

Thus ends the explanation of the Sāmaññakaṇḍa in this commentary on the Abhidhānappadīpikā, composed by the wise great minister Sirimahācaturaṅgabala, a lion among poets, who roams with knowledge attached to the great forest of all grammar.

Nigamanavaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Epilogue

1. “Saggakaṇḍo cā”tyādinā abhidhānappadīpikāyaṃ kapālatelavaṭṭisadisena kaṇḍattayena samaṅgitā dīpitā.

1. By the words beginning with "Saggakaṇḍo ca," it is shown that the Abhidhānappadīpikā is endowed with three sections, which are like a lamp's bowl, oil, and wick.

2. “Tidive”tyādinā toṭakena tassā payojanaṃ kathitaṃ. Tassattho – yo naro kattubhūto tidive devaloke, brahmaloke ca mahiyaṃ manussaloke, bhujagāvasathe nāgaloke cāti etesu tīsu ṭhānesu sannihitānaṃ [M 0.0618] sakalatthānaṃ sabbesaṃ abhidheyyānaṃ samavhayassa abhidhānassa dīpaniyaṃ pakāsaniyaṃ iha abhidhānappadīpikāyaṃ savanadhāraṇādinā kusalo cheko hoti, sa naro mahāmunino sammāsambuddhassa vacane suttābhidhammavinayasaṅkhāte vacane paṭu cheko hoti, paṭuttāyeva matimā nāma hotīti.

2. By the Toṭaka verse beginning with 'Tidive,' its purpose is explained. Its meaning is this: That person who, being the agent, becomes skilled and expert through hearing, remembering, and so forth, in this Abhidhānappadīpikā—which illuminates and reveals the collective designation of all things, all designata, situated in these three realms: namely, in the divine world (including the devaloka and the brahmaloka), in the human world on earth, and in the nāga world, the abode of serpents—that person becomes proficient and expert in the word of the Great Sage, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, which is classified as Sutta, Abhidhamma, and Vinaya. And precisely because of this proficiency, he is called wise.

3-9. Idāni yassa rañño vihāre vasitvā ayaṃ gantho viracito, tassa nāmaguṇanivāsakaraṇappakāravihāraguṇanāmādīni dassetvā attano ca nāmaguṇe dassetuṃ satta gāthā vuttā.

3-9. Now, seven verses are stated to show the name, virtues, residence, and manner of endowment of the king in whose monastery this book was composed, as well as the qualities and name of the monastery, and also to show the author's own name and virtues.

Tatra [M 0.0619] dutiyā bhujaṅgappayātaṃ nāma. Tāsaṃ ayaṃ sambandhādhippāyā atthavaṇṇanā – yo parakkamabhujo nāma bhūpālo rājā kāresi, rakkhesīti ca iminā sambandho. Kiṃguṇo so rājā? Guṇabhūsano saddhādiguṇālaṅkāradharo. Tejassī tejoyutto. Jayī arijayena yutto. Kesarivikkamo kesarasīho viya sūraguṇayutto, vīriyavā ca. Sa kattha nivāsī? So rājā laṅkāyamāsi laṅkānāmake dīpe nivāsanasīlo. Ciraṃ cirakālaṃ vibhinnaṃ tidhā vibhinnaṃ nikāyattayasmiṃ nikāyattayaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sammā nayena hetunā samagge samaggaṃ kāresi, kāritantoyaṃ karotīti kammiko, tathā sadehaṃva attano kāyaṃ iva niccādaro hutvā dīghakālaṃ mahagghehi ca paccayehi taṃ nikāyattayaṃ rakkhesi.

Among them, the second is in the Bhujaṅgappayāta meter. This is the explanation of the meaning, showing the intended connection of these verses: The connection is with this—'the king, the ruler named Parakkamabhuja, caused it to be made and protected it.' What were the qualities of that king? He was adorned with virtues, bearing the ornament of faith and other virtues. He was radiant, endowed with splendor. Victorious, endowed with victory over enemies. Valiant as a lion, endowed with heroic qualities like a maned lion, and energetic. Where did he reside? That king was in Laṅkā, accustomed to dwelling on the island named Laṅkā. For a long, long time, he rightly united the Saṅgha of monks—which had been divided, split into three Nikāyas—into harmony through proper guidance and reason. He was the agent who caused this to be done. Likewise, with constant care as for his own body, he protected that threefold Nikāya for a long time with costly requisites.

Tathā yena raññā yathā kittiyā attano saddhādikittiyā karaṇabhūtāya laṅkā attano nivāsanaṭṭhānabhūtā kammabhūtā sambādhīkatā saṅkaṭīkatā anokāsīkatā, tathā vihārehi gāmehi ārāmehi khettehi vāpīhi ca laṅkā sambādhīkatā.

Thus, just as by that king, by means of his fame arising from his own faith and other virtues, Laṅkā—his place of residence and the object of his actions—was made crowded, constricted, and without space, so too was Laṅkā made crowded with monasteries, villages, parks, fields, and reservoirs.

Tathā yassa rañño sabbakāmadadaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇaṃ anuggahaṃ patvā pāpuṇanahetu ahaṃ vibudhagocaraṃ paṇḍitavisayaṃ ganthakārattaṃ patto, tena raññā kārite pāsādagopurādivibhūsite, saggakaṇḍe devalokassa kaṇḍasadise, satoyāsayasmiṃ sādusalilāsayasamannāgate, paṭibimbite bhagavato nivāsanaṭṭhānajetavanamahāvihārassa paṭibimbabhūte, sādhusammate sādhuvihāroti sammate, sādhūhi vā sammate sarogāmasamūhamhi salilāsayabhikkhācārayuttagāmasamūhasamannāgate mahājetavanākhyamhi vihāre vasatā nivāsaṃ kubbatā santavuttinā santacārinā [M 0.0620] saddhammaṭṭhitikāmena dhīmatā atisayañāṇayuttena moggallānena sammāsambuddhassa dutiyaaggasāvakabhūtassa āyasmato iddhimato mahāmoggallānassa nāmadheyyena therena esā abhidhānappadīpikā racitāti.

Thus, because I attained the state of being a text-composer—a sphere for the wise and a domain for the learned—having received the incomparable favor of that king who grants all desires, this Abhidhānappadīpikā was composed by the elder named Moggallāna, who bore the name of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the second chief disciple of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, possessed of psychic powers. He, being of peaceful conduct, wise, desiring the stability of the true Dhamma, and endowed with supreme knowledge, composed it while dwelling in the great monastery named Jetavana. This monastery was built by that king, adorned with palaces, gate-towers, and so forth; like a section of the divine world; endowed with pleasant water reservoirs; a reflection of the great Jetavana Monastery, the dwelling place of the Blessed One; esteemed by the virtuous as a 'good monastery'; and furnished with a group of villages free from disease, suitable for alms-rounds and possessing water reservoirs.

Nigamanakathā

Concluding Remarks

Yadyatra [M 0.0621] dosoṇupamāṇasambhavo,

Guṇīsu vīdhimpi tathā vigāhate;

Yathā jalaṃ bhojanampi jantuvā,

Catuppado vāpyacaro kaṇaṇyapi.

If here there is the possibility of even a minute fault, so too does a little virtue find its way among the virtuous; just as water and food, even a tiny particle, is for a living being, a quadruped, or a wingless creature.

Asampavedidassanāya bhāsite,

Guṇo ca doso ca sadā vivijjare;

Tato budhā me navadhānatā bhavaṃ,

Khamantu dosaṃ guṇataṃ nayantu vā.

When something is spoken without full comprehension, both merit and fault are always discerned. Therefore, O wise ones, concerning this my new work, may you forgive the fault or else transform it into a virtue.

Yo sīhasūro sitakuñjarindo,

Rājādhirājā ahu tambadīpe;

Dubbāranāgādijito narindo,

Sukantabhīmādiguṇopapanno.

He who was a hero like a lion, a lord of white elephants, was the king of kings on Tamba Island; a ruler of men, victor over irresistible elephants and so forth, possessed of qualities such as loveliness and awesomeness.

Tannāmadheyyo tadanubbādajāto,

Saddhādiyutto catusetibhindo;

Nāgādithāmo atiduppasayho,

Uḷārapañño dhitimā yasassī.

Bearing his name, born of his lineage, endowed with faith and so forth, a breaker of the four fetters; with the strength of an elephant and more, very difficult to overcome, of vast wisdom, resolute, and glorious.

Tenāhamaccantamanuggahīto,

Anaññasādhāraṇasaṅgahena;

Saṅkhepatokāsimimaṃ visuddhi-

Saṃvaṇṇanaṃ sotuhitaṃ subodhaṃ.

By him I have been exceedingly favored with an incomparable patronage; briefly I have made this explanation of purity, beneficial and easy to understand for the listener.

Rājā pajaṃ rakkhatu sappajaṃva,

Dhammañca lokāpi samācarantu;

Pūrentu atthā supakappitā ca,

Kālena devopi pavassatūti.

May the king protect the people as his own offspring, and may the people of the world also practice the Dhamma; may well-conceived aims be fulfilled, and may the deva also rain in due season.

Abhidhānappadīpikāṭīkā niṭṭhitā.

The Sub-commentary on the Abhidhānappadīpikā is completed.
